# DEDICATION.

...finally led by these reasons, he has ventured to inscribe this work to your illustrious name. I believe the situation for men of my order and office <note>Witsius is referring to his role as a theologian and professor.</note> is such that they ought not only to keep an account of their time for themselves; but, since they live in the public light of all, they are also bound in a way to render an account of it to everyone; especially to those under whose protection and guardianship they are permitted to enjoy productive leisure. Since you now easily hold the chief place among these protectors, I must not hide that, after God the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deum Optimum Maximum," a standard honorific for God often abbreviated as D.O.M.</note>, I long to have my studies approved by you above all.

He whom the unique Savior <note>original: "Sospitator"</note> of the human race, Jesus, has consecrated to His ministry, it befits to strive with the utmost effort so that in enlarging His kingdom, promoting His glory, and securing the salvation of himself and others committed to his trust, he may appear to have left nothing undone. Whatever he is, whatever he has, whatever he is able to do, must be spent uniquely on Him. Especially regarding his time—a thing as fleeting and slippery as it is precious—he must keep the most diligent account, lest he be found guilty of misappropriating and misplacing it, and be deprived of a blessed eternity.

As often as I weigh these things in my mind—and I weigh them quite often—I shudder and tremble; and unless I considered that I have to do with a merciful Lord, indeed a most indulgent Father, my thoughts could not be separated from despair. For how great a part of life has slipped away while doing evil? How much while doing nothing? How much while doing something else? How unworthy is this of a man who professes the study of wisdom? How much more unworthy of a Christian, upon whom the industry of "redeeming the time" <note>A reference to the biblical exhortation in Ephesians 5:16 to use time wisely.</note> has been so accurately impressed? But by far most unworthy of a Theologian <note>term: "Theologo" (Theologian). In this context, a professional scholar of divinity and a minister of the church.</note>; whose entire duty consists in this: that he teach both by word and example how, through the diligent and pious use of a very short time, one must strive toward a glorious eternity. 

While my conscience itself wrings from me an honest confession <note>original: "confessionem"</note> of this truth, it does not, however, condemn me as if I had entirely grown numb to the duty imposed upon me, delighting in an idle silence. The opposite could be testified by so many nights spent awake, which [passed...] <note>The sentence continues onto the next page; the catchword "labo-" suggests the next word is "laboribus," meaning "spent in labors."</note>

...laborious days followed; and at times there was such a concentration of studies that my little body <note>original: "corpuſculum." Witsius often referred to his physical frailty or the toll his intense academic work took on his health.</note> was scarcely equal to bearing it. Only then did I seem to myself to truly live, when I devoted myself to searching out the hidden recesses and treasures of the sacred volumes <note>The Bible</note>; sparing no diligence by which I hoped to attain the mind of the Lord; gladly consulting all interpreters whom I judged to have progressed further than myself; claiming for myself from all of them with a grateful heart whatever recommended itself by a spark <note>original: "scintillatione"</note> of Divine truth; devoted to no sect, entangled in no faction, enslaved to no human name, but hanging from the mouth and nod of the Lord alone, and receiving the kingdom of God with the humble obedience of faith like a little child. 

In the same way and spirit that I learned those most sacred truths, I also taught them: whether in the Church, or in the School <note>The university or seminary setting</note>, whether publicly or at home. Never did I hold out the authority of any human name—much less my own, which I know to be meager, or rather nothing at all—as a screen for my teaching; I wanted nothing in the business of religion to be believed because it rested on the number of theologians, or the decrees of Councils, or the consensus of confessions <note>original: "formularum consensu," referring to official doctrinal statements</note>; but because God had revealed it in His word. To make disciples for Him alone—this was my work, this was my labor. 

Thus I also arranged it so that I might explain Divine truths as clearly as I could, both each one individually and all of them together, in that most elegant connection and sequence <note>original: "concatenatione"</note> which clothes them with the most beautiful appearance of heavenly Wisdom. Soon I would lead my listeners back to the sources themselves <note>The original Hebrew and Greek texts</note>, where they could hear God Himself teaching in His own tongue (as it were), those things which I had explained in my own words and in the language common to our times; and I forbade them to rest until they had penetrated into that sense which they would find could have been delivered by no speech more expressly and effectively than that which the Spirit of God used. And so my sole study has been to restore those things, which are found scattered throughout the rich variety of the Divine volumes as the subject required, each to its own place; so that from those woods better than cedar, and from silver and gold...

# DEDICATION.

...and with precious stones, arranged in a fitting order, the majestic temple of Wisdom <note>original: "Auguſta Sapientiæ ædes." Witsius uses architectural metaphors to describe the construction of a complete theological system.</note> might be built. However, I did not consider myself forbidden from occasionally treating a single point of doctrine at greater length, or dwelling longer on the explanation of some illustrious passage <note>original: "pericopæ," a term for a specific selection or excerpt of scripture used in teaching or liturgy</note> of the Sacred Scriptures. For in this way, I intended to reveal to my students how unsearchable is the wealth of wisdom contained not only in the whole, but also in every individual part; so much so that wherever you penetrate by digging, you find new treasures, no less valuable than those already found. 

There were times when I expounded the rites and ceremonies of the Old Testament; times when I explained the riddles of the Prophecies, or the memorable histories of both the Israelite and Christian people; and times when I interpreted entire Epistles written by the inspiration of the Divine Spirit. From time to time, I also ventured into the Antiquities <note>Historical studies of the ancient world, customs, and settings of the Bible</note> of both Churches <note>Meaning the religious life of the Old Testament/Jewish era and the New Testament/Christian era</note>, from which it seemed some light might shine upon more obscure divine oracles. 

And although I am so formed by nature and habit that I strongly shrink from disputes, I could not avoid occasionally drawing my weapons against those whom I saw abusing their talent and learning to attack God Himself, and attempting either to undermine His word with insulting fictions or to evade it with clever distortions. Yet I did this in such a way that I referred everything to the glory of God in Christ and to the exercise of true holiness. 

When I was reflecting on these things, I saw a large circle <note>original: "coronam," literally a crown or garland, used metaphorically to describe a gathered audience of attentive students</note> of most excellent young men attending my teaching. Most of them tried to catch what they heard with their pens, as each was more ready in mind and hand; for the lot of human weakness does not allow one to engrave everything on the memory, especially those things consisting of citations. But not even my own memory was sufficient for me, unless aided by written notes. From this, a certain necessity arose to record some things at greater length, so that I might have what I should deliver, and my listeners might have what I had delivered. For not everything could be retained from a single recitation, however clear; nor could they be so noted down by the students without some...

...so that many things might fall away, and some things not well understood might even be poorly recorded. And this is the true origin of my books: this was the goal, that I might benefit those who have been entrusted to my instruction. Not vain ambition, nor weariness of leisure, nor impatience with silence—amidst such a great crowd of surrounding occupations—have driven me to write; but rather the solid benefit of my students. Then also, it was so that their parents and friends, and others further removed from our association, and finally posterity itself—if indeed my writings survive the passage of time—might know in what manner I am accustomed to train my students, and on what course I run with them. From this same source, this Book of MISCELLANIES <note>original: "Miscellaneorum," referring to a collection of varied writings on different topics</note> now comes forth, which, with the respect that is due, I come to give and dedicate to You, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN. I have called them Miscellanies because of the diversity and variety of the Exercises, and because they are sometimes joined by no bond of necessity. Although in the treating of individual points, I have been most diligent in maintaining order, as far as my understanding allows. And indeed the first Book contains a complete treatise on the *Prophets* and *Prophecy*; where I occasionally had to undertake an examination of those opinions which, in this inquisitive age, are sold as a great part of higher wisdom; but they are entirely harmful to the word and Spirit of God. If they should be counted as wisdom at all, they belong to that wisdom which the Apostle James calls earthly, sensual, and demonic <note>James 3:15</note>. In the Dissertations on the *Tabernacle* and the *Priesthood of Aaron*, I sometimes have a matter to settle with SPENCER <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English scholar who argued that many Jewish rituals were adapted from Egyptian customs. Witsius strongly disagreed, favoring a more "divine" origin for these laws.</note>, a man certainly most learned, but who, in almost all the Mosaic institutions <note>The laws and religious structures established by Moses</note>, prefers to see the foolishness of the Egyptians rather than the never-sufficiently-praised wisdom of God, who was teaching His people the saving mysteries of faith through those things as if through shadows. He loves to derive the most sacred chapters of the Israelite religion from the foul pools of the Egyptians, rather than admit that they were ordained by God as types and figures <note>A "type" is a person or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow a reality in the New Testament</note> of more secret things. ...so that he might be able to profit in the reading and understanding of the Sacred Scriptures <note>Latin: *Sacrarum Literarum*</note>. Unless perhaps one wishes to except the final Dissertation, *On the Donatist Schism* <note>The Donatists were a 4th-century North African Christian group who argued that the church must be a church of "saints" and not "sinners." These works, however, such as they are, it seemed fitting to inscribe to your most Illustrious name. For this thing I have very weighty reasons; some of which are common to me and my fellow citizens, others are more personal. All of us as many as inhabit the Diocese of Utrecht <note>Latin: *Dioecesin Ultrajectinam*; referring to the administrative and ecclesiastical province of Utrecht in the Netherlands</note> owe veneration to your remarkable virtues, by which you stand out no less than by your authority and power, and you diligently watch over the welfare of all. And in whatever way each person is able, it is fitting to bear witness to that veneration both in word and deed. Allow it, therefore, to be said to you now, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, what all your modesty cannot forbid or avoid being said about you: allow me to serve in some way as a mirror and show you to yourself, and do not fear that I might consider less what your ears can bear than what is due to your virtues. Your intellect, which nature gave you capable of many great things, and which you yourself have most diligently cultivated with the studies of wisdom, as soon as your age permitted, opened the way for you to magistracy and honors. There it soon appeared how much strength you possessed, and what could be entrusted to your skill, and finally what great things were to be expected from your prudence once it had matured, confirmed by the experience of affairs. For those qualities which individually ennoble men one by one,

...of [honoring], before which you held all other things as secondary; to which was added that honor of bearing, dignity of countenance, courtesy of manners, and affable humanity. Since each of these traits is highly effective for winning over the hearts of men, when they were seen joined in you in such a happy union, they easily secured for you the love, reverence, and admiration of all. For that reason, adorned with the highest honors and called to the greatest affairs, you turned the eyes not only of your fellow citizens but also of your colleagues toward yourself, as they believed that those matters would finally result in success which were to be managed by your foresight.

But never did your Devotion to the Fatherland <note>Latin: *Pietas in Patriam*. In the Roman sense, *pietas* refers to a profound sense of duty and loyalty to family, country, and God.</note> manifest itself more clearly than during that fatal calamity when, subjected to the dominion of the French <note>Latin: *Gallorum dominio*; this refers to the French occupation of Utrecht in 1672 during the "Year of Disaster" (*Rampjaar*), when Louis XIV's forces invaded the Dutch Republic.</note>, the country seemed almost to have been given up for lost. I pass over in silence the services you then performed for the citizens in the presence of the enemy; those who experienced how great your authority was even there, to their own great benefit, are not silent about it. I must record this one thing, which posterity will always acknowledge with a grateful mind: when this most beautiful and pleasant city had been devoted to total destruction <note>Latin: *internecioni*; a term implying complete slaughter or annihilation.</note> by a cruel decree of the French court—to be plundered first by the soldiers, then devastated by flames, and buried under its own ruins—then you, the pillar of the Fatherland and a delay to the fates, through prayers, counsel, and every kind of service, obtained the revocation of that deadly sentence, and gained for the city, as it were, life out of death. By your prudence, you persuaded the enemy to believe that a ransom for the city <note>Latin: *redemtionem civitatis*; referring to the "fire-money" or tribute paid to the French to prevent them from burning the city as they retreated.</note> would be more beneficial to their own interests than its total destruction.

I will not say what gratitude was returned by certain individuals. It is better to pass over some things in silence, as they are disgraces to our history <note>Latin: *annalium nostrorum dehonestamenta*. The true fruit of right actions is to have performed them; nor is there any price for virtues worthy of them outside of the virtues themselves. Furthermore, the human condition is subject to these turns: that adversity is born from prosperity, and prosperity from adversity. It hides the seeds of both...

# DEDICATION.

God, and the causes of good and evil things, often lie hidden under different appearances. It was of such significance that the Republic lacked your presence for a short time <note>The author likely refers to a period of political tension or a temporary setback in Van Weede’s career before his rise to greater prominence.</note>, so that it would become clear that it cannot do without you. For soon, not only restored to your former dignity but increased with new honors, you were a wall and a defense for exhausted affairs; you settled those things which were disturbed; in war and in peace; in the military camp and in the senate; at home and abroad—everywhere powerful in counsel, faithful, and successful. The witnesses are your many embassies, carried out with such glory and with such benefit to the Republic, through which those excellent virtues of yours became famous even among foreign nations. Surely to you also was owed that eulogy which Cicero, in his work *Cato the Elder*, records as having been inscribed on the tomb of Atilius Calatinus <note>A Roman statesman and general during the First Punic War, famed for his integrity.</note>: **MOST NATIONS AGREE THAT HE WAS THE FOREMOST MAN OF THE PEOPLE.** There is, however, no greater proof of your merits than the fact that you proved them to the greatest of Princes, the King of Great Britain <note>William III of Orange, who was both Stadtholder of the Netherlands and King of England, Scotland, and Ireland.</note>, a most keen judge of talents. To that King, I say, whom the Divinity, moved by prayer, timely granted to the earth, so that he might free his Britain from the shackles and fetters that were being prepared for her; that he might sustain the tottering Netherlands <note>Latin: *Belgica*; at this time, the term was often used to refer to the Dutch Republic.</note>; and that he might, through his wisdom, virtue, and success, shatter the insane efforts of the enemies who conspired for the ruin of the state and religion. He is truly worthy of one to whom—as if to a bright and beneficial star—not only the British but also his own Netherlanders eagerly fly, most ready to expose themselves to the blades of assassins for his sake, and to lay down their bodies if a path to safety must be built for him through human slaughter.

One might doubt, **ILLUSTRIOUS SIR**, whether among all your titles you count any as more majestic than that, like Hushai the Archite <note>A biblical figure (2 Samuel 15) who was a loyal counselor and "friend" to King David, helping him against the rebellion of Absalom.</note> was to David of old, you deserve to be called **THE KING’S FRIEND** to **WILLIAM III**. This friendship is the more glorious to you because it is useful only to the public good. Indeed, your fortune possesses nothing greater than your ability, nor your nature anything better than your desire, to benefit as many people as possible.

# DEDICATION.

And since these great merits of yours are no less evident to me than to the rest of my fellow citizens, it is only right that they be acknowledged and proclaimed by me as well; your fame shall remain in the minds of the Belgians <note>original: "Belgarum"—at this time, the term was often used to refer to the inhabitants of the Low Countries (the Netherlands), not just modern-day Belgium.</note> and in the eternity of time. But there is also a more personal and private reason that has obliged me to record and commemorate your virtues. Indeed, through a close companionship of four months, it was granted to me not only to know those virtues more intimately, but also to enjoy them; this was when I served as chaplain <note>Latin: "a sacris"</note> to the Dutch embassy to Britain to see JAMES II, of which you were a major part. Then, with the public persona set aside—which a person can hardly maintain at all times even at home—I saw who you were within yourself. I learned, through no deceptive trial, what your mind, soul, and sincerity were like, not only regarding the State, but also regarding God and His worship; what reverence you had for His word, what zeal for truth directed toward piety, and finally, what care you had for preserving the Church in the purity of faith and the unity of peace.

From 그hat time on, I found access to you easy and gentle, and your ears were open to me. Just as I never wearied them with troublesome solicitations regarding matters that did not concern me, so I always found them favorable whenever I had to recommend either the cause of certain poor people or the affairs of Religion and the Church. For I believe those matters, concerning which I ever had any conversation with you, can be reduced to these two heads. Nor would I deny that it was a great comfort to my soul that you deigned to profess—so often and so extensively, even among leading men—that my ministry did not displease you, but rather that you approved of my integrity, simplicity, modesty, and the consistency of my life. Since I judged that the memory of these things ought to be preserved, I wished to insert them into this Dedication, by which I dedicate this work, whatever its worth, to your name.

Receive it, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS SIR, with your accustomed fairness and benevolence; receive it, I say, as a token of my perpetual [respect] toward you...

# DEDICATION.

as a lasting token of my respect. This is the only favor, this the only grace, which I now implore for myself and for my book. For I do not, as many are accustomed to do, demand the protection of your authority against detractors by means of an ambitious inscription. Your reputation is more sacred to me than to allow it to be exposed to the malice of others for my sake. And finally, those things which I have stated well, being safe under the protection of truth alone, will defend themselves; as for those things stated poorly, I would not even wish to defend them. Let them perish and vanish before the brighter radiance of a more serene light.

But you, **MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN**, live, flourish, and, enriched by the gifts of heaven, remain prosperous for many years. Add new and greater deeds to your most famous achievements, which shall be made eternal through all ages in titles and mindful annals <note>Latin: *fastos*—originally referring to the Roman calendar or list of consuls, but here used to mean historical records or the registry of great deeds.</note>.

# P R E F A C E .

These brief notes on almost any subject matter are those by which I discovered that the things I had treated more extensively could be explained, and some even more accurately and elegantly. However, it did not seem right to recommend this second edition of the work with such frequent changes that much of the grace or dignity of the first would be lost. It was received too kindly by the public for me to deserve poorly of fair buyers by depreciating the value of the copies they now own. Therefore, you will find few things corrected or polished in this edition, and even fewer added; for I have taken care that the page numbering remains consistent in both editions. But so that my progress would not be entirely lost to the public, and so that I might show my candor—which I consider a great ornament of learning—by praising others who have delivered better treatments than mine where the subject warranted it, I have cast some brief remarks into writing as a sample, which I now present in this preface.

<margin>Book I. Chapter I.</margin>
I. What the word "Prophet" signified among the people of God, I have explained at sufficient length in *Book I*, if I am not mistaken. I now wish to add <margin>Among the Egyptians, the high priest of sacred rites was called a Prophet.</margin> that among the Egyptians, the **high priest** was called a *prophet*; he was the one who presided over the other priests and the *pastophoroi* <term>pastophoroi: priests who carried the sacred shrines or images in processions</term>, and who distributed the temple revenues to the rest. *Epiphanius, Book III, Against Heresies:* <note>original Greek: παρὰ δὲ Αἰγυπτίοις προφῆται καλούμενοι τῶν ἀδύτων τε καὶ ἱερῶν ἀρχηγοί</note> "Among the Egyptians, those called prophets are the leaders of the inner sanctuaries and the sacred rites." To be sure, first in the temple procession went the *Singer*, then the *Horoscopus* <term>horoscopus: an observer of the stars who determined the correct times for rituals</term>, then the *Scribe* or *hierogrammateus* <term>hierogrammateus: a sacred scribe responsible for holy texts and symbols</term>, and afterwards the *Stolistes* <term>stolistes: the priest responsible for dressing the sacred statues and managing the vestments</term>. Finally, last of all walked the *Prophet*, carrying a water jar in his robe, as *Clement of Alexandria* teaches in *Book VI*. The Egyptians graced their chief priests with the name of "Prophets" because they believed certain secrets and mysteries were handed down by them. From this, those eager for foreign wisdom sought their intimacy. <note>original Greek: ἱστορεῖται Πυθαγόρας μὲν Σωγχῇδι τῷ Αἰγυπτίων ἀρχιπροφήτῃ μαθητεῦσαι</note> "It is recorded that Pythagoras was a pupil of Sonchis, the Egyptian Arch-prophet," according to the same *Clement in Book I*. And the other Clement <note>Referring to the author of the *Clementine Recognitions*, an early Christian work traditionally attributed to Pope Clement I.</note> in the *Recognitions, Book I*, not far from the beginning:

# P R E F A C E .
<meta>catchword: among</meta>

"I will seek Egypt," he says, "and there I will become a friend to the Hierophants <note>Priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>, or the Prophets who preside over the inner shrines." See *Ménage's observations on the Preface of Diogenes Laertius, Section 1,* and especially *Valois on Eusebius, Book 4, Chapter 8.* *Spartianus* (on page 65 of my copy) records that certain Greeks consecrated **Antinous** <note>The favorite of Emperor Hadrian, who was deified after his death</note> at the wish of **Hadrian**. Regarding this passage, *Casaubon* noted: *While other monuments of that consecration exist today, that one in Rome is particularly excellent:*

->TO ANTINOUS,<-
->WHO SHARES THE THRONE OF THE<-
->GODS IN EGYPT,<-
->M. ULPIUS APOLLONIUS,<-
->PROPHET.<-

*The man who dedicated this stone in honor of Antinous was a freedman of Hadrian, or of one of Trajan's relatives. He was, moreover, a Prophet—that is, a priest of Antinous. But because it is commonly believed that those endowed with the priesthood possess the power of divination, he does not call himself a priest or a flamen <note>A Roman priest dedicated to a specific deity</note>, but a Prophet.*

<margin>II. Bochart proves at length that the story of Jeremiah's belt was an actual historical event.</margin>
II. In Chapter III, Section IX, I briefly mentioned that it is not certain—as some argue—that the story of Jeremiah’s belt (which was placed at the bank of the Euphrates, rotted there, and was later taken up and worn by him again) should be explained as a prophetic vision rather than as a real historical event. Later, I came across the *Letters of Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note>, where this problem is treated more precisely. It is proved there, by both authority and logical arguments, that *Cyril* wrote well in his *commentaries on Hosea*: <term>No reasoning persuades us to reject the literal letter and to condemn the simple historical reality as mere fiction</term> <note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς ἡμᾶς ἀναπείθει λόγος παραιτεῖσθαι τὸ γράμμα, καὶ τῆς ἱστορίας τὸ εἰκαῖον καταψηφίζεσθαι</note>. There is no reason that should persuade us to repudiate the literal sense or to diminish the probability of the history by our own opinion. See, if you please, the very learned letter added to the *Sacred Geography, page 959 of the most recent edition.*

# P R E F A C E .

According to Theodoret <note>A 5th-century Bishop and influential Christian historian</note> in his *Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, Chapter 24*:
When Theodosius <note>Theodosius I (the Great), the last Emperor to rule over both the Eastern and Western halves of the Roman Empire</note> was about to fight against the Tyrant Eugenius <note>A usurper who attempted to restore paganism in the West</note> with only a small force of troops, he spent the entire night in prayer in a chapel situated on the peak of the mountain where he had his camp. Near dawn, sleep overcame him against his will. As he lay upon the ground, he seemed to see two men dressed in white garments and riding upon white horses. They told him to cast aside his fear and be of good heart, and at first light to take up arms and arrange his battle line for the fight. They said they had been sent as helpers and protectors; one was John the Evangelist, and the other was Philip the Apostle. Encouraged by this vision, the Emperor was inspired to offer prayers to God even more eagerly.

The same vision occurred to a soldier while he slept. When he told this to his centurion, he was led by him to the Tribune, and from the Tribune to the Master of the Horse <term>Master of the Horse: A high-ranking military commander, second only to the Emperor in the field</term>. Thinking he was bringing news of something new, the commander reported it to the Emperor. But the Emperor said: *“He did not see this for my sake; for I have already believed those who promised victory. But lest anyone should perhaps suspect that I, out of a desire for fighting, invented these things, the Helper of my empire revealed these things to him also, so that he might be a suitable witness to my account.”* For the common Lord had presented this vision to me first. Therefore, casting aside fear, let us follow the standard-bearers and leaders.

In short, when they came to the battle <note>The Battle of the Frigidus in 394 AD</note> and weapons began to be hurled from both sides, those protectors showed that what they had promised was true. For a violent wind, rushing from the opposite direction against the enemies, turned away all their arrows, javelins, and spears, so that all their weapons were carried off in vain. Added to this, an immense force of dust was carried with great force into their faces, forcing them to close their eyelids and attend to their endangered eyes. But the soldiers of Emperor Theodosius, suffering no inconvenience from that whirlwind, were slaughtering the enemy with spirited hearts.

IV. The unique privileges of Moses according to Jewish instruction.

IV. I have related the unique privileges of Moses above all other prophets in Chapter VII. The Doctors of the Hebrews value him so highly that, among the thirteen fundamental articles of their faith, they have formulated the seventh in these words, found in an elegant Instruction <note>original: Catechesis</note> titled *Sefer Lekach Tov* <note>original Hebrew: ספר לקח טוב; 'The Book of Good Doctrine'</note>, which has been reprinted several times in Amsterdam by the Jewish community: 

*That Moses was a man of the greatest stature in prophecy, surpassing all prophets who have ever existed from age to age; and that all other prophets who were before him, even the Patriarchs <note>The early biblical fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</note> themselves and their descendants, were lesser in dignity than he. He was the chosen of the God of Jacob, and through his hand, God gave to Israel the law of truth which restores the soul; and he reached a level in the knowledge of the Blessed God that no other man has ever attained.*

Furthermore, they maintain that there were four primary advantages <note>original Greek: Προτερήματα (Proterēmata)</note> belonging to Moses, listed in this order:

I. That, no matter who the prophet might be, the Lord does not speak with him except through an Angel, or some being separated from physical matter; whereas He spoke with Moses directly <note>original: oretenus; literally 'by mouth'</note>, just as it is said: *I will speak with him mouth to mouth.* (Numbers 12:8).

II. That for none of the other prophets did prophecy occur except in a dream, or a night vision, or during the day after a heavy sleep, to such an extent that all their senses failed them, as it is written: *In a vision I will make myself known to him, in a dream I will speak with him.* (Ibid. verse 6). But of Moses it is said: *Not so with my servant Moses.*

III. That in all the other prophets, when the prophetic influence <note>original: influxu prophetico; the divine inspiration entering the mind</note> came upon them, their senses either ceased to function or were certainly weakened. To Moses, however, no trembling or weakness occurred; rather, with his senses remaining strong, he related to God just as a man does to a friend speaking to him.

<margin>VI. Maimonides's notable commentary on the vision of God which Moses requested.</margin>

VI. But, they say, if he believed that God cannot be seen, why did he so earnestly ask to be admitted to the sight of Him? It is worth the effort to learn how *Moses Maimonides* <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> responded to that question; the most learned man *Ludovicus de Dieu* <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist.</note> presented his truly remarkable commentary from the *Treatise on the Foundations of the Law*, Chapter I, in his notes on *Exodus 33:18.*

*That is, he sought to know the truth of the essence of God to such an extent that he would hold Him known in his heart, no differently than if he had known this or that man whose face he had seen, or whose form he had engraved on his mind. Thus Moses sought that the essence of God might exist in his mind as distinct from the other essences of beings, so that he might know the truth of His essence as it is. Nevertheless, He revealed to him what no man knew before him, nor will any know after him; so that he attained something regarding the truth of His essence by which God was distinguished in his mind from all other beings: namely, in the same way that someone who had seen a person’s back, and had known his body and clothing, would have that person distinguished in his mind from the bodies of all other men.* <note>The author provides this Latin translation of the Hebrew text above to ensure the reader understands Maimonides's philosophical distinction: Moses didn't want to "see" God with eyes, but to "know" God's unique essence as clearly as we recognize a friend's face.</note>

<margin>VII. That Moses wrote the entire Pentateuch from the mouth of God as He dictated is a fundamental article of the Jewish faith.</margin>

VII. In the dispute regarding whether Moses is the author of the Pentateuch <term>Pentateuch; the first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy)</term>—which I have pursued at length in Chapter XIV—it is neither unpleasant nor useless to have explored the opinion of the modern Synagogue. They have included this view among those articles of faith which, if anyone denies even one, he is to be considered a deserter of the Jewish faith. This article is the eighth in order in the Catechism <note>Refers to Maimonides's "Thirteen Principles of Faith," which became a standard of Jewish orthodoxy.</note> just praised, expressed in this language: <gloss>That the whole Torah, in its entirety, from "In the beginning" <note>original Hebrew: *Bereshit* (Genesis 1:1)</note> until "in the sight of all Israel" <note>original Hebrew: *le-eyne kol Yisrael* (Deuteronomy 34:12), the final words of the Pentateuch.</note>, was written by Moses from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He; and there is no difference between the verse, "I am the Lord your God" <note>Exodus 20:2, the beginning of the Ten Commandments.</note> and the verse, "And Timna was a concubine" <note>Genesis 36:12; a seemingly minor genealogical detail.</note> and similar such verses; rather, the whole is equal, and all its verses and words are the word of the Lord and His commandments.</gloss> *That Moses wrote the entire Law absolutely, from the first word "Bereshit" to the final words, in the sight of all Israel, from the mouth of the Lord: and that there is no difference between the verse: "I am the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:2) and the verse: "and Timna was a concubine" (Genesis 36:12) and so on in similar cases: but that all these things are the voice and speech of the Lord, whose meaning is expressed by every verse and every single word.*

The Israelite Church thus professes two things in clear speech: first, that God is the author of the Pentateuch in all its parts and down to its individual words; second, that Moses was the writer of it all, who, by the inspiration of the supreme deity, committed it to enduring letters just as they were dictated to him. Maimonides records that Moses took care that every tribe was provided with a copy of the sacred volume thus written by him, in the Preface to his excellent work titled *The Mighty Hand* <term>Jad Chasaka; better known as the *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides's massive codification of Jewish law</term>: <gloss>Our teacher Moses wrote the whole Torah in his own handwriting before he died, and gave a scroll to each and every tribe, and placed one scroll in the Ark as a witness.</gloss> *Moses our Teacher described the whole Law with his own hand before he died, and presented a volume to each individual tribe: but one he stored in the Ark to serve as a witness, according to Deuteronomy 31:26.*

For that man exists in his mind as separate from all other men. So Moses sought that the essence of God might exist in his mind as separate from the other essences of beings; so that he might know the truth of His essence as it is. But God answered him that it is far beyond the mind of any living man—since he is composed of body and soul—to attain the truth of this matter as it is in its purity. Yet He revealed to him what no man knew before him, nor will anyone know after him; so that he attained something regarding the truth of His essence by which God was distinguished in his mind from the rest of beings: namely, in the same way that someone who had seen the back of a person, and had known their body and clothing, would have them distinguished in his mind from the bodies of other men.*

<margin>VII. That Moses wrote the entire Pentateuch from the mouth of God as He dictated it is a fundamental article of the Jewish faith.</margin>

VII. In the dispute over whether Moses was the author of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>—which I have discussed at length in Chapter 14—it is neither unpleasant nor useless to examine the opinion of the modern Synagogue. They have included this belief among those articles of faith which, if a person denies any one of them, he is to be considered a deserter of the Jewish faith. The article is the eighth in order in the previously praised Catechism, expressed in these words: <note>original Hebrew: "שכל התורה כולה מבראשית עד לעיני כל ישראל כלה כתבה משה מפי הק"בה ואין הפרש בין פסוק אנכי ה' אלקיך לפסוק ותמנע היתה פלגש וכדומה לזה' אלא כלה היתה שוה ודבר ה' ומימרו הם כל פסוקיה ודבריה"</note> *That the entire Law, from the first word "In the beginning" [Bereshit] to the final words "in the sight of all Israel," was written by Moses from the mouth of the Lord; and there is no difference between the verse: "I am the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:2) and the verse: "And Timna was a concubine" (Genesis 36:12) and others like it; rather, all are equal, and every verse and word is the speech and utterance of the Lord, whose meaning is expressed in every verse and every single word.* 

Thus, the Israelite community professes two things in clear speech: first, that God is the author of the Pentateuch in all its parts and every single word; and second, that Moses was the writer of them all, who, by the inspiration of the supreme divinity, committed them to lasting letters exactly as they were dictated to him. Maimonides records in the Preface to his excellent work titled *Jad Chasaka* <term>The "Strong Hand," also known as the *Mishneh Torah*, a comprehensive code of Jewish law written by Maimonides.</term> that Moses ensured each tribe was provided for with a copy of the sacred volume he had written: <note>original Hebrew: "כל התורה כתבה משה רבינו בכתב ידו : קודם שמת ונתן ספר לכל שבט ושבט וספר אחד נתן בארון לעד"</note> *Our Teacher Moses wrote out the entire Law in his own hand before he died, and gave a scroll to each and every tribe; and one scroll he placed in the Ark as a witness,* according to *Deuteronomy 31:26*.

<margin>VIII. Jean Le Clerc, having changed his opinion, acknowledges Moses as the writer of the Pentateuch.</margin>
VIII. But there is also something else in this Disputation <note>The author's larger academic work or argument.</note> which I believe it concerns my honesty and candor not to hide. Besides the opinions and arguments of Thomas Hobbes, Baruch Spinoza, and Richard Simon in that controversy, I brought forward and examined a completely new and unique opinion, by which the writing of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> was taken away from Moses and attributed to some unknown Samaritan priest. I had read this in a French book <note>referring to *Sentimens de quelques théologiens de Hollande* (1685)</note> which presents the judgments of certain Dutch theologians regarding Richard Simon’s *Critical History*. The author of that book is believed by public report to be Jean Le Clerc, a most learned man. Nor have I ever understood that this offspring of his intellect <note>meaning his authorship of the book</note> was ever denied by him. In that book, which he wrote in an epistolary style <note>written as a series of letters</note>, he sometimes plays his own part, and sometimes speaks as if in the name of some friend of his. I, without a worried observation of that distinction—which I believe he himself did not much demand to be noticed—simply called him Le Clerc for the sake of brevity. Since that time, there has appeared the same *Jean Le Clerc’s Philological Commentary on the First Book of the Prophet Moses.* Prefixed to it are three Dissertations. The title of the third is *On Moses as the Writer of the Pentateuch:* where, having changed tack <note>original Latin: *versa velificatione*, literally "having turned the sails," a nautical metaphor for changing one's mind or direction</note>, he defends almost the same opinion that we have put forward, and frees it from the difficulties by which it is usually burdened. I thought this should be mentioned here not only to vindicate my own sincerity but also for his own praise.

...Elisha spoke to Hazael in these words: <term>Say to him, "Not..."</term> <note>original Hebrew: *lo emor-lo*</note> <term>"You shall surely live; yet the Lord has shown me that he shall surely die."</term> <note>original Hebrew: *chayoh tichyeh ve-hir’ani Yehovah ki mot yamut*</note> These words are rendered variously in other languages due to the ambiguity of the particle <term>not</term> <note>Hebrew: *lo* (לא)</note>. Ordinarily, when written this way, it means "not." However, the Masoretes <note>the Jewish scholars and scribes who standardized the Hebrew Bible text between the 6th and 10th centuries</note> observed that there are fifteen places where it is indeed written as <term>not</term> <note>לא</note>, but it ought to be read—or at least understood—as if it were written as <term>to him</term> <note>לו</note>, which signifies "to him." They include this specific passage among those fifteen. If we set aside that Masoretic observation, Elisha's speech should be explained with this meaning: *Go, say, you shall not recover at all; for Jehovah has shown me that he shall surely die.* This is the version given by Junius <note>Franciscus Junius the Elder, a 16th-century Reformed theologian</note>, which our Dutch translators also follow.

However, many of the ancient interpreters, many of the Jewish Teachers, and several Christians have been more pleased by the Masoretic note. The Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> has: *Go, say to him, you shall be healed.* The Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> says: *Come, say, you shall surely live.* <note>original Greek: δεῦρο, εἶπον, ζωῇ ζήσῃ</note> The Chaldean, Syrian, and Arabic versions are in the same sense. This was also followed by Josephus in *Antiquities, Book IX, Chapter 2*: *The prophet ordered Hazael to report nothing bad to the king.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ προφήτης τὸν μὲν Ἀζάηλον ἐκέλευσε μηδὲν ἀπαγγέλλειν τῷ βασιλεῖ κακόν</note> 

The most illustrious man **Campegius Vitringa** <note>a Dutch theologian and Hebraist (1659–1722)</note>, in his *Sacred Observations, Book III, Chapter 16*, judges that the Masoretic explanation is to be preferred, based on these arguments:

I. Because Hazael, when reporting the Prophet’s words to his master Ben-hadad, repeats those very words <term>you shall surely live</term> <note>Hebrew: *chayoh tichyeh*</note>, omitting the negative particle <term>not</term> <note>לא</note>. It is not at all certain that Hazael reported the prophet's words in any way other than the prophet had spoken them.

II. The imperative verb <term>say</term> <note>Hebrew: *emor*</note> is most conveniently constructed with the following relative word <term>to him</term> <note>Hebrew: *lo*</note>. For it is entirely probable that Elisha would wish to make some mention of the person about whom he was speaking, and to whom certain words were to be delivered in his name. Thus, the elegance of the speech and its construction requires us to believe that Elisha said, <term>say to him</term> <note>Hebrew: *emor lo*</note>, referring to the king himself, and not simply <term>say</term> <note>Hebrew: *emor*</note>.

III. Added to this is the fact that the authors of the sacred punctuation <note>the Masoretes who added vowel points and accents</note> joined the particle <term>not</term> <note>לא</note> to the preceding word <term>say</term> <note>אֱמֹר</note> by a *Makkaph* <note>a Hebrew hyphen used to link words together grammatically</note>; by this they [indicated] clearly enough...

...clearly indicating that they wish the little word <term>not</term> <note>Hebrew: *lo* (לא)</note> to be understood here as <term>to him</term> <note>Hebrew: *lo* (לו)</note>. Thus far Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note>. But those who follow that interpretation involve themselves in a great difficulty, from which the way out is quite troublesome. For how could the most holy Prophet of God—having been consulted seriously and respectfully by a sick king—advise a royal minister to tell a useless lie, contrary to God’s clear revelation? Here the interpreters sweat much; and there is scarcely anyone who finds a satisfactory path for himself. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> almost gives up the fight when he comments thus: *if we follow this reading, there would be here not only dissimulation [concealing the truth], such as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> suggests, but something more, which was then considered permissible against foreigners and idolaters.*

But whatever may be said by that illustrious man, I do not believe it is right for anyone to induce another to lie; much less that such a thing would be consistent with the Prophet’s mission and the purpose of the divine oracle. Ben Gersom <note>Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator</note> certainly talks nonsense, contending that the Prophet did not want the oracle revealed to him from heaven to be reported to the king, lest it be said that the king died of fright upon hearing such a fatal sentence, and the cause of death be blamed on the Prophet. Others, therefore, prefer to think that the prophet spoke ironically, following the example of Micaiah in 1 Kings 22:15, who said to Ahab: *Go up and triumph, for the Lord will give it into the hand of the king.* <note>Micaiah spoke these words in mockery of the false prophets' flattery, knowing Ahab would actually fail</note>. 

Truly, even this is not quite fitting. For Elisha was not dealing with King Benhadad himself, such that the king could have understood the irony from the speaker's gestures or tone of voice—as Ahab easily understood. Marinus <note>likely referring to a contemporary biblical commentator</note> notes that the Prophet used an ambiguous expression, so that the word <term>Lo</term> <note>original Latin: *amphibola locutione*</note> could be understood as "not" or as "to him"; but Hazael understood it affirmatively. However, this contradicts the text: for the Prophet says expressly, "the Lord has revealed to me that he shall surely die." Others, therefore, argue more subtly: the king asked, "Will I recover from this illness?" The Prophet orders that he be answered precisely: "You will certainly recover." That is, this illness is not lethal, nor will it be the cause of your death in and of itself.

The reasons brought forward by the most distinguished *Vitringa* in defense of the Masoretic observation seem to me to be of little weight, if I may say so with all due respect to him. <meta>This page continues the philological and moral debate regarding Elisha’s prophecy in 2 Kings 8:10. The author is refuting an interpretation offered by a "Learned Man" (likely a contemporary critic) who argued that the envoy Hazael did not lie to King Ben-hadad, but accurately reported the Prophet's words. The author argues instead that Hazael deliberately manipulated the ambiguity of the Hebrew text to deceive the King.</meta>

-># PREFACE.<-

It was more consistent with Hazael's character that he be believed to have lied against his own religious convictions—which he undoubtedly did—than that a speech be attributed to the most pure Prophet which even in appearance favored a falsehood. "It is not established," says the *Learned Man*, "that Hazael reported the words of the Prophet differently than the Prophet had spoken them." On the contrary, I say, it is well-established that Hazael perverted the Prophet's meaning and reported to his master the opposite of that truth which he knew was contained in the prophecy. 

*Louis Cappel* <note>Ludovicus Cappellus (1585–1658) was a pioneering French Protestant scholar of Hebrew and biblical criticism.</note> notes acutely in his *Sacred Criticism, Book III, Chapter 10, Section 15*: "Unless perhaps one says that the Holy Spirit used the ambiguous word *lo* <note>The Hebrew word לא (meaning "not") sounds exactly like the word לו (meaning "to him"), a common source of puns and scribal confusion in the Bible.</note> here so that it might simultaneously express both Elisha's command and Hazael’s action, which was contrary to that command. For Elisha commanded that he should say, 'you will by no means recover'; but Hazael, because he knew such a message would be unwelcome to Ben-hadad, reported the opposite: 'you will altogether recover.'" 

Regarding the second point, I observe: The imperative verb *say* <note>Hebrew: אמור (amor)</note> is no less easily paired with the following negative particle *not* <note>Hebrew: לא (lo)</note> than with the relative particle *to him* <note>Hebrew: לו (lo)</note>. For it was not necessary for the Prophet to specify the person to whom these things were to be reported; the situation spoke for itself. One must have excessively fastidious ears to judge that the speech and its construction lack their proper grace when one hears the Prophet responding to Hazael, who was consulting him about his master's health: "Go, say, you shall by no means live." 

The Greeks <note>The authors of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, who are otherwise more studious of elegance, omitted the little word *to him* which the most learned man emphasizes here: "Come, say, you shall surely live" <note>original Greek: δεῦρο, εἶπον, ζωῇ ζήση</note>. What he notes in the third place concerning the *Maqqaph* <note>The term for a Hebrew punctuation mark similar to a hyphen used to link words together.</note> is almost nothing: for how tiny, how often non-existent is the force of that little line, except perhaps for the sake of sound; the most learned man knows better than I how indiscriminately it is placed or omitted, and how in the same construction it connects now these words, now others. To look no further, this very chapter provides us with an example. In the fifth verse, the words are joined thus: *and it happened as he was telling* <note>Hebrew: ויהי הוא־מספר (vayehi hu-mesapper)</note>, where the *Maqqaph* is between the last two words, whose joining the sense requires.

The Book of the Great Wisdom of Solomon <note>original: "Liber sapientiæ magnæ Salomonis"</note> (which is called the Book of Wisdom, and of which Rabbi Moses Nachmanides <note>A leading medieval Jewish scholar (1194–1270) also known as Ramban.</note> says in the Prologue to his commentary on the Law: *I saw a book written in Chaldean*, etc.; he cites words which are found in the Book of Wisdom, Chapter 7) seems to me—if it was not a translation—to have been composed by Solomon in the Chaldean language so that he might send it to some king living in the farthest reaches of the Orient. Truly, I do not think this is probable; but what forbids us from believing that Solomon was no less skilled in the Chaldean tongue than the courtiers of King Hezekiah <note>A reference to 2 Kings 18:26, where officials ask to speak in Aramaic (Chaldean) to avoid being understood by the common people.</note>? It is surely a weak argument that a book should be denied to Solomon simply because certain Chaldean words are found in it.

Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, at the end of Book 15 of his commentary on Isaiah, near the beginning of Chapter 57, writes thus: *The Jews believe that Isaiah prophesied concerning his own death, that he was to be sawn apart by Manasseh with a wooden saw; this is a most certain tradition among them. <margin>
XXIII. The horns of the altar provided the protection of refuge.
</margin>

XXIII. In the same *Dissertation*, §. 26, I briefly mentioned that the horns of the altar served as a refuge for criminals. But this matter requires a fuller explanation. That those who feared judgment—whether from private individuals or from the public—fled to the altar is manifest from Exodus 21:14. There, concerning one guilty of intentional murder, God says, *take him from my altar to be put to death.* <note>original: "ab altari meo rapito eum ad mortem"</note> That the horns of the altar were grasped by such people is witnessed by the history of Adonijah and Joab in 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. <note>The text cites 11. 28, likely a scribal or printing error for 2:28, the account of Joab's death.</note> However, the illustrious *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> observes that this was done more out of the custom of the nations than by the institution of the Law. And indeed, as far as I know, no Divine Law exists by which the altar is ordained to be an asylum. From the law just cited, the Hebrew Masters <note>Rabbinical scholars and commentators on the Torah.</note> not ineptly infer this one thing: that a killer who retreats to the altar by mistake <note>i.e., accidental manslaughter or "homicide from error"</note> is neither to be killed there, nor to be dragged from there to his death. But it is worthwhile to know by what narrow limits the consultants of Hebrew law circumscribe the immunity of the altar. They have formed various exceptions for themselves, some of which concern the *parts of the altar*, others the *persons* fleeing to it, others the *quality of the crimes*, and finally others the *stay* at the altar. They say that not the whole altar, not the sides, not the horns, much less the vicinity of the altar, but only the *roof* <note>The flat upper surface of the altar where the fire burned.</note>—that is, the upper part of the body of the altar—provided the protection of refuge. And they claim this applies not to just any persons, but only to *priests*; and not even to all of them, but only to a priest performing sacred rites on the very roof of the altar. Regarding the quality of the crimes, they warn that what has been said about the altar applies only to such killers as the cities assigned as *Asylums* <note>The six "Cities of Refuge" established in the Law of Moses for those who committed accidental manslaughter.</note> would otherwise have protected. Finally, they deny that it was permitted for one who had fled to the altar to *stay* there; rather, he was to be led from there to a city of refuge suitable for him. See *Selden's On the Law of Nature and Nations, Book IV, Chapter II*, where everything I have said is confirmed by the testimonies of the Hebrews. <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a renowned English polymath and scholar of Jewish law.</note> For my part, I do not think much of these technicalities of Hebrew law. However, since no Divine Law was provided for criminals [to find safety at the altar...]

<margin>XXIII. Whether the horns of the altar provided the protection of refuge.</margin>
XXIII. In that same *Dissertation*, section 26, I briefly mentioned that the horns of the altar <note>The "horns" were horn-like projections at the four corners of the ancient Israelite altar of burnt offering.</note> served as a refuge for criminals. However, that matter requires a more thorough explanation. It is clear from Exodus 21:14 that those who feared judgment—whether from private individuals or public authority—fled to the altar. There, regarding one guilty of voluntary murder, God says: *“take him from my altar that he may die.”* That the horns of the altar were specifically grasped by those in such a state is testified by the history of Adonijah and Joab in 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. <note>The original text cites 11:28, likely a scribal or printing error for 2:28, the passage describing Joab’s flight.</note> Yet the illustrious **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a foundational Dutch jurist and philosopher.</note> observes that this was done more out of the custom of the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the Greeks and Romans, whose temples often served as inviolable sanctuaries.</note> than by the instruction of the law. And indeed, as far as I know, no Divine Law exists by which the altar is decreed to be an asylum. From the law just mentioned, the Hebrew Teachers <note>Referring to the Rabbis and Talmudic commentators.</note> not ineptly deduce this one thing: that a killer by error <term>homicida ex errore|One guilty of accidental killing or manslaughter rather than premeditated murder.</term> who retreats to the altar is neither to be killed there, nor dragged from there to his death.

But it is worthwhile to learn within what narrow limits the Hebrew legal experts circumscribe the immunity of the altar. They have formed various exceptions, some of which concern the *parts of the altar*, others the *persons* fleeing to it, others the *nature of the crimes*, and finally others the *stay* at the altar. They say that not the whole altar, nor its sides, nor its horns—let alone the area surrounding the altar—provided the protection of refuge, but only the *roof*, that is, the upper surface of the altar’s body. Furthermore, they claim this was not for just any person, but only for *priests*; and not even all of them, but only for a priest who was *performing sacred rites* upon the roof of the altar itself. Regarding the nature of the crimes, they warn that what has been said about the altar applies only to those killers to whom the designated *Cities of Refuge* <note>Six cities established in the Mosaic law (Numbers 35) specifically to protect those who killed someone accidentally.</note> were intended to provide protection. Finally, they deny that it was permitted for one who had fled to the altar to *stay* there; instead, he was to be led from there to a city of refuge suitable for him. See **Selden**, *On the Law of Nature and Nations, Book IV, Chapter 11*, where all I have said is confirmed by Hebrew testimonies. <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English polymath and expert in Jewish law.</note> For my part, I do not place great value on these technicalities of Hebrew law. However, since no Divine law provides safety for criminals—

<margin>XXIV. With what intention the Patriarchs offered sacrifices, according to Abarbanel and Menachem.</margin>
XXIV. ...Although Cain could hardly bear <note>original: "dignè ferret"</note> that his brother’s sacrifice was preferred to his own—given that he had observed the rituals of sacrifice no less correctly than his brother, and that nothing he offered, whether in terms of the gift itself or the external method and ceremony of the offering, was less worthy or better produced than his brother’s—God warns him that it is not the offering itself that is to be considered here, nor whether it was performed correctly according to ceremonial law, but rather the person making the offering and whether they are given over to sin or not. XXVIII. I noted in Book II, Dissertation III, Section 5, that a man devoted to idleness was excluded from the Senate by Hebrew law. It counts idleness <note>Hebrew: *ha-battalah*</note> in the first place among the seven principal sins from which others usually sprout. It describes it thus: *Idleness is a wicked disease, by which a man is lazy and sluggish, so that he does not reach his perfection, and by which he disposes and directs his heart toward useless things, so that he is occupied neither in the Law, nor in the commandments, nor in the works entrusted to him. Moreover, whoever plays at* DICE, OR CARDS, AND SIMILAR GAMES, *commits this sin: because he is not occupied in things pertaining to the stability of the world. Yet it is forbidden for a man, as long as he lives in the world, to be occupied in anything other than the Law, or works of charity, or trade, or a craft and profession, through which the world is established. Whence also such a man is numbered among those who are not admitted to give testimony in a court of law.*

# FUNERAL ORATION
### ON THE DEATH OF HERMAN WITSIUS.

->Delivered at Leiden <note>Latin: *Lugduni Batavorum* is the Latin name for the city of Leiden in the Netherlands, home to its famous university.</note> on October 29, 1708 <note>Latin: *a. d. IV. # ORATION.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop-cap "E" at the beginning of the paragraph, decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Therefore, must our Academy <note>The University of Leiden.</note>, struck once again by the divine blow of heavenly lightning, threaten a most heavy fall? And with the double wound of its Head <note>Referring to the loss of prominent faculty members.</note> scarcely healed, is a third inflicted upon it that is by no means lighter? Therefore, does the City resound once again with laments and wailings, and call the whole Church, both near and far—which previously enjoyed the greatest brilliance of his light—to share in its grief? Therefore, have we come once more from the funeral rites, and gathered in this mourning assembly, which, through the signs of most justified grief thrusting themselves into everyone's eyes from all sides, drives away all vigor of mind? Therefore, even now must I speak to you, I who contemplate the magnitude of our common loss with a large stream of tears? I, who more than all others must be afflicted—having already lost the Great Spanheim <note>original: *Spanhemium*; Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701), a noted theologian.</note> and the Distinguished Trigland <note>original: *Triglandium*; Jacobus Trigland the Younger (1652–1705), a professor of theology at Leiden.</note>, those most dear men whom I once found teaching here to everyone's admiration, but whom it is no longer possible to see—am I now deprived of the sweetest and most useful companionship of the Most Celebrated Witsius? 

You, indeed, renowned man, were the one from whose praise my youthful studies received their first honor before a third of a century had even passed! You were the one who then sent me into the Most Holy Ministry of the Church with solemn prayers and advice, and after the passing of a single year, admitted me as quite a young man into the fellowship of the Franeker Chair <note>The University of Franeker was the second oldest university in the Netherlands, known for its theological faculty.</note> through your counsels! You were the one who, both in person and in absence, helped me with the most wholesome advice, and always showed a truly fatherly affection toward me! You were the one, the sole survivor of all the teachers—not only of Franeker during our first time together, but also of the Dutch <note>original: *Belgicarum*; during this period, "Belgica" was frequently used as the Latin name for the Netherlands.</note> Academies...

<header>ORATION</header>

And from the theologians of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the academic divinity faculties of the era.</note>, those who have passed away from here in succeeding years—the likes of Essenius, Vogelsang, Heidanus, Voetius, Burman, Alting, de Colonie, Arnold, van Diest, Hulsius, Wittich, du Moyne, van Wolzogen, and Spanheim—what and how great are these names! <note>These names refer to a "who's who" of 17th-century Dutch and Reformed theology, such as Gisbertus Voetius and Friedrich Spanheim.</note> You alone represented the whole Reformed World <note>original: *Orbe Reformato*; the international community of Calvinist churches and scholars.</note>, and you provided solace to me, your remaining companion, amidst the loss of so many illustrious men! 

But you were! And you are no longer among us now; you have been snatched away from me, from the Academy <note>The University of Leiden.</note>, and from the Church by the sudden onslaught of implacable death! And at this very time, when the world, rushing headlong toward its own destruction, most needed the abundance of your varied and most solid teaching, and the light of your unfeigned piety—at a time when your old age, with the vigor of your mind by no means worn away, had prepared you for divine wisdom and the common veneration of all. 

If ever the most grievous evils were to be feared for the Church and the world following the departure of great men—through whose surviving virtue those evils were held at bay, and whom a most wise God carries away so that He might not distress them with such things—now we can scarcely hope for anything good hereafter. We are left destitute of you, the pillar of our age against all the depraved impiety of doctrine and morals, and a true friend of God. 

But what am I doing? And where do the emotions of my troubled mind carry me? For I bestow praises upon the man to his face—praises which no one could justly deny him without exception, but which he, through his admirable modesty, refused ever to hear, and which, if he heard them, he would immediately bid me be silent. And what is more, I speak to him as if he were alive and present, though the Divine Hand has withdrawn him from us and raised him up eternally to see, hear, and enjoy heavenly things. 

And what is most significant: I might seem guilty of more than one offense against God and His servant through these complaints; as if I envied him his long-desired blessedness, or denied the thanks due to God for his long and joyful service, or distrusted His inexhaustible power in caring for His Church—a power most thoroughly proven through all the most difficult ages. 

It will be much better, therefore, if my speech, with a more composed mind, turns to you, Distinguished Peers <note>original: *A. P.*, likely *Amplissimi Patres* or *Auditores Prudentissimi*, formal addresses to the university audience.</note>. By recollecting the life of this Great Man—spent most happily on this earth for the good of the Church—I shall pay him his due, which can never be fully repaid, however much I may stammer in the doing. And you, now that the man's bones have been laid to rest, calm the useless waves of your troubled minds; attend not so much to me, speaking all too inelegantly, as to the matters to be discussed, which are of the highest merit.

# FUNERAL ORATION

Our **Witsius**, whom we have just carried to his grave, had parents who deserve the highest praise. His father was **Nicolaus Wits**, a man of most upright reputation among the people of Enkhuizen. He served the Church several times as a Deacon and later as an Elder, fulfilling both of these ecclesiastical roles with great faithfulness. He was also called to serve the State, and after various degrees of honor, he was elevated and distinguished by the offices of Treasurer and Burgomaster <note>original: *Quæstura & Consulatu*; in the Dutch Republic, a 'Consul' usually referred to a *Burgemeester* or Mayor</note>. In this magistracy, as in the whole conduct of his life, he behaved in such a way—staying far from those vices that often accompany high honors—that he was most dear to his fellow citizens for his modesty, gentleness, justice, unfeigned piety, and ancient simplicity.

Even now, the Church possesses a book of Sacred Songs imprinted with this man’s piety, by the reading or singing of which the Christian people may be variously built up. Furthermore, the city of Enkhuizen received from this most just governor another son, **Jacobus Wits**. The city quickly admitted him to the rank of judges (over whom he even presided), expecting him to follow in his father's footsteps. He was extinguished prematurely, leaving no male offspring, but from his daughters, one has a husband who is a most worthy Burgomaster of that same city and distinguished by other honors, **Nicolaus Ris**; the other has a son who is an eminent physician, **Henricus Ris**. This is in addition to his elegant daughters, in whose sweet company we have frequently seen their great-uncle <note>meaning Herman Witsius himself</note> rejoice while staying with us.

The mother of our elderly scholar was **Johanna**, a pious and prudent woman. She was the daughter of **Hermann Gerhard**, a man who was tested by many struggles for the sake of religion. After various misfortunes and many dangerous crises—and not without the manifest help of the Divine power—he was rescued more than once from the blades of encroaching enemies <note>Likely referring to the religious wars or persecutions of the Reformation era</note>, and eventually found a calm and faithful station in the Church of Enkhuizen. There, he taught the Gospel for over thirty years with great praise for his integrity, learning, zeal, and sacred, heart-swaying eloquence. He so loved that church of his in the Lord that, even when he was invited to the most flourishing and grandest churches in all the Netherlands <note>original: *Belgii*; referring to the Low Countries</note> with a much larger salary, he could not bring himself to ever desert it.

Born from such outstanding and Christian blood, our **Witsius** received a double spur <note>an incentive or motivation</note> toward all piety and virtue from his earliest days, especially when his parents, following their vows, consecrated their male offspring to the Giver of all things, God, for His most holy ministry...

# ORATION

Having been blessed with this child, the parents gave the little boy the name of his maternal grandfather <note>Hermann Gerhard, mentioned on the previous page</note>; at the same time, they prayed to God that the spirit of that great man might, in a sense, live again in his grandson Herman. They hoped that he—as parents' hopes and desires for their children are often great, and frequently bear the desired fruit—might be endowed with equal or even greater gifts and follow in his grandfather's footsteps.

From the family circumstances I have just described, you can easily gather the place where *Herman Witsius* was born: namely Enkhuizen, a significant and noble city of West Friesland <note>A region in the northern part of the province of Holland</note>. It was among the first Dutch cities to claim its liberty by a memorable example, shaking off the yoke of Spanish Tyranny. Once it was illuminated by the rays of divine and Evangelical Truth and embraced a purer worship of the Divine, it remained more tenacious of its untainted faith than its neighbors during the wicked disturbances of the Remonstrants <note>The Remonstrants were followers of Jacobus Arminius; their theological disputes with the Reformed Church led to great political and religious tension in the early 17th century</note>.

Although this city has, from ancient times, been more devoted to trade and navigation due to its close proximity to the sea, it has nevertheless produced many most faithful ministers of the churches for many years. Among these, I count my venerable father-in-law and most faithful pastor of Rotterdam, *Johannes Ursinus*; but in older times, the city also produced men outstanding in every branch of literature.

To say nothing of *Ruard Tapper*, a Professor of Theology at the University of Louvain and a most severe Inquisitor of "heretical pravity" <note>original: *hæreticæ pravitatis*; a technical term used by the Inquisition for heterodox beliefs</note> (as the Romans call it)—a man whose name was praised by some but hated by others, including many of his own citizens—Enkhuizen was the home of *Theodoricus Langius*. He taught Greek literature with great fame, first at Bordeaux in France and then at the Busleyden College <note>Also known as the *Collegium Trilingue*, a famous humanist center for the study of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew</note> in Louvain until the year 1578.

Also from Enkhuizen was *Franciscus Maelson*, a Doctor of Medicine renowned for his learning, eloquence, and wisdom in managing affairs. He was especially skilled in Greek literature, as is proven by his letters written in that language to Gemma Frisius <note>A famous mathematician and cartographer</note>, which were composed in a familiar yet elegant and polished style.

Finally, to pass over others, Enkhuizen-born was *Johannes Antonides van der Linden*, a most celebrated Professor of Medicine, first at Franeker and then here in our own University of Leiden. His son, an outstanding physician, and his daughter, married to our most distinguished former Consul Dorpius, still survive today. His grandfather, Henricus Antonides van der Linden, was also called from the ministry of the Enkhuizen church to inaugurate the University of Franeker and teach theology there by the Illustrious...

...was most wisely summoned by the noble and very powerful States of Friesland <note>The governing body of the province of Friesland</note> in the year 1585. Thus, even in his home city—a soil by no means sterile of good minds—there was no lack of illustrious examples of learning for our *Witsius* to set before himself as models to imitate.

He first began to see the light of day on the twelfth day of February, 1636. This year is particularly memorable for our purposes because, in that same month of February, by a public charter of the States of the Province of Utrecht <note>original: "Trajectinæ"</note>, the Illustrious Gymnasium (which had been prudently opened two years prior by the city's consuls and senate) received the rights and privileges of an Academy <note>This refers to the elevation of the school to the University of Utrecht</note>. It was in this very Academy that *Witsius* would later not only learn what was to be taught alongside others, but would also, for many years, teach others what he had learned from faithful instructors. I have also learned this regarding the man’s birth: that he, seeking the way to the light earlier than was proper, nearly killed both himself and his mother; and because of this, when he was born, he was so tiny and delicate that the midwife and the other women present predicted he would not survive <note>original: "non fore ei vitam vitalem", literally "that there would be no life worth living for him"</note>. But these women were then unaware of how great a man would come from that tiny babe, or how he would one day grow through divine grace—not so much in physical stature (which always remained quite small) as in the vigor of his mind, the greatness of his most useful labors, and the fame of his name throughout the entire world.

Following that great danger of his birth and his first moments of life, the care of his pious parents for the infant *Witsius* only increased. They by no means neglected this duty afterward; mindful of their vows, they raised the boy in a most holy manner. They instilled in him the precepts of Christian religion and piety almost with his mother's milk. As soon as he began to learn to speak, they shaped his untrained tongue to celebrate the praise of his Lord and God with stammering speech and half-formed words. Indeed, in the sixth year of his age, they introduced him to the city's public school to be imbued with the first elements of the Latin language. From there, after three years had passed and he had already been promoted to the Rector's highest class, his uncle Peter—the son of that Hermann whom I praised earlier—took him under his private and domestic discipline. That man was well-learned in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, and was also skilled in Philosophy, which he prudently applied not to empty or trivial subtleties, but to the clarification of reality and the exercise of rigorous Virtue; above all, however, he had devoted his primary efforts to Theology. He was living for himself in deep and secure leisure, free at that time from all public business, and to this [son] of his sister...
