### ORATION.

<meta>catchword: com-</meta>

He treated his nephew with the same singular affection as a son, educating him with such diligence that before his fifteenth year of age, he not only wrote and spoke Latin passably well, but could also readily interpret the Greek books of the New Testament and several Orations of Isocrates <note>A famous ancient Greek rhetorician</note>. He even rendered the Hebrew Commentaries on Samuel into Latin, demonstrating the etymology of words and the shifts in accents according to the rules of grammar. He also gained some taste of Philosophy from that discipline, having been taught Logic not superficially, but sufficiently for practical use, so that later, when he moved to the University <note>original: "Academiam"</note>, he required no teacher for that art. Furthermore, he learned the *Compendiums of Ethics* by Walaeus <note>Antonius Walaeus, a Dutch Reformed theologian</note> and Burgersdijk <note>Franco Burgersdijk, a Dutch logician whose textbooks were standard in the 17th century</note> during that same period. He did this so industriously that he knew by heart most of the maxims that frequently appear in Burgersdijk from the Ancients, whether they were in Greek or Latin. He ran through the *Elements of Physics* by the same Burgersdijk, and even sampled the subtleties of Metaphysics. And because he had in his uncle a strict <gloss>taskmaster</gloss> <note>original: ἐργοδιώκτην (ergodiōktēn)</note>, he had fixed in his memory most of the definitions and divisions of theological matters from Wendelin <note>Marcus Friedrich Wendelin, a German Reformed theologian known for his systematic handbooks</note>.

But above all, that man of ancient piety <note>Referring to the uncle</note> considered it his duty to accustom his nephew to the same devotion from his earliest childhood <note>original: "à teneris unguiculis", literally "from tender little nails"</note>. He himself used to have ready at hand notable sayings from both Divine Testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments</note> for almost everything that happens in common life. Whether rising, dressing, washing, walking, studying, or doing anything else, he frequently recited them in Hebrew or Greek, either as prayers, thanksgivings, or as reminders of his duty; and by both example and advice, he encouraged his young nephew to do the same. From this, it happened that even at that tender age, the boy made many Hebrew and Greek passages familiar to himself, which not even in old age did he forget. O, the rare happiness and industrious obedience of our *Witsius*! If such a thing were common today (and why should the truth not be spoken?), many would enter the University far better prepared than they are now when they leave the University for the common uses of life and the state.

When he had been equipped with these safeguards in his father’s house, in the year 1651, at the age of 15, it was decided that *Witsius* should be sent away to a University. Among them all, Utrecht <note>original: "Trajectina"</note> was chosen, which at that time flourished with men most famous in every branch of literature, a remarkable crowd of students, and excellent discipline. Especially [did he seek] that...

### FUNERAL [ORATION].

The theologians Gisbert Voetius, Carolus Maatsius, and Johannes Hoornbeck—great names of this century that cannot be disparaged—recommended him. But Maatsius had already passed away by the time our Witsius reached Utrecht <note>Utrecht is referred to by its Latin name, *Trajectum*</note>; at his funeral, Witsius heard Hoornbeck delivering a learned oration in memory of that most excellent colleague. Thus, having been made a citizen of the University of Utrecht, he made use of the guidance of Paulus Voetius in Metaphysics. Paulus was at that time a Professor of Philosophy and later a most celebrated Professor of Law, whose son, the famous <term>Jurist</term> <note>original: "JCto," an abbreviation for *Jurisconsulto*</note> Johannes Voetius, our own University has boasted of for many years even until now.

Furthermore, since he was especially delighted by the study of Oriental languages, he applied himself familiarly to the most illustrious Johannes Leusden, who taught those languages with incredible skill. Under Leusden's guidance, he interpreted almost the entire volume of the Hebrew Bible, as well as <margin>*</margin> the commentaries of Solomon Rashi <note>original: "Salomonis Jarchii." Renaissance scholars often referred to Rashi by this name</note>, Ibn Ezra, and Kimchi on Hosea, the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> Paraphrase of Jonathan on Isaiah, and that of Onkelos on a part of the Pentateuch. 

In addition, under the same teacher, he touched upon the secrets of the Masorah <note>The traditional system of notes on the Hebrew text of the Bible</note> and the thorny diction of the Talmud, studying the tracts *Sanhedrin* and *Makkot* edited by Johannes Cocceius, and the tract *Bava Batra* edited by Constantinus L’Empereur. From Leusden, he also drew the elements of the Syriac and Arabic languages, though he later cultivated Arabic less than all the others. 

Indeed, at Leusden’s urging, he proved how much he had progressed in Hebrew literature through a public demonstration. In the year 1654, he presented to the Academic assembly a Hebrew Oration, elegantly composed and most skillfully delivered by himself, following the example of a certain learned Hungarian, concerning the Messiah of the Jews and the Christians. 

Although he was almost entirely immersed in these linguistic studies, he by no means neglected the study of Theology, to which he knew all other things ought to be subservient <note>original: "ancillari," meaning to act as a handmaiden</note>. He diligently utilized the greatest masters and those most learned in the Sacred Scriptures in that sublime discipline—men whose most praiseworthy memory no lapse of time shall ever erase: Gisbert Voetius, Johannes Hoornbeck (who was then being called to our University in Leiden), Gualterus Bruinius (whose brilliance was like a shining but brief morning star intercepted by an unexpected death), and Andreas Essenius. 

From their instruction, combined with his incomparable domestic industry and true piety toward God, you will easily perceive for yourselves how much he progressed, even if I remain silent. Nevertheless, a desire arose in him to see Groningen as well, so that he might enjoy the company of the most celebrated Samuel Maresius there.

Setting out for there after the dog days of summer <note>The "dog days" (*ferias caniculares*) refer to the hottest period of summer, usually July and August</note> in the year 1654, he especially cultivated his study of Theology, content at that time with one *Doctor* and *Leader*. Under his direction, he practiced his preliminary exercises in holy sermons, which they call "Propositions," in the *French* language. In these, he offered such hope for himself to that Great Man that, despite his many and most heavy occupations, he deigned to purge those little declamations of *French* grammatical errors and *Latin* or *Dutch* <note>original: "Belgicis," referring to the Dutch language</note> idioms before they were recited in the College. Having thus completed a year at *Groningen*, and having obtained a travel-permit of the most honorable testimonial from the Theological Faculty, he considered *Leiden*. But because the plague was raging there, he decided to return to his beloved *Utrecht* <note>original: "Trajectum"</note>, so that upon the foundations of Theology—which had not only been successfully laid but already built up high—he might build further with gold, silver, and precious stones <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12, suggesting he was adding refined spiritual quality to his basic education</note>. Therefore, he not only diligently listened to the Professors of Theology teaching publicly and privately as before, but he also became very familiar with the most venerable man *Justus van den Bogaerdt*. He so esteemed Bogaerdt’s piety, prudence, and admirable gifts that he believed—perhaps with youthful enthusiasm, yet he believed it nonetheless—that no equal preacher was then living in the Church. From his sermons, conversations, and example, Witsius learned the inner workings of the Kingdom of God and the secrets of mystical and spiritual Christianity.

From him, he understood how much difference there was between that mere knowledge of theological matters—such as scholastic exercises, learnedly written books, and persistent study can confer upon minds devoid of the grace of true sanctification—and that heavenly wisdom which is acquired through meditating, praying, loving, and conversing familiarly with God. This wisdom is gained by the very taste and experience of spiritual things, and proceeding from the Spirit of God (who illuminates, convinces, persuades, and seals from within), it gloriously transforms the whole man into the most holy image of Christ. In short, he confessed that through the work of that most holy man, he was introduced by the Lord *Jesus* into his inner sanctuary <note>original: "penetrale"</note>, whereas before, lingering in the outer courtyard, he had been far too and foolishly pleased with himself. There, at last, he learned to renounce all vain presumption of knowledge, to sit humbly at the feet of the heavenly Master, and to receive the kingdom of God like a little child. Yet, lest you think that he so applied himself to the formation of all piety that he neglected his future academic studies, the theses he wrote concerning the Holy Trinity can and should prove otherwise...

However, because he thought he still lacked something of the elegance of that language, he next meditated on a journey into France itself, intending to visit the great men throughout that Kingdom so that he might also benefit from their presence.

following 1657, at the age of 21, having been lawfully called by the Church of Westwoud, **WITSIUS** was initiated into the ministry on the eighth day of July. This village is situated between Enkhuizen and Hoorn, at nearly an equal distance from both, and was joined in ecclesiastical matters to another called Binnenwijzend. There, for four years and some months, he served God with the greatest youthful enthusiasm. Nor was it with less success; for through frequent catechism <note>A method of teaching the principles of Christian religion through questions and answers</note>, most prudently adapting himself to the capacity of his students, he achieved such results that the boys and girls—both young and older—who were ignorant of all things when he first arrived, could not only answer skillfully regarding the principal heads of our religion, but also support their assertions with suitable testimonies from Scripture. They could even recite an entire sermon in order, with all its individual parts, when questioned, to both the joy and the embarrassment <note>A common theme in early modern biographies where the rapid learning of children "shames" the slower-learning adults</note> of their parents and the elders.

As the fame of such a faithful and capable Pastor spread far and wide, the Church of Wormer—in the same region of North Holland, quite numerous and celebrated, but at that time excessively disturbed by internal disputes—did not think they would find any other leader more suitable for settling their quarrels and building up their souls. And **WITSIUS** obeyed this call, transferring to its ministry in the month of October in the year 1661. He spent four years and six months there, arranging all things for Christian peace and the common salvation in such a way that he was equally loved by everyone and saw the most abundant fruit of his labor among them. For this reason, he did not allow himself to be drawn away by the people of Sluis in Flanders, who repeatedly urged him to explain the Gospel to them in both the Dutch and French languages. 

However, when the declared intentions of certain very prominent churches to call such an outstanding and useful man were most unfairly thwarted, a call from the people of Goes in Zeeland succeeded. Having moved there around Pentecost <note>The Christian festival celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit, occurring fifty days after Easter</note> in the year 1666, he so pleased everyone with his doctrine, character, and industry that he lived there in harmony and the most pleasant peace with his learned, pious, and most watchful colleagues. Two of these he venerated as fathers, and the third, his junior, he loved as a brother. He often protested afterward that no time in his whole life had been more tranquil or sweet, and more than once he wished to grow old in that peaceful harbor. But the people of Leeuwarden in Friesland did not allow this to happen, who [called him] to that [capital] of their nation...

### FUNERAL [ORATION]

In November of the year 1667, they called him with great longing to the splendid Capital <note>Leeuwarden, the capital of the province of Friesland</note>, so that such a brilliant light might shine not only in the Church, his Court, and the Council, but also before all the Frisians who gathered there from everywhere for the Assemblies <note>original: "Comitia," referring to the provincial states or parliamentary meetings</note> and the conduct of business. However, he finally arrived there in the month of April in the following year, 1668, as the people of Goes were very reluctant to let him go and drew out delays according to their custom. It can hardly be expressed with what vigilance, faithfulness, and wisdom he applied himself to the building, reviving, and governing of that Church. This was during a most difficult time, when enemies were rushing into the Netherlands <note>A reference to the *Rampjaar* or "Year of Disaster" in 1672, when the Dutch Republic was invaded by French, English, and German forces</note>, very quickly occupying many of its cities and terrifying and deeply unsettling all others; it was a time when there was a true need for minds and hearts that were no less wise than they were firm. Nor do I know—I who was at that time intent on my academic studies in my homeland of Friesland—of any other Man of God, either before or after him, whose labor in the Lord succeeded more happily, or who was more pleasing to the Church, the Nobility, and even the Court. For this reason, he presided for some time over the youthful studies of the Most Serene Prince of Nassau, the Hereditary Governor of Friesland, *Henry Casimir* <note>Henry Casimir II, Prince of Nassau-Dietz (1657–1696)</note>, who was extinguished all too prematurely. He also instructed that Prince's most illustrious sister, *Amelia*—who later married the Duke of Saxony-Eisenach—a most holy Princess, in matters of religion with remarkable success. He moderated the profession of faith <note>A public examination and confession of Christian doctrine required for full church membership</note> which both of them delivered publicly to the great edification of the Church, in the presence of their mother, the Princess *Albertine of Orange* <note>Albertine Agnes of Nassau, daughter of Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange</note>.

Hence, no one will be at all surprised that when the theological affairs of the University of Franeker seemed to have collapsed significantly—due to the injury of those most afflicted times and the passing of both the venerable old man Christian Schotanus and the recently installed Johann Melchior Steinberg—and since the truly academic and most ample gifts of our **WITSIUS** had been clearly seen by the Frisians through seven years of personal experience; no one, I say, will wonder that they designated him in the year 1675 to the Ordinary Professorship of Theology in their University, to be thus most happily restored. The Church of Franeker also most wisely seized this opportunity; being then deprived of its other Pastor, it most joyfully committed its most holy care to this designated Professor, whose pastoral gifts were so great and celebrated. Therefore, having accepted both of these calls at the same time, he came to Franeker; and after [being named] Doctor of Theology...

### SPEECH

<meta>catchword: Doctoris</meta>

After he had been announced to the Academic Senate by a fellow theologian, he was inaugurated as Professor of that same discipline on April 15th. He delivered a formal Oration to the tremendous applause of a vast crowd gathered from all over, in which he brilliantly described the *Idea of a True Theologian*. Indeed, he soon proved himself to be just such a man, alongside the venerable elder *Nicolaus Arnoldi* <note>Nicolaus Arnold (1618–1680), a prominent Polish-born Reformed theologian at Franeker</note>. Witsius always praised the integrity and eloquence of this very close colleague; likewise, I myself cannot recall that most excellent theologian without great praise and the most grateful affection due to him as my best teacher, mentor, and eventually, colleague.

Truly, from the church pulpit <note>original: *Suggeſtu*, the raised platform for preaching</note>, Witsius spoke with such gravity, elegance, piety, solidity, and usefulness that the people's long-standing lethargy was shaken off, and the stirrings of a new life openly revealed themselves in matters both great and small. Even his Academic Chair glowed with a most holy fire. A great number of "sacred youth" <note>students of theology</note> flocked to him from various and distant parts of Europe, desiring to gain both solid and pious wisdom; they eventually returned to their homes having made equal progress in both learning and devotion.

And so that he would not fail in any part of his duty or the expectations of those who had appointed him, he had barely set foot in the Academy before he set himself to writing, despite his many daily public and domestic tasks related to his dual roles as pastor and professor. Within a very short time, he published several works. In addition to selected academic disputations intended to strengthen the peace of the Church and a smaller treatise <note>original: *Diatriben*</note>, he produced two quite large and learned volumes for general use. These were very quickly distributed throughout the Netherlands <note>original: *Belgium*, often used in Latin at this time to refer to the Netherlands as a whole</note> and all of Europe, and they have since been reprinted more than once, being read then—and still today—with the highest praise.

Furthermore, whenever any extraordinary or serious matter arose—even regarding the schismatic followers of *Labadie* <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), a former Jesuit who founded a separatist pietist movement known as the Labadists</note>, who had then established their headquarters in Friesland—both the civil leaders and the church governors believed the matter should be settled through this man. 

These were the times when I myself, having returned to my homeland from the University of Leiden <note>original: *Academia Lugdunenſi*</note> and the sacred studies I pursued there, finally became known to our great theologian. Speaking on behalf of the ecclesiastical assembly, he examined my progress and praised it, recommending me as the pastor for the church at *Midlum* <note>a village located between the towns of Franeker and Harlingen</note>, solemnly commending that congregation to me from the pulpit. After a second academic examination before the Rector and the Senate...

<header>FUNERAL ORATION</header>

<sig>* f</sig>

<meta>catchword: ta</meta>

He <note>Nicolaus Arnold, mentioned on the previous page</note> decided that the title of Doctor of Theology should be conferred upon me, soon recommending me so highly to the Most Serene Prince and the most distinguished Governors that I was appointed by them as the third Ordinary Professor of Theology in that same year of [16]76. I cannot recall those years without proclaiming the happiness of my life, spent first as a neighbor and then in the intimate companionship of WITSIUS. In those days, as a young man, I was marvelously built up by his daily church sermons, spurred on by his academic lectures, instructed by his private conversations, and guided by his most wholesome advice and his most upright character; indeed, he assisted me in every way.

But the great radiance of the man caused neighboring peoples to envy the Frisians <note>The people of Friesland, the province where the University of Franeker was located</note> their long enjoyment of him, seized as they were by a great desire to have him for themselves. The Trustees of the University of Groningen and Ommelanden <note>original: *Groningo-Omlandicæ*</note> first attempted this at the end of the year [16]79. Seeking a worthy successor for the deceased Jacob Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a famous professor of Hebrew and Theology</note>—both for the Chair of Theology and Philology and for the university pulpit—they sent a Reverend man (who is still living) to Franeker to entice WITSIUS with honorable offers. 

But that effort met with no success at all; for once he had shared the matter with the Most High Prince and the other Trustees of the Frisian Academy—who protested that his services were most pleasing to them—he honorably and modestly excused himself to the people of Groningen. However, the people of Utrecht <note>original: *Trajectini*</note> very quickly followed the Groningers at the beginning of the year [16]80. After the death of the most celebrated Burmann <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a prominent Dutch theologian</note>, they judged that they needed a great man to increase the fame of their University and to protect the ancient piety of their Church. They knew full well that no one was better equipped for this than their own former student, WITSIUS. 

Therefore, they sent a most distinguished delegation to Franeker and earnestly requested that he be willing to relocate to adorn their University and Church. And the delegates obtained their request without too much difficulty, despite the great love with which the Frisians resisted losing such a useful man. He himself consented to the wishes of the citizens of Utrecht, led primarily by a religious conviction: since he acknowledged that he owed almost everything he had to that University and Church <note>Witsius had studied at Utrecht under Gisbertus Voetius</note>, he felt he must not fail to repay his debts with his services as a testimony of his grateful heart. After an honorable departure from the grieving Frisians, he came to Utrecht and was inducted into the ministry of that church on April 25th—the same day as our own Trigland <note>Jacobus Trigland the Younger (1652–1705), who became a professor at Leiden</note>—and four days later, into his Academic Professorship, having [delivered...]

He had, of course, many colleagues in the ministry of the Church who were shaped for doctrine, piety, peace, and Divine Zeal; among these old colleagues in the care of the Church of Leeuwarden <note>original: *Leovardiensis*</note> were *Petrus Eindhoven* and *Johannes Lastdrager*. In the University <note>original: *Academia*</note>, besides the aforementioned theologians—all most worthy of renown and laboring with him in the Lord for the honor of the Church—he had not only his friend *Johannes Leusden*, an excellent philologist, but also *Gerard de Vries* and *Johannes Luyts*, outstanding philosophers who diligently prepared the sacred youth for service in the Church. He had before his ecclesiastical pulpit a Christian Magistracy and an entire people who marveled at the power of his speech and experienced its various effects on their souls, moved toward religion. Before his academic and domestic chair <note>The professor's *cathedra* or seat of authority</note>, he had not only a vast "crown" <note>A common metaphor for a surrounding circle of attentive listeners</note> of excellent young men from every part of the world, who hung upon his most learned, solid, wise, and eloquent words, but also a great number of doctors themselves who flocked daily to learn from him. And so, seeing such great fruit from his work, he did not withdraw from any labors; he even spent many sleepless nights to remain useful to the University and the Church. Nor was it enough for him to bring forth his useful and varied doctrine in person—by preaching, lecturing, conversing, and debating—but he also laid out its treasures for the whole world, present and future, in many public and famous writings. These will endure and never perish unless solid doctrine and true piety themselves should pass away. Truly ungrateful, *Utrecht* <note>original: *Trajectum*</note>! if you ever forget the greatest merits of **WITSIUS**, who preserved your ancient piety and increased the splendor of your University to such a degree that I know not whether it was ever greater or will ever be as great in the future. Injudicious...

# FUNERAL [ORATION]
<sig>* f 2</sig>

Utrecht, how true to your name! <note>original: "vere Trajectum!" The orator is likely making a wordplay on *Trajectum*, the Latin name for Utrecht, which implies a "crossing" or a "path."</note> If you ever attempt to stand or raise your head by any other path than by nurturing and calling upon those men who follow the footsteps of your **Witsius** in the study of most holy truth, unfeigned piety, and Christian peace. Indeed, unfortunate Utrecht, if you should ever be deprived of those who sincerely represent your **Witsius**, you will not long stand nor preserve the ancient nobility of your glory; may God most kind avert all such things!

Yet I must still speak to the praise of the people of Utrecht, for they not only always recognized the wisdom and skill of the man in ecclesiastical assemblies, timely calling him to the highest honors in the Synods, but the leading men <term>Proceres</term> also testified by both deeds and words that his gifts were most proven and highly valued by them. It was from no other cause that the city twice honored him with the insignia of the highest office in their University <note>This refers to the office of Rector Magnificus, the rotating head of the university</note>, in the years **1686** and **1697**.

And I must by no means omit that in the year **1685**, when a most splendid embassy of the entire Belgian Republic <note>The United Provinces of the Netherlands</note> was decreed to **James II**, King of Great Britain—who was afterwards wretchedly seduced and ruined by the deceits of the French and the Romans <note>A reference to James II’s Catholicism and his alliance with Louis XIV of France, which led to his eventual overthrow in the Glorious Revolution</note>—that embassy was undertaken by our most illustrious **van Wassenaer**, Lord of **Duivenvoorde**, and the most excellent Ordinary Ambassador **van Citters**, as well as the most noble and illustrious **van Weede**, Lord of **Dijkveld**, a man of very useful deeds for the good of the fatherland. This latter man, I say, easily persuaded his colleagues in the embassy that no one other than **Witsius** should be chosen as their chaplain. They wished to present him to the English people as a theologian who was the pride of the Belgian churches, without any fear of causing offense or being met with contempt.

This plan of these illustrious men did not displease him; though he was quite sick in body, he went there eagerly. Having returned after a lapse of some months, he confessed that through his conversations with the **Archbishop of Canterbury**, the **Bishop of London**, and many other theologians—both those of the Episcopal <note>The Church of England</note> and the Dissenting <note>Non-conformist groups like Presbyterians and Congregationalists</note> disciplines—he had observed not a few things which contributed to the growth of his own learning and by which he was rendered more equipped in all wisdom. From that time on, the English did not hide that they had come to know **Witsius** so well that they thereafter held him in great love and high esteem.

After all these things, the fame of **Witsius**, most celebrated far and wide through the world, brought it about that [concerning] this greatest man in the University...

The Curators of this most illustrious [University] and the most distinguished Consuls of the city were seriously considering calling him to our **Leiden** <note>original: "Lugdunensem," referring to the University of Leiden</note> in the year **1698**. This was done so that they might timely prevent the loss that was feared due to the imminent passing of the great **Spanheim** <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701), a major figure in Reformed theology whose health was declining at the time</note>. Our excellent Governor and the most powerful King of the Britons, **William III**—a most happy Prince of immortal glory—was pleased by this same plan, owing to his constant piety toward God and his equal faith and prudence toward our Church and Academy. There was no delay, either in the decreeing and execution of the call to the office of Professor of Theology among us, or in his acceptance of the same. 

For although the people of Utrecht would have preferred otherwise, our **WITSIUS** had many serious reasons why he felt he should obey the invitation of the people of Leiden. He judged it to be entirely to the advantage of both himself and the Church that, being thereafter exempt from the labors of the pulpit <note>original: "á Suggestus Laboribus," referring to his duties as a regular preaching minister, which were physically demanding for his age</note>, he might spend his remaining elderly years more freely in service of the Academy. He was especially moved when he was informed of the will of the most powerful King through the illustrious Councilor of Holland, **Heinsius** <note>Anthonie Heinsius, the Grand Pensionary of Holland and a close confidant of King William III</note>. Subsequently, the King himself, having admitted him to an audience, kindly testified that it was pleasing to him that **Witsius** had complied with the call to the Leiden Chair—a call decreed on the King’s own recommendation—and he added a most generous promise of his Royal Favor, which he always fulfilled in deed thereafter.

When he arrived here, he held the inaugural ceremony for his office in this very place on October 16th—a most joyful occasion—delivering a serious and thoroughly elegant Oration in which he portrayed "The Modest Theologian" <note>Witsius's inaugural address at Leiden was titled *De Theologo Modesto*, emphasizing humility in scholarship</note>. With what faithfulness he held that same office here for a decade, with what diligence he worked, with what wisdom and prudence he taught, with what elegance he spoke, with what eagerness he disputed in debate, with what piety he lived, with what sweetness he interacted with others, with what brilliance he continued to write, and with what splendor he adorned the Academy—you all know these things so well, and they are so well-known to the whole world, that there is no need for my speech to dwell upon them at greater length here.

Indeed, he had scarcely spent one year among us when the Illustrious and Most Powerful States of Holland and West Friesland, upon the recommendation of the University leaders, entrusted the supreme care of their Theological College—where the noble foster-sons of their Republic grow for the benefit of the Church—to our **WITSIUS**, who was to lead their youth in the most peaceful manner. This appointment was in the place of the piously deceased Regent, **Marcus Effius**, while preserving all the honor and dignity of his Professorial office, which in the man...

However, **WITSIUS** accepted that new condition not very willingly; I know he would not have accepted it unless he had judged that he must comply with the pleasure of the States <note>original: "Ordinum," referring to the States of Holland and West Friesland</note> and spend himself in service to the Church. Nevertheless, he sustained the burden most faithfully and with the highest care, to the benefit and with the affection of the young men subject to him, just as he protected his very Professorship in the Academy. This continued until the year **1707**, on the **8th day of February**, when—on account of his advanced age and his strength being further worn down by heavy illnesses—he judged himself [unfit], more so than did the College itself or others aware of its affairs, who marveled at the man’s most constant alacrity, industry, and dexterity. In a meeting of the Curators and Consuls, despite their opposing wishes and the requests they made privately and publicly, and having rejected all the very great emoluments <note>financial benefits or salary associated with the office</note> which he received from it, he most modestly resigned from this second office. At the same time, according to his wish, he was granted immunity from the public exercises of his Professorial office in the Academy, for which the strength of his body was scarcely sufficient to perform according to ancient customs. Yet the most constant vigor of his eternal mind always remained, which he declared more than once when discussing this plan of his with me, concluding always that he would rather cease from his work than fail in it.

But truly, I scarcely think our **WITSIUS** would have been suited for such and so many labors, or that the Church and Academy would have had such and so many benefits from him, had he not found the most powerful aids and comforts at home. ### ORATION

[He married] the daughter of **Wessel van Borchorn**, a most honorable citizen and merchant of **Utrecht** <note>original: "Trajectini"</note> and a most worthy Elder of the Church, and of **Martina van Ysen**; he wed her in the middle of the summer of **1660**, after completing three years in the Holy Ministry. She truly excelled in a singular gentleness of spirit and in every civic and Christian virtue; she loved and honored her husband beyond the common measure. With her, he lived in the greatest harmony and sweetness for about twenty-four years in **North Holland**, **Zeeland**, **Friesland**, and **Utrecht**. Finally, in the year **[16]84**, after notable and long bodily infirmities, she was taken from her husband by a truly Christian death.

Next, I look upon the most joyful offspring which he had from this, his only wife—not so much the twin sons, long since taken by death, as the daughters, who were left to him until his final breath. These were, namely, **three daughters**, truly select and expertly formed through divine grace and the holy care of their parents, not only in Christian wisdom and piety but also in all elegance of speech and manners. First is **Martina**, who for some years has been the desire and the pride of her husband **Henricus Dibbets**, a most eloquent and distinguished Doctor in our Church at **Leiden**. Then **Johanna**, who for many more years has fulfilled the prayers and joys of her most noble husband **Lucas Walckier**, a Jurisconsult <note>original: "JCti," a legal expert or lawyer</note> and formerly a Judge and Senator of the **City of Utrecht**, and who, having served in the name of the **Amsterdammers** as a Prefect for the maritime affairs of the Belgians, is now a most worthy Assessor in the supreme administration of the territory of **Utrecht**. [May God long keep these two sons-in-law of our old man safe for the well-being of the Republic and the Church.] Finally, there is **Petronella**, who constantly remained at the side of her excellent father as his greatest comfort and aid, by no means suffering herself to be torn from him. Just before the final, fatal illness of her beloved father, she herself was sick with a most justified fear of imminent death, which caused her father such anxiety and paternal care that his own final fate might perhaps have been estimated as hastened by it, were it not also for the new joy which the life of his daughter—restored, as it were, from death—excited in him.

I will say this without fear of vanity <term>original: "praefiscine," an idiom meaning "without bringing ill luck" or "to speak without boasting"</term> and most truly: as much as the most loving father deserved from these three daughters through his tender care and cultivation of them from their earliest childhood <term>original: "a primis unguiculis," literally "from their first little fingernails"</term>, so also did these daughters—both before and especially after the death of their beloved mother—repay their most indulgent father with the debt of love, the constant observance of the most ready obedience after God, and the most longed-for and grateful service.

# FUNERAL ORATION

From all that we have already related concerning the life of our **Witsius** in its entirety, the admirable gifts and virtues of the man can be made sufficiently clear. In attempting to proclaim these with my own stammering tongue, I truly fear that I may diminish them too much. How great was the power of his Intellect in perceiving, investigating, and illuminating any matters, even the most abstruse; how great the sharpness of his Judgment in carefully discerning, determining, and arranging them; how great the tenacity of his Memory in preserving and recalling them; and how great the readiness of his most pleasant Eloquence in explaining, instilling, and urging them—all those who ever saw or heard the man know this well. 

His **Latin** elegance, attested to in all his sayings and writings, was no less than his **Dutch** eloquence <note>original: "Belgica Facundia"</note>, through which, when speaking from the pulpit with a most decorous moderation of gesture and voice, he carried away the souls of the faithful into a most holy assent, and struck even the incredulous and the impious themselves into amazement, shame, and fear. And just as no one will be found to have praised the late **Queen Mary** <note>Mary II of England, who died in 1694; Witsius was highly regarded by the Anglo-Dutch court</note> more worthily—as can be seen by reading the funeral sermon which he did not begrudge to the world—so too many sacred poems, which he sang for himself and others in most polished verses to the fitting praise of God and our Lord, ought to move a mind that is as learned as it is pious. 

Indeed, what branch of learning that forms and adorns a **Theologian** could you name for me in which he did not greatly excel? He brought with him to the Academy the necessary preparation in **Philosophy**, and in that place he increased it not a little; he was never to be caught by the tricks and sophistries of an unbelieving race, nor led away from sincere faith by the empty appearance of "greater wisdom" to either foster or tolerate the impious errors of the age. He exhausted all sacred **Philology** <term>philology: the study of language and literary texts</term>, both **Greek** and **Hebrew**, while simultaneously ranging very far into the secular elegances of **Latin**, **Greek**, and **Oriental** literature. From these he most skillfully gathered those things which might serve to properly illustrate Holy Scripture—yet in such a way that even here he prudently avoided every excess. 

He had the most thorough knowledge of **History**, both ancient and recent, ecclesiastical and civil, Jewish and Christian, local and foreign; and from it he always selected with the greatest care those things which could be of the most use for the present purpose. And he had learned **Theology** itself intimately in all its parts, being equally ready in establishing and defending truths and showing their connection as he was in refuting errors, discerning their origin, and weighing their significance. Sacred...

# ORATION

...an account of his learning that could be demanded from him or judged by anyone; I doubt whether anyone could be named as his equal, so thoroughly prepared was he for all those things by which he could assist the flocks and the youth committed to his care for the good of the Church. Even in his **Old Age**, he never withdrew himself from these duties, nor did he spare himself too much in times of illness. 

Furthermore, his modesty was truly singular. Not only did he occupy himself with the greatest care in handling Literature and the **Sacred Mysteries**, but he was also such that he was hardly ever pleased with his own work, even in those matters which he had spoken or written most successfully; he even distrusted the sincerity of his closest friends in their necessary praises of these works. Nor could anyone else be more content with his lot, even amidst adversities. He publicly testified at **Utrecht** <note>original: "Trajectinos," referring to the citizens or the university of Utrecht</note> with a loud voice that he would never wish to exchange his position in the Academy and the Church for royal dignity or imperial majesty. 

And to pass over his other virtues—or rather to embrace them all in one scope—he was a **true Theologian**, not in word only but in deed itself, always expressing his divine wisdom through sincere **Piety** toward God and his Savior. For he was constant in the public acts of sacred worship, attending with a most attentive mind to those things he heard. He was almost never more distressed than when the troublesome vigils of many nights occasionally made him drowsy during a service. He was diligent in **Domestic Exercises of Piety**, giving an example here for others to imitate in the fear of God. 

He was diligent in divine meditations on past, present, and future grace, not infrequently withdrawing himself from the most pleasant company of others for their sake. He was industrious in most holy prayers, both fixed <note>prayers performed at set times</note> and ejaculatory <term>jaculatoriis: short, spontaneous prayers "darted" upward to God in the midst of other activities</term>, and in these, the impulse and dictation of his own Spirit shone forth when they were heard. Finally, he applied himself energetically to this: that by fleeing all evil and studying the good, he might prove himself worthy of both God and men—through the past **Redemption through Christ** and, through this alone, the grace of God and a blessed eternity in heaven, which he always sighed for while holding the whole world in contempt.

I know well, **Distinguished Audience** <note>original: "A. P." for "Auditores Praestantissimi"</note>, that you will no longer wonder that this so eminent Theologian drew to himself and his teaching, wherever he might be, a great number of listeners. Many of these have long since been illuminating the most splendid Academies, Churches, and Schools of **Reformed Europe** with their own light, and many of them, now dressed in mourning [crowd]... <meta>catchword: turbam (crowd)</meta>

# FUNERAL ORATION

I seem to see before me an almost innumerable crowd of people from among the Belgians, Germans, Gauls <note>original: "Gallos," referring to the French</note>, Hungarians, Poles, Prussians <note>original: "Borussos"</note>, Swiss, and—separated from the rest of the world—not only the British, but even the Americans and the Indians <note>original: "Indos," likely referring to inhabitants of the Dutch colonies in the East or West Indies</note> themselves. You will not wonder, then, that he held learned and pious men everywhere bound to him above all others. Although I cannot name them all, I cannot remain silent regarding the venerable name of **Willem Selden** <note>original: "Guilielmi Seldeni"</note>, the truly renowned theologian of Enkhuizen, Delft, and finally The Hague. It is well known from his highly learned Dutch <note>original: "Belgicis"</note> and Latin works how busy he was even in his leisure; because of this man’s close merits, our **Witsius** once ensured that the citizens of **Utrecht** <note>original: "Trajectinis"</note> granted him the title of Doctor of Theology, even though he had not asked for it. 

Similarly, you will not wonder that many distinguished men desired to receive doctoral honors from him after they had already entered the service of the churches. Among these I must count not only **Jean Malnoë** <note>original: "Johannem Malnoëum"</note>, the great ornament of our Franco-Belgian <note>The Walloon or French-speaking Reformed Church in the Netherlands</note> Church, but also my own **Anton Klingler** <note>original: "Antonium Klinglerum"</note>, the venerable leader <note>original: "Antistitem"</note> of the Zurich churches for many years. Finally, you will not wonder that such a great theologian has left us such a vast multitude of highly erudite and useful books; I suspect it may be unnecessary to recite their names before you, as they are celebrated by everyone. 

Yet I would have you know that as early as the year [16]60 of the past century, while **Witsius** was still occupied in his first ecclesiastical post, he published *The Christianizing Jew regarding the Principles of Faith and the Holy Trinity* <note>original: "Judæum Christianizantem circa Principia fidei & SS. Trinitatem"</note>. Nor did he abstain from writing while in the Church of Wormer; in the year [16]65, he delivered to the Dutch his *Practice of Christianity* <note>original: "Praxin Christianismi"</note>, which included spiritual images of both the unregenerate man in what he has that is praiseworthy, and the regenerate man in what deserves to be rebuked and corrected. At Leeuwarden, he also prepared in the Dutch language *The Lord’s Dispute with His Vineyard* <note>original: "Litem Domini cum vinea sua"</note>, which he at the same time powerfully defended against opponents. From the labors of this man at Franeker, we have—besides other minor works later included in larger volumes—*The Economy of the Covenants of God with Men* <note>original: "Oeconomiam Fœderum Dei cum hominibus," Witsius’s most famous work on Covenant Theology</note>, which was also translated into Dutch by the Reverend Harlingius, a minister at Hoorn; as well as the *Sacred Exercises on the so-called Apostles' Creed* <note>original: "Exercitationes Sacras in Symbolum quod Apostolorum dicitur"</note>, which the venerable Costerus, a pastor at Delft, gave to the Dutch to read in their own language. At Utrecht there appeared the *Sacred Exercises on the Lord’s Prayer* <note>original: "Exercitationes Sacræ in Orationem Dominicam"</note>; the *Egyptian Studies* <note>original: "Ægyptiaca"</note> and *The Ten Tribes* <note>original: "Decaphylon"</note>, along with a *Discourse on the Legion* <note>original: "Diatribe de Legione"</note>...

# ORATION

...on the **Thundering Legion of Christians** <note>original: "Fulminatrice Christianorum," referring to a famous historical-theological debate about a 2nd-century miracle</note>; and the first volume of the **Sacred Miscellanies** <note>original: "Miscellaneorum Sacrorum"</note>, along with a good part of the second volume, besides certain even smaller works. Finally, at **Leiden** <note>original: "Lugduni"</note>, not only did the finished second volume of the *Sacred Miscellanies* come out, but here also were born the *Meditations* <note>original: "Meletemata"</note> which he himself called "of Leiden," which could also be added to the number of his **Selected Dissertations** <note>original: "Dissertationum Selectarum"</note>. All these writings are indeed not only so celebrated but also so polished, useful, and filled with various learning and piety, that they are most worthy of preservation <note>original: "cedro dignissima," literally "worthy of cedar," an idiom referring to the use of cedar oil to preserve scrolls from decay</note> and will commend the happiness of our age to far-off posterity.

Do you know, **distinguished listeners** <note>original: "A. P.," likely abbreviating "Auditores Praestantissimi"</note>, anyone among mortals more worthy of immortality than this Elder of ours? But he himself was born under the common law of nature, and his thin little body was already long ago conflicted by severe illnesses, from which a very grave fear of a much earlier departure sometimes flowed. Nor was there anything under divine providence, except a vigor of mind joined with piety, that kept him with us for so long; even with such complete use of his senses that not many months ago, while we were watching and listening, he read the **Greek Scriptures** printed in the smallest type promptly and easily by the light of the moon alone in the late evening, a feat which no one else could have performed. However, as his age grew heavier, he suffered at times the savage tortures of arthritis and the dire pains of kidney stones <note>original: "nephritidis à calculo"</note>. 

And about six years ago, in the Academic Chair and in the very act of an academic lecture, he was first struck by manifest but immediately vanishing signs of a sudden brain disturbance. And though these evils were softened by the good skill of the most famous physician **Frederic Deckers** <note>original: "Frederici Deckersii"</note>, they nevertheless threatened a return through light attacks from time to time: for a staggering and a weakness, indicating that the roots of the past evil were not yet uprooted, struck fear of a fatal disease coming from this eventually. To this, therefore, which had been foreseen for a long time (according to the account of the famous physician **Boerhaave** <note>original: "Boerhavenii"</note>), a fever gave the beginning at the first hour of the night on the 18th day of October, overwhelming him when he least expected it. When this was quickly extinguished, a total weakness remained in his body and a numbness in his mind, a sign of the affected brain. Considering these things himself, the most holy Elder predicted to me, to other friends, and to his doctor, with great tranquility of a constant mind, that these symptoms would be fatal. Nor did the apparent lightness of the illness change his prophetic judgment of death, as he predicted that the consequences of his advanced age and extreme debility could have no other outcome. And he was not wrong.

### FUNERAL ORATION

<sig>* g 3</sig>
<sig>To the Great God <note>original: "D. M.," likely abbreviating "Deo Maximo," a common dedication in late Latin orations, though it mimics the Roman "Dis Manibus" (To the Divine Spirits)</note></sig>

Indeed, as the charming images of a most sweet sleep lulled his senses by soothing them more and more, and after his final hour of life had signaled clearly enough to me—as I was encouraging him toward constancy of faith and hope with a prayer for divine Grace—he gave a new sign of that most blessed hope and heavenly longing he had so often testified to before. On the very first hour after noon on the 22nd day of October, he left this gentle life, which was fading away in a most mild decline, as peacefully as possible; and he most willingly passed from all labor and struggle to the joys prepared for him by his Lord, in the 73rd year of his age.

Thus lived, **distinguished listeners** <note>original: "A. P.," abbreviating "Auditores Praestantissimi"</note>, and thus died **HERMAN WITSIUS**, full of days and the good things of this life, but also full of its troubles. Truly he lives now, at last, truly in heaven with God, made a partaker through the grace of his Lord in a blessedness that will never end—for which we still aspire amidst mournful struggles. And he shall live again on the last day, so that even in a glorified body <note>original: "corpore decorato," literally "adorned body"</note> he may be with his Lord forever to proclaim His praises among the heavenly beings. Indeed, though dead, he will not cease to live among us, who will constantly honor his merits, and even to late posterity we shall learn from his example how to be truly wise and to act piously, for the Glory of God, the good of the Church, and our own Salvation. May God grant that we perform all this eagerly and without ceasing! 

Thus we shall truly adorn our "Sparta" <note>original: "Spartam... ornaturi," an ancient Greek idiom meaning "to do one's duty in the place where one is appointed"</note>, and one day we shall obtain the most generous rewards through His Grace in the joyful company of those now taken from us—the **Spanheims**, the **Triglands**, and the **WITSIUSES** <note>These were famous families of theologians at the University of Leiden who had recently passed away</note>, and indeed of all the blessed men and angels! May this same God preserve for Himself and most powerfully increase the Church, the Fatherland, and this University, and may He unite the surviving teachers most closely in the holy fear of His name. In place of those departing, may He now and always most kindly substitute the most worthy and useful men, who may carefully and successfully train the numerous youth for the public good, and greatly promote the Glory of the Supreme Deity, to whom alone it is fitting for all to offer sacrifice!

->I HAVE SPOKEN.<-

# SPEECH

...concerning the *Thundering Legion of Christians* <note>original: "Fulminatrice Christianorum"; this refers to Witsius's work on the historical miracle of the "Thundering Legion" of Roman soldiers</note>; and the first volume of the *Sacred Miscellanies* <note>original: "Miscellaneorum Sacrorum"</note>, along with a good portion of the second volume; besides certain other smaller works. Finally, not only did the completed second volume of the *Sacred Miscellanies* come out at Lyon, but here also were born the *Meditations* which he himself called *Leiden Meditations* <note>original: "Meletemata Leidensia"</note>, which could also be added to the number of his *Selected Dissertations*. Indeed, all these writings are not only so celebrated but also so polished, useful, and filled with various learning and piety, that they are most worthy of immortality <note>original: "cedro dignissima," literally "worthy of cedar oil," which was used in antiquity to preserve scrolls from decay</note> and shall commend the good fortune of our age to a late posterity.

Do you know, **distinguished listeners** <note>original: "A. P.," abbreviating "Auditores Praestantissimi"</note>, anyone among mortals more worthy of immortality than this old man of ours? But he himself was born under the common law of nature, and his frail frame <note>original: "corpusculum," a diminutive for "little body," often used affectionately or to show humility</note> was long ago struggled against by frequent and terrible diseases, from which the gravest fear of a much earlier departure sometimes flowed. Nor was there anything under divine providence, except a vigor of mind joined with piety, that preserved him for us so long; he even maintained such a complete use of his senses that, not many months ago, while we were watching and listening, he could promptly and easily read the Greek Scriptures printed in the smallest type by the light of the moon alone—something no one else could manage. However, as his age weighed more heavily, he occasionally suffered the sinister torments of gout <note>original: "Arthritidis"</note> and the dreadful pains of kidney stones <note>original: "nephritidis à calculo"</note>. And nearly six years ago, while in the academic chair and in the very act of delivering a university lecture, he was first struck by manifest though quickly vanishing signs of a sudden disturbance of the brain <note>original: "turbati subito cerebri"; likely a minor stroke or TIA</note>. And although these ills were eased by the fine skill of the most famous physician **Frederik Dekker** <note>original: "Frederici Deckerii"</note>, they nevertheless threatened to return through occasional slight attacks: for a staggering and a weakness—indicating the roots of the past evil were not yet uprooted—struck fear of a fatal disease coming from this eventually. Therefore, to this long-foreseen event [according to the account of the famous physician **Boerhaave** <note>original: "Boerhavenii"; referring to Herman Boerhaave, one of the most famous doctors in European history</note>] a fever gave the beginning at the first hour of the night on the 18th day of the month of October, overcoming him when he was not then expecting it. Once this fever was quickly extinguished, a total weakness of the body remained, and a torpor of the mind, which was an index of the affected brain. Considering these things himself, the most holy old man predicted to me, to other friends, and to his physician, with great tranquility of a constant soul, that they would be fatal. Nor did the apparent mildness of the disease change his prophetic sentence of death, as he foretold that the consequences of his advanced age and extreme weakness could have no other outcome. And he was not wrong.

His gifts and his praises—as he is mindful of his own—
grace was poured upon his lips like a honeycomb;
the power of a learned mind was his,
and an astounding judgment.
A sacred heart, Religion, and a Faith
devoted to the truth; a tongue speaking of God
and Christ in holiness; a brow
set against and hostile to the wicked world.
He mourned that all things were infected
by profane customs, that no limit was set
on crimes, and that faults increased daily
as the order of righteousness failed.
And mourning, he saw the iron times
of a collapsing world. For savage Strife <note>original: "Eris," the Greek goddess of discord.</note>
has long stirred up fraternal wars,
to set allied cities at enmity.
Therefore! Through all the regions of the fatherland
the torch of Discord burns with a swift whirlwind
of citizens, and the Fury <note>original: "Erynnis."</note>
herself, drunk, has applauded from her bosom.
Amidst the tumults and wars
drawn out further by the savage soldiery—which,
alas! for a long time have produced endless slaughters
with the pouring of purple blood.

Also translated as "Seer," from the root meaning "to see."</note></term> XIX. *How they are distinguished, we do not know.* XX. *Men of God.*

<margin>I. The purpose of the work.</margin>
May the Greatest and Best God command that which is glorious for Himself, saving for us, and useful for the studious youth and the whole Church—to whom we owe ourselves and all our belongings. [descrip]tion, because we not only fear, but also know for certain beforehand, that our speech as well as our thoughts will fall far below the excellence of the subject matter: and the reader may at times be indignant when he discovers that the noble arguments for speaking we have undertaken are not brought forth by us in a way that satisfies his wish and expectation. Nevertheless, we will strive diligently, so that we do not seem to have done nothing, or to have caused this trouble for ourselves and the reader in vain.

<margin>II. The linguistic study of words is useful.</margin>
II. But before we approach the *subject* itself, some things must be mentioned beforehand concerning the words which the Holy Spirit of God uses in this business. And although that first dissertation might seem at first glance to be only critical <note>In this context, "critical" refers to "criticism" in the sense of scholarly linguistic and textual analysis.</note>, and therefore sterile—suitable more for deterring than for attracting the reader—I would nonetheless dare to promise, provided he does not allow himself to be overtaken by a hasty weariness, that through these very linguistic observations, he will find himself led into an understanding of many difficult passages.

<margin>III. Nabi denotes a friend of God.</margin>
III. In the beginning, therefore, the word <term>Nabi <note>Hebrew: נביא. The most common term for a prophet in the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> occurs, which is used first of all in the history of *Abraham*, *Genesis 20:7*, where God, having rebuked King *Abimelech* for the abduction of *Sarah*, commands him to restore her to her husband *Abraham*, adding this reason: <note>original Hebrew: כי נביא הוא ויתפלל בעדך</note> *“for he is a Prophet, and he shall pray for you.”* It appears clearly enough that by <term>Nabi</term> is understood here one who is a *friend* and *intimate* of the supreme deity, whose injuries God recalls to His own mind as if almost done to Himself, and does not let them go unpunished, except by the intercession of the one who was harmed, and who is most powerful in his prayers. There is no doubt that the Psalmist alluded to this when, with the same intent, he called the Patriarchs <term>Nabiim <note>The plural form of Nabi.</note></term>, *Psalm 105:14–15*: *“He suffered no man to do them wrong; yea, he reproved kings for their sakes, saying: Touch not my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm.”* It is notable that they are called both *“God’s Anointed”* and *“Prophets.”* They were *Anointed*, certainly not with any physical oil—with which in later times, by God’s command, Priests and *Kings* were anointed (and are therefore called the *Anointed of the Lord*)—for we never read that such a thing was done to *Abraham*, or his son, or grandson. Yet they were “Anointed” by a remarkable grant of Divine goodness, by which He held them dear and distinguished to Himself, and enriched them with the abundance of His favor. And they were *Prophets*, that is, joined to Him by intimate familiarity: so that it would not be without punishment even for Kings to rashly harm them in any way. For this was given to *Abraham*, who is the first of all mortals whom we read to have been decorated with the name of *Prophet*, when God said to him: *“I will bless them that bless thee, and him that curseth thee I will curse.” Genesis 12:3.* We have

Using the examples of Abraham and the Patriarchs, he explains that prophecy is rooted in a special, protected relationship with the Divine rather than just ritual anointing.</summary>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>CONCERNING THE NAMES OF THE PROPHETS.</header>

Therefore, from the first use of this word, considered within its context, it follows that a <term>Nabi <note>Hebrew: נביא. The author is arguing that the core meaning of "Prophet" is "intimate friend."</note></term> is said to be one who is *God's familiar and intimate.*

<margin>IV. That friendship comprises three parts.</margin>
IV. But we do not yet have the whole picture. For that familiarity with God encompasses three things, all of which are contained within the scope of that word. Namely, *God speaks with His familiar friend*; and *he in turn speaks with God in prayers and thanksgivings*; and finally, he speaks *concerning God to others in the preaching of the Divine will.*

<margin>V. A. The disclosure of God's secrets.</margin>
V. This follows first from God's friendship: that God comes to His friend, reveals Himself to him, discloses His secrets to him, and informs him better about those things whose knowledge is useful or necessary for him. And this is what Christ promises to His friends in John 14:21: *He who loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and will show myself to him.* And again in verse 23: *My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him.* Again, in chapter 15:15: *But I have called you friends, because all things that I heard from my Father I have made known to you.* 

And from this "coming" of God to His friends, some Hebrew teachers derive the origin of the word we are discussing. For they maintain that <term>Nabi <note>Hebrew: נביא</note></term>, along with its related forms, comes from the root <term>Bo <note>Hebrew: בוא, meaning "to come" or "to enter."</note></term>, to come, to approach, or to enter; because God approaches such a person by the secret breath of the Spirit and indicates what is to come. Compare Ezekiel 2:2: *And the Spirit entered into me <note>Hebrew: ותבא בי רוח (va-tavo bi ruach)</note>—and I heard him who spoke with me.* Nor is it very different from what appears in this very 20th Chapter of Genesis, verse 3: *And God came to Abimelech in a dream of the night.* 

Certainly, Abraham could be called a *Nabi* by this name, as one to whom God frequently approached in His appearances, and whom He deigned to address with such friendly speech: *Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?* (Genesis 18:17). Indeed, the <term>Sod YHVH <note>Hebrew: סוד יהוה. This term implies both a "secret" and a "confidential circle" or "assembly."</note></term>—which refers to familiar interaction with God, and hence the disclosure of His secrets (for both are signified by the same word)—*is for those who fear Him* (Psalm 25:14). Such men *stand in the counsel of the Lord* <note>Hebrew: עמדו בסוד יהוה (amdu be-sod YHVH)</note>, being aware of His plans (Jeremiah 23:18, 22). And *the friendship of God was upon their tent* (Job 29:4). <note>original: "סוד אלוה עלי אהלם" (Sod Eloah alei ohalem)</note>.

<margin>VI. B. Conversation with God, especially in prayers.</margin>
VI. Furthermore, he who deserves to be called a *Nabi* must converse familiarly with God in prayers. For we see these two things joined: *He is a prophet, and he will pray for you.* And truly, the more excellent anyone was among the prophets, the more frequent and powerful he was in prayers. Take Moses as an example, by whose prayers the hands of God Himself were as if bound, so that God had to say to him, *Now therefore, let me alone* (Exodus 32:10). Or Elijah, at whose prayers the heavens withheld or poured out rain (James 5:17). And to this I would refer that word of the Psalmist in Psalm 99:6: *Moses and Aaron* among his priests <note>Hebrew: בכהניו (be-kohanav). The author glosses this as "among His familiar and distinguished ministers."</note>, *and Samuel among those...*

There is no doubt that the <term>Psalmist <note>The author of the Book of Psalms.</note></term> alluded to this when, with the same intent, he called the Patriarchs <term>Prophets <note>Hebrew: נביאים, the plural form "Nebi'im."</note></term> in Psalm 105:14–15: *He allowed no one to do them wrong; and he rebuked Kings on their account, saying: "Touch not my Anointed ones, and to my Prophets do no harm."* It is notable that they are called both the *Anointed* of God and *Prophets*. They are *Anointed*, certainly not with any physical oil—by which, in later times at God’s command, Priests and Kings were smeared, and are therefore called the *Anointed of the Lord*—for we never read of such a thing being done to Abraham, or his son, or his grandson. They were *Anointed*, however, by a notable indulgence of Divine goodness, by which He held them dear and extraordinary to Himself, and enriched them with the wealth of His favor. And they were *Prophets*, that is, joined to Him in intimate familiarity: so much so that not even Kings would be unpunished for rashly harming them in any way. For this was granted to Abraham, who is the first of all mortals whom we read was decorated with the name of *Prophet*, so that God said to him, *I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse.* (Genesis 12:3). <meta>This page continues the philological investigation of the word "Nabi" (Prophet). While the previous page established that the term first appears in the context of Abraham, this page breaks down the three specific characteristics of "prophetic friendship" with God: receiving divine secrets, engaging in powerful intercessory prayer, and eventually proclaiming God's will to others.</meta>

-># ON THE NAMES OF THE PROPHETS.<-

...therefore, from the first usage of this word considered in its circumstances, we conclude that a <term>Nabi <note>Hebrew: נביא. The author is arguing that the root of this word implies intimacy rather than just "predicting the future."</note></term> is said to be one who *is an intimate and familiar friend of God.*

<margin>IV. *That friendship encompasses three things.*</margin>
IV. But we do not yet have the full picture. For that familiarity with God encompasses three things, all of which are contained within the scope of that word. Specifically: *God speaks with His familiar friend*; and *he, in turn, speaks with God in prayers and thanksgivings*; and finally, *he speaks about God to others in the preaching of the Divine will.*

<margin>V. *A. The manifestation of the secrets of God.*</margin>
V. This is the first result of God's friendship: that God comes to His friend, reveals Himself to him, discloses His secrets, and informs him of those matters where knowledge is useful or necessary for him. And this is what Christ promises to His friends in John 14:21: *He who loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and will show myself to him.* And again in verse 23: *My Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him.* Again, in chapter 15:15: *But I have called you friends, for all things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.* 

From this "coming" of God to His friends, some Hebrew teachers derive the origin of the word we are discussing: for they argue that *Nabi* and its related forms come from the root *Bo* <note>Hebrew: בוא, meaning "to come, approach, or enter."</note>, meaning *to come, to approach, to enter*; because God approaches such a person by the hidden breath of the Spirit and indicates things to come. Compare Ezekiel 2:2: *And the Spirit entered [came] into me... and I heard Him speaking with me.* <note>Original Latin quoting Hebrew: *et venit in me Spiritus* — וּתָּבֹא בִי רוּחַ</note> Nor is it very different from what appears in this very 20th Chapter of Genesis, verse 3: *And God came to Abimelech in a dream of the night.* 

Certainly, by this name, Abraham could be called a *Nabi*: indeed, God frequently approached him in His appearances and deemed him worthy of such friendly speech: *Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?* (Genesis 18:17). To be sure, the <term>Sod Yehovah <note>Hebrew: סוד יהוה. This term carries a double meaning of "secret counsel" and "intimate circle."</note></term>—which refers to *the familiar commerce of God*, and consequently the *manifestation* of secrets (for both are signified by the same word)—*is for those who fear Him.* (Psalm 25:14). Such people *stand in the counsel of the Lord* <note>Jeremiah 23:18: עמדו בסוד יהוה</note>, knowing His plans. And *the friendship of God was upon their tent* <note>Job 29:4: סוד אלוה עלי אהלו</note>.

<margin>VI. *B. Conversation with God, especially in prayers.*</margin>
VI. Furthermore, he who deserves to be called a *Nabi* must converse familiarly with God in prayers. For we see these two things joined: *he is a prophet, and he will pray for you.* And indeed, the more excellent a man was among the prophets, the more frequent and powerful he was in prayer. Moses serves as the example, by whose prayers the hands of God Himself were, as it were, bound: so that God had to say to him, *Now therefore, let me alone* (Exodus 32:10). And Elijah, at whose prayers the heavens withheld or poured out rain (James 5:17). <margin>
VIII. Such things were also present in the early Christian Church.
</margin>
VIII. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> concludes, not without merit, that the same practice flourished in the early Christian Church, based on 1 Corinthians 14:26: "Each of you has a psalm." These extemporaneous hymns, he says, were often born from divine inspiration. Such was the hymn of Simeon, and Anna the widow, and—as is believable—the songs of Moses and his sister Miriam, and another by Moses, and by Deborah, and by Hannah (who was married to Elkanah), and the hymn of Isaiah in chapter 5. All those things which in later times came either from natural talent or from hard labor were then given to many people suddenly and by divine power, so that God's supreme kindness might be understood through it. Nor does that gift seem to have ceased entirely in later times. For unless I am mistaken, the words of Tertullian in his *Apology*, Chapter 39, pertain to this: "After the washing of hands and the bringing of lights, each is encouraged to sing to God in the midst of the assembly, either from the Holy Scriptures or from his own natural ability."

<margin>
IX. Which Satan imitated in his own initiates.
</margin>
IX. This was also imitated by Satan in his own initiates <note>The author uses the word "mystis," referring to those initiated into the secret "mysteries" of pagan religions.</note>. For the Gentiles also worshipped their gods with songs, which the ancient Romans called *Assamenta* <note>Latin: *Assamenta*, an archaic term for chants or songs sung by the Salii (priests of Mars).</note>. From this come the "Assamenta of Janus," the "Assamenta of Juno," and the "Assamenta of Minerva"—that is, private poems written for each of those individual gods. The Greeks had their *hymns*: both those with which they worshipped the gods to make them favorable—which they called *kletikous hymnous* <note>Greek: κλητικοὺς ὕμνους, "calling hymns" or invocations to bring a god near.</note> (in Latin, these are called *Indigitamenta* or *Carmina Calatoria*)—and those with which they called upon the "Vejoves" <note>Ancient Roman deities associated with ill-fortune or the underworld.</note> or sinister spirits to turn them away from doing harm, called *apotropaious hymnous* <note>Greek: ὕμνους ἀποτροπαίους, "turning-away hymns."</note> (in Latin, *Carmina Averruncalia*). Moreover, the lesser priests would sing these songs to their gods while seized by a certain <term>enthusiasm <note>From the Greek "enthusiasmos," literally meaning "having a god within." In this context, it refers to a state of divine possession or ecstatic inspiration.</note></term>. For as Proclus testifies, that hymn *Io Bacche* was "imbued with much shouting" <note>original: "βεβαπτισμένος πολλῷ φρυάγματι"</note>, and the *Dithyrambus* had "much of the divine breath" <note>original: "πολὺ τὸ ἐνθουσιῶδες"</note>. And the Corybantes <note>Dancers who worshipped the goddess Cybele with drums and loud music.</note>, according to Strabo in Book 10 of his *Geography*, were "filled with enthusiasm" <note>original: "ἐνθουσιαστικοί τινες"</note>, and were therefore held in the highest esteem among their people. For, as Strabo adds, "that enthusiasm seems to have a certain divine impulse and to come very close to the nature of soothsaying" <note>original: "ὁ ἐνθουσιασμὸς ἐπινευσίν τινα θεῖαν ἔχειν δοκεῖ, καὶ τῷ μαντικῷ γένει πλησιάζειν."</note>.

<margin>X. About speaking of God to others.</margin>

Indeed, *Rabbi Solomon* agrees with those who derive the word <term>Nabi<note>The standard Hebrew word for Prophet.</note></term> from *Nuv*; so that a "Prophet" becomes a preacher or teacher who brings forth the "germ" or fruit of the lips. How suitable this etymology <note>the study of the origin of words</note> is, I will not investigate now; let it only remain that a person is said to prophesy not only when they speak of mysteries and secrets through extraordinary revelation, but also when they speak of Divine matters through ordinary revelation—whether with the approval of the Spirit or otherwise in good conscience. With this in mind, Paul writes at length about prophecies in the Corinthian Church, and commands them to strive for the gift of prophesying above all other spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 14:1, 39). That is, he encourages the ability by which they are made fit to explain the Scriptures skillfully and to discuss Divine matters expertly.

He repeats this in 1 Timothy 2:12: *For I do not permit a woman to teach*. If a woman is not allowed to teach—indeed, not even to speak in the Church, but silence is commanded of her—by what logic is a "prophesying woman" introduced by Paul? And why is she given a mandate that she must not set herself to prophesying unless her head is first veiled?

### BOOK I. CHAPTER I.

<margin>It begins in the time of Samuel.</margin>
...to insert into the history. 1 Samuel 9:9: *In ancient times in Israel, everyone would say this when they were about to consult God: "Come, let us go to the <term>Seer</term> <note>Hebrew: עד הרואה (Ad Ha-Roeh)</note>"; for he who is today called a <term>Prophet</term> <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note> was in ancient times called a Seer.*

<margin>XVII. And by this observation, the appearance of a contradiction is removed.</margin>
XVII. If these matters are carefully considered, they are sufficient to resolve a significant difficulty which cannot fail to arise in the minds of readers when comparing the history of Samuel with the writings of Moses. For the history of Samuel seems to teach that the word <term>Prophet</term> <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note> was quite recent in those times, and that the word <term>Seer</term> <note>Hebrew: רואה (Roeh)</note> was used in its place in ancient times. Yet in the writings of Moses <note>The Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible</note>, at the very beginnings of the Israelite state, nothing is more frequent than the word <term>Prophet</term>; whereas the word <term>Seer</term> is not found there even once, as far as I know. Because of this, some conclude that the writing of the Pentateuch is somewhat later than the age of Samuel, since a name unknown to the ancient Israelites is frequently repeated there. However, if we weigh the matter fairly, we will find that the sacred history of Samuel does not deny that the word <term>Prophet</term> was also known and used by the ancients; it only teaches that around the time of Samuel, a meaning began to be attached to it through which it became a synonym for the word *Seer*. For in ancient times, it was used more generally, according to those concepts we have just explained: to signify a "friend of God" and an "interpreter of sacred things." But from that time on, in more frequent usage, it denoted a "searcher and discloser of hidden things," through whom God was consulted regarding those matters which mortals despaired of grasping unless God revealed them. Let these things now be said concerning the word <term>Prophet</term> and the name of the Prophet.

<margin>XVIII. The words <term>Visionary</term> and <term>Seer</term></margin>
XVIII. The names <term>Seer</term> <note>Hebrew: רואה (Roeh)</note> and <term>Visionary</term> <note>Hebrew: חוזה (Choseh)</note> are related, and they are joined to the name <term>Prophet</term> in such a way that they seem to say the same thing, but with a slightly different emphasis. 1 Chronicles 29:29 is especially relevant here, where it is recorded that the deeds of David were written *in the words of Samuel the <term>Seer</term> <note>Hebrew: הרואה (Ha-Roeh)</note>, and in the words of Nathan the <term>Prophet</term> <note>Hebrew: הנביא (Ha-Nabi)</note>, and in the words of Gad the <term>Visionary</term> <note>Hebrew: החוזה (Ha-Choseh)</note>.* I do not know if it is probable that these words were used distinctly in this way with a completely interchangeable meaning just for the sake of elegance; since these same titles seem to be attributed to the same persons elsewhere as well, and not without some emphasis. For Samuel is called "Seer" throughout 1 Chronicles 9:22 and 26:28; and Gad is called "Visionary" in 2 Samuel 24:11, 1 Chronicles 21:9, and 29:29. Likewise, Nathan is called "Prophet" in 2 Samuel 7:2, 12:25, 1 Kings 1:8, 10, 22, and many other places. Although both Samuel and Gad are called "Prophets" in some places, I do not find the honorific of <term>Visionary</term> bestowed upon Samuel, nor the title of <term>Seer</term> given to Gad.
