# ON THE NAMES OF THE PROPHETS.

<margin>
XIX. We do not know how they are distinguished.
</margin>
XIX. What, then, is the difference in meaning between these three names? To be sure, I confess that I do not know. Perhaps the critical method of Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and his focus on biblical philology.</note> might find a place here. He considers Samuel to be called a *Roeh* <note>original Latin: *Roeh videntem*</note>—a **Seer**—because of the Divine voice which he received face-to-face, as if from the very mouth of God. He suggests that those who spoke publicly were called **Prophets** <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note>. Finally, he suggests that the term <term>Beholder</term> <note>Hebrew: חזה (Choseh)</note> was used for all who received revelations, whether through ordinary study and meditation on the Scriptures or through extraordinary inspiration. If this distinction holds, the word *Choseh* would be the most general of all, signifying a person skilled in Divine matters through both their own diligence and the singular grace and inspiration of God. *Roeh* would be somewhat more specific, signifying one to whom God reveals hidden things through a prophetic vision. Meanwhile, it is common practice to use *Nabi* for an interpreter of the Divine will. However, it would have been desirable for the most distinguished Cocceius to have confirmed these points with examples and reasoning. He should have explained why the title *Choseh* is specifically attributed to Gad, the title *Roeh* to Samuel, and the title *Nabi* to Nathan; for all of them excelled in skillful talent, enjoyed Divine inspirations, acted as interpreters of God’s will, and were pointers toward hidden things. An industrious man must certainly strive to remain ignorant of as little as possible; yet an honest man must admit that, no matter how much diligence he exhausts, many things remain which he is forced not to know. And I truly desire my name to be counted among this latter sort of men.

<margin>
XX. Men of God. Add what is said in the Preface, Section I.
</margin>
XX. Prophets were also called **MEN OF GOD**. <note>See 1 Kings 13:1; 1 Timothy 6:11; 2 Timothy 3:17; 2 Peter 1:21.</note> They were called this because, in their sacred function, they do not belong to themselves, much less to other men, but are entirely God's. They conduct themselves according to His prescription and refer all things to His glory; they are such that no one can harm them without harming God in His ministers.

### BOOK 1. CHAPTER 1.

<margin>
It began in the time of Samuel.
</margin>
...to insert into the history. 1 Samuel 9:9: *In olden times in Israel, everyone said this when they went to consult God: “Come, let us go to the Seer” <note>Hebrew: עד הרואה (ad ha-Roeh)</note>; for he who is today called a Prophet <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note> was in olden times called a Seer.*

<margin>
XVII. And by this observation, a perceived contradiction is removed.
</margin>
XVII. If these things are carefully considered, they are sufficient to resolve a significant difficulty that cannot help but arise in the minds of readers when comparing the history of Samuel with the writings of Moses. For the history of Samuel seems to teach that the word **Prophet** <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note> was quite recent in those times, and that in its place, the word **Seer** <note>original Latin: *Roeh*</note> was used in antiquity. Yet, in the writings of Moses, at the very beginnings of the Israelite state, nothing is more common than the word **Prophet**; meanwhile, the word **Seer**, as far as I know, is not found there even once. From this, some conclude that the writing of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> is somewhat later than the age of Samuel, since a name unknown to the ancient Israelites is repeated there so familiarly. However, if we weigh the matter fairly, we will find it is not being denied in the sacred history of Samuel that the word **Prophet** was also known and used by the ancients. Rather, it is only being taught that around Samuel’s time, a meaning began to be attached to it by which it became synonymous with the word **Seer**. For in ancient times, the term was used more generally, according to the definitions we have just explained: to signify a "friend of God" and an "interpreter of sacred matters." But from that time on, in more frequent usage, it designated a "searcher and indicator of secret things," through whom God was consulted regarding those matters which mortals despaired of attaining unless God revealed them. Let these things now be said by us concerning the word **Prophet** <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note> and the name of the Prophet.

<margin>
XVIII. The terms *Choseh* and *Roeh*.
</margin>
XVIII. The names **Seer** <note>Hebrew: רואה (Roeh)</note> and **Beholder** <note>Hebrew: חוזה (Choseh)</note> are related; they are joined to the name **Prophet** <note>Nabi</note> in such a way that they seem to describe the same thing, but from a slightly different perspective. 1 Chronicles 29:29 is especially relevant here, where it is recorded that the deeds of David were written *in the words of Samuel the Seer <note>Hebrew: הרואה (ha-Roeh)</note>, and in the words of Nathan the Prophet <note>Hebrew: נביא (Nabi)</note>, and in the words of Gad the Gazer <note>Hebrew: החוזה (ha-Choseh); the author uses the Latin *Cernentis*, meaning "one who discerns" or "sees clearly."</note>.* I do not know if it is likely that these words were used distinctly in this way with an entirely interchangeable meaning just for the sake of elegance, especially since these same titles seem to be attributed to the same persons elsewhere, not without some emphasis. For Samuel is called **Seer** in various places (1 Chronicles 9:22; 26:28), and Gad is called **Gazer** (2 Samuel 24:11; 1 Chronicles 21:9; 29:29), just as Nathan is called **Prophet** (2 Samuel 7:2; 12:25; 1 Kings 1:8, 10, 22, and many other places). Although both Samuel and Gad are called Prophets in some places, I do not find that the title of **Gazer** is granted to Samuel, nor the title of **Seer** to Gad.

<margin>XIX. We do not know how they are distinguished.</margin>
XIX. What diversity of meaning, then, exists between these three names? Indeed, I confess that I do not know. He believes Samuel is called *Roeh* [Seer] <note>Hebrew: רואה</note> because of the Divine voice which he received face-to-face as if from the mouth of God; that "Seers" <term>חזים</term> <note>original: Chazim</note> refers to all who had revelations, whether through ordinary study and meditation upon Scripture, or through extraordinary inspiration. An industrious man must certainly strive to be ignorant of as little as possible: but an honest man must confess that, no matter how much diligence he exerts, many things remain which he is forced not to know. And I certainly desire my name to be counted among this class of men.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER II.

<margin>I. Definition of prophecy.</margin>
But we must finally approach the matter itself. I therefore define **PROPHECY** as follows: it is the **KNOWLEDGE AND REVELATION OF HIDDEN THINGS, WHICH A PERSON KNOWS NOT FROM THEIR OWN CLEVERNESS, NOR FROM THE REPORT OF OTHERS, BUT FROM A HEAVENLY AND EXTRAORDINARY REVELATION FROM GOD.** These points are worthy of being explained and proven somewhat more clearly.

<margin>II. In prophecy there is knowledge and revelation.</margin>
II. I say that for prophecy, a certain knowledge of things is required on the part of the prophet, and a revelation <note>The Latin *patefactio* implies an "opening up" or "uncovering" of what was hidden.</note> on the part of others with whom he communicates what he knows. The former is usually granted for the sake of the latter. For a prophet must first *stand in the council of God* <note>original: "in consilio Dei stare"</note>, and then proclaim the words he has heard to the people: as it says in Jeremiah 23:22. First, he must *have a dream* and *the word of God*—that is, the revelation—then *recount and speak it out*, as in verse 28: *The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully.* <note>original: "Propheta, penes quem est somnium, enarret somnium; & penes quem est verbum meum, eloquatur verbum meum vere."</note> For although it could sometimes happen that God revealed His hidden will to someone primarily for the instruction of the one to whom it was revealed—and who was held by no necessity to make it public—nevertheless, those are usually called "Prophets" in a specific sense through whom God manifests Himself to others as if through His messengers.

<margin>III. Of hidden things, both past,</margin>
III. Moreover, those things which are known through prophecy must be secret and hidden. It does not matter then whether they are *past*, *present*, or *future*. For even past things are sometimes known only through divine inspiration. Certainly, no one could have had a clear perspective on the order of the creation of the universe, as it is recounted by Moses, except from Divine revelation; and the one who first explained it to men must have been taught by God. And Daniel proved himself to be a prophet no less when he brought back to Nebuchadnezzar <note>The King of Babylon (r. 605–562 BCE).</note> such an accurate memory of a dream which he himself had forgotten, than when he explained those things which were foretold by the dream to happen in the passing of several centuries. Nor did that Samaritan woman <note>Referring to the account in the Gospel of John, chapter 4.</note> conclude poorly that Christ was a prophet from the fact that he had knowledge of her past life, even though he was joined to her by no previous acquaintance, and placed it before her eyes so clearly and without evasion (John 4:18, 19).

<margin>IV. As well as present.</margin>
IV. But even present things are among the objects of prophecy. For it was not with the eyes of the body, nor by the mere imagination of his own mind, but by the prophetic Spirit that Elisha saw his servant Gehazi <note>Gehazi was the servant of the prophet Elisha who secretly took gifts from Naaman, a Syrian general healed of leprosy, against Elisha's wishes (2 Kings 5).</note> when he was negotiating for the acceptance of gifts from Naaman the Syrian, who had been cleansed of leprosy by the help of Elisha's Lord (2 Kings 5:26). And by the same Spirit, Daniel...

->### ON PROPHECY.<-

...read that hidden writing, which had struck such terror into Belshazzar. *Daniel 5:8, 17, 25.* <note>In the biblical story, a mysterious hand wrote on the palace wall during a feast; only the prophet Daniel could interpret the message "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin."</note> What sort of writing it was is a matter of curious inquiry but is rashly defined by many. It is enough that it was such that Daniel’s communion with God was apparent from its reading and interpretation. Perhaps those letters were seen by no one except the King and Daniel. The Magi, with their incantations, could not make them visible, or at least readable, to themselves. It is not credible that those letters were entirely new and completely unknown to all mortals until then, or at least to the Chaldeans <note>The people of Babylon, famous in the ancient world for their study of astronomy and the occult.</note>, such that Daniel was the first to learn them and then taught the King. For how could he have convinced the King’s mind of their genuine reading so quickly and easily? Let this only be held: they were represented in such a way that they could not be read or understood without God intervening.

<margin>V. But especially future things.</margin>
V. Especially, however, *future* things belong to Prophecy—namely, *contingent* <note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to events that happen by chance or choice, rather than by a fixed law of nature.</note> and *free* events—most of all if they are predicted not just generally, but with the circumstances of persons, place, and time. And by this very thing, God proves His omniscience and firmly asserts His Divinity against the invented deities of the nations; because He Himself knows the future through Himself and reveals it to whom He wills. *Isaiah 41:21, 22, 23.*

<margin>VI. Known not from one's own cleverness.</margin>
VI. Moreover, this must also be observed: that it is required for prophecy that those hidden things are not known *by one’s own industry* or *cleverness*, nor by the speeches of *others* taught by God, but *by a heavenly and extraordinary revelation from God*. Not by the former: for *cleverness in investigating secret things makes one prudent, not a prophet*. And I think it is concerning such prudence and sagacity that the passage in *Proverbs 16:10* is to be understood: <gloss>An oracle is on the lips of the king; his mouth does not err in judgment.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: קִסֶם עַל שִׂפְתֵי מֶלֶךְ (qesem 'al-sipte-melek). The author is distinguishing between a King's natural intuition and a Prophet's supernatural revelation.</note> Regarding this sagacity or <term>shrewdness (eustochia)</term> <note>original Greek: εὐστοχία, meaning the ability to hit the mark or make a lucky guess.</note> in sniffing out hidden things, *Lipsius* <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a famous Flemish humanist whose works on political "monitions" or warnings were widely read.</note> collected some notable examples in *Politics, Monitions and Examples*, Book II, Chapter IX, Monition III. The Greeks used the word <term>divination (manteia)</term> <note>original Greek: μαντείας</note> and the Latins used the word *augury* with the same intent. Hence that old saying:
> The best seer is he who guesses well. <note>original Greek: Μάντις ἄριστος, ὅστις εἰκάζει καλῶς.</note>
> *I will deem him the best prophet who has conjectured well.* <note>The author provides a Latin verse translation of the Greek maxim attributed to Euripides.</note>
Hence also that of Ovid in *Tristia*, Book I, Elegy VIII:
> *Reason is an augury, and a conjecture of the future.*

<margin>VII. Nor by the information of others.</margin>
VII. Nor is prophecy derived from the information of others. For to know and explain in that way is the role of an *interpreter*, not of a Prophet strictly so called. Yet it can happen that God reveals the same thing, in almost the same words, to different Prophets and commands them to preach it; as is clear from a comparison of *Isaiah 2:2* with *Micah 4:1*, and *Isaiah 16:7* with *Jeremiah 48:29*.

VIII. But this is the point. For God claims this for Himself: that from the fullness of His own omniscience, He alone instructs His servants. <note>original: *Jes. XLIII. 12.*</note> **Isaiah 43:12**:
> *I have declared and saved and foretold, and there was no foreign god among you.*
Add also **Amos 3:7**: 
> *The Lord Jehovah does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the Prophets.*

<margin>IX. And that an extraordinary one.</margin>
IX. Nor is it without reason that I have called this not only a heavenly revelation, but an extraordinary one. It is the kind that Paul mentions happened to him regarding the mysteries of the Gospel; he did not receive it from a man through human instruction, nor was he taught it in such a way that he improved over time, but he knew it through the revelation of *Jesus Christ*, which suddenly made him fit for the very difficult task of the Apostleship. **Galatians 1:12**. For there is also a certain heavenly revelation through the Spirit of grace which happens to all the faithful; it consists in that inner illumination of minds by which the faith of God’s elect is produced in their souls. Concerning this, the same Paul says in **1 Corinthians 2:10, 12**:
> *But God has revealed them to us through His Spirit. To us—not only as Apostles, but also as believers. For he continues: We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that God has freely given to us.*
Since this spirit distinguishes the faithful from the people of this world, it must also be common to all the faithful. And indeed, Paul prays for the faithful Ephesians in **Chapter 1:17–18** that:
> *The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation through the knowledge of Him, the eyes of their minds being enlightened, to know what is the hope of His calling, and what are the riches of the glory of His inheritance among the saints.*
However, such people, although they may enjoy a certain immediate revelation, are not "Prophets" except in a very general sense and the loosest meaning of the word.

<margin>X. Certain distinctions.</margin>
X. For a greater clarification of these matters, certain distinctions seem necessary. In prophecy, one can distinguish between a <term>Gift (Donum)</term>—which happens even to private individuals and consists in the revelation of secret things—and an <term>Office (Munus)</term> <note>In this context, a 'Munus' refers to a formal, public role or "job" within the religious community, whereas a 'Donum' is a personal spiritual ability.</note>, which was an extraordinary function in the Church held by certain persons destined for it by a special Divine calling. Likewise, one must distinguish between the Revelation of a secret thing and the Impulse <note>original: *Agitatio*</note> to bring it forth to the public either by word, writing, or certain other symbols. Prophecy is also either *momentary*—occurring only on a specific occasion and then ceasing, such as with those seventy elders mentioned in **Numbers 11:25**:
> *And it happened that when the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did so no more.* <note>The "seventy elders" were chosen to help Moses lead the Israelites; their brief moment of prophesying served as a divine sign of their shared authority.</note>
Or it is *permanent*, such as can be seen in those who performed the prophetic office for many years and repeatedly had frequent revelations. However, none held prophecy...

### CHAP. III.

## On the Various Modes of Revelation.

*I. The modes of revelation are quite diverse. II. Sometimes God revealed His will by the instinct of His Spirit alone. III. Sometimes with the addition of symbols, which were occasionally presented to the external senses. IV. Here belong "lots." V. And the "Daughter of the Voice." VI. Examples of it. VII. Was it rejected with good reason? VIII. Sometimes symbolic objects were presented to the Imagination. IX. Of people who were awake. X. Which recommended themselves by the clarity of the representation. XI. But not always so clearly that they did not require an explanation. XII. Which was not always granted even to the Prophets themselves.*

<margin>I. The modes of Revelation are quite diverse.</margin>
It must be further noted that the MODES OF REVELATION were so varied that it is difficult to reduce them to specific classes in a fixed order. Far more learned men have labored greatly here <note>literally "sweated," meaning they put in intense effort</note>, and they have not all explained themselves in the same way. Therefore, we are not forbidden from attempting something after others have tried. Prophetic Revelation is either IMMEDIATE or MEDIATE. I call "immediate" that which proceeds from God in such a way that no created person <note>such as an angel or human messenger</note> intervenes. This, in turn, is either SIMPLE—carried out by the internal instinct of the Spirit alone—or SYMBOLIC—marked by the addition of certain symbols.

<margin>II. Sometimes God revealed His will by the instinct of His Spirit alone.</margin>
II. It seems beyond doubt that God’s holy men sometimes knew certain secrets for the sole reason that God willed them to know them, by that effective will through which He brings everything into existence. And just as He Himself is the purest Mind, so He can act intimately with the mind of a human through a secret conversation—one that is not heard or understood except by the mind to which, or rather in which, it occurs. To this point, unless I am mistaken, the final words of David lead us in **2 Samuel 23:2, 3**:
> *The Spirit of the Lord spoke IN ME. The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me.*
And elsewhere we read frequently enough of the word of God being in...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER III.

...to the Prophets; this is what **the Spirit of Christ within them indicated**, <note>original Greek: "ἐδήλου τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ"</note> the Spirit of Christ who was in them declared. **1 Peter 1:11**. Similarly, a sudden knowledge of the mysteries of the Gospel was given to the Apostles, as well as the knowledge of the languages in which they were to teach all nations without distinction. Nor did Paul receive the Gospel in any other way than through an internal revelation of Christ of this kind, when it pleased God to reveal His Son in him. **Galatians 1:12, 15, 16**. For although he both saw and heard something on the road toward Damascus, what he then saw and heard was a preparation of the mind toward teachability, rather than the Divine revelation itself by which he was shaped into such an exact expertise in the mysteries of the Gospel.

<margin>III. Sometimes Symbols are added, which are occasionally offered to the External senses.</margin>
III. At other times, however, God willed that SYMBOLS, or certain forms, be added. These were offered either to the EXTERNAL senses or to the IMAGINATION <note>the author uses the term "Phantasia" to refer to the mental faculty that receives internal images, as opposed to external physical sight</note>. Among the external senses, it pleased Him to affect especially *Sight* and *Hearing*, and sometimes even *Touch*; occasionally, all these senses at once. Luke records in **Acts 2:3** that "divided tongues as of fire" were seen sitting upon each of the Apostles. We all know that Hearing was the sense by which Adam perceived the voice of God walking in the garden. **Genesis 3:9**. Moses, when he had entered the Tabernacle of the congregation, heard a voice speaking to him from the mercy seat. **Numbers 7:89**. Likewise, a voice forced itself upon the ears of Samuel. **1 Samuel 3**. It is also certain that these two—sight and hearing—were sometimes so joined that those to whom God chose to declare Himself saw and heard something simultaneously. This occurred at the baptism of Christ, where the Holy Spirit was seen under the form of a dove, and the testimony of the Father concerning His only beloved Son was heard. **Matthew 3:16–17**. This also always took place in appearances of that kind where conversations were mixed in. **Genesis 18:17**. But God even affected *touch* sometimes along with hearing; we have an example of this in Daniel, **Chapter 10:9–10**, and in John, **Revelation 1:17**. All these senses concur at once in the story of Jacob. **Genesis 32**. He sees God in human form wrestling with him, he feels the socket of his hip being injured, and he hears that wrestler engaging in various conversations with him.

<margin>IV. To this belong Lots.</margin>
IV. To those things which affected the eyes we can refer DIVINATORY LOTS, the use of which was either in *consultations* for the detection of a hidden matter—as with Achan in **Joshua 7:14**, in Saul and Jonathan in **1 Samuel 14:42**, and in Jonah in **Jonah 1:7**—or in the *distribution* of inheritances, examples of which are in the book of Joshua; or finally in *election*, as in **Acts 1:26**. <margin>V. And the Daughter of a Voice.</margin>
V. To those things presented to the sense of hearing belongs the <term>Bat Kol</term> <note>Hebrew: בת קול</note> or **DAUGHTER OF A VOICE**. By this remarkable naming convention, the authors of the Targums <note>Aramaic translations/paraphrases of the Old Testament</note>, the Talmuds, and other Rabbis designate a certain species or degree of Divine oracles, taken from the <term>levels of the Holy Spirit</term> <note>Hebrew: מדרגות רוח הקדש</note>, as they say; or rather, a heavenly voice sent by God, which flourished especially during the time of the Second Temple. They call it the *Daughter of a voice* because Scripture calls it simply the *Voice*. The Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> say there is a certain Divine attribute called *Kol* <note>Hebrew: קול</note>, or "Voice"; its outward manifestation and revelation would then be the *Bat Kol*, the "daughter of the voice." Thus says Elias in *The Tishbite*. A commentary on the Talmud suggests that it was not the heavenly voice itself heard by men, but rather a kind of echo or reflection of it. See *Buxtorf’s Lexicon, page 321*. I agree more, however, with *Christian Schotanus* in *The Triumph of Scripture, Book II, Chapter VII*, who believes that <term>Kol</term> ("Voice") signifies the sound that strikes the air, while <term>Bat Kol</term> ("daughter of a voice") refers to the actual words and sayings expressed by that sound. Thunder is the voice of the Lord. Sometimes that voice was heard without the "daughter of the voice" being heard—that is, without the articulation of that sound into specific words. And in this way, perhaps, we should reconcile what is found in **Acts 9:7** with what is read in **Acts 22:9**. In the first passage, it is said that Paul's companions *heard the voice*, meaning an unarticulated sound; in the second, *they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me* <note>original Greek: τὴν δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν τοῦ λαλοῦντός μοι</note>, meaning they did not hear the speech distinguished into intelligible words.

This deserves to be compared with **Matthew 10:29**.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER III.

In the Prophets, this refers to that which **the Spirit of Christ within them made clear** <note>Original Greek: *ἐδήλου τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ*</note>; the Spirit of Christ *who was in them* declared it. 1 Peter 1:11. In this same way, the Apostles were suddenly granted knowledge of the mysteries of the Gospel, as well as the languages in which they were to teach all nations without distinction. Nor did Paul receive the Gospel in any other way than through an internal revelation of Christ of this kind, when it pleased God to reveal His Son in him. Galatians 1:12, 15, 16. For although he both saw and heard something on the road toward Damascus, what he then saw and heard was a preparation of the mind toward teachability, rather than that Divine revelation by which he was shaped into such an exact mastery of the mysteries of the Gospel.

<margin>III. Sometimes Symbols are added: which are occasionally presented to the external senses.</margin>
III. At other times, however, God willed that **SYMBOLS**, or certain outward forms, be added. These were presented either to the **EXTERNAL SENSES** or to the **IMAGINATION**. Among the external senses, it pleased Him to affect **Sight and Hearing** most of all, and sometimes even **Touch**; occasionally all these senses at once. Moses, when he had entered the Tabernacle of the meeting, heard a voice speaking to him from the mercy seat. Numbers 7:89. Likewise, a voice forced itself upon the ears of Samuel. 1 Samuel 3. It is also certain that these two were sometimes joined in such a way that those to whom God chose to declare Himself saw and heard something at the same time. This happened at the baptism of Christ; where the Holy Spirit was seen under the form of a dove, and the testimony of the Father concerning His only beloved Son was heard. Matthew 3:16, 17. This always took place in appearances of that kind where conversations were intertwined. Genesis 18:17. But God also sometimes affected **touch** together with hearing; an example of which we have in Daniel (Chapter 10:9, 10) and John (Revelation 1:17). All these things concur at once in the story of Jacob. Genesis 32. He sees God in human form wrestling with him, he feels his hip socket being struck, and he hears that wrestler engaging in various conversations with him.

To those things which affected the eyes, we can refer **DIVINATORY LOTS**, the use of which was for **consultations** to detect hidden matters (as with Achan, Joshua 7:14; with Saul and Jonathan, 1 Samuel 14:42; and with Jonah, Jonah 1:7), or in the **distribution of inheritances** (examples of which are in the book of Joshua), or finally in **elections**, as in Acts 1:26. <margin>XII. Which was not always granted even to the Prophets themselves.</margin>
XII. Indeed, it was not always so clear, for many specific details remained hidden, not only from the listeners but even from the Prophets themselves. This is what God said to Daniel in Chapter 12:4: *But you, Daniel, shut up these words, and seal this book until the determined time.* For God did not consider it necessary or useful for the Church that all of Daniel’s prophecies <term>vaticinia: predictions of the future or divine revelations</term> be understood immediately, until the time destined for their fulfillment either approached or the event itself lit a torch for the prophecies. Indeed, Daniel himself was forced to remain ignorant of some things (ibid. verses 8–9): *And when I heard and did not understand, I said, My Lord, what shall be the end of these things? And he said; go, Daniel: for these matters are shut up and sealed until the determined time.* And for this reason, the Prophets themselves diligently meditated upon their own prophecies to unearth their hidden meaning. 1 Peter 1:10–11.

BOOK I. CHAPTER IV.

## CHAPTER IV.

### On Ecstasy.

I. What ecstasy is. II. It is either Natural, III. Or Diabolical, IV. Or feigned by clever men, V. Or Divine. VI. Which sometimes follows revelation. VII. Sometimes precedes it. VIII. Paul's notable rapture. IX. Who speaks of himself as another, out of modesty. X. It is doubted whether he was present in heavenly things in the body or out of the body. XI. Certainly he heard unspeakable words <note>original: *ἄρρητα ῥήματα* (arrhēta rhēmata)</note>. XII. Greater than what is lawful for a mere man to say. XIII. Why the Church has not recounted them?

<margin>
I. What ecstasy is.
</margin>

ECSTASY can be related to those revelations represented through *symbols of the imagination* <note>original: *Symbola phantasiae*</note>. This word is derived from the Greek "to be moved out of place" <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐξίσαμαι* (apo tou existamai)</note>, as the scholar Stephanus <note>referring to the 16th-century lexicographer Henri Estienne</note> observes. It signifies generally the displacement of any thing from the state in which it was; but specifically, it refers to the mind. In that sense, it denotes either a great wonder or terror by which the mind is moved out of its ordinary state of tranquility (as seen in *Mark 5:42, 16:8; Luke 5:26*), or *such an alienation of the mind that, as the functions of the external senses cease, the mind itself is entirely ignorant of what is happening in the body, and is wholly occupied with intense and fixed thoughts.*

<margin>
II. It is either Natural,
</margin>

II. Sometimes it is purely NATURAL. This arises either from a disease affecting the brain in such a way that men lie as if dead for hours, or even several days, without sense or motion; yet, when they eventually return to themselves as if from a very deep sleep, they recount wonderful things they have seen. It can also arise from "vehement studies" <note>intense intellectual or spiritual focus</note>; some believe it is possible for a mind accustomed to deep meditation to occasionally immerse itself so deeply that it suspends the functions of the senses for a time. This is recounted of *Thomas Aquinas* <note>The 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note>, who had so accustomed himself to constant contemplation that he frequently fell into mental ecstasies where he appeared dead to those standing by. In the meantime, however, he was drinking in the hidden mysteries of the Divine scriptures, which he would communicate to others upon returning to himself. See, if you please, *Gualtperius* on Acts 10. *Cardanus* <note>Gerolamo Cardano, a Renaissance polymath</note> writes of himself in *Book VIII of "Varieties of Things," Chapter 43*, that he could pass into ecstasy whenever he wished, *so that he could hear the voices of those standing by only faintly, but not understand them; he did not feel a sharp pinch, and not even the pains of gout.* However, the credibility of this claim rests with the author.

<meta>Catchword: III. Ne-</meta>

->### ON ECSTASY.<-

<margin>III. Or Diabolical.</margin>
III. Nor does it seem that we should deny the existence of a certain DIABOLICAL ecstasy, occurring when a wicked spirit—seizing upon opportunities provided by <term>melancholic afflictions</term> <note>original Greek: μελαγχόλικα πάθη (*melancholika pathē*); in ancient medicine, these were physical imbalances thought to cause mental disturbances</note>—wondrously disturbs the brain. By weaving itself into the soul's mental images, the spirit impresses certain secrets upon the mind while it seems to be absent from the body—even things regarding the future or events happening in far distant places. Upon returning to themselves, these people recount these things as if they had seen them. Examples of this exist in *Peucer's "On Divination"* <note>Kaspar Peucer (1525–1602) was a German scholar who wrote a famous treatise on various forms of prophecy and magic</note> under the title *On Divine Possession* <note>original: "de Theomanteia"</note>.

<margin>IV. Or feigned by clever men.</margin>
IV. Although many consider it not improbable that many such states were feigned by clever men in order to win trust and veneration for their craft. This was wisely observed by *Maximus of Tyre* <note>a Greek philosopher and rhetorician of the 2nd century AD</note>, whose words are worthy of being recorded here, as they shed a significant light on this matter. <margin>See the preface, section 3.</margin> Thus he says in his *22nd Dissertation*: > *There was in Proconnesus a certain philosopher named Aristeas. At first, everyone disparaged his wisdom because he could point to no teacher. To counter this, he applied such a remedy: he claimed that his soul, having left his body, had sought heaven directly, from where he had traveled over all the lands of the Greeks and Barbarians, all the islands, the rivers, and the mountains, and finally had stopped at the borders of the Hyperboreans <note>a mythical people of the far north</note>. From here, he claimed to have observed all the rites and customs of all states, the characters of all lands, the changes of the air, the flooding of the sea, and the mouths of rivers; indeed, he claimed to have surveyed heaven itself much more easily than the lower regions. And yet, for this very reason, Aristeas obtained more credit than Xenagoras, or that famous Xenophanes, or anyone else who presented the matter just as it was.*

<margin>V. Or Divine.</margin>
V. But we are not now dealing with the *Natural* or the *Diabolical*, let alone those feigned by men themselves, but with truly DIVINE Ecstasy. This occurs when the Spirit of God, invading and filling the entire mind, keeps it—having been withdrawn from all commerce with the body for that time—entirely occupied with the contemplations and meditations of secret and divine things.

<margin>VI. Which sometimes follows revelation.</margin>
VI. This abstraction of the mind from the body, so to speak, seems to have happened sometimes after the initial representation of divine things; namely, when the soul was surrounded by such a great flash of majesty that, in its union with the body, it was unequal to such heavenly splendor. From this it happened that the body, lacking in strength—indeed, as if dead—lay without movement or sensation. We have an example of this in *Daniel 10:8-9* and *Revelation 1:17* <note>where the prophets collapse or fall as if dead when encountering a divine vision</note>.

<margin>VII. Sometimes it precedes.</margin>
VII. Sometimes it also preceded that representation, or was joined to the beginning of the representation, so that the mind in that state might lean entirely, without any distraction, toward the contemplation of the thing represented...

<margin>VIII. Paul's notable rapture.</margin>
VIII. But more than one rapture of Paul is recorded: for besides that one which Luke mentions in Acts 22:17, that other one is quite notable which he himself describes with no small gravity of words in 2 Corinthians 12:2, 3, 4. *I knew a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body, I know not; or whether out of the body, I know not: God knows;) such a one caught up to the third heaven. <margin>IX. Who speaks of himself as another, out of modesty.</margin>
IX. I do not think there is anyone who doubts that the Apostle is telling this about himself, even though he writes in the third person and seems to distinguish that man of whom he treats from himself in verse 5. For it is clear to anyone that this is done by the Apostle for the sake of modesty—avoiding as much as possible, and even trembling to speak of, the things that happened to him. But he also recognizes that the event was so great that it almost surpassed the human lot and condition of the servants of God on this earth.

<margin>X. And he doubts whether he was present in celestial things in the body or outside the body.</margin>
X. For he had been caught up into Paradise, even unto the third heaven, with such violence of the seizing Spirit that it was a matter of doubt to him: was he transported into heaven by a purely ecstatic representation, without any change of place, regarding both his body and soul; or was he truly carried away from the earth to the upper seats? And if that happened, did it occur to him with body and soul joined, as a whole <term>subsistent being</term> <note>original Greek: ὑφισάμενον (*hyphistamenon*); a philosophical term referring to the concrete, individual existence of a person</note>, or only as a soul separated for a time from the body? Since the Apostle defines nothing, let us not define it either. Let it suffice to observe that the clarity of this revelation was so great that he seemed to himself to have been present in those heavenly matters.

<margin>XI. Certainly he heard unutterable words.</margin>
XI. Furthermore, while he records none of the things he saw, he places a "fastening" <note>or a "bridle"</note> upon excessive curiosity; yet by telling what he *heard*, at least in general terms, he teaches us about great things. For he relates that he heard <term>unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter</term> <note>original Greek: ἄρρητα ῥήματα, ἅ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι (*arrhēta rhēmata, ha ouk exon anthrōpō lalēsai*)</note>. This sentence has much tormented the interpreters. If these words cannot be spoken, how could they be heard? For that which is heard is surely spoken. Then, if they cannot be spoken, why is it added that it is not lawful for them to be spoken by a man? For it would be in vain to forbid the reporting of things that cannot be said. Here, learned men flee to scholarly subtleties. For me, simplicity is pleasing. I do not think it necessary here

# ON ECSTASY.

...to be a confession of tautology <note>original: "ταυτολογίας"; meaning a needless repetition of the same idea.</note>. This can be avoided in two ways. Words are called unutterable <note>original: "ἄῤῥητα"</note> in respect to the one who had heard them. For to the one who was speaking, they were certainly utterable <note>original: "ῥητά"</note>. But he who had heard them calls them unutterable to himself, not because they could not be repeated at all, but because they possessed a greater power and significance than human speech could suffice to fully explain. He adds: *which it is not lawful for a man to speak*, namely in familiar conversation among men dwelling on earth; partly lest he detract from the majesty of such things through the humility of his own speech, and partly because it is fitting for those words to be heard in Paradise alone, as they are reserved for the age to come.

<margin>XII. Things too great for a mere human to be permitted to speak.</margin>
XII. However, I do not believe we should dismiss the interpretation of the most illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian who emphasized the historical unfolding of God's covenants.</note>: by which not only is every appearance of tautology removed, but great emphasis is added to the Apostolic discourse. He thinks that this part of the passage, *which it is not lawful for a man to speak*, should be referred to the one who was speaking to Paul: in this sense, that they were words of such great majesty that, being greater than man, they proved God was the author. There are certain words which Angels and Prophets can speak in God’s name. There are others which are so proper to God that they can by no means be transferred to creatures. Paul implies, therefore, that what he heard, he heard from the mouth of the Son of God himself.

<margin>XIII. Why did he not relate them to the Church?</margin>
XIII. But to what purpose did he hear them, if he was not allowed to communicate them to the Church? Some are inclined to answer that he spoke them, as if into the ear, to certain people initiated into a more secret wisdom. Yet that is not clear. It is better that we determine: I. These things were revealed to Paul for his own private consolation against the labors of his ministry, and did not contain anything regarding the common doctrine which it was in the interest of the Church to know. II. This very fact serves the benefit of the Church and the confirmation of our faith: that we hear the Apostle was caught up into Paradise and, having returned from there, became a witness that a place of blessedness exists, where he both saw Christ and heard remarkable and utterly admirable things from his mouth. III. Those things which are done in Paradise are so excellent that they can neither be set forth in human speech, nor can they be grasped by human minds in the darkness of our present age; for which reason we should strive to be admitted to their enjoyment in due time, rather than inquiring into them with a curiosity that will yield no profit. IV. Words are heard from Christ's mouth by which he is proved to be greater than man, God blessed forever.

## CHAPTER V.

# On Dreams.

*I. Dreams are either Natural or Supernatural. II. In the common course of His providence, God teaches many things to men through dreams. III. There are many and trustworthy examples of this matter. <margin>
I. Dreams are either Natural or Supernatural.
</margin>
Furthermore, God deigns to reveal Himself not only to those who are awake, but also to those who are SLEEPING. Concerning this matter, Eliphaz the Temanite speaks magnificently in the manner of the Easterners in Job 4:12-16. There is a very common distinction made so that some dreams are called NATURAL, and others SUPERNATURAL. The nature of our current project <note>The author's stated purpose for this treatise.</note> does not allow us to deal with the former at great length.

<margin>
II. In the common course of His providence, God teaches many things to men through dreams.
</margin>
II. This alone is worth investigating: whether, in the common course of His providence, God teaches mortals about things useful to them through dreams, and consequently, whether a prudent man ought to pay attention to his dreams. It is certainly true—with Scripture, Reason, and Experience conspiring in the same testimony—that *in the multitude of dreams there are vanities* (Ecclesiastes 5:6), and those who teach or learn the rules of <term>Oneirocritice</term> <note>The art or science of dream interpretation, from the Greek "oneiros" (dream) and "kritikos" (judge).</note> weary themselves with useless labor. Nevertheless, the observation of one's dreams is not to be entirely neglected by a man occupied with his affairs. For besides the fact that they can be indicators of both a hidden vice in the soul and of effectively working Divine grace (since the inner parts of the mind never reveal themselves more without pretense than in the silence and solitude of the night; Psalm 17:3), Divine providence also shows itself so wonderful in them that it causes things to come to the minds of dreamers which are especially conducive to Animal <note>Referring to the physical or biological life of the person.</note>, Economic <note>Relating to household management or one's social and financial station.</note>, and Spiritual life; and which, if they are compared with the eventual outcome, are the most brilliant testimonies of the Divine government over all things.

III. Of which matter there are very many [examples]
</margin>
III. All history is full of examples, both ancient and more recent; to turn up one's nose <note>original: "adunco suspendere naso"; a Latin idiom meaning to mock or treat with contempt.</note> at all of these is not po—

I will not waste the reader's time by recounting those things which are known to everyone and encountered everywhere. I prefer to mention a few cases that carry something truly memorable within them; from these, it will be clear how Divine providence plays a holy and wise role in human affairs.

<margin>IV. Peucer.</margin>
IV. Caspar Peucer <note>A famous German physician and reformer (1525–1602), who was the son-in-law of the great theologian Melanchthon.</note>, the celebrated son-in-law of the great Melanchthon, while languishing in the long-term filth of a most harsh imprisonment, seemed to himself in a dream to be attending the funeral of an illustrious woman. He dreamt he held in his own hand the rope by which the bell was pulled, which by chance he broke and threw down, proclaiming the words of <term>Psalm 124:7</term>: *the snare is broken, and we are escaped.* In the same dream, the words of God to Hezekiah from <term>Isaiah 38:5</term> were pressed upon him: *Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days.* The outcome proved both parts of the dream to be true. For a few days later, Anna, the wife of the Elector of Saxony—who had pursued Peucer with hostile hatred—passed away. The prisoner’s liberation followed shortly after her death. From that time, he lived for sixteen more years, enjoying excellent health and being heaped with honor and wealth.

<margin>V. Peiresc.</margin>
V. <term>Gassendi</term> <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher and scientist.</note> relates in his *Life of Peiresc* <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a renowned French humanist and antiquarian.</note> regarding the year 1609, that while on a journey between Montpellier and Nîmes, Peiresc dreamed and was heard to mutter something unusual. For this reason, <term>Rainier</term>, his traveling companion, woke him by asking if anything was the matter. Then Peiresc said, "Oh! What a pleasant and beautiful dream you have shaken me from!" When Rainier asked what it was about, he said, "I was dreaming that I was in Nîmes, and a goldsmith offered me a golden coin of <term>Julius Caesar</term> for the price of four <term>crowns</term> <note>original: "scutatorum," referring to the 'écu' or crown coin.</note>. I was just about to count out the money to him to have it, when you woke me so inconveniently, and both the goldsmith vanished from my sight and the coin from my hands." Afterward, giving no further thought to the dream, he arrived at Nîmes, and while lunch was being prepared, he took a walk through the city. By a truly astounding coincidence, behold, he ran into a goldsmith. When he asked the man if he happened to have anything rare, the man replied that he had a golden Julius Caesar. He asked for how much he would sell it; the man replied for the price of four crowns. He immediately paid that price, and having received the "Julius," he fulfilled his dream with wonderful good fortune. It is worth adding Gassendi’s judgment on this dream.

VI. "It was easy," he said, "for Peiresc to think of Nîmes, where he was going to arrive the following morning. He could have thought of that coin of Caesar, which while awake...

In a dream, he had heard these Greek words: "Avoid the ill-omened house"* <note>original: "Ἄιδι ἐν δυσφραίνῳ τῷ" — likely a phonetic or slightly corrupted transcription of a warning to depart from an unfortunate place.</note>. *Upon waking, he had written down the sound of those words in French letters. That following night, it collapsed. From what principle this dream is to be derived, and to what species it should be referred, I leave to be determined by those who profess a greater skill in these matters than I do. For me, it is enough to admire the provident care of God toward the human race, who instructs even those who are sleeping about their safety in such marvelous ways.*

<margin>VIII. Diabolical dreams.</margin>
VIII. **SUPERNATURAL** dreams are said to be those which have as their author some spirit operating from the outside. These are either **DIABOLICAL** or **DIVINE**. **DIABOLICAL** dreams are those which, though under the guidance of Divine providence, are nevertheless sent by a wicked and deceptive spirit to prophets, or to any other mortals, in order to deceive them. We read of these in Deuteronomy 13:1, Jeremiah 23:27, and 29:8. Among the Gentiles [pagans] there were also certain sacred places where they would spend the night to obtain dreams. Such was the temple of Amphiaraus, Amphilochus, Trophonius, and Aesculapius <note>Ancient Greek sites known for "incubation," where seekers slept in a temple hoping for a prophetic or healing dream from a god or hero.</note>. There, after certain purifications, a <term>cacodemon</term> <note>An evil spirit or demon, as opposed to a 'good' spirit (agathodaemon).</note> would show the sleepers medicines by which the sick might be healed, and would also answer regarding other matters. Frequent examples of these exist among historians, to be sought elsewhere.

# ON DREAMS.

<margin>IX. By what signs are they distinguished from others?</margin>
IX. Let us now discuss only this: by what signs diabolical dreams of this kind can be distinguished from others. Regarding this matter, the following points are generally observed by theologians. **I.** If they signify future events that are contingent <note>Occurring by chance or dependent on free will rather than natural necessity.</note> or depend on free choice, or otherwise depend on more hidden causes, the knowledge of which does not serve any useful purpose so much as a vain display of knowledge. **II.** If, under the appearance of divinity, they lead toward idolatry or superstition. **III.** If foul, filthy, or obscene things are presented to pious and chaste men, things which they abhor with their whole soul. See *Rivet in his Exercises on Genesis, Exercise 124.* <note>André Rivet (1572–1651) was a prominent French Huguenot theologian.</note>

<margin>X. Divine dreams, in great variety.</margin>
X. Divine dreams are those which, outside the common course of Providence, are sent by God to men in a special way for the certain revelation of hidden things. In such cases, sometimes both the *sleep* and the *dream* are from God, as in *Genesis 2:21* and *15:12*. Sometimes the sleep itself was natural, but the *dream* was <term>God-sent</term> <note>original Greek: θεόπεμπτον (*theopempton*)</note>, as in *Genesis 28:11-12*. The images represented in dreams were sometimes *Mute*, such as the cows and the ears of grain in Pharaoh's dream (*Genesis 41*); sometimes *Vocal* (*Genesis 20:3*); and sometimes *Mixed*, as in Jacob’s ladder (*Genesis 28:12*) and in the Macedonian man appearing to Paul (*Acts 16:9*). Occasionally, God chose to teach the sleepers immediately, giving the understanding of the dream along with the dream itself; at other times, he required the labor of another to intervene and explain the misunderstood dream, just as he employed Joseph for Pharaoh. Indeed, there are instances where he even willed the sleeper to be seized by a forgetfulness of the dream, so that he might win greater trust for its interpreter. The history of Nebuchadnezzar and Daniel proves this.

<margin>XI. Whether forgetfulness of his dream seized Nebuchadnezzar? <insert>forgetfulness?</insert></margin>
XI. For the most learned men—L’Empereur, De Dieu, Cocceius, <note>Constantijn L’Empereur, Louis de Dieu, and Johannes Cocceius were famous 17th-century scholars of Oriental languages and theology.</note> and any others—do not win my agreement when they explain the Chaldean <note>The language we now call Aramaic, in which parts of the Book of Daniel are written.</note> words of *Daniel 2:5*, <term>the matter has gone from me</term> <note>original Aramaic: מלתא מני אזדא (*milta minni azda*)</note>, not as a forgetfulness of the dream, but as the proclamation of a judicial sentence. It is as if the King had said: *An edict goes out from me; I so decree, proclaim, and pronounce.* For **I.** just as the word <term>davar</term> <note>original Hebrew: דבר</note> functions for the Hebrews, so does <term>milta</term> <note>original Aramaic: מלתא</note> for the Chaldeans: it signifies not only a "word," but also a "thing," "matter," or "business." And, not to wander too far, in this very passage it denotes the "business"—that is, the King's dream. For thus the Chaldeans say in verse 10: <term>there is no one among mortals on earth who can reveal the king's matter</term> <note>original Aramaic: די מלת מלכא יוכל להחויה</note>. And Daniel similarly, in verse 23: <term>you have made known to us the king's matter</term> <note>original Aramaic: מלת מלכא הודעתנא</note>. In these instances, <term>milta</term> certainly does not mean a royal edict, but the dream itself. **II.** Those same words do not seem to admit that interpretation so easily in verse 8, where, when the Chaldeans ask the King to tell the dream and promise then to provide its interpretation, the King responds: *I know for certain that you are trying to gain time, because you see* <term>that the matter has gone from me.</term> <note>original Aramaic: די אזדא מני מלתא</note>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER V.

...a word from me. To be sure, they repeatedly made the excuse that the king should first provide a recitation of his dream, and that they could not be forced to utter their oracles before then. They pressed this stalling tactic more confidently because they saw that the dream had escaped the king’s memory, and they hoped that in this way they would be freed from an interpretation that was full of danger. The King indignantly exposed the cunning of this plan. Is not this interpretation simpler than that other paraphrase which pleases *Louis de Dieu* <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642) was a prominent Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist known for his work on biblical commentary.</note>: *From your response I understand that you are only doing this to extend the time, because you surely see that death is looming over you from my decree—a death you hope to escape by prolonging the time.* For since the sentence of death had been pronounced no less against those who did not make the dream known than against those who did not interpret it, consideration of the royal decree against those not revealing it would have resulted in a plea for the mitigation of the punishment, due to the <term>impossibility</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀδύνατον (*to adynaton*)</note> of the demand, rather than a procrastination of a matter they were not promising for the future, but were counting <term>among things simply impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς ἁπλῶς ἀδυνάτοις (*en tois haplos adynatois*)</note>. 

III. Add also this: since the King was held by the greatest desire to understand the dream, why—when he utterly despaired of the Chaldeans' recollection of it—did he not eventually tell it himself, in case the Chaldeans might fulfill their promises and offer an interpretation in which the King's mind could find rest? For he preferred to be instructed in the meaning of his dream by any means possible, rather than to cut off every opportunity and hope of interpretation with untimely cruelty.

<margin>XII.</margin>
XII. Two questions deserve to be asked here: I. Why did God wish to reveal Himself in this singular manner at night and to those sleeping, since such a revelation seems obscure, uncertain, and poorly suited to the dignity of the Revealer and the things revealed, as well as to the benefit of the one receiving such a revelation? II. Next, by what characteristics are *Divine* dreams distinguished from *Natural* or *Diabolic* ones?

<margin>XIII. Why did God wish to reveal himself to the sleeping?</margin>
XIII. It is not very difficult to answer the first question. For the ultimate cause of this matter is the Divine will; to investigate its reasons is neither always safe, nor would one succeed by searching. Nevertheless, many things teach that it is wise here, as everywhere. For I. The mind during the nighttime, and in the silence of all things, seems better suited to receiving notions of spiritual things: not disturbed by objects from the outside acting upon it, nor distracted by a variety of other thoughts, nor agitated by the passions of the soul, but exposed in pure stillness to Divine influence. And it has been observed by students of nature that in sleep all objects seem larger, and the mind is more powerfully affected by them. II. Thus is shown the boundless...

### ON DREAMS. 27

[...the extended] <insert>power</insert> of God into the mind of man. We are unable to speak except to one who is awake; God speaks even to the sleeper. Not even the deep sleep of man is an obstacle to the Divinity whenever He wishes to imprint His notions upon the soul. **III.** We are taught that God is mindful of us even when we are mindful neither of God nor of ourselves. **IV.** No time should be withdrawn from God, and even while in bed one should find time for meditation on heavenly things. **V.** God requires a listener who is composed and teachable, not one who is arguing, grumbling, or disputing, but one receiving heavenly revelation without contradiction—just as images steal upon us in sleep. See more on this in *Rivet* <note>André Rivet (1572–1651) was a French Huguenot theologian; the work mentioned is likely his *Exercitationes in Genesin*.</note> in the *Exercise* just praised, and *Spanheim* in *Doubts, Part II, page 467* <note>Friedrich Spanheim (1600–1649) was a Professor of Theology at Leiden.</note>.

<margin>**XIV.** By what signs are Divine dreams distinguished from Natural or Diabolical ones?</margin>

**XIV.** This second question is somewhat more complex—at least for us, to whom such a wealth of extraordinary revelations in dreams has not been granted. It is believable that such clarity was present in these visions, and that such a convincing efficacy of the Holy Spirit was added, that they could not have doubted the matter. For they did not have to wait until the outcome matched the dream so that they might finally infer the Divinity of the dream from the meeting of the two through a series of arguments. Rather, they immediately perceived the presence of the Divinity in their soul and understood themselves to be warned by God. *Genesis 28:16, 17.* Thus, when *Jacob* woke from his sleep, he said: *“Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” Afterwards, moved by reverence, he said: “How awesome is this place! This place is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”* Compare *Job 4:12, 16.* *Augustine*, in his *Confessions, Book VI, Chapter XIII*, writes the following about his mother *Monica*: *“For she said she could discern, by a certain flavor* <note>original Latin: *sapore*. Augustine uses this to describe a spiritual "tasting" or intuitive sense of truth.</note> *which she could not explain in words, the difference between You revealing things and her own soul dreaming.”* Even *Pharaoh* and *Nebuchadnezzar* themselves seem to have perceived something extraordinary and Divine in their dreams, since they sought their interpretation with such great consternation and anxiety of mind.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER VI.

*I. 9. X. and Zechariah 2:3. XI. Which, however, does not provide a solid proof to the conscience. XII. XIII. Daniel 10:5 is more diligently examined. XIV. The name of the Lord could have been attributed by Zechariah to a created Angel. XV. It is not clear from the phrasing of Holy Scripture that the Holy Lord is being spoken of by Zechariah.*

<margin>I. Revelation was frequently made through Angels.</margin>
So far we have spoken about those types of revelation which occurred immediately <note>That is, directly from God without an intermediary.</note> from God to men; but others also exist which were brought to them **THROUGH THE INTERVENTION OF ANGELS**. This occurred whether the angels brought the entire message themselves, or whether God used their labor to present certain representations, which were made either to those who were awake or those who were asleep. Examples of these things are encountered everywhere and are very well known.

<margin>II. Specifically through Gabriel.</margin>
II. Here the *Angel Gabriel* performed a notable service for God, who foretold the future birth of the Messiah and many things pertaining to it, first to Daniel (Daniel 9:21), then also to Zechariah (Luke 1:19), and finally to Mary (Luke 1:26). I cannot agree with Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for "Federal Theology," which organized biblical history through various covenants.</note>, who thinks that *in Daniel 9:21 this name is not proper to a single Angel, but to all the myriads of Saints, from whom one speaks in the name of God to men concerning what is done to glorify God.* For Daniel distinguishes this Angel, marked by the name of Gabriel, from the others, and perceives that he is the same one he had seen before. And the Angel himself pointedly says to Zechariah, *I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God*; adding greater authority to his words by this emphasis, and showing that he is the same one who once revealed those tremendous mysteries to Daniel. Moreover, the name signifies either *Man of God*, according to some; or *the power of God* <note>original: "τὴν δύναμιν Θεοῦ"</note>, according to Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch humanist, diplomat, and theologian.</note> and others; or, as I would prefer, *God is my strength*. And thus this Angelic name contains a profession of a most significant truth: that the power of even the strongest creatures is situated in God, and is dependent upon Him in every way. When certain angels denied this truth because they wished to be their own masters, by that very act they became evil demons. And in this regard, the proud boasting of both ancient and modern Babylon is directly opposed to the Angelic confession. *Babylon considers its own force as its God* <note>original: "Babylon vim suam pro Deo habet."</note> (Habakkuk 1:11). The Angels, however, hold God as their force and virtue.

<margin>III. The Son of God sometimes appeared to the Prophets in the form of an illustrious Angel.</margin>
III. Many things persuade us that not only created Angels, but also the Son of God himself, the Lord of all Angels, sometimes appeared to the Prophets in the form of an illustrious Angel, and made known the secrets of God both through himself and through some ministering Angel.

<header>ON REVELATION THROUGH ANGELS.</header>

<margin>
IV. *As in Daniel 10:5, 6.*
</margin>
IV. Nor do I think we should interpret what appears in Daniel differently. Daniel 10:5, 6: *Lifting up my eyes I saw, and behold, there was a man dressed in linen garments, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz. His body was like sea-green beryl—or, as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian.</note> translates it, sardonyx—and his face like the appearance of lightning, his eyes like burning torches, and his arms and feet like the color of polished brass; moreover, the sound of his words was like the sound of a multitude.* And when Daniel had recounted his own trembling at the majesty of such an illustrious vision, he adds in verse 9: *then I heard the sound of his words*, which were undoubtedly announcing something worthy of such great majesty. Interpreters differ greatly as to which subject these illustrious attributes belong. Some among both the Ancients and Moderns understand it to be some glorious created Angel, Gabriel for instance, or, as *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought natural or historical explanations for biblical events.</note> prefers, Michael. However, this appearance is too magnificent to belong to a created Angel. Not even the Creator and Lord of all Angels presented himself to be seen with more august pomp. Exodus 24:10, Ezekiel 1:26, 27. Everything leads us to the Son of God, whether we look at the clothing, the habit of the body, the sound of the words, or the whole scheme of the apparition, or finally the consternation of the onlooker; all these things, I say, are similar to the apparition of Christ which John records as having happened to him at the beginning of his Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. Learned men have established this parallelism accurately enough: *Alcazar <note>Luis del Alcázar (1554–1613), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note> on the Apocalypse*, *A Lapide <note>Cornelius a Lapide (1567–1637), a Flemish Jesuit renowned for his biblical commentaries.</note> on Daniel*, and at great length *Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading Lutheran orthodox theologian.</note> in his Annotations on Grotius at this place*, bringing forward twelve reasons for this opinion.

<margin>
V. *Where another servant is joined to him.*
</margin>
V. I believe that the angel who touched Daniel with his hand, addressed him, and informed him—and who was likely Gabriel—must be distinguished from this appearing person (Verses 10, 11, 12). I. Because elsewhere two other Angels stood by that Man dressed in linen garments, like attendants to the Lord. Daniel 12:5, 6. II. Because these same tasks are attributed to Gabriel elsewhere. Daniel 8:18 and 9:21. III. Because the hand that strengthened Daniel was not, as is credible, made of bronze <note>original: "ahenea"</note>, such as the one described in verse 6, but rather soft and soothing, just as a human hand is wont to be. IV. Because the form of the one touching Daniel was *after the likeness of the sons of men*, distinct from the more august form of the one who stood opposite Daniel (verse 16). It is true, indeed, that Daniel does not narrate the distinction between the persons seen here with the same accuracy he employs elsewhere; nevertheless, the attributes themselves sufficiently assign the subject to the attentive reader. It is clear that two appeared to Daniel, whom he addresses distinctly by the name of Lord in verse 17: *How then can <term>the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord?</term>* <note>original Hebrew: עבד אדני זה לדבר עם אדני זה (ebed adoni ze l'dabber im adoni ze)</note>

# BOOK I. CHAPTER VI.

...how can I, the servant of this my Lord, speak with that my Lord? <note>Referring to Daniel 10:17.</note> For I believe the words are most conveniently explained in this way, when the pronoun "this" <note>original Hebrew: *zeh* (זה)</note> in both parts of the sentence refers to "my Lord." Previous arguments prove that of these two, one is Christ and the other is an Angel, his minister.

<margin>
VI. A similar example exists in Zechariah 1:8, 9.
</margin>
VI. I believe the same judgment should be made concerning that *Man* who appeared to Zechariah, riding on a red horse and standing among the *myrtle trees* that were in the hollow; behind him were *red, bay*—or, as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> prefers, *crimson*; Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant scholar of biblical animals and geography.</note> says *pale yellow*; and de Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch orientalist.</note> says *tawny*—and *white horses*. This figure is called the *Angel of the Lord*, and he is distinguished from another Angel who speaks to Zechariah. (Chapter 1:8, 9, 11). That *Man* is Christ, who is often designated by that same name, even by our prophet Zechariah in Chapter 6:12. In this scheme of apparition, he is a symbol of the future incarnation <note>original Greek: *ἐσαρκώσεως* (esarkōseōs)</note>. He sits upon a horse to denote the majesty of his lordship, his power, and his readiness to help his people. Compare Revelation 19:11. That horse is *red*, the color of blood, by which is foreshadowed the slaughter of enemies and the cleansing of the Church from sins through calamities. He stands *among the myrtles*, by which the Israelite Church is signified—not so much according to the flesh as according to the spirit—which is always green and always exhales a pleasant fragrance. And indeed, the myrtles are placed *in the deep* (or the hollow), that is, the Israelites in a lowly and afflicted state; he *stands* among them, protecting them by his gracious presence. Those who are *behind* him—the *red, bay, and white horses* with their riders—are ministering Angels, whose work God used in the governing of other nations. The different colors of these horses may designate the various fortunes of those nations: partly adverse, partly joyful, and partly mixed of both. These are like bodyguards and ministers behind the Angel standing among the myrtles, and they give an account of their expeditions to him as their Lord. Since Zechariah did not yet understand these things, he asked what they were; the *Angel speaking to him*—who usually leads him to an understanding of Divine mysteries—responds, *“I will show you what these are.”* But the *Man standing among the myrtles* preempts him; he takes up the explanation which the other Angel had promised, saying, *“These are those whom the Lord has sent to walk to and fro through the earth.”* Thus we have here two Angels instructing Zechariah: one conducts himself as the Lord—the Son of God himself—while to the other is assigned a specific duty, as it were, of speaking with Zechariah and explaining to him the secret meanings of the visions, of which frequent mention occurs in what follows.

<margin>
VII. And Zechariah 2:3, 4.
</margin>
VII. Most clearly, and without any ambiguity, the same thing is taught in Zechariah 2:3, 4: *And behold, as the Angel who was speaking to me went out, another Angel came out to meet him, and said to him, “Run, speak to that young man...”*

### ON REVELATION THROUGH ANGELS.

<margin>VIII. Cocceius thinks the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of an Angel. Daniel 10:5.</margin>
VIII. These matters seem to have been sufficiently explained in the way they are generally accepted among the Orthodox. However, the most celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and his focus on finding the presence of Christ and the Spirit throughout the Old Testament.</note> prepares other thoughts for his readers; he is of the opinion that the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of an Angel and instructed the Prophets. Regarding Daniel 10:5, he explains it as a Divine person who could be "sent," yet is distinct from Michael—the name used in this prophecy for Christ. This person, he argues, is the Holy Spirit. For God testifies everywhere that his works and the works of Christ are also the works of his Spirit; that the Spirit teaches the Prophets; and that he was obtained by Christ and is sent by him. Because the one speaking is distinguished from Michael, and since no ministering angel can claim that he stands alone against the Prince of Persia (that is, the Devil or the Devil's angel) with no helper except Michael, and finally because he indicates he was sent to Daniel, Cocceius concludes that this person is Divine, distinct from the Mediator <note>A title for Christ as the one who stands between God and humanity.</note>, dwelling in and giving life to men, and thus sent to men.

<margin>IX. And Zechariah 1:9.</margin>
IX. He makes similar observations regarding Zechariah 1:9. In the question asked, there is the title *My Lord* <note>original Hebrew: *Adoni* (אדני)</note>. No mention of this person precedes it. It immediately signifies that he was an Angel, distinct from the one who stood among the myrtle trees on the red horse. To him is attributed a specific office: namely, that he spoke to the Prophet. Zechariah calls this Angel his "Lord." We should consider Zechariah as a disciple of Moses and the Prophets, and notice in his wording <note>original Greek: *lexin* (λέξιν)</note> the influence of the Holy Spirit. In Psalm 110:1, David calls Christ his "Lord." What wonder is it if Zechariah calls the Spirit of Christ—who speaks in him and in all the prophets (according to 1 Peter 1:11)—his "Lord"?

<margin>X. Zechariah 2:3.</margin>
X. Again, regarding Zechariah 2:3 (or verse 7 according to the division used by Junius and Cocceius): In this second vision, the "interpreting angel" <note>Literally "the angel who spoke with me."</note> goes out, and another angel comes out to meet him. In this new vision, the interpreting angel again proceeds from heaven, and another angel meets him, dictating the things to be revealed to the prophet. These details are not without mystery. For why so many angels? And what is the meaning of this gathering of angels? It is the Spirit of Christ, stirring the prophets to the second vision, who receives from the Son—who is already preparing all things for his advent <note>original Greek: *parousian* (παρουσίαν), referring to the divine presence or second coming.</note> and thus, as it were, coming out from his holy dwelling—the things he is to announce to the Church through the Prophets.

<margin>XI. Which, however, he does not solidly demonstrate to the conscience.</note>
XI. Truly, these interpretations are very pious and do much to honor the Holy Spirit, whom the entire Orthodox Church worships as a Divine person co-eternal with the Father and the Son. They are also explained too learnedly and probably to be rashly rejected simply because they are new or perhaps not observed in this way by others. However, it is worth asking whether the most learned author has demonstrated them solidly enough to convince the conscience. That is something I cannot bring myself to affirm.

### BOOK 1. CHAPTER VI.

"the servant of this my Lord, to speak with that my Lord?" <note>original Latin: "servus Domini mei hujus, loqui cum Domino meo illo?"</note> For I think the words are most conveniently explained this way, when the pronoun *this* <note>Hebrew: זה (zeh)</note> in both parts of the sentence refers to *my Lord* <note>Hebrew: אדני (adoni)</note>. The preceding arguments prove that one of these two is Christ, and the other is an Angel, his minister.

<margin>VI. A similar instance appears in Zechariah 1:8, 9.</margin>
VI. I believe the same judgment should be made regarding that *Man* who appeared to Zechariah, riding on a red horse and standing among the *myrtle trees* that were in the hollow, *behind whom were red, sorrel*—or as Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian previously mentioned.</note> prefers, crimson; Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar and naturalist.</note>, pale yellow; and de Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch orientalist and theologian.</note>, tawny—*and white horses*; he is called the *Angel of the Lord*, and is distinguished from another Angel who speaks to Zechariah (Chapter 1:8, 9, 11). That *Man* is Christ, who is often designated by the same name, even by our Zechariah in Chapter 6:12. In this scheme of appearance, he is a symbol of his future incarnation <note>original Greek: ἐνσαρκώσεως (ensarkōseōs)</note>. He sits upon a horse to denote the majesty of his dominion, his power, and his readiness to help his people (Compare Revelation 19:11). This horse is *red*, the color of blood, which foreshadows the slaughter of enemies and the cleansing of the Church from sins through calamities. He *stands among the myrtles*, by which the Israelite Church is signified—not so much according to the flesh as according to the spirit—always green and always exhaling a pleasant fragrance. These myrtles are placed in a "hollow" or deep place, meaning the Israelites are in a humble and afflicted state; he *stands* among them, protecting them by his gracious presence. *Those who are behind him, the red, sorrel, and white horses* with their riders, are ministering Angels, whose labor God used in the governance of other nations. Their different colors may designate the various fortunes of those nations: some adverse, some joyful, and some a mixture of both. These are like bodyguards and attendants behind the Angel standing among the myrtles, and they give an account of their expeditions to him as their Lord. When Zechariah did not yet understand these things, he asked what they were; the *Angel speaking to him*—who usually introduces him to the understanding of Divine mysteries—answered, *“I will show you what these are.”* But the *Man standing among the myrtles* anticipates him, and takes up the explanation which the other Angel had promised, saying, *“These are they whom the Lord has sent to walk to and fro through the earth.”* We have here, therefore, two Angels instructing Zechariah: one who conducts himself as the Lord, the Son of God himself; to the other is attributed a certain duty, as it were, of speaking with Zechariah and explaining the hidden meanings of the visions to him, of whom frequent mention occurs in the following passages.

<margin>VII. And Zechariah 2:3, 4.</margin>
VII. This same thing is taught most clearly and without any ambiguity in Zechariah 2:3, 4: *“And behold, as the Angel who talked with me was going out, another Angel came out to meet him, and said to him, ‘Run, speak to this young man...’”*
