# CONCERNING REVELATION THROUGH ANGELS.

<margin>VIII. Cocceius thinks that the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of an Angel. Dan. 10:5.</margin>
VIII. These matters seem to have been explained sufficiently and are generally accepted among the Orthodox <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the established Reformed or Protestant theological consensus of the 17th century.</note>. However, the most celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> provides other thoughts for his readers, as he is of the opinion that the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of an Angel and instructed the Prophets. In Daniel 10:5, he interprets the passage as referring to a Divine person who is able to be "sent," yet is distinct from Michael—who in this prophecy is called Christ—and is therefore the Holy Spirit. For God testifies everywhere that his works and the works of Christ are also the works of his Spirit; that the Spirit teaches the Prophets; and that the Spirit was obtained from Christ and is sent by Him. Because the figure speaking is distinguished from Michael, and because no mere ministering Angel could say that he alone stands against the Prince of Persia (that is, the Devil or an angel of the Devil) and has no helper except Michael, and finally because he indicates he was sent to Daniel, Cocceius concludes that this is a Divine person. This person is distinct from the Mediator <note>A common title for Jesus Christ in his role as the link between God and humanity.</note>, yet dwells within men and gives them life, and is thus sent to men.

<margin>IX. And Zechariah 1:9.</margin>
IX. Similarly, regarding Zechariah 1:9, he observes the following: In the question, the title *my Lord* <note>original Hebrew: אדני (Adonai)</note> is used. No mention of this person precedes it. It immediately signifies that he was an Angel, distinct from the one who stood among the myrtle trees on the red horse: and he attributes to him a certain office, namely, that he spoke to him. He addresses the Angel as his Lord. Let us consider Zechariah as a disciple of Moses and the Prophets, and let us observe in his phrasing the *style* <note>original Greek: λέξιν (lexin)</note> of the Holy Spirit. David, in Psalm 110:1, calls Christ his Lord. What wonder is it then if Zechariah calls the Spirit of Christ—who speaks in him and in all the prophets (1 Peter 1:11)—his Lord?

<margin>X. Zechariah 2:3.</margin>
X. And again regarding Zechariah 2:3—or according to the division of Junius and Cocceius, verse 7: "In this second vision, the interpreting Angel goes out, and another Angel goes out to meet him." In this new vision, the interpreting Angel again comes forth from heaven, and another Angel meets him, dictating what must be revealed to the prophet. These things are not without mystery. For why are there so many Angels? And what is the meaning of this meeting of Angels? It is the Spirit of Christ, stirring for the second vision, who receives from the Son—who is already preparing all things for his *coming* <note>original Greek: παρουσίαν (parousian)</note> and is thus, as it were, coming out from his holy dwelling—those things which he may announce to the Church through the Prophets.

<margin>XI. Which, however, he does not solidly demonstrate to the conscience.</margin>
XI. Truly, these interpretations are very pious and do much to honor the Holy Spirit, whom the whole Orthodox Church venerates as a Divine person co-eternal with the Father and the Son. They are also explained with such great learning and probability that they should not be rashly rejected just because they are new and perhaps not observed in this way by others. Nevertheless, it deserves to be asked: has the most learned author demonstrated these points solidly enough to fully convince the conscience? For my part, I do not venture to affirm that.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>
XII. A more diligent examination of Daniel 10:5.
</margin>

XII. First, let us examine the passages found in Daniel. That most esteemed man <note>Referring again to Johannes Cocceius, the Dutch theologian.</note> acknowledges that the attributes given to the man described in Daniel <note>Daniel 10:5 describes a man clothed in linen with a belt of fine gold.</note> are such that the Book of Revelation says similar things about Christ, repeating and emphasizing several times what John saw in Christ. Therefore, the first thought that might occur to a reader skilled in Revelation, when finding similar descriptions in Daniel, is that these should also be understood as referring to Christ. A reader will be greatly confirmed in this thought if, recalling similar visions, they find that in all of them, there is no need to apply the description to any other Divine person besides Christ. Nor will a reader easily decide to understand the Holy Spirit here until it has been shown that the Spirit has presented Himself elsewhere in a prophetic vision to be seen in the form of some majestic Angel. Indeed, I do not recall such a thing being narrated in the Scriptures. Therefore, there must be powerful reasons to believe that, contrary to the usual custom of the Scriptures, the Holy Spirit is signified by this emblem here, when it is generally acknowledged that Christ is signified by the same or a very similar emblem elsewhere.

<margin>
XIII.
</margin>

XIII. On the contrary, he says, the reasons are immense. What are they, pray tell? He describes a person who *is no less than Divine*. I certainly grant that. But *that same person is distinguished from the Mediator* <note>The "Mediator" refers to Jesus Christ.</note>. That requires proof. It is proven, he says: *because in verse 13, that Angel distinguishes himself from Michael. Moreover, Michael is the Mediator.* I do not wish to deny either point now. But it remains to be proven that the Angel speaking in that verse is the same as the person described in verse 5. We have argued above, with arguments not to be despised, that the case is otherwise. He insists: *but no ministering Angel is able to say that he alone stands against the Prince of the kingdom of the Persians, and has no helper except Michael.* However, I say, that Angel does not say *he stands alone, and has no helper except Michael*; he says, *he stands against the Prince of the Kingdom of the Persians, and Michael came to help him.* And why could not some ministering Angel—take Gabriel, for instance—say that? Cannot such a one be designated by God to oppose the Devil or an angel of the Devil? If helped by Michael, is he not sufficient for frustrating the attempts of the Devil? Indeed, I would dare to say that this speech is more appropriate in the mouth of Gabriel than the Holy Spirit: since it is more fitting for the Mediator to come to the aid of Gabriel than to the aid of the Holy Spirit. From this I conclude there is no reason why we should depart from the accepted interpretation and transfer to the Holy Spirit those things which are said concerning the Son of God.

### CONCERNING REVELATION THROUGH ANGELS.

<margin>
The name of Lord could be attributed by Zechariah to a created Angel.
</margin>
XIV. Now let us consider what that most learned man <note>The author continues to critique Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his federal theology and interpretive methods.</note> noted regarding Zechariah. The weight of his argument consists primarily in this: that Zechariah addresses the interlocutor Angel—who is distinct from the Angel standing among the myrtle trees—by the name of "Lord." Furthermore, one must wonder why he—who otherwise argues so vehemently that the Church of the Old Testament was subject to Angels as if they were gods—now thinks it unbecoming for an Old Testament Prophet to call an Angel his "Lord." For indeed, those who are **so-called gods** are the same as those who are **so-called lords**, just as **there are many gods and many lords** (1 Corinthians 8:5). <note>Original Greek: λεγόμενοι Θεοί (legomenoi theoi) and λεγόμενοι κύrico (legomenoi kyrioi).</note> Secondly, the address "Lord" is a matter of common courtesy and was used in civil practice toward all those who displayed some mark of dignity; especially toward those who were considered teachers of the truth. Thus John in the Apocalypse, when one of the elders asked him, "Who are these clothed in white robes, and where did they come from?" responds, ***Sir [Lord], you know.*** (Revelation 7:13-14). If it was not unworthy of John to call one of the elders "Lord," why is it unworthy of Zechariah to give that name to one of the Angels? Add to this that, beyond controversy, a created Angel is addressed by this same title of honor in Acts 10:3-4. Where Cornelius, clearly seeing an Angel of God entering in a vision and saying to him, "Cornelius," gazed at him with fear and said, ***What is it, Lord?***

<margin>
From the phrasing of the Holy Scriptures, it is not clear that the Holy Spirit is called "Lord" by Zechariah.
</margin>
XV. But let us consider, says that most illustrious man, that Zechariah was a disciple of Moses and the Prophets, and let us observe the **diction** <note>Original Greek: λέξιν (lexin), meaning wording or style of speech.</note> of the Holy Spirit in his phrasing. Quite right, I say. But what is the diction of the Holy Spirit? David calls his "Lord" Christ. <note>A reference to Psalm 110:1, "The Lord said to my Lord."</note> Excellent. Therefore, the one whom Zechariah calls Lord is the Holy Spirit. This does not follow. At least, he says, it is not surprising if Zechariah calls the Spirit of Christ speaking within him "Lord." I admit it. But the question is: can this be proven from this passage by that line of reasoning? He who has learned from elsewhere that the Holy Spirit is eternal God with the Father and the Son cannot doubt that He is worthy to be addressed by the name of Lord. But what is being disputed now is whether, because Zechariah calls a certain Angel "Lord" and distinguishes him from Christ, it follows from this that the Angel is the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, is this **diction** <note>Original Greek: λέξις (lexis).</note> common in Moses and the Prophets, that the person of the Holy Spirit is called distinctly and by name first "Angel" and then "Lord"? I would be grateful if some examples of both ways of speaking were provided. Furthermore, what he notes regarding the meeting of Angels can be explained no less conveniently as referring to a ministering Angel, who, for all—

### ON THE PRIVILEGES OF MOSES.

<margin>God [reveals Himself] through vision and symbolic dreams.</margin>
...is understood: in the same way that God revealed himself to Ezekiel through the vision of the chariot and the field of dry bones, or to Jeremiah through the vision of the almond rod and the boiling pot. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a celebrated Jewish statesman and biblical commentator.</note> praises a certain scholar who observes that the word מַרְאָה <note>original: mar’ah</note>, which in the plural is מַרְאוֹת <note>original: mar’ot</note> meaning *mirrors* (Exodus 38:8), is distinct from the word מַרְאֶה <note>original: mar’eh</note>. This distinction teaches that every representation made to the other prophets was merely like an image shown in a mirror, which is: **A.** Only of the exterior, not the interior. **B.** Of certain movements and gestures, but not of a voice. **C.** Less accurate, for smaller and more subtle details are not seen as well in a mirror. **D.** Finally, it is only an image, not the thing itself. Perhaps Paul had this in mind? (1 Corinthians 13:12): <term>We see now as in a mirror, in a riddle, in part. <note>original Greek: Βλέπομεν ἄρτι ἐν ἐσόπτρῳ, ἐν αἰνίγματι, ἐκ μέρους</note></term> Next, God also reveals himself, **II.** To those sleeping, through a dream, presenting various sights, conversations, and actions to the imagination while they are resting at night.

<margin>IV. To Moses, mouth to mouth.</margin>
**IV.** The matter was different in the case of Moses. For, **I.** God speaks to him mouth to mouth. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Hebrew Bible.</note> translate this as <term>presence to presence <note>original Greek: ἐνώπιον ἐνωπίῳ</note></term>. John, in his second letter, verse 12, uses a somewhat more significant phrase: <term>to speak mouth to mouth <note>original Greek: στόμα πρὸς στόμα λαλῆσαι</note></term>. But this phrase seems, at least in this passage, to denote something more than פָּנִים אֶל פָּנִים <note>original Hebrew: panim el panim</note> or *face to face*, which is how God is read to have appeared to Jacob (Genesis 32:30) and to have spoken to the whole of Israel (Deuteronomy 5:4). Therefore, it signifies a familiar conversation, such as that of a friend to a friend, without fear or trembling (Exodus 33:11). Rabbi Menachem notes that there is also a certain difference in the manner of speaking: God addressed Israel *face in face* (Deuteronomy 5:4), but Moses *face to face*.

<margin>V. Through direct sight.</margin>
**V. II.** To him is attributed מַרְאֶה <note>original: mar’eh</note>, a *clear and distinct sight* of the things themselves. This sight: **A.** Is not only of the exterior, but also of the interior. For Moses, who was a faithful servant in the whole house of God, as the Jewish masters observe, had the right of approaching all the chambers, even the most inward. **B.** Is a perception not just of gestures and movements, but also of the voice, which was delivered to him while he was awake, since God spoke with him mouth to mouth. **C.** Through this, he knew all things deeply, unlike the others who, seeing symbols, did not understand everything they saw. **D.** Finally, through this, he looked into the things themselves rather than images, as the following points will also show.

<margin>VI. Although Mar'eh and Mar'ah are not always distinguished.</margin>
**VI.** It must certainly be admitted that this difference in the word is not observed everywhere. For the word מַרְאֶה <note>original: mar’eh</note> is sometimes used to denote enigmatic visions (Exodus 3:3) and is attributed to other prophets, such as Ezekiel (Chapters 11:24 and 43:3) and Daniel (Chapter 11). However, in this case, the matter itself demands that the distinction not be neglected.

**VII. III.** If—

## ON THE PRIVILEGES OF MOSES.

<margin>God reveals himself through symbolic vision and dreams.</margin>
...it is understood: in this way God revealed himself to Ezekiel through the vision of the chariot <note>A reference to the "Merkabah" or divine throne-chariot in Ezekiel 1</note> and the field of dry bones; and to Jeremiah through the vision of an almond rod and a boiling pot. Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and theologian</note> praises a certain scholar who observes that the word *mar'ot* <note>original Hebrew: מַרְאֹת</note>, which in the plural means **mirrors** (*Exodus 38:8*), is distinguished from the word *mar'eh* <note>original Hebrew: מַרְאֶה, meaning a sight or appearance</note> in such a way that we are taught that every representation made to the other Prophets was merely like an image shown in a mirror. This type of vision is: **A.** Only of external things, not internal. **B.** Of certain movements and gestures, not of a voice. **C.** Less accurate, for smaller and more subtle details are not seen as well in a mirror. **D.** Finally, it is only of an image, not of the thing itself. Perhaps Paul had this in mind? *1 Corinthians 13:12*: **"For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, in part."** <note>original Greek: Βλέπομεν ἄρτι δι' ἐσόπτρου, ἐν αἰνίγματι, ἐκ μέρους</note> Furthermore, God also reveals himself **II. To those sleeping**, through a *dream* at night, showing various sights, conversations, and actions to the imagination while they are in a deep slumber.

<margin>IV. To Moses mouth to mouth.</margin>
IV. The matter was different in the case of Moses. For, **1.** God speaks to him mouth to mouth. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translate this as "presence to presence" <note>original Greek: ἐνώπιον ἐνωπίῳ</note>. John, in his second Epistle, verse 12, uses a somewhat more significant phrase: **"to speak mouth to mouth."** <note>original Greek: στόμα πρὸς στόμα λαλῆσαι</note> But it seems that this phrase, at least in this passage, denotes something more than **"face to face"** <note>original Hebrew: פנים אל פנים (panim el panim)</note>, which is how God is read to have appeared to Jacob in *Genesis 32:30*, and how He addressed the whole of Israel in *Deuteronomy 5:4*. Therefore, what is signified is a familiar conversation, such as that of a friend to a friend, without fear or trembling (*Exodus 33:11*). Rabbi Menachem notes that there is also a certain difference in the mode of speaking: God addressed Israel **"face in face"** <note>original Hebrew: פנים בפנים (panim be-panim), Deuteronomy 5:4</note>, but He addressed Moses **"face to face."** <note>original Hebrew: פנים אל פנים (panim el panim)</note>

<margin>V. Through direct sight.</margin>
V. **2.** To him is ascribed *mar'eh* <note>original Hebrew: מַרְאֶה</note>, a **clear sight**, distinct, of the things themselves. This sight: **A.** Is not only of external things, but also of internal things. For Moses, who was a faithful servant in all the house of God, as the Jewish teachers observe, had the right to enter all the chambers, even the most private. **B.** It is a perception not just of gestures and movements, but of the voice, which was delivered to him while he was awake, since God spoke with him mouth to mouth. **C.** By this, he knew all things deeply, unlike the others who, seeing symbols, did not understand everything they saw. **D.** Finally, by this he looked into the things themselves, not just images; as the following points will also show.

<margin>VI. To what extent Mar'eh and Mar'ah are not always distinguished.</margin>
VI. It must certainly be admitted that this difference in the word is not observed everywhere. For the word *mar'eh* <note>original Hebrew: מַרְאֶה</note> is sometimes used to denote enigmatic visions (*Exodus 3:3*) and is attributed to other Prophets: to Ezekiel (*Chapter 11:24; 43:3*) and to Daniel (*Chapter 10*). However, in this case, the matter itself cries out that the distinction must not be ignored.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER VII.

<margin>VII. He contemplates the likeness of Jehovah.</margin>
VII. III. He beholds the likeness of Jehovah, which the Israelites are said not to have seen at Mount Sinai. Deuteronomy 4:12. <term>Temunah</term> <note>Hebrew: תמונה, meaning form, likeness, or representation</note> does not signify here the very essence of God, nor merely the brilliance of Divine Majesty as it will be seen by the blessed <note>Those in heaven</note>—which is neither lawful nor possible to grasp with the eyes in this mortal life. Exodus 33:20, 23. Rather, it refers to a certain exceptional ray of Divine splendor, perhaps shining forth in human form, such as the Apostles witnessed in Christ. John 1:14.

<margin>VIII. No one is his equal in miraculous works.</margin>
VIII. And just as he knew Jehovah in a unique manner, so also he was known, loved, and granted many points of preeminence by Jehovah above all others. Deuteronomy 34:10, 11, 12. No prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses, <term>whom Jehovah knew face to face</term> <note>original Hebrew: אשר ידעו יהוה פנים אל פנים</note>. This is true both in all the signs and wonders that Jehovah sent him to perform in the land of Egypt, etc., and in all the works of a strong hand and all the great and terrible deeds that Moses performed before the eyes of all Israel.

<margin>IX. Moses’s doctrine is the standard for everything to be said in the Church for all time.</margin>
IX. All of these things serve powerfully to commend the ministry of Moses. It is a ministry, I say, whose force was intended to endure through every age of the Church. Hence, not only did God recommend his authority anew through the last of the Prophets, Malachi—Chapter 4:4, *Remember the law of Moses my servant*—but also our Lord Jesus said that if anyone does not listen to Moses, they will not be persuaded even if someone were to rise from the dead. Luke 16:31. And Paul testifies that he was faithful in all the house of God, <term>as a testimony to the things that were to be spoken later</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς μαρτύριον τῶν λαληθησομένων</note>. Hebrews 3:5. Thus, everything spoken in the delivery of the New Testament doctrine must have its testimony in Moses, be examined according to the doctrine of Moses, and be confirmed by it. That saying of Isaiah always holds: Chapter 8:20, *To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.* All those things in the Gospel which are most spiritual are the figurative fulfillment of Moses. and since the Mosaic doctrine is a figure <note>A symbolic representation or "type" of something to come</note>, it contains within itself the testimony of its own fading away; but that glorious fading is itself its most ample confirmation.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER VII.

In his *Theologico-Political Discourse*, Chapter 11, page 26, **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was a Dutch philosopher whose work laid the groundwork for the Enlightenment, though he was often accused of atheism by his contemporaries.</note> contends that Moses believed *God is visible—that is, that this implies no contradiction on the part of the Divine nature.* For otherwise, he says, Moses would never have asked for such a thing. He maintains that God answered Moses according to Moses's own imagination when He said, *no one shall see me and live.* <note>A reference to Exodus 33:20.</note> Spinoza claims that God gave a reason consistent with Moses's own opinion. *For He does not say that this implies a contradiction on the part of nature, as the matter truly stands; but that it cannot happen because of human weakness.* These are the words of Spinoza. As for me, it matters little whom **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a prominent theologian and biblical critic known for his "Sentiments" which challenged traditional views on the authorship of the Pentateuch.</note> means by the "learned men" to whom he says he owes this consideration. For I have no intention of creating ill-will toward anyone by using the names of others. Instead, let us observe that which diminishes such ill-will. He contends, then, that these observations of his not only do not prejudice the authority of the Mosaic Laws—since they come from God and not from Moses—but even go far to confirm it. *For he who is well-persuaded of the simplicity of Moses (which the Latins would call "stolidity" <term>stolidity: a state of being dull, slow-witted, or lacking intelligence</term>) will more easily believe that these laws came from God than one who thinks Moses was capable of devising such laws himself.*

<margin>
XII. But he does an injury to Moses.
</margin>

XII. These points deserve to be weighed with a slightly more accurate examination. On this, I indeed agree with that most learned man: the authority of the Mosaic Laws is not to be judged by the natural talent of Moses. Those things he did as a Prophet are not to be assessed by any personal qualities he possessed, but are generally to be traced back to the revelation with which God favored him. But I confidently declare that a massive injury is done to that great friend and intimate of the supreme deity if he is burdened with the suspicion of such great stolidity without any probable reason. Especially if one is to believe he had not yet shed that stupidity after God had graced him with speech, a mission, and frequent miracles, and had approved his Prophetic ministry to the people. For this is where Le Clerc's arguments lead. If they do not prove this, they prove nothing. If, however, they are true, then the blasphemy of Spinoza will not wander far from the truth when he vomits these foul words with his impure mouth (on page 21): **Prophecy never made prophets wiser, but left them in their own preconceived opinions; and therefore we are not at all bound to believe them regarding speculative matters.** <note>original: PROPHETIAM NUNQUAM PROPHETAS DOCTIORES REDDIDISSE, SED EOS IN SUIS PRÆCONCEPTIS OPINIONIBUS RELIQUISSE...</note>

<margin>
XIII. Educated in the wisdom of the Egyptians from an early age.
</margin>

XIII. Is it probable that a man of noble birth, destined by God to handle the greatest affairs, brought up in the court of a most powerful King with great care and no less hope, and thoroughly taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians—a nation believed at that time to surpass all others in the skill of their intellect; I say, is it probable...

# ON THE PRIVILEGES OF MOSES.

...that he was of such great stupidity and sluggishness as **Clericus** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a theologian who suggested Moses was a "simple" man of his time.</note> seems to perceive in him?

<margin>XIV. And he is praised by this name in the sacred scriptures.</margin>
XIV. **Stephen the Protomartyr** <note>The first Christian martyr, whose speech before the Sanhedrin is recorded in Acts 7.</note> certainly did not judge him so. When he was about to recount the illustrious merits of Moses toward the Israelite people, he praises him primarily by this name: that having been raised by Pharaoh’s daughter as a son, he *was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians* (Acts 7:21–22). He surely would not have said this unless he believed that the arts of the Egyptians—according to the capacity of that age—comprised a great part of natural and civil Philosophy. We must especially note the occasion on which Stephen preached these things about Moses. Namely, certain men from the **Synagogue of the Freedmen** <note>original: "Libertinorum"; a group of formerly enslaved Jews or their descendants.</note> and others had disputed with Stephen and produced false witnesses who said they heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God (Acts 6:11). Against this slander, he offers his **Defense** <note>original: "Apologiam"</note>, in which he shows that he holds the most excellent views regarding Moses. Since he had many things to celebrate about him, he begins with this: that he was *educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.* Hardly could a more illustrious tribute of wisdom be given to any nation than was given to the Egyptians by this speech of Stephen.

<margin>XV. The wisdom of the Egyptians was highly esteemed, according to the capacity of those ages.</margin>
<margin>In *The Dream of Scipio*, Book 1, Chapter XIX. *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter XV. *Dream of Scipio*, Book 1, Chapter XXI.</margin>
XV. Sacred history agrees in 1 Kings 4:30. Where, when praising the incomparable wisdom of **Solomon** with just eulogies, it says that it was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the East, and **ALL THE WISDOM OF THE EGYPTIANS**. Unless that wisdom had been considered quite remarkable at that time, Solomon’s praise would have been diminished by such an absurd comparison. The Egyptians were believed to excel particularly in Natural and Civil wisdom. Regarding natural wisdom, **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Roman writer whose works preserved much classical knowledge.</note> calls the Egyptians the parents of all philosophical disciplines, whom **Plato** followed; he calls Egypt the "Mother of the Arts." Elsewhere, he testifies that the ancestors of the Egyptians were the first of all who dared to scrutinize and measure the heavens, invited by the opportunity of their location, since the sky—with its perpetual serenity—always allowed them to gaze upon it with an unobstructed view. The fame of their civil wisdom is indicated by that threat of God in **Isaiah**, where He declares that He will reduce all that wisdom to madness (Isaiah 19:11): *Indeed, the princes of Zoan <note>original: "Tzohanis"</note> are fools; the counsel of Pharaoh’s wise counselors has become brutish. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise"?* Yet all these things do not prevent that Egyptian wisdom from having been corrupted by a great mixture of magical superstition and foolish curiosity. But this at least is proved: that a man cannot be considered dull or stupid—by the standards of those times—who was taught the wisdom of the Egyptians from his early youth.

XVI. But Paul praises the wisdom of *Moses* on an even firmer foundation, specifically in Divine matters, many years before his mission to Pharaoh, while he discusses him in this manner: *Hebrews 11:24–27. By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Choosing rather to be mistreated along with the people of God than to retain the temporary enjoyment of sin. Accounting the reproach of Christ as greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians; for he looked toward the reward of the prize. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the King: for he remained steadfast, as one who saw him who is invisible.* It is the mark of wisdom to assign a just price to all things, and to have such power over one's own mind that, once that estimation is made, you compose the whole conduct of your life according to it. This *Moses* did when he was grown—that is, at forty years of age. It is the mark of wisdom to know God, and the Church, and the relationship of one to the other. This *Moses* knew. It was a mark of wisdom, and indeed an extraordinary one, to know the Messiah at that time, and to consider the fellowship in the <term>reproach of the Messiah</term> <note>original: "probrum Christi"; the suffering or shame associated with following the promised Savior.</note>. This *Moses* considered. It is the mark of wisdom to have the future reward of the prize so clearly perceived, and so deeply fixed in the mind, that in view of it, one considers the greatest things of his own age as abandoned. This *Moses* did. Finally, it is the mark of wisdom to see the invisible God with the eyes of faith and pious meditations in such a way that you are encouraged by that sight to perform works that are indeed beautiful, but also arduous. Thus *Moses* saw God. These things are surely far removed from that <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "ruditate"; implying a lack of refinement or intellectual simplicity.</note> of which **Clericus** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), the scholar whose views the author is refuting.</note> accuses him.

XVIII. <term>Le Clerc</term> <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Swiss theologian known for his critical approach to the Bible, whom our author is refuting.</note> continues: *Moses himself does not hide his slowness of tongue and his difficulty of speech.* But even if we grant that he was not very powerful in oratory, it does not therefore follow that he was destitute of the understanding of the greatest matters. There is a great difference between a Lawgiver and an Orator. And what, after all, is that eloquence which is especially required in a Lawgiver? Truly, it is not so much a readiness of tongue as the faculty of the mind to explain its own opinion in clear, transparent, and appropriate words. That Moses by no means lacked this is excellently proven by that long speech, most fit for teaching and persuading alike, which one reads he addressed to the Israelite people in the book of Deuteronomy. Nor was he unprepared with the flowers and ornaments of Oratory and Poetry, as is evidenced by those Songs, composed in the most affectionate language and with the most elegant words. Therefore, let the rivals of Moses’s praises cease to go about wearing down and diminishing the faculties of his mind based on a defect of the body, which he himself acknowledged.

### CHAPTER VIII.

## Is the power of prophesying natural to man?

I. *Three questions regarding the faculty of prophecy.* II. *Some argue that it is natural to man.* III. *First, because the memory of the past, which is undoubtedly natural, seems to be equally easy or difficult as the foreknowledge of the future.* IV. *Second, because prophecy also concerns things past and present.* V. *Furthermore, because many people approaching death have prophesied.* VI. *Finally, because the desire to know the future is innate in everyone.*

<margin>
I. Three questions concerning the faculty of prophesying.
</margin>

If we are led by any reverence for Divine revelations, it must not be doubted that God deigns to grant them to whomever He wishes at His own discretion: nor can any suitable cause be assigned as to why this person is more of a prophet than any other, except because it so pleased God. However, this fact does not prevent most learned men from asking: I. *Is the power of prophesying <note>original: "vaticinandi"</note> innate to the minds of men, such that they are no less equipped with some faculty by which they foreknow the future than that by which they remember the past?* II. *If that is not the case, is there at least in the temperament, genius, and character of this man a greater disposition toward prophecy than in that of another?* III. *Finally, could or should the prophets themselves have disposed and prepared themselves to receive the prophetic influence?* Regarding these questions, it will not be out of place to dispute somewhat more diligently.

<margin>
II. Some argue that it is natural to man.
</margin>

II. To begin with the first question: *Ammonius* <note>Ammonius of Athens, a philosopher and teacher of Plutarch.</note> in *Plutarch’s* treatise *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "De oraculis defectis"</note> fights with several arguments to show that the duty of divining, and this faculty by which the soul senses the future, is not foreign to its nature. These arguments were more extensively explained and more closely pressed by *Pierre Petit* <note>Petrus Petitus (1617–1687), a French physician, scholar, and poet.</note>, a Philosopher and Physician of Paris, in *On the Sibyls, Book I, Chapter VIII.*

<margin>
III. First, because memory of the past, which is undoubtedly natural, is seen to be equally easy or difficult as the foreknowledge of the future.
</margin>

III. First indeed, he argues in this way: since it is evident that our soul naturally remembers certain things, it is clear that it can know those things which no longer exist, but once were. Why then can it not also know those things which are not yet, but will be? And what distinction can be imagined regarding things that are equally non-existent? For the fact that we remember past things which no longer exist arises because certain "species" <note>In the context of Aristotelian philosophy, "species" refer to mental images or forms that represent objects in the mind.</note>—or figures of things—naturally present themselves to the mind; from the combination of these, and the application of those combinations to a certain time and sequence with the help of memory, the mind returns to a knowledge of things that were done long ago. These same species, moreover, can likewise serve for looking forward to future things. For it can hardly happen that anything occurs in future ages so unusual that it cannot be expressed through those species which we now hold in the mind—provided the mind knows how to compose those species, so that from them an appropriate prediction and announcement of one thing concerning another is produced, corresponding to the future event. In this, certainly, lies the difficulty and labor of divining the future; but it seems no less difficult to recall what has passed. Indeed, even of these past things, only the species seem to remain separately in the mind, to be compo—

# BOOK I. CHAPTER VIII.

...composition <note>original: "compositio"</note>, however, has long since vanished along with the existence and the perception of the things themselves. Therefore, since the mind, by its own faculty, brings about that composition, there seems to be an equal ease or difficulty in recalling a composition of forms made in past time as in exciting a new one from the phantasms <note>mental images or impressions</note> present in the mind, which might be suitable for the future outcome of things.

<margin>
IV. Secondly, because prophecy also concerns the past and the present.
</margin>

IV. This argument will strike more forcefully if we consider that divination—or, as theologians prefer to say, prophecy—extends no less to the past and the present than to the future.

->- - - For the seer knows all things,<-
->Those which are, which were, and which are drawn to come in the future.<-
<note>original: "Novit namque omnia vates, / Quæ fint, quæ fuerint, quæ mox ventura trahantur." A quote from Virgil’s *Georgics*, 4.392-3, describing the sea-god Proteus.</note>

How then does divination differ from memory regarding the past? Truly, there seems to be no difference in the things themselves, for it is common to all of them that they *were*. This alone is the difference: the seer says more about past and future things than any man, however excellent his memory, when he remembers. Otherwise, that difference is one of degree rather than of kind.

<margin>
V. Furthermore, because many approaching death have prophesied.
</margin>

V. The third reason is drawn from the experience of many who, as they approach death, prophesy; many examples of this are recorded. From this, Plutarch argues as follows: it is not likely that the soul gains some faculties and properties upon its departure from the body which it did not have before. It is much more likely that if it shows some power near death which it did not use before, it had that power as something innate, but obscured and hindered by the infection of the body; it then exerts this power when it begins to be released, and is less weighed down by the burden of the decaying limbs and humors <note>the four fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—once thought to govern human health and temperament</note>.

<margin>
VI. Finally, because the desire to know the future is innate to all.
</margin>

VI. The fourth argument is taken from the desire to know what will happen, which is innate in everyone. Hardly any other desire has attacked minds more vehemently. From this, it can be understood that the knowledge of the future is not naturally beyond the reach of man, but that the appetite of nature can be fulfilled, at least in some; otherwise, it would be in vain, and nature does nothing in vain. I pass over other arguments, as they are hardly, or not at all, worthy of our consideration.

<margin>
VII. But on the contrary, the consensus of the wise objects.
</margin>

VII. However, this opinion, however sharply defended, has already been condemned by the judgment <note>original: "calculis," literally "pebbles" used for voting</note> of almost all the wise; it is contrary to reason and is easily torn away from its foundations. Almost all the wise with one voice claim the foreknowledge of future things for God alone—I mean those things which are not so joined to the present and past that they can be foreseen by the skilled and the prudent, but those which depend on the free will of men or on fortune. > No seer among men living upon the earth

> <note>original: "Μάντις δ' οὐδείς ἐστιν ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων / Ὅστις ἂν εἰδείη Ζηνὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο." A Greek verse followed by the author's Latin translation: "Vates autem nullus est inter homines terræ incolas, / Qui noverit mentem Jovis Ægiochi."</note>

From this it follows that no mortal can foreknow future events of this kind except through Divine revelation. Socrates spoke excellently on this, according to Xenophon in the *Memorabilia, Book I*, near the beginning: he said that those who believe none of these things are divine, but rather that everything depends on human judgment, are mad <note>original: "δαιμονᾶν" (daimonân). Socrates suggests that relying solely on human reason for things that are beyond us is a form of spiritual madness.</note>. He used to say that if anyone refers nothing to the divine power, but instead attributes everything to human planning, they are out of their mind. Furthermore, he said it was necessary for men to learn what the gods wished them to know through study; but for those things which are not clear to men, they should try to inquire from the gods through divination. For the gods give signs to those with whom they are pleased.

The philosopher Celsus <note>A 2nd-century critic of Christianity</note>, as quoted by Origen in *Book VII*, emphasizes the same truth: *If by chance a Divine Spirit descending from God foretells divine things, it would be this Spirit proclaiming them; filled with this, men of old announced many good things.* Iamblichus, a philosopher of great renown among his peers, wrote a distinguished work *On the Mysteries*, in which he argues at length that the entire power of prophecy must be attributed to the one God. See, if you please, Huet’s *Demonstratio Evangelica, Axiom IV* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721) was a French bishop and scholar who sought to prove the truths of Christianity through logical axioms.</note>.

<margin>VIII. Supported by reason and experience.</margin>
VIII. But why do we pile up more testimonies, when both reason and experience dictate that there is no faculty in the human mind by which it can, by its own power, foreknow future events that are accidental or dependent on free will? For those events cannot be known in advance except through their causes—and specifically through all causes taken together and working toward a single effect. That joining of causes does not arise from nature, but from the free and secret decree of the Deity. Human deliberations are subject to this decree; it is impossible for anyone to know how these deliberations will turn out except for Him who holds the souls of men in His power. Indeed, the human mind does not even know what it will decide for itself when it is entangled in the deliberations of many, especially after examining reasons that were previously unknown to it. Iamblichus also saw this, arguing: *Therefore, it is impossible to judge certain events when we cannot grasp the convergence of all causes, unless we attain this through Divine inspiration.* Briefly: whoever foresees such a future effect must necessarily foresee it through its causes. <margin>IX. Responses to opposing arguments.</margin>
IX. Now let us turn to the arguments of the opposing view, which we will be able to dispatch briefly with a refutation. **How invalid the first argument is** is clear from the fact that the nature of past things is entirely different from that of future things. For past events have a certain, evident connection that has been proven by the event itself; memory represents this connection no less than it does the simple ideas of past things. This is indeed by a power that is entirely miraculous and astounding—the mechanics of which even the most subtle of Philosophers do not explain—but which every one of us experiences within ourselves. However, future contingent things <note>events that may or may not happen</note>, in respect to our knowledge, have no certain connection; instead, they are the kind of things that present themselves to our minds as being just as likely not to happen as to happen. All their connection lies hidden in the depths of fate, which our mind is not able to penetrate by itself. Experience teaches us that it is not very difficult to recall things that we know were done long ago, and whose connection we understood while they were occurring. But to form a connection for future things from simple ideas—a connection which depends on an impenetrable series of causes—is entirely unattainable <note>original: "ἀνέφικτον" (anepikton), meaning unreachable or beyond human power</note> for the human mind.

X. To the **Second** argument I respond that there is a most evident distinction between the divination of past things and memory. For memory concerns those things which were previously known to us. Divination concerns the unknown. These are distinguished not merely by degree, but by their entire category.

XI. To the **Third** argument: I would not deny that it has often happened that those who were near death have prophesied; however, that does not proceed from the fact that a faculty previously hidden in the soul finally begins to exert its strength. Rather, it is because the soul, then beginning to loosen itself from the chains of the body and being closer to communion with the divine <note>original: "numinis"</note>, is made more capable of those things which befit a pure mind. Among these is the ability to be more immediately influenced by God and the Intelligences <note>often referring to angels or celestial beings in early modern philosophy</note>, and to receive from their gift a new light of knowledge.

# WHETHER THE FACULTY OF PROPHESYING IS NATURAL.

...[knowing] future things, and especially those which are about to happen to oneself, whether it is implanted in the human mind by nature, or indeed whether it arises from a corrupt curiosity and meddlesomeness <note>original: "περιεργίᾳ" (*periergia*), meaning excessive curiosity or meddling in things beyond one's concern</note>; which ought to be corrected by a just submission of the soul under the divine training <note>original: "παιδαγωγίᾳ" (*paidagogia*), referring to the guidance or education provided to a child, here used for God’s discipline of man</note> of God. Indeed, Cicero, in Book II of *On Divination*, elegantly argues, as he usually does, that the knowledge of future things is not even useful for us humans. Specifically:

->*God in His wisdom shrouds the outcome of future time*<-
->*in a dark and misty night.*<-
<note>This poetic fragment is originally from Horace (*Odes* 3.29), quoted here by way of Cicero to illustrate that God intentionally hides the future for our benefit.</note>

The foreknowledge of evils decreed by God hastens our sorrows; it turns future misfortunes into present miseries. Truly, evils often torment us more through fear before they happen than through the senses after they have occurred. For we are accustomed to bear adverse circumstances more patiently than uncertain ones: we would rather fall once than hang in suspense for a long time. *Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.* Matthew 6:34. But let us grant that the desire to know what will happen to oneself is innate to man; it does not follow from this that such a desire can be satisfied by nature. The longing for the highest good and eternal happiness is also innate to the human mind: yet this is reached not by human strength, but by Divine grace. That not every innate desire can be naturally satisfied is manifest from this very example under discussion. It is assumed that the desire to know what will happen to oneself is innate to everyone. And yet, everyone admits that not all people possess that faculty of prophesying by which they might know the future, nor does even the most excellent of men foreknow all future things. Therefore, in some at least, that desire for foreknowledge is without effect, and thus far in vain; it is in vain for everyone regarding those things which they do not attain, however much they may labor to attain them.

<margin>I. A natural disposition for prophecy is believed by some to be: 1. Excellence of character and mind.</margin>
The second question is, whether in one man’s temperament, genius, and character, there is a greater disposition toward prophecy than in another? Here, it pleases some who defend the affirmative side to philosophize at great length. Their philosophical arguments were collected by the scholar we recently praised, *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar known for his work on ancient laws and the Sibylline Oracles</note>, in his work *On the Sibyl, Book 1, Chapter 10*. He considers the FIRST natural opportunity for prophecy to be an outstanding character and a sublimity of mind; those endowed with this are naturally drawn to the contemplation of Divine things, just as iron is drawn to a magnet. However, this propensity exists only in those who possess a naturally "great soul"; specifically, those who have obtained an excellent, lofty, and luminous power of mind. To those whom this has been granted as a singular gift of nature, they are judged to be naturally more fit for prophecy than all others. He admits, of course, that the prophetic light depends entirely upon God, yet in such a way that it is more fitting and consistent for it to be granted to illustrious geniuses. Since no one would deny that such was the character of *Plato*, *Pythagoras*, *Heraclitus*, *Parmenides*, *Anaxagoras*, *Aristotle*, and other wise men, who could deny that such men were naturally more fit for prophecy?

<margin>II. 2. The melancholic temperament.</margin>
II. THE SECOND thing which renders certain men more akin and fit for receiving that Spirit which makes prophets, is that temperament in which a great deal of black bile <term>atra bilis; the physical substance believed in ancient medicine to cause a melancholic personality</term> has accumulated in the body. *Petit* proves this in Chapter 11, not only by the authority and reasoning of *Aristotle*, but also by the examples of *Moses* and *Elijah*. These two stood out as the greatest of all Prophets of the Hebrew nation, yet both are so depicted in the Sacred Scriptures that it appears they were melancholics by temperament and bodily habit. Regarding *Moses*, he gathers this: First, from his love of solitude, by which it is likely he was driven to [tend] Jethro’s [flocks]...

### ON THE NATURAL DISPOSITION TOWARD PROPHECY.

...that so great a man [Moses] would tend the sheep of his father-in-law [Jethro] in the open fields. II. From his <term>slow speech and stammering</term> <note>original: "βραδυγλωσσίᾳ & ἰσχνοφωνίᾳ" (bradyglossia and ischnophonia)</note>, or rather his less fluent speech due to a hesitation of the tongue. The Philosopher <note>This refers to Aristotle, who famously linked melancholy with genius and certain physical defects.</note> notes that this defect is common to those of a melancholic temperament. III. From the fact that he remained unharmed for forty days without food on Mount Sinai. For although Petit easily believes he was sustained by Divine power, he nevertheless thinks it should not be entirely denied that there was something in his body by which he was naturally aided in enduring such a long fast. Indeed, there are some researchers of nature who believe this is a property of the "black humor" <note>Melancholy, or black bile, one of the four "humors" of ancient medicine.</note>: that it can preserve men for a long time without food. So much for *Moses*. He [Elijah] is also shown to have been remarkably melancholic, both from his manners and his <term>solitary wildness</term> <note>original: "θηριωδίαις" (theriodiais), referring to a beast-like preference for the wilderness</note>, since he preferred to live in places remote from human company—namely in unknown mountains and beside torrents—and also from the condition of his body. The author of the books inscribed *Melachim*, that is, *Kingdoms* <note>The Hebrew name for the Books of Kings.</note>—as Petit says, though he should have said *Kings*—depicts him in Chapter 4, Verse 1 (or as we usually number it, 2 Kings 1:8) as follows: *A hairy man and girded with a leather belt around his waist.* Most melancholic people possess such a physical appearance.

<margin>
III. Spinoza contends that prophecies are diversified according to the variety of temperament.
</margin>

III. *Spinoza*, the author of the *Theologico-Political Treatise* <note>The Latin text calls it "Discursus Historico-Politici," likely a variation or error in the title of Baruch Spinoza's 1670 work.</note> (Chapter 11, pages 18–19), proceeds somewhat further. He argues not only that a man's temperament is of great importance for prophecy considered generally, but that prophecies actually vary according to the nature of the specific temperament. *For instance, if a prophet was of a bilious <note>Yellow bile; associated with a choleric or angry temperament.</note> nature, victories, peace, and other things that move men to joy were revealed to him. For such men are often accustomed to imagining similar things. If, on the contrary, he was sad, then wars, punishments, and all manner of evils were revealed to him. And thus, as a prophet was merciful, gentle, angry, or severe, he was to that extent more fit for one type of revelation than another.* He further establishes this from Scripture in the following way. First, he says, it is clear from the case of *Elisha* (2 Kings 3:15), who, in order to prophesy to *Jehoram*, requested a musician; he could not perceive the mind of God until he was delighted by the music of the instrument. Only then did he predict happy things for *Jehoram* and his companions, which could not happen before because he was angry with the King. And those who are angry with someone are fit to imagine evils, but not good things, about them. A little later he continues: *To Ezekiel, who was impatient with anger, the miseries and stubbornness of the Jews were revealed (Ezekiel 3:14). And Jeremiah, being most sorrowful and seized by a great weariness of life, prophesied the calamities of the Jews. So much so that Josiah was unwilling to consult him, but rather a woman contemporary to him [the prophetess Huldah], as she, by her womanly nature, was more fit for God's mercy to be revealed to her (2 Chronicles 34).* But I return to *Petit*.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>III. The heavens and the position of the stars.</margin>
IV. The **third** point asserts that certain influences descend from the heaven itself and the positioning of the stars, which are favorable to the prophetic function we are discussing. <note>The author is likely continuing his summary of Samuel Petit’s *Miscellanea*, Chapter XIII.</note> For although he does not believe any faculty of the human intellect can reach that power which makes a prophet on its own, nevertheless, since God—the author of nature who disposes all things sweetly throughout the universe—willingly adapts His power to human natures and to the other things He employs, it should not seem absurd that He also uses the forces and arrangement of the stars (of which He Himself is the author). He may do this at times—indeed, quite often—to prepare the minds of men for Himself and to illuminate them with prophecy, provided it can be shown by some probable reason that such a power resides in the heavens. Moreover, philosophers of no small reputation <note>referring to respected scholars rather than "low-ranking" ones</note> admit that a person’s character is shaped by the disposition and influence of the stars, and that wondrous properties are born into the natures of remarkable individuals. If these traits come from the stars, why not divination? He does not, however, establish this as the primary cause of prophecy, as *Cardano* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who famously cast a horoscope for Jesus Christ.</note> did, but rather as a preparation, following *Pomponazzi* <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a philosopher who sought naturalistic explanations for miracles.</note>.

<margin>IV. The inhalation of subterranean vapors.</margin>
V. **Fourth**, he believes that the inhalation of subterranean vapors should be added to the other favorable conditions by which the mind is prepared for prophesying. In Chapter XIV, after having recounted a certain miracle from *Leonico Tomeo* <note>Niccolò Leonico Tomeo (1456–1531), a Venetian scholar.</note> that was commonly reported to have happened in recent years in the territory of Verona, not far from Lake Garda <note>original: "Benaci lacu"</note> toward the Alps, regarding the power of a vapor in a temple dedicated to the Blessed Mary in that region, he adds that he recorded these things all the more willingly so that the despisers of literature might cease to categorize as fables the many accounts of this kind found in the books of the Ancients, such as the famous vapor of the Delphic cave. He then explains the reasoning by which dwelling in such caves could dispose the soul toward prophesying. Clearly, the soul seems to be uplifted and nourished in no small measure by solitude, silence, and darkness itself. Added to this is the fact that the "horror" <note>In this context, "horror" refers to a sense of religious awe, dread, or trembling in the presence of the divine.</note> of the caves excites admiration and veneration in the soul. Hence, as *Marsilio Ficino* <note>A celebrated Renaissance philosopher who led the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> philosophizes, when the priests of the *Sibyls* and the *Pythia* withdrew into the cave of *Jupiter* or *Apollo*—where they believed the divinity itself was present—they thought upon the majesty of the god with such a stupor of admiration and veneration that their senses, imagination, and reason immediately suspended their own actions. Then the mind, exposed to the divinity alone—whether that was God or a Spirit <note>original: "Daemon"</note>—sensed the movements from above. Finally, regarding the exhalation of the earth, Petit does not believe this opinion should be entirely rejected, as it posits that a certain power resides in caves that is favorable to prophecy. This is explained by the way the melancholic humor—which is the most earthy, dry, and dense of all the bodily fluids—once heat is applied, renders men frantic and **ecstatic** <note>original: "ἐκστατικὺς" (ekstatikos)</note>, a state which is very close to di-

# ON THE NATURAL DISPOSITION TOWARD PROPHECY.

Aristotle teaches the preparation for <note>The OCR reads *vinandum*, but the context implies *divinandam*, "divining."</note> divining. If that property exists in that humor <note>referring to the "melancholic humor" or black bile discussed on the previous page</note> due to the nature of the earth that dominates it, how much more must we think it exists in the earth itself? These are the thoughts of *Petit*.

<margin>VI. In truth, the excellence of the mind contributes greatly to a more accurate perception of Divine matters.</margin>
VI. Regarding his rather elegant dissertation, let it not be a source of grievance if we also philosophize a bit more at length. No sane person can doubt that the more a mind is endowed with a superior and sublime faculty of understanding, the better suited it is for a more accurate and profound meditation on Divine matters. For that light instilled in the mind, increased by many exercises, extends itself to all objects to which it is applied. However, just as we assume that light to be natural, so it produces only a natural apprehension of Divine things; and that is, if you will, most excellent in proportion to that natural light and its correct use. I add that if it happens that a mind, endowed with such an extraordinary faculty of understanding, is illuminated by the *light of Divine grace*—which comes from the *regenerating and sanctifying Spirit*—it enters much more deeply into the knowledge of the mysteries of God than someone somewhat duller who might obtain the same degree of spiritual illumination. Finally, I do not think it should be denied that if the gift of prophecy is granted to someone who has obtained an excellent mental character and a great power of correct thinking from nature, he will observe Prophetic visions more distinctly, arrange them more orderly in his mind, and explain them more copiously and elegantly. For the gifts of grace, whether ordinary or extraordinary, do not remove, diminish, or hinder the gifts of nature; rather, they elevate them to nobler objects and more sublime operations concerning them. It is also clear from examples that the Spirit of grace, even when operating extraordinarily, adapts itself to the character of its ministers. Thus Isaiah, a man of royal stock and great genius, and Paul, refined by much learning, discuss the mysteries they were taught through prophecy with far more sublimity than Amos or Peter. <note>Amos was a shepherd and Peter a fisherman; the author contrasts their simpler styles with the sophisticated prose of Isaiah and Paul.</note> Yet, whether that sublime character of genius should therefore be called a "disposition" toward prophecy—that is indeed a question worthy of investigation.

<margin>VII. Yet, for this reason, it is not a disposition to prophecy.</margin>
VII. It seems otherwise to me: for since the gift of prophecy depends upon the pure, free, and generous grace of God, and is outside the order of natural things—being of a completely different kind from them—I do not think that any natural sagacity, however great it may be, is a "disposition" toward prophecy. For it would be necessary for it to be so either *from the nature of the thing* or *from some Divine constitution*. Yet it seems that neither can be said. Not from the nature of the thing; for of those things...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

...one natural preparation <note>original: "dispositio"</note> leads to another when things belong to the same category and order, such that one is a certain preparation of the subject for receiving the other. If, however, things differ entirely in their category, one is not a preparation for the other. That cleverness and agility found in certain birds, in monkeys, and in dogs—by which they surpass the slowness of oxen and swine by a long interval—is not a preparation for the human intellect. Nor is any degree of excellence in animal life a preparation for the spiritual life; because these things differ entirely in their category. For the same reason, a natural shrewdness of character <note>original: "sagacitas ingenii"</note> is not a preparation for prophecy; because the former belongs to the category of natural things, while the latter belongs to the category of supernatural things, which depend upon the free will of God. Furthermore, there is no Divine decree that establishes a link between excellence of character and prophecy. For God does not declare this through His word—in which no testimony of this matter is found—nor through His deeds. Those great geniuses of Plato, Pythagoras, Democritus, Aristotle, and their like, although so remarkably "prepared" for prophecy (as Petit believes), were left without that gift, while God deigned to grant it to cowherds and fishermen.

<margin>
VIII. But neither does it hinder prophecy.
</margin>

VIII. Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher whose radical views on the Bible and prophecy were often attacked by contemporary theologians.</note> differs greatly from Petit, but for a much more disgraceful reason.

> *Prophets, he says on p. 15, were not endowed with a more perfect mind, but with a power of more vivid imagination.*

Regarding Solomon, for instance, it is established:

> *that he indeed excelled others in wisdom, but not in the prophetic gift. Even those most prudent men, Heman, Darda, and Calchol, were not prophets; and on the contrary, rustic men, and those outside of all formal education—indeed even lowly women, like Hagar, the handmaid of Abraham—were endowed with the prophetic gift.*

These things are said by that impure man with the goal of depressing all prophecy below the level of the certainty and accuracy of philosophy.

<margin>
IX. What Spinoza calumniates.
</margin>

IX. But he compresses many falsehoods into few words. It is false that there were no prophets endowed with a more perfect mind than most mortals. Let Moses, Nathan, Isaiah, and Daniel—men of the greatest wisdom—serve as examples. It is false that Solomon was not a prophet, for God appeared to him at least twice. It is most false, and to be held as a foul calumny, what he writes elsewhere of Solomon on p. 27:

> *That no one in the Old Testament is found who spoke more according to reason about God than Solomon, who surpassed all of his age in his natural light.*

Thus far, he can be tolerated. But what he adds is blasphemous: **AND THEREFORE HE ALSO THOUGHT HIMSELF ABOVE THE LAW: FOR THE LAW WAS GIVEN ONLY TO THOSE WHO LACK REASON AND THE TEACHINGS OF THE NATURAL UNDERSTANDING.** Did Solo—

(2 Chronicles 27:9, Proverbs 4:4–5). Was the Law given only to those who lack reason and the instructions of natural intellect? Did Moses then lie when he said (Deuteronomy 4:6): *“You shall observe and do them; for this is your wisdom and your prudence before the eyes of the peoples, who, hearing all these statutes, will say, ‘This great nation is truly a wise and prudent people’?”* Did David lie, who, after discussing natural light and the knowledge of God through it in Psalm 19, spoke thus of the law of Jehovah in verses 8 and 9: *“The doctrine of Jehovah is perfect, restoring the soul; the testimony of Jehovah is true, bringing wisdom to the simple. The mandates of Jehovah are right, gladdening the soul; the precept of Jehovah is pure, enlightening the eyes”?* Indeed, he did so to such an extent that he testifies he was made wiser than all his enemies, more intelligent than all his teachers, and finally more prudent than the elders, solely by meditating on the precepts, testimonies, and commands of God (Psalm 119:98, 99, 100). Did Solomon himself lie when he wrote (Proverbs 6:23): *“The commandment is a lamp, and the teaching is light, and the corrections of instruction are the way of life”?* It is also false that Heman was not a prophet. For he is expressly called the “King’s Seer” <note>original: "Videns Regis"</note> (1 Chronicles 25:5).

<margin>
X. The power of the melancholic temperament for deep meditations.
</margin>

X. I easily believe that a temperament of the sort that draws mostly from black bile <term>black bile: in ancient medicine, one of the four humors thought to cause a "melancholic" temperament, often associated with both genius and depression</term>, provided it is not in excess, makes a man fit for deep, fixed, and sublime meditations, as physicists and doctors assert quite consistently. Nor would I deny that so great a force of imagination is sometimes found in melancholic men that they are driven into a natural ecstasy. Excellent and most worthy of reading is the letter of Hippocrates to Philopoemen, in which he discusses Democritus, whom his fellow citizens, the Abderites, thought was insane. In that letter, Hippocrates explains what the study of wisdom can achieve when it happens upon those who are stirred by black bile—a state that Democritus proved himself to be in by many signs. He compares the other desires of the soul to servants and handmaids rioting in a house; wisdom he compares to the mistress, who, as soon as she appears, causes the terrified servants to fall silent. And he shows how great the power of the soul is in such men; so much so that, ordering all disturbances to depart, it devotes itself solely to itself and its meditations. But let us present the words of Hippocrates themselves: *Whenever the mind, being tired by outward cares, wishes to rest—* <note>original Greek: Ὁκόταν ὁ νόος ὑπὸ τῶν ἔξω φροντίδων κοπιόμενος ἀναπαῦσαι θελήσῃ. ### BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

...when the mind releases the body, it quickly changes into a state of stillness. Then, rising upright within itself, it surveys the region of truth all around. In this place, there is no father, no mother, no wife, no children, no brothers, no relatives, no servants, no fortune—absolutely nothing of those things that produce an uproar. All disturbing things are excluded and stand back in fear; they do not even dare to approach out of reverence for those who dwell there. In that region dwell the arts, virtues of every kind, AND GODS, AND SPIRITS, <note>original: *dæmones*—in this classical context, these are "daemons" or guiding spirits rather than evil demons</note> and councils, and deliberations. <note>The author is quoting a famous (though likely apocryphal) letter attributed to Hippocrates regarding the "madness" of the philosopher Democritus, who was found dissecting animals to find the source of melancholy.</note> It is believed that Democritus, through his wisdom, migrated into this region. Consequently, no longer seeing those who are in the city, <note>original: *δοξάζεται μανίης νόσον, διὰ τὸ φιλέρημον*</note> he is thought to suffer from the disease of madness because of his love of solitude.

<margin>XI. Extraordinary symptoms of melancholy.</margin>
XI. The "sons of Physicians" <note>a common idiom for medical scholars</note> prove with many examples that Melancholy, if it suffers from excess, sometimes possesses those symptoms which are regarded as divination and prophecy by those less skilled in natural matters. However, the more experienced trace these to natural causes; once the imbalance of humors is cured, these symptoms cease of their own accord. Meric Casaubon <note>A 17th-century scholar and critic of religious "enthusiasm" or fanaticism</note> has a complete and lengthy chapter on this subject in his learned treatise *Of Enthusiasm*, written in the English language.

<margin>XII. To which supernatural causes sometimes mix themselves.</margin>
XII. But I add this also: it can easily happen that, by Divine permission, Demons abuse such conditions. To play games with men, they increase the imbalance of the humors and disturb the movement of the animal spirits <note><term>animal spirits</term>: In early modern medicine, these were believed to be very thin, subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to transmit sensation and movement.</note> in a disorderly fashion. They cause either foreign languages to be heard from the mouths of the sick, or secrets to be pronounced which, though unknown to men, are known to the spirits themselves. I cannot bring myself to deny that such things have happened, nor to refer them all entirely to natural causes. Indeed, I would not even wish to deny this: if pious men, who practice great intimacy with God, are seized by this disease, the Spirit of grace works in them according to the physical constitution of the person, and much more violent imaginations and emotions are born in the soul. Thus, they believe themselves to be present in the reality of things and speak of them in an almost prophetic manner; they say much about their raptures into Paradise, and about the sweetness of their consolations, of Divine love, and of heavenly glory...

<margin>XIII. Melancholy is not, however, a disposition toward prophecy.</margin>
XIII. All these points do not mean that an abundance of black bile <term>black bile<gloss>original Latin: atræ bilis. This is partly due to the same reasons we just provided regarding natural mental strength and excellence of character; and partly because a joyful, cheerful, and alert mind is certainly no less suited to receiving the prophetic influx than one that is sad and gloomy. It is a well-known Hebrew axiom that the <term>Shekhinah<gloss>Hebrew: שכינה; the Divine Presence or the indwelling of God</gloss></term> or the prophetic spirit does not rest upon a sorrowful soul. <note>This refers to the Jewish tradition that a prophet must be in a state of joy to receive revelation.</note> Certainly, we must not think that David, Heman, Asaph, and similar masters of music and famous singers were melancholic or hypochondriacal. Nor do I fear without cause that profane men—of whom there is a most plentiful crop in this age—will abuse such hypotheses to slander the things said about prophecy as nothing but the imaginations or delusions of melancholic men.

<margin>XIV. It is not clear that Moses was melancholic.</margin>
XIV. In his reasoning, <note>Likely referring to Pierre Petit (1617–1687), a physician and scholar who sought naturalistic explanations for biblical events.</note> Petitus is unjust toward *Moses* and *Elijah*; I am surprised that such improbable arguments fell from a learned man. Did Moses, who was accustomed to courtly life from an early age, prefer the shepherd’s life by some spontaneous inclination of the soul? Was he not forced to flee Egypt and hide to avoid the King’s anger when he settled with Jethro? While he stayed there, he took up tending sheep not from an abundance of black bile, but according to the custom of his ancestors—a life than which almost none is more peaceful. Furthermore, because it is known that certain melancholics were <term>slow-tongued<gloss>original Greek: βραδυγλώσσους (bradyglossous)</gloss></term>, is slowness of speech therefore a fit argument for melancholy? <note>Moses famously described himself as "slow of speech and tongue" in Exodus 4:10.</note> Do not those in whom either blood or phlegm predominates suffer from the same defect due to a more immediate cause? Finally, how absurd it is—not to say profane—to attribute what the sacred history tells of the miraculous forty-day fast to the properties of the "black humor" in any way? Surely it was not necessary for one sustained by Divine power outside the order of nature to be aided by the quality of his natural humors to endure such a long fast.

->## BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.<-

<margin>XV. Just as Elijah was not.</margin>
XV. Of the same [lack of] weight are the arguments by which one might contend that *Elijah* was melancholic. For the fact that he lived in the mountains and beside rushing streams happened partly because of the wickedness of men, whose fury he escaped in this manner, and partly by the command of God, who assigned such a dwelling place to him (1 Kings 17:3; 19:3–4). It is indeed said in 2 Kings 1:8, *ish ba'al se'ar* <note>original Hebrew: איש בעל שער</note>, **“A hairy man, or properly, a master of hair”**; however, interpreters disagree whether this refers to his physical appearance or to his clothes. And this latter view certainly seems somewhat more probable. It is at least certain that the Prophets wore hairy garments for their clothing (Zechariah 13:4). And John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, used the same kind of clothing (Matthew 3:4). Furthermore, the following details point toward this, as he is said to have been girded with a *leather belt*, which naturally matched the garment. But even if we grant Petitus <note>Likely Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a scholar who wrote on ancient customs</note> that Elijah was called a hairy man because of his long hair and shaggy beard, does it follow that he was melancholic just because he looked like that? By that same logic, one could conclude the same for Esau, Samson, Absalom, and who knows who else? It does not please us to be so "perceptive"—not to say reckless and bold—in judging the temperament of those who were so far removed from our own age and society; much less should we do so using such flimsy arguments.

<margin>XVI. Spinoza is refuted.</margin>
XVI. Least of all do we believe *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), the philosopher who argued in his *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus* that prophecy was a product of the imagination rather than pure intellect</note>, who argues that prophecies always varied according to the variety of temperament, such that only sad things were revealed to the sorrowful, only cheerful things to the happy, and threats to the angry. Moses, the mildest of all mortals, thundered the most dire threats and terrifying songs at the people of Israel by the instinct of the Divine Spirit. Isaiah sang of fates equally joyful and sad. That mournful Jeremiah predicted a happy return from the Babylonian captivity no less than the captivity itself. To Daniel, while he was sad and fasting, lying in sackcloth and ashes, Gabriel brought the most joyful news of the Messiah to come with all his benefits. Nor did revelation vary regarding the same subjects according to the temperament with which the seers were endowed; as if Josiah would have preferred to expect a pleasant promise of Divine mercy from a prophetess of a gentle nature <note>The prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22)</note> rather than from Jeremiah, who was of a sorrowful disposition. Had Jeremiah been consulted on the same matter, he would have answered the same as Huldah. Since Divine truth, which is always consistent with itself, cannot reveal contrary things about the same matter. All these [Spinoza's] arguments ultimately lead to this: that all prophecy is considered nothing but a strong imagination, of which the prophets themselves *did not have anything but moral certainty; and consequently, they could sometimes have been deceived*. <note>The term "moral certainty" here is used dismissively to mean a subjective feeling of being right, rather than absolute, objective truth.</note>
