-># ON THE NATURAL DISPOSITION TOWARD PROPHECY.<-

...they were able—indeed, they were truly deceived—and regarding which everyone is allowed to believe only as much as seems consistent with their own reason. We indeed shudder at these things as the very **depths of Satan** <note>original Greek: βάθη τοῦ Σατανᾶ; a reference to Revelation 2:24, often used to describe heretical or prideful "deep" knowledge</note>.

<margin>XVII. The position [of the stars] has very little power over the character of men, and none at all over prophecy.</margin>
XVII. I am fully convinced that the power which descends from the heavens and the position of the stars upon the character and nature of men is extremely slight, and for prophecy, clearly nothing at all. Since experience teaches that those who live under the same celestial influence are endowed with the most diverse characters and entirely contrary manners, how little is it that is owed to the stars? But if one must attend to the position of the stars only at the very moment of birth, what solid reason can be assigned why that momentary constellation, corresponding to the moment of birth, should imprint such power on the soul that another position of the stars, recurring very often, is not enough to change it? If the disposition of temperament, and from there the diversity of manners, depends on the moment of the constellation—since a delay of some time is required before the maternal fetus frees itself from the womb—from what point is the efficacy of the constellation to be calculated? From that moment when the fetus begins to emerge? Or from that when it has come forth whole into the **divine light of day** <note>original Latin: "in dias luminis auras," a classical poetic expression for being born</note>? But if the variation that happens around this point of birth is not so great as to induce a significant change in temperament, how is it that twins, Esau and Jacob, are of such different character and so contrary a nature? But let us grant that some power should not be denied to celestial influence regarding the temperament of man; what does this have to do with prophecy? Its every light is not from the position of the stars, but from the gracious and most free radiation of super-celestial light. *O incredible madness! For not every error is to be called folly,* <note>original: "O delirationem incredibilem! non enim omnis error stultitia dicenda est"</note> exclaims Cicero in this very debate.

<margin>XVIII. The same must be established regarding the inhalation of vapors from caves.</margin>
XVIII. The philosophizing that is established concerning the *inhalation of an underground spirit* <note>original: "subterranei spiritus haustu," referring to the ancient belief that prophets like the Delphic Sibyl inhaled volcanic or earthy gases to enter a trance</note> is ridiculous, and indeed seems to me unworthy of a Christian man. This is true: solitude tends to foster melancholy, and solitary leisure fills the mind with vain phantasms, which at first are wandering, but through frequent recurrence are fixed over time, so that the hermit finally convinces himself of many things which have no foundation except in his own empty imaginations. Nor do I deny that the brain can be affected in strange ways by vapor rising from the earth, especially from caves. But by no appearance can it be inferred from this what Petitus <note>Likely Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a scholar who wrote on ancient customs</note> contends: *that those terrestrial vapors which erupt more copiously from caves than from other places, instill something of a hidden energy into the mind to unravel the complexities of higher thoughts, and even [dispel] the darkness...*

<meta>This page continues the author's investigation into whether prophecy can be explained by natural phenomena. After dismissing astrology on the previous page, he now examines the theory that "earthly vapors" or the atmosphere of specific locations (like caves) can induce prophetic visions, citing and then critiquing the views of classical and Renaissance thinkers like Cardano, Cicero, and Plutarch.</meta>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

...for investigating future events. **Cardano** <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath who wrote extensively on medicine, mathematics, and the occult</note> plays the fool in his accustomed manner when, in *Book III on Dreams, Chapter 15*, after listing many things by which he believes the soul can be brought into that brilliance whereby it becomes capable of images through which future events may be imprinted upon it, he rejects the rest as ineffective and commends the suitability of caves for this purpose in these words: *“But nothing is more certain than caves, in which, due to the breath of the earth, far more diverse forms are observed by those who are awake than by those who dream without them.”*

<margin>
XIX. If such a place ever contributed anything to prophecy, it should be attributed not to nature, but to a deity or some spirit.
</margin>

XIX. Much more prudently, **Cicero** notes that the power of such a place, if it exists at all, is not natural but Divine. *“For what,”* he says in *Book II of On Divination*, *“is so Divine as a breath from the earth moving the mind in such a way that it makes it foresighted of future things, so that it not only perceives them long before, but even declares them in meter and verse? When, however, did that power vanish? Was it after men began to be less credulous?”* And **Dion Cassius** <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin</note>, where he recounts that **Nero**—whether angry at **Apollo** because he had given him unpleasant answers, or being insane in some other way—destroyed the place where the oracles were sought by killing men at the very mouth from which that breath emerged, calls that inspiration THE SACRED SPIRIT <note>original Greek: TO IEPON ΠΝΕΥΜΑ; original Latin: SPIRITUM SACRUM</note>.

<margin>
XX. A beautiful observation by Ammonius.
</margin>

XX. The dissertation of **Ammonius** in **Plutarch’s** work *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* (on my page 435) is quite memorable. *“If indeed,”* he says, *“our souls possess in themselves a power of divining which some quality of the air or wind excites, what is the purpose of the regulations for the Priestesses? And why is an oracle not given unless the whole sacrificial victim trembles from the bottom of its hooves while the liquid is poured over it during the libation, and it is shaken? Unless this happens, they say the oracle does not respond, and they do not bring in the Pythia <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi who delivered the oracles</note>.”* For since they assign most of the cause to a God or a spirit <note>original Greek: Θεῷ μὲν ἢ δαίμονι</note>, it is reasonable for them to do and believe these things; but as you describe it, it is not reasonable. For the vapor, whether the victim trembles or not, being present, would produce the divine inspiration and affect the soul similarly—not only that of the Pythia, but of anyone whose body it touched. Hence it is foolish to use only one woman for the oracles and to cause her such trouble, keeping her chaste and pure throughout her life. *“Yet certainly it is necessary, when they do these things and decree they ought to be done, that they ascribe the cause of them to gods or spirits. The way you were explaining the matter is not probable. For the vapor, whether the victim trembles or not, will strike a divine instinct wherever it is present and affect the mind: and this not only for the Pythia, but if it touches any body whatsoever. So it would be inept to use only one woman for the oracles, and to give her such a task, and to keep her chaste and untouched through her whole life.”*

XXI. But, to confess the truth, if there is any truth concerning inspirations of that kind...

### ON THE NATURAL DISPOSITION FOR PROPHECY.

I would not hesitate to attribute such reported phenomena to the illusions of evil demons,
<margin>XXI. Porphyry judiciously attributes these to evil demons.</margin>
who madden the credulous minds of men with wicked superstition. This was the view not only of the early Christians, but also of the wisest of the Pagans. **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who was often critical of Christianity but respected for his logic</note>, as cited in **Eusebius's** *Preparation for the Gospel*, dwells at length on this. He contends that oracles proceed from **Hecate**, **Serapis**, and similar beings; he allows them to come from no others except evil spirits. Indeed, at the end of his fourth book, he not only counts **Hecate** and **Serapis** among the evil demons but even identifies them as their leaders. In that same work (*Chapter XXI*), **Eusebius** records these words from **Porphyry**: *“Falsifying the appearance of the good gods,”* he says, *“and flatteringly enticing the multitude by inflaming human desires, they wish to be held in the place of the highest Gods themselves. Indeed, he says they were so cunning that they deceived even the wisest of the Greeks, the Poets and Philosophers, whom he admits were the cause of the common people's error. Furthermore, he asserts that the entire art of illusions was forged from their instructions.”* He concludes that: **they wish to be gods, though they are wicked demons. And as their presiding power seems to be the greatest god.** <note>original Greek: ὅπως θεοὶ εἶναι βούλονται, δαίμονες ὄντες φαῦλοι. Καὶ ὡς ἡ προεστῶσα αὐτῶν δύναμις δοκεῖ θεὸς εἶναι ὁ μέγιστος.</note> THESE SAME BEINGS, THOUGH THEY ARE WICKED DEMONS, STRIVE FOR DIVINITY, AND THUS THEIR LEADING POWER IS REGARDED AS THE GREATEST DEITY.

Porphyry pursues all these points in this manner. For this reason, he even denies that a wise man would either solicit demons or consult the prophets as they existed then, adding this sentiment, which is worthy of being preserved in cedar <note>An ancient expression meaning "worthy of immortality," as cedar oil preserved papyrus</note>: **The man who approaches God by himself, as if God were established in his own true inner being, will receive instructions concerning eternal life, having fled there entirely.** <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς δὲ δι’ ἑαυτοῦ προσιὼν τῷ θεῷ, ὡς ἐν τοῖς ἀληθινοῖς αὐτοῦ σπλάγχνοις ἵδρυται, περὶ τῷ αἰωνίῳ βίῳ λήψεται τὰς ὑποθήκας, ὅλως ἐκεῖ συμφεύσας.</note> THAT MAN ALONE, APPROACHING GOD BY HIMSELF—WHO HAS FIXED HIS SEAT WITHIN HIS OWN VESTIGES—AND FLOWING ENTIRELY TOWARD HIM, WILL DRAW FROM THAT SOURCE THE PRECEPTS OF ETERNAL LIFE. (*ibid. Chapter XIX.*) Who would have expected so much good from Porphyry?

<margin>XXII. But most of the histories of this matter are the fabrications of crafty men.</margin>
XXII. I go further, and I confidently profess that I regard most of what is told concerning the power of those vapors, and the oracles resulting from them, not so much as the illusions of demons but as the fabrications of crafty men. I do not take offense at **Petit** <note>likely Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar</note>, even if he translates these things with an odious name as one who hates literature; he considers many such things read in the books of the ancients—including that "breath" of the Delphic cave—to be mere fables. For my part, he may regard them as Sibylline leaves <note>A reference to the Sibyl's prophecies which were written on leaves and easily scattered; here meaning "worthless or legendary nonsense"</note>; provided that by the same effort,

->*He believes that raven Poets, and magpie Poetesses*<-
->*Sing the song of Pegasus.*<-
<note>A satirical quote from the Roman poet Persius, mocking those who claim divine inspiration for their mediocre work</note>

<margin>XXIII. Cicero’s observation.</margin>
XXIII. I do not possess so much credulity in my own house. Let us hear **Cicero**, speaking in the passage we just praised. But now I come to you:

# BOOK I. CHAPTER IX.

> O holy Apollo, who occupies the certain navel of the earth,
> From whence first escaped the savage, wild, and superstitious voice.
<note>original Latin: "O sancte Apollo, qui umbilicum certum terrarum obsides..." These lines are likely from a lost Roman tragedy, famously quoted by Cicero to describe the Delphic Oracle's reputation as the center (navel) of the world.</note>

For **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who was a staunch defender of the reality of divination and oracles.</note> filled an entire volume with such oracles—partly false, in my opinion; partly true by mere chance, as happens very often in any speech; and partly ambiguous and obscure, and so forth. A little further on: **Demosthenes**, who lived nearly 300 years ago, was already saying back then that the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The high priestess at Delphi who delivered the oracles.</note> "Philippized"—that is, she was essentially acting on behalf of Philip. By this, he meant to suggest that she had been bribed by King Philip of Macedon. From this, one may conclude that in other Delphic oracles, too, there was something insincere. But somehow those **SUPERSTITIOUS AND NEARLY FANATICAL PHILOSOPHERS SEEM TO PREFER ANYTHING RATHER THAN ADMITTING THEY ARE FOOLISH.** You would rather believe that something has vanished and gone extinct—which, if it had ever truly been divine, would surely be eternal—than simply refuse to believe things that are unbelievable.

<margin>XXIV. In the Delphic cave, everything was arranged for deception.</margin>
XXIV. And indeed, if there is anything divine in this vapor of the Delphic cavern, what reason can be given why the Delphic seat

> Has fallen silent, since kings feared the future
> And forbade the gods to speak?

As **Lucan** <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD) who wrote the epic poem *Pharsalia* about the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.</note> sang no less elegantly than emphatically in the *Pharsalia, Book V*. And if we look more closely into the Delphic cave, was not everything so arranged that the fraud would be easily transparent to those paying attention? The oracle itself, according to **Strabo**, was a hollow and deep cavern with an entrance that was not very wide. From it was emitted a spirit of divine madness, a <term>prophetic vapor</term> <note>original Greek: $\pi\nu\epsilon\tilde{\upsilon}\mu\alpha$ $\epsilon\nu\theta\upsilon\sigma\iota\alpha\sigma\tau\iota\kappa\acute{o}\nu$ (pneuma enthousiastikon)</note>. And, as **Plutarch** adds, this happened neither often nor at a fixed time, but at uncertain intervals. At those times, the chamber in which the consultants of the oracle were ordered to sit would be filled with a fragrance and a breeze, such as the sweetest and most precious ointments might pour forth from the inner sanctum, as if from a spring. (*On the Obsolescence of Oracles, near the end*). Meanwhile, the **Pythia** would mount the tripod placed over the opening of the cave, after the consultants had been moved away. If, by some singular indulgence, they were allowed to approach closer, their vision was so obstructed by the laurel branches with which the inner sanctums were hedged that no sharpness of the eyes could penetrate there. Add to this the darkness of the place, the incense smoke, and the subterranean chambers which crafty men could enter secretly to breathe whatever they wished into the Pythia’s ears. I shall not even mention now that the Pythia herself, equipped with the proper instruments, could have played her part—such as using a speaking tube to amplify her voice so that it seemed to sound greater than a human's.

<margin>XXV. As we have defendants who confess.</margin>
XXV. But why is there need for a long collection of evidence, when we have defendants who confess? Those very high priests of the shameful rites...

<header>ON THE NATURAL DISPOSITION TOWARD PROPHECY.</header>
<sig>H 3</sig>

...those who, no longer able to deny the truth, eventually confessed in public. **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian church.</note> provided an excellent commentary on this matter in the second chapter of the fourth book of his *Preparation for the Gospel*; from which I would like to select these few points: *“Yet anyone will easily perceive the sum and substance of the whole matter if he adds this one thing to what has been said: that many men of this kind, who displayed a singular divine inspiration—whom those people held as their chief interpreters of sacred rites, theologians, and prophets—not only in the past, but even recently in our own memory, and who were most famous for this divine wisdom, when they were dragged before Roman tribunals and driven by the force of interrogation, <note>original Greek: τὴν πᾶσαν ἐξεφώνησαν πλανὴν ἀνδρῶν ἀπάταις γενέσθαι, καὶ γοητείαν τετεχνασμένην τὸ πᾶν εἶναι ὁμολογήσαντες</note> cried out that the entire thing was a delusion born of the deceits of men, and confessed that the whole business was a sorcery contrived by art. They admitted that this entire genus of fraud was designed to deceive men, and the whole affair was a series of illusions composed with skill. Moreover, these men recorded the entire method of their secret plotting and the whole mockery of their malicious art in the public acts, using the very words with which they had previously exposed the matter.”* Thus, while paying the just penalties for their deadly fraud, they made public whatever was hidden, and they proved by the facts themselves, in the light of day, those things which are brought forth in our discourse.

<margin>XXVI. Conclusion.</margin>
XXVI. Go on then, **Petit**, <note>Likely referring to Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar known for his work on ancient laws and texts.</note> and say that those who refuse to bind their faith to those fictions are "haters of learning." Let us Christians finally be ashamed of what even the more perceptive Pagans were ashamed of; and far be it from us to suggest some subterranean breath or vapor <note>The author is attacking the "pneuma enthusiastikon," the belief that volcanic gases at Delphi caused the prophetic state.</note> endowed with such power that it could somehow make the mind foreknow the future. Let those "dispositions toward prophecy" depart, for having proceeded from such ineffective—or rather, non-existent—causes, they are themselves nothing.

# On the True Preparation for Prophecy.

VIII. The use of sacred music. IX. Prophecy obtained through prayer. X. God usually chose his prophets for himself from these schools. XI. Yet always according to His most free grace.*

Was there then nothing that ought to have been done by pious men, or that was actually done, by which they might [prepare] their minds for the influence of the Divine Spirit—

# BOOK I. CHAPTER X.

...how they would dispose or prepare themselves to receive the divine inspiration? This can be known from no other source but sacred history. By it, we are taught that from the earliest times of the Israelite state, there were schools in which the youth were trained in the knowledge of Divine matters.

<margin>
II. The first of these schools mentioned is at the hill of God: perhaps Gibeah.
</margin>

II. The first mention of these is under Samuel, who is recorded to have addressed Saul in this way in **1 Samuel 10:5**: *Afterward you will come to the hill of God itself, where there are garrisons of the Philistines; and it shall be that when you enter the city, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from that high place with a harp, a tambourine, a flute, and a lyre before them, and they will prophesy.* <note>The original Latin lists these instruments as "nablis, tympano, tibia, & cithara."</note> Which location this "hill of God" refers to is a matter of dispute among scholars. Some guess it was at *Kirjath-Jearim*, while others prefer *Gibeah*. It was called by this name either because the Ark was there at that time, or because there was a "high place" <term>high place: a "bamah" or elevated site used for worship</term> for sacrifices there, or because there was a synagogue and a gathering of young men training themselves in those things pertaining to the worship of the Divine. Yet, *the garrisons of the Philistines* were also there. It is probable that in the conditions of the peace recently struck between the Philistines and the Hebrews, this was included: that in the returned Hebrew cities—specifically in *Gibeah*—the Philistines would maintain a garrison. Thus, the Hebrews frequented these religious exercises in the very midst of the Philistines. This reflects well on both nations. For the Hebrews were not ashamed of their sacred rites, nor did they perform them more sloppily while among their enemies; nor are those Philistine guards recorded to have committed any hostile act against them. In this regard, they were more fair-minded than those who, not content with the name of "Christians," demand to be called *Most Christian*. <note>This is likely a satirical jab at contemporary European monarchs—specifically the Kings of France, who held the title "Most Christian King"—implying they were less tolerant of religious differences than the ancient Philistines.</note>

<margin>
III. The second school was at Naioth in Ramah.
</margin>

III. The second school was at *Naioth in Ramah* (**1 Samuel 19:19**). Now, *Ramah* seems to have been the homeland of Samuel, otherwise called *Ramathaim-Zophim* (**1 Samuel 1:1**). There are those who think the ending of the word represents a dual number, because Ramah was divided into two parts (much like Jerusalem) into an upper and lower city. The word *Zophim* <note>Hebrew: צופים</note> was added, which is translated as *looking toward*—either because the towns looked toward one another, or because it was in a high place (for *Ramah* <note>Hebrew: רמת</note> also signifies a high place), or because a tower was built there from which a view of distant places was visible. Others observe, somewhat more subtly, that *Zophim* denotes *watchmen* or *scouts*, and that prophets were distinguished by that name. For God says to Ezekiel in **Chapter 3:17**: *Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.* <note>Original Hebrew: בן אדם צופה נתתיך לבית ישראל (Ben adam tzopheh netatikha le-veit Yisrael)</note> From this, they infer that this city took its name from *watchmen*, because the *prophets* lived there, being men dedicated to the study of secret writings. Heinsius, in his *Sacred Exercises*, holds it as a certainty that from this the Greeks derived their word *sophoi* <note>Greek: σοφούς, meaning "wise men"</note>, and applied it first to astrologers, who observed the host of heaven and the rising of the stars from sublime and lofty places.

### ON THE TRUE PREPARATION FOR PROPHECY.

<margin>Book I. Chapter II.</margin> To me, all of these theories are nothing but conjectures—learned, if you wish—but I might add that they come from men who find it shameful to admit there is something they do not know. For my part, I think it better *to think so as to be sober-minded* <note>original Greek: φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν, a reference to Romans 12:3</note>. Naioth seems to have been a place near the city of Ramah, and thus belonging to it: a suburban field where the assembly of those prophesying either had their regular residence, or where Samuel was accustomed to retreat with his disciples for the sake of spirit or meditation. The Chaldean translation renders it as a *house of learning* <note>original: <term>Beth Ulpana</term>—an Aramaic term for a school or place of instruction</note>.

<margin>IV. The exercises practiced there.</margin> IV. Whatever the case may be, there was an assembly of prophets there, *and Samuel was standing as head over them* <note>original Hebrew: ושמואל עמד נצב עליהם</note>. Standing, he taught them, directed them, and, as it were, led the choir. The exercise of these prophets consisted primarily in being taught to celebrate God with sacred songs, both with the voice alone and with instruments. This training, however, encompasses many things: 
I. Mastery of sacred Music, both vocal and instrumental. 
II. Knowledge of the subjects for which God is to be celebrated: this pertains to God’s attributes, His virtues, and His works in the creation, sustenance, and governance of the universe. It specifically includes the notable wonders of Divine providence concerning Israel, the entire history of the nation, and finally the principal doctrines of the Israelite faith. For all these things are the subject matter of prophetic hymns. 
III. An ardent love of the soul toward God and sincere devotion, without which all religious music is cold and has nothing with which to commend itself to God. Thus, schools of this kind were nurseries of wisdom, religion, and piety; and from them, as is credible, came those great men—Nathan, Gad, Heman, Jeduthun, Asaph, and many others who outshone the rest in the Israelite church of that age.

<margin>V. The continuation of these schools in the kingdom of Israel.</margin> V. Such colleges, like a certain *remnant* <note>original Greek: λείψανον</note> of the *golden race* <note>original Greek: χρυσέης γένυς—a classical reference to a mythical, purer age of humanity</note>, survived even in the most corrupt times, not only in the kingdom of Judah but also among the ten tribes. The history of Elijah and Elisha proves this (**2 Kings 2:3, 5; 4:38**). Hence, there was such a great abundance of prophets under Ahab that Obadiah alone, while the persecution was raging, hid one hundred prophets, fifty in each cave (**1 Kings 18:4**).

<margin>VI. The Prophets taught all the people on Sabbaths and Festivals.</margin> VI. The prophets were accustomed to give special instruction to their disciples, who are called *sons of the prophets* <note>a Hebrew idiom referring to students or members of the prophetic guild</note>, but on feast days, they also taught the whole people, or at least those of the people who flocked to them. For in this way, that Shunammite woman used to hasten to Elisha, the man of God, on Sabbaths and New Moons (**2 Kings 4:22, 23**).

<margin>VII. Most especially...</margin> VII. By these exercises, the disciples of the wise were prepared to understand the law of God, the duties of piety and virtue, and the entire system of Divine wor-

# BOOK I. CHAPTER X.

<margin>...they prepared their disciples for the prophetic office.</margin>
...of the order of worship, so that they might teach Israel publicly and, with significant authority, sharply rebuke the vices of private citizens, the powerful, and the entire people; thunder the judgments of God; and promise rewards to those who do right. Those who do these things, acting in the prophetic manner, deserve to be called prophets.

<margin>VIII. The use of sacred Music.</margin>
VIII. Nor do I think it should be denied that that sacred *Music* was a way of preparing the mind and elevating it to receive the influx of Divine grace. Whether we believe that by that intense stirring of the passions, which the sweet-sounding instruments excited, the soul was as it were moved from its seat and more easily impelled by God with a prophetic spirit toward even extraordinary physical movements (in which signs of the present deity revealed themselves; which seems to have happened to those whose history is recorded in 1 Samuel 10:10 and 19:20–21). Or if we prefer to believe that the mind was calmed by some sweet music and those passions settled which hinder that gentle influx of the Divine Spirit. For it seems that Elisha requested a minstrel <note>The Latin *psalten* refers to a player of the psaltery or a musician.</note> to play before him for this end, so that he might pacify his mind—which was troubled (holily, indeed, but perhaps more vehemently than was just) by the king's impiety (2 Kings 3:15). Doubtless, he wanted some holy song to be sung before him, mixed with prayers and praises of God, by which the souls of the pious were then soothed and lifted up, becoming more fit to receive prophetic enlightenment, while God was moved to reveal what needed to be done.

<margin>IX. Prophecy obtained through prayer.</margin>
IX. For the prayers of the prophets also had great power here. Hence God Himself was the author of the command to Jeremiah that he should approach Him this way. Jeremiah 33:3: *Call to me, and I will answer you, and tell you great and hidden things that you do not know.* This turned out successfully for Daniel (Daniel 2:18–19).

<margin>X. From these schools God mostly chose His prophets.</margin>
X. Certainly these exercises of piety so pleased God that He granted the knowledge of secrets and of the future to many from that prophetic assembly. For even the "sons of the prophets" <note>The term "sons of the prophets" (<term>filii prophetarum</term>) refers to the students or disciples within these schools, rather than literal offspring.</note> living in Bethel and Jericho knew that Elijah would soon be taken up by Jehovah (2 Kings 2:3, 5). Indeed, it is not unlikely that God mostly selected from this group those whom He deemed worthy of the illustrious gift of prophecy and whom He would use as interpreters of His will among the people. Hence Amos tells of himself as a completely unusual case (Amos 7:14–15): *I was no Prophet*—meaning one of those great men who presided over those colleges, or at least had been in them for a long time—*nor was I the son of a prophet*—educated from childhood in the prophetic schools—*but I was a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit, not leading a prophetic life, [the life] of sacred...*

->CHAPTER XI.<-

## On the Impulse to Prophesy.

I. *The impulse to prophesy.* II. *Effected either by external command,* III. *Or by internal drive.* IV. *Why the prophetic word is called "more certain" by Peter.* V. *What "the day" and "the morning star" mean.* VI. VII. VIII. IX. *Personal resolution.* X. *The efficacy of the Divine act.* XI. *From where does such diversity in prophetic speech arise?* XII. *The wonderful eloquence of some.* XIII. *The wise simplicity of others.* XIV. *Prophets did not bind themselves strictly to specific words.*

<margin>I. The impulse to prophesy.</margin>
Up to this point, we have spoken of the <term>revelation</term> <note>original: "patefactione," referring to the act of making God's mind known</note> by which God indicated His mind to the prophets, and of the <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "dispositione," the mental readiness</note> and preparation of the soul for receiving that revelation. Now let us discuss that <term>Impulse</term> <note>original: "Agitatione," a stirring or driving force</note> by which the seers were driven to hand over to others the things they had learned from God. This impulse consisted partly of an express command and partly of an internal drive.

<margin>II. Effected either by external command.</margin>
II. Commands were very frequently given to the Prophets so that they might faithfully announce the things they had heard from God, without any concealment and without regard for the status of persons, just as they had heard them. Isaiah 58:1: *Cry aloud from the throat, do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet.* Jeremiah 1:17: *Therefore, gird up your loins, so that rising you may speak to them whatever I have commanded you; do not be dismayed by their faces, lest I confound you before them.* Ezekiel 3:17: *Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel; that you may hear a word from my mouth and warn them from me.*

<margin>III. Or by internal impulse.</margin>
III. To such commands, which appear everywhere, was added the internal impulse of the Spirit. Concerning this, Micah 3:8 says: *But truly I am filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord, and with judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin.* This impulse was so powerful...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "prophetic impulse" mentioned at the end of the previous page. The text moves from describing the internal psychological and spiritual pressure felt by prophets like Jeremiah to a detailed exegesis of 2 Peter 1:19 regarding the certainty of the "prophetic word" compared to direct sensory experience.</meta>

...driven, so that the Prophets were unable to resist it. Jeremiah 20:7-8: *“You enticed me, O Lord, and I was enticed; you were stronger than I, and you prevailed. I said, ‘I will not mention him or speak any more in his name,’ but in my heart there is something like a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I am weary from holding it in; I can no longer.”* <note>Jeremiah here describes the "prophetic fire," an irresistible divine urge to speak even when the prophet wishes to remain silent due to the persecution it brings.</note> Jeremiah elegantly compares this to the force felt by a man overcome by wine. Chapter 23:9: *“I am like a drunken man, and like a man whom wine has overcome, because of the Lord, and because of his holy words.”*

<margin>IV. Why is the prophetic word said to be “more certain” by Peter?</margin>
IV. Peter explains this whole matter carefully and copiously in 2 Peter 1:19, 20, 21; I wish to illustrate his words with a brief commentary. *“And we have a more sure prophetic word.”* <note>original Greek: "Kai echomen bebaioteron ton prophētikon logon."</note> He praises the prophetic word—that is, the whole doctrine preached by the men of God in the Church of the Old Testament. We also possess this word, still surviving by the grace of God in the sacred volumes; and indeed, it is “more sure,” or “firm,” as the Syriac translation has it <note>original Syriac: "dasharir"</note>, or “most firm” (using the comparative degree in place of the superlative, as in Acts 25:10, where “better” is used for “best”). Or, as I prefer because it better suits the simplicity of the phrasing, it is simply “firmer.” 

This comparison is made either to previous times (it is now firmer because it has been proven by the words and deeds of the Messiah and the outcome of events); or it refers to the estimation of the Hebrews (to whom the authority of the prophets was more certain than the report of Peter, who was merely recounting a heavenly voice heard by himself and his companions); or finally, it refers to the heavenly voice itself. For although that voice was of Divine—and therefore supreme—credibility <note>original Greek: "axiopistias," meaning the quality of being worthy of belief.</note>, it was done privately and before few witnesses. Thus, it might seem more subject to objections by others than the testimonies of Moses and the other prophets, through whom it had been established for many centuries that God had spoken. Certainly, those received oracles are the ordinary foundation and rule of faith, while those special revelations are extraordinary supports for a weak faith. <note>original Greek: "oligopistias," referring to a state of having little faith.</note> Therefore, in all other matters, one must always look back to those established oracles.

<margin>V. What are the “day” and the “morning star”?</margin>
V. *“To which you do well to pay attention.”* To “pay attention” <note>original Greek: "prosechein"</note> means to pull the mind away from all other things so that we keep it fixed on that one thing alone. Those who do this perform a beautiful, praiseworthy, pleasant, and useful act, worthy of a human and a Christian. *“...as to a lamp shining in a dark place.”* *“For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light.”* (Proverbs 6:23). <note>original Hebrew: "Ner mitzvah v’Torah or"</note> It shines in a squalid, foul place, devoid of all life and joy—the sort of closed-off places where no sunlight penetrates. Such a place is the entire world; such are the minds of all mortals, until they are illuminated by the light of supernatural revelation. *“Until the day dawns, and the morning star rises in your hearts.”* <note>The "morning star" (Greek: "phosphorus") refers to the internal illumination of the Holy Spirit that confirms the truth of the scriptures in the believer's heart.</note>

<meta>This page continues the exegesis of 2 Peter 1:19-20. The previous page discussed how the "prophetic word" is firmer than sensory experience. Here, the author explains the metaphors of the "day" and the "morning star," transitioning into the principle that prophecy does not originate from the prophet’s own private interpretation but from God.</meta>

# CONCERNING THE IMPULSE TO PROPHESY.

...in your <note>The text begins with the Greek word "hymōn" (your), completing the phrase from the previous page: "until the morning star rises in your hearts."</note> hearts. This can be understood as the day of grace, or the day of glory. Night once lay heavy upon both Paganism and Judaism. Through the Gospel, the day has shone upon both (Romans 14:12; Song of Solomon 4:6). This day dawns for the whole Church through the open preaching of the Gospel. The **Morning Star** <note>original Greek: "Phosphorus," literally "light-bringer," referring to the planet Venus as the morning star.</note> arises in the hearts of individuals when they are illuminated by the light of Christ’s grace, leading toward faith, sanctification, and joy. Christ is indeed the **sun**. Here, however, he acts as the **morning star**; driving away the shadows—though not yet all of them—and giving hope for the fullest light. To this very day, the prophetic word leads the faithful (Matthew 11:13). This is not because its use ceases afterward, but because the Gospel doctrine succeeds it, being much more illustrious and splendid—just as the rays of dawn surpass all torches and lamps. It was by this prophetic word that the dullness of dimming eyes had to be sharpened to meet such light.

Yet it is not absurd for us to think also of the day of glory. The promise of this is conceived in these words in Revelation 2:28: *And I will give him the morning star.* Since this is promised to the one who conquers and keeps the works of Christ until the end, it must refer primarily to the glory of the life to come. That is surely the dawn that will break at the daybreak of the blessed resurrection, when the faithful, awakened from the sleep of death, will joyfully behold Christ as the morning star, the herald of an imminent and beginning blessed eternity—a true and perfected day which shall have no evening. Indeed, as long as some squalor and darkness remain, so long do we have use for the prophetic word; until, translated to the light of glory, we shall need no lamp, enjoying most fully the communion of Him who said: *I am the root and the offspring of David, that bright and morning star* (Revelation 22:16).

<margin>VI. The proper interpretation.</margin>
VI. The Apostle confirms this warning of his by adding a notable reason: *knowing this first, that no prophecy of scripture is of one's own interpretation* <note>original Greek: "touto prōton ginōskontes, hoti pasa prophēteia graphēs idias epilyseōs ou ginetai."</note>. These words can be applied both to the first origin of prophecy and to the interpretation of prophecy that already exists. Among the Greek translators of the Old Testament, the word "to interpret" <note>Greek: "Epilyein"</note> corresponds to the Hebrew word *patar* <note>original Hebrew: פתר</note> (Genesis 41:12). Where the Hebrew text says, *to each man according to his dream he interpreted* <note>original Hebrew: "ish ke-halomo patar"</note>, the Septuagint <note>The standard Greek translation of the Old Testament used in the early Church.</note> has: *to the man according to his dream he interpreted* <note>Greek: "andri kata to enypnion autou epelysen"</note>. The subject there is the dream which Joseph explained, and the interpretation is praised because it proceeded not from natural sharpness of mind, but from Divine revelation. An "interpretation" <note>Greek: "epilysis"</note> is a *pithron* <note>Hebrew: פתרון, a solution or interpretation of an enigma</note>; a **private** <note>Greek: "idia"</note> interpretation is the interpretation of our own mind, an exposition of thoughts which we have formed for ourselves. **But truly, no prophecy is of its own interpretation.** Prophets are not interpreters of their own minds, but of the Divine mind. They do not set forth their own inventions or fabrications to men, but rather God's dictates.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XI.

VII. These things have been discussed aptly enough so far; yet they do not yet exhaust the full power of the words. **The opening of the mouth** <note>original Hebrew: *pithron peh*; original Greek: *epilysis tou stomatos*; original Latin: *apertio oris*</note> signifies an instigation to speak. Diviners are mute and keep their mouths closed until the **divine breath** <note>original Latin: *afflatus*, referring to a sudden breeze or breath of inspiration from a deity</note> arrives. Therefore, in the works of **Virgil** <note>A famous Roman poet (70–19 BC)</note>, it is said several times that their **mouths were loosened**. And Lycophron says in his *Cassandra*:
> He loosened the varied mouth of oracles, as before. <note>original Greek: Ἔλυσε χρησμῶν, ὡς πρὶν, αἴολον στόμα.</note>

Thus, prophecy is not of one's "own loosening," in the sense that the prophets spoke by their own natural instinct; rather, God loosened their mouths and impelled them to speak by His Spirit. Hence David says in Psalm 51:15 <note>The text cites verse 17, following a different numbering system</note>: **Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.** <note>original Hebrew: *Adonai saphathai tiphtach*</note> Similarly, Paul asks **that a word might be given to me in the opening of my mouth** (Ephesians 6:19) <note>original Greek: *hina moi dotheiē logos en anoixei tou stomatos*</note>, and Christ said to his disciples: **I will give you a mouth and wisdom** (Luke 21:15) <note>original Greek: *stoma kai sophian*</note>.

VIII. Yet it seems that even this does not satisfy the full force of the phrase. It is worth adding what was observed with equal erudition by **Cameron** <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a Scottish theologian known for his work on biblical interpretation</note>: **Release** <note>original Greek: *Epilysis*</note> can be rendered as **a sending forth**; just as when the barriers—which they call the **starting gates** <note>original Latin: *carceres*, the stalls for horses or runners at the start of a race</note>—are released, the runners burst forth onto the track to run. Indeed, prophets are said to "run" as the messengers and couriers of God. In Jeremiah 23:21 and Ezekiel 13:6-7, it is said: **They ran, and I did not send them.** In Greek, one might say: *They ran, and I did not release them* <note>original Greek: Ἔτρεχον κἀγὼ αὐτοὺς οὐκ ἐπέλυσα</note>. These expositions, which relate to the primary origin of prophecy, are supported by both what precedes and what follows in the text. A little earlier, Peter had praised the supreme firmness of the prophetic word. Now he assigns the reason and cause for this: because the oracles of the prophets are not human inventions, but Divine mandates. He teaches this here **by negation** <note>original Greek: *kat’ arsin*, meaning to explain what something is NOT</note>, and soon after **by assertion** <note>original Greek: *kata thesin*, meaning to explain what something IS</note>.

IX. Nevertheless, I do not object if the words we have explained so far are also applied to the interpretation of prophecy already in existence. For the prophecy of Scripture, which has proceeded from God, ought not to be explained according to human prejudices; nor according to the dictates of some vague philosophy; nor according to the opinion of any single man or assembly who claim a "dictatorship" in religion with sacrilegious daring; nor according to the desires of our flesh so that we might "sail with the wind" <note>An idiom for following one's own convenience or pleasure</note>; nor according to the stubbornness of our own private talent or character. All these things constitute a **private interpretation**. This point was also worthy of being emphasized and fits well with the preceding verses. Peter had praised those who pay attention to the prophetic word. Now he teaches how one must pay attention if we are to rightly recognize the light of truth: namely, that we should not grant anything here to our own individual intellect, nor bring ideas drawn from elsewhere into the Scrip-
ture...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of prophecy, transitioning from the "loosening of the mouth" to the specific way the Holy Spirit moves a prophet to speak. It addresses the internal mechanics of inspiration and the relationship between the Divine author and the human writer's individual style.</meta>

# ON THE IMPULSE TOWARD PROPHESYING.

[...not] let us bring [anything of our own]; rather, let us investigate the mind of God from Scripture itself, through its attentive consideration and comparison, guided by the same Spirit by whose inspiration it was written.

<margin>X. The efficacy of the Divine act.</margin>
X. For prophecy was never brought by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were **moved** <note>original Greek: φερόμενοι (*pheromenoi*); this word suggests being carried along, like a ship driven by the wind</note> by the Holy Spirit. This term is specific to this matter: for among the Greeks, such people are called **God-borne** <note>original Greek: θεοφόρητοι (*theophorētoi*); a term for someone "carried" or "possessed" by a deity</note>. The efficacy of this divine Spirit's act is so great that: I. He inspired the saints with the things they were to say. II. He powerfully impelled them to speak. III. In speaking, He directed them so wisely and certainly that they did not wander even the slightest bit in explaining His mind. To such an extent that the very words they brought forth must be held as the words of the Holy Spirit; and whatever simplicity, or precision, or power is detected in them—indeed, the entire wisdom of the whole discourse—must be reverently received by us as having proceeded from God. For Peter teaches all these things in those words of his: the emphasis of which is diminished by a wicked daring if we think of them as anything less significant.

<margin>XI. From where does such a great diversity of prophetic speech arise?</margin>
XI. Meanwhile, it must be observed that the character and style of speaking used by the **God-borne** prophets is very different, not only according to the subject matter but also according to the diversity of the speakers. **Jeremiah** <note>A prophet known for his "Lamentations" and plain, direct prose</note> narrates the things done in his time in one style, prophesies in another, and in yet another laments the sad fate of his people. And **Isaiah** <note>Often considered the most poetic and sophisticated writer of the Old Testament</note> greatly surpasses all others in the sublimity of his speech. I do not think this should be understood as if the Holy Spirit merely imbued the mind with a clear perception of the things to be explained and equipped the soul with a pious affection so that the prophet might strive to faithfully set forth what was revealed to him by God, while otherwise leaving it to the prophets' own diligence to adorn those things according to each one's own character and genius—as if the matters revealed were from God, but the style and character of the speech were from the prophets. But neither do I think it necessary to say or believe that the Holy Spirit dictated every single word to each of them by a certain **divine possession** <note>original Greek: ἐνθουσιασμῷ (*enthousiasmō*); a state of being "filled with the god" or a trance-like state</note> in such a way that no rational labor of the prophets intervened in meditating upon and arranging them. For from where, then, would come that diversity of style according to each prophet's talent and education? Rather, it is credible that the Holy Spirit acted with rational men in a rational way, such that, by accommodating Himself to the character of each, He employed their natural qualities for His own use and made them serve Him. Indeed, while they spoke in a manner agreeable to their own nature, they were so directed by the Spirit that they did not deflect at all from His intention. And thus Isaiah spoke in one way, and **Ezekiel** <note>An exiled prophet whose writing is marked by complex imagery and priestly concerns</note> in another, yet both spoke from God.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of prophetic style, moving from the general influence of the Spirit to the specific aesthetic qualities of the biblical text. It contrasts the high eloquence of prophets like Isaiah with the "unskilled" simplicity of the Apostles, arguing that both are divinely perfect.</meta>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>XII. The wondrous eloquence of some.</margin>
XII. The eloquence of certain Sacred Writers deserves its own praise; but the natural and unadorned simplicity of others possesses no less dignity; both are to be looked upon with equal reverence and an affection of piety. *Theodorus Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss reformer and linguist</note> elegantly praised the eloquence of Isaiah in his "Treatise on the Method of Learning Hebrew." He says: "A rhythmic composition of speech was not neglected by them, so that beyond common usage they expressed many things for the pleasure of the ears. A sufficiently certain proof of this will be the beautiful, well-composed words and tessellated mosaics <note>original: "emblemata tessellata"; referring to the intricate, interlocking poetic structure</note> of Isaiah in Chapter 25, which so soothe my ears that I do not think the tinkling composition of Isocrates <note>A famous Greek orator known for his polished, rhythmic prose</note> charmed with greater sweetness even the most delicate Greeks. And when I perceive the norms of the Rhetorical art, by which the charm of composition is measured—the allusion and repetition of words, similar endings, and the equality of syllables—I do not think I have Midas’s ears <note>In Greek myth, King Midas was given donkey ears for failing to appreciate the music of Apollo; Bibliander means he is not tone-deaf to the beauty of the text</note> here. For thus the most illustrious Orator in sacred eloquence spoke:* **On this mountain the Lord of Hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines, of rich food full of marrow, of well-refined, aged wines.** <note>original Hebrew: Isaiah 25:6. Bibliander is highlighting the rhythmic and repetitive sounds of the Hebrew text: "mishteh shemanim, mishteh shemarim, shemanim memuchayim, shemarim mezuqqaqim"</note> *I do not think anyone is of such a dull ear, or so adverse to sacred literature, that they would not confess that in this, and in countless others of that kind, the Hebrew language has its own charms and graces.*

<margin>XIII. The wise simplicity of others.</margin>
XIII. Elsewhere, however, in sacred speech, simplicity reigns, nor did Paul deny that he was **unskilled in speech** <note>original Greek: ιδιώτην τῶ λόγῳ (*idiōtēn tō logō*); 2 Corinthians 11:6. This refers to someone who is a "layman" or lacks professional training in Greek rhetoric</note>. This is certainly something Peter and John would have confessed just as much. But we must not allow anyone to abuse such a profession. Nor should we engage in the explanation of sacred literature in such a way as to think that a wise meaning cannot be drawn from it unless the words of the Divine writers are corrected, and an excuse is made for their "awkward" and "unskilled" speech. It is as if we, by our own skill in speaking and reasoning, were able to substitute another discourse by which the mind of the Holy Spirit might be better, more clearly, and more effectively explained than was done by these men of God. In truth, a person only truly progresses in reaching the mind of the Holy Spirit when they discover that the specific meaning they conceive is contained in those exact words so precisely that it could not be expressed more suitably. All our commentary must be directed toward this goal: not that the words of the Lord be exchanged for our own (which we might foolishly think are better), but so that the wisdom of the Divine speech may be made manifest to the conscience. If we do not yet happen to see this, let us confess our own lack of skill and our ignorance of sacred speech. For unless we wish to utterly undermine the Divine authority of the sacred scriptures, it must be firmly held that their words are the words of God. To ascribe a lack of skill to the words of God, as if they required our correction, is sheer profanity and horrendous blasphemy.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of prophetic speech, concluding the argument that the Holy Spirit does not dictate exact syllables but rather the essential meaning. It then transitions into Chapter XII, which focuses on symbolic actions performed by prophets, such as Isaiah’s nakedness and Hosea’s marriage, debating whether these were literal events or allegorical parables.</meta>

ON THE IMPULSE TO PROPHESY.

<margin>XIV. Prophets did not bind themselves strictly to specific words.</margin>
XIV. I would not dare, however, to press what has been said so far as if it were a fixed rule that the prophets always reported the exact same words and the same composition of speech to the people as they had heard them from the mouth of God. Indeed, the opposite seems possible to infer from the example of Moses, who recites the law he heard on Mount Sinai slightly differently in Deuteronomy than it appears written in Exodus. Here, he uses a certain freedom of his own, occasionally transposing words, exchanging some for others with the same meaning, omitting things well known from previous accounts, and adding others by way of interpretation—as will become manifest to those who compare them. Furthermore, when the Apostles and Evangelists relate the speeches of the Lord Jesus, even when they introduce him speaking directly, they do not use the same words the Lord used, because they do not even use the same words among themselves. And when they praise the words of the prophets from the Old Testament, they do not bind themselves to the same exact expressions. This observation is relevant so that we do not become "word-catchers" <note>original: "vocularum aucupes"; a metaphor for someone overly concerned with literal terminology rather than meaning</note>, as if Divine wisdom consisted in syllables. Let this alone be held: that when the prophets spoke under the prompting of the Spirit, they always spoke in the way the Spirit wanted them to speak, and always expressed the mind of the Spirit through their own speech.

---

## CHAPTER XII.

### On the Revelation of the Divine Will through Symbols.

I. *Prophets sometimes revealed the will of God through Symbols.* II. *Sometimes they were also commanded to employ things that seem to conflict with decency.* III. *Isaiah walked about naked.* IV. *That is, with his outer garments removed.* V. *Which was sufficient to serve as a sign.* VI. *Why he walked thus in Judea, when the sign was intended for the Egyptians and Ethiopians.* VII. *Was Hosea commanded to marry a harlot?* VIII. *It is not probable that this occurred in actual reality.* IX. *Nor did he join himself in lawful marriage to a woman who was formerly a fornicatress.* X. *Nor did he merely seem to himself to be joined to a prostitute in a prophetic vision.* XI. *But all these things are a pure parable.* XII. *The force of the prophetic phrasing is not weakened by this explanation.* XIII. *The emblematic names of the woman and the children lead to the same conclusion.* XIV. *Was Ezekiel truly required to lie on one side for so many days?* XV. *Reasons for the negative side.* XVI. *Reasons for the affirmative side.* XVII, XVIII, XIX. *Final Judgment <note>original Greek: 'Επίϰϱισις (Epikrisis); a critical decision or concluding assessment of the arguments</note>.*

->### BOOK I. CHAPTER XII.<-

<margin>I. Prophets sometimes revealed the will of God through Symbols.</margin>
But the Prophets were commanded to reveal the will of God not only through words, but also through certain **SYMBOLIC ACTS**, so that the matter signified might penetrate more deeply into the minds of the spectators. Thus, Jeremiah was commanded to prepare a yoke and straps for himself to place upon his neck and, through messengers staying in Jerusalem, to send them to neighboring kings as a sign of the wooden yoke of servitude to be undergone under the Babylonian Monarch. (Jeremiah 27). And Ezekiel was commanded to sketch the siege of Jerusalem on a brick (Ezekiel 4:1) and to shave off his hair and beard with a barber’s razor, dividing the hair into three equal parts using a scale (Chapter 5). He was also told to prepare for himself the gear of an exile and to move by day in the sight of the Israelites, then to dig a hole for himself through a wall and go out in the dark of night, so that he might serve as a portent to the house of Israel (Chapter 12). He was even told to set out a pot filled with meat and build a pile of bones under it, letting it boil as much as possible until the meat was consumed and the bones were scorched (Chapter 24). Other examples of this kind are found throughout the Prophets, which would be too tedious to dwell upon here.

<margin>II. Sometimes they were commanded to do things that seem to contradict decency.</margin>
II. However, one cannot pass over the fact that the Prophets were sometimes commanded to do things that seem hardly reconcilable with common decency—not to mention the dignity of the prophetic office—yet which were intended to serve as a portent to those to whom they were sent. It may certainly seem strange to see God’s decree to Isaiah in Chapter 20:2: *Go, and loose that sackcloth from your waist, and take off your sandal from your foot.* And Isaiah did so, *walking naked and barefoot.* What? Is it becoming for a respectable man, or worthy of a grave man, or fitting for a prophet, to expose himself naked to the sight of others and to present himself in such a state in the streets, in the market, and in the temple? There are those who argue that this was not done in physical reality, but only in a prophetic vision, such as <note>Maimonides (1138–1204) and Kimchi (1160–1235) were highly influential medieval Jewish scholars whose rationalist interpretations often viewed difficult biblical events as mental visions rather than literal history.</note> *Maimonides* and *Kimchi* among the Hebrews, whom some Christians also follow. But *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher who often argued for the literal historical truth of biblical narratives against purely allegorical readings.</note> argues at length against them, and his reasons seem more compelling.

<margin>III. Isaiah walked about naked.</margin>
III. For, first, Isaiah is not only commanded to strip himself, but is narrated to have actually stripped. Second, God shows this act of Isaiah to the people as a symbol of a future event (verse 3). Then the Lord said, *Just as my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot*, etc. Third, in this matter, he is presented to the people as a <term>מופת</term> <note>Hebrew: "môp̄ēt", meaning a wonder, sign, or miracle intended to demonstrate divine power.</note>, a *portent*—that is, an unusual thing which, by striking the eyes outside of common custom, stirs up wonder in the onlookers.

<margin>IV. That is, with the outer garments removed.</margin>
IV. What then? Did Isaiah truly walk about naked? Indeed, he was naked, for the sacred history explicitly states this. But he was not *entirely* naked in a way that would offend modesty. He took off his shoes; in

...in which there was nothing shameful. For in the East, in Greece, and even in Italy itself, it was customary for noble men to walk in such a manner. *Suetonius* mentions of Nero himself that he frequently walked barefoot. The prophet laid aside his **sackcloth** <note>original: *cilicium*; a garment made of coarse goat hair associated with prophets and mourners</note>, whether you understand this as the rough prophetic cloak he was accustomed to wear, or as a sign of mourning by which he had lamented the dismal state of the Israelite people. Once his outer garments were removed, he went out in public wearing only his inner tunic. Those who do this are said to walk **naked**. Thus, in *Virgil*: *Plow naked, sow naked* <note>original: "Nudus ara, sere nudus"</note>. *Mela* writes that the **Germans** mostly lived naked; *Tacitus* interprets this as having simply cast off their outer clothing. In *Xiphilinus*, regarding the life of the Emperor Elagabalus <note>referred to here as *Pseudantoninus*</note>, when the word *naked* <note>original Greek: γυμνός, *gymnos*</note> was used, it was followed by the phrase *waving a linen garment* <note>original Greek: σινδόνα διασείων, *sindona diaseion*</note>. I interpret 1 Samuel 19:24 in the same spirit, where it is recorded that Saul, having stripped off his clothes in the prophetic manner, acted before Samuel and was naked all that day and night. Likewise, the proud Michal reproached David, who was leaping and dancing before the Lord, for **uncovering himself** by laying aside his royal robes—though he was still dressed in a linen ephod—before the eyes of his servants and maids (2 Samuel 6:14, 20). And in Job, those are blamed who *strip the clothes from the naked* (Job 22:6). Finally, Peter is said to have been **naked** while engaged in fishing (John 21:7).

<margin>
V. Which was sufficient to serve as a portent.
</margin>
V. This kind of laying aside of the outer garment could suffice to signify the nakedness of the Egyptians and Ethiopians, with which they were to be carried away into captivity and exile; for it is right that the sign be less than the reality it signifies. Indeed, not even the captives themselves could expect total nakedness. The experience of our own wars still teaches us that certain individuals may be stripped of all their clothes by a victor. But what entire nation ever felt such harshness of war that all clothing was denied to them for a full three years? Certainly, the Prophet could be a **portent** <note>original Hebrew: מופת, *mofet*; a sign or wonder</note> to the people if he went about dressed quite differently than was his custom. To be seen entirely naked would not have been a portent <term>portent (mofet)<gloss>a miraculous sign or symbolic warning</gloss></term> fitting for prophetic gravity; rather, it would have been a disgrace and an insult to natural modesty. From this, I conclude that nothing was commanded of the Prophet that he could not perform while preserving his decency.

<margin>
VI. Why he walked thus in Judea, when he was meant to be a portent for the Egyptians and Ethiopians.
</margin>
VI. Furthermore, this point remains to be cleared up: since this entire matter concerns the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, why was it necessary for the Prophet to walk naked in **Judea**, where the Egyptians and Ethiopians perhaps never even heard a rumor of it? Why was he not sent instead to Egypt and Ethiopia to be a portent to those for whom he was prefiguring calamities? I answer: while the reality signified did indeed regard those foreign nations, the utility of the sign and the entire prophecy...

<margin>VII. Was Hosea commanded to marry a prostitute?</margin>
VII. There is another reason for that decree by which Jehovah addressed Hosea: 
> "Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom and children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking Jehovah." 

Hosea is read to have obeyed this command. Thus, departing, he took Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, who conceived and bore him a son (Hosea 1:2-3). Here interpreters diverge: some think these events actually happened in reality as they are narrated; others, that they happened to Hosea in a prophetic vision, whether while waking or sleeping, so that it seemed to him he did this by God’s command; others, that none of these things happened, but all have an emblematic and mystical significance. Amid such a variety of opinions, which can each seem valid to their respective authors, I shall explain through certain propositions what I consider to be—if not clearly and undoubtedly true—at least most similar to the truth and highly probable.

<margin>VIII. It is not probable that this happened in actual reality.</margin>
VIII. I. I consider it certain that the Prophet was not commanded to commit fornication with a prostitute, and from her procreate "children of whoredom"—that is, children born outside of his own line or from something other than a true marriage. **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian</note> defends this view, thinking the prophet did it without fault because of a Divine dispensation: just as the Israelites committed "theft" without crime <note>Referring to the Israelites taking the gold and silver of the Egyptians during the Exodus (Exodus 12:35-36)</note>, and Isaiah walked naked, because God commanded it. To me, however, this seems absurd. I. Because fornication is contrary to the most holy nature of God and the primordial law of marriage, and therefore cannot be commanded. The Israelites were not commanded to steal; rather, the property of the Egyptians—owed to the Israelites as wages for their labor—was given to them by God, the Supreme Lord, to be possessed by best right. Regarding Isaiah’s nakedness, I have just argued the matter. II. This would be foreign to prophetic dignity, and nothing would have rendered Hosea more contemptible to the people. III. It would oppose God's purpose, which was to sharply rebuke the people’s unspeakable **idolatry** <term>idolatria: the worship of idols, often compared in the Bible to marital infidelity</term> under the emblem of foul fornication. But how could that appear foul to the people which the Prophet did by God’s command?

<margin>IX. Neither did he join himself in legitimate marriage to a woman who was formerly a fornicator.</margin>
IX. II. I also do not think that Hosea married a woman in legitimate marriage who had previously been a prostitute, but who had turned from that filthiness of life to a sounder mind upon this marriage to the Prophet. I. Because this is explicitly forbidden to priests (Leviticus 21:7). The status of prophets seems to be the same: whether they are considered examples for the people or types of Christ. II. Because it is contrary to the text. For the children born from a wife who is now legitimate, although previously a harlot, [were...]

He is expressly commanded to love a woman who persists in adultery. *“Love a woman who is beloved by a friend and is an adulteress.”* <note>Hosea 3:1</note> III. This contradicts the prophet's purpose. For how can a woman, converted to chastity through a legitimate marriage, represent Israel, which is spiritually committing fornication and has remained obstinate in that fornication until now?

<margin>X. Nor did it seem to him in a prophetic vision that he was joined with a harlot.</margin>

X. III. Those who believe that Hosea was commanded to do this and performed it in a prophetic vision think less absurdly; they suggest it appeared to him that he took a harlot, was joined with her, and received from her "children of harlotry." For other things in prophetic visions—not actually done in reality but recounted to the people—are believed to have been set before them solely as an example. But even this does not win agreement. For the imagination of a thing base in itself is not honorable. Who would believe that God presented the image of a prostitute to the prophet, commanded him to embrace her, and that the prophet—stirred not by the remnants of a sinful nature, but by the Spirit of God—imagined himself mixing with a harlot, and then preached to the people that this had happened to him by God's will? Would this not have given the impious and mockers an occasion for laughter, and provided the pious a cause for offense?

<margin>XI. But all these things are a mere parable.</margin>

XI. IV. It seems most probable that these words contain a mere parable, in this sense: "These people boast that they are my wife and my children; but you, take up my persona and preach that they are as much a wife and children to me as if you took a prostitute from the filthiest brothel along with her bastards <note>original: "spuriis," referring to illegitimate children</note>; or as if a wife you married admitted others to her marriage bed and bore you children of fornication." And he did so; that is, he promptly executed the prophecy commanded to him for the people. Under the parable of a fictional woman, presented with emblematic names <note>Gomer and Diblaim</note>, and children who likewise have emblematic names <note>Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi</note>, he explained the will of God.

<margin>XII. Nor is the force of the prophetic phrasing weakened by this explanation.</margin>

XII. There is nothing in this opinion that offends, or that is not consistent with the holiness of the commanding God or the chastity of the obedient prophet. The whole difficulty lies in whether such an exposition satisfies the weight of the words the Prophet uses in this narration. Let us now attempt to show this. It should be observed, therefore, that it is the character of prophetic speech <term>characterem... prophetici sermonis</term> that they are sometimes commanded to *do* what they only have to *predict*, and which, in accordance with their prediction, will certainly come to pass. To Isaiah, God says in Chapter 6:10, *"Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy."* That is explained in Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 as: *"The heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears."* This indicates that it was not done by the work of Isaiah, but was truly predicted by Isaiah. <meta>This page continues the argument that the prophet Hosea's marriage was a symbolic parable. It explains that in biblical language, a prophet is often described as "doing" the thing they are actually only announcing, and analyzes the symbolic meanings of the names Gomer, Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi to support this interpretation.</meta>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XII.

...idiom, prophets are said to *do* what they merely announce. Thus, in 1 Kings 13:3, 5, that man of God who prophesied against the altar at Bethel is said to have *given a sign* <note>original: "edidisse prodigium"</note>, though he only announced it by the word of **the LORD**. Similarly, the Israelites are commanded to "set" <note>translated here as "give" or "pronounce"</note> a blessing on Mount Gerizim and a curse on Mount Ebal—that is, to *pronounce* them. Deuteronomy 11:29. In the same way, Hosea could be said to have "taken for himself a wife of whoredoms"—meaning he explained and presented that parable in such a passionate <note>original: "pathetico sermone," referring to the emotional and persuasive power of the speech</note> manner to the people that it served to convict them just as much as if the act itself had been performed before their eyes (which could not have been done decently).

<margin>XIII. The symbolic names of the woman and children lead to the same conclusion.</margin>
XIII. Regarding the names of the woman and the children born to her, because they are entirely symbolic <note>original: "emblematica"</note>, they lead us to think of a parable rather than a historical event. The woman's name is *Gomer*, a word that carries the meaning of both *completion* and *consumption* <note>The Hebrew root *gamar* implies finishing or coming to an end</note>. She could be called this either because of her "complete" beauty, or because she was equipped with all the arts of seduction, or even because she was soon to be destroyed. She represents Israel, which was enriched and adorned with many blessings by God, but was now nearing destruction. She is also called the daughter of *Diblaim*. *Debela* signifies a "cake of pressed figs," which were once considered delicacies; however, *Diblata* is also the name of a vast desert. Ezekiel 6:14. Thus, according to some, the name indicates that the cause of their luxury and ultimate ruin (or overthrow) was the pleasure arising from an abundance of all things. According to others, this mystical prostitute—the idolatrous Israel—has her origin in the "desert" (meaning the world) and will be reduced back to a state resembling a dry and fig-less wilderness.

The offspring born from this union similarly signify the future generations of Israel in different states. The first child, a male, is called יזרעאל *Jezreel*, which is the name of a city in the territory of the ten tribes where Jehu destroyed the family of Ahab (2 Kings 9). It signifies *a scattering to be performed by the Mighty God*. There is, therefore, in this name a symbolic denunciation of punishment to be inflicted not only on the house of Jehu, but on the entire people; their glorious name ישראל *Israel* <note>meaning "Prince with God" or "God strives"</note> is exchanged for the ominous name יזרעאל *Jezreel* <note>meaning "God sows" or "God scatters"</note>. The second child, a female representing a later and weaker age, is called לא רחמה *Lo-Ruhamah*, which means *she who has not obtained mercy*. Finally, the third, another male, is called לא עמי *Lo-Ammi*, meaning *not my people*, a meaning that is quite evident. Since all these names are clearly symbolic, it seems probable that this entire affair consisted of a mere representation rather than a literal fact. Consequently, the prophet was commanded to do nothing that would be contrary to modesty.

### ON THE REVELATION OF THE DIVINE WILL THROUGH SYMBOLS

<margin>
XIV. Did Ezekiel truly have to lie on one side for so many days?
</margin>
**XIV.** Interpreters also debate at length with what intention Ezekiel was commanded to lie on his left side and "bear the iniquity of the house of Israel" for three hundred and ninety days; and then to lie on his right side to bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days; bound with thick cords so that he could not turn from one side to the other. Meanwhile, he was to eat bread by measure and drink water by measure. For bread, he was to have a barley cake prepared over human excrement; however, when he pleaded against this, he was granted cow’s dung instead. *Ezekiel 4:4 and following.* The question is whether these things occurred only in a vision and were recounted to the people as a representation, or if they were commanded with the intent that they should actually be performed by the prophet? There are arguments on both sides.

<margin>
XV. Reasons for the negative side <note>The "negative side" refers to those who argue these events did not literally happen in the physical world.</note>.
</margin>
**XV.** Those who believe this consisted solely of a prophetic vision fight with these arguments: 
I. If these things happened in reality, one must imagine a miracle: for nature does not allow a person to lie on one side for so long. One would also expect that the Prophet, entangled in his own excrement after miserable and foul pains—becoming a horrific and abominable spectacle to Israel—would have perished in the most impure way, unless we believe the entire nature of things was miraculously overturned. Such a prodigy <note>original: "prodigium," a term for a supernatural omen or event</note> should not be asserted without the support of Scripture. 
II. From a calculation of the time, it can be gathered that Ezekiel did not lie down for that many days. The first revelation was made to him on the *fifth day of the fourth month in the fifth year from the deportation of King Jehoiachin.* *Ezekiel 1:1, 2.* This revelation occurred at least seven days later <note>original: "posterior," referring to the start of his ministry after a week of mourning</note>. *Ezekiel 3:15, 3:1.* Furthermore, it was in the *sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of that month, that Ezekiel sat in his house and the elders of Judah sat before him.* *Ezekiel 8:1.* Now, from the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, until the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year, only four hundred and thirteen days intervene. If seven days are subtracted from these, four hundred and six remain—whereas the days of lying on his side total four hundred and thirty. 
III. It seems altogether indecent for a prophet to be forced to actually eat a cake either kneaded with human excrement or cooked over it. Is it credible that the Greatest and Best God would treat His faithful servants so unworthily, when even the lowest of slaves could hardly be treated more unworthily by the cruelest of masters?

<margin>
XVI. For the affirmative side.
</margin>
**XVI.** But the other opinion is not without its own reasons. Those who follow it argue as follows: 
I. To that command, this second one is immediately joined, without any mark of distinction by which either the prophe-
