...[that the prophe]t was warned, or the reader is warned, that it must be understood otherwise; and that this was the mind of the Lord: that while the first <note>The visionary command.</note> was truly to be performed and was performed, the second <note>The physical action.</note> was established only in fantasy and imagination. 

**II.** This observation is even more pressing if one considers how both commands were so linked together that the first entered into the execution of the second. For in verse 6, the prophet is ordered *to set his face firmly toward the siege of Jerusalem, with his arm bared*. Surely God willed that in this reclining of his, he should fixedly gaze upon the brick on which he had sketched the siege of Jerusalem, and with his cloak thrown back, he should stretch out his ready arm, representing those who were about to attack Jerusalem with a fierce countenance and a ready hand. If that sketch was actually completed in fact, why should not the gazing at that sketch and the stretching out of the bared arm against the sketched Jerusalem likewise consist of actual deeds? 

**III.** The prophet is commanded to do all these things *before the eyes of the Israelites (verse 12)*; therefore, it was not in his imagination alone. 

**IV.** He is commanded to *prophesy* while reclining *(verse 7)*; certainly not with words, for *his tongue was stuck to the roof of his mouth, and he was mute.* Therefore, this prophecy consisted of deeds, through which he was given as a sign <note>The Latin "portento" here refers to a "wonder" or "sign" that points to a future event.</note> to the house of Israel. 

**V.** If all things were performed only in the imagination, there does not seem to have been such a great cause for pleading that the cake not be baked over human dung. The cause is undoubtedly greater if the prophet truly had to take food prepared in such a way into his own mouth.

<margin>XVII. Judgment <note>original: Ἐπίκρισις (Epikrisis), meaning a final decision or assessment.</note></margin>
**XVII.** To me, if anything is to be decided, these latter arguments seem stronger. Nor are responses lacking to the former [arguments]. 

**I.** The reclining of the Prophet on one side could be continued for so long without a miracle. Very learned men recount having seen—one, a noble paralytic lying on his back with wonderful patience for sixteen whole years; another, a certain madman bound with a chain, lying naked on the same side for entire days and nights for more than fifteen years. This was indeed hard for Ezekiel, and it ought to have been hard, so that he might represent the very heavy labors and troubles of the siege to the people; but what is it that a conscience of the Divine command and a mind hardened to patience cannot overcome? Especially if God, by His remarkable grace, diminishes the bodily distress and meanwhile soothes the mind with His most pleasant consolations. Nor should the rigor of this prophetic reclining be urged beyond measure, as if the Prophet were prevented—either by the Divine command or by his own ropes—from decently satisfying the necessities of nature. For that we should suppose this, neither reason nor the Prophet’s speech requires.

First, there is no shortage of interpreters—among whom is the most celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized the covenantal and symbolic nature of the Bible.</note>—who contend that three hundred and ninety days are assigned to the Prophet's reclining in total, within which forty days are specific to the tribe of Judah. *For, they say, it appears from verse nine that the entire duration is three hundred and ninety days: specifically the time during which he was to eat the prepared food.* Therefore, *in verse 6, we do not translate "when you have completed these, you shall lie on your right side," but rather, "and you shall complete these and lie down," that is: you shall complete these days in such a way that for forty days you lie on your right side, and then bare your arm and prophesy against Jerusalem.* These three hundred and ninety years are rightly thought to be from the division of the kingdom until the capture and burning of Jerusalem. If we follow this, every appearance of difficulty is removed. For between the thirteenth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, and the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year, somewhat more than three hundred and ninety days intervene. But let us take the maximum number of days; let us add the other forty to the three hundred and ninety, which joined together make four hundred and thirty: and these too can be found within the two markers just assigned. We need only recall to mind that every second or third year among the Hebrews was an <term>intercalary year<gloss>A year in which an extra month is added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar seasons.</gloss></term>, by the addition of a whole month. Let us suppose then—and nothing prevents us from doing so—that the fifth year mentioned in Ezekiel 1:2 had thirteen months; once again, the number of days in which Ezekiel was commanded to lie down is found.

XIX. III. Although God treats his servants with extraordinary love, and honors those who honor Him, this nevertheless does not prevent Him from occasionally commanding them to do something harsh, in which they serve as a <note>original: "portento"</note> sign or wonder to others. Among these must be numbered the command given to Ezekiel: which, however, is not to be interpreted as if human waste had to be kneaded into the dough of the cake or smeared upon it to be eaten with it; but rather that the cake was to be baked using that hardened material as fuel, to signify the <note>original: "inopia lignorum"</note> scarcity of wood. It is as if God had said: "So great will be the lack of wood and other things necessary for the comforts of life, that they will make a fire from the dung-pit." In this way they shall eat their "unclean" food until, lacking bread and water, they shall each be struck with orror and waste away in their iniquity. And you, Prophet, represent this to them in advance by such a preparation of your food. In this matter, there is no reason for us to retreat from the simplicity of the literal meaning. But perhaps we have lingered too long on this dispute.

# CHAPTER XIII.

->On the writing down of prophecies.<-

*I. Prophets were ordered to write their prophecies. II. A notable distortion of the command given to Isaiah on this matter. III. Refutation of that distortion. IV. Habakkuk 2:2 is explained. V. Jeremiah’s scroll submerged in the Euphrates. VI. The dual writing of prophecies: on tablets and in a book. VII. The collection of prophecies into a single volume; by whom it was done.*

---

<margin>I. Prophets were ordered to write their prophecies.</margin>
Things which are brought forth in bare speech and glide into the ears usually glide out of the mind again just as easily; they are fixed somewhat deeper if some symbol is added to the speech, striking the eyes as well. But even this impression fades over time. So that God might preserve the memory of his oracles intact through many successions of ages, he wisely ordered them to be shaped into WRITINGS <note>original: "SCRIPTIS"</note> that would endure for all time. Express mandates for this matter exist; and they are more well-known than is necessary to dwell upon them. See Exodus 17:14, Deuteronomy 31:19, Isaiah 30:8, Jeremiah 30:2, 36:2, 28.

<margin>II. A notable distortion of the command given to Isaiah on this matter.</margin>
II. That command by which God addressed Isaiah is quite remarkable. Chapter 8:1. *And Jehovah said to me, take for yourself a large scroll, and write in it with a human stylus, for Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz.* <note>The Hebrew name means "The spoil speeds, the prey hastens."</note> Which the most elegant Huetius <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar, author of the *Demonstratio Evangelica*.</note> twisted elsewhere with a monstrous distortion in *Demonstration of the Gospel, Proposal VII, Paragraph XV.* It will not be troublesome to append his words here. *The Prophet,* he says, *represents God not as one speaking plainly <note>original Greek: "εὐθυῤῥήμονα"</note>, but speaking with solemnity and modesty, using beautiful names for shameful things <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ τῶν κακεμφάτων καλοῖς ὀνόμασι χρώμενον"</note>, and setting himself the task of taking a wife and attending to children with her through metaphorical and honorable words. For the modesty of the Hebrew language was very great: so much so that it has no proper names for the genital parts and sexual matters, as observed by Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>. Therefore, he calls the wife a "large scroll"; he calls the "human stylus" that part of the body which cannot be named honorably. He orders him to write in it, "Quickly take the spoils, plunder quickly," that is, to beget a son with her who was to have that name. Isaiah therefore obeys God's command: "I took for myself," he says, "faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Berechiah, and I went to the Prophetess, and she conceived, and bore a son." Thus far Huetius.*

III. But what is "playing" at a serious matter, if this is not? The most learned man rightly praises the modesty of the Hebrew language. But metaphorical words of this sort, explained with that intent, I know not what shameful...

The very elegant Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French scholar and bishop.</note> twisted this into something else with a monstrous distortion in his *Demonstration of the Gospel* <note>original Latin: *Demonstratio Evangelica*</note>, Proposition VII, Paragraph 15. It will not be troublesome to record his words here. "The Prophet," he says, "represents God not as speaking **plainly** <note>original Greek: εὐθυῤῥήμονα (*euthyrrhēmona*)</note>, but **majestically** <note>original Greek: σεμνοπρεπῶς (*semnoprepōs*)</note> and modestly, **using beautiful names for unseemly things** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῶν κακεμφάτων καλοῖς ὀνόμασι χρώμενον (*epi tōn kakemphatōn kalois onomasi chrōmenon*)</note>; and by using metaphors and honorable words, God charges him to take a wife and attend to the procreation of children with her. For the modesty of the Hebrew language was very great, so much so that it has no proper names for the genital parts or functions, as has been observed by Maimonides. Thus, he calls the wife a 'large scroll'; he calls that part which cannot be named honorably 'the pen of a man.' He commands him to write in it: *Hurry to take the spoil, prey quickly*—that is, to beget a son with her, who was to have that name. Isaiah therefore obeys God's command: *I took for myself*, he says, *faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah; and I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.*" Thus far Huetius.

<margin>
III. Refutation of that distortion.
</margin>
III. But what is playing with serious matters if this is not? The most learned man [Huetius] rightly praises the modesty of the Hebrew language. But such metaphorical words, explained with that intent, produce a certain **unseem-** <note>original Greek fragment: κακεμ- (*kakem-*), likely completing as *kakemphaton*, meaning something ill-sounding or indecent.</note>

<sig>Vol. I. L</sig>

...sound **more shameful** <note>original Greek: φαυλότερον (*phauloteron*)</note> than if the Prophet had been instructed without such roundabout language about an honorable approach to a wife. Would it not indeed be far more honorable to say, "take a wife and labor to procreate children," than to use a transferred type of speech such as Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar known for his "Demonstratio Evangelica."</note> imagines for himself here? Above all, one must praise a modest mind which, when presented with simple words that signify something else entirely, is not easily led to think of those things which cannot be honorably named. If such an interpretation had slipped from any of us, what an uproar the parasites of the Roman Church would make! They would spread word of its novelty and immodesty with tragic exclamations. 

But I have no desire to dwell on harassing these men. The matter speaks for itself: a **large volume** <note>original Latin: *volumen magnum*</note> denotes paper, or parchment, or a tablet, which God wished to be large, either because of the multitude of things to be inscribed, or so that it might be more easily displayed when hung somewhere on a wall. He wants it written with a **human pen** <note>original Latin: *stilo hominis*</note>; by this phrase, the clarity of the writing is noted, as if He had said: "as clearly, plainly, and fitly for reading as can be done by a man." Isaiah obeyed this command when he ensured that both the Jews of his time, and all their posterity to this very day, and finally we ourselves with them, may read that prophecy.

<margin>IV. Habakkuk 2:2 is explained.</margin>
IV. The edict of God to Habakkuk is not different. Chapter 2:2. **Write the vision and make it plain on tablets, so that he who reads it may run.** <note>original Hebrew: *כתב חזון ובאר על הלוחות , למען ירוץ קורא בו*</note> It has been learnedly observed by a most celebrated interpreter that it is credible that it was no less customary among the people for the Prophets to set forth their writings publicly to be read—especially at their own homes—than it was for the Roman High Priests. Regarding whom, Cicero says in Book II of *On the Orator*: **The High Priest <term>Pontifex Maximus<gloss>The chief priest of ancient Roman religion.</gloss></term> committed all the events of each individual year to writing: he would publish them on a white board <note>original Latin: *album*</note> and set the tablet out at his home, so that the people would have the power to know them.** The Prophet here is also commanded to do this: to write the vision, explained and clearly set out on tablets, so that not only might any passer-by have the opportunity to read it, but also that anyone reading might be able to "run"—that is, to read quickly, sticking nowhere on account of the difficulty of the script.

<margin>V. Jeremiah’s volume submerged in the Euphrates.</margin>
V. There was something unique about that writing in which Jeremiah outlined the destruction of Babylon. He delivered this to Seraiah the Prince at the time he was going to Babylon with King Zedekiah. He gave him this additional task: that after the book had been read through, he should bind a stone to it and cast the book into the middle of the Euphrates, adding this song: **Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her, and they shall be weary.** Jeremiah 51:60 and following. The casting into the Euphrates...

<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XIII.</header>

...and the sinking of the book containing the fate of Babylon was a symbol of a fall from which Babylon was never to rise again. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian who wrote influential commentaries on the Bible.</note> compares this to that line from Horace:

-> *— — — as soon as the stones shall swim back from the deepest* <-
-> *shallows, having been lifted up, so that to return would be a sin.* <-
<note>original Latin: *simul imis saxa renarint / Vadis levata, ut redire sit nefas* (Horace, Epodes 16.25-26)</note>

He notes that this was modeled on the deed of the Phocaeans <note>The Phocaeans were Greeks who, fleeing Persian rule, swore never to return to their city until a mass of iron they threw into the sea floated again.</note>, who likewise—just like Seraiah <note>A high-ranking official and brother of Baruch, who carried Jeremiah's prophecy to Babylon (Jeremiah 51:59–64).</note> here—used a visible sign to accompany their words, as was the custom in that age, by throwing a lead plate into the sea. Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French Reformation leader.</note> noted, somewhat more usefully, that the Prophet did not look out for Seraiah alone with this action, but for all the faithful. For although this remained unknown for a long time, the Prince himself <note>Referring to Seraiah as a "prince" or high official of the court.</note> later confessed that this command had been given to him by Jeremiah, and that the book had indeed been thrown by him into the Euphrates. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "federal" or covenantal theology.</note> is the most subtle of all, if not perhaps more subtle than is right; *Because,* he says, *he wished this prophecy to be cast into the Euphrates with a stone, it seems to signify that it is enigmatic, and as if submerged in the deep, so that in its own time it might come forth into the light along with the truth itself.* I fear, I say, that this is more clever than it is solid. Since the book, submerged together with a stone, was never intended to come forth at any time, I do not see how the "coming forth" of the prophecy into the light was signified by this sinking. What follows is less displeasing: *Or it signifies that Babylon would be so abolished that it would be mentioned no more, and all the prophecies about it would no longer be cared for, since their fulfillment would no longer need to be awaited, the prophecy having turned into history.*

<margin>VI. The twofold writing of prophecies: on tablets and in a book.</margin>
VI. One observation still remains, which must by no means be overlooked in this place; namely, that the oracles were written by the Prophets for a twofold reason and with a double purpose: first on **open tablets**, to be fixed in a conspicuous place, so that after they were preached, they could be read publicly by anyone; and to this belongs what we just explained from Habakkuk: then in a **book**, so that they might endure for ages. Thus God spoke to Jeremiah in Chapter 30, verse 2: *Thus says Jehovah the God of Israel, declaring: write for yourself all the words, with which I speak to you, in a book.* Both methods are declared together to Isaiah in Chapter 30, verse 8, where this distinction is most evident: *Now come, write this on a TABLET among them, and engrave it in a BOOK; so that it may be for the times to follow, forever, even into the age.* Such a Prophetic Book, because it was inspired and dictated by God, is called the **Book of Jehovah**, in Isaiah 34:16: *Seek from the Book of Jehovah, and read: not one of these shall be missing.* That is, when that time has come, then take into your hands the volume of prophecies, of which Jehovah is the author...

<header>ON THE WRITING OF THE PROPHECIES.</header>

<margin>VII. The collection of prophecies into one volume, and by whom it was done.</margin>
VII. So far, indeed, it has been shown that individual prophecies were written down at almost the same time they were preached, by the command of God. However, it is not equally clear when, by whom, and in what manner the collection of these individual prophecies into a single book was made—whether this occurred during the prophets' own lifetimes and should be attributed to the authors themselves, or whether it should be credited to others. *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French theologian of the Reformation.</note> explains his view as follows in his *Preface to Isaiah*: *To this question,* he says, *none of the interpreters whose writings I have read so far responds. I, however, although I can hardly provide full satisfaction, will nevertheless say what I think. After the prophets had delivered a sermon to the people, they would gather a brief summary of it, which they would post on the temple doors so that the prophecy would be open to all and better known. When it had been posted for several days and was sufficiently known, it was taken down by the ministers of the temple and placed in the treasury, so that a perpetual monument of the matter might remain. It is likely that the books of the prophets were compiled from these; and this can be gathered from the second chapter of Habakkuk, if one weighs it correctly, and also from the eighth chapter of Isaiah. Indeed, those who have studied the prophets diligently and with judgment will grant me that their sermons were not always compiled in the proper order, but the volume was forged together as opportunity allowed. By the singular providence of God, however, it was brought about that through the work of the Priests—whose office it was to hand down prophecies to posterity (though they themselves were often most hostile to the Prophets)—these works have reached us.* He repeats almost the same points regarding *Isaiah* 8:2 and *Jeremiah* 51:64. Just as I cannot prove this opinion in all its parts with certain reasons, I also have no valid arguments to tear it down. We are forced to be ignorant of many things in such matters. Let us only proclaim the providence of God and give most grateful thanks to His immense goodness, because He has deigned to preserve His Divine prophecies—all of which bear the marks of Divinity within them—intact until our times for our instruction. Let us prefer to be humbly ignorant of the method of collection rather than to define it rashly, without the <term>trustworthiness</term> <note>original Greek: αξιοπισίαν (*axiopistian*), meaning credibility or historical reliability.</note> of Divine or human history.

<margin>I. All Antiquity believes the Pentateuch was written by Moses.</margin>
Since the discourse has now led us to speak of the impulse of the Holy Spirit, by which the Prophets were stirred to commit their Oracles to writing; and since Moses is the prince of Prophets, and the norm of his doctrine is the standard for all things that are to be spoken and heard in the Church of God at all times: it therefore seems worthwhile to deal specifically with his writings. This is now all the more necessary because we see men—famed for their erudition and who claim to be more skilled than others in solid Philosophy and sacred <term>Criticism</term> <note>In this context, "Criticism" refers to Biblical Criticism, the scholarly study and investigation of biblical writings to determine their origins and history.</note>—judging and writing about these books in a way far different than all antiquity has done until now. The accepted opinion of both Hebrews and Christians to this day is that Moses, commanded and instigated by God, is the author of those books which, famous under the title of the Pentateuch, are circulated in his name; if perhaps you except a few passages which are from a later, yet Divinely directed hand, and were slightly <term>interpolated</term> <note>Interpolation refers to the insertion of words or notes into a text by a later editor, often to clarify geographic names or historical facts for a later audience.</note> for the sake of better understanding.

<margin>III. Hobbes.</margin>
III. **HOBBES** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English philosopher famous for his political theory.</note> in his **Leviathan** *Part III. Chapter XXXIII.* contends that the books of Moses are named not after their Author, but after their subject; not because they were written by Moses, but because they concern Moses. However, he admits that **IT IS POSSIBLE THAT HE WROTE THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE NARRATED IN THESE BOOKS AS HAVING BEEN WRITTEN BY HIM**, namely the "Book of the Law," which, as it seems, is contained from *Deuteronomy Chapter XI to Chapter XXVII.*

<margin>IV. Proponent of the Pre-Adamite story.</margin>
IV. The famous proponent of the **PRE-ADAMITES** <note>This refers to Isaac La Peyrère, who argued in 1655 that humans existed before the biblical Adam.</note> maintains that those books which Moses himself had written have perished. In those books, he argues, Moses had narrated at length the annals of his Jewish people from their first origin and from Adam (the ancestor of the Jewish bloodline) down to his own times, and even the "genesis" or origin of all things before Adam was created; and that now only certain excerpts and haphazard notes of those works survive. *System of the Pre-Adamites, Book IV. Chapter I.*

<margin>V. Spinoza.</margin>
V. **SPINOZA** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a foundational figure of the Enlightenment who applied critical historical methods to the Bible.</note>, author of the *Theologico-Political Treatise, Chapter VIII.* <note>The Latin text reads "Historico-Politici," but this is a likely error for Spinoza's "Tractatus Theologico-Politicus."</note> admits indeed that almost everyone has believed Moses to be the writer of the Pentateuch. He claims that Aben-Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a medieval Jewish scholar whose subtle comments on the Torah were interpreted by later critics as early doubts about Mosaic authorship.</note>—whom he praises as a man of free-thinking spirit and no small amount of erudition—was the first of all he read to notice this prejudice, although he did not dare to explain his mind openly. Spinoza does not fear to profess openly that he fosters an opinion very different from the received one. He contends, therefore, that all the historical books we find in the sacred codex, which narrate events performed before the age of Ezra, have a single author, whom he suspects was Ezra. He guesses that Deuteronomy was the first of those books written by Ezra: partly because it contains the laws of the fatherland, which the people needed most, and partly because that book is joined to the preceding ones by no connection (as all the others are), but begins as a separate speech: *these are the words of Moses.* Then, he believes that Ezra applied his study to describing the complete history of the Hebrew nation, namely from the creation of the world down to the final devastation of the city, into which he inserted the book of Deuteronomy in its proper place. Spinoza adds, *perhaps Ezra called his first five books by the name of Moses because his life is chiefly contained in them, the name being taken from the more important part.* But in *Chapter IX.* he contends that Ezra did not put the final hand to those narrations: **NOR DID HE DO ANYTHING ELSE THAN COLLECT HISTORIES FROM DIFFERENT WRITERS, AND SOMETIMES MERELY COPY THEM DOWN, AND LEFT THEM TO POSTERITY NOT YET EXAMINED OR ORDERED: FINALLY, ALL THESE THINGS COLLECTED PROMISCUOUSLY AND ACCU-**

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

...WERE PRESERVED, SO THAT THEY MIGHT LATER BE EXAMINED AND PUT INTO ORDER MORE EASILY. Spinoza confesses he cannot guess what causes prevented Ezra from completing this work in all its parts, *unless perhaps it was an untimely death* <note>original: "nisi forte intempestiva mors"</note>. He maintains that these commentaries of Ezra—such as they are—have reached us only in a maimed and mutilated form, defiled by many errors; thus, we have nothing whole from ancient history, and nothing that does not require much correction. Spinoza sets all this out at length and, in his usual manner, strengthens his position with arguments and examples.

<margin>VI. Simon.</margin> VI. **RICHARD SIMON** <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and a pioneer of "Higher Criticism," applying historical methods to the study of the Bible.</note> proceeded in a slightly different manner in his *Critical History of the Old Testament, Book 1, Chapter 11*. He demands that everyone believe that from the time of Moses onward, there were certain <term>Scribes</term> <note>original: "Scribas sive Actuarios." These were public record-keepers or registrars.</note> or public registrars among the Israelite people. These were established by Moses himself, following the laudable custom of the Egyptians which he had observed while living in Pharaoh's court. These Scribes, protected by public authority, recorded the acts of the republic with as much diligence and faith as possible. From their lengthy commentaries and "elephantine volumes," those Sacred Writings which we now possess were later compiled as occasion allowed. Since this was done by various people, each of whom had their own purpose, Simon contends that this is why histories are sometimes poorly joined, and why repetitions are frequent, redundant, and tiresome.

In *Chapter 5*, he argues at length that Moses was not the author of the Pentateuch, and he accumulates many examples of repetitions. He claims these could only have originated from various compilers of the Pentateuch, where one compiler brought one <term>pericope</term> <note>original: "pericopæ." A pericope is a specific passage or extract from a text, often a story or lesson.</note> into the Sacred text from the vast commentaries of the Scribes, and another compiler brought in a different version of the same event. These sections, however poorly stitched together, were for some unknown reason accepted and left as they were by the Jewish Church. To this, another calamity was added: since the ancients wrote their volumes on scrolls, where the parts were joined by neither glue nor stitching but were rolled around cylinders and unrolled when needed, it could easily happen—and indeed did happen—that the parts of the volumes became confused. Because they were not put back in their proper places, the order of the sections was sometimes strangely and miserably disturbed. From this it follows that the most ancient history of the early world and the Israelite people is not from the hand of Moses, but was compiled from the commentaries of unknown Scribes by unknown men—certainly various and lacking in judgment—to whom, however, as if in mockery, the guidance of the Holy Spirit is attributed.

# WAS MOSES THE AUTHOR OF THE PENTATEUCH?

Nay, [Simon argues] that not even that compilation has come down to us in its entirety, but has been so disturbed by the confusion of the parts of the volumes that, unless the healing hand of Divine Criticism <note>original: "medica Divæ Critices manus"</note> intervenes, scarcely any wisdom worthy of God can be found in that ancient history. For this is where everything tends, if we wish to speak freely and without evasion. Meanwhile, lest Moses have nothing of his own here, the writing of the laws is attributed to him as Legislator, indeed out of a sort of noble-minded generosity.

<margin>VII. Le Clerc, who prefers to attribute it to a certain Samaritan Priest.</margin>
VII. **JEAN LE CLERC** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a Genevan theologian and man of letters, known for his critical approach to biblical studies.</note> proceeds by a different path, though in the same direction. He wished to appear to present us with the opinions of certain Dutch theologians regarding *Simon’s Critical History*. While he laughs at Simon’s "Scribes," he nevertheless agrees with him in stripping Moses of the authorship of the Pentateuch. But to whom should it be credited? Hear, or rather read, a marvelous and incredible thing: it would hardly find belief, unless one refused to trust their own eyes. Thus he writes on page 128 and following: *It is probable that the Pentateuch was composed at that time when the old characters of the Jews, in which it was first written, were better known than the new ones they had adopted during the Babylonian Captivity; and by an author who would be suspected neither by the Samaritans nor the Jews, and from whose hand both would receive it quite willingly. All these conditions meet in that Israelite Priest sent from Babylon to teach the new inhabitants of Palestine the rite by which the God of that region loved to be worshipped.* 2 Kings 17. *It is reasonable to believe that this priest, whether alone or assisted by others, in order to lead those unrefined peoples away from the insane opinion of polytheism* <note>original: "πολυθεΐας" (polytheias)</note>, *composed a history of the world created by the power of the one God, and an epitome of Jewish History up to the Law: so that it might become clear that there is only one God, namely the one whom the Israelites adore. Moreover, he wrote this history in Hebrew, in the ancient characters, either because he was not yet sufficiently skilled in the Chaldean language, or for some other cause unknown to us. It is difficult to determine the year in which these things were done; yet it seems to have happened after the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah. For in this year the Book of the Law was found, without which that Priest could not have put the finishing touch to his work: seeing as it makes up the greatest part of Hebrew history and was especially necessary for the instruction of the new Samaritans. If things are supposed to have happened in this way, it is easy to believe that those Priests who were at Jerusalem approved this history of the Bethelite Priest with their vote, since they found nothing in it except what was pious and consistent with Divine law and the truth of history. And in this way all the critical difficulties regarding the Author of the Pentateuch are removed. For in order for the Samaritans to receive the Pentateuch, it had to be written by an author not suspected by them; and so that they might have it in ancient letters...*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

Lest the Jews disdain to number it among their sacred books, it was fitting that it should have an author toward whom they were not so hostile as they were toward the Samaritans after the return from the Babylonian captivity. Finally, since things are found in the history of Genesis which demonstrate that its author had more contact with the Babylonian Empire than the Jews had before the captivity, it is necessary that he lived after Shalmaneser <note>Shalmaneser V, the Assyrian King who besieged Samaria (722 BCE).</note> deported the ten tribes into Assyria. Thus far the words of that most learned man <note>referring to Jean Le Clerc.</note>. I have chosen to render his own words at some length, lest I seem to have twisted an unexpected opinion into a mockery or the appearance of blasphemy: how far it truly is from such things, I will weigh and explain in its own place and with the seriousness it deserves.

<margin>VIII. But certainly Moses was a most famous writer.</margin>
VIII. What, however, should be decided about this whole business, we may judge no more surely or better than from the sacred letters themselves. From these it is now helpful to collect several points, which, arranged in order, will lead us little by little so that it is not difficult to define the question of the author of the Pentateuch. And this is first generally clear: that Moses was a writer, not only famous in his own time, but one whose monuments, contained in a book, were in the hands of the Israelites for many centuries after him. Those things which he wrote by God's command were of many different kinds.

(2 Chronicles 17:9): "They taught in Judah, having with them THE BOOK OF THE LAW OF JEHOVAH, and they went about all the cities of Judah, teaching the people."

The author is emphasizing that the ritual laws are so detailed they could not have been preserved by oral tradition alone.</note>; that no human memory would be equal to retaining them unless they existed as a written record. By whom, moreover, would they be better written than by him who both received them from God and delivered them to the people, and who urged their most accurate observation? BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

[...consecra]tion <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "-tione," likely completing the word "consecratione" from the previous page.</note> of the Levites is found in Numbers 3 and 8. Nor is there any precept of God pertaining to the Israelite religion of that time which Moses did not include in that book of his; since he is narrated to have completed all things by writing.

<margin>XII. Indeed, and prophecies as well.</margin> XII. But besides the commandments, Moses also wrote **PROPHECIES**, or the prediction of future events. These are found in Deuteronomy 28, 29, 30, and 31. <margin>XIII. And historical accounts.</margin> XIII. XIV. This command is very clearly expressed: if it is properly considered, it will lead us to the consideration of many other things. And first, I would like it to be noted that the history of the war against the Amalekites is no more memorable than those other wonders which God performed in claiming the Israelite people for Himself, both in Egypt and in the wilderness. If, therefore, God willed this memorial to be written in a book to be perpetual, and Moses consecrated it to eternity by his writing, what reason can be given why the same should not have been done regarding other works of God which far surpass this one in their marvelous nature? And of which it is said in Psalm 78:5–7: *He established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, when he commanded our ancestors to make them known to their children. That the next generation might know them, even the children yet to be born, and that they should arise and tell their children: And put their hope in God, and not forget the deeds of the mighty God.* Since, therefore, God willed His illustrious and prodigious deeds to be preserved in the memory of the Israelite people, and He Himself recommended writing in a book as the best remedy for assisting memory; by whom could that writing be done with greater faith, dignity, and authority than by Moses, who was himself a great part of these events, and was so often called to write by the express command of the deity?

XV. XVI. XVII. Add that the history is so interwoven with the Legislation and the covenant agreement for the Israelites that the latter cannot be explained without the former. Since, therefore, it is certain that the Legislation and the covenant agreement were described by Moses, and since these cannot be understood without the history of the Israelite nation; what a strange prejudice <note>original: "invidia", here meaning an ill-willed or unfair reluctance to grant credit</note> it is to deny Moses the writing of those things without which the things he undoubtedly wrote must necessarily be mutilated and incomplete!

XVIII. Finally, it must not be overlooked that in those things told concerning Abraham and God’s covenant with him—indeed, in the whole history of the Patriarchs as it is set out in the Book of Genesis—the foundations are laid for that covenant which God entered into with the Israelites through the mediation of Moses. Thus, all these things comprise one and continuous series of events; it is probable that they are also from a single hand, since they were all written with one purpose and all tend toward a single goal. And from whose hand rather than that of Moses, who so skillfully embraced these vast works of God and the connection of so many decrees within his great mind?

### XXII. Recapitulation of the proven theses.
<margin>XXII. Recapitulation of the proven theses.</margin>
XXII. Now let us collect those things which have been said. We have proven from the evident testimonies of Holy Scripture the following: I. That Moses, at God's command, was the most celebrated writer of his age among the people of God. II. That he wrote the Laws, which served as the standard of religion and all virtue for the Israelite people. III. Not only those laws contained in certain chapters of Deuteronomy, but also those appearing in the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. IV. Also many testimonies concerning Christ, most of which are found in the Book of Genesis. VIII. That the Book of Exodus is called "the Book of Moses" by Christ. IX. Indeed, that the entire Pentateuch, which was certainly read in the Synagogues during the time of Christ and the Apostles, is called "Moses" by James and Paul. X. And this is not because it is *about* Moses, but because it was *written by* Moses. If these things do not prove that Moses is the writer of the Pentateuch, by what reasoning can any ancient book finally be assigned its own author? I would dare to appeal to the conscience of all those with whom I now dispute, whether they can bring forward arguments—I will not say stronger ones, but even those having the appearance of similar value—for the person they themselves thrust forward as the writer of the Pentateuch?

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

...THE APOSTLES DID NOT COME INTO THE WORLD TO TEACH THE JEWS CRITICISM; IT IS NO WONDER IF THEY SPEAK ACCORDING TO COMMON OPINION. <margin>XXIV. Profanity convicted.</margin>
XXIV. Shame on that bold and reckless Criticism, which does not hesitate to place its own *conjectures*, as the critic himself admits, above the authority of the Apostles and even of Christ himself. For indeed, Christ and the Apostles were not "Doctors of Criticism" like those who today claim for themselves the kingdom of letters in every science; they were, however, Doctors of Truth, and they did not allow themselves to be deceived by common ignorance or the craftiness of the elites. Certainly, they did not come into the world to foster common errors and to fortify them with their own authority, spreading them far and wide—not only among the Jews, but among the peoples who depend solely on them. To sum it up in a word: whoever holds the Christian religion dear to their heart, and to whom the authority of Christ and the Apostles is sacred, will more willingly submit their faith to Christ and the Apostles when they speak of Moses as the author of the **Pentateuch**, than to all the *Hobbeses, Spinozas, Simons, and Le Clercs* <note>A list of prominent Enlightenment and rationalist thinkers: Thomas Hobbes, Baruch Spinoza, Richard Simon, and Jean Le Clerc.</note> who have ever existed, and to that entire race of profane critics with all their rash conjectures.

<margin>XXV. Simon refuted.</margin>
XXV. Thus far we have produced those arguments that stand for Moses; now we add that if one departs from Moses, no one else can be assigned who can be proven to be the author of the **Pentateuch** with any greater likelihood, let alone any certainty. For as to what *Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest often called the "father of biblical criticism."</note> argues at length regarding *Public Scribes* recording everything in daily acts—contending that they existed from the very beginning of the Republic, even in the desert—learned men have long since demonstrated that this is to be relegated to the "dream from the ivory gate." <note>A classical reference to false or deceptive dreams, originating from Homer and Virgil.</note> Nor has *Simon* been able to free himself from the objections of *Le Clerc* and others. To suggest that our sacred books were compiled from such public commentaries in so confused and unjudicious a manner as he claims is nearly blasphemy; and, whatever the pretext, it is said in mere mockery of the Scripture.

# WHETHER MOSES IS THE AUTHOR OF THE PENTATEUCH.

...[him] to walk in the ways of the Lord <note>original: "Jehovæ"</note>, by keeping His statutes, and His commandments, and His judgments, and His testimonies, as **IT IS WRITTEN IN THE LAW OF MOSES**. 1 Kings 2:3. And shortly after the captivity, that same book is praised as the ancient rule of religion. Ezra 3:2. **JUST AS IT IS WRITTEN IN THE LAW OF MOSES, THE SERVANT OF GOD**. And Ezra 6:18: **According to the prescription of THE BOOK OF MOSES**. Critics indeed dictate that these passages should not be understood as referring to the **Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, but to some other book of Moses—I know not which. They dictate it, I say, but they do not prove it. And indeed, everything cited in the places just mentioned is still found today in the Pentateuch. What forbids us, then, from thinking of that book in which all the citations are found? What commands us to imagine another one different from this?

XXVII. Truly, the *Samaritan Pentateuch* <note>A version of the first five books of the Bible preserved by the Samaritans, written in an older script.</note> is a powerful argument for its antiquity. This is especially true if it is believed, as many critics today wish, that the sacred books were first written in Samaritan letters—which letters Ezra changed for the newer and more elegant ones now in use. However, they say the Samaritan letters are not those belonging to the new colonists' homeland or ancestry, but are the most ancient Hebrew letters, retained by the Samaritans. It is well known how deadly a hatred existed between the Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity and the Samaritans; so much so that neither side wanted to accept anything sacred from the other. If, then, Ezra, or some <term>contemporary</term><gloss>σύγχρον</gloss><gloss>os</gloss> of his, had written the Pentateuch, how could it be that the Samaritans accepted a volume composed by their most bitter enemy with such great veneration as Divine? And how could they allow themselves to be forced to accept a work recently coming from the hands of a contemporary man as if it were Mosaic? How is it that the Samaritans have that volume recorded not in their own letters, but in the ancient letters of the Hebrews—which the Hebrews themselves, since that time, have not used except for the Assyrian or **Chaldean** <note>Aramaic or Babylonian</note> letters? These things do not hold together.

What madness is this, to suddenly elevate a *Samaritan Priest*, a man of no distinction and of no name, into the author of such a great work? Evidently, those greatest prophets whom the Jews and the ten tribes of Israel had possessed lacked that zeal [to write], so that a Samaritan man—a Schismatic, who had served the altar at **Bethel** <note>A city where the Northern Kingdom of Israel set up golden calves for worship, considered illegitimate by the author.</note> against God's command—[wrote] the history of the people of God from the creation of the world to the departure...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

...comes to be feared, I would not even wish to attend to other hypotheses—that is, to explain by some artifice how the text might best agree with them. Instead, let the text be considered in itself, as it is, and as it offers itself spontaneously to a mind occupied by no prejudices from elsewhere. To this habit I accustom myself as much as possible, secure in the knowledge that it cannot happen otherwise than that truth always harmonizes with truth. I frankly confess, therefore, that there are some things in the **Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> that do not seem to be attributable to Moses. However, I contend that these are few, and so small, that they do not prevent Moses from being established as the author of that book.

<margin>XXXII. Le Clerc collected many such points from his own mind.</margin>
XXXII. In seeking these out, unless I am mistaken, the most learned **Clericus** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a prominent Genevan theologian and biblical critic known for his skeptical approach to traditional authorship.</note> has surpassed the diligence of everyone else. He observes that three types of passages are found in the Pentateuch: I. Some things that are later than the time of Moses. II. Other things that must have been written during Moses' time. III. Finally, other things even earlier than Moses. Those which belong to the latter two categories do not contribute much to the present dispute. For it is generally confessed that those things which are either earlier than Moses, or occurred during his life, could have been written down by him. Only the first category [post-Mosaic additions] are now under our consideration. In this matter, we will follow him along his own path, subjoining to each of his arguments the points that the facts themselves dictate.

<margin>XXXIII. Genesis 2:11, 12 is examined.</margin>
XXXIII. For the **Pishon** <note>One of the four rivers flowing out of Eden.</note> is a branch of the Euphrates that carries into the Persian Gulf and brushes against those regions that were once called Chaldea, where **Hormuz** <note>An island and trading post in the Persian Gulf.</note> is now located. It is not credible, he argues, that Moses—who scarcely left Egypt—was equipped with such great skill regarding foreign regions. Still less is it credible that God revealed to him that the gold of that land was of good quality. 

I respond: I. This entire observation relies on a hypothesis which seems to me—if I may speak plainly—to be impious, and to utterly subvert the Divine authority of the sacred history. It is as if the Spirit of God did not teach the sacred writers certain things which they otherwise did not know of themselves. If that were true—if the sacred historians narrated nothing except what they sought out by their own human diligence—what then is the difference between the history of Genesis and the commentaries of **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian from the 1st century BCE who wrote a massive "Universal History."</note>? I would like this answered without evasion. II. Moses was not so unlearned, stupid, or dull as he seems to our critic. If Le Clerc, living in Amsterdam with his friends, knows so accurately that the Pishon is a branch of the Euphrates falling into the Persian Gulf near Hormuz, why could Moses not know the same in the most frequented court [of Pharaoh]...

<margin>XLII. Exodus 6:25, 26.</margin>
XLII. From the book of **EXODUS**, he [the Critic] noted the following. Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah relate no less significant things about themselves, and with no less grandeur of words.

For neither the word <term>Chose <note>original Hebrew: חוזה (Chozeh), meaning a visionary or seer</note></term>, nor <term>Roe <note>original Hebrew: ראה (Roeh), meaning a seer</note></term>, would have been suitable in that language. Nor, as far as I know, is there another word found in the Hebrew language that expresses its power. In the history of Samuel, however, we are not taught that the word <term>Nabi <note>original Hebrew: נביא, meaning prophet</note></term> only then began to be used for the first time, but rather that its meaning had changed slightly. Formerly, *Nabi* signified an intercessor before God and an interpreter of the Divine will; it is attributed to the Patriarchs in that sense, who, wherever they lived, practiced the worship of God, taught others, and prayed to God. It did not precisely denote a foreteller of future events—a meaning that began to be the primary one around the time of Samuel.

<margin>
XLIV.
Exodus
16:35.
</margin>
XLIV. The Author of the Pentateuch, so the Critic continues, narrates in **Exodus 16:35** those things which only happened after the death of Moses; as appears from **Joshua 5:11**: *The children of Israel ate manna forty years until they came to a habitable land; they ate manna, I say, until they reached the border of the land of Canaan.* I respond: I do not dare, as some do, to turn a clear and simple history into a prophecy <note>Some traditional commentators argued Moses wrote this through prophetic foresight; our author here disagrees</note>. I acknowledge, therefore, even here, a later hand.

<margin>
XLV.
Exodus
16:36.
</margin>
XLV. But I do not see why a later hand must be acknowledged in the following verse: *Now an Omer is one-tenth of an Ephah.* I hear the Critic saying that at a time when a certain measure is in common use among men, it is unlikely anyone would explain its quantity in other words. Observations of that kind only happen when the use of such a measure has ceased. But I respond: things that were known then are often narrated so that they might be known to posterity. And I remember that the Critic elsewhere complained, not without reason, that in the writing of history—to the great loss of posterity—those things are often omitted which are assumed to be most well-known to the present age. But how does our friend know that in the later centuries of the Israelite commonwealth the same measures were not still being handled by men? Or that the capacity of an Ephah was better known to them than that of an <term>Omer <note>The Latin text uses "Homer," but the biblical reference is to the Omer, a much smaller dry measure</note></term>? It is worth comparing what the sacred history records God saying to Moses: **Numbers 3:47.** *You shall take five shekels for each head; you shall take them according to the sanctuary shekel: that shekel is twenty gerahs.* Note that God Himself explains the value of a shekel to Moses by means of <term>gerahs <note>The Latin text uses "obolos," a Greek coin, to translate the Hebrew "gerah," the smallest unit of Hebrew currency</note></term>. For it belongs only to one equipped with powerful arguments to say that this parenthesis was inserted into the Divine speech by some unknown later writer.

<margin>
XLVI.
Deuteronomy 1:1.
</margin>
XLVI. These things the Critic noted from Exodus; from the books of **LEVITICUS** and **NUMBERS**, nothing. But a few things from **DEUTERONOMY**.

# IS MOSES THE AUTHOR OF THE PENTATEUCH?

It begins at Chapter 1: *These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel* <margin>li</margin> <note>original Hebrew: בעבר הירדן (*be-ever ha-Yarden*)</note> **beyond the Jordan**. From this, the Critic concludes that this book was written in Palestine, in respect to which the desert is "beyond" or "across" the Jordan. I respond: The word *ever* properly denotes **in passage**, or **at the crossing**; and *ever* signifies a part or a place positioned nearby, and can be translated as much as **on this side** as **beyond**, according to the requirements of the subject. In 1 Samuel 14:41, Saul speaks thus: *be you* <note>original Hebrew: לעבר אחד (*le-ever echad*)</note> **on one side**, *and I and Jonathan my son will be* <note>original Hebrew: לעבר אחד (*le-ever echad*)</note> **on the other side**. From this it is plain that the word *ever* denotes **a certain side**; however, it must be gathered from the nature of the matter being discussed which side is designated. There are places where it designates the nearer part: as in 1 Kings 4:24. Where it is said of Solomon, *For he ruled over* <note>original Hebrew: בכל עבר הנהר (*be-chol ever ha-nahar*)</note> **all the region on this side of the River**, which <term>Junius <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a prominent Huguenot theologian and biblical translator</note></term> well translated as, *in the entire closer part of the river, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings* <note>original Hebrew: עבר הנהר (*ever ha-nahar*)</note> **on this side of the River** *who were around the river itself*. The river in question is the Euphrates, so called <term>antonomastically <note>a figure of speech where a general epithet or title—like "The River"—is used to refer to a specific, well-known person or thing</note></term>, as a comparison with verse 21 proves. Moreover, the Euphrates was the boundary of Solomon's empire to the East; nor indeed did his rule extend to all those things or those kings who were *beyond* the Euphrates. From this it is established that *ever ha-nahar* denotes there the nearer part of the river. The same meaning holds in Deuteronomy 3:8, where not a historian, but Moses himself speaks: *So we took at that time this land from the hand of the two kings of the Amorites* <note>original Hebrew: אשר בעבר הירדן (*asher be-ever ha-Yarden*)</note> **who were at the crossing of the Jordan**, that is, on this side of the Jordan. If *be-ever* signified "across," and a historian living in Palestine had written it from that perspective, he would have recklessly corrupted the words of Moses, attributing to him a speech that is by no means suitable to the place where the speech was held. Add to this Joshua 5:1 and 9:1. It is well known that the book of Joshua was written after the Israelites had crossed the Jordan. It is likewise well known that the kings mentioned there reigned on that side of the Jordan where the Israelites were then living. And yet those same kings are said to have been <note>original Hebrew: בעבר הירדן (*be-ever ha-Yarden*)</note> **beyond the Jordan**. This must necessarily be translated as **on this side of the Jordan**. <term>Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who defended the Bible against early modern critics</note></term> judiciously turned the argument of these cavillers back upon them. In Genesis 50:10, these words are read: *And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is situated* <note>original Hebrew: בעבר הירדן (*be-ever ha-Yarden*)</note> **beyond the Jordan**. And then in verse 11: *Therefore the name of that place was called the Mourning of Egypt, which is* <note>original Hebrew: בעבר הירדן (*be-ever ha-Yarden*)</note> **beyond the Jordan**. According to the hypothesis of the Critics, the phrase must be explained in respect to Canaan, where they claim the writer of the Pentateuch lived. Now, if Ezra or anyone else wrote the Pentateuch in Canaan to the west of the Jordan, and *ever* always signifies "across," these places would certainly have to be sought to the East of the Jordan; however, it is established that they are situated to the West of the Jordan. On the contrary, if Moses was the author of the book...

BOOK I. CHAPTER XIV.

...we say that, since he wrote these things when the crossing of the Jordan by the Hebrews had not yet occurred, he assigned these places to the west of the Jordan, as he ought to have done. From this it follows that the word <note>original Hebrew: בעבר (*be-ever*)</note> is of ambiguous meaning, and is employed sometimes to denote the further side and sometimes the nearer side. The force of this argument <term>Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Dutch theologian and biblical critic known for his skeptical approach to traditional authorship.</note></term> is unable to evade unless the hypothesis is changed: by asserting that the writer does not use the word *be-ever* in respect to himself, but in respect to the Egyptians and those coming from Egypt by the route of the desert. But <term>Huetius <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who defended the Bible against early modern critics.</note></term> argued, as he was bound to do, from the hypothesis itself.

<margin>
XLVII.
*Deuteronomy* 3:14.
</margin>
XLVII. There is also something else that produces difficulty. *Deuteronomy* 3:14: *Jair, a son of Manasseh, took all the region of Argob* etc. *and called them after his own name, the villages of Jair,* **UNTO THIS DAY**. This seems hardly capable of being said in the time of Moses, because the events narrated here happened only a few months before Moses's death. I respond: I confess it seems that this parenthesis was inserted later to explain the speech of Moses.

<margin>
XLVIII.
Conclusion.
</margin>
<margin>
*Add what is said concerning this argument in the Preface, Section VII.*
</margin>
XLVIII. And these are the points which the most learned Clericus saw fit to note, so that from them he might prove that the Pentateuch was not composed by Moses. If all these things are examined without prejudice, as is only fair, only four places in the entire volume will remain in which some interpolation must be acknowledged. Indeed, the interpolation is so slight that it consists either in the change of a single small word or in the addition of a very brief little story, for which the occasion was provided by the very words of the ancient writing. However, such a tiny amount cannot support the weight of such a monstrous demand: that, against all the faith of Antiquity, and against the authority of the Apostles and of Christ, the authorship of the Pentateuch should be stripped from Moses.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>The majesty of the revealing God.</margin>
It is as difficult for us to explain how the prophets were able to know that the revelations made to them were distinguished from all diabolical illusions and melancholic imaginations <note>Early modern thinkers often attributed false visions to "melancholy," a condition thought to be caused by an imbalance of bodily fluids affecting the mind and creating vivid, false fantasies.</note>, as it is for them to explain it to us. It seems certain that there was present in them a certain majesty, and a splendor of incomparable light and glory, which was worthy of God when He addresses His own people. This was sometimes so great that the prophets, unable to bear it, were significantly disturbed in both mind and body—whether they were awake or asleep.

<margin>III. And the recognized remarkable light of the revelation itself.</margin>
III. If it pleased the Supreme Power to act more familiarly at times, and to peacefully address the soul without the display of external symbols, it is believable that such a force of light was present—penetrating the inner recesses of the mind—that they could not fail to see the Author of Light within that light. Anyone knows the voice of a parent, a brother, or another close relative from the kind of signs that prove themselves to the consciousness with indubitable evidence, even if they cannot be so easily explained to others for their conviction. The address of God to the soul is arranged in the same way. The friends of God hear and know the voice of God, and easily distinguish it from the voice of anyone else.

<margin>IV. Why was the voice of God speaking first unknown to Samuel?</margin>
IV. I confess that God was not immediately recognized by Samuel <note>Referring to the story in 1 Samuel 3, where the young boy Samuel hears God calling him at night but assumes it is his mentor, the High Priest Eli.</note>. But that happened by a singular dispensation of Divine providence. I will not say now that Samuel was very young, nor that he was unaccustomed to being addressed by God, and that the words of the address were very few, consisting only of the name of the person addressed. I would rather have these two points considered: I. In that address, there was no revelation of any secret, but an awakening of a sluggish mind toward readiness and attention. At the time when future things were being signified, then Samuel knew that God was speaking to him. II. In the beginning, God did not want him to know it; so that the youth, approaching the Priest in that simplicity and candor of his mind, would in no way be suspected; but the Priest would be convinced that nothing here was being done by cunning or by a secret pact. As it happened, the Priest soon did not doubt that God had spoken to Samuel, and he reverently received the words of Samuel as Divine oracles.

<margin>V. The divine fittingness of the things revealed.</margin>
V. Added to this is the fact that sometimes the wisdom, holiness, sublimity, and divine fittingness <note>original: "θεοπρέπεια" (theoprepeia) — a theological term for what is appropriate to the character and nature of God.</note> of the things revealed were so great that they soon insinuated themselves into the mind as having proceeded from God. This happened most especially when the minds of the friends of God were admitted to the holy contemplation of the mysteries of faith, in which that excellence of truth unfolds itself, so that not even the heavenly spirits <note>A reference to angels.</note> could be sated by the meditation upon them. At such times, there converge the majesty of the revealing God, the splendor of the revelation, and the super-celestial light of the things revealed; the mind is so surrounded on all sides by the rays of all these things, that in such great

# ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

<center>...may exult in such a brightness of the Divinity flashing everywhere, with the most pleasant *plerophoria* <note>original: πληροφορίᾳ; a Greek term meaning "full assurance" or "complete certainty," often used in a theological context to describe absolute conviction in faith.</note>.</center>

<margin>VI. Which, however, did not always immediately prove itself to the conscience.</margin>
VI. But this does not hold true in every revelation. For although God never manifests anything of Himself that is not worthy of His divine power, it could nevertheless happen that the prophets recognized the divine nature of the revelation even if the *theoprepeia* <note>original: θεοπρέπεια; a Greek term referring to "that which is fitting for God" or "divine decorum." The author is saying the prophet knows God is speaking, even if the command seems strange or "unlike" God at first.</note> of the matter revealed was not yet manifest to their own conscience. Take Ezekiel as an example: he recognized that it was God speaking to him when he was told, "You shall prepare a cake upon cakes of human excrement in the sight of Israel." Yet, he was so far from thinking the execution of that command was worthy of God or himself that he pleaded against it with a careful prayer (Ezekiel 4:12, 14). Similarly, Peter, in his ecstasy, did not doubt that God was speaking to him, but he did not see the rightness of the matter revealed at first glance. Therefore, when he was ordered to rise, kill, and eat whatever animals he saw without distinction, he replied:

> By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.

(Acts 10:13, 14). In such revelations, the conviction of Divinity does not arise from a consideration of the thing revealed, but from the clarity of the revelation itself, the majesty of the one revealing it, and a secret power that draws out the firmest possible assent.

<margin>VII. It does not seem possible for prophets to be led into error by any Divine revelations.</margin>
VII. It remains to be investigated whether prophets could be certain that they would never be led into error by the revelations made to them. Certainly, if we rightly consider God’s Truthfulness, His Goodness, and the purpose of revelation, it seems hardly possible that any mortal could be deceived by any Divine revelation. For God’s most sacred Truth is utterly foreign to all fraud and deception. God’s most indulgent Goodness does not allow one who commits themselves to His word to be led astray from the path of truth. The purpose of revelation is for man to know God and His will. By what reasoning, then, could it be that God would misuse His own revelation to indicate something that is agreeable neither to His nature nor His will? These things are so clear, and prove themselves so evidently to the conscience, that they expel all fear of the contrary.

<margin>VIII. But a saying of God creates a difficulty. Ezekiel 14:7, 9, 10.</margin>
VIII. Nevertheless, there is no shortage of both certain sayings and examples of revelations that cause hesitation <note>original: "scrupulum"; literally a "scruple" or a small sharp stone in one's shoe, meaning a cause for doubt or unease.</note>. Regarding the sayings of God, there is a memorable and wonderful passage in Ezekiel, Chapter 14, verses 7, 9, and 10: *“Anyone from the house of Israel, or from the foreigners who sojourn in Israel, who separates himself from following me, taking his dung-gods <note>A literal translation of the Hebrew term for idols used in Ezekiel, emphasizing their filthiness.</note> into his heart, and sets the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face: when he comes to a prophet to consult me through him...”*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

...as I am Jehovah, I WILL ANSWER HIM BY MYSELF. But if the prophet is enticed <note>original: *pellectus*; suggests being lured or persuaded into a course of action.</note> to speak a word, I JEHOVAH HAVE ENTICED THAT PROPHET <note>original: *EGO JEHOVA PELLEXERO PROPHETAM IPSUM*; from Ezekiel 14:7-9. This difficult passage suggests God "deceives" a prophet as a form of judgment.</note>, and stretching out my hand against him, I will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. Thus they shall bear the punishment of their iniquity; the punishment of the inquirer and the punishment of the prophet shall be equal. Here, in clear speech, God declares that he sometimes answers an inquirer, not according to the truth of the matter, but according to the corrupt disposition of the inquirer. This does not happen through the fraud or fallacy of a malevolent prophet lying in God's name; rather, God answers through Himself and entices the prophet to speak those words, so that it results in punishment for both the inquirer and the prophet.

<margin>IX. And the complaint of Jeremiah. Chapter IV. 10</margin>
IX. Jeremiah’s complaint in Chapter 4:10 is not far removed from this word of God to Ezekiel. *And I said: Ah, Lord God,* surely you have greatly deceived <note>original Hebrew: אכן השא השאת (*akhen hasha hasheta*); an emphatic construction meaning "surely deceiving you have deceived."</note> *this people and Jerusalem, saying, "Peace shall be for you," when the sword has reached even to the soul.*

<margin>X. As also the history of Balaam, Numbers XXII.</margin>
X. An example also occurs in the story of *Balaam* <note>A famous biblical account of a prophet-for-hire who was eventually stopped by a talking donkey and an angel.</note> in Numbers 22. The messengers of the King of the Moabites come to Balaam. Balaam asks God whether he should go with them. God refuses. Balaam stays home. The messengers persist—others come, more honorable than the first. Balaam consults God again. The oracle responds that he should go. Verse 20: *And God, coming to Balaam at night, said to him: "Since these men have come to call you, rise up and go with them."* Balaam obeys the command. He sets out, but on an ominous journey, and with God being indignant. *And so Balaam, rising in the morning, saddled his donkey and went with the princes of the Moabites. But the anger of God was kindled because he went, and the Angel of Jehovah stood in the way to be an adversary against him.* Why does God thus command Balaam to go, and yet at the same time is angry that he obeys the oracle?

<margin>XI. And that of the Israelites, Judges XX.</margin>
XI. In the same way, the oracle seems to have deceived the Israelites in Judges 20:18. *They went up to the house of God to consult God and said: "Who among us shall go up first to this battle against the Benjaminites?" Jehovah replied: "Judah first."* They obey the oracle. But they are slaughtered in a foul carnage of twenty-two thousand men. Again they consult the oracle, after lamentations and prayers: *they ask, "Shall I go again to battle against the children of Benjamin my brother?" Jehovah replied: "Go up against him."* With what success? Again eighteen thousand men of the Israelites are laid down. Must we not recognize some deception here as well?

XII. Certainly these matters are not without difficulty, which we will nevertheless attempt to remove, so that the glory of the God of Truth and Goodness may remain intact...

# ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

...remains hidden. Therefore, to begin with that discourse found in Ezekiel, the following points must be observed in it.

I. It is not a matter here of the friends of God, nor of upright men who, endowed with a sincere love of truth, long to hear it from God’s own mouth. Rather, it concerns the wicked, who *have brought their own filth into their soul* <note>original: *stercora sua in animum suum induxerunt*; here "filth" refers to idols, often called "dung-gods" in a derogatory sense in the Hebrew Bible</note>—that is, they hold things of no value as idols—and *set the stumbling block of iniquity before themselves*. This means they cherish their favorite errors, stumbling into them so that they sin more and more, acting perversely and receding further from the way of truth and salvation. When these people come to consult God, they do not do so with the intention of being instructed in the truth, but rather so that they might find some pretext in the word of God for their errors and depraved desires. God threatens these men, acting as a just Judge and Avenger of such a wicked soul, that they will be answered according to their filth—that is, according to their own depraved desires. For it is just *that those who refused to receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, for this reason God sends them a powerful delusion, so that they might believe a lie.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:10–11</note> It is just, I say, that those *to whom it did not seem good to acknowledge God, God should give them over to a mind devoid of all judgment.* <note>Romans 1:28; the author uses the Latin *mentem omnis judicii expertem*, usually translated as "reprobate mind."</note>

XIII. II. It should be noted that these things are candidly foretold by God through the prophet to those men, with the intention that they might not be deceived; a warning is added so that they might turn themselves from those wickednesses of theirs, and thus escape this just, yet terrible judgment. *Verses 4 and 5: To seize the house of Israel in their own heart. Therefore say to the house of Israel, "Thus says the Lord Jehovah: Repent, and turn your minds away from your dung-gods," etc.* After such a rebuke, threat, and admonition, those who persist in wallowing in their own filth have only themselves to blame if they are subsequently led astray.

XIV. III. When Jehovah says that he will answer by himself, he does not say it with the intention of bringing forth any word containing a falsehood, in which there is error or deception. Rather, by his unsearchable wisdom, he will so temper his most holy words that those who hear or read them without a love of truth, and with a soul full of depraved desires, will find in those words things which they may abuse to confirm themselves in error. Thus, every occasion for twisting the words of God to their own destruction is not taken away from them.

XV. IV. When God adds that the prophet is enticed <note>original: *pellectum*; lured or persuaded</note> to speak a word by which such consulters are deceived, and that he has been *enticed by Himself*, he is speaking of a prophet who is similar to those consulting him. Such a prophet, loving the wages of iniquity, also loves to [indulge] them in their errors and...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

...to flatter his own desires, and proves himself worthy of that same judgment. God entices him, not by breathing a lie into him—in the way He inspires truth in His friends—but by directing all things through His most holy providence so that many occasions for straying are suggested to him. By abusing these occasions maliciously or recklessly, he is both deceived himself and deceives others. Indeed, it is not without God's providence that teachers of lies often possess great talent, learning, memory, and skill; they have these things from God. Nor is it without God that they notice things which can serve as material for **sophisms** <note>original Greek: *σοφισμάτων*; these are clever but fallacious arguments used to deceive</note>, and that such things come to their clever minds which can be plausibly brought forward to disguise an error. If these things are considered as they should be, there is nothing in this entire discourse that is contrary to Divine Truth and Goodness; rather, it is a declaration of God's just judgment upon those who love darkness more than light. This is done with the intention that they might be turned from the love of falsehood to the love of truth, and thus escape the just vengeance of the Divinity.

<margin>
XVI. On Jeremiah 4:10.
</margin>

XVI. These matters had to be explained at somewhat greater length, since the core of the difficulty was located here; in the remaining points we may now be briefer. As for Jeremiah, when he complains that the people and Jerusalem were deceived by God, he is referring to the sermons of those <insert>false</insert> prophets who promised all things would be secure and prosperous for the people, and especially for Jerusalem (which was the last of all to be captured). He attributes this to God insofar as God had allowed those prophets to lie in such a way, even using His name as a pretext, and did not always punish them immediately. Moreover, he considers God as a Just Judge who gave over a rebellious people—resistant to true warnings and desiring flattering things, however false—to be mocked by the smooth talk of those deceivers.

For He wished both Himself and His people Israel to be celebrated through Balaam, and for Balak to be struck down, as it were, by his own sword. God does not disapprove of the fact that Balaam went, but that he went with an evil intent. For he went greedy for gold, and hoped that somehow he might manage to obtain the promised reward and find the opportunity to curse the people of Israel. This is clear from the response of the Angel, who was rebuking...
