# ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

...should we imagine such a thing in our minds, especially in Divine matters—where it would be the height of impiety to treat the fulfillment of <margin>fulfillment of prophecies</margin> prophecies in a playful or deceptive way? Nevertheless, all faith that relies on such an assertion, since it relies only on the testimony of a man—even one who is honest and worthy of credit, and indeed who is most *trustworthy* <note>original Greek: *ἀξιόπιστος* (axiopistos)</note> among men—is still only human faith, which ultimately rests on the authority of human testimony. However, something more is required here: for the prophets wanted their words to be received as oracles, with that faith which is owed only to Divine utterances. Therefore, the testimony of God Himself must be added, so that Divine authority may be granted to the words of that prophet. Now, God provides this testimony in more than one way.

And first, certainly, when He builds trust in later prophecies through the fulfillment of earlier ones. Indeed, the fulfillment of prophecies, by the order of Divine providence, is a real testimony by which it is established that the prophecies to which the event responded in such a way are from God. From this it further follows that God wills that he to whom He has revealed Himself so familiarly, and whose predictions He has confirmed by the manifestation of the event itself, should be recognized as a prophet by His people. Finally, it is deduced from this that it would not be consistent with the goodness of God to allow men who love truth and virtue to be deceived thereafter under the pretext of His name by one whom they have recognized and received as a prophet by His own command or recommendation. We are taught all of these things in the history of Samuel. <margin>1 Samuel 3:19-20.</margin>

> *And Samuel grew, and Jehovah was with him, and He let none of his words fall to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a Prophet of Jehovah.*

<margin>XXII. We find one instance where the prophet of Bethel used the name of God to cover a lie.</margin>
XXII. Yet we find one instance where a certain prophet used the name of God to cover his own lie. God had sent a man <note>The "Man of God" from Judah mentioned in 1 Kings 13.</note> to foretell the profanation of the altar at Bethel, and had given him this command: that he should neither eat bread nor drink water in that place. Having been invited at great length by the king himself, he religiously obeyed the command of the deity. However, it happened that a certain old Prophet was living in Bethel at the time, whose sons told him what had been done. He pursued the man of God, caught up with him, and enticed him to return; when the man refused because of the divine prohibition, the old prophet replied: *"I also am a prophet, as you are; and an Angel spoke to me by the word of Jehovah, saying, 'Bring him back with you to your house, that he may eat bread and drink water';"* BUT HE WAS LYING TO HIM. The good man, in his ancient simplicity, believed the lie, but to his own great misfortune. For while he was sitting at the table, *the word of Jehovah came* to the prophet <note>original Hebrew: *אל הנביא* (el ha-navi)</note>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

...which he returned <note>original Hebrew: *אשר השיבו* (asher hashibo)</note> to the prophet who had brought him back, who was commanded to say to his overly trusting companion: "Because you have rebelled against the decree of Jehovah and have eaten bread and drunk water... your corpse shall not come into the tomb of your ancestors." And soon, as he departed, a lion killed him; standing by the corpse along with the donkey upon which the prophet had sat. Travelers passing by reported in the city that the body of a man lay in the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. Here, the old man, upon learning this, ordered his sons to saddle his donkey and reached the place where the corpse remained unharmed by the lion. Having picked it up and carried it back to the city, he placed it in his own tomb with mourning and honor. He even performed a funeral lamentation: **"ALAS, MY BROTHER!"** He also commanded his sons that when he died, they should place his bones next to the body of that prophet. For he knew it would certainly come to pass what the word of the Lord had declared through that prophet against the altar of Bethel and all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria. (1 Kings 13).

<margin>
XXIII. The Masters argue in vain over the name of this prophet.
</margin>
XXIII. For my part, I do not approve of the idle curiosity <note>original Greek: *περιεργίας* (periergias)</note> of the Hebrew Masters who anxiously inquire and rashly define who this old prophet might have been. The Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note>, because the text says "a certain prophet" <note>original Hebrew: *נביא אחד* (navi echad)</note>, makes his name "Chad," or *Unus* (One). Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a prominent medieval Jewish commentator</note> testifies that in certain manuscripts it is read "Micah is his name" <note>original Hebrew: *מיכה שמו* (Michah shemo)</note>, and that this is found in the words of the Masters. Some, however, say that he was Amasiah, the priest of Bethel. Others, that he was the prophet Iddo or Addo. Again, some say he was Jonathan, the son of Gershom. These are all nonsense and trifles <note>original Latin: *Liræ & gerræ* — an Erasmian idiom for foolish talk</note> from men demanding to be wiser than what is written.

<margin>
XXIV. Although he was a liar here, he was truly a prophet.
</margin>
XXIV. Yet I do not agree with Lyranus, Dionysius, Hugh, Cajetan, Vatablus <note>A group of influential medieval and Renaissance biblical commentators</note>, and many others who, following Josephus, assert that he was a false prophet. Theodoret <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and bishop</note> argues better; he proves that he was a true prophet, even though he used false words with the Man of God. First, because God predicted through him to the Man of God what was going to happen to him. Second, because he is called nothing else but a "Prophet" in Scripture. Third, because he believed the predictions concerning Josiah. Furthermore, he does not seem to have been entirely devoid of piety, since he recognized the justice of the Divine judgment in that man, performed the funeral rites for him, and wished to be buried in the same grave.

<margin>
XXV. Whatever his motive for lying was,
</margin>
XXV. But with what intention did the old man strive so vehemently to bring the prophet to his table? Josephus—followed by Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado, also known as Abulensis, a 15th-century Spanish bishop and commentator</note> and others—suspects an evil trick by which he wished to destroy that excellent man. The Glossa <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> states: "This false prophet was the chief of the priests, and was greatly cherished by the King as a divine man. # ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

...and that he <note>King Jeroboam</note> might kill him as a malicious evildoer, he <note>the Old Prophet</note> devised a plan to deceive the man of God. He acted quite craftily so that, while the man transgressed God's command, he would incur His wrath (as happened later, when he believed a man more than God). By these means, the things he had predicted would be shown to be false, and thus he could persuade the King, just as he did. However, these theories do not align with the facts we have just proven to be much more probable. It is more likely that this persistent, friendly pressure arose from a sense of humanity, civility, and affection toward the man of God. When the old man saw that he could achieve nothing, he finally added a lie to his prayers—one which he perhaps thought was merely a "dutiful lie" <note>original: *mendacium officiosum*; a historical theological term for a lie told to be helpful or polite</note>, although the outcome proved it was fatal to his guest.

<margin>XXVI. Certainly he sinned remarkably.</margin>
XXVI. But with whatever intent he did this, he certainly bound himself to a massive crime, from which a prophet ought always to be most distant—especially when he testifies that he is speaking in the name of God. Meanwhile, the terrifying judgments of the Divine Power reveal themselves here; they are to be marveled at rather than scrutinized too closely. Certainly, the lie of the Prophet of Bethel seems to be a far greater crime than the other man’s reckless gullibility. Yet, the poor man paid for the latter so severely, while we do not read that the former was punished in an exemplary way. Nevertheless, the old man’s deadly lie is marked with "black coal" <note>original: *atro carbone*; a Latin idiom for a mark of infamy or eternal disgrace</note> to his eternal shame for his misplaced helpfulness.

<margin>XXVII. God made use of his lie to confirm the truth.</margin>
XXVII. God would not have permitted this unless He intended to make use of it <note>original: *abuti*; here meaning "to employ for a different purpose"</note> for the confirmation of the truth. For **I.** By the occasion of this lie, it was made clear to all the people that the outcome would certainly correspond to the words God spoke to the prophet. From what they saw fulfilled, they were to judge the rest. **II.** This entire history should have struck a massive terror into Jeroboam. For if a reckless meal—guilty of nothing except that it was against the prohibition of God, even though a contradictory command from another prophet was presented as a pretext—was punished so severely, what punishment was not owed to Jeroboam for his so insolently desecrating the worship of the Mosaic religion? I credit this observation to Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential theologian</note>, who expressed it in these words: "For if the taking of food against the divine command, done not out of pleasure but out of deception, brought such punishment upon a righteous man, into what kind of punishments will they fall who, having abandoned the God who made them, worship the images of mindless animals?" <note>original Greek: *Εἰ γὰρ τροφῆς μετάληψις παρὰ τὴν θείαν ἐντολὴν γενομένη...*</note> **III.** The fact that the Prophet’s corpse remained unharmed, with the lion itself standing by like a guardian, taught that this man was under God’s care. He had punished him as a transgressor, yet He willed him to be honored as a Prophet, whose predictions by this very...

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

Thus, the Bethelite Old Man’s lie branded him with infamy; it harmed only the overly trusting Man of God; but through the work of Divine providence, it served remarkably to confirm and publicize the truth.

<margin>
XXVIII.
Sometimes God seals a prophet's mission with miracles.
</margin>
XXVIII. FOURTHLY. God is also to be considered to bear clear testimony to a prophet when He seals his mission with a portent and a miracle. For since miracles are operations of a kind that exceed the laws of nature, they are always proofs of Divine omnipotence. *“It is the God of Israel who alone performs wonders.”* <note>original Latin: *Deus Israelis est, qui facit mirabilia solus*</note> Psalm 72:18. It is not probable that God would lend His omnipotence to wicked men to confirm a lie and deceive the pious. Therefore, if someone says they come in the name of God to say or do something notable for God’s people, and they prove this mission with an effect in which the "finger of God" <note>original: *digitus Dei*; a biblical idiom for divine power</note> clearly shines forth, no reason can be given why they should not be received with the obedience of faith as one sent by God. 

God dealt with the people of Israel in this way when He sent Moses to liberate them from Egypt. For when Moses said, *“But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice; for they will say, ‘The Lord has not appeared to you,’”* Jehovah responded that he would be equipped with the power to perform a portent before their eyes, *“so that they may believe,”* He said, *“that Jehovah, the God of their fathers, appeared to you.”* If one portent is not enough, He adds a second: *“This will happen,”* He said, *“if they do not believe you or listen to your voice and the first sign, they may believe the voice and the second sign.”* Indeed, He even adds a third, so that even persistent stubbornness might be subdued to the submission of faith. Exodus 4:1, 2, 5, 8, 9. Nor was that effort without success. For when Moses performed those signs before the eyes of the people, the people believed. verses 30, 31. 

The widow of Zarephath <note>original: *Sareptana*</note> was convinced by the same argument; when Elijah had raised her son from the dead, the woman said to him, *“now I know by this experience that you are a man of God, and the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”* 1 Kings 17:24. Naaman also, recently cured of his leprosy by a miracle, returned to the man of God and acknowledged that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, and he honored Elisha as a great minister of that God. 2 Kings 5:15.

# ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

<margin>XXIX. The use of which is principal in a double case.</margin>
XXIX. Two things, however, must be observed here; the first of which is that it was not necessary, nor fitting for Divine wisdom, to confirm the missions of all prophets—much less their prophecies—with miracles; but that their principal use was in a double case. I. When someone comes equipped with a unique mandate to deliver an extraordinary and great message in God’s name, or to perform a completely unusual ministry: especially if he is sent to organize the entire form of religion. II. When something once commanded and established by God Himself is to be abolished <note>original Latin: *abrogandum*; to repeal or annul a law</note>, and another form of Divine worship is to be substituted for it.

<margin>XXX. First, when a Prophet is sent to organize the entire form of religion.</margin>
XXX. If someone comes in the name of God to perform something unusual, or to stir the people to perform unusual things, and to shape all the ceremonies of religion, reason seems to require that he also possess unusual evidence—signs that convince the mind of the Divine mandate he carries. For there is great danger on both sides, whether one believes a man presenting such a mandate, or does not believe him. If he is believed rashly and without sufficient reason, there is the danger that minds seduced by the deceptive grandiosity of an idle or malicious man <note>original: *maleferiati hominis*; literally "a man keeping holiday badly," meaning someone idle or up to no good</note> may be reduced to such straits that they pay the just penalties for their thoughtless credulity. If the mandate is not believed, yet actually has God as its author, there is the fear that one might bring the wrath and vengeance of the scorned Deity upon one's own head. Therefore, it is necessary for such a "delegate" of God <note>original: *mandatarium*; a person acting on behalf of another</note>, so to speak, to confirm his mission with arguments by which a prudent and cautious mind may be put at ease, and anyone who refuses to believe may be stripped of every appearance of a just excuse. It is hardly possible to achieve this more effectively than by the display of miracles, which make it manifest to all observers that a present Divinity is with such a man. This is the reason why Jehovah equipped Moses with so many miracles.

<margin>XXXI. Second, if a form of worship once established must be discarded.</margin>
XXXI. But the necessity for miracles is no less when a form of worship established by God comes to be changed. For since that form which is to be discarded <note>original: *antiquanda*; to be treated as old or obsolete</note> was supported by miracles, the force that moves the previous one out of its place must be of no less efficacy: and the mind must be convinced of this later part of the Divine will with at least equal evidence. In that case, miracles are not opposed to miracles in a way that some blunt the validity of others; no more than the Divine will is opposed to itself. But, as God disposes all things sweetly according to the immensity of His wisdom, as is fitting for each age; and by His eternal counsel He determined to prescribe some things for a time that were suitable to that time, for those...

For this reason, Christ and the Apostles proved their doctrine—in which the old Mosaic worship was being made obsolete—with such stupendous wonders. They did this to make it publicly clear that they were sent by God for the proclamation of the Gospel no less than Moses was sent for the proclamation of the Law. *While God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.* Hebrews 2:4.

<margin>

Miracles were

XXXII. Moreover, we see that it has occurred at times that, through the wickedness of kings and the lethargy of the people, there has been a significant departure from the straight path of religion. This might happen through a change in ceremonies or the mixing of religion with idolatry. Whenever this happened, it seemed right to the Deity to oppose the encroaching vices of the age with certain remarkable men who, having rebuked the impiety as it deserved, called their listeners back to pure worship. In such cases, a sharp repetition and insistence upon Divine institutions should certainly have been enough; however, because the people and their leaders were not just drifting, but rushing with great momentum toward impiety, God willed to fortify the rebukes of His faithful servants with new miracles. 

The history of Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel who famously set up golden calves for worship</note> provides a memorable example: when he had corrupted religion with many of his own institutions and built an altar at Bethel against God's command—to alienate the people's hearts from the Temple at Jerusalem—a prophet was sent to him. This prophet predicted that a son named Josiah <note>A later king of Judah known for his major religious reforms</note> would be born to the house of David, who would sacrifice the priests of the high places upon that altar and burn human bones upon it. To grant credibility to this prophecy, he performed a wonder that very day, saying, *“This is the sign that the Lord has spoken: behold, this altar shall be split apart, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.”* And as he spoke, the altar was split, and the ashes were poured out from the altar, according to the wonder which the Man of God had performed by the word of the Lord. 1 Kings 13. 

Later, when Ahab was reigning and Jezebel <note>The Phoenician queen who promoted the worship of Baal in Israel</note> was raging, the affairs of religion were in a most wretched state; Israel was vehemently rebuked by the voice of Elijah. But so that the schemes of Jezebel, the frauds of the priests of Baal <note>term: Baaliticorum; relating to Baal, a Canaanite deity</note>, and finally the vanity of all idolatry might be exposed to the confusion of everyone, God intervened with a miracle. Fire descended from heaven and burned up the soaking-wet sacrifices, consuming the wood, the stones, and even the dust itself. Seeing this, the people cried out, *“The Lord, he is God; the Lord, he is God.”* 1 Kings 18:39.

If it should please God on other occasions to perform miracles through His servants, or concerning them—as it is established has frequently been done—this must be attributed to the infinite goodness of the Divine power, which with such great mercy supports human weakness **exceedingly abundantly** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ (*hyper ek perissou*), a phrase often used in the New Testament to describe God’s overflowing grace</note>. obviously false
doctrines.

XXXIV. From this also follows what I wish to be observed in the second place: after God has clearly explained His will and sealed it with a miracle, no wonders are to be valued—no matter how much they present themselves under the appearance of miracles—which are put forward in support of a contrary doctrine. For it must remain a fixed principle that what He Himself has stamped with the seal of true miracles cannot but have proceeded from God; and what openly opposes truth so confirmed cannot but be false. Consequently, a wonder produced to confirm an opposite doctrine is not a true miracle, but the illusions of deceptive spirits, which God permits to happen in this way to test the constancy of His own people. 

For example: God had proven to the people of Israel by the most certain and well-tested miracles that religious worship is owed to Him alone; this ought to have been certain and beyond doubt for the Israelites. The Devil, who is the "god of this world," has his own **initiates** <term>mystas: originally referring to those initiated into secret Greek religious mysteries; here used for priests of false idols</term>, through whom he might entice some of the Israelites to his own worship. Lest he should seem inferior to the God of Israel, he himself produces certain signs through these initiates of his, with which he plays wonderful and wretched tricks upon the senses and minds of mortals. God does not even wish these to be attended to. Deuteronomy 13:1, 2, 3. Nor indeed are they worthy of attention. For since the falsity of the doctrine they are used to confirm can be clear from a comparison with the true doctrine, and since God never misuses His power to confirm a lie, it is rightly concluded that those marvels are illusions and tricks—surpassing, perhaps, human strength and skill, but not the Devil’s. And it is easier to incline the mind to this conclusion when one considers that God Himself forewarned of such fraud, and of the reasons why He sometimes allows it to be constructed by the Devil. Compare Matthew 24:24, 2 Thessalonians 2:9.

for the Prophets

...mitigated by repentance. II. It could have been possible that the King spoke with Gehazi, while he was still a leper, by maintaining a proper distance: just as Naaman the leper came with his retinue to the door of Elisha's house to negotiate with him about the cure of his leprosy (2 Kings 5:9-10). Similarly, those four lepers called out to the gatekeepers of the city of Samaria and reported that the siege was lifted and the Syrian camp deserted (2 Kings 7:8). Also, ten men who were lepers met Christ, and standing far off, they cried out, *Jesus, Master, have mercy on us* (Luke 17:12). It seems that Moses did not forbid every kind of conversation with lepers, but only living together with them. However, these ways of reconciling the accounts <note>The author is addressing a chronological problem: how King Jehoram could speak familiarly with Gehazi in 2 Kings 8 if Gehazi had been cursed with permanent leprosy in 2 Kings 5.</note> are hardly satisfying to the mind. For Elisha’s curse is quite eloquent and explicit, in which he denounces perpetual leprosy not only for Gehazi, but also for his descendants; it seems unlikely that such a short delay of the disease could satisfy the curse. Nor is it probable that the king would have wanted to speak with a leper. Furthermore, the conversation was quite long and familiar, taking place in the court—where that noble woman whose son Elisha had raised from the dead came to appeal to the king—rather than in an open field. Therefore, it is very unlike the examples cited where lepers are said to have called out to others from a distance. It remains, therefore, III. for us to believe that this conversation of the king with Gehazi was established before his affliction, and is narrated through a certain <term>hysterologia</term> <note>original: "ύστερολογία"—a Greek rhetorical term for a "later-account," where events are placed out of their chronological order for thematic reasons</note>, out of its proper place, without preserving the order of time. For simply because the cure of Naaman and the punishment of Gehazi were mentioned first, it does not mean they happened first. Examples of similar chronological displacement are frequent and obvious to everyone in the Holy Scriptures; there is no need for us to linger on listing them now.

## BOOK I. CHAPTER XV. ##

Ananias, whom Peter did not even threaten with death. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD) known for his allegorical interpretations of Scripture.</note> thinks that Ananias was so struck by such a heavy rebuke that he died from excessive shame and sorrow. But it is truer to say that Peter's voice was the **moral cause** <note>original: "caussam uti vocant moralem." In theological logic, a "moral cause" is an action (like a command or prayer) that moves God to act, even though the human speaker has no power of their own.</note> of this miracle, which God performed at his word. God willed to make the authority of the Apostles, the power of the Gospel, and the Divinity of the Holy Spirit illustrious through such a stupendous work. Although the spirit of the Gospel is disposed entirely toward gentleness and kindness, God nevertheless willed that at the beginning of its preaching, some terrifying examples should stand out, so that fear might be struck into stubborn men. And this is what is said in **verse 11: Great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.**

XXXVIII. But Paul also showed himself no less terrible toward Elymas the Sorcerer. When Paul was explaining the way of God to the Proconsul <note>original: "Proprætorem." Sergius Paulus was the Roman governor of Cyprus.</note> Sergius Paulus, Elymas interrupted with shameless words, striving to turn the Proconsul away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, set his eyes on him and is said to have addressed him thus: *O full of all deceit and all malice, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you shall be blind, not seeing the sun for a season.* Immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking *some to lead him by the hand.* **Acts 13:9, 10, 11.**

XXXIX. There are those who refer the **Rod** mentioned in 1 Corinthians 4:21 to this power: *What do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod?* On this subject, that most distinguished man **William Saldenus** <note>Guilielmus Saldenus (1627–1694), a Dutch Reformed theologian and close friend of the author.</note>, the most faithful and sweet of my friends, published a very learned Dissertation. Certainly, that power seems to belong here which is magnificently proclaimed in 2 Corinthians 10:3, 4, 5, 6, where the Apostle ends with these words: *And being ready to punish all disobedience.* To be sure, the Church at that time lacked the protection of a Civil Magistrate; yet the minds of mortals are so constituted that, if all terror is absent, they can scarcely—if at all—be kept to their duty. For this reason, Christ granted his Apostles a miraculous power of punishing. Meanwhile, it was wisely observed by Calvin: *Since miracles for the most part ought to reflect the nature of Christ, who is entirely gentle, sweet, beneficial, and merciful; therefore, rare examples of a different power were produced by the Apostles.* Nor should it be thought that they were equipped with this power whenever they pleased to take revenge on someone; rather, *the same Spirit of God who thus armed them was also the director of its right and lawful use.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how divine missions are authenticated. While the previous page focused on the "terrifying examples" of miracles performed by the Apostles Peter and Paul to establish their authority, the author now pivots to a difficult question: how did the Old Testament prophets gain credibility when they performed no immediate miracles?</meta>

<header>ON THE MARKS OF TRUE PROPHECY.</header>

...if a proclamation is strengthened by a present miracle, or if the mission of a Representative of the Divine Will <note>original: "exemplaris Numinis"</note> burns bright through vengeance against the stubborn, it is no wonder if he wins great authority among the people. It must be admitted, however, that this does not happen to all Prophets. 

<margin>How did they prove their mission, they for whose sake no miracle was performed?</margin>
And what do they have to offer, who set forth their first prophecy? Those for whose sake no miracle has yet been performed? Whose prophecies have not yet been sealed by God, neither by the outcome of events nor by any other means? Let us take Isaiah, or Micah, or Jeremiah, when they were called by God to the prophetic office and held their first sermons to the people. Or let us take Jonah, sent to the Ninevites to predict their imminent destruction. How did they prove their mission and win trust for their words among the people of Israel? How did the latter, a foreign man, persuade a most powerful city to admit his message as a heavenly oracle? What crime would it have been if they had argued that the prophets and prophecies should first be tested—about which nothing had yet been established for them—before they received words that were perhaps pious, but nonetheless human, as the dictates of the Supreme Deity?

Here I confess that I am stuck <note>original: "hærere," meaning to be at a loss or hesitate.</note>, and I see scarcely any path open to escape. Must we say that the men whom God admitted to the prophetic office were so distinguished for wisdom and piety, and so well known to their fellow citizens and countrymen, that no suspicion of fraud could fall upon them? That they came forth from the Schools of the Prophets <note>Groups or guilds of students who studied the law and spiritual discipline under a master prophet.</note> and provided evidence there of their familiar communication with God? That their first sermons were founded on the Mosaic doctrine <note>The Law of Moses.</note> and contained rebukes and threats, or exhortations and promises, which were bound to prove themselves to the people's conscience? And that there was present such a majesty and efficacy in their speaking, which we now cannot imagine for ourselves, but which they nevertheless perceived without difficulty, since they were permitted to look upon and hear them in person?

As for Jonah, must we say that he explained at length to the Ninevites what had happened to him in his hesitation and flight—how he was swallowed by a whale, returned to the land after three days, and finally reached the city by a repeated command—and that he narrated this with such gravity of moving speech <note>original: "pathetici sermonis." In the 17th century, this meant speech capable of stirring deep emotion and conviction.</note> that he found trust among men convicted by the conscience of their crimes? Finally, since those prophetic sermons showed the right path of virtue by which predicted calamities might be avoided or promised goods obtained, was it not certainly safest to offer them obedience as if they had come from heaven, until the fates themselves explained themselves more clearly? Indeed, all these things can be said, and truly they have their weight.

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

But whether these arguments are sufficient to remove every difficulty deserves more careful consideration. No further thoughts occur to me now, but I find through experience what I warned at the beginning: there will always remain something in which I do not satisfy myself, much less expect to satisfy others.

<margin>XLI. The outcome does not seem to match many prophecies.</margin>
XLI. In the meantime, a great difficulty reveals itself, which I believe should be resolved as conveniently as possible. Since the truth of prophecies is to be judged by their outcome, why is it that the outcome does not match many prophecies? God Himself warns of this in the book of Jeremiah: *At whatever moment I speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, that I will pull up, break down, and destroy: if that nation against which I have spoken turns from its evil, I also will repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it. And at whatever moment I speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, that I will build and plant it; if it does what is evil in my eyes by not listening to my voice, I in turn will repent of the good with which I said I would benefit it.* <note>original: "Jer. XVIII. 7. 8. 9. 10." This passage establishes the principle of "conditional" prophecy, where God's stated plan may change based on human response.</note>

<margin>XLII. But in those cases, a silent condition lies underneath.</margin>
XLII. To remove this doubt <note>original: "scrupulus," literally a small sharp stone that causes discomfort in a shoe; a metaphor for a lingering doubt or hesitation.</note>, predictions must be distinguished so that some are considered absolute, while others are suspended upon a certain condition. The former must always be fulfilled; the latter are fulfilled only when the condition upon which they are suspended exists. Indeed, speaking accurately and philosophically, all are always fulfilled—even the conditional ones. For, as students of Logic <note>original: "Logicorum filii," literally "sons of the Logicians," a common academic idiom for those trained in formal reasoning.</note> know, the truth of a conditional statement does not consist in the truth of the prior part or the result, but in the connection between the two. For example: let us take this prediction: *if Israel constantly obeys the commands of its God, it will enjoy prosperity for many centuries in the peaceful possession of the land of Canaan.* That promise remains true, even if Israel neither obeys nor prospers in the land. Nor does Israel have the right, based on this promise, to expect any prosperity unless obedience has come first. Furthermore, it should be observed that such a condition is sometimes expressed in plain speech, and sometimes implied to be understood silently. Where it is expressed, there is no difficulty. But in threats or promises, even when not expressed, a condition must frequently be understood. And this is what the words of God in Jeremiah mean: in which, however, God speaks in a popular way after the manner of humans, as if led by regret <note>original: "pœnitudine," a term the author uses to describe God "changing His mind," though he notes this is a human way of speaking.</note> He changes His word and plan. How these things ought to be understood in a way worthy of God—that He is unchanging—is something we learned as children.

<margin>XLIII. What kind of prophecy it is</margin>
XLIII. Let us illustrate the matter with one or two examples. Isaiah said to King Hezekiah <note>original: "Hizkiæ Regi"</note>: *set your household affairs in order, for you shall soon die, and not...*

### ON THE SIGNS OF TRUE PROPHECY.

<margin>Hezekiah—concerning the death of Hezekiah.</margin>
you shall live no longer. <note>original: "Jeſ. XXXVIII. 1." This refers to Isaiah 38:1, where the prophet tells the King to set his house in order because he is dying.</note> Yet it happened otherwise: for Hezekiah was recovered from his illness and lived for fifteen years more. What should be said here? **Molinaeus** <note>Pierre du Moulin (1568–1658), a prominent French Huguenot theologian and author of "Vates" (The Prophet).</note> in *The Prophet, Book I, Chapter VI,* believes that Isaiah answered in this way before the counsel of God was fully perceived. And therefore, he was soon ordered to correct what he had pronounced in error. But that great man does not seem to have noticed how Isaiah began his speech; for coming to the king, he said, *"Thus says the LORD."* <note>original: "ſic ait Jehova."</note> Certainly, given Isaiah's virtue and faithfulness, he would not have dared to use God's name and authority for his own word without consulting Him. To me, it seems there is no doubt that Isaiah said whatever he said by God’s command and according to God’s mind. What then? He indicated that the disease from which the king suffered was lethal by its own nature, and that it was certain he would shortly die from it. But there was a <term>hidden condition</term> <note>original: "subintelligebatur conditio," an implied or understood requirement not explicitly stated in the text.</note> understood: unless, through remarkable repentance and powerful prayers, he might obtain a miraculous cure from God. Hezekiah certainly understood the matter this way; nor did he think he was hearing an irrevocable sentence of imminent death. Instead, turning his face to the wall and with many tears, he implored the mercy of God, and not in vain. And for this reason, Isaiah was sent to him with repeated instructions, not to "correct" what he had wrongly pronounced without consulting God, but to more fully explain the mind of the Lord and to demonstrate how great the power of repentance and prayer truly was.

<margin>XLIV. And on the destruction of the Ninevites.</margin>
XLIV. Let us also add the history of Jonah; who was sent to the Ninevites to preach, *"Yet forty days, and then Nineveh shall be overthrown."* <note>Jonah 3:4.</note> To all appearances, this prediction seemed absolute: yet there was nonetheless an underlying condition—unless the Ninevites should remarkably repent. If they were not fully convinced that such a condition existed, they at least suspected it. Hence they turned themselves to prayers and fasting, saying, *"Who knows if God will turn and repent, so that He may turn away from His fierce anger and we do not perish?"* <note>original: "quis ſcit, an reverſurus ſit, & pœniteat Deum..." (Jonah 3:9). Here, "repent" in reference to God means a change of intended action rather than a confession of sin.</note> And in truth, God "repented" of the evil which He had said He would inflict upon them, and He did not inflict it. <note>Jonah 3:10.</note> That is, by the very act, He showed that this condition had been underlying the prediction: that if they performed penance for their crimes, they might exchange them for a better way of life.

<margin>XLV. How absolute predictions can be distinguished from those that depend on a silent condition.</margin>
XLV. Meanwhile, it remains to be asked: how can one distinguish whether a prediction is absolute, or whether it is suspended upon a condition that is kept silent? ### BOOK I. CHAPTER XV.

...by certain circumstances. If we look at the nature of things, those prophecies are absolute which fall into these categories: 

I. Those by which specific events are foretold with their particular circumstances and the definition of time, place, manner, and persons. Such was the prophecy about the altar at Bethel being profaned by Josiah, involving the burning of priests and human bones; the prophecy about the occupation of Babylon by Cyrus, the commander of the Persian and Median army; and the prophecy about the coming of the Messiah in the flesh, born in Bethlehem of a Virgin and from the Royal family, though reduced to poverty, etc. For the gathering of so many specific details, which no human wisdom could ever join together, cannot come from anywhere else but the counsel of God; He set these forth for the very purpose of proving by the event that He is endowed with a foreknowledge that senses all things before they happen.

II. Those by which the internal disposition of the soul is foretold, whether it be wicked and abnormally deviating from duty, or praiseworthy and holy. For example, when it is predicted that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened so that he does not let Israel go, or that the Israelites will turn away from the path shown to them by Moses, or that eyes will be blinded and the minds of many will be covered with a callous <note>The author uses the image of a "callus" (thickened skin) to describe a mind that has become insensitive or stubborn to spiritual truth.</note> so that they do not receive the Messiah and His Gospel. Or on the contrary, the prophecies about their conversion in the "latter days" <note>original: "noviſſima dierum," a biblical phrase referring to the end of the current age or the era of the Messiah.</note>, about the circumcision of the heart, about the law being placed in their minds and inscribed on their souls, about the recognition of the Messiah, and also about the calling of the nations <note>original: "vocatione gentium," referring to the conversion of the Gentiles to Christianity.</note> and their conversion from the unspeakable worship of false gods, and many other things of that kind. For these events actually serve as the conditions upon which other things depend, but they themselves do not depend on any condition.

III. Those by which things are foretold that are in the hand and judgment of God alone, and which clearly cannot be changed by any human variation. Such are the predictions of miracles to be performed by Christ and His Apostles; the coming of Christ to the final and universal judgment; the burning of the universe, the resurrection of the flesh, and similar matters.

IV. Finally, those by which things are foretold that surpass the shrewdness of human plans and the direction of <term>secondary causes</term> <note>In the philosophy of this period, God is the "First Cause." "Secondary causes" are the natural laws, physical forces, or human choices that God uses to bring about his will.</note>, and which, when considered in themselves, are devoid of all probability and likelihood. For the more they are removed from human senses and the usual arrangement of secondary causes, the more clearly they represent the counsel of God, who wants the glory of His works attributed to Himself. And here the harsh but spirited saying of **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) known for his provocative defense of faith against Greek philosophy.</note> holds true: **I BELIEVE BECAUSE IT IS IMPOSSIBLE** <note>original: "CREDO QUIA IMPOSSIBILE EST"</note>—impossible, that is, in the judgment of the flesh and the plans of men. The more improbable the return from the Babylonian captivity and the rebuilding of Jerusalem seemed, the more certain its prediction had to be considered. For indeed, thus says the Lord: *I am He who*

XLVI. Furthermore, it can be gathered from certain specific circumstances which predictions are to be understood in an absolute sense—namely, those which God has confirmed either by a **Miracle** or by an **Oath**. For since those predictions that presuppose a condition of duty (either fulfilled or neglected) more easily prove themselves to the conscience by their own fairness, and represent a connection of events consistent with both Divine and human nature, it seems less necessary for God to change the order of nature by performing a miracle to confirm them. When He does perform a miracle, it is to be expected that His omnipotence will surely provide the predicted thing, and that He will never "repent" <note>In this theological context, "repentance" refers to God changing His declared plan or mind, rather than a confession of sin.</note> of His prediction.

An **Oath**, however, declares the immutability of God’s counsel regarding the matter for which it is employed; it excludes everything that is sometimes attributed to God under the name of "repentance." God himself teaches this in Psalm 89:35–36: *Once have I sworn by my Holiness, I will not lie to David: His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before me.* It is true that God usually makes promises of this kind dependent on the condition of obedience; but here He declares that no transgressions of the house of David will be such that they make the promise, sanctioned by an oath, void. As the preceding verses imply (verses 30–33): *If his children forsake my law... then I will visit their transgression with the rod... but my lovingkindness I will not utterly take from him, nor will I lie against my faithfulness.*

Finally, this prediction is so <term>ἀμεταμέλητος</term> <note>original: "ἀμεταμέλητος" (ametamelētos) — a Greek term meaning unchangeable, irrevocable, or without regret.</note> that it is in no man's power to alter it in any way. Jeremiah 33:20–21: *Thus says Jehovah: If you can break my covenant of the day and my covenant of the night, so that there should not be day and night in their season; then also may my covenant with David be broken.* Paul teaches the very same thing most clearly in Hebrews 6:17–18: *In this matter, God, willing more abundantly to show to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, guaranteed it with an oath; so that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong consolation.* It is true, of course, that God requires the heirs of the promise to hold fast to the hope set before them with constant faith. But it is no less true that God so governs their minds by His omnipotent grace that they do not shamefully de[sert]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("de-") and continues on the next page.</note>

# ON THE PROPHETS BEFORE THE LAW.

<margin>
I. Three periods of the prophets.
</margin>
So far we have dealt with Prophets in general: now it pleases us to weave together the **HISTORY OF THE CHIEF PROPHETS**, and to inquire when the gift and office of prophecy began, how it was continued, and finally whether and when it ceased? Indeed, one may distinctly consider three periods of time in which God dispensed prophecy in different ways. I. **BEFORE THE MOSAIC LAW.** II. **UNDER THE LAW.** III. **UNDER THE GOSPEL.**

<margin>
II. The first of men was the first of the Prophets.
</margin>
II. **BEFORE THE LAW**, he who was the first of men was also the first of the Prophets. For to **ADAM**, created in His own image and dwelling in great familiarity with Him, God offered Himself above all else to be known—both according to those things which nature can teach about God, and those which are learned only from gracious revelation. To this latter category, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, must be referred the subsistence of the one and individual unity in three persons <note>A reference to the doctrine of the Trinity being revealed even to Adam</note>. To him also He revealed the order of the creation of the universe, the formation of his spouse from his rib while he slept, the prohibition against tasting of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and other things which it was necessary for him to know, as one to whom God had entrusted dominion over the things He had created. After the fall, however, He rebuked him with just indignation, pronounced sentence, and narrated at length the evils with which he and his posterity were to be punished. Finally, He comforted him with a most pleasant address, in which, though in very brief words, the sum of the entire Gospel is contained—which we have explained more fully elsewhere <note>This likely refers to the "Protoevangelium" in Genesis 3:15, the first promise of a redeemer</note>. It is believable that God thereafter delivered this promise, first uttered in enigmatic speech, somewhat more clearly to **ADAM**, who, having grasped it with living faith as a most precious deposit, carefully preserved it and did not neglect to communicate it to his sons and grandsons. These things are inferred from the commentaries of Moses <note>The Book of Genesis</note> and the nature of the matter itself, through no difficult collection of evidence.

<margin>
III. The teaching of the ancient Hebrews concerning Adam's book.
</margin>
III. The Masters of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis</note> say that a certain book, containing celestial wisdom, was delivered to Adam by the "Lord of secrets." They say he attempted to carry it with him out of Paradise; but it was snatched away just as he had exited and was taken up into heaven. Soon, however, it was restored at his supplication, on the condition that he communicate the wisdom contained therein to his posterity. At first glance, these things seem ridiculous: but they contain the teaching of the Ancients, and teach the following truths through parabolic speech. I. That the knowledge of Divine things in the state of integrity <note>The state before the Fall</note> was communicated to Adam, partly through <term>manifestation</term> <note>original Greek: φανέρωσιν (phanerōsin)</note>, as far as <term>that which may be known of God</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ γνωσὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ (to gnōston tou Theou)</note> is concerned, and partly through the <term>revelation of mysteries</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν μυστηρίων (apokalypsin tōn mystēriōn)</note>. II. That this knowledge was for the most part lost by the just judgment of God, by which he vindicated His most holy...

<margin>VI. Did Jude take his tradition regarding Enoch’s prophecy from these sources?</margin>
VI. And yet, it is a wonder that some wish to claim that the **Blessed Jude** fetched this prophecy of **Enoch** from such a futile, trifling, and in every respect **Apocryphal** writing. To me, this seems in no way probable. For the Apostle certainly did not intend to detract from the faith and reverence of his most holy letters, in a matter of the greatest importance, by the allegation of an absurd script. Furthermore, **Jude** does not say that **Enoch** "wrote" thus; nor is there found in the book which is called "of Enoch" <note>The author is referring to the various fragments of the Book of Enoch known in the 17th century; the full text was not rediscovered in the West until later.</note> even a trace or a footprint <note>original: "vola vel vestigium"</note> of this prophecy. This was learnedly demonstrated with many reasons by the recently praised **Heidegger**. <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss theologian who wrote extensively on the history of the patriarchs.</note>

<margin>VII. Or was it rather from the Mosaic history?</margin>
VII. But from where, then, did the Apostle draw the prophecy of **Enoch**? The most celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a leading 17th-century Dutch theologian famous for his "Covenant" or "Federal" theology.</note> conjectures that **Jude** gathered it from the **Mosaic history** <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>. *For*, he says, *it is well established from the sacred scriptures that Enoch prophesied. For **Jude** ascribes a specific formula of prophecy to **Enoch** which cannot be learned from **Moses**. I should believe, therefore, that **Jude** had these things from a well-known and admitted tradition of that time: which he knew to be true through the Spirit as his teacher, and worthy to be consecrated to eternity in this Epistle of his.

**BOOK I, CHAPTER XVI.**

...to be disturbed again by a flood, nor to wipe out the human race by waters. This plan he set forth under the name of a **covenant**, and confirmed it with the solemn sign <note>The Latin *sacramento* here refers to a sacred pledge or visible symbol.</note> of the rainbow formed in the clouds.

<margin>IX. An absurd opinion regarding the natural necessity of the universal flood.</margin>
IX. At this point, even as I hurry along, a new and—as I certainly judge—absurd opinion forces a delay upon me; of such ideas, this present century has produced a most abundant crop. There are those who refer the Flood—which sacred history testifies was sent by an angry God to wash away the sins of mortals—to purely natural causes in such a way that they argue it happened with no less necessity at that specific time than do the eclipses of the sun or moon at their fixed seasons. To achieve this, they imagine such a fabric of the universe that, out of chaos, according to the **rules of motion**, through the passage of time and a long series of natural causes, a well-ordered world finally had to emerge—as indeed it did. But they conceive the original constitution of the universe then formed much differently than it is now. And because of their incredible cleverness of mind, they depict it no less accurately than if they had been present to witness it with their own eyes and diligent care. They are unconcerned with what **Moses** reported about the creation of the world in the span of six days, provided that the dictates of their own **Philosophy** remain safe and sound <note>original: "farta tecta," a Roman legal term meaning "tight and roofed," used here to mean keeping a theory intact.</note>. Although **Moses** was perhaps not entirely unskilled in their philosophy (which is added out of modesty), he nevertheless thought it sufficient to record his history in a plainer manner <note>original: "crassiori Minerva," literally "with a thicker Minerva," an idiom for a simple, practical understanding as opposed to subtle academic theory.</note>, suited to the capacity of the Israelite people and as it served the establishment of religion. From that form of the universe, they deduce the necessity of the flood according to the eternal **rules of motion**; and they do so with such a neat concatenation of causes that they could not have a clearer view of it if they had formed it themselves, or had at least been present as advisors to God while He was forming it.

<margin>X. This view is refuted.</margin>

> *They became vain in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened. While they claim to be wise, they have become fools.* Romans 1:21-22.

For whatever they may boast, they neither know the fabric of the world from their own philosophy, nor do they understand its dissolution. To defend both, they build for themselves a universe out of ideas fluttering in their empty brains, the likes of which no mortal has seen, nor Scripture taught—indeed, the form of which is openly contrary to the narrative of Scripture. It would be a wonder if God did not say to them what he once said to **Job** out of the whirlwind:
> *Who is this that darkens counsel with ignorant words? Gird up your loins now like a man; and what I ask of you, make known to me. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who arranged its dimensions, since you are so knowledgeable? Or who stretched a measuring line upon it?* Job 38:2-5.

# ON THE PROPHETS BEFORE THE LAW.

...taught in the humble school of the prophets and Apostles, we believe Moses—or rather God—as he narrates, and through faith we understand, <margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin> *that the world was framed by the word of God, so that the things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.* And while we understand these things by faith, we look down from on high, laugh at, and detest all that "unwise wisdom" <note>original Greek: *ἄσοφον σοφίαν* (asophon sophian), a play on words suggesting a foolish or pseudo-wisdom.</note> of proud philosophy, and the delirious reasonings of a maddened wisdom; certain that the foolishness of God is wiser than all human wisdom. We believe the same Moses: that just as it was not nature, but sin, that brought death to man; so it was not nature, but the crimes of the human race, that brought this horrendous slaughter upon the whole world. God sent the flood, not because the laws of nature and the order established by Himself then required it, but because He saw the wickedness of man increase on the earth, <margin>Genesis 6:5</margin> *and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.*

XI. Indeed, I hear it said by sharp-witted men <note>The author is likely referring to early modern "physico-theologians" or Cartesian thinkers who tried to explain miracles through natural laws.</note> that God, to whom all His works have been known from eternity, so balanced the weights of the "great machine" of the universe that these two coincided at the same time: the remarkable wickedness of men, and the collapse of the laborious mass. This is indeed true; but it does not satisfy the emphasis of the Mosaic narrative. For it does not join the impiety of men and the terrifying fall of the world in the way that the crimes of mortals and the "silences of the moon" <note>original: *lunae silentia*, a classical poetic term for the period when the moon is not visible, used here to mean a natural, inevitable astronomical event.</note> are joined; but rather as a meritorious cause <term>meritorious cause: a legal or theological term for an action that deserves a specific reward or punishment as a direct consequence</term> is joined with its effect. Meanwhile, it is certain that God, who had determined to permit the wickedness of men to rise to that peak of impiety at that time, and who had decreed to wash away the sins of men with a universal flood, also so established the order of the universe from the beginning that at that same time there would be sufficient material for as much water as was required to cover the earth. But for us mortals, however much we may swell with the opinion of our own wisdom, it is not therefore necessary to know where that water came from, how it was moved, and what was finally done with it. It is enough to acknowledge that all things are ready at the Divine nod. In this terrifying judgment of God, let those things remain which cannot be explained by us according to the order of nature. As many of us as are Christians—not by profession of a name, but in the truth of the matter—we believe the sacred scriptures even in those things whose full reason we do not grasp.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.

XIII. And when the Gospel was to be preached—by which men are allured to communion with God in Christ—the Jews having been rejected, the message went to the descendants of Japheth. It was in their own languages that the most sacred volumes of the Christian religion were published. Thus it was granted to Japheth to dwell in the tents of Shem: that is, to be admitted to the communion of the Church, which before the coming of the Messiah had been limited to the family of Shem. For although God excludes the children of neither Shem nor Ham from the Church, it is certain that the faith of Christ has flourished most greatly since the age of the Apostles in Europe and in those parts of Asia which fell to the lot of Japheth. ### ON THE PROPHETS BEFORE THE LAW.

Histories testify to this: namely, those parts of Asia which the Canaanites had long possessed were eventually conquered by the Greeks and Romans <note>The author interprets the expansion of the Greeks and Romans (descendants of Japheth) into the Levant and North Africa as the fulfillment of Noah's prophecy in Genesis 9.</note>. <margin>XV. Next in this series follow Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</margin>
XV. From that time, God conversed quite familiarly with **ABRAHAM**, **ISAAC**, and **JACOB**, whose history is very well known. However, they are too lengthy to be recounted here, let alone explained.

<margin>XVI. Those who appeared in the form of three men were not prophets of those times.</margin>
XVI. There are some among the Hebrew teachers—including *Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson* <note>original: "R. Levi Ben Gerson"; also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note>—who, when they read that three men were seen by Abraham and received with hospitality (Genesis 18), explain this as referring to three prophets of those times, such as *Shem*, *Eber*, and others. They also observe that while they stayed with Abraham, they are called only by the appearance of "Men," but when they are with Lot, they are called "Angels." They argue this is because, strictly speaking, they were not sent to Abraham, since he himself was a prophet—and a prophet is not usually sent to another prophet. However, they claim that with Lot, to whom no prophecy had ever fallen, they took on the name and dignity of Angels. 

Yet these are empty speculations and the cold inventions of men who misinterpret the words of Scripture rather than explaining them soundly. Many points are piled up here that are patently false. It is false that those whom God sent to overthrow the Pentapolis <note>The "Five Cities" of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah.</note> were merely human men; such a task is not usually entrusted to men. It is false that they were not sent to Abraham, but only to Sarah; they spoke far more with him than with her. It is also false that this is the reason for the different names—that Abraham was a greater prophet than those who approached him, and therefore it was not fitting for them to be designated by the most worthy name of "Angels" in his presence, though they rightly bore it with Lot as one less worthy. For the Scripture progresses from the appearance of the thing to its true nature. Because they appeared to Abraham in the form of men, they are called "men" here. Because in truth they were not men but Angels, they are thereafter distinguished by the name of "Angels." Whether they were created Angels, or whether some greater mystery lay hidden under that appearance <note>A reference to the "Theophany," where many Christian theologians argued one of the three men was the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>, has been discussed by us elsewhere.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>
XVII. Did prophecy happen to Lot?
</margin>

XVII. But this also deserves to be examined: whether they are correct who deny that any prophecy happened to **Lot**? For since he left his native soil and everything usually sweet in one's fatherland with an eagerness equal to **Abraham's**, led solely by devotion to the Divine; and was celebrated by the name of justice, and dear to God in a singular way; it is not incredible that God occasionally appeared to him for the nourishment of faith and piety. Certainly, God now speaks to him no less than to Abraham through Angels, informs him of the imminent destruction of Sodom, shows the way of salvation, instructs him with His precepts, and rescues him not without a miracle from the flames of the doomed cities. But the other things that sacred history relates concerning him, his wife, and his daughters, are such as should strike readers with amazement. They clearly demonstrate how incredible the corruption of human nature is, which cannot be tamed by any wonders; how strong the remnants of vice are even in pious men; how immense is the goodness and mercy of God, still acknowledging as His own those who, through their crimes, show themselves most unworthy of such great favor; finally, how inscrutable is the judgment of God, who just now exempted those from the punishments of a wicked city, only to leave them soon to themselves, so that they might pollute themselves with the contagion of similar crimes <note>The author refers to the events in Genesis 19, where Lot's escape from Sodom is followed by the moral collapse of his family in the wilderness.</note>.

<margin>
XVIII. Joseph the Prophet.
</margin>

XVIII. Among the sons of **Jacob**, **Joseph** stood out for the gift of prophecy: whom God, while still a youth, informed through remarkable dreams about the things that were to happen to him, his brothers, and his entire family. He also equipped him with an admirable skill for interpreting dreams: not that which the followers of <term>Oneirocritices</term> <note>The Greek term for the "art of dream interpretation." The author distinguishes between secular/superstitious dream analysis and Joseph's divine revelation.</note>, a most vain art, boast of; but that which, proceeding from the Spirit of God, penetrates into the knowledge of His secrets. By using this gift, he proved himself commendable to **Pharaoh** and admirable to his wise men; thus, he was the author of salvation during the seven-year famine, not only for **Egypt** and the neighboring nations but especially for his father's family.

<margin>
XIX. Are Ethan and Heman, grandsons of Judah, the authors of Psalms 88 and 89?
</margin>

XIX. Among the descendants of Jacob in Egypt lived <term>Ethan</term> <note>Meaning "enduring" or "ancient."</note> and <term>Heman</term> <note>Meaning "faithful."</note>, sons of <term>Zerah</term>, who was the son of **Judah**. (1 Chronicles 2:6). Now, these men are believed not only to have been renowned for the sake of wisdom—so much so that **Solomon** is compared with them in 1 Kings 4:31—but also gifted with the Prophetic Spirit and the authors of certain Psalms. For Psalm 88 is inscribed as <note>original Hebrew: משכיל להימן האזרחי</note> *A didactic ode of Heman the Ezrahite*. And Psalm 89 as <note>original Hebrew: משכיל לאיתן האזרחי</note> *A didactic ode of Ethan the Ezrahite*. That these men are the same as the sons of Zerah just praised by us is defended, after others, by the most excellent <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist and scholar of the Bible's historical chronology.</note>. These are his words in *Chronicle of Times, Vol. 1, p. 24*:

> In these days of bitterness and misery lived two sons of Zerah, or Ezrahites,

### ON THE PROPHETS BEFORE THE LAW.

*...Zarchites*, **Heman** and **Ethan**, (1 Chronicles 2:6), who had the Spirit of the Lord upon them in the middle of all their afflictions, and wrote Psalms **88 and 89**. The former of these laments sadly over their present calamity, while the latter sings extensively of the mercies of God in the midst of this calamity and predicts their liberation. This is the proper place and order for these **Psalms**. Again, in the *Handful of Gleanings from Exodus, Section II* <note>The author is citing John Lightfoot’s *A Handful of Gleanings out of the Book of Exodus* (1643), a work of biblical chronology and commentary.</note>: these two Psalms are the oldest fruits of writing that the world can show; for they were recorded many years before **Moses** was born, by two men who fathered children under this **Egyptian** servitude and affliction: **Heman** and **Ethan**, the sons of **Zerah**. In **Psalm 88**, **Heman** deplores the distress and calamity of **Israel** in **Egypt** in a most emotional meter; for this reason, he titles this **Elegy** *al machalat le’anot* <note>original Hebrew: על מחלת לענות</note>, "upon the sickness because of affliction." Because of this, he and his brothers are called the "sons of **Machol**" <note>original Hebrew: בני מחול (bene machol). In 1 Kings 4:31, these men are noted for their wisdom.</note> in 1 Kings 4:31. In **Psalm 89**, **Ethan** sings extensively of their liberation based on the promise in Genesis 15, predicting that the fury of the Red Sea would be calmed (verse 9) and *Rahab* (or **Egypt**) would be crushed (verse 10), and that the people would hear the joyful sound <note>Latin: *clangorem*, literally a "clanging" or "shouting," often referring to the trumpet blast associated with the giving of the Law or religious festivals.</note> of the Law (verse 15).

<margin>
XX. Are there others of the same name who flourished in the time of David?
</margin>

XX. However, these points, though learnedly observed, do not seem certain or solid; indeed, they are not even probable. For others of the same name are mentioned who were put in charge of sacred songs during the time of **David** and **Solomon**. There exists a certain **HEMAN**, the grandson of **Samuel** (1 Chronicles 6:33): *Heman the Musician, the son of Joel, the son of Samuel.* He was also a prophet (1 Chronicles 25:5): *Heman, the king's seer, in the words of God to lift up the horn*—whether we understand this as a musical instrument or, as I would prefer, as the strength of the kingdom of **David and the Messiah**. Compare Psalm 132:17 and Luke 1:69. At that same time, there was also a certain **ETHAN**, a **Levite** by birth, descended from the offspring of **Merari** (1 Chronicles 6:44), who is joined with **Heman** and **Asaph** as the singers appointed by **David** (1 Chronicles 15:17).

<margin>
XXI. Why this is more probable.
</margin>

XXI. It is far more probable, however, to attribute these Psalms to those men—since they contain such express mentions of **David** and his kingdom—than to those who lived before **Moses** was born. For to whom would it seem believable that the will of God regarding the Kingdom of **David**, and the **Messiah** as the son of **David**, was revealed to men living under **Egyptian** oppression? Even **Samuel** did not know this when he was sent to anoint one of the sons of **Jesse**; and **David** himself did not know it until those happy origins were revealed to him through **Nathan**. **Lightfoot** does indeed point out an exception in **Psalm 99, verse 6**, arguing that a prophetic mention of **Samuel** was made by **Moses**. But he proves that this was a **Psalm of Moses** by no argument other than the authority of the **Hebrew** <note>Referring to the tradition of the Jewish Rabbis.</note> scholars. This, however, is of little weight...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.

...himself, who is ignorant of this? It is much more probable that the wisdom of Solomon is compared with those who flourished in his own time and were appointed to great affairs, rather than with those who, many centuries before him, spent a miserable life in a dismal prison-house <note>Latin: *ergastulo*, referring to the slave-labor conditions of Egypt.</note>, and about whom sacred history elsewhere records nothing except their bare names. I do not hide the fact that an obstacle remains: that **Heman** and **Ethan**, who flourished in David's time, were Levites, not sons of Zerah; yet the authors of these Psalms are called **Ezrahites**. But it is assumed too freely—which is itself uncertain—that the surname "Ezrahite" must designate a son of Zerah. There may be another reason for that naming, unknown to us. 

If, however, one prefers to admit for certain that the sons of Zerah were famous for wisdom, and that "Ezrahites" signifies the same as "Zerahites," the conjecture of **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> seems not to be despised: that Heman and Ethan the Levites, being wise men, were surnamed Ezrahites because they were equal in wisdom to those ancient sons of Zerah—as if you were to say, Heman and Ethan were "Zerahites reborn." Or if this is less pleasing, it could be thought that these Psalms were composed by David or another contemporary writer and presented under the names of Heman and Ethan the Ezrahites because they contain an explanation, application, and amplification of the doctrine and prophecy brought forth by those ancients and preserved until now in the memory of the godly, to which other similar things were added according to the needs of the time. **Cocceius** is not averse to this opinion, nor does **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist and clergyman.</note> disapprove.

<margin>XXII. Job truly existed in the nature of things.</margin>

XXII. Most interpreters believe that **Job** lived during the time of the Israelites' stay in Egypt and was a man of great fame in Arabia. For I do not think we should listen to those who argue that no Job ever existed in the nature of things, but transform his entire history into a fictional drama and a parable, devised for the purpose of training Israel in virtue and constancy. Certain Talmudists trifle with this idea among many others; they dispute in the *Bava Batra* <note>A tractate of the Babylonian Talmud dealing with legal and historical traditions.</note>: "Job never existed and was never created, but was a parable" <note>Original Hebrew: איוב לא היה ולא נברא אלא משל היה. The Latin in the text reads "Propheta non fuit" (He was not a prophet), though the Hebrew specifically names Job.</note>. 

Indeed, it is not fitting for Jews to speak thus, nor is it permitted for Christians to believe so. For both Ezekiel (Chapter 14:14) and James the Apostle (Chapter 5:11) mention Job as a man of the highest integrity, holiness, and patience, who no less illustrated the Church by his virtue than **Noah**, or **Daniel**, or **Elijah**, with whom he is recorded in the same series and as an equal example. And the history itself is so written that it differs greatly from a mere drama, tragicomedy, or parable. For all the characteristics of true history concur here:

...especially the personal names of the individuals, the regions, the friends, and the daughters. These are not ingeniously invented, as is common in fictional tales, but are known from the sacred scriptures and even from foreign writings, and they perfectly fit both that age and history. <margin>History of Job, Chapter I.</margin> This argument was learnedly pursued by the most celebrated man, Friedrich Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701) was a Calvinist theologian at Leiden who wrote on biblical history and chronology.</note>, in a very erudite work, which was also celebrated with well-deserved praise by Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar known for his "Demonstratio Evangelica."</note>.

<margin>XXIII. Ancestry: Was he an Edomite?</margin>
XXIII. If Job truly existed, then, what was his **ancestry**? Most believe, both among the Ancients and the Moderns, that he was an *Idumæan* <term>Idumæan: An inhabitant of Edom, the region south of the Dead Sea settled by the descendants of Esau.</term>, descended from Esau; they are led to this primarily by these reasons. I. That *Job* is *Jobab*, one of the Kings from the posterity of Edom (Genesis 36:33). II. That *Uz* was the grandson of *Seir*, from the line of *Dishon* (Genesis 36:28). From this comes the name of the land which *Job* inhabited, a part of Idumæa (Lamentations 4:21): *Rejoice, daughter of Edom, dwelling in the land of Uz.* III. That among the friends of Job is named *Eliphaz the Temanite*: it can hardly be doubted that he was descended from Esau, for the son of Esau was *Eliphaz*, and the son of Eliphaz was *Teman* (Genesis 36:10, 11). Hence the name of the region (Amos 1:12; Jeremiah 49:7). However, whether this Eliphaz is called a "Temanite" from his ancestry or from his location is uncertain; but for this matter, it is the same.

<margin>XXIV. Was he from Nahor?</margin>
XXIV. But those who trace *Job* from *Nahor*, the brother of Abraham—to whom were born the sons *Uz*, *Buz*, and *Chesed* (Genesis 22:21, 22)—seem to fight with stronger arguments. I. Because the seat of the family was named after *Uz*, the firstborn of Nahor and the prince of the family; and this is *Ausitis* <note>original: "Ausitis." A Greek name for the land of Uz, often associated with the Arabian desert.</note> of Arabia, not of Syria, nor Palestine, nor Idumæa. This was assigned with great arguments by the recently praised Spanheim. II. Because from Nahor was born *Buz*, from whom either the land or the city took the name "Buz," from which came *Elihu the Buzite* (Job 32). This man was joined to Job by both proximity and the bond of blood, and was likewise an inhabitant of Arabia Deserta. III. Because from the same Nahor was born *Chesed*: whence those raiders, the *Chasdim* <term>Chasdim: The Hebrew term for the Chaldeans.</term>, mentioned in Job 1:17. These were similarly neighbors to Job; though according to the condition of the region and the nature of the tribe—now with the added impulse of Satan—they were prone to plunder.

<margin>XXV. Was he from Kethura?</margin>
XXV. Nor are there those lacking who derive Job from *Abraham* himself, and count him among the grandsons of *Kethura* <note>Kethura was the woman Abraham married after the death of Sarah; her descendants are traditionally linked to various Arabian tribes.</note>; they rely on the following reasons. I. That from the same Kethura arose another of the friends or kinsmen of Job, *Bildad the Shuhite*, also an inhabitant of Arabia, undoubtedly from *Shuah* or *Suchus*, born to Abraham (Genesis 25:2). At least from this it is gathered that Job’s lineage can be estimated to be from Kethura just as much as from Esau and Nahor, from whom his other friends were descended. II. That from the same Kethura was sired, through *Jokshan*, *Seba* or *Sheba* (Genesis 25:3).
