<margin>
XXVI. Uncertainty.
</margin>
XXVI. These matters, having been so debated by the most learned men, perhaps leave the reader more uncertain than they found him. Even those who have applied the most diligent effort to the investigation of these things see more to reject than to approve; and when they have searched through all the shelves of their own industry, they leave the judgment of opinions to the reader, hardly daring to decide for themselves. Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701), a Dutch theologian.</note>, than whom no one has treated these matters more accurately, confesses that it is difficult to define which of the last two opinions should be chosen, since each rests upon its own defenses and its own probability. It is not permitted for us to know everything. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian and famous Hebraist.</note> says: *Let each person judge these things as he wishes. It is enough that it is clear by all signs that Job was not from the people of God chosen and set apart from all nations—namely, from the sons of Israel—and yet he was from a people in whom the knowledge of the true God and His word was not yet extinct.* <note>original: "De his judicet quisque, ut volet. Satis est, omnibus signis constare, Jobum non fuisse de populo Dei electo..."</note>

<margin>
XXVII. Credible that he lived before the Law was given.
</margin>
XXVII. But at what **TIME** did Job live? Here too the opinions of the Doctors <term>Doctors: Here referring to "Doctors of the Church" or high-level academic theologians.</term> vary. Some believe that Job lived before the Israelites' departure from Egypt, and thus was prior to Moses; others believe he lived after the departure, around the time of the wandering in the desert; others finally place him after Moses, under the Judges, or even in a later age. Each of these views, with their respective arguments, can be seen in Spanheim's work. To me, none seem to be of such a kind that they certainly establish what is required. However, the greatest probability lies with those who argue that Job lived very close to the age of the Patriarchs <note>The Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> and was older than the given Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Torah or the Mosaic Law given at Mount Sinai.</note>.

<margin>
XXVIII. The author of the book concerning Job is unknown.
</margin>
XXVIII. Nevertheless, you should not conclude by any necessity of sequence that the **BOOK OF JOB** is of the same antiquity. Regarding its author, whatever some may rashly determine, nothing is certain. The opinion of most learned men seems not improbable: that notebooks or records were written by Job himself or by his friends, in which they recorded the whole matter (certainly as far as the substance is concerned) in their own language—that is, in Arabic or old Syriac. From these records, by the action of Divine providence, some holy man endowed with the Spirit of God, and with that same Spirit as his guide, collected those things which we now have and adorned them in the Hebrew tongue to be added to the sacred Canon. This is gathered from the "Arabisms" and "Syriasms" <note>Linguistic features or loan-words originating from Arabic or Syriac rather than pure Hebrew.</note> which Bochart, Pococke, Hottinger, Walton, and others most skilled in Oriental languages have detected in great number in this book.

<margin>29. As well as the time of its writing.</margin>
XXIX. Exactly when the book was written is equally uncertain. Those who are currently considered the leaders of the Critics <note>The author refers to early biblical critics of the 17th century who began questioning traditional dating of scripture.</note> believe they can detect an era later than the time of David and Solomon. However, they rely on weak arguments, as is the case with most critical claims. On the other hand, the arguments for a much greater antiquity are not necessarily any stronger. Nevertheless, it is credible that the book was written before the time of Ezekiel, who, in Chapter 14:14, clearly looks back upon the history of Job.

<margin>30. The Divine Book is improperly subjected to the censure of critics.</margin>
XXX. Whatever the case may be, a great disservice has been done in this century by those who have so boldly subjected this Divine book to their harsh <note>original: "plagosae," literally "beating" or "scourging."</note> censure. If they had wished, they could have already seen most of their petty objections refuted in the works of Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701), a Dutch theologian mentioned on the previous page.</note>, whom we have praised so often; a response to their other points would be easy enough if we were currently addressing that matter.

<margin>31. Job was a Prophet.</margin>
XXXI. This one point now serves our purpose: that in that age, outside the communion of His covenanted people, God had a man in Arabia who was not only endowed with a true knowledge of Him and shining with many illustrious virtues, but whom God also deigned to address with repeated speeches. God proved by His very actions that this man was an intimate friend whose prayers carried great weight. Finally, God set him before that age as an example: a PROPHET great and venerable in both deed and word. His prophecies regarding Christ—the "Preserver of Men" <note>original: "Servatore hominum," translating the Hebrew נוצר האדם (Notzer ha-Adam)</note> and the "Redeemer" <note>original: "Goele" (Goel), a Hebrew term for a kinsman-redeemer who vindicates a relative.</note> who is restored to life, the conqueror of death, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life—are so outstanding that you will hardly find more magnificent prophecies in any of the prophets of those centuries.

<margin>32. In vain do the Rabbis object.</margin>
XXXII. Certainly, those among the Hebrew Teachers <note>Referring to various Rabbinic commentators.</note> are mistaken when they dictate that Job was an unlearned man, since Scripture nowhere specifically calls him "wise" or "knowing"; they argue that if he disputed skillfully in some places, it must be attributed to the natural luck of his genius. Truly, Job himself indicates clearly enough that he was considered a wise man by the people of his era when he recounts that not only did young men rise for him, but even the elderly stood up, and princes fell silent, and those who heard his eloquent words called him blessed (Job 29:8, 9, 11). Eliphaz testifies to this even more clearly in Chapter 4:3–4:
> Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have strengthened the trembling knees.
And certainly, Job was not inferior to Eliphaz, who in verse 12 attributes immediate Divine revelation to himself.

<margin>33. The lineage of Balaam.</margin>
XXXIII. BALAAM was not far removed from the era of Job; if we look at his lineage, he was the son of Beor from Pethor (Numbers 22:5).

->### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.<-

<margin>
And his native soil.
</margin>
He whom Moses calls Beor <note>original: בעור (*Be’or*)</note>, Peter—writing from Babylon—calls Bosor (2 Peter 2:15). For the Chaldeans sometimes pronounce the letter *Ayin* <note>The Hebrew letter ע</note> as an 'S,' a practice that the Greeks also occasionally imitated. Pethor was a town in Syria, as he himself says in Numbers 24:7: *The King of the Moabites has summoned me from Syria.* This is certainly that Syria which, because it is situated between the Euphrates and the Tigris, is called Mesopotamia, or "Between the Rivers." Hence it is called Pethor of Mesopotamia (Deuteronomy 23:4), which is by the river (Numbers 22:5), specifically situated next to the Euphrates, where the Pacoria of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Roman geographer.</note> is located. For Agostino Steuco <note>original: "Augustinus Steuchus" (1497–1548), an Italian Old Testament scholar and Vatican librarian.</note> does not win agreement when he argues that "Pethor" <note>original: פתורה (*Pethorah*)</note> is derived here from the verb meaning "to explain," "to interpret," or "to solve a riddle" <note>original: פתר (*patar*)</note>, suggesting that Balaam was regarded at that time as a sort of interpreter of dreams and an explainer of enigmas to whom kings from all sides would send letters and consult on all most obscure matters. I do not deny that the word *Pethora* can elsewhere signify an interpretation or the solution of a riddle. However, in this passage, everything makes it clear that it is the name of a city. Abraham had once lived in that same region and had worshipped false gods (Genesis 24:4, 10; Joshua 24:2). Jacob had served there on account of his wife and had fathered all the Patriarchs there, with the sole exception of Benjamin. Hence the Israelite people confessed that their father was a "lost Syrian" (Deuteronomy 26:5). From that shared life with the Patriarchs, certain remnants of the true religion remained in some families, though they were almost entirely smothered by a great deal of superstition. For this reason, Balaam—unless perhaps he was a descendant of Keturah <note>Abraham's second wife, whose descendants lived in the East.</note>—was imbued with some knowledge of the true Divinity, but he corrupted it with superstitious and magical arts, which was a common vice among those living in the East (Isaiah 2:6).

<margin>
XXXIV.
By profession
indeed a
diviner.
</margin>
XXXIV. Balaam was certainly by profession a "diviner" <note>Hebrew: קוסם (*kosem*), a term for someone using forbidden methods to see the future.</note>; for so he is called in Joshua 13:22. Now, a diviner is one who promises knowledge of secret and future things, to be acquired by arts that are not good. For this reason, God prohibited his people from every kind of divination (Deuteronomy 18:10), and He detests it as an abominable crime (1 Samuel 15:23): *Because rebellion is as the sin of divination.* Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> frequently calls him a <term>Mantis</term> <note>original: Μάντιν, a Greek term for a soothsayer or seer.</note>. Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> calls him most famous in that art and very powerful in harmful incantations. Philo Judaeus <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria (c. 20 BC–50 AD).</note> calls him *a man celebrated for divination, who had been initiated into all forms of the mantic art* <note>original: Ἄνδρα ἐπὶ μαντείᾳ περιβόητον, ὃς ἅπαντα μὲν ἐμεμύητο τῆς μαντικῆς εἴδη</note>. Philo denies that he was blessed with the gift of prophecy, but rather that he excelled only in those types of vaticination <note>A formal word for predicting or prophesying.</note> which were held in high regard among the gentiles at that time, such as predicting droughts, rains, and plagues...

...and other things of that kind he predicted; but most of all he was corrupted by the science of <term>augury<note>original: "scientia augurali"; the practice of interpreting omens, such as the flight of birds or celestial signs, to predict the future.</note></term>. Nearly all the ancient writers agree with this same opinion.

<margin>XXXV. But he was also a prophet.</margin>
XXXV. It must not be denied, however, that he was endowed with the gift of PROPHECY at that time when the knowledge of God in Syria had not yet completely faded away. For although he was accustomed to using many deceptions and fallacies, he nevertheless sought and obtained counsel and foreknowledge of the future from God, not from demons; and God addressed him in a nightly vision no less familiarly than one of his own servants; yet only in this particular matter. It was wisely observed by *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French theologian of the Reformation.</note> that God willed such figures to exist among the profane <note>In this context, "profane" refers to the Gentile nations living outside of the specific covenant of Israel.</note> nations so that some sparks of light might glitter in the darkness, and thus the excuse of ignorance might be removed. This occurred especially before the Law was given, because God had not yet distinguished his chosen people from foreigners by this mark <note>Presumably referring to the formal Mosaic Law or the distinct religious identity of Israel.</note>.

<margin>XXXVI. Origen wrongly conjectures that the doctrine of the Messiah was spread among the nations through him.</margin>
XXXVI. *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar.</note> proceeds further than is justified, conjecturing that just as the prophecies of *Balaam* were inserted into the sacred volumes by *Moses*, they were even more fully recorded by those who then inhabited *Mesopotamia*, among whom he was held in high esteem and who are known to have been students of his art. From this he further infers that the class and institution of the <term>Magi<note>The "Wise Men" from the East mentioned in the New Testament.</note></term> flourished in the Eastern regions from him; and that having all that *Balaam* had prophesied recorded among them, they also possessed the writing concerning the star rising out of Jacob and the scepter proceeding from Israel which he had foretold. Since the *Magi* had these records in their possession, it followed that when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood the prophecy was being fulfilled better than the Israelite people themselves; and therefore they came, sought him out, and immediately worshiped him. But these things are uncertain, or rather, false. For such knowledge and expectation of the Messiah did not thrive among the profane nations.

<margin>XXXVII. Certain Rabbis also wrongly equate him to Moses.</margin>
XXXVII. The Masters of the Hebrews are hyperbolic, as they often are, almost equating *Balaam* in the degrees of prophecy to *Moses* himself. They argue over the saying in *Deuteronomy 34:10*: *No prophet has arisen again* IN ISRAEL *like Moses.* <note>original: "Non surrexit propheta amplius IN ISRAEL sicut Moſes."</note> Not in *Israel*, they say; but among the nations of the world, one did arise. And who was he? *Balaam*. But *Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson* <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note> observed more correctly that in many respects *Balaam* was inferior not only to *Moses*, but also to the rest of the prophets of Israel; indeed, he was infamous for those vices which make him unworthy to be included in the catalog of honorable men.

<margin>XXXVIII. His prophecies...</margin>
XXXVIII. Regarding his PROPHECIES, which *Moses* deigned to record, they indeed narrate the fates of the people of Israel and other neighboring peoples; they even [foretell] something about the Messiah...

<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.</header>

<margin>
They are inferior to the saints.
</margin>
they say; yet if we compare them with other prophecies, and the songs of holy men and women, we will find them to be far inferior. For even if he explained great things that were to happen in the world, he did not glorify the name of God, nor did he explain the justice of God and his kingdom. From this we can also learn how much difference there is between the saving knowledge of God and that which Balaam possessed; and between the prophecy concerning Christ and the kingdom of justice, and that by which the fates of kingdoms are known—the kind with which both Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar were gifted. Therefore, he ought not to be counted among those prophets whom God set over his Church. For their purpose was not only to predict some future events, but especially to announce God's covenant by which he reconciles men to himself, and to adapt all their prophecies to that end. Balaam’s method was far different, as he brought forth only bare prophecies without any <term>seasoning of doctrine<note>original: "doctrinæ condimento"; the author suggests that Balaam's words lacked the moral and spiritual instruction found in true biblical prophecy.</note></term>. As *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential Reformer.</note> and *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for "Covenant Theology."</note> have excellently commented.

<margin>
XXXIX.
He was wicked in character.
</margin>
### XXXIX.
In the habits of the man there are also many things which clearly demonstrate a profane character. For he shows himself in this: I. Intolerable vanity and ambition, preaching about himself more than about God and the grace of God within him. The <term>boastful rhetoric<note>original: "Thrasonici sermonis cothurni"; literally "the buskins (theatrical boots) of Thrasonic speech," referring to Thraso, a stock character of a bragging soldier in Roman comedy.</note></term> of his speech tends toward this: *The word of Balaam, son of Beor, and the word of the man whose eyes are opened, who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down, but having his eyes uncovered.* Numbers 24:3, 4, 15, 16. II. A <term>cursed hunger for gold<note>original: "Sacra auri fames"; a classical Latin idiom from Virgil meaning an accursed or insatiable greed.</note></term>: for no matter how much he boasted that he despised the offered treasures of the Moabite King, he nevertheless openly showed in every way that the "reward of unrighteousness" was loved by him (2 Peter 2:15) and that he was deceived by it (Jude verse 11). Hence those repeated tricks of sacrifices, to see if in any way he could obtain the power to curse the people of God. III. A fear rather of a servile mind trembling at the whip of God, than a reverence for the Divine Power joined with a love of His holiness, such as becomes the children of God. For he had to be subdued by threats lest he speak anything other than what pleased God; his mind meanwhile panted for those things by which he could actually obtain the prize he had swallowed in hope. IV. Hatred toward the Israelites. For although he proclaimed their happiness with sought-out praises, and predicted it would continue through the passing centuries, and was forced to confess the vanity of his own art concerning them, he nevertheless looked upon all these things with an envious mind. Hence that deadly counsel by which he harmed them more than if he had cursed them with all his songs. V. A reckless profanity of mind, shining forth from that same counsel.

<header># ON THE PROPHETS BEFORE THE LAW.</header>

<margin>*The peak of a plan fatal to the Hebrews.*</margin>
When he had discovered that his efforts were not prevailing against the Israelites, he became the architect of a plan for the Midianites and Moabites to expose their daughters and daughters-in-law to the lustful embraces of the Israelites. These women, coached by their parents in the arts of the prostitute, were to lure them into the <term>shameful worship of Baal<note>original: "propudiosum Baalis cultum"; referring to the cult of Baal-Peor, which often involved ritual prostitution.</note></term>. Both *Philo* and *Josephus* <note>Philo of Alexandria and Flavius Josephus, two of the most important Jewish historians of the first century.</note> have embellished this counsel of Balaam with great elegance of speech. And indeed, it did not lack its own fatal success. For while the Israelites were staying at Shittim, the Moabite and Midianite virgins—clever, well-dressed, and beautiful—were sent into their camps. They offered themselves readily to the Hebrew youths, and once they had inflamed their passions and received promises of stable marriage, they finally responded that they would only comply on the condition that the men would cross over to the worship of the same gods in whose lands they were settling. The reckless Israelites obeyed. They allowed themselves to be invited to the sacrificial feasts, ate <term>food sacrificed to idols<note>original: "idolothytis"; from the Greek "eidolothuton," meaning meat that had been offered to a pagan deity.</note></term>, joined themselves with *Baal-Peor*, and worshipped that object of shame. Because of this, the anger of God was kindled against the people, for He would not tolerate such a foul apostasy. He commanded Moses to take the leaders of this great crime and <note>original: "affigere ad solem"; literally 'to fix to the sun,' meaning to execute or hang them in public view.</note> expose them in the open, after they had first been stoned, as the law regarding idolaters commanded. The other judges, appointed in a certain number, also killed whoever among their own groups had joined with *Baal-Peor*. *Numbers 25*. This is how much the diabolical cunning of Balaam cost the Israelites—an event which God, many centuries later, recalls to their memory in *Micah 6:5*: *“O my people, remember now what Balak king of Moab planned, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, that you may know the righteous acts of Jehovah from Shittim to Gilgal.”*

<margin>XLI. *Therefore his memory is abominable in the Church.*</margin>
### XLI.
And indeed, Balaam deserved for the memory of his name to be abominable throughout the entire Church of God, and to serve as a type of those who, by favoring the lusts of the flesh, seduce His people away from the chaste love of God. For this reason, the Lord reproaches the Angel of the Church at Pergamum, *“because you have there those who hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed to idols, and to commit fornication.”* *Revelation 2:14*. Moreover, he paid the deserved penalties for his crime: he was slaughtered by the sword of the Israelites along with the Midianites. *Numbers 31:8*.

<margin>XLII. *Those who change Balaam into Elihu are merely babbling.*</margin>
### XLII.
Even if there were nothing else but this wickedness of character, it would be enough to show that those who make Balaam (so often condemned in sacred scripture) the same person as <term>ELIHU</term> are far distant from the truth. Elihu, the friend of Job, always spoke so piously and wisely about God. But there are many other reasons besides which prove that tradition to be vanity and a lie. I. The names are very different in both sound and meaning. אליהוא *Elihu* <note>Hebrew: "Elihu," meaning "My God is He."</note> is a name of the best omen, and...

<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XVI.</header>

[The name Elihu] signifies *My God is Himself*, a brief symbol of great faith and hope. <term>Balaam<note>original: "בלעם Bileam"</note></term> means "the swallowing of them," or "the destruction of the people," an omen of the worst kind; for he truly attempted this with a most destructive plan. **II.** Their ages do not match at all, for Elihu was a contemporary of Job, who likely preceded the Exodus of the Israelites by almost an entire century. Balaam, however, flourished among his own people toward the end of the wandering in the desert. **III.** Nor is their lineage the same. For the one was a *Buzite*, of his father *Barachel*, from the family of *Nahor*; the other truly had *Beor* as his father, whose origin is uncertain—perhaps from the nation of the Keturahites, in Pethor. **IV.** Finally, they have nothing in common. For the one was a holy man, everywhere displaying a love of truth, a reverence for the divine, and a heart steeped in noble integrity. The other was a scoundrel, impious in both doctrine and deeds. No probable reason can be assigned for such a shameful <term>metamorphosis<note>original: "μεταμορφώσεως" (metamorphoseos)</note></term>, by which Elihu could be transformed into Balaam.

<header>CONCERNING THE PROPHETS IN THE DESERT.</header>

<margin>**I.** The four periods of time under the Law.</margin>
The times **UNDER THE LAW** can be further divided into various periods: **I. IN THE DESERT.** **II. IN CANAAN.** **III. DURING THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.** **IV. AFTER THE RELEASE FROM CAPTIVITY.**

<margin>**II.** In the desert, Moses, the prince of prophets, gave rise to the origin of "mythical" theology.</margin>
**II. IN THE DESERT**, he who was the author, founder, and legislator of the Israelite Commonwealth under God was also easily the prince of all the prophets who lived under that <term>economy<note>The term "economy" (oeconomia) here refers to the specific way God managed His relationship with humanity during the time of the Mosaic Law.</note></term>. This man is **MOSES**, whose preeminences, praised by the Supreme Deity Himself, I have recently explained. If I wished to pursue his history, it would fill not just a few pages, but a massive volume. So greatly do his birth, his deeds, his passing, and his burial teem with wonders. A small portion of these matters, through a widely spread fame, was scattered through almost all the nations of the whole world—not only neighboring ones but remote ones as well—and supplied a great deal of material for the "mythical" <note>original: "fabulari." The author refers to how pagan nations adapted the historical life of Moses into their own myths and legends.</note> theology of the Gentiles. As *Huetius* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who argued in his "Demonstratio Evangelica" that many figures in pagan mythology were actually distorted versions of Moses.</note> showed at great length in his *Demonstration of the Gospel*, he measured out arguments and examples of this matter to the Christian world, not by a small measure, but by the whole "barn," as they say. He might have better served the cause, and perhaps his own reputation, if he had shown himself a slightly more sparing steward of his own erudition and <term>wide reading<note>original: "πολυαναγνωσίας" (polyanygnosias)</note></term> in this area. For in such a great hodgepodge of ancient myths which he gathered from everywhere, it is impossible that many things are not found that have only a very thin resemblance to the history of Moses, and which are compared to it through a very weak <note>original: "frigida," literally "cold" or "spiritless."</note> collation. We leave those things to their own value, content to have pointed out the place where anyone who is captivated by such things can be filled to satisfaction. We love more solid matters: and from only the first and the last appearance made to Moses, we shall select those things which seem most notable and which come closer to our purpose.

<margin>**III.** His Teacher was the Angel of the Lord.</margin>
**III.** The first of all the appearances narrated to have happened to Moses is found in Exodus III. At this point, I wish only to observe what Teacher Moses had as his Instructor and the author of his prophecies. It was the **ANGEL OF THE LORD** <note>original: "ANGELUS JEHOVÆ"</note>, who appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a certain bush (verse 2). Yet this Angel, greater than all other angels, is several times called **LORD** <note>original: "JEHOVA"</note> in the progress of the history, and says of himself, *"I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob"* (verse 6). Who is that but the Son of God? He "did not consider it robbery to be equal with God" <note>original: "οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ" (ouch harpagmon hēgēsato to einai isa theō). A reference to Philippians 2:6.</note>. He is the Angel of God through a voluntary arrangement in such a way that He is simultaneously God; He is a messenger in such a way that He is simultaneously the Lord. Those things which Orthodox interpreters [say] are well known...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVII.

...against the blasphemies of Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was a theologian who founded Socinianism, a system that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ. The author is using Jewish texts to argue that the idea of a divine Mediator was present in Hebrew tradition long before the New Testament.</note> have been gathered from these and similar words of scripture.

<margin>**IV.** Whom Menahem recognizes to be Michael, the God of Bethel, and the High Priest of the heavens.</margin>
**IV.** But these same truths from the Instruction of the Ancients are still found even now in the writings of certain Hebrews. *Rabbi Menahem* <note>Menahem Recanati (late 13th–early 14th century), an Italian rabbi and kabbalist known for his mystical commentary on the Torah.</note> writes thus concerning this Angel: *This was Michael, and he is called the Angel of the Lord, not of God. Again: this Angel is the Angel Goël <note>original: "Goël." Hebrew for "Redeemer."</note>, the Redeemer, who said to Jacob that he was the God of Bethel: this is the one of whom it was said, "And the Angel of his presence saved them."* Genesis 48:16; 31:11, 13; Isaiah 63:9. In a few words, that Rabbi has encompassed many great matters. He calls this Angel *Michael*, whom the Masters of the Hebrews agree indeed excels all others; but in what that excellence consists, they have not equally investigated. *Rabbi Menahem* does not speak badly when he says he is the **HIGH PRIEST OF THE HEAVENS**, *who offers the prayers of the righteous to God: the CELESTIAL HIGH PRIEST, who represents the souls of the righteous in the sight of the Divine.* The same is the <term>Angel of Redemption<note>original: "מלאך הגואל" (Malakh ha-Goel).</note></term>, whom the Rabbis admit to be God Himself; certainly our Menahem, writing on Genesis 48, hints at the **Divine Majesty** <note>original: "השכינה" (ha-Shekhinah). In Jewish tradition, the Shekhinah represents the dwelling or settling divine presence of God.</note> when he says, *"The Angel who redeemed me."* Indeed, the name of "Redeemer" is among the titles of God. Psalm 19:15; Isaiah 43:1; 47:4. Nor does this Angel hide his own Deity when he says to Jacob in clear speech: *"I am that God of Bethel, where you anointed the pillar, and where you vowed a vow to me."* Genesis 31:11, 13. And therefore, as our Menahem has most beautifully observed: Moses implores his goodwill as a fountain of grace and blessing. Deuteronomy 33:16: *"May the favor of him who dwelt in the bush come abundantly upon the head of Joseph."* Where the <term>Targum Onkelos<note>The standard Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah.</note></term> has: *Whose glorious majesty dwells in the heavens, and who appeared to Moses in the bush.* <note>original Aramaic: "דשכנתיה בשמיא ועל משה אתגli באסנא"</note> Finally, Menahem adds that the same is called the *Angel of the Face* <note>Often translated as the "Angel of His Presence."</note>, who both continually beholds the face of God, and in whom God offers His own face to be beheld by men for joy and salvation—who, in short, is the very face of God.

<margin>**V.** A notable passage of Nachmanides concerning him.</margin>
**V.** Those things which *Moses Nachmanides* <note>Moses ben Nachman (1194–1270), also known as Ramban, a leading medieval Jewish scholar and philosopher.</note> of Girona commented regarding Exodus 23 surely deserve to be included here; for they contain the pure doctrine of the Ancient Church concerning a certain Angel who is the very Supreme Deity. Often translated in English bibles as the "Angel of his presence."</note> This is surely that Angel WHO IS THE FACE OF GOD, of whom it was said in Exodus 33:14: *MY FACE shall go before [you], and I will cause you to rest.* Finally, it is that angel of whom the prophet speaks in Malachi 3:1: *And the Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple, even the Angel of the covenant whom you desire.* 

A little later: Consider carefully what these words mean: *MY FACE SHALL GO BEFORE [YOU].* For *Moses* and the *Israelites* always desired the primary Angel; however, they were not able to truly understand who he was. For they did not perceive it from others, nor did they sufficiently grasp it through prophetic insight. And yet, that the "Face of God" signifies *God himself* is widely acknowledged among all interpreters. He means to say, unless I am mistaken, that there lies beneath this doctrine a great secret <note>original: "ingens arcanum"</note> which the *Israelites*—indeed, not even *Moses* himself—were ever able to comprehend in all its fullness; and concerning which no one will ever form any clear thoughts for himself, except one who is well-versed in the comparison of the scriptures: namely, how there can be a certain Angel of God who is also God himself.

<margin>**VI. Metatron of the Kabbalists.**</margin>
**VI.** The Talmudists call this Angel by the strange and foreign name **METATRON**. Thus *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> says regarding Exodus 23:21: *Our Rabbis say: He is Metatron, whose name is like the name of his Teacher: namely God, the Almighty.* <note>original: "שדי" (Shaddai). One of the primary Hebrew names for God, meaning "The Almighty."</note> For by <term>Gematria|A traditional Jewish system of interpretation that assigns numerical values to Hebrew letters. If two words have the same value, they are considered to be mystically connected.</term> *Shaddai* <note>original: "שדי"</note> makes 314; the letters of the word *Metatron* <note>original: "מטטרון"</note> make the same amount. 

The things which *Rabbi Bechai* <note>Bahya ben Asher (13th century), a Spanish rabbi and kabbalist known for his "fourfold" method of biblical interpretation.</note> comments on regarding the same name and passage are very clear, although they are marred by certain trifling observations. He says he is called *Metatron* because that name encompasses two meanings: namely, **Lord** <note>original: "אדון" (Adon)</note> and **Messenger** <note>original: "שליח" (Sheliah)</note>. The meaning of "Lord" comes from the speech of the Rabbis, who call a Lady or Mistress a *Matrona* <note>original: "מטרונה" (Matrona). A loanword from Latin/Greek into Hebrew.</note>. The meaning of "Messenger" comes from the speech of the Greeks, who call a Messenger *Menytor* <note>original: "מנטטור" (perhaps referring to the Greek Μηνύτωρ, meaning an informer or one who reveals).</note>. Indeed, there can even be a third meaning in it, that of **Guardianship** or **Guardian**. For the *Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has *Matrat* <note>original: "מטרת"</note> ("Guard") in place of the Hebrew word *Mishmeret* <note>original: "משמרת"</note> ("Watch"). 

From these etymologies, it is clear that he is himself both the Lord and the Messenger of the Lord, and he has the same name as his Lord. He is the Lord of all things that are beneath him: for all the hosts of the upper and lower worlds are under his judgment and under his hand; he is the Messenger of him who is above him, and who made him to rule over all things, and appointed him Lord of his house, and Ruler of all his possessions. However, you must observe that the reason for the meaning of "Lordship" is doubled in him: and...

<margin>VII. The kernel of true doctrine.</margin>
VII. Let us separate the precious from the worthless, and leaving behind the foolish etymologies of the more recent Rabbis like hollow shells, let us reserve for ourselves only the kernel of sound doctrine: the sum of which is that a certain Angel of God is praised in the scriptures who is himself God; and who was the Teacher of Moses. <margin>VIII. The final moments of Moses.</margin>
VIII. Moses had this same Angel as a leader throughout the entire course of his life; and indeed, even in his final moments. For after he had set forth the whole will of God to the people, and had encompassed the destiny of the Israelite nation in a most excellent Song, and finally had prayed for all favorable things for the individual tribes with a prophetic spirit, he prepared himself for death at God's warning. He therefore ascended from the plains of the Moabites into Mount Nebo, to that summit which the sacred scriptures call Pisgah. Josephus <note>The Jewish-Roman historian Flavius Josephus.</note> adds on his own account that this was done while the entire multitude of the Israelite people accompanied him, pouring forth such weeping that Moses himself was moved by compassion and dissolved into tears. Meanwhile, by a gesture of his hand to those further away and by his voice to those nearby, he signaled that they should not follow his departure with such a great testimony of grief. The people obeyed: and once they were dismissed along with the elders, Moses remained alone on the summit of the mountain, situated opposite Jericho, as if in the middle between the northern and southern boundaries of the land.

The very learned <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a renowned English churchman and Hebraist known for using Rabbinical literature to explain the New Testament.</note> observes that these things were done at the beginning of the fortieth year of the Israelites' journeying in the wilderness: and from this he concludes that Moses' primary crime consisted in this: that his mind wavered concerning God's promise about entering into the land after forty years. After that water has now departed, must water be brought forth by us from another cliff? O you rebels, have you brought the matter to this point through your murmuring, that there is a need for a new station in the wilderness, and a new cliff must be opened, which may grant you water for your long stay, as Horeb used to do? Must our stay in the wilderness be started anew now, when we hoped our labor had reached its end, and thus we will never leave this wilderness?* And at the same time he struck the cliff twice, out of indignation and anger. And so they did not believe the promise about entering the land after forty years; nor did they sanctify the Lord before the eyes of the people, to confirm them in the faith of that promise: but they nearly shook out whatever good spirit was in them, and thus spoke thoughtlessly with their lips. And for that reason they were excluded from the land of Canaan. Thus says <term>Lightfoot</term>.

<margin>X. Which was preceded by a view of the promised land.</margin>
X. Nevertheless, Moses had this last fruit of his labor in this life: that he saw the land which God had sworn to the fathers. Namely, He wished for joy to be stirred up in him from the faithfulness kept with the fathers. But He did not wish that he himself should either complete the work of the people's liberation, which he had begun, or see it completed by another. There are few to whom this is given. Most enter into the labors of others. Therefore, it is no cause for resentment for any of us to depart from here to the heavenly fatherland before we have seen the fruit of our labor in this land. For the same happened to Moses: not to lead Israel into possession of the promised inheritance. This is a learned and pious observation of <term>Cocceius</term> <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who developed "Covenant Theology," emphasizing the historical progression of God's plan.</note>. ### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>XI. Is this death to be understood in its literal sense?</margin>
XI. After all these things had been thus accomplished, Moses the servant of Jehovah died in the land of the Moabites, <gloss>according to the mouth of Jehovah</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: *al pi Yehovah*</note>. *And he buried him in that same valley, in the land of the Moabites, opposite Beth-Peor, and no one knows his burial place to this day. Deuteronomy 34:5-6.*

§. 6. There is an inquiry among the learned as to whether "death" here signifies the separation of the soul from the body, or a <term>transmutation</term> <note>A change or transformation into a spiritual state without the usual process of decay.</note>—the kind expected by those whom the day of the Lord shall find alive (*1 Corinthians 15:51*). Likewise, they debate whether "burial" should be understood as the placing of the body in the earth, or a <term>metathesis</term> <note>original Greek: *metathesis*; a removal or translation from one place or state to another.</note>—that is, a transposition of the body along with the soul—which is indicated to have occurred near the valley by the mountain. In the *Yalkut* <note>The *Yalkut Shimoni*, a medieval compilation of Jewish midrash (scriptural commentary).</note> and the *Sifre* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, an old opinion of some is recorded that Moses did not die, but stands and serves in heaven. <term>Josephus</term> <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> says: <gloss>“He wrote in the holy books that he died, fearing lest, because of the excellence of his virtue, they might dare to say he had departed to the divine realm.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: "γέγραφε δ' αὐτὸν ἐν ταῖς βίβλοις τεθνεῶτα, δείσας μὴ δι' ὑπερβολὴν τῆς περὶ αὐτὸν ἀρετῆς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον αὐτὸν ἀναχωρῆσαι τολμήσωσιν εἰπεῖν."</note> <term>Jerome</term> <note>St. Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, writing on Amos 9, says: <gloss>“He ascended with Moses, whose burial place could not be found on earth because he had ascended into heaven.”</gloss> But these ideas lead us away from the simplicity of the history; its words concerning the death and burial of Moses are too clear to be set aside by far-fetched interpretations. Meanwhile, it seems evident from *Matthew 17:3* and *Luke 9:30* that Moses was in a state of life when he appeared with Elijah before the Lord Jesus to confirm the faith in the resurrection. However, the time of his personal resuscitation remains unknown.

<margin>XII. In what sense did he die "at the mouth of Jehovah"?</margin>
XII. But his <term>euthanasia</term> <note>In the historical sense, this refers to a "good" or peaceful death, free from agony and full of grace, rather than its modern medical meaning.</note> is worthy of note. He knew the time, place, and manner of his death, which he encountered neither by external force, nor disease, nor old age, but by the sole will of God separating the soul from the body. He was not dragged unwillingly, nor did he set out in fear to the place where he knew he must die. Instead, with a calm mind and a composed spirit, he committed himself and all he possessed to the Divine power, expiring as if in God's very embrace. The Sages of the Hebrews looked toward this when they said of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam that they died <gloss>by a kiss</gloss> <note>original: "osculo"</note>, or while being kissed. For Scripture testifies of Moses and Aaron that they died <gloss>according to the mouth of Jehovah</gloss> <note>original: "AD OS JEHOVÆ"; Hebrew: *al pi Yehovah*</note> (*Numbers 33:38; Deuteronomy 34:5*). They believe the same regarding Miriam, even though Scripture does not say so explicitly because she was a woman. They believe the meaning of this expression is that they died from an excess of love, in the apprehension, taste, and sensation of some Divine pleasure that surpasses the lot of this mortal life. And they compare this to what the Bride says in *Song of Solomon 1:2*: *“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,”* where the grasping of the Creator is joined with the highest love of God,

<margin>XIII. Secretly buried by God.</margin>
XIII. But in his BURIAL, something happened to Moses that happened to no other mortal before or after him. For God himself took upon himself the entire care of the funeral, to be managed without the intervention of any human work. *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his writings against heresies.</note> testifies from ancient tradition that God made use of the service of Angels. *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> does not disagree: *he was buried with no one present, clearly not by mortal hands, but by immortal powers* <note>original Greek: "ἐτάφη μηδενὸς παρόντος, δηλονότι χερσὶν οὐ θνηταῖς, ἀλλ’ ἀθανάτοις δυνάμεσι"</note>; by this phrase, he designates the Angels. God also willed the place of burial to be unknown to all mortals—indeed, even to the evil demons themselves—and certainly inaccessible. *R. Solomon Jarchi* <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval commentator on the Hebrew Bible.</note> relates from the traditions of the ancients that the grave of Moses had been prepared since the six days of creation to atone for the crimes of Peor <note>Referring to the idolatry of the Israelites at Baal-Peor.</note>, and that it is one of those things created *between the suns* <note>original Hebrew: *bein ha-shemashot*</note> in the twilight of the Sabbath eve. Others pass down that Moses buried himself: or at least that the earth opened itself, and once Moses had entered and died, it closed up and returned to its former state, and from that cause his burial place remained unknown. *Cedrenus* <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> adds: *From that time until this very day, a bright cloud overshadows that place, obscuring and walling off the sight of those looking on, so that they might not know his grave forever.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐκ τότε οὖν καὶ μεχρι τοῦ νῦν φωτοειδὴς νεφέλη ἐπισκιάζει τὸν τόπον ἐκεῖνον..."</note> Otherwise, these and similar things passed down outside of scripture are the inventions of audacious men.

XIV. We shall more usefully inquire why God willed the grave of Moses to be hidden with such care. These seem to be the primary reasons for that matter. I. <margin>
XV. The dispute between Michael and the Devil over the body of Moses.
</margin>
XV. For to this matter belongs a fragment of ancient history which Saint Jude inserted into his Divine Epistle (verse 9), whether he took it from Hebrew tradition or elsewhere. It says: *But Michael the Archangel, when contending with the Devil he disputed about the body of Moses,* <note>Jude 1:9 refers to a story from the "Assumption of Moses," a non-canonical Jewish text.</note> *did not dare* <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἐτόλμησε"</note> *did not bring himself* to cast a mark of curse upon him, but said, *The Lord rebuke you.* The parties in this dispute are, on one side, Michael the Archangel—that same prince of Angels who is also Lord, and who was the teacher and leader of Moses from the beginning; on the other side is the Devil, the "world-ruler" <note>original Greek: "κοσμοκράτωρ" (kosmokrator); a term used in the New Testament to describe spiritual powers of evil.</note>, Michael’s adversary in all things. The subject and cause of the dispute was the body of Moses. Michael wished to hide it, looking out for the rest of his servant and intending to prevent superstition and idolatry; the Devil, however, wished to bring it out into the open so that, by mocking the remains of the Prophet, he might lure the people into idolatry. In that dispute, it is believable that the Devil spewed out many blasphemies against God and Michael. Michael, however, *did not dare* or *did not bring himself* <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἐτόλμησε"; the author notes that "non sustinuit" or "non animum induxit" are better shades of meaning here.</note> (for Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), a distinguished English scholar and theologian.</note> has proved with several examples that "to dare" <note>original Greek: "τολμᾶν"</note> sometimes carries this meaning) to cast a mark of curse upon him. This was not because he feared the Devil, but because he wished to act in all things with propriety, to rightly uphold the character of the Angel he had assumed, to show himself as the very opposite of the Devil, and to leave an example of patience for the humans to whom these things were to be revealed. Nor is this unworthy of the Majesty of such a great Angel: for in Zechariah 3:2, the Angel of Jehovah (who is himself Jehovah) said to Satan, *The Lord rebuke you.* And perhaps Jude gathered from this that, because Michael's "purpose" <note>original Greek: "φρόνημα"</note> is always the same, he spoke similarly in that struggle as well, and did not pronounce judgment in any other way than by calling for the judgment of the Father.

The shepherds themselves, emerging in amazement, spread the scent far and wide from their otherwise filthy garments. Stirred by the novelty of the event, they reported everything they had seen and found to the Patriarch of the Maronites <note>The Maronites are an Eastern Catholic Christian group primarily based in Lebanon.</note> living on Mount Lebanon at the Monastery of Saint Mary—which they call *Kanobeen Kadischa Mirjam* <note>The Monastery of Our Lady of Qannubin, the historic see of the Maronite Patriarchs.</note>. This Patriarch, named *Mataxat*, was convinced by the evidence of the unusually sweet scent <note>The "odor of sanctity" was historically considered a proof of a holy person's presence.</note>. Therefore, having sent two priests there (among whom was *Aben-Useph*, a man excelling in learning and prudence), they found the monument, upon which was inscribed in Hebrew letters: **MOSES THE SERVANT OF THE LORD**.

Elated by the magnitude of such a miracle, as it appeared, the Patriarch petitioned *Morat* Bassa <note>Murad Pasha, an Ottoman governor.</note> of Damascus with prayers that the custody of the discovered tomb be granted to him.

But the *Greeks*, the *Armenians*, the *Franciscans*, and finally the *Jews*, opposed them. These groups, though at odds with one another, competed in the court of the Mufti and the Vizier <note>High-ranking officials in the Ottoman government in Constantinople.</note> using money and bribes to claim the tomb they believed to be that of *Moses*.

The *Jews* especially contended that the *Tomb of Moses* belonged to them. They argued that nothing would be more glorious among the titles of the Turkish Emperor than to be the Lord of three tombs: that of *Muhammad in Mecca*, *Jesus Christ in Jerusalem*, and *Moses on Mount Nebo*.

But the *Jesuits* eluded the efforts of all others through their own clever arts. By offering great gifts, they obtained an order that the tomb and the entrance itself be sealed, and that no one be allowed to approach it *under penalty of death*.

Thus *Morat* Bassa, having sent the Sanjak-beys <note>District governors in the Ottoman Empire.</note> of *Jerusalem* and *Safed*, ordered the mountains to be blocked and the tomb to be closed.

The *Jesuits* themselves, however, having entered into a conspiracy with the *Druze* <note>An ethno-religious group in the Levant.</note>, endeavored to secretly remove the body of *Moses* from the tomb and transport it to Europe. They promised themselves—not without reason—that this would bring great sanctity and immense wealth to their religious order.

They had already opened the tomb itself with much labor, only to find it **empty**, containing no body or remains. While they were whispering among themselves in astonishment—deliberating whether to take the whole tomb or, because its size made that impossible, to carry off parts of it—the matter was meanwhile betrayed to the Sanjak-beys of *Jerusalem* and *Safed*. Quickly sending cavalry under *Jafer Aga*, they overtook the Jesuits in the very act, who were then severely punished. The Sanjak-beys then blocked the tomb with massive stones so that it would be inaccessible in the future.

This caused great turmoil in the court at Constantinople, and led to questions among the learned: what should be decided regarding this tomb of Moses?

But a certain learned Jew, *Jeconias Ben Gad*, living in *Safed*, showed in a complete book written on this subject: that it was not of *Moses the Servant* [of the Lord] <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "Do-" suggests the next page completes the word "Domini" (of the Lord).</note>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>
XV. The dispute between Michael and the Devil over the body of Moses.
</margin>
XV. To this point belongs a fragment of ancient history, which—whether taken from Hebrew tradition or elsewhere—the holy Jude inserted into his Divine Epistle at verse 9: *But Michael the Archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, did not dare* <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἐτόλμησε" (ouk etolmēse)</note> *[or did not bring himself] to pronounce against him a railing accusation, but said, "The Lord rebuke thee."* The parties in this dispute are, on one side, Michael the Archangel—that same prince of angels who is also the Lord, and who was the teacher and leader of Moses from the beginning; on the other side is the Devil, the "ruler of the world" <note>original Greek: "κοσμοκράτωρ" (kosmokratōr), a term for a powerful spiritual being exercising worldly influence</note>, the adversary of Michael in all things. The subject and cause of the dispute was the body of Moses; Michael wished to hide it, caring for the rest of his servant and intending to prevent superstition and idolatry. The Devil, however, wished to bring it out into the open, so that by mocking the remains of the Prophet, he might entice the people into idolatry. In that dispute, it is believable that the Devil spewed many blasphemies against God and Michael. Michael, however, *did not dare*, or *did not bring himself to* (for Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), a renowned English scholar and theologian known for his work on Greek linguistics</note> has proved with several examples that "to dare" <note>original Greek: "τολμᾶν" (tolman)</note> can sometimes mean this), to cast upon him a mark of malediction. This was not because he feared the Devil, but because he wished to act in all things with decorum, to properly maintain the character of the Angel he had assumed, to show himself most unlike the Devil, and to leave an example of patience for the men to whom these things were to be revealed. Nor is this unworthy of the majesty of so great an Angel: for in Zechariah 3:2, *the Angel of Jehovah, who is himself Jehovah, said to Satan, "The Lord rebuke thee."* And perhaps it was from this that Jude concluded—since his "mindset" <note>original Greek: "φρόνημα" (phronēma)</note> is always the same—that in that struggle he spoke similarly, and did not pronounce judgment in any other way than by demanding the judgment of the Father.

</margin>

Therefore, following the goats as guides, they came to precipices of immense depth, within which they found a valley of small circumference but most pleasant, into which the descent was very difficult, through the rocks...

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XVII.

...that this was the tomb of the [servant of the] Lord, but rather belonged to another Moses who lived many centuries later. And so, the belief regarding the discovery of the tomb of Moses vanished once more. Thus far, the account of Hornius <note>Georg Horn (1620–1670), a Dutch historian and geographer who wrote extensively on biblical history and the origins of nations.</note>.

<margin>XVII. The mystery of this whole matter.</margin>
XVII. But let us return to our purpose. It is not probable that in these singular works of Divine providence—within a Dispensation <term>Economy (Oeconomia): The historical arrangement of God’s dealings with humanity, specifically the religious system of the Mosaic Law.</term> that was entirely symbolic and significant—there was no underlying mystery. This must be investigated through the analogy of the scriptures. 

**I.** It is not for nothing that neither Aaron the High Priest, nor Moses the Lawgiver, led the people into possession of the holy land, but both passed away before it was accomplished; instead, that introduction was entrusted to Joshua. Does this not evidently teach the *weakness and uselessness of the ancient priesthood and law? For the Law made nothing perfect, but a better hope was introduced, through which we draw near to God* <note>original: Heb. VII, 18. 19.</note>. 

**II.** The death of Moses, occurring alongside the entry of the people into the rest of the land of Canaan—brought about by Joshua the son of Nun, the executor of the Mosaic covenant—indicated the *vanishing* <note>original Greek: ἀφανισμόν (aphanismon), meaning disappearance or abolition.</note>, obsolescence, death, and fading away of the Mosaic Dispensation. This was to be joined with the entry of the people into the rest of the new testament, brought about by Jesus, the Son of God and Mary, the guarantor of a better covenant. 

**III.** The burial of Moses signifies the total abolition of the Dispensation which has once vanished, so that it shall never live again or be restored; not even when the Israelite people, having finished the days of their rejection, are readmitted to the communion of Divine grace <note>original: Jer. III. 16. XXXI. 32.</note>. 

**IV.** The fact that the death of Moses happened *at the mouth of the Lord* <note>A literal translation of the Hebrew idiom meaning "by the command of the Lord."</note>, and his burial was provided by the Lord Himself, signifies that the abolition of the Mosaic Dispensation would occur according to God's will and predictions, to be carried out by the work of the Messiah Himself. *In the middle of the week, the Messiah shall abolish sacrifice and offering* <note>original: Dan. IX. 27.</note>. 

**V.** The dispute between Michael and the Devil over the body of Moses <note>A reference to the Epistle of Jude 1:9.</note> is a figure of those disputes which arose between the Apostles, the defenders of Christian liberty, and the stubborn Jews and False Apostles who urged the necessary observation of Mosaic ceremonies even in the Christian Church, pressing the Gentiles converted to the faith of Jesus under the same yoke. For those False Apostles, deceitful workers, what else were they but *ministers of Satan transforming themselves into Apostles of Christ?* <note>original: 2 Cor. XI. 13.</note> *They say they are Jews, and are not, but are the Synagogue of Satan* <note>original: Apoc. II. 9.</note>.

<margin>XVIII. Aaron was also a Prophet.</margin>
XVIII. Among the prophets in the desert, AARON, the brother of Moses, must also be included. He was not only a prophet for Moses and an interpreter of his mind, but also for God. For so God says in Exodus IV. 15: *I [will be with your mouth and his mouth]...*

## BOOK I. CHAPTER XVII.

...bowing down, they showed honor to God. <note>Commentary on Exodus 24:1–2</note> It was not yet the time for everyone to approach God indiscriminately and with great familiarity, as if they were already a "royal priesthood." This event was only a foretaste of the **manifestation of God** <note>original Greek: tēs epiphaneias tou Theou</note>; which, as the most celebrated Interpreter rightly notes, had to be made known to Israel through suitable witnesses. This was so they might know who had given them the precepts, to what hope all those symbolic figures were leading them, and finally, what kind of divine manifestation they should expect. For to those who ascended, it was granted to look upon the God of Israel—not indeed in His absolute essence, but in a certain symbol of His present Majesty and Grace. Indeed, it seems probable to me that He appeared in the form of a man standing on a jeweled floor, just as Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel saw God. For the words of the text suggest this when they mention the "feet" of God. Nor is this contradicted by what Moses says in Deuteronomy 4:15: *“For you saw no form on the day that Jehovah spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire.”* For in that passage, he is speaking of a different time—namely, the day the Law was given—and of different people; for that speech is directed to the whole nation, who saw nothing of God then, rather than to the elders specifically, who must certainly have seen some form of God if they saw His feet.

<margin>
XXII. Namely, the Son of God to be clothed in human flesh.
</margin>
XXII. Here again, some of the Hebrew Interpreters hold a notable tradition from the ancient teachings. Recanati, as cited by Alting, writes the following on the first verse of this chapter: *“The Blessed Great God ordered him to ascend to Jehovah; that is, to Metatron, who is sometimes called by the name of God, and signifies the **Shekhinah** <note>original Hebrew: Shekhinah, referring to the Divine Presence dwelling among men</note>, being called by that name.”* It is as if he had said: "Ascend to the place of glory where the Angel Redeemer is." This is correct. They saw the Son of God, the Angel Redeemer, who promised that He would dwell in their midst. In this apparition, there was a prelude to the **incarnation** <note>original Greek: ensarkōseōs</note>, through which it would come to pass that He would be seen present, eye to eye.

<margin>

According to Ruëus in his *Booklet on Gems*, sapphires are distinguished by a heavenly blue color, and the best ones also shimmer and sparkle with golden points. The Greek author agrees: *“The sapphire is a stone having flakes of gold as if in the shape of the letter sigma.”* <note>original Greek: Saptheiros lithos echon spiladas chrysion hōs en sigmasi</note> See Salmasius in his notes on Solinus, page 93. Certainly, it was once of great value. For this reason, elsewhere the Throne of God is seen in the likeness of a sapphire stone. <note>Ezekiel 1:26</note> This signifies the glorious Majesty of God, of which He wishes to make the Church a participant, according to the measure of its capacity. # ON THE PROPHETS IN THE DESERT.

...its stones, *and I will lay your foundations with Sapphires.* <note>Isaiah 54:11</note> There is a reason why those Sapphires had the appearance of *bricks* <note>original Latin: *laterum*, referring to the rectangular shape of bricks or tiles</note>. In part, this pertains to their beauty, for it implies the great size of the Sapphires, their orderly shape, and their purpose as a kind of floor spread beneath God. In another part, it regards the Israelites themselves. It is believed that God wished to use this symbol to call to their memory the slavery they had served in Egypt, where they were forced to make bricks from mud. But now, from slaves they had become a free people, the people of God, whom God walked among as if with His own feet—*the stones of the Sanctuary, their sapphire-like polish.* <note>Lamentations 4:1, 7</note> Furthermore, it is added that there appeared under God’s feet something like *the very body of heaven in its brightness*, which signifies both the purity of Divine holiness and the splendor of His grace. Just as a cloudy sky is a sign of Divine anger. <note>Jeremiah 4:23, 28; Zephaniah 1:15</note> Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology"</note> interprets the *Sapphire* as a *Carbuncle* <note>a red gemstone, often associated with glowing coal or blood</note>; and having made that assumption, he continues: *the floor, in the likeness of a carbuncle, signifies a kingdom founded in blood.* The clarity signifies <term>purity and integrity</term> <note>original Greek: *to eilikrines kai akeraion*</note>.

<margin>
XXIV.
What does it
mean that
they ate
and drank
having seen
God?
</margin>
XXIV. Finally, it follows that *God did not stretch out his hand against the chosen nobles of Israel*, namely to punish or take vengeance. For they had not approached the presence of the Deity with reckless daring against a command, but had been ordered to come closer along with Moses and Aaron. And *having seen God, they ate and drank.* Some interpret this as a fault, as if they had forgotten such great honor and immediately returned to the pleasures of this animal life. Others interpret it simply to mean that they remained among the living and returned unharmed from the sight of such great glory; whereas otherwise the accepted opinion was that those who saw God would soon die. The Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystical scholars</note> explain it more subtly as the nourishment of the soul, which is often presented under the image of physical food. They say the elders were nourished by the radiance of the *Shekinah* <note>the visible manifestation of the Divine Presence</note>. For if secondary causes <note>natural things like food and drink</note>, when applied, provide nourishment, how much more so the approach to the First Cause <note>God Himself</note>. *They nourished their eyes on the splendor of the Shekinah, like the Angels who carry the Throne of God’s glory, which is the nourishment of the soul and its delight.* See *Alting* <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a German Hebraist and theologian</note>. Yet those seventy were not so spiritual: for among those who approached, it is believable that there were some who later bound themselves to the crime of the golden calf. To me, it seems these things were done according to the ancient rite, in which banquets were provided after the ratification of a covenant. <note>Genesis 26:30; 31:54</note> Thus God here also prepared a banquet for those joined to Him in covenant, so that they might eat and drink before His face—whether of the remains of the peace offerings, or of Manna, or some other food, which could not be lacking to God. This was a proof of peace...

XXV. Then also seventy other elders prophesied.
</margin>

XXV. But neither should we overlook in this history the **OTHER SEVENTY ELDERS OF ISRAEL**, who were joined to Moses by the will of God when he complained of the excessive burden of governing. Regarding them, God said to Moses in Numbers 11:17: *“I will take of the spirit that is upon you and will put it upon them; thus they shall bear the burden of the people with you, and you shall not bear it alone.”* This was very pleasing to Moses, who, as he was commanded, gathered seventy men from the elders of the people and stood them around the tent of meeting, there to be consecrated as if to God. This was so they would recognize that they would perform the office of judges in God’s name, and that judgment itself is not so much of men as it is of God. <note>Deuteronomy 1:17</note> *Then the LORD <note>original Latin: *Jehova*</note> descending in a cloud spoke to him, and taking from that spirit which was upon him, he bestowed it upon those seventy elder men. Not that those things shared with them were taken away from Moses, but that they were each made partakers of their own portion of the same spirit with which Moses had been gifted.* The Chaldean <note>referring to the Aramaic Targum, a translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> paraphrases <note>original Greek: *paraphrazei*</note>: *“and he multiplied from the spirit that was upon him, and gave to them.”* <note>original Aramaic: *ve-rabbi min rucha d’alohi*</note> But Rabbi *Salomo* <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> illustrates the matter with an elegant comparison. *“At that hour,”* he says, *“Moses was like a lamp placed on the top of a stand, from which all the others are lit, without any loss—not even the smallest—to its own light.”* <note>original Hebrew: *lamah Moshe domeh ba-otah sha'ah...*</note> That spirit which was given to them was the author and giver of wisdom, prudence, equity, justice, gentleness, and the other virtues required in judges and governors of a commonwealth. But it also produced something unusual in them: namely, that they *prophesied*. That is, either by Divine impulse they broke out into praises of God, or they spoke skillfully and to the amazement of their listeners about the most excellent and Divine matters in a very solemn discourse that far exceeded their previous aptitude and the common lot of the Israelites—*declaring the mighty works of God.* <note>original Greek: *apophtheggontes ta megaleia tou Theou*</note> Thus, from both the subject matter and the manner and style of the speech, it was clear that they were moved by the Spirit of God. This, however, happened only on that day. *For they did not continue to prophesy.* <note>Numbers 11:25</note> Nor was it greatly necessary for the ordinary performance of their duty. It sufficed—

<margin>XXVI. Eldad and Medad; Joshua is indignant, but Moses approves.</margin>

XXVI. Furthermore, a memorable thing occurred: two men, **ELDAD** and **MEDAD**, although they were among those enrolled, had remained in the camp and had not presented themselves at the tent of meeting. This was perhaps because they shrank from the burden of governance, preferring the quiet of private life; or perhaps out of modesty, because they judged themselves unworthy of public duties—just as for the same reason Saul hid himself among the baggage <note>referring to 1 Samuel 10:22</note> when he was to be sought for the kingship. Or it may have been for some other reason unknown to us. The Hebrew teachers <note>referring to the Rabbinic tradition and Midrash</note>, who claim to know everything, recount Moses’ entire deliberation on this matter and the order of this enrollment—beyond what is found in the sacred history—in roughly this way: 

Moses thought to himself: "If I take six men from each of the twelve tribes, there will be seventy-two, two more than the required number of seventy. If I take five from each, ten will be missing. If I take five from some tribes and six from others, it will stir up envy among the tribes." To avoid this, he took seventy-two small scrolls, seventy of which were inscribed with the word *Zaken* <note>original Hebrew: זקן, meaning "Elder"</note>, while the remaining two were either blank, as some relate, or inscribed with the word *Chelek* <note>original Hebrew: חלק, meaning "Portion" or "Part"</note>. After he had mixed them in a box, he ordered everyone to draw a scroll. To the one who drew a scroll inscribed with the name *Zaken*, he said: *"God has already sanctified you."* To the one who drew a blank or otherwise inscribed scroll, he said: *"God does not want you; what can I do for you?"* They claim this was the lot of Eldad and Medad, who were thus excluded from the dignity and office of the Senate <note>the author uses the Roman term 'Senatus' to describe the assembly of elders</note>. However, they were not excluded from the sharing of the spirit, for they also prophesied in the camp. Joshua was indignant and asked Moses to restrain them, but he did not succeed. Instead, he received a response worthy of Moses, and worthy of being remembered through all ages: 

> *"Are you envious on my account? Would that all the Lord's <note>original Latin: Jehova</note> people were prophets, with the Lord putting his spirit upon them!"*

<margin>XXVII. A passage from James chapter 4:5 illustrated by this occasion.</margin>

...unlikely from the history just set forth. Moses is commanded to lay hands on him <note>referring to Joshua</note>. This ceremony is commonly used in consecrations (Numbers 8:10) and was followed by an even more abundant measure of the spirit (Deuteronomy 34:9). For Joshua, son of Nun, was full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands upon him. Furthermore, Moses is commanded to stand him before Eleazar the priest and the whole assembly, so that he might be recognized by everyone and all might be witnesses to the commands being entrusted to him. For he was to be instructed in these commands before their very eyes. Those commands appear in Deuteronomy 31:7–8. After Moses proclaimed these, God added His own (Deuteronomy 31:14–15). For God said to Moses: "Behold, your days are near when you must die; call Joshua and present yourselves at the tent of meeting, so that I may instruct him." Therefore, Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves at the tent of meeting. And Jehovah appeared in the tent in a pillar of cloud, with the pillar of cloud standing over the entrance of the tent. Here indeed something prophetic happened to Joshua, in that he was instructed in his commands by God Himself without the intervention of any other creature. God adds: "You shall impart to him some of your glory, so that the entire assembly of the children of Israel may listen to him." This may be appropriately understood as the excellence of the gifts of soul and body, and the resulting venerable Majesty which would strike the eyes of the people with a remarkable appearance and turn their minds toward reverence. 1 Chronicles 29:25 deserves to be compared here: "Jehovah magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, bestowing upon him a royal Majesty such as had not been upon any king before him in Israel." The Chaldean interpreter <note>referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> and other Hebrew Teachers <note>the Rabbis of the Talmudic and Midrashic tradition</note> think here of that extraordinary brightness with which Moses' face shone, which they claim was shared with Joshua so that God might make him venerable to the Israelites through such a remarkable sign of His favor.

<margin>
II. Yet in such a way that it was simultaneously taught that he was lesser than Moses.
</margin>

II. Rabbi Menachem <note>Menachem Recanati, a 14th-century Italian rabbi and kabbalist</note> observes very well that it was not said, "you shall impart *your* glory," but "*from* your glory" <note>original Latin: *de tua gloria*</note>. From this, the Elders <note>the ancient Jewish sages</note> have handed down the tradition that the face of Moses was like the face of the sun, while the face of Joshua was like the face of the moon. But what is added next is especially noteworthy: "He shall stand before Eleazar the Priest, that he may consult him concerning the judgment of the Urim before Jehovah; at his word they shall go out," etc. Two things are implied by these words: first, that in the performance of his office, and especially in military affairs, Joshua was to do everything according to the decree of Jehovah. Since God Himself was the supreme King and Commander of the people, Joshua was to serve only as His legate. Second, that God ordinarily indicated His will to the Priest through the judgment of the Urim <note>the Urim and Thummim were sacred lots or objects kept in the High Priest's breastplate used to determine God's will</note>. From this it follows that Joshua did not possess that same familiarity with God that Moses had, which allowed him, whenever he wished, to [consult] God immediately...

...it was permitted to approach God; nor had he used the benefit of prophetic instinct so frequently.

<margin>III. Although God often deigned to address him with His word.</margin>
<margin>Joshua 1:1.</margin>
III. Nevertheless, God deigned to honor him several times with this honor, so as to address him directly: and indeed, immediately after the death of Moses. The **Talmudists** <note>Scholars of Jewish law and tradition who compiled the Talmud</note>, in their usual manner—that is, boldly—define this as having occurred after the thirtieth day from Moses' death, since the Israelites wept for the funeral of Moses for thirty days. They take this for granted, assuming that a person's mind, occupied by either mourning or any other disturbance, cannot be inspired by the **prophetic Spirit** <note>The divine influence or "instinct" that allows a person to receive revelation</note>. But *Masius* <note>original: "Masius"; referring to Andreas Masius, a 16th-century scholar known for his commentary on Joshua</note> considers it more likely, and not without reason, that as soon as Moses had departed from this life, Joshua immediately applied his whole mind to the thought of managing the government entrusted to him; and while he was turning many things over in a hesitating mind, he was uplifted by this Divine address. It is not believable that this consisted of some articulated speech falling into his ears, but rather an illumination of the mind, so that he perceived the things mentioned in his soul no less than if all those words had been pronounced clearly in his presence with a distinct voice; and at the same time, he understood that this illumination came to him from God. For then God is said to speak words to Joshua, or any other **prophet** <note>original: "vatem"</note>, when He so informs their minds with the notions of those things that they not only see the matters themselves in their mind as if present and placed before their eyes, but simultaneously understand that this stirring of their mind is heavenly, and they are affected no differently than if they heard God speaking with them in the clearest voice. But at other times also, God addressed Joshua: Chapter 3:7, 4:1, 15, 5:2, 9, and elsewhere quite often.

<margin>IV. The appearance which occurred to him near Jericho, very similar to the one by which Moses was honored.</margin>
IV. But more illustrious than the rest is that appearance of God which occurred to Joshua near Jericho, and is recorded in Chapter 5:13 and following. This comes very close to the vision that had once been presented to Moses in the bush. And, as has been most learnedly observed by *Masius*, there seems to have been a similar reason for both, and the same purpose of God in both: so that the mind of each Commander, at the very beginning of their conduct of affairs, might be simultaneously strengthened with certain confidence and restrained from insolent arrogance, while they were taught that the arduous and difficult commands they were undertaking were to be carried out by God’s counsel, will, and power, and not by their own strength or wisdom. But see how wisely God offered Himself to be seen by His servants under a different emblem. For the nature of the different tasks to be performed required that different appearances be offered to them. Moses—who had to struggle with a cruel master of the people <note>Pharaoh</note>, and even with the very elements of nature, in Egypt, in the sea, and in the wilderness—saw the bush, namely the people of whom he...

V. But who is that armed man? He calls himself the PRINCE OF THE ARMY OF JEHOVAH. It is clear enough that an Angel is indicated by this title. But which Angel? Who, if not the one concerning whom God spoke these words to Moses: *Behold, I send an Angel before you, to keep you in this way, and to bring you into that place which I have prepared.
