This Angel is the eternal Son of God, to whom belongs all the power of the name of Jehovah, the perpetual Prince and director of the people of God. Again, it is pleasing here to listen to the teaching of the ancient Hebrews, the remnants of which exist in the **Book of Tanchuma** <note>original: "Libro Tanchuma"; a collection of homiletic teachings on the Torah known as the Midrash Tanhuma</note>: from which the most learned **Masius** <note>original: "Masius"; Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish scholar and expert in Hebrew and Syriac</note>—who has been rightly praised by us several times—noted down the following points. God said to Moses, BEHOLD I SEND AN ANGEL BEFORE YOUR FACE. But *Moses* responded, I do not want an Angel, but I want you yourself. Furthermore, *Joshua* the son of *Nun*, when he first saw the Angel, said, ARE YOU FOR US, OR FOR OUR ADVERSARIES? Then the Angel said to him, I, he said, AM THE PRINCE OF THE ARMY OF THE LORD. NOW I HAVE COME. As if he were saying, *“I am now present for the second time, so that I may lead the Israelites into the possession of their inheritance. For I had also come when Moses your Teacher was the Commander. But he, when he saw me, did not want me to go with him, but pushed me away from himself.”* As soon as *Joshua* had heard these things, he fell on his face, and worshipping him, said, WHAT DOES MY LORD SPEAK TO HIS SERVANT? These words have something of the truth, but under coverings and with a mixture of error, as is common in Jewish writings. It is true that Moses once rejected an Angel offered to him by God. Exodus 33:2, 12, 13, 14, 15. However, that was not this Angel whom God had promised in Exodus 23:20. Far be it that *Moses* rejected him! He asked for him to go with him when he said, IF YOUR FACE DOES NOT GO BEFORE US, DO NOT COMMAND US TO DEPART HENCE. For, as we recently heard from the **Gerundensian** <note>original: "Gerundensi"; referring to Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides or Ramban, a medieval scholar from Girona</note>, the Angel of the Covenant, the Angel of the Face, is the very face of God. This is the same Angel whom God, having promised him to Moses, now also presents to Joshua. He is the same who dwelt in the bush: who demands from Joshua, as a demonstration of reverence, what he once demanded from Moses, *that he take off his shoe*.

they observe a distinction. To Moses it was said, *take off your shoes from your feet*, using the plural number: but to Joshua, *take off your shoe from your foot*, in the singular. Isaac **Arama** <note>original: "Isaac Aramæus"; a 15th-century Spanish rabbi and philosopher known for his work 'Akedat Yitzchak'</note> attributes this to the fact that <margin>The removal of shoes.</margin> Moses was burdened with a double care, both of which he was commanded to cast from himself onto God; whereas Joshua had only one. Another Jew, well-versed in the philosophy of the **Kabbalists** <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> named **Bahya** <note>original: "Bahya"; likely Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish scholar</note>, thinks the difference in number refers to the more abundant understanding of things with which Moses was to be informed by God above Joshua, and to the higher rank by which he was to be admitted more closely into God's familiarity. But, as **Masius** judiciously observes, these points are more clever than they are firm.

He also solemnly renewed the covenant between God and Israel, writing the promises of the people in the **BOOK OF THE LAW OF GOD**. Finally, he erected a stone under the oak tree which was near the sanctuary of God, so that this stone might serve as a witness for them, lest they should lie to their God. Joshua 24. Many things converge here that are most worthy of note, in which the wisdom of Joshua—or rather the instinct of the Divine Spirit—shines forth remarkably. And first, indeed, is that he summoned the leaders of the people to the *field of Shechem*. For it was there that **Abraham**, when he first reached Canaan after leaving his homeland, built an altar to the God who appeared to him. Genesis 12:7. And truly, that very place must have moved their minds not a little, where perhaps the footprints of Abraham still remained, and where he first of all had been initiated into that religion and those sacred rites which Joshua was now instilling in his grandsons, who had become heirs of the land. Next, it should also be noted that all these things were performed by Joshua through a prophetic impulse: for he begins his speech with the formula solemn to the prophets: **THUS SAYS THE LORD** <note>original: "SIC AIT JEHOVA"</note>, and introduces the Lord himself speaking in the first person, as the Grammarians say. Furthermore, it is memorable that he wished not only to write down the words of this covenant, following the example of Moses, but to **WRITE THEM IN THE VERY BOOK OF THE LAW OF GOD**, namely that which was kept and preserved at the side of the Ark of the Covenant as a witness—

<margin>VIII. Whether he is the author of the book bearing his title is not entirely certain.</margin>
VIII. Whether he also wrote his own history, and this very book which we now possess, is a matter of debate among the learned; and as is common in matters that are not clear, the arguments on both sides are not particularly firm. At the very least, it seems to me that the reasoning of **Huetius** <note>original: "Huetii"; referring to Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and prominent scholar</note> cannot withstand the weight of a solid demonstration. From the words just praised—*Joshua also wrote all these words in the volume of the law of the Lord*—he infers the following: He says that if one pays attention, these words surely signify that Joshua, following the example of Moses, committed his deeds to writing and added his book to the end of the book of the law written by Moses, just as it is now joined to it. But, I say, if one pays attention, they will easily discover that the passage does not concern the entire history of Joshua, but rather the repeated solemn enactment of the covenant; nor is the discussion there about joining another volume to the volume of the law, but about the volume of the law itself, in which this repetition of the covenant was inscribed. Furthermore, most of the arguments brought forward by the opposing side are such that they can be avoided by a sufficiently convenient response. Therefore, let me be permitted to **withhold judgment** <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epechein); a term from Skeptic philosophy meaning to suspend assent or judgment when evidence is balanced</note>.

IX. > I made you go up from Egypt, and I brought you into this land which I had promised by oath to your ancestors, and I said: I will not make my covenant with you void forever. Wherefore I also say, I will not expel them from before your face; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you.

Upon hearing this, the people, moved by the consciousness of their crimes, broke out into profuse tears, from which the name stuck to the place. For **Bochim** in Hebrew signifies *those who weep*. Judges 2:1—-.

### ON THE PROPHETS IN CANAAN

<margin>II. 7.</margin> II. Because he is said to have ascended from Gilgal. For those from above descend, they do not ascend: and they descend from heaven, not from Gilgal, or any other earthly place. III. Because he is not read to have disappeared anywhere. IV. *Jonathan the Chaldean Paraphrast* <note>original: "Jonathan Chaldaeus Paraphrastes"; refers to the author of the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note>, who lived around the times of Christ, further confirms this: for he *paraphrases* <note>original: "παραφράζει"</note> this passage thus: THE PROPHET ASCENDED ON A MISSION FROM BEFORE THE LORD FROM GALGALA. *Learnedly*, says *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a highly regarded Flemish Protestant scholar of Old Testament and Hebrew studies</note>, *as always*. For in a simple historical narrative, the Angel of Jehovah <note>original: "Angelus Jehovae"</note> does not usually denote a human Prophet without any additional description, especially in those most ancient times of the Israelite people, when Prophets were called "men of God." I do find, indeed, a prophet described as an "Angel of God." But I do not find that where an "Angel of God" is said to have appeared or come, a Prophet is the intended meaning.

<margin>XI. But the Son of God.</margin> XI. And indeed, this Angel here uses language that is suitable not for a man, nor for any created Angel, but for Jehovah himself: for that Jehovah, I say, who is also the "Angel of Jehovah" <note>Many theologians of this period identified the "Angel of the Lord" as the "Pre-incarnate Christ" or the Son of God</note>. For he attributes to himself the fact that he led the people out of Egypt, and introduced them into Canaan, and that he does not wish to expel the remaining Canaanites. These things belong only to that Angel in whom the name of Jehovah is, and who, appearing to Joshua, testified that he was the Captain of the hosts of the Lord. For to imagine a Prophet speaking as the person of him whose messenger he is <note>i.e., speaking in the first person as if he were God himself</note> does not fit the style of Scripture. Prophets are accustomed to preface their words with: *Thus says Jehovah*. This is not found here, nor do we dare to add it of our own accord. As for his being said to have "ascended from Gilgal," this pertains to the *form* <note>original: "σχῆμα"</note> of the appearance. He first appeared in Gilgal, and from there he moved to this place. Moreover, he conveniently came from that place where he had stayed for a long time for the protection of the camp, and was even then believed to stay. This was especially effective for refreshing the memory of the benefits received there and of the covenant renewed through circumcision. That he is not recorded to have disappeared is a minor point: for neither is the disappearance of that Angel narrated who was seen by Joshua. The authority of Jonathan the Paraphrast is not of such great weight as to override sounder reasons.

<margin>Judges VI. 11.</margin> <margin>XII. Who appeared to Gideon and the parents of Samson.</margin> XII. In a not very dissimilar manner, the Angel of the Lord appeared to GIDEON (Judges 6:12) and to the PARENTS OF SAMSON (Judges 13:3, 9, 11), whom they wrongly thought to be a *Man of God*. Otherwise, the word of Jehovah was rare in the times of the *Judges*, and there was no "open vision" (1 Samuel 3:1). (*)

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>An anonymous prophet sent to Eli.</margin>

There are even those who understand him to be *Samuel* himself. Most importantly, the first appearance of God to Samuel is not only narrated in the following chapters, but is clearly later than this prophet's declaration; Samuel's vision is actually a repetition and confirmation of it. <margin>XIV. Samuel, Nathan, Gad, Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun.</margin>

It is much more consistent to believe that the deeds of the Prophets were inserted into the history of David’s reign; and elsewhere, too, Prophets are praised as the writers of the histories of their own time. ## ON THE PROPHETS IN CANAAN.

**[The words] of David and of Asaph the seer.** Note that **Asaph** is not only called a "Seer" <note>original: *Videntem*; a term for a prophet who receives divine visions</note>, but he also left behind written words in which Jehovah was to be celebrated no less than by the words of David. Only one Psalm carries the name of **Heman**, namely Psalm 88; we recently argued against *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist and clergyman</note> that this should be attributed to a contemporary of David. Heman was certainly the *King’s Seer*. 1 Chronicles 25:5. The name of **Jeduthun** is found in the titles of three Psalms: 39, 62, and 77.

<margin>XV. David also a Prophet.</margin>
XV. But King **David** himself is also a great name among the Prophets. For Peter speaks of him in this way in *Acts 2:30–31: Being therefore a PROPHET, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne; he, seeing this before, spoke of the resurrection of Christ.* And truly, such clear prophecies concerning Christ exist in the Psalms of David that one can learn from them almost everything that must be held regarding His person, offices, states, and benefits. Many passages belonging here are frequently cited in the New Testament by Christ and the Apostles—not merely as an elegant allusion, but as a solid proof and confirmation of the matters being discussed. But most worthy of eternal record <note>original: *cedro dignissima*; literally "worthy of cedar oil," used in antiquity to preserve precious manuscripts</note> are the last words of David, in which he both professes himself to be a prophet and explains, in a divinely inspired speech, those blessings which encompass the covenant of grace founded in the Messiah. 2 Samuel 23:1–3: *The saying of David the son of Jesse, the saying, I say, of the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet Psalmist of Israel. The Spirit of Jehovah spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue. The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me, etc.*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

"...lifted his heel against me" <note>original: *versus me calcem*; a reference to Psalm 41:9, traditionally applied to the betrayal of Jesus</note>. Without a doubt, says the **Critic**; he was thinking of one of those who notably supported **Absalom** <note>the son of David who led a rebellion against him</note> in his uprising; consider **Ahithophel**, perhaps, or someone else like him: and it is clear that he is speaking of an event that had already happened to him. And **THIS VERY EVENT INSPIRED THOSE WORDS IN HIM** which noted the betrayal of **Christ** by one of his own Apostles: as is evident from *John 13:18.* The Author of Psalms 69 and 109—**WHETHER IT WAS DAVID, OR ANYONE ELSE—DID NOT INTEND**, as it is reasonable to believe, in his own mind to prophesy something that would happen many centuries later to one of the disciples of **Jesus**, when he was striking his enemies with the most dreadful curses; meanwhile, **Peter** proceeds to apply certain words from those Psalms to the traitor **Judas**. *Acts 1:20.* No great light of understanding is needed to perceive that this Author’s intention was not to speak of **Judas**; **NOR WAS HE INSPIRED BY A SPIRIT OF MERCY**, when he broke out into this deadly song: *Set a wicked man over him, and let an accuser stand at his right hand, etc. Psalm 109:6 and following.* **WITH NO EFFORT IT IS SEEN THAT THESE ARE ONLY THE WORDS OF A MAN MOVED BY VEHEMENT ANGER, AND BURNING WITH AN EXTREME DESIRE FOR REVENGE**, such as neither the Law of **Moses** would permit, nor the Gospel of **Christ** would endure. And therefore, that Theologian <note>likely referring to a rationalist critic of the era</note> is indignant that there was an interpreter of great name who wrote in the summary of the Psalm that **David**, **AS A FIGURE OF JESUS CHRIST**, driven by a singular zeal, demanded vengeance from God upon his enemies. *But, where, he asks, do they find that Christ cursed his enemies in this manner? Have they forgotten the words with which, near death, he so mercifully interceded for the most wicked of mortals? Were not the worst of all his adversaries, and the sworn enemies of the Gospel, those who with criminal minds and hands fixed him to the cross? Yet, he was so far from thundering deserved curses upon them that, on the contrary, he implored the grace of his Father for the pardon of such great crimes. I confess, he continues, that I do not understand the Christian religion if it permits such curses, and if through it one may demand such horrible vengeance from one’s enemies, as we see done by the author of this and other Psalms.*

<margin>XIX. David spoke of Christ with foreknowledge.</margin>

But since that "type" was established by Divine counsel, and the things that happened to the "type" were intended to prefigure those things which were to come in the <term>ANTITYPE</term> <note>The fulfillment of a prophecy or prefiguration, specifically Christ</note>; the narrative of the event seen in the "type" is not a matter of chance similarity, but by Divine design, it is a true prediction of the thing to be fulfilled in the "antitype." Nor is there any reason for us to believe that God did not, by that same design, so direct the speech of the prophets that it first signified those things which were lesser in the "type," while more strongly expressing those things which were to be greater in the "antitype." ### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

...happened, and that there was no more secret meaning in the words which the Spirit dictated to him? Certainly, **Peter** testifies that the Spirit of **Christ**, acting as a messenger within the prophets, caused them to **SEEK AND SEARCH OUT** those things that were to happen to **Christ**, *both his sufferings and the glory that would follow them* <note>original: "tam perpeſſiones illius, quam gloriam eas conſecuturam"</note> (1 Peter 1:10-11). Furthermore, the comparison made in this regard between **David** and **Caiaphas** <note>Caiaphas was the Jewish High Priest who presided over the trial of Jesus; the author is likely responding to an argument that David, like Caiaphas, spoke words he didn't fully understand.</note> is truly unjust. And yet even this **Caiaphas**, though he did not know it, did not prophesy without **God's** hand. It was not merely the nature of the business being discussed—as those critics wish to claim—but the remarkable providence of **God** that dictated those words to him. For **John** implies this when he reminds us that he *was the High Priest of that year*.

<margin>XX. And indeed by the inspiration of God.</margin>
XX. II. Furthermore, it is entirely intolerable that he <note>Referring to the critic Jean Le Clerc.</note> denies that the **Spirit of God** inspired either the words or the meaning to **David** when he produced those prophecies about **Christ**. These views are diametrically opposed to the clearest teaching of **Christ** and the **Apostles**. The **Apostles** testify that **GOD SPOKE THROUGH THE MOUTH OF DAVID HIS SERVANT** (Acts 4:25), and **Christ** himself says that **DAVID SPOKE THROUGH THE HOLY SPIRIT** (Matthew 22:43). Nowhere are we taught that the **Psalms of David** are to be so distinguished that he spoke some through the **Holy Spirit** and others without the **Spirit**, or by the instinct of another spirit that is contrary to the **Holy Spirit**.

<margin>XXI. Prophecy is properly contained in the words themselves.</margin>
XXI. III. If the things **David** sang came only from his own poetic talent, thinking only of his own affairs, to which other events concerning **Christ** only accidentally correspond; I would confidently say that those are no more prophecies about **Christ** than if I were to tell a part of the Gospel history using a "cento" <term>A 'cento' is a poem made up of various lines or fragments from another author, such as Virgil, rearranged to create a new story.</term> compiled from the verses of **Virgil**, and then try to sell that cento as a prophecy. Is this how **Christ** and the **Apostles** would have acted? Is this worthy of their wisdom and power? Is this worthy of the **Gospel**? The very phrasing used by **Christ** and the **Apostles**, when they adapted the words of the **Psalms** to their own purpose, indicates that a true logic of prophecy lay beneath them. If verse 10 of **Psalm 41** dealt with nothing but **David's** own affairs, was it appropriate for **Christ**, when he predicted the betrayal of **Judas**, to use this speech: **IT IS NECESSARY THAT THE SCRIPTURE BE FULFILLED**, *he who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me* (John 13:18)? # BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

...memory is elegantly preserved by these enigmatic names. Furthermore, **AGUR**—that is, Solomon, now recovered through true repentance—introduces a speaker: *The man to Ithiel and Uchal* <note>original Hebrew: *Ha-geber le-Ithiel ve-Uchal* (Proverbs 30:1)</note>. *The Man* <note>original: *Ha-geber*</note> is a name derived from strength, and denotes a robust man, a hero. *Ithiel* is explained by most as having the letter "L" as a prefix indicating a recipient, and they then translate *Ithiel* as *God is with me*. However, the most renowned Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note> thinks that the "L" belongs to the root word, and that the name is composed of *Leithi* and *El*, meaning *I have labored* or *I have been exhausted for God’s sake*. *Uchal* signifies *I have prevailed*. Thus, these names would enigmatically describe a man who, endowed with the greatest talent and mental strength, wrestled with God to know and embrace Him with the greatest labor and exhaustion, and eventually "conquered," so that he truly knew and embraced God.

<margin>XXVIII. A confession of his own dullness is not unworthy of the wisest Solomon.</margin>
XXVIII. Such a man—whether it be Solomon himself or anyone else endowed with those faculties—must say, *I am more stupid than any man, etc.* <note>Quoting Proverbs 30:2: "Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man."</note>; that is, he must issue a confession of his own ignorance, stupidity, and natural blindness. This shows that the knowledge of the secrets of God, and of His counsels and ways, surpasses the reach, insight, and talent of the human mind. And indeed, this is how things truly stand: the wiser someone is, the more clearly they perceive their own dullness when they apply themselves to contemplating Divine matters. For when one considers the great works of God, so great a Maker, and the Son of such a Maker—and considers also the depths of the Divinely revealed Word—all senses immediately vanish. All reason and every sharp point of our talent fails us, to such an extent that in these great contemplations, even the wisest person seems cast down below the common lot of men, and the splendor of such great light obscures the entire vision of the mind's eye. Therefore, is this confession of his own dullness unworthy of the wisest Solomon? Does it contradict the profession of wisdom he makes elsewhere? He could glory in the Lord regarding the wisdom granted to him by God when making a comparison not so much with Divine things, but with other men.

# ON THE PROPHETS IN CANAAN.

...admonition of his duty, so that he might conduct himself in a manner befitting a minister of God, and one who knows himself to be God’s special possession.

<margin>XXX. The Book of Proverbs must be held as Canonical.</margin>
XXX. To this book, which includes the Proverbs of Solomon under whatever name, the entire Church—both Hebrew and Christian—attributes Divine and Canonical authority. In this, they follow the lead of the Apostles, who on several occasions cite passages from this book in the New Testament, and indeed do so as part of Divine Scripture. Thus, Paul in *Romans* 3:10, 15, testifies that it is **WRITTEN**, *their feet are swift to shed blood*, which is taken from *Proverbs* 1:16. Add also *Romans* 12:20 compared with *Proverbs* 25:21; *Hebrews* 12:5-6 compared with *Proverbs* 3:11-12; and *James* 4:6 compared with *Proverbs* 3:32. I omit other examples. Rightly, therefore, "the whole choir of the ancients called the Proverbs of Solomon 'all-virtuous wisdom'" <note>original Greek: *panareton sophian*</note>, as recorded by **Eusebius** in his *History, Book IV, Chapter XXV*. Furthermore, **Theodore of Mopsuestia** <note>A 5th-century bishop and theologian whose views on the human elements of Scripture were often controversial.</note> was marked by that name because he contended that "Solomon uttered those proverbs not from the grace of prophecy, but only from human prudence"; he was condemned in the **Fifth Council of Constantinople** around the **Year 551**.

<margin>XXXI. Though torn apart by unworthy insults from a recent Critic.</margin>
XXXI. A certain recent **Critic** <note>Likely referring to Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous biblical critic who questioned traditional views of inspiration.</note> thought he should proceed quite a bit further; he not only acknowledges no Divine inspiration in *Proverbs*, but does not even perceive anything remarkable in them. He says, "They are moral maxims which any honest man could say **WITHOUT INSPIRATION**. Indeed, infinitely many are found among them which are nothing but popular proverbs, in which there is indeed good sense, but **NOTHING DIVINE**. Household warnings occur in great number, which simple women and peasants everywhere know. Oh, how trivial!" But he even ventures to judge some as lacking wisdom and being unworthy of the Spirit of God: specifically those found in Chapter 30:18-20 <note>These verses describe "four things too wonderful for me," such as the way of an eagle in the sky.</note>. He says, "It must be frankly confessed that something better could have been said without the Prophetic Spirit. Those who believe that the Spirit of Prophecy uttered such things do not value the Spirit of Prophecy at its true worth." Indeed, he does not stop even here. He does not fear to criticize other parts as contrary to charity and the Gospel, in which category he places the warning about not rashly acting as a guarantor <note>term: *spondendo* / Suretyship (promising to pay another's debt)</note> for others, which is repeated several times: Chapters 6:1, 17:18, 22:26, 27:13. And he thinks himself witty and elegant when he jokes that our merchants, even without being warned, observe this religiously enough; finally ending that dispute with a mocking speech: "It was not very necessary, as it seems to me, for God to send Prophets to teach mortals thrift in the administration of their means..."

<margin>
XXXII. By whom it is seriously defended.
</margin>

XXXII. It is easy to notice where these arguments lead—no longer through winding paths, but by a straight road. Namely, if the Book of Proverbs contains nothing Divine; if the infinite number of sayings therein are nothing but common street-talk, which common women and peasants everywhere know; if others contain very little wisdom or good sense, such that better things are easily said; if some, finally, do not sufficiently agree with the charity and liberality commended by Christ: what remains but that a book of such a character be cast down from the canon <note>The "canon" refers to the official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture.</note> of Divine writings? That it should hardly be numbered among the wise and good? Or even that it be banished "to the market of stale and cold things" <note>original Greek: *eis tēn tōn heōlōn kai psychrōn agoran*</note>, into the street that sells frankincense and perfumes? <note>This is a literary reference to a place where failed books were sold to shopkeepers to be used as wrapping paper for spices.</note> What then? Is it mere boastfulness <note>The author uses the term "Thrasonism," referring to Thraso, a braggart soldier character from Roman comedy.</note> when the author of Proverbs testifies at the very opening of the work that these are *to know wisdom and instruction, to perceive the words of understanding; to receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity; to give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion.* And again in Chapter 8:5-7: *O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart. Hear; for* I WILL SPEAK EXCELLENT THINGS; *and the opening of my lips shall be right things. For my mouth shall speak truth* etc. Was the writer of the sacred history <note>Referring to the biblical author who recorded Solomon’s life in the Books of Kings.</note> destitute of judgment and out of his mind when he praises the incomparable wisdom of Solomon even for his proverbs? Or did all those things which contain such great wisdom perish, with only those being collected and preserved in which a tiny bit of good sense is perceived by the more subtle Critics? I wish the Critic here had followed his own Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who wrote extensively on the Bible.</note>, who established that this book is a selection <note>original Greek: *eklogēn*</note> of the best maxims: and that all things contained in it are ethical <note>original Greek: *ēthika*</note>, pertaining either to the precepts of morals or of prudence, yet in such a way that these and those always look back toward the worship of God. Is it permitted for a Christian man to deny that anything Divine is in that book which Paul, James, and Peter praise as a part of Divine Scripture? Does the divinity of the book get in the way of warnings regarding household prudence <term>Oeconomicæ prudentiæ</term> <note>From "o अर्थव्यवस्था" (oikonomia), meaning the management of a household or estate.</note>, known even to peasants and common women? Yet true wisdom and virtue are of the widest extension, and nothing is so small that it is not directed by them; nothing is so humble that it does not provide material and occasion for more sublime thoughts. By your faith, Critic: is there anything Divine in the speech of Isaiah which appears in Chapter 28:23 and following, where he begins with no small magnificence of words: *Give ye ear, and hear...*

"Give ear and hear my voice; hearken and hear my speech. Does the plowman plow all day to sow? Does he furrow and harrow his ground? XXXIII. And what do you find worthy of your criticism in Proverbs 30:18-19? <note>These verses describe "four things too wonderful for me": the way of an eagle, a serpent, a ship, and a man with a maiden.</note> Is there not indeed—in that lofty and swift flight of the eagle through the sky, in such agility and entanglement of the serpent and the winding of its coils, in the whole business of navigation, and in the loves of spouses to be joined in marriage—some hidden mystery? Is it not a mystery whose immediate causes, most singular reasons, and the special leadings of Divine providence the human mind cannot attain? Does not God himself number the eagle and its flight among his great works in Job 39:27-30? Is not the passage of ships through the sea also celebrated by David in Psalm 104:26, as providing an opportunity to see the works of God and his wonders in the deep (Psalm 107:23-24)? Is it not a stupendous thing which is seen in the marriages of people previously unknown to each other, joined by wondrous ways beyond the intention of either, and soon bound by such great love that it surpasses all devotion toward brothers, sisters, and even parents themselves? Is it unworthy of a wise man to profess his ignorance here, and to be amazed at these great works of Divine providence? Is it unworthy of the Spirit of God to train his people in this humility? Is a profession of ignorance more unseemly in the mouth of Agur <note>The attributed author of Proverbs 30.</note> than in the mouth of Asaph? <note>A Levite singer and composer to whom many Psalms are attributed.</note> For Asaph also wrote of himself:
> *I was as a brute, who was ignorant; I was like Behemoth, a great beast, before you.* Psalm 73:22.

XXXIV. Finally, what is there in the warnings against rash financial surety <term>surety: the act of taking legal responsibility for someone else's debt</term> that deserves to be picked apart? For it is not Solomon’s intent to forbid financial sponsorship at every time and in every case. Rather, he calls away thoughtless youth and other ill-advised squanderers of their resources from the rashness of guaranteeing debts, by which they might harm themselves and their families, and sometimes even the very person for whom they stand surety. Is this not a part of economic prudence? Is it unworthy of the Spirit of God to exhort his people to this form of wisdom and virtue as well? Does not Christ's [instruction] to his disciples tend toward the same end...

BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

...commanded <note>original Latin: *jussum*</note> that the remaining fragments be gathered so that nothing should perish? <note>A reference to Jesus’ command after the feeding of the five thousand in John 6:12.</note> Yet Christ also commended generosity and praised the Samaritan who stood as a guarantor for the wounded guest. This is true. But a wise thriftiness provides the very means by which you are able to be generous. A reckless pledge, by which you strip yourself of your goods to make someone already wealthy even richer, takes away that which you would have much more wisely spent on the poor, or promised on their behalf. I felt I owed this defense of the Divine Proverbs of Solomon against the audacity of modern Criticism.

<margin>XXXV. Calumnies against the Ecclesiastes of Solomon.</margin>
XXXV. Nor is it any more difficult to refute the objections the Critic has seen fit to raise against Solomon's other book <note>The Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>; in which he notices nothing prophetic. He does not think it probable that *the Spirit of God would wish to set out the reasonings and arguments of the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect known in the time of Jesus for denying the resurrection and the immortality of the soul.</note>, or even worse views, at such great length and in all their effectiveness*, only to refute them in a mere two or three words. He observes that *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch scholar who suggested Ecclesiastes was written later than Solomon’s time.</note> argued that while Ecclesiastes was written under Solomon's name, it was actually by someone else who lived in Chaldea. *This conjecture*, he says, *if it be true, means this book is nothing more than a sort of intellectual play by those who were in the Babylonian Captivity.* He adds that *he knows a certain man highly skilled in Sacred Criticism who suspects the author of this book was imbued with those opinions regarding the immortality of the soul and the future life which the Sadducees later held.* Yet, he himself thinks it better to determine nothing regarding this question.

<margin>XXXVI. Arguments Refuted. See also the Preface, Section XII.</margin>
XXXVI. To me, however, those who recognize Solomon as the author of this book, and acknowledge its subject and matter to be upright and holy, seem to hold a much more wholesome and sacred view. Indeed, the author must be the most deceitful of all mortals unless he is Solomon. For who besides Solomon was the son of David and King in Jerusalem? Who grew to such power and such wisdom that he surpassed all who were before him in Jerusalem? Who was supplied with such great wealth that he could complete those grand works in which this author testifies he indulged his heart? All these things are so unique to Solomon that they cannot be ascribed to anyone else. Grotius conjectures, indeed, that the writer lived in Chaldea, but he does so with no suitable argument. For in his belief that he can prove this from Chaldean words, he is mistaken. Even granting that some Chaldean words occur here, it proves that the author was not ignorant of that language; it does not prove he was in Chaldea. And how many, and what, are these Chaldean words? He finds only four in his Annotations. I. <term>סיר</term> <note>original Hebrew/Chaldean: *sir*</note>, a Pot. Chapter 7:6. But it is clear this is Hebrew from Exodus 16:3. II. <term>אביונה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *abiyyonah*</note>, Chapter 12:5 <note>Often translated as "desire" or "caper-berry."</note>, but this too is Hebrew, derived from the word "to will" <note>original: *abah*</note>.

XXXVII. Furthermore, the aim and theme of the book <note>The Book of Ecclesiastes</note> is entirely pious and holy. For it teaches the vanity of all human affairs, thoughts, affections, and even of wisdom itself; it condemns the restless curiosity and inconstancy of minds; it urges *euthymia* <note>original Greek: εὐθυμίαν; meaning a state of cheerfulness or tranquility of mind</note>, and the joyful use of God's gifts, which cannot be separated from a good conscience and the pursuit of those works that please God; and in that matter, it places the greatest happiness of this life. Meanwhile, it lifts the soul to higher things, warning that even in the use and fruit of pleasure, the memory of Divine judgment must be retained. Finally, it concludes in a manner worthy of the wisest Prophet: *The sum of the matter, all these things having been heard:* REVERE GOD HIMSELF, AND OBSERVE HIS COMMANDMENTS, FOR THIS IS THE WHOLE OF MAN. FOR GOD HIMSELF SHALL BRING EVERY WORK INTO JUDGMENT, WITH EVERY HIDDEN THING; WHETHER IT BE GOOD, OR EVIL. Is this the work of a Sadducee or an Epicurean? <note>Philosophical groups often accused of denying the afterlife or divine providence.</note> Those opinions which are scattered here and there, and which seem to sound negative or appear inconsistent, are, when considered in their proper context and explained as they ought to be, both true and consistent with others, and are all to be referred to the same goal.

<margin>XXXVIII. Insults against the Song of Songs.</margin>
XXXVIII. The Critic treats Solomon's third book, which is called the SONG OF SONGS, with no greater kindness. XXXIX. But if this is not turning the most sacred things into something profane, absurd, and ridiculous, what is? The poem itself bears Solomon's name. All sacred history records that Solomon was the wisest of all men. If indeed [he sang of] nothing but his own...

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

...and of some female friend of his, were he to sing of these loves in this song with a style so turgid and comparisons so enormous, I do not know how he could maintain his reputation for wisdom with this work; and indeed, it would be a poem more worthy of some Polyphemus <note>A Cyclops from Homer's Odyssey, used here to suggest a crude or monstrous character</note> than of the wisest, most refined, and most polished of Kings. What also was the mind of the Church, that it should guard with such diligence, as a most precious deposit, so turgid an <term>Idyllion</term> <note>A short poem, often pastoral</note> which in no way deserves to be compared with the <term>Bucolics</term> <note>Pastoral poems</note> of Theocritus and Virgil, or the <term>Epithalamiums</term> <note>Wedding songs</note> of Catullus, and in which there would scarcely be a grain of sound mind unless greater things lay beneath? Alas, what coals instead of treasure! <note>A Latin proverb meaning something that seems valuable but turns out to be worthless</note> The very name ***Song of Songs*** <note>original: *Cantici Canticorum*</note> indicates its excellence: but what excellence is there in it if it were nothing but a love song, revealing too openly the secret mysteries of nuptials and the soft whispers of lovers at night, with a <term>cothurnated</term> <note>Tragic or elevated; from the 'cothurnus' or high boot worn by ancient tragic actors</note> style and with the most daring and utterly unusual metaphors?

It is traditional in sacred matters to designate the closest and sweetest union of Christ and the Church, and their chaste loves, by the likeness of marriage; to call Him the bridegroom and beloved, and her the bride; especially in sacred songs. Psalm 45. Isaiah 5:1. This is truly the ***Song of Songs***, forged from many songs—indeed, embracing all songs and revealing their sum and marrow—in which, as if in a center, the remaining songs unite and harmonize. Thus, the nucleus of the sacred songs was gathered by Solomon into this poem. And indeed, there is discovered here a perpetual <term>dialogue</term> <note>original Greek: διαλογισμός, meaning a conversation or reasoning</note> of Christ, the Church, and His Ministers. 

Now the Church speaks words suited to her state at different times, expressing her charity, faith, hope, and burning desires; sometimes also joy and gladness, thanksgivings, and the boastings arising from them; at times the incomparable beauty of her bridegroom, and the incredible sweetness of his love; sometimes also complaints and prayers; and there are places where words of mutual encouragement intervene. Christ responds to the Church, signifying what He works in her at each time according to the diversity of her states: sometimes He raises a lament, sometimes He encourages, sometimes He consoles. If the words are explained with this mind, then they are most beautiful, most charming, and full of the best meanings. Then the poem will be worthy of its title, worthy of Solomon, worthy of the Church which guards and reads it, and worthy of the Holy Spirit who inspired it. These things we say on behalf of Solomon and his Divine writings.

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETS IN CANAAN

<margin>that bold Criticism.</margin>
All the Holy Scriptures [so the critics claim] were written without any inspiration, indeed by upright men and those most removed from any desire to lie, who declared the truth as far as they knew it and followed the most faithful records they could find; yet they were men subject to error even in writing, who—relying on different authors or through a lapse of memory—sometimes relate the same events in different ways, not without manifest, palpable, and irreconcilable contradictions. Some *Psalms* bearing the name of David are [according to these critics] born from anger and a desire for revenge rather than from the Spirit of God. In the *Proverbs* of Solomon there are many commonplaces, of which a Critic might easily have said better things without any divine inspiration. The *Song of Songs* has nothing mystical about it, but is similar to the rustic and giant-like song of Polyphemus <note>A reference to the crude, monstrous Cyclops from Greek mythology, used here to describe a style the author's opponents find unrefined</note>. If we proceed in this manner, how little of the Divine will finally remain? O wretched Church, who has until now guarded, kissed, and venerated such low-value writings as if they were a most precious treasure! Or rather, O bold and impious Criticism, which attributes to itself so much authority over Divine matters, and so wickedly snatches away the supports of the faithful’s faith and their most pleasant delights!

<margin>XLI. Of the following Prophets, some left writings, others did not.</margin>
XLI. But let us pursue the order of the Prophets, who are found to have been numerous in that and the following times; therefore, they must be discussed briefly, lest this commentary grow to an immense size. I find, however, that there were two kinds: some left no writings behind them which, having been brought into the Archives of the Church, still survive today; others are better known for the writings that still exist. I shall briefly present a catalog of the former, observing the chronological order in which they prophesied, and will soon speak of the others.

The same man, when his eyes were dim with old age, prophesied with a most solemn speech to the wife of Jeroboam—who was asking about the health of her sick son—not only of the son's death, but also the horrific slaughter of Jeroboam’s family and the destruction of the kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 14). When Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, held power in Jerusalem, <margin>Shemaiah.</margin> SHEMAIAH the prophet flourished, whose speeches to the King are recorded (2 Chronicles 11:2, 12:5). ...at that place he addressed the people with these words: *“Thus says God: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the Lord, He has also forsaken you.”* Having formed a conspiracy, they stoned him with stones by the King’s command in the courtyard of the house of the Lord. 2 Chronicles 24:20–21. This was the detestable ingratitude of King Joash, who owed his life, his kingdom, and all his prosperity to Jehoiada, the father of Zechariah. Therefore, Zechariah, receiving a reward so unworthy of his virtues and merits, and moved by a most righteous indignation as he was dying, said: **MAY THE LORD SEE IT, AND REQUIRE IT.** <note>Latin: *Videbit Jehova, et requiret.* A common biblical expression calling for divine justice or an accounting of a crime.</note> And certainly the Lord saw it, and He required it. As for the ungrateful King, after he had been tortured by the most grievous diseases, certain conspirators killed him in his bed of sickness. 2 Chronicles 24:25.

<margin>XLV. *Anonymous.*</margin>
XLV. Amaziah, the son of Joash, showed himself more obedient to an **ANONYMOUS** Prophet. When Amaziah had hired a hundred thousand Israelites for a hundred talents of silver to fight with him against the Edomites, a Man of God came to him, declaring that he should dismiss the Israelites, for the Lord was not with them. He told the king to let go of all the money he had spent, trusting in the kindness of God, who was prepared both to grant victory to his own forces and to enrich him with even greater wealth. He obeyed the command and ordered the Israelites to depart, however much they were incensed. 2 Chronicles 25:7. Later, when because of the crimes of King Ahaz the Israelites had led away two hundred thousand of their kinsmen as captives—women, boys, and girls—and were carrying off a massive amount of plunder to Samaria, <margin>Oded.</margin> a prophet of the Lord named **ODED** appeared there. Meeting the victorious crowds, he explained to them the wrath of God against the Jews; though the Israelites had been His ministers and executioners, they had not acted without great crime of their own. He was the authority who convinced them to release that captive multitude, lest the heat of Divine wrath overflow upon them as well. That event occurred during the reign of Pekah, son of Remaliah, over the Israelites, at the same time that *Isaiah* prophesied. 2 Chronicles 28:9. We gather from 2 Chronicles 33:18 that under the reign of Manasseh there were several **SEERS** <note>Latin: *Videntes*. A term for prophets who received direct visual revelations or "visions."</note> who spoke to him in the name of the Lord God of Israel. The last of those whose writings we do not possess, as far as I recall, is <margin>Uriah.</margin> **URIAH**, the son of Shemaiah from Kiriath Jearim. He appeared as a prophet in the time of Jehoiakim, using almost the same words as *Jeremiah*. When he fled to Egypt, King Jehoiakim had him brought back and struck him down with a sword, casting his corpse into the graves of the common people. Jeremiah 26:20.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XVIII.

<meta>catchword: another</meta>

<margin>XLVI. The Letter of Elijah to Jehoram.</margin>
XLVI. And these are the Prophets whose writings no longer exist, about whom we might have something to suggest. However, I cannot pass over entirely untouched *that letter which Elijah is said to have written to Jehoram, the king of Judah* (2 Chronicles 21:12), since it is well established that he was taken up into heaven while Jehoshaphat, the father of Jehoram, was still living and reigning; for it is read in 2 Kings 3:11 that Elisha was consulted after Elijah had been taken away. There are those who, pressed by this difficulty, think that Elijah, the author of this letter, was a different person from that famous Tishbite <note>original: *Thisbite*. Referring to Elijah’s hometown, Tishbe.</note>; or even that Elisha, the disciple of Elijah and heir to his Spirit, came in the name of his master. But neither of these seems probable to me. For it is not established by the records of any history that there was another prophet of the same name as Elijah in the kingdom of Israel at nearly the same time; nor is he distinguished here by any note from that great Prophet. There is also no example of Elisha, who is frequently mentioned in history, being designated by the name of Elijah. We should not rashly resort to such things as to invent unusual figures of speech at our own whim.

XLVII. What then? Some have believed that this letter was written by Elijah after he had been snatched away from human affairs. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch humanist and jurist whose theological commentaries were widely influential.</note> thinks this is no more to be wondered at than what is written in 2 Maccabees 15, where Judas Maccabeus is said to have seen in a divinely sent dream the Priest Onias and the Prophet Jeremiah praying for the people. But aside from the fact that this is cited from an apocryphal and legendary writing, the reliability of which rests with the author, the reason for the difference is manifest in itself. For there is a great difference between whether the saints in heaven pray for the pious dwelling on earth, or whether they write letters in heaven with pen and ink, or by any other means, to be delivered to those who are guests in this lower part of the world. Not that I think it could not happen, if indeed it pleased the Divine Power; for many things must be believed by us that are not a little more wonderful. But I judge that miracles are not to be established unless God teaches them. *It is ridiculous*, says *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic sources to explain the Bible.</note>, *to think with the Jews that Elijah sent these letters from heaven after he had been taken up there. Works, Vol. 1, p. 85, in the Chronicle of Times.*

XLVIII. It is more credible, therefore, that the letter was written by Elijah before his translation <note>original: *raptum*. Referring to his being "caught up" into heaven in a whirlwind.</note>, even though it was delivered to Jehoram later. For he could have foreseen by a prophetic spirit the things that Jehoram was going to do, just as Elisha foresaw what Hazael would do after he gained possession of the kingdom of Syria. Nor is it improbable that Elijah entrusted this writing to Elisha, so that he might share it with Jehoram at the proper time; just as certainly...

The author rejects theories of a "second Elijah" or a heavenly courier, suggesting instead that Elijah wrote the letter in advance through prophetic foresight.</summary>

XLIX. *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English Hebraist who specialized in reconciling biblical chronologies.</note> weaves the sequence of history together in this way: *While Moab was rebelling against the king of Israel, King Jehoram requested the help of Jehoshaphat to restrain the rebels. <margin>L. *As the Hebrew republic declined toward destruction, the prophets committed their oracles to writing.*</margin>

L. Now let us pass to those prophets who, at the instigation of the Spirit of God, committed their oracles to "living pages" <note>original: *victuris chartis*. Literally, "papers that will live," referring to enduring written works.</note>. We find this happened most especially as the affairs of the Israelites were verging toward their destruction, because of the horrifying crimes with which they were binding themselves. For around those times, God raised up a continuous series of prophets, both in the kingdom of Israel and of Judah, who would remind the rebellious people of their duty not only by word of mouth but also by writing, and would transmit both their crimes and God’s threats to posterity in everlasting monuments. This was so that all generations might see the ingratitude and abominations of that people, as if carved into eternal tablets with an iron pen and a diamond point <note>A reference to Jeremiah 17:1.</note>; and so that they, seized by holy fear, might not commit similar acts. Moreover, here is the order of those Prophets.

Junius <note>Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a prominent Huguenot theologian and biblical scholar.</note> refers him to the final years of Josiah, so that he would have lived at the same time as Jeremiah. The *Seder Olam* <note>An ancient Hebrew chronological work.</note> refers him to the times of Manasseh, which Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and commentator.</note> also indicates. <margin>53. The uncertain era of Obadiah.</margin>
53. OBADIAH: At what time he may have prophesied cannot be said with certainty. Most of the Hebrews are of the opinion that he was the governor of Ahab’s palace, of whom we read in 1 Kings 18, and that he was an Edomite by birth and a convert. But none of this is probable. For the sacred history praises that Obadiah not for the excellence of prophecy, but for his piety alone. And if he had been a Prophet, in what way could he have both held a position at court and enjoyed the favor of the king at a time when Jezebel was mistress of affairs and was seeking to put all the prophets of Jehovah to death? However, it appears from the prophecy itself that in the time of this Prophet, the affairs of the Jews and especially of Jerusalem were greatly afflicted, and that the Edomites promoted and increased that affliction. For *strangers had carried away captive the forces of Jerusalem, and foreigners had entered into his gates; and had cast lots upon Jerusalem; and then Edom was as one of them.* [Obadiah 1:11]. On account of which thing, he predicts great calamities for them. When these things happened to Jerusalem—whether they should be referred to the Babylonian captivity, or to earlier times when the city was plundered by Shishak <note>original: *Sisacum*</note> king of Egypt (1 Kings 14:25), or by the Philistines and Arabs (2 Chronicles 21:16, 17), or by Joash king of Israel (2 Chronicles 25:21)—is uncertain. In favor of the first opinion is the fact that he uses almost the same words used by Jeremiah in Chapter 49:14, and thus he would have been a contemporary <note>original Greek: *σύγχρονος*</note> of Jeremiah around the times of the Babylonian captivity. But it seems to argue against this, again, that no mention at all is made of any such prophet who existed at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, or after it, when men of the first rank <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword *tæ* completes the word *notæ*.</note>

<margin>54. Zephaniah.</margin>
54. ZEPHANIAH prophesied during the time of Josiah, as seen in Chapter 1:1. He is believed by some to be the great-grandson of King Hezekiah. However, it is uncertain whether the Hezekiah listed among his ancestors was the king himself. It is not unbelievable that his prophecy falls at the beginning of Josiah's reign, before the work of religious reform had fully progressed. For in Chapter 1:4–5, he sharply lashes out against those who worship the host of heaven upon the rooftops, and those who swear by the Lord <note>original: *Jehovam*</note> and by Malcham; he threatens that God will cut off the remnant of Baal, and the names of the idol-priests <note>original: *poparum*; referring to the *Chemarim* or non-Levitical priests</note> along with the regular priests.

<margin>55. Jeremiah.</margin>
55. JEREMIAH began to prophesy in the thirteenth year of Josiah while he was still quite young; he acted as a prophet to the people of God for forty years, just as Moses did. Specifically, he served eighteen years under Josiah, eleven under Jehoiakim, and eleven under Zedekiah. This is the calculation of Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and rabbinical scholar known for his work on biblical chronology.</note>. Junius <note>Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian.</note>, however, counts at least forty-two years. And just as Moses was present as a teacher to the people in the wilderness for that great span of forty years until they entered the land promised to them, so Jeremiah acted as the teacher of the people in their own land for the same length of time, until they were driven out into the "wilderness of the nations." Thus, he is the last of the prophets in the land of Canaan before the Babylonian captivity, of which he was not only a prophet but also a witness. Concerning his death and burial, Elmakin <note>George Elmacin (al-Makin ibn al-’Amid), a 13th-century Coptic Christian historian whose *Ecclesiastical History* was a common source for Eastern traditions.</note> records these things in his *Ecclesiastical History*, page 128: *Jeremiah, like Habakkuk, went into Egypt and prophesied against Egypt, saying that Nebuchadnezzar, the King of Babylon, would move against Egypt, kill its people, and burn the shrines and gods of the Egyptians. And because he did not cease prophesying against Egypt, Babylon, Tyre, Sidon, and the Ammonites, he was overwhelmed by stones and died, and was buried in Egypt. They also say that Alexander, when he entered Egypt, carried the body of Jeremiah with him to Alexandria and buried it there.* But these accounts are partly uncertain and partly quite improbable.

<margin>
I. The four stages of the Babylonian Exile. The first.
</margin>

There were three stages of the Babylonian Captivity or Exile, or, as I prefer to reckon them, four. The first exile occurred in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, at the end of the third year of Jehoiakim, or the beginning of the fourth. For this is how Daniel and Jeremiah must be reconciled. Daniel, in Chapter 1, verse 1, relates that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem in the third year of Jehoiakim; clearly at the end of that year. Jeremiah, in Chapter 25, verse 1, refers the same event to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, evidently at its beginning. 

Now, Nebuchadnezzar was the son of Nabopolassar, who increased the Babylonian kingdom—which he had received as a modest realm—through force of arms. He added Egypt, Coele-Syria, and Phoenicia to it, greatly aided by the courage of his son Nebuchadnezzar, who immensely surpassed his father in the size of the empire and the glory of his deeds. Jehoiakim was the third-to-last king of Judah, the son of Josiah, and the brother of Jehoahaz (whom Pharaoh Necho removed from the throne and led away into Egypt). He was also the father of Jehoiachin (or Jeconiah), who succeeded him on the throne, and the brother of Zedekiah, the last king of the Jews. Having been placed over the kingdom by the King of Egypt, he was his tributary. He was a worthless man, steeped in vices. 

Nebuchadnezzar undertook his first expedition against this king while his father was still alive and ruling over the Babylonians, as the most learned men have observed by comparing sacred history with secular accounts. He is nevertheless called "King" by Jeremiah and Daniel because he was sent on this expedition by his father with Royal power, and was a full partner in his father’s sovereignty. Therefore, after routing the Egyptians and being drawn by the strategic advantage of the location, he invaded Jerusalem, which had been subjugated by the Egyptians four years earlier and was now a dependency of the Egyptian kingdom. At this time Daniel, along with his companions and a portion of the temple vessels, was deported. Jehoiakim, however, by committing himself to the protection of the Babylonians, remained in the kingdom.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>II. The second.</margin>
II. **The second deportation** occurred after the rebellion of Jehoiakim <note>King of Judah, r. 609–598 BCE; he was a tributary to Babylon but rebelled in favor of Egypt.</note>. For once the Egyptians had been defeated and the Babylonians were farther away, the people expected the restoration of the kingdom with such confidence that the king dared to revolt against Nebuchadnezzar after years of servitude. However, the outcome was that he was led away toward Babylon in chains (2 Chronicles 36:6). Yet it seems he never arrived there; instead, having died on the journey, he was either cast out onto the road or lightly covered with earth without being mourned, and thus was buried with "the burial of a donkey" <note>original: *sepultura asini*; a reference to Jeremiah's prophecy that the king would be dragged and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem.</note> (Jeremiah 22:18–19 and 36:30). At that time, along with Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar deported three thousand and twenty-three Jews (Jeremiah 52:28).

<margin>III. The third.</margin>
III. **The third abduction** took place under Jeconiah <note>Also known as Jehoiachin, son of Jehoiakim.</note>, who succeeded his father Jehoiakim but reigned for only three months and seven days. When Jerusalem was besieged, he went out voluntarily and surrendered himself, his mother, the princes, and the courtiers into the power of the king of Babylon. At that time, the king deported all the most distinguished of the Jews, leaving behind only the "dregs of the people" (2 Kings 25:10; 2 Chronicles 36:10). Jeconiah himself was punished with a long imprisonment (2 Kings 25:30). It was then that *Mordecai* (Esther 2:5–6) and *Ezekiel* (Ezekiel 1:1–2) were deported.

<margin>IV. The fourth.</margin>
IV. **The fourth** and final deportation fell during the reign of Zedekiah, who was the uncle of Jeconiah and was appointed as successor by Nebuchadnezzar. For those most wretched of the Jews who had remained in their own land, being proud of their possession, boasted that they alone were the true seed of Abraham, while they despised the exiles as profane and impure (Ezekiel 33:24). Indeed, they were so pleased with this line of thinking that Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, sending legates into Egypt to ask for horses and soldiers (Ezekiel 17:15). He also entered into treaties against Nebuchadnezzar with the neighboring kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, through their ambassadors who came to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 27:3). Therefore, when Nebuchadnezzar saw Palestine burning with these new uprisings, he decided there should be no delay before the combined strength of these nations could unite. He came into Judea with a powerful army, besieged Jerusalem—the stronghold of the war—attacked it, destroyed it, burned the temple, and either killed the people or led them away. The king's sons were slaughtered before his very eyes, and then his own eyes were plucked out; bound with two bronze shackles <note>original: *numellis chalibeis*; iron or steel leg-restraints</note>, he was deported to Babylon (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 52).

<margin>V. A mark of mercy,</margin>
V. It cannot be doubted that these things happened to the Jews by the most just judgment of God on account of their crimes. However, the bill of divorce <note>original: *libellum repudii*; a legal term for a writ of separation, here used metaphorically for God's covenant with the people.</note> for the people had not yet—

# ON THE PROPHETS IN THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.

<margin>That God gave prophets even to the captives.</margin>
...had given a certificate of divorce <note>original: *repudii libellum*; a biblical metaphor for God casting off Israel due to their unfaithfulness</note>: and for that reason, He granted prophets even to the exiles, to serve as their instruction and solace. He had indeed called the land of Canaan His own land. In it, He had possessed a house and a people. But, when He began to lead the people out from it, He went, as it were, into exile with them, and He gave them prophets in the midst of the nations, in an impure land, and displayed visions to them that were indicators of the greatest matters. He was signifying even then that the time was pressing on in which He would ride through the desert and hold His kingdom over the nations throughout the whole world; and that the Jews who had remained in Jerusalem and still saw the Temple did not have as much cause for boasting as those who were in captivity.

<margin>VI. A portrait of Ezekiel.</margin>
VI. There were two prophets in particular who were given to them at that time: Ezekiel and Daniel. Ezekiel was of the tribe of Levi, from a priestly family, the son of Buzi, and was himself also a priest (Ezekiel 1:3). The name <term>Ezekiel</term> <note>original Hebrew: יחזקאל (*Yechezqel*)</note> signifies "God will act strongly." It is believable that his pious parents, in those most corrupt times, bore witness to their faith and commended the same to their children by bestowing such emphatic names. Although the father of this prophet was called <term>Buzi</term> <note>original Hebrew: בוזי (*Buzi*)</note>, which means *my shame*, because those times were full of shame and insult, he nevertheless hoped that God would support the pious by His power and uphold the covenant of His grace with a strong hand. But we should not linger only on the name. Greater things must be said: for this man of ours was truly distinguished in learning and character. Thus, even setting aside the gift of prophecy—which is incomparable—he deserves to be compared with other illustrious writers because of his most beautiful <term>conceptions</term> <note>original Greek: ἐννοίας (*ennoias*); referring to his deep thoughts or mental flashes</note>, elegant comparisons, and great skill in many matters, especially architecture.

<margin>VII. The time in which he prophesied.</margin>
VII. He began to prophesy in the fifth year after his own deportation with Jeconiah <note>Jeconiah, also known as Jehoiachin, was the young king of Judah exiled in the second wave of the captivity around 597 BCE</note>, thirty-four years after Jeremiah began. This is also called the "thirtieth year" (Ezekiel 1:1), whether measured from the beginning of the reign of Nabopolassar <note>The father of Nebuchadnezzar and founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire</note>, or from the Passover celebrated by Josiah and that remarkable reformation, or from his own birth; or perhaps because all these events fell within the same year and can therefore be considered together. At this time, the Spirit came upon him, and by a river in Babylonia <note>The river Chebar</note>, he saw the heavens opened, just as Christ at a similar age had them opened for Him by a river in Judea (Luke 3:21–23). He proceeded to prophesy to the Jews in Babylon at the same time that Jeremiah was prophesying to them in Judea. The beginning of his prophecy fell in the middle of the reign of Zedekiah, when the state of Judea was still peaceful. Nor were there lacking <term>False Prophets</term>, who promised all sorts of flattering things to the people: that Jeconiah would be brought back and the Babylonian yoke would be cast off. Thus, amidst the complacency of men,

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

...and had to contend with false prophets—Jeremiah in Judea, and Ezekiel in Babylonia. It is believed that he prophesied for about twenty years.

<margin>VIII. The subject matter of his prophecies.</margin>
VIII. The prophecies themselves overflow with great mysteries, expressed for the most part in a style that is enigmatic and symbolic, and therefore somewhat obscure, except to those who are attentive and well-practiced. Before all else, he saw the Son of Man sitting upon the Throne of God, with the holy Angels ministering to Him in the governance of the universe and the Church. He proceeds to predict, through both words and symbols, the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple because of the crimes of the Jews. He prophesies concerning the overturning of the present and future crown, so that the kingdom might be handed over to the <term>Messiah</term> <note>original: *Messiæ*; the "Anointed One" promised in Jewish scripture</note>. He also sings of the fates of the Ammonites, Moabites, Tyrians, Egyptians, and Edomites. Having dismissed the unfaithful shepherds, he promises that the great and most faithful Shepherd of souls shall be raised up. He foretells the return of Israel to their land, the reunion of all the tribes, and a restoration that is like a resurrection from the dead. Furthermore, he describes the wars of the Church against <term>Gog</term> <note>a symbolic enemy of God's people mentioned in Ezekiel 38-39</note>, as well as the New Spiritual Temple to be built by Christ, the Holy City, and the inheritance shared by both Israelites and <term>Proselytes</term> <note>converts to the faith</note>. If these things are rightly understood, they lead the mind into the contemplation of the greatest matters, most worthy of being revealed by God to His people through the prophets.

<margin>IX. Their authenticity, wrongly called into doubt by some.</margin>
IX. It is a very bad thing, therefore, that is recorded in the Talmudic Tractate on the *Sabbath* <note>original: *Sabbatho*; referring to the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Shabbat 13b</note>: that certain ancient Rabbis debated rejecting the book of Ezekiel and removing it from the <term>Canon</term> <note>the official list of inspired books in the Bible</note>, because they thought they detected several things in it that did not agree well with the Law of Moses. They would indeed have done so, had it not been for a certain <term>Ananias</term> <note>referring to Hananiah ben Hezekiah, a scholar of the 1st century AD</note>, who promised he would reconcile all the discrepancies, and did so. But it is well that our faith does not depend on the judgment of foolish men. If any prophecies possess proofs of their <term>authenticity</term> <note>original Greek: *γνησιότης* (gnēsiotēs)</note> and Divinity, these certainly do. There is a very great agreement between these and the prophecies of Jeremiah, who was prophesying at the same time but in a very distant place; and also with the most Divine *Apocalypse* of John. Indeed, many events have already sealed their truth. The quibbles and slanders of the <term>Theologico-Political</term> <note>a reference to Baruch Spinoza and his controversial 1670 work *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus*, which critiqued the divine origin of the Bible</note> arguer against this part of the sacred volumes also fall fruitlessly; they have been rightly rebuked by others.

<margin>X. Epiphanius’s fable regarding his death and burial.</margin>
X. Epiphanius—or whoever is the author of the book *On the Lives of the Prophets*—relates the death and burial of Ezekiel in this manner. He was killed in Babylon, the author says, by a leader of the people in the station where he presided, because he had rebuked the leader for the worship of idols. He was then buried in the field...

### ON THE PROPHETS IN THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.

After a few things are interposed, he continues thus: *The holy man lies in the region of the Syrians, and many used to flock to his tomb for the sake of prayer. When a frequent gathering of Jews had occurred there at his memorial, the Chaldeans, fearing they might rise against them, decided to make an attack on them and kill them. In addition to these things, the prophet, having voluntarily undertaken prayers, supplied a most abundant supply of fish to feed those already consumed by hunger; and for many who were failing, he obtained life from God.* It is tiresome to write more: they are so fabulous and Apocryphal.

<margin>XI. And those of Benjamin.</margin>
XI. He, after speaking of the Tower of Babylon, says that on its border, at the bank of the Euphrates, there stands the Synagogue of the blessed prophet Ezekiel, where across from the Synagogue are sixty towers, and between each one is a Synagogue. In its courtyard is a chest for the sacred books; and behind the Synagogue, the tomb of Ezekiel the son of Buzi: over which hangs a large dome of most beautiful workmanship, which <term>Jechoniah</term> <note>also known as Jehoiachin, a king of Judah taken captive to Babylon</note>, king of the Jews, built with thirty-five thousand Jews who followed him when he was released from prison by <term>Evil-merodach</term> <note>the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar</note>. This place on one side faces the river Chebar; on the other, the Euphrates. Moreover, Jechoniah and all who accompanied him are seen carved on the wall—Jechoniah in the first place, and Ezekiel in the last. That place remains a sanctuary to some extent to this day: for here they flock from the most remote places for the sake of praying, from the beginning of the year until the <term>Feast of Expiation</term> <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement</note>, and they celebrate with great joy. . . . . *There, on the Day of Atonement, they read from a large book produced there, which the prophet Ezekiel wrote with his own hand. Over Ezekiel's tomb a lamp burns day and night, from the time when he himself lit it: and to this day those who followed him repeatedly change the wicks and add oil.* . . . . Even the sons of the nobles among the <term>Muhammedans</term> <note>Muslims</note> come there to pray, because of their burning love for the blessed prophet Ezekiel; and they call the place the HABITATION OF ELEGANCE. Thus far Benjamin: let the credit for this history rest with him. As for me, I am but one of many who are skeptical; nor do I easily surrender my belief to narratives of that kind. Let us be content to know those things about Ezekiel which the sacred scriptures hand down. The rest are trifles <note>original: *gerræ*; a Latin term for nonsense or "stuff and nonsense"</note>, destitute of all authority.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>...taken away.</margin>
...of the year, and in the third year of Jehoiakim, according to Daniel 1:1. This was so clearly noted by Daniel himself, not only for the sake of the credibility of the matter and historical accuracy, but because from that point the calculation of those seventy years must begin, which the Babylonian captivity was destined to last. It also serves to show with what great goodness God sent Daniel ahead with his companions—who would find favor with the King—for the subsequent benefit of the people who were to be taken captive later. Let us also briefly narrate the history of this Prophet: first speaking of the man himself, then of his writings.

<margin>XIII. Etymology of his name.</margin>
XIII. His name was Daniel <note>Hebrew: דניאל</note>, which is not far from *Dan* <note>Hebrew: דן</note>, of whom Rachel says in Genesis 30:6: *God has judged my cause* <note>original Hebrew: *dananni Elohim*</note>. It means, therefore, *God is my Judge*, or *my Avenger*. By this name, as if by a symbol, his pious parents testified to their hope in God, especially in their perplexing affairs, whether public or private, and they wished this son to be a witness of that hope by his name. David had one of his sons with this name (1 Chronicles 3:1) by Abigail; and Ithamar <note>a son of Aaron the High Priest</note> had someone among his descendants with this name (Ezra 8:2).

<margin>XIV. Lineage.</margin>
XIV. His lineage, if not Royal, was at least noble. This is gathered partly from 2 Kings 20:18 and partly from Daniel 1:3. In this, the sovereign <note>original Greek: *ἀνυπεύθυνος* (anypenthynos), meaning "not held to account" or "unanswerable"</note> freedom of Divine providence comes to be adored by us; which at times indeed chose the lowliest from among the common people to enrich with the gifts of His heavenly grace—such as <term>Amos</term> <note>a shepherd-prophet</note>, <term>Elisha</term> <note>a plowman-prophet</note>, and the Apostles—but at other times also made the illustrious nobles of this world powerful through gifts in the Church.

<margin>XV. Age.</margin>
XV. His age fell during the beginning, the duration, and the end of the seventy-year Babylonian captivity. At this time, <term>Ancus Marcius</term> and <term>Tarquinius Priscus</term> <note>legendary early kings of Rome</note> ruled over the Romans. Over the Medes ruled Astyages and Cyaxares. Over the Babylonians, Nebuchadnezzar with his successors. Over the Persians, Cyrus. Over the Lydians, Croesus. During this time also, the three most powerful kingdoms of the Assyrians, Jews, and Chaldeans, and their three capitals—Nineveh, Jerusalem, and Babylon—were cut down. The <term>Seven Sages of Greece</term> <note>a title given to seven 6th-century BC philosophers and statesmen, such as Solon and Thales</note> also flourished around this time, as Pererius <note>Benedictus Pererius, a prominent 16th-century Jesuit commentator</note> observes.

<margin>XVI. Character.</margin>
XVI. He was endowed with a character capable of all disciplines (Daniel 1:4). This was aided by the diligent instruction of the Chaldeans (verses 19, 20), but was especially taught by God (ibid. verse 17; Daniel 4:5, 6; 5:11). Hence he was famous for his reputation for wisdom even among neighboring nations (Ezekiel 28:3). To his learning was added exceptional piety toward God (Daniel 1:8). He possessed a spirit that bore either prosperity or adversity with equal strength (Daniel 5:17), an uncorrupted loyalty toward the King (Daniel 6:4), and constant devotion toward his own nation (Daniel 9).

# ON THE PROPHETS IN THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.
