<margin>
XVII. Way of life.
</margin>
XVII. In his **WAY OF LIFE**, the first thing to be noted is I. **THE DOMESTIC ASPECT** <note>original Greek: *ΤΟ ΟΙΚΟΝΟΜΙΚΟΝ* (To Oikonomikon)</note>. Here the question is asked whether he was celibate or married. *Cornelius à Lapide*, a Jesuit scholar, determines this confidently: *He preserved untainted virginity,* he says, *even unto death, as* **ALL** *confess*. Many of the ancients thought of him as a <margin>eunuch <note>Hebrew: *saris*</note></margin> "eunuch" in this way. Nor are the Jews at variance with this, who hand down the tradition that he was a *Spado* or *eunuch* <note>Hebrew: *saris*</note>, based on *Isaiah 39:7* compared with *Daniel 1:6*. But here, logic certainly escapes them. For the word *saris* does not always denote someone castrated; rather, because such men were often appointed to the highest honors, it can refer to any *leading man and courtier*. See *Genesis 37:36*, where *Potiphar* is called a *saris* <note>court official</note>, yet it is well established that he was joined to a wife—and one who was quite unruly at that. Whence the *Targum* <note>an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> rightly translates it as a *magnate* <note>Aramaic: *rabba*</note>, and the Septuagint <note>the Greek Old Testament</note> sometimes translates it as a *ruler* <note>Greek: *dynastēn*</note>. Indeed, the Hebrew *saris*, the Chaldean *rabana*, the Syriac *mhaimna*, and the Greek *eunouchos* all share the same meaning <note>referring to a trusted official or chamberlain</note>. It is probable, therefore, that Daniel was called by this name not by reason of a mutilated body, but because of his secretarial office, and that he was in fact married. For in *Ezekiel 14:14*, he is joined with Noah and Job, both in respect to his pious intercession and in respect to his offspring. II. **THE POLITICAL ASPECT** <note>original Greek: *ΤΟ ΠΟΛΙΤΙΚΟΝ* (To Politikon)</note>. He held the highest dignity after the King under *Nebuchadnezzar* (*Daniel 2:48-49*), though he seems to have been deprived of this under *Belshazzar* (*Daniel 5:11, 16*). But he was restored by the same and held in the greatest honor by *Darius the Mede* (*Daniel 6*) and *Cyrus the Persian* (at the end of the same chapter). III. **THE ECCLESIASTICAL ASPECT** <note>original Greek: *ΤΟ ΕΚΚΛΗΣΙΑΣΤΙΚΟΝ* (To Ekklēsiastikon)</note>. Here we must consider what place he occupied in the sacred assembly of the people of God.

<margin>
XVIII. Whether he is to be numbered among the Prophets.
See Preface §. XIV.
</margin>
XVIII. The question arises here, *whether Daniel should be numbered among the Prophets*, or, as the Jews prefer, among the *Hagiographa* <note>the "Holy Writings," the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible</note>. For the Hebrews are accustomed to distinguish between *Prophecy* <note>Hebrew: *Nevi'im*</note> and the *Holy Spirit* <note>Hebrew: *Ruach Ha-Kodesh*</note>. They attribute the *Holy Spirit* to one who speaks like any other man, with the full function of all his senses, yet is stirred by the Spirit of God, which illuminates the mind and suggests words of truth, confession, and praise. They call it *Prophecy*, however, when the use of the senses is taken away from a person—whether they are awake or asleep—so that, being carried away, they either see visions or hear a voice speaking to them. Based on this distinction, they strike Daniel's writings from the register of *prophecies* and reduce them to the rank of the *Ketuvim* <note>Greek: *Hagiographorum*</note>, to which they assign a somewhat lower value.

<margin>
XIX. Reasons of those who deny it.
</margin>
XIX. They fight for this view with these arguments. I. That although an Angel allowed himself to be seen by him and imbued him with knowledge of future things, it was done through a dream, and he did not perceive the Angel within himself; which is required for true prophecy. II. That...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

...[that he] was a Eunuch. Moreover, the Lord forbade such persons from entering his assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). It is far from the case, then, that such men could perform a Prophetic office. III. Because he lived not in the manner of the Prophets, but in the manner of Great Men <note>original Latin: *Magnatum*; referring to high-ranking nobles or court officials</note>. IV. Because it is not clear that he preached publicly in the Church <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia*; here referring to the assembly of the faithful or the congregation of Israel</note>. These are the arguments of the Hebrews <note>The author is referring to certain Jewish traditions, such as those in the Talmud, which categorize the Book of Daniel in the "Writings" (Ketuvim) rather than the "Prophets" (Nevi'im)</note>.

<margin>
XX. The Assertion.
</margin>
XX. There are many things, however, which command us to believe that Daniel was not only a prophet, but an exceptional one among the prophets. For I. Jesus, the Prince and Lord of all Prophets, expressly honors him with the title of PROPHET (Matthew 24:15). II. All the requirements of prophecy are present in him, and indeed in the most excellent way: whether we consider the things he foretold, which were great and good in themselves and the knowledge of which is most useful to the human race and especially to the people of God; or the circumstances of the events revealed to him with all their accuracy; or the manner of revelation, in which both the Majesty of God and His familiarity with the holy seer clearly shine; added to this is the clear explanation of the riddles and symbols represented to him by the Angel. III. Since the representation of the Messiah and His kingdom, along with the matters pertaining to it, is the very soul of Prophecy; hardly anyone is found among the prophets who has discussed more concerning Him, or more clearly and decisively. So much so that the closer he was to the days of the Messiah, the more conspicuously he both knew and announced them. IV. The Jews themselves support this when they return to their senses <note>The author suggests that when Jewish historians are not being polemical, they admit Daniel's rank</note>. Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book X, last chapter, not only calls him "one of the greatest prophets" <note>original Greek: *Ἕνα τῶν μεγίστων προφητῶν* (Hena tōn megistōn prophētōn)</note>, but even prefers him over others. "For," he says, "he did not only continue to prophesy future things as the other prophets did, but he also determined the time in which these things would come to pass; and while other prophets foretold calamities, and because of this were disliked by kings and the multitude, Daniel was a prophet of good things for them." Jacchiades <note>Joseph ben Yahya, a 16th-century Jewish commentator</note> also—whose commentary on Daniel was published with observations by Constantinus l'Empereur <note>A prominent 17th-century Dutch scholar of Hebrew</note>—writes on Chapter 1, verse 17, that he "attained the highest boundary of prophecy" <note>original Hebrew: *הגיע לקצה גבול נבוא* (higgi’a l’ketzeh gevul nevu’ah)</note>.

<margin>
XXI. These things being proven, the others are refuted.
</margin>

# ON THE PROPHETS IN THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.

It cannot be proven by any scriptural testimony, nor by any induction of examples, that such a violent seizure was common to all prophets, as in most of them no evidence of it exists. Furthermore, even if this were entirely certain, it is remarkable to find interpreters so foolish as to use that weapon against Daniel; for it is established that he was sometimes so overwhelmed by the magnificence of his visions that his appearance was changed and corrupted, and he lay like a dead man as his strength failed him. *Daniel* 7:28, 8:17 & 27, 10:8. For the speech of the Angel, with which he addressed him, and his standing upright, certainly took place in a prophetic vision. In such a matter, all the senses rest from their functions, and that influence comes upon the rational faculty, and from there it is diffused into the imaginative faculty, and in this way it fulfills and completes its work.*

Thus far Maimonides. If indeed the power of prophetic vision cannot be better declared by any other example than that of Daniel, what is Daniel lacking in this regard that would cause him to be judged inferior to the other prophets?

XXII. Furthermore, it is also a vain claim that he did not see the Angel instructing him except in a dream. For God spoke thus of the prophet in Numbers 12:6: *In a vision I will make myself known to him; in a dream I will speak with him.*

A physical defect inflicted upon the body by force does not set limits on Divine grace. Of this, there exists this notable promise in Isaiah 56:3, 4, 5: *Let not the eunuch say, "behold I am a dry tree." For thus says Jehovah regarding the eunuchs who keep my sabbaths, and choose that in which I delight, and take hold of my covenant; I will even give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name, better than that of sons or daughters.* To be sure, there is a prohibition for those castrated in Deuteronomy 23:1, regarding entrance **into the assembly** <note>original Hebrew: בקהל (*bi-qahal*), referring to the congregation of Israel.</note>...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

<note>original Hebrew: *beqahal Yahweh*</note> to enter the assembly of the Lord. But it is well known that most of the Hebrews, with the support even of the most learned Christians, explain that phrase in such a way that it denotes the right of marrying an Israelite woman. If we follow this explanation, there is nothing in that law that stands in the way of our purpose.

XXIV. Furthermore, the grace of prophecy does not take away political dignity; nor does it always require <term>an austere lifestyle<note>Greek: *to sklērodiaiton*; a term referring to a harsh or ascetic way of life, such as that of a hermit or monk.</note></term>. Nothing forbids the same man from both flourishing in the friendship of princes and acting as a prophet at the same time. It would go poorly for prophets if no one could bear the honor of this name unless he walked with a staff and a pouch—as if filth produced wisdom and a sound mind. Moses, who was the prince of Prophets, was also the supreme ruler of the Israelites. To the High Priest of the Hebrews, whose dignity in the republic was second only to the prince, the gift of prophecy sometimes fell. Finally, there is a frequent saying of the masters: <note>original Hebrew: *she-ein ha-nevu'ah shorah ella al adam ashir*</note> *“Prophecy does not rest except upon a wealthy man.”*

XXV. Regarding what they say about the public ministry of the Church, it must be held that a distinction should be made (as we also advised above) between the *gift of prophecy* and the *prophetic office*. It is possible that God deems someone worthy of the former while not calling them to the latter. Furthermore, it is not clear to us what Daniel may or may not have said in the assemblies of the people of God. Just as we should affirm nothing on that matter, we have nothing to stubbornly deny. Certainly, he taught the Church, and still teaches it even now, through his Divine writings. And these things had to be said now for the defense of Daniel, as a distinguished Prophet, against the quibbles of the Jews.

XXVI. Scripture is silent regarding his death and burial. Epiphanius and Dorotheus report that he fell asleep in peace in Babylon and was magnificently entombed in a royal cave, and that his tomb was very well known to everyone in Babylon until that day. However, those books regarding the lives of the Prophets are <term>pseudepigraphal<note>Latin: *pseudepigraphi*; works falsely attributed to a specific author, in this case, the early Church fathers Epiphanius and Dorotheus.</note></term> and falsely ascribed to those authors, as we also indicated before. We know that Daniel was in Susiana by the Tigris in the third year of Cyrus (*Daniel* 10:1, 4). At that time, he was very old. That he then returned to Babylon and ended his days there...

<margin>XXVII. Concerning this story of Benjamin.</margin>
XXVII. The account of Benjamin <note>referring to Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> on page 86 agrees so far, placing Daniel’s tomb in Susa by the Tigris River, and he relates a story about it that is more wonderful than true. Specifically, he claims that on the side of the Tigris where the great prophet’s tomb is located, there are riches and an abundance of all things; but on the other side, there is a kingdom of poverty. From this, envy and disputes arose among the neighbors, until finally a deal was reached between those exhausted by the fighting on this condition: that Daniel’s casket would change locations alternately, being on this side of the river one year and on the other the next. They stood by their promises and agreed pacts on both sides until Senigar Saas, the great Emperor of the Persians, arrived there. Thinking it unworthy that the Prophet's casket be rolled about from place to place in this way, he ordered the Jews and <term>Ishmaelites<note>A historical term used here to refer to Muslims.</note></term> to measure an equal distance from both sides and place Daniel’s casket in a glass shrine, suspending it from the middle of a bridge with iron chains. He testifies that it hung there until his own time. Regarding the location of the tomb, Abulfeda—a previously <term>unpublished<note>original Greek: *anekdotos*; referring to a manuscript not yet printed or widely distributed at the time of the author's writing.</note></term> Arab writer cited by Schickard in his *Notes on the Dissertation concerning the festival of Purim*—agrees. "Susa," he says, "is a very ancient city in <term>Khuzestan<note>original Latin: *Chusistan*; a province in southwestern Iran.</note></term>, where the tomb of Daniel the Prophet is located."

<margin>XXVIII. And Petachiah.</margin>
XXVIII. Rabbi <term>Petachiah<note>Petachiah of Regensburg, another 12th-century traveler who documented Jewish communities.</note></term> subscribes to Benjamin’s little story; the same Schickard provides his words from his *Itinerary*, chapter 9: "They showed me the urn of Daniel. At first, it was on the other side [across the river] where there is every abundance, prosperity, and blessing. Therefore, those living on this side of the river were saying, 'Because that Holy Man is not buried with us, our land lacks a blessing.' From this, continuous wars arose among them, so that now one side and now the other, as victors, would seize the urn for themselves; until finally the elders settled the dispute by setting up iron supports in the middle of the river and suspending the urn from there with chains. The urn is entirely made of bronze, jutting out from the middle of the structure ten <term>cubits<note>original Latin: *ulnis*; a historical unit of measurement roughly the length of a forearm.</note></term> above the waters, so that it can be seen from afar like beautiful glass. The local Jews tell that if a ship is carried under it and carries honest men, they pass through unharmed; but if not, they are sunk in the waters. Therefore, they are afraid to sail beneath it."

BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

...through study, effort, art, or formal teachings. Whatever is known in this way comes from divine inspiration. The wise <term>Chaldeans<note>In this context, a class of scholars and astrologers in ancient Babylon.</note></term> rightly said to the King: *it is not within the power of any mortal to show these things; they are known only by the gods, whose dwelling is not in the flesh.* (Daniel 2:10-11). This was even confessed by Nebuchadnezzar himself in verse 47: *In truth,* he said, *your God is the God of Gods, and the Lord of Kings, and a revealer of mysteries, since you were able to reveal this secret.* Indeed, what is told throughout the book of Daniel if not the transactions of heaven? He often sees himself among the angels, speaks with them, and learns the fates of nations. In short, he truly managed to transcend his mortality—a fact not hidden even from the lords of the world who treated him with such familiarity. (Daniel 5:11, 12, 14).

<margin>XXXI.II. Antiquity.</margin>
XXXI. It is a sign of antiquity that Daniel's prophecies are most clearly shown to have been written by Daniel himself in Chapter 7:1-2. *Then he wrote the dream, and told the sum of the words.* As the speaker, Daniel said: *I saw in my vision by night, etc.* And again in Chapter 12:4: *But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal this book until the determined time; many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.* From this, it is established that not only were some prophecies written down here and there by Daniel, but they were also collected into a book—a book intended to endure through the passing centuries for the increase of knowledge as many read through it.

<margin>XXXII. Vainly attacked by the Talmudists.</margin>
XXXII. Therefore, the <term>Talmudists<note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note></term> talk nonsense in the <term>Gemara Bava Batra<note>A specific section of the Babylonian Talmud dealing with legal traditions and the history of the biblical canon.</note></term> Chapter 1, where they claim that the volume of Daniel was compiled by the Men of the Great Synagogue. They argue it was not permitted to commit prophecies to writing outside the Holy Land. Much more truthfully, <term>Josephus<note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works are vital for understanding ancient Jewish history.</note></term> writes in *Antiquities, Book 10, Chapter 12*: <note>original Greek: τὰ βιβλία ὅσα δὴ συγγραψάμενος καταλέλοιπεν Δανιῆλος ἀναγινώσκεται παρ’ ἡμῖν ἔτι καὶ νῦν.</note> *The books which Daniel wrote and left behind are read among us even now,* which provides us with certain proof that God shared His conversations with him. Furthermore, the reasoning the Talmudists bring forward is openly contrary to the Scriptures, which expressly testify that certain prophecies were written in <term>Chaldea<note>The region in southern Mesopotamia where Babylon was located.</note></term>—not only Daniel’s, as I have just shown, but also Ezekiel’s. See Ezekiel 1:1. That these were written by Ezekiel himself is clear from the fact that he speaks <term>in his own person<note>original Greek: αὐτοπροσώπως; meaning the author speaks as himself, "I," rather than being described by a later narrator.</note></term>. But this pretext also contradicts sound reason. For if God does not consider it beneath Himself or His oracles to communicate them to prophets outside the Holy Land—and if the prophets explained those same things aloud to the people there—why should it be forbidden to do so in writing?

...that it was composed in Judea in the age of [Antiochus Epiphanes], he blasphemously asserts, by some unknown author falsely claiming the name of Daniel for himself, who predicted events that had happened up to that time as if they were future occurrences. Furthermore, he claims that events which were truly in the future were announced through ambiguous and false prophecies. But **Josephus, Book XI, Chapter VIII**, is sufficient to refute him, where he records that the prophecies of Daniel were shown to Alexander the Great by the High Priest Jaddus <note>Jaddua, the High Priest mentioned in Nehemiah 12:11, who according to legend met Alexander the Great outside Jerusalem.</note>.

<margin>XXXIV. And Spinoza.</margin>
XXXIV. Even under the pretext of wisdom, the *Theologico-Political Philosopher* <note>A reference to Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) and his controversial "Tractatus Theologico-Politicus."</note> acts insanely, judging that the book of Daniel only appeared long after the temple worship was restored by Judas Maccabeus. He offers no probable reason, except that it seems so to him. He proceeds in a very intricate manner. He admits the last five chapters are undoubtedly Daniel's. He suspects the earlier ones were taken from the chronological books of the Chaldeans. He adds that the book of Ezra is connected to Daniel, and Esther to that, from which he concludes all have the same author, to which he adds Nehemiah as a supplement. These are bold, profane, and foolish divinations <note>original: *hariolationes* — wild guesses or nonsensical predictions.</note>.

<margin>XXXV. III. The Original Language.</margin>
XXXV. III. THE ORIGINAL LANGUAGE is *Hebrew* in Chapter I and the first three verses of Chapter II. From there until the end of Chapter VII, it is *Chaldean* <note>Now commonly referred to by scholars as Aramaic, the administrative language of the Babylonian and Persian Empires.</note>. Afterward, it returns to *Hebrew*. The additions concerning *Susanna, Bel and the Dragon*, and the *Hymn of the Three Children* <note>These are the "Deutero-canonical" or Apocryphal parts of Daniel found in Greek versions but not the Hebrew Bible.</note> exist only in *Greek*. What is the cause of this diversity? Many say it was done deliberately, so that through the Chaldean chapters, the Chaldeans might have a record of what happened to their kings, while in the following five, the Hebrews might be taught the mysteries of what would happen after the destruction of the Babylonian empire. But the entire volume was written for the Church, not for the Chaldeans. A very small part of the seventh chapter deals with the Chaldeans, while it explains things that will happen to the world and the Church until the final times. And yet, it is written in the Chaldean idiom.

<margin>XXXVI. Huet's wild guesses.</margin>
XXXVI. Huetius <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar known for his work on biblical transmission.</note> believes he has "outwitted the experts" <note>original: *cornicum oculos fixisse*, a Latin idiom meaning to deceive the most eagle-eyed or to do something incredibly clever.</note> when he conjectures that *the entire book was first written in Chaldean in Chaldea; then translated into Hebrew by the returning Jews for the benefit and use of their nation, and this by public authority; finally, it was translated into Greek by the author of the ancient interpretation, by Aquila, Theodotion, Symmachus, and others. From this, he says, it happened that in poorly preserved and mutilated copies (which could easily happen among a people devastated by so many ruins, exiles, and fires), when scribes came to reassemble the work, they were forced to fill in what was missing in the Hebrew copy from the Chaldean one; thus this ambiguous offspring arose. Regarding the additions of Susanna, etc., because they were pleasant to read and suited to the common understanding, he thinks it happened that they were widely celebrated among the Hellenists* <note>Greek-speaking Jews.</note>*, and especially the Alexandrians, whose genius...*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.

...Hebraisms, you say, occur here in several places. So be it, what then? Must we therefore acknowledge some Divine authority for this book? Not even you yourself would bid us conclude so. But at least, you say, the fair reader will therefore admit that these narratives were first conceived in Hebrew. Let him admit it: what profit do you gain from that? Have not more recent Hebrews also played the fool in their own language? Could not Hebrew **pseudepigrapha** <note>Pseudepigrapha: works falsely attributed to a historical figure or a biblical era.</note> also have been forged? But fairness does not persuade us to admit what you wish us to admit. Why could this little story not have been first conceived by some **Hellenist** <note>A Greek-speaking Jew, often one living outside of Judea.</note> in the Greek language, but one that drew quite a bit from Hebrew? There is no book in the New Testament that does not abound with Hebraisms. Must it therefore be admitted that they were all first conceived in Hebrew? Where was your mind, most learned *Huet*, when it pleased your soul to argue in this way? Did you not recall that thing which almost all of our people have objected against the authority of these narratives, and which *Jerome* records was objected to him in his own time by one of the Hebrew Teachers: namely, that there exist in them tropes of Greek elegance to which no Hebrew words could ever correspond, and which prove they were not translated from elsewhere, but first conceived in the Greek language? You know the **pun** <note>original: *paranomasiam* — a play on words.</note> derived "from the mastic tree" and "from the holm oak." <note>original: *apo tou schinou kai apo tou prinou*. This refers to the famous Greek wordplay in the Story of Susanna (Daniel 13:54-59). The judge puns on the names of the trees: the "mastic" tree (*schinos*) leads to "splitting" (*schisai*) the witness, and the "holm oak" (*prinos*) leads to "sawing" (*prisai*) him. These puns only work in Greek, not in Hebrew.</note> But do you know the Hebrew names of trees that would allow such a thing? Who would not rather think these are from some Greek trickster’s pleasantry <note>original: *suaviludio* — a charming or playful trick or literary game.</note> than sought from Hebrew?

XLII. As for what *Huet* adds—that the Jews do not oppose the truth of the story of Susanna—I do not know if he can sufficiently prove it. *Jerome, in his preface to Daniel*, testifies that he experienced the opposite: <note>original: *Audivi ego quendam de præceptotibus Judæorum...*</note> *I heard a certain one of the Jewish teachers when he mocked the story of Susanna; and he said it was fabricated by some Greek or other.* The author of *Zemach David* <note>David Gans (1541–1613), a famous Jewish chronicler and astronomer. His book, *The Sprout of David*, is a history of the Jewish people.</note> shows that the same mind still resides with his people in Book II, Number 330: <note>original: *Historia Susannæ, filiæ Chilkiæ...*</note> *The history of Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, as it is recorded in the book of Susanna, was received through tradition by them—namely, the Christians—but not by us.* Moreover, the reason *Huet* boasts for the loss of the Hebrew edition, we have shown above to be of no account at all.

<margin>
I. Daniel does not seem to have presided over Judea after the captivity.
</margin>

->BOOK I. CHAPTER XIX.<-

Some Hebraisms <note>idioms or stylistic features characteristic of the Hebrew language</note>, you say, occur here. Fine, what then? Must we therefore recognize some Divine authority in this book? Even you yourself would not command us to conclude that. But at least, you say, the fair reader will admit on that account that these narratives were first conceived in Hebrew. Let him admit it: what gain do you derive from that? Have not even more recent Hebrews written foolishly in their own language? Could not Hebrew <term>pseudepigrapha</term> <note>writings falsely attributed to a biblical figure or antiquity</note> also be forged? 

But fairness does not urge us to admit what you wish us to admit. Why could this little story not have been first conceived by some Hellenist <note>a Greek-speaking Jew of the Diaspora</note> in the Greek language, but one that drew quite a bit from Hebrew? There is no book in the New Testament that does not abound with Hebraisms. Must it therefore be admitted that they were all first conceived in Hebrew? Where was your mind, most learned Huet, when it pleased your soul to argue in this way? Did you not recall that point which almost all of our people have raised against the authority of these narratives, and which *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> mentions was already raised in his own time by one of the Hebrew teachers: namely, that there exist in them certain figures of Greek elegance <note>original: "Græcanicæ elegantiæ tropos"</note> to which no Hebrew could ever correspond, and which prove they were not translated from elsewhere, but first conceived in the Greek language? 

You know the <term>paronomasia</term> <note>a play on words or pun</note> derived from "the mastic tree" and "the holm oak." <note>This refers to a famous Greek pun in the story of Susanna. When the elders are questioned separately about which tree Susanna was under, one says a mastic tree (*schinos*), and Daniel replies that an angel will cut (*schisein*) him; the other says a holm oak (*prinos*), and Daniel replies the angel will saw (*prisein*) him. These puns only work in Greek, not Hebrew.</note> But do you know the Hebrew names of the trees which would permit such a thing? Who would not rather think these things came from some Greek trifler's amusement than being sought from a Hebrew source?

XLII. As for what *Huet* adds—that the Jews do not oppose the truth of the story of Susanna—I do not know if he can prove it sufficiently. *Jerome, in his preface to Daniel*, testifies that he experienced the opposite: *“I heard a certain one of the teachers of the Jews when he mocked the story of Susanna, and said it was fabricated by I-know-not-which Greek.”* That the same mindset still resides in his people today is shown by the author of *Zemach David* <note>A famous Jewish chronicle by David Gans, published in 1592</note> (Book II, No. 330): *“The story of Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, as it is recorded in the Book of Susanna, is received by them—meaning the Christians—through tradition; but not by us.”* Moreover, the reason Huet boasts for the loss of the Hebrew edition—that it was simply lost over time—we have shown above to be of no account at all.

<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XX.</header>

...of [such] piety, wisdom, and authority that it seems he could not have remained unnoticed. It is more likely that he flourished in favor and power under Darius the Mede, Cyrus, and their successors, and managed the affairs of the Israelites abroad among those lords of the world.

<margin>II. Haggai was not a heavenly spirit, but a man.</margin>
II. Jerome is the authority for the fact that some once believed **HAGGAI** was not a man, but an Angel clothed in human form and sent from heaven to stir men toward their duties and the study of piety. They were led to this reasoning because in Chapter 1:13 he is called <note>original Hebrew: *Malak Yehovah be-malakut Yehovah*</note> the **Messenger of the Lord in the Lord’s mission.** But there is an old complaint that nothing is so foolish that it has not been said by some "wise" person. Who, even moderately skilled in sacred literature, does not know that the name "Angel" <note>The word *Angelus* in Latin and *Malak* in Hebrew literally means "messenger," referring to a job description rather than a biological species.</note> refers not so much to nature as to office? Just as it sometimes denotes heavenly spirits whom the supreme deity uses for his ministries, so elsewhere it is used to designate men upon whom he has imposed the task of teaching. A most eloquent passage exists in Malachi 2:7: *The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and the law shall be sought from his mouth; for* **HE IS THE MESSENGER OF THE LORD OF HOSTS.** And indeed, Haggai is called a Prophet, which is a title for men, not heavenly spirits; and he is joined with Zechariah as being of the same kind and order. Ezra 6:14.

<margin>III. Zechariah son of Berechiah: is he the one mentioned in Isaiah 8:2?</margin>
III. **ZECHARIAH** was the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo. Zechariah 1:1. Was he the son of that Iddo who lived in the time of Rehoboam <note>The son of Solomon and first king of Judah</note> and recorded his deeds in writing? 2 Chronicles 12:15. The logic of the timeline does not seem to allow this. For between Rehoboam and Darius, under whom Zechariah prophesied, at least 240 years intervene. From this it follows that Iddo, Zechariah’s grandfather, was either a different person from that one, or Zechariah descended from that famous Iddo only after several intervening generations. Since he is said to be the son of Berechiah, interpreters have asked whether he is the same one mentioned by Isaiah in Chapter 8:2: *I took to myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest, and **ZECHARIAH THE SON OF JEBERECHIAH.*** Likewise, is he the same as the one mentioned by our Lord in Matthew 23:35: *That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of **ZECHARIAH, SON OF BERECHIAH,** whom you killed between the temple and the altar.* These are worthy questions to be treated with care.

<margin>IV. Isaiah deals with witnesses of the prophecy he published.</margin>
IV. As for the first question, it must be weighed above all else what matter Isaiah brought witnesses for. On this point, the learned scholars go their separate ways. Some understand them to be witnesses of the *marriage* completed by the Prophet,

<header>CONCERNING THE PROPHETS AFTER THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.</header>

...for which ten witnesses were ordinarily required; but here two were employed, who were very well known and most worthy of trust. Others think of these as witnesses to a birth; so that no one could falsely claim that a girl had been born and a male child secretly substituted for her. Some also think of them as witnesses to a name given to the son of the Prophet during circumcision, acting as if they were godparents. But all these explanations seem rather weak. Better are those who believe the Prophet is dealing with witnesses to a prophecy he had published.

<margin>V. Or those who would testify that all things were predicted exactly as they happened.</margin>
V. This, again, can be understood in two ways: either that he took witnesses for himself who would testify that all things were predicted exactly as they were being foretold; or that he praised certain men by name who, moved by the same <term>divine inspiration<note>original: "numinis instinctu"; refers to the internal drive or "instinct" provided by God to the prophets.</note></term>, would predict the same thing. The most serious theologian, **Zacharias Ursinus** <note>A 16th-century German Reformed theologian, famous for his work on the Heidelberg Catechism.</note>, explained the first view accurately and clearly:

<note>original: "Quum in præsentia non inveniret fidem Propheta apud populum, rejiciebat dijudicationem litis inter se & populum infidelem, ad impletionem vaticinii, utpote quæ demonstratura erat, si sequeretur tempore prædicto, Jesaiam vera & à Deo profecta oracula edidisse, & contra, si non responderet eventus prædictioni, fuisse vanum & impostorem. Ne autem, si fierent prædicta, populus eludere posset oracula, quasi vel non essent edita, vel non sic essent edita sicut res evenissent, vel non certa Dei patefactione, sed casu essent hæc prædicti: neve Jesaias, si non fierent quæ prædicebat, posset subterfugere crimen imposturæ & pseudoprophetiæ, negando se hæc prædixisse; ideo testes adhibet, quorum auctoritas apud populum erat exceptione major..."</note>

*“Since at that time the Prophet did not find faith among the people, he deferred the judgment of the dispute between himself and the unfaithful people to the fulfillment of the prophecy. This fulfillment would demonstrate—if it followed at the predicted time—that Isaiah had uttered true oracles that came from God; conversely, if the outcome did not match the prediction, it would show he was a vain man and an impostor. Furthermore, if the predictions came to pass, the people might try to mock the oracles, claiming they were never published, or not published in the way events actually turned out, or that they were predicted by chance rather than by a certain revelation from God. Likewise, if the things he foretold did not happen, Isaiah might try to escape the charge of imposture and <term>false prophecy<note>original: "pseudoprophetia"</note></term> by denying he had ever predicted them. Therefore, he employs witnesses whose authority among the people was beyond reproach. If the predictions did not happen, they would testify against Isaiah that he had predicted false things; but if they did happen, they would testify for Isaiah and against Ahaz and the people, stating that Isaiah had predicted these things exactly as they occurred, in the name of the Lord, with certainty and constancy, even at his own risk. Consequently, his oracles were true and divine, while the manifest impiety and blasphemy belonged to Ahaz and the people, who had despised the word of God spoken through the mouth of Isaiah and accused him of lying.”* **Musculus** <note>Wolfgang Musculus, a Reformer known for his biblical commentaries.</note> holds similar views, and **Calvin** is not far off.

<margin>VI. And then by Uriah and Zechariah, men contemporary with Isaiah are to be understood.</margin>
VI. However, those who set things up this way must necessarily understand these honored witnesses to be certain men of great reputation among the people, living in Jerusalem at the same time as Isaiah. Therefore, they believe **URIAH** the Priest is the one who served as High Priest in the time of **Ahaz** and was the minister of his idolatry, building the Damascene altar in the temple of Jerusalem by the king's command (2 Kings 16:10). They argue he is called a "faithful witness" not because of his own virtues, but because of the authority he held among the people due to the dignity of his office. Ursinus adds: it seems he also employed this Uriah...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "faithful witnesses" mentioned in Isaiah 8. While the previous page introduced the problem of who these witnesses (Uriah and Zechariah) were, this page critiques the common historical identifications and explores a grammatical argument suggesting the witnesses were future prophets appointed by God.</meta>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XX.</header>

...so that he, who was himself a despiser of the prophetic oracles, might shortly after be compelled, willing or not, to bear witness to their truth. However, they think **ZACHARIAH** *son of Jeberechiah* was the father-in-law of *Ahaz*, and the maternal grandfather of *Hezekiah*, who is mentioned in 2 *Kings* 18:2 and 2 *Chronicles* 29:1. And I find that most interpreters concede to this opinion.

<margin>VII. Which is not without its own difficulty.</margin>
VII. Yet this view seems to suffer from certain difficulties of its own. First, since Isaiah proclaimed this entire prophecy of his not only with a public voice before the King and the people, but also, at God’s command, wrote it with his own hand in a scroll, and—as *Calvin* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French theologian whose commentaries were standard references for Reformed scholars.</note> maintains—took care to have it posted on the doors of the temple to be preserved thereafter in the Archives; why was there a need for witnesses to testify that these things had been so predicted by Isaiah? Isaiah’s own hand and writing testified most powerfully of all for itself. Secondly, the prophecies whose certainty was at stake were not all, nor even most of them, to be fulfilled while Isaiah and his contemporaries were still living: how then, from the eventual outcome, were those witnesses supposed to answer either for or against Isaiah? Not to mention that *Uriah* the Priest <note>Referring to the high priest during the reign of Ahaz who complied with the king's idolatrous changes to the temple.</note>, a man who was a <term>prevaricator<note>A person who speaks or acts in an evasive way; here, one who betrays his religious duty.</note></term>, a slave to the whims of an impious King, and an unfaithful servant to his Supreme Lord, seems an enemy of Isaiah and unworthy of the title *faithful witness*; nor is it certain whether *Zachariah*, the father-in-law of *Ahaz*, was the son of *Jeberechiah*, since the name of his father is nowhere published.

<margin>VIII. Or those who would confirm Isaiah's prophecy with a similar one.</margin>
VIII. Therefore, so that these difficulties may be avoided and the words of the Prophet may have a significant emphasis, they seem not inconveniently explained as referring to those who were going to prophesy similar or identical things; being designated here by their own names, they were going to strongly confirm the oracles of Isaiah. Nor do I think we should disregard the observation of *Abravanel* <note>Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a renowned Jewish statesman and philosopher whose biblical commentaries were highly regarded by Christian Hebraists.</note>, which he owes to the ancient teachers: that this verse is not so much the speech of the prophet as the speech of God, such that God is acting to summon witnesses for Himself. To this, another point can be added: that the Hebrew words <note>original: "וְאָעִידָה לִּי עֵדִים נֶאֱמָנִים" (Ve-aidah li edim neemanim)</note> "And I will call for myself faithful witnesses" properly sound as if they designate a future time; therefore, they are best translated as *and I shall summon for myself faithful witnesses*. This was also well noted by the <term>interlinear version<note>A type of translation where the English (or Latin) word is placed directly below the original Hebrew or Greek word to show the exact correspondence.</note></term>, rendering it: *And I will cause faithful witnesses to testify for me*. For under the letter ו (Vau) there is no point which the Grammarians call "conversive"; therefore, the verb in the future tense remains in its future meaning. This is all the more certain because in the nearest verses, both preceding and following, the grammatical analogy in the punctuation of the <term>vau conversive<note>A grammatical feature in Biblical Hebrew where the prefix "and" flips a verb's tense from future to past or vice versa.</note></term> is exactly observed. Who, then, are those witnesses whom either the Prophet or God testifies will be summoned? These are the praised...

# ON THE PROPHETS AFTER THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.

...prophecy <note>Completing the word "prophetiam" from the previous page's catchword.</note> are praised: I. By reason of their name. II. By reason of their Testimony. III. By reason of their faith in testifying.

<margin>IX. These appear to be Uriah son of Shemaiah, and Zechariah the Prophet.</margin>
IX. The names of the witnesses are Uriah the Priest, and Zechariah son of Jeberechiah. What is more appropriate here: to think of men who are otherwise unknown, or one who is even infamously known <note>Referring to the historical Uriah the Priest who cooperated with King Ahaz's idolatry, mentioned on the previous page.</note>, who could contribute hardly anything to the confirmation of this prophecy? Or should we think of those who are mentioned elsewhere in the Sacred Scriptures with the highest praise under these same names? Who would doubt that the latter is preferable, unless something stands in the way? We shall soon show that nothing stands in the way. Furthermore, praise is given to Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath Jearim, who, when he had prophesied against Jerusalem and the land of Judah, was forced to flee into Egypt; he was brought back from there by King Jehoiakim and put to death by the sword (Jeremiah 26:20). It is not explicitly stated that this Uriah was a Priest, but neither is anything said that would lead to a suspicion of the contrary. Besides this Uriah, the most famous is Zechariah son of Berechiah, whose prophetic book we possess, and who prophesied under Darius. Indeed, the names Barachiah and Jeberechiah differ by only a single small letter, which introduces no change in meaning; they are rightly considered one and the same name. These men are surely worthy to be employed as witnesses.

<margin>X. Because they prophesied the same things as Isaiah.</margin>
X. But how could they be witnesses for Isaiah? This must now be explained, which I hope to do most clearly. We must look at what Isaiah prophesies in these chapters. He had predicted to the Jews the coming of the Messiah to his people, and the nature of the time in which He was to be born; likewise, he had predicted the calamities which Ahaz was bringing upon himself, the people, and his house, to be inflicted by the Assyrians—namely Tiglath-Pileser and Sennacherib, the Kings of Assyria—to whom Nebuchadnezzar <note>King of Babylon (r. 605–562 BCE), who destroyed the First Temple.</note> can be added. For after the Monarchy of the Assyrians was transferred to the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians.</note>, the Chaldeans sometimes appear under the name of "Assyrians." Finally, he had predicted the restoration of the land to its former abundance, so that the mountains which were once cultivated with a hoe—where no one had dared to go before—would then be places for the driving of oxen and the treading of sheep; that is, fertile and secure pastures, without fear of wild beasts or enemies. All these things were confirmed by the testimonies of Uriah son of Shemaiah, who prophesied with such constancy concerning the devastation of the land of Judah; and Zechariah son of Berechiah, who, living after the Babylonian captivity was ended, most brilliantly predicted the multiplication of the people in the land, the blessing of the earth, and the coming of the Messiah at that specific point in time. Because these men [agreed] in the same prophecy with Isaiah...

<margin>XI. And this with remarkable faith and constancy.</margin>
XI. Finally, since we have shown the manner in which they were summoned as witnesses, it is clear in itself why they are called *faithful witnesses*. For they were such, both by reason of their virtues and the authority they possessed, and by reason of their fearless constancy in delivering their prophecies. From this I conclude: our *Zechariah*, the son of *Berechiah* <note>original: "Barachiæ"</note>, was praised by *Isaiah* long before he was born.

<margin>XII. With the agreement of the Talmudists.</margin>
XII. The *Talmudists* do not differ much from this opinion in the *Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Makkot, folio 24, pages 1 and 2*. From this, *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist who used Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note> excerpted these points for *Matthew 23:35*: It is written, *I will cause to be witnessed for me faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Berechiah* (note that it is written *Berechiyahu* with a final "u" <note>original: ברכיהו. This refers to the fuller theophoric spelling of the name in Hebrew.</note>). *But what is the reason why Uriah is joined with Zechariah? For Uriah lived during the time of the First Temple, while Zechariah lived during the Second.* However, the *Scripture* attaches the prophecy of Zechariah to the prophecy of Uriah. *By Uriah it was said: "Therefore Zion shall be plowed as a field." By Zechariah it is written: "Old men and old women shall yet sit in the streets of Jerusalem." When the prophecy of Uriah is fulfilled, the prophecy of Zechariah will also be fulfilled.* It is added in *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a prominent Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> that these were the words of *Rabbi Akiva* to *Rabban Gamaliel*, *Rabbi Joshua*, and *Rabbi Eliezer the son of Azariah*, who were so satisfied by this explanation that they burst forth in congratulation with these words: *Akiva, you have comforted us; Akiva, you have comforted us.* <note>original: עקיבה נחמתנו עקיבה נחמתנו</note>

<margin>XIII. And by the Paraphrast. See also the Preface, § XV.</margin>
XIII. The *Paraphrast Jonathan* <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Prophets.</note> is of nearly the same mind: *And I will cause to be witnessed before me faithful witnesses: the curses which I said I would bring in the prophecy of Uriah the priest, which behold, have come to pass. In the same way, all the comforts which I said I would bring in the prophecy of Zechariah, the son of Jeberechiah, I am about to bring.* <note>The author provides the Aramaic text followed by a Latin translation, both rendered here into English.</note> In short: they agree in understanding this Zechariah to be our Prophet.

<margin>XIV. Is the Zechariah whom Christ praises in Matthew 23:35 our prophet?</margin>
XIV. Did the Lord also speak of the same man in Matthew 23:35? That must now be investigated further. These arguments support the idea: I. That not only was his own name *Zechariah*, but also his father’s name was *Barachiah*. By this father's name he is distinguished from other *Zechariahs* mentioned in *Scripture*. For we do not find any other *Zechariah, son of Barachiah*, anywhere else in the sacred writings.

...we determine. <note>original: "nimus", likely completing "statuimus" from the previous page.</note> II. <margin>XV. Was he the Son of Jehoiada?</margin>
XV. Therefore, others prefer to believe the Savior was speaking of *Zechariah* the son of *Jehoiada*, of whom we read in 2 Chronicles 24. They are led by these arguments: I. Because sacred scripture mentions no other Zechariah being killed. It does not seem likely that Christ would bring up something uncertain and obscure, but rather a matter thoroughly proven to everyone. II. Because the location of the murder fits. For it took place in the open air, in what the Hebrews call the *chatzer* <note>original: חצר</note>, the Greeks the *aulē* <note>original: αὐλὴν</note>, and *Josephus* the *hypaithron* <note>original: ὕπαιθρον</note>, in which the Altar of burnt offerings stood; so that a certain part of the courtyard lay between the Altar and the House of the temple, which Christ calls the *naon* <note>original: ναὸν, referring to the inner sanctuary</note>. *Josephus* also names this place in the same way in his history *On the Capture [of Jerusalem]* Book 5: "between the altar and the temple" <note>original: μεταξὺ τοῦ βωμοῦ καὶ τοῦ νεώ</note>. In the *Babylonian Talmud*, in the chapter on the measurements of the Temple, it is said that the space between the porch and this Altar was 22 cubits. III. Because Christ is dealing with a murder that is to be exemplarily avenged. Now, this Zechariah, when he was dying, said: *May the Lord see it, and require it.* IV. Because the Jews themselves observed that the death of this Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, was memorable for its singular nature and the vengeance that followed—adding also, according to their custom, little fables, which those who enjoy such things can find in the works of *Lightfoot*. That Christ seems to be speaking of one who was killed *most recently* by the Jews, and in this way he is contrasted with *Abel*. But after Zechariah son of Jehoiada, Uriah was killed under the first temple; and under the second temple, and indeed very recently, John the Baptist, who was greater than all the prophets.

<margin>XVI. Was it another man killed by the Zealots shortly before the final siege?</margin>

This was immediately followed by the siege, as can be seen in Josephus.* <note>Hugo Grotius was a 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian who often sought historical and linguistic parallels in scripture.</note> *Cocceius* expresses this even more confidently in his commentaries on this passage: WITHOUT A DOUBT THIS IS A PROPHECY CONCERNING ZECHARIAH THE SON OF BARUCH, whom the Zealots—having set up a mock High Sanhedrin of seventy men—condemned though he was innocent, and killed in the Temple itself, as Josephus narrates in his *History of the Jewish War*. However, an objection arises: it seems difficult to turn the words of Christ, who speaks in the past tense, into a prophecy about the future.

<margin>XVII. Not entirely clear.</margin>
XVII. These points are debated by learned men on both sides with some degree of probability. Each opinion has its own reasons to defend itself. Each is also pressed by its own difficulties. For my part, let everyone be free to embrace the one they judge to rest upon more solid arguments, and whose difficulties they hope to resolve with less trouble. That last opinion, though it does not seem to me to be "without a doubt" preferable to the others as *Cocceius* dictates, should not be set aside as if it were devoid of all probability. For his reasons are not worth nothing, nor is the difficulty unsolvable. Christ knew what was to come, and predictions of future events are frequently set forth in the words of the past tense. Finally, Christ, speaking in Hebrew, could have used a participle which carries no fixed determination of time, which Matthew wisely expressed with the Aorist <note>The Aorist is a Greek verb tense usually indicating past action, but the author argues it was used to translate an ambiguous Hebrew structure.</note>. That could be understood in the sense of either the future or the past.

# ON THE PROPHETS AFTER THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY. #

<margin>Haggai and Zechariah prophesied under Darius: was it Hystaspis or Nothus?</margin>
Zechariah prophesied. Concerning *Haggai*, it is said in Chapter 1, verse 1: *In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by Haggai the Prophet to Zerubbabel, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Anno secundo Darii Regis..."</note> Concerning *Zechariah*, likewise at the beginning of his book: *In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah.* From this it is clear that there was only a two-month interval between their prophecies. However, which Darius this might be—in whose second year they began to prophesy—whether DARIUS HYSTASPIS or DARIUS NOTHUS, is a matter of great controversy among the learned. <note>Darius I (Hystaspis) ruled c. 522–486 BCE, while Darius II (Nothus) ruled c. 423–404 BCE. This distinction changes the biblical timeline by a century.</note> The history of the kings of Persia, as handed down by the Greek writers, is a most intricate matter; to reconcile these writers among themselves and with Divine History is beyond our strength, and perhaps beyond human capability. I shall not even attempt so arduous a task. But mindful that I write for young students, to whom my labor is dedicated, I will strive to clearly explain some of the principal opinions of the most learned men—whose authority in the Church is now great—so that the students may understand them clearly and judge the reasons for each in their own way.

<margin>XIX. So that it may be determined, the sequence of the Persian kings must be maintained.</margin>
XIX. It must therefore be held above all else that the prophecies of both *Haggai* and *Zechariah* were prepared so that they might encourage Prince Zerubbabel and Joshua the High Priest, along with the Jewish people, to resume and complete the building of the temple, which had been interrupted for many years. It should also be known that this building project was sometimes forbidden and sometimes permitted by various Persian kings, in whose power the Jews were at that time. Those times cannot be properly distinguished unless we represent to ourselves a certain sequence of the kings of Persia. That sequence is constructed either from *Scripture* or from Greek authors, who are then compared with *Scripture* in various ways.

<margin>XX. This sequence is derived from Scripture according to Cocceius.</margin>

For *Achaschuerosch* <note>The Hebrew form of Ahasuerus.</note> and *Cyaxares* are the same name. Perhaps *Xenophon* applied the father's name to the son. The second is DARIUS HYSTASPIS, whom *Ezra* places after Cyrus in *Chapter 4:5*. He is followed by AHASUERUS, that is, XERXES (Ezra 4:6), the fourth King from Cyrus and the third of Cyrus's successors. He is followed by ARTHACHSCHAST, that is, ARTAXER-

### ON THE PROPHETS AFTER THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY. ###

The Jews, by the grant of <term>Cyrus</term> <note>Cyrus the Great, who allowed the Jews to return from exile in 538 BCE.</note>, began to lay the foundations in the first year—though he should have said the second year, according to Ezra 3:8—of the Babylonian Monarchy itself. Despite their rivals' futile resistance, they continued the construction for 46 years or more, until they were prohibited by the edicts of <term>Xerxes</term> and <term>Artaxerxes Longimanus</term> <note>Artaxerxes I.</note>, as gathered from Ezra 4. From that time, the work ceased until the second year of <term>Darius Nothus</term> <note>Darius II.</note>; in his sixth year, it was completed, although the final finishing touch was eventually applied in the seventh year of <term>Artaxerxes Mnemon</term> <note>Artaxerxes II.</note>. Thus, the total time in which they were occupied in building the temple, until the sixth year of Darius, is 117 years: part of which is attributed to work, and part to the cessation. Approximately 68 or 70 years are to be attributed to the cessation. This is the view of <term>Burman</term> <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch theologian.</note> in his *Commentaries on Ezra 4*.

<margin>XXII. The arguments of those who understand the king to be Darius Nothus.</margin>
XXII. It is not my pleasure to compare every detail, as that would be a task of immense labor; I only wish to point out now that these prophecies are referred to the second year of **DARIUS NOTHUS**. <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar of chronology.</note> contends the same, as does <term>Sethus Calvisius</term> <note>A German astronomer and chronologer.</note> after Scaliger, who argues this case at length in his *Introduction*, Chapter 42, though from different principles than <term>Cocceius</term> or <term>Burman</term>. This is their principal argument: in <term>Zechariah</term> Chapter 1, verse 12, the interceding Angel says:
> Lord God of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have treated harshly for these seventy years?
In the same book of Zechariah, Chapter 7, verse 3, it is narrated that two years before the completion of the temple, in the fourth year of **King Darius**, certain envoys from **Babylon** consulted the priests and prophets as to whether the Church should continue weeping, "as I have done," it says, "for many years." In God’s response, however, those years are said to have been seventy (verse 5):
> When you fasted in the fifth and seventh months, **FOR THESE SEVENTY YEARS**, etc.
It does not seem possible for this to be understood as the years of the Babylonian Captivity, for those had long since passed by the time of Zechariah, however one calculates it. It is evident, then, that it deals with those years which only now reached their end. For they ask whether they should now return from their seventy-year fast to a more joyful way of life. From this, it is inferred that the years understood are those that elapsed after the captivity ended but during a period of distress, which gave cause for fasting and lamentation. Those years cannot be found in the age of <term>Darius Hystaspis</term> <note>Darius I, who reigned much earlier.</note>, for then only about fifteen years of fasting had occurred since the return to the land due to the prohibition of the temple's construction. But they are perfectly found in the time that passed between the beginning of Cyrus and the reign of Darius Nothus. Thus do these most learned men defend their opinion.

XXIII. Most others, however, take a completely different view: and by Darius...

BOOK I. CHAPTER XX.

<margin>...of those who argue for Hystaspis.</margin>
Those who favor the king praised by Ezra and the prophets understand him to be **DARIUS HYSTASPIS** <note>Darius I, who ruled from 522–486 BCE. "Hystaspis" refers to his father, Hystaspes.</note>. They fight for this view with these reasons. I. From the first year of Cyrus, when the edict for the building of the temple was promulgated, to the sixth year of *Darius Nothus* <note>Darius II, who ruled much later, from 423–404 BCE.</note>, when it was finished, there pass—according to *Scaliger* and *Calvisius*—**one hundred and thirteen years**; according to *Burman*, **one hundred and seventeen**; according to *Cocceius*, **one hundred and forty-two**. In this entire space of time, and for some time both before and after, <term>Zerubbabel</term> held the Princedom and <term>Joshua</term> the High Priesthood. Such a long duration of governance, in both the Church and the State, has never been heard of regarding any mortal in any century. From this, it is concluded that such a great interval did not occur between the beginning and the completion of the temple as there is between the start of Cyrus and the sixth year of *Darius Nothus*. II. In *Haggai* Chapter II:3, it is recorded that some of the Jews had seen the splendor of the first Temple and compared the glory of the second to it, as it was in the seventh month of the second year of Darius. If this were understood to be *Darius Nothus*, it would be necessary for those Jews who saw both temples at the same time to have lived at least beyond **one hundred and eighty years**, which shrinks from all probability. Thus argue those who fight for *Darius Hystaspis*.

<margin>XXIV. What can be opposed to the former arguments.</margin>
XXIV. These reasons deserve to be weighed against one another; so that this may be done more carefully, I wish to subjoin some considerations which can be opposed to each. To the argument concerning the 70 years having elapsed in the second year of *Darius*, there are various responses. However, the most probable solution to the difficulty seems to be this one, which <term>Theodoret</term> <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 CE), an influential bishop and biblical commentator.</note> first pointed out, and many learned men after him have approved. Specifically, that the "seventy" is double: one of the **Jerusalem captivity**, the other of the **Jerusalem desolation** and the **burned temple**. The former began in the *first year of Nebuchadnezzar* and ceased in the *first of Cyrus*; the latter began in the *nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar* and ceased in the *second of Darius Hystaspis*, when, after some interruption, the temple began to be restored. The matter itself almost speaks for the fact that these last 70 years are understood in *Zechariah* VII. Certainly, that history cannot be referred to the years of the Babylonian captivity of which *Jeremiah* speaks in XXV:11–12 and XXIX:10. For those had already ceased 17 years earlier; and if the Jews had fasted because of the captivity, they would have ceased to fast once the captivity was ended. Yet they had fasted until the second, even the fourth year of *Darius*. Therefore, the cause of the fasting was different—namely, the sad consideration of a temple burned and not yet restored. This is also demonstrated by the occasion of the embassy itself. For when they saw the work of the building of the Temple proceeding so beautifully, they thought they should ask—

XXV.
What about those who came later.

XXV. On the other side, regarding the argument drawn from the incredible longevity of **Zerubbabel** and **Joshua**—if *Darius Nothus* were to be understood—*Calvisius* <note>Sethus Calvisius, a German chronologist and astronomer</note> responds that the opposing view is burdened by the same absurdity. For although from the second year of the Monarchy of *Cyrus* to the sixth year of *Darius Hystaspis* no one counts more than twenty-two years, and in this way the difficulty regarding the age of *Zerubbabel* and *Joshua* seems resolved, yet what is avoided in them must be admitted in **Nehemiah**, **Ezra**, and **Sanballat**. For *Nehemiah* is believed to have lived until the times of *Alexander the Great*: because in *Chapter XII:11, 22*, he names the High Priest **Jaddua**, who is certain to have been a contemporary of *Alexander*. Likewise, *Ezra* seems to have lived near the end of the Persian Empire: for in *Chapter X:6*, he is said to have entered the chamber of *Johanan*, the father of *Jaddua*. After *Broughton*, *Nisbet* urges this argument more strongly, having considered the birth of *Ezra*. *Ezra*, they say, was the son of *Seraiah* (*Ezra VII:1*). But *Seraiah* was killed by *Nebuchadnezzar* before the captivity (*2 Kings XXV:18*). Therefore, if *Ezra* was born before the destruction of Jerusalem, and in the seventh year of *Artaxerxes Mnemon* <note>Artaxerxes II, who reigned much later than the first Artaxerxes</note>—the year he returned from Babylon to Jerusalem—he would have had to be over two hundred years old. Finally, there was also the great longevity of *Sanballat*: for he, the leader of the <term>Cutheans</term> <note>A term often used for Samaritans</note> in the time of *Nehemiah*, extended his life to the times of *Alexander the Great*, with whom he held great favor, obtaining for his son-in-law *Manasseh* the ability to build a temple on Mount **Gerizim**, which would be almost equal to the one in Jerusalem. Since, therefore, such great longevity is found in *Nehemiah*, *Ezra*, and *Sanballat*, what is the reason to deny the same, or consider it incredible, in *Zerubbabel* and *Joshua*? Especially since *Joshua* and his friends are called *men of portent* <note>original Hebrew: אנשי מופת (*anshe mofet*), usually translated as "men who are a sign" or "men of omen"</note> (*Zechariah III:8*).

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XX.

> Long ago, when the Temple was being founded, many elders wept, seeing its smallness. In the meantime, so many years have flowed by. If, therefore, there is someone among you now of such an age that he can still remember the former building, does this Temple not seem as nothing to you? Certainly, if those who saw it were alive, they would consider this as nothing.

He adds, however: *it is credible that many among the people could have remembered the former Temple under Hystaspis* <note>Darius I, who ruled 522–486 BCE</note>. Yet he does not think that reasoning is so great that he would abandon his opinion regarding the building of the second Temple under Darius Nothus <note>Darius II, who ruled 423–404 BCE</note>: to which he believes himself compelled by greater reasons.

<margin>
XXVII.
What might be answered in response to these exceptions.
</margin>

XXVII. But to these things, many points are again put forward by others, by which they think the force of those observations can be neutralized. Regarding Nehemiah, those who emphasize his long life allow themselves to believe that Artaxerxes, under whom Nehemiah was appointed Governor of Judea, was not *Longimanus* <note>Artaxerxes I "Long-hand"</note>, but *Mnemon* <note>Artaxerxes II "The Mindful"</note>, the son of Darius Nothus. However, from the twentieth year of Longimanus to the twentieth year of Mnemon there are at minimum sixty years, which may thus be subtracted from the alleged longevity of Nehemiah. But since that hypothesis is not admitted by those who argue the temple was built under Hystaspis; that response may indeed seem to hold weight against *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous scholar of chronology</note>: but in truth, it does not remove the difficulty. For that *Artaxerxes* who sent Ezra and Nehemiah to Jerusalem followed that Darius who established the edict regarding the building of the Temple (Ezra 6:14). On this point, both sides agree. Therefore, those who ascribe that edict to Darius Hystaspis must necessarily understand *Artaxerxes* to be Longimanus. And thus, the argument sought from the longevity of *Nehemiah* remains unshaken so far. Therefore, another answer must be sought. Surely an elderly *Nehemiah* could have looked upon *Jaddua* <note>The High Priest mentioned in Nehemiah 12</note> as a youth. Let us suppose *Jaddua* became High Priest in his thirtieth year: and at the time of *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great</note> he was ninety years old, which is not rare among High Priests: from that hypothesis, it is possible that Nehemiah died sixty years before Alexander's monarchy, and yet lived for some time with *Jaddua*. And thus, the age of *Nehemiah* would have nothing extraordinary about it.

XXVIII. The difficulty concerning *Ezra* is greater. But even that is diminished by observations that are not to be despised, whether we look at the beginning or the end of his life. It cannot be proved from the fact that he is called the son of *Seraiah* that his life began before the destruction of Jerusalem, even though *Seraiah* was slaughtered by *Nebuchadnezzar* before the captivity. # ON THE PROPHETS AFTER THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY.

...it is certain that Seraiah <note>The High Priest executed by Nebuchadnezzar II during the fall of Jerusalem</note>, who was killed by Nebuchadnezzar, was the ancestor of **Ezra**; however, many men named **Seraiah**, even from the priestly line, are mentioned by **Ezra** and **Nehemiah**. It does not follow that because **Ezra** is called the **son of Seraiah**, he was his immediate son. For in **Ezra 7:3**, **Azariah** is said to have been the son of **Meraioth**: although between **Azariah** and **Meraioth**, no fewer than seven generations are skipped for the sake of brevity in **1 Chronicles 6:7, 8, 9**. **Ezra’s** goal was to demonstrate that his ancestors were of the priestly line. He achieves this by indicating he is descended from **Seraiah**: which is true, whether he was a grandson or a great-great-grandson. Therefore, nothing can be concluded about the beginning of **Ezra’s** life from the name of **Seraiah**. 

Furthermore, it is not established that his life was extended nearly to the end of the Persian Empire based on the fact that he is said to have **entered the chamber of Johanan, the father of Jaddua** <note>original: "intrasse cubiculum Joanan patris Jadduæ"</note>. **Ezra 10:6.** For **Johanan** could have been quite young at that time. Moreover, the act of **Ezra** praised there is the last of those recorded in Scripture. According to the lifespans of many High Priests, more than a hundred years could easily have passed from the youth of **Johanan** to the old age of **Jaddua**. And thus far, the arguments for that prodigious longevity of **Ezra** fail.

## XXIX. 

Regarding the age of **Sanballat** <note>The Governor of Samaria who opposed Nehemiah</note>, in which the primary hope of **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a 16th-century Dutch scholar who revolutionized historical chronology</note> and **Calvisius** <note>Sethus Calvisius, a German astronomer and chronologer</note> lies, the response is as follows. Assuming that **Nehemiah** came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of **Mnemon** <note>Artaxerxes II "the Mindful," ruled 404–358 BCE</note>, which is indeed **Scaliger’s** opinion, **Sanballat’s** age would have nothing extraordinary about it. Suppose he were twenty years old in the twentieth year of **Mnemon**: from there to the fifth year of **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great</note> is not more than fifty years, so that when **Sanballat** died at the siege of Tyre, he would be no older than seventy. 

But this response, again, is based on the hypothesis of the person being answered, not on the person answering. Thus, the difficulty remains. For if **Sanballat** opposed **Nehemiah** in the twentieth year of **Artaxerxes Longimanus** <note>Artaxerxes I "Long-hand," ruled 465–424 BCE</note>, he must have been a man of mature age since he was endowed with such great authority. But let us suppose he was twenty: it is necessary that at the siege of Tyre he would have been one hundred and thirty years old. **Scaliger** and **Calvisius** defend such longevity as being quite ordinary for that time. 

However, **Cappellus, Petavius, Torniellus** <note>Prominent 17th-century theologians and chronologists</note>, and others, rather than admitting this, posit a double **Sanballat**: one who opposed **Nehemiah** in the twentieth year of **Longimanus**, and whose son-in-law was driven from the temple by **Nehemiah** in the days of **Darius** (not **Codomannus** <note>Darius III, the last King of Kings of the Persian Empire</note>, as **Scaliger** thinks, but **Nothus** <note>Darius II</note>. **Nehemiah 12:22**); and a second who was the son or grandson of the first, or at least shared his name. It was this second one’s daughter, **Nikaso**, whom **Manasseh** (the brother of the High Priest **Jaddua**) had taken as his wife; for this reason, he was expelled not by **Nehemiah**, but by his brother **Jaddua**. There were, therefore, two **Sanballats**—

## XXX. 

The argument from **Haggai 2:4** does not seem possible to be brushed aside by **Scaliger’s** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> explanation. For the words are clear and eloquent: *Who is there among you who remains, who saw this house in its former glory? and what do you see it as now? is it not in your eyes as nothing?* Who, unless they were already occupied by prejudices from elsewhere, would understand this speech of the prophet in any other way than that he addresses those who were granted the chance to see both houses—the first Temple and the second—and to make a comparison between the two? No more transparent than these are the things narrated in **Ezra 3:12-13**. See, if you please, **Robert Baillie’s** *Theological and Chronological Work*, page 159.

<margin>XXXI. The matter is obscure.</margin>

## XXXI. 

And so we have disputed these matters at somewhat greater length so that younger students may learn not to determine anything rashly, nor to immediately hold as certain and indubitable whatever they have perhaps heard from some recent Master. Reasons must be weighed; authority should be forced on no one. Let neither side create a prejudice. It is a matter of prudence sometimes to respond: **IT IS NOT CLEAR** <note>original: "NON LIQUET"</note>. Let me be permitted that same response here. If, however, something must be said, the reasons that fight for **Darius Hystaspes** <note>Darius the Great</note> seem stronger.

<margin>XXXII. Both Haggai and Zechariah poured forth remarkable oracles concerning the Messiah.</margin>

## XXXII. 

In the prophecies of both **Haggai** and **Zechariah**, many things exist concerning the **Messiah** as if he were already approaching. And indeed, **Haggai** illustrates the mystery of the adorable Trinity, representing the Lord of hosts as being present with his people through his Word and his Spirit (**Chapter 2:4-5**). He also promises a greater glory to the second house, since it would enjoy the presence of the **Messiah**, who was foreshadowed in ancient times by the Ark. He shows that that time is not far off (**verses 6, 7, etc.**). **Zechariah** records these same things, but also many other points pertaining to the kingdom of the Messiah and the signs of the times, for the narrating of which there is no time now. **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian famous for "Covenant Theology"</note> explained the general goal of **Zechariah** quite well: *namely, that it is to lead the people back to repentance, to strengthen them against impending temptations and afflictions, to confirm them in the faith and expectation of the Mediator, and to prepare the people to receive him; and to equip us with the greatest arguments by which we may recognize him, so that we may preserve the truth of faith concerning the righteousness which is in him, be patient in the struggles of the Church, and by faith conquer the world raging against Christ.*

...they concluded that he was a heavenly being, as I also noted regarding the *Prophet Haggai*. Some of the Jews pass down that he was *Mordecai*, others *Ezra*, and some even *Zerubbabel* or *Nehemiah*; all of these suggestions are based on flimsy or non-existent reasons. It is more likely that the name belongs to a specific man whose personal history is unknown to us. Nor can one say with certainty in what age he prophesied. It is clear, however, that he prophesied when the Temple was already built, because he mentions it as a complete structure in Chapter 1:10. Indeed, it appears clearly enough that he lived in the time immediately following the building of the temple: namely, the period in which Israel was still under Governors <note>original: *Duces*</note>, such as *Zerubbabel* and *Nehemiah*. He rails against unlawful marriages in Chapter 2:11, which are also discussed in *Nehemiah 13:23, 28*; against the embezzlement of tithes in Chapter 3:8, mentioned in *Nehemiah 13:10, 11*; and against other profanations in Chapter 1:13 and 2:8, which appear in *Nehemiah 13:15*. He concludes by turning the people toward the study of Moses, and toward the expectation of Elijah the precursor and the Messiah, the "sun of righteousness." After his departure from this world, the spirit of Prophecy also departed and was, as it were, a stranger among the Jews until the dawn of the Gospel began to shine.

<margin>XXXIV. Regarding the Prophetic Office, but not the grace of Prophecy.</margin>
XXXIV. This cessation should be understood as applying to the formal prophetic office in such a way that we do not deny that certain revelations occurred to specific individuals, by which they were informed of matters regarding either their private or the common welfare. For there do not seem to be sufficiently valid reasons to stubbornly deny credit to reputable historians who record such events.

<margin>XXXV. What is said to have happened to Jaddo.</margin>
XXXV. It is well known what *Josephus* <note>The Jewish historian Flavius Josephus</note> records as having happened to *Jaddo the High Priest* <note>original: *Jaddo Pontifici*</note>, when *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great</note>, enraged at the Jews, was moving quickly toward Jerusalem after the capture of Gaza. At that time the High Priest, turning many things over in his trembling mind to no avail, ordered public supplications and sacrificed victims to God, entrusting the public safety to Him. On the night immediately following the sacrifice, God appeared to him in a dream, commanding him to be of good courage and to open the gates with the city decorated <note>original: *coronata*, literally "crowned" with garlands</note>; he commanded that the people should go out to meet the King in white garments, while he himself, with the rest of the priests, should go in the solemn vestments of his order, secure in God's providence. How happily this turned out for him and for the whole Jewish people has been explained by me more fully elsewhere.
