<margin>XXXVII. And regarding Manahem.</margin>
XXXVII. It is a memorable story that *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> tells in the *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 15, Chapter 13*, in these words: *“There was a certain Essene <term>Essene: A member of a Jewish sect known for communal living and strict religious observance.</term> named Manahem, who was not only of an honest life and proven character by the testimony of men, but truly also possessed the gift of the prophetic spirit granted by God. This man, seeing Herod while he was still attending school with other boys, greeted him as 'King of the Jews.' Herod, thinking he was being mocked or that he was not well known to the man, corrected his words, claiming he was just one of the common people. Then Manahem smiled and, with a gentle tap, stroked him on his backside <note>original: "posteriora ejus permulcens"</note> rather than striking him, and said: 'Indeed you shall reign, and you shall rule fortunately; for so God wills. Remember Manahem’s words, which should remind you of the changeability of fortune. For nothing is more fitting for you to contemplate than justice, piety, and fairness toward your fellow citizens. But I know you will not do this, as I know what is to come: for you will be unmindful of both divine and human law, although otherwise you will be most fortunate and worthy of eternal glory. Yet you will not be hidden from God, who will rebuke you with a heavy punishment at the end of your life.' Herod did not value these words highly at the time, as he then hoped for no such thing. Later, however, having been raised to the kingdom and such great success by prosperous events, when he was at the height of his power, he summoned Manahem and asked about the length of his reign. Manahem gave no certain answer, but when the King asked whether it would last ten years, he said, 'and twenty, and thirty,' and so he left the fated end undetermined. Herod, content with even this, dismissed Manahem with a handshake, and from then on, he always held the Essenes in high regard. Although these things seem to exceed belief, it nevertheless seemed right to point them out to the reader, because there are many of that kind to whom the Divinity deigns to open His decrees and counsels because of their upright character.”* Concerning the same Manahem, these words are found in the *Juchasin <note>original: "Juchasin" refers to the Sefer Yuchasin, a 16th-century work of Jewish history by Abraham Zacuto.</note>, folio 29, column 2*: *“Manahem was a great wise man, like a Prophet, and he uttered many prophecies. He predicted to Herod, while he was still a minor, that it would happen that he would reign. And when he did reign, he summoned him, who also predicted that he would continue to reign.”*

...more than thirty years. Moreover, he reigned for thirty-seven years. And so we have brought the history of the prophets very close to the times of the Gospel.

<margin>XXXVIII. Prophets also came forth from Galilee.</margin>
XXXVIII. We conclude with this observation: the Lord has deemed any Israelites worthy of the grace of prophecy, without distinction of tribe or family. *I raised up prophets from your sons; is it not so, O children of Israel?* says the Lord (Amos 2:11). In the Gospel according to John, Chapter 7:52, the chief priests and Pharisees are said to have told Nicodemus: *Search and know that no Prophet has arisen from Galilee.* But we have searched, and we have discovered that this was asserted by them rashly and falsely. For *Nahum* was an *Elkosite* <note>A native of Elkosh; Jerome identifies this as a village in Galilee.</note>, whose homeland in the time of Jerome was a village in Galilee still known by the same name. *Jonah* was from *Gath-hepher* (2 Kings 14:25). Moreover, Gath-hepher is located in the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 19:13), and consequently in Galilee. For it is well known that this tribe held a part of Galilee.

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.

<margin>He was [a priest], not its High Priest.</margin>
...some have judged. But they are in great error. For it appears from the list of High Priests of that time that our Zechariah had no place among them. Indeed, the very words of Luke prove that opinion to be false. For Luke is accustomed to calling High Priests <term>archiereas</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀρχιερέας* — a specific title for the leading priests or the High Priest</note>. See Chapter 3:2 and Acts 4:6. However, he calls this man simply a <term>hierea</term> <note>original Greek: *ἱερέα* — a general term for a priest</note>, even adding the pronoun <term>tis</term> <note>original Greek: *τις*</note>, meaning "a certain priest." No one would speak this way regarding the High Priest. Add to this that Zechariah performed his duties in his turn and by lot. The High Priest, however, performed all the sacred rites at all times. Nor should it be thought that because Zechariah is said to have "burned incense," he therefore entered within the inner veil into the Holy of Holies, where it was forbidden for any mortal to set foot except the High Priest. For this passage concerns the daily incense-burning on the golden altar of incense, which was in the Holy Place, outside the inner veil, where the priests performed their duties daily.

<margin>IV. Nor was he his Deputy.</margin>
IV. Indeed, it is not even credible that he was the Deputy of the High Priest, whom the Hebrew masters call the <term>Sagan</term> <note>Hebrew: *סגן* — the second-in-command who could step in if the High Priest became ritually impure</note>; for the history contains nothing that leads us there, and certainly he did not fill the place of another in this function, but maintained the turn of his own order. I would not, however, wish to fight with the argument used by Scultetus in *Evangelical Exercises, Chapter 6*, that a deputy was not substituted for the High Priest except on the Day of Atonement, so that if something happened by which he appeared defiled, that other person would enter the sanctuary in his place; but as soon as the Day of Atonement had passed, that deputy would immediately resign. So indeed says <term>Cunaeus</term> in *The Hebrew Republic, Book 2, Chapter 6*. But it has been observed by other most learned men that the dignity of that deputy was perpetual, such that the one who was the closest heir to the High Priesthood held it until he succeeded the High Priest himself. See, if you please, <term>Selden</term> in *On the Succession to the High Priesthood, Book 2, Chapter 1*, and <term>Buxtorf</term> in his *Talmudic Lexicon* under the word *Sagan*. <term>Lightfoot</term>, on Luke 3:2, teaches that the Sagan was not so much a Vice-High Priest as a "Super-priest"; and that he was the same as the <term>mamoné</term> <note>Hebrew: *ממונה* — a prefect or overseer</note> or prefect of the temple, whose office was not <term>ephemeron</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐφήμερον* — temporary or lasting only a day</note>, but perpetual, or at least annual. He pursues this more extensively in *On the Ministry of the Temple, Chapter 5*. Let it suffice, therefore, to hold Zechariah as a priest; let us not dream of any greater dignity without cause.

<margin>V. It fell to him by lot to perform the incense-burning.</margin>
V. When the turns of the sacred ministry reached the Division of <term>Abia</term> <note>The "Division of Abijah" was one of the 24 rotating shifts of priests established by King David (1 Chronicles 24)</note> to which he belonged, the duty of performing the incense-burning fell to him by lot. For all things in the daily ministry were distributed by lot both to the priests and to the Levites: who would perform which ministry, who [would offer] the whole...

->### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.<-

...who would offer the burnt offering, who the peace offerings, who would serve in the morning, who in the evening, who would slaughter the sacrifice, who would pour out the blood, who would clear the ashes from the altar, and who would offer the incense. That lottery used to take place in the chamber known as **Gazith** <note>original Latin: *Gazith*; the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Sanhedrin met and priestly duties were assigned</note>, which had the form of a great Basilica. The priests, however, most greatly desired that it might be permitted to them *to offer the incense themselves*; for it was understood that everything would succeed well and according to the heart's desire for the one who had offered the incense. Indeed, it was wisely established that the distribution of duties should be done *by lot* <note>original Latin: *forte*</note>: both so that no quarrels would arise in the selection of duties, and so it might be taught that every person must eagerly undertake whatever vocation God—to whom the lot belongs—has entrusted to them.

<margin>VI. When Gabriel appeared to him.</margin>
VI. Therefore, while Zechariah was performing this function in the Temple—that is, in that part of the sacred building which is called the **Holy Place** <note>original Latin: *Sanctum*; the outer chamber of the sanctuary containing the golden altar, lampstand, and table</note>—an Angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. In former times, God was accustomed to suggest His will to the priest from the Ark; but now, there was no Ark, and no Oracle spoke. Instead, an Angel appeared, whom it is hardly certain had ever been seen or heard in that place before that day.

<margin>VII. Promising a son from his barren wife.</margin>
VII. This Angel promised a son to Zechariah by his wife Elizabeth, who was already advanced in years. This son was to be a cause of joy and exultation not only to Zechariah himself, but to many others; the Angel then set forth his remarkable gifts and exceptional duties in a most eloquent speech. We do not have the time now to dwell on all of these. This, however, is worth noting: the appearance of the Angel to announce the miraculous birth to an old woman, long barren, was employed by God most wisely (as He does all things) so that He might foster faith in the miracles regarding the birth of His own Son from a Virgin, which was soon to come. For a person will more easily believe that the invisible God could show Himself clothed in human flesh if they have also beheld an equally invisible Angel; and why should one doubt that a most chaste and immaculate virgin could give birth, when one learns that an aged woman, barren and utterly unfit for bearing children, has brought forth a child?

<margin>VIII. But Zechariah pays for his unbelief with an ominous silence.</margin>
VIII. In this matter, however, Zechariah’s faith faltered; he had to pay for this defect with a truly unusual punishment. For, having been commanded into silence by the Angel, he was rendered mute until the day his wife bore him the promised son. It is no small part of the wisdom of the righteous to compare the actions of God with one another, and to observe with foresight how the last things correspond to the first. The rite of burning incense is, in the opinion of the Jews, of the highest sanctity among the offerings. Yet it began with ignorance and inadvertence, and turned out most unhappily for the first priests <note>A reference to Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10, who offered "strange fire" and were consumed</note>. See **Leviticus 10**. And now, as the era draws to a close, the rite is tarnished by unbelief, which [robbed] the one offering the incense of the use of his tongue...

->### ON THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.<-

...dismisses. Is it not most clearly taught in this way, the **weakness and uselessness** <margin>the weakness and uselessness</margin> <note>original Greek: *τὸ ἀσθενὲς καὶ τὸ ἀνωφελές*; a reference to Hebrews 7:18 regarding the limitations of the Old Covenant law</note> of the ancient priesthood? It was the duty of the priest, once the sacred rites in the Temple were completed, to bestow the name of God upon the people with a solemn song of blessing. <margin>*Num. VI. 24. 25. 26.</margin> <note>Numbers 6:24–26 contains the "Priestly Blessing": *The Lord bless you and keep you...*</note> The entire multitude of the people, remaining outside in prayer, expected this from Zechariah. But he falters; and emerging after a delay longer than usual, he meets the common expectation with an unforeseen and unhoped-for silence. Entirely unable to speak, he fails them, to the astonishment of everyone. The order of the Prophets had already fallen silent long ago; now, even the Priest who was to give the blessing becomes mute. This was so that through this silence, a place might be made for the **Greatest of Prophets** <note>John the Baptist</note>, who was soon to proclaim the hidden designs of God regarding the salvation of the human race, and for the **High Priest** <note>Jesus Christ</note>, who would shortly bring about the true atonement of souls and lasting blessings. It was also so that the minds of mortals, suspended in expectation of such great things, might be stirred to listen to his words by the amazing silence of the others.

<margin>IX. Which he soon breaks with a remarkable prophecy.</margin>
IX. On the eighth day from the birth of his son, when friends were disputing over the infant's name, Zechariah—still mute—asked for a writing tablet and wrote that his name would be **JOHN**, just as the Angel had commanded. Immediately, *Zechariah’s mouth was opened, his tongue loosened, and he spoke, blessing God.* The mouth that unbelief had shut, faith now opens. And he who had been prevented from blessing the people begins his speech with a blessing of God. Indeed, *filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesied*, and in a noble song, he joyfully celebrates the now-imminent fulfillment of the Divine promises, the prosperous success of his son who was to prepare the way for Christ, and other matters pertaining to this. Thus, in Zechariah, the gift of prophecy which had long been dead is miraculously reborn.

<margin>X. The legend of the martyrdom of Zechariah.</margin>
X. Concerning the other deeds of Zechariah and his death or martyrdom, sacred history <note>i.e., the Bible</note> contains nothing. The "Father of Annals" <note>likely a reference to the historian Baronius, or a general reference to early chroniclers</note> attempts to fill this gap from human writings. Relaying a story from Peter, the Bishop of Alexandria, he says that because Zechariah had hidden his son <note>John</note> who was sought for slaughter, he was ordered by Herod to be killed between the temple and the altar. Another cause for his death is added from Cyril of Alexandria: that *being led to the knowledge of hidden things by a prophetic spirit, since he rightly understood the mystery of the Virgin regarding her extraordinary birth, he did not bar the uncontaminated and most pure mother from that place in the temple which was designated by law for Virgins (for that place was midway between the altar and the temple). Therefore, when they heard that the King of all creation was proceeding to a human birth by Divine counsel, fearing lest they should come under the power and command of that King, they killed him who had testified to these things about the birth, sacrificing the priest.*

### BOOK 1. CHAPTER 21.

<margin>XI. And the miracles that followed.</margin>
XI. But miracles were also not to be lacking from this martyrdom. They are told in this way: the stones of the temple, sprinkled with **Zechariah's** blood, preserved the indelible marks of his death. This is attested by **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155 – c. 220 AD</note>, who writes the following in his work *Scorpiace* <note>The "Antidote for the Scorpion's Sting," a treatise written to encourage martyrs</note>: *Zechariah is slaughtered between the altar and the temple, leaving eternal stains of his blood upon the flint stones.* <note>original: "Zacharias inter altare & ædem trucidatur, perennes cruoris sui maculas filicibus adfignans."</note> However, **Jerome** <note>The scholar famous for translating the Bible into the Vulgate Latin</note> laughs mockingly at this, attributing it to the simplicity of believers rather than historical truth. He writes—I know not how piously, but certainly as follows: *Simpler brothers among the ruins of the temple and the altar, or in the exits of the gates leading to Siloam, point out red stones and think they were polluted by Zechariah’s blood. We do not condemn the error, for it arises from a hatred of the Jews and the devotion of faith.* But hear also another miracle from a letter which the **Emperor Valentinian** is said to have written to the Bishops of Asia, and which appears in the work of **Theodoret** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century Church historian</note> in his *Ecclesiastical History, Book 4, Chapter 7*. There, among other things, the Prince says: *Lest you incur those losses which belong to the Testament of Christ, consider what happened regarding Zechariah’s blood: for those murderous men—together with the pestilential demon who was a partner in that slaughter—were handed over to the punishment of death and perished, torn apart at the arrival of our heavenly King, Jesus Christ.* Yet these accounts are **Apocryphal** <note>writings of questionable authorship or authenticity</note> and are not worthy of belief.

<margin>XII. Joseph addressed by an Angel.</margin>
XII. To **JOSEPH** also, the betrothed of the Blessed Virgin, a divine oracle was delivered in the manner of the prophets. It happened on this occasion: when he had discovered by certain signs that **Mary** was pregnant, and being ignorant of the cause of the pregnancy, he formed a plan to leave her secretly. For since he was a just man and a great lover of his ancestral laws, he did not think it fitting for his honor or modesty to admit a "polluted" woman into a chaste marriage bed. However, because he loved the girl who was betrothed to him and had greatly revered her other virtues until then, he did not wish to accuse her publicly or expose her to disgrace. He decided it was better to give her a bill of divorce <term>repudii libellum</term> <note>A legal document of separation; Joseph sought a "quiet" divorce to protect Mary's life, as the law could demand a public trial and harsh punishment for perceived infidelity</note> without a legal outcry and without infamy, known to no one except those who needed to know. As he was weighing these plans in his mind, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, *Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit, etc. Matthew 1:20, 21.* <note>original: "Josephe, fili Davidis, ne metue accipere Mariam uxorem tuam. Nam quod in ea genitum est, ex Spiritu Sancto est &c."</note> Joseph easily recognized that this dream was sent to him by God, because he was being instructed about his own private thoughts, which are known only to God. Therefore, having woken up, he did as the Angel had commanded him. But the Angel appeared to him a second time during his rest, ordering him to flee to **Egypt** with the young child **Jesus** and his mother, to avoid the traps and the fury of **Herod**, and to stay there until the Angel commanded his return.

<margin>XIII. Was the Prophet Simeon the son of Hillel?</margin>
XIII. It would be a sin to omit **SIMEON** here, a just and devout man, *waiting for the consolation of Israel, upon whom the Holy Spirit rested. It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. He came, therefore, led by the Spirit, into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, he took him into his arms, blessed God, and said: Now Lord, you let your servant depart, etc.* <note>The "Nunc Dimittis," a traditional Christian canticle</note> Luke 2:25 and following. A question arises among scholars: was this Simeon the son of Hillel, who is so celebrated in Jewish history? To judge this in order, first the history of that Simeon must be told; then it must be compared with Luke’s narrative, and a conclusion formed from the comparison of both.

<margin>XIV. The history of Simeon, son of Hillel.</margin>
XIV. The history of Simeon is as follows. His father was Hillel, called "the Babylonian" because he had come from Babylon at the age of forty. For forty more years, he applied himself to the study of the law in Jerusalem. For another forty, he ruled Israel. His family was most noble; at that time, hardly any other deserved to be placed before it. He was a <term>Prince from the house of David</term> <note>original Hebrew: "נשיא מבית דוד" (Nasi mi-beit David)</note>, descended from Shephatiah, the son of Abital, as mentioned in 2 Samuel 3:4. This, however, is only to be understood regarding his maternal lineage. Hillel the elder was the head of the family of Princes, the head of the Academy and the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem</note>; and this family dignity continued through him, his sons, and his grandsons, even to the tenth generation. His son Simeon, the heir to his father’s dignity, was the first of all we read about to be distinguished with the title <term>Rabban</term> <note>A title of higher honor than 'Rabbi', usually reserved for the heads of the Sanhedrin</note>, and was the father of Gamaliel <note>The famous teacher of the Apostle Paul</note> mentioned in Acts 5:34. He lived during the era when Christ was born. It is worthwhile to add the words of Ganz in <term>*Zemach David*</term> <note>"The Branch of David," a historical work by the Jewish chronicler David Ganz, published in 1592</note>, *Part II, for the Year 3761*: "Jesus the Nazarene was born in Bethlehem of Judea, a mile and a half from Jerusalem, in the year 3761 after the creation, which is the 42nd year of Caesar Augustus; and according to this calculation, his birth fell in the days of Rabbi Simeon, son of Hillel." <note>original Hebrew: "ישוע נוצרי נולד בביתלחם יהודה פרסה ומחצה מירושלים בשנת ג' אלפים ותש" סא ליצירה והיא שנת מב" לקיסר אוגושטו ולפי חשבון זה היה לדתו בימי ר' שמעון בן הלל"</note> Simeon also seems to have been a man of ancient integrity and simplicity, who believed that virtue was found not in polished speech, but in deeds shaped by the standard of equity and justice. For among his own sayings, this is also praised: *Speech, however sharp* <note>The Hebrew text continues: "is not the main thing, but the action" (לא המדרש הוא העיקר אלא המעשה)</note>

<margin>XV. Comparison with the narrative of Luke.</margin>
XV. Indeed, if these details are compared with what Luke narrates about his Simeon, they align: I. The Name. II. The place of residence. III. The age. IV. The integrity of his life. V. From these points, Scultetus, Lightfoot, Alting, and other most learned men conclude that the Simeon mentioned by Luke was indeed the son of Hillel, the father of Gamaliel, and the President of the Jewish Senate. They even believe that the very silence of the Talmudists regarding him supports this theory. The reason for this silence was likely nothing other than a "Vatinian hatred" <note>A classical idiom for intense, implacable hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius</note> which the compilers of the Talmud held toward Jesus of Nazareth. Because this Simeon was the first of all the residents of Jerusalem to recognize Him, and not only made a public confession about Him in the Temple but also informed Herod when he was inquiring about the Messiah’s birthplace—for one can hardly doubt that he, as the chief of all the scribes, was consulted, and indeed consulted above all others—all his words and deeds were condemned to eternal oblivion. Only his name survived, preserved by the necessity of the Hillelian genealogy; in the same way, the memory of others was shrouded in silence for this very reason. Thus argues *Alting in Shilo, Book IV, Chapter XXI.*

<margin>XVI. It does not provide sufficiently certain arguments to prove they are the same person.</margin>

Jairus is called the *ruler of the Synagogue* (Luke 8:41). Joseph of Arimathea is called a *Senator, a good and just man* (Luke 23:50). <margin>XVII. John the Baptist: did he prophesy before he was born?</margin>
XVII. John the Baptist must be numbered among the greatest of the Prophets, by his own merit and by Christ’s estimation; most of the Ancient Fathers say that he prophesied before he was even born. Indeed, the Gospel history testifies to this concerning him: when the pregnant Mary came to his own pregnant mother, upon hearing Mary’s greeting, *the babe leaped in Elizabeth’s womb, and she, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out with a loud voice and said: "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting sounded in my ears, the babe leaped for joy in my womb."* Luke 1:41–44. He had not drawn this knowledge from the senses, for he was deprived of their use until this point. Nor had he received it from his parents, for they had not yet seen Him. Nor from any instruction, of which he was entirely lacking. But by the immediate operation, power, and sanctification of God, it was brought about that this herald and forerunner of the Lord...*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.

...that he even knew his Lord before he knew anything of the world outside himself, and indicated by a dance the one whom he could not yet announce with mouth or voice; and that he had faith before he had **hearing** <note>original Greek: ἀκοήν (*akoēn*). The author is referencing Romans 10:17, "Faith comes by hearing."</note>, from which faith normally arises—indeed, before he had received the Word of God, through which **the hearing** <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀκοή (*hē akoē*)</note> exists. Thus God is capable beyond what we can comprehend. I confess that all these things have been said learnedly, elegantly, movingly, and even piously: and therefore it did not trouble me to record them here.

<margin>
XVIII. It does not seem to be so.
</margin>

XVIII. I doubt, however, whether these things can be proven from the sacred text. To me, having weighed it diligently, it seems thus: That leaping of the infant in the womb of Elizabeth had something singular and extraordinary about it, which she herself, taught by the Spirit of God, perceived to point toward something else. For it was not her own joy, arising from the sight and friendly greeting of her sweetest kinswoman, that was the cause of the leaping in the fetus; rather, the mother herself was preceded by the fetus, and by its leaping and extraordinary movement, she learned that something singular was happening to her—that the mother of her Lord was coming to her. It does not follow from this that the little infant, not yet born, recognized Jesus coming in Mary, or that he taught this to his mother Elizabeth. It is also not said that the infant was filled with the Spirit. It is only said that Elizabeth, from the extraordinary movement of the infant, gathered that something extraordinary was happening, and she herself, by the teaching of the Holy Spirit with which she was suddenly filled, prophesied concerning Mary, the mother of Christ.

Has a man who speaks this way deserved, Cornelius à Lapide, that you should write of him: "Calvin thinks this movement and leap of John was merely natural"?

# ON THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.

...[concerning his] birth, that famous prophecies were issued about him. For he is the *voice of one crying in the wilderness.* <margin>*The voice of one crying.*</margin> This "voice of one crying" is what Isaiah spoke of in Chapter 40:3: *The voice of one crying in the wilderness, of one preparing the way of Jehovah*, which he also applied to himself in John 1:23. He is a *Voice*, that is, a loud, clear, and faithful herald, reporting nothing but the words of God: a pure voice, teaching always through his speech, life, food, clothing, and finally all his actions. He is of one *Crying*—that is, God—who at that time most powerfully urged everyone toward repentance, and was soon to be heard in the proclamation of the Gospel to the ends of the earth. Note, it does not say *a crying voice*, but the voice *of one crying*, so that the cry is first God's, while John is only the Echo, the repercussion of that cry; and his preaching is truly the <term>Daughter of the Divine Voice <note>original Hebrew: בת קול (*Bat Kol*); a Jewish traditional term for a heavenly voice or a secondary echo of divine revelation.</note></term>. *The voice of one crying in the wilderness*, both literally and mystically. For he preached in the wilderness of Judea (Matthew 3:1). And all of Judea at that time was like a mystical wilderness: filled with wild beasts, stumps, thorns, briers, logs, and stones, bearing no fruit for God. The sum of his preaching tended toward this: that for *Jehovah*—that is, the Messiah clothed in human flesh, coming to his people—a way might be prepared, and souls might be stirred to receive him.

XXI. God speaks of the same in Malachi 3:1. <margin>XXI. *The Messenger Preceding the Angel of the Covenant.*</margin> *Behold, I will send my Angel <note>The author uses the Latin "Angelum," meaning messenger, to refer to John the Baptist as a precursor.</note>, a messenger, a herald, who will come very soon after Malachi, the last of the prophets; who shall prepare the way before my Face*, that is, before the Messiah, in whom God graciously displays his face for sinful men to contemplate; the Hebrews themselves, as was recently shown, approve of this explanation. *And the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to his temple; even the Angel of the covenant, in whom you delight.* That Lord is the Messiah: whom David also in the Spirit calls his Lord in Psalm 110. He is the same *Angel of the Covenant*, sent to preach, confirm, and seal the covenant of grace with his death; and to provide the promises of that covenant for the chosen. For whose coming all who awaited the consolation of Israel had panted for so many centuries. He shall come, to be seen and heard by the people; into his temple, built for his honor and worship; he is the Lord of the temple himself, and of all the prophets who were his forerunners. *He shall come suddenly.* Sooner than expected: certainly while the temple was still standing, so that he might carry out judgment there. Now, who is there to whom these things apply, if not Christ and his immediate precursor, John?

XXII. To the same point belong the words in Chapter 4:5, 6. <margin>XXII. *The Elijah of Malachi.*</margin> *Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the coming of the great and dreadful day of Jehovah* etc. This is to be understood regarding the day of the Messiah’s coming...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.

The Jews themselves can hardly deny this <note>original: "vix ipsi negaverint Judæi"</note>. Matthew 17:10. However, there is no necessity for us to understand that "Elijah" must be that specific Tishbite <note>Elijah is called "the Tishbite" after his hometown, Tishbe.</note> who was taken up into heaven in a whirlwind. It often happens that proper names of this kind are applied to other persons because of some similarity they share with them. Thus, the *Messiah* is called *David* in Jeremiah 30:9, Hosea 3:5, and Ezekiel 34:24. Likewise, *Jehu* is called *Zimri* in 2 Kings 9:31 <note>Zimri was a notorious usurper; Jehu is compared to him because he also overthrew a king.</note>. *John the Baptist* is the *Elijah* of the Gospels, being most similar to Elijah in his spiritual gifts, his office, and his way of life—indeed, he is greater in all things. Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14; 17:12. In the most corrupt times, Elijah was deterred by no danger from setting the sins of the King and all the people before their very eyes. The same spirit appeared in John. Because of this eminent zeal, some people fabulate <note>The author is likely referring to Jewish mystical or midrashic traditions regarding the transmigration of souls.</note> that the soul of *Phineas* <note>A priest in the Book of Numbers known for his zeal for God.</note> entered into *Elijah*. Nor is it improbable, as *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> thinks, that it was said by the ancients that *Elijah came in the spirit of Phineas*; at least, this was the meaning of that expression. Even among the Jews themselves, it is not sufficiently agreed whether that ancient Elijah himself is to come. *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note>, in his work *The Laws Concerning Kings* <note>original: "Hilcat Melachim"</note>, *Chapter XII, § 2*, disputing the arrival of Elijah, says: *No one knows how all these things and other similar matters will happen until they actually occur.* And more expressly, *Menasseh Ben Israel* <note>A prominent Portuguese rabbi and diplomat in the 17th century.</note> in *On the Resurrection of the Dead, Book III, Chapter VII*: *Whatever the case may be, A CERTAIN PRECURSOR WILL COME, who will turn hearts and prepare them well, lest the earth be struck with a curse.*

<margin>XXIII. Prophet of the Most High.</margin>
XXIII. Furthermore, that Angel who announced John’s birth to Zechariah also proclaimed how great he was destined to be. Luke 1:14 and following. And Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied about the newly born child:
> And you, little child, will be called the PROPHET OF THE MOST HIGH: you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, and to give knowledge of salvation to his people through the forgiveness of their sins. Luke 1:76–77.

He solemnly inaugurated his prophetic office in the thirtieth year of his age. For in the 15th year of *Tiberius Caesar*, when *Pontius Pilate* was governor of Judea, under the High Priests *Annas* and *Caiaphas*, THE WORD OF THE LORD CAME TO JOHN, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness. Luke 3:1 and following. By this same formula the ancient seers were sent forth. Jeremiah 1:2; Ezekiel 6:1. And the same is repeated for John. Since the time of Malachi, the order of prophets had been extinct; so much so that for many years no one had instructed the people by such an impulse of the Word of the Lord. Now, that order is restored, beginning with John.

<margin>XXIV. Than whom none among those born of women is greater.</margin>
XXIV. Jesus himself held John in such high esteem that he pronounced that *among those born of women, no one has arisen greater than John*: namely, in gifts, holiness, the sublimity of his teaching, and the dignity of his office. For it was given to him to be the closest herald <note>original: "Ante-", likely "Antetrans", though the catchword indicates "am-"</note> to the Messiah...

<margin>XXV. With the exception, however, of him who is the *lesser* <note>original: "μικρότερος" (mikroteros)</note> in the kingdom of heaven.</margin>
XXV. But it is remarkable what the Lord soon adds: *the lesser one <note>original: "τὸν μικρότερον" (ton mikroteron)</note>, he who is minor in the kingdom of heaven, is greater than he.* This is usually explained as referring to the least minister of the Christian Church, to whom it is given to preach the Gospel of fulfillment: who would be called *greater than John*, not by reason of the Prophetic Spirit, Holiness, Zeal, or similar gifts, but by reason of his ministry, because he can explain the whole mystery of our salvation much more clearly than was ever done by John. But I do not know if we should reject the opinion of those who, by *the lesser one* in the kingdom of heaven, understand Christ himself, so called because he was younger in age and later in his ministry: in which sense James the son of Alphaeus was called *the small* <note>original: "ὁ μικρὸς" (ho mikros)</note>, Mark 15:40, that is, the younger, in respect to James the son of Zebedee, who was *the Greater*. For it might seem strange that the Lord Jesus, who throughout this whole discourse of his proclaims all these excellent things about John, should then, where you would least expect it, make him less than the least of his disciples. But the matter itself suggests that, however much he might extol John, he nevertheless testified that he [John] was less than himself [Jesus]. John himself proclaiming: *he who comes after me is preferred before me, because he was before me.* John 1:15. Nor can anyone claim this explanation is a novelty, unless they are ignorant of what *Epiphanius*, *Chrysostom*, *Euthymius*, and *Theophylact* <note>These are early Church Fathers and prominent biblical commentators from the 4th through the 12th centuries.</note> have commented, along with many learned men after them.

<margin>XXVI. The *austere lifestyle* <note>original: "Τὸ σκληροδίαιτον" (To sklērodiaiton)</note> of John.</margin>
XXVI. John displayed something singular in the whole arrangement of his life: as in his *place of dwelling*, so in his *clothing* and *food*, presenting an example of sorrowful repentance <note>original: "pœnitentiæ luctuoſæ"</note>. He *lived* not in crowded cities, but in the *wilderness*, far from all the pomp and splendor of the world. Not indeed in the manner of Hermits among wild beasts, but where he had the opportunity of preaching repentance <note>original: "resipiscentiæ"; a theological term for a change of mind or heart.</note>. Yet in such a way that by this example it might be taught that the grace of God and his kingdom were not bound to the earthly Jerusalem, the tangible Mount Zion, and the Sanctuary made by hands, but that even the wilderness was to be inhabited by God; and those men, who until now had been like a fruitless desert, would become God’s place and city. For *clothing* he had a *camel-hair garment*, rough, hairy, woven from the hairs of a camel, crude and uncombed, not softened, groomed, or spun into thread. Such a garment is called a *hairy cloak* <note>original Hebrew: "אדרת שער" (adderet sear)</note>. Zechariah 13:4. Which John bound with a *leather belt*, which, by tightening the haircloth garment, increased its austerity: in this also he was like Elijah. His *food* was *locusts and wild honey* <note>original: "ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι ἄγριον" (akrides kai meli agrion)</note>. Some understand this [the locusts] as referring to the tips of branches,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of John the Baptist’s ascetic lifestyle and his dual identity as a priest and a prophet, following the previous section's comparison between John and Christ.</meta>

<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.</header>

...others imagine other things. But I do not see why we should depart from the most common meaning of the word. For it is a very well-known fact that *locusts* served as food not only for individuals, but even for entire nations. To these he added wild honey, which was found without cultivation in the mountains, forests, and crevices of rocks, or dripped naturally from the trees. Thus his diet matched his clothing; it was not sought out or prepared by art, but was what the wilderness provided of its own accord—raw and meager. However, he did not affect this type of diet out of superstition (for I believe that when he was among citizens or the king, he did not require locusts), but rather he wanted to be a model of extraordinary frugality. Furthermore, he drank neither wine nor any intoxicating drink, following the example of the *Nazirites* <note>original: "Naziræorum"; individuals in the Bible who took a vow of holiness which included abstaining from wine and cutting their hair.</note>.

<margin>XXVII. Religious abstinence from wine: whether it represents, in a certain way, the state of innocence.</margin>
XXVII. The observation of the most learned *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English Hebraist who used Rabbinic literature to interpret the New Testament.</note> is worth noting: He supposes it to be highly probable that the vine was that tree whose fruit God forbade man to eat in Paradise—a point which certain Hebrew masters determine without any hesitation. From this he infers that the Nazirite vow—a most exacting institution, a large part of which consists in religious abstinence from all products of the vine—recalls something of the state before sin and outlines it in a certain way; just as leprosy, the most unclean of uncleannesses <note>original: "immunditiarum immundissima"</note>, best outlines the state of sin.

<margin>XXVIII. How that way of life could be consistent with the priesthood.</margin>
XXVIII. Since John was the son of a priest and a priest by right of birth, and since priests were required to be clothed in linen garments, to stay in the Temple at fixed times, and to eat from the sacrifices; the question is rightly asked: how could his dwelling in the desert, and food and clothing so different from common custom, be compatible with the priestly institution? To resolve this difficulty, I believe it should be noted that John was a Prophet by a singular Divine decree. Now *Prophets*, in the performance of their duty—which depends entirely on God’s impulse—are above common laws; this can be proven by many arguments from the history of Samuel. Furthermore, he was not only a priest, but also a *Nazirite*; and that not by his own choice, but by Divine ordination. Moreover, ordinary laws yielded to the Nazirite vow. Add to this that in such a great multitude of priests, John's presence in the temple was not so strictly required that he would not have plenty of time left for the proclamation of his baptism. Finally, in the exercise of their duty, priests were indeed commanded to clothe themselves in white robes <note>original: "stolis se albis amicire"</note>, which it is reasonable to believe John likewise did in that case; but outside of their sacred function, they were not restricted to any specific form of clothing.

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL #

<margin>XXIX. *John’s office.*</margin>
XXIX. The principal duty of John was to preach the *baptism of repentance for the remission of sins* <note>original: "Baptismum resipiscentiæ ad remissionem peccatorum"</note>, to warn his listeners that they should eagerly embrace the *Kingdom of Heaven* which was already at the doors, and finally to point out the Messiah who was present and to turn the souls of all toward him. Nearly all the teachers of religion who existed at that time were disputing over food, drink, washings, tithes, sacrifices, and external rituals of that kind, as if the "prow and stern" <note>original: "prora... & puppis"; an ancient idiom meaning the beginning and the end, or the most vital parts of a matter.</note> of the whole religion were situated in these things. Indeed, they frequently rendered the clearest commands of God void by their human and hypocritical institutions, all while swelling with a proud presumption of their own righteousness. John, however, establishing a far different path, called his listeners away from external things to the soul, from ceremonies to morals, from human institutions to Divine commands, and from an arrogant opinion of perfection to a humble confession of sins and a zeal for repentance. The Hebrew Masters <note>A reference to the Rabbis or religious leaders in Jerusalem.</note> used to extol themselves in an insane manner because of their temple, its proud foundations, and its external apparatus. John, far from Jerusalem in the wilderness, preached the kingdom of heaven and a completely different state of affairs under the Rule of the Messiah, whose distinguished privileges are justice, peace, and joy through the Holy Spirit. He proclaimed that this was now imminent and would soon be revealed. He also came to bear witness to the light; he commanded that they should believe in him who was to come after him. When he saw him already present, he pointed him out with his finger, saying: <term>BEHOLD THE LAMB OF GOD WHO TAKES AWAY THE SINS OF THE WORLD</term> <note>original: "ECCE AGNUS DEI QUI TOLLIT PECCATA MUNDI"</note>. He exalted him as infinitely above himself, confessing he was unworthy to untie his sandal straps. Finally, he compared his whole ministry to this: that as Christ increased, he himself should decrease, just as the heavenly sun outshines all the stars. His baptism served to confirm all these things; by it, the Jews themselves—as if they were new converts <note>original: "proselyti"</note>—were initiated into the approaching kingdom of heaven, having offered a confession of sins, the practice of penitence, and a profession of faith in the Messiah for the remission of sins.

<margin>XXX. *His Martyrdom.*</margin>
XXX. In the performance of this most holy duty, with a great gathering of the people, he proceeded fearlessly until he was cast into prison by Herod and, for reasons known from the Gospel, was beheaded—sealing his heavenly teaching with his pure blood. This was the end of that great man, whom not only the Gospel writings but also the histories of the Jews <note>A reference to the historian Flavius Josephus, who provides a non-biblical account of John's execution.</note> praise with great accolades. The piety of this man deserves that what has been recorded about him should be read everywhere with great pleasure. Therefore, I will also take care to include here what

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI. ###

Josephus, the *Chronicle of the Kings of the Second Temple*, and the *Sprout of David* <note>original title: "Zemach David"</note> have all written about him.

<margin>XXXI. Mentioned by Josephus.</margin>
XXXI. *Josephus, Antiquities, Book XVIII, Chapter VII* <note>In modern editions, this is typically Book 18, Chapter 5</note> contains these words: *The Tetrarch* <note>A governor of one-fourth of a province; here referring to Herod Antipas.</note> *put to death John, who was nicknamed the Baptist. He was an excellent man, who urged the Jews toward the pursuit of virtues—especially piety and justice—and at the same time toward the washing of baptism. He taught that such a rite would only be pleasing to God if they did not merely abstain from one or two sins, but if they first purified their souls through righteousness and then added the purity of the body. Because great crowds gathered around him, for the common people were eager for such teaching, Herod feared that the man’s great influence might lead to some form of rebellion, as they seemed ready to do anything based on his advice. Herod judged it better to remove him before any new trouble arose, rather than waiting for things to become disordered and then repenting when it was too late. Thus, John was sent in chains to Machaerus* <note>A hilltop fortress in modern-day Jordan.</note> *and was ordered to be killed there. Following this deed, it was the opinion of the Jews that Herod’s army was destroyed by an angry God as a punishment.*

<margin>XXXII. And by Hebrew Historians.</margin>
XXXII. In the *Chronicle of the Kings of the Second Temple, page 54, column 4*, these words appear: <note>original Hebrew: גם אנטיפוס הרשיע והתעיב מכל אשר היו לפניו...</note> *Antipas also acted impiously and committed more abominations than all who were before him; he took the wife of his brother Philip away from him, though she had already borne children. Rabbi John the High Priest* <note>original: "R. Jochanan Cohen Gadol." Medieval Jewish sources often referred to John the Baptist as a "High Priest" or "Rabbi," sometimes conflating different historical figures.</note> *rebuked him for this abomination, and Antipas struck him and put him to death.* The *Sprout of David* <note>A 16th-century Jewish history by David Gans.</note> *Part I, for the year 1770 of the era of the family* <note>referring to the era of the Seleucids or a specific Jewish dating system used by the author.</note> says: *Herod Antipater, whom some call the Tetrarch, was the son of the first Herod and the brother of Archelaus, and was the third king from the House of Herod. He too was an evil man and a destroyer; he killed many of the Sages of Israel with the sword. He took the wife of his brother Philip for himself while Philip was still alive. John the High Priest, because he had rebuked him for this crime, was killed by the sword along with many of the Sages of Israel. These testimonies agree sufficiently with the Gospel history regarding the name of the Baptist and the practice of baptizing (Matthew 3:1 and following), and regarding the cause of his imprisonment and death (Matthew 14:3, Mark 6:17, Luke 3:19–20).*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of figures in the Gospels by transitioning from John the Baptist to the prophetic role of Jesus himself. It compares Jewish expectations of the Messiah's prophetic status with the reality of Jesus's ministry.</meta>

->### ON THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.###<-

It is the Lord; nor did any others possess wisdom, except from the *Jews*, through His Spirit. Moses promised the Messiah under the title of PROPHET. <margin>Like Moses, or greater.</margin> Deuteronomy 18:15. Although modern teachers <note>The author refers to contemporary Jewish scholars of his time who might interpret this differently.</note> now twist these words to another meaning, it was a settled opinion among the Jews that the Messiah would be a Prophet—not merely secondary to Moses, but his equal, or rather, his superior. Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> makes him equal to Moses in his *Treatise on Repentance, Chapter IX, near the end*: *That King who shall arise from the seed of David will be endowed with more wisdom than Solomon, <note>original Hebrew: ונביא גדול הוא קרוב למשה רבינו</note> and he will be a great Prophet, close to Moses our Teacher; and therefore he will teach all the people and instruct them in the way of the Lord, and all nations shall come to hear him.* The Ancients went even further, whose saying was praised by Abravanel <note>Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and commentator.</note> in *Commentary on the Latter Prophets, folio 78, column 1*: <note>original Hebrew: רום מאברהם ונשא ממשה וגבה ממלאכי השרת</note> *Higher than Abraham, more exalted than Moses, and loftier than the ministering angels.* Nor should we leave unmentioned the Kabbalistic <note>Referring to Jewish mystical tradition.</note> observation of *Baal Hatturim* <note>The "Master of the Rows," a title for Jacob ben Asher, a 14th-century scholar noted for his numerical analysis of the Torah.</note> who points out that the 15th verse of the 18th Chapter in Deuteronomy begins *and ends with the letter Nun*, which is the sign for the number fifty. This is *to signify that the fifty gates of understanding would be known to the Prophet promised there*, of which they believe only forty-nine were open to Moses. Likewise, they note that ten words are contained in that same verse, *to signify that this Prophet must be obeyed no less than the Decalogue* <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. While this collection of trivia may seem frivolous, the underlying truth is most certain.

<margin>XXXIV. *Such is our Jesus.*</margin>
XXXIV. Furthermore, the Hebrews were unable to conceive of anything so magnificent regarding the excellence of prophecy in their *Messiah* that our JESUS did not surpass it by an immense margin. Regarding his Prophetic office—in all its parts and its preeminence—I remember that I, following other theologians, also outlined this in my *Tenth Exercise on the Apostles' Creed, section 13 and following*. I do not think it necessary to repeat those points here.

<margin>XXXV. *Whose preaching is sometimes distinguished from prophecy.*</margin>
XXXV. I add only this one thing now: sometimes the preaching of Jesus is so distinguished from prophecy that it seems to be contrasted with it. Daniel, recounting the duties and benefits of the Messiah, numbers among them the <note>original Hebrew: חתם חזון ונביא</note> *sealing up of vision and prophet.* Daniel 9:24. *Vision* denotes the foretelling of a future thing. *Prophet* denotes the one upon whom the task of foretelling the future thing rests. The *sealing of the vision* is its consummation through fulfillment, by which the present reality itself is substituted for the foretelling. The same seems to be taught in Habakkuk 2:3: *For the vision is yet for an appointed time.* That mode of teaching, which consists of prophetic preaching and symbolic prefiguration, shall last until <note>original Greek: τὴν προθεσμίαν</note> the appointed time and <note>original Greek: πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου</note> the fullness of time, as mentioned in Galatians 4:2, 3, 4. <note>original Hebrew: ויפח לקץ</note> *And he shall speak to the end*, which is to say, he shall come. *The end* denotes the final part of <note>original Greek: τῆς προθεσμίας</note> the appointed time, <note>original Hebrew: אחרית הימים</note> the end of days.

BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.

...the days, the last of these days <note>original Greek: ἔσχατον τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων</note>. Then shall come the Herald <note>original Hebrew: מבשר (Mebasser)</note>, for *Louis de Dieu* <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642) was a prominent Dutch orientalist and theologian known for his work on Middle Eastern languages.</note> observed that this is a noun, not a verb. Now, this Herald signifies a witness of a present reality. This is Christ. Of whom this saying also stands: *Matthew 11:13. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.* With this, the axiom of the Jews agrees, provided it is understood correctly: *All the Prophets did not prophesy except for the days of the Messiah.* <note>original Hebrew: כל הנביאים לא מתנבאים אלא לימות המשיח</note> This was not meant as if no ancient prophecies spoke of things to happen after the appearance of the Messiah (for they extend even to the consummation of the ages); or as if the gift of prophecy would cease with the Messiah (for then it ought to have flourished anew); or that the Messiah himself and his disciples would predict no future events (for they describe the fate of the Church until the final judgment). Rather, it was meant in this sense: that what the Prophets predicted concerning the Messiah, and the kingdom of heaven, and eternal blessings, have their fulfillment in Christ: *in whom all the promises of God, as many as there are, are Yes and Amen. 2 Corinthians 1:20.* Once he has been revealed, it will no longer be said, "Wait, he will come," but, *Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord whom we have waited for; we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation. Isaiah 25:9.*

> At about the same time lived Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is lawful to call him a man. For he appeared to them alive on the third day, just as the divine prophets had predicted this and many other marvelous things about him. And even to this very day, the tribe of Christians named after him has not failed.

Over this passage, the most serious disputes occur among critics: some arguing for its <term>authenticity</term> <note>original Greek: γνησιότητι (genuineness or authenticity)</note>, and others against it. It pleases me first to play the role of a spectator here, and then finally to offer my judgment according to my own liberty, which whoever wishes may follow.

### CONCERNING THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.

*Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book I, Chapter XI; Demonstration of the Gospel, Book III, Chapter VII; Jerome in the Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers; Isidore of Pelusium, Book IV, Epistle 225; Sozomen, Book I, Chapter 1; Cedrenus; Nicephorus, Book I, Chapter XXXIX; Suidas under the entry "Josephus."* <note>These are citations of ancient and medieval historians who accepted the passage about Jesus in Josephus as genuine.</note> And thus it has been handed down to us in a continuous series.

III. There is also reason on this side, and more than one. 1. For it is not probable that Josephus, a most diligent writer when he was following the history of the Jews, remained silent about that man who stirred up the greatest movements among that people, founded a sect after his own name, and declared himself to be the Messiah, for whose arrival the whole nation of the Jews was then gasping. 2. Since he considered *John the Baptist* and *James the Brother of God* <note>original Greek: ἀδελφόθεον (adelphotheon). James the Just was traditionally called the "Brother of the Lord."</note> worthy of his praise, is it believable that he thought Jesus Christ—whose name was far more famous—unworthy of mention? 3. This point is even more pressing if we consider that in praising *James*, to make him more distinguished, he wrote that he was the BROTHER of JESUS, WHO WAS CALLED CHRIST; whom, evidently, he knew to be far better known. For thus Josephus’s words run in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book XX, Chapter VIII: Ananus the Younger calls a council of judges, and having brought before it the BROTHER OF JESUS CHRIST, JAMES by name, and certain others along with him, having accused them as guilty of impiety, he delivered them to be stoned. This deed was deeply displeasing to all the good men in that city and to those who were devoted to the laws.* 4. In the judgment of those who have a keen critical sense <note>original Latin: "nasum habent Criticum," literally "those who have a critical nose."</note>, the color of the wording and the thread of the discourse agree; they are clearly of the kind typical of Hellenistic writers <note>Greek-speaking Jews of the period</note>. One may also observe certain expressions familiar to Josephus. Thus says Huet <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721) was a prominent French bishop and intellectual who defended the authenticity of this passage.</note> in the *Demonstration of the Gospel, page 47 of the Amsterdam Edition.*

<margin>XXXVIII. Why it is rejected by others.</margin>

XXXVIII. On the opposing side, the case is fought with these arguments: 1. Many of the earliest defenders of the Christian sect never defended their cause with this testimony. Not *Justin Martyr*, not *Tertullian*, and not *Photius*, who published a summary and critique of Josephus's work. They would not have omitted this passage <note>original Greek: ῥῆσιν (rhēsin)</note> if it had been known to them or held as genuine. 2. *Origen* openly wrote in more than one place that Jesus was not recognized as the Christ by Josephus; *Theodoret* asserted the same. And the matter speaks for itself. Since Josephus intended to apply the prophecies about the Messiah—whether out of flattery or from his own conviction—to the Emperor Vespasian, how could he have said of Jesus: *“This was the Christ”* <note>original Greek: ὁ χριστὸς οὗτος ἦν (ho christos outos ēn). This is the most controversial sentence in the Josephus passage, as it seems to be a confession of faith unlikely for a practicing Jew.</note>? 3. Josephus was born of a *priestly* family and was devoted to the *Pharisaic* sect, whom Christ had set himself to attack above all others; therefore it is not likely that praise was given by Josephus to one who had afflicted Josephus’s own associates with the gravest insults. 4. ### XLI. Regarding the SECOND point.
*Origen* and *Theodoret* <note>two influential early Christian theologians</note> are to be understood in this way: they deny that Josephus ever approved of the opinion that established Jesus as the Christ. We believe this as well. For Josephus was not a Christian, but a Jew. He acted here in the role of a Historian, reporting those things that common rumor carried, without interposing his own judgment. This is how the words "he was the Christ" <note>original Greek: ὁ χριστὸς οὗτος ἦν (ho christos outos ēn)</note> should be understood—that is, he was so-called by common title. This is much like how Josephus elsewhere called James "the brother of Jesus, the one called Christ" <note>original Greek: ἀδελφὸν Ἰησοῦ, τοῦ Χριστοῦ λεγομένου (adelphon Iēsou, tou Christou legomenou)</note>. This is especially true since, in speaking of Christ, he used words that Pagans are accustomed to use for their Heroes and for men who surpass the common lot of humanity.

### XLII. Regarding the THIRD point.
Josephus shows in many ways that he was not driven by a great zeal for his own religion. Why should he not have handed down these accounts of Jesus in order to earn the praise of an impartial Historian? After all, he either believed—or pretended to believe—that Vespasian <note>the Roman Emperor who destroyed Jerusalem</note>, the mortal enemy of the Jewish nation, was the Messiah. There is a very sharp observation by *Cloppenburg* <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652), a Dutch theologian</note> in his *Letters to Cappel* (Works, Vol I, p. 161) that Josephus's mention of Christ in that place was of such a kind that, consistent with Jewish treachery, it held a blasphemous connection with the following story. That following story is even more unconnected <note>original Greek: ἀπροσδιόνυσος (aprosdionysos), a Greek idiom meaning "nothing to do with Dionysus," or irrelevant</note> to the narrative than the mention of Christ. Cloppenburg suggests that Josephus, by using a parallel involving a woman named Paulina—who in his opinion was impregnated by a god but in reality by the "spirit of the world"—intended to mock the faith of Christians regarding the conception of Jesus Christ from a virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit. See, however, *Cappel* <note>Louis Cappel (1585–1658), a French Protestant scholar</note> arguing against this on page 165.

### XLIII. Regarding the FOURTH point.
Why should the passage not be considered coherent? In the preceding sections, Josephus made mention of a sedition moved by the Jews against Pilate on the occasion of the standards <note>Roman military ensigns</note> which he had brought into the city bearing the image of Caesar. In the following sections, he tells the story of Decius Mundus and Paulina <note>a Roman scandal where a man tricked a noblewoman into sex by pretending to be the god Anubis</note>, which occurred in the foul rites of Isis at Rome. Both events happened in the same era in which Christ lived. What could prevent a Historian from remembering Christ between these two narrations? Does that Roman story of Mundus and Paulina pertain more to the affairs of the Jews than this account of Christ? And granted, even if these narrations do not flow together perfectly: what is more familiar even to the most excellent historians than to heap together diverse narrations as the variety of events requires, without seeking a formal bridge between the topics? The leading historians—*Thucydides, Polybius, and Livy*—do this very often, especially in matters upon which they do not wish to dwell, as *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a renowned classical scholar</note> observes regarding this very passage of Josephus (Exercise 11, No. 11). <margin>XLIV. Spanheim has written most extensively about the Apostles.</margin>
XLIV. To Christ, as Lord of the Prophets, must be joined the **APOSTLES**, who were themselves the primary ministers, witnesses of his life, doctrine, miracles, death, and resurrection. They were enriched with the most abundant gifts of his Spirit as Teachers of the Universe, who propagated the Gospel to the ends of the habitable world—to put it briefly, they were more than Prophets under the Economy of the New Testament. Regarding their name, institution, office, preeminences, and number, we would have many things to say, were it not that the greatest glory of our Order, **FRIEDRICH SPANHEIM**, had already taken up that material in his *Historico-Theological Dissertation on the Apostolate and the Apostles*. There, he treated this whole business so extensively, eruditely, and elegantly that it is far better to send the reader there than to cause trouble for ourselves and others with a repeated writing, which could never approach the abundance and elegance of Spanheim’s Dissertation.

<margin>XLV. They were also Prophets.</margin>
XLV. It is now especially worthy of consideration how the Apostles are Prophets, though they are otherwise distinguished from the Prophets. They are certainly Prophets in this: I. Because they learned Gospel truths from the immediate revelation of the Divine Spirit, promised to them so often by Christ and granted so abundantly. II. Because, under the impulse and direction of the same Spirit, they set forth the truths they were taught, whether by voice or by writing. III. Because they did this in the languages of any nations and peoples, the skill of which the efficacy of the Divine Spirit infused into them in a single moment. IV. Because they confirmed that doctrine of theirs with miracles, the likes of which no ages had seen anything equal or similar, and by which it was necessary for all spectators to be seized with admiration. However, they are distinguished from the Prophets strictly so called in that the greatest part of their function did not consist in the prediction of future things, but in the proclamation of the Gospel of fulfillment. They explained the Christian religion most excellently: they taught the systematic connection <term>synarmologia</term> <note>original Greek: συναρμολογία (synarmologia); refers to the fitting together or internal consistency of a system of thought</note> of its parts most accurately; they demonstrated it most evidently (where it was necessary) by bringing forth testimonies and arguments from the Old Testament; and those things which were so hidden in allegories—

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL #

...allegories and types established by God in that ancient Economy <note>The "Economy" refers to the theological system or divine administration of the Old Testament</note>, so that they could not be understood or divined except by the extraordinary help of the Spirit, they interpreted them miraculously. However, this did not prevent them from sometimes performing the office of prophets by foretelling future events, as we find Paul, Peter, and John did in their epistles. They were, moreover, greater than all the *Prophets* in this respect: while the inspiration <note>original Latin: afflatus</note> of the prophets came and went as it pleased God, that light which was divinely infused into the minds of the Apostles accompanied them perpetually.

<margin>XLVI. Whether David prophesied concerning them in Psalm 68:27, 28.</margin>
XLVI. It is helpful now to inquire whether David prophesied anything concerning the Apostles of Christ and the tribes from which they were to be born in *Psalm 68:27, 28*. There, the words from the Junian version <note>A Latin translation of the Bible by Franciscus Junius and Immanuel Tremellius, highly regarded by scholars of this period</note> read as follows: *In the congregations bless God, the Lord, you who are from the fountain of Israel. There is Benjamin, the small one, and their ruler; the princes of Judah and their assembly; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.* Theodoret <note>A prominent 5th-century bishop and commentator</note> and others among the Ancients have applied these words to the Apostles. Nor are there lacking more recent authors who agree. This opinion, supported by new pillars <note>original Latin: tibicinibus, meaning supporting arguments</note>, is explained in roughly this manner by Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a German philologist and theologian</note> in his *Schilo, Book V, Chapter 20*, and in his commentary on this Psalm in the second volume of his works. In this prophetic Psalm, the glorious ascension of Christ into heaven is described, along with the events that followed it. Among these is the blessing of the Lord <note>original Hebrew: במקהלות (bam-maq-he-loth)</note>, *in the great assemblies*—the vast gatherings not of just one people. In this verse, therefore, those who were to be the heralds of Divine praise are described. They are designated by the tribes of Israel from which these heralds were to take their origin.

There, BENJAMIN is placed first, and by him is designated PAUL, who arose from that tribe. He is called <note>original Hebrew: צעir (tsair); original Greek: νεώτερος (neōteros)</note> *the younger* or *minor*, because just as Benjamin was the last of the sons of Jacob, so Paul himself was the last of all to be called to the Apostleship; for which reason he calls himself the *least* and *one born out of due time* (1 Corinthians 15:8, 9, 10; Ephesians 3:8). The word <note>original Hebrew: רדם (radam)</note> is added, which is never repeated elsewhere. This is either a simple word denoting an *ecstatic* person <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐκστάσει (en ekstasei)</note>—and indeed, from the root for "sleep" comes the word for *being overwhelmed by a deep ecstatic sleep*. In that case, it most accurately outlines the *Calling* of Paul, which occurred in an ecstasy (Acts 9:3, 12), and his *Confirmation* in office, which likewise occurred in an ecstasy (Acts 22:17; 2 Corinthians 12:1). Alternatively, the word is a compound and means *he who rules them*, not with the power of a master, but of a father and teacher (1 Corinthians 4:15). This was a prerogative not of domination, but of labor beyond his fellow servants (1 Corinthians 15:10; 2 Corinthians 11:5, 23). To him are added the *Princes* <note>original Hebrew: שרים (sarim); original Greek: προεστῶτες (proestōtes) or ἡγέμενοι (hēgemomenoi)</note>. And specifically the *Princes of Judah* <note>original Hebrew: רגמתם (rigmatam)</note>. This word is a *hapax legomenon* <note>A term that appears only once in a given text or language</note> designating a *heap of stones*. A *stone*, moreover, is called the *stayer and preserver of something*.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI. ###

[...served.] <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page</note> Thus Joseph in Genesis 49:24 is called the *Stone of Israel* <note>original Hebrew: אבן ישראל</note>. A *heap of stones* denotes many from the same tribe, who are colleagues in the same work. From the tribe of *Judah* were these Apostles: I. *James the Less*, the brother of the Lord (Galatians 1:19), the son of Alphaeus and Mary (Mark 15:40), who was the sister of Mary, the mother of Jesus (John 19:25). II. *Jude*, the brother of this James (Jude 1:1). III. *James the Great*, and IV. *John*, the sons of Zebedee and Salome—which is gathered from Matthew 27:56 compared with Mark 15:40—whom they say was the sister of Joseph, the husband of Mary. V. *Simon the Zealot*, or *Canaanite*, whom antiquity believed to be the uterine brother <note>A brother born of the same mother</note> of James the Less and Jude. VI. *Judas Iscariot*, whose homeland *Kerioth* is numbered among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:15). Next, mention is made of the *princes of Zebulun*. To this group should be referred: I. *Peter*, II. *Andrew* his brother, III. *Philip*—all born in *Bethsaida*, a city of *Galilee* in the tribe of *Zebulun* (John 1:45). IV. *Bartholomew*, who many believe is the same person as *Nathanael*, both because of his friendship with Philip (John 1:46 compared with Matthew 10:3) and because *Nathanael* is named among the Apostles in John 21:2. Now, *Nathanael* was from *Cana of Galilee* in the territory of *Zebulun* (ibid). Finally, the *princes of Naphtali*. *Matthew*, of *Capernaum*, as it seems from Matthew 9:9, which city is in that tribe. There remains *Thomas*, or *Didymus* <note>A Greek name meaning "the Twin"</note>, of whose lineage nothing is clear. These are the views of *Altingius* <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a noted Dutch professor of Hebrew and theology</note>; which, if they are not entirely convincing, are certainly learned.

<margin>XLVII. Prophets of the New Testament.</margin>
XLVII. In the order immediately following the Apostles are numbered the *Prophets* (1 Corinthians 12:28): *And God has appointed some in the Church: first Apostles, secondarily Prophets.* So also in Ephesians 4:11: *And He gave some as Apostles, and some as Prophets.* Compare Ephesians 2:20 and 3:5. "Prophets" here denotes those who, being endowed with a singular skill in the sacred scriptures and an extraordinary gift of the Spirit, interpreted the ancient prophecies. They compared the things reported as done by the Apostles and Evangelists with the ancient predictions, showing from them that things had to happen in this way, and thus demonstrating the truth of the Gospel from Moses and the Prophets. They are distinguished from the *Apostles*: not because the Apostles were not prophets—which they surely were, as we have demonstrated, in the most excellent manner—but because certain prophets were not Apostles. Moreover, they are joined to the Apostles because they confirmed the truth of the Apostolic preaching from the ancient oracles. It is believable that such Prophets in the church at Antioch were *Barnabas* and *Simeon* who was called *Niger*, and *Lucius of Cyrene*, and *Manaen*, who had been brought up with *Herod* the Tetrarch, and *Saul*: unless perhaps they were also gifted with the faculty of foretelling the future...

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL. #

...they were endowed. *Acts 13:1.* Such were also **JUDAS** and **SILAS**, who, since they were prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with much speech. *Acts 15:32.* And indeed, there must have been in them both a great dignity of office and a great abundance of the Spirit, since they are placed as intermediaries between the Apostles and the Evangelists. For just as they are second after the Apostles, so when the Apostles are set aside, they are counted as first. It is clear that their duty—which consisted of the solid confirmation of the Gospel through the ancient oracles of the prophets—was most noble. For this task, exceptional gifts were required: a vast knowledge of the matters of the Christian religion, of the wonderful harmony that exists between its parts, and of the prophetic emblems and riddles <note>original: *aenigmatum*</note> through which the matters of the Gospel were represented in ancient times; furthermore, they required a great ability to explain these things for the building up of the church. These gifts did not come to the prophets so much through practice and study as through some extraordinary inspiration of the Spirit and by a "Divine touch," <note>original: *virgula Divina* — literally "a divine little rod," a metaphor for a miraculous stroke of inspiration or a gift from God</note> as it is often called. Yet, this singular grace of God did not hinder that diligence which everyone was bound to apply toward the attainment of the most excellent gifts. Hence it happened that, just as in the ancient Israelite Church, so too in the first Christian Church, the use of prophetic exercises was frequent.

<margin>XLVIII. The most ancient manner of prophetic exercises.</margin>
XLVIII. I believe that those things which Paul commands in *1 Corinthians 14:29 and following* should be understood as referring to these kinds of prophetic exercises. There, he wishes for *only two or three prophets* to speak in the Church—specifically in succession on one day—so that the listeners are not overwhelmed by a multitude of speakers. To others, however, who are endowed with similar skill, he allows the right to judge whether the prophecies are being set forth in the proper way and order, in keeping with the intention of the ancient prophets, and whether each is properly applied to its subject. For in such an exposition of prophecies, there must be a demonstration to the conscience. The Apostle adds that if something *has been revealed to another sitting nearby, the first should be silent*. For he did not want the one who was speaking to think that he had entered the office of speaking in such a way that he would not be willing to listen in turn, even if his own speech were interrupted. This was according to the ancient custom among the Jews; in the Synagogues, in the chambers, and in the courts of the Temple, familiar discourses were held in which the opportunity was given for questioning, judging, and expressing one's own thoughts in turn. As the most learned man **CAMPEGIUS VITRINGA** <note>Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian; the work mentioned is his study on the ancient synagogue</note> shows at length in *Chapter 11 of his The Ancient Synagogue*. Furthermore, he who asked for permission to speak, while the other remained silent, was required to have a <term>revelation <note>original Greek: ἀποκάλυψιν (*apokalypsin*)</note></term>, that is, a distinct knowledge of the truth from Divine information—

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI. ###
