<margin>
XLIX.
In what sense the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.
</margin>
XLIX. For *the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 14:32.</note> This can be understood in two ways, and in both senses it is true and fits the Apostolic purpose. First, the spirit of a prophet is subject to the one prophesying. No one should pretend to defend their own disorder <note>original: *ἀταξίαν* (ataxian) — a state of chaos or lack of discipline</note> by claiming they are so driven by the spirit that they cannot wait their turn. The Apostle says it is not so with those whom God employs in sacred exercises. Those possessed by Pythonic spirits <note>original: *Pythonici* — refers to the pagan oracles, like the Pythia at Delphi, who were believed to be possessed by a spirit and often acted in an uncontrollable frenzy</note> were accustomed to be so carried away and driven that they were not in control of themselves. But the gifts of God, although they do not originate from a man’s will, are nevertheless governed by his will regarding the action, and they easily allow for the time and delay necessary for good order. Therefore, the Spirit subjects His gifts to the wisdom and counsel of the prophets, so that they may use them decently and at the proper time. Thus, this reasoning of the Apostle refers to the rule: *let the first one be silent.* <note>1 Corinthians 14:30.</note>

But this passage can also be explained with this intent: *that the spirits of the prophets who are speaking are considered subject to the other prophets who are listening.* Because, as a most celebrated interpreter <note>likely referring to a Reformer like John Calvin or Hugo Grotius, common in scholarly texts of this period</note> rightly says, *the Holy Spirit does not, through His gifts, make a prophet proud, arrogant, or shameless; rather, He coordinates one gift with another gift and makes us listen gladly to others. For God does not give everything to one person, but distributes His gifts among many, so that no one can say: "I do not need you." And thus the spirit subjects itself in a way to the prophets—namely, so they may judge for themselves what is their own and what is not; what He has given to a certain prophet, and what he still lacks.* And so this reasoning would especially regard the rule: *Let others judge.*

<margin>
L. Agabus, the proclaimer of future things.
</margin>
L. Yet there was no lack of prophets in the strictest sense of the word, whose role it is to foretell hidden and future things. Such a man was **AGABUS**, who indicated through the spirit that a great famine would occur throughout the whole world, *which also took place under Claudius Caesar. Acts 11:28.* The same man, taking Paul's belt and binding his own hands and feet, said: *Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt in this way, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. Acts 21:11.*

For when the Apostles first traveled across the world and did not stay for long durations in individual places, they could not know by human means which of the new converts were suitable to be appointed as overseers of the churches. Since this matter was of the greatest importance, they were aided either by the spirit of "discerning of spirits" or by the warnings of prophets concerning certain...

Paul took him as a companion after he had been approved and recommended by the testimony of the prophets, consecrated by the laying on of hands, and enriched with the greater gifts of the spirit; and now he urges him to fight the good fight, just as the prophets had predicted he would do.

<margin>52. The Revelation of John.</margin>
LII. I say nothing of THE REVELATION OF JOHN <note>original: *Johannis Apocalypsi*</note>, for who would dare deny that it is a most excellent prophecy of the things that are to happen in the world and the Church until the end of all things? Meditation on this work has so occupied the most learned writers of our age that I can omit a longer dissertation on it without any loss to the reader. It will suffice now to point out that John acted as a prophet in the Apocalypse to such an extent that nothing in the Old Testament can be compared with it; so magnificent and splendid were the visions presented to him, framed in wondrous symbols and divinely adapted to depict future events, as was later proved by the outcome. I say these visions were admirable—divided into so many parts, composed of so many images, varied as if with colors and paintings, and finally illustrated with so many figures and displays of men, animals, and other things. These were represented to him not once or twice, but following one after another, and they surpassed in their wonder all the inspirations <note>original: *afflatus* — a divine breath or "breathing upon" by the divine</note> of the ancient Prophets. As *Moses Amyraldus* <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), an influential French Protestant theologian known for his work on divine decrees</note> well judged in his *Preface to the Psalms*.

<margin>53. The dignity and office of the Evangelists.</margin>
LIII. After the Prophets, the EVANGELISTS are numbered, according to <term>Ephesians 4:11</term>. Their office has a great affinity with the prophetic office, although it was a little lower in grade and dignity. But just as it was an extraordinary office, consisting in being companions and co-helpers to the Apostles in preaching or even writing the Gospel, so it is fair to believe that they were furnished with some extraordinary gifts. The first of these was such a power of the spirit that it preserved them from all error, so that wherever they directed their minds in the meditation of theological matters, they perceived the truth without any danger of erring. In this respect, they surpassed the condition of ordinary Pastors and Teachers. The second is that, since the Evangelists were set over the Christian Churches...

<margin>
54. Stephen, filled with the Holy Spirit, and his face shining like an Angel.
</margin>
LIV. The things told concerning STEPHEN are more memorable than can be omitted in a history of the Prophets of the New Testament. He was indeed from the order of Deacons, but many things were granted to him by divine gift which otherwise did not pertain to that order. For he himself, like an Evangelist or some Prophet, performed great wonders and signs among the people and preached the word of the Gospel with such effectiveness that none of his adversaries could withstand the wisdom and the spirit by which he spoke. Finally, he spoke with such gravity and grace that all who sat in the Jewish council, looking intently at him, saw his face as if it were the face of an Angel (Acts 6). This extraordinary beauty of countenance not only commended the dignity of the speaker but gave an illustrious testimony to the innocence of this most holy man. For in this way, God showed that Stephen was not doing wrong to the Law of Moses, since He adorned his face with the same majesty of brightness that the Israelites had once been stunned by in Moses; nor was anything preached by him that was contrary to the law brought by Angels, since God made his face most similar to an Angelic one.

LV. Truly his final speech was worthy above all others to be included by Luke in the Acts of the Apostles. Indeed, it does not merely contain a narration of very well-known events, but is a most wise <term>Apology<note>Here "Apology" is used in the classical sense of an *apologia*—a formal, reasoned defense of one's position or beliefs.</note></term>, in which he argues from the entire governance of God regarding the Israelite people that nothing is taught by him that is not fundamentally consistent with the Divine mind. He was accused of blasphemy against the Temple and the Law, because he had said that Jesus of Nazareth would destroy the Temple and change the rites which Moses had handed down. He himself, repeating the matter from the beginning, showed that the substance of the promise made to the Fathers did not consist of the Temple or the rites to be observed there—indeed, not even the possession of the land of Canaan itself, since Abraham...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Stephen’s defense speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7). The previous page established Stephen as a man filled with the Holy Spirit, performing signs and speaking with a wisdom his opponents could not resist. This page explains the theological strategy behind his long historical narrative and defends its accuracy against modern critics.</meta>

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>ON THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL.</header>

[Abra]ham, and his son and grandson, lived in that land as if it were not their own; and the Patriarchs who followed with their descendants, who were heirs to the promise made to Abraham, were able to be either weighed down by affliction in a foreign land or enjoy honors there, without losing the essential substance of the promise. He also shows that the principal promises were made to Abraham before he was given the sign of circumcision—a point which Paul also emphasizes elsewhere. Likewise, he shows that the Israelites were doing nothing new in his own time by clamoring against God when He spoke to them through His ministers; for their ancestors had similarly clamored against Moses himself, whose honor they now claimed to hold so dear to their hearts. Furthermore, he points out the late arrival of the Temple, which was only built much later by Solomon; he emphasizes God's own clear declaration that He takes little delight in a building made by human hands. From this, Stephen concludes that they act most wickedly by placing so much holiness and religious importance in the Temple and its rituals alone, while simultaneously persecuting the prophets who teach the truth. Therefore, he argues, it should not be held against him as a crime if he had mentioned something regarding the future destruction of that Temple.

<margin>56. The speech is troubled by the unjust censure of a recent critic.</margin>
LVI. I do not deny that in this long speech there occur several things which, at first hearing, one might hardly discern where they are leading; and other things which seem to deviate slightly from the literal letter of the Mosaic narrative. But Stephen did not deserve this censure from an arrogant critic: <note>The author is likely defending Stephen against early Enlightenment biblical critics who questioned the historical accuracy of the New Testament speeches.</note> *“Saint Stephen was indeed full of the Spirit of the Gospel when he recited that speech which appears in Acts 7; nevertheless, he seems to have mixed in many historical matters that pertain nothing to the case being discussed, and which can hardly be reconciled with the history of the Old Testament. Nor are there wanting learned men who think that Stephen, through a failure of memory <note>original: "lapsu Mnemonico"</note>, confused certain things that should have been kept distinct.”* Truly, one must attribute very little to the Holy Spirit (with which Stephen is recorded to have been not only imbued, but filled) to suggest that the Spirit allowed such a lack of discernment <note>original: *ἀκρισίαν* (akrisian)—a lack of judgment or critical sense</note> and failure of judgment in the mind of this defender of the faith that he poured out many things beside the point, not discerning what favored his own cause. Or to suggest such a weakness of memory that he incorrectly narrated the best-known events. What kind of "fullness of the Holy Spirit" is this—the very gift Christ promised as the greatest mark of His generosity—if it provided less to these Men of God than a moderate amount of diligence and skill provides to the least of the modern critics? <margin>
LX. Stephen’s wondrous vision.
</margin>
LX. Especially wondrous is what happened to Stephen after he delivered this very grave speech before the Jewish council. For then, full of the Holy Spirit and with his eyes fixed on heaven, he saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and that Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." <note>Acts 7:55–56. The "Son of Man" is a title Jesus frequently used for himself, often associated with his role as judge and redeemer.</note>

<margin>
LXI. What the "opening of heaven" signifies.
</margin>
LXI. These matters deserve some <term>lingering study <gloss>Greek: ἐπιμονήν (epimonēn), a rhetorical term for dwelling on a point for emphasis</gloss></term>. What exactly is meant by the report that he "saw the heavens opened"? This way of speaking occurs not only here, but also in Ezekiel 1:1, Matthew 3:16, Acts 10:10, and Revelation 4:1 and 19:11. However, interpreters diverge in explaining it, as usually happens with obscure matters. Some refer this to lightning and flashes of light, by which the atmosphere <note>original Latin: "æther"</note> seems to be divided and opened to men. This manner of speaking is not unusual for poets. Thus Silius Italicus says in Book I:

> ...and with the pole broken, the fiery sky flashes. <note>original Latin: "rupto-que polo micat igneus æther"</note>

Statius says in the *Thebaid*, Book I:

> ...the jagged lightning bolts tremble, and the sky is burst open by a sudden flash. <note>original Latin: "abrupta tremiscunt Fulgura & attritus subita face rumpitur æther"</note>

Ovid says in the *Fasti*, Book II:

> From here it thunders; from there the sky is split by fires sent forth. <note>original Latin: "Hinc tonat, hinc missis abrumpitur ignibus æther"</note>

Others conceive of a *Chasm* <note>A gap or opening in the atmosphere.</note> or a hiatus, such as natural philosophers explain in works on *Meteorology* <note>The study of atmospheric phenomena, based on Aristotelian science.</note>; specifically, when the outermost and highest parts of the air are condensed and become brighter so as to limit the view, while the middle air, remaining thinner, is not seen as usual. Then, a sort of gap and opening of the sky presents itself to the eyes of the spectators. Others argue that a real fissure occurred in the highest heaven, a pulling apart of parts that were previously continuous. Finally, others think it signifies the removal of all impediments that could delay the sharp edge of sight, so that the saints might see what God wanted them to see. When nothing is seen in a clear sky except that glowing height, the sky seems closed; but when something is discerned in the vault, or above it, or descending from it, the sky appears to be opened by the manifestation of that object.

LXII. It is not my habit to determine anything rashly in a doubtful matter; but if I may be allowed a conjecture, I would think the explanation of this phrase can vary according to the variety of circumstances. When Ezekiel writes that the heavens were opened to him, if something...

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header># ON THE PROPHETS PRAISED IN THE GOSPEL</header>

Concerning what was presented to his physical eyes, it is not unreasonable to imagine lightning, or at least a flash very similar to lightning, except that it was more lasting. For the prophet himself seems to lead us to this conclusion in <note>Ezekiel 1</note> verse 4: *I saw, therefore, when behold a stormy wind came from the North, a great cloud and a fire enfolding itself, and a brightness surrounding it, etc.* In the baptism of Christ, recorded in Matthew 3:16 and Mark 1:10, something seems to have happened beyond the natural order, which was not unlike a <term>chasm <gloss>Latin: Chasmati; a term used in early meteorology to describe a literal gap or "opening" appearing in the sky</gloss></term>, so that a certain opening was visibly perceived in the highest region of the air, from which the appearance of a dove descended. For it is not necessary, nor even likely, that either a literal dove or the appearance of a dove was formed in the highest heaven and descended from there. In ecstatic visions—in which it is not the things themselves that are presented to the senses, but rather emblems of things presented to the imagination—the "opening of the heavens" is not a physical reality, but exists in the imagination of holy men. This is how I interpret Acts 10:10, Revelation 4:1, and 19:11. In this history of our Stephen, I believe there was either a real parting of the physical parts of the upper sky, or at least those parts of the heavens that limit our sight were made transparent, so that he could penetrate with his eyes to see those bodies which are in the highest heavens.

<margin>LXIII. How he saw the glory of God.</margin>
LXIII. But what did he behold there? The **glory of God**, that is, a certain light, brilliance, and extraordinary brightness, which is the symbol of Divine Majesty. Compare Exodus 24:10, Ezekiel 1:27, Luke 2:9, and 2 Peter 1:17 with Matthew 17:5. He saw this with his physical eyes, which he kept fixed intently on heaven. But there was also the addition of an attentive contemplation of the mind, which penetrated through external symbols to secret and spiritual matters. For he was "full of the Holy Spirit," by whose help three things were accomplished: 
I. That he might nobly lift his eyes from lower things to higher things, from which this glory of the Divinity could shine upon him. 
II. That he might have eyes fit to behold and endure such great light; for otherwise, in this mortal state of ours, the dullness of human eyes is unequal to the task. <note>See Daniel 10:7 and Acts 9:7, where humans are overwhelmed by divine light.</note>
III. That he might be able to keep his mind fixed on the contemplation of heavenly things, even while so many great circumstances surrounded him which would have distracted and disturbed the meditations of even the most constant man.

<margin>LXIV. And the Lord Jesus standing at the right hand of God.</margin>
LXIV. But besides this, he saw the Lord **Jesus**: he, I say, while standing on the earth, saw Jesus in the heavens. For the Lord did not leave heaven to become closer to him. <note>Acts 1:11, 3:21.</note> This was able to happen because his faculty of sight was increased and amplified in a wonderful way by Divine omnipotence. <header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XXI.</header>

It should not seem incredible that He who gave man the skill and art to see distant things as if they were near, and small things as if they were much larger—through the help of <term>telescopes</term> and <term>microscopes</term>—could have given Stephen such sharpness of sight that he was able to look out from the earth and see those things being carried out in the heavens. Moreover, he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God; that is, adorned with Royal Majesty, closest to God—indeed, even with Divine Majesty and glory. Perhaps he also saw Him literally positioned to the right of that splendid brilliance which was set before his eyes. Finally, he saw Him *standing*: this was to signify the Lord's ready promptness to protect and strengthen Stephen, and to receive his spirit. Compare this to Micah 5:4: *And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: ועמד ורעה (ve-amad ve-ra'ah)</note>; and Daniel 12:1: *Michael, who stands over the children of your people* <note>original Hebrew: העומד על בני עמך (ha-omed al bene ammekha)</note>. The Greeks also call helpers <term>parastatai <gloss>literally "those who stand beside"</gloss></term>. Thus, this extraordinary vision created great consolation for Stephen; it was for him a foretaste of celestial glory.

<margin>LXV. What happened prophetically to Cornelius and others from the common body of the faithful.</margin>
LXV. But even to the common people among the faithful, at that beginning of the New Testament, certain prophetic gifts were granted. Cornelius the <term>Centurion <gloss>a professional officer of the Roman army</gloss></term>, one of those *Gentiles who piously worship the Divine* <note>original Hebrew: חסידי אומות עולם (Chassidei Umot Ha-olam), a term for "righteous among the nations"</note>, not only saw an Angel (by whose speech he was assured that his prayers had been heard and his alms were pleasing to God), but having been instructed in the principles of the Christian religion by Peter, he was suddenly seized—along with his household—by a miraculous inspiration of the Spirit, to the astonishment of those watching. Indeed, the faithful of the circumcision <note>Jewish Christians</note> who had come with Peter were amazed that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even onto the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues (previously unknown) and magnifying God (Acts 10:45–46). The disciples of John the Baptist were honored with the same benefit of Divine grace; when Paul laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and **PROPHESIED** (Acts 19:6). That this was frequent enough in those first times of Christianity can be gathered from 1 Corinthians 12, where the Apostle discusses at length the various <term>charismata <gloss>spiritual gifts or "favors" granted by God</gloss></term> of the Holy Spirit, which He distributes to individuals as He wills.

<margin>I. The infallibility of the Apostles in teaching is of great importance to the Christian cause.</margin>
I. Since the Apostles were appointed by Christ as the teachers of the universal Church, and we must attribute all received Gospel doctrine to them, we must first of all carefully inquire: were they led in teaching and writing by such a certain and unwavering direction of the infallible Spirit that their doctrine never wandered from the truth? For although the Christian Church has always held this as indubitable and as a principle of its faith, nevertheless in this unhappy century of ours, it has begun to be brought into controversy by men of great but perverted intellect. Hence, the necessity has been placed upon us first to explain the truth clearly, then to stoutly defend and vindicate it.

<margin>II. They reached it only by certain definite stages.</margin>
II. And indeed, it is very well known from Gospel history that the Apostles, when they were first called by Christ, were quite unlearned <note>original Latin: "rudes," meaning unrefined or raw.</note> in heavenly doctrine. Indeed, even after they had enjoyed the discipline of Christ for three years, they had not been so thoroughly scoured of the "rust" of errors and prejudices that they did not harbor absurd opinions regarding the nature and character of the kingdom of God. These opinions they scarcely—or perhaps not at all—set aside before His ascension into heaven. Rather, until that time, they occupied the benches of students rather than the chairs of Teachers <note>The author uses a classroom metaphor: the *subsellia* (benches/lower seats) versus the *cathedras* (the professor's chair).</note>. Except that they had to undergo a kind of apprenticeship for their future Apostleship during that time. For to them it was...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXII.

Judea had to be traversed for the sake of announcing the arrival of the kingdom of heaven: for which purpose they needed both a certain power of performing miracles and the light of knowledge by which they might surpass the condition of the other disciples. Truly, after they were imbued with power from on high on the day of Pentecost, and with the Spirit descending upon them from heaven filling them, they were suddenly changed into different men; and they were furnished with those endowments by which they might be rendered entirely fit for the function of the office entrusted to them, and now to be performed. *They began to speak in various tongues*, which they had never learned, just as that Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2:4); and in all those tongues they preached the mighty works of God <note>original Greek: τὰ μεγαλεῖα τοῦ Θεοῦ (*ta megaleia tou Theou*)</note>. <margin>III. It does not extend to individual actions.</margin>
III. However, this does not seem to extend to individual actions. This occurred although in the sum of their doctrine, even regarding that same article <note>Referring to a "point" or "article" of faith, specifically the relationship between Jewish law and Gentile converts.</note>, there was the most exact consensus among them.

<margin>IV. In doctrine itself, the Spirit revealed to them what the timing required.</margin>

<margin>VII. Le Clerc.</margin>
VII. The Author of the *Critique of Simon’s Critical History* <note>Referring to the work *Sentimens de quelques théologiens de Holland* (1685), a response to Richard Simon's pioneering work of biblical criticism.</note>—whom for the sake of brevity we shall call Le Clerc—did not hesitate to align himself with Spinoza in many respects. He circumscribes the entire infallibility of the Apostles within these specific boundaries: **I.** They clearly perceived the general principles of the Jewish Religion, which they had learned from their earliest years. **II.** They had also distinctly heard from Christ, and clearly understood, the doctrine of the Gospel, which is comprised of a few articles that are clear, easy to understand, and can be easily retained in the memory. **III.** They had seen Christ's miracles, His resurrection from the dead, His ascension into heaven, and so forth. **IV.** Since they knew these things with certainty, they also narrated what they had seen and heard infallibly. That is, in my opinion, they acted in good faith, lying about nothing against their conscience. **AND IN THIS MATTER CONSISTED THEIR INFALLIBILITY.** In the *Apology* for this opinion of his, on page 228, he explains it thus:

> **THIS SPECIES OF INFALLIBILITY IS EASILY UNDERSTOOD, PROVIDED ONE OBSERVES THAT A GOOD MAN, ENDOWED WITH A GOOD FACULTY OF UNDERSTANDING AND WELL-INFORMED IN RELIGION, WHO DOES NOT THROW HIMSELF INTO THE DANGER OF FREQUENT OR PROLONGED REASONING, CAN HARDLY EVER ERR, AS LONG AS HE REMAINS IN SUCH A DISPOSITION AND PERSISTS IN THAT PATH.**

He adds **V.** That it could, moreover, have been possible that the "spirit of miracles" <note>original: "spiritus miraculorum"</note> which Jesus sent to them strengthened their memory and opened their minds in a way incomprehensible to us. But it is certain, he says, that this spirit did not lead them in such a miraculous way that we are obliged to receive whatever they said or wrote with the same reverence as the words of Christ. Furthermore, he attacks that idea of infallibility—which is said to arise from the perpetual guidance of the Holy Spirit in their preaching or writings—with these arguments in particular: 

I. That it has no foundation in Scripture itself, nor in any promise of Christ. II. That neither the Apostles regarding themselves, nor the ancient Christians regarding the Apostles, held such an opinion of infallibility. III. That the Apostles sometimes erred in their opinions, their preaching, and their defenses <note>original: "Apologiis"</note>, no less than in their actions. IV. That they themselves sometimes distinguish their own dictates from the dictates of the Holy Spirit. V. That such infallibility belongs to Christ the Lord alone.

X. These are the subtleties with which the ill-employed refinement of human intellect wickedly snarls against God; yet no great labor is required to wash them away. For, I: There is a reason in the world why Christ assigned the assistance of His Spirit to the Apostles most especially at that time when they had to plead the cause of the Gospel before princes and judges—the arbiters of life and death. It is because at such times the minds of men—even the most constant orators and the most eloquent speakers—are usually unhinged by terror. II. So far from the perpetual assistance of the Spirit being excluded here, it is instead most strongly confirmed. Yet, I do not suppose He indicated by this that He would not similarly be present with him against other enemies. He teaches the opposite himself in verse 7 and 8: *To whatever I send you, go; and whatever I command you, speak. Do not be afraid of them: for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.* Furthermore, Christ promised the Apostles that *He would give them a mouth and wisdom, which* ALL WHO OPPOSE THEM *will not be able to contradict or resist* (Luke 21:15). Therefore, the sense of this passage is: not only may you be at ease in the ordinary course of your duties, but you shall not lack the assistance of the Spirit even then, when all things usually fail even the most stout-hearted. # ON THE INFALLIBILITY OF THE APOSTLES IN SPEECH #

As Hugo Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian whose commentaries on the Bible were highly influential in the 17th century.</note> rightly notes, God provided both wisdom to the mind and eloquence to the mouth; this speech was not artificial <note>original: "calamistratum," literally meaning "curled with a branding iron," referring to an overly ornate or affected rhetorical style.</note>, but reflected the very nature of naked truth with simple gravity. Grotius also excellently advised that this promise should be compared with **Exodus 4:12**. In that passage, God encourages Moses, whom he was sending to the Israelites and Pharaoh, with these words: *“Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and will teach you what you are to speak.”* Indeed, who would doubt that God promises to Moses here exactly what the Prophets possessed when they spoke in His name? And who would doubt that those words of Moses ought to have been accepted as so many divine oracles, both by Pharaoh and by the Israelites?

IV. It is utterly false to claim that the "Holy Spirit" denotes merely a holy disposition of the mind. Here again, Grotius speaks excellently. Lest the Apostles be terrified by such great dangers, Christ promises them a great help: *“not angels, but the Spirit of God itself, than which nothing greater could be promised.”* And the facts themselves speak. For in **Matthew 10:20**, it is called the *Spirit of the Father*, and it is distinguished from the Apostles' own disposition and natural aptitude: *“It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father.”* Can a person's natural aptitude for speaking be contrasted with the person themselves speaking? And what would be the sense of those words if they meant: "it is not so much you who speak, as that holy disposition of your mind which the Gospel generates"? Finally, the Spirit being discussed here is the one Christ promised as a representative <note>original: "vicarium," suggesting the Holy Spirit acts as Christ's deputy or substitute on earth.</note> for Himself. Every rule of reason forbids us from explaining this as a mere "disposition of mind." Nor does the "Spirit of God" or "of the Father" signify a mere habit of our soul in any passage of scripture. Let it be granted to Jean Le Clerc <note>original: "Clerico." Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a Genevan theologian known for his critical approach to the Bible, which often downplayed traditional views of inspiration.</note> that phrases like the *Spirit of slumber, Spirit of fear,* or *Spirit of fortitude* <note>original: "Spiritus soporis, Spiritus timoris, Spiritus fortitudinis."</note> denote a disposition of mind resulting in sleep, fear, or strength. But what does that have in common with the *Spirit of the Father* and the *Spirit of God*? Would the latter mean a disposition of mind that *makes* one the Father or God? For that is what the similarity of the phrase would require if Le Clerc’s logic were followed.

<margin>
XI. Christ's saying in John 16:13 is watered down by Le Clerc.
</margin>

XI. Regarding **John 16:13**, our author <note>Referring back to Le Clerc.</note> observes: I. *That this is not to be understood in its full rigor, as if the Apostles knew everything.* II. *That the manner of speaking is quite figurative and improper, as the following parts of the verse imply. Therefore, the words should not be pressed too hard.* III. That this is the simplest sense: *“After you have received the spirit of miracles, it will teach you what else you need to know, whether through visions or by calling to your memory what I said before; so that you may understand the meaning and know what needs to be done in the future.”* (Compare **John 14:26**). IV. *Furthermore, the spirit of miracles does not immediately make one infallible.* An example is found in the Corinthians in **1 Corinthians 12:8**, *who nevertheless were not infallible teachers of the truth for that reason,* but required the instruction of the Apostle for the correction...

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XXII. #

...of vices, the solution of doubts, and the refutation of errors. Therefore, [our opponent argues] a perpetual and infallible leading of the Spirit was not taught, since the outcome did not always seem to correspond to such a promise.

<margin>XII. Honestly set forth by us.</margin>
**XII.** We, however, shall observe things more useful for the clarification of this passage. I. *In general.* It is a very poor method of interpretation to use excessive subtlety to thin out the emphasis of words, so that those things said with a magnificent display of language in the Sacred Scriptures are reduced to a meager meaning. The Socinians <note>The Socinians were a rationalist sect that denied the Trinity and often sought to minimize the supernatural elements of the Bible in favor of moral teachings.</note> follow this manner of commenting more than others. Would that our opponent’s complaint about the "highly figurative" way of speaking did not stem from that same principle! Even though what is figurative here is extremely emphatic. It was hardly worth mentioning that absolute omniscience is not promised to the Apostles here; who would be so insane as to dream of such a thing? The Lord’s promise must be understood according to the "subject matter," as they say. Yet, let it not be thought that with grand words, which naturally create thoughts of the greatest things in the mind, He intended to promise only small, common, or mediocre things. That would not be consistent with the Lord’s sincerity, nor with the inexhaustible wealth of His goodness, which never lacks something to bestow.

**XIII.** II. There is no reason to restrict what is said here about the Spirit to a *Spirit of miracles*. For the text concerns that Spirit whom Christ promises as his own substitute; who is the *Advocate* <note>original: "παράκλητος" (paraklētos), often translated as Comforter, Counselor, or Advocate—one who stands alongside to help.</note> in verse 7; who pleads Christ’s cause before the world, certainly not through miracles alone, but also through the other works of His grace: the conversion, sanctification, consolation, and strengthening of the elect; and who pleads the cause of the faithful before God (Romans 8:26). Thus, He is the opposite of the *Accuser* <note>original: "κατηγόρῳ" (katēgorō), referring to Satan as the accuser of the brethren.</note> (Revelation 12:10). And He is the *Spirit of Truth*, not only because He confirms the Gospel with miracles, but because He instills it into the souls of mortals by an internal, secret, and effective means (1 Corinthians 2:10, 12; Ephesians 1:17). He is promised here as a *Guide* <note>original: "ὁδηγὸς" (hodēgos), a leader or conductor on a journey.</note>, in allusion to the pillar of fire and cloud, which did not allow the Israelites to wander astray in the desert (Compare Isaiah 63:11–14).

**XIV.** III. A "Spirit of miracles" does not immediately make a person infallible; nevertheless, even our Author [Le Clerc] would not deny (p. 257) that whatever that Spirit confirms by His miracles must be accepted as infallible doctrine. Furthermore, it is not just some part of the Apostles' doctrine, but the whole of it—just as they embraced it in both their preaching and their Epistles—with all its inferences and arguments (2 Thessalonians 2:15: *whether by word or by letter* <note>original: "εἴτε διὰ λόγου εἴτε δι’ ἐπιστολῆς" (eite dia logou eite di' epistolēs).</note>).

->### ON THE INFALLIBILITY OF THE APOSTLES IN TEACHING.###<-

<note>original: "ἀληθῶς" (truly)</note> [The word] was truly confirmed by miracles. (Mark 16:20; Acts 14:3; Hebrews 2:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:5).

<margin>XV.</margin>
**IV. More Specifically.** The Apostles can be considered in two ways: according to what they had in common with the rest of the faithful, or according to what was unique to them as Apostles. In both respects, this promise was fulfilled for them, always maintaining the proper proportion for each role. As believers, they had the Spirit of Truth as their Master: <note>original: "ἀψευδῆ" (unfailing or truthful)</note>, who led them—just as the pillar of cloud and fire led the Israelites—into all truth necessary to be known for salvation. That is, by an effective illumination of their minds, He directed them so that they could not fall into errors that would overturn their salvation. This, in truth, happens to all the faithful (1 John 2:20, 27). But beyond this, something grander was promised to them as **Apostles**. As the <term>Teachers of the Universal Church</term><note>The author emphasizes that the Apostles were not just local leaders, but authorities for the entire global body of Christians.</note> and exceptional Prophets of the New Testament, greater gifts were due to them so that they might be rendered fit for their duty. 

Furthermore, the dignity and authority of that office demanded that they themselves were most fully persuaded that they taught nothing but the truth. It also required that their listeners could receive everything they taught—about the entirety of the Christian religion, at any time or in any manner, whether by word of mouth or in writing—boldly and without fear of error. For this to be possible, Christ promised them the Spirit as a guide into all truth which they would have occasion to announce. For unless you assume the <term>infallible assistance</term><note>The theological concept that the Holy Spirit prevented the Apostles from making errors when teaching the core doctrines of the faith.</note> of the Spirit in all Apostolic doctrine, everything must necessarily be unstable. The Church is built on the **Foundation of the Apostles** (Ephesians 2:20, 21). How solid could it be if that foundation were not firm and stable? And how could it be firm if it were assumed the Apostles were subject to error in their teaching? Paul states this beautifully in 1 Corinthians 12:7: <note>original: "Ἑκάστῳ δὲ δίδοται ἡ φανέρωσις τοῦ πνεύματος πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον" (To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good)</note>. "To each is given the declaration of the Spirit for the common benefit." That is, to each person, a measure of the Spirit is granted according to how they can be most useful to the Church in the parts entrusted to them. 

The function of the Apostles was the first of all in the Church; in dignity, it even surpassed the function of the Prophets (verse 28). Since, therefore, they were more exceptional than all others, they were also equipped with more excellent gifts. They were more excellent than the Prophets in this: while the Prophets had their inspirations at certain times, the Apostles—who had to teach constantly—possessed those inspirations constantly while teaching. For this was "for the common good."

<margin>
*Do the events narrated in Acts 15 undermine Apostolic infallibility?*
</margin>
For neither did the ancient Christians, nor the Apostles themselves, hold that opinion regarding infallibility. Why is that? *It is evident from Acts 15. Certain Jews who had become Christians ordered that Gentiles, along with their profession of Christianity, should undergo circumcision. Paul and Barnabas sharply opposed that opinion; however, their authority was not so great as to impose silence on those Judaizers. Although Paul was second to none of the Apostles, they still did not yield to him; the Church at Jerusalem had to be consulted. There, the Apostles were gathered with the Elders; first they conferred and disputed among themselves (verses 6–7), then Peter and James gave their opinions, and finally they concluded by common vote what should be done. If the Church of that time had recognized Paul as an infallible Teacher, it would not have been necessary to send to Jerusalem. If all the Apostles had been filled with the Spirit of infallibility, they would all have been of the same opinion; without any dispute, they would have chosen only one person to pronounce the oracle in the common name of all. So says that author on page 249.* <note>The "author" being quoted here is Jean Le Clerc (Clericus), a prominent 17th-century theologian who challenged traditional views on biblical inspiration.</note>

<margin>
XVII.
It is shown that they do not undermine it.
</margin>
XVII. Let us examine this matter a little more closely. <note>literally: "Let us rub this ear of grain a little," a metaphor for careful investigation.</note> **I.** It is absurd to form a judgment about Apostolic Authority based on the opinion of these Judaizers; for having barely been imbued with the first elements of Christianity, they were still heavily influenced by the stubbornness of their nation and the blind zeal of their sect. For they were <term>from the sect of the Pharisees</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς αἱρέσεως τῶν Φαρισαίων"</note> (verse 5). They were believers by profession, but <term>false brothers</term> <note>original: "ψευδάδελφοι"</note>, falsely using the name of the Apostles and acting as disturbers of the Churches (verse 24). These are the same ones of whom Paul speaks in Galatians 2:4: "false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring free men into bondage." Clericus is welcome to praise these men as the authors of his own opinion, as far as we are concerned. **II.** It is true that Paul did not overwhelm the Church simply by the authority of his Apostleship; for the Apostles were accustomed to teach in such a way that they commended themselves to every man’s conscience <term>by the manifestation of the truth</term> <note>original: "τῇ φανερώσει τῆς ἀληθείας"</note> (2 Corinthians 4:2). This is also what Christ the Lord did, not always putting forward His own authority, but setting it aside to appeal to Moses, to the Scriptures, and to other arguments (John 5:39, 46, 47; Matthew 22:31, 32). Nor—despite the nonsense Spinoza speaks <note>Baruch Spinoza, whose "Tractatus Theologico-Politicus" argued that Apostles reasoned like ordinary men rather than speaking as infallible prophets.</note>—does it undermine Prophetic authority when one persuades by reasoning and arguments the things he says; for God Himself pleads the cause of His Divinity in this way against idols and their patrons, and invites them to produce their own arguments (Isaiah 41 and 44). **III.** The fact that the Church at Antioch decided that some of their members should go to Jerusalem did not arise from their having a bad or doubtful opinion regarding the faith and authority of Paul, but so that the rest [of the Apostles might be heard] for the purpose of convicting the Judaizers...

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XXII. #

...occupied with their own [concerns], he governed their minds with his secret power in the act of judging, so that what seemed best to them was, in reality, the dictate of the Holy Spirit. Nor did they write without consideration: *It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.* <note>Acts 15:28. This phrase is central to the author's argument that the Apostles’ decisions were divinely sanctioned.</note> For two things were being claimed by the "Judaizers" <note>Early Christians who believed that converts to Christianity must follow the Law of Moses, including circumcision.</note>: first, the opinion of the Spirit expressed in the ancient oracles <note>The Old Testament scriptures.</note>; and second, the authority of the Apostles who were in Jerusalem. Both claims are denied here. It seemed one way to the Holy Spirit, who leads us into the true sense of the ancient oracles; and it seemed the same to us, for whom it is a matter of religion not to go against the Spirit. Therefore, they warn in verse 24 that they *had given no such command* <note>original Greek: ΟἷΣ Οὐ ΔΙΕΣΤΕΙΛΆΜΕΘΑ</note> to those thoughtless zealots of the Mosaic Law by which they were troubling the peace of the Churches.

II. We do not directly infer the perpetual infallibility of the Apostles from this passage alone; it is enough to show that nothing contrary to it can be inferred, and that this fact remains: what they decreed here and now, they decreed by the dictate of the Holy Spirit. Thus, that decree was to be received by the Church with the obedience of humble faith no less than any Prophetic oracle. And what reason is there for us to conclude that, regarding other dogmas of faith of equal or greater weight, they were less informed and directed by the Holy Spirit than they were concerning this **disputed question**? <note>original Greek: πρόβλημα — referring to the specific controversy of whether Gentile converts needed to follow Jewish law.</note> However, the infallibility of the Apostles arising from the Spirit’s direction is not to be shared with all the Elders and the entire Church of Jerusalem. For these others, having heard the dictate of the Spirit in and through the Apostles, offered their own consent, as was appropriate.

III. It is fitting for the **New Testament dispensation** <note>The "New Economy" or the era of the Gospel as opposed to the Old Testament Law.</note> that the Apostles do not always speak with that same rigor with which the Ancient Prophets spoke. Finally, no reason can be given why this phrase should be considered unworthy of a Divine oracle: *You will do well—that is, you will do a thing pleasing to God—to observe these things.* <note>Acts 15:29</note> A similar expression, as Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> himself notes, occurs elsewhere when dealing with things that are of Divine command, such as in Philippians 4:14 and 3 John verse 6. And there was a special reason why the letter was concluded in this way; namely, because it contained some things that were more a matter of prudent advice to be observed for a time <note>Referring to the temporary prohibitions on certain foods to avoid offending Jewish Christians.</note> than a universal commandment.

XXI. **Response I.** We ourselves have observed previously that the Holy Spirit did not reveal every truth to the Apostles all at once, but rather for the common good <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον</note> (1 Corinthians 12:7), only as far as the usefulness of the Church required. Since God himself refuted the error they had conceived regarding the Apostle, who would now step forth to defend their mistake?

XXII. Our opponent <note>Referring to Jean Le Clerc</note> continues. For: **I.** The concealment of a true and useful doctrine—one that ought to be preached in those circumstances and whose concealment causes others to stumble—is a human weakness that does not fit those you believe to be mere "organs of the Spirit." **II.** This way of acting used by Peter suggested the necessity of observing circumcision to the Gentiles no less than if he had taught it in words. **III.** It is probable that Peter and Barnabas believed this dissimulation was lawful for them, unless you prefer to say they acted wickedly against their own consciences. And thus, some "stumbling" must be acknowledged even in their understanding of doctrine.

For he had been taught this by the divine oracle in Acts 10:19, 20. He had also taught this to the people of Jerusalem in Acts 11.

Therefore, there was no error in any specific dogma <note>original: "dogmate"; here referring to a settled point of religious doctrine</note>. For he was not teaching anything different regarding this matter than he had previously. **II.** All of Peter's confusion concerned the circumstances of the act itself, where the guidance of prudence belongs. Prudence teaches us to "be all things to all people," even "to the weak as if weak" (1 Corinthians 9:20, 22). Peter believed this principle applied here, so as not to offend the circumcised <note>meaning Jewish Christians</note>, since he was their primary Apostle. Paul, on the other hand—more perceptively and more truly—judged that more scandal was born from this poorly timed accommodation. Therefore, this entire controversy was not about the **Doctrine of Christian Liberty**, but about its use in this specific time and place. In this, Paul perceived the rules of prudence better. We admit, therefore, Peter’s error here—not only in the deed itself, but also in his judgment—yet it was an error concerning a specific action, not concerning any head of doctrine. **III.** We do not attribute a "metaphysical infallibility" to the Apostles, nor do we believe they were mere "instruments of the Spirit" <note>original: "Organa Spiritus"</note> like a flute in the mouth or hand of a musician. Rather, we believe that whenever they taught, they were so clearly informed by the Holy Spirit that they never pushed forward an error in place of Gospel truth. Meanwhile, they also used their own intellect, judgment, meditation, and counsel; these faculties were not removed, but were holily and powerfully governed by the Holy Spirit. Having noted this before, we now repeat it.

These things are unworthy of any Christian; that he used an absurd and foolish excuse, if not a deceitful one: for even if he were ignorant that he was the high priest, he himself confessed that he was a magistrate. That he interpreted the mind of Moses poorly and against the Gospel, as if he had forbidden speaking evil of a magistrate in such a way that he permitted speaking evil of a private person: consequently, he suffered as an <term>evildoer <note>original: κακοποιὸν; a criminal or wrongdoer</note></term>, and finally betrayed the cause of the Gospel before everyone here. (1 Corinthians 4:12, 13): *being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it; being defamed, we entreat.* Can such lack of self-control and imprudence coexist with the Spirit of <term>power and of love and of a sound mind <note>original: δυνάμεως καὶ ἀγάπης καὶ σωφρονισμοῦ; referring to 2 Timothy 1:7</note></term>, which he claims for himself? <margin>XXVI. *He does not admit that he sinned in any way.*</margin>
XXVI. III. I am not unaware of how differently learned men interpret Paul’s defense <note>original: "Apologiam"; here meaning a formal legal or logical defense, not an admission of guilt</note>. It was a hard saying, indeed, but true. <term>Burden <note>original: משא (massa); a Hebrew term often used for a prophetic oracle or a "heavy" message of judgment</note></term>. *Grotius says well:* He uses the right of a prophet. For I. It is the role of prophets to freely rebuke not only leading men, but also Kings (1 Kings 18:18; 2 Kings 3:13; Isaiah 1:10, 23; Ezekiel 21:25). II. It is also their role to announce God’s judgments to the wicked (See Isaiah 22:17, 18; Jeremiah 22:18, 24, 28). The Apostles, however, were prophets, and more. Therefore, Paul rightly rebuked the man’s hypocrisy and did not indeed call down God’s judgments <note>meaning he did not wish for them out of malice</note>, but announced them. <term>God is about to strike you <note>original: Τύπτειν σε μέλλει; Paul's specific words to Ananias in Acts 23:3</note></term>. The outcome confirmed the prophecy. For, as *Grotius* observes, Ishmael son of Phabi was substituted as High Priest not long after this time, though it is uncertain whether Ananias died or was removed. Therefore, the origin of this speech was not the lack of self-control or anger of Paul, but the Prophetic Spirit. See a similar case in Acts 13:9-11. Nothing here is against the institution of the Gospel, but all is from Apostolic authority (2 Corinthians 10:2-6). Nothing is against the example of Christ, but according to it (Matthew 23:27).

Yet he had not sinned against it, since he was neither obliged to recognize Ananias as a Ruler, nor was his speech a slur: for it did not proceed from an evil mind, but from a better and higher principle. And thus this defense is wise, prudent, and holy; containing mysteries that, at that time and place, were not to be explained too clearly, lest he provoke their minds beyond the matter at hand. By this observation, all the <term>sophistications <note>clever but false or misleading arguments</note></term> of our author fall away.

XXX. I respond. 1. If there were any force to this argument, it would have to proceed from one who believes Christ was a mere man and a simple minister of God. I do not know, however, if <term>Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and biblical critic known for his skeptical views on the total inspiration of Scripture</note></term> has so far forgotten himself that he has brought his mind to openly profess that. We speak openly, having removed all <note>original Greek: "κρυπτοῖς τῆς αἰσχύνης"</note> *hidden things of shame*, and we recognize Christ not only as a Prophet, but as the Lord of the Prophets. And in this regard, He is infinitely greater than all the Prophets. Hebrews 3:3, 5. 2. Our opponent will not deny prophetic inspiration to the Prophets when they were engaged in their duty. Was it therefore permitted for them to speak in the same way and tone (as he says) in which Christ spoke? Certainly not. John 3:31, 34. God had reserved certain words to be spoken by Christ alone: <note>original Greek: "Ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι"</note> *Things which it is not lawful for a man to utter.* 2 Corinthians 12:4. Let the matter itself be weighed, which is manifest even without these testimonies to all those who, with us, acknowledge the eternal Deity of Christ. 3. The Apostles also sometimes spoke in such a way that they come very close to that phrasing of Christ’s which is full of authority. Galatians 5:2: <note>original Greek: "ἸΔΕ' ἘΓΩ' ΠΑῩΛΟΣ ΛΕ'ΓΩ ὙΜῖΝ"</note> *BEHOLD, I, PAUL, SAY TO YOU.*

Concerning certain things, an express command of the Lord had been heard long ago, such as regarding divorce. Compare Matthew 5:32; 15:7. Concerning other things, no command had existed until now. Of the former, Paul says, *not I say*, meaning "you are not hearing this from me for the first time," but *the Lord* said it long ago. Of the latter, *I say, not the Lord*, that is, Christ has commanded nothing on this matter so far. I am the first to set forth the mind of the Lord. Not, certainly, from his own reasoning alone, but by the instinct of Christ. For he did not lack <note>original Greek: "δοκιμὴ τοῦ λαλοῦντος ἐν αὐτῷ Χριστοῦ"</note> *proof of Christ speaking in him.* 2 Corinthians 13:3. Similarly in verse 25: *I have no command of the Lord.* That is to say, one expressed long ago that binds everyone universally. <note>original Greek: "Γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι"</note> *But I give my judgment*, that is, I suggest a counsel of prudence regarding what is expedient here and now. ->### ON THE PROPHETESSES.<-

<margin>
I. *Miriam holds the primary place among the prophetesses.*
</margin>
It has pleased the Supreme Being to adorn not only the male sex but also the female with the grace of Prophecy; for not only Prophets but also PROPHETESSES are praised in sacred history. It is now my pleasure to present a series of them, so that nothing is lacking from this work. The primary place among them is held by MIRIAM, the sister of Aaron and Moses, distinguished by the title of PROPHETESS in Exodus 15:20. That which is *Miriam* to the Hebrews is called *Mariam* <note>original Greek: Μαριάμ</note> by the Greeks and *Maria* <note>The English name Mary</note> by the Latins.

<margin>
II. *The etymology of that name.*
</margin>
II. There is much debate among the learned concerning the <term>etymology <note>the study of the origin and history of words</note></term> of this name, especially from the time when superstition and idolatry concerning the Mother of our Lord <note>The Virgin Mary</note> began to prevail. Because of this, even against all rules of grammar and the resisting spirit of the Hebrew language, many writers have carved various meanings out of this name which they believed should be attributed to their "Goddess" <note>A polemical reference to the Catholic veneration of the Virgin Mary, whom the Protestant author suggests is treated like a deity.</note>. Certain masters of the Roman Church have made themselves look ridiculous in this regard; there is no need for me to waste effort now in refuting their trifles. *Angelo Canini*, a man most skilled in Oriental literature, derives it from the root *rum* <note>original Hebrew: רום</note>, and therefore wishes it to signify *exalted, sublime, or eminent.* But that seems to me to be a somewhat far-fetched derivation, though *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius, a famous Flemish Protestant biblical scholar</note> does not reject it. *Gomarus* <note>Francis Gomarus, a Dutch theologian</note> fetches it from the word *meri* <note>original Hebrew: מרי</note>, meaning "rebellion," which, when joined with the suffix of the third person plural, makes *Miriam*, "their rebellion"; just as that complete word appears in Nehemiah 9:17. Others think of the root *marar* <note>original Hebrew: מרר</note>, from which comes *marah* <note>original Hebrew: מרה</note>, "bitter," and they claim she was so named because of bitterness. So says the author of the *Life of Moses*: "And her name was called Miriam, because at that time the Egyptians, the sons of Ham, began to make the lives of the children of Israel bitter." <note>original Hebrew: ותקרא שמה מרים כי בעת ההיא החלו המצרי' בני חם למרור חיי בני ישראל</note>. *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English Hebraist</note> joins both meanings. "The word," he says, "properly and openly indicates both the rebellion of the Jews and also their bitter affliction." They were punished greatly and harshly because of the sins of Israel in Egypt at the time when Miriam received this name. As far as I am concerned, everyone is free to judge such etymologies and the reasons for the names given as they wish. To me, if no other evidence is added from elsewhere, nothing seems more uncertain.

<margin>
III. *Why she is called the sister of Aaron.*
</margin>
III. This Mary is called the *sister of Aaron*. Why not *of Moses*? He answers: because Aaron was older and born immediately after Miriam. It can be added that she had lived more closely with him, in the same house or certainly the same neighborhood; whereas Moses spent his youth in the palace, removed from the company of his own people and regarded as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, and then was absent abroad for forty whole years among the Midianites. It could also have happened that Miriam and Aaron...

-># ON THE PROPHETESSES<-

<margin>I. Miriam holds the primary place among the prophetesses.</margin>
It has seemed good to the Supreme Power to adorn not only the male sex, but also the female sex <note>original: *sequiorem sexum*, literally "the following sex," a common early modern Latin expression for women</note> with the grace of Prophecy; for in sacred history, not only Prophets but also PROPHETESSES are praised. Now, so that nothing is missing from this work, I am pleased to present a list of them. Among these, the first place is held by MIRIAM, the sister of Aaron and Moses, who is distinguished with the title of PROPHETESS in Exodus 15:20. The name which is *Miriam* in Hebrew is *Mariam* <note>Greek: Μαριάμ</note> in Greek and *Maria* in Latin.

<margin>II. The etymology of her name.</margin>
II. There is much debate among the learned regarding the etymology <note>the study of the origins of words</note> of this name, especially since the time when superstition and idolatry concerning the Mother of our Lord grew strong. Because of this, many writers—ignoring all rules of grammar and the spirit of the Hebrew language—have carved many meanings out of this name which they believed should be attributed to their Saint. <note>original: *Divae suae*, a term the author uses to critique the high veneration of the Virgin Mary in the Roman Catholic Church</note> Certain masters of the Roman Church have shown themselves to be ridiculous in this regard, but I should not waste my effort now in refuting their trifles. *Angelus Caninius* <note>A 16th-century Italian linguist and scholar of Oriental languages</note>, a man most skilled in Oriental literature, derives the name from the root *rum* <note>Hebrew: רום</note>; therefore, he argues it means "exalted," "sublime," or "eminent." But that seems a bit far-fetched to me, though *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Protestant scholar of Hebrew</note> does not reject it. *Gomarus* <note>Francis Gomarus (1563–1641), a famous Dutch theologian</note> traces it from the word *meri* <note>Hebrew: מרי</note>, meaning "rebellion," which when joined with the plural suffix makes *Miryam* <note>Hebrew: מרים</note>, "their rebellion"; just as that complete word appears in Nehemiah 9:17. Others think of the root *marar* <note>Hebrew: מרר</note>, from which comes *marah*, "bitter," and they claim she was so named because of bitterness. This is the view of the author of the *Life of Moses*: "And her name was called Miriam, because at that time the Egyptians, the sons of Ham, began to make the lives of the children of Israel bitter." <note>original Hebrew: ותקרא שמה מרים כי בעת ההיא החלו המצריי׳ בני חם למרור חי׳ בני ישראל</note> *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an influential English Hebraist</note> combines both meanings. He says, "The word properly and clearly indicates both the rebellion of the Jews and also their bitter affliction." They were punished severely for the sins of Israel in Egypt at the time Miriam received this name. For my part, everyone is free to judge such etymologies and the reasons for given names as they please. To me, if no other evidence is added from elsewhere, nothing seems more uncertain.

<margin>III. Why she is called the sister of Aaron.</margin>
III. This Miriam <note>Latin text uses *Maria*</note> is called the "sister of Aaron." Why not the sister of "Moses"? He <note>The author likely refers to a specific commentator or the biblical text itself</note> answers: because Aaron was older and born immediately after Miriam. It can be added that she had lived more closely with him, in the same house or certainly in the same neighborhood; whereas Moses, removed from contact with his own people and regarded as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, spent his youth in the court, and then was away in a foreign land among the Midianites for forty entire years. BOOK I, CHAPTER XXIII.

...she might have been born of a different mother than Moses; for this reason, she was called the sister of Aaron rather than of Moses. Among the Rabbis of the Roman School <note>Likely referring to the Jewish community in Rome or scholars associated with that tradition</note>, there are those who gather from this that Miriam was an unmarried virgin, because she is identified by her brother rather than a husband. Yet that argument is quite weak and contrary to the opinion of the Hebrews, who do not doubt Miriam's marriage, as we shall soon understand: *Josephus* records that *Hur*, who is joined with Aaron in Exodus 24:14, was her husband.

<margin>VI. The name of Prophetess applies to her in the full force of the word.</margin>
IV. We must now chiefly consider the fact that she is called a <term>Prophetess</term> <note>Hebrew: *nebi'ah*</note>. This is not in the same sense as Isaiah's wife in Isaiah 8:3, who took this name from her husband; just as among the ancient Christians, the wife of a Bishop was called a *Bishopess* <note>original: *Episcopa*</note>, and the wife of a Presbyter a *Presbyteress* <note>original: *Presbytera*</note>. Rather, she is called so because the qualities proper to Prophets also applied to her. Those are said to "prophesy" who explain the mysteries of religion, who proclaim Divine praises under the impulse of the Spirit, who devote themselves to holy prayers, and who speak in the manner of the prophets. There is none of these things which does not fit Miriam. Yet even greater things must be considered here. It is one thing for some act of prophesying to be attributed to someone; it is another for them to be honored with the title of Prophet. Therefore, when we hear her called a Prophetess, it must be established that she was taught secret matters by an extraordinary inspiration of the Spirit, and that she taught the people of Israel what she had learned. God himself, in counting the benefits bestowed upon Israel, includes the fact that He gave them *Moses, Aaron, and Miriam* as teachers and leaders of the people in the desert (Micah 6:4). Nor could Miriam restrain herself from taking more spirit from this than was proper, saying to Moses along with Aaron: 
> *Has the Lord spoken only through Moses? Has he not also spoken through us?* (Numbers 12:2) 
And in this matter, she was not refuted by Moses or by God.

<margin>V. Her unjust quarrel with Moses.</margin>
V. But learn from this very thing how even the most brilliant lights are sometimes obscured by a dark cloud of imperfections. This same Miriam—this Prophetess, this leader of the Israelite people—indulging her passions too much and envying Moses, quarreled unjustly with him and drew her brother Aaron into sharing the same crime with her. A *Cushite* woman <note>Historically, "Cushite" usually refers to people from the region of Ethiopia or the upper Nile, but the author here argues for an Arabian location</note>, whom Moses had taken as his wife, gave the occasion or pretext for the dispute. It is believable that *Zipporah* is understood by this name; though she was actually a Midianite, she is called a *Cushite* here because the Midianites inhabited part of that region which the Sacred Scriptures call the land of *Cush*. The *Great Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer</note> has asserted with very probable arguments that this was not Ethiopia, but Arabia. But what was it about this Cushite woman that displeased them so much? There are those who believe...

### ON THE PROPHETESSES.

...that she <note>Likely referring to Zipporah, Moses' wife</note>, being proud of her marriage to such a great man as Moses was, demanded that she be preferred over Miriam—whom God had nevertheless placed ahead in the leadership of the people. It is a simpler explanation, however, that Miriam took offense at Moses’ marriage to a foreign woman and urged for a divorce, so that he might instead join himself to an Israelite woman.

<margin>VI. Jewish legends regarding the causes of the dispute.</margin>
VI. Here, the Hebrews have left us wonderful traditions, which smack more of the character of a carnal people than they approve themselves by any likelihood of truth. They weave a tale that Zipporah was present with Miriam when it was announced to them that Eldad and Medad <note>Two elders who received the spirit of prophecy while remaining in the camp; see Numbers 11</note> were prophesying in the camp; Zipporah is said to have remarked: *Woe to their wives; for once they have begun to prophesy, they will abandon their spouses, just as my husband abandoned me.* Miriam, being indignant and believing an injustice was being done to Zipporah—to whom the "marital debt" was not being paid—reported the matter to Aaron and rebuked Moses along with him. As is often the case in "women's matters," the woman pleaded the cause more fervently. Others say that Miriam was not indeed ignorant of this separation of the marriage bed before, but had hidden her feelings because she believed her brother was exhausted by the burden of governing the people. However, once he had obtained seventy colleagues to help him carry the weight of leadership, she judged this neglect of his wife to be intolerable. And to this they refer those words: *HAS THE LORD SPOKEN ONLY THROUGH MOSES?* <note>original Latin: "Tantunme per Mosen locutus est Dominus?"</note> *Is he so unique in his law of holiness that he has the right to abandon his wife? HAS HE NOT ALSO SPOKEN THROUGH US? Yet we do not break off our marriages for that reason, nor do we forget the mutual faithfulness we owe our spouses, even if they are not prophets. We are permitted to have communion with God without such a separation; therefore, such abstinence is not necessary for Moses if it causes injury to his wife.* But perhaps we have lingered too long in the smoke of these trifles.

<margin>VII. Miriam’s Leprosy.</margin>
VII. This grumbling so displeased Jehovah that, once Moses was vindicated, His anger burned against the disputants. He struck Miriam, the leader of this act, with a most heavy and foul leprosy. With this punishment, God avenged the contempt shown to Moses without any favoritism. From this example, and others like it, Paul impressed this warning upon his fellow Hebrews, which must also be engraved upon our own minds: Hebrews 12:25. *See that you do not refuse Him who speaks: For if those did not escape who refused Him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from Him who speaks from heaven.*

<margin>IX. Deborah:</margin>

Others prefer *Lappidoth* to be a descriptive title, so that she is called a “woman of splendors,” illuminated by Divine brilliance. Nor are there wanting those who interpret her as a “woman of lamps,” because she might have prepared lamps for use in the sanctuary. These are mere play and trifles. It is more credible that she was the wife of a certain Lappidoth, a man otherwise unknown.

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIII.

...[the commander] of his army, like some brute beast, should be so shamefully slaughtered; and that the most sacred laws of hospitality were violated; and sincerity and faith profaned by feigned kindness and a calculated, false smoothness of speech: in short, that this whole deed smells more of the spirit of a furious and treacherous woman than of an honorable and modest matron. <note>This opening paragraph summarizes the arguments of critics who found Jael’s deception of Sisera to be immoral or "unladylike" by the standards of the time.</note>

XV. However, the things done by Jael and praised by Deborah are not to be judged by the common law of humanity or alliance. Something singular, extraordinary, heroic, and divine must be recognized here, which surpasses the ordinary rules of what is honorable. The war on the part of the Israelites was just. Sisera was a public enemy: an oppressor of God’s people, already broken by Divine power, devoted to a curse, and proscribed by God. Having been made certain of this through the Spirit, Jael dared a great and memorable deed. Since she was a Kenite <note>A member of a nomadic tribe related to Moses’ father-in-law</note>, she indeed enjoyed peace with the King of Hazor; yet not every peace implies a treaty of friendship. It could be that the family of Heber, whose wife Jael was, had merely bought off harassment with a tribute. This Kenite woman was bound by more and tighter bonds of friendship to the Israelite people; it was permissible for her both to betray and to destroy their common enemy. Since this was lawful, it does not seem unlawful to use those means which were suitable for achieving that end: such as receiving him into her home, refreshing him with drink, inducing sleep, and many other things of that kind. In these things, there is no more fault than in other **stratagems** <note>original: "stratagematis"; tactical deceptions used in warfare</note>, which in military service are not only permitted but even praised. Jael indeed feigned something and concealed something; but this is not absolutely forbidden.

XVI. The chief difficulty lies in this: that these words seem hardly able to be cleared of the charge of lying: *Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not fear* <note>original: "diverte Domine mi, diverte ad me, ne timeto." This is Jael's invitation to Sisera in Judges 4:18.</note>. For it can hardly be understood otherwise than as the speech of someone promising safety. To tell the truth, I do not find a way to fully excuse it. It is the case with almost all human actions—even those performed at the prompting of the Spirit—that something of our own is easily added, and the impulse does not restrain itself carefully enough within those boundaries which the holiness of the Divine law has otherwise prescribed. By this, a **blemish** <note>original: "nævus," literally a mole or birthmark; used here to mean a moral imperfection</note> is indeed brought upon a good action, but its entire praise is not taken away. Therefore, that heroic spirit of Jael, surpassing her sex, could be praised by Deborah—a spirit by which, incited by God himself, she removed a proud enemy; even if in the whole undertaking of that action something may be found which is not entirely free from fault.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on famous prophetesses from history and scripture. # CONCERNING PROPHETESSES.

<margin>
XVII.
The story
of the Theban
Sphinx: was it
modeled on the
history of
Deborah?
</margin>
XVII. To some, it seems that the *Theban Sphinx* was modeled after the example of Deborah. The Sphinx, said to be a daughter of royal blood, was described as having the body of a *Lion* but the face of a *human*. The Boeotians <note>An ancient Greek people from the region of Boeotia</note> called her *Phix*; she is said to have sat upon Mount Phicion, where she wove together riddles and enigmas. Having been appointed as a judge of disputes regarding the succession of the kingdom, she punished those who lost their cases with death. Socrates <note>Likely Socrates of Rhodes, a later historian, rather than the famous philosopher</note> referred to her as *a prophetess uttering obscure oracles* <note>original Greek: χρησμολόγον δύσγνωσα μαντευομένην</note>. These details seem to bear a certain resemblance to the history of Deborah, such that they might be believed to be taken from it. For:
I. *Phix* is a Phoenician word with a Greek ending, derived from *Pikkeah* <note>original Hebrew: פקה</note>, meaning "one with open eyes," "wise," or "a seer." This word is found in Exodus 4:11 and 23:8. Both Deborah and the Sphinx earned their names because of their wisdom and sagacity.
II. Both lived upon a mountain.
III. Both were seers.
IV. Both were judges of disputes.
V. Both were equally powerful in wisdom and strength. This is the significance of the image of the *Lion* and the *human*. Clement of Alexandria, in his *Miscellanies, Book V*, says the Sphinx was a symbol of *strength combined with intellectual skill* <note>original Greek: ἀλκῆς τε μετὰ συνέσεως</note>.
VI. Both put many enemies to death. For the slaughter of the Canaanites under Deborah's leadership was recorded by the Phoenicians, in whose sight these deeds were performed, and this could have provided the occasion for the legends about the Sphinx's ferocity. Thus argue certain very learned men; however, if someone prefers to consider this a clever play of the mind <note>An intellectual exercise or imaginative theory rather than a hard fact</note>, they will not find me strongly opposing them. See, if you please, *Bochart’s Canaan, Book I, Chapter XVI*.

<margin>
XVIII.
Hannah’s 
prophecy
concerning
the Messiah.
</margin>
XVIII. I hasten now to Hannah, the mother of Samuel, whose song, recorded in 1 Samuel 2:1 and following, is no less elegant and eloquent than it is fertile with mystical meanings. Most learned men have explained it with subtle commentaries, which I do not have the time to examine now. This much certainly seems clear to me: the entire context of her speech is far too magnificent to be referred solely to her arguments with her rival Peninnah, or to the son granted to her by the Lord. To say nothing of the rest, it is obvious in verse 10 that an outstanding prophecy concerning Christ exists. For while she represented in her mind that miserable servitude which the Israelites suffered under the yoke of the Philistines—which is an image of a much harsher servitude under the power of sin and the Devil—she ascended in her thoughts to the Messiah King, who was to liberate the people and claim the kingdom and dominion over his own. Concerning him, she sings in these words:

> *Those who contend against the Lord shall be broken in pieces; against them he will thunder in the heavens. The Lord will judge the ends of the earth: for he will give strength to his King, and will exalt the horn of his Anointed.*
