### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>
XIX. A brief explanation of the paraphrase.
</margin>
XIX. Those who contend against Jehovah are all the enemies of the kingdom of God, who consult together against the Lord and *his Anointed* <note>original Latin: Unctum ejus</note> (Psalm 2:2). Specifically, these were those wicked Jews, the worst of all mortals, who were always stirring up new controversies against Christ and his disciples and inciting the minds of the Gentiles against them. To them, she denounces destruction (Compare Luke 19:27 and 20:16) and foretells that God will thunder from heaven against each of them—that is, he will demonstrate his wrath from heaven through terrible effects (Compare Psalm 50:3 and 97:3, 6). She adds that *Jehovah will judge the ends of the earth* by sending many plagues everywhere upon rebellious men, especially upon the inhabitants of the land of Israel (Matthew 24:7, 21 and 19:28). *He will give strength to his King*. In the time of Hannah, there was no king in Israel. But she had learned that the Messiah would be King, and she predicts that he will act prosperously with God's favor (Psalm 110:2 and 89:22). *And he will exalt the horn of his Anointed*. This is exactly the same sentiment found in Psalm 132:17, 18 and Luke 1:69 <note>In biblical language, the "horn" is a symbol of strength and salvation</note>.

<margin>
XX. Also applied to the Messiah by the Hebrews.
</margin>
XX. The Masters of the Hebrews <note>Jewish rabbis and scholars</note> also recognized a prophecy concerning the Messiah in these words. The *Chaldean* <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> intends that no one else is designated here but the one who, having triumphed over Magog—the last of the enemies—would reign. For thus he <term>paraphrases</term> <note>original Greek: παραφραζει</note>: <note>original Aramaic: יי יעביד פורענות מן הגוג וממשירית עממין חטופין דאתן עמיה מסיפי ארעא ויתן תוקפא למלכה וירבי מלכות משיחיה</note> *The Lord shall take vengeance upon Magog, and upon the army of rapacious nations who come with him from the ends of the earth; and he shall give strength to his King, and shall increase the Kingdom of his Messiah.* *Kimchi* <note>David Kimchi, a prominent medieval Jewish scholar</note> is also eloquent on this point: <note>original Hebrew: המלך הוא המשיח ואמרה חנה זה על דרך נבואה או דרך קבלה כי היתה קבלה אצלם כי עתיד להיות מלך בישראל וחתמה השירה הזאת בדברי המלך לפי שזכרה מפלת הרשעים והם אויבי ישראל ואמרה כי האל יתן עז למלך ישראל שיושעו ישראל על ידו מיד אויביהם</note> *This King is the Messiah. Hannah spoke these things through prophecy or through tradition. For there was a tradition among them that there was to be a king in Israel; and she sealed this song with words concerning this King, because she remembered the fall of the wicked, who are the enemies of Israel, and she said that God would give strength to the King of Israel, so that through his hand the Israelites might be saved from the hand of their enemies.*

<margin>
XXI. Huldah.
</margin>
XXI. But the name of <term>Huldah</term> the Prophetess is also great and memorable; she flourished during the reign of <term>Josiah</term>. Both her person and her prophecy are described in 2 Kings 22:14 and 2 Chronicles 34:22. Regarding her person, she was the wife of Shallum. Chaste marriage is so far from displeasing God that he blesses not only virgins, but also married women, whenever it pleases him, with his intimate communion and the virtue of prophecy. This Shallum, or perhaps his parent or grandfather, whose names are not the same...

# CONCERNING THE PROPHETESSES.

...are always depicted in literature, or perhaps he himself, following his father and grandfather, was the שומר הבגדים <term>keeper of the robes</term> <note>original Hebrew: shomer ha-begadim</note>. I believe these were the sacred robes used in the Temple, the custody of which was assigned to certain Priests. The Hebrews record that there were seven chambers at the seven gates of the Temple where the sacred vessels and garments were stored; they also say there were seven men to whom the care of these gates and chambers was committed. In later times, these men were called אמרכלין <term>Amarkalin</term> <note>officials or trustees of the Temple treasury</note>, or as others read, *Immarcalin*, who had under them three vicars known as גזברין <term>Gizbarin</term> <note>treasurers</note>. Regarding these, see *Lightfoot* on *The Temple Service*, Chapter 5, Sections 3 and 4. It appears that Shallum was among these officials.

<margin>
XXII. Her place of residence.
</margin>

XXII. Huldah lived in Jerusalem במשנה <gloss>in the second part</gloss> <note>often translated as the "Second Quarter" or "district"</note>. This is interpreted in various ways. Some apply it to the city itself. Jerusalem was divided into three parts: the *first* was the City of David on Mount Zion, where the royal palace stood; the *second* was adjacent to it on Mount Moriah, where the Temple was located; and the *third* was the outermost part. These scholars argue that Huldah's house was in that middle section. Others believe *Mishneh* was the proper name of a specific street or neighborhood in Jerusalem. There are also those who contend it was a place near the Temple where the learned gathered to debate and confer on the Law and its meaning, which later writers call a בית מדרש <term>Beth Midrash</term> <note>a House of Study</note>. For *Mishnah* refers to the tradition that interprets the Law. However, as with many ancient and obscure matters, nothing can be determined with certainty. I have observed that one of the Temple gates bore the name of Huldah. Whether this relates to our prophetess in some way, I confess I do not know. Whoever wishes may consult *l'Empereur* in his commentary on the *Middoth* <note>a treatise on Temple measurements</note>, pages 1 and 2. This much I know: she was held in such high esteem among her people that they record that no person, man or woman, was ever buried within the walls of Jerusalem—except for the House of David—save for her alone. See *Solomon Jarchi* <note>the medieval commentator Rashi</note> on 2 Kings 22.

<margin>
XXIII. The Prophecy.
</margin>

XXIII. Certainly, she was a prophetess of such great dignity that King Josiah, anxious about his own fate and that of the kingdom, sent to inquire of her. To the kingdom, she predicted destruction, because they had forsaken Jehovah and burned incense to foreign gods. But to the King, because his heart had been softened upon hearing the words of the Law, and because he had torn his clothes and wept before Jehovah, she ordered these things to be announced:

> Therefore, says Jehovah, behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace, so that your eyes shall not see all the evil that I am about to bring upon this place.

<margin>
XXIV. Did it match the outcome?
</margin>

XXIV. The first part of the prophecy, which concerns the kingdom, presents no difficulty. However, the outcome does not seem to correspond entirely to the second part. For the prosperity and piety of the King ended in a mournful death...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIII.

...was concluded. Pharaoh Necho, the King of Egypt, set out with his forces against Carchemish, a town situated on the Euphrates. Josiah met him with a chosen band of Judeans, threatening war. Necho sent messengers to him, saying, *“What have I to do with you, King of Judah? I have not come against you, but against the house with which I am at war. God has commanded me to make haste. Stop interfering with God, who is with me, lest He destroy you.”* <note>original Latin: "quid mihi tecum, Rex Judææ? In te non sum profectus, sed domum cum qua mihi bellum est..." This exchange is recorded in 2 Chronicles 35:21.</note> Josiah refused to obey this saving warning—which truly was from God, though we do not know by what means it was revealed to Necho. Battle was joined in the valley of Megiddo, where Josiah fell from a wound. Carried to Jerusalem in the "second chariot" <note>A spare or secondary royal carriage often used for transport rather than combat.</note> which he had, he was laid in the tomb of his ancestors, with all Israel and Judah mourning; the prophet Jeremiah also composed a lamentation along with other prophets. Can one who dies by such a sad fate truly be said to *“be gathered to his grave in peace”*?

XXV. Yet we must distinguish between the "private peace" of the king, which he himself disturbed by a reckless war, and the "public peace" of the kingdom. The Prophetess <note>Huldah</note> had promised the latter, not the former. This is shown by the following words: *“lest your eyes see the evil which I am about to bring upon this place.”* Often, a timely death is a blessing, even if it is joined with some bitterness. On this subject, the poet *Juvenal* sang elegantly in his *Tenth Satire*:

> *Priam would have gone to the shades of Assaracus <note>An ancestor of the Trojan royal house.</note> with Troy still safe,*
> *With great solemnity, with Hector carrying the funeral bier*
> *And on the shoulders of his remaining brothers, amid*
> *The tears of the Trojan women, as Cassandra began*
> *To let out the first wails of mourning, and Polyxena tore her cloak,*
> *If only he had died at a different time, before*
> *Paris had begun to build his daring ships.*
> *What, then, did his long life bring him? He saw everything*
> *Overturned, and Asia falling by fire and the sword.*
> <note>original: "Incolumi Troja Priamus venisset ad umbras..." This passage from the Roman satirist Juvenal argues that King Priam would have been happier dying before the Trojan War destroyed his city and family.</note>

God’s Providence acted so that Josiah would not see similar things in his own kingdom; he fell in war, yet amidst the profuse tears of his people, he was laid in the royal tombs of his ancestors. And thus, the prophecy of Huldah maintained its truth.

<margin>
XXVI.
Mary,
Mother of
the Lord.
</margin>
XXVI. When we come to the records of the New Covenant, among all other women, MARY, the mother of the Lord, raises her head immensely high. How the Angel Gabriel appeared to her, foretelling the most joyful conception and the saving birth of the Son of God, is a matter well known to everyone. No less celebrated by the mouths of all is the song with which she, moved by the Spirit, celebrated the praises of God, the Best and Greatest. If this song is compared with that of Hannah <note>The mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 2), whose song shares themes and structure with Mary's Magnificat.</note>, a very great affinity and a most delightful harmony will be revealed to the observer.

# ON PROPHETESSES.

<margin>XXVII. Elizabeth her kinswoman.</margin>
XXVII. Nor should we pass over ELIZABETH, who, with the same Spirit as her teacher, recognized and proclaimed the Lord before He was even born, while His mother, being pregnant, was visiting her. Although this Elizabeth was "of the daughters of Aaron" <margin>Luke 1:5, 36.</margin> she is nevertheless called a relative of Mary in the same chapter, verse 36—and Mary is known to have been from the tribe of Judah. In this matter, there is no contradiction. For nothing prevents Mary’s mother from having been of the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron; indeed, there are some among the ancient writers who record that she was Elizabeth’s sister. It is also possible that Elizabeth’s mother or grandmother was of the tribe of Judah, and thus related to Mary’s father by a close blood-relationship, even if her own father or grandfather was of the tribe of Levi. For a family, according to the very well-known Jewish genealogical rule, is reckoned from the father, not from the mother. 

As for the objection some raise—that it was forbidden for Israelites to marry outside of their own tribe—this is an unfounded assumption; at the very least, it was not a universal law. We find no such prohibition in the sacred records. In fact, there are examples to the contrary. Aaron the Levite married the daughter of Amminadab, the sister of Nahshon <note>original Latin: "filiam Aminadabi, sororem Nahessonis." This marriage linked the priestly line with the princely line of Judah.</note>, who was a prince of the sons of Judah (Exodus 6:22; 1 Chronicles 2:10). If you argue that this happened before the giving of the Law, here is another example from after the Law: Jehoiada the Priest—and consequently a Levite and a descendant of Aaron—took as his wife the daughter of King Jehoram, who was of the tribe of Judah and the House of David (2 Chronicles 22:11). If you insist that more was allowed to the Priests and Levites than to the other tribes, I will not demand to see the documents of such a "privilege" (though I could by right), but I will simply point out that this is enough to resolve the difficulty we are discussing. For, under this hypothesis, Elizabeth’s father, a descendant of Aaron, could have taken a wife from the family of David, and thus she would be a relative to Mary’s parents. 

But we see the same thing in other tribes as well. Certainly David, a man of Judah, had as a wife the daughter of Saul, a Benjamite. No law to the contrary is found. For Numbers 36:6 is a determination for the specific case of <term>heiress-daughters</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπικλήροις (epiklerois). These were daughters who inherited their father's estate because there were no sons.</note> to whom the entire inheritance passed because the male line had died out. Their marriages were restricted not only to their own tribe, but to men of their own family, to keep the land within the clan. Such a specific ruling confirms general freedom of marriage rather than removing it. Furthermore, it is not unlikely that Mary herself was such an <term>heiress-daughter</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπίκληρον (epikleron).</note>, and for that reason she was betrothed to Joseph as her nearest kinsman.

<margin>XXVIII. Anna, daughter of Phanuel.</margin>
XXVIII. Furthermore, ANNA, DAUGHTER OF PHANUEL, of the tribe of Asher, is explicitly honored with the title of Prophetess in Luke 2:36. In her history, several things occur which, in our observation...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the lineages of New Testament figures, transitioning from Elizabeth to Anna the Prophetess. It explains the etymology of her name and her family’s origins in the tribe of Asher, refuting the idea that no prophets could come from Galilee.</meta>

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIII.

...are worthy of our attention. In the name of *Anna*, there is the meaning of *grace*; in *Phanuel*, the *sight of God*; and in *Asher*, the meaning of *blessedness* <note>original Latin: "In Annæ vocabulo, gratiæ, in Phanuelis, conspecti Dei, in Afer, beatitudinis significatio est." The author is using the Hebrew etymologies of these names to highlight their spiritual significance.</note>. And truly, among the many blessings that flowed into her from the fountain of Divine grace, this is the greatest: that she saw *God* clothed in human flesh face to face. In that vision, she found the summit and the very essence of *blessedness*.

<margin>XXIX. From the tribe of Asher in Galilee.</margin>
XXIX. But how was someone from the tribe of *Asher* living in *Jerusalem*? Were the genealogies of the tribes scattered by the Assyrian captivity actually preserved? And did those people return to their homeland? They certainly returned, as many as wished to do so; *for by the decree of Cyrus, the opportunity to return was granted to all who were of the people of God* <note>See 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–4; and Ezra 7:13.</note>. It is indeed believable that the Israelites of the northern kingdom lost their public genealogical records, which were kept in the Archives—unlike the Jews of the southern kingdom, whose genealogical books were maintained until their return to the land and beyond, as seen in the books of Ezra, Nehemiah, and the first book of Chronicles. However, this did not prevent many Israelites from knowing which tribe they belonged to through private family records. Thus, it is well known that the Apostle *Paul* was of the tribe of Benjamin, and this *Anna* of ours was of the tribe of *Asher*. Yet they were perhaps unable to produce an uninterrupted record of their kin from the public catalogs. Perhaps even Anna, although she knew she was from the tribe of *Asher*, could not show the exact line of descent through sons and grandsons in a straight line from the root of her tribe. For this reason, after the return from the Babylonian captivity, the division of the land was handled differently for the ten northern tribes than it was for the Jews of the south. To the latter, their ancestral homes and seats were assigned because their family trees were well known. This could not be done for the former. Those who were known to be from the tribe of Zebulun were permitted to live in the ancient territory of Zebulun, and so it was for the others. However, the distribution of property among them was by no means as accurate as it had been in the past. I have discussed this matter more diligently in Chapter 5 of my work *On the Decapolis* <note>original Latin: "Decaphyli."</note>. It is not without purpose that we are reminded that Anna arose from the tribe of *Asher*. From this, it is clear she was a *Galilean*, for the *Asherites* occupied part of *Galilee*. And thus, once again, the observation of the Pharisees—that *no Prophet ever arose from Galilee*—is proven false <note>John 7:52.</note>.

<margin>XXX. The Prophetess.</margin>
XXX. For indeed, *Anna* was both a *Galilean* and a *Prophetess*. Scholars debate whether this title should be understood in a loose or a strict sense. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> suggests it denotes *a woman who was occasionally visited by the Holy Spirit*. *Others*, he says, *had formerly been Prophetesses by ordinary office, such as Deborah; but that kind of Prophet in either sex had ceased by that time*. <meta>This page continues from page 292, completing a sentence regarding a counter-argument about the cessation of prophecy. It focuses on Anna the Prophetess, her lifestyle as a "holy widow," and the linguistic roots of her service in the Temple.</meta>

### ON THE PROPHETESSES.

<sig>Oo 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: with fastings.</meta>

...contends to the contrary, that prophecy had indeed ceased for approximately four centuries, but began to flourish again at the dawn of the Gospel. Our subject, Anna, came from her native soil in the territory of Asher to Jerusalem, partly as one *devoted* <note>original: *devotam*</note> to God so that she might more readily find time for prayer in the Temple, and partly as a *prophetess*, to fulfill that office in the capital city. This view seems supported by the title of *Prophetess*, which refers not just to an occasional act but to a formal office, and by the fact that in verse 38 she is said to have spoken about Christ to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.

<margin>XXXI. A widow who never remarried.</margin>
XXXI. It was also among her praises that she was a widow of eighty-four years, having lived with her husband for only seven years. It has been considered a great honor for a woman among almost all nations not to seek a second marriage, so that she might not seem to have *loved the state of marriage more than her husband*; a sentiment Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) who wrote about the customs of the Germanic tribes.</note> recorded regarding the Germans. The early Christians, although they could not show that remarrying was prohibited by any decree of Christ, nevertheless discouraged it. For this reason, presbyters <note>Early church leaders or elders.</note> did not wish to be present at the celebration of second marriages, lest they seem to approve of them.

<margin>XXXII. Constant in the Temple.</margin>
XXXII. But her extraordinary piety surpassed all other praises: *she did not depart from the temple, worshipping God with fastings and prayers, day and night*. This too must be explained from Hebrew antiquity. In Exodus 38:8, women are praised <term>who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting <note>Hebrew: *ha-tsaba’oth asher tsaba’u pethach ohel mo‘ed*. This refers to women who served or "processed" in an organized fashion at the entrance of the sacred tent.</note></term>. The Greeks translate this as: *the women who fasted, who fasted by the doors of the tabernacle of witness* <note>original Greek: τὰς νηστεύσασας, αἳ ἐνήστευσαν παρὰ τὰς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς τοῦ μαρτυρίου.</note>. Junius <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a prominent Reformed theologian and biblical scholar.</note> translates it as: *the women coming together in troops, who assembled in troops at the door of the tent of meeting*. A similar expression appears in 1 Samuel 2:22, *the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting*. The Greeks there say: *those standing by the doors of the tabernacle of witness*. Junius, as before: *the women who assembled in troops at the doors of the tent of meeting*. 

It could also be aptly translated as: *observing the appointed times*, for the word <term>tsaba <note>Hebrew: צבא. Usually meaning "host" or "army," it also refers to a "waiting" or "service" in a religious context.</note></term> signifies both an "organized troop" and a "station," or the "fixed turns of service." As in Numbers 8:25, *and he shall return from the sequence of the service* <note>Hebrew: *ve-shub mi-tsaba ha-‘abodah*. This describes the retirement of Levites from their organized duties.</note>. This does not mean that such women performed some official priestly duty in the temple; rather, their <term>liturgy <note>Greek: *leitourgia* (λειτουργία), meaning public service or religious duty.</note></term> consisted of fastings and prayers—at least, this was the greatest part of their service. And this is perhaps the reason why the Greeks called these "serving women" *those who fasted* <note>Greek: τὰς νηστεύσασας</note>, using a more liberal interpretation that explained the custom and ancient practice rather than the literal force of the word. These matrons did this not perpetually (which the management of a household would not allow), but at fixed times. Yet widows were able to do more than married women; being freed from such domestic cares, they were permitted to continue their *ministry*, so that they *did not depart from the temple, devoting themselves to prayers and fastings*.

BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIII.

...with fastings. Our Anna was of this sort. However, this is to be understood reasonably, allowing for a rhetorical exaggeration <note>original: *hyperbole*</note>. For due to the necessities of nature, the need to take food, and other duties of social life, she had to leave the temple at times. It is noted only that she was there very frequently and with the greatest persistence. Thus Aaron and his sons are commanded in Leviticus 10:7:

> *Do not go out from the door of the tabernacle of meeting, lest you die.*

And Luke says of the Apostles in his Gospel, 24:53:

> *And they were <note>original Greek: διὰ παντὸς (dia pantos)</note> at all times in the temple, praising and blessing God.*

Unless perhaps Anna possessed some unique privilege, whereby a room in the temple was granted to her as a Prophetess to live in. For that there were rooms of this kind around the temple, which it was lawful for women also to inhabit, is shown by the history of Joash, who was rescued from the fury of Athaliah: whom Jehoshabeath, the wife of the High Priest Jehoiada, hid with his nurse in a bedroom, so that he remained hidden in the house of God for six years. 2 Chronicles 22:11, 12.

<margin>XXXIII. The four prophesying daughters of Philip.</margin>
XXXIII. **THE FOUR DAUGHTERS OF PHILIP THE EVANGELIST** close the ranks: who were virgins who prophesied. Acts 21:8, 9. In my opinion, they were gifted not only in the singing of divine praises and in remarkable skill for interpreting the Scriptures, but also with the ability to predict the future. For it pleased God to ennoble the beginnings of the Gospel in this way: so that the truth of that remarkable promise might be established by every means:

> **YOUR DAUGHTERS ALSO SHALL PROPHESY; AND UPON MY HANDMAIDENS I WILL POUR OUT MY SPIRIT IN THOSE DAYS, AND THEY SHALL PROPHESY.**

Acts 2:17, 18.

<margin>I. Whether the gift of Prophecy, and the Prophetic office, still last in the Church?</margin>
Hitherto we have woven together the catalog of Prophets of both sexes, as far as it was permitted to follow the guidance of the sacred writings. It remains now to be asked whether, after the departure of the Apostles from the earth, the gift of prophecy and the prophetic office ceased in the Christian Church; or whether, having continued for some centuries, they gradually failed; or finally, whether they still last—though perhaps more rarely—and will last in the Church until the end of the age?

<margin>II. Testimonies of the Fathers concerning their own age. Of Justin.</margin>
II. If we consult the ancient teachers of the Christian religion, many of them, and the most weighty, testify that the faculty of Prophecy still flourished in their own age. They do this not only in passing and perfunctorily, but also when they are disputing with their sharpest adversaries, whom it would have been most difficult to deceive <note>original: *os oblinere*, literally "to smear the mouth," a Latin idiom meaning to trick or silence someone</note>. JUSTIN, the Philosopher and Martyr, in the dialogue which he held for two days with Trypho the Jew, believed that this point should not be omitted by him. For he speaks thus on page 308 of the recent Cologne edition: <note>original Greek: Παρὰ γὰρ ἡμῖν καὶ μέχρι νῦν προφητικὰ χαρίσματά ἐστιν. ἐξ ὧ δ καὶ αὐτοὶ συν-</note> *“For among us even until now there are prophetic gifts; from which you yourselves ought to understand...”*

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.

"...you ought to know that the things which were formerly in your race <note>referring to the Jewish people</note> have been transferred to us." <note>original Greek: "νιέναι ὀφείλετε, ὅτι τὰ πάλαι ἐν τῷ γένει ὑμῶν εἰς ἡμᾶς μετετέθη"</note>. For among us, even until now, prophetic gifts still exist; from which you also ought to understand that those things which were once in your race have been transferred to us. Eusebius also noted this passage in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, Chapter XVIII. Where he says of Justin: "He writes that even until his time, <term>prophetic charismata</term> <note>spiritual gifts or divinely inspired powers</note> shone forth in the Church." <note>original Greek: "γράφει δὲ ὡς ὅτι μέχρι καὶ αὐτοῦ χαρίσματα προφητικὰ διέλαμπεν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας"</note>. Indeed, he writes that the gifts of prophecy still flourished in the Church during his own age.

<margin>III. Of the Gallic Churches under Antoninus Verus.</margin>
III. We owe to the same Eusebius a large part of the Letter which the Churches in Gaul <note>modern-day France</note> sent to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia concerning the deeds of their martyrs under the Emperor Antoninus Verus. Something must be excerpted from that Letter which pertains to our subject. It goes as follows: A certain Alcibiades, one of the number of those martyrs, followed a hard and austere way of life; admitting no food at all, he was accustomed to live only on bread and water. When he was placed in prison and wished to maintain the same way of living, it was revealed to Attalus—after the first combat he had completed in the Amphitheatre—that Alcibiades was not doing rightly or in proper order by refusing to use the creatures of God <note>i.e., food</note> and thus becoming an example of a stumbling block to others. Alcibiades therefore obeyed, and thereafter began to use all foods indiscriminately, giving thanks to God. Having narrated these things, the Gallic Brothers add: "For they were not unvisited by the grace of God, but the Holy Spirit was their counselor." <note>original Greek: "Οὐ γὰρ ἀνεπίσκεπτοι χάριτος Θεοῦ ἦσαν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἦν σύμβολον αὐτοῖς"</note>. For Divine grace had not deprived them of its presence, but they had the Holy Spirit as their advisor. Book V, Chapter III.

<margin>IV. Of Miltiades.</margin>
IV. Miltiades <note>an early Christian apologist</note>, in the same Eusebius, Book V, Chapter XVIII, enumerating the prophets of the New Testament—Agabus, Silas, and the daughters of Philip—adds Ammia of Philadelphia, Quadratus, and several others; subjoining this universal sentiment: "For the Apostle <note>likely referring to Paul</note> deems it necessary that the prophetic gift should exist in the whole Church until the final coming." <note>original Greek: "δεῖν γὰρ εἶναι τὸ προφητικὸν χάρισμα ἐν πάσῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ μέχρι τῆς τελείας παρουσίας ὁ Ἀπόστολος ἀξιοῖ"</note>. Indeed, the Apostle is the authority that the gift of prophecy ought to remain in every Church until the very last advent of the Lord.

<margin>V. Of Origen.</margin>
V. Concerning his own time, Origen writes as follows in Book I of *Against Celsus*, pages 34 and 35: "And even traces of that Holy Spirit, which was seen in the form of a dove, are still preserved among Christians. They cast out demons, perform many healings, and see certain things regarding the future according to the will of the Word. And even if Celsus—or the Jew whom he introduced—mocks what is about to be said, it shall nevertheless be said: that many, as if against their own will, have come to Christianity, some spirit having suddenly turned their mind from hating the Word to being willing to die for it, by appearing to them in a vision, whether awake or in a dream. For we have recorded many such things which, if we were to write them down..."

# ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES

> <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸι αὑτοῖς παρατυχόντες..."</note> If they themselves were present and saw it, we would be a laughingstock to the unbelievers, as if we ourselves were inventing these things just as they suspect others do. But God is witness to our conscience, that we wish to establish the divine teaching of Jesus not through false reports, but through some various working of power.

Indeed, even today, traces of that Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove, are preserved among Christians; they cast out demons, perform many healings, and foresee future things by the will of God. Celsus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and critic of Christianity</note> may mock what is said, or the Jew introduced by him in his writing may mock it, yet it shall be said nonetheless: many were drawn to the Christian religion almost against their will, a certain spirit suddenly changing their intellect from the hatred they held toward the Word, so that by His grace they did not hesitate to meet death after visions were offered to them, whether while sleeping or awake. **FOR WE HAVE SEEN MANY SUCH THINGS**, which if we were merely to recount **WHAT HAPPENED IN OUR OWN PRESENCE**, the unbelievers would burst into laughter, thinking that we, like those they already suspect, were making things up. **BUT GOD IS WITNESS TO OUR CONSCIENCE** that I endeavor to commend the Divine Teaching of Jesus not with false little stories, but with various examples of proven effectiveness. This is surely the clearest testimony of prophecy still lasting in the Church.

<margin>VI. Of Cyprian: concerning himself.</margin>
VI. At the same time Origen lived, **CYPRIAN** <note>Bishop of Carthage and a major Church Father, d. 258 AD</note> also lived, who in his 11th Letter of the 6th Book (according to the order of the Oxford Edition; number 7 in Pamelius’s edition; or Book 4, Letter 4 in Erasmus’s edition), which is addressed to the Priests and Deacons, records several of his own visions. Although the first of these contained nothing extraordinary that any Christian might not easily know from Scripture, he nevertheless said he felt compelled to share it with the brothers. For he says:
> For you ought to know what most persuaded and compelled me to write these letters to you (just as the Lord deigns to show and reveal): it was said in a vision, "Ask and you shall receive."

Then after that, a command was given to the standing people, that they should ask for certain designated persons. In their asking, however, there were discordant voices and differing wills, and this greatly displeased Him who had commanded them to ask. He also adds a second vision concerning a net-fighter <term>retiarius</term> <note>A type of Roman gladiator who fought with a net and trident, here used as a symbolic figure in a dream</note>. For he says, that too was shown:
> that a father of a family was sitting, with a youth sitting at his right hand; this youth was anxious and somewhat sorrowful with a kind of indignation, sitting with his cheek resting on his hand, with a mournful face. But another, standing on the left side, carried a net, which he threatened to cast so that he might catch the surrounding people. And when the one who saw it wondered what this might be, it was told to him: the youth sitting at the right was saddened and grieved because his commands were not being observed; but the one on the left rejoiced, because an opportunity was being given to him by the father of the family for power...

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.

...to take the opportunity for raging. **Cyprian** <note>Bishop of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), a major figure in early Latin Christianity</note> himself provides the explanation of the vision, so that we might not remain in doubt. *And we saw fulfilled,* he says, *what had been shown: that while we despise the Lord’s precepts, and do not keep the saving commands of the law given to us, the enemy received the power of doing harm, and covered with the cast of a net those who were poorly armed and less cautious for resisting.* <note>original Latin: "Et vidimus impletum... jactu retis operiret."</note> Indeed, that same letter relates even a third vision concerning the imminent liberation of the Church in these words: *Finally, to his smallest servant—even though he is beset by many sins and is unworthy of His regard—He nevertheless deigned to command, out of His goodness toward us: "Tell him," He said, "to be secure, for peace is coming; but because there is a short delay in the meantime, there are still some who remain to be tested."*

In the history of every age, almost infinite examples are found of such revelations made to martyrs; if I wished to spend effort collecting them, I would have to write a massive volume.

<margin>VIII. Gregory Thaumaturgus.</margin>
VIII. **Gregory** was a student of Origen; he was given the title **Thaumaturgus** <note>from the Greek for "Wonder-worker"</note> because of the miraculous works he is said to have performed. **Phadimus**, then the Bishop of the Church of Amasea, practically compelled him into the Bishopric of the Church of Neocaesarea. Phadimus was a man "to whom there was a certain foreknowing power from God by the Holy Spirit." <note>original Greek: "ᾧ θεόθεν ἐξ ἁγίου πνεύματος προγνωστική τις δύναμις ἦν."</note> As **Gregory of Nyssa** <note>A 4th-century Bishop and theologian who wrote a life of Gregory Thaumaturgus</note> attests, there was within him a certain divine power of foreseeing the future granted by the Holy Spirit. After accepting the Bishopric, Gregory was anxious in mind and conflicted over which path he should most preferably walk, turning the matter over for a long time. While keeping a night-long vigil over these cares, it is said that someone clearly appeared to him in human form, with an elderly face and shape, reflecting a certain venerable, sacred, and Divine beauty in the grace and composition of his clothing; he carried a great power in the grace of his countenance and the arrangement of his figure. He announced that he had appeared to Gregory by Divine command so that the truth of the pious faith might be revealed. Stretching out his finger, he showed him another image in the form of a woman, greater and more venerable than the human condition allows. At the same time, a light shone forth—though the night was dark—along with those who appeared...

Shall I not place him with the Apostles and Prophets—a man who lived in the same spirit as they, and who followed the footsteps of the Saints throughout his whole life, and who maintained the vigor of Gospel living as long as he lived? Indeed, I would say this: we would surely do an injustice to the truth if we did not count that soul among those who are joined to God. He shone forth like a distinguished and great lamp in the Church of God, and through the help of the Spirit, he held a terror against the power of demons. For he had received such grace for the "obedience of faith among the nations" <note>A reference to Romans 1:5</note> that, having started with no more than seventeen Christians, he joined the entire population—both urban and rural—to God through knowledge. He even turned the courses of rivers in a different direction, commanding them in the great name of Christ, and he dried up a marsh that was providing a cause for war between greedy brothers. INDEED, HIS PREDICTIONS OF THE FUTURE ARE SUCH THAT HE IS IN NO WAY INFERIOR TO THE OTHER PROPHETS. But it would be altogether too long to review the miracles of this man, who, because of the excellence of the gifts which the Spirit worked in him—in every virtue, sign, and wonder—was called **ANOTHER MOSES** <note>original: "ALTER MOYSES"</note> even by the enemies of the truth themselves.

<margin>
XI. Theodoret on his own time.
</margin>

XI. <margin>
XII. Joel seems to have promised a perpetual gift of prophecy to the Church, in the opinion of some.
</margin>

XII. Indeed, there is no lack of pious and learned men who believe that the gift of prophecy was promised by God to the Church for every age. In this matter, they especially urge the prophecy of Joel, cited by Peter in *Acts 2:16, 17, 18*: *This is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: "And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. And indeed upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out my spirit, and they shall prophesy."* Note I: Visions, dreams, and prophecies are promised here, arising from the operation of the Spirit being poured out abundantly. II: These prophecies are to be understood as extraordinary revelations, such as happened to the Apostles and were frequent in the primitive Church, as is generally admitted. For Peter explains that prophecy by those things which had happened to them on the day of Pentecost. III: Yet something more is promised, or at least something different from what was granted to the Apostles.

-># ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES<-

For here exists a promise of visions and dreams. In that outpouring of the Holy Spirit with which the Apostles were gifted, there were not dreams or visions, but a more sublime—that is, an internal—illumination, by which they were made knowledgeable of many languages and the deepest mysteries in a single moment. Therefore, the fulfillment of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinii"</note> extends further, so that the Holy Spirit might reveal mysteries in the New Testament through dreams and visions as well. IV. This promise was made for "the last times." Do we not know that "the last times" designates the entire course of the Gospel? V. The outpouring of the Spirit *upon all flesh* extends to the final day of judgment, as seen in verse 20. VI. Communion with this Spirit is promised to all those far in the future. Verse 39: *For the promise is made to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off, whomever the Lord our God shall call.*

<margin>XIII. What experience is believed to have proved up to our own age.</margin>
XIII. Consistent with this prophetic text, a catalogue of visions, revelations, divine dreams, and prophecies can be woven through all the centuries of the Church. Our venerable VOETIUS <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a Dutch Reformed theologian known for his immense learning</note> contributed much to this subject from the richest storehouse of his immense reading. *Select Disputations, Part II, pages 1055 and following.* And in this our own age, there have been figures like *Drabitius, Kotter, and Paniatovia* <note>Mikuláš Drabík, Christoph Kotter, and Christina Poniatovia were 17th-century visionaries whose "Lux in Tenebris" prophecies were widely debated</note>, who were held as distinguished prophets by men of the greatest weight, even after a serious and accurate examination of the facts. I say nothing for now of that wonderful dispensation of the Divine Spirit which is said to have happened to certain ministers of the Gospel and other exceptionally pious men in Scotland; or of those raptures and ecstasies in which, very recently in France, boys and girls are recorded to have spoken things that were marvelous and almost beyond belief <note>A reference to the "French Prophets" or Camisards, a Huguenot group in the Cévennes known for ecstatic prophecy around 1688</note>. Of these, the most learned and celebrated JURIU <note>Pierre Jurieu (1637–1713), a prominent French Protestant theologian who defended the authenticity of these modern prophecies</note> showed himself to be a most fierce defender.

<margin>XIV. It does not seem entirely deniable that the gift of Prophecy flourished until the third or fourth century.</margin>
XIV. But however much confidence we see in many things being narrated, I do not think it a sin to subject them to a more accurate examination. My view is this: God, the Best and Greatest, certainly granted Prophets to the Church at the beginning of the Gospel, who were moved by His Spirit in a singular way. Together with the Apostles, and even for some time after their departure from the earth, they watched over the propagation of the saving doctrine and confirmed their mission with wonders: for the nature of those times seemed to require this. Nor do I deny that such distinguished men of God existed even in the third and fourth centuries of the Christian era; for it would be harsh to strip all credibility from the pious Fathers <note>The early Christian writers and leaders of the first few centuries</note> who constantly narrated such things about the men of their own age and acquaintance.

XV. Yet I do not think it necessary, for that reason, to accept everything without distinction

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>
What is narrated by the Church Fathers is not to be admitted indiscriminately.
</margin>
...we should not admit everything. The style of most of the Church Fathers <term>Patres; the influential early Christian theologians and bishops of the first several centuries</term>, being adapted to a declamatory <note>original: "declamatorium," referring to a rhetorical style intended for public performance rather than strict historical accuracy</note> way of speaking, overflows with hyperbolic exaggerations. Unless these are assisted by a more charitable interpretation, they do not present a just and true idea of events to the mind. Nor should it be hidden that quite a few of the Fathers suffered from excessive credulity; they imprudently seized upon, and even more imprudently narrated—in that grand style of speaking to which they were accustomed—things that they could have known were not sufficiently investigated, if only they had chosen to attend to them with better judgment. No one is ignorant of this, unless they are a stranger to reading the Fathers, or are endowed with the same credulity as they were. Furthermore, because men were so greatly pleased with themselves regarding visions and apparitions, they easily persuaded themselves that things proceeded from an extraordinary operation of the Divine Spirit which could have actually arisen from a powerful and fixed imagination, according to the ordinary course of nature. Indeed, what we have just heard Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage</note> narrating about his own visions does not seem so grand that it could not have naturally come into the mind of a man full of such thoughts.

<margin>
XVI. The Judgment of Voetius.
</margin>
XVI. Lest I seem more difficult than is just, I will add the judgments of two Great men, to which I fully subscribe. The first is our venerable VOETIUS <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note>, who in his *Select Disputations, Part II, page 1059*, speaks in these words:
> Regarding the predictions of Melito, Methodius, Gregory of Neocaesarea, called the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgi"</note>, and such Holy Men in the primitive Church, I freely admit they were not maliciously fabricated, or demonic. But whether they were Divine, I do not think it is a sin to doubt; or at least to leave the matter undecided. Whatever the case may be, I do not at all admit that eulogy by Basil <note>Basil the Great (330–379 AD)</note> as it is too hyperbolic; for he attributes the same spirit to Gregory the Wonder-worker as to the Apostles and Prophets; and he claims that in predictions of the future, Gregory was in no way inferior to the Prophets, and compares him with Moses. Nyssen <note>Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395 AD), Basil's brother</note> does the same in his life of Gregory. See also the *Exposition of Faith* by the same Gregory, which Gerard Vossius <note>a prominent 17th-century scholar</note>, the provost of Tongeren, asserts was received by revelation from John the Evangelist and is held by the Eastern Church. But no one who knows what authority Augustine attributed to the writings of the Fathers will believe that the whole Church believed this to be so. Thus far Voetius.

### ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES

...without end, which are attributed to him <note>Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–270 AD), known as "the Wonder-worker"</note> by [Gregory of] Nyssa in his *Life*, and everywhere by Basil himself, Theodoret, Socrates, Evagrius, Suidas, etc.; from which he received the name of "Thaumaturgus" <term>Thaumaturgus; Greek for "wonder-worker" or "miracle-worker"</term> and of "a second Moses." Certainly, many things in Nyssa's account breathe a certain old-womanly credulity <note>original: "anilem quandam credulitatem," a disparaging term used by early modern scholars to describe superstitious or uncritical belief in folk-tales</note>.

<margin>
XVIII.
The promise of Joel does not imply a perpetual continuation of the Prophetic office.
</margin>
XVIII. However, let it be granted <note>original: "esto," a rhetorical concession</note> that Prophetic men flourished in the Church for a while, and that a specific time when they ceased cannot be assigned; nevertheless, I do not think there is found in the sacred scriptures any declaration of the Divine will by which He established that the prophetic office should continue in the Church. For that promise which appears in Joel <note>Joel 2:28-32</note>, repeated by Peter <note>Acts 2:17-21</note> and recently praised by us, seems to look elsewhere. It is a solemn custom for the Prophets in the Old Testament to express both the duties and the benefits of the faithful of the New Testament using formulas of this kind—drawn from the duties of the highest value among the Jews, and from the benefits which that ancient people most greatly desired.

Thus, the duties of spiritual and rational worship under the Economy of the New Testament <term>Oeconomia Testamenti Novi; the "New Testament Dispensation" or the way God manages the world and the Church after Christ</term> are described as "ascending the mountain of the house of the Lord," "building an altar to Him," "offering incense and a pure gift," "slaughtering victims," and "celebrating Sabbaths"; and many other things of this sort occur. The benefits destined for the Christian Church are described with similar expressions. Those which Joel uses belong to this same category. To be sure, under the Old Testament, prophecies, dreams, and revelations flourished, with God making Himself known immediately. This is now transferred to the Economy of the New Testament, so that by a prophetic phrase, the abundance of light and knowledge of God, and progress in it, might be designated. This was to be so great that the ordinary faithful <note>original: "fideles gregarii," the "rank-and-file" believers as opposed to the leaders</note> of the New Testament, when compared with the ordinary faithful of the Old Testament, would surpass them by as long an interval as once existed between the Prophets and other men from the common people.

Compare promises on the same subject in Isaiah 11:9 and Jeremiah 31:34, and their fulfillment in 1 John 2:27. Meanwhile, God willed that an excellent and extraordinary evidence of that matter, and a kind of down payment <note>original: "arrham," a legal term for a deposit or pledge</note>, should exist in that incredible outpouring of the Spirit with which the Apostles were endowed <note>original: "mactati," which can mean sacrificed or honored; here used to mean enriched or blessed</note>; of which He also made certain others in those first times participants, and in which the very words of the prophecy are fulfilled just as they sound <note>original: "sic ut tinniunt," literally "just as they ring/clink," meaning the literal fulfillment of the words</note>. From these events, the faithful might gather by firm reasoning what they might expect from the Divine wealth. Faith in this explanation is confirmed, to pass over other things, by Peter's address to the Jews in verses 38 and 39: *Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is made to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off...*

He interprets the miracles of the Apostolic age as a "down payment" or literal sign of this broader spiritual enlightenment.</summary>

<page-num>302</page-num>
<header>BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.</header>

<margin>The things narrated by the Fathers should not be admitted indiscriminately.</margin>
...that we should admit everything. The style of most of the Fathers, adapted to a declamatory <term>declamatory; a rhetorical style common in the ancient world designed for emotional impact and persuasion rather than historical precision</term> manner of speaking, is full of hyperbolic exaggerations. Unless these are assisted by a kinder interpretation <note>original: "benigniore interpretatione," meaning we should read them with a grain of salt or look for the underlying moral truth rather than literal fact</note>, they do not present a just and true idea of things to the mind. Nor should it be hidden that many of the Fathers suffered from excessive credulity; they rashly seized upon, and even more rashly recounted—using that magnificent style of speaking to which they were accustomed—things which they could have known were not sufficiently explored, had they only wished to pay attention with greater judgment. No one is ignorant of this, unless they are a stranger to reading the Fathers, or endowed with that same credulity themselves. To this is added that, since these men were quite pleased with themselves regarding visions and apparitions, they easily persuaded themselves that things proceeded from an extraordinary operation of the Divine Spirit, which could have arisen from a vehement and fixed imagination according to the ordinary course of nature. Certainly, those things which we just heard Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an influential early Christian writer</note> relating about his visions do not seem so grand that they could not have come naturally into the mind of a man so full of such thoughts.

<margin>XVI. The judgment of Voetius.</margin>
XVI. But lest I seem more difficult than is fair, I will add the judgments of two great men, to which I fully subscribe. The first is our venerable **VOETIUS** <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a leading Dutch Reformed theologian known for his immense scholarship</note>, who in his *Selected Disputations, Part II, p. 1059*, speaks in these words: *“Concerning the predictions of Melito, Methodius, and Gregory of Neocaesarea (called the 'Wonder-worker'), and such holy men in the primitive Church, I freely admit they were not maliciously fabricated or demonic. However, whether they were Divine, I do not think it is a sin to doubt—or at least to leave the matter undecided. Whatever the case, I do not at all admit that eulogy of Basil as it is too hyperbolic; for he attributes the same spirit to Gregory the Wonder-worker as to the Apostles and Prophets, and says that in his predictions of the future he was in no way inferior to the Prophets, even comparing him to Moses. Gregory of Nyssa does the same in his 'Life' of Gregory. See also the 'Exposition of Faith' of that same Gregory, which Gerard Vossius, the provost of Tongeren, asserts was received through a revelation from John the Evangelist and is held by the Eastern Church. But no one who knows what authority Augustine attributed to the writings of the Fathers will believe that the whole Church believed this to be so. Thus far Voetius.”*

<margin>XVII. And of Spanheim.</margin>
XVII. To whom no one worthier can be joined than **FRIEDRICH SPANHEIM** <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Younger (1632–1701), a professor of theology and church history at Leiden</note>, whose judgment concerning *Gregory* stands as follows: *Introduction to the History of the New Testament, 3rd century, p. 332. “Many things falsely bear the name of this Gregory, such as the 'Exposition of Faith' against the Arians, supposedly received from a revelation of John and the Virgin Mary... Learned men rightly doubt the 'Canonical Epistle' attributed to him. But they doubt much more regarding the wonders and miracles, which are almost without...”*

<header>ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES</header>

...without end, those things attributed to him by Gregory of Nyssa in his *Life of Gregory*, and throughout by Basil himself, Theodoret, Socrates, Evagrius, Suidas, etc., from which he received the name "Wonder-worker" <note>original: "Thaumaturgi"</note> and "another Moses." Many things in Gregory of Nyssa certainly breathe a sort of old-womanly credulity <note>original: "anilem quandam credulitatem," implying stories that are more like superstitious folk tales than historical facts</note>.

<margin>XVIII. Joel’s promise does not imply a perpetual continuation of the Prophetic office.</margin>

XVIII. Indeed, even if it were granted that Prophetic Men flourished in the Church for some time, and that a fixed date for when they ceased cannot be assigned; nevertheless, I do not believe that any declaration of the Divine will is found in the Holy Scriptures by which He decreed to continue the Prophetic office in the Church. For the promise that exists in the Book of Joel <note>Joel 2:28-29</note>, repeated by Peter <note>Acts 2:17-21</note> and recently praised by us, seems to point in another direction. It is customary for the Prophets in the Old Testament to express both the duties and the benefits of the faithful in the New Testament using formulas drawn from those offices held in highest esteem among the Jews, and from those benefits which that ancient people most desired. Thus, the duties of spiritual and rational worship under the New Testament Dispensation <term>Dispensation; from "Oeconomia," referring to God's plan or system for managing human affairs in a specific era</term> are described as "climbing the mountain of the house of the Lord," "building an altar to Him," "offering incense and a pure gift," "slaughtering victims," and "celebrating Sabbaths"—along with many other such examples. And the benefits destined for the faithful of the Christian Church are described with similar expressions. To this same category belong the words used by Joel. Truly, under the Old Testament, prophecies, dreams, and revelations flourished, with God revealing Himself directly. This is now transferred to the New Testament Dispensation, so that by a "prophetic phrase," an abundance of light and knowledge of God—and progress within it—is signified. This was to be so great that the ordinary faithful <note>original: "fideles gregarii," meaning the rank-and-file members of the congregation</note> of the New Testament, compared with the ordinary faithful of the Old Testament, would surpass them by as great a distance as once existed between the Prophets and other common men. Compare promises on the same theme: Isaiah 11:9, Jeremiah 31:34, and their fulfillment in 1 John 2:27. Meanwhile, God willed that an exceptional and extraordinary proof of this matter—a sort of down payment <term>down payment; from "arrha," a legal term for a deposit or earnest money securing a contract</term>—should exist in that incredible outpouring of the Spirit with which the Apostles were endowed. He made others participants in this in those early times, and in this, the very words of the prophecy were fulfilled in a literal sense <note>original: "sic ut con-tinniunt," literally "as they ring out" or "echo exactly"</note>, so that from these events the faithful might gather by firm reasoning what they could expect from the Divine abundance. To omit other points, Peter’s address to the Jews in verses 38 and 39 gives credit to this explanation: *“Repent and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins: and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is made to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off...”* <note>Acts 2:38-39</note>

BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.

...things to come, etc. Is there any mortal so intensely favoring the continuation of the Prophetic office <note>original: "Prophetic muneris"</note> in the Christian Church that he would demand the spirit of Prophecy be promised to all believers and those baptized? Or if he were to assert this, would he not be openly refuted by the actual outcome of events? Once these things are correctly observed, the arguments produced from this prophecy fall away of their own accord, so that there is no need to respond to each one individually.

<margin>XIX. Nor does the Church need it after the completion of the canon of the Scriptures.</margin>
XIX. Just as God did not declare His will regarding the continuation of the Prophetic spirit and office in the Church, so too the Church has no need for them. For after the doctrine of faith—spread far and wide among all nations by the Apostles and apostolic men—was contained within the sacred volumes to form a most sufficient canon of faith and conduct, we no longer have a great need for any prophecy. It is enough for the faithful that, having implored the help of the Spirit, they search the inexhaustible wealth of Scripture, where they will find most abundantly whatever is required for the acquisition of complete salvation. If any Prophets were still to be raised up in the Church, it would be for one of several purposes: I. Either for the end that they might teach something superior to Scripture, or at least add something to it which has not yet been revealed by the Prophets and Apostles; II. Or because there are many things in the dogmas of Scripture and the prophecies of the Prophets blocked by great obscurity, such that God might impart their interpretation to us through these men; III. Or so that, by some heroic prudence and fortitude of spirit, they might both gird themselves for difficult tasks and encourage others—things which are, however, outside the sphere of a common calling; or finally, so that they might predict certain events whose knowledge would bring great utility to the Church, which nonetheless could not be sensed beforehand except by the Spirit of God. For *Moses Amyraldus* <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a prominent French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur.</note> judiciously observed that all the reasons for which God would show these extraordinary men—worthy of the name of prophets—to the rest of mortals must be referred to these points. Yet the same *Amyraldus* proves in a lengthy discourse that none of these things are suitable, let alone necessary, for the Dispensation <term>Dispensation; "Oeconomia," referring to the structured plan of God's dealings with humanity in the New Testament era</term> of the New Testament: *in his Preface to the Psalms*. Acknowledging with gratitude what we borrow from him, we shall strive for brevity.

<margin>XX. For there remain no new dogmas to be added to those handed down there.</margin>
XX. And as far as the first cause is concerned, it cannot be admitted by those who are, as is proper, persuaded of the perfection of the Divine writings and their sufficiency for complete wisdom. And indeed, unless one wishes to utterly subvert them, one ought to believe them when they testify about themselves that they speak the wisdom
of God

# ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES #

...of God among the perfect <note>Referring to those mature in the faith, as in 1 Corinthians 2:6.</note>, because they reveal mysteries into which the heavenly spirits themselves <note>original: "cœlestes genii"; referring to the angels mentioned in 1 Peter 1:12 who desire to look into the Gospel.</note> desire to look; because they make known that manifold wisdom of God to the commands and powers that are in the heavens; and because they are able to make us wise for salvation, so that the person of God may be perfect, fully equipped for every good work. And what more should we expect? Whoever demands to know more, and promises another Gospel besides that which we have received, let him know that we stand with Paul, who asserts that there is no other Gospel and warns us not to desire to know high things. <note>original: "Μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ᾽ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν" (Romans 12:3). Translated: "Not to think of oneself more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment."</note> And what, pray tell, is found in any kind of writing, by anyone who called himself a prophet or was regarded by others as a prophet, that deserves to be added to our undoubtedly Divine Books? What does it contain of momentous, heavenly, or Divine truths conducive to faith, piety, and salvation that does not already exist there? Whatever I have ever found anywhere from those who treat the doctrine of the Scriptures with contempt, as if it were the mere "raw elements" of wisdom, consists either of blasphemous fictions, or superstitious old wives' tales, or a pompous grandiloquence of speech in which there is not even a crumb of good sense. We, for our part, are content with that measure of the Spirit which so prepares our minds by its power that we do not seek to divine or reveal anything new ourselves, but only to understand for our salvation those things which have been revealed in Scripture. And when we learn these things with the Spirit as our Teacher, then we consider ourselves to be <term>prophesying</term> <note>The author defines "prophesying" here as the inspired interpretation of existing Scripture rather than the delivery of new divine messages.</note>, and we give thanks to God that He fulfills Joel’s prophecy <note>Joel 2:28, which promised that "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."</note> in us in this manner. Therefore, for this reason certainly, we do not need Prophets to teach us other truths besides those which exist written in the sacred volumes.

<margin>XXI. It is not permitted to expect a new prophetic revelation to clarify the obscurities of Scripture.</margin>
XXI. Furthermore, it is not necessary for Prophets to be given to us for the purpose of interpreting obscure dogmas of the Scriptures or the riddles of the prophecies with an inspiration of the Spirit similar to that with which they were originally written. For the Providence of the Divine power has so arranged the Scripture that it is its own interpreter. Diligent people, aided by that common grace of the Spirit which is supplied to all the faithful, are able to attain its meaning—as much as is sufficient for salvation—by applying careful scrutiny and a comparison of passages with one another. Everywhere you see this scrutiny and comparison of the Scriptures recommended to their readers; you do not see them directed toward new prophecies to provide light for the ancient oracles. John, in his <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>—a book than which no other more abstruse exists in all the Divine volumes—does not promise a new revelation of its meaning;

### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV. ###

...but *he pronounces those blessed who read, and those who hear, the words of this prophecy, and observe those things which are written in it*: Chapter 1:3 <note>Revelation 1:3</note>, suggesting that its meaning can be understood through reading and hearing.

<margin>XXII. Those who have claimed this for themselves have mostly provided nothing that could not proceed from common diligence.</margin>
XXII. And indeed, those who boast that they have their interpretations from some Divine inspiration ought to prove them not only by the remarkable evidence of truth, but also by some wonderful quality that moves the minds of men beyond the ordinary. For if there is nothing in the interpretation of a passage of scripture that could not proceed from a man who is learned, pious, sharp, and nourished by the reading of sacred scripture, it is right to assign that interpretation not to a prophetic breath <note>original: "adflatui Prophetico"; refers to direct divine inspiration</note>, but to the common grace of the Holy Spirit. Why should we resort to miracles when the daily Providence of God satisfies our minds? Furthermore, if we inspect the commentaries of those who have attributed Divine inspiration to themselves, or the dictation of Angels, we not only find nothing in them so wonderful that it exceeds the common lot of truly great theologians; but we mostly find that they fall far below the commentaries of others in judgment, accuracy, and solidity—men who, having implored God's help, applied only their own industry.

<margin>XXIII. In these pretended revelations, the genius of the writer usually shines through more than the character of the Divine Spirit. As is clear in the formula of the Wonder-worker.</margin>
XXIII. Besides the fact that in these "dictates of the spirit," as they are presented, the genius and character of the writer shine through far more clearly than the character of the Divine Spirit. For an example, let us take the exposition of the adorable Trinity, which they say the Apostle John dictated to Gregory the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Gregorio Thaumaturgo"; a 3rd-century bishop known for miracles</note> by the command of the Blessed Virgin: is there not in the whole of that speech more of Gregory, or some other theologian of that age, than of John? Truly, the Orthodox who were imbued with the study of philosophy spoke in almost that form at that time; John did not speak thus, whose style is much simpler and more worthy of the venerable mystery.

<margin>XXIV. And in the revelation of Poniatovia concerning the Adorable Trinity.</margin>
XXIV. In the *History of the Revelations of Christina Poniatovia* <note>original: "Christinæ Paniatoviæ"; a 17th-century Polish visionary whose revelations were published by Comenius</note>, in Revelation XIX, a wonderful sketch of the Holy Trinity is narrated, explained with those emblems and phrases that belong to this current age. For she says thus:
> *The* LORD *came to me, covered in a garment shining beyond measure, so that eyes could hardly bear it. And soon there also approached the* ANCIENT ONE, *likewise in a white garment. A third person preceded them, similar in stature to them, yet entirely ignited like a flame, whom I had never seen in such an image. And the Lord said to me: Behold, we whom you have before your eyes come to you today so that we may show you our distinction, and yet our unique essence, equality, and the power of our Divinity. The name of this one (pointing to the old man) is the* ANCIENT OF DAYS: *This one (pointing to himself) is named the* WORD OF THE FATHER

# ON THE CONTINUATION OF THE PROPHETS AFTER THE APOSTLES #

...Eternal: These things, however (pointing to that fiery person) are called **HEAVENLY FIRE**, and the **SPIRIT** proceeding from both. You see, therefore, three distinct persons: yet one, true, undivided, immortal God of one essence. For the *Son* dwells in the *Father*, and the *Father* in the *Son*, and the *Holy Spirit* in the *Father* and the *Son*: and so that one God dwells in himself, just as he revealed himself to you mortals in his most holy word. To you, however, for an easier understanding of this Divine mystery, these three persons are shown, so that when you see three persons, you may see *only one God*, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. And again, when you see one person, you may see all three persons, because they are undivided and dwell within one another <note>This concept of mutual indwelling is known in theology as "perichoresis" or "circumincession."</note>. These things indeed have the style and character of a Catechetical instruction <note>A "Catechism" is a summary of religious doctrine used for teaching</note>: but whether God himself spoke these words about himself, I do not know if those who are accustomed to the expressions of Scripture can be persuaded.

<margin>
XXV. On Kotter’s Angelic Sermon, and his Paraphrase of the Lord’s Prayer.
</margin>

XXV. In the *Revelations of Christoph Kotter, Chapter 40* <note>Christoph Kotter (1585–1647) was a German visionary whose prophecies were popular during the Thirty Years' War.</note>, there exists an "Angelic Sermon" regarding the excellent triple title of *Christ*, which the Angels themselves explained. These titles are: **MAN OF WISDOM** (a name by which, however, I do not remember Christ being called in the Sacred Scriptures), **LION OF THE TRIBE OF JUDAH**, and **STANDING IN THE MIDST OF THE SEVEN CHURCHES**. Afterward is added a Paraphrase of the Lord’s Prayer, dictated to *Kotter* by the Angels. In which, however—whether in the sermon or the paraphrase—anyone would detect *Kotter* himself; that is, a man endowed with mediocre theological skill and occupied by intense thoughts regarding certain objects. But that sublime and Divine quality, for the sake of which Angels ought to have been sent from heaven, and which should surpass the meditations of pious men (lacking prophetic revelation) by a great distance, one will not find. These things are said by me so that, through the presentation of examples, it may be clear that from those who were considered "prophets" of these later times, nothing at all has come forth for the explanation of scripture and the mysteries of faith that could not have been better observed by others without extraordinary revelation.

---

<margin>
XXVI. Luther, prudently content with the written word, abstained from visions and apparitions.
</margin>

XXVI. Prudently, therefore, *Martin Luther*, content with the written word of God and the common assistance of the spirit, neither desired dreams, visions, or apparitions of Angels for himself, nor cared for those boasted of by others. His words, excerpted from his commentaries on *Genesis*, are worthy of being read here as well. *Thus he says on Genesis 37: "Because I am not fit for having or interpreting dreams; nor do I seek that faculty or knowledge for myself, and I have made a covenant with my Lord God, that he send me neither visions, nor dreams, nor even Angels. For I am content with this gift, that I have the holy scripture, which abundantly teaches and supplies all things."* <note>Luther famously emphasized "Sola Scriptura" (Scripture Alone) as the sufficient source of divine truth.</note>

### BOOK 1, CHAPTER 24 ###

...which are necessary both for this life and for the life to come. In this Scripture I believe and rest, and I am certain that I cannot be deceived. Nor do I disparage the gifts of others, if God should perhaps reveal something to someone beyond Scripture through dreams, through visions, or through Angels. Let them indeed be gifts: but they are things I neither care for nor desire. For I am moved by that infinite multitude of illusions, tricks, and impostures by which the world was horribly deceived through Satan for a long time under the Papacy <note>The author is referring to the Roman Catholic Church system under the Pope</note>; furthermore, I am moved by the sufficiency of Holy Scripture; if I do not give faith to it, I certainly will not easily believe an Angel, a vision, or a dream. 

But as I said, this reasoning is peculiar to me, by which I would not dare to prescribe anything to others. For I have more than enough revelations when I know what must be believed, what must be hoped for, what must be advised to others, and by what means this life should be lived piously and honestly. And this, according to my meager ability, I gladly share with others, so that they too might know and understand the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, the Creed <note>original: *Symbolum*</note>, the Lord's Prayer <note>original: *Orationem Dominicam*</note>, etc. 

*The same work, regarding chapter 40, leaf 61.* I have often said that from the beginning of my cause, I always asked the Lord not to send me dreams, or visions, or angels. For many fanatical spirits have attacked me, of whom one boasted of dreams, another of visions, another of revelations, by which they strove to teach me. But I replied that I did not seek such revelations, and if any were offered, I would not place faith in them. And I prayed with burning vows that God would give me a certain sense and understanding of Holy Scripture. For if I have the Word, I know I walk in the right path, and cannot easily be deceived or err. 

And I truly prefer a "Davidic" understanding <note>Refers to the deep, prayerful understanding of Scripture characteristic of King David in the Psalms</note> over prophetic visions, which I believe even David did not greatly desire. But see how certain a sense Scripture possesses. The fanatics with their dreams tried to push me first one way then another, and if I had listened to any of them, I would surely have had to change my type of doctrine thirty or forty times. But when I rejected them all, they shouted that I was stubborn and headstrong, and they let me go. Therefore, I pay no heed to visions and dreams, and although they seem significant, yet I despise them, and am content with the certain sense and faith of Holy Scripture. Because if I have the Word, I am certain that God and the Angels are present with me; if not visibly, yet instilling their rays, and directing me in the way of truth. This is my opinion, which I do not change.

...so that the Mass might be entirely abolished, a certain scribe objected that all the examples he had previously cited to prove that **is** is used for *signifies* were parables, but that no example had been brought forward in which a simple figure of speech <note>original: *tropus*</note> was present, such as he was imagining in the words of the Lord’s Supper. This anguish seemed to disturb me greatly, just as dreams are sometimes wont to play tricks in the deceptive night (for we are telling nothing other than a dream as far as we are concerned, although what we learned through the dream is not trivial, thanks be to God, for whose glory alone we bring these things forth). Immediately as this vision appeared, I woke up and leaped from my bed. I first examined the passage in the Septuagint* <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> *from every angle, and I discussed it before the whole assembly to the best of my ability, etc.* Friedrich Spanheim the Elder, in his *Disputation on Enthusiasm, Thesis xvi*, concludes that this dream of Zwingli was sent by God <note>original Greek: *theopempton*</note> both because of the occasion, the material suggested, and its holy application toward establishing a most true doctrine. Whatever the case may be, it was done piously by Zwingli that he recognized a certain Divine guidance in this matter.

...God raised up, under the name and power of the <term>Judges</term><note>The biblical leaders of Israel before the era of Kings, such as Samson or Deborah, who were believed to be directly inspired by God.</note>, those who, being equipped with extraordinary commands, performed unusual works. At times also the Kings, whom He considered as His vicars and legates, He warned through prophets what needed to be done. But since no such <term>Theocracy</term><note>A form of government where God is recognized as the immediate ultimate authority.</note> now exists in the world, and kingdoms and Republics are governed by their supreme powers—albeit under the guidance of Divine providence—God has left it to individuals to judge what is useful, first by the rules of equity and justice, and then by the rules of prudence. And those are mistaken who expect that God will set forth His mind concerning specific events or ways of acting through Prophets by an extraordinary oracle. For anyone to attempt to disturb the public peace and tear down those things which have God as their author, they would need a clearly extraordinary calling, one that proves itself with so many arguments that the mind is entirely certain of God's will in an undertaking so dangerous and which, without such a calling, would be utterly wicked. New prophets cannot generate this certainty, no matter how much confidence they have, whether they twist ancient prophecies to current events by their interpretations or offer new oracles.

<margin>XXIX. Müntzer's Prophecies were the destruction of himself and many others.</margin>
XXIX. How much destruction false prophets brought upon innocent but dangerously credulous men in the last century is a very well-known matter. Thomas Müntzer stands as the prime example of all of them. From a preacher of the Gospel, he became a prophet; first he boasted that he had been taught from the scriptures that at some time the wicked princes and magistrates would be removed and new, pious ones substituted in their place. Then, he preached that he had been warned by God that *now* was the time in which such a great thing ought to be completed. Finally, he claimed that this task had been divinely imposed upon him, so that he might be the leader and auspice of that greatest work. Therefore, having gathered a huge multitude, chiefly of rural folk, when he saw that he must clash with the forces of the princes, he is said to have encouraged them to battle in the manner of a Prophet with this speech:

> I most certainly confirm to you that God will be with us, and the victory shall be ours: for He Himself promised it to me in person—He, I say, who cannot deceive or lie—He commanded that I should undertake the matter in this way, by changing the magistracy.
