### ON THE CONTINUATION OF THE PROPHETS AFTER THE APOSTLES ###

**Volume I. Sig. Rr**

...word, and the faith given to me regarding it, I hold nothing dearer in this life. *Bending my knees before God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, I pray that he might not desert the work begun in us, but keep me and you—whoever you are, grafted into the root of Christ—blameless, and cause me and you through death not to come into judgment, but to pass into life: where the sun shall not fall upon us, nor any other heat, and where the Lord shall wipe away the tears from our eyes, etc.* So may the Ruler of Heaven, Earth, and Sea, God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit, blessed forever and ever, be merciful to me and to you who read these things. Amen.

<margin>XXXI. Yet the outcome does not correspond to his prophecies.</margin>

XXXI. To anyone reading these things, spoken with such a magnificent display of words, would not some terror or horror be struck into them? Yet the outcome, and the history of events carried out in the European world from the year 1643, which do not correspond at all to those prophets, offers a strong testimony against that confidence; indeed, as I judge, it refutes them with an irrefutable argument. From the many examples I could bring forward, it is pleasing now to pick out just a few. In *Revelation* 30, God is said to have instructed the Seer <note>The "Seer" (Videns) refers to Nicolaus Drabík, whose visions were famously published by Comenius.</note> with these commands:

> *Take up a journey to the Prince (of Transylvania, Rákóczi <note>George I Rákóczi (1593–1648), a Protestant Prince of Transylvania who fought against the Habsburgs.</note>) and say to him that you are sent by Me, your Creator and his, so that you may anoint him before the entire army, which I have gathered to him, and proclaim him King of this land. But you shall first deliver a sermon on the words of the second Psalm: "I have anointed my King," etc. Meditate on that sermon immediately: and when it is finished, you shall pour the oil of anointing, of Balsamine oil (which you will find in the Prince's court), in the sight of the whole people, upon the head of the Prince. Soon after, however, let the Prince summon the Nobles of the land, and let him order a Crown to be prepared, and a day to be set for his Coronation, to be performed in Bratislava <note>original: "Posonii"; the Latin name for the city of Pressburg, modern-day Bratislava, where Hungarian kings were crowned.</note>, in the presence of the inhabitants of the land: at which you also will be present. When this has been done, I will strike the hostile army with a great slaughter, just as I told you before, that I would remove them just as stones and wood are usually cleared from the road.*

Indeed, these things are clear and wrapped in no ambiguity of words. But what was the outcome? The Seer himself explains it in *Revelation* 32. He sets out to the Prince: he is not even admitted to his sight. The court preacher reports that the Prince said peace had now been made between himself and the Emperor <note>The Holy Roman Emperor, head of the House of Austria.</note>, and that it could not be broken; if the Seer wished to return home, now was a convenient opportunity. Thus he departs with nothing accomplished. The Prince dies shortly after. Is it not evidently clear from this that this command concerning the Anointing and Coronation of the Prince of Transylvania was a mere illusion, not a heavenly oracle? Is this how God is accustomed to act with His Prophets, whom He ever sent to anoint Kings in His name? Did He not Himself bring it about through His Providence, that they should carry out what they were commanded? Was it worthy of God to instruct Drabík with these commands at the time when the Transylvanian Prince had made peace with the Austrian house—a house which Drabík claimed was devoted to destruction?

->### BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.<-

...since this whole business of anointing and coronation pertained to the destruction of the House of Austria? <note>The House of Austria refers to the Habsburg dynasty, the primary Catholic power in Central Europe at the time.</note>

XXXII. I hear it argued in excuse: that all these things were offered to the Prince of Transylvania <note>George II Rákóczi (1621–1660), who succeeded his father and was often the target of Drabík’s prophetic encouragements.</note> only conditionally—under the law that he show himself ready and eager for the Divine commands, and that he undertake the expedition against the enemies of God without hesitation. But it had already been said to the Seer <note>original: "Videnti"; referring to the visionary Nicolaus Drabík.</note> before, in *Revelation 15*: *Know therefore, Prince, that the hour of your birth has already come*: AND THAT I HAVE CHOSEN HIM, AND NO OTHER, SO THAT IN MY NAME HE MAY ASSIST THE NATIONS RAISED UP BY ME TO OVERTHROW THE HOUSE OF AUSTRIA and *to abolish the Idolaters, with all their abominations.* <note>Protestant visionaries of this era frequently labeled the Roman Catholic Church and its rituals as "idolatry."</note> These nations could indeed carry this out without him: YET I HAVE DECREED TO MAKE HIM A PARTAKER OF THAT HONOR IN THIS NATION, AND NO OTHER. Now, God does not decree anything under an uncertain condition. Whomever He chooses for the performance of such a great work, He also disposes his will and mind in such a way that he serves His counsel. God does not choose anyone on the condition *if* they are willing, but by His choice, He *makes* them willing. Let Cyrus be the example, whom God had chosen for the destruction of the Babylonian Monarchy and the liberation of the Israeli people; God instilled in him such a mind that he fulfilled all His pleasure, and God strengthened his right hand to lay low nations before him, and girded him though he was unknown to Him. *Isaiah 44:28; 45:1, 5.* And with what crime, finally, did Rákóczi bind himself, by which he might have forfeited the crown of Hungary promised to him and his? Was it because he preferred to take political prudence into his counsel rather than the dictates of Drabicius? For I see this being reproached against him everywhere. Yet I do not see what evil there is in that. Truly, it is right for us to hold Divine oracles as always more authoritative than all human counsels. But before all things, it must be established that those things being peddled as oracles are indeed what they are said to be. We owe such reverence to the dictates of God that we must not rashly admit anything as dictated by God which does not demonstrate itself by evident proof. By what miracle, then? (which can rightly be demanded in such a state of affairs) or by what other suitable reason had Drabicius—an unknown man—proved to the Prince that he was sent by God for the announcement of such great things?

XXXIII. Let us add another point. In *Revelation 47*, it is predicted that the end of the kingdom of the Beast <note>The "Beast" is a common apocalyptic reference to the Papacy or the Holy Roman Empire.</note> and the idolaters would be in that very year. *Act manfully: for I, Jehovah, speak,* THAT ALREADY IN THIS YEAR *the measure of the cruelty of the Idolaters against my worshipers under the sun has been filled.* A little later: *I, the Alpha and Omega, laid the foundations of that reigning Harlot: I ALSO HAVE NOW put an end to her in the counsel of my heart.* Moreover, this revelation was made on November 19, 1650. On the following day, a new revelation is said to have occurred to him,

# BOOK I. CHAPTER XXIV.

...the patrons of recent revelations are, if I may speak openly, that for me a single Paul is better and more certain than a hundred Drabíks. To this declaration I add this: that the modesty of Paul, his circumspection, and that prudent and holy reluctance with which he introduces the revelations made to him <note>The author refers to 2 Corinthians 12, where St. Paul speaks humbly of his visions in the third person.</note>, seems to me far more worthy of a Prophetic spirit than this boasting and vaunting of Drabík.

<margin>
XXXVI.
Jurieu's kind judgment concerning him and those like him.
</margin>

XXXVI. Indeed, I wish that the Reverend and most learned man *Pierre Jurieu* <note>A prominent 17th-century French Protestant theologian known for his studies on the Apocalypse.</note> had not placed such high value on these recent prophecies, as he expressed his opinion in these words in the Preface to his commentary on the Apocalypse:

> *“I find,”* he says, *“in the Prophecies of Kotter, Christina Poniatowska, and Drabík, published by Comenius <note>Jan Amos Comenius, the famous Czech educator and theologian, compiled these prophecies in a work titled 'Lux in Tenebris' (Light in Darkness).</note>, something great and wonderful. Kotter, who holds the primary place among these three, is grand and magnificent: the images of his visions are marked by such nobility and majesty that those which occurred to the ancient Prophets hardly possessed anything more excellent. They are also joined together in an admirable way, so that one supports the other without any contradiction. It surpasses my understanding how a manual craftsman could embrace so many and such great things in his imagination without Divine aid. That two-year period of Christina’s prophecy is, in my judgment, a series of miracles the likes of which have not been seen since the age of the Apostles. Indeed, I find nothing more admirable even in the lives of the greatest prophets than what happened to this maiden. Drabík is also memorable for his own grandeur, though he suffers from much obscurity. These three prophets agree in this: they predict the imminent destruction of the Antichrist’s kingdom. Yet, on the other hand, so many and such great stumbling blocks present themselves that one would hardly dare to rely on them with a quiet mind.”*

So says the most illustrious *Jurieu*. His judgment in Drabík’s case deviates greatly from the judgment of God, if the things we just heard Drabík saying about the clarity and evidence of his revelations are true.

<margin>
XXXVII.
My <term>evaluation<gloss>original: *epikrisis* - a Greek term for a final judgment or critical assessment</gloss></term>.
</margin>

XXXVII. I conclude thus: these persons must be committed to God, and no necessity is imposed upon me to determine whether they wickedly fabricated all these things (which charity forbids me to suspect), or whether they were illusions of the imagination arising from melancholy <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was seen as a physical imbalance that could cause vivid, sometimes false, religious hallucinations.</note> or some other cause; or indeed whether something of the Divine was present, though not without a mixture of illusions to which melancholic temperaments are easily prone. However, I trust I shall not be judged a criminal by my God if, content with the revelations of the Scriptures, I leave all more recent prophecies in their place, to be proven or refuted by the outcome. I will allow myself to be driven by no such prophecy to either fear or hope anything vehemently; much less will I, having overstepped the boundaries of my calling, set my hand to a dangerous work.

-># ON THE CONTINUATION OF PROPHECY AFTER THE APOSTLES<-

XXXVIII. Neither, however, would I wish to deny on that account that it frequently occurs that pious men, devoted to Divine worship in a singular way and admitted to a closer and more intimate friendship with the deity, are taught by Him about future and secret things. The knowledge of these things is exceedingly useful for the stirring up of piety, the consolation of the soul, the strengthening of faith and hope, and the exercise of prudence. All history of every age is full of such examples. Nor do I see any reason why faith should be denied to upright and godly men, most worthy of belief, when they occasionally narrate such things about themselves for the glory of God. Yet, not everything that is told should be rashly accepted. For in such matters, it can easily happen that men are either mocked by phantasms, or that strange affections proceed from a condition of the brain and the temperament of the humors <note>The author refers to the theory of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, or finally, that fictions are sold as facts. Into which of these categories the recent little stories **CONCERNING THE FRENCH BOYS AND GIRLS** <note>This refers to the "Little Prophets" of the Cévennes (the Camisards), a Protestant movement in France starting around 1688 where children claimed to speak under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.</note> should be placed, I do not think it is a sin to doubt. However, if any revelations do happen to some, they serve more for their own private information than as a rule of faith or action for others, let alone for the Church. They themselves, perhaps from that internal light with which they are illuminated by the Spirit, are able to discern that these things happen to them Divinely; but they lack the arguments by which they might prove the Divinity of the revelation made to them to the consciences of others.

<margin>XXXIX.
Epilogue.</margin>
XXXIX. And so I have discussed these matters, according to the grace granted to me, concerning this most grave subject. In this, I am so far from hoping that I have satisfied others, that I have not even satisfied myself. Many things occur here which require accurate, long-lasting, and very fixed meditation, as well as a careful comparison of facts. I frankly confess that I do not have enough talent for this task, nor have I had enough leisure in this most laborious kind of life. There are also some things of which one can hardly form a just idea in the mind unless one has learned by experience. I do not hide the fact, however, that nothing of a prophetic nature has ever happened to me. Besides the diligent scrutiny of the Sacred Scriptures—than which nothing is sweeter or more pleasant—the anointing proceeding from that Holy One is sufficient for me, which teaches all things <note>A reference to 1 John 2:20, "But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth."</note>, and of which the kindness of the Divine deity imparts some portion to individuals who revere Him. If I have occasionally investigated the opinions of other learned men more freely, and have boldly said what I judge to be more true, it was not done out of a desire for contention, much less from an inability to control my mind, and least of all from malice or bitterness; but solely out of a love for the truth, and to protect the authority of the Divine oracles. It happened beyond my intention that this commentary of ours grew to such a great bulk. If the abundance and variety of the subject matter does not prove or excuse this to the Reader,

<margin>Add, if you please,

XIX. XX,
XXI.</margin>

<margin>
1. The structure of the Tabernacle teaches no fewer things about Divine virtues than the structure of the Universe.
</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring a bird standing among floral and scrolling leaf motifs.</image-desc>

The structure of the Divine Tabernacle is worthy of our consideration, for in it we have the heart and center of all Ceremonies; indeed, all of them had to be celebrated either within it or with a view toward it. God, who gave only six days to the creation of the whole Universe, spent forty days instructing Moses in the model of the Tabernacle, because in it was to be seen the idea of the World of Grace—a work far more admirable than the first. Moses spent only one or two chapters describing the structure of the visible world, but six times as many explaining the structure of the Tabernacle. This serves to remind us that no less attention should be paid to this than to the former; for from its consideration, the virtues of God in Christ will shine upon us. And certainly, pious men have always placed great value on dwelling in this Tabernacle (Psalms 23:6; 27:4; 42:2; 84). Yet they could not see as many mysteries in it as we Christians do by the grace of God, to whom the key to the riddles <note>original: "ænigmatum clavis"</note> has been given, and its genuine...

->BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.<-

the genuine use was demonstrated beforehand by Paul. He certainly spoke of many things; but not, as he himself declares, of every single detail (Hebrews 9:5), implying that similar things could be said about those he passed over in silence. Thus, he leaves room for the exercise of our own diligence.

<margin>II. Not all of its mysteries were so fully explained by Paul that others do not still remain to be investigated.</margin>

II. For it is not right to think that only those things mentioned by Paul possessed hidden meanings, or that our labor in searching out the rest will be spent in vain. Paul himself provided great arguments against believing such a thing when he testified generally that the Mosaic institutions <note>The laws, rituals, and structures established by Moses.</note> contain a "shadow," the *body* of which is found in Christ (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 10:1). Regarding this entire Tabernacle <note>The portable sanctuary used by the Israelites in the wilderness.</note>, he asserts in clear words that it was a *pattern of a greater and more perfect one, not made with hands*, nor of this earthly creation; and regarding the activities performed in the tabernacle, he says they were *patterns of the things in the heavens* (Hebrews 9:9, 11, 23, 24). 

Furthermore, no one who places a just value on Divine wisdom will easily persuade themselves to believe that a few small instructions—those seen explained in the pages of the New Testament—exhaust the entire doctrine of ancient mysteries so completely that the rest were given to no purpose. They would have been given in vain if they possessed no deeper meanings. Indeed, they would also be in vain if those meanings—once we ceased to be taught by the living voices of the Apostles and Prophets—could never again be investigated by any mortal, or demonstrated by comparing these most skillfully crafted "pictures" with their original model <note>original: "prototypo"</note>. 

We owe immortal thanks to Divine Goodness because it has itself gone before us on this path of unfolding these riddles <note>original: "aenigmatum"</note>, even selecting some for their mystery that perhaps no one would have ever thought of. It is our duty to benefit from such an excellent education, growing in the sagacity and prudence of the righteous. We should not merely marvel at these treasures that we now see unlocked before our eyes, but we should use that "golden key" <note>A metaphor for the method of Christological interpretation used by the Apostles.</note> with foresight to unearth those treasures which we are certain lie hidden in other compartments of the same ark. 

And although we may not be able to explain every single detail in a way that is proven by obvious demonstration when taken in isolation, it is nonetheless generally established that in all the Mosaic ceremonies—as if in different images of one great painting—Christ and His Church are depicted. The more diligently we notice and assign these similarities, the more clearly we place the wisdom of God in the light. It cannot be by accident, or outside the intention of the Great Artist, that such a vast number of analogies is found between the "painting" and its subject. In this regard, the most learned men of our century <note>Refers to 17th-century contemporary biblical scholars.</note> have served the studies of younger men excellently; we freely profess that we have been greatly helped by their industry, first to the glory of God, and then to their own praise.

<margin>III. Allegorical application is our model.</margin>
III. Furthermore, so that it is not necessary for us to wander off again into this dispute regarding the allegorical interpretation of Mosaic institutions <note>The laws and structures established by Moses</note>, I wish to clearly set forth our own opinion on the matter. I cannot do this more elegantly than in the words of Moses Amyraldus <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a prominent French Protestant theologian</note>, in the Preface he wrote for his commentaries on the Psalms of David. There, after discussing the Divine art by which the Apostles explained the symbols of the Old Testament in a truly marvelous way, he continues as follows:

> *What the Apostles achieved in this genre serves as a model, by whose standard all other theologians should conform their thoughts and meditations in this study. In this regard, it is necessary to exercise caution: just as the Apostles were sparing in this study, we must avoid excess. As they followed the main points, as it were, and rejected trivial hair-splitting <note>original Greek: λεπτολογίαν (leptologian)</note> because they did not wish to display their own cleverness, but rather to serve the edification of the Church and the confirmation of the truth, so should we omit those things which are too flimsy and stick to the "body," as it were, of significant matters. Finally, just as they demonstrated the truth of their interpretations by nothing other than the clear evidence of the similarity that exists between the interpretations and the things from which the allegories are drawn; so let us likewise draw out the proofs of our explanations. Otherwise, the subject of symbols is slippery and ambiguous; when human ingenuity indulges itself beyond measure, it wanders and runs off into various empty flights of fancy <note>original: "meteorismos," referring to lofty but groundless speculations</note>, in which it seems to play rather than to act seriously and religiously.*

But let us return from this detour back to the main path.

<margin>IV. Besides the Levitical Tabernacle, there was also Moses’ Private and David’s Public Tabernacle.</margin>
IV. Let us proceed, then, to the matter at hand. It must be understood beforehand that THREE sacred Tabernacles are mentioned to us. I. THE PRIVATE TENT OF MOSES, erected outside the camp after the making of the golden calf <note>original Greek: μοσχοποιΐαν (moschopoiiun)</note>: this is indeed called the "Tabernacle of Meeting," because there God met with Moses and displayed His glory for the Israelites to see. Exodus 33:7. However, this is different from the one God had destined for public worship, which Moses did not pitch for himself, but for God. Exodus 40:34–35. Nor was it built immediately after the crime of the golden calf, but in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month. Ibid, verse 2. II. THE PUBLIC TENT OF DAVID: into which he transferred the Ark of the Covenant from the house of Obed-Edom, erected on Mount Zion. 2 Samuel 6:17; 1 Chronicles 16:1. III. THIS LEVITICAL TABERNACLE, which we must now discuss, and the pattern of which was shown to Moses on the mountain.

<margin>V. The history of the Levitical Tabernacle.</margin>
V. I wish to set before your eyes, in a single glance, the various fortunes of that Tabernacle. After it was duly finished with all its instruments, Moses erected and initiated it. Exodus 40. Then, having been dismantled several times, it shared the common journeys of the Israelites in the desert, carried by the Levites who were consecrated for that service. Numbers 4. After the entry into Canaan, it was first placed at Gilgal. Joshua 4:18–19. From there it was moved to Shiloh.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

Once the Ark was captured by the Philistines, God rejected and despised Shiloh <note>original: "Siluntem"</note> (Jeremiah 7:12, Psalm 78:60) and the Tabernacle was moved to Nob, as can be gathered from 1 Samuel 21:1. In the time of David and Solomon, it was located at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3), until it was transferred with all its utensils into the Temple (2 Chronicles 5:5).

<margin>VI. Things to be noted.</margin>
VI. But let us consider more accurately the individual details pertaining to this Tabernacle of the Law <note>The Levitical Tabernacle</note>, and indeed distinctly: I. THE MATERIAL. II. THE FORM, or the Idea shown from heaven. III. THE PARTS. IV. THE MYSTICAL SIGNIFICANCE.

<margin>VII. The material of the Tabernacle was collected from the voluntary offering of the Israelites.</margin>
VII. God willed the MATERIAL of the Tabernacle to be gathered for Him from the voluntary offering of the Israelites, from whom He required gold, silver, bronze, and blue, purple, and double-dyed scarlet fabrics; and fine linen <note>original: "lignum xylinum," literally "wood-linen," a term for fine cotton or flax</note>, and goat’s hair; also ram skins dyed red, and violet-colored skins <note>original: "pelles melium"; traditionally translated as badger or dolphin skins, the exact animal remains a subject of scholarly debate</note>, and the finest cedar wood <note>The author uses "cedar," though the Hebrew text specifies Shittim or Acacia wood</note>, and oil for the light, and fragrant herbs for the anointing oil, and spices for the incense, and onyx stones, and stones for setting (Exodus 25:2–7). When the Israelites heard this, everyone whose heart moved him and everyone whose spirit stirred him willingly brought an offering to the Lord for the work of the Tent of Meeting. Men came with women, bringing brooches, earrings, rings, and pendants—all kinds of gold objects. Others brought silver, bronze, and the finest cedar wood; others blue and purple fabrics, and many more things of that kind. The leaders, moreover, brought precious stones with such readiness and generosity that because more than enough was being offered, the people were restrained from giving more by Moses' command (Exodus 35:21 and following; 36:3 and following). I do not wish now to trouble every single word with critical diligence, as they are rendered differently by different translators. For when you have exhausted yourself with much labor and heard every scholar arguing their own case, you will be more uncertain than before. We are pursuing greater matters.

<margin>VIII. To which was added a prescribed tribute of a half-shekel to be paid by each person.</margin>
VIII. Besides this voluntary offering, a *tribute* <note>A mandatory tax</note> was prescribed for the people, to be paid by all for atonement and to be set aside for the service of the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 30:11–16). All Israelites from twenty years old and upward were to be counted, without exception: Priests, Levites, converts, and freedmen. However, women, infants, and slaves were not included. The tax was a half-shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. Most Hebrew Masters <note>Rabbinical authorities</note>, and many Christians among them, have maintained that the *Shekel of the Sanctuary* <term>Shekel of the Sanctuary: A standard unit of weight or currency kept at the Tabernacle to ensure honesty in transactions</term> was twice as large as the one in common use. But more recent scholars, having weighed the matter better (as it seems), teach that the shekel designated by this name is one that is correct in both value and weight, corresponding—

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE

...according to the pattern that was preserved in the sanctuary; just as <term>Justinian</term> <note>The Byzantine Emperor Justinian I (r. 527–565 AD), famous for his legal code, also regulated trade standards</note> ordered that weights and measures be kept in the most sacred church of every city. This reasoning is well-supported. For the <term>shekel</term> <note>original: "siclus"</note> of the Sanctuary is defined as twenty <term>obols</term> <note>original: "obolis"; in the Hebrew text, these are called 'gerahs'</note>. Leviticus 27:25. Nowhere else is another value established for it, nor is there any reason why they should have differed. On the contrary, the prophet Ezekiel (Chapter 45:12), while urging the princes to practice law and justice and to use just weights and measures, considers no other than the twenty-obol shekel as the standard for common use as well. Furthermore, the most ancient shekel coins that still exist today are almost all of the same weight, and they are worth nearly half an <term>Imperial Thaler</term> <note>original: "Imperialem [Dalerum]"; a standard silver coin used across Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries</note>. *That fixed price was neither to be increased nor decreased*: the same amount was to be paid by the rich and the poor; even if, as the Hebrew scholars say, one had to obtain it by begging or by selling their own clothes. *Its use* was for the daily ministry and for the atonement of souls. *Its necessity* was to prevent a plague from spreading among them. This is what the Hebrews say happened in the time of David, when a plague raged among the people because the payment of this tribute had been neglected. Whether this was an annual census or a one-time contribution for the first construction of the Tabernacle will be discussed more conveniently elsewhere.

<margin>IX. The amounts which made up the grand total.</margin>

**IX.** It will be more worthwhile now to observe how great a total sum this census produced. Moses teaches this in Numbers 1:46. The total number counted was six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men. Therefore, an equal number of half-shekels were paid: making a total of 301,775 whole shekels. This makes up one hundred <term>talents</term> <note>A talent was the largest unit of weight in the Bible, roughly equivalent to 75–100 pounds</note> and 1,775 shekels (Exodus 38:25). To these, add the gold collected from voluntary contributions, which was twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels (verse 24). These figures are better understood if they are reduced to our own modern calculations. This conversion, however, is carried out in various ways. <term>Tremellius</term> and <term>Junius</term> <note>Immanuel Tremellius and Franciscus Junius, 16th-century scholars famous for their Latin Bible translation</note> calculate the total value of the gold so that it exceeds 5,560,450 Imperial Thalers. The silver, they calculate, exceeds 1,922,887 and a half Imperial Thalers. Others calculate as follows: 29 talents of gold make 664,912 <term>Hungarian florins</term>. Add the 730 gold shekels, which correspond to 5,579 Hungarian florins. The total sum of gold collected would be 670,491 Hungarian gold coins, according to the calculations of <term>Georgius Agricola</term> <note>1494–1555; a German scholar known as the "father of mineralogy"</note> in his book *On the Price of Metals*. As for the silver, they reduce the one hundred talents to 203,600 Hungarian florins. Add the seventy talents of bronze from Exodus 38:29, which make 2,036 Hungarian florins. <term>Willem Goeree</term> <note>A 17th-century Dutch author who wrote extensively on biblical architecture and Jewish history</note>, whose diligence in such matters is to be praised, follows a different method of calculation. He thinks the tribute from the Israelite census, of one hundred talents and 1,575 <note>The author likely means 1775, matching the biblical text mentioned above</note> silver shekels, was worth 60,355 <term>Flemish Pounds</term>, or...

<margin>VIII. To which was added the prescribed tribute of half a shekel to be paid by each person.</margin>
VIII. In addition to this voluntary offering, a *tribute* was imposed on the people, to be paid by everyone for atonement and to be set aside for the ministry of the tent of meeting (Exodus 30:11–16). All Israelites from twenty years old and upward were to be counted: without exception, this included Priests, Levites, <term>proselytes</term> <note>Converts to Judaism</note>, and freedmen. However, women, children, and slaves were not included. The *tax* was half a shekel, according to the "shekel of the sanctuary." Most of the Hebrew Masters, and many Christians following them, have maintained that the <term>Shekel of the Sanctuary</term> <note>original: "Siclum Sanctuarii"</note> was twice as large as the one in common use. But more recent scholars, having weighed the matter better (as it seems), teach that this name designates a shekel that is just and honest in both value and weight, and which corresponds...

than the pattern which was kept in the sanctuary: just as *Justinian* <note>Flavius Justinianus, the 6th-century Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law</note> ordered measures and weights to be kept in the most sacred church of every city. And reason supports this. For the <term>shekel of the Sanctuary</term> <note>original: "siclus Sanctuarii"</note> is defined as twenty <term>obols</term> <note>original: "obolis"; these correspond to the Hebrew 'gerah', the smallest unit of weight/currency</note> in *Leviticus* 27:25. Nor is any other value established for it anywhere else; nor was it necessary for one to be established: for what reason would there be for them to be different? Indeed, *Ezekiel* in Chapter 45:12, urging the princes to exercise law and justice and use just weights and measures, considers no other than the twenty-obol shekel as just, even in common use. To this is added that the most ancient coins of shekels which still exist today are almost all of the same weight: and are worth about half an <term>Imperial Thaler</term> <note>original: "Imperialem [Dalerum]"; a large silver coin used throughout the Holy Roman Empire</note>. That defined price was neither to be increased nor decreased: the same amount was to be paid by the rich and the poor; even if, as the Hebrews say, one had to acquire it by begging or selling one's clothes. Its **Use** was for the daily ministry and for the atonement of souls. Its **Necessity** was to prevent a plague from spreading among them. This, the Hebrews say, happened in the time of David when a plague raged among the people because the payment of this tribute was neglected. Whether this was an annual census or contributed only once at the first building of the Tabernacle will be more conveniently discussed elsewhere.

<margin>IX. These things joined together formed a vast sum.</margin>
IX. It will be better now to notice how great a sum this census produced. *Moses* teaches this in *Numbers* 1:46. All those numbered were *six hundred three thousand five hundred and fifty*. Therefore, the same number of half-shekels were paid: or 301,775 whole shekels. These make up one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels (*Exodus* 38:25). To these, add the gold collected from voluntary contributions, twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels (verse 24). These are better understood if they are reduced to our own calculation. This, however, is calculated in different ways. *Tremellius* and *Junius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius and Franciscus Junius, influential 16th-century Protestant biblical scholars</note> calculate the sum of gold in such a way that it exceeds the value of *five million, five hundred sixty thousand, four hundred fifty Imperial Thalers*. Of silver, however, the value exceeds *nineteen million, two hundred eighty-eight thousand, eight hundred eighty-seven and a half Imperial Thalers*. Others calculate it thus: 29 talents of gold make 664,912 <term>Hungarian florins</term> <note>original: "florenos Ungaricos"; a high-purity gold coin widely used for international trade</note>. Let 730 gold shekels be added, which correspond to 5,579 Hungarian florins. The entire sum of gold collected would be 670,491 Hungarian gold pieces, according to the calculation of *Georgius Agricola* <note>A 16th-century German scholar often called the "father of mineralogy," who wrote extensively on metals and weights</note> in his *Book on the Price of Metals*. They reduce the one hundred talents of silver to 203,600 Hungarian florins. Let the seventy talents of bronze from *Exodus* 38:29 be added, making 2,036 Hungarian florins. *Goeree* <note>Willem Goeree, a 17th-century Dutch author who wrote on Jewish antiquities and architecture</note>, whose diligence in such matters is to be praised, follows another method of calculation. He thinks the tribute of the Israelite census, of one hundred talents and 1,575 <note>The text here says 1,575, though the biblical record in Exodus 38:25 and the author's earlier calculation mention 1,775</note> silver shekels, was worth 60,355 <term>Flemish Pounds</term> <note>original: "Libras Flandricas"</note>, or...

Or 130 <term>tons of gold</term> <note>original: "Tonnas auri"; in the 17th-century Netherlands, a "ton of gold" was a standard unit of account representing 100,000 guilders/florins, not a measure of physical weight.</note>, and about 5,950 florins.

<margin>X. Where the Israelites obtained such great wealth in the desert.</margin>
X. Since these amounts almost surpass belief, it is rightly asked where the Israelites—who had been crushed by harsh slavery and extreme poverty in Egypt, and were now wandering in the desert—could have obtained such a great supply of materials and such abundance of wealth. First, it is probable that at least some among Israel had reserved for themselves no small amount of the ancient wealth of their ancestors; this could especially have been the case among the descendants of Joseph. Furthermore, it is certain that they carried many things out of Egypt which had been given to them by their hosts and neighbors, as seen in <term>Exodus 12:35–36</term>. Nor is it incredible that something was added to them from the spoils of the Egyptians, whose corpses—along with their garments and whatever precious things were on them—were washed onto the shore by the waves of the Red Sea <note>original: "mari Erythræi"; literally the Erythraean Sea, the classical name for the Red Sea.</note>. Moreover, the desert itself perhaps supplied some things, specifically the wood they required. There are even those who assert there was a forest near Sinai from which trees were cut down. <term>Abarbanel</term> <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a renowned Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note> conjectures that neighboring nations also brought merchandise for sale into the camps of the Israelites. But this is outside of the Scripture: for no one is recorded to have come to the Israelites in the desert except Jethro and his kin; all others were afraid to approach because of the slaughter of the Egyptians and the Amalekites. And truly, we must proclaim here the mercy of God toward His people, who enriched them with His blessings before they served in Egypt, and endowed them with riches as they exited the Egyptian workhouses. Likewise, we see the generosity of the people toward God in return, for they held nothing so dear that they would not most gladly consecrate it to His divine power.

<margin>XI. What hidden significance lies beneath this.</margin>
XI. Many things meet here that are worthy of remembrance. I. That God willed every kind of material, and of very different rank and price, to be collected for the construction of His <term>Tabernacle</term> <note>The portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites.</note>: not only gold, silver, and bronze, but also wood, items spun from wool or hair, and the skins of animals. These things, though joined in such diversity, contributed greatly not only to the integrity of the Tabernacle but also to its ornament and beauty. This is exactly how it is with those in whom God dwells through His Spirit; whom He Himself places in different positions, equips with different gifts, and employs in different duties and ministries, making them parts of His spiritual home. This home, composed of such diverse elements, rises up not only more orderly but also more decorative. II. That He willed this offering to be voluntary and spontaneous, prescribing to no one by a fixed law what or how much they ought to offer. Thus He is delighted by the offerings of His people...

...willingly on the day of your power, in the beauties of holiness. **Psalm 110:3.** And He wishes all things to be prepared, *so that it may be a matter of generosity, and not as something extorted; not out of sorrow or necessity: for God loves a cheerful giver. 2 Corinthians 9:5, 7.* III. Because that offering is called <term>Terumah</term> <note>Hebrew: תרומה; literally an "uplifting" or "heave-offering," referring to a gift dedicated to God</note>, an exaltation, a separate thing that is raised up, a sacred gift devoted to the *Most High*, and is applied to those uses for which none can be more eminent. Indeed, the highest honor of those things we possess is found in this: that they are freely given to God, to be spent on His ministry. We abuse our goods whenever we force them to serve either avarice, pride, or pleasures. But we extol them to the greatest loftiness of their use when we consecrate them to the Divine. IV. Nor should it be omitted that they contributed not only material, each according to their means, but that everyone applied their *skill* and all their industry to prepare the things they offered; not even the women were excepted, whose industry led them to weave with their own hands, and they brought spun yarns of hyacinth-blue and purple. **Exodus 35:25.** Thus it is right to consecrate to God not only our resources and wealth, but also our intellect, industry, and every skill: so that what is most excellent in us may be spent with all eagerness on adorning the Church of God. Nor is there anyone among those who belong to the people of God who is not able to provide something in his own place and order.

XII. Furthermore, although God is greatly delighted by a *voluntary offering*, He nevertheless commanded a *tribute* to be paid to Himself as *Lord and King* out of debt: so that the Israelites might acknowledge that they owed not only their possessions, but even their life to God, and by this performance of <term>homage</term> <note>The feudal act of acknowledging oneself as the vassal of a lord; here, the author uses it to describe Israel's relationship to God</note> they might redeem the use of the same. They were to profess, moreover, that no one is the master of his own head and life; but all equally acknowledge one Lord, God, who by a singular benefit had joined them to Himself as a people. But even greater things seem to lie beneath this. I. Since this tribute *is given for the expiation of souls*, it is a figure of that true <term>ransom</term> <note>Greek: λύτρου (lytrou); a price paid for the release of a captive or the redemption of a soul</note>, consisting not of gold or silver, but of the precious blood of the Son of God, by which we are redeemed from the wrath and curse of God. II. And since it was of such low value, worth scarcely a fourth part of an <term>Imperial coin</term> <note>Latin: "Imperialis"; likely referring to the Reichsthaler, a standard European silver coin in the 17th century</note>; by that very fact it was proved to be only a symbol. Otherwise, both Scripture and reason teach that the value of the soul is infinitely more precious. **Psalm 49:8, 9.** III. Since it had to be paid equally by everyone, just as much by the poor as by the rich; we are taught that with God there is no respect of persons, and that the souls of all are equally dear to Him; one and the same <term>ransom</term> <note>Greek: λύτρον (lytron)</note> was paid by Christ for all the elect; the same need must be confessed by all, and the same right exists for all with respect to daily expiation, and finally, it happens to all...

<margin>XIII. The Form of the Tabernacle.</margin>
XIII. From the consideration of the material, let us move to the **FORM** of the Tabernacle. God Himself showed this to Moses, *revealing the pattern from heaven*, according to which He commanded every single part to be most exactly fashioned. **Exodus 25:9, 40; 26:30.** For those are deceived and they deceive others, whoever argues that Moses constructed this portable dwelling of God in the desert after the example of what he had seen in Egypt, and in order to accommodate the crude intellect of his Israelites. Indeed, the most learned **Spencer** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an influential theologian who argued that many Jewish rituals were "accommodated" from Egyptian pagan customs to prevent the Israelites from backsliding into idolatry</note> does not win my belief, however much he contends with a lengthy discourse that the coarseness of that age, and religion confirmed by the long-standing use of the nations, gave origin to this Divine Tabernacle. *“For since,”* he says, *“it was the custom among the Egyptians and other nations to carry about the images of their Gods, or their symbols, placed in chariots, small shrines* <note>original Greek: ναΐσκοις (*naiskois*)</note>, *or tents; either so that they might worship them with singular honor, or that they might have them as inseparable companions of their journeys and dangers: and since it was not so easy to abolish that custom, hence it seemed good to God to stoop to the custom and measure of the age, to dwell in a Tabernacle, and even to hand over a Tabernacle to be carried about by His ministers.”* He especially thinks that the **TABERNACLE OF MOLOCH** and **CHIUN** <note>References to Amos 5:26 and Acts 7:43, which describe the Israelites carrying the "tent of Moloch" and the "star of the god Chiun/Rephan" during their desert wanderings</note> gave the occasion for this matter: and he is quite detailed in describing that similarity and affinity which existed between the Tabernacle of the Testimony and the Tabernacle of Moloch. From this he concludes, *“God allowed the Israelites a tabernacle to be carried around so that, by rites bearing the image of ancient custom, He might entice them to His worship and bind them closely to Him.”* (*Dissertation on the Origin of the Tabernacle*). However, no matter with how much confidence these things are said, they lead the mind away from the simplicity of the Mosaic narrative, which mentions no such thing; away from the purity of Divine worship, which has nothing in common with the monstrous superstitions of Moloch; away from the intention of God, who willed that the customs of His people should not be in any way similar to the customs of neighboring nations, but most separate from them; and finally, away from the meditation on far more sublime and far more excellent things, which this entire dissertation of ours will invincibly show the Tabernacle was intended to signify. Certainly, God willed that nothing of Egyptian wisdom—indeed, not even any human wisdom whatsoever—should intervene here, except insofar as it served to execute most accurately those things which were commanded. **Exodus 31:6.** *I have put skill into the mind of every industrious person, so that they may make all that I have commanded you.* Thus we are taught: I. We must dare nothing in the matter of religion from the inventions of our own reason; but all things must be required according to the Lord’s prescription. **Colossians 2:22, 23.** II. All the shrewdness of our reason must be so submitted to God that, judging what He Himself has prescribed to be best, we never correct His commands according to our own judgment, but execute them exactly as they were commanded...

...let us strive to perform [these things] most exactly. "Observe therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom and your understanding." <note>Deuteronomy 4:6</note>. III. Since the design <note>original: *idea*</note> descended from heaven to be shaped on earth, it is taught by that very fact that those earthly things are *copies of the heavenly things* <note>original Greek: *ἐπουρανίων ὑποδείγματα*</note>, HEAVENLY PATTERNS. <note>Hebrews 9:23</note>.

<margin>XIV. The Court.</margin>
XIV. Now let us survey the **PARTS** of the Tabernacle, each with its own equipment, beginning from the exterior so that we may gradually reach the more secret areas. And first, we encounter the **COURT**; the description of which is found in Exodus 27:9–19 and 38:9 and following. It was an ample space, open to the sky, surrounding the Tabernacle (though not so that the Tabernacle occupied the precise center), and it was formed from eyeleted curtains of interwoven linen <note>original: *xylino internexo*, referring to fine cotton or linen</note>, in such a way that they were translucent and full of holes; so that the Israelites, or any others standing outside, could see the things being done within. These curtains were hung upon columns which had bronze bases and were furnished with silver hooks and bands. At the gate of the court, there was a covering of twenty cubits made of violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and interwoven linen, of embroidered work <note>original: *opere phrygiano*, literally "Phrygian work," a style of intricate embroidery</note>. From this, it appears that even the outermost materials and craftsmanship of the sacred Tabernacle were splendid.

<margin>XV. One or many.</margin>
XV. Whether the Court was *one* in number or *several* is debated among scholars. Moses mentions only one, but it was hardly of such great size that it could hold the entire crowd of Levites with their ministries, let alone the innumerable multitude of the Israelite people; and David speaks of the *courts* of the Lord several times in the plural. <note>Psalms 65:5; 84:3; 96:8</note>. Furthermore, if this is not to be understood from the character of the Hebrew language, which uses the plural number to indicate the excellence of a thing, it is probable that in the desert and in the first times of the Israelite Republic there was only one court, where the priests performed sacred duties with selected Levites. Whether those Israelites who wished and were able stood by, I see questioned by learned men and diligent investigators of these antiquities. But when the Israelites had obtained more peaceful settlements in Canaan and the Tabernacle was fixed at Shiloh—where the Masters of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis and Jewish commentators</note> relate it was surrounded not only by its curtains but also by a wall—it is not incredible that another court for the people was joined to that Court of the Priests. At least in the time of David, that there was an assembly of the people in the Court is proved clearly enough by the Psalms just cited. In the Temple, all acknowledge at least a double Court. <note>2 Chronicles 33:5; 1 Kings 6:36; 7:12</note>. One for the *Priests* <note>2 Chronicles 4:9</note> and the other for the *people*, to which a third was added, certainly in the Temple of Herod, namely the *Court of the Gentiles*.

->## BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.<-
<meta>catchword: pious</meta>

<margin>XVI. The Bronze Altar of Burnt Offerings</margin>
XVI. Belonging to the equipment of the Court are the **BRONZE ALTAR OF BURNT OFFERINGS** and the **BASIN**. We have the architectural plan <note>original: *sciagraphiam*</note> of the Altar in Exodus 27:1, 2, and following. Its material was made of Shittim wood <note>original: *lignum Sittim*, likely Acacia wood</note>, or the finest cedars, which was ordered to be overlaid with bronze. Its shape was *square*, with a length and width of five cubits, and it stood three cubits high. It had horns on its four corners, as well as bronze utensils, a bronze grating and network, and poles overlaid with bronze to be inserted into bronze rings so that it might be portable. It was to be placed in the open air, within the Court, before the gate of the tent of meeting (Exodus 40:6). It served for all the sacrifices which were to be burned either in whole or in part upon it; and this was done only by the sacred fire—that is, the fire which descended from heaven (Leviticus 9:24)—which was to be fed daily with such diligence that it might seem eternal (Leviticus 6:9, 12). However, a notable difficulty occurs regarding this matter. Specifically, God commanded the Levites, who were to carry the Altar during the travels of the Israelites, to sweep away the ashes and spread a purple cloth over it, placing all its utensils upon it, and covering it with a covering of badger skins <note>original: *pellibus melium*, referring to the 'tahash' skins mentioned in the Bible, often translated as badger, porpoise, or fine leather</note> (Numbers 4:13, 14). But how could the fire be preserved under a double covering? Or how, if the fire were kept, were the coverings not burned? The difficulty grows if one considers that such a journey was sometimes extended for several days. Here the Jews, according to their custom, flee to miracles, telling how it was achieved by Divine omnipotence so that the fire lived without fuel or air under the purple cloth, and the cloth remained unharmed as if it covered no fire at all. But just as it is a matter of religious duty for us not to doubt even with the slightest hesitation the miracles we find recorded in the sacred volumes; so we are not very quick to admit those which are handed down only by human authority, especially Jewish authority—that is, of very dubious reliability. It is far more credible to say that in such a case, the fire was removed from the altar and placed in pots along with its ashes, and there nourished with necessary fuel until it was replaced on the altar (Compare Exodus 27:3). The fable concerning the sacred fire being kept in a cave after the destruction of the temple by the Babylonians and restored by Jeremiah was learnedly refuted by John Rainolds <note>Rainoldus (1549–1607) was an influential English Puritan scholar and translator of the King James Bible</note> in *Lectures on the Apocryphal Books, cxxxiii*. This Altar was a place of *Refuge* <note>or sanctuary</note> for one who had sinned by error: a fact which the Hebrews gather from Exodus 21:14, though they limit it with many restrictions, which anyone who wishes to see may find in Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 11*.

<margin>XVII. The Basin.</margin>
XVII. The architectural plan of the Basin exists in Exodus 30:18–21. Its material was likewise made of bronze, just like the Altar. But it had this remarkable feature: that bronze was collected from the mirrors of the women who assembled in troops at the gate of the tent of meeting (Exodus 38:8). Certainly the pious...

# ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

certain pious women, led by a singular devotion, were **assembling** <note>original: צֹבְאֹת (*tzov'ot*), a Hebrew term suggesting a gathered troop or host performing service</note>, performing a kind of sacred service around the tent—not this *Levitical* one, which had not yet been built, but the *tent of Moses*, where God used to meet and speak with *Moses* (Exodus 33:7). Later, they would assemble at the Levitical Tabernacle at appointed times in groups for prayers and other exercises of religion (cf. 1 Samuel 2:22). Those women, according to the custom of the age, possessed their own mirrors made of polished and shining bronze, which indicated what was decorous or unseemly on the face, and by which they were accustomed to arrange their hair, ribbons, and whatever other head-ornaments they possessed. These mirrors, which had once served only for the cleanliness of the body and perhaps for womanly vanity, they now contributed with a willing heart to a more sacred use, so that the sacred basin might be fashioned from them for the cleansing of the ministers of God. *Moses does not describe the form of the Basin.* However, it is more than probable that it was so designed that it had certain taps or pipes <note>original: *epistomia* or *fistulas*</note> in its lower parts, from which clean water could be released repeatedly whenever there was a need. For it is unseemly that the uncleanness of many should be washed away by the same water, which would have already been made impure by the first washing. Fresh water was always poured in during the morning, whether from a spring or a well—it matters not, provided it was clean and of pure color. The *use of the Basin* was this: that Aaron and his sons, that is, all the priests about to perform sacred rites, should wash their hands and feet; this was not to be neglected, unless they wished to pay for it with their lives. The *location of the Basin* was between the Altar and the tent of meeting, so that it might be ready for necessary use.

<margin>XVIII. The Tent with its coverings.</margin>
XVIII. From the Court, let us attentively consider the Tent itself. Here, first, the outermost **COVERING** <term>TEGMEN</term> of the Tent presents itself to the eyes, which is called *mikseh* <note>original: מִכְסֶה</note>, made of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering of badger skins <note>original: *pellibus melium*, referring to the 'tahash' skins; the exact animal is debated, often identified as porpoise or fine leather</note> as a covering on top (Exodus 26:14). This served to cover the roof, not the sides. II. Beneath these coverings was the **TENT** <term>TENTORIUM</term>, called *ohel* <note>original: אֹהֶל</note>, consisting of eleven curtains made of goat's wool, or as others prefer, goat's hair, to be joined together by bronze loops (ibid. verses 7–13). III. Then followed the **TABERNACLE** <term>TABERNACULUM</term> strictly speaking, called *mishkan* <note>original: מִשְׁכָּן</note>, in which the Lord dwelt: consisting of ten very precious tapestries, made of interwoven linen, and blue, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, which were filled with Cherubim of most artistic workmanship; these were fastened to upright boards of the finest cedar wood by their blue cords and golden loops (ibid. verses 1–6).

<margin>XIX. The Holy Place, with its furnishings.</margin>

XX. The **HOLY OF HOLIES** was the innermost and most sacred part of the Tabernacle, separated from the *Holy Place* by a most skillfully crafted veil, called the *Parokhet* <note>original: פרוכת</note>, and referred to by the Apostle as *the second veil* <note>original: τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα (to deuteron katapetasma)</note> in Hebrews 9:3. The excellent analogy between the things signified and their "type" <note>A "type" is a historical person or event intended by God to foreshadow a future reality</note>: which becomes manifest through a diligent comparison of the individual parts.

# ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

<meta>Tt 2</meta>
<meta>catchword: words</meta>

...while [representing] the visible Heavens. The *Court* represented the world of the earth. The *Table* with the *twelve loaves* represented the *twelve signs* of the Zodiac. The *Lampstand* with its *seven lamps* represented the *seven planets*. The four colors of the curtains represented the four Elements of the World. <note>The ancient theory that all matter is composed of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> This was also the opinion of *Josephus*, who stated <note>original Greek: "τὴν διαμέτρησιν τῆς σκηνῆς πρὸς μίμησιν τῆς τῶν ὅλων Φύσεως γεγονέναι"</note> *that the proportioning of the tabernacle was made in imitation of the nature of the universe.* (Antiquities of the Jews, Book III, Chapter 5). Truly, those who philosophize so coldly about the Tabernacle, and think nothing here of the *Messiah* and his dwelling among his people through the Spirit, turn the Tabernacle of God into the Tabernacle of *Moloch*; <note>A Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice; the author is suggesting that stripping the Tabernacle of its Christian spiritual meaning is a form of idolatry.</note> nor do they have a much better faith in God than those who worship Moloch.

<margin>XXIII. A somewhat better view: Political.</margin>
XXIII. A little more probable, and not to be entirely despised, is the observation of those who notice that God, as the King of the Israelite people, wished to dwell in this Tabernacle as if in some Royal palace. Indeed, God said: <note>original Hebrew: "ועשו לי מקדש, ושכנתי בתוכם"</note> *And they shall make for me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in their midst.* (Exodus 25:8). <margin>A. XXV</margin> Upon these words of the Law, *Moses Nachmanides* <note>A leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic, also known as Ramban (1194–1270).</note> commented quite skillfully:
> <note>original Hebrew: "ועשו בית וכלים כמקדש מלך ובית ממלכה: ושכנתי בתוכם בבית ובכסא הכבוד אשר יעשו לי שם"</note> *They shall make a house and vessels, like the sanctuary of a King and a royal house. And I will dwell in their midst in the house and upon the throne of glory which they shall make for me there.*

But we have spoken more copiously on this matter elsewhere, where we explained the <term>Theocracy</term> <note>A system of government in which God is recognized as the immediate ultimate ruler; here referring specifically to ancient Israel.</note> of the Israelite people. Now it is pleasing to hear the Jews discussing this, especially the one I just praised, *Isaac Abarbenel*, <note>A Portuguese Jewish statesman and philosopher (1437–1508) who wrote extensive commentaries on the Bible.</note> whose words on Leviticus 25:8 <note>likely a citation error in the original for Exodus 25:8</note> are as follows:
> *The sanctuary of God has various names: The Tent of Meeting, the Dwelling Place of the Lord, the Dwelling Place of the Testimony, and the Sanctuary of the Lord. It is called the Tent of Meeting because in the desert it had the appearance of a tent constructed of curtains and boards. It is called the Dwelling Place* <note>original Hebrew: "מפני שכינה שם, השם שכונה" — Mishkan</note> *because the Divine Majesty* <note>The Shekhinah, or the manifest presence of God.</note> *dwelt in it. It is called the Dwelling Place of the Testimony because the Book of the Laws and the Tablets were stored in it, which were a testimony between the Israelites and their heavenly Father. Finally, it is called the Sanctuary* <note>Miqdash</note> *because it was forbidden for the uncircumcised and the unclean to enter there.*

And a little further on:
> *In this Palace were the Table, the Lampstand, and the Altar of Incense, as things suitable for the service of the King of the world. Not that He, to whom all praise is due, has any need of these things—far be it from us to think so! But so that it might settle deeply into the minds of the people that the Lord their God moved in the midst of the camps of the Israelites.*

XXIV. But of all the Hebrews I have seen, *Rabbi Shem Tob* <note>Shem-Tov ben Joseph ibn Shem-Tov, a 15th-century Spanish philosopher.</note> followed these matters most fully in his notes on the *Guide for the Perplexed*, Part III, Chapter 45. Of which...

<meta>This page continues the quote from the Jewish scholar Moses Nachmanides (begun on the previous page), who interprets the Tabernacle as a royal palace for God as King. It then transitions into the author's own mystical and Christian interpretation of the Tabernacle’s Outer Court.</meta>

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

it will not be wearying to append his words. *God*, he says, *to whom be praise, commanded such a house to be built for himself, just as a Royal house is wont to be. In a royal house, these things are found: Some who guard his palace; others who perform duties pertaining to the Royal dignity, who prepare the feasts and provide other things necessary for the King. Others, finally, who sing daily with voice and stringed instruments. There is also in the royal house a place established for preparing food. Likewise, a place where perfumes are burned for him. There is also a table, and likewise a chamber proper to himself, where no one sets foot except he who is second to him, or whom he holds among his dearest. In the same way, God willed all these things to be in his house, lest he should yield in any matter to the Kings of the earth. For he is the Great King, though he does not indeed stand in need of these things; but from this the reason for the daily sustenance given to the Priests and Levites easily shines forth, being that which every King is accustomed to supply to his ministers.* AND ALL THESE THINGS AIMED AT THIS: THAT THE COMMON PEOPLE MIGHT UNDERSTAND THAT THE KING, NAMELY THE LORD OF HOSTS, DWELT AMONG US. <note>The "Lord of Hosts" (Dominus Exercituum) is a common biblical title for God, emphasizing His sovereignty over both heavenly and earthly armies.</note> *For he is the Great King, to be feared by all nations.* Thus far that Hebrew scholar. <note>Referring to Moses Nachmanides, the 13th-century philosopher mentioned on the previous page.</note>

<margin>
XXV. The mystical meaning of the Court.
</margin>

XXV. I confess that these things have been noted not inconveniently. However, they fulfill by far the smallest part of those things which ought to be meditated upon by pious hearts on the occasion of the Tabernacle. Let us, as becomes Christians, strive for something somewhat more sublime; and in the first place, let us seek out the mystical significance of the **COURT**, and of those things which were contained in the Court. <note>The "Court" or *Atrium* refers to the large, enclosed outdoor area surrounding the Tabernacle tent where the altar of burnt offering stood.</note> I. The **COURT** is a figure of the Church according to its external administration and visible form: by which all those are encompassed who make a profession of faith and observe external worship, whether they do so sincerely or hypocritically. It is worth comparing Revelation 11:1–2, where the Court, distinct from the Temple and not to be measured by John but "cast out," seems to denote the great multitude of men which the scope of the Church was to include, and which would claim for itself the name, dignity, and privileges of the Church. II. The **Amplitudo** <term>Amplitudo (breadth/size)</term> of the Court can signify the future dilation and expansion of the visible Church. Nor is it incredible that Isaiah alluded to this in Chapter 54:2: *Enlarge the place of your tent, and let the curtains of your habitations be stretched out; do not hold back; lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes.* III. The **Planks** with the curtains hanging from them, separating the court from all those parts of the earth which remained excluded, denote the separation of the people of God from all outsiders who are alienated from the knowledge, worship, and covenant of the true God (Numbers 23:9; Deuteronomy 33:28). IV. The **Veil** spread over the entrance warned that the way of entry into the Church is not open to all, except to those professing faith and repentance; and that there is a need for reverence and sobriety for those who would approach God

BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

T 3

...placed in the Courtyard, outside the Tabernacle, before the entrance of the tent of meeting. This location served not only for the sake of dignity and cleanliness—ensuring the sanctuary was not daily defiled by blood, smoke, and ashes—but it was also a figure of the offering of Christ, which was to be carried out publicly in the sight of all. The sacred fire, descending from heaven and to be preserved perpetually, is an emblem of the eternal Spirit through whom Christ offered himself blameless to God (Hebrews 9:14). This is that spirit which sanctifies all victims and makes them acceptable to God (Romans 15:16): *That the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Spirit.* Without this Spirit, whatever is offered—no matter how great a show of zeal is made—is profane and abominable. As seen in Isaiah 50:11 <note>The Latin text cites Jes. i. 11 (Isaiah 1:11), but the quoted text "En vos omnes..." is actually Isaiah 50:11.</note>: *Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who encircle yourselves with firebrands: walk in the light of your fire, and in the firebrands that you have kindled. This shall you have from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow.*

<margin>XXVII. The rite of its expiation.</margin>
XXVII. Also worthy of consideration is the rite of expiating <note>In this context, "expiation" refers to the ritual cleansing or consecration of an object to make it fit for holy use.</note> the Altar, prescribed in Exodus 29:37-38. It had to be expiated by: I. The slaughter of a young bull. II. The sprinkling of blood. III. Anointing with holy oil. Thus it became a "Most Holy thing," so that whatever touched it became holy. Expiation presupposes sin; but what sin burdened the Altar, which had seen no use until now? Certainly, it was crafted by men, whose hands and minds were not sufficiently pure. Therefore, God willed that it be expiated first, before it was employed for sacred rites. By this, the minds of the Israelites were to be convinced that something which, from its very origin, was polluted and required expiation, could not provide true atonement. Instead, they were to look to Him who, born by the power of the Most High and conceived by the Spirit of God, is the Holy One <term>preeminently</term> <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐξοχὴν (kat' exochen)</note>, requiring no expiation for Himself. Thus, this Altar, considered in itself, belonged to the "weak and beggarly elements of the world"; in this regard, it did not represent Christ but stood in opposition to Him. Yet, there is a figure of Christ in the fact that by its touch it sanctified those things moved toward it. For it belongs to Christ—who did not obtain this through some ceremonial anointing, but from that fullness of the Spirit with which He was drenched—to sanctify our offerings, our prayers, and indeed our very selves, so that we might receive from Him as much as suffices for our own sanctification.

<margin>XXVIII. The mystery of the Laver.</margin>
XXVIII. Who could doubt that the LAVER <note>A "laver" is a large basin or vessel used for ritual washing.</note> also pertained to that purification of souls which we have from the spirit of Christ? Christ is that *fountain opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness* (Zechariah 13:1). Feet and hands are symbols of our actions; since God willed that they be washed so diligently—threatening even the penalty of death to those who did otherwise—we are taught that in the worship of God, purity is required in all actions, both external and internal (Isaiah 1:16; Psalm 26:6; 2 Corinthians 7:1).

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

<margin>XXVIII.</margin>
XXVIII. 1. Nor should we overlook the allegory of *Gregory*, observed in his *Seventeenth Homily on the Gospels*; he notes that the Bronze Laver was made from the mirrors of the women, by which he intends to signify repentance. Thus, the Law is understood through the mirror, as it reveals our stains <note>See James 1:23, 25, where the Word of God is compared to a mirror showing a man’s natural face.</note>. However, the Laver and the water contained within it signify remorse and tears. The location of the Laver near the Altar of Burnt Offerings reminds us of the union of the blood and the Spirit of Christ—the former for justification, the latter for sanctification. The Altar with the blood of the victims served to signify justification; the Laver with its water served to signify sanctification.

<margin>XXIX. Of the Tabernacle itself.</margin>
XXIX. From the Courtyard, let us step into the TABERNACLE: but only with that reverence which is owed to those most sacred rites. Let us survey these mysteries in such a way that, starting from the more general, we may gradually descend to the more specific details. The most general thing of all that the tabernacle could signify is the gracious indwelling and presence of God in Israel <note>Exodus 29:45-46: "I will dwell among the children of Israel and will be their God."</note>. To this would be added that other dwelling of God in Christ, and through Christ in his people. Concerning this, Isaiah 8:14 says: The Lord, who is a stumbling block to both houses of Israel, shall become for a sanctuary <note>original Hebrew: למקדש, *le-mikdash*</note>. <note>See also Zechariah 2:14, John 1:14, and Revelation 21:3.</note>

XXX. More specifically, it signifies I. THE HUMAN NATURE OF CHRIST, which is also called a Temple. The analogy is as follows: I. Just as the Deity dwelt in the tabernacle in a shadowy way, so in Christ "dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" <note>Colossians 2:9</note>. II. Just as the tabernacle was humble on the outside but precious on the inside, so the external form of Christ appeared contemptible to the eyes of the flesh <note>Isaiah 53:2-3, Philippians 2:7, Romans 8:3, Psalm 22:7</note>. However, his internal nature, to be discerned by the eyes of faith, is most glorious <note>John 1:14, 2 Peter 1:17, Hebrews 1:3</note>. III. Just as there was Divine speech in the tabernacle, so God addresses us through the Son <note>Hebrews 1:1</note>. He is therefore called the *Word*, because he revealed <note>original Greek: ἐξηγήσατο, *exegesato*, meaning to lead out, explain, or make known</note> the Father to us <note>John 1:18</note>. IV. Just as the tabernacle was taken down and set up again, and finally brought into the temple to rest there, so the body of Christ, dissolved by death, was raised up on the third day <note>John 2:19</note>, and afterward was received into heaven for eternal rest.

XXXI. II. THE CHURCH OF THE ELECT. For I. That also is the House of God <note>1 Timothy 3:15, 1 Peter 2:5, 1 Corinthians 3:16</note>, in which God promised He would dwell <note>2 Corinthians 6:16, Matthew 28:20</note>. II. Just as the tabernacle consisted of various parts of quite unequal dignity, yet skillfully joined together by its straps and rings, so the Church is gathered from people of every age, sex, nation, language, and condition—quite unequal in their duties and gifts, yet joined by the same Spirit, faith, and charity, and arranged in a fitting order <note>Psalm 122:3</note>.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

The placement of the Altar in the Courtyard, outside the Tabernacle and before the entrance of the tent of meeting, was not only for the sake of beauty and cleanliness—ensuring the sanctuary was not daily defiled by blood, smoke, and ash—but it was also a symbolic representation of the offering of Christ, which was to be carried out publicly in the sight of all. The sacred fire, descending from heaven and to be kept burning continually, is an emblem of the eternal Spirit through whom Christ offered himself blameless to God <note>Hebrews 9:14</note>. This is the same spirit that sanctifies all sacrifices and makes them acceptable to God <note>Romans 15:16: "That the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost."</note>. Without this Spirit, whatever is offered, no matter how great the appearance of zeal, is profane and abominable. As written in Isaiah 50:11: *Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who encircle yourselves with firebrands: walk in the light of your fire and in the firebrands you have kindled. From my hand this has come to you; you shall lie down in pain.* <note>original: "En vos omnes accendentes ignem, circumcingentes malleolis: ite in focum ignis vestri, & in malleolos quos succendistis. E manu mea est hoc vobis, in dolore jacebitis."</note>

<margin>XXVII.
The rite of its expiation.</margin>
XXVII. Also worthy of consideration is the rite for the expiation <note>The process of cleansing or making an object holy and fit for divine use.</note> of the Altar, prescribed in Exodus 29:37–38. It had to be expiated by: I. The slaughtering of a bullock; II. The sprinkling of blood; and III. Anointing with holy oil. Thus, it became a "Most Holy" thing <note>original Latin: "Sancta Sanctorum," literally "Holy of Holies," here referring to the high degree of sanctity assigned to the altar.</note>, so that whatever touched it became holy. Expiation implies the presence of sin; but with what sin was the Altar burdened, since it had not yet been used? Certainly, it was constructed by men, whose hands and minds were not sufficiently pure. Therefore, God willed it to be expiated first before it was employed for sacred duties. This was intended to convince the minds of the Israelites that an object which required expiation due to the pollution of its very origin could not provide true atonement. Instead, one must look to him who—born by the power of the Most High and conceived by the Spirit of God—is the Holy One *par excellence* <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν," meaning pre-eminently or in the highest sense.</note>, needing no expiation himself. In this way, the Altar considered in itself belonged to the "beggarly elements of the world" <note>A reference to Galatians 4:9, implying physical rituals that lack inherent spiritual power.</note>; in that respect, it did not represent Christ but was contrasted with him. However, it serves as a figure of Christ in that by its touch it sanctified those things moved toward it. For this belongs to Christ—not that he attained it through some ceremonial anointing, but that he might sanctify our offerings, our prayers, and indeed ourselves from that fullness of the Spirit with which he was imbued, so that we might receive from him what is sufficient for our own sanctification.

<margin>XXVIII.
The mystery of the Laver.</margin>
XXVIII. Who could doubt that the LAVER <note>The large bronze basin used by priests for washing.</note> also pertained to that purification of souls which we have from the spirit of Christ? Christ is that fountain opened to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness <note>Zechariah 13:1</note>. Feet and hands are symbols of our actions; since God willed that these be washed so carefully by all—even threatening the penalty of death for those who did otherwise—we are taught that the purity of all actions, both external and internal, is required in the worship of God. <note>See Isaiah 1:16, Psalm 26:6, and 2 Corinthians 7:1.</note>
