### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Nor should we overlook the allegory of Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), a highly influential Pope and theologian known for his symbolic interpretations of Scripture.</note>, observed in his *Seventeenth Homily on the Gospels*. He notes that the Bronze Laver was crafted from the mirrors of the women, which he interprets as a symbol of repentance. In this view, the mirror represents the Law, which reveals our blemishes <note>James 1:23, 25: "For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass..."</note>, while the basin and the water contained within it represent compunction <note>A feeling of deep regret or remorse</note> and tears. The placement of the laver near the Altar of Burnt Offerings reminds us of the connection between the blood and the Spirit of Christ: the former for justification <note>Being made right before God</note> and the latter for sanctification <note>The process of being made holy</note>. The Altar, with the blood of the victims, served to signify justification; the Laver, with its water, signified sanctification.

<margin>XXIX. And of the Tabernacle itself.</margin>
<margin>XXIX.</margin>
Let us now step from the Courtyard into the TABERNACLE: but only with that reverence which is owed to those most sacred rites. In examining these mysteries, let us begin from the general aspects and gradually descend to the more specific. The most general thing the tabernacle could signify is the gracious indwelling and presence of God among Israel <note>Exodus 29:45, 46</note>. To this is added that other dwelling of God in Christ, and through Christ, within his people. Regarding this, Isaiah 8:14 says the Lord, who is a stumbling block to both houses of Israel, shall become "for a sanctuary" <note>original Hebrew: *le-miqdash* למקדש</note>. See also Zechariah 2:14, John 1:14, and Revelation 21:3.

<margin>XXX.</margin>
More specifically, it signifies **I. THE HUMAN NATURE OF CHRIST**, which is also called a Temple. The analogy is as follows:
I. Just as God dwelt in the tabernacle in a shadowy way, so in Christ dwells the whole fullness of the Godhead bodily <note>Colossians 2:9</note>.
II. Just as the tabernacle was lowly on the outside but precious on the inside, so the external form of Christ appeared contemptible to the eyes of the flesh <note>Isaiah 53:2, 3; Philippians 2:7; Romans 8:3; Psalm 22:7</note>. However, his internal nature, perceived by the eyes of faith, is most glorious <note>John 1:14; 2 Peter 1:17; Hebrews 1:3</note>.
III. Just as there was Divine speech in the tabernacle, so God addresses us through his Son <note>Hebrews 1:1</note>. He is called the Word for this reason: because he "has explained" <note>original Greek: *exegesato* (ἐξηγήσατο), meaning to interpret, reveal, or lead out the meaning of</note> the Father to us <note>John 1:18</note>.
IV. Just as the tabernacle was dismantled and then set up again, and finally brought into the temple to rest there, so the body of Christ, dissolved by death, was raised again on the third day <note>John 2:19</note> and afterwards taken up into heaven for eternal rest.

<margin>XXXI.</margin>
**II. THE CHURCH OF THE ELECT.** For:
I. It too is the House of God <note>1 Timothy 3:15; 1 Peter 2:5; 1 Corinthians 3:16</note>, in which God has promised he will dwell <note>2 Corinthians 6:16; Matthew 28:20</note>.
II. Just as the tabernacle consisted of various parts of very unequal dignity, yet were skillfully joined together by their straps and rings, so the Church is gathered from people of every age, sex, nation, language, and condition. Though they are quite different in their duties and gifts, they are nevertheless joined by the same Spirit, faith, and love, and arranged in a harmonious order <note>Psalm 122:3</note>.

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

...placed in the Courtyard, outside the Tabernacle, before the entrance of the tent of meeting, was intended not only for the sake of dignity and cleanliness—so that the sanctuary would not be defiled daily by blood, smoke, and ashes—but it was also a <term>figure</term><note>A "figure" or "type" is a person, object, or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> of the offering of Christ, which was to be carried out publicly in the sight of all. The sacred fire, descending from heaven and to be kept burning continually, is an emblem of the eternal Spirit through whom Christ offered himself unblemished to God <note>Hebrews 9:14</note>. This is that spirit which sanctifies all victims and makes them acceptable to God, as seen in Romans 15:16: *That the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Spirit.* Without this Spirit, whatever is offered—no matter how great the appearance of zeal—is profane and abominable. 

> *Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who encompass yourselves with torches: walk in the light of your fire, and in the torches that you have kindled. This you shall have from my hand: you shall lie down in sorrow.* <note>Isaiah 50:11. The author uses this to warn against "strange fire" or human-made religious zeal as opposed to the "sacred fire" of the Holy Spirit.</note>

<margin>XXVII. The rite of its expiation.</margin>
XXVII. Also worthy of consideration is the rite of <term>expiating</term><note>Expiation refers to the act of making amends or purification for sin.</note> the Altar, prescribed in Exodus 29:37–38. It had to be expiated: I. By the slaughter of a young bullock. II. By the sprinkling of blood. III. By anointing with sacred oil. Thus it became a "Holy of Holies," so much so that whatever touched it became holy. Expiation presupposes sin; but with what sin did the Altar labor, since it had seen no use until now? Certainly, it was crafted by men, whose hands and minds were not sufficiently pure. Therefore, God willed that it be expiated first before it was employed for sacred duties. By this, the minds of the Israelites might be convinced that a thing which required expiation from its very origin could not provide true expiation itself. Instead, they were to look toward Him who—sown by the power of the Most High and conceived by the Spirit of God—is the Holy One <note>original: *κατ' ἐξοχὴν* (kat' exochen), meaning "preeminently" or "par excellence"</note>, standing in need of no expiation. Thus, the Altar considered in itself belonged to the *weak and beggarly elements of the world*; in this respect, it did not represent Christ but stood in opposition to Him. Nevertheless, it serves as a figure in that it sanctified those things moved toward it by its contact. For that power belongs to Christ—not acquired by some ceremonial anointing, but from that fullness of the Spirit with which He was drenched—so that He might sanctify our offerings, our prayers, and indeed ourselves, so that we might receive from Him enough for our own sanctification.

<margin>XXVIII. The mystery of the Laver.</margin>
XXVIII. Who could doubt that the LAVER also pertained to that purification of souls which we have from the spirit of Christ? Christ is that fountain opened to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for separation from uncleanness <note>Zechariah 13:1</note>. The feet and hands are symbols of our actions; since God willed that these be so carefully washed by all—even threatening the punishment of death to those who did otherwise—we are taught that the purity of all actions, both external and internal, is required in the worship of God. <note>Isaiah 1:16; Psalm 26:6; 2 Corinthians 7:1</note>.

# ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE TABERNACLE OF LEVITICUS.

VII. 1. Nor should we look down upon the allegory of *Gregory* <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and Doctor of the Church known for his influential biblical commentaries.</note>, who observes in his *17th Homily on the Gospels* that the Bronze Laver was crafted from the mirrors of women <note>Refers to Exodus 38:8, where the women gave up their polished bronze mirrors to make the basin.</note>; by this, he intends to signify repentance. Just as the *Law* is understood to be a mirror that reveals our stains (*James 1:23, 25*), the laver and the water it contains represent remorse and tears. The location of the laver near the *Altar of Burnt Offerings* brings to our minds the union of the blood and the Spirit of Christ—the former for our justification (being made right with God) and the latter for our sanctification (being made holy). The Altar with the blood of the victims served to signify the former; the Laver with its water signified the latter.

<margin>
XXIX.
And of the 
Taber-
nacle 
itself.
</margin>
XXIX. From the Courtyard, let us step into the TABERNACLE: but only with that reverence which is owed to those most sacred mysteries. Let us survey these mysteries by starting from the general and gradually descending to the more specific. The *most general meaning of all* that the *tabernacle* could signify is the gracious indwelling and presence of God within Israel (*Exodus 29:45, 46*). To this is added a second dwelling of God in Christ, and through *Christ* in His people. Regarding this, Isaiah (*8:14*) says: **The Lord**, who is a stumbling block to both houses of Israel, shall become <term>as a sanctuary</term> <note>original Hebrew: *לְמִקְדָּשׁ* (le-miqdash)</note>. (*Zechariah 2:14, John 1:14, Revelation 21:3*).

XXX. *More specifically*, it signifies I. THE HUMAN NATURE OF CHRIST, which is also called a Temple. The *analogy* is as follows: I. Just as God dwelt in the tabernacle in shadows, so in Christ the whole fullness of the Deity dwells bodily (*Colossians 2:9*). II. Just as the tabernacle was plain on the outside but precious within, so the external form of Christ appeared contemptible to the eyes of the flesh (*Isaiah 53:2, 3; Philippians 2:7; Romans 8:3; Psalm 22:7*). However, the internal nature, which must be discerned by the eyes of faith, is most glorious (*John 1:14, 2 Peter 1:17, Hebrews 1:3*). III. Just as there was Divine speech in the tabernacle, so God addresses us through His Son (*Hebrews 1:1*). He is therefore called the *Word*, because he <term>has revealed</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐξηγήσατο* (exēgēsato), meaning to lead out, explain, or make known fully.</note> the Father to us (*John 1:18*). IV. Just as the tabernacle was taken down and set up again, and finally brought into the temple to rest, so the body of Christ, dissolved by death, was raised again on the third day (*John 2:19*), and afterward taken up into heaven for eternal rest.

XXXI. II. THE CHURCH OF THE ELECT. For I. This too is the *House of God* (*1 Timothy 3:15, 1 Peter 2:5, 1 Corinthians 3:16*), in which God promised He would dwell (*2 Corinthians 6:16, Matthew 28:20*). II. Just as the tabernacle consisted of various parts of quite unequal dignity, yet skillfully joined together by its straps and rings, so the Church is gathered from people of every age, sex, nation, language, and condition—though they are quite different in their duties and gifts, they are nonetheless joined by the same Spirit, faith, and love, and arranged in a beautiful order (*Psalm 122:3*).

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

*III.* Just as in the Tabernacle, so also in the Church there is a revelation of **God**. *Romans 16:25, 26; 1 Corinthians 2:9; Ephesians 3:10.* *IV.* Just as the tabernacle was **lowly** on the **outside**, regarding its condition in this world and the persecutions it faces, yet it is **beautiful within**. *1 Corinthians 1:26; Psalm 45:14; Song of Solomon 1:5, 6.* *V.* Just as the tabernacle wandered through uncertain **dwelling places** in the world, so too does the Church, until it is brought into the heavenly sanctuary. *VI.* Just as the tabernacle, though **taken apart**, was held together again: so also the bodies of the faithful, though dissolved by death, shall be raised to glory. *1 Corinthians 15.*

XXXII. The MATERIALS of the Tabernacle, selected by God, are undoubtedly useful for teaching something regarding the truth. However, we have not yet grasped every single detail. The thoughts of a most learned interpreter <note>This likely refers to Johannes Cocceius or a similar 17th-century federal theologian who popularized these allegorical interpretations.</note> seem to come closest to the truth. **Fine linen**, or the flax of the curtains, and the **cedar** planks seem to signify the humanity of Christ, according to which He is the fruit of the earth. *Isaiah 4:2.* To the **blue** color of the curtains <note>original: "hyacinthino"</note> corresponds the grace of Christ, than which nothing is sweeter to the mind: just as nothing is more pleasant to the eyes than the color of the sky, due to its tempered light. To the **purple**, which does not shine, corresponds an external and apparent humility. To the **scarlet**, the blood of Christ. The **coverings** taken from animals signify the preservation of this tabernacle through death, specifically the death of Him who offers Himself as a victim, and in that offering is made like those animals. The **silver bases**, which support the upright boards of the tabernacle, signify the *righteous decree* <note>original: "τό δικαίωμα" (to dikaiōma); here meaning the legal satisfaction or merit</note> of Christ, upon which every dwelling place of God for sinners is founded.

<margin>
XXXIII.
And the Saints.
</margin>
XXXIII. Now let us proceed to the interior of the Tabernacle, where we first encounter that place which is called the HOLY PLACE. This was a figure of the **Church Militant** <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christian community currently living on earth, struggling against sin and trial, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven.</note> on earth. The analogy is as follows: I. In name, for the Church of God is also **Holy**. *1 Corinthians 3:17; 2 Corinthians 6:14; 1 Peter 2:5; Ephesians 5:27.* Yet it is so in such a way that its holiness is of a lower order than that of Christ and the **Church Triumphant**: just as the **Holy Place** was less than the **Holy of Holies**. *Philippians 3:12.* II. The Holy Place was separated from the Courtyard by its veil, which was made according to the prescription of God with most skillful workmanship. The Church is separated from the world. *Romans 12; Song of Solomon 4:12.* This is not by certain futile gestures or **will-worship** <term>original: ἐθελοθρησκείαις (ethelothrēskeiais); refers to self-imposed religious rites or "voluntary worship" that lacks divine authorization</term>; but by the commands of God and inimitable piety. III. All the priests in their order had the right to enter the Holy Place, provided they were not legally impure. All the faithful without distinction have a right to the privileges of the Church, provided they strive for purity of heart and hands. *Psalm 24:4.* For Christ has made all these people **Priests** unto God. *Revelation 4:10; 1 Peter 2:5; following Isaiah 61:6.* IV. In the Holy Place, the priests ministered to God. *Hebrews 9:6.* In the assembly of the brothers, worship pleasing to Him is offered. *Psalm 42:5; Hebrews 10:25.* V. In the Holy Place there was both **light** and **bread**. Both...

# On the MYSTERIES of the LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

The grace of God provides the Church with light, by which she may see, walk, and work; and bread, for her satisfaction. VI. There was no way to the Holy of Holies <note>The inner sanctuary where the Ark of the Covenant was kept.</note> except through the Holy Place. Likewise, there is no way to the state of glory except through the state of grace. Hebrews 12:14.

<margin>XXXIV. The golden table.</margin>
XXXIV. In the Holy Place was the **GOLDEN TABLE** with **TWELVE LOAVES**. This is described in Exodus 25:23. The material was partly of the finest cedar wood and partly of gold plating the cedar. Regarding its form, it had a golden crown and rim, and carrying poles made of cedar wood overlaid with gold, to be inserted into four rings by which it could be carried. All the utensils of this table were also to be made of pure gold. Twelve loaves of bread were to be placed upon it (Leviticus 24:6), to be arranged every Sabbath, and then eaten by Aaron and his sons as a <term>Holy of Holies</term> <note>A Hebrew superlative meaning "most holy" or "most sacred portion."</note>, and this was to be done in the Holy Place. (Ibid. verses 8, 9).

<margin>XXXV. Its mystery.</margin>
XXXV. These things also signify the Messiah, who is the bread of life to his own (John 6:48, 51) and simultaneously the Table, since in him all the sweetness of Divine grace is bestowed and offered to us. John 1:16, 17.

XXXVI. But more specifically, the **TABLE** is a figure of the Gospel word and the Sacraments, in which Christ is presented to the faithful. 1 Corinthians 10:21. It was golden, along with all its equipment; because Christ himself, his word, and the sacraments—however worthless they may seem to the people of this world—are nonetheless infinitely more precious than all the treasures of the world. Matthew 13:44, 45; Philippians 3:8. There was once great pride among the Romans regarding their tables, and great luxury regarding their food. Regarding the former, see Pliny, Book 13, Chapter 15. Regarding the latter, see <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous 16th-century humanist scholar.</note> Lipsius *On the Greatness of Rome*, Book 4, Chapter 7. But that incredible arrogance is mere nonsense compared to this spiritual and heavenly preparation, of which even the smallest crumb could not be redeemed by any treasures of the Persians. Memorable is that sacred Table which the Emperor Justinian <note>The Byzantine Emperor who rebuilt the Hagia Sophia in the 6th century.</note> made for the celebration of the Lord's Supper and dedicated in the Church of Saint Sophia in Constantinople. <note>Also known as the Hagia Sophia.</note> Cedrenus <note>George Cedrenus, a Byzantine historian.</note> describes it in these words: *“Then he also made the sacred table, <note>original Greek: έργον άμίμητον</note> an inimitable work. For it was made from gold, silver, every kind of stone, wood, metal, and other species—whatever the earth, the sea, and the whole world produce. When he had collected from all of them those things which are the best and most precious in abundance, and those of lesser value more sparingly, he cast them into the mold. And he completed it as a cast-type, from which it appeared so varied that it struck those looking at it with amazement.”* Around the table, this inscription was read: <note>original Greek: ΤΑ ΣΑ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΣΩΝ ΣΟΙ ΠΡΟΣΦΕΡΟΜΕΝ ΟΙ ΔΟΥΛΟΙ ΣΟΥ, ΧΡΙΣΤΕ, ΙΟΥΣΤΙΝΙΑΝΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΘΕΟΔΩΡΑ, Α ΕΥΜΕΝΩΣ ΠΡΟΣΔΕΞΑΙ ΥΙΕ ΚΑΙ ΛΟΓΕ ΤΟΥ ΘΕΟΥ</note> "WE YOUR SERVANTS, O CHRIST, JUSTINIAN AND THEODORA, OFFER TO YOU YOUR OWN FROM YOUR OWN; FAVORABLY ACCEPT THESE, O SON AND WORD OF GOD."

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

->JUSTINIAN AND THEODORA: TAKE THESE THINGS GRACIOUSLY, O SON AND WORD OF GOD.<- <note>This likely refers to a dedicatory inscription on an altar donated by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora, which the author uses as a point of contrast.</note> I do not disapprove of this testimony of a grateful mind and affection of piety. However, I doubt whether such a precious table was sufficiently mindful of the simplicity of the Christian cause. The value of the Christian faith is not to be established in some external display, but in the inestimable excellence of spiritual and secret things, which are perceived only by the mind and faith. 

But I return to the Mosaic table, which was also surrounded by a golden Crown. This was because its equipment was entirely Royal—*the bread of the mighty* <note>original: "Panis potentum," often translated as "the bread of angels."</note> *Psalm 78:25.* It was furnished with all necessary equipment, because through Christ not only is the sweetness of Divine grace offered to us, but also those things by which we are able to accept this grace and turn it to our use. He both offers us his grace and confers the faith by which we receive that grace. The table was provided with rings and poles for carrying; for Christ, in the Gospel, passes from place to place so that he may visit all parts of his dominion.

<margin>
XXXVII.
And the loaves of presence.
</margin>
XXXVII. **THERE WERE TWELVE LOAVES**, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. For Christ is abundantly sufficient as food for his entire Church. *All in all. Colossians 3:11.* These, like an offering made by fire, *Leviticus 24:7*, were set back before the face of God. This is because the virtue of Christ’s sacrifice is continually before God, *Hebrews 9:24*. Every Sabbath the Priests replaced them with fresh ones. Christ must be frequently brought to our memory through the preaching of the Gospel: proposed now in this way, now in that, sometimes plainly, and sometimes, as of old, wrapped in ceremonies, so that he may always be like fresh food, most pleasing to our palate. *Compare Matthew 13:53.* This should happen especially every Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>: just as that day is named after him, so also the day itself, and in memory of him, ought to be sacred to us. For he himself clearly showed himself to be seen by John on that day. *Revelation 1:10.* The fact that it was lawful for no one to eat these loaves except the Priests alone signifies that no one has communion with Christ except those who serve God, separate themselves from the world, and offer their bodies to the Deity. *1 Corinthians 10:21.* That they were only to be eaten in the **Holy Place** teaches that all things pertaining to Christ are to be held as sacred. *1 Corinthians 11:27, 28, 29.*

The golden Lampstand.
</margin>

Its architectural outline <note>original: "scíagráphia"</note> is found in *Exodus 25:31.* The material was solid gold, weighing an entire talent, which is sixty pounds. Its form was such that six branches came out from the lampstand's central shaft <note>original: "lychnuchi scapo"</note>, each with three bowls resembling the appearance of an almond, with one ornamental knob <note>original: "malo," literally 'apple'</note> and a flower. In the whole lampstand there were seven Lamps, burning with pure olive oil...

### On the Mysteries of the Levitical Tabernacle.

...pure oil, of which it is spoken in Chapter 27:20, 21. There were also snuffers and trays made of gold for removing the waste from the lamps. It was the duty of the priests to light it every evening (Leviticus 24:2, 3) and to extinguish it in the morning (1 Samuel 3:3).

XXXIX. Regarding the *mystery* in general, this observation is relevant: that throughout the administration of His covenants, God has everywhere joined together symbols of *light* (for knowledge) and *food* (for nutrition). In the first covenant [in Eden], there was the Tree of Knowledge and the Tree of Life. In the desert, there was the pillar of fire and the Manna. Here [in the Tabernacle], there is the Lampstand and the Table. In the New Testament, there is Baptism—called *enlightenment* <note>original: "φωτισμὸς" (phōtismos)</note> by the ancient fathers—and the Holy Supper. We stand in the greatest need of both: food for living, and light for acting wisely.

XL. More specifically: the LAMPSTAND is a figure of the *Church*, which, being illuminated by the light of Christ, holds that same light out to others (Revelation 1:20, 2:5; Zechariah 4:2). The faithful are not only illuminated, but are themselves *Light* (Ephesians 5:8). They shine both with the light of God’s *wisdom*, which is made known even to the angels through the Church (Ephesians 3:10), and with the splendor of *Holiness* (Matthew 5:16). Both are joined together in Philippians 2:15, 16. But it must be understood that this light of the Church is borrowed; she does not possess it of herself (John 1:8, 9). She is a lampstand, not the *Sun* (Revelation 12:1). She is clothed with the Sun and crowned with a crown of twelve stars. All her light is communicated from Christ, *who is the Dayspring from on high* <note>original: "Oriens ex alto," a reference to the rising sun or dawn in Luke 1:78</note>, and is spread through the Apostles.

XLI. The material, which is *gold*, signifies: I. *Participation in the Divine nature* (2 Peter 1:4). For in these sacred emblems, gold represents the Deity and the eternity of Christ. II. The excellence of the Faithful (Lamentations <note>original: "Thr." refers to Threni, or Lamentations</note> 4:2), specifically the excellence of *Wisdom* (Job 28:15, Proverbs 3:14), of Faith (1 Peter 1:7), and of *Sanctity* (1 Peter 3:3, 4). For the Lampstand is fashioned in respect to these very qualities.

XLII. The OIL is the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:27). The foolish virgins also had lamps, but without oil. Unregenerate men who profess Christ indeed have some knowledge of the mysteries of God, but it is not that vivid knowledge which comes from the Holy Spirit, and therefore it is not true knowledge. For they remain fools (Matthew 25:3). This light is not acquired by any human skill (1 Corinthians 2:14). Those who surround themselves with the sparks of their own fire shall lie down in sorrow (Isaiah 50:11). To be sure, all illumination is from the Holy Spirit as God (Job 35:10, 11), and is sometimes present in a singular way even in the one performing the work (Hebrews 6:4). Nevertheless, that alone is to be esteemed as the precious and sacred oil which is from the Holy Spirit, as the Spirit of Christ; it does not only illuminate, but also sanctifies. This is called *gold* in Zechariah 4:12.

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

->JUSTINIAN AND THEODORA: ACCEPT THESE THINGS GRACIOUSLY, O SON AND WORD OF GOD.<-
<note>original: "JUSTINIANUS ET THEODORA : QUÆ BENEVOLE ACCIPE, FILI ET VERBUM DEI." This is a famous dedication found on the altar of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, gifted by the Emperor and Empress.</note>

I do not find fault with this testimony of a grateful soul and this display of piety. Yet, I doubt whether such a costly table was entirely appropriate for the simplicity of the Christian faith. The value of our faith should not be judged by any outward display, but by the priceless excellence of spiritual and hidden matters, which are perceived only by the mind and through faith. But I return to the Mosaic table, which was also encircled by a golden *Crown*. This was because its arrangement was entirely Royal. It is the *Bread of the mighty* <note>original: "Panis potentum." A reference to the Manna or heavenly bread.</note> (Psalm 78:25). It was furnished with all necessary equipment, because through Christ, we are offered not only the sweetness of Divine grace, but also the means by which we can accept this grace and put it to our use. He both offers us His grace and grants us the faith by which we receive that grace. The table was equipped with rings and poles for carrying. For Christ, in the Gospel, moves from place to place, so that He may visit all parts of His dominion.

<margin>
XXXVII.
*And the bread of presence.*
</margin>
XXXVII. THERE WERE TWELVE LOAVES, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. For Christ is abundantly sufficient as food for His entire Church. He is *all in all* (Colossians 3:11). These loaves, like a "fire offering" (Leviticus 24:7), were placed *before the face of God*. This is because the power of Christ’s sacrifice is continually before God (Hebrews 9:24). Fresh loaves had to be set out by the Priests every Sabbath. In the same way, Christ must be frequently called to our memory through the preaching of the Gospel: presented now in this way, now in that—sometimes plainly, and sometimes, as in the old days, wrapped in ceremonies—so that He may always be like fresh food, most pleasing to our palate (cf. Matthew 13:53). This ought to be done especially on every Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>: just as the day is named after Him, so should the day be sacred to us in His memory. For He also clearly presented Himself to be seen by John on that day (Revelation 1:10). The fact that it was not lawful for anyone to eat these loaves except for the *Priests* alone signifies that no one has communion with Christ except those who serve God, set themselves apart from the world, and offer their bodies to the Divine (1 Corinthians 10:21). The fact that they were to be eaten only in the *Holy Place* teaches that everything pertaining to Christ must be held as sacred (1 Corinthians 11:27, 28, 29).

<margin>
XXXVIII.
*The golden lampstand.*
</margin>
XXXVIII. Directly across from the Table, on the Northern side, was the LAMPSTAND. Its design is described in Exodus 25:31. The material was *solid gold, weighing an entire talent, which is sixty pounds*. Its form was such that six branches extended from the shaft of the lamp-holder itself, each with three bowls shaped like almonds, a knob, and a flower. In the entire lampstand there were seven *Lamps*, burning with pure olive oil,

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

Uu 2

<margin>XXXIX.</margin>
XXXIX. This observation pertains generally to the **mystery**: that throughout the administration of His covenants, God has everywhere joined together the symbols of **light**, **His mystery**, and food for nourishment. In the first [covenant in Eden], there was the Tree of **Knowledge** and the Tree of **Life**. In the desert, there was the pillar of fire and the Manna. Here, there is the Lampstand and the Table. In the New Testament, there is Baptism—called <term>Illumination</term> <note>original: "Φωτισμός" (Phōtismos). A common Greek term used by early Church Fathers to describe the spiritual enlightenment granted through baptism.</note> by the Ancients—and the Holy Supper. We stand in the greatest need of both things: nourishment for living, and light for acting wisely.

XL. **More specifically**: THE LAMPSTAND is a figure of the **Church**, which, having been illuminated by the light of Christ, also holds that same light out to others (**Revelation 1:20, 2:5; Zechariah 4:2**). The faithful are not only illuminated, but are themselves Light (**Ephesians 5:8**). They shine both by the light of the **wisdom of God**, which is made known through the Church even to the Angels themselves (**Ephesians 3:10** <note>The original OCR reads "3:20," but the context of wisdom being shown to angels refers to Ephesians 3:10.</note>), and by the splendor of **Holiness** (**Matthew 5:16**). Both are joined together in **Philippians 2:15, 16**. But it must be understood that this light of the Church is borrowed, and she does not have it from herself (**John 1:8, 9**). She is a lampstand, not the Sun (**Revelation 12:1**). She is clothed with the Sun and crowned with a crown of twelve stars. All her light is from Christ, **who is the Dayspring from on high** (**Luke 1:78**), communicated through the Apostles.

XLI. The **Material**, which is **gold**, signifies: I. **Participation in the Divine nature** (**2 Peter 1:4**). For in these sacred emblems, gold represents the Deity and the eternity of Christ. II. The **Excellence of the Faithful** (**Lamentations 4:2**), specifically the excellence of **Wisdom** (**Job 28:15; Proverbs 3:14**), of **Faith** (**1 Peter 1:7**), and of **Holiness** (**1 Peter 3:3, 4**). For it is in respect to these things that it is a Lampstand.

XLII. THE OIL is the Holy Spirit (**1 John 2:27**). The foolish virgins also had lamps, but without oil. Unregenerate men, though they profess Christ, possess some knowledge of the mysteries of God, but it is not that vivid knowledge which comes from the Holy Spirit, and therefore it is not true knowledge; for they remain foolish (**Matthew 25:3**). This light is not acquired by any human skill (**1 Corinthians 2:14**). Those who surround themselves with the sparks of their own fire "shall lie down in sorrow" (**Isaiah 50:11**). To be sure, all illumination comes from the Holy Spirit as God (**Job 35:10, 11**), and sometimes in a singular way even in those who are being moved by Him (**Hebrews 6:4**). Nevertheless, that alone should be esteemed as precious and sacred oil which comes from the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of Christ; it does not only illuminate, but also sanctifies. This is called **gold** in **Zechariah 4:12**.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

XLIII. **The six branches proceeding from one stem, and the seven lamps**, represent individual Churches, each conspicuous with its own light; they are members of the same universal Church, with which, joined by one Spirit, they constitute one undivided whole. The **bowls**, moreover, and the **knops** <note>original: "mala," literally "apples," referring to the decorative spherical ornaments on the Menorah</note>, and the **flowers**, and the **tongs**, etc., signify the various ministries of the Church by which she is rendered beautiful. **1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11, 12; Romans 12:6–8.** These things, though they may seem lowly to the world, are nevertheless **golden** and precious in the sight of God. **Psalm 84:11.**

XLIV. **The lampstand was lit toward evening.** In the "evening of the world," a more brilliant light was destined to arise. **Jeremiah 30:24; Daniel 12:4.** It shone only **by night** and was extinguished **in the morning**. By this, it seems to be signified: I. That as long as the use of that lampstand remained, it was still night, and the promised day had not yet arrived. Until Christ, it was night—not only for the Gentiles, but also for the Jews. That night passed away with the arrival of Christ. **Romans 13:12.** Once the true light had arisen, that lampstand had to be extinguished, and all Levitical worship was to cease. II. That all illumination of the Church through the ministry of the Word is restricted to the state of this present life, and will cease with the rising of the light of glory. Peter’s words in **2 Peter 1:19** can be understood in both ways.

XLV. **It was the duty of the priests to light the lamps daily.** This pertains partly to our High Priest, Christ, who radiates a continuous flow of light into His own people (**Isaiah 49:6; Luke 2:32**); and partly to the Ministers, upon whom it is incumbent to promote the light of the Church both by the clarity of Sacred doctrine and by the exemplary holiness of their lives, as well as by the lawful use of discipline, to remove everything that obscures that splendor. In **Zechariah 4:3, 13**, by the two olive trees, the "two sons of oil"—that is, the double order of the anointed, the Prophets and the Apostles—seem to be understood.

<margin>XLVI. The Altar of Incense.</margin>
XLVI. Next follows the ALTAR OF INCENSE, the <term>outline</term> <note>original: "Sciagraphia," a Greek-derived term for a preliminary sketch or architectural drawing.</note> of which is found in **Exodus 30:1–10**. In this, note: I. The **Material**, which was the finest cedar <note>often identified as shittim or acacia wood</note>, covered with gold. **verses 1, 3.** II. The **Form**. It was required to be square (**verse 2**) with horns proceeding from it, golden rings, poles, etc. **2, 3, 4, 5.** III. The **Location**. It was to be placed before the inner veil, in front of the mercy seat. **verse 6.** IV. The **Use**. This is presented <term>positively</term> <note>original: "θετικῶς" (thetikōs)</note>: 1. Regarding the **action**, Aaron shall burn incense upon it. **verse 7.** 2. Regarding the **time**: In the **morning**, when the lamps are prepared (that is, cleaned); and in the **evening**, when they are to be lit. And this was to be done daily. **verses 7, 8.** It is also presented <term>negatively</term> <note>original: "ἀρνητικῶς" (arnētikōs)</note>: no **foreign incense**, nor any **burnt offering**, **grain offering**, or **drink offering** was to be offered there. **verse 9.** Only once a year were the horns to be sprinkled with the blood of the sin offering, on the Day of Atonement.

# ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

->Uu 3<-

XLVII. This Altar also generally signifies *Christ*. **Hebrews 13:10.** Just as He offered Himself to God as a "fragrant offering" <note>original Greek: "eis osmēn euōdias"</note>, **Ephesians 5:2**, <margin>The mystery of this.</margin> so He also continually intercedes for us with His most sweet prayers. **1 John 2:1.** He makes our own prayers pleasing to God. **John 16:24.** Just as this altar was distinct from the altar of burnt offering—which was in the court, outside the outer veil, **Exodus 27:1**—it likewise signified the same Christ, but from a different perspective. That altar represented Christ offering Himself for our sins on the cross; this altar represents Him *interceding* for us.

XLVIII. The *wood* of this altar is fit to signify the humanity of Christ, while the *gold* signifies His eternity and Divine excellence. The altar of burnt offering was covered with *bronze*, because Christ was in a total state of humiliation while He was offering Himself for our sins. **Hebrews 9:26–28.** This altar is overlaid with *gold*, because His intercession is full of majesty and is primarily carried out in a state of glory. **Romans 8:34; Hebrews 1:3.**

XLIX. The *form*, being square and identical on all sides, denotes that Christ *is the same yesterday, today, and forever*, **Hebrews 13:8**, and is equally accessible to those approaching Him from the four corners of the world. **Isaiah 45:22.** The *carrying poles*, by which it could be carried from place to place, signify that Christ is present with His Church in every place, **Matthew 18:20, 28:20**, even in the islands, **Revelation 1:9**, in the furnace, **Daniel 3:25, 28**, in the den, **Daniel 6:23**, and in prison, **Acts 16:25.**

L. The *location* of this Altar is in the innermost part of the *Holy Place* <note>original: "Sanctum"</note>, where it was forbidden for the people to look in, and where only the Priests were occupied. In contrast, the altar of burnt offering in the court was exposed to the eyes of everyone. Christ, offering Himself on the cross during the feast of Passover, was seen by all the people; but when pouring out prayers for His own, even in this life, He withdrew to a secret place on the mountain. **Matthew 14:23; Luke 21:37.** And after His sacrifice, He was not to be seen by the people who had crucified Him, yet He was in the midst of those whom He had atoned for. **Acts 10:41.**

LI. The *incense* <note>original: "odoramenta," literally "fragrant things"</note> signifies: I. *The intercession of Christ*. Which, relying on His sacrifice, is most pleasing to God the Father, and is continual and perpetual. II. *The prayers and thanksgivings of the Saints*. **Revelation 5:8; Psalm 141:2.** Regarding these, we are taught: *I. They ought to be daily*, morning and evening. **Psalm 55:18; Daniel 6:11; Colossians 4:2.** *II. Only according to the will of God.* **1 John 5:14.** *III. Kindled indeed by the fire of zeal*, **Romans 12:11**, but not by *strange* <note>original: "peregrino," referring to fire not taken from the sacred altar</note> fire. **Isaiah 50:11.** *IV. Without presumption of one's own merits*, relying solely on the dignity and merit of Christ. For it was forbidden to offer sin offerings <note>original: "propitiatoria"</note> on this altar. Christ alone makes our prayers pleasing to God, both by His merit (signified by the blood sprinkled on the altar annually) and by His *intercession*. Compare **Revelation 8:3.**

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

<margin>
LII. The Mystery of the Interior Veil.
</margin>

LII. Let us now approach the **INTERIOR VEIL**, which distinguished the *Holy of Holies* from the *Holy Place*. Regarding its significance, we can speak with great confidence, as the Apostle Paul has gone before us as our guide. It signified three things.

I. *The visible heaven*, through which the Lord Jesus passed. **Hebrews 4:14.** This is the heaven that the hope of the faithful, following Jesus, penetrates. **Hebrews 6:19–20.** For, **first**, just as this veil hid those things that were within, so too the visible heavens—the limit of our current sight—hide the things that are inside, so that we are unable to see them <term>ὀφθαλμοφανῶς</term> <note>original Greek: "ophthalmophanōs," meaning "visibly" or "to the naked eye"</note>. God has set His glory above the heavens. **Psalm 8:2.** Our life is still hidden with Christ in God. **Colossians 3:3.** For us to perceive heavenly things, it is necessary for the heaven to be opened and drawn aside. **Revelation 4:1.** 

**Second**, the veil, which was exceptional in its material and craftsmanship, suggested to those looking upon it that the interior things were far more excellent. This visible heaven, fashioned with much skill, **Psalm 8:4; 19:2**, ought to instill in us thoughts about the excellence of the superior palace, of which this heaven is merely the outermost and lowest floor. 

**Finally**, just as the curtain was frequently folded up during the transport of the tabernacle and eventually became useless once the Temple was built—perishing entirely along with the Temple—so also these visible heavens will one day be "folded up like a garment," **Psalm 102:26**, and "pass away with a roar." **2 Peter 3:10, 12.** This will occur when God reforms the entire universe into a more majestic temple for His glory.

LIII. II. *The ceremonies of the Law*, by which the mysteries of the Gospel were largely covered. For just as the outer veil barred the common people, so this interior veil barred the Priests themselves from gazing upon the secrets and from familiar access to the Throne of Grace. The veil placed over the face of Moses served the same purpose. **2 Corinthians 3:13.** There was a double use for these ceremonies: 
1. *To foreshadow and prefigure Christ.* **Colossians 2:17.** In this respect, they were a great privilege of the Israelite Church over the Gentiles. **Isaiah 42:21; Hosea 8:12; Romans 9:4.** 
2. *To envelop the promises of grace in their own obscurity.* For most people, sticking to the "bark" <note>the outer shell or literal meaning</note>, did not penetrate to the "kernel." The faithful saw nothing except obscurely and through a cloud. In this respect, the ceremonies were a <term>ἥττημα</term> <note>original Greek: "hēttēma," meaning a "deficiency" or "disadvantage"</note> of the Ancient Church compared to the New.

LIV. III. *The flesh of Christ.* **Hebrews 10:19–20.** 
**A.** Just as the veil covered the glory of Jehovah lurking within, so the "form of a servant" <note>the human nature assumed by Christ</note> covered the glory of Christ’s Divinity. **Philippians 2:6–7.** For this humility was so great that it was a "stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles." **1 Corinthians 1:23.** 
**B.** Just as the veil was by no means lacking in its own value and artistry, so also the flesh of Christ was holy and <term>ἀμίαντος</term> <note>original Greek: "amiantos," meaning "undefiled" or "pure"</note>. **Hebrews 7:26.** It was adorned not merely with the image of Cherubim—that is, angelic holiness—but with the image of the Divine. It is a perfectly fashioned exemplar of all sanctity. 
**C.** Just as there were Cherubim on the veil, so around Christ

# On the Mysteries of the Levitical Tabernacle

Angels frequently hovered around Christ as a man: at his birth (Luke 2:13), after the temptation (Matthew 4:11), in his agony (Luke 22:43), and in the tomb (Matthew 28:2). **D.** Just as there was no entrance to the sanctuary except through the veil—and that being drawn aside—so no entrance is given into heaven except through the flesh of Christ, which had to be broken by death. Not because no one was saved before Christ's death, but because they were saved only through and because of it (Hebrews 2:9–10; 9:15). Hence also, when Christ died, the **veil** <note>original Greek: *tò katapétasma*</note> was torn (Matthew 27:51). All obstacles being removed, heaven itself was opened to all nations.

<margin>LV. *The Sanctuary. Hebrews 9:24.*</margin>
LV. The **HOLY OF HOLIES** was a **type** <note>In biblical studies, a "type" is a person, thing, or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of the highest heaven (Hebrews 9:24). For there is: **I.** The most perfect holiness (Isaiah 63:15). **II.** The Throne of God (Isaiah 66:1). **III.** Incredible glory (Psalm 8:1), with which no gold of this world can be compared. **IV.** The realities signified by the *ark*, the *mercy seat* <term>mercy seat: the golden lid of the Ark where God's presence was said to dwell</term>, the *Cherubim*, and the rest of the items present there (Hebrews 12:22–24).

<margin>LVI. *Of the Ark of the Covenant.*</margin>
LVI. But let us examine these things somewhat more closely. The structure of the **ARK** is described in Exodus 25:10. The material was *of Shittim wood* <term>Shittim: likely wood from the acacia tree, known for its durability</term>, or of the most excellent cedars. That wood, fashioned into the form of a chest, was covered inside and out with the purest gold. The length was two and a half cubits, and the *width a cubit and a half*. It was surrounded by a golden molding. Four golden rings were set into the corners. Two *poles* were inserted into these, made indeed of cedar wood but overlaid with gold, so that it could be carried wherever necessity required. For it had to be carried on the *shoulder*; it was not permitted to place it on a *wagon* (1 Chronicles 13:7 and following, compared with 15:12, 15). Moreover, the Hebrews assert that it was carried by the Levites in such a way that those carrying it had their faces turned toward the ark from both sides, so that no one turned their back to it.

<margin>LVII. *The Tablets of the Testimony stored within it.*</margin>
LVII. The use of the ark was for *storing the testimony*. By this is understood the **Tablets of the Covenant**, which are also called the Tablets of Testimony (Exodus 31:18). This is because they were clearly the testimony of the Covenant entered into between God and Israel: by which God witnessed His will, which He commanded the Israelites to follow; and the Israelites witnessed their own eagerness, by which they had promised obedience. From this, the ark itself is called the *Ark of the Testimony* (Exodus 30:6). And even the entire Tabernacle takes its name from it. However, these were not the Tablets which Moses had broken out of holy indignation because the covenant had been violated—those originally made by the hand of God—but those which Moses had fashioned out of stone at God's command, similar to the first ones, and inscribed by God Himself with the same words as the first. For as to the claim some argue, that the fragments of the first tablets were placed in the Ark, either alone or joined with the later ones; that is not only beyond the Scripture, but against it.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

For so the words of Moses hold in Deuteronomy 10:1 <note>The text cites verse 12, but the quote corresponds to the beginning of the chapter.</note>: *At that time the Lord had declared to me: "Hew for yourself two stone tablets like those first ones were, and come up to me on the mountain, and you shall make for yourself a wooden ark: so that I may write on those tablets the same words that were on those first tablets which you broke: THEN YOU SHALL PLACE THEM IN THAT ARK."* Unless perhaps it is to be understood—as I see very learned men also suggest—as referring to another ark, purely of wood, without any gold covering, in which the tablets of the second writing were stored until the other one, to be covered everywhere with gold, was completed by Bezalel <note>Bezalel was the chief artisan of the Tabernacle, endowed by God with special skill.</note>. Furthermore, there was nothing in the ark, at least in the time of Solomon, except the two stone tablets which Moses had placed there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). As for what happened to the first ones <note>The original tablets smashed by Moses in anger at the Golden Calf.</note>, with scripture being silent, we are not unwillingly ignorant.

<margin>LVIII. The Propitiatory Lid with the Cherubim</margin>
LVIII. Furthermore, a *mercy seat* <term>mercy seat: from the Latin 'propitiatorium,' the golden lid of the Ark where atonement was made</term> *made of pure gold was placed* upon the Ark. And two golden Cherubim, made from the lid itself as a continuous work, covered it with their wings, with faces turned toward each other in such a way that they looked down together toward the mercy seat. Regarding the form of the Cherubim, there is great dispute among interpreters. If anyone wishes, he may see what I have discussed with some diligence on that matter in my work *On Egyptian Antiquities* <note>original title: "Ægyptiacorum"</note>, Book II, Chapter 13. This one thing is certain: they were winged living creatures. But of what species, with how many wings, with how many faces they were endowed, and what the form of the rest of the body was, there is a deep silence in the writings of Moses. Therefore, perhaps it will be best of all to profess a modest ignorance here. *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> prudently defined them thus in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book III, Chapter 6*: <note>original Greek: Ζῶα πετεινὰ, μορφῇ οὐδενὶ τῶν ὑπ’ ἀνθρώπων ἑωraμένων παραπλήσια</note> *Winged living creatures, similar in form to none of those seen by men, which Moses had seen represented on the throne of God.* And elsewhere, in *Book VIII, Chapter 2*: <note>original Greek: Τὰς δὲ χερουβεῖς οὐδεὶς ὁποῖαί τινες εἰπεῖν οὐδὲ εἰκάσαι δύναται</note> *As for the Cherubim, no one can say or even imagine what kind of figure they were.* On the mercy seat, in the middle of the two Cherubim, was the *Throne of Divine Majesty*, from which He gave oracles to those consulting Him (Numbers 7:89).

<margin>LIX. The Location of the Ark.</margin>
LIX. The *ordinary place of the ark* was within the veil, in the Holy of Holies (Exodus 26:33). While the Tabernacle was standing, the ark was taken from there whenever the Israelites were to set out, so that it might scout out a place of rest for them (Numbers 10:33), and so that it might be a comfort to them as a symbol of the Divine presence, and a terror to their enemies (verse 31). After it was brought into the temple, it was never removed from there except with the destruction of the temple (Psalm 132:13–14; 2 Chronicles 5:9; 1 Kings 8:8). For this reason, the temple is called the *rest of the Lord and of the Ark of his strength* (2 Chronicles 6:41) and a *place of rest for the Ark of the covenant of the Lord* (1 Chronicles 28:2). Eventually, the Levites were even relieved of the burden of carrying it (2 Chronicles 35:3).

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

<margin>LX. What happened to the Ark after the destruction of the Temple.</margin>
**LX.** Since the sacred records are silent regarding what happened to the Ark after the destruction of the temple, a most fertile ground for storytelling was born here for the overly curious interpreters, both Jewish and Christian. The Jews imagine that King Solomon, when he had learned from the responses of the prophets that the temple would one day be leveled to the ground by the Babylonians, constructed obscure and intricate vaults beneath the floor of the temple where the ark could be safely hidden when danger was imminent. They claim this was observed by Josiah, who—having been informed of the impending slaughter of Jerusalem by the reading of the Mosaic law and the prophecy of the prophetess Huldah—timely hid the Ark in that cavern, along with Aaron’s rod, the **Urim and Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim: mysterious objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will</term>, and the remains of the **Manna** in the Golden Urn. In this spirit, they interpret 2 Chronicles 35:3: *Josiah said to the Levites: "Place the Holy Ark in the place which Solomon, the son of David, built."* <note>original: "Josias Levitis dixit: ponite Sanctam arcam in loco quem Salomon, filius Davidis ædificavit."</note> How far these things are from the true sense of sacred history is obvious to anyone, unless they are dulled by a thick head and stupor.

<margin>LXI. According to Epiphanius.</margin>
**LXI.** **Epiphanius** <note>Saint Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a Church Father known for his writings against heresies and his collection of saintly biographies.</note>—if indeed it was Epiphanius—wanders even further from probability; his fable in the *Book on the Lives of the Prophets, Chapter VIII*, goes roughly like this: Jeremiah, he says, rescued the Ark and its contents before the temple's destruction and hid them away, swallowed up within a rock. Then, to the standing elders of the people and the priests, he said:
> *The Lord has gone from Sinai into heaven; and from there He shall return with holy power. And this shall be the sign of His coming: namely, when all nations shall worship the wood.* <note>The "wood" here is a common early Christian reference to the wooden Cross of the crucifixion.</note>
After this, he added:
> *No one among the priests or prophets shall reopen this Ark except Moses, the chosen of God: and Aaron alone shall spread out the tablets which are within it. Furthermore, in the resurrection, the Ark shall rise first of all, and shall break forth from that rock, and be placed upon Mount Sinai. Then all the saints will flock to it, everywhere awaiting the Lord, and they shall flee the enemy who plots their death.*
Having said these things, Jeremiah, pressing with his finger, imprinted the name of God upon the stone and sealed it, and that figure remained fixed as if it had been carved with iron. Presently a cloud covered that rock. Neither does anyone know that place, nor to this day has anyone been able to read the name; nor will anyone ever be able to until the end of the world. That rock is situated in that wilderness where the Ark first existed, between those mountains where Aaron and Moses lie. At night, a cloud rests upon that place like fire, similar to the things that happened in ancient times, to signify that the glory of God shall never depart from His law. Thus far Epiphanius.

<margin>LXII. According to the truth of the matter.</margin>
**LXII.** For the rest, these stories are all apocryphal and destitute of any appearance of probability. It is more probable, as others believe, that the Ark burned together with the Temple. Even if that too might seem strange—why, when the other utensils of the Temple were transferred to Babylon—

->BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.<-

For these are the words of Moses in Deuteronomy 10:1, 2: *At that time the Lord had commanded me: Hew for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones, and come up to me on the mountain, and make for yourself a wooden ark; so that I may write on those tablets the same words that were on those first tablets which you broke: THEN YOU SHALL PLACE THEM IN THAT ARK.* <note>The author is quoting the Latin Vulgate or a similar scholarly translation of the Hebrew text.</note> Unless perhaps this is to be understood—as I see most learned men also prefer—as referring to another ark, made purely of wood without any gold covering, in which the second tablets of the law were kept until the final one, which was to be covered with gold on all sides, was completed by **Bezalel** <note>Bezalel was the master craftsman appointed by God to build the Tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 31).</note>. Furthermore, there was nothing in the ark, at least in the time of Solomon, except the two stone tablets which Moses had placed there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). As for what happened to the first [broken] tablets, since the Scripture is silent, we are not unwilling to remain ignorant.

<margin>LVIII. The Mercy Seat with the Cherubim.</margin>
**LVIII.** Additionally, a *mercy seat* <term>Mercy Seat: From the Latin 'propitiatorium,' the golden lid of the Ark where God's presence was said to dwell</term> made of pure gold was placed upon the Ark. And two *golden Cherubim*, made of hammered work from the lid itself, covered it with their wings, their faces turned toward one another in such a way that they both looked down toward the mercy seat. There is a great dispute among interpreters regarding the form of these Cherubim. If anyone is interested, they may see what I have discussed with no small diligence on that matter in my work *On Egyptian Affairs, Book II, Chapter XIII.* One thing is certain: they were winged living creatures. But as to their species, how many wings they had, how many faces they were endowed with, and what the form of the rest of their body was, there is a deep silence in the writings of Moses. Therefore, it is perhaps best for everyone to profess a modest ignorance here. **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide essential context for the Second Temple period.</note> prudently defined them thus in *Antiquities, Book III, Chapter VI*: *Winged creatures, in form like none of those seen by men, which Moses had seen depicted on the throne of God.* <note>original Greek: Ζῶα πετεινὰ, μορφῇ οὐδενὶ τῶν ὑφ' ἀνθρώπων ἑωραμένων παραπλήσια</note> And elsewhere, in *Book VIII, Chapter II*: *Regarding the Cherubim, no one can say or even imagine what kind of form they had.* <note>original Greek: Τὰς δὲ χερουβεῖς οὐδεὶς ὁποῖαί τινες εἰπεῖν οὐδὲ εἰκάσαι δύναται</note> On the mercy seat, in the midst of the two Cherubim, was the *Throne of Divine Majesty*, from which God gave oracles to those who consulted Him (Numbers 7:89).

<margin>LIX. The Location of the Ark.</margin>
**LIX.** The ordinary *location* of the ark was within the veil, in the **Holy of Holies** <term>Holy of Holies: The innermost sanctum of the Tabernacle and later the Temple, accessible only to the High Priest once a year</term> (Exodus 26:33). While the Tabernacle stood, the ark was taken from there whenever the Israelites were to set out, so that it might scout out a place of rest for them (Numbers 10:33), and so that it—as a symbol of the Divine presence—might be a comfort to them and a terror to their enemies (verse 31). After it was brought into the Temple, it was never removed from there until the destruction of the Temple (Psalm 132:13, 14; 2 Chronicles 5:9; 1 Kings 8:8). For this reason, the Temple is called the *resting place of the Lord and of the Ark of His strength* (2 Chronicles 6:41) and a *place of rest for the Ark of the covenant of the Lord* (1 Chronicles 28:2). Consequently, the Levites were relieved of the burden of carrying it (2 Chronicles 35:3).

### Concerning the Mysteries of the Levitical Tabernacle.

<margin>60. What happened to the Ark after the destruction of the Temple.</margin>
**LX.** What became of the Ark after the destruction of the Temple, since the sacred records are silent, has given rise to a very rich abundance of storytelling for overly inquisitive interpreters, both Jewish and Christian. The Jews imagine that King **Solomon**, having learned from the responses of prophets that the Temple would one day be leveled by the Babylonians, built obscure and intricate vaults beneath the Temple floor where the Ark could be safely hidden when danger loomed. They claim this plan was followed by **Josiah**, who—having been warned of the imminent disaster of Jerusalem by reading the Mosaic law and by the prophecy of **Huldah** the prophetess—timely hid the Ark in that cave, along with **Aaron’s** staff, the **Urim and Thummim** <term>Urim and Thummim: Sacred objects used by the High Priest to inquire of God's will</term>, and the remainder of the **Manna** in the Golden Urn. In this spirit, they interpret 2 Chronicles 35:3: *Josiah said to the Levites: Place the holy ark in the house that Solomon the son of David built.* How far these ideas are from the true meaning of the sacred history, anyone can see, unless they are dulled by "phlegm and stupor" <note>A common early modern medical metaphor suggesting that a physical imbalance of "humors" made a person mentally slow or unable to perceive the truth.</note>.

<margin>61. According to Epiphanius.</margin>
**LXI.** **Epiphanius** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD) was a Church Father. The work cited here, *The Lives of the Prophets*, is now generally thought to be by a different, later author.</note>—if indeed it was Epiphanius—wanders even further from probability. His legend, in the *Book on the Lives of the Prophets, Chapter 8*, goes roughly like this: **Jeremiah**, he says, rescued the Ark and its contents before the destruction of the Temple and hid them inside a rock which swallowed them up. Then, while the elders of the people and the priests stood by, he said: *The Lord has departed from Sinai into heaven; and from there He will return with holy power. And this shall be the sign of His coming: namely, when all nations shall worship the Wood <note>original: "lignum" – This is a traditional Christian reference to the wood of the Cross.</note>.* Next, he added: *No one among the priests or prophets shall reopen this Ark except **Moses**, the chosen of God; and **Aaron** alone shall unfold the tablets that are within it. Furthermore, at the resurrection, the Ark shall rise first of all and break forth from that rock, and it will be placed on Mount Sinai. Then all the saints will flock to it, waiting for the Lord everywhere, and they will escape the enemy who plots their death.* Having said these things, Jeremiah marked the stone with the name of God using his finger, and that shape remained fixed as if it had been engraved with iron. Soon a cloud covered that rock. No one knows that place, nor has anyone been able to read the name to this day; nor will anyone ever be able to until the end of the world. That rock is situated in the wilderness where the Ark first existed, between those mountains where Aaron and Moses lie. At night, a cloud rests on that place like fire, similar to the things that happened in ancient times, to signify that God’s glory will never depart from His law. Thus far Epiphanius.

<margin>62. From the truth of the matter.</margin>
**LXII.** However, these accounts are all **Apocryphal** and lack any appearance of probability. It is more likely, as others believe, that the Ark burned along with the Temple. Even if it might seem strange why, when the other Temple vessels were carried across to Babylon...

BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

...[why] he caused [the treasures] to be carried away by **Nebuchadnezzar**, yet neglected the **Ark**, which surpassed everything else in value, craftsmanship, and the estimation of its holiness. Unless, perhaps, this very estimation of its holiness, and the memory of what once happened to the Philistines <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 5-6, where the Ark caused plagues and disasters for the Philistines who had captured it.</note> in the past, frightened the minds of the Babylonians away from violating the **Ark**: at least to the point that they preferred to leave it to the common fate of the **Temple** rather than carry it away with them at great risk to themselves. On this matter, the most learned lectures of **Reynolds** <note>John Reynolds (1549–1607) was a prominent English Puritan scholar; the work cited is *De Libris Apocryphis* (On the Apocryphal Books).</note> on the Apocryphal Books, Lecture 136 and those following, deserve to be consulted. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the **Ark** was missing from the **Second Temple**: for although the Jews fashioned another similar to it, it lacked the ancient holiness and the visible symbol of the Divine Presence. But perhaps we have pursued these matters at somewhat greater length than was necessary.

<margin>63. Spencer derives the religious use of the Ark solely from the sacred chests of the Egyptians.</margin>
**LXIII.** Now let us inquire into its mystical significance. If we believe the most learned **SPENCER** <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was a pioneer in the comparative study of religion. His influential work argued that God adapted Egyptian rituals for the Israelites to prevent them from returning to paganism.</note>, the **ARK**, insofar as it was a sacred construction fashioned in the shape of a chest, derived its origin from the sacred chests of the pagans, of which there is frequent and obvious record among the ancients. *Since the Gentiles,* he says, *were accustomed to make Arks, consecrated to the mysteries of their gods, out of cedar, and to make them conspicuous and venerable with gold or ivory: it is easy to believe that the God of Israel granted golden Cherubim, and an Ark likewise distinguished by cedar and much gold, lest a perverse envy should prick their minds when they saw the images, chests, and other sacred objects of the heathens shining everywhere; and lest their childish minds be offended by a simple worship that fell below the pomp of heathen superstition.* <note>original: "Quum enim Gentiles Arcas... offenderentur."</note> And this reason alone seems to him so significant that he cannot bring himself, in his mild spirit, to do anything but be gravely angry with those who, *dazzled by the splendor of the Ark, are accustomed to flee toward Allegory (THAT USUAL ASYLUM OF IGNORANCE, he says, when the difficulty of the Mosaic text presses).* See, if you please, the cloud of impetuous speech he pours out upon those who think that institutions of that kind proceeded from God for the sole reason *that they might signify, by way of some more recondite mystery, that He is to be worshiped with a pure mind.* See *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book III, Chapter I, Dissertation v, Section iv. And as if it were not enough to have warned of this so seriously once, he strikes the same anvil with greater vehemence in Section VIII. There, when he had framed an objection for himself—that the singular holiness and decoration of the **Ark** would suggest it was a **type** <term>Type: A person, object, or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</term> of some most sacred thing, and drew its origin from some heavenly pattern rather than the mystical chest of the heathens—he opens his mouth to answer that argument in this way: *From a weapon so blunt,* he says, *we have nothing much to fear.* FOR WHO IS POSSESSED OF SO HAPPY A GENIUS THAT HE CAN ASSIGN ANY HEAVENLY THING FORESHADOWED BY THE TYPE OF THE ARK, AND [PROVE] HIS OPINION WITH SOME PROBABLE ARGUMENT, OR THE TESTIMONY OF SCRIPTURE...

# ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

[...TO] ESTABLISH? Many indeed assert that something <term>more mystical<note>original: "μυστικώτερον" (*mystikōteron*)</note></term> underlies the Ark, and they turn completely bitter unless we grant blind faith to their pronouncements, which are supported only by a thin resemblance. But (*to speak plainly*) I loathe and shun that profane breed of interpreters who toy with God's sacred things, and mold the institutions of the Law—like wax images—into the forms and ideas of all things according to their own whim. As far as the Ark is concerned, I leave it to the judgment of the prudent reader whether the opinion of those WHO BELIEVE THE ARK WAS INSTITUTED ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM OF THE AGE—and who bring forward many well-supported arguments—is not more likely than the opinion of those WHO ASSERT THE ARK WAS GIVEN TO FORESHADOW CERTAIN GOSPEL MYSTERIES, even though they cannot confirm that opinion with even a shadow of reason?

<margin>LXIV. That he derives the Cherubim from their bull-shaped idols.</margin>
LXIV. It is also remarkable to say how he philosophizes concerning the **CHERUBIM**. He proves that their appearance closely approached a calf-like form by this reason among others: because certain idols, displaying the form of oxen or calves, held that very place and use among the more ancient nations which the Cherubim held among the Israelites. For it is known to everyone familiar with the Scriptures that the Cherubim served a dual purpose: namely, to be a seat and throne for God, and so that this crude people, led by their senses, might have a symbol of God's presence and carry Him about as He sat upon the Cherubim. And among the more ancient pagans, *idols* made in the likeness of beasts—most often bulls—and placed in the <term>inner sanctuaries<note>original: "adytis," the most sacred, restricted parts of a temple.</note></term>, were the seats of the gods from which their responses were given. From these facts he draws this conclusion: *Since, therefore, the idols of the Nations, having the place and use of the Cherubim, bore primarily a calf-like form, there is reason for us to believe that the Cherubim of the Hebrews also closely approached that same form.* For it is consistent with reason that sacred images serving nearly the same end and use should be considered not to have differed much in their forms. *In the same place, Chapter IV.* Meanwhile, he maintains that the form of the Cherubim was such that **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a Jewish historian. In his *Antiquities of the Jews*, he famously claims that no one can describe the actual shape of the Cherubim.</note> was ashamed of it; for that reason, Josephus concealed their true figure (which he knew the pagans would turn into matter for mockery) under a word of uncertain meaning. He wisely abstained from describing it in open words to avoid scandal, aware that the Gentiles would regard it with no less laughter and ridicule than the *Ass's Head* <note>original: "Caput Asininum." This refers to a common ancient anti-Jewish and anti-Christian slander (onolatry) which claimed they worshipped the head of a donkey.</note>. *In the same place, Chapter IV, Dissertation 5, Section II.* From this he then further concludes that the symbols and idols of Egypt especially provided the occasion for instituting the aforementioned forms of the Cherubim. He explains it thus: *The Israelites, accustomed to the idols of the Egyptians, loved them more intensely and clung more tenaciously to the worship of those formed in the likeness of calves. Since, therefore, that people followed idols of calf-like form with such blind and headlong zeal, it seems probable that God [fashioned] idols, in...*

### On the MYSTERIES of the LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

...ESTABLISH? Many indeed assert that something <term>more mystical<note>original Greek: μυστικώτερον (mystikōteron)</note></term> lies beneath the Ark, and they fly into a total rage unless we grant a lazy faith to their dictates, which are supported only by a thin resemblance. <margin>LXIV. As well as the Cherubim from their bull-shaped images.</margin>

LXIV. It is also wonderful to say how he <note>Referring to John Spencer, the subject of this critique.</note> philosophizes about the CHERUBIM. Meanwhile, he maintains that the form of the Cherubim was such that <term>Josephus<note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note></term> was ashamed of it; he argues that Josephus therefore concealed their true figure—which he knew the Pagans would turn into material for mockery—behind a word of uncertain meaning. He prudently abstained from describing the figure in open words for the sake of avoiding scandal, being aware that the Pagans would hold it in no less laughter and ridicule than the <term>Ass’s Head<note>original: Caput Asininum. ...fashioned primarily in the forms of calves, he <note>John Spencer</note> wished to grant them; since He <note>God</note> instituted so many laws adapted to their customs, and derived certain sacred rites used among the Egyptians into His own worship. When the Israelites also prepared for their journey to the promised land, and, in the Egyptian manner, demanded a visible sign of the God who was to set out with them; God granted them the Ark and the Cherubim, to be carried about with them, so to speak, and willed all sacred rites to be performed in their presence. Ibid. Section IV.*

<margin>
LXV. And their mystical significance from the Symbolic Theology of the Egyptians.
</margin>
LXV. Indeed, that most learned man does not deny that the Cherubim were mystical and symbolic figures, and monuments of certain more hidden truths; but he also contends that in this respect they borrowed their origin from the multiform symbols and <term>Hieroglyphics<note>The author uses this term in the 17th-century sense: as symbolic or "sacred" pictures believed to hide deep philosophical secrets.</note></term> of the Egyptians. For since in earlier ages, symbols, enigmas, parables, figures, and especially Hieroglyphics, were considered a primary part of knowledge, it is reasonable to believe that God, yielding to the pursuits of the age, placed the Cherubim in the Tabernacle as emblems and hieroglyphics of more secret things; so that His sacred rites might be more pleasing to those who had some taste for more secret literature, and might not seem to yield to Egyptian rites even in the appearance of wisdom. Finally, he concludes generally: *Egyptian symbols and the more obscure signs of things seem to have given occasion to the typical rites of the Jews, and to many laws of Moses, which contain the kernel of some mystery beneath the husk of the literal sense. Section V.*

<margin>
LXVI. A serious refutation of that opinion.
</margin>
LXVI. These things the far more learned man dictates with great confidence; bearing those who speak against him with annoyance, as he himself confesses. However, the favor or anger of any mortal is not of such value to us that we should speak timidly on that account for the truth, piety, and honor of our most sacred religion. Let him hear, therefore, if perhaps these writings should ever reach his eyes, let him hear, I say, the Most Reverend man—not what bile, or spite, or a mind enslaved to superstition has dictated, but what <term>Batavian candor<note>original: "Batavus candor." For I have learned from many experiences that it has sometimes happened even to the wisest of mortals that, when either by a singular inclination of the mind, or perhaps even by chance, they have stumbled upon some opinion which pleased their mind more than others, they treat it as [sacred]...

...carry around some idol of the mind in their eyes, mouth, and pen: they believe it meets them almost everywhere; they imagine they see it in nearly all objects; and, if the objects are different, they wrap them in such a form that they appear to approach most closely to the image of their beloved idea. There is no lack of examples by which I could prove this observation; but I shall spare myself the ill-will and the labor. The most renowned *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian whose work suggested that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian "superstitions" to steer the Israelites away from outright idolatry.</note> provides an example in himself. Once he convinced his mind that God transferred several things from the sacred rites of the Egyptians into His own religion—so that He might accommodate the crude nature of the Israelite people, who were accustomed to such things, and keep them obedient and away from the horrid idolatry of neighboring peoples (as if they were attracted and occupied by certain toys <note>original: *crepundiis*, literally "rattles" or "children's playthings"</note>)—he soon began to fall so desperately in love with this opinion of his that he explained it more prolifically, extended it more widely, and defended it more sharply than any mortal before him. He does not stop at a few tiny details: this learned man sees Egyptian things everywhere, and perceives the Israelite rites only through them and as being composed in their image. However absurd, indeed even shameful, the Egyptian rites may be, they are nevertheless considered worthy to have given the occasion and origin to the Mosaic institutions. No matter how sacred the Mosaic institutions are—even the *Holy of Holies* <note>original: *Sanctitas Sanctitatum*</note> itself, as the Scripture speaks—this does not prevent them from being compared, as if they were certain tolerable follies, with the ridiculous things <note>original: *γελοίοις* (geloiois)</note> and the shameful parts <note>original: *ἀιδοίοις* (aidoiois), referring to the phallic or indecent imagery in Egyptian paganism</note> of the Egyptians, which modesty forbids me to state in plain words. And by this reasoning, it is judged that the wisdom of God the Legislator is better served, and a more "recondite" <note>Hidden or esoteric</note> doctrine is taught, than if someone were to prudently compare those things—as types, figures, and shadows—with the heavenly truth revealed in the Gospel.

LXVII. I cannot hide, nor is there any reason why I should hide, that it grieves my soul to see learned men thus abuse their letters and their leisure. What? Would the Israelites have had to lack the principal part of their religion unless it had first pleased the Egyptians to go mad? Did God act through His institutions so that the Israelite people (if you remove the idolatry) would seem to approach the Egyptians as closely as possible in their religion? Did He not everywhere emphasize to the Israelites that they must not act in the matter of religion according to the institutions of the nations from which they came, or to which they were going, or which they otherwise had as neighbors surrounding them? Did He not separate them from the rites of those nations with infinite precepts; even in those things which, considered in themselves, are neither good nor bad, and whose entire goodness or badness depends solely on the will of the Legislator? Is not the entire Mosaic Law a *fence of a middle wall* <note>original: *septum parietis intergerini*, an allusion to Ephesians 2:14, referring to the "middle wall of partition" that separated Jew from Gentile</note> and an enmity, separating Israel...
