### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

->350<-

...from the Nations? Was it not a massive vice of the Israelites that they adhered to the profane rites of the Egyptians with an excessive inclination of a dull mind? Were they not sharply rebuked for this matter by Moses and the later Prophets? And would God have tolerated this vice in them, and even fostered it (for surely it could not be cured in this way) by indulging them so that they had almost all sacred rites similar to those of the Egyptians, with this only distinction: that, by changing certain small details, the Israelites did in honor of the One God what the Egyptians did in honor of Isis or Osiris, Apis or Serapis? <note>These are major Egyptian deities: Isis (motherhood/magic), Osiris (death/resurrection), Apis (the bull-god), and Serapis (a Greco-Egyptian sun/healing god).</note>

LXVIII. See where we are sliding. The Pagans had a sacred chest, <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾗ τὸ Διονύσȣ αἰδοῖον ἀπέκειτο</note> *in which the private parts of Dionysus were stored*. They also had another used in the *mysteries* of Ceres, *containing within more trifles and toys than a child's box*. They also had, in the revelries of Bacchus, chests and huge snakes crawling out of ivy. Finally, the Egyptians had a chest which, *capable of secrets, deeply hid the covered things of a magnificent religion*. <note>The author is mocking the idea that the Ark of the Covenant was merely a "holy version" of these pagan containers.</note> Since the Israelites were greatly delighted by these and similar things, Spencer argues that the indulgence of the Divine granted that they too should have a sacred chest, but one to be furnished with more holy monuments. Is this how one treats the pestilential disease of a mad little people? Images of bulls were the seats of the Gods among the more ancient Heathens. This was immensely pleasing to the Israelites fresh out of Egypt. What did God do? He indulged them with Cherubim, in a form coming very close to that of a bull; about which *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Jewish historian.</note> was afterwards so ashamed that, fearing the infamy of the rumored "worship of an ass's head," <note>A common anti-Semitic slur in antiquity was that Jews worshipped the head of a donkey in their sanctuary.</note> he prudently disguised the figures of the Cherubim. If that be true, oh, how much more prudent than Moses (for I do not dare say God)—more prudent than Moses, I say, was *Josephus*!

For what Moses once gave to the Israelites in imitation of Gentile rites, *Josephus*, with his foresight (praised by *Spencer*), concealed for the sake of avoiding scandal and to protect his religion from mockery. That people pursued images of calf-like form with headlong zeal, and demanded a visible sign of God going with them in the desert. "Come," says God, "let this also be granted to the people: let them have Cherubim for that purpose." But why, *Spencer*, did God take it so badly when the same thing had recently been provided by Aaron according to the people’s wishes? <note>Referring to the Golden Calf incident in Exodus 32.</note> Or is the only difference that Aaron complied with the people's wishes of his own accord, while God kept Moses busy with the same task soon to be done by Divine command? The Egyptians used to lift the Tabernacle of Moloch <note>Moloch: a deity mentioned in the Bible, often associated with child sacrifice and portable shrines.</note> and the images of Gods onto their shoulders; the Israelites had watched this with great pleasure. Behold again God’s "indulgence": He does not allow them to lack a portable Tabernacle and an Ark with Cherubim to be carried by the Levites. But what is this, if not turning the Tabernacle of God into the Tabernacle of Moloch, or at least...

For what small difference does it make, if the mysteries are removed, whether some Tabernacle displays an image of the *Sun* or of a *calf*? <note>The author refers to the Golden Calf incident; he argues that without its divine meaning, the Tabernacle is no better than a pagan idol.</note> You are indignant, *Spencer*, that the *Devil is called the ape of God*: <note>original: "Diabolum Dei simiam vocitari." I am not usually accustomed to dispute with such vehemence of speech: but the nature of this matter is such that it does not allow itself to be handled with soft fingers. I would fear that God might reproach me for lukewarmness, unless my mind grew hotter than usual against such foreign ideas.

<margin>LXIX. Spencer's arguments are examined.</margin>
LXIX. But *Spencer* believes he has nothing to fear from all these points, since he has supported his opinion with such solid reasons. Solid reasons? Let us see which ones. First, he confirms with many examples that the use of sacred Chests <note>original: "Cistarum"</note> existed among the *Egyptians*, *Trojans*, *Etruscans*, *Phoenicians*, *Greeks*, *Romans*, and almost every nation. No one denies this, but it contributes nothing to the matter. He continues: *reason suggests that religious instruments of this kind should be judged to have surpassed the Mosaic Law in antiquity*. On the contrary, I say, reason suggests that proof of that antiquity must be demanded before it is believed. For neither *Plutarch*, nor *Eusebius*, nor *Suidas*—whose testimonies *Spencer* praises—say anything about such a great antiquity for these Sacred Arks; nor, if they did say so, would they be sufficiently suitable authors. Let us grant that in the rites of *Osiris* or *Bacchus* <note>original: "Liberi Patris," an epithet for the Roman god Bacchus/Dionysus.</note> there was the use of some Ark; let us even add that the worship of Osiris and Bacchus is older, if you like, than the Mosaic Law: it does not follow from this that the use of the Ark was contemporary with the very beginning of the worship of Osiris or Bacchus. For, as tends to happen in such things, superstitions are heaped upon superstitions little by little. Nor is there anyone who can assign the beginnings of the Sacred Chests, if you depart from this Mosaic one.

LXX. *But who,* says Spencer, *who is even slightly sane would say that those nations learned the model for their Arks from the long-obscure and despised nation of the Jews?* Indeed, I do not need to say that, nor, if I did say it, do I trust that I would be held less sane by prudent men. Superstition is a widespread thing, and it easily creeps into the minds of men who are naturally inclined toward it. Nor is a chest a thing so removed from common human use that it could not have occurred to the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>Priests or officials who interpreted sacred mysteries.</note> and leaders of many nations to employ it in their own rites; even if one knew nothing of the other, or only through a confused rumor...

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

->352<-

...might have heard. And indeed, the Ark of the Israelites was so renowned for such stupendous miracles among neighboring nations that it is no wonder if the religious practice of some Ark spread first to them, and then from them to more remote peoples. This much is certain: almost all religious *Chests* <note>original: "Cistas"</note>, at least those of the Greeks and Romans, are later than the Mosaic age, and for that reason, they are cited here with no appearance of truth.

LXXI. Finally, even if it were most thoroughly proven—which has not yet been proven—that the Sacred Chests of the Egyptians preceded the Mosaic age and were not unknown to the Israelites, the matter would still not be settled. For it remains to be proven that God, in order to gratify the Israelites who were fond of Egyptian rites, gave them the Ark out of respect to those customs. That, however, as I judge, can never be proven. On the contrary, the opposite has been proven by us. For God willed His people to be most separated from neighboring nations in matters of religion, and especially from the Egyptians. There must have been another reason, then, why He granted the Ark with the Cherubim to the Israelite people, even if the Egyptians once had something similar. And what probable reason can be imagined, except that through those symbols He might instruct His people concerning the greatest mysteries?

<margin>LXXII. Spencer's unjust hatred toward Allegories.</margin>
LXXII. Here *Spencer* flares up beyond measure. He pursues *Allegories* with a horrible whip, as if they were a common asylum of ignorance; protesting that he hates that profane class of interpreters. If he means bold, inept, and cold allegories—by which historical, natural, or moral matters are led away from the simplicity of truth, contrary to God's intention, and turned into I-know-not-what types of secret things—he will certainly not have me speaking against him. But if he denies that *the Ark and similar ceremonies of the Mosaic Law are shadows of the mysteries of the Gospel*, and if he maintains that *this opinion cannot be proven by even a shadow of reason*, I profess that I would rather endure anything than allow that wisdom to be stripped from divine institutions.

<margin>LXXIII. It is proven that the whole Mosaic Ministry looked toward the Messiah.</margin>
LXXIII. What? Is not the whole ministry of Moses designed to lead one, as if by the hand, to the Messiah and His justice and grace, to be grasped by faith? Why then does Paul say in Romans 10:4: THE END OF THE LAW IS CHRIST, FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS TO EVERYONE WHO BELIEVES? Does not "the Law" denote the entire Mosaic doctrine, as in John 1:17? Moreover, Christ is its End. In every way: both by reason of *limit* <note>original: "termini"</note>, because in His appearing <note>original Greek: "ἐπιφανείᾳ" (epiphaneia)</note> the Economy of Moses began to cease (Luke 16:16); and by reason of *intention*, because through its enigmas it shows the truth which is in Christ. The Law HAD A SHADOW OF THE GOOD THINGS TO COME, *not the very body of things* (Hebrews 10:1). And by reason of *consummation*: both because Christ perfectly fulfilled whatever was either commanded or prefigured in the law:

...was: because it is as if the sum and soul of the law, and, as they say, the <term>quintessence</term> <note>Literally "the fifth essence," referring to the purest or most concentrated part of something.</note> of it. LXXIV. A distinguished passage of Paul on this matter exists in **2 Corinthians 3:13**, where he recounts that *Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not look intently at the end of what was being abolished.* <note>Original Greek: πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἀτενίσαι τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ τέλος τοῦ καταργουμένου.</note> *Lest the children of Israel should look,* or as others prefer, *since they did not direct their eyes toward the end of that which is now removed as useless.* What is that "thing being abolished"? It is the glory of Moses’ face (verse 7). Moreover, that was a symbol of that ministry, which was not to be deprived of its own glory (verse 9). Yet it had to cease, so that it might make room for a more glorious ministry, which is the *ministry of the Spirit* (verses 9, 10, 11). What is the "end" of that which is abolished? With almost all interpreters agreeing, it is Christ, that Lord to whom Israel shall turn once the veil is removed (verse 16). What is the "veil placed over the face of Moses"? It is that obscure and perplexed method of teaching used by Moses, through which it happened that the dull and blinded Israelites, clinging to external things, did not penetrate to the inward mysteries.

The observation of <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in his *Guide for the Perplexed* (Book III, Chapter IX) deserves praise, and was also praised by <term>Grotius</term> <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note>: *The Law was given on a cloudy day, to signify the veil which takes away from our eyes the prospect of truth.* Finally, all things tend toward this: that we may be taught that the goal of the Mosaic doctrine was indeed to lead the Israelites to the contemplation of the Messiah. But such was their dullness that, since they were unequal to bearing that glorious light, some veil of more obscure information had to be applied, by which it happened that they saw less of the Messiah.

<term>Camero</term> <note>John Cameron (c. 1579–1625), a Scottish theologian known for his work on the relationship between the Old and New Testaments.</note> judiciously followed this whole reasoning of type and mystery. The matter comes down to this: Moses’ face shone because it had been turned toward God; that is, the Ministry of Moses, insofar as it is referred to the mind and counsel of God, is altogether splendid and illustrious, and leads clearly enough to Christ, who is the true light. But a carnal people cannot bear that splendor; therefore, the law is veiled to a carnal people until the Spirit approaches to take away the veil. Then even Moses himself is not conscious of his own splendor: for it does not belong to Moses, insofar as he is a minister of the <term>letter</term> <note>Referring to the "letter of the law" as opposed to its spiritual meaning.</note>, to explain the mysteries of the Gospel, the knowledge of which is from the spirit of grace, which causes more to be understood from the doctrine of Moses than the mere sound of the words rings out. When Moses returned to God, he laid aside the veil; so also the Israelite people, when they turn themselves to the Lord, will lay aside the veil of their heart and see the glory...

**2 Chronicles 8:11**. Hence its veneration was so accurately provided for that the eyes of all were barred from the sight of it; and because of it, when it was violated by the curiosity of eyes alone, a vast and almost incredible slaughter occurred at Beth-shemesh (**1 Samuel 6:19**). And *Uzzah* paid with his death for his reckless touch, though it proceeded from veneration (**2 Samuel 6:6-7**). If other things in the Tabernacle were typical <note>Functioning as a "type" or prophetic symbol.</note> and had their own mysteries, is it believable that this item lacked a mystery—this which was the most Holy of all, and by whose holiness the rest were sanctified? Is it believable that it was so carefully placed in the very inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle for the sole reason that the Israelites might have a chest in their sacred rites just as the Egyptians, Phoenicians, Etruscans, and worshipers of Bacchus were accustomed to hide their shameful things in a chest?

...he explicitly records that these things held meanings of more secret matters, mentioning the **Ark of the Covenant** <note>original: *Arcam pacti*</note> covered all over with gold, and the glorious **Cherubim** overshadowing the **Mercy Seat** <term>Mercy Seat: The gold lid of the Ark, known in Hebrew as the *Kapporet*, where God was said to dwell</term> in Hebrews 9:4–5. Indeed, he warns there that he will not speak of these things individually; but by that very statement, he implies that there is no lack of things that *could* be said. And elsewhere he said something that deserves to be remembered here. <margin>a Heb. 4:14–16</margin> *Having therefore a Great* **High Priest** <note>original: *Pontificem Magnum*</note>*, who has passed through the heavens; let us approach with freedom of speech the* **Throne of Grace**. <margin>b</margin> In all these things, I believe no one would deny there is an allusion to the Mosaic institutions. Our *Jesus* corresponds to the High Priest of the Hebrews; the *passage of Jesus through the heavens* corresponds to the *entry of the High Priest through the veil*. The *approach of the faithful*, imploring and expecting God’s help, corresponds to the *approach of the Israelites to the Tabernacle* at the <margin>c</margin> time when the High Priest entered into the inner shrine. But to what does the "Throne of Grace" correspond? To what, if not the **Ark of the Covenant** placed in the innermost Sanctuary? Certainly, Jeremiah teaches that the **Sanctuary** <note>original: *Sacrarium*; the Holy of Holies</note> was regarded as the throne of God. Chapter 17:12: *A throne of glory, a throne of the Most High from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary.* Add to this Ezekiel 43:7. But within the **Sanctuary**, that name was most properly owed to the **Ark** and its "Propitiatory" cover, upon which the Cherubim sat and, from above, the Cloud rested—in which God manifested His presence. Leviticus 16:2; Exodus 25:22. For this reason, God is also said to *ride upon the Cherubim* (Psalm 18:10) and to *dwell* or *sit between the Cherubim* (Psalm 80:1), and they themselves support the throne of God (Ezekiel 10:1). From this, it is concluded that just as the **High Priest** was a "Type" <note>A symbolic foreshadowing</note>, and his entry *through the veil* was a type, and the **Holy of Holies** <note>original: *Sanctum Sanctorum*</note> was a type; so also the **Ark** was a type. Its placement in the Holy of Holies signified that **Throne of Grace** of which Paul speaks—that is, the love and grace of God reconciled to us in Christ, which He gloriously displays in heaven, from where He hears the prayers of suppliants and kindly bestows help upon them.

LXXVIII. But John also provides a powerful argument in Revelation 11:19, where he recounts that the *temple was opened in heaven*, and the **Ark of the Covenant** *was seen in the temple*. What does "temple" signify here? Certainly the **Church** <note>original: *Ecclesia*</note>, in which God dwells through the manifestation of grace and glory. I will not argue now whether this refers to the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth</note> or the Church Triumphant <note>The Church in heaven</note>. That is a deeper inquiry and is not necessary for this case. But if the temple signifies the Church, then the **Ark** must also signify something that pertains to the glory and happiness of that Church. Indeed, in that spiritual and Heavenly Church, there is nothing that corresponds to an imitation or monument of **Egyptian superstition** <note>A reference to the author's opponent, Spencer, who argued the Ark was copied from Egyptian customs</note>; rather, there are far more majestic things which the Ark was Divinely destined to signify. To be sure, the *Ark being seen in the Temple*—a thing never permitted while the ancient tabernacle still held its station—signifies...

If all these things are considered with a clear mind, and with affections and prejudices set aside as is proper, I appeal to your conscience, *Spencer*, <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an influential theologian who argued that many Jewish rites were adapted from Egyptian customs. <margin>
LXXIX.
*The Mystery
of the
Ark.*
</margin>
LXXIX. Having finished this general dispute, we shall proceed with a calmer step and an untroubled foot into a more specific inquiry into those things which were prefigured by the Ark: relying on those foundations which we established at the beginning of this dissertation in Paragraph III. The **Ark**, therefore, signifies Christ, who is the "body" <note>Colossians 2:17</note> of all the shadows. I. *Its material*, partly of wood and partly of gold, is fit to represent His two natures. The wood represents the human nature, according to which He is the *fruit of the earth* <note>Isaiah 4:2</note>. Yet, it was incorruptible <note>original Greek: ἄσηπτον (*asepton*)</note>, subject to no decay; not even when He was dead and placed in the tomb <note>Psalm 16:10</note>; just as Pliny ascribes eternity to *Cedar* in Book XIII, Chapter V. Gold can be a *symbol of Deity*: in respect to its solidity, purity, brightness, and value, denoting the eternity, holiness, and glory of Christ, while simultaneously teaching us what place He should hold for us—namely, that we should count all things as loss and dung compared to Him. Because *only gold* was visible, and the *wood* covered within and without by gold was not seen, some believe they detect this mystery: that Christ had not yet been made conspicuous in the flesh, but His manifestation <note>original Greek: ἐπιφάνεια (*epiphaneia*)</note> remained until then wrapped in the precious promises of God. II. *The form of the Ark*, by which it was suited for guarding treasure, can call to our minds that Christ is the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and every kind of happiness are hidden: from whose abundance the elect may take grace for grace. III. *The Golden Rim* <term>Rim: The *Zēr*, a decorative molding or crown around the top of the Ark</term> surrounding the Ark, appears to be a type of the Crown and Kingdom of Christ. IV. *The Tables of the Covenant*, placed within the Ark, signified that Christ would have the law of God in the midst of His bowels <note>in His heart; Psalm 40:8</note>, and would fulfill every requirement of righteousness <note>original Greek: δικαίωμα (*dikaioma*)</note> for His elect. V. *The Poles*, inserted into four golden rings for carrying the Ark, most conveniently signify that Christ, through the preaching of the Gospel, along with all His grace and glory, would be carried to the four corners of the world. VI. *The Rest of the Ark* was in the Holy of Holies, especially after it was brought into the Temple; the Rest of Christ is in the Sanctuary not made with hands, after He entered into those things which are within the veil <note>Hebrews 6:19–20</note>, to remain there eternally <note>Acts 3:21</note>.

### On the Mysteries of the Levitical Tabernacle.

<margin>LXXX. And of the mercy seat.</margin>
LXXX. Just as the entire Ark did, so especially the **MERCY SEAT**—the atonement cover—represented Christ, in that He covers our sins and restores us to favor with God. For *God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself* (2 Corinthians 5:19). This mercy seat was fashioned from pure gold but placed upon a wooden ark, which teaches us what it is that added price and value to Christ's satisfaction: namely, the infinite dignity of His Divinity. The tablets of the Law were covered by the mercy seat; when the people of Beth-shemesh gazed upon them uncovered, even for a moment when the lid was removed, they brought a horrific slaughter upon themselves (1 Samuel 6:19). Through the atonement of Christ, all our iniquities—by which we have violated both tablets of the Law—are covered, so that they may never come into God's sight to condemn us. But if we should dare to look upon the Law apart from Christ’s satisfaction, we will find nothing in it but the terrible sentence of eternal curse. Upon the Mercy Seat, God showed the presence of His Majesty, and from there He gave gracious answers to the people. In the merits of Christ, a "throne of grace" has been established, which anyone rightly imploring Divine help may approach with confidence and the hope of being heard. God dwelt there in a cloud (Leviticus 16:2), in whose darkness rays of Divine splendor flashed. This is that indwelling which the Hebrew Masters express with the famous word <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>original: שכינה, meaning the "Divine Presence" or "Dwelling"</gloss>. What else did this signify but the fullness of the Deity dwelling bodily in the man Christ? In the past, the cover was located in the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle, behind the veil, hidden from all eyes, since the atonement had not yet been made. But now, God <term>set Him forth</term> <gloss>original: προέθετο (*proetheto*)</gloss> and exposed Christ to the eyes of all as a <term>propitiation</term> <gloss>original: ἱλαστήριον (*hilasterion*), referring to the mercy seat or the means of atonement</gloss> in His blood (Romans 3:25), since whatever was required for atonement has now been perfectly fulfilled.

<margin>LXXXI. And of the Cherubim.</margin>
LXXXI. That the <term>Cherubim</term> <note>Celestial winged beings who serve as guardians of God's throne.</note> were emblems of the Angels has been more extensively explained and proven by us elsewhere. Now we shall consider them only insofar as they had their place on the Mercy Seat. Since they were attached to it, and since the mercy seat signifies Christ, why should we not take this occasion to reflect that the Angels are bound to the ministry of Christ by a constant law and a perpetual, unchangeable will? (John 1:52). Indeed, they themselves have no need for atonement, since they are pure of every crime and stain; nevertheless, Christ reconciled us to those who always stand on God's side, and He reconciled them to us, so that we might merge into one heavenly commonwealth with the Angels (Hebrews 12:22). With bowed faces, they gazed at the mercy seat, thus demonstrating their desire to <term>look into</term> <gloss>original: παρακύψαι (*parakypsai*), meaning to stoop down or bend over to see more clearly</gloss> the mysteries of our redemption (2 Peter 1:12). There were two of them, with their faces turned toward one another, yet in such a way that each looked down upon the cover of the ark. This position of theirs...

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

...teaching [us] beautifully (for the *conduct* <note>original Greek: politeia; refers to the "citizenship" or way of life</note> of the Angels serves as an example for us) how the Faithful, of both the Old and New Testaments, ought to look upon one another with eyes of *equal honor* <note>original Greek: isotimos</note> and mutual charity, yet look together toward Christ.

<margin>LXXXII. The golden urn.</margin>
LXXXII. Also deserving of its own consideration is the **GOLDEN URN** in which the **MANNA** was stored, concerning which a command exists in Exodus 16:32. God ordered a certain measure—which the Hebrews call a *Homer*—of that food with which the Israelites were miraculously sustained for forty years in the desert, to be placed in a bowl or urn and kept in safe-keeping, so that future generations might have a monument of that wondrous food on which their ancestors lived in the desert, and might marvel at the powerful and good providence of God toward them. *Concerning the material of the Urn*, Moses handed down nothing. Hence, different people guess different things. *Rabbi Bechai* <note>Rabbi Bahya ben Asher, a 13th-century Spanish commentator</note> believes a guess should be made from the name <term>tsintsnet</term> <gloss>original Hebrew: צנצנת</gloss>, the etymology of which teaches that it was a *cold vessel*, and <term>matsnenet</term> <gloss>original Hebrew: מצננת</gloss> *cooling*. This implies that what was preserved in it was kept cold and was consequently suitable for long-term storage; such a vessel is said to be *earthenware* <note>as in Jeremiah 32:14</note>. Others here suggest bronze, iron, or lead. *Abarbanel* <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> divines that it was *glass*, so that what was kept inside could be seen from the outside. The Greeks called it a <term>golden jar</term> <note>original Greek: stamnon chrysen</note>. The Apostle <note>the author of the Book of Hebrews in the New Testament</note> followed this, and rightly so. Since all the vessels of the outer sanctuary were made of gold, how much more is it to be believed of those things which were consecrated in the innermost shrine? Whether the etymology taken from "coldness" is of any value is rightly doubted. But even if it were granted, it fits gold no less than earthenware or glass. Certainly, a great miracle in this matter ought to have struck the minds of the Israelites: that the manna, which otherwise rotted and swarmed with worms if kept until the next day, remained uncorrupted for nearly nine centuries, until the burning of the first Temple.

<margin>LXXXIII. Whether it was placed inside or beside the Ark.</margin>
LXXXIII. Where in the Sanctuary this urn was placed is not entirely clear, except that Aaron was ordered to place it *before the face of the Lord*—<term>before the testimony</term> <gloss>original Hebrew: liphnē ha-edūt</gloss> (Exodus 16:33). But whether by *the testimony* one should understand the *tablets of the testimony* (the Ten Commandments), which are also called *testimony* in an absolute sense (Exodus 30:6; 40:18), or the *Ark* itself which guarded those tablets (which also seems to be called the *testimony* in Exodus 30:36), remains uncertain. A comparison of two passages, which seemingly contradict each other, increases the difficulty. 1 Kings 8:9, the sacred History testifies that *there was nothing in the Ark except the tablets of the law*. But Paul in Hebrews 9:4 writes that *besides those tablets, there was in the Ark the golden urn with manna, and the rod of Aaron which blossomed*. The Interpreters sweat greatly over this; but there are two primary ways of reconciling these views, and I can hardly say which of the two should be preferred over the other.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the sacred contents of the Ark of the Covenant, specifically addressing the scholarly debate over whether the Golden Urn of Manna and Aaron’s Rod were stored inside the Ark or merely alongside it, based on a comparison of Old Testament accounts and the Epistle to the Hebrews.</meta>

->On the MYSTERIES of the LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.<-

### LXXXIV.
Some believe that the urn along with the rod were indeed enclosed within the cavity of the Ark at the beginning of the Tabernacle's existence. **Jacob Alting** <note>Jacobus Alting (1618–1679) was a German Hebraist and theologian known for his work on biblical antiquities</note>, in his usual learned manner, explained this view and attempted to make it seem probable. He believes, therefore, that while Moses was still alive, these items were deposited *inside the Ark* in the order they would appear if the lid were removed: first, the **urn of manna**, which was placed at the side of the tablets and, because it was taller, stood out above the rest due to its shape and caught the eye; then **Aaron’s rod**, stretched out over the tablets, the width of which provided space for its branches, flowers, and fruits, and which had to be placed at the very top; for if anything had been placed on top of it, the pressure would have spoiled the beauty of the flowering rod; finally, in the lowest position, the **stone tablets of the covenant**, which were put in first and covered the greater part of the floor, and could not be damaged by the flowering rod placed upon them. From this observation, the order of the Apostolic listing <note>A reference to Hebrews 9:4, where the author lists the contents of the Ark</note> gains clarity. Nor does the Apostle seem to include all these things within the cavity of the Ark without authority, since Aaron was commanded to deposit the urn not "before the ark of the testimony," but "before the testimony" <note>original Latin: *coram testimonio*; "The Testimony" usually refers specifically to the stone tablets of the Law</note>: which is also commanded regarding **Aaron’s rod** in *Numbers 17:10*. "The Testimony" ordinarily signifies the tablets of the pact.

As for the fact that in the time of Solomon—the period discussed in *1 Kings 8:9*—these things were arranged a little differently, the reason for that is not obscure. When the Ark was being carried about, it would have been less convenient for all these things to have been left inside its cavity: especially when it was carried into the camp while the Israelites were fighting against the **Philistines**. At that time, it fell into the power of the enemy: and though it was returned to the Israelites, it remained for some time outside the Tabernacle (where the urn and rod were kept in safekeeping, in a quite separate place) until the Temple was built and the Ark was carried into it and placed in the inner sanctuary. By that time, nothing had been preserved in it for a long while except the tablets, whereas formerly in **Shiloh** those other items were also contained within it. And indeed, these things are said not without probability. 

Certainly, these views seem preferable to me over the notes of **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, who believes that in the age of Moses the Urn with the Manna and Aaron’s rod were indeed in the Ark; but with the passage of time, *fearing that the rod might suffer rot and the manna might suffer mold, they were removed from the ark and kept in a place lacking wind and sun. And when Solomon’s temple was built, they were not replaced in the Ark for the same reason, but in a subterranean vault, as the Ancient Rabbis write.* However, this is to diminish the magnitude of the miracle in the preservation of the Manna without any necessity, or even without any probable cause. For with the same ease that it was kept incorrupt by God for several years, with that same ease all mold could have been kept from it for many centuries.

### LXXXV. 
To others, however, a different method of reconciliation is more pleasing.

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological debate regarding the positioning of the sacred items related to the Ark of the Covenant. # BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.
<meta>catchword: LXXXVII.</meta>

*Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a renowned Flemish Protestant Old Testament scholar and Hebraist.</note> observed regarding Exodus 16:34 that among the Hebrews and those who write in a Hebrew style, the particle **IN** sometimes carries the meaning of *at, near,* or *beside*. To prove this, he cites Joshua 10:11 and Judges 18:12. Another learned man very appropriately adds Joshua 5:13, 1 Kings 17:3, Jeremiah 13:5, and Colossians 3:1. Therefore, the phrase **IN WHICH**, in this context, may also mean *at* or *beside which Ark*. However, Drusius himself raises a difficulty that he admits he is unable to resolve. He says that everything would be agreeable were it not for the words that follow: **THE TABLETS OF THE COVENANT**. For those were certainly **INSIDE** the Ark. It is not very probable, he argues, for the word **IN** to carry two different meanings in the same sentence <note>i.e., meaning "beside" for the urn and rod, but "inside" for the tablets</note>. Despairing of a solution, Drusius adds, *Beware, therefore, of following this interpretation.* But *Jacobus Cappellus* <note>Jacques Cappel (1570–1624), a French Huguenot theology professor and Hebrew scholar.</note> considers that difficulty so slight that he believes Drusius is "looking for a knot in a bulrush" <note>A Latin idiom (*nodum in scirpo*) meaning to find a difficulty where none exists.</note>. For what, he asks, prevents us from saying in one and the same verse that things are *in the Ark*, whether they are beside it or inside it? Just as we say people live *in Rome*, whether they dwell *near* the city or *within the city itself*? Another adds: Paul was no less permitted to speak this way than we are when we say, for example, that *skin, flesh, bones, and intestines are in the human body*; here, **IN** is used with the same general meaning, but with a certain latitude of application.

<margin>LXXXVI. *The Mystery of the Hidden Manna*.</margin>
### LXXXVI.
Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 10:3 that some mystery lies beneath the **MANNA**, where he calls it *spiritual food*; that is, as *Augustine* well interprets it, *signifying something spiritual*. And Christ explains at great length in John 6:32 that He is *that true bread which comes down from heaven*, which was prefigured by the Manna. We have elsewhere followed the analogies between the two in great detail, which we do not care to repeat here. What must be primarily considered now is what was signified by the *preservation of the Manna in the golden Urn* and its *setting aside before the face of Jehovah*. This does not seem difficult to discover. Namely, Christ—who had descended from heaven to be the bread of life for sinful man—was taken up into heaven again, gifted with immortality, and now enjoys the presence of God in the Sanctuary not made with hands, rejoicing in a glorious and eternal life. Hence, communion with Christ in glory is called *eating the hidden manna* in Revelation 2:17, a manifest allusion to this very thing we are now discussing. It is an allusion most elegant and full of mysteries. For: 
I. That which is most vital in this participation of Christ's sweetness *is reserved with Christ in heaven* (Colossians 3:3; 2 Timothy 1:12). 
II. No worldly man knows the sweetness of this (John 14:17). Indeed, not even the faithful themselves know it until they experience it (1 John 3:2). 
III. Finally, this communion is not merely for a day, like the daily manna, but is perpetual; just like that manna which, set aside before the Lord, was immune to rot, mold, and worms.

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.
->Vol. I. Z z<-
<meta>catchword: LXXXVIII.</meta>

<margin>LXXXVII. Whether Aaron’s Rod was the same as the Staff of Moses.</margin>
LXXXVII. We have already heard several times of the **ROD OF AARON** placed beside the Golden Urn, which had miraculously budded. Its history is recounted in Numbers 17 and is known to all. God willed to confirm the authority of the Aaronite Priesthood against the seditious grumblings of **Korah** <note>Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron’s leadership in the desert; the budding rod was a divine sign that Aaron’s family alone was chosen for the priesthood.</note> and his associates through this miracle: that a dry staff cut from an **Almond tree**, inscribed with the name of Aaron, suddenly—in a single night—produced flowers and fruit. He commanded that this staff be preserved "before the testimony" <note>original: "coram testimonio" — referring to the Ark of the Covenant or the Tablets of the Law.</note> as a perpetual memorial of that event, so that the honor of the priesthood would be certain for Aaron and no longer subject to controversy. 

There are those who believe that this staff was the very same one that Moses had carried for some time, the instrument of so many miracles; regarding this, some of the Hebrew teachers babble wonderful and incredible trifles. They imagine that this staff was cut from that tree which God showed to Moses in the desert to make the bitter waters of **Marah** drinkable <note>See Exodus 15:23-25; "Marah" means bitter in Hebrew.</note>. They claim this tree came from a shoot of the **Tree of Life**, which angels supposedly gave to **Seth** <note>The third son of Adam and Eve.</note> when he was sent by his father to Paradise to beg God for the forgiveness of sins. They say the angels taught Seth at that time that as soon as this shoot sprouted, God’s mercy would descend upon him and the closed gates of heaven would be opened. Seth, therefore, supposedly planted this shoot in the desert, from which Moses later plucked his staff. From this same tree, they claim, the bronze serpent was hung, which God intended for the salvation of the whole world to be achieved in the time of the Messiah. 

If we cannot suspect that some hidden mystery lies beneath this fable—drawn perhaps from ancient oral instruction and explained through a parabolic story—it must be admitted that such inventions are as unworthy of men using their reason as they are worthy of a nation whom we see, with pity, deserted by God and surrendered to its own dullness. 

However, to return to the matter at hand, I find that several serious men agree with the Hebrews thus far: they believe Aaron’s budding rod was indeed Moses’s miraculous staff. They are led to this primarily by the reasoning that in Numbers 20:8 and following, Moses, by Divine command, **took the rod from before the Lord**—that is, the one stored in the sanctuary—which in verse 11 is called the **rod of Moses**. Since the rod set aside in the presence of the Lord is called the rod of Moses, they infer that Aaron’s name had been inscribed on Moses’s own rod, and that this same staff, after so many miracles, budded no less miraculously. This opinion, drawn from **Rabbi Chaskouni** <note>Hezekiah ben Manoah, a 13th-century French rabbi and exegete known for his commentary "Chizkuni."</note> and other Hebrew Masters, is embraced by the most celebrated and judicious theologian **John Owen** <note>Johannes Ouvvenus (1616–1683), a leading English Puritan and theologian.</note> in his learned commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews; and upon this foundation, he builds many mysteries.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION I.

LXXXVIII. However, one may doubt whether that argument is entirely solid. For it is clear from **Numbers 17** that the individual leaders of the various tribes brought their own rods; the tribe of **Levi** also brought its rod, to be inscribed not with the name of Levi, but with the name of **Aaron**. There is no evidence in that history that provides even the slightest suspicion that this rod was the staff of **Moses**. Indeed, it was not given by Moses, but was given to Moses by the leader of the Levitical tribe to be placed in the Tabernacle of the meeting. For the words of verse 6 say: *“And when Moses had spoken to the children of Israel, all their leaders gave him rods, one for each leader according to their paternal houses, twelve rods; and the rod of Aaron was among their rods.”* Furthermore, it would not have been such a suitable proof for overcoming the stubbornness of the complaining **Israelites** <note>The Israelites were questioning why Aaron's family alone held priestly authority.</note> if Aaron's rod had been of a different kind than the rods of the other tribes. In that case, what is recorded to have happened would have been attributed to the unique nature of that specific rod, rather than to a miracle <note>original: "portento"</note> powerful enough to settle the controversy. Furthermore, although it is certain that Aaron's rod was placed "before the testimony," <note>That is, in front of the Ark containing the Ten Commandments.</note> is it sufficiently certain that the staff of Moses—the monument of so many miracles—was not also placed there for a time by God's command, so that he might take it up again? I admit the Scripture says nothing express on that matter; but the words of the sacred history in **Numbers 20:9** seem to hint at something of the sort. And certainly, that staff with which Moses struck the rock in **Horeb** (**Exodus 17:5–6**), which was a shepherd’s crook and a traveler's staff, seems more suited for that task than a rod sprouting leaves, flowers, and fruit, which could easily be damaged by striking a rock. Therefore, it could have been Moses's staff which he is said to have "taken from before the **Jehovah**" <note>The Divine Presence in the Tabernacle.</note> in Numbers 20, even if it was not the rod of Aaron. Whatever the case may be, let the matter remain uncertain rather than building grand mysteries upon such a weak foundation.

<margin>
LXXXIX. It is said to be preserved in Rome and elsewhere among the sacred relics, along with the Urn of Manna.
</margin>
LXXXIX. **Onuphrius** <note>Onuphrio Panvinio (1530–1568), an Augustinian friar and historian famous for his works on Roman antiquities.</note>, in his book *On the Seven Churches of the City*, testifies that the Rod of Aaron, together with the **Urn of Manna**, still exists in **Rome** in the Church of the **Holy Savior** <note>Commonly known as the Basilica of Saint John Lateran.</note>. Nor is Onuphrius the only one to assert this; even **Pope Sixtus V**, in the book titled *The Wonders of Rome*, confirmed the matter with his own privilege as true and certain. For it is recorded there that in the **Lateran Church** in Rome, among other relics, are the **Urn of Manna** and the **Rod of Aaron**. But the **French** also show the same at the **Holy Chapel** <note>The Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.</note> in **Paris**, the **Spanish** at the Church of the **Holy Savior**, and finally the people of **Bordeaux** at the Church of **St. Severin**, according to **Calvin** in his *Treatise on Relics* <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the Protestant reformer, wrote a famous satirical "Treatise on Relics" mocking the multiplication of holy objects in Europe.</note>. The reality itself speaks to how shamelessly fraudulent these things are.

<margin>
XC. Its Mystery.
</margin>
XC. Let us follow that which is solid. The Rod of Aaron, as it pertains—

### ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE LEVITICAL TABERNACLE.

[The rod] pertained to confirming the authority of the Priesthood; thus, no less than Aaron himself with his priesthood, it bore a **type** <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of the *Priest and Priesthood of Christ*. Christ is the *rod* <note>original: "virga"</note>, arising not only from the cut-off trunk of *Jesse* <note>original: "Isai"</note>; Isaiah 11:1. but also himself cut off from the land of the living: Isaiah 53:8. and yet soon after death he blossomed again, and became the tree of life, having buds, flowers, and fruit all at once: producing new fruits every single month. Revelation 22:2. And of his priesthood, as it is most pleasant, so also there is a perpetual greenness, vigor, and efficacy: since he is a priest *according to the power of an indestructible life*. Hebrews 7:16.

<margin>XCI. *The Volume of the Law.*</margin>
XCI. Finally, next to the Ark in the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adyto," the Holy of Holies</note>, by the command of God, the VOLUME OF THE LAW was placed, written by the hand of Moses himself, so that it might be there as a witness; yet it was to be brought out every seven years, at the appointed time in the year of remission <note>The "year of release" or Sabbatical year, when debts were forgiven.</note>, during the feast of Tabernacles, so that it might be read before all Israel appearing before the face of Jehovah. Deuteronomy 31:24, 25, 26 and 10, 11. However, it is believable that before the Book was deposited in the sacred place, several **copies** <note>original: "apographa"</note> of it were made, diligently compared with the **original** <note>original: "autographo"</note>, which were kept in the hands of the priests and served for daily use. Just as it is also believable that by the *Book of the Law* here is understood not only *Deuteronomy*, but the entire complex of Mosaic Laws which are also found in the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers: and why should we not believe the entire <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> is meant? Its histories also, full of so many miracles, greatly served the edification and conviction of the Israelites; and, hardly less than the Laws themselves, they were able to stand as a witness against them. From these things it is clear with what great reverence God wanted his sacred dictates to be preserved in the most holy place: so that each of the Israelites might learn to piously and religiously store the oracles of the Divine Law in a pure heart, which is the sanctuary most pleasing to God. Thus God commanded in Deuteronomy 6:6:

> AND THESE WORDS WHICH I COMMAND YOU TODAY SHALL BE IN YOUR HEART.

Thus David performed in Psalm 119:11:

> IN MY MIND I STORE UP YOUR WORD, THAT I MIGHT NOT SIN AGAINST YOU.

<margin>
I. Whether sacrifices are of human invention or Divine command.
</margin>
<margin>
Outram, *On Sacrifices*, Book I, Chapter 1, § v. <note>William Outram (1626–1679) was an English theologian whose work compared Jewish and Christian sacrificial systems.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
Spencer, *On the Origin of Sacrifices*, Chapter III, Section II. <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was a scholar who argued that many Hebrew rituals were adapted from earlier Egyptian or "pagan" customs under Divine guidance.</note>
</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'H' decorated with a winged figure and floral flourishes.</image-desc>

**H**e who has inspected the sacred volumes of Moses, even with a fleeting glance, cannot be ignorant of the fact that pious men, almost from the very beginning of the world’s age, performed sacred rites to GOD by offering those things which the goodness of the Divine power had granted to them for food. But it is not equally agreed upon among the learned whether that method of performing sacred rites should be credited to **HUMAN INVENTION** or to **DIVINE COMMAND**. There are those who believe that the earliest humans were so instructed by the light of nature that they saw a visible honor and worship ought to be rendered to God, and that this could best be done if each person returned to God, by a sacred ritual, the best of what they possessed. They argue this was the origin of those sacrifices which, because they are returned to God for benefits received, are usually called **EUCHARISTIC** <note>original: "EUCHARISTICA"; from the Greek for "thanksgiving."</note>. To this was added the opinion, stemming from the unrefined nature of that early age, that God would grant all things to those who gave gifts—as if, in the manner of humans, He could be soothed by presents, or felt obligated by any bounty to "settle the score" with them. From this, they say, began the sacrifices called **EYKTIKA** <note>original: "'ΕΥΚΤΙΚΑ'"; Greek for "precatory" or "prayer-based."</note>, or **PRECATORY**. Indeed, the ancients practiced a kind of bargaining with God, and they dealt with Him as if He were a moneylender who gave only so that He might receive. Furthermore, the idea took hold of the minds of those early mortals that God could be appeased by sacrifices no less than men are by gifts. This provided the occasion for **HILASTIC** <note>original: "HILASTICIS"; Greek for "propitiatory" or "expiatory."</note> or **PROPITIATORY** sacrifices. For just as men usually present a gift to a King or some great noble when they seek to soften his anger (as in Proverbs 21:14: *“A gift in secret pacifies anger”*), so also the Ancients used sacred gifts for the same purpose, believing they were just as effective for appeasing God as they were for man. Although all these ideas were quite unrefined and coarse, God nevertheless indulged the simplicity of the early centuries to such an extent that, having regard for the good intention from which they proceeded, He accepted them as a worship pleasing to Himself.

<margin>
II. The history of Moses mentions nothing explicitly on this matter.
</margin>

**II.** However, as much as this opinion has great authors to support it, and however much it defends itself with a great apparatus of learning, nevertheless, from [my] mind...

### ON THE PRIESTHOOD OF AARON AND CHRIST.

<margin>Outram, Book 1, Chapter 1, § v. <note>William Outram (1626–1679) was an English clergyman whose work "De Sacrificiis" compared Jewish and Christian sacrificial systems.</note></margin>
...I could not bring myself to agree with him. I admit, indeed, that no express command from God regarding the act of sacrificing exists in the most ancient history written by Moses <note>The author refers to the Book of Genesis.</note>; not even in that place where he first mentions sacrifices. But I do not believe that this silence is a valid argument for those who prefer to attribute the origin of sacrifices to men rather than to God. For as long as Moses affirms neither side, the matter must remain undecided. Indeed, many great things were done in the first ages of the world of which he, striving for the utmost brevity, makes not even a single word of mention. Nowhere in his history did he record the prophecy of Enoch, nor the daily troubles of Lot arising from the wicked customs of the Sodomites, nor the pious warnings of Noah (all of which are nevertheless praised by other sacred writers). Nor indeed—which is much more relevant—did he record the sacrifices of Cain and Abel for the purpose of explaining the core doctrine of sacrifice; rather, he mentioned them to trace the origin of Cain’s hatred toward Abel and that wicked fratricide. Thus, it is less surprising if he neglected to teach their origin, since he only touched upon them in passing.

<margin>III. Nevertheless, no worship can be pleasing to God which He Himself has not commanded.</margin>
III. Since, therefore, this controversy remains undecided by the history of Moses, let us see what arguments may be supplied from other sources. And this, I believe, will be granted to me by everyone: that the religious practice of sacrifice, performed piously by pious men, was pleasing and acceptable to the Supreme Being. Moses testifies to this many times, and God demonstrated it by His very actions. I add that the principal part of external worship consisted in sacrifices and the prayers and thanksgivings joined to them. Indeed, scarcely anything else pertaining to this matter can be shown from primitive antiquity. Now, it is consistent with the Wisdom, Holiness, and Majesty of God that He should not allow anything to be attributed to Him as a major part of religion which He Himself did not command. Who among men has known the mind of the Lord, or has been His counselor, that he should determine by his own ingenuity what God ought to regard as acceptable? Who, conscious of his total dependence on God, would presume to make a part of holy and religious <term>worship</term> <note>original Greek: θρησκείας (thréskeias); referring to the formal acts of religious observance.</note> that which he did not learn from God to be holy and pertaining to religion? As if it were placed in the judgment of a foolish and sinful man to confer holiness upon some thing or action which God—whose pattern and will are the sole norm of all holiness—did not confer upon it. Finally, the supreme Majesty of God as Ruler demands that, just as He alone is to be religiously worshiped, it belongs to Him alone to prescribe the manner in which He wishes to be worshiped. Hence, at all times, that worship has been condemned which mortals have fashioned out of their own heart. Truly, this was the crime of Jeroboam: to introduce something into religion <term>which he had devised from his own heart</term> <note>original Hebrew: אשר ברא מלبو (asher bara millibbo); a reference to 1 Kings 12:33, where King Jeroboam institutes a new festival and priesthood of his own making.</note>.

### BOOK II, DISSERTATION II.

...in his own heart. (1 Kings 12:33). Concerning such people, God says with indignation, *Who has required these things from your hands?* (Isaiah 1:12). He disapproves of all reverence that anyone is taught by the commandment of men (Isaiah 29:13 <note>The OCR cites verse 15, but the text refers to 29:13: "their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men."</note>), proclaiming, *In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.* (Matthew 15:9). Just as Paul also condemns those things *which are prescribed from the commandments and doctrines of men, although they have an appearance of wisdom in <term>will-worship</term> <note>original: ἐν ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ (en ethelothrēskeia)</note>, and voluntary devotion.* (Colossians 2:22-23).

<margin>IV. "Will-worship" condemned by Paul.</margin>

IV. I am well aware that the most illustrious Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an influential English scholar who argued that many Jewish rituals were adapted from existing "pagan" customs rather than being entirely unique divine revelations.</note> despises this reasoning as a "blunt sword" that does not deeply wound his cause. Since it is easily apparent to anyone paying attention that the Apostle *understood the term "will-worship" in a sense that was not bad*, as has been proven by Hammond and Grotius <note>Henry Hammond and Hugo Grotius were prominent 17th-century theologians and biblical critics.</note>; nor can anyone accuse every form of worship flowing from human ingenuity and institution alone of being superstition, without condemning the very generation of *the sons of God*—the Church, I mean, both Jewish and Christian—which is manifest by many examples to have offered worship pleasing to God through rites devised only by human ingenuity.

V. However, to start with that last point, I would indeed dare to strenuously deny that the Church, whether Jewish or Christian, ever forced upon God as a major part of religion something He did not command, yet which He accepted nonetheless. And I would wish for that to be demonstrated not by *many examples*, as is so confidently asserted, but by even a single one. I am not speaking of small and indifferent circumstances of worship <note>referring to "adiaphora," or minor details like the color of a cloth or the time of a meeting</note>, but of a notable part of worship. This commandment of the Lord, which Moses delivered to the people of Israel in Deuteronomy 12:32, is of eternal truth: *Whatever I command you, be careful to do it; you shall not add to it nor take away from it.*

VI. Now let us consider Paul's mind. It is certain that Paul argues against those who follow the "commandments and doctrines of men" <note>original Greek: ἐντάλματα καὶ διδασκαλίας ἀνθρώπων</note>, whatever pretext the idle teachers of superstition may use to recommend them. For they are accustomed to claim as a pretext that these things contain a "show of wisdom" <note>original Greek: λόγου σοφίας (logou sophias)</note>, secret meanings, the beauty and harmony of religion, and a guiding hand toward greater and more sublime things. Likewise, they claim that there is *will-worship* <note>original Greek: ἐθελοθρησκεία (ethelothrēskeia)</note> in them, a term which Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> and Grotius correctly explain through the Hebrew term <term>Nedavot</term> <note>original: נדבות. This refers to "freewill offerings" described in the Old Testament, which were voluntary gifts to God.</note>, meaning worship *voluntarily undertaken*. It is used here in a sense that serves the defense and recommendation of such institutions. They used to say that a fervent religion is not content with those things that are necessary; that the honesty restricted by rules is of little virtue; that something more and of one's own accord must be attempted by one who is zealous for a more sublime piety; that God held <term>Nedavot</term> (freely offered gifts) as pleasing; and thus they recommended their own institutions, about which...

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of human innovation in religious worship. Building on the condemnation of "will-worship" from the previous page, the author now turns to the biblical example of Abel to prove that true worship must be based on a specific command from God rather than human ingenuity.</meta>

# On the Priesthood of Aaron and Christ.

...no law of God exists. So they claim, indeed. But the Apostle [Paul] teaches that those pretexts and outward displays are futile, and mere sophistries of Satan, by which human inventions in Divine matters are disguised: against which he very diligently warns Christians. Briefly, he teaches that all <term>will-worship</term> <note>original: ἐθελοθρησκείαν (*ethelothrēskeian*), a term used in Colossians 2:23 to describe self-imposed or man-made religious practices.</note>, colored by whatever pretext, in all those things which are of human invention, is displeasing to God.

<margin>VII. The faith by which Abel offered a sacrifice pleasing to God rested upon God's command and promise.</margin>

VII. But let us return to the sacrifices. Paul provides a strong argument for their Divine institution in Hebrews 11:4: **BY FAITH ABEL OFFERED TO GOD A BETTER SACRIFICE THAN CAIN.** Here, above all, we must inquire what the Apostle understands here by **FAITH**. We can learn this more certainly from no other source than from the Apostle himself. At the beginning of the chapter, he describes faith thus: *Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.* <note>original: ἔστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων (*esti de pistis elpizomenōn hypostasis, pragmatōn elenchos ou blepomenōn*)</note> By these words, he teaches that faith contains hope, which certainly rests upon the promise of God and the command to believe; and indeed such a hope that deserves the name <term>substance</term> <note>original: ὑποστάσεως (*hypostaseōs*), meaning the underlying reality or firm foundation.</note>, that is, a most firm, solid, and unshakable thing, which "stands under" the things hoped for and promises them to itself—as if undergoing every danger and risk of ambiguity—or it "stands them up," representing them as if one already possessed them. He further teaches that in faith there is <term>evidence</term> <note>original: ἔλεγχον (*elenchon*), a word implying a proof or a conviction that results from a demonstration.</note>, a "demonstration" and a convincing argument, and a "conviction" of the mind arising from such an argument; so much so that the believer has no less certain a foundation for his faith than a mathematician has for those demonstrations which appear to the mind as most evident. Such an evident demonstration and such a strong conviction can have no other foundation than the infallible truthfulness of God, who testifies about Himself and His will. Moreover, such faith differs greatly from any kind of persuasion by which someone, without any indication of the Divine will, presumes on his own that he is performing something pleasing to God. Furthermore, it should be observed that Paul says, not that Abel lived by such faith, or was righteous, but that he *offered* by such faith, so that faith was the starting point of the offering. Now, since the faith described by Paul rests on the command and promise of God, it follows that Abel offered by the command of God, and expected that such a sacrifice would be pleasing to God according to the promise. Let this also be added: that through faith Abel offered a *better sacrifice*, so that the reason why it was more acceptable to God than Cain's offering is found in Abel's faith. Moreover, a persuasion that arises from the mere presumption of one's own invention, and is joined with a gross ignorance of God, neither deserves the name of faith nor can make any duty pleasing to God.

VIII.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

<margin>
VIII. This is very far from such an ignorant persuasion as Spencer attributes to the ancients.
</margin>
VIII. Once these things are duly observed, the objections of the most learned *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English theologian who argued that many Hebrew rituals were adapted from earlier "primitive" or pagan customs—a view the current author strongly opposes.</note> fall of their own accord. He dictates that the faith which made Abel's gift worthy of the title of a **more excellent sacrifice** <note>original: <term>πλείονος θυσίας</term> (*pleionos thysias*), from Hebrews 11:4.</note> was a persuasion so firm and deeply fixed concerning God's inclined affection toward all the pious, and the most ample rewards to be conferred on those living piously, that he modeled his life according to the rules of piety, and gave not only his goods but himself to God. But indeed, the Apostle [Paul] here does not treat faith insofar as it is a general principle of a righteous life, but specifically insofar as it was the principle of a **good sacrifice**. It remains to be asked: upon what foundation did the Patriarchs' persuasion rest concerning God's favorable mind toward their sacrifices? For since—as that most learned man [Spencer] himself very well argues—it is manifest to the human mind, even when only slightly imbued with knowledge of the Divine nature, that in sacrifice considered in itself there is nothing by which it could be of any value with God; it is necessary that something else must be added from elsewhere to produce the persuasion that victims could provide a **fragrant aroma** <note>original: <term>ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας</term> (*osmēn euōdias*), a phrase often used in the Greek Bible to describe a sacrifice pleasing to God.</note> to the God of Spirits, and that God willed to regard rituals smelling merely of blood in the place of worship and obedience. The only thing remaining for that most learned man is this: *If sacrifice*, he says, *is viewed as a sign of a mind devoted and bound to God, it takes on, as it were, a new face and appearance; and the Patriarchs, from their innate knowledge of Divine goodness and grace, could easily persuade themselves that God would kindly accept a gift of this kind, offered with a grateful and devoted mind.* Meanwhile, he does not deny that the flesh of the offered beast, the less it suited the nature of God, the more it suited the "rudeness" <note>Meaning the primitive or unrefined state of early humanity.</note> of the first men. He adds that if nothing incongruous, nothing absurd, nothing savoring of the simplicity of more ancient times could be perceived in rituals and religions of this kind, there would be room for suspicion that they exceeded the genius of those times. But I confess it exceeds my own genius and capacity to understand how a persuasion joined with such "rudeness" and lazy ignorance of God—in which so many incongruities and absurdities meet as if in a formed battle-line—could be honored with the name of **faith**; a faith which not only itself might merit pardon and grace, but might also render other duties proceeding from it pleasing to God. To me, certainly, it is not pleasing to judge the piety and religion of the ancient people so meagerly and contemptuously.

<margin>
IX. Moreover, it was faith in the Sacrifice of the Messiah.
</margin>
IX. But we have not yet exhausted all the strength of our argument. **To offer a sacrifice by faith** signifies more and greater things than we have asserted thus far. That faith by which Abel obtained the testimony of righteousness is faith in the promise concerning the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, but whose heel would in turn be crushed by the serpent. For all of Paul's argumentation leads to this: that righteousness before God is from faith in the **Messiah**. Abel, therefore, offering by faith, did not think that the sacrifice pleased God in itself, or was pleasing because of a pious intention of the mind, or was in any way effective for satisfaction for sin, or the obtaining

### Concerning the Priesthood of Aaron and Christ.

the right to life. For if the Apostle [Paul] understood this as faith in a general sense, he would contradict himself, since he disputes the opposite throughout the entire Epistle. Rather, by sacrificing sheep and offering their fat, Abel testified that he believed that for righteousness—that is, for the right to eternal life—a sacrifice of **fragrant aroma** <note>original: *boni odoris*; a reference to the "pleasing aroma" of sacrifices in the Old Testament, signifying God's acceptance.</note> was necessary, one that was better than the blood and fat of cattle. Therefore, in his own offering, he meditated upon a superior offering, to be provided in its own time by the **seed of the woman** <note>A reference to Genesis 3:15, interpreted by Christians as the first prophecy of the Messiah (Christ) who would defeat the serpent.</note>. Because Cain did not attend to this, or perhaps thought it of little value, he was destitute of that skillful faith; hence, Abel's offering was superior to that of Cain. All these things imply a revelation from God concerning sacrifices and their ultimate purpose.

<margin>X. Even the somewhat more refined pagans recognized that sacrifices do not please God in themselves.</margin>
**X.** Let us examine this matter a little more closely. To judge God according to human character—as if He were one who is delighted or appeased by gifts and presents—is a wretched, foul error, unworthy of a pious man. For, as the most illustrious *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), whose work *De Legibus Hebraeorum* suggested that many Jewish rites were adapted from pagan customs.</note> judiciously argues, the material of sacrifices—**the flesh of cattle, the pouring of blood, and other such things**—is so cheap and so far removed from the supreme Majesty of God, that no one (unless they were entirely simple and ignorant of things) could fail to judge that sacrifices were plainly superfluous and utterly unworthy of God. Indeed, the more refined pagans were so far from believing that sacrifices were consistent with the nature of their gods, that they were not infrequently struck by wonder as to how a rite so grim, and so foreign to the nature of the gods, could have entered the hearts of men, spread so far, and clung so tenaciously to their customs. Since this is the case, how can it seem probable that the holy Patriarchs, who were friends and intimates of God, were imbued with such a foul error—one from which even the Gentiles, who were destitute of all communion and commerce with the divine, recoiled? Who would believe that sacrifices offered from such a foolish opinion could have pleased God? Or rather, would not God have been indignant that He was so judged by human character, as if gifts were considered to carry no less weight with Him than they do among men?

<margin>XI. The Patriarchs therefore considered something else in them: what could it be, other than the sacrifice of the Messiah? See also the Preface, § XXIV.</margin>
**XI.** Since, therefore, sacrifices did neither please God for their own sake, nor were the Patriarchs so dull-witted <note>original: *bardi*</note> as to believe they did, there must have been another reason why the Patriarchs were bound by such a religious devotion to sacrifices, and why God testified that they were pleasing to Him. What truer reason can be devised than that sacrifices were **symbols and figures** of other things, which would more closely agree with the nature of God and the wise meditation of pious men? Furthermore, since such sacrifices were also offered as were intended for propitiating the deity and expiating sins, what could they more suitably signify than that true sacrifice of the Messiah, which alone is fit for this purpose? And what is more worthy of the friends of God than, on the occasion of their offerings, to turn the thoughts of their minds toward that goal? Finally, what forbids—

## BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.
->S-6.<-

should we decide that these things were otherwise? Did the Patriarchs entirely ignore the doctrine concerning the future propitiation through the Messiah? Were they deprived of every Gospel, or any understanding of it? Were their sacrifices, especially the **propitiatory** <term>hilastica: from the Greek *hilastikos*, referring to sacrifices intended to appease God or atone for sin</term> ones, not fit for prefiguring the sacrifice of Christ? Why would they be less so than the sacrifices instituted later by the Mosaic law? Was it not a pious act for those offering to reflect upon the Sacrifice of Christ? Is this not a view worthier of the Patriarchs than those delusions from which the Gentile nations should shrink? Does not such a meditation deserve the name of "faith" more than some vague persuasion, based on no probable reason, about appeasing God with gifts? Finally, can anything be imagined that more worthily serves as the reason why the God of Spirits graciously accepted these animal victims?

<margin>XII. It is probable that Adam’s leather tunics were the hides of animals offered to God.</margin>

XII. But let us not stop even here. The first sacrifice of which explicit mention exists in the Holy Scriptures is the sacrifice of Abel. However, many things persuade us that it was not absolutely the first. Indeed, Moses records it in such a way that he seems to be speaking of a practice already customary at that time. Let us therefore press on further. And here, indeed, nothing occurs so certain that it can be presented as a mathematical demonstration; yet there is a conjecture of such great probability as can rightly be desired in this kind of historical inquiry. After God had consoled the first humans with the first promise of the Messiah, and of the salvation to be granted on His account, He made for Adam and his wife leather tunics, with which He clothed them (Genesis 3:21). Those skins were the hides <note>original: *exuviae*; literally "spoils" or "shed skins," referring to the remains of the animals.</note> of living creatures. But how did they die? Was it by a natural death? That does not even have the appearance of truth. Were they slaughtered so that their meat might rot upon the surface of the earth or beneath it? Or so they might serve as food for man or other animals? None of these options commends itself to the mind as probable. What remains, then, except that we determine it consistent with the truth that God, already from that time, dedicated the proclamation of the **Covenant of Grace** not without the shedding of blood? This was done so that the fat with the meat might be burned in His honor, while the skins were given to Adam, as to the first Priest. This appears to be the origin of that law which appears in Leviticus 7:8: *“When the Priest offers anyone's burnt offering, the skin of the burnt offering which he offered shall be that Priest's.”*

<margin>XIII. The mystery of this matter.</margin>

XIII. He who wishes to see no mystery in these things should not envy us for seeing it to the honor of Divine wisdom and goodness; let us believe that these things were so performed by God and written by Moses for the wisest of reasons. Whatever clothing man had devised for himself <note>A reference to the fig leaves Adam and Eve used to cover themselves.</note> could not cover him in such a way as to withstand the eyes of God. Whatever a sinner may labor to achieve through his own industry and **science falsely so-called** <note>original: *falsi nominis scientia*; a reference to 1 Timothy 6:20, suggesting human reasoning apart from revelation.</note>, he will accomplish nothing that can reconcile him to God, wherever he may appear before the tribunal of God. *“Their webs are like spiders' webs; they shall not become garments, nor shall they cover themselves with their works”* (Isaiah 59:5-6).

# On the Priesthood of Aaron and Christ.

->§. 6.<-

Section 6. Suitable garments were a gift of Divine mercy. The righteousness by which our sins are covered *is from God.* <note>Philippians 3:9</note>. From the spoils of mortality and the remains of slaughtered living beings, the bodies of the first-formed <note>original: *protoplastorum*, referring to Adam and Eve</note> were covered. The garment of grace, by which the "body of sin" is covered, comes from the very death of Christ; nor can that righteousness, which makes us accepted by God, be established without the intervention of that death. Surely it is Christ’s role to say to his own: *I counsel you to buy from me white garments, that you may be clothed, so that the shame of your nakedness does not appear.* <note>Revelation 3:18</note>.

<margin>XIV. The distinction between clean and unclean animals existed before the flood and pertains to sacrifices.</margin>
XIV. But a not-to-be-despised argument for this view is supplied by the distinction between *clean and unclean animals*, which was already known to Noah before the flood; a fact that sacred history clearly hints at. <note>Genesis 7:2, 8 and 8:20</note>. Moreover, those animals were considered clean which were given to man for food and were sacrificed to God on the altar. For God willed these two to be joined, partly so that man might more clearly demonstrate his gratitude to God by offering what had been given to him for the preservation of his life—and was therefore most dear—and partly so that the substitution of the sacrifice for the man might be more clearly taught. For man, by offering the supports of his own life, seems to offer life itself.

Furthermore, this distinction of living beings must have originated either from man or from God. If it was devised by men, they were led to it either by natural reason or by mere superstition. But natural reason does not teach that any animal created by God is unclean in itself. For if it were unclean by nature, it would remain unclean always, everywhere, and to everyone. And in what would that natural uncleanness consist? Is it because all "unclean" animals provide food that is unhealthy for the body? But the medical arts and the daily experience of all nations contradict this. Or is it because they rub some uncleanness onto the souls of men? But who would believe that deer and goats—especially in those hot regions—offer fewer provocations to vice than, for example, rabbits or hares?

If, therefore—since nature does not teach it—men devised the distinction between clean and unclean animals by their own ingenuity, to what can this be attributed except to some vain or scrupulous superstition? But how can it be that such a superstition would deserve such solemn approval from God as is expressed—to say nothing of other instances—at least in the Mosaic law? It remains, therefore, that this distinction of animals was established not by men, but by God Himself: for reasons not natural or moral, but ceremonial, and depending on the will of the Supreme Lawgiver. Regarding these matters, Cunaeus <note>Petrus Cunaeus (1586–1638), a Dutch scholar known for his work on the Hebrew state</note> elegantly writes: *On the Hebrew Republic, Book II, Chapter XXIV. Many things are placed there in the list of the impure, not by the dictate of nature or reason, but*
