# On the PRIESTHOOD OF AARON AND CHRIST.

...I would be. Therefore, this oil was like a ring and seal of Moses, the chief of Prophets, by which the King and the Priest were to be sealed, so much so that by its power they were made disciples of Moses and could boast that they were the work of his hands.

LVIII. However, these claims are not of such evident truth that they do not deserve a more accurate examination. First, concerning the claim that serves as the foundation for the rest—that the sacred oil was prepared by Moses himself—this not only cannot be proven from the sacred scriptures but is even contradicted by them. For Moses did not apply his own hand to the work, nor did he mix those types of spices with the perfumer's art; instead, he entrusted that task to Bezalel <note>Bezalel was the master craftsman chosen by God to construct the Tabernacle and its furnishings.</note> along with the others. Thus, this oil is listed among the works of Bezalel in Exodus 37:29: *He also made the holy anointing oil and the pure, fragrant incense with the work of a perfumer.* <note>original: "Fecit quoque oleum ipsum unctionis sanctae opere pigmentarii."</note> Furthermore, it is not certain that this oil was manufactured only once. For if the words of the text are properly considered in Exodus 30:31, 32, and 33, a repeated preparation of the oil for the sacred use for which it was destined by God is not forbidden; what is forbidden is only the preparation of a *similar* ointment for private and profane use. 

How many miracles must be imagined for the use of that single preparation to have sufficed for so many centuries? There was indeed a large amount of *spices*, namely 1,500 shekels <note>The shekel was a standard unit of weight; here the author calculates the total weight of the various spices listed in Exodus 30.</note>, or as many half-ounces, which according to the calculation of Schickard <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635), a German polymath and professor of Hebrew known for his studies on biblical weights and measures.</note> grow to 47 of our pounds. But very little *oil* was added, specifically one Hin <note>A Hin is an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, roughly equivalent to 5 liters or 1.3 gallons.</note>; therefore, the total volume of the ointment could not have been very large, because after the dregs of the spices were removed, only the aromatic essences were extracted. 

Moreover, scented substances tend to evaporate even if they are very tightly sealed—especially if the vessel containing them must be opened frequently. Add to this that this ointment was used for a great many things: for not only men, but also many vessels of the sanctuary were smeared with it: the Ark of the Testimony, the Table, the Lampstand, both Altars, the massive Basin, and finally the Tabernacle itself (Exodus 30:27). Nor were a few tiny drops sprinkled with a stingy hand upon the person being anointed; rather, it was poured liberally upon the head, so that it flowed down through the beard and onto the edges of the garments (Psalm 133:2). 

Hence, it is a wonder if it sufficed even for the first anointing, let alone that it would have sufficed to continue for so many centuries. Nor should this ointment—which was made according to God's prescription but by human hands and art—be compared with the *hidden Manna* <note>The jar of manna kept inside the Ark of the Covenant as a permanent memorial.</note>, which was a miraculous work of God to be preserved in memory of another miracle. It should instead be compared to the composition of the incense mentioned in Exodus 30:34 and following, which no one doubts had to be remade whenever it ran out. These points lead me to believe that the stories the Hebrew Masters <note>The author refers here to the Rabbinic tradition and the Talmudic sages.</note> hand down concerning the miraculous continuation and preservation of this oil should be counted among fables. It does not please us, nor is it truly permitted,

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

(Since the exact method is not expressed by Moses, it is supplied in various ways by different interpreters.) *Two hundred and fifty shekels of fragrant cinnamon, the same amount of fragrant cane <note>Also known as calamus.</note>, and five hundred of cassia, to which had to be added a Hin of olive oil. The preparation was to be made according to the art of the perfumer. The Hebrews describe the method in this way: He takes the quantity of each species determined by God and crushes each separately; then he mixes them all and soaks them in pure, sweet waters until all their essence is extracted. Afterward, he pours in a Hin of olive oil, or twelve Logs <note>A 'Log' is an ancient liquid measure; twelve logs are roughly equivalent to several liters.</note> (that is, as much as seventy-two eggs contain) and cooks it together over a fire until the waters evaporate and the ointment remains. He stores this in a vessel for posterity.*

<margin>LVII. Whether the oil, having been prepared once by Moses himself, lasted until the time of Josiah.</margin>
**LVII.** It is worthwhile to recognize what the Masters of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis and Jewish sages.</note> have handed down regarding this ointment; Abarbanel <note>Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a celebrated Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator.</note> has expounded their opinion extensively and judiciously in his commentaries on this passage. The summary comes to this: they maintain that it was prepared by Moses himself with his own hands because God said, **YOU TAKE FOR YOURSELF.** <note>original: "TU ACCIPE TIBI" — quoting Exodus 30:23.</note> *That is: You, you yourself shall take these things and make the oil and the anointment, and let no other mortal dare to make it as long as the earth exists.* Because no one else was to make anything similar to it, they maintain that by Divine power—and not without a remarkable miracle—it was preserved for a thousand years. For if you take away the miracles, it would not have been possible by the nature of things for it to last so long and suffice for so many uses, as the Rabbis themselves admit. *Did not many miracles happen,* they ask, *to the oil of anointing from its beginning to its end? In the beginning, there were no more than twelve Logs: yet with it were anointed the tabernacle and its vessels, Aaron with his sons for all seven days of their consecration, as well as the High Priestly successors and the Kings. Surely it was destined to be durable, just as it is said in Exodus 30:31: This shall be a holy anointing oil to me* <term>HOC</term> <note>original: "זה" (Zeh) meaning 'this'.</note> *throughout your generations.* The little word <term>HOC</term> ("This") is worth 12 according to <term>Gematria</term> <note>Gematria is a traditional Jewish system of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters; the letters of 'Zeh' (Zayin=7, He=5) sum to 12.</note>, which was the number of Logs. Rabbi Jehuda said: *How much was consumed by dripping? How much did the aromatic roots absorb? How much did the heat dissipate?* Yet they say that Moses, helped by the power of God, secured a lasting quality for this oil, just as he did for the Manna that was to be kept in the Golden Urn. Indeed, they say he even caused this oil to convert the surrounding air into its own nature, and thus it increased itself. Nor was there a lack of mystery in this matter. To be sure, God the Best and Greatest established a double government among the Israelites: one human, namely that of the Kings, who are the supreme moderators of the people; the other Divine, which is that of the Priests, the ministers of God. He willed that both should depend on the mouth and law of Moses. For that reason, He commanded that Moses himself should prepare the sacred oil to be preserved for the generations of the Israelites; and that he should anoint the first Priests with his own hand, while Kings should be anointed with the oil prepared by him—and this usually by a Prophet, the successor of Moses.

### LVIII.

But these matters are not of such evident truth that they do not deserve a more accurate examination. And first indeed—regarding the foundation upon which everything else is built, namely that the sacred oil was made by Moses himself—this not only cannot be proven from the sacred scriptures but is even opposed by them. For Moses himself did not put his hand to it, nor did he mix those species of spices with the perfumer's art, but he entrusted that work to Bezalel <note>Bezalel was the chief artisan of the Tabernacle, endowed by God with special wisdom and skill.</note> along with the others. Hence this oil is counted among the works of Bezalel. Exodus 37:29 says: *He also made the holy anointing oil by the work of a perfumer.* Furthermore, it is not certain that this oil was prepared only once. For if the words of the text in Exodus 30:31-33 are properly considered, they do not forbid a repeated preparation of the oil for the sacred use to which it was destined by God; they only forbid the preparation of a similar ointment for private and profane use. 

How many miracles must be imagined for the use of that single preparation to have sufficed for so many centuries? There were indeed quite many spices—namely 1,500 shekels, or as many half-ounces—which according to the calculation of Schickard <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635), a German polymath and professor of Hebrew and astronomy.</note> amount to 47 of our pounds. But very little oil was added, namely one Hin <note>A 'Hin' is an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, roughly 4 to 6 liters.</note>; therefore the total measure of the ointment could not have been very great, because after the dregs were left behind, only the scents were extracted into the oil. Furthermore, scented substances tend to evaporate, even if they are very well sealed; especially if it becomes necessary to open the vessel in which they are contained quite often. 

Add to this that this ointment was used for very many things: for not only men, but also many vessels of the sanctuary were smeared with it: the Ark of the Testimony, the Table, the Lampstand, both Altars, the very large Basin, and finally the Tabernacle itself (Exodus 30:27). Nor were a few small drops sprinkled with a stingy hand upon the person being anointed; but it was poured liberally upon the head, so that it flowed down through the beard and onto the edges of the garments. 

<margin>Psalm 133:2.</margin> Hence it is a wonder that the oil sufficed even for the first anointing, let alone that it should have sufficed to continue through so many centuries. Nor should this ointment—which was indeed made according to God's prescription, yet by human hands and art, and served frequent uses through many centuries—be compared with the "Hidden Manna," which was a miraculous work of God preserved in memory of another miracle. Rather, it should be compared with the composition of incense described in Exodus 30:34 and following; no one doubts that when the incense ran out, another similar batch had to be prepared. These reasons cause me to think that what the Masters of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis and Talmudic sages.</note> hand down regarding the miraculous continuation and preservation of this oil should be numbered among fables. It does not please us, nor indeed is it permitted...

<margin>
59. The method of anointing in the shape of the Greek X.
</margin>

### LIX. 

They report that the METHOD OF ANOINTING was as follows: with the oil poured over the head, a figure like the Greek *Caph* <note>The author uses "Greek Caph" here, but the context and the following sentences clarify he is referring to the Greek letter *Chi* ($\chi$)</note> was made by the finger of the anointer in the middle space between the eyes or eyebrows. In this matter, the *Priestly* anointing was distinct from the anointing of *Kings*, which was usually done in the shape of a *crown*. On this point, nearly all the Hebrew Masters agree. But the figure of the "Greek Caph" does not seem to have been so well known to them. Some think of their own Hebrew letter; and from this, they carve out mysteries. Let us hear *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a renowned Jewish statesman and biblical exegete</note> again: *The form of the Priest's anointing,* he says, *was like the letter כ [Caph]; so that it might be taught that he is a minister of God, appointed by God to stand and minister to Him in His Sanctuary. For Caph denotes כהן [Kohen], "Priest," since it is the first letter of that word.* After a few intervening words, he adds: *It is also possible that the figure of the letter Caph was used in anointing the Priest to teach that it is his duty to serve God with his hands. For כ [Caph] signifies "hand" to the Hebrews.* Others speak more clearly of the *Greek Chi*, the shape of which ($\chi$) is similar to that cross which is commonly called the "Saint Andrew’s Cross." If you wish, see those who discuss these matters: *Schickard* in *The Law of the King*, Chapter 1, Theorem 4, with the observations of *Carpzov*; *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> in *Succession of the Pontificate*, Book II, Chapter 9; *Simeon de Muis* in *Various Sacred Matters* on Exodus 30; and many others who for the most part take their material from these same sources.

<margin>
60. Persons to be anointed.
</margin>

### LX. 

The PERSONS TO BE ANOINTED were undoubtedly: I. AARON. II. HIS SUCCESSORS in the HIGH PRIESTHOOD. Hence any High Priest was called <gloss>the anointed priest</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: כהן משוח, "Kohen Mashuach"</note>. Leviticus 4:3, 5, 16. In this matter, there was a notable difference between the anointing of High Priests and Kings, which the Talmudists explain in the *Jerusalem Gemara* <note>The commentary portion of the Jerusalem Talmud</note> on the tractate *Horayot*, folio 47, column 3, in these words: *A King who is first appointed had to be anointed; but the King’s son, who succeeded to the kingdom, did not necessarily have to be anointed (unless perhaps because of a rival faction, and so that the disagreement between competitors might be settled). But truly the High Priest, even if the Son of a High Priest, had to be anointed for ten generations.* That is, according to the law, forever. III. THAT CAMP PRIEST, whose role was to give courage to the whole army by his exhortation, and to solemnly dismiss the others who enjoyed the privilege of being absent: whom they therefore call <gloss>the anointed of war</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: משוח מלחמה, "Mashuach Milchamah"</note>. *Schickard* has learnedly collected many things concerning his office in Chapter 5, Theorem 17.

...distinguished by sacred garments; they deny he was *distinguished by anointing* <note>original: מרובה משחה (*merubbe mishchah*); a Hebrew term referring to a High Priest who was "multiplied" or "amplified" by the anointing oil, as opposed to one who was merely "multiplied by garments"</note>. <margin>
62. Whether the common Priests were also anointed.
</margin>

LXII. Whether the COMMON PRIESTS <note>original: *gregarii sacerdotes*; literally "rank-and-file" priests, referring to the descendants of Aaron who were not the High Priest</note>—the sons of Aaron—were also anointed is a matter of debate among the learned. There is no lack of great men, most skilled in these matters, who deny it; they are led by these reasons in particular: I. Because the High Priest alone is called the *Anointed Priest*, and is distinguished from the others by that title (Leviticus 21:10). II. Because anointing is commanded in the consecration of the High Priest, but it is omitted in the consecration of the Priests (Exodus 29:7, 8, 9). <margin>Add Preface §. XXVI.</margin> III. Because the same is observed in the execution of the command (Leviticus 8:12). The celebrated *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "federal theology"</note> even found a mystery in this lack of anointing.

> It was not fitting, he says, that those to whom the right of entering the Holy of Holies was denied should have a fleshly anointing. Where the Holy Spirit of promise is, there is the Holy of Holies. Again, here there was a sign of imperfection <note>original: τῆς ἀτελείας (*tēs ateleias*)</note>. For where not only Israel, but even the Priests themselves lack the anointing which grants the right of entering the earthly Holy of Holies, there surely the Spirit of promise has not yet been given, without whom no one can draw near to God, and in whom we draw near to God as our father.

Others, however, affirm it: among whom is *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a polymath and English jurist who wrote extensively on Jewish law</note>. In his work *On the Succession to the High Priesthood*, Book II, Chapter IX, he writes as follows:

> In the very institution of the Priesthood, by which Aaron and his descendants were consecrated, not only he himself, but also his sons were anointed, and that for seven continuous days; just as they were also clothed in a solemn rite. As is clear in Exodus 29:29: *The sacred garments that belong to Aaron shall be his sons' after him, to be anointed while wearing them and to be consecrated in them for their ministry.*

But, to tell the truth, the passage cited does not seem to apply here. For this does not concern the Priests who were Aaron's associates, but rather his successors in the High Priesthood. Somewhat more explicit is Exodus 30:30:

> You shall also anoint Aaron and his sons; thus you shall consecrate them so that they may serve me in the Priesthood.

LXIII. In deciding this controversy, if I may be permitted to offer my own opinion, I think some distinction is necessary. The High Priest was anointed in one way, and the Priests in another. The High Priest was drenched on the head with holy oil, in the manner just explained (Exodus 29:7). However, the Priests were only lightly sprinkled on their sacred garments with oil mixed with the blood of the sacrifices. Moses teaches this in Exodus 29:21:

> Then, taking some of the blood that is on the altar and some of the anointing oil, you shall sprinkle Aaron and his garments, and his sons and the garments of his sons with him; thus he and his garments shall be holy, as well as his sons and the garments...

The author concludes that while the High Priest was fully anointed on the head, ordinary priests were merely sprinkled with a mixture of oil and blood.</summary>

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

...of his sons with him. This was also diligently observed in the execution of the command. *Leviticus 8:30.* From this it appears that Aaron received a twofold anointing: one that he possessed as his own, by which he became the **High Priest**, with **pure oil** poured upon his head; and another which he held in common with his sons, by which he was a **Priest**, with **oil and blood** sprinkled upon his garments. Furthermore, all the Hebrew authorities agree on this: the High Priests were always anointed successively as long as the sacred oil was available; but no **common priests** <note>original: *sacerdotes gregarios*; literally "rank-and-file" priests, referring to the descendants of Aaron who did not hold the High Office</note> were anointed, except for the immediate sons of Aaron. This was because their descendants were considered to have been sufficiently anointed in the persons of their ancestors.

<margin>
64. The Mystery of anointing.
</margin>

LXIV. It is also easy to transfer these things to our Jesus: who is the **Messiah** <note>original: המשיה (*Ha-Mashiach*)</note>, the **Christ** <note>original: Ὁ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ (*Ho Christos*)</note>, the **ANOINTED** one above all others. The **sacred OIL** signifies the fullness of the Deity dwelling in Him bodily, and the most abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit with which He was enriched. *Isaiah 61:1.* The fragrance of the oil represents the sweetness of grace, of the gifts and consolations of the Holy Spirit, by which the faithful are drawn to the love of Christ. With the same oil that **Aaron** was anointed, the **tabernacle** was also anointed, along with all its vessels. Likewise, all those in whom Christ dwells through a mystical habitation are partakers of His anointing, and that anointing makes their ministries pleasing to God. *2 Corinthians 1:21–22; 1 John 2:20, 27.* It was a sin to apply that sacred oil to any common or profane use. The world does not receive the Holy Spirit. *John 14:17.* It is the greatest impiety to simulate the Spirit in deceitful actions that mimic His character with an outward appearance, or to use Him as a pretext for the desires or impulses of the flesh. The oil poured upon the head, flowing down from there onto the beard, signifies the fullness of Christ's grace, communicating Himself to the members of His mystical body. *Psalm 133:2–3; John 3:34.* The manner of anointing in the shape of the Greek letter **X** <note>Jewish tradition describes the High Priest being anointed with a sign like the Greek letter *Chi* (Χ), likely representing the word "Christ" or "Anointed" in later Christian interpretation</note> either signifies nothing, or leads us directly to the cross, which our High Priest was destined to endure for the expiation of our sins. *Hebrews 12:2.* Because the High Priest was anointed in a special way, differently from the common priests, we may consider whether we are taught by this that Christ has no partners in His **Mediatorial office**—not even those closest to Him, namely the Apostles and their like. Yet, because He did in some sense have the other Priests as partners in Anointing, it teaches that the faithful are anointed by the Divine Spirit for a **spiritual and mystical priesthood**. *1 Peter 2:5.* The lack of external oil during the time of the **Second Temple** <note>The "Holy Oil" of Moses was said to have been hidden or lost during the Babylonian exile, so priests in the Second Temple era were consecrated only by their garments</note> may signify the imminent cessation of the Ceremonies, so that they might give way to an **unchangeable priesthood** <note>original: ἀπαραβάτῳ (*aparabato*); a Greek term from Hebrews 7:24 meaning a priesthood that does not pass to another</note> and to a true and mystical anointing that shall never fail.

<margin>
65. The offering of the triple Sacrifice for Aaron and his sons.
</margin>

LXV. Finally, the consecration included the **OFFERING** of a triple sacrifice for Aaron and his sons. *Exodus 29:10; Leviticus 8:14.*

# ON THE PRIESTHOOD OF AARON AND CHRIST.

### 399

The first sacrifice, consisting of a young bull, was a sin offering <term>piaculare: an expiatory sacrifice intended to appease divine anger</term>, serving as a certain ransom <note>original Greek: *λύτρον* (*lytron*)</note> by which they were first of all to be purified. The second consisted of a ram and was a burnt offering <term>holocaustum: a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire as a gift to God</term>, by which they might be commended to God, being wholly devoted to His service. The third was also a ram, for a Peace Offering <term>sacrificium Salutare sive Pacificum: a sacrifice for well-being or fellowship</term>, to which a sacred feast was attached so that they might be grafted into the family of God. Rabbi Levi ben Gerson <note>A renowned 14th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator, also known as Gersonides</note> discusses these victims excellently; his commentary is most worthy of being included here. He advises that the logic of the order in which these sacrifices were performed must be observed. For first of all, the sin offering was made for the expiation of sins: of which nothing but a certain amount of fat was offered to the most Holy Presence, because the offerers were not yet worthy for God to receive a gift or tribute from them. But after they had been purified, so that it might be understood they were devoted to the sacred ministry, they sacrificed the burnt offering to God, which was given entirely to the altar. After the burnt offering, they offered a sacrifice similar to a peace offering (of which a portion is usually given to God and a portion to the offerers) for this purpose: so that it might be clear they had by then been received into God’s favor to such an extent that they might share a common table with Him. Isaac Abarbanel <note>A 15th-century Jewish statesman and theologian</note> has similar points in his commentaries on Exodus 29. See William Outram <note>A 17th-century English clergyman and scholar who wrote extensively on sacrificial rites</note>, Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.

<margin>LXVI. The right ears and right thumbs of the Priests were stained with the blood of the ram.</margin>
LXVI. Furthermore, the right ears of all the Priests, and the thumbs of their right hands and the big toes of their right feet, were to be stained with the blood of that ram which was offered as a peace offering. *Exodus 29:20.* By this it was signified that it is the duty of Priests: I. To listen with their ears to the command of God. II. To have their hands ready for His service. III. To walk with swift feet in the ways of the Lord. IV. And to do all these things with a sincere intention and in the most exact manner. For just as the right side is the most noble and best suited for acting, so it is also a symbol of faith and sincerity.

<margin>LXVII. The rest of that ram went partly to God and partly to Moses.</margin>
LXVII. Finally, these things having been performed, Moses placed the fat of the aforementioned ram—the tail, the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, both kidneys, and the right shoulder—as well as one loaf of bread, one cake mixed with oil, and one unleavened wafer, into the palms of Aaron and his sons; and placing his own hands under their hands, he waved all those things in every direction <note>This refers to the "wave offering," a ritual gesture where the items were moved toward the altar and back to symbolize presenting them to God</note>, offering them to God, the owner of all things; and once offered, he soon burned them upon the altar. However, the breast of the same ram, waved in the same manner, he took for himself, having performed the duties of a Priest. *Leviticus 8:25 and following.*

<margin>LXVIII. The mystery of these things.</margin>
LXVIII. And it is to be believed that these things also pointed to something deeper. But, as often happens elsewhere with types <term>types: historical figures or events in the Old Testament seen as foreshadowing Christ in the New Testament</term>, a certain "change of persons" must be noted here. Since this offering was performed by Moses, and he was now acting as a Priest, Moses in this matter took on the role of Christ, who by His own offering sanctifies those who approach God.

It identifies Moses as a "type" of Christ in his role as the mediator of these rituals.</summary>

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

#### 400

Aaron with his sons represents the *elect* <note>Those chosen by God for salvation or special service</note>, who cannot perform services pleasing to God, nor be admitted into the fellowship of His family and grace, unless they have first been cleansed by the blood of Christ. Furthermore, in the *victims offered*, there is a figure of Christ. In the *expiatory bull* <term>juvenco piaculari: a young bull sacrificed to make amends for sin</term>, the Famous Interpreter <note>Referring to Johannes Cocceius, mentioned later on the page</note> believes that the mortality and patience of Christ are shown, as well as the fact that he was intended as food for men. In the *Ram of the burnt offering*, he commands the same to be considered: the male sex, and the nature and character of that animal. The *male sex* denotes strength and power. The *sheep kind* indicates a distance from inflicting injury <note>A reference to the gentleness and innocence of the lamb</note>. The *imposition of hands* on both sacrifices foreshadows that our sins were imputed to Christ, and that we must lean upon Him through faith. The *Feast of the Peace Offering*, to which Aaron was admitted, denotes the communion that all mystical Priests have with Christ, their Altar (Hebrews 13:10). 

The fact that *blood was smeared on the right ear*, as well as on the *thumbs of the right hands and feet*, signifies that the Priest who was *figured* <note>represented symbolically</note> by them has ears pierced for obedience <note>original: "aures perforatas"; a reference to the servant who chooses to stay with his master forever in Exodus 21:6, symbolizing Christ’s total obedience</note>, hands ready to take hold of those given to Him by the Father, and feet swift in the ways of the Lord to help His own. It also signifies that the intellect, will, and affections of no men are sanctified except by His blood (Hebrews 9:14). 

The fact that *Moses places the fat, the tail, and the other parts of the ram used for the peace sacrifice*, along with the things joined to them, *upon the palms of Aaron*, demonstrates the weakness of the Aaronic priesthood. Aaron and his sons do not themselves offer that by which they are sanctified as Priests, but another does it. They merely hold something in their hands and wave it before Jehovah, in which God takes delight. Man cannot approach God to offer a sacrifice pleasing to Him unless it is handed to him by a greater Priest. Moses now performs the duties of this greater Priest in this symbolic figure. See the most renowned *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who emphasized the "covenants" and saw many Old Testament rituals as direct shadows of Christ</note> pursuing all these points at length regarding Exodus 29. Even if it cannot be proven that every single minute detail was prefigured in this way, surely no one, I think, would deny that these things can be piously contemplated on this and any other occasion. And who will begrudge the faithful and the lovers of Christ that they, through the Mosaic institutions—which they know were at least generally intended for this purpose—ascend to the meditation of spiritual and heavenly things in Christ?

<margin>LXIX. It is the duty of the Priests to approach God.</margin>

LXIX. Thus far we have seen the *Consecration of the Priests*, by which they are initiated into their office; now let us weigh the FUNCTION of the office itself. This can be considered either *Generally* or *More Specifically*. Generally, the Sacerdotal Function consists in this: that they APPROACH GOD—that is, they converse familiarly with God, they are the ministers closest to God, occupied in the things of God which must be conducted before God Himself. For they are described thus...

<margin>LXX. The word "Priest" denotes a Minister of the King.</margin>
LXX. The word itself, <term>Cohen</term> <note>Hebrew for Priest</note>, implies this. For it signifies a *minister closest to the King*. Furthermore, since Kings are of two different kinds—some earthly, and one Heavenly, who is the King of the whole universe—both have their <note>original Hebrew: "Cohanim"</note> *priests* or *ministers*. Thus the sons of David are called *Priests* <note>Hebrew: "Cohanim"</note> in 2 Samuel 8:18. <margin>LXXI. Christ, being closest to God, has the right of access for all.</margin>
LXXI. Truly, Christ is both closest to God and <note>original Hebrew: "Gever amiti"</note> *the Man who is His companion.* Zechariah 13:7. Moreover, Priests approach God in such a way that they handle the affairs of the people before God, as beautifully observed by the Apostle in Hebrews 5:1. The Prophet is <term>God's Legate</term> <note>An official messenger or ambassador sent from God to the people</note> to the people. Haggai 1:13; 2 Corinthians 5:20. The King is <term>God's Vicar</term> <note>A deputy or representative exercising God's authority on earth</note>. 2 Chronicles 19:6. The Priest is the <term>People's Patron</term> <note>An advocate or protector representing the people's interests before God</note>. Thus also Christ is a *merciful and faithful High Priest in those things which must be done before God* (Hebrews 2:17), *to appear before the face of God for us* (Hebrews 9:24).

<margin>LXXII. Three parts of the Priestly function.</margin>
LXXII. More specifically, three things pertain to the priestly function:

Likewise, the Lord said to Moses: *Take for yourself sweet spices, stacte and onycha...*

Whoever makes anything like it to enjoy its smell shall be cut off from his people. <note>This passage translates Exodus 30:34-38, describing the *Ketoret* or sacred incense.</note> The Hebrews explain these things somewhat more clearly: instead of the four species of spices praised by Moses, they count fifteen, in this proportion: Stacte <note>oil of myrrh</note>, Onycha <note>aromatic shell</note>, Galbanum, and Frankincense, 70 pounds each. Myrrh, Cassia, Spikenard, and Saffron, 16 pounds each. Costus, 12 pounds. Cinnamon, 9 pounds. Cinnamon bark <note>original: *cassia lignea*</note>, 3 pounds. These, collected into one sum, make 368 pounds. This allows one pound for each day of the year, so that for the entire year there remain three residual pounds, which are used for the Day of Atonement. That incense, by which prayers are signified, is a most holy thing to God. For nothing is more holy or more proper to God than the devoted offering of prayers: it is a crime, under penalty of extermination, for these to be alienated and offered to one who is not God.

<margin>74. The manner of offering gifts.</margin>
**74. THE MANNER OF OFFERING GIFTS**, or grain offerings <note>original: *ferta*</note>, was this: all were prepared from barley or wheat flour; to some, wine was added, but to others it was not. Those which were augmented by a libation of wine were to be kneaded with oil and seasoned with salt, without leaven and without honey. Leviticus 2:11. God willed that leaven be absent, if we believe Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, so that no delay would be caused by waiting for fermentation. Honey was excluded lest the Priests, while touching it, should anticipate the eating by licking their fingers. Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> considers that by this precept the Israelites were distinguished from idolaters, who were accustomed to add leaven and honey to their offerings. Baal Hatturim <note>Jacob ben Asher, a 14th-century biblical commentator</note> relates this to moral character. "Leaven," he says, "denotes the evil inclination <note>original: *figmentum malum*</note>, which corrupts everything; the same is signified by honey, insofar as that corruption is sweet to a corrupt man." Salt, however, is the *Salt of the covenant* (Numbers 18:19) because it is a sign of the covenant and of its constancy. Furthermore, grain offerings of this kind were always to be joined with some type of animal sacrifice <note>original: *victimarum*</note>, never to be given without a sacrifice: and together with the burnt offerings they were to be consumed by fire as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. Numbers 28 and 29. Grain offerings not augmented by wine libations were either leavened or unleavened <note>original: *azyma*</note>. Leavened offerings, such as those loaves of the firstfruits on the Day of Pentecost (Leviticus 23:17) and those used in the thank-offerings <note>original: *Eucharisticis*; here referring to the *Shelamim* or peace offerings</note> (Leviticus 7:13), were indeed to be presented to God, but were by no means to be burned on the Altar; instead, they went in their entirety to the Priests. For it was not lawful to burn leavened feast-meals on the altar. Leviticus 2:10. No offering which you offer to the Lord shall be made...

# ON THE PRIESTHOOD OF AARON AND CHRIST.

...leavened: for you shall burn no leaven nor honey as a gift consumed by fire for the Lord <note>original: *Jehovæ*</note>. Some of the *unleavened bread* was given partly to the Priests and partly to the Altar. 

As, for example, the firstfruits of the harvest to be offered at the feast of Passover. Regarding these, the Masters of the Hebrews <note>The Rabbis and Jewish sages</note> teach as follows: from three bundles of grain, three *seahs* <note>a biblical unit of dry measure</note> of barley were threshed in the Temple Court; from those threshed, winnowed, ground, and roasted seeds, one *Omer* <note>about 2.3 liters</note> was selected. This was mixed with one *log* <note>about 0.3 liters</note> of oil and increased by adding a handful of frankincense. First, it was held out toward all the quarters of the world, as if to God the creator of all, then partly given to the Altar and partly to the Priests. Before this feast was rendered to God, no one was allowed to taste new grain. *Leviticus 23:14.*

<margin>
75. The offering of sacrifices belonged partly to the owners.
</margin>

75. **THE OFFERING OF SACRIFICES** <note>original: *Victimarum*</note> was formerly twofold: one part belonged to the *Owners of the Sacrifices*, and the other to the *Priests*. The former is completed in three acts. I. That the victim be brought to the door of the tent of meeting. *Leviticus 1:2-3: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: when any of you offers an offering to the Lord... he shall offer it at the door of the tent of meeting.* II. That by the laying on of hands it be consecrated to God and substituted for the one offering. *Ibid. verse 4: And he shall lean his hand upon the head of his burnt offering, so that it may be accepted for him to make atonement for him.* III. That it be slaughtered by the person offering it. *Verse 5.* Maimonides <note>The 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> in *Biat Hammikdas* <note>Entering the Sanctuary</note> Chapter 9, Section 6: *The slaughtering of sacrifices by laypeople (who are not of the house of Aaron) is legitimate, even for the most holy things; but the receiving of the blood, and the actions that follow it, belong to the Priesthood.*

<margin>
76. Part belongs to the Priests.
<term>Terumah</term>
<term>Tenufah</term>
</margin>

76. The Priestly Offering similarly has three parts. Of which, I. is the offering of the blood, the fat, and the choice portions <note>original: *prosectorum & ablegminum*</note>, which were applied by the Priest to the altar. *Leviticus 3:2-3.* II. The waving toward all the quarters of the world: which is usually called *Tenufah* <note>a wave offering</note> and *Terumah* <note>a heave offering</note>. *Exodus 29:27, Leviticus 10:14-15.* These are distinguished by the Hebrew Masters in this way: *Terumah* is the waving upward, while *Tenufah* is the waving performed forward and backward, and to the right and left. By these rituals, the sacrifice was duly presented to God who fills all things—and what else?—who watches over and possesses all things. Thus *Rabbi Bechai* <note>Bahya ben Asher</note> on *Leviticus 8*: <note>original Hebrew: מוליך ומביא למי שארבע רוחות העולם שלו מעלה ומוריד למי שהשמים וארץ שלו</note> *He moves it forward and backward to Him to whom the four quarters of the world belong; he moves it upward and downward to Him who is the Lord of heaven and earth.* *Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson* <note>also known as Gersonides</note> adds that the waving pertained to this: <note>original Hebrew: להורות על השם יתעלה השגיה בעליונים בתחתונים בכל פנות שהם בו</note> *that we may understand that the providence of God (may He be exalted) is present in the highest and lowest things, in every corner where they exist.* However, the Illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian</note> explains these differently; he may be consulted in his Lexicon under the words *Terumah* and *Tenufah*. III. Finally, the third part of the Priestly offering is the burning by the sacred fire on the Altar.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

<margin>
77. The Daily and Annual offering of incense.
</margin>
77. **THE OFFERING OF INCENSE**, or <term>incense-burning</term> <note>Latin: *suffitio*</note> is twofold: one is to be performed daily, morning and evening; the other is performed every year on the Day of <term>Atonement</term> <note>Yom Kippur</note>. For the daily incense-burning, unless the Jewish records deceive us, three Priests were employed, perhaps chosen by lot. To the first, the task was given to sweep the ashes of the golden altar into a certain golden vessel. To the second, to take glowing coals from the bronze Altar of Burnt Offerings and, having placed them in a certain fire-pan, move them to the golden altar. When these two had exited the temple, the third priest—prompted by the Overseer standing outside—would take the incense from the censer with his hand and cast it onto the altar's hearth. Once this was done, he also exited the Temple—that is, the Holy Place—but only after he had adored the divine presence dwelling there by bowing his body toward the Holy of Holies with the greatest reverence. At the same time that the incense was being burned by the Priest, the people themselves, each standing in their own place, performed their prayers (Luke 1:10), while the Levites meanwhile sounded trumpets and sang in harmony. This took place in the morning and evening when the lamps were tended (Exodus 30:7–8). And truly, while the lamp of the Word is being lit, prayers ought to be added. The annual incense-burning was not performed by just any Priest, but by the <term>High Priest</term> <note>Latin: *Pontifex*</note> alone, in the <term>Holy of Holies</term> <note>the innermost chamber of the Temple</note>, within the veil, on the solemn Day of Atonement. At that time, carrying the censer of incense in his left hand and the fire-pan with glowing coals in his right, he entered the innermost sanctuary. Having entered and set down the fire-pan from his hand, he cast the incense onto the coals; once the sanctuary was filled with a dense cloud, he stepped back out into the outer sanctuary gradually and walking backward.

<margin>
78. Three songs of solemn prayers to be recited by the High Priest on the Day of Atonement.
</margin>
78. They desired **PRAYERS** to be added to all offerings, both from the offerents themselves and from the Priests. This was done most significantly on the **DAY OF ATONEMENT**, during that great annual sacrifice. Regarding this, the Masters <note>the Rabbis and scholars of the Talmud</note> recount three distinct formulas of prayer used by the <term>High Priest</term>. In the first, which took place beside the <term>sacrificial bull</term> <note>the young bull offered for sin</note>, he confessed his own sins, those of his household, and those of the entire family of Aaron.

> *I beseech You, Lord, we have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have rebelled in Your sight, I, and my household, and the sons of Aaron, Your holy people. I beseech You, Lord, forgive now the sins, iniquities, and rebellions by which we have sinned, committed iniquity, and rebelled in Your sight, I and my household, and Your holy people. As it is written in the Law of Moses Your servant, where it is said: "on this day there shall be an atonement for you, and a cleansing from all your sins; before the Lord you shall be cleansed."*

To this prayer of the High Priest, the Priests would respond with this short song: **Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever.** <note>original Hebrew: *Baruch shem kavod malchuto l’olam va’ed*</note>. In the second formula, which was used regarding the goat to be led away into the wilderness, the <term>High Priest</term> would pray for all the people.

> *I beseech You, Lord, Your people Israel has sinned, committed iniquity, and rebelled in Your sight.*

# On the Priesthood of Aaron and of Christ

> *I beseech You, Lord: forgive now the sins, the transgressions, and the rebellions with which Your people, the house of Israel, has sinned, transgressed, and rebelled in Your sight; as it is written in the Law of Moses Your servant, where it is said: On this day there shall be an expiation for you, and a cleansing from all your sins; you shall be cleansed before the Lord.* <note>original: "Obsecro Domine, remitte nunc peccata..." This is the traditional confession of the High Priest on Yom Kippur.</note>

To these prayers the people responded as described above. See 2 Maccabees 1:23 for another form of sacrificial prayer. There was also a third prayer of the High Priest on the Day of Atonement. When he entered the <term>inner sanctuary</term> <note>the Holy of Holies</note> to offer the incense and fill the room with a thick cloud, he would step backward toward the people into the outer sanctuary and commend the people to God in this way:

> *May it please You, Lord, that if this year be a hot one, it may also be rainy; that the scepter may not depart from the house of Judah; that Your people Israel may not lack for food; and that the prayers of the wicked may be rendered void.*

<margin>79. Many things worthy of observation regarding the Priestly Blessing.</margin>
79. Regarding the <term>Priestly Blessing</term> <note>Numbers 6:24–26, often called the Aaronic Blessing</note>, several points arise that are most worthy of observation. First is the circumstance of time. After Israel had been received into God’s covenant, the sanctuary properly established, the people arranged in order around it, and sanctified in that order, the Law concerning the Blessing was brought forth. Surely, *the one who looks into that perfect law of liberty and remains in it, being not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, that person, I say, shall be blessed in his work.* (James 1:25). The observation of Rabbi Menachem of Recanati <note>A 13th-14th century Italian Kabbalist</note> is beautiful: *The reason,* he says, *why the blessing is mentioned after the Tabernacle was erected is this: because from the superior and heavenly Tabernacle, an abundance of blessing flows down into that which is lower and earthly.* Nor should we overlook that, according to the Teachers, the Priestly Blessing was performed only in the morning, never at the hour of the <term>Mincha</term> <note>the afternoon offering</note>. (Maimonides, *Treatise on Prayers*, Chapter 14, Section 1).

80. They also believe much is contained in the little word **thus**, which begins the command for the blessing: **Thus you shall bless the children of Israel.**
**Thus**: by lifting up the hands.
**Thus**: in the <term>holy tongue</term> <note>Hebrew</note>.
**Thus**: with the face turned toward the people.
**Thus**: in a loud voice.
**Thus**: with the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>the sacred four-letter Name of God, YHWH</note> clearly pronounced, if the blessing occurs in the sanctuary. Outside the sanctuary, they did not pronounce this most holy name. Indeed, even in the sanctuary itself, the pronunciation ceased after the death of <term>Simeon the Just</term> <note>A famous High Priest during the Second Temple period</note>. They also believe it was a sin to add a fourth blessing to this triple one, even though similar blessings are found elsewhere in the sacred scriptures—such as that in Deuteronomy 1:11: *May the Lord God of your fathers make you a thousand times more than you are, and bless you.*

77. THE OFFERING OF INCENSE, or the burning of spices, is twofold: one to be performed daily, morning and evening; the other annually, on the Day of Atonement. For the daily incense offering—unless the Jewish traditions mislead us—three <term>Priests</term> <note>These roles were assigned by lot as described in the Mishnah, tractate Tamid.</note> were employed, perhaps chosen by lot. At that time, carrying the censer of incense in his left hand and a brazier with burning coals in his right, he would penetrate into the innermost sanctuary. Having entered there and set down the brazier from his hand, he would cast the incense onto the coals; then, once the sanctuary was filled with a thick cloud, he would step out toward the outer sanctuary gradually and moving backward.

### LXXIX. Concerning the PRIESTLY BLESSING

<margin>79. Many things worthy of note regarding the Priestly Blessing.</margin>
79. Concerning the **PRIESTLY BLESSING**, several things occur that are most worthy of observation. First is the circumstance of time. After Israel had been received into the covenant of God, the sanctuary rightly established, the people placed in order around it, and sanctified in this order, the Law concerning the Blessing was brought forth. Surely *he who has looked into that perfect law of liberty, and has remained in it, because he was not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, he, I say, shall be blessed in his work.* (James 1:25). Beautiful is the observation of Rabbi Menachem of Recanati <note>A 13th-14th century Italian Kabbalist and commentator</note>. He says the reason why mention of the blessing was made after the <term>Tabernacle</term> <note>The portable dwelling place of God's presence</note> was erected is this: because from the higher and heavenly Tabernacle, an abundance of blessing flows down into that which is lower and earthly. Nor should it be overlooked that, according to the Masters <note>The Jewish Sages</note>, the Priestly Blessing was only performed in the morning, never at the hour of the *Mincha* <note>The afternoon or evening offering</note>. *Maimonides, Treatise on Prayer, Chapter 14, Section 1.*

### LXXX. Regarding the little word "THUS"

80. They also believe that much is contained in the little word **THUS**, which introduces the command for the blessing: **THUS YOU SHALL BLESS THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL.** "Thus," meaning by raising the hands. "Thus," in the holy language, which is Hebrew. "Thus," with the face turned toward the people. "Thus," in a loud voice. "Thus," with the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter sacred name of God, YHWH</note> expressed, if the blessing is done in the sanctuary. Outside the sanctuary, they did not pronounce this most holy name. Indeed, even in the sanctuary itself, it ceased to be pronounced after the death of Simeon the Just <note>A High Priest during the Second Temple period, often identified as Simon II</note>. They also believe it was a sin to add a fourth blessing to this triple blessing, however much it might be found elsewhere in the sacred scriptures—for example, that which appears in Deuteronomy 1:11: *May the Lord God of your fathers make you a thousand times more than you are, and bless you.*

LXXXIII. In all parts of the priestly function, there is nothing that Christ did not exactly perform. For I. through the *eternal Spirit he offered himself* to God without blemish, *that by his blood he might cleanse the conscience from dead works*: Hebrews 9:14. And by a single offering he perfected forever those who are sanctified. Hebrews 10:14. II. He PRAYED for his own on earth. John 17:10. And even now he prays for them in heaven. LXXXIV. But these matters deserve to be explained a little more closely. Not only the offering of livestock, but also of GIFTS <note>Original: "MUNERUM," referring to non-animal offerings</note>, was instituted for obtaining the expiation of sins. This can be gathered, partly from that terrible sentence pronounced by God against the family of Eli, that it would not come to pass that *the iniquity of the house of Eli be expiated* <note>original Hebrew: בזבח ובמנחה — "by sacrifice or by grain offering"</note> *by sacrifice or by gift.* 1 Samuel 3:14. And partly from the counsel David suggests to Saul: *If Jehovah has stirred you up against me, let him smell a gift,* 1 Samuel 26:19. That is, see that something is offered to him that is pleasing, so that he, being appeased, may free you from this persistent melancholy. Furthermore, if typical expiation could also be obtained by a sacred offering, it must necessarily have a respect to Christ; in which respect all the force and virtue of the ceremonies is founded. But it also follows that there is something in the offering of Christ that corresponds to the *Mincha* or *Gift* <term>Mincha (a Hebrew term for a grain offering or voluntary gift to God, as distinguished from a blood sacrifice)</term>. ### On the Priesthood of Aaron and Christ.

...explained what pertains to the offering of the *Sacrifice of Christ*. Let it only be noted now that the purest *fine flour* <term>simila: the finest wheat flour used in the "Mincha" or grain offering</term>, from which the Offering was made, can signify the most exact purity of Christ. The *Oil* signifies the communication of the Holy Spirit. *Frankincense* represents the most pleasant scent of the gift, and God’s acceptance of it as something pleasing. The *Burning* <note>Original: "Crematio"</note> on the altar signifies the death of Christ for the atonement of sins. Finally, the fact that a portion of the gift was given to the Priests signifies the communion of the faithful with Christ in the sharing of his merits.

<margin>85. By which the faithful, sanctified through him, are also represented.</margin>
LXXXV. <margin>86. And the duties of piety to be performed by them.</margin>
LXXXVI. Finally, certain duties of piety are also noted, which are to be carried out by religious people toward God, toward themselves, and toward their neighbors. Toward God, *through prayers and thanksgivings.* For these are compared to the offering of gifts. Psalm 141:2: *Let my prayer be set forth before you as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.* In Malachi Chapter 1:10-11, after God had protested that he takes no pleasure in the offering of an external gift unless it is commended by the piety of the one offering it, he soon adds: *From the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name shall be great among the nations, and in every place incense shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering.* To this corresponds that word of Paul in 1 Timothy 2:1: *I desire therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands, without anger or dispute.* Even those offering the gift were reminded of their own crimes and were compelled to a humble confession of their guilt. For just as the slaughter of animals included a confession of our obligation to death, so too did the sacred consumption of those things which were otherwise given to us for the sustenance of life. The pouring out of oil and wine, and the burning of fine flour, salt, and frankincense, signified the same thing as the slaughter of an animal. BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

They base this observation on the Mosaic phrase: *When a soul offers an offering of a gift to the Lord* <note>Original Latin: "Anima quum offert oblationem muneris Jehovae," citing Leviticus 2:1. The author highlights that the Hebrew text uses the word "soul" (Nephesh) to refer to the person offering.</note>. This interpretation is perhaps a bit subtle. Yet, gifts of liberality bestowed upon the needy are also compared to these offerings in Hebrews 13:16: *But do not forget to do good and to share.* For God is pleased with such sacrifices. Elsewhere, Paul also calls these "a sweet-smelling fragrance, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God."

<margin>87. In the offering of the sacrifice of Christ, there are three stages.</margin>
LXXXVII. In the *Offering of Christ* as a SACRIFICE, just as in other sacrifices, *three stages* must be distinctly considered. First, those living victims were offered at the door of the tent of meeting (Leviticus 1:2-3); *secondly*, they were slaughtered for the honor of God and placed upon the altar, to be consumed by fire either in whole or in part; *finally, the blood of some was carried into the innermost sanctuary.* In the same manner, Christ offered himself: first, while alive and healthy, when he traveled of his own accord to the place where he knew he would be led as a <term>piacular victim: a sacrifice offered to appease divine justice and atone for sin</term> to judgment and soon to the cross (Luke 18:31), and he voluntarily presented himself to God in the face of imminent death. This is what he says in John 17:19: *For them I sanctify myself* <note>Original Greek: "ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐγὼ ἁγιάζω ἐμαυτὸν"</note>, meaning, *for them I offer myself to God as a victim.* For the term "to sanctify" <note>Hebrew: קדש (qadesh); Greek: ἁγιάζειν (hagiazein)</note> sometimes carries the same weight as "to offer" (Leviticus 22:2-3, Deuteronomy 15:9). Nor does it admit any other suitable meaning in this passage. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> excellently explains these words, *I sanctify myself*, as *I offer a sacrifice to you* <note>Original Greek: "προσφέρω σοι θυσίαν"</note>. Secondly, he offered himself through *suffering and dying* and pouring out his blood; to that end, he was led outside Jerusalem, just as those victims which most closely prefigured him were to be burned outside the camp and the city (Hebrews 13:11-12). For it is unbeatably concluded from the Apostle’s argument in Hebrews 9:26-28 that the offering of Christ consists in his passion and death; there he proves that Christ had to sacrifice himself only once at the end of the ages to do away with sin, because otherwise he would have had to suffer many times since the foundation of the world, and because he died only once, just as it is appointed for men to die once.

This sanctification was performed not so much by the altar itself as by the sacred fire, which, having descended from heaven, was a figure of the Holy Spirit. <margin>89. The learned observation of Cloppenburg.</margin>
LXXXIX. Meanwhile, one should not disregard the learned and subtle observation of Cloppenburg <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652) was a noted Dutch Calvinist theologian</note>, that Christ was sanctified through that very curse of which the cross was the symbol. Indeed, the mystery of <term>expiation: the act of making amends or reparation for guilt or sin</term> lay in the fact that victims were consecrated through a Curse: for it was necessary to devote them to a curse in order to obtain a blessing from God. And thus Christ made atonement for us, having himself become a **curse** <note>original Greek: "κατάρα" (katara)</note>, when he sanctified himself for us, and was sanctified by the Father through sufferings. Hebrews 2:10. See Cloppenburg’s *Sacrificial Schools* in *Gleanings of Problems*, VI. The flames with which he was burned are the Zeal for Divine glory and an incredible charity toward his brothers. Psalm 69:10. To these was added the baptism of fire kindled by the wrath of God against our sins. Luke 12:50.

<margin>90. The third part of Christ's offering is his entry into heaven.</margin>
XC. Finally, in the third place, Christ offered himself when he brought his own blood into the sanctuary not made with hands—that is, into heaven itself—and presented it to his Father. Hebrews 9:12. This matter is worthy of being clarified by a somewhat more extensive dissertation. God teaches in express words in Leviticus 17:11 that the blood of beasts is considered their soul <note>The Hebrew word "Nephesh" can mean both "soul" and "life-force," which the author is connecting to the physical blood</note>, because it is the vehicle of life, and that this same blood is substituted for the soul of the sinful man offering the victim, and has therefore been given upon the altar to make atonement for souls. Therefore, when the Messiah is considered as the <term>antitype: the reality or person foreshadowed by an earlier symbol or "type"</term> of the victim offered for atonement—just as the blood of the victim stands for the soul, in its place and stead—so in turn the soul of the Messiah is called "blood" whenever he appears under the emblem of a brute animal, namely the slaughtered Lamb. 1 Peter 1:19; Revelation 5:6, 7:14. Conversely, his blood is sometimes called "soul" when he is represented as a rational agent who offers something in accordance with his pledge. Isaiah 53:10, 12. Thus, soul and blood in this matter are **equivalent in power** <note>original Greek: "ἰσοδυναμοῦντα" (isodynamounta)</note>. Therefore, just as the blood of goats and calves was brought into the inner sanctuary at the time when the body of the victim was dead, so also the blood of Christ was brought by himself as the Priest—with his Divinity performing the office of the High Priest—into the sanctuary not made with hands; while the body remained outside, set apart in a clean place outside the camp. For in this way the analogy between the <term>type: a symbolic person, object, or event in the Old Testament</term> and the antitype must be preserved, in the assignment of which the Apostle certainly did not err. Moreover, that blood can be nothing other than the soul of Christ; which, when he had poured it out, having torn the veil of his flesh (Hebrews 10:20), at which time also the veil of the Temple was torn (Matthew 27:50), he brought into heaven. Afterward, Christ presented not only the soul, but also the very body of the slain victim in heaven before God...

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.

...stood present before God. For he is in heaven not only as our High Priest, but also as a "Lamb that was slain." <note>original: Apocalypse 5:6</note>. Why, then, should that presentation of the victim before God not be considered part of his offering?

<margin>
91. The effect of the offering is the full expiation of sin.
</margin>

XCI. The *purpose and effect* of the offering is the complete <term>expiation: the act of making amends or reparation for guilt</term> and the blotting out of our sin. <note>Hebrews 1:3; 1 John 3:2</note>. For God placed our sins upon Christ just as he would upon a sacrificial victim; and so Christ, by a voluntary pledge, took them upon himself. He satisfied the debt so fully—having received them from the Father and taken them upon himself—that he truly and perfectly *atoned* for them. Hence, among the benefits of the Messiah, we find listed "to make an end of sins." <note>original Hebrew: "kaphar avon" from Daniel 9:24</note>. It is worth including here the words of the Hebrew Lexicon called the *Aruch* <note>A famous dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash compiled by Nathan ben Jehiel in the 11th century</note> under the entry for *kaphar* (atonement) on folio 76, at the end: *Wherever it says, "Behold, I am for atonement," the meaning is, "Behold, I am in his place to bear his iniquities," as if he were saying, "I take his sins upon myself so that I may atone for them."* Moreover, Christ atoned for our sin so fully that it can no longer be charged to the faithful as punishment—a benefit even the ancients possessed by virtue of the offering that was to be completed in its own time. Consequently, there is no longer a place for the demand of a "handwriting of debt" <note>original: "chirographi," referring to a legal bond or record of debt</note>, nor for the confession of guilt as if one were not yet atoned for, which occurred in the repeated animal sacrifices. This is the fruit of the completed offering. <note>Colossians 2:14; Hebrews 10:2</note>.

<margin>
92. Ephesians 5:2 is explained from the inner secrets of the Mosaic rituals.
</margin>

XCII. And for this reason, Christ is said to have given himself for us as "an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor." <note>original Greek: "ΠΡΟΣΦΟΡΑΝ καὶ ΘΥΣΙΑΝ τῷ Θεῷ εἰς ΟΣΜΗΝ ΕΥΩΔΙΑΣ" from Ephesians 5:2</note>. These words of Paul have much greater emphasis than they seem to at first glance; they cannot be explained except from the inner secrets of the Mosaic institutions. This has been excellently demonstrated by Jacob Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679) was a Dutch linguist and theologian</note> in his *Heptad IV, Dissertation 5, sections 19 and 20.* Specifically, in the Old Testament, only those sacrifices were said to be a "pleasing odor" to God to which *oil and frankincense* had been added. <note>Leviticus 2:2, 9, 16</note>.

<margin>
Add Preface § XXVII.
</margin>

But for sacrifices for sin, it was forbidden *to add frankincense and oil.* <note>Leviticus 5:11</note>. Nor are they said to have been a "sweet-smelling savor." This is because they could indeed "commemorate" sin, but they could not truly "remove" it. To be sure, the victim for sin was often burned; it was food for the wrath of God, which, though it would otherwise have consumed the sinner, poured out its power upon the substitute to destroy it. Sometimes the victim was given to the Priests as food, who in that way "incorporated" the sin and took the guilt of the people upon themselves <note>Leviticus 10:17</note>; this was to show that, eventually, the Priest and the victim would be one and the same person, as was fulfilled in Christ. However, because such a victim for sin was the object of Divine wrath, it was not permitted to add *frankincense* to it, because...

...that it would not be a "sweet-smelling aroma," nor would God find satisfaction in it as something that makes amends. For this reason, the person making the offering was not allowed to eat any part of it. Instead, another sacrifice was used—the "peace offering"—which was joined by a meal offering, incense, wine, and oil. This was done after the guilt was cleared to testify to the grace of a reconciled God and to a joyful fellowship. <note>Leviticus 23:19–20</note>. The matter is different in the sacrifice of Christ, in which it is right that everything is as perfect as possible and complete in all its parts. There, we find a true **SACRIFICE FOR SIN & GUILT** <note>original Hebrew: "Chatat" and "Asham"</note>; and for this reason, it is called a **SACRIFICE** <note>original Greek: "Thysia"</note>. But at the same time, there is an **OFFERING** <note>original Greek: "Prosphora," the word Greeks typically use to translate the Hebrew "Mincha"</note>, which is a <term>Meal Offering: an offering of grain or flour</term>, always accompanied by oil, incense, wine, and a liquid offering; because of this, it was a "sweet-smelling aroma" to God. In truth, Christ was a victim for sin in such a way that he bore the brunt of Divine anger; but he did so in a way that Divine justice was fully satisfied. There was present the *incense of good pleasure*, and the *wine of joy* followed after. To this most pleasant fellowship, all the faithful are admitted as participants in that mystical and truly peaceful banquet.

<margin>93. The tearing of the veil is proof that the atonement is complete.</margin>
XCIII. It is also very much worth noting, as a most learned man has beautifully observed, that a remarkable proof of the <term>expiation: the act of making amends for a crime or mistake</term> performed by Christ is found in the *tearing of the veil*. The veil stretched over the <term>Holy of Holies: the innermost part of the Tabernacle where God's presence dwelt</term> symbolized how sins, like a dividing wall, block sinners from approaching God. However, on the solemn Day of Atonement, when the blood of the sacrificial goat was shed, the veil would yield for the High Priest about to enter the inner sanctuary, opening the way to represent the atonement being made before God. However, because sin was not truly removed in this way, but only shown in a symbolic figure, the veil would return to its place and its previous use once the priest left, once again barring access to the sanctuary. But after Christ had completed the atonement on the cross, as he was about to enter the heavenly sanctuary to present his atoning blood there, the veil did not merely move aside for a moment. Instead, it was torn and shredded—not by human hands, but by Divine power—as if to show it would have no use from then on, eternal redemption having been obtained. These observations seem to me so beautiful, so learnedly noted, and so helpful for illustrating God’s wisdom in His laws and works, that I wish them to be read in my own writings no less than in those of the most famous *Alting* <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch professor of Hebrew and theology</note>. I include them on the condition that the glory of the discovery remains untouched for him, provided he was the one who found it.

->### BOOK II. DISSERTATION II.<-

...we learn this nowhere more certainly or safely than from *Revelation 8:3-4: Then another Angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the Throne. And the smoke of the incense with the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the Angel in the sight of God.* No one was permitted to burn incense except for the priests <note>Numbers 16:40</note>. When King Uzziah rashly took this duty upon himself, he paid for it with lifelong leprosy <note>2 Chronicles 26:19; the original text cites verse 1, but the narrative of the leprosy occurs later in the chapter</note>. From this, it follows that the Angel, carrying a censer in his hand and offering incense, is a Priest. Moreover, this role fits none of the Angels except the "Angel of the Covenant" <note>original Latin: *Angelo Fœderis*, a title often used by theologians to identify Christ as the divine messenger of God's promise</note>, the Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

This Angel was seen by John as standing at the Altar—not the bronze altar of burnt offerings which was located outside, but the Golden Altar of incense, which is before the Throne of God in the Holy Place, facing the Ark. In the ancient Tabernacle and Temple, a veil or curtain was positioned between the altar and the Ark. But here, the scene is shown to John somewhat differently. By the death of Christ, the veil was torn. John sees both the Golden Altar and the Throne of God at once, with the veil removed.

That Priest-Angel held a *golden censer with much incense.* By this *incense*, some understand the *satisfaction and merits of Christ*, because he is said to have *offered himself as an offering for a sweet-smelling aroma* <note>Ephesians 5:2</note>. However, we have just shown that this refers not to the *incense*, but to the <term>Mincha: a grain or meal offering that accompanied animal sacrifices</term>. Prayers correspond to the incense, as John himself explains. 

Furthermore, the incense was prepared *from various spices.* In the same way, there are many themes for devoted prayers, and many emotions are mixed within them in a pleasing harmony. The scent of these spices was most delightful; nothing is more acceptable to the Divine than holy prayers. The fact that the spices had to be crushed seems to pertain to the afflictions by which the soul, holily humbled, is rendered more ready for the exercise of prayer. This was not lacking even for Christ himself: *who in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard, was delivered from his fear* <note>Hebrews 5:7</note>, and *being in agony, he prayed more earnestly* <note>Luke 22:44</note>.

Two types of prayers seem to be mentioned here: those which belong more specifically to the Priest-Angel, and those of the saints, to which the Priest-Angel adds his own. The former are called *much incense*; in this, they are partly similar to the ancient incense offerings, which were made from many spices, and partly different. In ancient times, only a handful—about half a pound—was burned at a time. Christ's prayers, however, are both frequent and commend many great things to God the Father. It is somewhat more obscure when it says *these incenses were given to him.* Does this refer to the office of High Priest imposed on him by the Father, with the connotation of acceptance—so that the meaning is...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Christ’s priestly work in the heavenly sanctuary, specifically interpreting the imagery of the incense and the golden altar in Revelation chapter 8 by comparing it to the historical rituals of the Jewish Temple.</meta>

->### ON THE PRIESTHOOD OF AARON AND CHRIST<-

Should we believe the Father assigned this duty to Christ the Mediator so that, after he had offered himself as a sacrifice, he might also offer prayers for his people? Such prayers, proceeding from the Father’s own command, could not fail to be most pleasing to Him. Or should we refer this to the various turning points in the history of the Church, which provide the occasion for Christ’s prayers? In this view, "incense" is said to be given to him whenever the many calamities of the Church provide an opportunity for intercessory prayers. Or—which I would prefer—is this simply an allusion to the ancient custom where a certain measure was taken from the store of incense prepared for the whole year and given to the priest about to perform the offering? This was done either by the **Prefect of the Temple** <note>the official in charge of the daily operations and security of the Jerusalem Temple</note> or whoever else was tasked with that care. At the very least, these portions of incense are given—that is, as I believe, *added*—to the prayers of all the saints, both those who are already in heaven and those who are still on earth. It is from Christ’s intercession that their prayers receive all their fragrance, grace, and power. Christ takes these prayers brought to him, joins them to his own, and offers them to the Father, making them acceptable to Him. The symbol of this is the *smoke of the incense and the prayers of the saints, ascending from the hand of the Angel before God. Meanwhile, silence was made in heaven for half an hour, and the Angels prepared themselves to sound the trumpets.* This too is drawn from ancient ritual. For the people, standing back at a distance from the portico, maintained a deep silence while occupied with pouring out their prayers, until the priest had finished the sacred rites at the altar. During this time, the **Levites** <note>the assistants to the priests who also served as the Temple choir and orchestra</note> would sound their instruments. Thus, while Christ intercedes for his own, the Church, suspended in expectation of great works, waits with hope and patience for the unfolding of the Divine counsel, until God indicates what He is about to do by the sound of trumpets.

<margin>95. Christ's intercession is full of authority.</margin>
95. Christ's intercession is not a "bare" plea for us, not unlike the prayers that the faithful owe to one another. Rather, it is the glorious representation of that will of Christ by which we are made holy; it rests upon the dignity of his person and the effectiveness of his sacrifice. It is powered by the virtue of the righteousness he completed for us and the sacred covenant by which he gained the right not only to pray for some grace on our behalf, but even to *demand the nations as his inheritance; Psalm 2:8. To demand them, I say, as a due reward and the price of his labor. Isaiah 49:4.* Hence, he speaks with a certain authority that would be unseemly for anyone else besides the Son of God and the guarantor of such an excellent covenant. He says in *John 17:24: "Father, those whom you have given me,* <note>original Greek: θέλω (*thelo*)</note> **I will** *that where I am, they also may be with me."* Indeed, this intercession is of such dignity, authority, and efficacy that it can no more be transferred to another than can the atonement for sins itself, upon which it rests and with which it is joined in an inseparable partnership. *1 John 2:1-2.* For it is a **theandric** work <note>original Greek: θεανδρικόν (*theandrikon*); a theological term for an action performed by Christ as the "God-man," involving both his divine and human natures</note>, in which there concurs not only the human will of Christ, through the representation of the right he has acquired—

XCVI. Furthermore, we must observe here the correspondence of Christ's prayers with those we mentioned that the High Priest of the Hebrews poured out on the Day of Atonement <note>The most solemn day of the Jewish year, also known as Yom Kippur, involving purification for the people's sins</note>. Just as a triple prayer is attributed to that priest, so also we find that Christ, in the final part of his Priestly duty, prayed three times in a principal way. First, when he was already on the verge of offering himself (John 17). Then, in his very passions, which taken together constitute his offering; this happened several times but is condensed into one formula in Psalm 22. Finally, after he entered the "holy of holies not made with hands" <note>A reference to Heaven itself, contrasting with the physical Temple in Jerusalem</note>. There, by his intercession, he obtains that the Church—refreshed in the heat of persecutions by the dew and rain of spiritual consolations—may be *like a watered garden* (Jeremiah 31:12). He prays that his spiritual kingdom may be perpetual, *as long as the sun exists, and while the moon lasts, throughout eternal generations* (Psalm 72:5) <note>original Latin: "quamdiu erit Sol, & durante Luna, in generationem æternam"</note>; *that the soul of the priests may be saturated with fatness, and his people satisfied with his goodness* (Jeremiah 31:14). Finally, he prays that all the wishes and efforts of his enemies may be in vain (Isaiah 54:14, 17). In that prayer of Christ which John records in Chapter 17, we also find that Christ maintained a specific order: first, he prayed *for himself* (verses 1–5); then *for the Apostles*, who were his in a singular way and constituted his immediate family (verse 6 and following); and finally *for the whole people*, and all those who would believe (verse 20 and following).

<margin>

can bless
another in the
same way
that Christ
does.
</margin>
XCVII. Similarly, the Priestly BLESSING of Christ differs in its entire nature from that by which either the pious bless one another, or church leaders call down all favorable things upon the Church. For the latter consists in mere words and the sincerity of the one making the vow; it is a plea to God that He might do good to men. But Christ's blessing is accomplished by actual deeds and a real communication of spiritual goods. He does not ask for these from another, but takes from those things which are his own to impart them to us. Ezekiel 46:18: <note>original Hebrew: "מֵאַחֻזָּתוֹ יַנְחִיל אֶת בָּנָיו"</note> *he shall give an inheritance to his sons out of his own possession.* (Compare John 16:14, 15).

All the
mysteries of the
priestly
blessing are
fulfilled in the
Blessing of
Christ.
</margin>
XCVIII. Indeed, Christ is the one whom *God raised up and sent, so that* He might BLESS *us, and turn every one of us from our wickednesses* (Acts 3:26). He began the very beginnings of his Teaching with the most excellent blessings (Matthew 5) <note>The Beatitudes, such as "Blessed are the poor in spirit"</note>. And when his ministry on earth was completed, *lifting up his hands, he blessed his disciples. And it happened that while he was blessing them, he was parted from them and carried up into heaven* (Luke 24:50, 51). It is very notable that when his arrival into the world was near, a priest of the Aaronite line <note>Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist</note>, about to bless the people, suddenly and by a miracle became mute (Luke 1:21, 22).
