->### On the Priesthood of Aaron and Christ.<-

21. 22. ...this was to signify that the end of that priesthood was near, and that another priest of a more excellent order was to be expected, in whom all the nations of the earth would be blessed. And here, the observation of the *Rabbis* <note>Jewish scholars and teachers of the law</note> comes to our use: that the Aaronic Priests would indeed bless the people in the *morning*, but they never blessed them at the time of the *evening* sacrifice. This was reserved for these last times (Hebrews 1:1), when in the very evening of the world, God spoke heavenly blessings to us through his Son.

XCIX. Nor is it for nothing that *Rabbi Menachem* <note>Menachem Recanati, a 13th-century Italian rabbi and kabbalist often cited by Christian scholars</note> advised that every blessing descends from the heavenly tabernacle into the earthly one. The *Earthly Tabernacle* is a figure of the Church dwelling on earth. The *Heavenly* signifies God’s seat in the heavens. In Christ, we have such a High Priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens. *A minister of the sanctuary, and of that true Tabernacle, which the Lord set up, and not man* (Hebrews 8:1-2).

C. Nor does it seem to be without mystery that the great name of JEHOVAH was to be expressly pronounced in the priestly blessing; for in those things which Christ did out of his benevolent affection toward us, there is a clear notification of the name of God, in all the power of its meaning (John 17:6). *Then God was known by his name Jehovah to the mystic Israel* (Exodus 6:2).

CI. Highly <term>mysterious</term> <note>original Greek: "mustēriōdēs"</note> is the triple repetition of the name *Jehovah*; nor should we reject the note of *Rabbi Menachem* concerning the triple variation of accents on that same word. What could be more appropriately signified by this than the adorable <term>Trinity</term> <note>The Christian doctrine of one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note> of Divine persons in one Deity, from whom, as if from a perennial fountain, every blessing is derived upon us? Compare 2 Corinthians 13:14 and Revelation 1:4-5. The first <term>pericopa</term> <note>a short passage or selection from a text</note>, **MAY JEHOVAH BLESS YOU AND KEEP YOU**, is very fittingly referred to the **FATHER**: of whom Paul writes in Ephesians 1:3, *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ.* And to whom Christ himself says in John 17:11, *Holy FATHER, KEEP them through your name.* The second <term>pericopa</term>, **MAY JEHOVAH MAKE HIS FACE SHINE UPON YOU, AND BE GRACIOUS TO YOU**, pertains to **CHRIST**, who is the *light of the world* (John 8:12) and of the *heavenly Jerusalem* (Revelation 21:23). His face *shines like the sun* (Revelation 1:16), and in his face is the light of the knowledge of the glory of God (2 Corinthians 4:6). In him is most fully completed that <term>paroemia</term> <note>a proverb or wise saying</note> of the wisest King in Proverbs 16:15: *In the light of the King's face is life, and his favor is like a thick cloud of the late rain.* In him, finally, are the *surpassing riches of grace* (Ephesians 2:7), *which reigns through righteousness unto eternal life* (Romans 5:21). The last <term>pericopa</term>, **MAY JEHOVAH LIFT UP HIS FACE TOWARD YOU, AND GIVE YOU PEACE**, since it signifies the application of grace and the communication of peace and joy, is fittingly applied to the **HOLY SPIRIT**, *through whom the kingdom of God is to us righteousness, and peace, and joy* (Romans 14:17).

<margin>I. Three types of Sanhedrins.</margin>
I. In the Republic of the Hebrews, from all ancient history, it is said that there were three types of Judicial Assemblies: of which one deserves to be called the **Smallest**, the second the **Larger**, and the third the **Greatest**.

<margin>II. The Smallest consists of three judges.</margin>
II. The **Smallest** consisted of only **Three** judges: a number which those skilled in Hebrew law subtly draw out from the sacred scriptures in their own fashion. First, they observe that the name אלהים <note>original: *Elohim*</note>—usually meaning God—when attributed to men, is used only of judges who have been duly ordained in the land of Israel. Thus says *Maimonides* <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> in his *Treatise on the Sanhedrin, Chapter 4, Paragraph 4:*

> The name <note>original: *Elohim*</note> is not applied except to a court of law <note>original: *Beth Din*</note> that has been ordained in the Land of Israel alone.

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

The name *Elohim* <note>original: "Elohim"; in Hebrew, this name for God is also used to refer to judges, magistrates, or "mighty ones" acting with divine authority</note> was not applied except to an assembly of judges properly ordained in the land of *Israel*. Furthermore, they note that the plural form of that name also implies a plurality; and indeed, a plurality that cannot be satisfied by just two people. For they hold this as an axiom of indubitable certainty: a judicial assembly cannot consist of an even number, because in a disagreement of opinions, nothing can be concluded with equal votes. Therefore, so that a matter can be decided, at least three are required. For if one of two judges said, *He is guilty*, and the other said, *He is innocent*, a third was required to increase the weight of one opinion and tip the scales. See *Buxtorf's Talmudic Lexicon, column 2513* <note>Johannes Buxtorf was a famous 17th-century scholar of Hebrew and Jewish law</note>.

<margin>III. *And it was found in those cities which have fewer than 120 inhabitants.*</margin>
III. This kind of three-man assembly <term>Triumviral: a court or committee consisting of three men</term> took place in those cities where fewer than one hundred and twenty inhabitants—that is, heads of households—were found. And it was believed to be sufficient for settling the disputes that belonged to that local forum. However, as *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204) was a preeminent Jewish philosopher and legal scholar whose work codified much of Jewish law</note> advises, it was more praiseworthy and honorable if more people were employed as witnesses and inspectors of the case to be discussed and the future judgment; these could be increased to the number of eleven if a disagreement arose.

<margin>IV. *Established either by public Authority or by the consent of the litigants.*</margin>
IV. These three-man judges were appointed either by public *Authority* or by the private consent of the litigants. By public authority, the Great Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme legal and religious assembly of ancient Israel</term> provided judges for individual towns and villages, according to the divine precept in *Deuteronomy 16:18: You shall appoint judges and officers in all your gates, which the Lord your God gives you, throughout your tribes, who shall judge the people with righteous judgment.* But sometimes these three-man judges were also chosen for a specific occasion; partly from a *Compromise*, or a common agreement of the litigants (similar to the use of arbitrators in a contested jurisdiction), and partly from the choice of a single individual where an act of voluntary jurisdiction was to be exercised. For so it stands in the *Sanhedrin, Chapter III, Section I: Monetary cases are judged by three. Each of the parties chooses one judge for himself, and they together select a third. This is the opinion of Rabbi Meir. But the Sages decreed that the two judges should select the third.*

<margin>V. *Requirements for the Triumvirs. Add Preface, Section XXVIII.*</margin>
V. They used less strictness in appointing three-man judges than in judges of a higher order; nevertheless, they required certain things without which it was not lawful to be counted even among the Triumvirs. Let us hear *Maimonides* again in *Sanhedrin Chapter XI: In the judges of the three-man colleges, although not everything is required as strictly as in the elders of the superior assemblies, nevertheless, it is necessary that those seven qualities be present in each: namely, I. Wisdom. II. Modesty. III. Fear [of God]. IV. Hatred of profit. V. Love of Truth. VI. Being loved by fellow people <note>original Hebrew: "אהבת הבריות להם" (Ahavat habriyot lahem); literally, "the love of the creatures for them," meaning they should be well-liked and respected by the community</note>. VII. That they have a good reputation.*

# ON THE SANHEDRINS OF THE HEBREWS.

...they are excluded. This is stated in the *Sanhedrin*, Chapter III, Paragraph III: "These are disqualified: I. <note>original: "המשחק בקוביא"; literally "one who plays with cubes"</note> **The Gambler**. II. **Usurers** <note>Those who lend money at interest.</note>. III. **Those who teach pigeons to fly**. IV. **Traders of the fruits of the seventh year**." The reasons for this rule are as follows. **The Gambler** does not acquire his goods in a lawful manner, because he does not work for the public good—an obligation that rests upon all mortals—and he conducts his affairs by luck; however, luck does not confer legitimate ownership. For when the transfer of ownership occurs not by full consent, but while the owner is grieving the loss, it is considered a form of robbery. As for **Usurers**, the Hebrew legal experts decree that they deny the God of Israel as if by a signed contract. **Those who train pigeons for flight competitions** were presumed to be raising decoy birds to lure away others' pigeons, thereby causing injury to their neighbors. Finally, the **fruits of the seventh year** <note>The Sabbatical year (Shmita) in which the land of Israel was to lie fallow; its produce was intended for communal use, not for commercial profit.</note> were granted for use, not for gain.

<margin>VII. Provided, however, that those who truly repented were admitted.</margin>
VII. Nevertheless, all these people could eventually be admitted if they abandoned their ways, provided they proved their repentance with suitable evidence. They say the repentance of gamblers is proven when they break their dice and will not play even for no stakes. The repentance of usurers is proven when, by drawing up formal documents, they begin to shun their former habit so thoroughly that they do not even lend their money for interest to foreigners. *Coccejus* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> discusses this matter learnedly in his notes on this passage.

<margin>VIII. Cases to be decided by the Triumviri <term>Triumviri: a local court or committee consisting of three men</term>.</margin>
VIII. The matters that belong to the court of the Triumviri are generally <note>original: "דיני ממונות"; *Judicia pecuniaria*</note> **monetary judgments**; likewise disputes concerning injury, damage, or "half-damage." This refers to whether full damage must be repaid—as when a man or an ox known to be dangerous causes harm—or only half of the damage given, as when a previously tame ox causes harm. They also handle cases regarding double, quadruple, or quintuple restitution. They rule on violence and seduction—that is, regarding the sexual assault or fraudulent seduction of an unbetrothed woman. They judge cases of defamation, the intercalation <note>The practice of adding an extra month or days to the lunar calendar to align it with the solar year.</note> of the month and the year, and many more matters of that kind. Finally, they add that the Triumviri also had the right to decree the punishment of flogging. The remaining details are too minor to pursue with a more extensive commentary.

<margin>IX. The Sanhedrin of 23 men, established with remarkable subtlety.</margin>
IX. We come now to the **Greater** Judicial College, consisting of TWENTY-THREE men. They arrive at this number with great subtlety by twisting various passages of the Sacred Scriptures in the following way. In *Numbers 35:24–25*, it is said, "Then the <note>original: "עדה"; *coetus*</note> **congregation** shall judge... and the congregation shall rescue." Behold, they say, two "congregations": one judging and the other rescuing; that is, twenty men in total. This is because a "congregation" (or *edah*) consists of ten men. From where is this proven? From *Numbers 14:27*: "How long shall I bear with this evil **congregation** of those who murmur against me?" If you remove Joshua and Caleb from them—since they were not involved in the wicked murmuring—ten remain. But what is the reason for adding three more? From that...

BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

This is understood from Exodus 23:2: *Do not follow the majority to do evil.* <note>original Latin: "Ne sequaris plures ad mala."</note> From this it is inferred that the majority must absolutely be followed in doing good. It is further added: *yielding after the majority.* <note>original Latin: "post plures inclinando."</note> For a person should not be inclined toward evil in the same way they are toward good. One may pronounce a judgment in favor of "good" <note>In this context, "good" refers to an acquittal or a merciful ruling.</note> based on the opinion of a single judge; however, one may not pronounce a judgment for "evil" <note>That is, a conviction or harsh penalty.</note> unless the votes of two judges outweigh the rest. Since a court of judges must not consist of an even number, one more must be added to these. Thus, you have the twenty-three members. These details are found in the *Sanhedrin, Chapter I, Section VI.* Yet, what are these but the empty subtleties of men's wit and leisure, or—what is most shameful of all—the abuse of God's own word for something of no use?

<margin>X. A summary of those things which pertain here.</margin>
X. They maintained a council of twenty-three men in all the larger towns where there were more than 120 heads of families. However, Rabbi *Nehemias* <note>A 2nd-century Jewish scholar (Tanna) known for his work on the Mishnah.</note> asserts there must be 130, so that the number corresponds to the "commanders of tens" <note>referring to the administrative breakdown suggested by Jethro to Moses.</note>. In *Jerusalem*, however, there were two Sanhedrins of this kind: one had its seat at the Temple Mount, and the other at the Temple Court. Distinguished men from the smaller cities were called to the first; from there, they were transferred to the second, serving as a sort of <term>storehouse</term> <note>original Latin: "promtuarium"; a reserve of qualified officials.</note> from which the most expert judges were provided for the **Great Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme religious and legal body of ancient Israel, consisting of 71 judges.</note>. We shall teach this more extensively in its proper place. No one was admitted into this order except the most excellent of the Israelites, those endowed with the gifts that *Jethro* recommended to Moses; we will have to speak of these more at length when we describe the members of the Great Sanhedrin. In the council of twenty-three, **every kind of case** was discussed, with a few exceptions that were reserved for the Great Sanhedrin.

<margin>XI. The manner of sitting.</margin>
XI. The manner of sitting was as follows. It represented the shape of a half-circle, the middle seat of which was occupied by the President <note>The "Nasi" or Prince of the court.</note>. To his right sat the Vice-President <note>The "Av Beit Din," literally "Father of the House of Judgment."</note>. To his left, as some believe, sat a Sage <note>The "Chacham."</note> distinguished above the rest. Then, the remaining colleagues sat on either side. At both ends of the semicircle, a Scribe was stationed. Below them sat three rows of those called the "disciples of the Sages," such that each row contained twenty-three disciples—the same number as the judges. In each row, they sat according to their rank in knowledge. If a disagreement arose among the judges such that it became necessary to ordain one of the disciples to increase the number <note>to break a tie or reach a required majority</note>, they would ordain the one who excelled in the first row. Then, the first person in the second row would rise and take the lowest seat of the first row to fill the vacancy. Similarly, the first of the third row would take the lowest seat of the second. Finally, they would select one person from the common people and place him in the lowest seat of the third row. Thus, through actual practice, the disciples learned the law and were made fit to be substituted into the places of those who died or became too old to serve.

# On the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews.

<margin>XII. Josephus is at odds with the Talmudic scholars regarding the number of judges.</margin>
XII. *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> discusses these matters with great learning, as is his custom, based on the decrees of the Talmudic scholars. However, these details are vastly different from those which *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD) was a first-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> included in his history. For in his *Antiquities, Book IV, Chapter VIII*, he introduces *Moses* speaking with these words: "In every city, let seven men rule, who have practiced both virtue and a zeal for justice. To each authority, let two ministers from the tribe of the Levites be given." <note>original Greek: ’αρχέσθωσαν δὲ καθ’ ἑκάστην πόλιν ἄνδρες ἑπτὰ, οἱ καὶ τὴν ἀρετὴν καὶ τὴν περὶ τὸ δίκαιον σπουδὴν προσησκηκότες. ἑκάστῃ δὲ ἀρχῇ δύο ἄνδρες ὑπηρέται διδόσθωσαν ἐκ τῆς τῶν Λευϊτῶν Φυλῆς.</note> *Sigismund Gelenius* <note>A 16th-century scholar known for his Latin translations of Greek classics.</note> translates this as: *Let seven men of proven virtue and practitioners of justice preside over each town. To each magistrate, let two ministers from the tribe of the Levites be assigned.* This poses a profound puzzle <note>original Latin: "crucem... figunt," literally "fixes a cross," a metaphor for a difficult problem.</note> for the learned. Indeed, what should be said? Could *Josephus* have been ignorant of such obvious matters, not only of his own people but of his own era? Could he have been mistaken, or did he intend to deceive, concerning the number of judges in the individual cities of his nation? Or is it believable that the Talmudists, regarding a matter so clear and uncontested as long as their republic stood, would so consistently peddle nothing but their own dreams, with no profit in lying?

<margin>XIII. Grotius’s reconciliation.</margin>
XIII. The illustrious *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch legal theorist who often sought to harmonize conflicting historical sources.</note> believes he has found a method of reconciliation; it will not be out of place to present his own words. Thus he writes *on Matthew 5:21: Since all the Hebrews say the assembly of these judges consisted of twenty-three, it seems strange to many that Josephus, to whom nothing of his ancestral customs was hidden, seems to establish only seven. But Josephus himself seems to me to untie this knot when he says in the following words: "To each magistrate, let two ministers from the tribe of the Levites be assigned." For by "authority" <note>Greek: ἀρχὴν (archēn)</note> he understands the individual office-holders, to each of whom were added two assessors skilled in the law, whom Josephus calls assistants <note>Greek: ὑπηρέτας (hyperetas)</note>, which in Hebrew is "Shotrim" <note>Hebrew: שוטרים (officers or officials)</note>. Therefore, seven citizens of the place were the judges; additionally, there were fourteen assessors, who were mostly chosen from the Levites. One or two others seem to have been added as supernumeraries.* Thus far *Grotius*.

<margin>XIV. Not a solid argument.</margin>
XIV. But, if we wish to speak the truth, the knot remains untied. First, it is quite debatable whether *Josephus* means by "authority" the individual office-holders, or rather the office of the magistrate itself, or the seven-man council as a whole. For it is not clear from any other source that two ministers were granted to each individual; however, it is a very certain matter that there were two ministers—scribes—for the councils. Secondly, it is difficult to count ministers among the judges. For the "Shotrim" <note>officers</note> or "assistants" <note>Greek: hyperetai</note> were never among the number of judges. Nor was there any difference in dignity among the colleagues regarding judicial power. Finally, even if all these points were granted (which, however, seem hardly grantable), the difficulty still remains. For by *Grotius’s* calculation, only twenty-one are produced. BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

...whether one or another detail is added, they are said without merit. Why so? It is not only here, but frequently that the Talmudists <note>The rabbis and scholars whose discussions are recorded in the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> agree poorly with *Josephus*: especially in this matter of the Sanhedrins. As to whose authority carries more weight, now is not the time to decide. Let it suffice to have observed that those who do not wish to bow to every little story of the Talmudists regarding their judges should not be condemned for ignorant stubbornness.

<margin>XV. There was no appeal from the minor councils to the major ones.</margin>
XV. We hasten toward the consideration of the GREAT SANHEDRIN: for the sake of which everything so far has been said, as it were, in advance. But this must first be observed with diligence: the minor councils were not so subordinate to the major ones that an appeal <note>original: *provocatio*; the legal process of moving a case to a higher court for a new decision.</note> was granted from the former to the latter. It is believed that specific cases were entrusted to each; on the condition that whatever they judged would be ratified. The judgments of the Courts of Three <note>original: *Triumvirum*</note> concerned monetary matters and things that did not touch upon life; and the Courts of Twenty-Three <note>original: *Vigintitrium virum*</note> decided on capital matters and those involving life. For the rest, they are said to have been coordinated, not subordinated: so that any legal breach might be closed immediately, rather than gaping further or longer through an appeal. Indeed, the Great Sanhedrin was not established for appeals: since it was not the litigating parties, but the judges themselves who referred there what seemed difficult to them. And here too was a brief decision of the controversy, which it was a sin to speak against. These things will be shown from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> shortly hereafter.

<margin>XVI. Selden and Leusden praised.</margin>
XVI. Now let us deal with this Sanhedrin itself with as much diligence as we can. I do not have much new material with which to illustrate this notable part of Jewish Antiquity: but I will collect those things which have been noted here and there by others, and present them in a condensed form, arranged in an orderly fashion, for my young students. The man of stupendous erudition, JOHN SELDEN, surpassed the diligence of all others in this matter with his thick work *On the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews* <note>original: *De Synedriis Hebræorum*</note>: but because it seems written only for the most learned men, it is by no means suited to the grasp and use of studious youth. For, if I may say so with all due respect to that Great Man, that work is so stuffed with citations, so distended with excursions—learned ones, indeed, who would deny it?—but often long-winded, and sometimes having little to do with the matter he is treating, even intricate and obscure. It is finally written in such a character and style that it demands a mind subdued to attention and patience by long practice, and a stomach capable of swallowing much boredom. Our people love clarity combined with brevity, the praise for which is indeed owed to the most famous man JOHANNES LEUSDEN, once my most helpful teacher in Philological <note>The study of language in historical literary sources.</note> matters. He published a Dissertation on the Sanhedrins in his *Mixed Philologist* <note>original: *Philologo suo Mixto*</note>; which I cannot help but recommend to the reader on this occasion. Nevertheless, it has not deterred me from...

### ON THE SANHEDRINS OF THE HEBREWS.

...I would not be commenting on these things anew. For there is a well-worn Hebrew proverb: *he who forbids a disciple to speak his opinion after his Master has spoken acts just as if he were barring a son of the family from seeing his father’s inheritance.* Nor will it be troublesome to that most refined man <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary scholar like Selden or Grotius with whom the author occasionally disagrees.</note> if I should pursue certain matters more extensively in a somewhat freer discourse, and even disagree in a few small points. “The doors of the Muses are open to all.” <note>original Greek: Ἄφθονοι αἱ Μουσῶν θύραι. A classical Greek idiom meaning that knowledge and inspiration are not restricted to one person.</note>

<margin>XVII. The order of things to be discussed.</margin>
XVII. I shall proceed in this order: first, I will set forth what the Hebrew Masters, and the most learned of the Christians among them, have handed down concerning the Great Sanhedrin; then, I will candidly bring forth my own *opinion* as to what I judge to be consistent or inconsistent with the truth in this entire history.

<margin>XVIII. The name Mechokek.</margin>
XVIII. Let us begin with the names by which either the entire Senate or the individual Senators are believed to have been designated. In the first place, the name *Mechokekim* <note>original Hebrew: מחוקקים; translated as "lawgivers" or "decree-makers."</note> occurs, first used in the prophecies of Jacob where he sings the fates of his sons. *Genesis 49:10*: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah,* **and a Lawgiver** <note>original: מחוקק (Mechokek)</note> **from between his feet.** For that word, Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> has *Scribe*. The Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> says: *Teachers of the Law.* Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel.</note> says: *Scribes teaching the law.* The etymology is as follows: *Mechokek* is derived from *Chakak*, a word which signifies *to write* or *to engrave* (either with a chisel or a pen), and also *to decree* or *to establish*, because statutes and decrees are usually written down. Thus *Isaiah 10:1*: *Decreeing statutes of vanity.* *Proverbs 8:15*: *Princes decree justice.* Therefore, *Mechokek* can mean: I. A *Scribe*, who is occupied with writing, whether in preparing it or explaining it. II. A *Lawgiver*, who issues statutes and decrees. The first seems more ecclesiastical, the second more political. But since both powers were joined in Moses and in the elders established by Moses, the *Mechokekim* are conveniently understood to be the Elders and Leaders of the people of Israel who, sitting in the chair of Moses, interpreted the law and compelled the people to observe it. Thus Moses himself is called *Mechokek* in *Numbers 21:18*, as are the Leaders of the people, the *Lawgivers of Israel* in *Judges 5:9*. David also says: *Judah is my lawgiver* (Psalm 60:10), because since the King himself was from the tribe of Judah, many men—and the most skilled ones at that—were admitted into the senate from that same tribe.

<margin>XIX. Of the Elders.</margin>
XIX. At other times they are called the ELDERS OF ISRAEL. <note>original Hebrew: זקני ישראל (Ziknei Yisrael)</note> *Exodus 4:29, 15:3, Deuteronomy 31:9.* It is clear that the name itself denotes age, yet with a connotation of authority and power. We have the most ancient example of this in *Genesis 24:2*: *Abraham said to his servant, the Elder <note>original: Presbyterum, seu seniorem</note> of his house, who was in charge of all that he had.* The Jerusalem Targum explains...

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

...explains <note>original Aramaic: עבד יהוה שלוטא (*ebed Yahweh shalota*)</note> as "His principal servant, or one who rules." Not only among the Hebrews, but also among most other Eastern peoples, the title of "elder" was a title of authority. Thus we read of Pharaoh’s servants, the "elders of his house," and all the "elders of the land of Egypt" (Genesis 50:7). And of the "elders of Midian" and of the "Moabites" (Numbers 22:4, 7). Many other points relevant to this have been gathered by <term>Selden</term> <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> in *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 1, Chapter 14.

<margin>
XX. Those who are said to have been ordained by the laying on of hands.
</margin>
XX. It is especially noteworthy that after the Law was given, certain individuals were admitted into the order of elders through a unique procedure and ceremony. Specifically, to those venerable for their age and wisdom, the power or license to judge any cases of Hebrew law was granted through the "laying on of hands," which they call <term>Semicha</term> <note>original Hebrew: סמיכה; the formal process of rabbinic ordination.</note>. This was not done so that a person would immediately exercise judicial power by this creation alone, but rather to declare him capable of holding judicial offices. From this order of elders—and in no other proper way—one could then be admitted into the order of Judges, whether of the Great Sanhedrin or a Lesser Sanhedrin. <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal codifier.</note> is explicit on this matter in *On the Sanhedrin*, Chapter 4. The same rule applies to any Lesser Sanhedrin and the Court of Three: namely, that anyone admitted to them must be created through the laying on of hands by another who was previously created in the same way. "Moses our Teacher thus created Joshua, according to what is written in Numbers 27:23: *And he laid his hands upon him, and commissioned him.*" Therefore, this is the <term>Semichat Ha-Zekenim</term> <note>original Hebrew: סמיכת הזקנים</note>, or the "laying on of hands of the elders," by which one is made an elder. Because of this, scholars believe Paul was referring to this in 1 Timothy 4:14, when he attributes to Timothy the "laying on of hands of the <term>Presbytery</term>" <note>original Greek: ἐπίθεσιν τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ Πρεσβυτερίου (*epitheton ton cheiron tou Presbyteriou*); in this context, the council of elders.</note>. Whatever the case, we see "the Sanhedrin and the whole council of the children of Israel" <note>original Greek: τὸ Συνέδριον καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ (*to Synedrion kai pasan ten gerousian ton huion Israel*)</note> joined together in Acts 5:21 <note>The OCR citation "Act. iv. 21" appears to be a typo for Acts 5:21.</note>. And the whole assembly of judges is called the "Presbytery" (Acts 22:5) and the "Council of Elders of the people" <note>original Greek: Πρεσβυτέριον τοῦ λαוῦ (*Presbyterion tou laou*)</note> (Luke 22:66). In short, if this observation holds, while not all who were made elders by the laying on of hands were Senators, all Senators had to be first admitted into the order of elders.

<margin>
XXI. *Shophetim*, or Judges.
</margin>
XXI. The term <term>Shophetim</term> <note>original Hebrew: שופטים; Judges.</note> is quite proper; the sacred scriptures speak of them sometimes in the plural, and sometimes specifically as if of one individual. Thus Moses decrees in Deuteronomy 19:17: *Then the two men between whom the controversy is shall stand before the Lord, before the Priests and the Judges who shall be in those days.* And in 2 Chronicles 19:5, it is related that <term>Jehoshaphat</term> <note>A King of Judah known for his judicial reforms.</note> appointed judges in the land throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city. Commentators explain this as referring to the Council of Twenty-Three (verse 8). And also in Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat appointed some of the Levites and Priest...

-># BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.<-

It was not only among the Hebrews, but also among most other Eastern peoples, that the name "elder" was a title of authority. Thus we read of Pharaoh's servants as the **elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt** (Genesis 50:6). We also read of the **elders of Midian and of the Moabites** (Numbers 22:4, 6). <term>John Selden</term> <note>A famous 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> has gathered many other examples relevant to this point in his work *On the Sanhedrin, Book 1, Chapter 14*.

<margin>XX. Those who are said to be ordained through the laying on of hands.</margin>
XX. It is especially important to observe that, after the Law was given, certain individuals were admitted into the order of elders through a unique method and ceremony. Specifically, to those who were venerable in age and wisdom, the **Power** or **License** to hear any case of Hebrew law was granted through the laying on of hands, which they call **Semicha** <note>original: סמיכה</note>. This was not done so that a person would immediately exercise judicial power by virtue of this creation alone, but rather to declare them eligible for judicial appointments. Only from this order of elders could someone be properly chosen—and not otherwise—to join the ranks of the Judges, whether in the Great or the Lesser <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme and local legal councils of ancient Israel.</note>. <term>Maimonides</term> <note>The preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and legal codifier.</note> is explicit on this matter in *Sanhedrin, Chapter 4*: "The same right applies to **any Lesser Sanhedrin and the Court of Three**, namely, that everyone admitted to them must be created through the laying on of hands by another who was previously created in the same way. **Moses our Teacher** created **Joshua**, according to what is written in Numbers 27:23: *And he laid his hands upon him, and gave him a charge.*" This is, therefore, the **laying on of hands of the elders** <note>original: סמיכת הזקנים (*semikhat ha-zekenim*)</note> by which an elder is created. For this reason, scholars believe Paul was referring to this in 1 Timothy 4:14 when he attributes to Timothy the **laying on of hands of the Council of Elders** <note>original Greek: ἐπίθεσιν τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ Πρεσβυτερίου (*epithesein ton cheiron tou Presbyteriou*)</note>. Whatever the case may be, we see that **the Sanhedrin and the whole senate of the sons of Israel** (Acts 4:21) <note>original Greek: τὸ Συνέδριον καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ</note> are joined together. The entire assembly of judges is called the **Council of Elders** <note>Presbytery</note> in Acts 22:5, and the **Council of Elders of the people** in Luke 22:66. In short, if this observation holds true: while not all who were created elders by the laying on of hands were Senators, all Senators had to be first admitted into the order of elders.

The Sacred Scriptures sometimes speak of them in the plural, and sometimes specifically as if referring to one individual. Let us hear <term>Maimonides</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist whose codification of Jewish law is cited here.</note> in his *Treatise on Rebels*, Chapter I, Section IV: *If any doubt arises for someone in Israel, he consults the Sanhedrin that is in his own city. If that body is able to release him from the difficulty, it is well; if not, the one who asks, together with the Sanhedrin or its delegates, goes up to Jerusalem, and they ask the Sanhedrin that is at the Temple Mount. If this body settles the matter, it is well; if not, they all come to the Sanhedrin that is at the Temple Court; which, if it can, unravels the difficulty. If it cannot, the Great Sanhedrin was to be consulted by all together; and everyone had to abide by its determination.*

<margin>
XXIV. Whose final sentence is held as ratified.
</margin>
XXIV. Regarding what God says: *the Judge who will be in those days*, they explain it in this way. If the **Great Sanhedrin** has determined any cause by its judgment, according to the religious conviction of its mind; and other Judges in the same Sanhedrin, as time passes, should decide the same cause differently because of reasons that seem more probable to them, and should retract the former sentence, the retracted one is considered void. Each individual sentence holds its own force at the time it was issued. And if we follow this interpretation, whatever <term>Grotius</term> <note>Hugo Grotius, the Dutch jurist mentioned on the previous page.</note> comments regarding an extraordinary **Suffete** <note>A term for an ancient supreme magistrate, derived from the Hebrew word for "Judge."</note>, however learnedly, is beside the point.

<margin>
XXV. The "Sufes" of the Carthaginians seems more likely to be from *Tsopheh* <note>צופה</note> than from *Shofet* <note>שופט</note>.
</margin>
XXV. Nor is it entirely certain whether the **Suffetes** of the Tyrians and Carthaginians were so named by the Hebrews as *Shophetim* <note>original: "Sophetim"; Hebrew: שופטים, meaning "Judges".</note>. The conjecture of <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a French religious scholar and leader in historical chronology.</note>, <term>Drusius</term> <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant divine and Hebrew scholar.</note>, and <term>Selden</term> <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and polymath known for his studies of ancient Jewish law.</note> is not improbable: that the etymology of that word is from the Hebrew *Tsopheh* <note>צופה</note>, which means a **watcher**, an **overseer**, an **inspector**, or a **bishop** <note>The author uses several Latin terms for "overseer": *speculator, Ephorus, Epoptes, Episcopus*.</note>. For the highest magistrate of the Carthaginians was called *Sufes* in the singular number. <term>Festus</term> <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> says: *Sufes was the name of the Punic magistrate.* And <term>Paulus</term> says in the same place: *Sufex, a consul; in the Punic tongue.* <term>Seneca</term> also in *On Tranquility of Mind*, Chapter III: *You do not wish to administer the republic unless as a Consul, or a Prytane, or a Ceryx, or a Sufes.* The same is proved by the bronze inscriptions of the Africans, which Selden presents. Now, *Sufes* is not so conveniently derived from *Shofet* <note>שופט</note> (for it is unusual for the letter 't' <note>Hebrew letter Tet (ט)</note> to be changed into an 's') as it is from *Tsopheh* <note>צופה</note>; for nothing is more common than for an 's' to be joined to the end of words ending in 'e'. Drusius, in his confident way, says: *Sufe*, he says, becomes *Sufes*, just as *Mamre* becomes *Mamres*; *Hause*, *Hauses*; *Jamre*, *Jamres*. For the Greeks add a <term>sigma</term> <note>The Greek letter 's' (σ).</note> to names ending in *a, e,* or *u*. Nothing is more certain. Such great confidence does not quite please me. I would rather say: these things are not improbable. However, some difficulty exists in the plural number. For from *Tsopheh* <note>צופה</note> comes *Tsophim* <note>צופים</note>, from which *Sufetes* differs greatly. Yet Selden seems to resolve that difficulty, observing that the plural termination is from the character of the Latin rather than the Punic language; for the Latins, just as they made *Magnetes* from *magnes*, so from *Sufes* they made *Sufetes*. But these things are mentioned in passing.

# Of the Councils of the Hebrews.

<margin>XXVI. Ridiculous Etymology.</margin>
XXVI. Recent names for this assembly are **The Great House of Judgment** <note>original: "Beit Din ha-Gadol"</note> and **Sanhedrin**. Some Masters of the Hebrews derive foolish etymologies for this latter word from their own language. There are those who absurdly claim it is composed of *San* and *Haderin*. They say *San* denotes the Law given at Sinai, as if *San* were derived from *Sinai*. *Haderin*, meanwhile, they say refers to those who "repeat," because they repeated the law by interpreting it, explaining it beautifully, and applying it. Others joke that senators are called *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Sanhedrin"</note> because they "hate favoritism" <note>original: "sonei panim be-din"</note> in judgment. Others, finally, claim the name means they are "haters of gifts" <note>original: "sonei doronot"</note>. This is all nonsense. It is clear that the word is Greek <note>The word "Sanhedrin" is a Hebraized version of the Greek "sunedrion," meaning a sitting together or council.</note>, which they adopted after the Macedonian reign, like many other words, slightly bending it to the nature of their own language.

<margin>XXVII. Council</margin>
XXVII. Among the Greeks, the word *Council* <note>original Greek: "Sunedrion"</note> signifies either the assembly of Judges itself (as in Matthew 26:59 and Acts 5:21), or the place of the assembly, such as a Senate-house. Thus Herodian writes concerning Pertinax in Book II, Chapter III: *When day arrived, he went down to the council of the senate.* <note>original Greek: "hēmēras en katalabousēs, katēlthen epi to sunedrion tēs boulēs."</note> Again, in Book VII, Chapter 10: *They gathered, then, not indeed in the Senate-house where they were previously accustomed, but in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter.* <note>original Greek: "sunēlthon en ouk eis to sunēthes sunedrion, all' eis ton tou Dios neōn kapetoliō."</note>

<margin>XXVIII. The Great Synagogue is not the Sanhedrin.</margin>
XXVIII. The most learned <term>Schickard</term> <note>Wilhelm Schickard (1592–1635) was a German polymath and professor of Hebrew who wrote extensively on biblical law.</note>, in *On the Royal Law of the Hebrews*, Book I, Theorem II, thinks the Sanhedrists were also called the **Men of the Great Synagogue** <note>original: "Anshei Knesset HaGedolah"</note>. He believes Ezra was among them, along with Daniel, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, and other illustrious men of those times. However, that gathering was very different from the Sanhedrin. For it is said to have consisted of 120 men, not 71. Nor was it a permanent body; rather, it ended with Simeon the Just, who went out to meet Alexander the Great. This is calculated to have happened in the 40th year after the building of the Second Temple. Finally, it was intended for one specific task: namely, the restoration of the Scriptures and the Church after the return from Babylon. It did not attend to ordinary trials, nor did it preside over the government of the people. See <term>Buxtorf</term> <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629) was a celebrated Christian Hebraist whose works were standard texts for studying Rabbinic literature.</note> in *Tiberias*, Part I, Chapter 10.

<margin>XXIX. But rather a fabrication of the traditionalists.</margin>

<header>BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.</header>

*...among the Jews there flourished practices of an unknown author, attributed to the Men of the Great Synagogue <note>The Great Synagogue, or "Anshei Knesset HaGedolah," is traditionally held to be a council of 120 prophets and sages established by Ezra in the 5th century BCE.</note>, which nevertheless in reality have nothing but a human origin, and hold a primary place among the traditions of the Pharisees, referred to under the false title of being divinely inspired <note>original Greek: "theopneustōs"</note>. For the Great Synagogue lived neither at one time nor in one place, and for that reason it was not a "Synagogue" in the true sense, but is a fiction of the Traditionalists, who could otherwise find no connection of tradition <note>original Greek: "paradōseōs," referring to the unbroken chain of oral law transmission</note>. Thus the mass of Jewish history rests on a slippery foundation, even regarding those parts of it upon which many and very great other things are usually built, as if upon the most explored truth.*

<margin>XXX. The main heads of things to be said regarding the Sanhedrin.</margin>

XXX. Furthermore, let us progress from the names to the consideration of the MATTER itself: and let us refer those things which are especially memorable to certain heads. Therefore, these following points especially deserve our attention. I. THE FIRST INSTITUTION OF THE GREAT SANHEDRIN. II. THE PERSONS TO BE CHOSEN INTO IT. III. THE ELECTION <note>original: "cooptatio"</note> ITSELF. IV. THE AUTHORITY OF THIS SENATE. V. THE PLACE OF ASSEMBLY. VI. THE TIME. VII. THE CONTINUATION and SUCCESSION OF THE SANHEDRIN.

<margin>XXXI. The Institution of the Sanhedrin.</margin>

XXXI. THE INSTITUTION OF THE GREAT SANHEDRIN, according to Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a highly influential Dutch jurist and theologian often cited in legal history.</note> and many other very learned men, both among the Hebrews and the Christians, is understood in this manner. Just as twelve tribes and twelve tribal leaders <note>original: "phylarchæ"</note>, or prefects of the tribes, were established in memory of the twelve sons of Israel; so, in memory of those heads of households whom Jacob led into Egypt, seventy or seventy-two leaders were set over the people to care for their affairs, as far as the royal commands of Egypt permitted. These, because of the age from which they were selected, were called *elders*, from which comes the Greek term for a council of elders <note>original Greek: "gerousia"</note>, and the Roman term *Senate*. Among these elders, before all others, Moses is ordered to explain the commands which he had received from God (Exodus 3:19), which he indeed did in Exodus 4:29. From their number also seem to have been those from whom the Egyptian taskmasters <note>original Greek: "ergodiōktai," literally "work-drivers"</note> demanded an account of the daily labor (Exodus 5:14). Afterward, by Jethro’s advice, judges were established in the desert to judge minor cases, while the investigation of greater matters was reserved for Moses (Exodus 18:21, 26). Nevertheless, those ancient seventy remained, who represented the entire Israelite people in the solemn confirmation of the covenant, and whom God himself honored with a sight of his glorious majesty and admitted to his table (Exodus 24). However, they were endowed with very diminished or absolutely no power of judging: the proof of which is that Moses, when ordered to approach the mountain peak to enjoy closer communication with the divinity, declared to the Elders: *wait for us sitting here, until we return to you. Behold, Aaron and Hur are with you; whoever has something to say, let him go to them.* Where Moses clearly, in place of his absence <meta>catchword: his own</meta>

in his own time, he delegates his judicial roles not to those <term>Seventy</term>, but to Aaron and Hur.

XXXII. A little while later, when Moses complained that he alone could not bear the burden of the supreme judgments and petitions, God spoke to him thus: *Numbers 11:16. Gather for me <term>Seventy</term> men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and its officials, and bring them to the tent of meeting that they may stand there with you.* From this it appears they already had care over the people's affairs; but now God, equipping them with a new Spirit—specifically a judicial one—commands them to bear part of the burden which Moses alone had sustained until now: that is, as we have said, the burden of supreme judgments and petitions. And this is believed to be the first, solemn, and indeed Divine institution of the <term>Great Sanhedrin</term> <note>The Great Sanhedrin was the supreme legal council of ancient Israel, acting as both a high court and a legislative body.</note>.

<margin>XXXIII. Which is believed to have happened at almost the same time as the institution of the Areopagus among the Athenians.</margin>
XXXIII. Very learned men have judged it not at all unworthy of note that at the same time the <term>Seventy</term> judges of the Hebrews were established in the desert, the Areopagite judges were instituted among the Greeks at almost the same time to decide on the greatest cases, both criminal and civil. For Moses led the people of God out of Egypt during the reign of Cecrops <note>A mythical king of Athens, often used by early modern historians as a chronological marker to sync Biblical and Greek history.</note>, King of the Athenians, as most chronologists agree. Furthermore, under the same Cecrops—as Eusebius reports in his *Chronicles*—*it was called the Areopagus, and a court was established there* <note>original Greek: "ἄρειος πάγος ἐκλήθη, καὶ δικαστήριον καλέσθη"</note>. Indeed, so great was the authority and splendor of that Areopagite court that Isocrates, in his *Areopagiticus*, asserts it *rightly excelled all the councils of all Greece* <note>original Greek: "πασῶν εἰκότως διενεγκεῖν τῶν ἐν τοῖς Ἕλλησι Συνεδρίων"</note>.

<margin>XXXIV. Three things to be observed regarding the Sanhedrins.</margin>
XXXIV. Regarding the PERSONS constituting the <term>Sanhedrin of the Hebrews</term>, these three things must be weighed: I. NUMBER. II. TRIBE. III. REQUIRED QUALITIES.

<margin>XXXV. The Number of 70 with their leader.</margin>
XXXV. Concerning the NUMBER, Caesar Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Catholic cardinal and ecclesiastical historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> discusses it thus under *the Year 31, section 10: There was indeed among the Jews a college composed of Elders and Magistrates, which was called by them the Sanhedrin, and it consisted of <term>Seventy-one</term> men. You have the origin of this, instituted by God through Moses, in the Book of Numbers, Chapter 11, when God commanded Moses to choose <term>Seventy</term> men whom he knew to be the Elders and Masters of the people. This college of Elders, with two others joined who played the parts of Eldad and Medad (who, although they had remained in the camp, had nevertheless prophesied, being inspired by the same spirit), the number <term>Seventy-two</term> always persisted among their descendants.* Many among the Catholics, and even Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar who specialized in Semitic studies and the Old Testament.</note> and Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian famous for laying the foundations of international law.</note> among the Protestants, uphold this same opinion.

BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.
<meta>catchword: XXXVII.</meta>

Indeed, there is a constant tradition that every <term>Great Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme legal and religious council of the Jewish people, serving as both a high court and a legislative body.</note> consisted of seventy men, over whom a Prince <note>Original: *Princeps*, likely referring to the *Nasi*, the presiding head of the Sanhedrin.</note> was to be placed; just as Moses was placed over the first seventy, he completed the number at seventy-one. And *Selden*, in his work *On the Sanhedrins, Book II, Chapter IV* <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of Hebraic law whose works were standard references in the 17th century.</note>, confirms this opinion as more truthful with many arguments.

---

<margin>XXXVI. The Tribes: although none had an exclusive right, the Priests nevertheless predominated.</margin>

### XXXVI.

Men were chosen for the <term>Senate</term> <note>The author uses the Latin term *Senatus* to describe the Sanhedrin, drawing a parallel to the Roman governing body.</note> from any of the <term>tribes</term> of Israel without discrimination, provided they were found suitable for such great dignity. Indeed, we have just observed that those first seventy represented the whole of Israel. <margin>Deuteronomy 17:8.</margin> However, it can be gathered that the Priests played the most prominent roles here—not by a right of birth or the pre-established dignity of the priestly function, but because they were considered more fit than the others. It is believable that at the beginning of the Republic <note>Meaning the Hebrew Commonwealth or state.</note>, most people from the other tribes voluntarily withdrew from that burdensome dignity, which was inconvenient for them but far more suitable for the Priests and Levites.

Specifically, once the Israelites had entered the possession of Canaan and each had received his own fields to cultivate, they were so occupied by farming that they did not care to be free for public judgments at the neglect and detriment of their household affairs. But no portion of land was given to the entire tribe of Levi to cultivate; thus, they could not use this excuse. Therefore, those who had leisure from agriculture could more conveniently be free for public service. This is the first reason.

To this, a second is added: that leisure gave the Levites the opportunity to meditate on the law of God and to exercise themselves in its study, especially since they were established as the Teachers of the people by Divine ordinance. <margin>Deuteronomy 33:10.</margin> Hence, a necessity was imposed upon them to acquire a ready expertise in Divine laws and judgments.

But a third cause is also not lacking. We shall show a little later that this assembly was restricted to the place where the Tabernacle of God was located. Now, the Priests, as well as the Levites, always had to be present in great numbers around the Sanctuary for the ministry imposed upon them; thus, by the power of their office, they were forced to live in the place where the assembly was to be held. This was far more inconvenient for others. Finally, there were no fixed salaries for the function itself, nor any action of the treasury so that they could enjoy the fines. Hence, the office of judge was not so sought after, because it was without profit—indeed, it was joined with the loss of household property. The Levitical tribe and the Priests, however, had especially large incomes—namely, tithes from the entire harvest and other offerings—through which they were abundantly provided for. It was with good reason, therefore, that the duty of judging was entrusted to the Priests and Levites, at least so that they made up the greatest number. And these, finally, are the true causes of this matter.

<summary>This page explains that the Great Sanhedrin consisted of 71 members (70 plus a presiding Prince) and argues that Priests and Levites dominated the council because their lack of land-ownership and their central location at the Sanctuary gave them the necessary leisure and expertise.</summary>

### On the SANHEDRINS of the HEBREWS.

<margin>XXXVII. No inherent right to the Sanhedrin.</margin>

XXXVII. Otherwise, Levites and Priests, as such, had no inherent right to the Sanhedrin over any of the rest of the Israelites. Not even the <term>High Priest</term> <note>Original: *Pontifex*. The supreme religious leader of the Israelites.</note> himself, by virtue of his office, was a member of the Sanhedrin as such, unless he was deemed suitable and had been legally admitted to it. Indeed, if Priests and Levites were not found to be equipped with the appropriate gifts, **even if the entire Senate consisted of Israelites from other tribes, it was permissible**; <note>Original Hebrew: *אפי' היו כולם ישראל הרי זה מותר*. This emphasizes that merit and knowledge of the law were more important than priestly lineage.</note> according to the inquiry of **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist whose codification of Jewish law is a primary source for this text.</note> in *Sanhedrin, Chapter 1.*

<margin>XXXVIII. Sanhedrists in the time of David and Jehoshaphat.</margin>

XXXVIII. David seems to have chosen many from the tribe of Judah for the Senate, whom association with the court had made capable of managing affairs. And this is believed to pertain to what is written in *Psalm 60:10: Judah is my Lawgiver.* In the time of Jehoshaphat, the Senate consisted of both Priests and other leading men, the heads of paternal families. Specifically praised are **Amariah, the Chief Priest, the leader in every matter of the Lord, and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the leader in the house of Judah, in every royal matter.** *2 Chronicles 19:8, 11.*

<margin>XXXIX. Whether the councils of Priests and Princes were distinct.</margin>

XXXIX. Elsewhere, however, the Council of Priests seems to be distinguished from the Council of Princes: for the Priests and Prophets demanded Jeremiah be put to death as a capital criminal, whom nevertheless the Princes of the house of Judah, presiding at the entrance of the New Gate of the Lord, acquitted. *Jeremiah 26:10, 11.* To resolve this difficulty, **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian often called the "father of international law."</note> offers two responses. **I.** It might appear to be more a dispute among colleagues themselves—of the sort described in *John 7:50* and *Acts 5:35*—rather than a formal accusation where others were acting as judges. **II.** There were many Priests outside the Senate, and if any of them took on the role of an accuser, they removed from themselves the power of judging.

<margin>XL. The King was not admitted into the Sanhedrin.</margin>

XL. But although the way to the Sanhedrin lay open to all honored men, they excluded the King. For thus says **Maimonides** in *Sanhedrin, Chapter II, § 4:*
> The King of Israel is not admitted into the Sanhedrin, because it is not permitted to disagree with him, or to contradict his word.

Yet they do admit the High Priest, provided his wisdom is not unequal to his dignity. The Kings of the Davidic line, although they were not usually admitted into the Sanhedrin either, nevertheless sat and judged the people themselves.

<margin>XLI. To which, however, Proselytes were admitted.</margin>

XLI. Finally, it is worth noting that not only was access to the Sanhedrin open to all Israelites without tribal distinction, but even **Proselytes** <note>Converts to Judaism who were not born into the Israelite tribes.</note> themselves were admitted. This the Talmudic scholars prove by the examples of the descendants of **Jethro** <note>The Midianite father-in-law of Moses.</note> and **Sennacherib** <note>The Neo-Assyrian king; tradition holds that some of his descendants converted and became famous Jewish scholars.</note>. Jethro was a Midianite; and yet his descendants earned the right to sit in the <term>Chamber of Hewn Stone</term> <note>Original: *conclavi cæsi lapidis*. This was the dedicated hall on the Temple Mount where the Great Sanhedrin held its sessions.</note>. **Shemaiah** and **Abtalion** were of Babylonian origin, descendants of Sennacherib, and yet they were Rectors of the Academy and Presidents of the Sanhedrin. *Sanhedrin, Chapter XI.* See also *Rabbi Abraham in Kabbala, folio 27, column 4.*

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

<margin>XLII. *Qualities required in the Sanhedrin members. Stated Negatively*.</margin> XLII. The Masters describe the qualities required in judges in two ways. I. **Negatively** <note>Original Greek: *Ἀρνητικῶς* (Arnetikos). This refers to the list of attributes that disqualify a person from serving.</note>. II. **Positively** <note>Original Greek: *Θετικῶς* (Thetikos). This refers to the attributes a judge must possess.</note>. They deny that the following can be lawfully co-opted into the Sanhedrin: I. One exhausted by old age. This they measured not so much by years as by a defect of bodily or mental strength. For that most famous and long-lived **Rabban Jochanan ben Zakkai** <note>A primary Jewish scholar of the late Second Temple era and a key figure in the development of the Mishnah.</note>, having been co-opted into the number of the Sanhedrin at eighty years old, participated in judgments until his 120th year, and was finally even the Prince of the Great Sanhedrin. II. A eunuch or emasculated man, because they are judged to be more cruel—not only by the Hebrews, but also by the Romans. For thus says **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a Latin court poet.</note> in *Book 1, Against Eutropius*:

> ->-- A eunuch is moved by no sense of duty, --<-
> ->He cares for neither family nor children; mercy is for those<-
> ->Who are like themselves, and a shared loss binds their spirits.<-

III. One who lacks offspring, which usually encourages mercy. IV. One who has not yet reached the proper age. The Masters differ in defining this. A Talmudic Gloss on the Babylonian **Gemara** <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary on the Mishnah.</note>, **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with the Great Council and legal proceedings.</note> Chapter 10, says no one is fit for deciding matters before they have reached forty years of age. But **Rabbi Abihu**, in the name of **Rabbi Jochanan**, when discussing the distinction between monetary and capital judgments, thinks thus: *Even one younger than twenty years, or whose two hairs of puberty have not yet appeared, properly exercises monetary judgments, but by no means capital ones.* Whether, indeed, upon reaching the twentieth year, one was immediately considered of an age fit for capital judgments by those who spoke thus, is not entirely clear. The conjecture of **Selden** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English polymath and jurist who wrote extensively on Hebrew law.</note> is probable: that the law regarding forty years was regularly observed, so that only where a more distinguished knowledge of the Law supplemented their age were younger men co-opted. V. One who does not practice a craft useful to human society. For it is held unlawful for a man to occupy himself entirely with other things <gloss>except in the Law and deeds of kindness, or trade, or a craft, or some work that contributes to the public good</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *אלא או בתורה וגמילות חסדים או בסחורה ואומנות ומלאכה שיש בהן ישוב של עולם*</note>, as **Obadiah Bartenora** <note>A 15th-century Italian rabbi famous for his commentary on the Mishnah.</note> teaches from the decrees of the Ancients. VI. One who suffers from a notable physical deformity. For example, if he were blind or one-eyed.

<margin>XLIII. *Stated Positively*.</margin> XLIII. On the contrary, in the assessors of the Great Sanhedrin, they required the following: I. That they be <gloss>of distinguished stature</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי קומה* (Ba'alei komah)</note>. II. <gloss>Of distinguished wisdom</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי חכמה* (Ba'alei chokhmah)</note>. III. <gloss>Of distinguished appearance</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי מראה* (Ba'alei mareh)</note>. IV. <gloss>Of a proper age verging toward old age</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי זקנה* (Ba'alei ziknah)</note>. V. <gloss>Not unskilled in magic</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי כשפים* (Ba'alei keshafim)</note>. VI. <gloss>Fluent in seventy languages</gloss> <note>Original Hebrew: *יודעים בשבעים לשון* (Yode'im b'shivim lashon)</note>, so that there is no need to hear through an interpreter. That they require skill in magic is elegantly hissed at by **Cunaeus** <note>Petrus Cunaeus (1586–1638), author of *The Hebrew Republic* (De Republica Hebraeorum).</note> in *Book 1, Chapter 12*. # On the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews.

...and are utterly ridiculous. For the claim that exactly seventy languages exist in the world is a piece of **Rabbinic pleasantry** <note>Original Latin: *Rabbinicum suaviloquium*. The author is suggesting that the Rabbis often used poetic or exaggerated speech rather than literal fact.</note>; truly, for one man to be equipped with the knowledge of so many languages exceeds the human lot, let alone that every single Senator should have attained such great skill. Nor does this Talmudic decree agree with **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, who discusses the prohibition of the study of foreign languages among his people. *“I,”* he says, speaking of his own nation's customs with some pride, *“by the confession of my fellow tribesmen, am exceptionally well-versed in our ancestral teachings. I have also applied myself to Greek literature with some success, although the ancestral custom did not allow me to attain an exquisite mode of pronunciation. For our people do not look up to those who have spent time on many languages, because they consider that a profane study, common to slaves and freeborn men alike. Rather, they only vote to declare as wise those who have attained such great skill in the Law and the sacred letters that they are able to interpret them.”* <margin>Antiquities of the Jews, Book 20, Chapter 9.</margin> Nor do I doubt that Josephus deserves more credit here than the Talmudists.

<margin>XLIV. The most ancient mode of election.</margin>
XLIV. The **co-optation** <note>The process of electing or appointing someone into a group.</note> of judges into the Sanhedrin consisted partly of *Election* and partly of the *initiation of the elected*. The most ancient election is said to have been performed in this manner. <margin>Gemara Sanhedrin, Chapter 1, Section 6.</margin> When God said to **Moses**: *Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel,* Moses thought about how he was to accomplish this. For, he said, "If I choose six from each tribe, there will be two extra. If I choose five, ten will be missing. If I choose five from one tribe and six from another, I will cause envy among them." What did he do? He selected six from each tribe, then he placed seventy-two **slips** <note>Original Latin: *pittacia*. Small pieces of parchment or paper used for drawing lots.</note> into an urn—seventy of which were inscribed with the word **ELDER** <note>Original Latin: *SENIOR*.</note> and two of which were blank—and he ordered each man to draw one. To him who drew **ELDER**, Moses said: "God has long since sanctified you." To him who drew a blank tablet, he said: *"God does not require you; what can I do for you?"* This method of choosing is the first and most ancient of all.

<margin>XLV. A more recent mode.</margin>
XLV. As the ages passed, when the Hebrews were granted peaceful enjoyment of their land, they say that Senators were admitted into the **Great Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme council and court of the ancient Israelite nation, composed of 71 members.</note> in this way: certain men were sent from the Great Sanhedrin throughout the whole land of Israel to inquire who was wise, God-fearing, humble, of proven sagacity in discerning matters, and favored by the people. They would make such a man a judge in his own city. From there, they promoted him to the **Sanhedrin of 23** <note>A smaller regional court.</note> which sat at the entrance to the Temple Mount. From there, he was co-opted into the one that sat at the door of the Court; and from there, finally, to the Great Sanhedrin. Sometimes, judges were also co-opted or substituted outside the usual order by Kings and others to whom the supreme command was committed, when the colleges were restored after some period of decline. In these cases, not only votes but sometimes **lots** were employed—if we are to believe **Philo**. <margin>Philo, *On Judges* <note>Original Greek: *περὶ δικαστ.* (Peri dikast.)</note></margin>

BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

<margin>XLII. Qualities required in the Sanhedrin. Negatively.</margin>
XLII. The Masters describe the **QUALITIES** required in Judges in two ways. I. **Negatively** <note>Original Greek: *'Αρνητικῶς* (Arnetikos)—defining something by what it is not.</note>. II. **Positively** <note>Original Greek: *Θετικῶς* (Thetikos)—defining something by its required attributes.</note>. They deny that one can be lawfully co-opted into the Sanhedrin if they are:

I. **Worn out by old age.** This they judged not so much by years as by a defect of strength in the body or mind. For that most famous and long-lived **Rabban Jochanan ben Zakkai** <note>A primary Jewish scholar of the 1st century AD who played a key role in preserving Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple.</note>, having been co-opted into the number of the Sanhedrin at eighty years old, participated in judgments until his 120th year, and was eventually the Prince of the Great Sanhedrin.

II. **A Eunuch**, or one emasculated, because they are deemed to be more cruel—a view held not only by the Hebrews but also by the Romans. Thus says **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus, a Roman court poet (c. 370–404 AD).</note> in Book I of *Against Eutropius*:

> ->*--A eunuch is moved by no piety,*<-
> ->*Nor does he care for lineage or children; clemency is bound by*<-
> ->*similarity toward others, and a shared loss binds their souls.*<-
> <note>Original Latin: *Eunuchus nulla pietate movetur, Nec generi natisve cavet; clementia cunctis In similes, animosque ligant consortia damni.* The poet argues that because eunuchs cannot have families, they lack the natural empathy that comes from fatherhood.</note>

III. **One who lacks offspring**, which usually serves to stir a person toward mercy.

IV. **One who has not yet reached a proper age.** The Masters differ in defining this age. The **Talmudic Gloss** <note>Explanatory notes on the Talmudic text.</note> on the Babylonian Gemara, *Sanhedrin* Chapter 10, says no one is fit for deciding matters before he has reached the age of 40. But **Rabbi Abihu**, in the name of **Rabbi Jochanan**, where the distinction between monetary and capital judgments is discussed, judges thus: *Even one younger than twenty years, or who has not yet grown two pubic hairs, may rightly exercise monetary judgments, but by no means capital ones.* Whether, however, once the twentieth year was completed, they were immediately considered fit by age for capital judgments by those who spoke thus, is not entirely clear. The conjecture of **John Selden** <note>A famous 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> is probable: *That the law regarding 40 years was regularly observed, so that where a more distinguished knowledge of the Law compensated for age, even younger men were co-opted.*

V. **One who does not practice a craft useful to human society.** For it is held illicit for a man to occupy himself entirely in other matters, **except in the Law and acts of kindness, or in trade, or craftsmanship, or some work that contributes to the settling of the world** <note>Original Hebrew: *אלא או בתורה וגמילות חסדים או בסחורה ואומנות ומלאכה שיש בהן ישוב של עולם*. This reflects the Jewish value of *Yishuv Ha'olam*, or contributing to the sustainability of civilization.</note>: as **Obadiah Bartenora** <note>A 15th-century Italian rabbi famous for his commentary on the Mishnah.</note> teaches from the decrees of the Ancients.

VI. **One who suffers from a significant physical deformity.** For example, if he were blind or one-eyed.

<margin>XLIII. Positively.</margin>
XLIII. Conversely, they required the following in the assessors of the Great Sanhedrin:

I. That they be **men of stature** <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי קומה* (Ba'alei Komah)</note>, meaning of impressive height.
II. **Men of wisdom** <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי חכמה* (Ba'alei Chochmah)</note>, of distinguished wisdom.
III. **Men of appearance** <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי מראה* (Ba'alei Mar'eh)</note>, of distinguished form.
IV. **Men of old age** <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי זקנה* (Ba'alei Ziknah)</note>, of a proper age verging toward seniority.
V. **Men of sorcery** <note>Original Hebrew: *בעלי כשפים* (Ba'alei Keshafim)</note>, meaning not unlearned in magic.
VI. **Knowing seventy languages** <note>Original Hebrew: *יודעים בשבעים לשון* (Yodim b'shiv'im lashon)</note>, so that it is not necessary to hear through an interpreter.

For that exactly seventy languages exist in the world is a piece of Rabbinic flowery speech <note>original: *Rabbinicum suaviloquium*</note>; truly, for one person to be equipped with the knowledge of so many languages exceeds the human lot, let alone that every single Senator should have attained such great expertise. Nor does this Talmudic decree agree with Josephus, who discusses the prohibition of the study of foreign languages among his people. *I, he says, in the manner of his own nation and quite boastfully: For I, by the confession of my fellow tribesmen, am remarkably well-versed in our ancestral teachings; I have also applied myself to Greek literature with some progress, although our national custom did not permit me to attain an exquisite manner of pronunciation. For our people do not respect those who have mastered many languages, because such a study is considered profane among them, and common to slaves as well as to the free-born. They only pronounce as "wise" those who have attained such great expertise in the Law and the sacred letters that they are able to interpret them.* <note>Quoted from Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 20, Chapter 9.</note> Nor do I doubt that Josephus here deserves more credit than the Talmudists.

<margin>XLIV. The most ancient mode of Election.</margin>
XLIV. The **APPOINTMENT** <term>Cooptatio; the formal process of electing a new member into a body by the existing members</term> of Judges into the Sanhedrin consisted partly of *Election* and partly of the *Initiation of the Elected*. The most ancient election is said to have been performed in this manner. From the *Gemara Sanhedrin*, Chapter 1, Section 6: When God said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel," he wondered how he would accomplish it. For, he said, "If I choose six from each tribe, there will be two extra. If I choose five, ten will be missing. If I take five from one tribe and six from another, I will provoke envy among them." What did he do? He selected six from each tribe, then he placed seventy-two small slips of paper into an urn—seventy of which were inscribed with the word **ELDER**, while two were left blank—and mixed them together. He ordered each man to draw one slip. To him who drew **ELDER**, he said: *the Lord has long since sanctified you*. To him who drew a blank slip, he said: *God does not require you; what can I do for you?* This method of choosing is the first and most ancient of all.

<margin>XLV. A more recent method.</margin>
XLV. As the ages passed, when the Hebrews were permitted to enjoy peaceful affairs in their own land, they say Senators were admitted to the Great Sanhedrin in this way: certain men were sent from the Great Sanhedrin throughout the entire land of Israel to seek out who was wise, God-fearing, humble, of proven sagacity in discerning matters, and well-liked by the people. They would make such a man a judge in his own city. From there, they promoted him to the Sanhedrin of Twenty-Three, which sat at the entrance to the Temple Mount. From here, he was co-opted into that which sat at the door of the Court <note>referring to the *Azarah* or inner courtyard of the Temple</note>; and from there finally to the Great Sanhedrin. Sometimes Judges were also appointed and substituted outside the usual order by Kings and others to whom the supreme command of affairs was entrusted, especially when the colleges were being restored after some period of decline. In these cases, not only votes but sometimes lots were employed—if we are to believe Philo in his treatise *On the Judge* <note>Original Greek title: *Περὶ δικαστοῦ* (Peri dikastou)</note>.
