->### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.<-

<margin>
XLVI. Initiation performed by the laying on of hands.
</margin>
XLVI. *The Initiation or Ordination of those elected was performed by the laying on of hands*; which I believe was distinct from the ceremony by which someone was created an Elder. For by this rite, as I mentioned above, Senatorial dignity was not bestowed; rather, it merely declared that the man was fit to be admitted into the order of Senators. They derive this ceremony from Moses, who initiated Joshua into his office in this manner according to Numbers 27:23. This laying on of hands was performed either by a <term>Triumvirate</term> <note>A small committee or court of three men</note> appointed for that purpose by the Sanhedrin itself; or by the full Sanhedrin; or finally by a single Senator who took two other colleagues as his associates. From the time of Hillel, it became the rule that no one was considered legitimately ordained without the authority of the Prince of the college: though the number of three men was still strictly observed in every ordination. To the laying on of hands, these words were usually added: <note>original Hebrew: אֲנִי סוֹמֵךְ אוֹתְךָ וּתְהִי סָמוּךְ</note> *I ordain you, and be you ordained.* They considered it a divine violation to perform this rite outside of the Holy Land, since its full power was confined within the borders of Palestine.

<margin>
XLVII. For which a solemn ritual formula was later substituted.
</margin>
XLVII. Eventually, this laying on of hands, which had been the custom for a long time, ceased. Instead, a certain ritual formula <note>original: *carmen*, literally a "song" or "chant," but here referring to a fixed legal declaration</note> was recited in prescribed words; Maimonides says it was of this kind: <note>original Hebrew: הֲרֵי אַתָּה סָמוּךְ וְיֵשׁ לְךָ רְשׁוּת לָדוּן אֲפִלּוּ דִינֵי קְנָסוֹת</note> *Behold, you are ordained, and power is given to you to exercise judgment, even in cases of criminal penalties.*

<margin>
XLVIII. The President and Vice-President of the Sanhedrin. See also the Preface, Section 29.
</margin>
XLVIII. Thus far I have discussed the members of the Great Sanhedrin. It must not be omitted that two, or as some prefer, three men stood out above all the rest. The first of these was the President, who was called <note>original Hebrew: נָשִׂיא בְּכָל מָקוֹם</note> *the Prince in every place*, or simply <note>original Hebrew: נָשִׂיא</note> *Prince* (Nasi), or <note>original Hebrew: רֹאשׁ</note> *Head* (Rosh), or <note>original Hebrew: מוּפְלָא</note> *The Distinguished One* (Mufla). The second after him was the <term>Vice-President</term>, called <note>original Hebrew: אַב בֵּית דִּין</note> *Father of the House of Judgment* (Av Beit Din). His seat was at the right hand of the Prince. Some add a third, called the <term>Sage</term> <note>original Hebrew: חָכָם; Hakham</note>, whose place was at the left hand of the Prince.

<margin>
XLIX. To whom a third was added, by the name of Sage.
</margin>
XLIX. Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note> brought forward clear testimony on this matter from the Talmudic Gloss, in his notes on the Sanhedrin, Chapter 4, Number 13. The *Nasi*, or Prince, is he who has the authority to publicly interpret the Law. The *Father of the House of Judgment* is the leader of the Judges, by whose mouth disputes are decided. The *Sage* is he who excels among the teachers, with whom one communicates regarding matters to be done, being skilled in the meanings and reasonings of the Law. He sits at the left of the Prince. Rabbi Judah the Holy, when dying, distributed these three offices such that he appointed his son Gamaliel as Prince, bequeathed the persona of the Sage to his other son Simeon, and made Rabbi Hanina the Father of the Senate. To these three, according to their degrees of dignity, degrees of honor were also shown. When the Prince enters, all the people rise, and they do not sit back down until he himself commands it. When the Father of the Senate enters, they form two rows for him...

...is received by those standing. When a Sage <note>Latin: *Sapiens*; here referring to a high-ranking scholar or member of the Sanhedrin</note> enters, one stands while another sits.

<margin>L. Authority of the Sanhedrin.</margin>
L. The **Authority** of this Sanhedrin was by far the greatest, whether one considers the matters they handled, the persons over whom they presided, or finally the *value and effectiveness* of the sentences they pronounced.

<margin>LI. Matters to be handled there.</margin>
LI. The **Matters** dealt with in the Great Sanhedrin were of every kind: Private and Public; Ecclesiastical and Political. For the Church was so intertwined with the State that both constituted a single body; and the form of Government was *Theocratic* <note>A system where God is recognized as the supreme civil ruler and His laws form the basis of the state</note>, where the supreme Sovereignty remained with God, and the remaining Magistrates were nothing but God’s Ministers. I have dealt with this subject specifically elsewhere. It was therefore the duty of the Senators to travel throughout all Judea, to inspect the assemblies of the people, and to establish Magistrates in the towns: to deliberate on waging war, on crushing enemies, and on extending the empire. The Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> also attribute to them the power of appointing the King. But it is also established that the business of religion was entrusted to them. They believe that a certain Kabbalah <note>original: *Cabbalam*; referring to the oral tradition or "received" doctrine of mysteries</note>, or doctrine of mysteries, was handed down by hand from the very beginnings of the Republic, the entire force and authority of which rested with them. Furthermore, it was their role to establish certain statutes concerning sacred matters and to devise certain methods by which the Law would be explained. *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> encompassed most of the things that had to be decided by the Great Sanhedrin in these words: *They do not appoint a King except by the decision of the Great Sanhedrin of 71 men. They do not ordain minor courts for individual tribes or cities except from the mouth of those same 71. They do not condemn an entire tribe to be expelled, nor a false Prophet, nor a High Priest to capital punishment, except in the same Great Senate. However, monetary cases are judged by three men. But they do not declare an elder rebellious, nor overturn an apostate city, nor make a woman suspected of adultery drink the bitter waters <note>Referencing the "Sotah" ritual from Numbers 5:11–31</note>, nor expand the city or the temple courts, nor go out* <term>למלחמת הרשות</term> <note>original Hebrew: *l’milchemet ha-reshut*; an optional, discretionary, or voluntary war</note> *into a war of power (that is, a spontaneous, voluntary, or arbitrary war which is undertaken* <term>כדי להרחיב גבול ישראל ולהרבות גדולתו ושמעו</term> <note>original Hebrew: *kedei leharchiv gvul yisrael u-lerbot gedulato u-shmo*; so that the borders of the Israeli kingdom may be expanded, and its greatness and fame increased</note> *to expand the borders of the Israelite kingdom and increase its greatness and fame) or to measure the location of a slain person <note>A ritual performed when a body was found between cities to determine responsibility</note>, except by the will of the aforementioned Council, as it is said in Exodus 18:22: "Whatever is Great, let them bring to you."* See *Schickard on Royal Law, Chapter I, Theorem II. And Cocceius on the Sanhedrin, Chapter I, section v.*

<margin>LII. Persons subject to jurisdiction.</margin>
LII. The **Persons** who were subject to the jurisdiction of the Great Sanhedrin were of every kind and dignity, with not even Prophets or High Priests—nor even, if we believe the Rabbis, Kings—being exempt. Regarding the **False Prophet** <note>Latin: *Pseudo-Propheta*</note>, this caution of Jewish law exists: *They do not punish a False Prophet with death in the assembly that is in his own city, nor in the assembly in Jabneh <note>Also known as Jamnia, a significant center of Jewish learning</note>, but they lead him to the Great assembly which is in Jerusalem, and they keep him until...*

And they execute him during the festival, as it is said, *And all Israel shall hear, and fear, and shall no longer act in such a manner.* <note>original: "et omnis Israël audient, & metuent, & non pergent amplius ad eum modum facere"; referencing Deuteronomy 17:13</note> And from this, light is shed upon the saying of the Lord in Luke 13:33: *It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside of Jerusalem.* <note>original: "Non contingit ut Prophetæ pereat extra Hierusalem"</note>

<margin>LIII. The High Priests.</margin>
LIII. Concerning the **High Priest**, they teach the following: *The High Priest judges and is judged; he gives testimony, and testimony is given against him.* <note>Quoted from the Mishnah, Sanhedrin Chapter 2, Section 1</note> However, no one judged him in capital cases except the Great Sanhedrin. Furthermore, the power of the Sanhedrin over the High Priest extended so far that, on account of various offenses and the pollutions that easily occur, he could be beaten with leather straps. Once he had undergone this punishment, <term>חזור לגדולתו</term> <gloss>he was restored to his majesty</gloss>. However, in the case of the <term>ראש הישיבה</term> <gloss>Prince of the Sanhedrin</gloss> <note>Literally "Head of the Academy"</note>, this was tempered so that if he were thus flogged, <term>אינו חוזר לשרותו</term> <gloss>he was not restored to his office</gloss>.

<margin>LIV. The Kings.</margin>
LIV. Finally, the Talmudic scholars subject the **King** himself to the Sanhedrin, such that he could be corrected and brought into order by it, even by flogging. This was done, however, only for three specific crimes prohibited to him: namely, if he multiplied wives beyond eighteen; if he multiplied horses beyond what was sufficient for his chariot (for they deemed even leading one around for mere pomp worthy of lashes); and finally, if he multiplied wealth for himself to leave in private treasuries. These points are confirmed in the very expressive words of the Talmud by Wilhelm Schickard in *On Royal Law* <note>original: "de Jur. Reg."</note>, Chapter 6, Theorem 7, and by John Selden in *On the Sanhedrin* <note>original: "de Syned."</note>, Book III, Chapter 9, although other opinions are brought forward to the contrary.

<margin>LV. Especially those of the House of David.</margin>
LV. But the Hebrews distinguish the Kings who were of the House of David from the Kings of Israel. In honor of the former, they testify that because they knew the law and their own obligation, they did not consider that humiliation and legal submission to be shameful to themselves. However, they reproach the latter <note>The Kings of the northern Kingdom of Israel</note> for pride and arrogance, as they refused to subject themselves to the law; for this reason, to avoid scandal, the Masters judged that they should be left to themselves and to God.

<margin>LVI. A Talmudic tale regarding this matter.</margin>
LVI. Nor are there lacking short stories by which they persuade themselves that the angry Divinity demanded punishment from the Senate when they did not defend their authority over Kings with enough spirit. In the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary</note> of Sanhedrin, Chapter 2, this little tale is read: The servant of King Jannaeus (who was from the Hasmoneans, the brother of Aristobulus and son of Hyrcanus) had committed a murder. Simeon son of Shetach urged the Sages to take notice of it and hold a trial concerning him. They sent word to Jannaeus: *Your servant has committed murder.* He sent the servant to them. They sent word to him again: *You must also present yourself and receive the testimony: for concerning masters, the law says: let the owner of the ox come and stand next to his ox.* <note>Referencing Exodus 21:29</note> (For servants are compared to cattle). He came and sat down. Then Simeon son of Shetach—

# Concerning the SANHEDRIN OF THE HEBREWS.

Shetach turned to him and said:
> "King Jannai, stand up on your feet; then the testimony will be spoken concerning you. Do not think you are standing before us, but before Him at whose command the world came into being. For it is written: *Then both the men between whom the controversy is shall stand.*" <note>original: "stabuntque duo isti viri quibus lis est"; referencing Deuteronomy 19:17</note>

Then the King replied:
> "Not by your command," he said, "but according to what your colleagues shall determine."

The President then looked to his right to see if he had any supporters; but they kept their faces fixed on the ground out of fear. Turning to his left, when he saw that they likewise did not dare to lift their faces, he said:
> "O you thinking men! It will come to pass that He who knows the thoughts of men will take vengeance upon you."

Immediately, the angel Gabriel struck them to the ground, so that they all breathed their last. Also very well known is the history of *Herod* being called to judgment by the Sanhedrin, which *Josephus* pursues at length in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 14, Chapter 17.

<margin>LVII. Whether the punishment of lashes is contrary to Royal Majesty.</margin>
LVII. Since those things we have recounted regarding the punishment of lashes to be inflicted on a King by the sentence of the Sanhedrin seem diametrically opposed to **Royal Majesty**, highly learned men see a difficulty arising here: by what reasoning might they soften such a harsh assertion? They observe, therefore, that this punishment was not formerly regarded among the Jews as flogging is among us today, but rather like the fines which are exacted even from the most noble without infamy. This is not only urged by *Schickard*; but also by *Hugo Grotius* in his work *On the Law of War and Peace*, Book 1, Chapter 3, Paragraph 10.
> "I see," he says, "that the Hebrews agree that lashes were inflicted upon a King who sinned against those laws written concerning the King's duty. But among them, these were free from infamy, and were undertaken voluntarily by the King as a sign of repentance: and therefore he was not beaten by a public executioner, but by one whom he himself had chosen, and he set the limit to the lashes at his own discretion."

LVIII. But it has been well noted by others that *Josephus* in *Antiquities*, Book 4, Chapter 8, calls it a <term>most shameful punishment</term> <note>original Greek: τιμωρίαν αἰσχίστην / timorian aischistēn</note>, illiberal, infamous, and most foul, and one that is least suitable for a <term>free man</term> <note>original Greek: ἐλευθέρῳ / eleutherō</note>. And indeed, if anyone considers those things which *Schickard* himself commented on regarding this kind of punishment, he will easily notice that it is a thing most unworthy of Royal Majesty to be condemned, by a sentence of the Sanhedrin, to lashes inflicted with a bull-hide strap upon the chest, between the breasts, on the back, and on both shoulder blades. But we have thus far only been setting forth the decrees of the Hebrews, not yet inquiring into their truth.

<margin>LIX. The sentence of the Sanhedrin was executed without any appeal.</margin>
LIX. Let us proceed, therefore, to examine those things which pertain to the authority of the Sanhedrin. The latest of these consists in the irreversible <term>validity</term> <note>original: "valore"</note> of the <term>sentence</term> <note>original: "sententiæ"</note> pronounced by the Senate. This <term>validity</term> is proved in various ways. First, by this reasoning: if anyone were condemned by the Senate, he would be handed over to punishment without any appeal, to such an extent that it was not lawful even for the King himself to exempt him from the judgment.

<margin>LX. Whose justice so that—</margin>
LX. In order, however, to make the justice of their sentence manifest to the whole people—

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

<margin>They took remarkable care to ensure that the process was manifest to the people.</margin>
...might perform, and so they might achieve the true purpose of punishments, which is the preservation of public peace and the restraint of crimes; they ordered that when a defendant was led to execution, a herald should go before him, crying out with a loud voice: "This man goes to his punishment, by which he undergoes this death: because he committed this crime, at this time, in this place: and N. N. <note>The names of the specific witnesses</note> are witnesses to this matter: if anyone knows anything that could benefit the defendant, let him come and bring it forward." Furthermore, someone stood before the doors of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and court of the ancient Israelites</note> holding a cloth or linen cloth in his hand, which he would wave if anyone took up the defense of the accused; upon seeing this, another person, sitting on a horse not far from there, would gallop to bring back the condemned man. Indeed, if something occurred to the defendant himself that he had not yet brought forward for his defense, he was allowed to return four or five times: and so that his words on the way might be more accurately weighed, they assigned two of the disciples of the wise to accompany him. *Sanhedrin Chapter VI, § 1.*

<margin>LXI. What they also falsely claim was observed regarding the execution of Jesus.</margin>
LXI. I cannot omit on this occasion, although it is a complete fabrication, what the Talmudists <note>The authors and compilers of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> relate concerning our Jesus—who was wickedly demanded for the cross by their ancestors. *Babylonian Gemara, Sanhedrin Chapter VI.* "There is a tradition," they say, "that Jesus was hanged on the eve of Passover, and a herald went before him for forty days crying out: 'This man goes out to be stoned, because he performed sorceries, and persuaded and seduced Israel; whoever knows a defense for him, let him come forward and produce it.' But no defense was found. Therefore they hanged him on the eve of Passover." *See Lightfoot on Matthew 27:31.*

<margin>LXII. Punishment for contumacy: Flogging.</margin>
LXII. Furthermore, it was not only those sentences by which someone was condemned to death that were carried out, but whatever else was established by the Sanhedrin regarding any matter was held as valid, and those who went against it or spoke against it were severely punished. For they had their <term>Shotrim</term> <note>original Hebrew: שוטרים; "officers" or "enforcers"</note> **Enforcers**, who, equipped with sticks and leather straps, compelled subjects to observe the decree established by the judges; they were the executors of the punishment decreed for rebels. They call this <term>Makkat Mardut</term> <note>original Hebrew: מכת מרדות</note> **flogging for rebellion and contumacy** <note>willful disobedience or resistance to authority</note>. This was far more severe than the legal flogging for the violation of some Divine law, even though the latter was also quite harsh. For the accused was bound to a pillar in such a way that he neither stood entirely nor sat, but hung as if bent over. Then the executioner, placed behind him and standing on a stone, struck him—stripped naked to the navel—with a calfskin strap split into four, alternating strikes on the front and back in a ratio of three to two <note>original: "proportione sesquialtera"; referring to the distribution of the 39 lashes: 13 on the chest and 26 on the back</note>. One of the judges would command the striking, another would count the blows, and a third would chant the justice of the punishment. Nevertheless, there was a certain predefined number of blows for this legal flogging, and it was not permitted to go beyond forty. However, that which is called the flogging of contumacy, which awaits those who transgress the prohibitions of the scribes, depended on the discretion of the judges...

### ON THE SANHEDRINS OF THE HEBREWS.

...and according to the nature of the crime, the punishment was either increased or decreased; it could even proceed to the death of the guilty party. It was not carried out with a whip, but with a staff. <note>The author distinguishes between *flagellum* (a whip often used for religious or corrective discipline) and *baculus* (a wooden staff or rod used by civil authorities).</note> See Buxtorf, *Talmudic Lexicon*, page 1252. This flogging was the standard practice when someone refused to obey a decree of the Sanhedrin in matters of lesser importance.

<margin>LXIII. Sometimes Death.</margin>
LXIII. However, if one resisted the court in a more serious matter, the death penalty was established for the defiant person. This is derived from Deuteronomy 17:12:
> *But the man who acts arrogantly, so as not to listen to the priest who stands to minister there to the Lord your God, or to the judge: that man shall die, and you shall take away that evil from Israel. So that all the people may hear, and fear, and not act arrogantly thereafter.*

<margin>LXIV. To be inflicted on the Rebellious Elder.</margin>
LXIV. And from here come those Talmudic regulations concerning the <term>Zaken Mamre|Rebellious Elder</term>: a man who, even if he himself were a judge and a member of the Sanhedrin, was to be punished with death if it were proven that he had acted defiantly according to his own opinion against the decrees of the Sanhedrin. Nor did any kind of excuse for his defiance benefit him; not even if he could prove with unanswerable arguments that his opinion had been approved by the Sanhedrin in ancient times and had openly prevailed among their ancestors. For the most recent decree of the Sanhedrin was always to be preferred. How they derive this from the words of Divine Law was shown by us above in § XXIV. The experts in Hebrew law urge this so severely that they deny it was lawful for the Sanhedrin itself to grant pardon to the defiant one: <note>original Hebrew: "kedei shelo yirbu machlokot beYisrael"</note> *lest, of course, the diversity of opinions be multiplied in Israel,* says Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> as cited in Selden, *On the Sanhedrin, Book III, Chapter III.* By these means, the authority of the Great Sanhedrin was abundantly safeguarded.

<margin>LXV. The location of the Sanhedrin was initially varied.</margin>
LXV. Now let us look at the LOCATION. This is believed to have varied according to the circumstances of the times. In the age of Moses, it is said to have been <note>original Hebrew: "lifnei petach ohel moed"</note> *at the door of the tent of meeting* (Numbers 11:24). After the Israelites entered the Holy Land, they say it had various seats, now in one place, now in another, but always where the Tabernacle was located: in Shiloh, in Mizpah, Gilgal, Nob, Gibeon, and at the house of Obed-Edom; and finally in Jerusalem. Where it sat during the time of the First Temple <note>The Temple of Solomon, destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE.</note> is not sufficiently established. But the Masters assert for certain that its seats were joined to the Temple, understanding the phrase "the place which the Lord chose" to refer to both the Temple itself and the nearby seats of the Sanhedrin. Shortly before the destruction of the Temple by the Chaldeans, Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Rabbinic scholar.</note> thinks (*Description of the Temple, Chapter IX*) it can be concluded that the chamber of the Sanhedrin was near the Eastern Gate of the Temple, above the chamber of the gatekeepers. In Jeremiah 35:4, these words occur: *I brought the Rechabites to the house of the Lord, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was near...*

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

...near the CHAMBER OF THE PRINCES, which was above the chamber of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the keeper of the threshold. Regarding these "Princes," the author says we cannot understand them to be those belonging to the royal family; for what would the sons of Jehoiakim have been doing here? They lived in the Royal Palace of Zion, and the path by which they came to the Temple led to the Western gate, which was called Shallechet and Coponius; whereas this gate, of which the son of Shallum was the keeper, was the Eastern gate, as appears from 1 Chronicles 9:17–18. Therefore, by "Princes," we must understand the Great Men of the Sanhedrin, the <term>Rulers of the people</term> <note>Acts 4:8; original Greek: Ἄρχοντες τοῦ λαοῦ</note>, whose judicial seat was near the Eastern Gate, or the Shushan Gate, specifically above the chamber of the Gatekeepers. Here they sat during the time of the First Temple. So says Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Rabbinic scholar</note>; I will not say now how firmly he holds this; I will only point out that Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher and legal scholar Moses Maimonides</note> held a different view. For he maintains that from the very first construction of the Temple by Solomon, the <term>Chamber of Hewn Stone|Lishkat Haggazith</term> <note>original Hebrew: לשכת הגזית</note> was built for the Sanhedrin to sit in, located in the Court of Israel on the Southern side of the Temple. See Selden, Book II, Chapter 15, § 4. But all these matters are of uncertain reliability.

<margin>LXVI. Under the Second Temple, in the most celebrated Chamber of Hewn Stone.</margin>
LXVI. It is more certain that in the Second Temple there was a chamber of that name destined for this use. It was so called because it was paved with precious stones carved with great skill. In its form, it resembled the appearance of a Great Basilica, of which Rabbi Solomon Ben Virga speaks in the *Schebet Jehuda* <note>The "Scepter of Judah," a 16th-century history of the Jews</note> as follows: <gloss>And there was a house called the Chamber of Hewn Stone; it is said that whoever has not seen its construction has never seen a magnificent building.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: ושם בית נקרא לשכת הגזית ומי שלא ראה בניינה : אמרו שלא ראה מעולם בנין מפואר</note> This, Gentius, in his *History of the Jews* (page 362), rendered in a luxuriant style: "Here was that most famous senate house, celebrated throughout the whole world, which the Hebrews were accustomed to call in their own language **LISCAT HAGGAZITH**: the splendor and magnificence of this building were so great that the entire world seems to have nothing like it or second to it." This is perhaps too hyperbolic. The founder of this chamber is said to have been Simeon Ben Shetach, who was the Vice-President of the Sanhedrin when Judah Ben Tabbai was President, in the sixth generation after Ezra, during the reign of Jannaeus the Hasmonean. Part of this court was on sacred ground; the other part was on profane <note>non-consecrated</note> ground. Consequently, it had two doors. One was on the sacred side, through which the Prince entered with his assessors; the other was on the profane side, through which the defendant was led in. The assembly of Judges was in the profane part, because no one was permitted to sit in the Temple Court except for Kings from the family of David. The sacred part was distinguished from the profane by the height of the floor.

<margin>LXVII. From which it departed of its own accord forty years before the destruction of the Temple.</margin>
LXVII. Forty years before the destruction of the Temple, the Sanhedrin is said to have left this place and changed its stations ten times. The reason given for this move is this: they believed that as long as they sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stones, they were bound to deliver judgment on all cases brought before them; and that all their judgments bound everyone...

<meta>The catchword "gare" at the bottom of the page is the end of the Latin word "obligare," meaning "to bind" or "to obligate."</meta>

# On the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews

...to judge the Jews. But since they were now being crushed by the heavy yoke of Roman rule, by which their power was diminished in many ways, and since crimes and murders were increasing immensely, and assassins—protected by the favor of the Roman Governor—were being snatched away from justice, so that they could not restrain such insolence in the manner of their ancestors, they believed it better for them to yield their location. However, because it was not lawful to pronounce a capital sentence anywhere else, they returned to that chamber whenever necessity urged it. They say this also happened in the trial of Jesus and in similar cases.

<margin>LXVIII. Whether John 19:13 implies that Pilate had his Tribunal in this chamber?</margin>
LXVIII. When **Selden** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> had recounted these things from the Talmud (*Book II, Chapter xv, § iv*), he added: "Certainly we are openly taught from the Gospel that the sentence was passed by them in the **Lithostrotos** <note>Greek: *Lithostrotos*, meaning 'The Pavement'</note>. From this it seems to be clearly inferred—whether we look at the reason for the name or the authority of those Hebrews there—that the *Lithostrotos* itself, so called in Greek, was the place of the Great Sanhedrin, or the Chamber named for its pavement. For the Greek words regarding Pilate in John 19:13 are: *he sat down on the judgment seat, in a place called the Pavement* <note>original Greek: ἐκάθισεν ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος, εἰς τόπον λεγόμενον λιθόστρωτον</note>; just as if it had been very well known that the tribunal or court seat was in that place, as in the **Chamber of Hewn Stone** <note>original Hebrew: *Liskath Haggazit*</note> itself."

<margin>LXIX. This is not likely.</margin>
LXIX. I see that **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English scholar who specialized in using Rabbinic texts to explain the New Testament</note> concedes to the same opinion; however, this does not satisfy me at all. For the sacred Gospel History contains nothing from which it can be concluded with any appearance of certainty that Pilate ascended the seat dedicated to the Jewish Senate in the Temple Courtyard. Only a similarity of the Greek name occurs here. But nothing prevents us from believing that there were several places in Jerusalem paved with stones. Indeed, **Josephus** <note>The 1st-century historian Flavius Josephus</note> says that Pilate's tribunal was *in the great stadium* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ σταδίῳ</note>, or in a covered <term>colonnade|xystus</term>. And if there is any similarity in the Greek name, the argument sought from it is overturned by the dissimilarity of the Hebrew name. For who ever heard of the Court of the Hebrew Senate being called **Gabbatha**? And what place, I ask, would a Roman Governor have held in the Jewish Sanhedrin? For he could not sit together with the Jewish Senators, since he was neither the President, nor the Vice-President, nor a part of the Senate. Nor could he have his own Roman Senate there. The Jews would not have suffered either, nor would the Romans have wished it. It is, therefore, far more probable that Pilate had his own tribunal. But back from the detour to the main path.

<margin>LXX. The Form of the Session.</margin>
LXX. THE FORM OF THE SESSION was as follows: They all sat in a semicircular shape, just as we observed regarding the court of twenty-three men. In the middle was placed the seat for the **Prince** <note>The *Nasi*, or President of the Sanhedrin</note>. To his right sat the **Father of the House of Judgment** <note>The *Ab Beit Din*, who served as the vice-president</note>. To his left sat the **Wise Man** <note>The *Chacham*, a high-ranking legal expert within the court</note>. The rest sat on either side in their order of rank, such that the more dignified were closer to the Prince. There stood by the **Scribes**; according to most, there were **two**: one on the right, who wrote down the votes of those acquitting;

BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

...the other on the left, who recorded those voting for condemnation. *Rabbi Judah adds a third*; one who would write down both sides, so that the count of each group might be established with greater certainty. The accused was introduced through the door on the secular side <note>The "profane" or non-sacred side of the chamber</note>, before the judges. At his right hand was the <term>Master of the Lawsuit</term> <note>Hebrew: *Ba'al Din*; here referring to an advocate or accuser</note>, who spoke either for him or against him, as referenced in Psalm 109:31 and 6, and Zechariah 3:1. The sentence was pronounced within the court after the parties were called inside. The one who was eldest among the judges, having addressed the parties by name, would say to one, "*You are innocent*"; and to the other, "*You are liable*." For this reason, it was not permitted for any of the judges, upon leaving, to say: "*I judged in your favor, but my colleagues condemned you; but what could I do? My colleagues outvoted me*." They judged that whoever did this fell under the saying of Solomon in Proverbs 11:13: "*He who reveals a secret is a slanderer*."

<margin>LXXI. Time.</margin>
LXXI. Finally, something must be mentioned regarding the TIME OF THE SESSION. They convened daily (though on Sabbath days they met in the Synagogue on the mountain, so they would not appear to have gathered for the purpose of holding a legal trial) and they sat from the time of the morning <term>continual sacrifice</term> <note>The *Tamid*, or daily offering</note> until the evening continual sacrifice; so that their session and the time of Divine worship never coincided. The morning sacrifice was slaughtered at dawn; the evening one was ordinarily slaughtered at the half-eighth hour <note>Approximately 2:30 PM</note> and offered at the middle of the tenth hour <note>Approximately 3:30 PM</note>. However, it was not considered necessary for all seventy-one elders to be present at all times, unless the gravity of the matter required everyone's presence. Otherwise, if anyone had business elsewhere, it was lawful for him to be absent and return; provided, however, that no fewer than twenty-three judges were always sitting.

<margin>LXXII. Continuity of the Sanhedrin.</margin>
LXXII. Regarding the CONTINUITY and SUCCESSION of the Sanhedrin, these traditions are handed down: its beginning, as I have noted, is placed in the wilderness; where **Moses**, while he lived, performed the role of Prince. After the people were led into the land of Canaan and **Joshua** died—who was Prince of the Sanhedrin after Moses—God occasionally appointed Judges outside the usual order, who had the right of judging even without the Senate. But in times when He had raised up no such leader, it was necessary to have recourse to the Senate, in which the High Priest was usually the most prominent figure, a fact which **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and scholar</note> takes as certain; he refers this to Deuteronomy 17:8–9: *To the Priest or the Judge*. Meanwhile, **Selden** <note>John Selden, the English legal scholar previously mentioned</note> himself considers it beyond doubt that the use of ordinary courts, and thus of Sanhedrins, was sometimes interrupted by disturbances, whether from foreign enemies or domestic strife. And as for what Grotius claims—that it lasted until the times of Herod through a perpetual process of co-opting new members—Selden advises that this must be qualified by the interruptions which, according to the crises of the times and the state of affairs, were various and many. (Book II, Chapter 5, § I & III). In the times of Eli, Samuel, and Saul, there is indeed no mention of the Senate in the sacred scriptures; nevertheless, the Hebrews hand down that Samuel received the teaching of the law...

# On the SANHEDRINS of the HEBREWS.

<margin>a</margin> ...received [authority] from Eli and his Sanhedrin; and David from Samuel and his Sanhedrin. Indeed, where we read in 1 Samuel 6:19 that the men of Beth-shemesh were struck down in the time of Samuel because they profaned the Ark with an improper gaze, among the people there were <note>original Hebrew: שבעים איש חמשים אלף איש — *shiv'im ish hamishim elef ish*</note> **seventy men and fifty thousand men**; this number seventy is interpreted by the Teachers <note>The Rabbinic Sages</note> as referring to the Great Sanhedrin. For this reason, *Jonathan* <note>The Aramaic paraphrase known as the Targum Jonathan</note> translates it this way: <note>original Aramaic: וקטל בסבי עמא שבעין גברא ובקהלא חמשין אלפי גברא — *ve-qatal be-sabei amma shiv'in gavra uve-qahala hamshin alfin gavra*</note> **And he slew seventy men from the elders of the people, and fifty thousand men from the assembly.**

LXXIII. We also read in both Talmuds <note>The Jerusalem and Babylonian collections of Jewish law and tradition</note> that *Saul* was the Prince of the Sanhedrin, and his son *Jonathan* was the <term>Father of the Sanhedrin</term> <note>Hebrew: *Av Beit Din*; the second-ranking presiding officer of the court</note>. *Selden* <note>John Selden, a 17th-century legal scholar</note> adds in Book II, Chapter XVI, Section IV: "As long as and to the extent that the kingdom—whether of Judah or Israel—retained its own customs before the disasters of the exile, the Prince of the Sanhedrin and the King were usually the same person, following the example of Moses, who was the first Prince." *Maimonides* <note>The medieval philosopher and jurist</note> states that *David* was a member of the body of the Great Sanhedrin. And when *Benaiah*, the son of Jehoiada, is described as being in charge of the <term>Pleti and Creti</term> <note>The Cherethites and Pelethites, King David’s elite royal guard</note>, Rabbi *Levi ben Gerson* interprets this as a reference to the members of the Great Sanhedrin, according to the mind of the Sages. They were called *Creti* <note>original Hebrew: שכורתים דבריהם — *she-kortim divreihem*</note> **because they 'cut' their words—that is, they gave brief and decisive commands**; and *Pleti* <note>original Hebrew: שמופלאים במעשיהם — *she-mufla’im be-ma’aseihem*</note> **because they were 'wonderful' in their deeds.** Under the reign of King *Jehoshaphat*, there is an explicit mention of a Senate, whose Prince at that time seems to have been *Amariah* the High Priest, while *Zebadiah, son of Ishmael*, served as the "Father" (2 Chronicles 19:8). During the reign of *Jehoiakim*, son of Josiah, the "Princes of Judah" are narrated to have sat at the entrance of the "New Gate" of the Lord to judge the case of *Jeremiah* (Jeremiah 26:10–11). Moreover, there is a constant tradition that the authority to judge a Prophet belonged specifically to the Great Sanhedrin. Under King *Zedekiah*, the authority of this venerable Senate appears to have been quite powerful, as the King himself declared that he could do nothing against them (Jeremiah 38:4–5). Through *Ezekiel*, it is also said of the Priests, as the leaders in that Senate, in Chapter 44:24: **"In legal cases they shall maintain the law; they shall judge according to my laws, statutes, and decrees."** Yet a little earlier, the same *Ezekiel*, describing the corruption of the people, specifically mentioned the Great Senate, naming seventy elders and their leader *Jaazaniah* (Chapter 8:11). These same people are believed to be the "Officials" with whom King *Jehoiachin* of Judah went out to surrender to the King of Babylon, and who were deported with him to Babylon (2 Kings 24:12).

LXXIV. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, the influential Dutch jurist</note> argues that there is no doubt that these Seventy elders retained their authority among the Jews during the Babylonian exile. They certainly retained their status as *heads of the paternal families* during that time (Ezra 1:5, 8:16, 9:1).

LXXV. Upon returning home, judicial power was granted to them by King Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:25–26). [And that] *Ezra* himself [was] the prin...

Time.

LXXI. Finally, something must be said regarding the <term>TIME OF ASSEMBLY</term>. They sat daily (except on the Sabbath days, when they met in the Synagogue on the Mount, so as not to appear to be meeting for the purpose of holding a trial), and they sat from the perpetual morning sacrifice until the perpetual evening sacrifice; thus, their session and the time of Divine worship never coincided. The morning sacrifice was performed at dawn; the evening sacrifice was ordinarily performed at the eighth and a half hour <note>Approximately 2:30 PM</note> and offered at the ninth and a half hour <note>Approximately 3:30 PM</note>. However, it was not considered necessary for all seventy-one Senators to be present at all times, except when the gravity of the matter required the presence of everyone. At other times, whoever had other business was permitted to leave and return, provided that no fewer than twenty-three were always sitting in attendance.

### Concerning the COUNCILS of the HEBREWS.

<margin>a</margin> ...received [authority] from Eli and his Sanhedrin <note>The Great Council</note>: and David from Samuel and his Sanhedrin. Indeed, where we read in 1 Samuel 6:19 that the people of Beth-shemesh were struck down during the time of Samuel because they had desecrated the Ark with a profane inspection, the text says: **seventy men, fifty thousand men** <note>original Hebrew: *shiv'im ish hamishim elef ish*</note>. This number of seventy is taken by the Rabbinic Masters to refer to the Great Sanhedrin. Hence, *Jonathan* <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets</note> paraphrases it thus: **And he killed seventy men from the Elders of the people, and fifty thousand men from the assembly.** <note>original Aramaic: *Ve-katal be-sabei amma shiv’in gavra u-ve-kahala hamshon alfei gavra*</note>.

LXXIII. It is also recorded in both versions of the Talmud <note>The Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds</note> that Saul was the Prince of the Sanhedrin, and his son *Jonathan* was the Father of the Sanhedrin <note>The "Father of the Court" was the second-highest ranking member</note>. *Selden* <note>John Selden, a famous 17th-century legal scholar</note> adds in Book II, Chapter XVI, Section IV: *For as long as and to the extent that the kingdom, whether of Judah or Israel, retained its own customs before the misfortunes of the captivity, the Prince of the Sanhedrin and the King were usually the same person—unless I am mistaken—following the example of Moses, who was the first Prince.* *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> states that David was part of the body of the Great Sanhedrin. And when *Benaiah*, son of Jehoiada, is said to have been in command over the **Pelethites and Cherethites** <note>2 Samuel 8:18; traditionally the King’s bodyguard</note>, *Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson* interprets this, according to the mind of the Masters, as referring to the men of the Great Sanhedrin. They were called **Cherethites** <note>Hebrew: *Creti*</note> **because they cut short their words, or pronounced their decrees briefly** <note>original Hebrew: *she-kortim divreihem*</note>; and **Pelethites** <note>Hebrew: *Pleti*</note> **because they were wonderful in their deeds** <note>original Hebrew: *she-mufla’im be-ma’aseihem*</note>. Under the reign of Jehoshaphat, there is express mention of the Senate, of which the High Priest *Amariah* seems then to have been Prince, and *Zebadiah*, son of Ishmael, the Father. (2 Chronicles 19:8). Under *Jehoiakim*, son of Josiah, the Princes of Judah are said to have sat at the entrance of the New Gate of the Lord to judge the case of *Jeremiah*. (Jeremiah 26:10–11). It is a constant tradition that the judgment of a Prophet belonged specifically to the Great Sanhedrin. Under *Zedekiah*, the authority of the Senate appears to have been quite venerable, with the King himself declaring he could do nothing against them. (Jeremiah 38:4–5). Through *Ezekiel*, it is also said of the Priests, as the chief men in that Senate in Chapter 44:24: **In controversy they shall stand in judgment; and they shall judge it according to my judgments: and they shall keep my laws and my statutes.** Yet that same *Ezekiel*, shortly before, describing the corrupt morals of the people, specifically mentioned the Great Senate, naming seventy elders and their leader *Jaazaniah*. (Chapter 8:11). These same men are believed to be understood by the name of **Officers**, with whom *Jehoiachin, King of Judah* went out to the King of Babylon, and who were deported with him to Babylon. (2 Kings 24:12).

LXXIV. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> says there is no doubt that during the Babylonian exile, these Seventy retained their authority among the Jews. Certainly, they had the heads of the paternal families at that time. (Ezra 1:5; 8:16; 9:1).

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

...had been the leader, as the Rabbis <note>original: *Magistri*</note> argue in various places. Antiochus threw everything into chaos; later, once liberty was restored by the Hasmoneans <note>The Jewish dynasty that rose to power after the Maccabean Revolt</note>, the supreme authority over all affairs rested with this Senate. For this reason, even the Royal Scepter was kept in the Courtroom.

<margin>
LXXVI. Its authority was diminished by various degrees around the time of Herod.
</margin>

LXXVI. This order remained until the time of Herod the Great, though its authority was gradually diminished in various ways. **I.** By Gabinius, the governor of Syria; who, after Pompey's victory in 55 BC, split the Senate into five parts. He established four other councils in *Gadara, Amathus, Jericho, and Sepphoris*, though they did not have equal power to the one in Jerusalem. These councils were instituted more for the administration of the republic than for judicial matters, and remained subordinate to the Jerusalem Senate. *Josephus, Antiquities, Book XIV, Chapter X.* **II.** By Herod; who, having been forced to answer for his actions in Galilee before King Hyrcanus, later became King himself and removed those judges, as well as the King, with the exception of one man, Sameas <note>Likely referring to the sage Shammai or Shemaiah</note>. Herod held him in honor because of his justice, and because later, when the city was besieged by Herod and Sosius, Sameas advised admitting Herod, arguing that because of their sins they could not escape his rule. *Josephus, ibid, Chapter XVII.* However, *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English Hebraist</note> intervenes with strong arguments from the Talmud, suggesting that not all of them were killed. *On Matthew 2:4.* **III.** Through those various migrations from the Chamber of the Temple <note>The Chamber of Hewn Stones, where the Sanhedrin met</note>, which were discussed above in section LXVI. **IV.** By the removal of the power of capital judgment by the Romans. For when Judea was reduced to a province, it seems to have been established—as in the other provinces of the Roman Empire—that the Senate could not put anyone to death without the consent of the Roman Governor, even while its other judicial powers were preserved. Most scholars refer here to *John 18:31* <note>"It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death"</note>. This is also linked to the confession in the Talmud that capital judgments were taken away from the Senate forty years before the destruction of the Temple. However, *Selden* <note>John Selden, a prominent legal scholar</note> and *Lightfoot* interpret this to mean it happened because of the frequency of murders; since the Senate could not properly punish them, they preferred to abandon their chamber (outside of which such matters could not be judged) so as not to judge at all. Thus, the authority of the Sanhedrin was not extinguished by the Romans, but put to sleep by its own members.

<margin>
LXXVII. It lasted, however, even after Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus.
</margin>

LXXVII. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> believes that this Senate completely perished when Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus. The Hebrews, however, say otherwise; they record that after the destruction of the Temple, *Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai* and *Rabban Gamaliel II* presided over the Sanhedrin at *Yavne* <note>Latin: *Jafne*</note>. *Rabban Simeon*, the son of Gamaliel, is said to have returned to *Usha*. *Rabbi Judah the Holy*, when the Sanhedrin had meanwhile moved to the neighboring city of *Shefaram* <note>Latin: *Sephacham*</note>, transferred it to *Beth-Shearim*. When he fell ill, he was transported to the city of *Sepphoris*, located three leagues from the village of *Nazareth*. Finally, as they relate, with...

...lived on familiar terms with the Emperor Antoninus Pius at Tiberias. <note>The text likely refers here to Rabbi Judah the Prince (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi), the redactor of the Mishnah, who according to Jewish tradition had a close relationship with a Roman Emperor named "Antoninus."</note> See *Cocceius, Commentary on the Gemara of Sanhedrin, Chapter 1, Section 13, Note 9.*

<margin>
LXXVIII. A catalog of the Presidents from the Babylonian captivity until the end.
</margin>

LXXVIII. In order for the reader to have a fuller knowledge of this history, it is helpful to attach a catalog of those who are recorded to have presided over the Sanhedrin from the return from the Babylonian captivity until its destruction. The Hebrews list them in this order:

I. **EZRA**: Who went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Darius. *Ezra 7:8.* This was twenty-four years after the people’s return from Babylon. According to the calculations of certain Hebrew chronologists, he lived until the year in which **Alexander the Great** came to Jerusalem. He died on the tenth day of the month of *Tebeth* <note>The tenth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly December/January</note>, and thus he lived through the transitions of both the Babylonian and Persian Monarchies.

II. **SIMEON THE JUST**, of whom his countrymen tell wonderful stories: that in his time, the scarlet wool on the head of the scapegoat turned white <note>A miraculous sign that the sins of the nation were forgiven on Yom Kippur</note>; that the lot for the scapegoat always came up in his right hand; that the western lamp <note>The central lamp of the Temple Menorah</note> was never extinguished; and that the altar fire always flamed pleasantly. They say that after his death, the power of that fire was greatly diminished. Some identify him with *Jaddo* (Jaddua), but *Josephus* clearly distinguishes them, placing Simeon after Jaddua, with an *Onias* between them.

III. **ANTIGONUS OF SOCHO**. This was his teaching:

> Do not be like servants who serve the Master for the sake of a reward; but be like servants who serve without looking for payment, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.

Two wicked disciples, *Sadoc* and *Baithos*, twisted this into an impious meaning, denying eternal life and the resurrection of the dead. They were the patriarchs of the *Sadducean* heresy <note>The Sadducees were a Jewish sect that rejected the oral law and the doctrine of the resurrection</note>.

IV. **JOSE (JOSEPH) BEN JOEZER**, from *Zeredah* (which was the home of Jeroboam, *1 Kings 11:26*), who had as his Vice-President **Jose ben Jochanan** of Jerusalem. Here the *Talmudic* records begin to name them in pairs—that is, a **President** <term>Nasi: the head of the Sanhedrin</term> and a **Vice-President** <term>Av Beit Din: literally "Father of the Court"</term>. It is not that there were no Vice-Presidents before this, but rather that their names have been lost to time; just as there were others after **Hillel**, though they are never named by the Jews.

V. **JOSHUA BEN PERACHIAH**, President; **NITTAI OF ARBELA**, Vice-President. Joshua lived in the time of King *Jannaeus* <note>Alexander Jannaeus, a Hasmonean king known for his conflict with the Pharisees</note>, a cruel man. Because the King persecuted many of the sages who did not favor his faction with extreme cruelty, Joshua was forced to flee to Alexandria. He was finally recalled through the intercession of **Simeon ben Shetach**.

VI. **JUDAH BEN TABBAI**, President; **SIMEON BEN SHETACH**, Vice-President. It is this Simeon who is believed to have established the **Chamber of Hewn Stone** <note>original: *Conclave cæsi lapidis*; the Hall within the Temple where the Great Sanhedrin met</note>.

VII. **SHEMAIAH**, President, and **ABTALION**, Vice-President. These two were kinsmen and descendants of Sennacherib <note>Referring to a tradition that they were converts or descended from converts</note>, but their mothers were Israelites.

VIII. **HILLEL**, President, and **SHAMMAI**, Vice-President; men most celebrated in their own time...

Teachers of the Law. IX. **RABBAN SIMEON** the son of **HILLEL**. Some believe this was the same man who recognized Christ, took him in his arms, and preached about him. *Luke 2.* <note>The text identifies this Simeon with the biblical figure who performed the Presentation of Jesus in the Temple.</note> X. **RABBAN GAMALIEL**, son of *Simeon*. Under his discipline, Paul was educated. He presided over the Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews</term> when Christ was condemned. However, whether he was present at that specific time remains uncertain. XI. **RABBAN SIMEON**, son of *Gamaliel*. He perished in the destruction of the Temple; and his son would also have been killed had not *Rabban Jochanan Ben Zaccai*, who was in the Emperor's favor, obtained his life through his pleas. Even though the Temple was destroyed, the Sanhedrin survived, though in a weakened state; it continued to have Presidents until its final dissolution. Thus follows XII. **RABBAN JOCHANAN BEN ZACCAI**: whose Sanhedrin sat at *Yavne*. <note>original: "Jafne". Yavne became the center of Jewish leadership after the fall of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> XIII. **RABBAN GAMALIEL** of *Yavne*, Son of Rabbi *Simeon*, whom Rabbi *Jochanan Ben Zaccai* rescued from death. But since he was a minor when his father died, he could not succeed him immediately; therefore, *Jochanan* occupied his place. When Jochanan passed away, *Gamaliel* was made heir to his father’s dignity. XIV. **RABBAN SIMEON**, son of *Gamaliel*. XV. **RABBI JUDAH**, son of *Simeon*, surnamed **THE HOLY**. He compiled the *Talmudic Mishnah*. <term>Mishnah: the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</term> XVI. **RABBAN GAMALIEL**, son of *Rabbi Judah*. With him, the title *Rabban* ceased, and the Sanhedrin was extinguished. *Lightfoot, Description of the Temple, Chapter 22.*

<margin>
LXXIX.
These Talmudic histories regarding their Sanhedrins are not of established truth.
</margin>

LXXIX. Thus far, we have set forth what the followers of Talmudic doctrine have handed down concerning their Sanhedrins. Now let us see what must be determined regarding them based on the actual truth. For it must not be thought that so much authority is to be attributed to the Hebrew Masters that we should immediately admit as certain whatever they pleased to invent regarding the antiquities of their nation. It has been proven by infinite examples that—whether from ignorance of ancient history or from a foolish desire for fabrication and nonsense—many things occur in their writings that provoke either the anger or the laughter of the more learned. Nor are there lacking highly ERUDITE men and critics of sharp discernment who believe that no such "Great Sanhedrin" as described by the *Hebrews* ever existed in their commonwealth, except perhaps from the times of the *Hasmoneans*; <note>The Hasmonean dynasty ruled Judea from roughly 140 BC to 37 BC.</note> let alone that it continued by a perpetual co-option of new Senators from *Moses* all the way to *Herod* or the end of the *Israeli Republic*. They support this opinion of theirs with so many and such great arguments that they seem to me very difficult to ignore for anyone from whom they seek agreement. Therefore, so that the readers of my works may themselves be able to judge what should be decided about this whole business, I will gladly undergo the trouble of first examining the reasons usually brought forward for the continuation of the Sanhedrin, and then I will set forth those which argue against it.

<margin>
80. Those whom one ought not to believe, except insofar as they are confirmed by the Holy Scriptures.
</margin>

80. I do not think anyone well-versed in the Talmudic writings <note>The Talmud is the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> will be so far removed from fairness as to command that something be believed for the sole reason that it has been handed down by the Rabbis. This is especially true if the matters are of the greatest antiquity, preceding the age of those masters by a long series of centuries. It is only right that something be brought forward from ancient records by which their commentaries may be granted, if not the evidence of certainty, then at least some appearance of truth and some degree of probability. However, if we go back to the beginnings of the Israelite Republic <note>The author uses 'Republic' (Respublica) in the classical sense to describe the organized political community of ancient Israel.</note>, no ancient records remain except the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, it must be investigated above all whether those Scriptures teach anything about such a Great Sanhedrin and its continued existence. The Hebrews certainly believe so, and many among the Christians, even the greatest of men, have believed them; but they were led by quite weak reasons. This will become clear from an examination of them.

<margin>
81. The arguments of those who affirm this are examined.
</margin>

81. They say that, in memory of those heads of households whom Jacob led into Egypt, <term>70</term> or <term>72</term> were appointed as prefects over the people to care for their affairs, as far as the royal commands of Pharaoh allowed. But from where do they get this, if not from guesswork? For Moses says <term>not a peep</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲ γρύ" (oude gry). A classical idiom meaning "not even a syllable" or "absolutely nothing."</note> about that matter. He indeed mentions the Elders of Israel, whom he was commanded to address in Egypt: but that they presided over the people with authority, or that they were <term>70</term> in number, and that this was in memory of those who came into Egypt with Jacob—truly, he does not mention that. Nature itself teaches all nations that singular reverence is owed to those who are older in age; and therefore, if any controversy arises, one should recur to those who, endowed with experience in many matters and less subject to those passions which the boiling blood of youth is wont to excite, are rightly believed to be more fit for giving counsel. It is probable that those who are called the "Elders of Israel" were of this sort, possessing authority through persuasion rather than the power of commanding. The argument for this is that once the people were asserted into liberty and led into the wilderness, these elders presided with no power. For Moses alone decided everything at the beginning. Those who in **Exodus 5:14** are called <term>officers</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שֹׁטְרִים" (shotrim). These were foremen or minor officials.</note> or "Moderators of the children of Israel," were not judges administering the republic, chosen by the Israelite people; rather, they were ministers of Pharaoh’s tyranny, appointed by his taskmasters to urge on and ensure the daily quota of labor. I admit that in **Exodus 24:1, 9**, seventy Elders of Israel are praised: but it must be observed that they are called <term>70 from the Elders</term>; therefore, there were many more to whom that name applied, and from whom these were chosen—not for a Magistracy, but to be present with Moses at this solemn enactment of the covenant. Indeed, the words of Moses himself, also cited above, take away from them the authority of a Magistrate: verse 14: *But to those Elders he said: Wait for us here, sitting [until we return]...*

-> # Concerning the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews. <-

<margin>
LXXX.
Those who ought not be believed, except insofar as they are confirmed by the sacred writings.
</margin>

LXXX. I do not think anyone well-versed in the **Talmudic** <note>The body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law and legend.</note> writings will be so far removed from fairness as to command that something be believed solely on the grounds that it was handed down by the **Rabbis**. This is especially true if the matters are ancient, preceding the age of those masters by a long series of centuries. It is only right that something be brought forward from ancient records by which their commentaries might be granted, if not the evidence of certainty, at least some appearance of truth and probability. However, if we go back to the beginnings of the **Israelite Republic**, no ancient records remain except for the **Sacred Scriptures**. Therefore, it must be investigated above all else whether those Scriptures teach anything about such a **Great Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation.</note> and its continuation. The Hebrews certainly believe so, and many among the Christians, even the greatest of men, have believed them; but they were led by very weak arguments, as will become clear from an examination of them.

<margin>
LXXXI.
The arguments of those affirming this are examined.
</margin>

LXXXI. They say that, in memory of those heads of families whom **Jacob** brought into Egypt, seventy or seventy-two overseers were set over the people to look after their affairs as far as the royal commands of the Pharaoh permitted. But from where do they have this, if not from guesswork? For **Moses** says not a single word <note>original: "οὐδὲ γρύ" (oude gry) — a Greek idiom meaning "not even a grunt," or absolutely nothing.</note> about that matter. He does indeed mention the **Elders of Israel**, whom he was commanded to address in Egypt: but he does not mention that they presided over the people with authority, or that there were seventy of them, or that this was done in memory of those who came into Egypt with Jacob. Nature itself teaches all nations that a singular reverence is owed to those who are older in age; therefore, if any controversy arises, people recur to those who—endowed with experience in many things and not so liable to those passions which the boiling blood of youth is accustomed to stir up—are not undeservedly believed to be more fit for giving counsel. It is probable that those who are called the **Elders of Israel** were such men, possessing the authority to persuade rather than the power to command. The proof of this is that, once the people were asserted into liberty and led into the desert, these elders presided with no power. For in the beginning, Moses alone decided everything. Those who are called **Moderators** <note>original: "שֹׁטְרִים" (Shotrim) — often translated as officers or overseers.</note> of the children of Israel in **Exodus 5:14** were not judges administering the republic, chosen by the Israelite people: but were ministers of **Pharaoh’s** tyranny, appointed by his taskmasters to urge on and oversee the daily quota of labor. I confess that in **Exodus 24:1, 9**, seventy Elders of Israel are praised: but it must be observed that they are called seventy *of* the Elders; therefore, there were many more who held that title and from whom these were chosen—not for a Magistracy, but to be present with Moses in this solemn enacting of the covenant. Indeed, the very words of Moses, also praised above, take away the authority of a Magistracy from them: in verse 14, *He said to those Elders: wait for us here until...*

**BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.**

...until we return to you. Behold, Aaron and Hur are with you; whoever has a matter to be discussed should go to them. <note>Exodus 24:14. Moses says this before ascending Mount Sinai.</note> Thus, so far, there is nothing that has the appearance or even the first rudiments of a Great Sanhedrin.

LXXXII. Furthermore, the judges whom Moses appointed on the advice of **Jethro** <note>Moses' father-in-law, a Midianite priest.</note> cannot be referred to any Sanhedrin. For these were neither a council of three, nor of twenty-three, nor of seventy <note>These are the standard sizes for different levels of Jewish courts according to later Rabbinic law.</note>; rather, they were capable men out of all Israel, leaders among the people, chiefs over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. **Exodus 18:21, 25.**

LXXXIII. What is recounted in **Numbers 11:16** comes closer, where it is clear that, by God's command, an assembly of seventy men was established to bear the burden of the people together with Moses. However, this question remains: does this assembly match everything that the **Talmudists** <note>The Jewish sages and scholars of the early centuries CE who compiled the Talmud.</note> claim about their Sanhedrin? Was it established for the purpose of being perpetual? Was it actually continued through so many centuries by a repeated succession of Senators? Was it endowed with such authority over High Priests and Kings? Were those specific cases they describe reserved for it? And many other such claims. Truly, the Mosaic history contains nothing about these matters; nor is it right to believe the **Rabbis**, who add whatever they wish from their own minds regarding things equally unknown to them as to us. Indeed, several things occur in the Mosaic narrative that suggest matters were not as the Masters <note>A common term for the Rabbinic authorities.</note> hand down. The occasion for establishing this Senate was the people’s murmuring against Moses; hence Moses’ complaints to God—that he had not conceived nor given birth to this people, that he was not sufficient to carry them, and finally, that he was not equal to the envy which this rule brought upon him. God, wishing to favor Moses, joined to him seventy of the Elders of Israel, to be imbued with the same Spirit as Moses, to carry the burden of the people with him. Should this not be most conveniently understood as follows: that they were to relieve Moses of a great part of the envy, and by their plurality, as more immediate witnesses of Moses’ actions, they might prevent or restrain such murmurings of the people? For ordinary judgments seem to have been sufficiently provided for by previous arrangements. And this very history testifies that the people did not lack Elders and Officers, from whose number these were chosen. Since the cause for establishing this assembly ceased with the death of Moses and the entry of the people into **Canaan**, what prevents us from suspecting that the assembly itself also ceased? Certainly, we read nothing of its continuation in the Sacred Volumes.

LXXXIV. For as to what God says in **Deuteronomy 17:9**: *And you shall come to the Levitical priests, and to the judge who will be in those days, that you may consult them, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: ובאת אל הכהנים הלוים ואל השפט אשר יהיה בימים ההם</note>—this is not fit to produce in the mind any idea of a perpetual Great Sanhedrin. There

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that the Great Sanhedrin, as described by later Jewish tradition, did not exist during the periods of the Judges or the early Kings of Israel. He argues that the leadership groups mentioned in the Bible were temporary or regional, not the perpetual high court claimed by the Talmudists.</meta>

### On the SANHEDRIN OF THE HEBREWS.

Priests are praised as legal consultants, and some Judge—either an ordinary official or an extraordinary one raised up by God—is mentioned as the person to whom one must go for a decision. However, regarding the specific number of a perpetual and uniform Senate, or the determination of specific cases that would belong to it, there is absolutely nothing in the text. Indeed, the controversies mentioned here—"between one type of homicide and another, between one lawsuit and another, between one physical injury and another" <note>original: "inter caedem & caedem, inter litem & litem, inter plagam & plagam"</note>—were not cases specifically reserved for a Great Sanhedrin, but were matters that could be decided by any other judges whatsoever.

LXXXV. It is indeed narrated that **Joshua**, when he was advanced in age, gathered all the tribes of Israel in the field of the Shechemites, after he had called together the *Elders of Israel, and its Chiefs, and its Judges, and its Officers*, so that they might present themselves before God. **Joshua 24:1.** But there is nothing here that forces us to think of a Sanhedrin. Rather, the words suggest that these Elders, Chiefs, and Judges were summoned by Joshua to Shechem from their individual tribes and cities for this extraordinary business, and were then dismissed, each to his own possession (**verse 28**); it does not suggest that they constituted a single standing body of a Senate that was constantly available to Joshua.

LXXXVI. As for the stories the Hebrews <note>The author refers here to the Rabbinic tradition and the Talmudists.</note> invent regarding the Sanhedrins over which Eli, Samuel, Saul (with Jonathan), David, and other Kings supposedly presided, these betray themselves by their own absurdities. The arguments brought from the sacred scriptures to support them are mere mockeries, unworthy of the dignity of a serious refutation. With what appearance of truth can they claim that **Saul** was the President of the sacred assembly and make **Jonathan** the "Father of the Court"? <note>A specific title in the Sanhedrin, *Av Beit Din*.</note> They use the same logic to transform the *Cherethites and Pelethites* <note>King David's elite foreign bodyguard.</note>—who were actually Praetorian soldiers—into members of the Sanhedrin. How can it be that the Prince of the Sanhedrin and the King are now claimed to be the same person over a long period of time, when elsewhere these same authors deny the King a place in the Sanhedrin, lest he should influence other Senators to his side by the authority of his vote? David could sing, *Judah is my Lawgiver* (**Psalm 60:10**), even if he was not thinking of a Sanhedrin. For from that tribe he was able to find and select prudent and wise men, joined to him partly by kinship and partly by close relationship, through whom he might protect the rights of his Majesty and the Kingdom, even if they were not enrolled in a formal Sanhedrin. **Jehoshaphat** in **2 Chronicles 19** did indeed institute judges in the cities of Judah, and specifically in Jerusalem; but there is no mention here of the Seventy-two or the Seventy. That very institution shows that there was no existing Sanhedrin in the kingdom at that time. Add to this that the Hebrews attribute to the Sanhedrin itself the power to choose its own successors at its own discretion, yet here the King claims whatever authority that is for himself. In **Jeremiah 26:10** and **35:4** and elsewhere, <term>שרים</term> (*Sarim*) or **Princes** are mentioned: but why should we not understand by that name the Chiefs of the people, the "men of the purple," or courtiers? Who could possibly infer the existence of such a Sanhedrin from such a general term using certain logic?

Tom. I. Lll

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION III.

The seventy men shown to Ezekiel in Chapter 8:11 certainly were not endowed with the Spirit of God, nor were they fit for those offices which the Rabbis attribute to the Sanhedrin. Had things fallen so low that those who were commanded above all to root out idolatry—not just a few of them, not just the majority, but all of them in a conspiracy—became leaders of the people into the most foul and wicked idolatry? O brilliant guardians of ancestral traditions, defenders of the Mosaic laws, and depositories of the Divine Kabbalah! <note>The author is using heavy irony here to mock the idea that these corrupt men mentioned in Ezekiel could have been part of a divinely ordained high court.</note> The *Heads of families* <note>original: "Capita familiarum"</note> mentioned in the Book of Ezra do not signify Sanhedrin members, but rather the principal men in each family, as the matter itself demonstrates. Thus, from the examination of all those testimonies usually brought forward to prove such a Sanhedrin as the Talmudists <note>Scholars and teachers of the Jewish Talmud.</note> describe to us, I believe it is clear that neither individually nor collectively do they suffice for a solid demonstration of that matter.

<margin>87. There are many reasons that suggest no such Sanhedrin existed before the Babylonian Captivity.</margin>

LXXXVII. On the contrary, there are many reasons which make it highly probable that no such Sanhedrin existed in the Old Republic of the Israelites. Not in the time of JOSHUA, who governed the Republic by his own authority, without consulting any Sanhedrin in matters of war or peace. Not in the time of the JUDGES, who administered affairs by God’s order and command, with no mention ever of a Sanhedrin. If a Judge raised up by God was lacking, there was no governing authority. Everyone thought they could do whatever they pleased. **Judges 21:25.** Where then was a Sanhedrin of such great power? Not in the time of SAMUEL. For he alone judged Israel with supreme power, traveling now here, now there, as the necessity of the matter required. And he did not appoint any Sanhedrin members, but rather his *sons* as Judges. When they failed to perform their duty as was proper, the *Elders*—that is, the more honored men of the people—came to Samuel seeking a King. **1 Samuel 8:4.** Samuel does not discuss that petition with a Sanhedrin, but with God alone. Nor in this entire business of choosing a King—which, if anything, belonged to a Sanhedrin—did any votes of a Sanhedrin intervene; rather, everything was carried out by the will of God through Samuel alone. Not under the KINGS. For which of the Kings was ever appointed, deposed, or corrected by a Sanhedrin? As the Kings were, so for the most part were the people; we never read that a Sanhedrin carried any weight. The "Right of the King" was described by Samuel. **1 Samuel 8:11 and following.** What business did the Sanhedrin have here with the King? Even if there were nothing else, it is clear from this that what the Masters <note>The author refers here to the Rabbinic teachers.</note> rave about regarding the Sanhedrin's power over Kings—even to the point of flogging them—is mere fiction.

LXXXVIII. <header>BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.</header>

Indeed, at this time, the scrutiny of ancient prophecies <note>original: "vaticiniorum"</note> is particularly timely, provided it is undertaken modestly and soberly and directed toward its legitimate end. Let there be no profane curiosity in such inquiries, nor a reckless boldness in defining things—especially those things which, since they are still in the future and hidden in the secrets of fate, will best be understood when the event itself becomes the teacher. Therefore, seeing others busily engaged in this, I also felt an inclination to examine those things which I found attributed to the *Turks* by celebrated interpreters of the Scriptures. I did not think it would be unwelcome to my students if I communicated these findings to them, arranged in a certain order.

II. It seemed best to organize the work in this way: first, to report the expositions of the *most learned* men with the utmost faithfulness and integrity; *then*, to subjoin the reasons by which those expositions were strengthened by their authors, or seemed to me capable of being strengthened; *furthermore*, I would explain more fully through historical records <note>original: "historiarum monumentis"</note> those things believed to pertain to the fulfillment of these prophecies, which the interpreters, according to the nature of their work, have only pointed toward with a finger; *finally*, using my own liberty, I would judge and disclose what I approve of or find lacking in each interpretation, candidly and modestly, according to my custom and without malice toward anyone. These matters I followed through with no small diligence in public lectures some years ago. However, since that work requires great care for its full presentation—which my current occupations do not allow—I am pleased to present just one *specimen* of our commentary in this exercise. In it, we shall inquire: WHETHER ANYTHING REGARDING THE ORIGIN AND PROGRESS OF THE MUSLIM EMPIRE WAS PREFIGURED IN THE SEVENTH CHAPTER OF DANIEL.

<margin>III. A very famous interpreter believes that the Turkish Empire is represented by the Leopard.</margin>
III. For a very famous interpreter of our age claims to have found in the emblem of the LEOPARD <term>Leopard; original: "Pardo"</term> a prophecy that ought to be referred to this subject. The words of Daniel in verse 6 are as follows: AFTER THIS I LOOKED, AND BEHOLD, ANOTHER LIKE A LEOPARD, AND IT HAD FOUR WINGS OF A BIRD ON ITS BACK; AND THAT ANIMAL HAD FOUR HEADS, AND DOMINION WAS GIVEN TO IT. <note>original: "POSTEA VIDI, ET ECCE ALIUD UT PARDUS..."</note> That these words pertain to the Turkish Empire is gathered from more than one class of reasons. I. Because the series of this vision and its connection with what precedes leads us there. II. Because this description can be applied to no other empire. III. Because everything fits the Turkish Empire exactly. Let us explain each point more carefully.

<margin>IV. Drawing the connection of this vision to that point.</margin>
IV. The sequence and connection of this vision, according to the mind of the celebrated interpreter, are as follows: the goal of the Holy Spirit in this chapter is to teach that four kingdoms would precede the Kingdom which Christ, with His Church,
