### CONCERNING THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

...it will have its own in all lands. That is surely the glorious kingdom, which will consist in the gathering of many and great peoples to the Christian Church; in the subduing or removal of enemies who persecute the truth of the Gospel; in the increase of heavenly wisdom, holiness, joy, and all the gifts of the Spirit; in the abundance of all blessings, even those pertaining to this life, such as are worthy and fitting for the children of God who are kindly regarded by their Father; and finally, in that manifestation of Divine glory and majesty over the faithful, which—however much the world may snarl in opposition—shall wring this confession from it: that Christ reigns in the Church, and the Church in Christ. This is that kingdom described in verse 27: *And the kingdom, and the power, and the majesty of the kingdoms under the whole heaven were given to the people of the Saints.* However, those four kingdoms, which are to immediately precede this kingdom of Christ, belong to the times of *that Fourth Empire*, which was represented to *Nebuchadnezzar* <note>The King of Babylon who dreamt of a statue made of four different metals (Daniel 2).</note> by the legs and feet. Therefore, it is important to observe how this vision of *Daniel* agrees with or differs from the revelation that occurred to *Nebuchadnezzar* in his dreams.

<margin>v. And its relationship to the dream of Nebuchadnezzar.</margin>
V. In the statue of *Nebuchadnezzar*, a synopsis <note>original: σύνοψις</note> of all times is presented through four notable Empires. These follow in this order: the *Babylonian*, *Persian*, *Greek*, and *Roman* Empires. It was also noted that under the *fourth* Empire, Christ would arise, and that he, after he had emerged from his own people, would possess a great kingdom and would finally shatter all opposing kingdoms. However, because great changes were destined to happen in the world while that image stood—or rather, during the final part of the Empire denoted by it—and so that the faithful would not lack instruction concerning those changes, and so that in their own time the *Jews* might be even more powerfully convinced of the kingdom of Christ, another four kingdoms were presented in this 7th chapter. These were to exist in the world before the people of Christ would obtain the kingdom. Thus, many things are explained pertaining to the *fourth* Empire, of which there was either no representation, or a very obscure one, in that earlier image.

VI. But if we think the subject of this riddle <note>original: "aenigmatis"</note> is exactly the same, why is there no mention here of the stone cut from the mountain, as there was in Chapter II, but only a mention of the judgment of Christ carried out under the fourth beast? This is surely a strong argument that all these kingdoms follow the appearance of Christ; nor can the *Persian* or *Greek* Empire be understood through any of these animals. It seems much less possible for the *Babylonian* to be understood: for this dream was shown to *Daniel* in the first year of *Belshazzar*, who was the last King of the *Babylonian Monarchy*.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

Moreover, it was not then the proper time for the *Babylonian Empire* to be depicted in a vision.

<margin>VII. And the designation of the time attributed to the four Beasts.</margin>
VII. Furthermore, one might call what appears in verse 17 almost a final argument: *These great animals, which are four, are four Kings, who SHALL ARISE from the earth.* Since these kings are said to be about to rise, it is clear that none of them existed at the time of *Belshazzar* <note>Latin: Balthazar. The last king of Babylon, during whose reign Daniel received this vision.</note>. If anyone should wish to object to this observation, pointing out that the representation of the Babylonian empire was shown to *Nebuchadnezzar* <note>The King of Babylon (r. 605–562 BC) who dreamt of a statue made of four metals.</note> as he was thinking about future things in the *Golden Head*: let him know that quite different things are said here than there. It is not said there that four empires would exist on the earth, and specifically following a storm of winds blowing on the sea, as it is here. But concerning the first Empire, it is said there: *Chapter II. 38. You are that head of gold*; and concerning the second, verse 39: *And after you shall arise another kingdom.* From this it is concluded that those kingdoms now described by Daniel are those of which none existed while *Belshazzar* was reigning.

<margin>VIII. Finally, the emblem of the great sea tossed by storms.</margin>
VIII. Add that the world is offered here to Daniel as a *Sea*, and indeed *tossed by winds*. In an emblem, the sea signifies *the world without the peaceful cultivation of the Gospel, where there is no sowing of the word of grace, no harvest of the fruits of the Spirit.* The Earth, contrasted with the sea, denotes that part of the world where *the Gospel is peacefully preached*. Therefore, it is signified that throughout this time there would be no *earth or place of habitation for the Church where sowing could take place, or where fruits could be gathered*. It is necessary, then, that the cursed Jewish people—who are *that great mountain burning with fire*, Revelation 8:8 (from which the stone was cut that grows into a great mountain, Daniel 2:34, 35, 45)—*be cast into the sea* before these Kingdoms arise. Furthermore, the *force of the winds upon this great sea* denotes all the commotions in the world through which the *Babylonian, Medo-Persian*, and likewise the *Greek* Empires were overturned: as well as that commotion by which the *Great Mountain was cast into the Sea*, or the *Jewish War* <note>The First Jewish-Roman War (66–73 AD), resulting in the destruction of the Temple.</note>; and thereafter all the wars which the *Romans* waged before they took up the name of Christ. But also those movements through which those four kingdoms came to exist. Thus the meaning of the riddle will be this: the unfruitful world will be shaken by great movements; and many kingdoms will be overturned. Then, finally, a kingdom will arise which will emerge, as it were, from the sea, and will stand upon the land, when the world will have the appearance of the *fruitful land* <note>original Hebrew: תבל (Tebel), usually referring to the inhabited, productive world or the earth as a fertile place.</note>, and will receive the sowing of the word. Then there will still be three other Kingdoms. And only then will the *Kingdom of the Church* be given. These points had to be emphasized more at length so that it might be established from the notation of time that the Empires treated here are those which follow the revelation of Christ and the destruction of the Jewish people, and which more closely precede the glorious Kingdom of Christ on earth. Among these Empires, there can be little doubt that the *Turkish* <note>The Ottoman Empire, often a focal point for Reformation-era prophetic interpretation.</note> power also has its own place.

<margin>IX. The other Beasts, in his view, are not suitable for designating the ancient Monarchies.</margin>
IX. It is not only the notation of time that leads us here, but the very emblems of the Holy Spirit are such that they can scarcely, if at all, be applied to those ancient Monarchies. Since all these kingdoms are compared to one another in such a way that one cannot be understood without the other, necessity itself compels us to point out something about each one, so that the place the *Turkish Empire* <note>The author is likely referring to the Ottoman Empire, which was a dominant power during the time this text was written.</note> should hold among them might be more clearly established. First, it must be proved that the other Empires mentioned here can be so suitably explained that they fall into times far removed from the affairs of the Turks. However, they would be removed from them if, as many believe, the LION meant the *Babylonian*, the BEAR the *Persian*, and the LEOPARD the *Greek* Empire. Therefore, that opinion must be refuted before all else. It is refuted in this manner:

<margin>X. The Lion is not the Babylonian Monarchy.</margin>
X. What is said of the LION and its two wings, their de-feathering <note>Latin: *deplumatio*. The plucking of wings or loss of plumage, interpreted here as a gradual loss of power.</note>, its being lifted up on its feet, and a man’s heart being given to it (Daniel 7: verse 4), does not appear to fit the *Babylonian Empire*. For the arguments made to this end, both by Jews and others, to make these things seem spoken of the Babylonian Empire, are forced. The *Babylonian Empire* was not split in two. Nor did any "de-feathering"—that is, a slow diminishing of glory and strength—take place; rather, it collapsed suddenly. Nor was it, after de-feathering, set upon its feet like a man—that is, reduced to such smallness that it stands as if on a human footprint. For the space covered by the body of an upright man is tiny compared to the space a Lion covers with two wings spread out. Moreover, it cannot be said of the Babylonian Empire that it was diminished and yet left remaining for a time. For the whole was transferred at once by an overthrow from the *Babylonians* to the *Medes* and their *Persian* allies. This observation is of the greatest importance to the case we are making. Indeed, from the correct understanding of this first emblem, the understanding of the others also depends.

<margin>XI. The Bear is not the Persian, nor the Leopard the Greek.</margin>
XI. And indeed, the BEAR, a foul animal, and not at all lovable or honorable, seems hardly appropriate to express that wealthy and magnificent *Monarchy of the Persians*. And, as should suffice here, if the *Lion* does not signify the *Babylonians*, as has just been proved, the *Bear* does not signify the *Persians*. Nor does the LEOPARD signify the *Greeks*. For those Empires are designated which followed one another in immediate succession.

<margin>XII. Nor is the fourth animal the Roman.</margin>
XII. Neither can that FOURTH animal, *dreadful and terrible and exceedingly strong*, denote the whole *Roman* Empire, which certainly existed before the *Turkish* one. For it must be noted that Chapter 13 of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> alludes to this Prophecy. Here is the *Lion*, the *Bear*, the *Leopard*, and another marvelous beast. The Apocalypse attributes to its own Beast something

There is no need to gather many arguments, since an open, simple, and seamless explanation—which corresponds exactly to historical events and the words of the riddle—proves itself by its own merit. According to the mind of a most celebrated Interpreter, it works in this way: The Lion, whose strength, power, and nobility are great, represents the *first Christian Empire*, specifically that of Constantine and his successors. That Beast passed itself off as the Church, was held to be the Church, and was even worshiped. The Eagle is the standard <term>insigne: the military symbol or eagle-standard carried by Roman legions</term> of the Roman army. The wings denote the two great parts that constituted that Empire: the *East and the West*. Compare Revelation 12:14: *There were given to the woman two wings of a great eagle*, which means the two *kingdoms of the Roman Empire*. By the "plucking of the wings" <note>original: *deplumatio*</note>, it is clear that the diminishing of the Empire in both parts, East and West, is signified. This diminishing of the Christian Empire was brought about by the two following animals, alongside which it stood for a time, though in a weakened state. And this

is what is said, *and it was lifted up from the earth, and set on its feet like a man.* It occupied a small space: just as the space of a human footprint is tiny if it is compared to the space which a Lion occupies *with expanded wings.* And *the heart of a man was given to it.* That people ceased to rule and wage wars, and turned itself toward disputations, rhetorical arts, philosophy, and other things which men handle who are not like wild beasts. Thus the Greeks and Romans, as the Empire decreased, devoted themselves to human speculations and discourse. And in this way, all things fit best with the Empire of Constantine and his successors.

<margin>XIV. The Bear: the kingdom of the Goths, who were addicted to the Arian heresy <note>Arianism was a major theological dispute in the early church regarding the nature of Christ's divinity; the Goths were famous converts to this version of Christianity</note>, as well as the Vandals and the Lombards.</margin>
XIV. There follows in the vision another, second animal, like a BEAR, which was raised up on one side. This is understood as the kingdom of the *Goths*, who were addicted to the *Arian* heresy, as well as the *Vandals* and the *Lombards*. This kingdom was more ignoble than the first, and more savage. And so it was said to it, *arise, devour much flesh.* <note>original: "surge, comede carnem multam"</note> This boundary, this limit for it, was described by God. Once it has devoured much flesh, it ceases to be. For if any remnants of the kingdom of the *Goths* remain, they are included in another Beast.

<margin>XV. The fourth animal: the Empire of Charlemagne and his successors in Germany and Gaul.</margin>
XV. It cannot be obscure to a man well-versed in history what times we have now reached, in which the *LEOPARD* <note>original: "PARDUS"</note> ought to have obtained its kingdom. However, before we deal with that—about which we must primarily establish our discourse—come now, let us consider the Empire of the fourth animal; between which and the two preceding ones, the kingdom of the *Leopard* must intervene in the middle, at least as far as its beginnings. The **Muhammadan Kingdom** <note>The early Islamic Caliphate</note> introduced a mixed religion, ignorantly forged from a blend of Paganism, Judaism, and Christianity. # On the Four Beasts of Daniel.

<margin>XXI. And four heads.</margin>
XXI. But the animal also had *four heads*. These signify four principal dynasties. For that many are observed in this Empire. First, the Caliphs of *Baghdad*, in *Syria*. Second, the *Egyptian* Sultans with the *Mamluks* <note>A caste of warrior-slaves who eventually seized the throne of Egypt</note>, in *Africa*. Third, in *Asia*, the *Sultans of Iconium* <note>The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, located in modern-day Turkey</note>. Fourth, in *Greece*, the *Ottoman Turks*.

<margin>XXII. History of the Caliphs of Baghdad and Damascus.</margin>
XXII. The history of these *Caliphates* is briefly as follows. In the beginning of the *Muslim* reign, there was only one *Caliph*. That word signifies *Successor*, and preeminently <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἐξοχὴν"</note> a *Successor in the kingdom*, from which it happened that the *Muslim* Emperors are called simply *Caliphs*. They were also the supreme heads of sacred matters, holding the same position among the Muhammadans as the *Pope* does among Christians: as was observed by *Benjamin* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> in his *Itinerary*, page 64. Regarding this passage, L'Empereur <note>Constantine L'Empereur, a noted scholar of Oriental languages</note> noted that the *Caliphs* conducted themselves in both *Political and Ecclesiastical* affairs in such a way that they personally carried out the duties of both types; they even delivered sacred sermons, which could be confirmed by various examples from *Elmacinus* <note>George Elmacin, a 13th-century historian of the Arab world</note>. The first *Caliphs*, as well as *Muhammad* himself, had the seat of their Empire in the city of BAGHDAD, built from the ruins of *Seleucia and Babylon* at the confluence of the *Euphrates and Tigris*. Later they moved to *Damascus*. However, during the reign of *Marvan II*, who was the nineteenth after Muhammad, someone in Persia from the descendants and branch of *Abbas*—descended from *Abu Bakr*, the father-in-law of Muhammad—named SAPHA or ABUL ABBAS, boasting that he was full of divine spirit and inciting servants against their masters, defeated first the general of Caliph *Marvan*, then *Marvan* himself, and transferred the Caliphate, or sacred empire, to his own family in the year 751 <note>The text uses the archaic numeral IɔCCLI for 751</note>. From this discord, the *Muslim* kingdom was gradually split in two, and two claimed the name of *Caliph* for themselves. One of them moved the seat of the Caliphate back from *Damascus to Baghdad*: and from there he administered the affairs of the *Saracens* through *Syria*, *Persia, and Arabia*; this was, of course, our Sapha or Abul Abbas with his descendants.

<margin>XXIII. In Egypt.</margin>
XXIII. Later, another from the line of *Ali* <note>original: "Halys"</note>, who was the son-in-law of Muhammad, fixed the seat of the Caliphate in EGYPT and AFRICA. For ABDALLA, tracing his lineage from *Ali*, crossed into Africa around the year 808 (as the Archbishop of Tyre <note>The chronicler William of Tyre</note> counts it), and having occupied those regions, he first called himself *Mehedim* <note>The Mahdi, or "Guided One"</note>, as if the *Leveler*, and occupied Sicily with an invincible fleet. Then, having assumed the name of Caliph, he did not wish to appear as a successor of Muhammad—whom he detested—but as the successor of *Ali*. His grandson *Abuthamimus* <note>The Fatimid Caliph Al-Mu'izz</note>, whom others call *Elcainum*, having subjugated Egypt, founded *Cairo* <note>original: "Alcairum"</note> near *Memphis* <note>original: "Menalum"</note>, so named as if it were the "Compeller" <note>The name Al-Qahira means "The Victorious" or "The Conqueror"</note>, by another...

## BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

under the name of *Babylon of Egypt* <note>original: "Babylonem Ægyptiam"; refers to the Roman fortress of Babylon in what is now Old Cairo</note>, and there he established the new seat and court of the *Caliph*. This *Cairene* <note>The Fatimid Caliphate</note> Caliphate persisted until the time of *Shirkuh* <note>original: "Sarraconem"</note> and *Saladin*, who brought the last Caliph in *Egypt* to an end in the year 1173. It happened in this manner: The last of the Caliphs of *Egypt*, being harassed in war by *Amalric*, the sixth King of *Jerusalem*, sought aid from the Sultan of *Syria*, *Nur ad-Din*. He sent an army under the leader *Shirkuh*, which expelled the Christians from all of *Egypt*. This *Shirkuh*, enticed by the wealth of the region, suddenly attacked the Caliph, stripped him of his kingdom, and left him in charge only of sacred rites. Named the *King and Sultan of Egypt*, he established his royal seat at *Cairo*. His nephew through his brother, *Saladin*, abolished the *Cairene* Caliphate—which had already lasted 230 years—and placed himself under the protection of the *Caliph of Baghdad* as the legitimate Pontiff <note>In this context, "Pontiff" refers to the supreme spiritual authority or High Priest of Islam</note>. The Romans <note>Western Europeans</note> call him *Saladin*, but to the Arabs he is *Salah ad-Din*. That name signifies the "restorer of religion."

<margin>XXIV. The end of these gave rise to the Kingdom of the Mamluks.</margin>
XXIV. The origin of the MAMLUKS is traced back to his reign; their Empire in *Egypt* was thereafter notable. To the Arabs, *Mamluk* signifies a slave, an acquired thing, or a servant, whether they are "bought for silver" <note>original Greek: "ἀργυρώνητος"</note> or "captured in war" <note>original Greek: "αἰχμάλωτος"</note>, as *Schindler* advises in his *Pentaglot Lexicon*, and *Joseph Scaliger* in Book III of his *Isagogic Canons*, in the notes on the Dynasty of the Caliphs. The Mamluks, therefore, were purchased bodyguards and servants. For when *Saladin* saw the softness of the *Egyptians*, he detested it. In order to have soldiers he could oppose to the *Europeans* living in *Syria*, he had previously sent every year to the *Circassians*—who live near the *Meotian* marsh <note>The Sea of Azov</note> and were perpetually fighting with the *Tartars*—and bought many select captive youths. He trained them in arms for the exercises of war, but in such a way that they also learned the *Muhammadan* religion. With these soldiers, in the year 1187, he drove the Christians out of *Palestine*. After *Saladin* died, his eight sons (except for *Nur ad-Din*, who claimed dominion over *Aleppo*) were seized and killed by *Saphadin* <note>Al-Adil</note>, his brother. The grandson of Saphadin (through his son *al-Kamil* <note>original: "Melabadino"</note>), named *As-Salih Ayyub* <note>original: "Melechsala"</note>, was the fifth *Sultan of Egypt* of this stock. Having been defeated by the Christians in great battles and distrusting the *Egyptians*, he sought protection chiefly from the *Mamluks*. He chose an excellent band, purchased at no great price, from among the *Tartars*, *Turcomans*, and *Circassians*—who at that time had entered *Armenia* and *Asia* through the *Caspian Gates* and had sold the *Cuman* <note>original: "Comanos"</note> people (who belong to *Cappadocia*) into slavery <note>original: "sub corona vendiderant," literally "sold under a crown," a Roman idiom for selling war captives</note> after defeating them in battle. He opposed these Mamluks to his enemies, and even captured *Louis IX*, the King of *France*, alive at *Damietta* after a great battle in the year 1250. See *Hottinger* on the 13th century, page 196, and *Micrælius*, *Syntagma Politicum*, Book III, Section XI. But these very Mamluks, not long after this victory was won, murdered *As-Salih Ayyub* and invaded the kingdom, and from their own number, after holding...

### ON THE IV BEASTS OF DANIEL.

taking their shared race into account, they chose a *Turkmen* <note>original: "Turquimenium"; likely referring to the first Mamluk Sultan, Izz ad-Din Aybak, of Turkic origin</note>, whom different people call by different names, to preside over the vast kingdom of the Egyptians. They continually restored and greatly increased their army from the *Mamluks*—men who, kidnapped from their own lands, were circumcised after renouncing Christ. A law was established that no one should be admitted to the kingdom or the rank of soldier except those born to Christian parents and imbued with the Christian religion who had afterwards bound themselves to the *Muhammadan* religion <note>Islam</note>. They ruled until they were defeated by *Selim* <note>Sultan Selim I of the Ottoman Empire</note> in the year 1517 and yielded to the *Ottomans* [Othmanidis]. <margin>
XXV. The Caliphate of Iconium.
</margin>
XXV. *Kutlumush*, a kinsman of *Toghrul Beg* <note>original: "Tangrolipicis"; refers to the founder of the Seljuk Empire</note>, laid the foundations of the ICONIAN Caliphate <note>The Sultanate of Rum, based in Iconium, modern-day Konya</note>. His son *Suleiman*, having occupied *Nicaea*, tore apart the *Byzantine* Empire on all sides and fought fiercely with varying fortune against *Godfrey of Bouillon* <note>A leader of the First Crusade</note>. His great-grandson *Kilij Arslan* [Clizaſthlanes] reduced the Emperor *Manuel Comnenus* to the greatest straits; and penetrating even into *Phrygia*, he struck the greatest terror into all the Greeks. But because he had divided the entire Empire among his four sons in his last will, they later possessed little strength due to their divided forces. His grandson was *Alauddin* [Aladinus], who greatly expanded the *Iconian* kingdom. His son, *Ghiyath ad-Din* [Gajazadinus], whom historians testify to have been a Christian, lived during those times when the *Tartars* <note>The Mongols</note>, having spread their forces to the four corners of the world far more swiftly than *Alexander the Great* once did, subdued the principal parts of the world. Among the other kingdoms, they also brought the Sultanate of *Iconium* in *Caria* under their power, despite the vain resistance and the unhappy meeting of *Ghiyath ad-Din* in battle.

<margin>
XXVI. The Ottoman Dynasty.
</margin>
XXVI. The affairs of the OTTOMAN Dynasty are better known than the others. *Osman*, or *Othman*, gave it its beginning around the year 1313 <note>The traditional start date is often cited as 1299; 1313 may refer to a specific expansion</note>. He was born under the omen of dreams and occupied several provinces of Asia Minor, establishing his royal seat in the city of *Prusa*, or *Bursa*. His successors transferred the Imperial seat first to the Thracian city of *Adrianople*, and then to *Constantinople* itself. This occurred in the year 1453, when *Mehmed II* [Mahumetes II] captured that city. This same Ottoman family remains the ruling house among the *Turks* today; and from this comes the name of the *Ottoman Porte*, which is most widely accepted everywhere.

<margin>
XXVII. Under which the Leopard received dominion.
</margin>
XXVII. These four Dynasties, therefore (so that our discourse may finally return to where it diverted), seem to be conveniently understood as the four heads of this Beast <note>Referring to the Leopard in Daniel 7:6</note>. Although we cannot be certain whether yet another Dynasty is to arise among that people, it is sufficient that there are four heads until it receives dominion. For the prophet <note>original: "vates"; referring to Daniel</note> is warned that this, too, shall come to pass.

# ON THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

<margin>
Gulich,
*Sacred Hermeneutics*
Part Two,
Section 95.
</margin>
Prophecy is only a single and continuous body of speech, in which things that come before and things that follow are connected in only one order and series until the end. The method of Prophecy is to return from the end to the principles. Thus, it often pours out the same order of events multiple times and in many ways. What one prophecy says more briefly and as if in a summary—for easier distinction and a firmer memory—another follows through more clearly and with more parts. Certainly, all things pertaining to a particular matter cannot be signified by one single emblem; therefore, God's Wisdom and Kindness use several, so that what was lacking in one picture (no matter how skillful) might be supplied by another no less skillful.

XXXI. It is not necessary to dwell long on this observation, since the whole *Revelation of John* <note>original: *Johannis Apocalypsis*</note> supplies us with the clearest argument. I can express this no better than in the words of that most celebrated Interpreter himself. He says: <margin>On Revelation 1, Section 16.</margin>
> He who compares these parts with one another not too carelessly will clearly see that they deal with the same things in different ways, and that the same things are narrated as if they occurred multiple times. This is the most certain sign that the thread of Revelation is not one single line continued through the whole book, but is, as it were, folded back several times. For things belonging to the earliest times are not shown only in the first chapters, and those of the last times in the last chapters; rather, those distinct sections encompass both the first and the last things—except where episodes <note>original Greek: $\epsilon\pi\epsilon\iota\sigma\acute{o}\delta\iota\alpha$ (epeisodia), referring to incidental scenes or digressions</note> exhibit some more illustrious part of the Prophecy in a new way.

XXXII. But why do we seek examples from elsewhere when we can find them in our own *Daniel*, where they are frequent enough despite the book's brevity? Do we not see the same **Babylonian Monarch** depicted now under the emblem of the **Golden Head**, and soon after under the **Tall and Branching Tree**? Do we not see the same **Dynasty of the Medes and Persians** delineated at one time by the likeness of the **Ram** having two high but unequal horns? The same **Monarchy of the Greeks** represented sometimes through the **Bronze Belly and Sides**, and other times through the **He-Goat** with a **Great Horn** that was soon broken, in whose place four smaller horns arose? Is not the same **Antiochus Epiphanes** signified now by the enigma of the **small horn** (which nonetheless magnified itself excellently toward the South, toward the East, and toward the **glory itself** <note>A reference to the land of Israel</note>), and at other times by the enigma of **someone despised**, to whom they had not granted Royal Majesty, who nevertheless would occupy the kingdom through flatteries while coming in peace? I cease to recount more, as these are known to everyone.

### CONCERNING THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

<margin>Sacred Hermeneutics <note>The study of the principles of interpreting biblical texts.</note>, Latter Part, § 95.</margin>
Prophecy is a single and continuous body of discourse, in which preceding and following events are connected in only one order and series until the end. The method of Prophecy is to return from the end to the beginnings—so says Gulichius <note>Abraham Gulichius (1642–1679) was a Dutch theologian known for his "analytical" method of interpreting prophecy.</note>. Therefore, it frequently presents the same order of things in many different ways. What one Prophecy says briefly and, as it were, in a compendium <note>A concise summary.</note> for easier distinction and more reliable memory, another executes more clearly and in more parts. Evidently, all things pertaining to a certain matter cannot be signified by a single emblem <note>A symbolic picture or vision.</note>; therefore, the Wisdom and Kindness of God uses many, so that what was lacking in one picture—however skillfully made—might be supplied by another no less skillful.

<margin>On Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> I, § 16.</margin>
XXXI. There is no need for us to dwell long on this observation, since the entire *Apocalypse of John* provides us with the clearest evidence: which I shall express in no better words than those of the most Famous Interpreter <note>Likely referring to Johannes Cocceius or Gulichius himself, who argued that Revelation repeats its timeline multiple times.</note> himself. He says:
> *Whoever compares these parts among themselves with some diligence will clearly see that they deal with the same things in one way and then another, and that the same events are narrated as if they happened many times. This is a most certain sign that the thread of the Apocalypse is not one continuous line throughout the whole book, but is, as it were, folded back several times. For the first chapters do not show the things of the earliest times while the last chapters show things of the final times; rather, these distinct sections embrace both the first and the last things, except where interludes* <note>original: ἐπεισόδια</note> *exhibit some more illustrious part of the Prophecy in a new way.*

XXXII. But why do we seek examples from elsewhere rather than from our own *Daniel*, where they are frequent enough given the brevity of the volume? Do we not see the same *Babylonian Monarch* <note>Nebuchadnezzar.</note> depicted now under the emblem of the **Golden Head** <note>In the vision of the great statue in Daniel chapter 2.</note>, and soon after under the emblem of a **Tall and Branching Tree** <note>In the vision of Daniel chapter 4.</note>? Is not the same *Dynasty of the Medes and Persians* outlined at one time by the likeness of a **Ram having two high but unequal horns** <note>In Daniel chapter 8.</note>? Is not the same *Greek Monarchy* figured sometimes through the **Belly and Thighs of Bronze** <note>Daniel 2:32.</note>, and at other times through the **He-goat** with a **Great Horn**—but one soon broken, in whose place four smaller horns arose <note>In Daniel 8, representing Alexander the Great and his successors.</note>? Is not the same *Antiochus Epiphanes* <note>A Hellenistic king of the Seleucid Empire who persecuted the Jews.</note> signified now by the riddle of the **little horn** which magnified itself greatly toward the South, the East, and toward the "pleasant land" <note>Israel; see Daniel 8:9.</note>; and at another time by the riddle of a **certain despised person** to whom they had not given royal majesty, but who would come in peaceably to seize the kingdom through flatteries <note>Daniel 11:21.</note>? I cease to recount more, as these are known to everyone.

<margin>
Is it the same thing—yet not quite the same—that was shown to Daniel and to Nebuchadnezzar?
</margin>
Why should four animals of unusual shape be represented to Daniel? It was in God's interest to reveal these things to Nebuchadnezzar <note>The King of Babylon who had the dream of the Great Statue.</note> so that He might assert His omniscience, His omnipotence, and the fearsome Majesty of His divine power before that proud Prince. It was also in Nebuchadnezzar's interest to have some perspective on the fates of the kingdoms that would succeed him, so that by looking ahead to the future he might reign more prudently; that by remembering the past he might give thanks to God; and finally, that by recognizing the instability of all things, he might learn not to put his trust in the present.

But it was of the greatest importance to the Church that the very things they had learned, in a sense, from the dream of a profane man as reported by Daniel, they might learn again—and more fully—from a new vision granted to the most holy prophet himself. It was repeated to confirm their faith, and expanded for their more abundant instruction. For these emblems <note>The symbolic animals: the lion, bear, leopard, and terrifying beast.</note> contain many details that were not prefigured in that way by Nebuchadnezzar’s statue. Therefore, unless something else stands in the way, it should by no means be considered improbable that the fates of the same Monarchies are now being represented to Daniel which were represented to Nebuchadnezzar at another time and under a different image.

<margin>
XXXIV.
For it is no obstacle that there is no mention here of the stone cut from the mountain.
</margin>
XXXIV. But, says the **Most Learned Man** <note>This likely refers to a contemporary scholarly opponent who argued that Daniel 7 must describe a later time period than Daniel 2.</note>, there is a primary obstacle: no mention is made here of the *stone cut from the mountain* <note>original: "lapidis de monte excisi". A reference to Daniel 2:45, traditionally interpreted as the Kingdom of Christ or the Church destroying earthly empires.</note>, as there was in chapter II. He argues this is a significant enough reason to believe all these kingdoms follow the appearance of Christ. However, what seems like a significant argument to that Most Learned Man appears to me to be utterly small and weak. Just as in the **Apocalyptic Emblems** <note>The symbols found in the Book of Revelation.</note> that warn of the same events, yet are not all identical, so it is here. The Most Learned Man himself judges that the seven *Letters*, the seven *Seals*, and the seven *Trumpets* agree with one another in such a way that they describe the history of the same time period in order. Yet how many things are written in the *Letters*, and sounded through the *Trumpets*, about which the *Seals* say nothing? 

Is it permitted for me to conclude in this way: because nothing appears in the first *Seal* regarding the persecutions and patience of the Church, nor anything about the loss of their first love (which are discussed in the first *Letter*); and nothing about the hail and fire mixed with blood, or the storms by which the Jewish Republic was tossed before the peace they had with the Romans was dissolved (which are proclaimed by the first *Trumpet*); therefore, this is a significant enough argument that the first Letter, Seal, and Trumpet do not describe the exact same times? Certainly, such a conclusion would not be permitted—neither by the logic of the Most Learned Man, nor by right reason. This is because different things can be said about the same events and the same times. Let that same logic be applied to the argument we are now examining. In both places—in Chapter II as well as Chapter VII of Daniel—the same kingdoms are described, as will be proven by comparison; but not all the same things are predicted about those same kingdoms. In this vision, however, the Spirit of God found it sufficient to assume those things as a foundation, intending to explain more fully those matters which pertain to His glorious kingdom. <margin>XXXV. Or that it might not seem timely for the rise and progress of the Babylonian empire to be depicted under the reign of Belshazzar.</margin>
XXXV. There is a greater argument brought forth from the consideration of timing. Certainly, this dream was presented to Daniel in the first year of Belshazzar <note>original: "Balthazar"</note>, who was the last ruler in the **Babylonian Monarchy**. Was it then timely to depict the rise and progress of the **Babylonian** empire in a vision? This objection certainly has an appearance of validity: but it will vanish once we observe that it sometimes happens in prophecies that present and past things are represented for the sake of continuity and the link with future things.

<margin>XXXVI. For prophecy is accustomed to represent past things because of their link with future things.</margin>
XXXVI. In the **Revelation** <note>The Apocalypse of John</note> this is most evident. It was given to **John** while he was an exile on **Patmos**, during the time of **Domitian**, after **Jerusalem** <note>original: "Hierosolyma"</note> had been destroyed; yet, at that time, the birth of **Christ** was represented to him, as well as the oppression of the **Jewish Commonwealth** by **Pompey**, **Gabinius**, and **Herod**, who had taken authority away from the judges: the reduction of **Judea** into a province of the **Romans**: the resurrection of **Christ** from the tomb and death, and His ascension into heaven—at least if we follow the commentary of the Most Learned Man <note>A reference to Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a famous federal theologian known for his work on prophecy.</note> on *Revelation 12*. Again, in the opening of the first seal, the first preaching of the Gospel was represented, which took place during a time of world peace: and in the opening of the second seal, the taking away of peace from the Jewish people by **Gessius Florus**, the procurator of the Emperor **Nero**, who was the first to ignite the Jewish war. *Revelation 6:1-4.* Let me now ask in my turn: was it then "untimely" to depict for **John** in a prophetic vision those things which he himself had already witnessed with his own eyes and ears? It was, without a doubt, timely, because it so pleased Divine wisdom. Nor is the reason obscure; for in this way the connection <term>nexus</term> of things is shown; events which are found to have already happened provide faith for those yet to happen; and in all things taken together, the harmony of Divine wisdom shines most clearly, while He indicates the end from the beginning. *Isaiah 46:10.*

<margin>XXXVII. As Cocceius himself observes.</margin>
XXXVII. But no one has solved the difficulty he raised better than the Learned Man <note>Cocceius</note> himself; for these words of his are more than sufficient. *Observe*, he says, *that the Apocalyptic visions do not only display things which were to be in the future after the time of the vision; but also those which already stood out then. For, to use an example, in Chapter 12, the advent of Christ and His Ascension into heaven are displayed: which had already happened then. He derives future things from past events, and displays the whole order of the affairs of the kingdom.* Just as, when **Nebu-**

<margin>Why should the same things, yet not exactly the same, be shown to Daniel as were shown to Nebuchadnezzar?</margin>
Why should four animals of unusual shape be shown to Daniel? It was in God's interest to reveal these things to Nebuchadnezzar to assert His omniscience, His omnipotence, and the fearsome majesty of His divinity before that proud Prince. It was also in Nebuchadnezzar's interest to have some perspective on the fates of the kingdoms that would succeed him; thus, looking toward the future, he might reign more prudently; mindful of the past, he might give thanks to God; and finally, recognizing the instability of all things, he might learn not to trust in present circumstances. But it was of the greatest interest to the Church that the same things they had learned, through Daniel’s reporting, from the dream of a profane man <note>Referring to the pagan King Nebuchadnezzar.</note>, they should learn a second time, and more fully, from a new vision given to the most holy prophet. Unless some other obstacle exists, it should by no means be considered improbable that the fates of the same Monarchies are now represented to Daniel which were represented to Nebuchadnezzar at another time and under a different image.

<margin>XXXIV. For it is no objection that no mention is made here of the stone cut from the mountain.</margin>
XXXIV. But, says the most learned man <note>The author is likely addressing a specific scholar, such as Joseph Mede or Grotius, who held a different view of prophetic timelines.</note>, a primary objection is that no mention is made here of the *stone cut out of the mountain* <note>original: "lapidis de monte excisi"; this refers to the Kingdom of God in Daniel 2:45.</note>, as there was in Chapter II. He argues this is a significant enough reason to believe all these kingdoms follow after the appearance of Christ. However, what seems a significant argument to that most learned man appears to me quite meager and weak. For just as in the Apocalyptic emblems <note>The visions found in the Book of Revelation.</note> which warn of the same events, not all the details are identical; so it is here. That most learned man believes that the seven *Letters*, the seven *Seals*, and the seven *Trumpets* agree with one another in such a way that they describe the history of the same time period in order. Yet how many things are written in the *Letters* and sounded by the *Trumpets* about which the *Seals* say nothing? Is it permitted for me to conclude in this way: because nothing appears in the first *Seal* regarding the persecutions and patience of the Church, or the loss of their "first love" (which are discussed in the first *Letter*); and nothing is said of the hail and fire mixed with blood, or the storms by which the Jewish Commonwealth was shaken before the peace they held with the Romans was dissolved (which are heralded by the *First Trumpet*); is this a significant enough argument to say that the first Letter, Seal, and Trumpet do not describe the exact same times? Surely such a conclusion would not be allowed, neither by that learned man nor by right reason. For different things can be said about the same events and the same times. Let that same logic be applied to the argument we are now examining. The same kingdoms are described in both places, in Daniel Chapter II as well as Chapter VII, as will be proven by comparison; but not all the same things are predicted about those same kingdoms. In this vision, however, the Spirit of God was content to assume them, intending to explain more fully those things which pertain to His glorious kingdom. Prophecy is not accustomed to repeating everything, even when it *repeats much*.

<margin>
XXXV. Or that it might not seem timely for the rise and progress of the Babylonian Empire to be depicted under the reign of Belshazzar.
</margin>
XXXV. A greater argument is drawn from the *consideration of time*. To be sure, this dream was shown to Daniel in the first *year of Belshazzar*, who was the last king in the Babylonian Monarchy. Was it then timely to depict the rise and progress of the Babylonian Empire in a vision? This objection certainly has the appearance of truth, but it will vanish when we observe that it sometimes happens in prophecies that present and past things are represented for the sake of continuity and connection with the future.

<margin>
XXXVI. For prophecy is accustomed to represent past events because of their connection with the future.
</margin>
XXXVI. In the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> this is most evident. It was given to John while he was exiled on Patmos during the time of Domitian, after the destruction of Jerusalem; yet even then, the birth of Christ was represented to him, along with the oppression of the Jewish Republic by Pompey, Gabinius, and Herod, who had taken authority away from the judges. It showed the reduction of Judea into a Roman province, the resurrection of Christ from the grave and death, and His ascension into heaven—at least if we follow the commentary of the Most Learned Man <note>A reference to Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a famous Dutch theologian known for his "federal theology" and his work on the Book of Revelation.</note> on Revelation 12. Again, in the opening of the first seal, the first preaching of the Gospel performed in the peace of the world was represented; and in the opening of the second seal, the removal of peace from the Jewish people by Gessius Florus, the procurator for Emperor Nero and the first to ignite the Jewish War (Revelation 6:1–4). May I now ask in my turn: was it then timely to depict to John in a prophetic vision those things which he himself had already experienced with his own eyes and ears? It was, without a doubt, because it so pleased Divine wisdom. But the reason is not obscure; for in this way the connection of things is shown. Things that are discovered to have already happened provide faith for those yet to happen; and in all these things taken together, the harmony of Divine wisdom shines most brightly while it indicates *the end from the beginning* (Isaiah 46:10).

</margin>

For, to use an example, in Chapter 12, the coming of Christ and His Ascension into heaven are displayed, which had already happened by then. It leads future events out of past deeds and displays the whole order of the matters of the kingdom.*" Just as, when Nebuchadnez-

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

[Nebu]chadnezzar, what would happen in the future, and God wished to show it to him (Daniel 2:29). He saw an image whose head was he himself (verse 38). What remains but for us to apply this observation to our present purpose? When God wished to show Daniel the order of the Empires in which the affairs of the Church were to be entangled—so that future events might be deduced from what had already occurred—He first presented to him the image of the Babylonian Empire, even though it was then verging toward its end. Indeed, without considering the Babylonian Empire, the rise of the Medo-Persian Empire could not be properly understood.

<margin>XXXVIII. Those things which are future in most of their parts are spoken of as being absolutely in the future.</margin>
XXXVIII. "Quite right," you might say, "unless there were a very strong obstacle in what the text expressly says: that the four Beasts are four Kings **WHO SHALL ARISE FROM THE EARTH** <note>Daniel 7:17</note>. From this, it seems clear that none of them existed at the time of Belshazzar." However, it must be understood that a vision of this kind is like a complex whole; since the majority of its parts are in the future, the whole is said to be in the future through a common figure of speech called *synecdoche* <note>original: "synecdoche" — a rhetorical device where a part represents the whole or vice versa.</note>. The Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> of John again provides us with examples. Its first and universal inscription reads: *The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show to His servants: **THINGS WHICH MUST SHORTLY COME TO PASS.*** And yet, a subdivision of the matters treated appears in Chapter 1:19: *The things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter.* Similarly, in Chapter 4:1, John sees an open door in heaven and hears a voice like a trumpet speaking with him, saying: *Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be hereafter.* Yet you would wrongly conclude from this word that none of those things existed in John's time. For among the things shown, some were then existing, and many had been done long before.

<margin>XXXIX. This was also noted by Cocceius.</margin>
XXXIX. Let it not be a burden to set down again the words of that Most Learned Man <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and his focus on biblical prophecy.</note>, which we approve of wholeheartedly. He says: "There are some things in this Prophecy that were already standing; some were imminent, which would occur in an uninterrupted series until all were fulfilled. At the beginning, he said: 'things which must happen quickly.' Nevertheless, in those things which he saw, he included things that were already then in existence, as he says in verse 19: *ha eisi, kai ha mellei ginesthai meta tauta* <note>original Greek: "ἃ εἰσι, καὶ ἃ μέλλει γίνεσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα" — "the things which are, and the things which are about to happen after these."</note>." *The things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter.* Properly speaking, an <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>original: "Ἀποκάλυψις" — literally an "unveiling" or revelation of hidden things.</note> or revelation pertains to those things which had not yet happened, and the revelation looked chiefly to these; but it shows them connected with their already existing beginnings, lest the reader should remain in doubt as to when those future events would occur and what the order of things was.

<margin>XL. A similar example in Daniel 2:29.</margin>
XL. As we have done several times now, let us return from the Apocalypse to Daniel, in whom we find a twin and related example. In Daniel 2:29, when the Prophet was about to explain the subject of the dream that had been presented to Nebuchadnezzar, he began as follows: *As for thee, O King, thy*—

### ON THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

...your thoughts rose upon your bed concerning what would happen hereafter; and He who reveals secrets has made known to you what is to be <note>Daniel 2:29</note>. Certainly, anyone who wishes to infer from this that nothing the King was warned about existed at the time of his dream would be acting with too much haste. For where Daniel explains the individual parts of the vision, he divides the things represented into those that are present and those that are future in verses 37, 38, and 39. Regarding the present, he says: *You, O King, are that head of gold.* Regarding the future: *After you shall arise another kingdom, etc.* 

To be sure, a most learned man <note>The author likely refers to a contemporary scholarly opponent here.</note> objects that one thing is said here and another there; but, I ask you, what is the difference? He insists that it is not said *there* <note>Referring to the vision in Daniel 7</note> that the four Empires are things of the future. On the contrary, I argue that the entire point of the dream is stated to be the revelation of future things. Nevertheless, Daniel demonstrates from the matter itself that not everything is to be assigned to the category of the future for that reason. 

From this we form a strong argument: some visions are proposed under a general title of "future things" which, as a single whole, encompass many parts, some of which may already be present or even past, while the majority are future. Therefore, when the Angel says to Daniel in Daniel 7:17: *These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, who shall arise from the earth,* we will properly interpret it, according to the prophetic style, as follows: This vision of the four beasts represents to you a series of four great Empires, which shall arise one after another. This remained true even if the first already existed, since the second was soon to be born from its ruins.

<margin>XLI. It is incorrectly concluded from the emblem of the Sea that the Jewish people were dispersed among the nations before the rise of these Empires.</margin>

XLI. Nor is there any support for this new explanation in the fact that this world is presented to Daniel as a Sea, and indeed one *tossed by the winds.* It is suggested that this riddle signifies a world without the peaceful worship established through the *Gospel.* From this, a second conclusion is drawn: that during this time there would be no land or place of habitation for the *Church.* And a third: that it was necessary for *that great mountain burning with fire*—that is, the cursed Jewish people—to have been *thrown into the sea* (Revelation 8:8) before these kingdoms arose. 

However much I have sharpened the edge of my intellect here, I have been unable to detect any probable connection between the premise and the conclusion. Just because the sea is tossed by winds, does it therefore follow that no land exists? Is it not possible for four Empires to arise from the sea—that is, if you wish, from the midst of Gentilism <note>original: "gentilismo" — the state of being a Gentile or pagan, outside the biblical covenant.</note>—even if there is some land where God has His seed and harvest? Why can empires not arise from the sea unless a mountain is first thrown into the sea (meaning the Jews dispersed among the Gentiles)? Did not those ancient Monarchies—the Babylonian, Medo-Persian, Greek, and Roman—arise from the sea in this sense? That is, did they not arise from those parts of the world where there was no worship of the Gospel?

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

<margin>XLII. *The Sea here signifies a collection of peoples.*</margin>

XLII. However, even this has not persuaded that most learned man <note>likely referring to a contemporary scholarly opponent who argued for a strict literal distinction between sea and land</note> that "the Sea" is opposed to "the Earth" in this sense here. I am not disputing now what might be the case elsewhere. Here, certainly, Daniel does not distinguish the earth from the Sea in that way. For the animals he saw rising from the Sea in verse 3 signify the *Kings arising from the Earth* in verse 17. Therefore, the Sea is an emblem <note>a symbolic representation</note> of the Earth here. Specifically, Prophecy calls a collection of many great peoples the *Sea*, or a multitude of waters. *The Sea itself rose against Babylon, it shall be covered by the roar of its waves* <note>Jeremiah 51:42</note>. Revelation 17:15 says: *The waters you saw, where the Prostitute sits, are peoples, and crowds, and nations, and languages.* Isaiah 8:7 states: *Behold, the Lord will cause the waters of that river, strongest and widest, to rise against them: the King of Assyria and all his glory.* Jeremiah 46:7–8: *Who is this that rises like a stream, like rivers whose waters are stirred? It is the Egyptian, who rises like a stream.* Add also Psalm 124:4–5 and 144:7. And so, these animals arise from the Great Sea, that is, from the indiscriminate mass of many men and peoples; four Empires were born, and they showed themselves to be seen in a tumultuous world, which serves as a vast theater of shifting fortunes.

<margin>XLIII. *The Winds signify great armies.*</margin>

XLIII. Furthermore, the *Winds, which made an onset upon this great sea*, signify great, swift, and powerful armies, wandering through the world, rushing at everything in their path or in opposition, leveling them, stirring great movements in the world, and giving those empires their origin, preservation, activity, or even their end. For Prophecy uses the emblem of Winds in this sense. Jeremiah 4:11–12 says: *At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem: a clear wind from the high places in the desert, a way to the daughter of my people; not for winnowing, nor for cleansing; a full wind, stronger than those, shall come for me.* This denotes the army of the Babylonians (as can be gathered from verses 6 and 7) about to bring destruction to the towns situated on the hills, and even to the temple itself down to its very floor, as if a wind had carried it away. Again, in Jeremiah 49:36: *I will bring against the Elamites the four winds from the four ends of the heavens, and I will scatter them into all those winds, so that there will be no nation where someone driven out from Elam does not reach.* This riddle of the winds is explained in the following verse: *and I will make the Elamites terrified before their enemies, and before those seeking their life.* Again, in Jeremiah 51:1: *Behold, I am about to rouse against Babylonia, and against those who inhabit the heart of those rising against me, a destroying wind.* This is explained in verse 2: *And I will send against Babylonia winnowers <note>original: "ventilatores" — those who separate grain from chaff, used here to describe soldiers who scatter a population</note>, who will winnow her.* Finally, Hosea 13:15: *The East Wind <note>original: "Eurus"</note> will come, the wind of Jehovah rising from the desert, and its fountain will be put to shame, its stream will dry up: he will plunder the treasure of all desirable vessels.*

# ON THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

<margin>XLIV. Why the same Empires were represented to Nebuchadnezzar in the form of a Human Statue, and to Daniel under the form of beasts.</margin>
XLIV. So far, therefore, we have encountered nothing that prevents us from explaining Daniel’s vision as referring to those four ancient Empires. Let us see if the remaining details also align. It is not without reason that these Empires are presented to the holy Prophet under the form of *Beasts*. For here the Prophet beholds what Nebuchadnezzar had not seen. To the latter <note>King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, as described in Daniel chapter 2</note>, the future Empires were shown under a *Human* face—stately, grand, and splendid—because he held Empires in high esteem and regarded them as his Gods, who were typically worshipped through statues. But to Daniel, these same things appear under the image of *Wild Beasts*; for the Prophet knew that all those Empires were instruments of idolatry, and consequently of the Devil. Furthermore, many things perpetrated within them were irrational, inhuman, and monstrous; though they may be adorned with the beautiful pretext of the <term>Commonwealth</term> <note original: "Reipublicæ">In this context, it refers to the organized state or political order, which rulers often used to justify their actions</note>, they are nonetheless more worthy of beasts than of man.

<margin>XLV. Scripture compares the Assyrian kingdom to a Lion.</margin>
XLV. The first Beast, like a LION but equipped with Eagle's wings, what it signifies the Holy Spirit Himself sufficiently explains; for He more than once depicts the Kingdom of the ASSYRIANS and BABYLONIANS with this comparison. Of the Ninevites <note>The capital of the Assyrian Empire</note> it is said in Nahum 2:11–12: *Where is the lions' den, and the pasture of the young lions? Where the Lion, the Lioness, and the Lion's cub used to go, with no one to make them afraid? The Lion tearing enough for his cubs, etc.* After the Babylonians had conquered these, they themselves are called Lions. Isaiah 5:29: *Their roaring is like that of a monstrous Lion, and roaring like young lions they shall growl, and seize the prey, and carry it off to the forest, and no one shall rescue it.*

<margin>XLVI. Eagle's wings are attributed to the same for their swiftness.</margin>
XLVI. Eagle’s wings denote the speed of the victories with which the Babylonians traversed not only neighboring but also the most distant nations. Isaiah 5:26–27: *Behold, they come swiftly, with speed. None shall be weary, none shall stumble among them; they shall not slumber nor sleep; neither shall the belt of their loins be loosed, nor the strap of their sandals be broken.* Jeremiah 4:13: *Behold, he comes up like clouds, and his chariots like a whirlwind; his horses are swifter than Eagles.* Jeremiah 48:40: *For thus says Jehovah: Behold, he shall fly like an Eagle, and spread his wings over Moab.* Jeremiah 49:22: *Behold, like an Eagle ascending he shall fly, and spread his wings against Bozrah.* Add Ezekiel 17:3: *A great eagle with large wings, long-winged, full of feathers, which had divers colors:* which the Lord Himself teaches was spoken concerning the king of Babylon in verse 12. Indeed, it is not unlikely that the ancient Assyrian Kings had a golden eagle with extended wings as a Royal ensign—as the Persian Kings did after them—and that Scripture alludes to this when it designates them by the name of Eagles. However, there is no necessity for us to conclude that the Empire was divided <note original: "bifidum">literally 'split in two'</note> simply because two wings are attributed to it, since the requirement of the riddle is fully satisfied by the meaning of swiftness.

XLVII. The plucking and tearing out of the wings, by which they were accustomed to [raise themselves] from the earth...

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the first beast in Daniel’s vision (the lion with eagle’s wings), specifically focusing on the meaning of the wings being plucked and the beast being given a human heart and standing on human feet, signifying the decline of the Babylonian Empire after Nebuchadnezzar.</meta>

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

<margin>The plucking of the wings signifies a loss of ornament and speed.</margin> [The act of plucking the wings] signifies a reduction of splendor, swiftness, and strength; whether this happens slowly or suddenly is not entirely relevant to this matter. Certainly, *Cicero* did not imply a slow deprivation of his dignity when he wrote to *Atticus*: *those who had clipped my wings do not want them to grow back* <note original: "qui mihi pennas inciderant, nolunt easdem renasci">. It is well established that after Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian Empire lost much of its authority. In place of boldness came fear; in place of speed came sluggishness; in place of victories came frequent retreats, accompanied by disasters. In Nebuchadnezzar’s descendants—as almost all historians note—hardly any sparks of the ancient courage or nobility shone forth. None of them are found to have even thought about extending the borders of the Empire; but while they vied with each other in surrendering to laziness and lust, from that point onward all things began to ebb and slip backward. See, if you please, *Josephus in the first book of Against Apion*.

<margin>XLVIII. The feet and heart of a man signify slowness and cowardice.</margin> XLVIII. To the same point belongs the statement that the beast *stood on its feet like a man*, and that *the heart of a man was given to it*. *Feet* are contrasted with *wings*; *standing* with *flying*; *man* with the *eagle*; the *heart of a man* with the *spirit of a lion*. This teaches us that a restraint was placed upon that course of victories; once that eagle-like flight of Nebuchadnezzar was finished, his successors were equipped not with wings, but only with feet. With these, they did not run to invade further territories, but stood still, content with their ancestral wealth—not out of a sense of justice, but through sheer inertia—acting neither with foresight nor courage. *Man* here is not contrasted with the *Lion* as a "rational animal" is to a "beast," but as someone unversed in war <term>imbellis</term> and idle compared to the strong and high-spirited. For the Lion is a symbol of courage. *Judges* 14:18: *What is stronger than a lion?* *Proverbs* 30:30: *A lion, the strongest among beasts, who does not turn back for fear of anyone.* Hence, concerning *Saul and Jonathan* in 2 *Samuel* 1:23: *They were swifter than eagles, and stronger than lions.*

However, "Man" is sometimes a name used to denote a lack of military spirit. *Isaiah* 2:22: *Stay away from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for of what value is he?* But this weakness is most notably indicated by the word *Enosh* <note original: "אנוש">Enosh</note>, which Daniel uses here. It is a name for man derived from deplorable misery, for *Enosh* signifies one who is sick and incurable. It was for this reason that Seth named his son. *Genesis* 4:26. The Church prays in *Psalm* 9:21 that her enemies may experience this through their own ruin: *let the nations know they are but men* <note original: "ידעו גוים אנוש המה">yedu goyim enosh hemmah</note>. The *Heart of a Lion* is an intrepid spirit. 2 *Samuel* 17:10: *Even the most valiant, whose heart was like the heart of a lion.* In Greek, you would say this with the single word *leontothymon* <note original: "λεοντόθυμον">lion-spirited</note>, or *thymoleonta* <note original: "θυμολέοντα">lion-hearted</note>; just as the poets call Hercules and Achilles "lion-hearted." The *Heart of a Man*, if compared to a Lion, is mere smallness of soul; a *sick and languishing heart* <note original: "לב אנוש">lev enosh</note>. *Jeremiah* 17:9.

XLIX. This <term>metamorphosis</term> <note original: "μεταμόρφωσιν">transformation or change of form</note>, if we may call it that, the Babylo—

### ON THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

...the Babylonians. Those once fierce and strong lions under Nebuchadnezzar, having soon put aside all their ferocity, served the Persians in abject slavery, just like spiritless men and trembling slaves. Xenophon
<margin>Xenophon notes this regarding the conquered Babylonians.</margin>
<margin>Xenophon notes this "proclamation."</margin>
<margin>Cyropædia, Book VIII.</margin>
*Cyrus proclaimed that the Babylonians should till the land, pay tribute, and serve those to whom each of them had been assigned. But he ordered that the Persians, and those who shared in his rule, and as many of the allies as chose to remain with him, should be spoken to as masters of those they had received.* <note>original Greek: "Κῦρος Βαβυλωνίους μὲν τὴν γῆν ἐργάζεσθαι... προηγόρευε διαλέγεσθαι."</note> Cyrus decreed that the Babylonians must work the fields, pay taxes, and show obedience to those to whom they were individually handed over. However, he commanded that the Persians, their partners, and those allies who wished to stay with him, should speak as masters to those placed under them. What is "violent" or forced in this explanation, as a certain most learned man charges? On the contrary, what could be said that is more consistent with the style of the Scriptures and the actual events of history?

<margin>L. The Bear is the emblem of the Medo-Persian empire.</margin>
L. If the Babylonian Empire is signified by the Lion, as we have proven from the clarity of the analogy, then the facts themselves dictate that the **MEDO-PERSIAN** empire, which succeeded the Babylonian, is to be understood by the **BEAR**. Nor is the analogy obscure. The **BEAR** is slower, more awkward, and less noble than the Lion, yet it does not yield to the Lion in greediness, cruelty, or ferocity. In the same way, the Medo-Persian Empire was somewhat inferior to the Babylonian in its virtues and successes. For this reason, in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, *a Silver Breast is placed beneath the Golden Head*. I will pass over many other comparisons for now, which can be seen individually in the works of their respective authors, for that is not our current task.

<margin>LI. To which everything said of the Bear fits perfectly.</margin>
LI. As for the statement that the beast *stood on one side* <term>ve-lishtar chad haquimat <note>A transliteration of the Aramaic/Hebrew phrase וְלִשְׁטַר חַד הֳקִמַת from Daniel 7:5, meaning "it raised itself up on one side."</note></term>, it allows for various interpretations. It does not seem far-fetched to understand this as the humble beginnings of the Persians, who were confined to their mountains—*like bears lurking in mountain dens* <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἀν’ ὤρεα φωλάδες ἄρκτοι"</note>—living far removed from trade with other nations. They owed the first fame of their name and empire to Cyrus. But soon, with new courage filling their hearts, they joined the Medes to themselves, then subjugated the Babylonians, and forced many other nations to obey them.

LII. And this is what is hinted at by those *three ribs* which this Bear held in its mouth between its teeth. These clearly represent three great and powerful kingdoms located at three corners of the world: the West, the North, and the South. For the vision in the following chapter lends light to this enigma; there, the same Persian Empire is shown under the symbol of a *Ram*, striking with its horns toward the *Sea* (that is, the West), the *North*, and the *South* (Daniel 8:4). To the West belong the islands of the Mediterranean Sea, most of which were subject to the Persians, as can be seen from Xerxes' war against the Greeks. Who—

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the first beast in Daniel’s vision—the Lion representing the Babylonian Empire. It focuses on the symbolic "plucking of wings" and the "human heart" given to the beast, representing the decline of the empire after the death of Nebuchadnezzar.</meta>

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

<margin>The plucking out of the wings signifies a reduction in ornament and swiftness.</margin>
The plucking out of the wings denotes a reduction of ornament, speed, and strength; whether this happens slowly or suddenly does not particularly matter to the point. Certainly, *Cicero* did not mean a slow loss of his dignity when he wrote to *Atticus*: *those who had clipped my wings do not want them to grow back.* <note>original Latin: "qui mihi pennas inciderant, nolunt easdem renasci."</note> It is well established that after Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian Empire lost much of its authority. In place of spirit, fear succeeded; in place of speed, laziness; in place of victories, frequent flights along with disasters. Hardly any sparks of the ancient courage and nobility shone forth in the descendants of Nebuchadnezzar, as historians everywhere note. None of them are found to have even thought about extending the borders of the Empire: but while they vied with one another in surrendering to idleness and lust, from that point everything began to flow away and slide backward. See, if you will, *Josephus in the first book of Against Apion*.

<margin>XLVIII. The feet and heart of a man signify slowness and weakness in war.</margin>
XLVIII. To the same point belongs the statement that the beast *stood on its feet like a man*, and *that the heart of a man was given to it*. Feet are contrasted with wings; *standing* with flight; *man* with the *eagle*; and the *heart of a man* with the *spirit of a lion*. We are taught that a delay was cast into that course of victories; once that eagle-like flight of Nebuchadnezzar was finished, his successors were equipped not with wings, but only with feet. With these, they did not run to invade further lands, but stood still, content with their ancestral wealth—not out of a sense of justice, but out of mere laziness: doing nothing with foresight, nothing with spirit. *Man* here is not contrasted with the *Lion* as a rational animal is to a beast, but as someone weak and lazy is to one who is brave and high-spirited. For the Lion is a symbol of strength. Judges 14:18: *What is stronger than a lion?* Proverbs 30:30: *A lion, the mightiest among beasts, who does not retreat for fear of anyone.* Hence, concerning Saul and Jonathan in 2 Samuel 1:23: *They were swifter than eagles, and stronger than lions.* However, *Man* is sometimes a name for weakness in war. Isaiah 2:22: *Stop trusting in man, who has but a breath in his nostrils; for of what account is he?* Most especially, this weakness is noted by the word <term>אנוש (Enosh)</term>, which Daniel uses here. It is a name for man taken from "deplorable misery." For <term>אנוש (Enosh)</term> signifies *sick and incurable*. It was for this reason that Seth named his son. Genesis 4:26. The Church prays that enemies may experience this to their own shame and ruin in Psalm 9:20: <note>original Hebrew: "ידעו גוים אנוש המה"</note> *let the nations know they are but men.* The *Heart of a Lion* is an intrepid spirit. 2 Samuel 17:10: *Even the bravest, whose heart is like the heart of a lion.* In Greek, you might call this in a single word <term>λεοντόθυμον (leontothymon)</term> or <term>θυμολέοντα (thymoleonta)</term>, "lion-spirited"; poets call Hercules and Achilles <term>θυμολέοντα</term>. The *Heart of a man*, if compared to a Lion, is mere pusillanimity <note>faint-heartedness or cowardice</note>; <term>לב אנוש (lev enosh)</term> is a *sick and languishing heart*. Jeremiah 17:9.

### CONCERNING THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.

<margin>Which Xenophon notes regarding the conquered Babylonians.</margin>
...the Babylonians. Those lions, once fierce and strong under Nebuchadnezzar, soon laid aside all their ferocity. Like unwarlike men and trembling slaves, they served the Persians in dejected servitude. Xenophon <note>Xenophon was a Greek historian and soldier, a student of Socrates.</note> writes that Cyrus ordered: <note>original Greek: "Κῦρον Βαβυλωνίας μὲν τὴν γῆν ἐργάζεσθαι, καὶ τοὺς δασμοὺς ἀποφέρειν, καὶ θεραπεύειν τούτους οἷς ἕκαστοι αὐτῶν ἐδόθησαν. Πέρσας δὲ, καὶ τοὺς κοινωνοῦντας, καὶ τῶν συμμάχων ὅσοι μένειν ᾑροῦντο παρ’ αὐτῷ, ὡς δεσπότας ὧν ἔλαβον, προηγόρευε διαλέγεσθαι."</note> *the Babylonians were to work the land, pay the tributes, and serve those to whom each of them had been assigned. But he proclaimed that the Persians, and those who shared with them, and whichever allies chose to remain with him, should speak as masters over those they had received.*

<margin>Cyropaedia, Book VIII.</margin>
Cyrus decreed that the Babylonians must till the fields, pay tribute, and yield obedience to those to whom individuals had been handed over. However, he ordered the Persians, their partners, and whichever allies wished to stay with him, to speak as Lords to those they had received as their subjects. What is "violent" in this explanation, as a certain Most Learned Man <note>likely a reference to a contemporary scholarly critic, such as Hugo Grotius</note> charges? Rather, what could be said that is more consistent with the style of scripture and the actual historical events?

<margin>L. The Bear is the emblem of the Medo-Persian Empire.</margin>
L. If the Babylonian Empire is denoted by the Lion, as we have proved from the clear analogy; then the matter itself speaks to the fact that the **MEDO-PERSIAN** Empire, succeeding the Babylonian, is to be understood by the **BEAR**. The analogy is not obscure. A **BEAR** is slower, more clumsy, and less noble than a Lion; although it does not yield to the Lion in its greed, cruelty, and savagery. Likewise, the Medo-Persian Empire was somewhat inferior to the Babylonian in its virtues and successes. Hence, in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the Silver Breast is placed below the Golden Head. I will remain silent now regarding many other comparisons which can be seen individually in their respective authors. For we are not dealing with that matter at this moment.

<margin>LI. To which all things predicted of the Bear perfectly apply.</margin>
LI. As for the statement that the beast *stood on one side* <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: ולשטר חד הקימת (u-le-setar chad haqimat)</note>, it admits of various interpretations. It does not seem far-fetched to understand this as the humble beginnings of the Persians, who were hemmed in by their mountains—*like bears lurking in mountain dens* <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἀν’ ὤρεα φωλάδες ἄρκτοι"</note>—and once lived removed from trade with other nations. They owed the first fame of their name and empire to Cyrus. But soon, with new courage entering their hearts, they joined the Medes to themselves, then subjugated the Babylonians, and forced many other nations to obey them.

LII. And this is what is hinted at by those *three ribs* which this Bear gripped in its mouth between its teeth. These signify great and powerful kingdoms situated at three points of the compass: the West, the North, and the South. For the vision in the following chapter lends light to this enigma; there, the same Persian Empire is displayed under the symbol of a **Ram**, striking with its horns toward the *Sea* (that is, the West), the North, and the South (verse 4). To the West belong the islands of the Mediterranean Sea, most of which can be seen to have obeyed the Persians during the war of Xerxes against the Greeks. Which—
