### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

[To the territories already mentioned] add Syria, Cappadocia, and Asia Minor. Toward the South, the Persians attacked Egypt, Arabia, India, Ethiopia, and Libya. And finally, toward the North, they conquered Scythia, the peoples of the Black Sea, Lydia, Armenia, the Iberians <note>This refers to Caucasian Iberia, located in modern-day Georgia, not the Spanish peninsula.</note>, the Albanians, the Colchians, the Caspians, and others.

LIII. It is added that it was said to this Bear: *Arise, devour much flesh.* This was certainly spoken by God, who on more than one occasion attributed the stirring up of the spirit of the Medes and Persians to Himself as the author. *Isaiah 13:17–18:* 
> Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who shall not regard silver, and as for gold, they shall not delight in it. Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eye shall not spare children. 

*Jeremiah 51:11:* 
> Jehovah has raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes: for his device is against Babylon, to destroy it. 

Isaiah also mentions Cyrus by name, two hundred years before he was born, in Chapter 45:1–3. Thus says Jehovah to his Anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two-leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut. 
> I will go before you, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron. And I will give you the most hidden treasures, and the most secret riches of secret places: that you may know that I, Jehovah, who call you by your name, am the God of Israel.

LIV. Thus, therefore, it was said to this Bear by God: *devour much flesh.* For the "devouring of flesh" represents the seizing of desired persons and things. Compare *Numbers 23:24: He shall not lie down until he eats of the prey, and drinks the blood of the slain.* Also *Revelation 17:16: They shall make her desolate and naked, and shall eat her flesh.* What is "forced" or "violent" here? What has not been sought, confirmed, and illustrated from the analogy of the scriptures?

<margin>LV. The Roman Empire corresponds to the Fourth Beast.</margin>
LV. The application of the FOURTH BEAST to the ROMAN EMPIRE is equally easy: partly to that ANCIENT and PAGAN empire, and partly to the ANTICHRISTIAN and PAPAL one. Regarding the latter, the Most Learned Man <note>A recurring reference to a scholarly contemporary, likely Hugo Grotius, whom the author is refuting.</note> will not dispute with us. But what prevents those former characteristics from being attributed to the Ancient Empire? Was it not *dreadful*, and *terrible*, and exceedingly *strong*? It was certainly more so than the empire of Charlemagne and his successors, which settled far below that ancient Greatness. Did it not have iron teeth—that is, audacity, cruelty, and an insatiable greed, equipped with those weapons which were remarkably prepared for harming and plundering? Does it not fit the description that it *devoured, and broke in pieces, and stamped the residue with its feet?* Compare *Daniel 2:40.* Three things especially are attributed to this Beast in this entire description: **I. Strength.** **II. Cruelty.** **III. Rapacity.** All of these were exceptional in the Ancient Roman Empire.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four beasts from the Book of Daniel, specifically transitioning from the Persian Bear to the fourth beast, which the author identifies as the Roman Empire. The focus here is on the strength and subsequent cruelty of Rome.</meta>

# On the Four Beasts of Daniel

<margin>LVI. Similar to it in Strength</margin>
LVI. Regarding the strength and power of this beast—from which its very name is derived—no one holds any doubt. Jerome, in Book II of his work *Against Jovinianus*, writes: "**Powerful City**, interpret your own name; a city of strength, a Mistress City, a city praised by the voice of the Apostle." The name **Rome** signifies **Strength** <term>rhōmē: ῥώμη</term> among the Greeks, or **Sublimity** <note>original: "Sublimitatis"; likely referring to the Hebrew root *ramah* (high/exalted)</note> among the Hebrews. The poetess Erinna <note>Modern scholars often attribute this "Hymn to Rome" to the poetess Melinno rather than Erinna.</note>, as cited by Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous Flemish philologist and humanist.</note>, writes of Rome itself:

> “For of all, you alone, most powerful one,
> Bring forth great spear-wielding men,
> Just as the fertile field of Demeter <note>The Greek goddess of the harvest and agriculture.</note>
> Sends up a harvest from the earth.”
> 
> In short, among all peoples, you produce
> A mighty offspring for wars; and as from the wide
> Earth the crop rises, you yourself abound
> In a harvest of men.

Examples of this are well-known from all of history; if you wish, you may see specific instances in Lipsius’s *On Roman Greatness*, Book IV, Chapter IV.

<margin>LVII. Cruelty</margin>
LVII. However, from that same history, one can find examples of unbelievable savagery and cruelty. They practiced this not only in war—where the mind is often not in full control of itself—but even after treaties were signed and during times of peace. The clemency of *Julius Caesar* is often praised; yet, according to Plutarch in his *Life of Caesar*, during the Gallic War (which lasted nine years), Caesar "destroyed a million souls with his own hands" <note>original: μυριάδας ἑκατὸν ἐν χερσὶ διέφθειρεν; Plutarch actually writes that a million were killed and another million enslaved.</note>—that is, he killed ten hundred thousand men by force of arms. The Caucaei <note>A Celtiberian people in central Spain, often associated with the town of Coca.</note>, a powerful people of Spain, were unable to match Roman arms and violence and so sent pleading ambassadors to the camp of General *Lucullus*. They were willing to make peace and a treaty under any conditions. Lucullus demanded hostages, a hundred talents of silver immediately, and a specific number of auxiliary cavalry. All these demands were met diligently and submissively. He then commanded further: that they receive two thousand soldiers into their city to serve as a garrison. This, too, was done. But those soldiers were secretly ordered to seize the walls and gates. Once they had done so, Lucullus brought in the rest of the army. A trumpet signal was given to slaughter the elderly, children, men, and women without distinction. Thus the town was plundered and destroyed; twenty thousand people were murdered in an act of supreme wickedness. The crime of *Sulpicius Galba* was no less degenerate. Entering Lusitania <note>A Roman province in the western Iberian Peninsula, primarily modern-day Portugal.</note> as an enemy, he began devastating the land. The inhabitants were bewildered, as they were unaware of any cause or fault on their part. They sent ambassadors and renewed their previous treaties. Galba received them and even expressed pity that they were being so afflicted. "But," he said, "perhaps poverty drove you to raid for plunder and take up the appearance of war; I will provide a remedy. I will divide you into three groups, and in a field..."

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

"...and I will settle you on fertile soil, where you may spend the rest of your lives happy and safe. Come with your wives and children; I shall assign such a valley and such a part to you." The wretched people come, happy and secure, and were divided into three groups. When he had approached the first group, he ordered them to lay down their arms, as if they were friends and allies. Once these were laid down, he sent in his soldiers and, though the people implored for good faith and the gods, he killed them to a single man. The same was done quickly to the second and third groups, even before the news of the crime could reach them. So much for **Cruelty**.

<margin>LVIII. On Rapacity.</margin>
LVIII. Indeed, the *Rapacity* of the Propreters, Proconsuls, and Governors in sucking dry and plundering the provinces was unbelievable.

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 8.</margin>
->-- *They used to bring back in deep ships*<-
->*Hidden spoils, and more triumphs from peace than from war.*<-

*Lipsius* <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a renowned Flemish humanist and scholar.</note> writes elegantly: *The poets invented certain Harpies who would tear apart or defile everything with their touch and claws; in reality, these were those Roman Governors. Every "Best and Most Beautiful" man behaved in such a way that he carried all the spoils of war home with him. Demades <note>An Athenian orator known for his wit and corruption.</note> was once accustomed to say, whenever he went to the Tribunal or a Magistrate's office, that he was going to a "golden harvest." Believe me, those men went, and each one promised himself the Golden Fleece of Colchis like a modern Jason. Have you read those accounts by Cicero regarding that one man, Verres? <note>Gaius Verres, a Roman magistrate infamous for his extreme corruption and exploitation of Sicily.</note> Most things were similar in others, and the wretched provincials were nothing but prey and spoil to their governors.*

<margin>LIX. And trampling underfoot what he could not turn to his own use. Book XLV.</margin>
LIX. Furthermore, let us learn from the example of *Lucius Paulus*—who was considered among the best of citizens—how they trampled under their feet what they could not devour (that is, turn to their own use). It was determined that he should plunder the whole of *Epirus* <note>A region in the Balkans.</note>, because they had sided with *King Perseus* <note>The last king of the Macedonians.</note>. What does he do? In the very words of *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note>: He sends Centurions into the individual cities, who were to say they had come to lead away the garrisons so that the *Epirots*, like the *Macedonians*, might be free. He summoned ten leading men from each city. *After he had commanded them that the gold and silver should be brought forth into the public treasury, he sent cohorts through all the cities, so that they arrived at all of them on the same day. Orders had been given to the tribunes and centurions regarding what was to be done. In the morning, all the gold and silver was collected; at the fourth hour, the signal was given to the soldiers to plunder the cities. And the prey was so great that four hundred denarii <note>A standard Roman silver coin.</note> were divided among the cavalry, and two hundred to the infantry. One hundred and fifty thousand human heads [slaves] were led away. Then the walls of the plundered cities were demolished; there were about seventy such towns. Moreover, all these things were done by order of the Senate.* Is this not first swallowing down whatever you can with greedy voracity, and then trampling the remainder underfoot? For when nothing remained of the things that could be transported, they vented their rage on the wretched walls and roofs, and ordered them to be demolished. Lest you think this was rare, *Polybius* <note>A Greek historian who recorded the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> teaches that this was a solemn custom of cruelty among the Romans. *For they seem,* he says, *to do this for the sake of causing terror. Therefore...*

### On the Four Beasts of Daniel.

...which is frequently seen when the Romans capture cities: not only are men killed, but even dogs are cut apart, and the limbs of other living creatures are hacked off.

<margin>LX. The shape of this Beast, which differs from the others.</margin>
LX. Furthermore, Daniel testifies that this Beast was *unlike* <note>original: *dissimilem*</note> the others he had seen before. At this point, interpreters first consider the visible appearance of this Beast—how it differed from the others—and then the difference in what it signifies. Some Jewish scholars speculate that it was a *Wild Boar*, based on the argument of Psalm 80:13: *The wild boar from the forest uproots it, and the creatures of the field feed on it.* However, a boar does not possess such ferocity compared to a Lion, a Bear, or a Leopard, nor such strength that it could fulfill the power of those things predicted about this Beast, which is more monstrous than all the rest. Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (c. 1535–1610), a Spanish Jesuit theologian known for his commentaries on Daniel.</note> guesses that this Beast can be compared to that *Indian* creature mentioned by Aristotle in *Book II of the History of Animals, Chapter 1*, citing Ctesias of Cnidus <note>A Greek physician and historian of the 5th century BCE.</note>. He calls it a *Manticore*, which has a triple row of teeth on both sides, the size and feet of a lion, the face and ears of a human, blue-gray eyes, a reddish color, and a tail armed with a sting like a wild scorpion. It shoots out its stingers, has a voice not unlike a pipe or trumpet, runs with no less speed than a deer, and is so wild it can never be tamed, possessing a particular appetite for human flesh. But since Scripture is silent, it is a matter of prudence to define nothing. If there is room for conjecture, it is not unlikely that John was shown nearly the same beast in *Revelation 13:1–2*, in which the parts of the others were mixed together: a body like a leopard, feet like a bear, and a mouth like a lion. This was to signify that both the virtues and the vices of all the others were present in this one alone.

<margin>LXI. In what way the Roman Empire differed from the rest.</margin>
LXI. And indeed, the Roman Empire was different from the rest. First, because it was not governed in only one way. All the other empires were <term>Monarchies</term> <note>Systems where a single person holds supreme power.</note>. This one, however, you may see governed at times as a Monarchy, at times as a Democracy, and at times as an Aristocracy. Sometimes there were Kings; once these were driven out, there were Consuls, then the <term>Decemvirs</term> <note>A ten-man commission established to compile the laws of Rome.</note>, then Consuls again with a Dictator added; finally there were Princes, while the Consuls, Tribunes of the plebs, and other names of magistrates remained in the meantime. Second, because under this Empire, the Antichrist had to be revealed, and almost the whole world had to take on a far different appearance than it had held before. And so, step by step, we are led to see Rome as once Pagan, and now Antichristian. For both are explained by the same common symbol, and they are one Empire. This is clear from Nebuchadnezzar’s dream. We believe, along with a Most Celebrated Interpreter, that the things which follow in Daniel are to be understood as referring to Antichristian Rome. There is no necessity for us to dwell on these points now.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

...and I will settle you on rich soil, where you may spend the rest of your lives in a blessed and safe state. Come with your wives and children: I shall assign you to such a valley, and to that particular region." These wretched people came, joyful and secure, and were divided into three groups. When the general had approached the first group, he ordered them to lay down their arms as if they were friends and allies. Once they were disarmed, he sent in his soldiers and slaughtered them to a man, even as they implored his good faith and the Gods. <margin>LVIII. On Rapacity.</margin>
LVIII. Indeed, the *Rapacity* <note>original: *Rapacitas*; greed or the act of seizing by force.</note> of the Pro-praetors, Proconsuls, and Governors in exhausting and pillaging the provinces was incredible.

->—they carried back in deep ships—<-

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 8.</margin>
> *Hidden spoils, and more triumphs won from peace [than from war].* <note>Juvenal's 8th Satire critiqued the Roman nobility for plundering the very provinces they were meant to protect.</note>

Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous Flemish philologist and humanist.</note> elegantly writes:
> *The poets invented certain Harpies who would snatch or defile everything with their touch and claws; in reality, these Roman Governors were those very things. Even the best and most handsome among them behaved in such a way that they brought the spoils of every war home with them. Demades <note>An Athenian orator and contemporary of Demosthenes.</note> used to say, whenever he went to the Tribunal or a Magisterial office, that he was going to a "golden harvest"; believe me, these men went, and each one promised himself he was a Jason reaching Colchis <note>The mythical land of the Golden Fleece.</note>. Have you read what Cicero wrote regarding that one man, Verres? <note>Gaius Verres, a Roman magistrate notorious for his extreme misgovernment of Sicily, whom Cicero prosecuted.</note> Most such things were found in the others as well, and the wretched provincials were nothing but prey and spoil to their governors.*

<margin>LIX. And that which it could not convert to its own use, it trampled with its feet. Book XLV.</margin>
LIX. However, let us learn how they trampled with their feet what they could not devour—that is, what they could not convert to their own use—through the example of Lucius Paulus <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, a Roman general and statesman.</note>, who was held to be among the best of citizens. He was destined to plunder the whole of Epirus because they had sided with King Perseus. What did he do? In the very words of Livy:
> *He sent centurions into each city, saying they had come to lead away the garrisons so that the Epiriotes might be free, just like the Macedonians. He summoned ten leading men from each city. When he had commanded them to bring forth their gold and silver into the public square, he sent cohorts throughout all the cities, arranged so that they would arrive at all of them on the same day. Orders had been given to the tribunes and centurions on what was to be done. In the morning, all the gold and silver was collected; at the fourth hour, the signal was given to the soldiers to plunder the cities. The booty was so great that four hundred denarii were divided among the cavalry and two hundred among the infantry. One hundred and fifty thousand human beings were led away into slavery. Then, the walls of the plundered cities were razed; these were about seventy towns. All these things were done by order of the Senate.*

Is this not first devouring whatever you can with greedy voracity, and then trampling the remainder with your feet? For when nothing remained of the things that could be transported, they vented their rage on the wretched walls and roofs, and ordered them to be destroyed. Lest you think this is an isolated case, Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period who chronicled the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> teaches us that this was a solemn custom of the Romans in their cruelty. He says they seem to do this *for the sake of inspiring terror. Therefore*

### On the Four Beasts of Daniel

...as is frequently observed when the Romans capture cities: not only are the people slaughtered, but even the dogs are butchered, and the limbs of other animals are hacked off.

<margin>60. How the appearance of this Beast differed from the others.</margin>
LX. Furthermore, Daniel testifies that this Beast was *unlike* <note>original: *dissimilem*</note> the others he had seen before. Regarding this, interpreters first consider the *visible appearance* of this Beast—how it physically differed from the others—and then the diversity of what it signifies. Some Jewish commentators guess it was a *Wild Boar*, using the evidence of Psalm 80:13: *The boar from the forest uproots it, and the creatures of the field feed on it.* <note>In the Latin Vulgate and some Hebrew numbering, this is Psalm 79:14. The "it" refers to the vine of Israel.</note> However, a boar does not possess such ferocity or strength compared to the Lion, the Bear, or the Leopard that it could exhaust the power of the things predicted about this Beast, which is more monstrous than all the rest. Pererius <note>Benedictus Pererius (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian and commentator.</note> conjectures that this Beast could be compared to that *Indian* creature mentioned by Aristotle (citing Ctesias of Cnidus) in Book II, *Chapter 1 of the History of Animals*. He calls it the *Mantichora*, <note>A legendary creature similar to a sphinx.</note> which has *three rows of teeth on each side, the size and feet of a lion, the face and ears of a human, blue-grey eyes, a blood-red color, and a tail armed with a sting like a wild scorpion, capable of launching its grown-on quills like arrows; its voice is not unlike a flute or a trumpet, its speed is no less than that of a deer, and its ferocity is so great it can never be tamed, having a particular appetite for human flesh.* But since Scripture remains silent, it is the part of wisdom to define nothing. If there is room for conjecture, it is not unlike the truth that the beast shown to John in Revelation 13:1–2 was essentially the same, in which the parts of the others were blended: a body like a leopard, feet like a bear, and a mouth like a lion—to signify that both the powers and the vices of all the others were present in this one alone.

<margin>61. In what way the Roman Empire was different from the others.</margin>
LXI. And indeed, the Roman Empire was different from the rest. First, because it was not governed in only one way. All the other empires were monarchies. This one, however, you may see governed now as a monarchy, now as a democracy, and now as an aristocracy. At times there were Kings; once these were driven out, there were Consuls, soon Decemvirs <note>A ten-man commission in the Roman Republic.</note>, then Consuls again with a Dictator added; finally, there were Emperors <note>original: *Principes*</note>, while the offices of Consuls, Tribunes of the People, and other titles of magistrates remained in place. Second, because under this Empire the Antichrist had to be revealed, and almost the entire world had to take on a far different face than it had before. Thus, we are gradually led to the point where we see Rome as once *Pagan* <note>original: *Gentilem*</note> and now *Antichristian*. For both are represented by the same common symbol, and they are one and the same Empire. This is evident from Nebuchadnezzar's dream. We agree with a most celebrated interpreter that the things which follow in Daniel are to be understood as referring to Antichristian Rome. There is no necessity for us to dwell on these matters now.

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

<margin>LXII. The analogy between the Leopard and Alexander.</margin>
LXII. We proceed now to the **LEOPARD**: with which, alongside nearly all interpreters, we believe the kingdom of the **MACEDONIANS**, or the **GREEK MONARCHY**, is most elegantly prefigured. This is suggested not only by the order of the visions, according to the principles we have just laid down, but also by the suitability of the analogy. <margin>Bochart, *Hierozoïcon*, Book III, Chapter VII.</margin> <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a famous scholar of biblical animals.</note> Namely: I. Just as the Leopard *is small in stature* (for the males hardly equal the size of a calf, and the females do not exceed the size of a moderate hunting dog) but is supreme in spirit and strength, so that it does not fear to engage with the Lion or any of the tallest wild beasts; so Alexander, *almost a petty king*, dared to attack the King of Kings with a meager force—that is, *Darius* <note>Darius III, the last King of the Achaemenid Empire of Persia.</note>; whose kingdom extended from the Aegean Sea all the way to the Indians. II. No animal is swifter than the Leopard: likewise, Alexander utilized such speed in conducting his affairs that he subdued a great part of the inhabited world in twelve years. The much slower growth of the *Muhammadan Empire* <note>The early Islamic conquests.</note> cannot be compared with this celerity. It is one thing to subject almost the entire world to oneself in a twelve-year period; it is quite another to subdue the provinces of Arabia, along with some neighbors, in the space of a decade, as we noted above regarding *Muhammad*. Alexander’s mother, *Olympias*, had dreamed that a thunderbolt was born from her womb. Consequently, *Apelles* <note>The renowned court painter to Alexander the Great.</note> skillfully painted him holding a thunderbolt in his hand, which moves rapidly against obstacles with the greatest force. And it is well known what he replied when asked how he could execute such great things in so small a space of time: namely, <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἀναβαλλόμενος</note> *“By delaying nothing.”* III. The variety of spots on the Leopard, according to *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian.</note>, signifies the diverse character of Alexander: for he was at times merciful, and at others cruel; sometimes temperate in his diet, and at others a drunkard; sometimes abstinent, and at others indulging in his passions. According to others, the spots signify the diverse customs of the nations over which he ruled; or even the arts, actions, and frauds of the Greeks, whose character was varied and ready to assume any appearance for the sake of their interests. IV. They say that *Leopards* are captured not by force, but by craft, when they are *heavy with wine*. Hunters, having observed the Leopard's hiding places, place bowls filled with wine there. The leopards are soon drawn out from their caves by the scent; they drink the wine most greedily, and after they have grown warm with the unmixed wine, they play together and rush headlong into lust; then, drunk and exhausted by mating, they fall into a deep sleep; once asleep, they are captured. A verse from *Oppian's* fourth book of the *Cynegetica* <note>A poem on hunting from the 2nd or 3rd century AD.</note> supports this:

> *Panthers too have been tamed by the gifts of Bacchus,* <note>Bacchus is the Roman god of wine.</note>
> *when deceitful hunters pour out a deceitful drink.*
<note>original Greek: Παρδάλιας καὶ δῶρα Διονύσοιο δάμασσαν, θηροφόνων δολερῶν δολερὴν πόσιν οἰνοχοοῦντων</note>

And indeed, Alexander the Great, [who had conquered] so many enemies...

<header>ON THE FOUR BEASTS OF DANIEL.</header>

Everyone knows that the victor often succumbed to wine, and finally died overcome by it. <note>original: "vino saepe succubuisse, tandemque vino oppressum interiisse." This refers to the historical tradition that Alexander the Great died after a period of heavy drinking in Babylon.</note> For other analogies that are usually praised by others—perhaps more with ingenuity than with solid substance—look to the works of *Pererius*, *Sanctius*, *Cornelius a Lapide*, and others. <note>These were prominent Jesuit biblical commentators of the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>

<margin>LXIII. The four wings are a symbol of the greatest speed.</margin>
LXIII. THE FOUR WINGS which the Leopard had on its back denote **SPEED**; this was twice as great as the swiftness of the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians, represented by the first beast (the Lion).</note>. For, as *Jerome* <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> says, nothing was faster than Alexander’s victory. From the Illyrian and Adriatic seas all the way to the Indian Ocean and the River Ganges, he traversed the world more through victories than through battles: and in six years he subjugated part of Europe and all of Asia for himself, even as far as India. Indeed, *Darius* wrote to Alexander that he would grow old just by traveling through such vast lands, even without a battle. *Curtius, Book IV, Chapter V.* <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian who wrote a biography of Alexander the Great.</note> Unless you prefer to understand the four wings as Alexander's four Generals, along with their armies, by whose work and assistance he conquered so many regions.

<margin>LXIV. Four heads, as many kingdoms.</margin>
LXIV. THE FOUR HEADS denote those **FOUR KINGDOMS** into which his Empire was divided after Alexander’s death. This is shown more fully in Chapter VIII:8: *And that male goat grew exceedingly great: but when he was strongest, that great horn was broken, and four grew up in its place toward the four winds of heaven.* This is, according to the Angel's explanation in verses 21–22: *And that young goat is the King of Greece. And the great horn between his eyes is the first king. And since it was broken, and four stood up in its place: Four kingdoms shall stand up from that nation, but not with his power.* For although after Alexander's death his successors fought amongst themselves and the Empire was torn into many small states <term>dynasties|local ruling powers</term>—some count ten—nevertheless, four major kingdoms encompassed the most civilized part of the human race: namely **Macedonia**, **Asia Minor**, **Syria**, and **Egypt**. *Antipater* occupied Macedonia, *Antigonus* Asia Minor, *Seleucus* Syria, and *Ptolemy* Egypt. <note>These successors are known historically as the Diadochi.</note>

<margin>LXV. Alexander recognized that the power given to him was from God.</margin>
LXV. Nor does it lack its own emphasis when it is added that **POWER WAS GIVEN** to this beast. This is because it happened beyond all natural reason and beyond the expectation of all men that such a tiny handful of soldiers achieved so much. For who would have thought, when he crossed the sea, that he would become the victor of Asia and the entire Orient? In his army there were 32,000 infantry, no more than 5,000 cavalry, and 180 ships. With this small force, it is uncertain which is more admirable: that he conquered the whole world, or that he even dared to attack it. This much is certain: he himself, compelled by the force of truth, attributed his victories to God, if the account by *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>—which we have praised elsewhere—is not mistaken.

<margin>LXVI. "Sultan" denotes any power you choose.</margin>
LXVI. Let the wise reader now judge whether our explanation of this Divine riddle—in which we refer the Leopard to Alexander and his successors—is not at least as clear (to ask for nothing more than what is fair), as easy, and as plain as that which commands us to think of the <term>Muslim Empire</term><note>The author is likely responding to contemporary 17th-century interpreters who tried to apply biblical prophecy to the Ottoman Turks.</note>. For as to what some urge regarding the word **שָׁלְטָן** <note>original: "שָׁלְטָן" (sholtan). An Aramaic word meaning dominion, power, or sovereignty.</note> **SOLTAN**, as if that power of the Turks were designated by it rather than any other power because the Turkish Emperors are still called "Sultans"—that, to put it very mildly, is of little weight. For that word is quite general; it denotes any empire or any commander. Indeed, not to wander far, it is used in this very Chapter. In verse 12, it is attributed to the Beasts: <note>original Aramaic: "ושאר חיותא העדו שלטנהון" (ve-shear chayuta he'du sholtanehon)</note> *And concerning the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away.* In verse 14, it is applied to the Son of Man; in verse 16, to the fourth beast; and in verse 27, to the people of the saints of the most High. Nor is it surprising that this nation, whose language is related to Hebrew and Chaldean <note>The author refers to Arabic, which shares the same Semitic root for "ruler" or "authority."</note>, has retained that name for itself.

<margin>LXVII. Disadvantages of the new interpretation.</margin>
LXVII. And so, unless I am mistaken, we have shown that our expositions, never faltering, always proceed with an unhindered foot, once the difficulties have been removed which the Most Celebrated Interpreter <note>Likely a reference to a specific scholar like Joseph Mede or Hugo Grotius, who were famous for their prophetic commentaries.</note> saw fit to cast in the way. Now, let it be permitted to set forth candidly what we find lacking in his own interpretation. I will say nothing now of the *Novelty* of the discovery, which, although it should not be rashly preferred to the ancient and approved views, tends to win favor rather than provoke suspicion, given the current temperament of men. I prefer to weigh the matter itself.

LXVIII. In this regard, it seems to me exceedingly harsh that he wishes these Animals to be "replicated" in the **Apocalyptic Beast** <note>The Beast from the Book of Revelation (chapter 13), which combined the features of a leopard, bear, and lion.</note>, which is composed of these four as if fused together. From this it would follow that the Arian nations <note>Germanic tribes like the Goths and Vandals who followed the Arian heresy, which denied that Jesus was of the same substance as God the Father.</note>—savage and of a dark color, that is, abominable for their denial of the greatness of Christ—represented by the emblem of the **Bear**, and the Empires of the Muslims, or the **Caliphs**, in Syria, Egypt, Asia, and Greece, figured by the symbol of the **Leopard**, would belong to the Apocalyptic Beast in such a way that they constitute nearly half of it. However, I do not see by what reasoning this can be defended or reconciled with the other hypotheses of that Most Learned Man.

<margin>LXIX. Definitions of the Apocalyptic Beast.</margin>
LXIX. For what is that Apocalyptic Beast to whom the Dragon gave his power? Let us hear the definitions of the Most Learned Man himself. In his *Treatise on the Church and Babylon*, section 74, he responds to this question as follows:

> "It is certainly easy to say. For if the **DRAGON** is Satan, armed and clothed with the strength and power of the Roman people who openly worshiped him, then surely the **BEAST**, to whom the Dragon yields his throne, is the **MULTITUDE TRIUMPHING IN THE NAME OF CHRISTIANITY BUT NOT IN TRUTH**, and usurping that same power."

### Of the Four Beasts of Daniel

Alternatively, just as the Roman people, while openly worshiping the Devil and attacking the Christian religion, are counted as the Dragon of seven heads; so too the Roman people, in every part of the Roman Empire, **BEARING THE CHRISTIAN NAME BEFORE THEM, AND EITHER SPEAKING OR HEARING THE WORDS OF THE FOUNDATION** <note>original Latin: "verba fundamenti," referring to the fundamental doctrines or creeds of the Church.</note> and allowing them to be spoken, yet not understanding them, and not believing in Christ with a right and true faith, but following the opinions of men and calling upon a human name, is the Beast. A little later: What therefore remains, except that the people called "Christian," having a throne on earth and possessing the power of the City of the Dragon, is distinguished from the Holy City by the fact that it does not hold the true faith? And how could the Beast not denote the people called "Christian," when the second Beast, which exercises all its power in its presence, bears horns like a Lamb? By this is surely denoted a likeness to the Lamb in hypocrisy, or a usurpation of those things which belong to the true Lamb—whether these be the two Testaments (<italic>as Primasius argues</italic> <note>Primasius of Hadrumetum was a 6th-century North African bishop whose commentary on Revelation was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>) or the power of opening and closing <note>The "power of the keys" to heaven and hell.</note>. Add to this from the commentaries on Revelation 13, § VII: Under the name of the Beast rising from the sea, he depicted the Christian Republic, which appeared to be the Church and the very Kingdom of God—which the martyrs awaited, and into which the Apostle says we must enter through many tribulations (Acts 14:22)—when, in fact, it was the Beast and a persecutor of the saints. Again, in *On the Church and Babylon*, § LXVII: In the first place, I do not think it can be doubted that this Beast upon which the Harlot sits in Revelation 17 is the same as the one otherwise called in Revelation the Beast rising from the Abyss, or from the sea (Rev 11:7; 13:1). The Harlot, however, according to our Author, is that hierarchical order of the Roman Church: or, to say it in his own words, the Multitude of those teaching errors and subjecting to themselves the people who are called Christian and are the Beast, being joined together among themselves by laws and authority. Ibid. § LXXVI: Furthermore, that woman is described in Revelation 17:4 as clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls—understand this as "adorned." Where, by "purple and scarlet," the <italic>Learned Man</italic> understands the name of Christ who came in the flesh and shed his blood for the Church; by "gold," the name of the Holy Spirit, whose assistance the Harlot claims for herself; by "precious stones and pearls," the Saints, the Righteous, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Martyrs, who are named by her.

<margin>70. Neither the Arian Heresy nor Muhammadanism can be part of it.</margin>
70. For that group was never seen to be that Kingdom of God into which one must enter through many tribulations; it did not speak the "words of the foundation," since their doctrine is—as the Ancients well said—a **God-denying heresy** <note>original Greek: *ἀρνησίθεος αἵρεσις* (arnēsitheos hairesis).</note>. It did not have the Harlot as its occupant—that is, the Clergy of the Roman Church—by whom it was always condemned, cast out, and from the Church's sacred boundary...

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION IV.

...was expelled from the city boundaries. Much less does <term>Muhammedanism|An older European term for Islam</term> form a part of the Beast, for it neither puts forward a Christian name, nor sits upon those seven mountains <note>A traditional reference to the seven hills of Rome.</note>, nor possesses the power of the City of the Dragon; it does not have the horns of the Lamb, nor is it sat upon by the Whore; it is neither a Christian Republic nor was it ever seen as the Kingdom of God. In short, it possesses nothing at all from the definition of the Beast.

<margin>LXXI. The Apocalyptic Beast corresponds only to Daniel’s Fourth Beast in some of its parts.</margin>
LXXI. What then? The four beasts of Daniel are not "replicated" <note>original Latin: "replicantur," meaning folded together or repeated.</note> within that single Apocalyptic beast, as our Author says. Rather, the Apocalyptic beast corresponds to Daniel’s fourth beast, at least regarding some part of it; it explains many things about it more significantly and copiously, as those times had now become nearer, which to Daniel—being far removed from them—remained unpronounced. An accurate comparison of both images, such as the most noble *Launay* <note>Pierre de Launay (1573–1661), a French Protestant scholar who wrote extensively on the Apocalypse.</note> established, will place this observation in a clear light:

I. Daniel, after he had described three beasts—the first like a *Lion*, the second like a *Bear*, and the third like a *Leopard*—says the fourth was different from the three prior ones, but he remains silent on what appearance it actually had. John, however, explains it by teaching that three species converged into one, such that the *trunk* of the body resembled a *Leopard*, the *feet* a *Bear*, and the *mouth* a *Lion*.

II. Both Daniel and John attribute *ten horns* to this Beast.

III. Both explain these as *ten Kings* who would rise and reign (Daniel 7:24; Revelation 17:12).

IV. Both detect in this beast a *mouth speaking great things and blasphemies against the Most High* (Daniel 7:8, 25; Revelation 13:5).

V. Daniel saw the horn of this beast *wage war with the saints and prevail over them* (Daniel 7:21). John says, *it was given to him to wage war with the saints and to conquer them* (Revelation 13:7).

VI. Daniel says the saints were to be delivered into his hand *for a time, and times, and half a time* (Daniel 7:25), which is three and a half years. John says, *power was given to him to act for forty-two months* (Revelation 13:5), which amounts to the same length of time (Compare Revelation 12:14).

VII. Daniel says *that Beast was slain, and its body perished, and was delivered to the burning of fire* (Daniel 7:11). John says, *And the Beast was captured, and with it the False Prophet, and both were cast alive into the lake of fire burning with sulfur* (Revelation 19:20).

Such great conformity between the two sufficiently proves that they deal with the same subject. Therefore, the four beasts of Daniel are not "replicated" in the one Apocalyptic beast: and thus the argument of that most learned man derived from that premise completely collapses.

<margin>LXXII. The new exposition does not sufficiently distinguish the wings of the Leopard from the heads.</margin>
LXXII. Furthermore, this also deserves consideration: whether he distinguishes the *four wings* from the *four heads* of the Leopard sufficiently well. By the *wings*, he understands the four great parts of the Roman Empire which were torn away by the Muslims: Syria, Asia, Africa, and Greece.

<margin>III. Moloch, a common name for the Gods of the Orientals.</margin>
III. He whom the ancient Orientals worshipped with the sacrifice of children is everywhere called MOLECH or *Moloch* in the Sacred Scriptures. Most contend that this was *Saturn*, others *Mars*, and some *Mercury*. ### On the Worship of Moloch.

III. Different nations each had their own individual Moloch. In 1 Kings 11:7, **Molech** is called the "abomination of the children of Ammon." This does not mean the idol belonged uniquely to them; for other nations also had <note>original: מלכם (m-l-k-m)</note> **their own Melech** <note>"Melech" is the Hebrew word for "King."</note>, as written in Zephaniah 1:5. Furthermore, the Gods of the Sepharvaim are called <term>Adramelech|Magnificent King</term> and <term>Anamelech|Responding God</term> (2 Kings 17:31). The former signifies a **Magnificent King** or **God** (similar to how the Philistines spoke in 1 Samuel 4:8 of the <note>original: אלהים אדירים (elohim adirim)</note> **Magnificent Gods**), while the latter signifies a **Responding God**. The Romans might have called him **Oracular Jupiter**. The God of the Tyrians and Sidonians was called **Melkarthos** <note>original: Μελκαρθος</note>, derived from <note>original: מלך קרתא (Melech Kartha)</note> **King of the City**, or the **City-guarding God** <note>original: ὁ πολιεῦχος θεός (ho polieuchos theos)</note>. Athenagoras, in his *Embassy*, testifies that the Carthaginians worshipped **Amilkan** <note>Known to us as the name Hamilcar</note>, which is <note>original: המלך (Ha-Melech)</note> **The King**, or perhaps <note>original: המלכה (Ha-Malkah)</note> **The Queen**, or **Kingdom** <note>original: Basilèa / Basilèian</note>. And those who are called the **Gods of Hamath**, **Arpad**, and **Sepharvaim** in Isaiah 36:19 are each called the <note>original: מלך (Melech)</note> **King of those cities** in 2 Kings 19:13.

<margin>V. However, it seems to have been worshipped primarily under that name alone.</margin>
V. From all of this, I conclude that **Molech** is a common name that various Eastern nations bestowed upon their Gods—specifically that one whom they considered the supreme among the Gods, and to whom they therefore judged that the best of all sacrifices, namely human ones, should be offered. This seems most particularly referable to the **Sun**, who is the **King of the heavenly host**, just as the Moon is the <note>original: מלכת שמים (Malkat Hashamayim)</note> **Queen of Heaven**.

<margin>VI. A difficult passage from Amos. Chapter 5:26.</margin>
VI. I would like to take this opportunity to explain a difficult passage in Amos 5:26, which was quoted by the blessed Stephen in Acts 7:43, insofar as it serves our purpose. The words of Amos are as follows: <note>original: ונשאתם את סכות מלככם ואת כיון : צלמיכם כוכב אלהיכם אשר עשיתם לכם</note> **"But you carried the tabernacle of your King [Melech] and the pedestal of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves."** *Junius* translated it in this manner: *"Indeed, you carried the tabernacle of your Melech, and the base of your images; the Star of your God, which you made for yourselves."* Stephen the Protomartyr inserted it into his Defense thus: *"Indeed, you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the Star of your God Remphan, figures which you made to worship them."* To properly and orderly investigate the meaning of these words, three things seem to require explanation: I. What is to be understood by <note>original: מלככם (Malkekhem)</note> **Melecum**, or **your King**. II. What it means to **Carry** the <note>original: סכות (Sukkoth)</note> **tabernacles** of that god. III. In what way this is attributed to the **Israelites**.

<margin>VII. Where Moloch is understood as the King of the Israelites.</margin>
VII. By **Melecum** or **your King**, an earthly king is not understood, as I believe everyone acknowledges. Nor is it God, the Heavenly King; for it could not be imputed to them as a vice that they recognized God as their King. Rather, it refers to the **Sun**, whom the Easterners called sometimes **Baal** (or **Beal** in Syriac), sometimes **Melech**, and at other times **Moloch**. This is evident: I. From ancient versions. For the Syriac and Arabic have **Melech**, and the Septuagint has **Moloch**. II. From the quotation by Stephen, who not only uses the phrase **"the tabernacle of Moloch"**;

BOOK II. DISSERTATION V.

...but from this, he also proves that the Israelites performed worship to the **host of heaven** <note>This refers to the stars and planets, often personified as a celestial army.</note>. (verse 42). III. This is proven from the matter itself. For <note>original: כיון כוכב אלהיכם</note> **Kiun, the star of your God**, is joined to it. <note>Amos 5:26</note>

<margin>VIII. Saturn is meant by Kiun.</margin>
VIII. Furthermore, <note>original: כיון</note> **Kiun** signifies **Saturn**, who in the Arabic and Persian languages is called <note>original: כיואן</note> **Keivan**. Properly, it denotes that power of a deity which grants existence, nature, and fitness to all things. The Hebrew root <term>Kun|To be established</term> in its basic form <note>the Kal stem</note> means to be prepared or arranged. In Arabic and Syriac, it means "to become." In other verb forms <note>the Hiphil and Piel stems</note>, it means to cause to exist, to generate, or to implant a nature. The Syrians use the word **Kejana** to mean "nature." The ancients attributed this to Saturn because he was the author of all existence, nature, and fitness. **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** writes in Book 1: <note>original: Τοῦτον τὸν δαίμονα...</note> "This divinity, whom the Romans call Saturn, is the giver and fulfiller of all happiness to men... and has encompassed the nature of the world."

<margin>IX. Called Remphan by the Egyptians.</margin>
IX. Moreover, whom other Easterners called **Kiun**, the Egyptians called **Remphan**, or **Rephan**; as **Salmasius** and **Louis de Dieu** have shown regarding Acts 7. From this, the translators <note>referring to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> acted wisely: while translating the Bible in Egypt, they substituted the name **Remphan**, which was very well known to the Egyptians, for the Hebrew **Kiun**, which was unknown to them. It appears, however, that both names—**Kiun** (or **Remphan**) and **Moloch**—refer to the same celestial body, though in a different form and manner of worship, just as the **Moon** and **Diana** are related among the Greeks. **Moloch** took the form of a **King**, while **Kiun** took the form of a **Star**. But whether we consider **Remphan** to be the same as **Moloch** or distinct from him, it is clearly evident here that the discussion concerns one who belongs to the **host of heaven**.

<margin>X. The Tabernacle of Moloch was a small shrine or a portable carriage.</margin>
X. But what is <note>original: סכות, ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ Μόλοχ</note> the **Tabernacle of Moloch**? 
I. **Grotius**, **Hammond**, and others think that <term>naiskoi|small shrines</term> are meant here—miniature portable chapels fashioned in the likeness of a temple. **Casaubon** and **Grotius** have proven with many testimonies from the ancients (regarding Acts 19:24) that such small boxes containing tiny idols were used in idolatrous worship. In that passage, Luke mentions **silver shrines of Artemis**, made in the shape of a temple, in which an image of **Diana** (or the **Moon**) was stored. 
II. **Selden** understands it as a larger tabernacle, constructed of light and portable material, containing the image of **Moloch**. Indeed, the Chaldean text explains it this way: "and you carried the tabernacle of your King [Moloch] in pairs." Also, **Philo of Byblos**, quoted in **Eusebius**, mentions a <note>original: ναῶ ζευγηφορουμένω</note> **shrine carried by a yoke** belonging to the Great God of the Phoenicians. 
III. **Louis de Dieu** and others (from whom **Selden** does not differ much) interpret it as a <term>Thensa|A ceremonial carriage</term> or a **Litter**. A **Thensa** was a vehicle or a platform made of ivory or silver, often covered by a veil, on which the images of the Gods were carried around, especially in processions. **Servius**, commenting on the 6th book of the *Aeneid*, mentions <term>xoana|carved images</term>—small statues that were carried in litters.

### ON THE WORSHIP OF MOLOCH.

...on palanquins <note>The Latin 'lectica' refers to a portable litter or sedan chair used to carry images of gods in processions.</note>, and moved by the bearers themselves, they poured forth prophecies, a practice found among both the Egyptians and the Carthaginians. Whatever the case may have been (for these things do not differ much from one another), it pertained to an idolatrous rite to carry around that certain tent in honor of the God to whom it was dedicated, and whose image was enclosed within it. Indeed, that tabernacle was not only a receptacle in which the enclosed Moloch was carried, but it was the idol itself: an image of the heavens, in which the sun, 그at great King of the stars, is contained as if in a tabernacle.

<margin>XI. What else Psalm 19:5 seems to indicate.</margin>
XI. It is a probable conjecture of *Louis de Dieu and Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English Hebraist who argued that many Jewish rites were adaptations of Egyptian customs.</note> that the Psalmist alluded to this in Psalm 19:5: <note>original Hebrew: לשמש שם אהל בהם</note> **"In them he has set a tabernacle for the sun."** For here, he seems to silently mock the religious madness of the heathens, who, by carrying the sun around in their narrow little tabernacles—the very sun for whom God placed a tabernacle in the heavens—did not so much worship him as dishonor him.

<margin>XII. Whether this idolatry is attributed to the Israelites literally or in a hidden sense.</margin>
XII. But in what way can all these things be attributed to the Israelites? Most interpreters connect the words of the Prophet <note>Amos</note> with the preceding verses so that they refer to the time of the Israelites' wandering in the desert. Some of them contend that these things were literally done by the Israelites in this manner; others flee to more hidden or mystical meanings.

<margin>XIII. Spencer proves this point.</margin>
XIII. *Spencer* maintains that the Israelites retained those corrupt opinions with which they had been imbued in Egypt while they were in the desert. Consequently, they dedicated to themselves those Egyptian idols as if they were their own, which were most suited to the condition of people wandering through the wilderness. Therefore, they thought it wise to worship *Osiris* primarily in the form of *Moloch*; for Osiris, according to *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic blend of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, credited with ancient wisdom.</note>, was believed to be the overseer of the bodies of every nation and the author of power and strength, who might restore their strength during a most difficult journey. Furthermore, *Kiun*, or *Saturn*, seems to have been the "God of Hospitality" <note>original Latin: Deus Hospitalis</note>, who took under his protection those who were poor and lacked a fixed home. Hence, the Israelites thought he was the one who most needed to be appeased at that time. Finally, small images and portable tabernacles—minimal hindrances to travel—were very well-suited to the condition of those wandering. Spencer does acknowledge the silence of Moses on this matter, but says the testimony of Amos is sufficient.

<margin>XIV. Cocceius, after others, holds this view.</margin>
XIV. However, because it seems hardly probable that the Israelites would dare to commit such nefarious idolatry in the presence of Moses, nor were they ever rebuked by Moses by that name (as far as we read), others believe that *Amos* was not noting the external deeds of the Israelites so much as their *inner spirit*. It is as if he had said: "You served the Tabernacle of the living God in outward appearance, but in reality, you worshipped *Moloch*, whom you made your own by your impiety." So says *Ju-*

...nius and Tremellius. This was excellently explained by de Dieu in his commentary on *Acts 7*, and after him by Cocceius. The main point comes down to this: the Jews did not relate the Mosaic Tabernacle with its Cherubim to the proper goal—namely, to Christ and the blessings to be provided through him—but instead considered it, as their doctors still do today, as a representation of the world and nature. Please see my *Dissertation on the Levitical Tabernacle*, Section 22. Anyone who considers the Tabernacle of God only in this way, and thinks nothing of the Messiah and his benefits, turns it into the *Tabernacle of Moloch*, and possesses no better faith in God than one who worships *Moloch*. And whoever carries the *Tabernacle of God* with that mindset, as the Israelites did through the Levites, does not offer a worship more pleasing to God than if he were carrying the *tabernacle of Moloch*.

<margin>XV. Our judgment.</margin>
XV. Although these points are cleverly argued, I do not know why the simplest interpretation seems to me to be the best of all, provided nothing stands in the way. In this case, nothing at all stands in the way except for the silence of Moses. However, that difficulty can be removed in various ways. It should be noted that Moses did not report everything about the Israelites in Egypt or the wilderness that is found in other Prophets. An example of this is *Ezekiel 20:7–8*, where God recounts that he commanded the Israelites living in Egypt *that each person should cast away the detestable things from before his eyes, and not defile themselves with the dung-gods of Egypt;* yet in their rebellion, they refused to obey him. The Mosaic history contains nothing about this matter. In verse 24, God reproaches the Israelites in the wilderness because their eyes followed the dung-gods of their fathers; those were the gods of the Egyptians (see verse 7).

XVI. Verse 26 is cited by some: *They passed through all that opens the womb.* <note>The author is discussing a controversial passage in Ezekiel 20 regarding the sacrifice of children.</note> But this seems to refer to something else. For the phrase "by fire" is not added, nor is it credible that all the firstborn of the Israelites were consecrated to Moloch. I do not disapprove of Cocceius’s explanation, who translates that phrase thus: *I declared them impure with their gifts, when all that opens the womb was passed through.* This "passing through" <note>original Latin: traductio</note> was not done by the Israelites, but by God. Nor is a passing through fire noted, but rather for the purpose that one might be sacred <note>original: 'facer', likely a typo for 'sacer' (sacred or set apart)</note> to God. God made every firstborn pass over to himself (*Exodus 13:12*). In their place, he then took the Levites (*Numbers 3:4*). And thus all the rest were declared impure, as they were barred from the ministry of the tabernacle. Dathan’s speech—that *all the people are holy*—was displeasing to God.

XVII. Furthermore, it is not necessary that these things be explained concerning the Israelites in the wilderness. For they can be applied to later generations as a more immediate cause of the Assyrian captivity <note>The "transportationis Assyriacæ" refers to the forced exile of the Israelites by the Assyrian Empire.</note>. It is as if God were saying: *Your parents did not offer sacrifices to me in the wilderness, and they perished because of their evil ways; but you are much worse than they.* They murmured against me; you [worship] other gods,

### On the Worship of Moloch

You introduced gods, and indeed the most shameful ones. Therefore I will cause you to go into exile, etc. So says Grotius, and thus no difficulty remains.

<margin>XVIII. *To "pass through the fire" sometimes signifies only a ritual of purification.*</margin>

XVIII. And let these things said about *Moloch* suffice. Now let us look at his most accursed *Sacred Rites*. These are explained by the phrase *passing through the fire* <note>original Hebrew: העביר באש, *ha'avir ba'esh*</note>. This signifies two things. I. The lesser of the two: a *passage through the fire*. Two pyres were built, between which a child was led either by priests or by parents, or was ordered to leap through the flames, so that having been thus purified, expiated, and solemnly dedicated to *Moloch*. The Greeks translated it this way in *Deuteronomy 18:10*: "there shall not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or his daughter in the fire" <note>original Greek: οὐχ εὑρεθήσεται ἐν σοὶ περικαθαίρων τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ ἐν πυρί</note>. And not without reason. For: I. the word <note>original Hebrew: העביר, *he'evir*</note> has that meaning in *Exodus 13:12*: "And you shall set apart to the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: והעברת ליי׳, *ve-ha'avarta l'Adonai*</note>. II. The purifications and consecrations of the ancients' idols were, for the most part, performed by *fire*. Those initiated into the rites of *Mithras* <note>An ancient mystery religion centered on the god Mithras, popular in the Roman Empire</note> were compelled, among other troublesome ceremonies, "to pass through fire and through cold" <note>original Greek: διὰ πυρὸς παρελθεῖν καὶ διὰ κρύεος</note>. So too the *countryfolk* of old *Rome*, when they would leap through a large fire of straw and hay, believing themselves to be purified by these *Palilia* <note>An ancient Roman agricultural festival aimed at cleansing sheep and shepherds</note>. To which these verses apply:

> And soon, through the burning heaps of crackling straw,
> You shall throw your active limbs with a swift foot.

Even the early Christians, who had not yet completely shed their paganism, were accustomed to light huge bonfires at the *New Moons* and leap through the flame; for this reason they were rebuked by *John Chrysostom* and the *Council of Trullo*. See *Grotius* on *Deuteronomy 18:10*. From which *Spencer* took his ideas. Add *Ainsworth* on *Leviticus 18:21* and *Beyer's additions to Selden*.

<margin>XIX. *Sometimes it also signifies actual burning.*</margin>

XIX. II. It signifies *slaughter and burning* as a burnt offering <term>holocaust: a religious animal sacrifice that is completely consumed by fire</term>. For the *Canaanites* and their neighboring peoples were accustomed to put their children to death in honor of their gods. Indeed, when most serious public disasters were feared, the kings of the nations would sacrifice the son they loved most to appease the anger of the gods (*2 Kings 3:27*). From there, it passed to private individuals (*2 Kings 17:31*). And from the Gentiles to the *Kings of the Israelites*. *2 Kings 16:3*: "*Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel; and he even sent his son through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations, which Jehovah had expelled from before the face of the Israelites*." On this passage, *Josephus* <note>A first-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> says: "He offered his own son as a burnt sacrifice according to the customs of the Canaanites" <note>original Greek: ἴδιον ὁλοκαύτησε παῖδα κατὰ τὰ τῶν χαναναιων ἔθη</note>. Although others interpret it differently and apply it to *Hezekiah*, who reigned afterward. See *Spencer*, page 316. Perhaps he made one merely pass through the fire as a rite, but burned others. *2 Chronicles 28:3*. Compare the example of *Manasseh* (*2 Chronicles 33:6*). Many of the people were guilty of the same crime. This is clear from *Jeremiah 19:5*, *7:31*; *Ezekiel 16:20-21*, *23:37*; and *Psalm 106:38*.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION V.

<margin>XX. Its method.</margin>
XX. The method is described in various ways. The summary is essentially this: Moloch was a hollow image with the face of a calf <note>original: "facie vitulina"</note> and outstretched hands. The priests would heat this image with fire; they would then place the infant into its hands until the child was consumed by the flames. Meanwhile, drums <note>original: "tympanis"</note> were beaten so that the wailing of the infants would not be heard. Moreover, those wicked priestlings had persuaded the people that by offering one such infant, the others would be safe and the entire family would enjoy prosperity. See Drusius on *Acts 7*.

<margin>XXI. In the valley of Hinnom, from which the name Gehenna comes.</margin>
XXI. These sacred rites were performed in Tophet, in the *valley of the sons of Hinnom*. <note>Jeremiah 32:35; 2 Kings 23:10</note>. It is believed that *Tophet* was named after the *drums* <note>original: "Tympanis"; the Hebrew word "toph" means drum</note>. From this valley of *Hinnom* comes the name *Gehenna*. This is a very well-known matter. It was there that the ultimate impiety was committed. After the site was defiled by Josiah <note>7th-century BCE King of Judah who instituted religious reforms</note> as recorded in *2 Kings 23:10*, the place became an object of horror to everyone. They would cast filth and carcasses there, and a perpetual fire was kept burning to consume the refuse and bones. From this comes the "Gehenna of fire" <note>original: "gehenna ignis"</note> mentioned in *Matthew 5:22*.

<margin>XXII. Which and how many crimes concur in these rites.</margin>
XXII. God severely **FORBADE** this impiety to his people. <note>Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 18:10</note>. The penalty of death was added. <note>Leviticus 20:2</note>. The reasons for the prohibition were: I. Because that rite was *contrary to the law of nature and to the duty of parents toward their children*. <note>Psalm 106:38</note>. II. It was *sacrilegious*. For they were stealing children—who were born to God and consecrated to Him through circumcision—and sacrificing them to a demon. <note>Ezekiel 23:37</note>. III. It was *magical*, usually connected with the consultation of demons. Thus, both are forbidden together in the same passage <note>Deuteronomy 18:10</note> and are narrated as having occurred together. <note>2 Kings 17:7, 21:6</note>. IV. It was *propitiatory*, intended to ward off evils <note>original: "averruncanda mala"</note>. This is something demons could not do, nor did God wish to be appeased with human victims, lest it should lead to the obscuring of the sacrifice of Christ. <note>compare Micah 6:7</note>. For it is clear enough that the sacrifice of beasts provides only a symbolic or "typical" expiation; regarding human sacrifices, something else might be incorrectly presumed <note>the author suggests human sacrifice might be mistaken for a truly effective payment for sin, a status reserved for Christ alone</note>.

<margin>XXIII. From which, however, something good can be learned.</margin>
XXIII. Yet something **GOOD** can be learned even from this profane rite. I. It is innate in humans to realize it is not fitting for the Divine to show itself favorable to sinners unless a suitable victim intervenes. II. The sacrifice of cattle is not sufficient for this purpose. <note>Micah 6:6-7</note>. III. Our children ought to be consecrated to God, and a public profession of that fact should be made. IV. Nothing ought to be so dear to us that we would not willingly spend it for the sake of the Divine.

It explains the transition of the Valley of Hinnom into the metaphorical "Gehenna" (Hell) and outlines the theological reasons why God strictly prohibited these rites.</summary>

# DISSERTATION VI,

### ON

## THE PRESENT AND FUTURE AGE.

I. *The importance of this dissertation.* II. *The argument.* III. *The same thing can be referred to the present and future age from different perspectives.* IV. *The "Future World" among the Hebrews denotes the state of souls after death.* V. *As also for Paul in 1 Timothy 6:17, 19.* VI. *And 2 Timothy 4:10.* VII. *And Ephesians 1:21.* VIII. *Finally, also for Christ in Matthew 12:32.* IX. *By "future world," the Hebrews also understand that which follows the resurrection of the dead.* X. *As also Christ and the Apostles.* XI. *Does it also refer to the days of the Messiah?* XII. *Maimonides teaches that the Hebrews, or at least some of them, felt this way.* XIII. *Rabbi Elias.* XIV. *Menasseh Ben Israel.* XV. *The Ancients: in Berakhot and Sanhedrin.* XVI. XVII. *Tanchuma.* XVIII. *The saying of Rabbi Huna.* XIX. *Of others.* XX. *Bava Batra.* XXI. *Midrash Kohelet.* XXII. *With very clear explanations.* XXIII. *Rabbi Samuel does not disagree.* XXIV. *Nor those who refer the days of the Messiah to this world.* XXV. *Scripture certainly calls the Kingdom of the Messiah a "new world."* XXVI. *Owen's notable commentary on 2 Peter 3:5, 13.* XXVII. *The first period of that New World.* XXVIII. *The second.* XXIX. *The third.* XXX. *The end of these days.* XXXI. *The end of the appointed time.* XXXII. *The "consummation of the ages" denotes the end of the Mosaic Economy.* XXXIII. *The "habitable world to come" is the Church of the New Testament.* XXXIV. *Which is also rightly called the <term>oikoumenē</term> <note>original Greek: οἰκουμένη; referring to the "inhabited" or "civilized" world</note>:* XXXV. *And is called "future."* XXXVI. *And is subject to Christ, not to Angels.*

<margin>I. *The importance of this dissertation.*</margin>
The distinction between the "present age" and "the one to come" <note>original Greek: τοῦ αἰῶνος τοῦ νῦν καὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος; Hebrew: הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, *ha-olam ha-zeh ve-ha-olam ha-ba*</note>—that is, the PRESENT & FUTURE WORLD—is very frequent, both in the mysterious oracles of the Divine scriptures and in the commentaries of the Hebrews. Since a genuine explanation of this phrasing can shed a great deal of light on many testimonies of the Scriptures, I believe I will perform a service not unwelcome to students of hidden wisdom if I investigate and discuss it a little more diligently.

<margin>II. *The argument.*</margin>
II. *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius, a 16th-century Flemish Protestant Hebraist</note> has briefly encompassed the summary of those things I have to say, while commenting on Matthew 12:32 in these words:

<header>BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI.</header>

->*The future age is threefold, as Don Isaac Abarbanel <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a prominent Jewish statesman, philosopher, and Bible commentator.</note> noted in the book entitled The Possession of the Fathers <note>A reference to Abarbanel's work *Nachalat Avot*, a commentary on the Ethics of the Fathers.</note>. The first is the* AGE OF THE MESSIAH. *The second is* AFTER THIS LIFE. *The third is* AFTER THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD.<-

<margin>
*III. From a different perspective, the same thing can be referred to the present and the future age.*
</margin>
III. However, the moments of time are always to be considered such that the beginning of the age called "future" is judged to coincide with the end of that "present" age which corresponds to it in meaning. For example, when the "future age" denotes the days of the Messiah, the "present age" is the name given to the time that runs up until the manifestation of his kingdom. When, however, the "future age" refers to the condition of separate souls after this life, the "present age" flows for each individual until the end of this physical <term>animalis</term> <note>The author uses "animalis" in the Latin sense of "pertaining to the breath/soul of a living creature," essentially meaning our current biological life.</note> life. Finally, whenever the "future age" designates the status of both mankind and the entire universe after the resurrection of the dead, the "present age" encompasses whatever time passes until the universal renewal of all things. Hence it is clear that, from a different perspective and without any contradiction, one and the same thing can be referred to both the present and the future age. Nevertheless, lest calculations be confused, a student of accuracy must always attend to the comparison of the present age with the future, while maintaining the logical consistency of the definition. But we must clarify and confirm each individual meaning, in such an order that our discourse, having begun from the clearer and more widely accepted points, may end with those that are more a matter of controversy.

<margin>
*IV. For the Hebrews, the "Future World" denotes the state of souls after death.*
</margin>
IV. First, therefore, the Sages of the Hebrews understood the "future world" to mean the state of souls after death. This was the intent of Tanchuma <note>A collection of Jewish homilies (Midrash) on the Torah.</note> on page 52: <note>original Hebrew: עה"ב לאחר שיצא האדם מן העולם הזה</note> *The future world exists when a man has departed from this world.* And Moses Maimonides <note>The 12th-century philosopher also known as Rambam.</note> fights with many arguments against Moses Gerundensis <note>The 13th-century scholar also known as Nahmanides or Ramban.</note> to prove that the future world is that into which each person is received after death—not indeed regarding the body, but regarding the soul. For he says in the *Laws of Repentance* <note>A section of Maimonides' legal code, the *Mishneh Torah*.</note>, Chapter VIII: <note>original Hebrew: העולם הבא אין לו גוף וגויה אלא נפשות צדיקים בלבד בלא גוף</note> *In the future world there is no body or physical form, but only the souls of the righteous separated from the body.* Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> likewise on 1 Samuel 25:29 says that according to the opinion of Jonathan, this is the interpretation of the passage: <note>original Hebrew: נפש אדני צרורה בצרor החיים לעולם הבא</note> *the soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living, in the future age.* To the same effect is that from the Zohar <note>The foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note> on Genesis, page 5, column 2: *What is the Sabbath day?* <note>original Hebrew: דוגמת ארץ החיים שהוא עולם הבא עולם הנשמות עולם הנחמות</note> *A likeness of the land of the living, which is the future world, the world of souls, the world of consolations.* It would be a waste of effort to use excessive diligence on such a clear matter.

# ON THE PRESENT AND FUTURE AGE.

<margin>
V. See also
1 Tim. 6:17, 19.
</margin>
V. I believe that Paul wrote in the same spirit in 1 Timothy 6:17 and 19: <note>original: "τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι παράγγελλε"</note> *command the RICH in THIS AGE*, that they should not be high-minded, etc., storing up for themselves a good foundation <note>original: "εἰς τὸ μέλλον"</note> *for the FUTURE*, so that they may take hold of eternal life. With this saying of Paul, one may compare a rather elegant little story found in the *Midrash Ruth* <note>The Midrash Ruth is a traditional Jewish homiletic commentary on the Book of Ruth.</note>, folio 42, column 2. The summary of it is as follows: *Of two men who had lived wickedly and impiously in this world, one repented and was counted among the assembly of the righteous in the future world; the other was counted among the wicked. The latter, complaining about his lot since they had both been bound by the same crimes, received this answer: "The other man repented before death." To which he replied, "Allow me to go and repent now also." But the answer came again: "O most foolish of men! Do you not know that this world (that is, the world of souls into which he had passed) is like the Sabbath, on which—according to the opinion of the Hebrews—it is not permitted to prepare food, while the world from which you came is like the Eve of the Sabbath? If a man does not prepare on the Eve of the Sabbath, what shall he eat on the Sabbath? Furthermore, this world is like the sea, and the world from which you came is like the dry land. If one does not prepare while on the dry land, what shall he eat at sea? Moreover, this world is like the desert, and the world from which you came is like the inhabited land. If one does not prepare in the inhabited land, what shall he eat in the desert?"*

<margin>
VI. And
2 Tim. 4:10.
</margin>
VI. To the same category I would refer 2 Timothy 4:10: *Demas has deserted me*, <note>original: "ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα"</note> *having loved the PRESENT AGE*, that is, this physical <term>animalis</term> <note>Referring to biological life or the life of the senses rather than spiritual life.</note> life. Fearing dangers and inconveniences, he surely looked out for the time of his own life. Hesychius <note>Hesychius of Alexandria was a 5th-century grammarian who compiled a famous dictionary of obscure Greek words.</note> correctly states: <note>original: "Αἰών, ὁ βίος τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ τῆς ζωῆς χρόνος"</note> *Aeon (Age) is the life of men, the span of time of a life.* This can be confirmed by comparing Mark 4:19 with Luke 8:14.

<margin>
VII. And
Eph. 1:21.
</margin>
VII. And why should we not interpret Ephesians 1:21 in the same sense? There we read that Christ was raised far above all *rule and authority*, and *power*, and *dominion*, and *every name that is named* not only in THIS AGE, but also in the FUTURE. It is as if the Apostle were saying: Christ is much more sublime than all the Angels, whatever eminent titles they may enjoy; and if there are even more majestic names for Angels which we, having joined their company, will only learn in the future age, Christ rules over those as well. This stands unless one prefers to follow the most celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian famous for "Covenant Theology."</note> in understanding "this age" as the *Old Testament*, where there are great names like *Angels*, *Prophets*, *Moses*, and the *High Priest*; and "the future age" as the *New Testament and the kingdom of glory*, where the <note>original: "διαφορώτερον ὄνομα"</note> *more excellent name* of Christ is most clearly demonstrated. But we shall discuss that meaning shortly.

### BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI.

<margin>
VIII. Finally {
Christ
Matthew
12:32.
</margin>
VIII. Perhaps from this first interpretation <note>Referring to the "world of souls" after death but before resurrection.</note> some light may shine upon that famous saying of Christ in Matthew 12:32: *It will not be forgiven* **NEITHER IN THIS AGE** *nor* **IN THE FUTURE**. Even though—following the lead of Saint Mark in Chapter 3:29—we may safely interpret this as *he never has forgiveness* <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔχει ἄφεσιν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα"</note>, the observation of Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> and others should not be dismissed. It appears that Christ deliberately named both ages to strip away from the Jews the persuasion with which they flattered themselves regarding the most serious crimes. For they believed that sins committed by those who persevered in the profession of Judaism were forgiven either through simple repentance (for sins against positive commands), or on the solemn Day of Atonement (for sins against negative commands), or through the punishments of this life (for those carrying the penalty of death or excision), or at least *after death*, whether immediately or after some delay, for those committed with contempt for the Divine Majesty. And from this comes the common proverb, <term>Kaparah Mitah</term> <note>original Hebrew: כפרה מיתה</note>, *death is the atonement for sins*. You will find the words of the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> pertaining to this, translated into Latin, in *Lightfoot’s commentary on this passage* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English Hebraist who explained the New Testament via Talmudic parallels.</note>. The Jews therefore believed that certain crimes are expiated and forgiven in this age, and others *in the future*—namely, the age of souls—either through death itself or through the sufferings following death. Regarding these matters, see *Menasseh [Ben Israel] on Creation, Problem XVII*. To these crimes they attached the blasphemy of the Divine name. For so it stands in the **Sanhedrim, Folio 37, column 3**: *For him by whom the name of God is profaned or blasphemed, repentance has no power to suspend judgment, nor the Day of Atonement to expiate, nor inflicted lashes or chastisements to wipe it away; but all these only suspend the judgment, and death wipes it away.* Thus they say: but on the contrary, Christ teaches that there is no reason for profane despisers of the Holy Spirit to flatter themselves with any expiation, either of *this* or of the *future age*, whether through or after death.

The Gerundese <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar from Girona.</note> fights for this meaning. To avoid the nausea of wordiness, I would like to add a few notes from *Menasseh Ben Israel, On the Resurrection of the Dead, Book III, Chapter 1*. # CONCERNING THIS AGE AND THE FUTURE ONE.

Notable and very famous is that passage which appears in the prayer composed by the Great Assembly: *these are its words.*
