*There is no comparison with you in* **THIS WORLD**, *O Lord our God; nor is there anyone besides you, our King, in the* **LIFE OF THE FUTURE AGE**; *nor will there be any besides you, our Redeemer, in the* **DAYS OF THE MESSIAH**; *nor is there anyone like you, our Savior, in the* **RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD**. After some further points, *Menasseh* <note>Menasseh ben Israel (1604–1657), a leading Portuguese rabbi and diplomat.</note> proceeds thus: "And this is also effectively proven by that illustrious passage read in the *Tractate Sanhedrin* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with judicial procedures and the afterlife.</note>: *where it is said that none of those who deny the resurrection shall be a partaker of the future age; and the reason is added why he shall not be a partaker, namely this:* <note>original Hebrew: "הוא כפר בתחית המתים לפיכך לא יהיה לו חלק בתחית המתים"</note> *Whoever denies the resurrection of the dead, by the very fact that he denies it, shall not be a partaker of the resurrection.*" Thus far *Menasseh*. Let these excerpts from the Hebrew authors suffice for now.

<margin>
X. As Christ and the Apostles [taught].
</margin>
X. Excellently to this point, the Lord *Jesus* says in Luke 20:34, 35, 36: *The children of this age* <note>original Greek: "Οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου"</note>, **THE SONS OF THIS AGE** *marry and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy to attain* **THAT AGE** *and the* **RESURRECTION FROM THE DEAD**, *neither marry, etc., and they are the children of God, since they are* **SONS OF THE RESURRECTION**. Add Mark 10:29, Luke 18:29, 30, and especially Titus 2:12, 13: *Let us live piously in the* **PRESENT AGE**, *expecting that blessed hope and the* **GLORIOUS APPEARING** *of the glory of that great God and our Savior, namely Jesus Christ.* Which *appearing of glory* <note>original Greek: "ἐπιφάνεια τῆς δόξης"</note>, if not exclusively, then certainly most especially, is to be understood as the radiance and flashing of the approaching kingdom of glory at the final coming of Christ for the resurrection of the dead and the last judgment.

<margin>

</margin>
XI. A greater difficulty seems to exist for some regarding the third meaning, *concerning the Days of the Messiah*. And he adds: if anyone wishes to be more fully informed on this matter, he should go to Abarbenel <note>Isaac Abarbenel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher.</note> in the book *The Inheritance of the Fathers* <note>Latin: Nachalat Abbot</note>, *the Chapter of Ben Zoma*: which Abarbenel, also praised by Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Hebraist.</note>, oh how I wish I had him at hand now! XIV. Menasseh Ben Israel.

XIV. That is, he says, whoever is raised shall enjoy the blessedness of that future age, or shall obtain a portion of the Holy Land when it is distributed among the tribes. XVII. But we do not lack further evidence. Let us hear again from the *Tanchuma, folio 9, column 2:* <note>The Tanchuma is a collection of homiletic midrashim (interpretations) on the Torah.</note> The Holy God, Blessed be He, says to Israel: *In this world you fear because of your transgressions; but in the future world, when there will be no evil inclination <note>Hebrew: Yetzer Ha-Ra</note>, you will be concerned only with the good stored up for you, as it is said: afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king. Hosea 3:5.* <note>original: "In hoc mundo vos timetis... Davidem Regem suum."</note> Do these things also refer to anything other than the days of the Messiah? I would like this to be compared with the *Sepher Abkat Rochel* <note>The "Book of the Powder of the Merchant," a medieval work on Jewish eschatology.</note>, which in the tenth consolation of the times that will come under the Messiah, also proclaims this as a distinguished good: *The Holy One, Blessed be He, is destined to remove the evil inclination and every evil thing from Israel.* <note>original Hebrew: עתיד הקב״ה להסיר יצר הרע וכל דבר רע מישראל</note> Nor does Gerundensis <note>Moses ben Nahman, also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270).</note> disagree in his commentary on *Deuteronomy 30:6.*

<margin>XVIII. The saying of Rabbi Huna.</margin>
XVIII. It is worthwhile to excerpt something again from *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist and clergyman.</note>, who in his *Chronicles of the Times of the New Testament, Section IX,* has these words: Rabbi Huna speaks of three ages, the last of which is the **Age of the Messiah**, about which he says: when it comes, the Blessed God says, "It now falls to me to establish a new creation." They also call this time the **future age** <note>Hebrew: Olam Ha-Ba</note>, because of the change in things they expected then, as if a **New World** had been created. *Tanchuma, folio 77, column 3:* IN THE FUTURE AGE I WILL SEND MY MESSENGER QUICKLY, AND HE WILL PREPARE THE WAY BEFORE ME. Is there still any reason to doubt?

<margin>XIX. Of others.</margin>
XIX. Certainly, all doubt must yield to those things which *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his covenant theology.</note> noted on the title of *Psalm 92.* "The Sabbath day," he says, "can be understood as the time of the New Testament, in which the grace and truth of God exhibited through Christ are represented, the yoke of legal servitude having been taken away." Thus *Hebrews 4:9* refers to a "Sabbath rest." <note>Greek: sabbatismos</note> And so the **Ancient Rabbis** thought *that this Psalm pertains to the time to come, an age which is entirely Sabbath and rest; and these are the days of the Messiah.* <note>original Hebrew: שהוא על העתיד לבא לעולם שכלו שבת ומנוחה והם ימי המשיח</note>

However, those expressions **the world to come** <note>Hebrew: Olam Ha-Ba</note> and **the future age** <note>Hebrew: Atid La-Vo</note> have the same meaning, as noted by Elijah Levita in *Tishbi* under the word *Atid*.

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI.

Rabbi Hezekiah says: "Every law that you learn in this world is mere vanity if it is compared with the **LAW OF THE FUTURE AGE**." <note>original Hebrew: "כל תורה שאת לומד בעולם הזה הבל היא לפני התורה של עולם הבא"</note> But the Law of the future age is the Law of the Messiah. <margin>XXII. With the most articulate explanations of both the Talmudists and the Targumists, I have their words.</margin>
XXII. But why should I fight with inferences, however evident they may be? Since I have the articulate words of both the Talmudists <note>The scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> and the Targumists <note>The authors of the Targums, which are Aramaic translations and expansions of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. <margin>XXIII. Nor does Rabbi Samuel disagree.</margin>
XXIII. I am certainly not unaware of that well-known saying of Rabbi Samuel <note>Samuel of Nehardea, a prominent 3rd-century Jewish scholar in Babylonia.</note>, which is frequently repeated in the Talmud: "**There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah except for the subjection to foreign kingdoms**." <note>original Hebrew/Latin: "אין בין העולם הזה לימות המשיח אלא שעבוד מלכיות. Perhaps these many testimonies of the Hebrews might seem to have been piled up with more labor than necessary in a clear matter. But let the reader know that there was once a man most learned in these letters who took it upon himself to stubbornly deny, in a circle of erudite men, that any Hebrews existed who understood the "future age" as the age of the Messiah. This gave me the occasion to prove that meaning more at length.

<margin>XXIV. Neither do those who refer the days of the Messiah to this world.</margin>
XXIV. In the meantime, I will by no means deny that many testimonies of the Jews can be produced in which they speak of the days of the Messiah as belonging to this world: but these are easily reconciled with those I have just cited, based on the foundation we laid in Theme III. Specifically, if someone has in mind that meaning of the "present and future world" according to which the "future" begins with the resurrection of the dead, it is necessary for him to refer the times of the Messiah to the present world: yet he does not by that very fact overturn the other meaning of that distinction, according to which the times of the Messiah are called a part of the "future age." For statements to be contradictory, it is necessary—according to the rules of Logic—that the affirming and denying parties speak of the same thing, in the same respect, and in the same manner.

# ON THIS AGE AND THE FUTURE ONE.

...those who call the Kingdom of the *Messiah* the beginning of the New Age strive to prove this. <margin>He calls the kingdom of the Messiah new.</margin> In the Prophet *Haggai*, at the time when God says he will send him who is the *Desire of all nations* for the *World*; he adds that he will shake the heavens and the earth, and the *sea*, and the *dry land*. Hag. II. 6. Likewise in *Isaiah*, Chapter LXV. 17: *For behold, I am about to create new heavens and a new earth: and these former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they come to mind.* Again, Chapter LXVI. 22: *Those new heavens and the new earth, which I am about to make, stand before me.* This agrees with Revelation XXI. 1: *And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea is no more.* Nor is that saying of Peter inconsistent, 2 Peter III. 13: *But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise. All things tend toward this: that through the Messiah, a new face of things must be brought to the world, from which it is permitted to consider the beginning of another age.*

<margin>XXVI. John Owen’s remarkable commentary on 2 Peter III. 5. etc.</margin>
XXVI. I cannot bring myself to deprive the readers of this Dissertation of the very learned commentary which that most excellent man, *John Owen* <note>John Owen (1616–1683) was a highly influential English Puritan theologian and academic administrator at Oxford.</note>, provides on this last passage of Peter in his commentaries titled *Theologumena* <note>A work on the history and nature of theology.</note>, Book III, Chapter 1. He observes that the Apostle in verses 5, 6, and 7 mentions a double world: *that old one which perished by water*, and the one present at that time which was to be consumed by fire; after the destruction of which, he announces the entrance of a third world in verse thirteen: <term>But we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells.</term> <note>original Greek: "Καινὸς δὲ ὀυρανὸς καὶ γῆν καινὴν κατὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα αὐτῶ προσδοκῶμεν ἐν οἷς δικαιοσύνη κατοικεῖ."</note> The Apostle is not dealing with the visible Heaven or Earth in terms of their physical substance in either place. For when the old world was destroyed by water, the framework of the heavens and earth nevertheless remained. Therefore, that *World* consisted of the men living in the world. Once they were deleted by the flood, another *world* had to be established for the proper carrying out of the worship of God. Moreover, God laid the foundations of this World in the family of Noah: the entire fabric was completed by the establishment and furnishing of the *Jewish Church*. And that was the world which Blessed Peter predicted was then and there to be dissolved by fire, namely, in the prophetic style. So we read in Isaiah, Chapter fifty-one, verses fifteen and sixteen: *I am the Lord your God, who divided the sea, so that its waves roared, the Lord of hosts is his name, and I have put my words in your mouth, and I have covered you in the shadow of my hand: that I may plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth, and say to Zion, "You are my people."* Therefore, at that time when God, dividing the sea and leading his people out of Egypt, entrusted them with the word or law along with the solemn prescription of his worship—forming them into a Church for himself—he instituted and perfected this new world, that heaven and those earths. At the time when Peter wrote, this *World*, that is, the *Jewish Church* which was now apostate <note>A term used here to describe the rejection of the new Christian covenant by the established Jewish religious system.</note>, hurried toward its destruction by fire; not otherwise than that old World rushed headlong into the flood. By the fire...

# BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI.

Rabbi Hizkias says: <note>original: "כל תורה שאת לומד בעולם הזה הבל היא לפני התורה של עולם הבא"</note> "All the Law that you learn in this world is mere vanity compared to the **LAW OF THE FUTURE AGE**." For the "Law of the future age" is the Law of the Messiah. It is explained in this way in Chapter 11, verse 8: "All the Law that a man learns in this world is vanity <note>original: "לפני תורתו של משיח"</note> compared with the **LAW OF THE MESSIAH**."

<margin>XXII. With very clear explanations.</margin>
XXII. But why do I struggle with logical deductions, however evident they may be? For I have explicit words from both the Talmudists <note>The compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> and the Targumists <note>Translators or commentators who provided Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. A gloss of the Talmud on Sanhedrin, Chapter 11, cited by Joseph de Voisin in his notes on Raymond Martini's *Dagger of Faith* <term>Pugio Fidei; a famous 13th-century polemical work by Raymond Martini used to argue for Christianity using Jewish texts</term> page 356, speaks in this manner: <note>original: "כל דלית לי׳ חלק לעו״הב היינו . אין להם חלק לעולם הבא"</note> **THEY HAVE NO PORTION IN THE FUTURE AGE, THAT IS, IN THE DAYS OF THE MESSIAH.** Furthermore, the Targum on 1 Kings 4:33 says: <note>original: "בעלמא הדין ובעלמא דאתי דמשיחא"</note> "In this world, and **IN THE FUTURE AGE OF THE MESSIAH**."

<margin>XXIII. Nor does Rabbi Samuel disagree.</margin>
XXIII. I am certainly not unaware of that famous saying of Rabbi Samuel, which is repeated quite often in the Talmud: <note>original: "אין בין העולם הזה לימות המשיח אלא שעבוד מלכיות"</note> "*There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah, except for the subjection to kingdoms.*" <note>This refers to the political independence of Israel vs. being ruled by foreign powers.</note> However, even this distinguishes the days of the Messiah from this world and suggests a new argument to us; it is far from favoring those who think otherwise. It might seem that I have piled up too many Hebrew testimonies for a matter that should be clear. But let the reader know that there was once a man most learned in these letters who took it upon himself to stubbornly deny, in a circle of learned men, that any Hebrews existed who understood the "future age" as the age of the Messiah. This gave me the occasion to prove that meaning more at length.

<margin>XXIV. Nor those who refer the days of the Messiah to this world.</margin>
XXIV. Meanwhile, I will by no means deny that many testimonies of the Jews can be produced in which they speak of the days of the Messiah as belonging to *this* world. But these are easily reconciled with those I have just cited, based on the foundation we laid in Section III. That is to say: if someone has in mind the definition of "present" and "future" world where the "future" one begins only with the resurrection of the dead, that person must necessarily refer the times of the Messiah to the present world. However, that does not by itself overturn the *other* meaning of that distinction, according to which the times of the Messiah are called a part of the "future age." For statements to be truly contradictory, it is necessary—according to the rules of Logic—that the person affirming and the person denying be speaking about the same thing, in the same respect, and in the same manner.

<margin>XXV. Scripture certainly refers...</margin>
XXV. But whatever the case may be regarding the Hebrew Doctors; it certainly cannot be denied that in the expressions of both the Sacred Prophets and the Apostles...

# OF THIS AGE AND THE FUTURE.

...those who maintain that the Kingdom of the Messiah is the beginning of the New Age rely [upon this].
<margin>
He calls the Kingdom of the Messiah "new."
</margin>
In the Prophet Haggai, at the time when God says he will send him who is *the desire of the nations for the world*; <note>original: "Mundum est desiderium gentium" — a variation on Haggai 2:7, usually rendered as "the desire of all nations shall come."</note> he adds, that he will shake the heavens & the earth, & *the sea, & the dry land*. Haggai 2:6. Likewise in Isaiah, Chapter 65:17: *For behold, I am about to create new heavens, & a new earth; and these former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they come to mind.* Again in Chapter 66:22: *Those new heavens, & the new earth, which I am about to make, stand before me.* This agrees with Revelation 21:1: *And I saw a new heaven & a new earth. For the first heaven & the first earth had passed away, & the sea was no more.* Nor is that saying of Peter inconsistent, 2 Peter 3:13: *But we look for new heavens, & a new earth, according to his promise.* All things tend toward this: that through the Messiah a new face of things is to be brought upon the world, from which one may consider the start of another age.

<margin>
XXVI.
John Owen's
notable
commentary
on 2 Peter 3:5
etc.
</margin>
XXVI. I cannot bring myself to deprive the readers of this Dissertation of that most learned commentary, which that most excellent man, *John Owen*, provides on this last passage of Peter in his *Theological Treatises*, Book III, Chapter 1. <term>Theologumena; "Theologumena Pantodapa," a famous 1661 work by the English Puritan theologian John Owen discussing the history of religion.</term> He observes that the Apostle in verses 5, 6, and 7 mentions a double world: that old one which perished through water, and the one present at that time to be consumed by fire; after the destruction of which, he announces the entry of a *third* in the thirteenth verse. <note>original: "Καινὸς δὲ οὐρανὸς καὶ γῆν καινὴν κατὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα αὐτοῦ προσδοκῶμεν ἐν οἷς δικαιοסύνη κατοικεῖ" — "But we look for a new heaven and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells."</note> The Apostle does not treat the visible Heaven or Earth in respect to their physical substance in either place. For even when the old world was destroyed by water, the framework of the heavens and the lands nevertheless remained. Therefore, that *world* consisted of the men living in the world. When they were destroyed by the flood, another *world* had to be erected for the proper performance of God’s worship. Moreover, God laid the foundations of this World in the family of Noah: the entire structure was completed by the erection and adornment of the *Jewish* Church. And that was the world which Blessed Peter foretold was to be dissolved immediately by fire; namely, in the Prophetic style. Thus we read in Isaiah, Chapter 51, verses 15 and 16: *I am the Lord your God, who divides the sea, so that its waves roar—the Lord of hosts is his name—and I have put my words in your mouth, and protected you in the shadow of my hand: to plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth, and to say to Zion, you are my people.* At that time, therefore, when God, dividing the sea and leading his people out of Egypt, entrusted to them the word or the law with the solemn prescription of his worship, forming them into a Church for himself, he instituted and perfected this new world—that heaven and those earths. At the time Peter wrote, this World—that is, the Jewish Church now become apostate—hastened toward the destruction of fire; not unlike how that old World threw itself into the flood. ->### BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI.<-

With the destruction of the Temple and the city, the structure of that world was dissolved. However, because it was not yet **the end of the age** <note>original Greek: $\tau \tilde{\eta} \ \alpha \iota \tilde{\omega} \nu o \varsigma \ \sigma \upsilon \nu \tau \acute{\varepsilon} \lambda \varepsilon \iota \alpha$ (tēs aiōnos synteleia)</note>, the Apostle commands the faithful to look for another world—new heavens and a new earth—according to God’s promise. That promise is found in Isaiah, chapter sixty-five, verse seventeen; and in the same words in chapter sixty-six, verse twenty-two. *Behold,* he says, *I am about to create new heavens and a new earth, and these former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they come to mind.* In these passages, the Prophet depicts the state of the Church after the coming of Christ; namely, at that time when God would take Priests and Levites from among the Gentiles, as the words in the twenty-first verse of the final chapter state—that is, when the Gospel ministry would be established. For this reason, that state of the Church before the conflagration of this second world was designated the "age to come" and the *world to come*; as Paul teaches us in the *Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter two*, verse five, and also in *chapter six, verse five*. Thus, that *first* or ancient world perished through the flood of water; the Apostle foretells that the *second*, which was present at that time, would perish by fire; and he confirms that the future world would endure until the consummation of the age. Thus far, **Owen**. <note>John Owen (1616–1683) was a prominent English Puritan theologian; the author here is summarizing Owen’s "Theologumena Pantodapa."</note>

<margin>
XXVII.
The first
period of that
New World.
</margin>
XXVII. Whatever one may think of this exposition, which we offer to the learned to be weighed, all these prophecies certainly describe for us the Kingdom of the Messiah; yet they have various stages and periods of their fulfillment. God began to *shake the heaven and the earth* when, once the profane idolatry of the Gentiles was removed and the men of the whole world were stirred by the preaching of the Gospel and raised up in uncommon hope, He also demolished Jerusalem and the Temple—where He had held the throne of His glory. With the beauty of the land struck by a curse, He abolished, both by law and by deed, the *weak and beggarly elements of the old world*. <note>An allusion to Galatians 4:9, referring to the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament.</note> He introduced that state in which *neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but a **new creation*** <note>original Greek: $\kappa \alpha \iota \nu \dot{\eta} \ \kappa \tau \iota \sigma \iota \varsigma$ (kainē ktisis)</note>, and all nations without distinction enjoy the privileges of the spiritual kingdom. In short: *where the old things have passed away, and all things have been made new.* 1 Corinthians 5:17. <note>The author likely intends 2 Corinthians 5:17.</note> See, if you please, Hebrews 12:26-27, along with the commentaries of **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major French Protestant reformer and scholar.</note> and the **Dutch**. <note>Refers to the "Statenvertaling" or the Dutch Authorized Version's marginal notes, highly regarded in the 17th century.</note> Isaiah’s prophecies are also of such a kind that at least their beginning precedes the final coming of Christ, as will be clear to those who examine them.

<margin>
XXVIII.
The second.
</margin>
XXVIII. But beyond this first innovation, we also expect a second renewal of the world under the auspices of the Messiah. This will occur when, naturally, the Antichrist has been cast down from his throne, the destroyers of the earth have been destroyed, the Israelites have been converted, and the Church is surrounded by a great light of knowledge, holiness, and consolation. The world will then be gifted with remarkable abundance and, as it were, *life from the dead*. Romans 11:12, 15. These happy times...

# ON THIS AGE AND THE FUTURE #

...the times of Revelation 21 are portrayed in their living colors. On that chapter, I would wish the reader to consult the very learned commentary of Jonas le Bui, also known as Launaeus. <note>Jonas le Bui (Jean de Launoy, 1603–1678) was a French theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to church history.</note>

<margin>XXIX. Third.</margin> XXIX. Finally, the *ultimate* renewal of the world will follow, when it is entirely liberated from the slavery of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. Nature waits for this revelation with "outstretched neck" (as it were) <note>original Latin: *exserto capite*; a metaphor for eager expectation</note>, sighing and laboring in birth together until this very time (Romans 8:19ff). This is what Peter was primarily looking toward. Since the renewal of the world was to be begun at the first coming of the Messiah, continued under his guidance, and completed at his final "appearance" <note>original Greek: *ἐπιφάνειᾳ* (epiphaneia)</note>, this condition of time is most rightfully called the *future age* <note>original: *futurum seculum*</note> when compared to the ages that came before.

<margin>XXX. The end of these days.</margin> XXX. We should also not overlook that the coming of the Messiah is everywhere placed "in the end of days" <note>original Hebrew: *בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים* (be-acharit ha-yamim)</note> (Isaiah 2:1) or "at the end of these days" <note>original Greek: *ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων* (ep’ eschatōn tōn hēmerōn toutōn)</note> (Hebrews 1:1). This properly signifies *during the very last of these days* which were passing while the ceremonial worship was still standing and the "elements of the old world" were still in force. From this, it is established that shortly after that arrival, new days belonging to a new age are to be reckoned.

<margin>XXXI. The end of the appointed time.</margin> XXXI. A very similar phrase is found in Habakkuk 2:3: "The vision will still be for an appointed time," and "there will be a herald" <note>original Hebrew: *יָפֵחַ* (yaphach), which the author interprets as a 'witness' or 'herald'</note> AT THE END "who will not lie." The "vision" there signifies prophetic preaching, accompanied by a symbolic demonstration. That was to endure until the "set time" <note>original Greek: *προθεσμίαν* (prothesmian)</note> and the "fullness of time" mentioned in Galatians 4:2–4. All the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John (Matthew 11:13). It belongs to the Messiah to "seal the vision and the prophet" (Daniel 9:24), which is to say, to abolish them by proving them true. He is promised here under the name *Herald* <note>original: *יָפֵחַ* (yaphach)</note>, who is an Indicator, a Proclaimer, or a Witness (compare Proverbs 6:19, 12:17). He does not merely predict future things but narrates the truth and the reality of what has been done. He is said to be coming "at the end" <note>original Hebrew: *לקץ* (la-qetz)</note> of the pre-established term. From this point, the epoch of the second age must begin.

<margin>XXXII. The consummation of the ages marks the end of the Mosaic Economy.</margin> XXXII. And indeed, Christ came and sacrificed himself "at the consummation of the ages" <note>original Greek: *ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων* (epi synteleia tōn aiōnōn)</note> (Hebrews 9:26)—that is, at the end of the prior time. For there were still to be "the coming ages" <note>original Greek: *αἰῶνες ἐπερχόμενοι* (aiōnes eperchomenoi)</note> in which God would show "the surpassing riches of his grace" (Ephesians 2:7). He could have sent Christ at the end of days in such a way that the resurrection of the dead followed immediately. But he willed that the "year of grace" begun by Christ's mission (Isaiah 61:2) should extend through many centuries, so that he might more illustriously reveal the magnitude of the riches of his kindness to the world through such a long duration of time.

<margin>XXXIII. The world...</margin> XXXIII. Nor do I doubt that in Hebrews 2:5, by "the world..."

->### BOOK II. DISSERTATION VI. ###<-

<margin>The Church of the New Testament is the habitable world to come.</margin>
By "the world to come" <note>original Greek: οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν (oikoumenēn tēn mellousan)</note>, which the Apostle asserts is subject to Christ and not to Angels <note>Hebrews 2:5</note>, he understood the Church of the New Testament, in which the kingdom of the Messiah is fully revealed. For regarding the age following the final judgment, he testifies that Christ will then hand over the kingdom to God the Father, and the Son himself will be subjected to Him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24, 28). Indeed, the argument that Cameron <note>John Cameron (1579–1625), a Scottish theologian</note> subtly raises—that the state of the Church as it is on this earth cannot be called the "habitable world," much less the "one to come"—is of little value. He claims that the world is a desert for the Church, and that the "habitable world" of the Church is in heaven, just as the Israelites' was in the land of Canaan.

<margin>XXXIV. Which is also rightly called the "habitable world."</margin>
XXXIV. I do not deny, of course, that the state of the Church on earth, if compared with the heavenly state, holds some likeness to a desert. Nevertheless, the Church of the New Testament, when compared with that of the Old, can be appropriately called the *habitable world* <note>original Hebrew: תבל (tebel); Greek: ἡ οἰκουμένη (hē oikoumenē)</note>, and it is called so more than once in the sacred writings. Before the "appearance" <note>original Greek: ἐπιφάνειαν (epiphaneia)</note> of Christ, the Jewish state was like a desert. For this reason, John is called "the voice of one crying in the wilderness" (Isaiah 40:3)—not only literally <note>original: γραμματικῶς (grammatikōs)</note>, because he frequently taught in desert places, but also mystically <note>original: μυστικῶς (mystikōs)</note>, because the people to whom he was sent had the appearance of a desert and an unsown land. But concerning the kingdom of Christ, it was predicted in Isaiah 35:1–2: *The desert and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose. It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing: the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it, the excellency of Carmel and Sharon.* And again in Psalm 93:1: *The Lord reigns, he is clothed with majesty; the Lord is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself:* **the habitable world is also established** <note>original Hebrew: אף תכון תבל (aph tikon tebel)</note>, that it cannot be moved. Even the "blind" Jews <note>a common period polemic referring to those who did not recognize Jesus as Messiah</note> cannot fail to see that this Psalm, along with the others up to the hundred and first, pertains to the future and speaks of the days of the Messiah. For so says the commentary *Kav Venaki* <note>A 17th-century Jewish commentary by Isaac Aboab da Fonseca</note>, following Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval Jewish rabbi and biblical commentator</note>. In the same manner, Psalm 96:12–13 says: *Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice before the Lord: for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge* **the habitable world** *with righteousness, and the people with his truth.* That is, he will purge his Church of hypocrites and manifest his righteousness, which is the foundation of all salvation, and for its sake, he will vindicate his people, fulfilling for them the promise made to the Fathers. It is clear, therefore, that the New Testament Church is called the "habitable world."

<margin>XXXV. And it is called "future."</margin>
XXXV. But it can also be called the *habitable world to come* <note>or "future habitable world"</note> for a twofold reason. First, with respect to the time that went before, and the "traditions" <note>original Greek: παραδοσίας (paradosias)</note> of the Ancients:

<keywords>World to Come, Church of the New Testament, Messiah, Habitable World, Tebel, Oikoumene, Isaiah, Psalms, David Kimchi, Kav Venaki</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "habitable world to come" (Hebrews 2:5), specifically concluding the argument that this term refers to the Church under the New Testament rather than a post-judgment state.</meta>

...[no]... <note>Continuing from previous page: "...no [less than the desert through which Israel traveled]."</note> : in what way Christ—even while present, and having been perfected through his suffering and introduced into glory—is called **TO COME** <note>original Latin: FUTURUS</note> in respect to the first Adam (Romans 5:14). II. Because at that time when the Apostle was writing these things, while the temple, the Levitical hierarchy, and the Jewish civil state <note>term: Politia (Polity); refers to the organized government and social structure of the Jewish people at the time.</note> were still standing, the revelation of the Kingdom of the Messiah in full liberty was something expected more than something already at hand. For this reason, he calls his own age, in which sacrifices and gifts were still being offered, the **PRESENT TIME** <note>original Greek: τὸν καιρὸν τὸν ἐνεστηκότα (ton kairon ton enestēkota)</note>, in contrast to the time immediately approaching, which he calls the *time of correction* <note>original Greek: καιρὸς διορθώσεως (kairos diorthōseōs)</note> (Hebrews 9:9-10). Therefore, by reason of the New Testament, the Church was called by the Apostle *the habitable world to come* <note>original Greek: ἡ οἰκουμένη ἡ μέλλουσα (hē oikoumenē hē mellousa)</note>.

<margin>XXXVI. And it is subject to Christ, not to Angels.</margin>
XXXVI. While he denies that this Church is subject to Angels, he should by no means be thought to be asserting this regarding the Ancient Church. For he is entirely focused on this: to make the Doctrine of Christ as commendable to us as possible. The magnificent praises with which he adorned Christ's person in the preceding chapter serve this end. Next, he established the great excellence of the Gospel over the Law. Now he emphasizes this point: that the Father has conferred upon him the empire of the habitable world—an honor that was never conferred upon any of the Angels. He makes notable mention of the *world to come* because, since its condition is far more excellent than what went before, it was very relevant to illustrating Christ’s dignity to observe that he alone is the Lord of the Church in its most perfect state. What does this imply about the subjection of the Old Testament Church under Angels? Indeed, I remember having spoken copiously on this matter elsewhere. *And so enough has been said on these matters.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταύτῃ (Kai tauta men dē tautē); a common scholarly formula used to wrap up a point.</note>

He marveled that they questioned and answered in a proper order and with balance, showing a spirit of cooperation. They did not stubbornly cling to what they had once decided if it was shown to be false, nor did they shy away from addressing contradictions; rather, they strove to press their proposal as much as possible, yet when reason required it, they were not afraid to change their minds and admit the truth. With a clear conscience and without pretense, their hearts open to God, they joyfully accepted whatever was proved by the demonstrations and teachings of Holy Scripture.

The result of this discussion was exactly what the excellent Prelate <note>Referring to Dionysius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century bishop known for his moderate approach to church controversies.</note> had hoped for. Indeed, the champion and most fierce defender of that doctrine, a man named Coracion, not only yielded—confessing himself defeated by the truth—but also solemnly promised, in front of all the Brothers present, that he would never mention that opinion again, having realized its emptiness through the opposing arguments. The other Brothers rejoiced at this meeting, and at the humility and agreement shown toward everyone.

I wish that all who argue about our modern controversies would approach them with that same spirit and handle them with that same method. They should be certain of this one goal: to embrace and defend whatever is shown to be true—whether it has been said a hundred times before or is being heard for the first time—based on the evidence of the truth itself in the sight of God, putting aside all partisan zeal, <note>original: "χωρὶς προκρίματος, μηδὲν κατὰ πρόκλισιν"</note> *without prejudice, doing nothing out of partiality*.

BOOK III. CHAPTER I. On the sense of the APOCALYPTIC LETTERS.

->ON<-

# THE SENSE OF THE APOCALYPTIC LETTERS.

## CHAPTER I.

### The Occasion for the Writing, and the Status of the Controversy.

*I. Great is the difficulty of the Sacred Apocalypse. II. The reason for this difficulty is sought partly from the writing itself, III. which was wisely so arranged by God; IV. and partly from the condition of man. V. Yet it is our duty to search the Apocalypse diligently. VI. For it sets forth many beneficial things which are obvious to all: VII. nor should we despair of understanding the more hidden things. VIII. Nevertheless, it must never be presumed that we have attained everything. IX. What is disputed today concerning the sense of the Apocalyptic Letters. X. Not whether those seven cities of Asia existed? XI. Nor whether those Letters are common to the whole Church regarding their use? XII. Nor whether those Churches can in some sense be called types of others? XIII. Nor finally whether the totality of the Church is figured in some way by their sevenfold number? XIV. But rather, whether these seven Letters are historically and dogmatically adapted to the state of the particular Churches to which each is inscribed, like the rest of the Apostolic letters? XV. Or whether they prophetically and symbolically figure the seven periods of the Universal Church in order? XVI. The sum of the controversy.*

<margin>Great is the difficulty of the Sacred Apocalypse.</margin>
It is a common complaint, among both the Ancients and Moderns, that the Apocalypse of Saint John—truly a majestic and Divine writing—is enveloped in a very many-layered and thick mist of enigmas. This complexity does not merely exercise the wits of even the sharpest interpreters but tires them; indeed, it sometimes throws them into despair of ever attaining its genuine meaning.

<margin>Eusebius, Church History, Book VII, Chapter XXV.</margin>
Some of the Ancients, as Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, <note>Dionysius of Alexandria (died 264 AD) was a student of Origen and a significant figure in early Christian theology, known for his critical evaluation of the style of the Book of Revelation.</note> testifies, said that the work was "unknown and incomprehensible," <note>original Greek: "ἄγνωστον καὶ ἀσυλλόγισον"</note> and even "that it was not an Apocalypse [Revelation] at all, being exceedingly and thickly covered by the veil of ignorance." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ἀποκάλυψιν εἶναι, τὴν σφόδρα καὶ παχεῖ κεκαλυμμένην τῷ τῆς ἀγνοίας παραπετάσματι." Dionysius was highlighting the irony that a book titled "Revelation" seemed so obscured.</note>

<margin>Letter 103 to Paulinus.</margin>
Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate, often remarked on the density of Scripture.</note> says that the Apocalypse "has as many secrets as it has words." Ansbert, <note>Ambrosius Ansbertus (died 784 AD) was a Carolingian monk whose commentary on Revelation was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> in the most holy prayers which he prefixed to his commentary on the Apocalypse, describes the oracles contained within it as

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book III, Chapter I, focusing on the inherent difficulties of interpreting the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse). It completes the thought from page 311 regarding the testimony of historical scholars on the text's complexity.</meta>

<header>BOOK III. CHAPTER I.</header>

...called it the "obscure paths of enigmas." <note>This likely refers to Jerome or another Early Church Father mentioned on the preceding page.</note> And in the Preface of that same work, he speaks thus in his modesty: *The things we strive to reach for contemplation are higher than our understanding; the things we proceed to consider are beyond our strength; the things we are forced to pass through to unravel are difficult for our genius.* Nor was Ribera <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591) was a Jesuit scholar whose commentary on Revelation became a standard reference.</note> wrong, in the Prologue to his commentaries, when he says that *the Apocalypse is a great and spacious sea, full of storms and tempests, in which all human wisdom is swallowed up.* And how few interpreters are there who have not uttered similar sentiments?

<margin>II. The reason for this difficulty is sought partly from the writing itself.</margin>

II. This difficulty, however, proceeds from more than one cause: it must be sought partly from the writing itself, and partly from the condition of those reading it. For the matter of the writing is extremely sublime; the style is symbolic and enigmatic; and there are frequent allusions to the mystical and not yet fully understood visions of the ancient Prophets—especially Ezekiel and Daniel—with which this book prophesies either the same things, or similar things that correspond to those ancient ones as "types" <note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note>. Indeed, almost every prophecy suffers from its own particular obscurity; both because its expression is usually enigmatic <note>original: ἀινιγματώδης (*ainigmatōdēs*), meaning "riddle-like" or "full of puzzles."</note>, and because events occurring at different times and places often bear such a great resemblance to each other and to the prophetic words that you are left in doubt as to which event the prediction should be applied. Furthermore, if the prophecy has not yet been confirmed by the actual event, the difficulty is even greater: for we can hardly grasp, or even hold in our thoughts, the way in which future facts will one day explain this enigmatic sketch of Divine fates. For the most part, God speaks indefinitely about the future, such that He keeps the specific moments, places, persons, and other circumstances within His own power; if anyone tries to determine these by their own imagination, they are almost certain to be proven rash and foolish by the eventual outcome. Even the Prophets themselves sometimes did not understand their own visions, so much so that they required an Angel as a guide and interpreter.

<margin>III. Wisely so arranged by God; In his 6th Homily on Ezekiel.</margin>

III. Nor did God wish to exercise His servants in this way without reason. For just as this difficulty prevents a disdain for Divine wisdom—as if it were too common <note>original: *proletariæ*, meaning "low-class" or "plebeian"; here suggesting that if the Bible were too easy, people would not respect its depth.</note>—so too are the pious driven by that same difficulty to a confession of their own ignorance and dullness, to a more diligent searching, and to a more earnest devotion to prayer. Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> says beautifully: *The very obscurity of God's words is of great utility; because it exercises the mind so that it may be expanded by the effort, and the exercised mind may grasp what the idle mind cannot.* It serves another even greater purpose, *because if the understanding of the sacred Scripture were open in all things, it would become cheap; in certain more obscure places, it refreshes the soul with a sweetness of discovery that is all the greater because the soul was exhausted by the labor of the search.*

<summary>The author explains why the Book of Revelation is so difficult to interpret, citing its symbolic style, its relationship to Old Testament types, and God's intentional design to humble readers and encourage deeper study.</summary>
<keywords>Apocalypse, Ribera, Prophet Ezekiel, Prophet Daniel, Gregory the Great, biblical interpretation, symbolism, divine wisdom, prophecy</keywords>

# On the Meaning of the APOCALYPTIC EPISTLES.
<sig>Ttt</sig>

<margin>IV. The cause of difficulty is to be sought partly from the condition of man.</margin>

IV. But much of the cause for difficulty also lies within man himself. For after the fall into sin, we all suffer from such a dullness of mind that it clearly grows dark and goes blind when facing divine and heavenly things. Added to this, in many people, is a lazy sluggishness and a contempt for the hidden treasures of divine wisdom, which cannot be found except by digging and diligent searching. There are even some who, while proclaiming themselves content with the clear teachings of the Scriptures and the common doctrines of faith, do not believe it is worth their effort to examine the hidden depths of the Prophecies—depths that often withdraw from even those who search them. Others, after they have applied themselves to reading and meditating on some of the sacred prophecies, are frightened by the almost immense labor that must be endured: the investigation of prophetic phrases, symbols, and riddles, as well as the study of events that have occurred in the Church and throughout the entire world, and the comparison of those events with the prophecies. Prejudices also hinder many, preventing them from seeing things that otherwise would not be entirely obscure. And finally, the desire to examine the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> is clearly extinguished in some by the overly ingrained opinion of its impenetrable obscurity. For such a person imagines that the exposition of the Apocalypse is like the *squaring of the circle* <note>original: "quadraturam circuli" — a mathematical problem that was famously impossible to solve using only a compass and straightedge; here used as a metaphor for an impossible intellectual task.</note>, of which it is often said: *it is knowable, but not yet known.* They believe that without a unique revelation from God, the Apocalypse is utterly incomprehensible. Hence, the modesty of those who have chosen to write nothing by way of commentary on the Apocalypse is often praised above the laborious busywork of other interpreters.

<margin>Salmerón, Prelude 4. Pereira.</margin> <note>Alfonso Salmerón (1515–1585) and Benito Pereira (1535–1610) were prominent Jesuit theologians and biblical commentators.</note>

<margin>V. It is our duty to search the Apocalypse diligently.</margin>

V. However, since all Scripture is divinely inspired and prepared entirely for the perfecting of the man of God, there is nothing in it—nothing at all—that may be rightfully neglected by a man who reveres God, or set aside as if it did not concern him. Indeed, there are places where the study of prophecies is explicitly commended: 1 Thessalonians 5:4 and 2 Peter 1:19. And regarding the Apocalypse specifically, Chapter 1:3 states: *Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this Prophecy, and keeps those things which are written in it.* The Lord wants these things to be read privately and heard in the Church—where they should also be explained in sermons—and kept, both in the treasury of a sanctified memory and in the practice of a holier life. To those who do this, He promises the greatest happiness. Whoever seeks that happiness ought not to think that meditation on the Apocalypse is foreign to his own concerns.

<margin>VI. For it also sets forth many beneficial things which are obvious to everyone:</margin>

VI. For it weaves together the marrow-filled mysteries <note>original: "Sacramenta" — here used in the broader sense of "sacred mysteries" or "hidden truths."</note> of the Church, as I remember Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> saying somewhere. And even if it is not understood in every part, it nevertheless has precepts of holiness scattered throughout; it has excellent encouragements toward constancy in faith and piety; it has the surest promises of a reward to be given to those who stand firm; and it contains the message of Divine judgment, both upon the Church and...

<summary>This page argues that while human sin, laziness, and prejudice make the Book of Revelation difficult to understand, believers have a spiritual duty to study it because all Scripture is divinely inspired and offers moral guidance and promises of blessing.</summary>

### BOOK III. CHAPTER I.

...against its enemies, a most illustrious demonstration; it contains a most brilliant description of the glory that is to be bestowed upon the Church, both in this and in the future age; it has the sweetest songs of Saints and Angels, in which they lead us in the praise of Divine virtues; finally, it is full of such sentiments that everywhere exhale the sweetest scent of holiness. And indeed, these things have been set out openly for all until now, and are fit to bring great benefit to the soul, even if one does not follow every detail *minutely* <note>original Greek: λεπτομερῶς (leptomerōs)</note>. Nor are these things obvious only to those who, shaped by schools and practiced in libraries, belch out the wisdom acquired in Academies and porticoes: but also to the simple, the unrefined, the unpolished, and the common folk <note>The author uses the Latin *idiotis*, referring to people without formal academic training rather than its modern derogatory sense.</note>, who are entirely occupied with the crossroads, the street corners, and the weaving looms—to borrow these words from Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>.

<margin>
On the Testimony of the Soul, chapter 4.

Letter LXIV to Constantius.
</margin>
Rightly might you apply specifically to the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> what *Ambrose* <note>Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD) was the Bishop of Milan and a highly influential figure in the early Church.</note> says generally about Scripture: *“It is a sea, having within itself profound meanings, an abyss of prophetic riddles. Many rivers enter into this sea. There are, therefore, sweet and clear streams; there are also snowy fountains that leap up into eternal life; there are good words like honeycombs, and pleasing sentiments that irrigate the minds of the listeners with a certain spiritual drink and soothe them with the sweetness of moral precepts.”* And these things perhaps suffice for the edification of those among the faithful who are of the common people.

<margin>VII. Nor is the understanding of more hidden things to be despaired of.</margin>
VII. Meanwhile, it is the duty of the learned to examine each detail more carefully and to take pains to dig out the truth lying hidden at the bottom. Following the example of Daniel, Chapter VIII:15: *“And it happened when I, Daniel, saw that vision, I sought understanding”* <note>original Hebrew: וָאֲבַקְשָׁה בִינָה (va-avakshah binah)</note>. Nor should the obscurity of the proposed matters discourage the mind; rather, it ought to sharpen one's diligence.

<margin>Chrysostom, Homily XL on Job.</margin>
> For the truth in the Scriptures is not hidden, but obscure; not so that those who seek it may not find it, but so that those who are unwilling to seek it may not find it: so that it may pertain to the glory of those who found it because they desired it, and sought it, and found it; but to the condemnation of those who do not find it, because they neither desired it, nor sought it, nor found it. <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an Archbishop of Constantinople famous for his eloquent preaching.</note>

That promise of God in Daniel Chapter XII:4 serves as a comfort to the diligent: *“Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be increased.”* And again, verse 10: *“None of the wicked shall understand, but the wise* <note>original Hebrew: הַמַּשְׂכִּילִים (ha-maskilim) – referring to those who are discerning or teachers.</note>, *or those being instructed, shall understand.”* And surely the Spirit of God would never have wished the book of the Apocalypse to be written and published unless He also wished it to be understood eventually.

<margin>Ribera in the Preface.</margin>
What hinders us then from also humbly knocking at the doors of Divine Wisdom, and with a certain pious and religious boldness of a faithful mind, going to Christ—the best of all friends—who gave this Apocalypse to his servant John to make it known to his servants? And in the middle of the night of this obscure and sacred darkness, let us ask for the “loaves of understanding” <note>A reference to the Parable of the Friend at Night (Luke 11:5-8), where a neighbor asks for bread at midnight.</note>, which we may set before either our own age (if God so wills) or future ages?

# On the Meaning of the APOCALYPTIC LETTERS.

<margin>
VIII. Yet we must never presume that we have grasped everything.

VIII. Furthermore, we must proceed with caution in this matter, and with a certain sacred fear and trembling; lest, through laziness, we choose to remain ignorant, or through arrogance, we presume to have attained a full understanding of everything. For no matter how much diligence we apply, there will be no shortage of things about which we must say what Zechariah <note>The prophet Zechariah from the Old Testament.</note> replied to the Angel when asked if he knew the meaning of those things: *I know not, my Lord.* Zechariah 4:13. Let no one easily imagine that they have explored those things which were revealed to John himself <note>The Apostle John, the traditional author of Revelation.</note> only after many and bitter tears. Revelation 5:4. Let us rejoice in those things we have been given to understand; let us wonder at the rest with religious devotion, and investigate them with both humility and diligence. In a manner both holy and modest, Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Alexandria (died 264 AD), a bishop known for his scholarly approach to scripture.</note>, whom I recently praised, says:

<margin>
Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, Chapter XXV.

> <note>original Greek: Μείζονα δὲ τῆς ἐμαυτοῦ φρονήσεως τὴν ὑπόληψιν... And so I feel that certain Divine mysteries are covered by human words, discerning this not so much by my own judgment as believing it by faith. And therefore, I do not reject what I do not understand, but I admire it all the more, the less I am able to grasp it.

<margin>
IX. What is the controversy regarding the meaning of the Apocalyptic Letters?
</margin>

IX. But since the duty of a faithful interpreter is to shed light on obscure things, he must above all take care not to cast darkness or fog over things that are clear by using interpretations that are more clever than solid. Whether those who contend that the letters written in Christ's name to the seven Churches of Asia Minor are prophetic are doing exactly that, remains a question. They argue that these letters contain, in order, a <term>mystical description</term> <note>A "mystical" or "spiritual" interpretation suggests that the text has a hidden meaning beyond the literal history of the seven ancient cities.</note> of the whole Universal Church through its seven periods. This has been asked before, and it deserves to be asked again now. For since the study of Prophecies, which lay as if half-dead for a long time, now seems to be flexing its muscles again, the meaning of these letters has begun to be treated—should I say carefully, or perhaps too curiously? Nor did I think it out of place to bring the arguments of both opinions, equipped with all their defenses, into the field, as it were. I shall do so with such lack of bias that, until I have deployed all the forces on both sides, arranged the <term>phalanxes</term> <note>An ancient military formation; here used as a metaphor for organized arguments.</note> of each party with all my skill, and shown the reader "spears threatening spears" <note>A poetic reference to Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, describing a civil war where similar weapons face each other; used here to show how balanced the opposing arguments are.</note>, it will be difficult, or rather impossible, to judge which side I favor.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
X. The question is not whether those Seven cities of Asia actually existed.
</margin>

X. First, the state of the controversy must be properly defined. The question is not whether the seven cities of Asia mentioned in *Revelation chapters 1 and 2* and the Churches of Christ within them existed in John's time; or whether the names of those cities and everything said about them should be interpreted merely as something symbolic, symbolic <note>original: "hieroglyphicum," referring to sacred symbols</note>, and dramatic—just as some have wrongly transformed the *History of Job* into a tragicomedy and a drama. On both sides of the debate, it is accepted as an indubitable truth that those Churches actually existed in the mentioned Asian cities at that time. By a singular grace of the Divine <note>original: *numinis gratia*</note>, they were made the guardians not only of their own individual heavenly Letters, but of the entire Sacred Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>.

<margin>
XI. Nor is it whether those Letters are common to the whole Church in their application.
</margin>

XI. Nor is it a matter of dispute whether the contents of those Letters are intended for the use of the entire Christian Church. For just as the Letters to the Romans, Corinthians, and Ephesians—and even those to individual persons, such as Timothy, Titus, and Gaius—were addressed to them specifically and by name, they were nonetheless dictated and intended by God for the edification of the whole Universal <note>original: *Catholicæ*</note> Church. Thus, every individual believer ought to consider what was said to the Romans or to Timothy for the instruction of faith or the correction of behavior as being said to themselves. The same principle applies here. What *Jesus* said to his disciples, he said also to us, and to everyone: *Mark 13:37. And whatever things were written before were written for our instruction; that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. Romans 15:4.*

<margin>
XII. Nor whether those Churches can be called types of others in some sense.
</margin>

XII. Indeed, I do not believe it is even disputed whether those Asian Churches—in their virtues and vices, as well as in God's judgments upon them—can be called <term>types</term> <note>A "type" is a historical person, event, or thing that serves as a prophetic pattern for something else in the future.</note> and figures of certain subsequent Churches. This is meant in the same sense that the Apostle writes concerning the Hebrews in *1 Corinthians 10:6: "Now these things were our types, that we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted." And again in verse 11: "Now all these things happened to them typically: but they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come."*

<margin>
XIII. Nor finally, whether the totality of the Church is figured in some way by their number seven.
</margin>

XIII. Nor do I believe the heart of the controversy lies in whether the totality <note>original: *universitas*</note> of the entire Universal Church is represented by that seven-fold number of Asian Churches, such that the Church of every age might contemplate its own image in one of these letters (or perhaps in several at once) as if in a mirror. On this point, I find that interpreters of every group generally agree.

While these matters certainly serve as a warning to the universal church and should be wisely applied for the edification of other assemblies in other centuries where similar conditions prevail, they are no more to be transformed into allegories or prophecies of future events than the letters of Paul to the Romans or the Ephesians.

<margin>
XV. Or do they, in fact, Prophetically and Symbolically arrange seven periods of the Universal Church?
</margin>
XV. But those who have more recently and laboriously commented on the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> contend that the subjects of those letters are no less prophetic than the subjects of the seven seals and the seven trumpets, to which each letter corresponds in order. They maintain that those Churches of Asia are not to be considered so much in themselves as emblems and types of the entire Christian Church across seven distinct and successively ordered periods of time; they argue the names of each church contribute to this, as they are symbolic. Thus, the first, which is **Ephesus**, represents the condition of the primitive Church, beginning from Christ’s ascension into heaven and ending with the death of the Apostles around the end of the first century; this period was, as is fitting, the purest and most chaste of all. The second, **Smyrna**—which is named after Myrrh <note>original: "a Myrrha," a bitter but preservative resin</note>, a bitter but health-giving spice—responds to the second and third centuries; it is a figure of the suffering Church, tested by many martyrdoms. The third, **Pergamum**, figures the state of the following three centuries, from the Year 300 or 325 to the Year 600 or 606, at which time the Church began to exist in a "towered and vast city," that is, the Mystic Babylon <note>The author refers to the rise of the Papacy or the institutionalized Roman church</note>, to which Pergamum corresponds. The fourth, **Thyatira**, encompasses several centuries up until the time of the Reformation; during these "breathing-spaces" of the centuries, the Church was harassed by cruel afflictions and was, as it were, immolated <note>sacrificed</note> to God. The fifth, **Sardis**, is an emblem of the Church which—having renounced communion with the Anti-Christ and restored a purer worship of the Divine in some measure—was nevertheless defiled by many vices and, above all others, by a foul "hatred of brothers" <note>original Greek: $\mu\iota\sigma\alpha\delta\epsilon\lambda\phi\acute{\iota}\alpha$ (misadelphia)</note>, such as has been found in the Churches devoted to Luther <note>The Lutheran churches</note>; unless one prefers to refer the Bohemians and Hussites <note>Followers of Jan Hus, a pre-Reformation reformer</note> to this period. Therefore, it is said of the Church of Sardis, *that it lives in name only, but in reality is dead*. The sixth, **Philadelphia**, responds to the Reformed Church, which is slightly later in time but purer in Doctrine, more accurate in Discipline, more constant in afflictions, and far more excellent in Brotherly Love. <margin>XVI. The Heart of the Controversy.</margin>
XVI. To summarize the matter briefly, this is the question: *Are the Letters of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> Historical, Doctrinal, and Hortatory <note>providing encouragement or advice</note>, describing the state of the Asian Churches as it was then, with encouragements, warnings, and promises suited to that state—just like the other Apostolic Letters? Or are they in fact Prophetic, Allegorical, and Emblematic, foretelling the future state of the Church, much like the Seven Seals and the Seven Trumpets, which these Seven Letters match in their prophecies and allegories?* Theologians and interpreters generally hold the first view; several more recent Learned Men argue for the latter. Let us weigh the arguments for each opinion.

# THE FIRST ARGUMENT.

<margin>XVII. Ancient names of cities and regions are symbolic.</margin>
XVII. Those who fight for the Prophetic and Allegorical sense proceed as follows. First, they bid us observe that nothing is more frequent in the Sacred Scriptures than to use the names of ancient regions, or even nations, to mystically signify gatherings of men who belong to much later times and dwell in entirely different places. Thus, under the names of Zion or *Jerusalem*, *Israel* or *Judah*, the Church of the New Testament is denoted; while by the terms *Sodom*, *Egypt*, *Babylon*, and *Tyre*, Antichristian *Rome* is frequently indicated. Since this observation is of great weight for the understanding of prophecies, it will be neither useless nor unpleasant to illustrate it with certain notable examples.

<margin>XVIII. The mystery of Babylon.</margin>
XVIII. Before his fall, he appeared to be a *most bright Star* (though in reality he was a murky star, a wandering star <note>original: "δνοφερὸν, ἀστὴρ πλανήτης" (dnopheron, astēr planētēs), referencing Jude 13</note>), and a *Son of the Dawn*, boasting that he emerged with the very daybreak, or the first dawn of the Gospel light, amid the darkness of the world. And he speaks in his heart, doing all things *according to his own will* <note>original: "κατ᾽ ἰδίου θέλημα" (kat' idiou thelēma)</note>: "I will ascend into heaven," meaning, by my own counsel I will exempt myself from all judgment, both Ecclesiastical and Political, to which those who stand upon the earth are subject; "and I will exalt my throne above the stars of God," meaning I shall have a Throne, and sit upon it, far superior to all the stars of God—both the Priests and Elders of the Old Testament and the Ministers of the New; and "I will sit *upon the mount of the congregation*," according to that word of the Apostle in 2 Thessalonians 2:4: *so that he sits in the temple of God* <note>original: "ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καθίσαι" (hōste auton eis ton naon tou Theou kathisai)</note>; "in the sides of the North," where the tables were located upon which the sacrifices were slaughtered (Ezekiel 40:39) and the table of the bread of presence (Exodus 26:35). That is to say: I will conduct myself as a Priest, appointed by God for this purpose, to offer and see that offerings are made for the sins of the people, and I shall attribute all supreme power to the Sacrament of the lordly bread. And "I will ascend into the heights of the clouds," which are the source of dew and rain, to which the word of God is compared,

<margin>XIX. The Moabites.</margin>
XIX. In the same way, the **MOABITES** in Isaiah chapters 15 and 16 signify the Jews who were visited by Christ and invited to share in his kingdom, yet became the persecutors of the Apostles and the faithful. They are called Moabites because they were partly inhabitants of the land of Moab, and partly because they were joined to the Moabites in their superstition and spirit. <margin>XXI. Gog and Magog.</margin>
XXI. Similarly, in Ezekiel Chapter 38, **GOG**, as if a *roof* <note>original: "tectum"</note>, symbolically denotes one who places himself in the middle between God and men (just as a roof comes between heaven and earth). These mountains are the Alps. The Land of Israel, or the Church, is **Germany**. From there, the east is reached most quickly by ships for those who travel from Germany and the whole North. Moreover, *Gog was buried at Trent*, along with all his multitude; for the Council gathered there by Gog produced such decrees by which it showed that Gog, and all who act with him, are plainly dead and blinded so that they cannot see the truth. To those decrees, the Council added anathemas <note>formal curses or excommunications</note> by which the Romans separated themselves from the communion of those passing toward Zion—that is, from Israel, or the **Evangelical Church**. Since that is called the land of the living, while they place themselves in the land of death and destruction, they are rightly said to be burying themselves.

<margin>XXII. *It is not surprising, therefore, that in the Prophetic writing the names of Asian cities should likewise be interpreted symbolically.*</margin>
XXII. There are almost infinite other things of this kind which, safely neglected or perhaps even despised by the ancients, could not escape the sharp industry of more recent scholars. This is all the more true because those very people who stand for the literal sense are forced to explain what is said about Jezebel in the letter to the Thyatireans as a riddle. If nothing else, this at least is proved from what has been said: those who interpret the names of Cities in a Prophetic book symbolically—as is done elsewhere without fault and not without praise for subtlety—commit nothing foreign to the interpretation of the Apocalypse.

<margin>
XXIII. The entire Apocalypse is a single Letter addressed to the Universal Church.

XXIII. *Secondly.* To approach the present controversy more closely, it must be noted that the entire Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> has the character of *a single Letter* <note>original: "unius Epistolæ"</note> which is addressed to the Universal Church. For it is not without reason that (contrary to what usually happens in the Apostolic letters written to individual Churches) the address is not directed first to these seven specific Churches; rather, from the very beginning, a blessing is pronounced upon *all who read, and hear, and keep the words of this prophecy.* (Rev. 1:3). These words imply that this letter is "Catholic" <note>The author uses "Catholic" in its original Greek sense of "Universal," referring to the whole Christian world across all time, rather than the Roman Catholic denomination.</note>—intended for all Churches of all ages. Furthermore, when John begins the fourth chapter after finishing these specific Letters, he does not break the established order as if he were turning his discourse toward other Churches. Instead, using the same method, he explains and applies to those same Churches the themes of the seven seals, the seven trumpets, and whatever else the Apocalypse contains. All these things are concluded with a general closing, in the manner customary for Letters, in Rev. 22:21: *The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.* Thus you may know that this is finally the end of the entire Universal Letter.

# ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE.

The glory of the Lord, and his very insignia, are displayed when he is said *to walk in the midst of the seven golden lampstands* <note>A reference to Revelation 1:13 and 2:1</note>. But what does this mean? Is he present with his favor, Spirit, and help only to the churches of Asia? Did he not promise the same to all his people, even until the end of the age? Why then would he wish to be titled only after those seven churches? This cannot be; it is not in keeping with the dignity of such a great King. Just as it would be unbefitting for a Lord of three Kingdoms and more than a hundred domains to write the names of only seven provinces or cities on his coat of arms and to take his title from them, so it is here. Furthermore, what of the fact that the Holy Spirit himself is called *sevenfold* because of the seven churches? This was surely not merely because of those specific churches in Asia. For if, perhaps, the cities of Philippi or Colossae had been included among them, would John then have recorded eight or nine Spirits? The sacred text itself teaches the contrary in Revelation 5:6: namely, that these are the *seven spirits which are sent out into all the earth*, and this is undoubtedly true for all times and ages. All these things sufficiently prove that a more majestic mystery lies beneath those emblems, and one that should not be restricted within the boundaries of the Asian churches.

### ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE.

...Like a wreath of palm-like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, beyond all the powders of the merchant <note>This is an allusion to Song of Solomon 3:6, often interpreted as the Church ascending from the wilderness of persecution.</note>. This signifies the patience of the faithful during persecution and their martyrdoms, which spread their fragrance far and wide, much like the smell of sacrifices or incense. <margin>XXX. What Pergamus signifies.</margin>
XXX. **PERGAMUS** signifies a *citadel*, as Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian who compiled a famous lexicon.</note> notes: "Pergamus: the acropolis of Troy" <note>original Greek: "Πέργαμος ἡ ἀκρόπολις τῆς Ἰλίϰ"</note>. Such was the Church in the Roman Empire after the time of Constantine the Great.

<margin>XXXI. What Thyatira signifies.</margin>
XXXI. The **THYATIRAN** Church signifies "she who is sacrificed and vexed" <note>original Greek: "τὴν θυομένην καὶ τειρομένην" (tēn thyomenēn kai teiromenēn). The name *Bamah* <note>A Hebrew word for "High Place," often used for unauthorized places of worship.</note> does not declare more clearly how vain a "high place" is in Ezekiel 20:29 than this Church reveals its nature through its own name. The word *Bamah*, if you consider the sound of the voice, is "Ba mah" <note>original Hebrew: "בא מה"</note>. It signifies, "Has it come? What?" As if to say: "Do you think anything truly comes of that place? And what is it that comes to it? God does not come there. Only you go there." What, then, is *Bamah*? It is certainly nothing. This is the subtle observation of a most learned man regarding Ezekiel 20:29 <note>likely referring to the theologian Johannes Cocceius</note>. For it is the Church we have seen subjected to many contentions, reproaches, vexations, punishments, and every kind of harassment within an Empire that was Christian in name only, under the tyranny of the Antichrist.

<margin>XXXII. What Sardis signifies.</margin>
XXXII. **SARDIS** was the capital of the Lydians, once the royal palace of Croesus; it aptly signifies the Church in the Christian Empire raising its head higher than usual. For once the Reformation was begun by Luther, several secular Princes devoted themselves to the useful work of the Church. However, some clergy—by a very poor example—arrogated to themselves lordship over their brothers while the Church was still in its infancy. Furthermore, the *measuring line* of the Word of God, according to which His temple must be built, was again placed into the hands of the workers. Finally, the *remnant* of the spiritual Israel was gathered, and amidst a foul corruption of morals, some survived who did not soil their garments.

**XXXIII.** Within the riddle of **PHILADELPHIA** <note>original Greek: Φιλαδελφία</note> is contained the character of the true Church: *brotherly love*. Just as this love makes brothers in Christ pleasant and joyful to one another, sharing in each other's blessings and burdens, it also implies the avoidance of those who are not true brothers, so as to avoid division and false teaching. Furthermore, the city of Philadelphia was situated in a dangerous location; even when it was most flourishing, it was sparsely populated. Its citizens lived scattered in the fields, fearing the frequent tremors of the city. How perfectly this name fits the Reformed Church <note>This refers to the "Calvinist" or "Presbyterian" branch of the Reformation</note> that arose after the German Reformation (the "Sardian" era); that is, the churches of Switzerland, Swabia, Geneva, France, the Netherlands, and Scotland. For just as this church is truly pious because of its brotherly love, it is also humble and obscure, stripped of almost all worldly power and human prestige. In this way, it is the exact opposite of *Pergamum*—the proud and towered city. Its citizens, though joined in spirit and will, and living under nearly the same laws and institutions regarding matters of importance, nevertheless live scattered in few places and separated from one another. They are always exposed to great danger because of the power and multitude of the enemies who surround them, growling and gnashing their teeth.

---

<margin>
XXXIV.
The meaning of Laodicea.
</margin>

**XXXIV. LAODICEA**, a great and wealthy city on the river Lycus, was founded by Antiochus, the son of Stratonice, and named *Laodicea* in honor of his wife, Laodice. The name implies a "leader of the people" <note>original: "princeps populorum"</note> who would dictate justice and bring forth laws. If we follow the interpretation of Brightman <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607) was an influential English clergyman whose work "A Revelation of the Revelation" argued that the Seven Churches represented historical stages</note>, this city is a type of a Church that is Reformed in its doctrine, yet swollen with its own wealth and worldly pride. He points to the **Anglican Church** <note>The Church of England</note> as an example, where the Bishops are peers of the Realm. In honor, they are superior to many nobles; in wealth, staff, the magnificence of their buildings, and all other worldly pomp, they are equal to the highest Earls. Their Deans, Archdeacons, Prebendaries, and Chaplains—by accumulating many "benefices," as they call them—equal at least the rank of Squires in their annual income. Alternatively, according to others, the Laodicean era signifies the Church of the very last days, in which God will execute *Judgment* among the peoples.

---

<margin>
XXXV.
It is concluded that it is impossible for these ecclesiastical affairs to match these symbols so exactly without divine intent.
</margin>

**XXXV.** Since it is now clearly evident from what has been explained at some length how harmoniously the names of these cities represent the distinct conditions of the Churches according to their historical periods, who would not recognize the wisdom of the Divine Spirit? He leads His people to the contemplation of these signified truths through such elegant symbols. Could it happen by chance, and without the intent of the Divinity, that the things done (or yet to be done) in the Church should agree so exactly with the symbolic names used by God?

# ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE.

### SEVENTH ARGUMENT.

<margin>
XXXVI.
The outcome
confirms the
Prophetic
