</margin>
XXXVI. Seventh. Reality itself speaks, and the actual outcome of history adds such credit to this prophetic interpretation that it compels even the most stubborn to agree. It is simply inconceivable how the contents of these letters could exhibit such an accurate map of all the changes that have befallen the Church of the New Testament, unless that had been the intent of the Holy Spirit. Let us briefly survey the themes of each individual church.

<margin>
XXXVII.
In the Letter
to the Ephesians
is the
transformation
of the Apostolic
Church.
</margin>
XXXVII. Could the condition of the Apostolic Church be described more clearly than it was in this Letter to the Messenger <note>original: "Angelum"</note> of Ephesus? You see there the praised works of piety and the labor exhausted by the Apostles in propagating the Gospel; they divided the world among themselves and filled every land with the proclamation of Christ. You see their patience, both in bearing with those who were weak and in eagerly undergoing afflictions—as is evident from the martyrdoms of Stephen and nearly all the Apostles, and the persecution of the Church under Claudius, Nero, Domitian, and others. You see their turning away from evil and their flight from it, examples of which are found in *Acts 5:5, 10; 8:23; and 13:8, 10, 11.* You also see the scrutiny of the False Apostles, with whom Paul had frequent struggles, as did John with Ebion and Cerinthus <note>Ebion and Cerinthus were early heretics who challenged the divinity of Christ in the 1st century</note>. Nevertheless, they are blamed for the loss of their "first love," examples of which are found among the Galatians (*Galatians 3:3*), the Corinthians (*1 Corinthians 1:5*), the Hebrews (*Hebrews 10:32, 33*), and Demas (*2 Timothy 4:10*). Conversely, they are praised because they hated the works of the Nicolaitans, which are similarly hateful to Christ. To be a "Nicolaitan" is to form a sect and to take the name of a man instead of the name of Christ. This is exactly what the Apostle forbids in *1 Corinthians 1:12*. It is certain that after the earliest times, men arose who followed a human name; it is even more certain that later those emerged who wished to belong more to Peter than to Christ, and who made the human name of the successors of Peter the principle of their faith. It is certain that the deeds of such men are not good. It is certain that the Head of that sect can be called "Nicholas" in a riddle, or in Hebrew "Balaam," so that it is, as it were, <term>Baal-am</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעל עם</note>—Lord of the people. Nicholas signifies <term>he who conquers the people</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ νικῶν τὸν λαὸν</note>, one who overcomes the people as if they were <term>inferiors</term> <note>original Greek: ἥττονα</note> and makes them subjects and slaves. Thus, the primitive Church is praised because it turned away from such efforts of <term>those seeking preeminence</term> <note>original Greek: Φιλοπρωτευόντων; refers to leaders who love to put themselves first</note>. Compare *3 John verses 9, 10.*

to the

times nearest
to the Apostles
are prefigured.
</margin>
XXXVIII. Furthermore, who does not see that the times which immediately succeeded the Apostles are prefigured in the Letter to the Smyrnaeans? The Church is presented there as greatly afflicted and destitute, yet wealthy in regard to the Spirit and the Kingdom of God. Such was the condition of the Church after the times of the Apostles (*1 Corinthians 1:26, 27, 28; Hebrews 10:24*). In the most recent wars, which [afflicted] all of Judea...

### BOOK III. CHAPTER II.

...who had devastated everything were miserably impoverished. Christ’s closest kinsmen were mocked and despised by Domitian because of their poverty. Many others were banished to islands and condemned to the mines—a punishment reserved for slaves—living a life more painful than death. A certain Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (r. 314–335 AD), who according to legend was hiding in a cave on Mount Soracte to escape persecution before being summoned by Emperor Constantine.</note> was brought out from a cave, just as Joseph was from prison, and raised by Constantine to the highest dignities in the Church. Yet, being full of God, wealthy in the treasures of His grace, and rich in the abundance of spiritual comforts, they equaled the wealth of kings in their spirits. Mention is also made of the *Blasphemy of the Jews*, that is, the slander by which the Jews of ancient times made Christians hateful to the Gentiles. *Justin Martyr* and *Eusebius* testify to this slander. Finally, the affliction of "ten days" is predicted. This refers either to the ten general persecutions, or to the final one under *Diocletian*, which lasted for ten years. The learned observation of *Louis Cappel* <note>Ludovici Capelli (1585–1658), a French Protestant scholar and clergyman.</note> deserves no small praise. He says, *"Ten days consist of 240 hours. Now, if you calculate the years from 85 AD—around the time of the second persecution under Domitian and the banishment of the Apostle John to the island of Patmos, where he wrote these things—up to the year 325 AD, when Licinius was removed by Constantine, there are precisely 240 years."* For the things attributed to the Smyrnaeans pertain to the universal Church of those centuries.

The Church
of Pergamum
is the type for
the following

XXXIX. The subsequent centuries are presented in the Letter to *Pergamum*. The Church of that time is said to dwell where the *Throne of Satan* is. This should be compared with Chapter 13:2, where it is said that *the dragon gave his Throne and his power to the beast*. By this act, the Church dwelt where the Throne of Satan was. For the "Beast" signifies a multitude that is "animalistic" <note>The author uses "animalem" here to mean "carnal" or "soulish," as opposed to "spiritual."</note> under the name of Christian, and reigning in the world. This thought leads us to the "great city," the Roman Empire, in which Constantine ensured that all things were subjected to the Christian name. More clearly, the Throne of Satan is the Throne of the Antichrist, reigning now in Christian Rome, just as the Dragon had previously reigned in pagan Rome. Furthermore, what is added regarding *Antipas*, Christ's faithful Martyr, is a prophetic riddle. Antipas is a shortened form of <term>Antipatros</term> <note>original: ἀντίπατρος</note>. This signifies something like <term>isopatron</term> <note>original: ἰσόπατρον</note>, <term>equal to the father</term> <note>original: ἴσον τῷ πατρί</note>. It is well known from dictionaries that the prefix <term>anti</term> in composition sometimes denotes likeness or equality. No name could have been more aptly fashioned to signify the defenders of the <term>homoousion</term> <note>original: τῶ ὁμοουσίω; the theological doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, established at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, whose role it is to say the Son is *equal to the Father* (John 5:18). That martyr—or rather, all the defenders of this doctrine—were then "slaughtered" by legal decree, and some were harassed and killed by the Arians, whose patrons were Constantius and other Emperors of the East. The Church of that time is rebuked because it held those teaching the *Doctrine of Balaam and the Nicolaitans*. For on the occasion of the Arian controversies, the Roman Pope, even among those

The Catholics began to be held in higher esteem. In the Council of Nicea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the orthodox Nicene Creed and organized the early Church hierarchy.</note>, the ancient custom was confirmed that Churches should be under individual Bishops, Bishops under Metropolitans, and the prince of Metropolitans in the West should be the Roman Pope. Thus, at the same time, the truth of the Gospel was confirmed against Arius <note>The priest whose teachings led to Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, and the imperious doctrine of Balaam and the Nicolaitans <note>Groups mentioned in Revelation 2 interpreted here as symbols of ecclesiastical corruption and hierarchy.</note> was established.

<margin>XL. In the letter to Thyatira, the Waldenses are described.</margin>
XL. In the *Letter to Thyatira*, praise is given to *charity*, *ministry*, *faith*, *patience*, and *latter works more abundant than the first*. The *Waldenses* <note>A medieval proto-Protestant movement that emphasized poverty and the authority of the Bible.</note> point to these as if with a finger; their Churches, famous after the rise of the Antichrist, have had few equals since the age of the Apostles in purity of faith, heat of charity, zeal for ministry, patience in persecutions, and the abundance of most excellent works. But the Church of that time is also blamed because *it permitted the woman Jezebel to teach*, etc., not sufficiently resisting the *system of false Prophets*, and the head of them all, the *Antichrist*. Time for *repentance* was given to this Jezebel when God delivered the Roman Popes, along with the flock they ruled, from the harassments of the Arians under Gratian in the year 382 AD and Theodosius in 388 AD, and from the incursions of both the Saracens and the Goths, and granted them a huge victory over the Turks through the leader John of Austria <note>Leader of the Holy League fleet at the Battle of Lepanto (1571).</note> in the year 1571. This was, as it were, the final moment of Divine patience toward them. Since this Jezebel did not repent, God *threw her into a bed of suffering*: afflicting the city of Rome and all of Italy with various torments through the Vandals, Goths, Huns, Saracens, and Muhammadans. It is also worth remembering here everything that has happened since the beginning of the Reformation, and into what straits God has recently thrown the persecutors and the Roman clergy. Finally, He threatens that *He will kill her children with death*, that is, He will abolish the beast "by the brightness of His coming." <note>original: "τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ" — a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:8, describing the destruction of the Antichrist at the Second Coming.</note> Compare chapter 11:18 and 19:20.

<margin>XLI. The Church of Sardis exhibits the likeness of the Lutheran Church.</margin>
XLI. Does not the *Letter to Sardis* describe the *German Church* fresh from the Reformation? There, *many had the name of being alive*, because they were separated from the society of Jezebel, or the Great Harlot; yet they did not possess the reality of life itself. They said and wrote much, and showed zeal for the truth, and did many things that the living do; but since they did those things more from the shame of having their falsehoods exposed than from a love for the truth, and consequently did not enjoy the sweetness of a good conscience, *they were in truth dead*. It is also clearly stated in verse 3 that most Doctors of the Church, while opposing the doctrine of Jezebel, did not retain what they had received and heard, but added new inventions, such as the new dogma of ubiquity <note>The Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s physical body is present everywhere, particularly in the Eucharist.</note>, which troubled the Church. There are also other such matters of the Synergists <note>Those who believed that human will cooperates with divine grace in regeneration, a controversial topic in 16th-century Lutheranism.</note>,

...and new opinions concerning **Justification**. <note>The doctrine of how a person is made righteous before God, a central debate of the Reformation.</note> Meanwhile, a few had remained there who *had not defiled their garments*, namely through hatred of their brothers, new doctrines, and the stumbling block given to the dying. Certainly, hatred and violated peace are completely repugnant to the purity of Christians. Consider the vision of Montanus, the African confessor mentioned by Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian; the reference is to his "Ecclesiastical Annals."</note> *in Book 11 of the Annals, for the year 262 AD, section 14.* To those it is promised that they shall walk with Christ in white, which signifies the peace to be given to the Church for the justification of their cause.

XLII. The Philadelphian Church corresponds to our Reformed Church.

XLII. The Church of **Philadelphia** clearly corresponds to our **Reformed** Church. To her an *open door* was given, that is, the opportunity of preaching the doctrine of truth, with all human power and Diabolical fraud striving against it in vain. She indeed *had little power*, which was especially evident in our own **Netherlands** <note>original: "Belgio." In the 17th century, "Belgium" typically referred to the Low Countries/Netherlands as a whole.</note>; her affairs, reduced to the very brink of ruin, seemed ready to involve all who favored her in the same destruction. Nevertheless, she *kept the word of Christ* and *did not deny His name*, constantly persevering in the truth once it was recognized. This continued until *those who say they are Jews*—the most powerful Monarchs who falsely boast that they are the true people of God, and who had stood as the oppressors of the Lord’s afflicted—were forced to *come and worship before her feet*. This means they were compelled to make peace with those regions in which the Church exists, renouncing all their claims; and indeed even to profess in words that God *has helped them*.

XLIII. Laodicea represents the condition of the final times.
</margin>
XLIII. The Church of **Laodicea** represents the condition of the final times. And the pious observe with grief the beginnings of that blamed time in **England**, **France**, the **Netherlands**, and where not? Are not those who recently wished to reconcile religions with great effort <note>A reference to "Irenicism," movements seeking to find common ground between Catholics and Protestants, which the author views as a compromise of truth.</note> an example of this lukewarmness? And what is said to the Angel of the Church of the final time—to whom should it seem more directed than to those who specifically call themselves **Bishops**, and who conclude from these very letters that in each individual Church there ought to be individual Bishops such as they themselves are? Let them see how they will prove themselves to be **fervent** <note>original Greek: "ζεσός" (zestos)</note> and not *lukewarm*. Let them watch out lest they be vomited out of the Lord’s mouth. But why should we look elsewhere for what reveals itself too much in the Netherlands? Where (as someone said), *the zeal for truth barely draws a sickly breath: and, what is the heart of the matter, life does not correspond to doctrine, but deviates from it by the whole width of heaven. There, those very men who are hailed as Patrons of the truth fear more for themselves and their own reputation—lest they suffer any loss—than they fear for the Truth. Hence, if you call their words and deeds to an examination, you will find almost nothing of sincere and solid Theology, but only **political word-maneuvers** <note>original Greek: "λογοδρομίας" (logodromias) - literally 'word-races' or rhetorical gymnastics.</note> and Meanders <note>Labyrinthine or winding paths, named after the Greek river.</note>, by means of which they attempt to escape unharmed. <margin>XLV. Many things in these Epistles do not suit the Churches of those times.</margin>
XLV. *Eighth.* Every doubt should be removed by the demonstration showing that many things are contained in these epistles which, according to the literal sense, either cannot be applied to the specific Churches to which they were addressed except by force and without foundation, or even not at all; yet they are evidently true in that universal period of the Church which corresponds to the Church named in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. The supporters of this opinion work out the details of this demonstration in the following way.

<margin>XLVI. Which is demonstrated by examples.</margin>
XLVI. In the Epistle to the **Ephesians** there is mention of the **Nicolaitans**. In order to apply this to the Ephesian Church, the ancient writers—doubtless taking the opportunity of this passage—handed down as history, though it was mere guesswork, a story of the Nicolaitans. They say their heresy was that it was permissible to commit fornication and to use women indiscriminately, even those who were married. Some trace them back to **Nicolas**, a Proselyte <note>A convert to Judaism, then to Christianity; one of the first seven deacons.</note> of Antioch from Acts 6:5. Of him they say that, when he was accused of jealousy toward his most beautiful wife, he wished to leave her and prostitute her to everyone. Thus they think he was the author of such profanity: and they hand down that he said, as Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of heresies.</note> writes, *'unless one indulges in lust every day, he cannot share in eternal life.'* <note>original Greek: εἰ μὴ τις καθ᾽ ἡμέραν λαγνεύει ζωῆς οὐ δύναται μετέχειν αἰωνίου</note> Others [suggest] another [origin] of this sect...

For it is not believable that such absurd thoughts, alien not only to Christian piety but even to civil uprightness, could have occurred to a holy man approved by the Apostles with so little or no provocation. *Gomarus* <note>original: "Gomarus." Finally, what *throne*, what glorious kingdom with Christ on this earth, did the *Laodiceans* obtain? How much better, simpler, and more certain is it to explain all these things enigmatically?

### FIRST ARGUMENT

L. <margin>L. No Prophecy is of private interpretation.</margin> And **first indeed it must be observed in general, that no prophecy of the Scriptures is** of private interpretation <note>original Greek: ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως; see 2 Peter 1:20</note>, so that it would be permitted for any mortal to loosen its knots at his own will. For what Peter calls "interpretation" <note>Greek: ἐπίλυσις (epilysis)</note> here is the same as what the Hebrews call *pithron* <note>original Hebrew: פִתְרוֹן; a solution or interpretation of a dream</note>, and what Daniel calls *mesharei kitrin* <note>original Aramaic: מְשָׁרֵי קִטְרִין; "the loosening of knots," used in Daniel 5:16 to describe the solving of difficult problems</note>. Since prophecy was not brought by the will of man, but was dictated by the Holy Spirit, it is a sacrilege to explain it in any way other than according to the intention of that same Holy Spirit. Every genuine interpretation of prophecy possesses a **demonstration to the conscience** <note>original Greek: ἀπόδειξιν πρὸς τὴν συνείδησιν</note> and a **conviction of the soul** <note>original Greek: ἔλεγχον</note>—a sense that the Holy Spirit intended to indicate by the words of the prophecy the very thing we are thinking about them. Unless this happens, the soul has no place to rest. From this it follows that it is by no means permitted for us to imagine allegories, types, symbols, and prophetic enigmas where the words of a passage are plain, the history is evident, and the sense is simple; nor does God teach us, either here or elsewhere, that He wished to foreshadow something more hidden and far in the future by those plain words and evident history. If any dare to do so, they make their listeners and readers empty; **they speak a vision of their own heart, not from the mouth of Jehovah.**

LI. <margin>LI. Frequent allegories are poured out by curious minds. According to Letter 104.</margin> Excessive zeal for allegory has always displeased wise men in the Church. For if anywhere, certainly here there is a great need to restrain the "itch" of human curiosity, which often, if offered even a tiny crack of opportunity, permits itself an enormous amount, and uses the right of metaphor shamelessly, daring more than modesty allows. To whom has Origen not been offensive in this regard? He was noted by Jerome (who otherwise indulged himself too much in this area as well) as an interpreter who was always allegorical and fled from the truth of history, and who thought the sharpness of his own wit were the **sacraments** of the Church. <note>In this context, Jerome is accusing Origen of treating his own clever ideas as if they were sacred, divinely-instituted mysteries.</note>

# ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

...is the nature of a <term>type</term><note>A "type" is a biblical person, object, or event (usually in the Old Testament) that is understood to prefigure or symbolize a future reality (the "antitype," usually Christ or the Church in the New Testament).</note>, which depends on nothing else than Divine institution. The most celebrated Coccejus <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who emphasized how the Old Testament points toward the New.</note> states excellently:

<margin>In Jeremiah 22:8.</margin>
> *If Scripture does not indicate that we ought to see in one thing the image of another, even if different things explained by Scripture have some similarity and conformity, we cannot however assert that this is a type and figure of that, unless that conformity is demonstrated from a comparison of the Scriptures. Once demonstrated, indeed, the Wisdom of God is revealed; but without that demonstration, it is reckless to argue from the form of a preceding thing, as if it were a type, to the form of a following thing.*

<margin>
LIV. Unless the testimony of Divine institution is added, either explicitly or implicitly.
</margin>
LIV. Therefore, so that we may know something to be spoken allegorically <note>original Greek: αλληγορούμενον (allegoroumenon); used by St. Paul in Galatians 4:24 to describe the story of Sarah and Hagar</note> and to have the nature of a type, it is necessary that either God has expressly testified this concerning that matter; or He has declared it concerning some category of things under which that matter is included as a species; or He refers one to the other by a manifest allusion of words; or He at least silently hints at it by His own reasoning; or finally, He proclaims certain things about that matter which, as far as the letter and the sound of the words go, are not fulfilled in that thing—whose fulfillment, therefore, must be sought in a different matter, yet one which corresponds to the thing about which they were first spoken. Furthermore, since these observations are of great use for the genuine interpretation of the Scriptures and are not foreign to the present business, it will not be out of place to dwell on this meditation for a little while, and to illustrate those things which might seem somewhat obscure in such brevity with a more expansive explanation and suitable examples.

<margin>
LV. For sometimes God expressly declares this about a certain thing.
</margin>
LV. *First*. There are places where God expressly testifies that He has ordained something as a type of another thing. Thus, the *bronze* serpent raised up by Moses is interpreted by Christ as referring to Himself lifted up on the cross. We know—because the Spirit Himself declares it in the Scriptures—that Melchizedek was a figure of Christ; that the Red Sea represented Baptism; the manna brought down from heaven, spiritual food; the water flowing from the struck rock, a mystic drink; Sarah and Hagar, and Mountains Sinai and Sion, represented the two covenants or Testaments; and that the stay of Jonah in the belly of the fish, from which he emerged alive, foreshadowed the burial and resurrection of Christ. Typical explanations of this kind are no less certain than if the thing itself had been stated in so many words, without the detours of types.

<margin>
LVI. Sometimes He asserts this regarding a category in which many special things are contained.
</margin>
LVI. *Second*. There are also places where God does not assert this so specifically about a certain thing, but nevertheless has testified it concerning that category of things under which this thing is included as a species. For example, it is established concerning the Mosaic Ceremonies in general that they are shadows of future things, of which the "body" <note>Referring to Colossians 2:17: "These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance [body] belongs to Christ."</note> is Christ. Whatever, therefore, pertains to those Ceremonies, even if we do not find it specifically applied to Christ, is nonetheless to be interpreted enigmatically and symbolically, and compared with those things which are said of Christ or...

<meta>This page continues the criteria for identifying "types" in the Bible. On the previous page, the author argued that something is a type only if God has indicated it as such. This page explores how that indication can be implicit through wordplay or the logical structure of Apostolic arguments.</meta>

# BOOK III. CHAPTER III.

...or mentioned in His <term>mystical body</term><note>The Church, considered as the spiritual body of Christ.</note>, and they have an analogy corresponding to those ceremonies. For it must not be thought that all <term>types</term><note>A prophetic person, object, or event in the Old Testament that prefigures something in the New Testament.</note> are explicitly <note>original Greek: διαῤῥήδην (diarrheden)</note> explained in Scripture and applied to their subject: the Apostle himself confesses that he did not speak of everything in detail. *Hebrews 9:5.* It seemed sufficient to the Holy Spirit to warn generally that all Mosaic institutions are spoken <term>allegorically</term><note>original Greek: ἀλληγορούμενα (allegoroumena); meaning they have a deeper symbolic meaning.</note>, and to illustrate this with certain examples; through these, He showed the way in which one must proceed in the elucidation of symbols, and handed over the key to unlock those hidden things. Other matters of the same kind are left to human diligence to investigate.

<margin>LVII. Sometimes through a wise allusion to more material things, He leads us into the knowledge of spiritual things.</margin>
LVII. *Thirdly*. It happens sometimes that God, while discussing a spiritual matter, recalls us to the memory of something more physical and material through a manifest allusion of words; by this very act, He shows that the physical thing was a certain symbol of that spiritual and mystical reality. Thus we know that the visible creation of this world, as it is narrated by Moses, is a type of the **new creation** of the faithful and the establishment of the Church: because the logic of our entire restoration is frequently explained using phrases and similarities drawn from the first creation. The **new man** is said to be *created according to God*. *Ephesians 4:24.* And the faithful are called God's *workmanship* <note>original Greek: ποίημα (poiema), from which we get the word "poem."</note>, *created in Christ Jesus*. *Ephesians 2:10.* And the entire mystical body of Christ is called a *new creature*. *2 Corinthians 5:17.*

<margin>LVIII. Sometimes He hints at or assumes something is typical by the very method of His argument.</margin>
LVIII. *Fourthly*. It happens sometimes that the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures does not so much openly assert that certain things are typical, as He hints at it and silently assumes it through the mode and method of His reasoning. For example, when the Apostle argues from the types of *Sarah*, *Hagar*, *Melchizedek*, etc., against the Jews, he assumes this premise—as if it were granted by both sides and known to the Hebrews from their ancient <term>Catechesis</term><note>The basic oral instruction or teaching given to early Christians and Jewish converts.</note>—namely, that God wished to present an elegant picture, worthy of the precision of such a great Artist, in the memorable persons of the **Old Instrument** <note>A term for the Old Testament.</note>, to whom several remarkable things happened outside the ordinary course of nature. By this picture, Christ along with His mystical body was to be sketched out. *Galatians 4:12.* <note>The author likely refers to the argument starting in Galatians 4:21 regarding Sarah and Hagar.</note> Having laid this foundation, he soon descends with a certain Divine skill to the explanation of specific types. For he does not overwhelm them by his own Apostolic authority and *credibility* <note>original Greek: ἀξιοπιστίᾳ (axiopistia)</note>, but convinces them with the evidence of reasons and the ease of his deduction; arguing only from things already conceded or clear in themselves. From this method of arguing, it is rightly concluded that those other memorable persons, whose typical significance is nowhere expressly explained—such as *Abel*, *Enoch*, *Noah*, *Abraham*, and many similar ones—were types of Christ in many things that happened to them or were performed by them.

LIX

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the criteria for identifying types and allegories in Scripture. The previous page discussed how God uses wordplay and manifest allusions to link physical things to spiritual realities. This page provides a fifth logical rule: if the description of a person or event in the Old Testament is too grand for the historical figure itself, it must refer to a greater "Antitype," specifically Christ.</meta>

# ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

<margin>LIX. Finally, if something is predicted of a matter that is either not fulfilled, or not fully fulfilled in it, one must consider the <term>Antitype</term><note>The reality or person prefigured by a symbol (the "type"). For example, if the sacrificial lamb is the type, Jesus is the antitype.</note>.</margin>
LIX. Fifth and finally: If it happens that something is spoken concerning a thing whose *fulfillment* we do not find in the matter that seems to be indicated at first, it is necessary for us to turn our eyes elsewhere. We must investigate whether something else is signified through that first thing, in which the truth of that statement may be most fully seen. For this must be held as a fixed and settled rule for us in the interpretation of the Scriptures: in the word of God, no word is placed in vain, and nothing is ever said so grandly that the truth of the matter does not correspond to it exactly. The Sacred writers are far removed from the puffed-up grandiloquence of those who—as Herodian says at the beginning of his *History*—"handed down insignificant and small deeds, through the excellence of words, with a glory greater than the truth" <note>original Greek: εὐτελῆ καὶ μικὰ ἔργα, λόγων ἀρετῇ, δόξῃ παρέδωκαν τῆς ἀληθείας μείζονι</note>, raising thin and humble matters far above the reliability of truth through the artifice of writing. It is not as if we should ever think we owe God an apology for speaking imprudently, awkwardly, or more liberally than is just. That alone is a true and solid understanding of Scripture which makes manifest to the conscience the wisdom and prudence of God speaking; so that you could not imagine anything more just, holy, and worthy of God in the matter signified, nor anything more charming, beautiful, and fitting in the manner of speaking. Therefore, when those things which are present in a certain subject fall far below the magnificence of the Divine word, the necessity is imposed upon us to think of another subject in which all the predicates are most fully verified. Paul provides an example of this in Hebrews 11:6–9 <note>The author likely intended to cite Hebrews 2:6–9, which discusses Psalm 8; Hebrews 11 discusses faith.</note>. He considers those things said in Psalm 8 regarding man and the son of man, and he observes that at least some of the descriptions are much too grand for their full truth to be demonstrated in any <term>mortal man</term><note>original Hebrew: אֱנוֹשׁ (*enosh*), referring to man in his frail or fallen state.</note> subject to hardship. From this, he concludes that these things must be explained as referring to Christ. In the same way, those things said in Psalms 2, 16, 22, 45, 69, 72, and the Song of Songs, are understood to be said not so much of David or Solomon (even if certain small parts seem to fit them in a thinner sense) but of Christ, for whom they were the forerunners of His spiritual kingdom. For, according to the rule of Logicians, subjects are such as their predicates allow them to be. However, those predicates are greater than a "mere man" <note>original Greek: ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (*psilo anthropo*)</note> and a sinner. But in Jesus Christ and His Church, they are so recognized that the magnitude of the reality far exceeds the grasp of the words. In the same way, one may infer that Tyre, Babylon, etc., in the Prophets are symbols of other assemblies, if the things predicted of those cities were not fulfilled in them exactly as they were predicted.

<margin>LX. None of all these things have a place here.</margin>
LX. These are the laws of allegorical and typical interpretations. If anyone, by despising or neglecting these laws, indulges his own wit and devises mystical senses for himself, so that those things which are <term>enigmas</term><note>original Hebrew: מְלִיצוֹת (*melitzot*), meaning parables, proverbs, or mocking poems that require interpretation.</note>...

...whoever transforms plain speech into <term>riddles</term><note>original Hebrew: חִידוֹת (*chidot*), meaning puzzles or dark sayings</note> and enigmas does not teach the meaning of God, but thrusts forward the figments of his own brain, and, as Jerome says, *wanders in a frenzied error within the Scriptures*. Therefore, only one thing seems able to be said in favor of the allegorical and prophetic interpretation of those Letters: that not all things contained in them were fulfilled in the Asian Churches—from which, according to the fifth law, a necessity arises to think of another subject. The writing of these Letters belongs to the execution of that command, in which "the things that are" are set forth. However, these things are only revealed to John after he was carried up into heaven, following the dictation of these letters which he had received while on earth. LXII. They do not pay proper attention to the methodical arrangement of the entire work, which corresponds most skillfully in both order and phrasing to the proposed division, according to the interpretation we have given.

<margin>LXIII. For there is a most wise reason for this order.</margin>
LXIII. Moreover, what is more accurate than this division? What is more harmonious than this arrangement? What is wiser than this order? What is more suitable or probable than that explanation which makes these virtues of God and His word manifest? Indeed, the soul of a Christian man, about to approach the contemplation of the secret counsels of God with familiarity, ought above all to be imbued with the knowledge of Christ the Lord. This is so that he may hold His Majesty in reverence, look up to His eyes—which see the deep and hidden things of the heart—and tremble at His words. Then, it is necessary for him to descend into himself and conform all his affairs exactly to the will of Christ: stirring up faith, charity, patience, and the other Christian virtues if they are fading, and diligently restoring whatever had collapsed in the practice of Christianity. Then, finally, he will be fit to stand in the counsel of Jehovah, be admitted into the inner sanctuary of God, and become a partaker of His secrets. For *the secret of Jehovah is for those who fear him.* Psalm 25:14. *He who loves me,* says the Lord Jesus, *will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.* John 14:21.

BOOK III. CHAPTER III.

Daniel 12:10: *Many shall be purified, made white, and refined, but none of the wicked shall notice; yet the wise shall understand.* <note>original: "sed intelligentes animadversuri sunt"</note> Because Abraham observed the way of the Lord by doing justice and righteousness, and was an authority for his people to do the same, the Lord said He could not hide from Abraham what He intended to do. In that same order, by the command of Christ, John prepares the minds of those to whom the Apocalypse was first entrusted to understand the hidden things of the prophecies. First, he recounts to them what he had just learned of the Majesty of Christ from His marvelous appearance; then he emphasizes those things which lead to the correction of morals and the practice of the Christian life, placing before their eyes a kind of mirror of themselves; after all these things, he explains the series of fates—recounting in prophetic speech what is to happen to the Church, what the future lot of its enemies will be, and in what way all things shall finally be concluded by the glorious coming of Christ.

### THIRD ARGUMENT.

<margin>LXIV. John governed and ruled the Churches of Asia.</margin>
LXIV. THIRDLY. Nor can it be said that there is no cause why John was specifically commanded to warn these Churches by name, and to make them the guardians of his entire Apocalypse. It is certainly not because he was the first to found and establish those Churches; for it is well known that such praise is owed to Paul. Rather, it is because he stabilized and ruled them after Paul’s departure or death, and held them committed to his own care and inspection. Indeed, all of Antiquity agrees that in his old age, John undertook the administration and care of the Asian Churches, which had been founded by the preaching of Paul and excellently instructed in piety; he did this so that they might not fall away from the sincere faith they had once received through the arts of the many heretics active in that region. He lived in Ephesus before his exile to the island, and from there he was sent in chains to the Emperor Domitian by the proconsul of Asia, accused of <term>impiety</term><note>In this context, *impietas* often refers to the Roman legal charge of failing to worship the state gods or the Emperor.</note>. Returning from exile, he again established his seat and home for his affairs at Ephesus and governed the neighboring Churches. He even set out to the bordering regions, appointing Bishops in one place, rightly organizing entire Churches in another, and everywhere diligently performing the office of an Apostle. He lived in Asia for a very long time, even until the era of <term>Trajan</term><note>Roman Emperor, reigned 98–117 AD.</note>; as <term>Eusebius</term><note>The "Father of Church History," writing in the 4th century.</note> records from the accounts of *Irenaeus* and *Clement of Alexandria*. To this, *Tertullian*, *Epiphanius*, *Jerome*, and others agree with one voice. See *Baronius* at the years 44, 97, and again 99 AD.

Rather, it was because he stabilized and ruled them after Paul's departure or death, and held them committed to his own care and inspection. Indeed, all of Antiquity agrees that John, in his old age, undertook the administration and care of the Asian Churches <note>This refers to the Roman province of "Asia" in modern-day Turkey, not the entire continent.</note>—which had been founded by the preaching of Paul and excellently instructed in piety—lest they should fall away from the sincere faith they had once received through the arts of the many heretics active in that region. He lived at Ephesus before his exile on the island [of Patmos], and from there he was sent in chains by the proconsul of Asia to the Emperor Domitian, accused of impiety. <note>“Impiety” in this Roman context usually meant a refusal to participate in the imperial cult or state religion.</note> Returning from exile, he again established his seat and home for his affairs at Ephesus and governed the neighboring Churches. He even set out to the surrounding regions, here appointing Bishops, there rightly organizing entire Churches, everywhere diligently performing the duty of an Apostle, and living for a very long time in Asia until the times of Trajan; as *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> records from *Irenaeus* and *Clement of Alexandria*. *Tertullian*, *Epiphanius*, *Jerome*, and others agree with one voice on this. See *Baronius* <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian who wrote the "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> at the year 44 AD, and again at the years 97 and 99.

<margin>
LXV. And this is the reason why he was ordered to write to them by name.
</margin>
LXV. There is therefore no reason for anyone to ask why these Churches, rather than any others, were warned through heavenly letters sent by John, and were made the depositories of the entire Revelation (which nonetheless concerns the universal Church); even though they were neither larger nor more famous than many others,

->## ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.<-

...and some of them, not surviving long after, would have seen and experienced very few of the things predicted in the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>? For besides the fact that the sole will of the most free and wise Divinity suffices for every reason, the cause is not hidden as to why several letters, and an entire book, having John as their Author, were addressed to the Asian Churches, which the same John had already presided over for many years, and was to preside over in the future. For what was more appropriate and just than that he should instruct by a rich writing that would last for all ages those whom he had taught with his living voice? Nevertheless, he knew that the use and benefit of this work—not circumscribed by their borders or their times—would overflow into the entire Church of Christ.

<margin>
LXVI. The Churches to which the Letters were addressed could not have understood themselves as anything other than the ones being praised or blamed in them.

### FOURTH ARGUMENT.

LXVI. FOURTHLY. The very subjects of the Letters are such that the Churches, reading the letters addressed in their own names, could not have thought otherwise than that they themselves were being blamed or praised in them, and that a narration of the things happening among them was being established. Could it have been possible that the Church of the Pergamenes <note>The church in Pergamon, one of the seven cities addressed in Revelation</note>, reading what was written to it from heaven—that it "dwells where Satan has his throne," and that "Antipas, Christ’s faithful martyr, was killed among them," and that they "have those who hold the doctrine of Balaam and of the Nicolaitans"—could it have been possible, I say, that in reading this, they would think that Satan's throne was no more present among them than in other cities of the Roman world? Or that they had never seen any Antipas <note>Tradition holds Antipas was the first bishop of Pergamon, martyred under Domitian</note>, or heard of a man who praised the eating of things sacrificed to idols <note>original: "idolothytorum"</note> and fornication <note>original: "scortationem"</note> as lawful things, or found any sect under the name of the Nicolaitans? Instead, would they think that by those verbal riddles, things were being hinted at which would happen in far distant places after several centuries? Would they not, in their simplicity, have said to John: "What throne of Satan, what Antipas, what followers of Balaam, what Nicolaitans are you telling us about, whose faces we have never seen and whose names we have never heard? Who can understand riddles of this kind?" And so of the rest.

<margin>
LXVII. Nor was it right for them to refer those things said to them to other places and times.
</margin>

LXVII. And as for the rebukes, exhortations, promises, and threats addressed to the individual Churches, ought they not to have believed them to be spoken to themselves, named specifically, and directed at them? Was it permitted for the Laodiceans to interpret those things noted in their Letter regarding their era and arrogance in such a way that they pertained no more to themselves than to their neighbors, the Philadelphians, but only foretold what the Reformed Church would sin, for example, in England or Belgium <note>original: "Belgio," referring here to the Low Countries</note>, after fifteen or more centuries? Who would doubt that by such an irrelevant interpretation <note>original: "commento," literally a fabrication or invention</note> in the greatest...

<margin>
LXVIII.
What some nonetheless wish to claim.
</margin>
LXVIII. This weapon of argument could be considered cast in vain if the learned men with whom we clash in this dispute were of the opinion that everything contained in these Letters was first written and fulfilled literally in the Asian Churches, and then typically represented other Churches through a certain logic of <term>correspondence <note>original: συστοιχίας (*systoichias*), meaning a parallel arrangement or structural alignment between two things</note></term>. This was the opinion of the most praised *Brightman* <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607), an English clergyman who argued that the Seven Churches represented the history of the Christian Church from the Apostles to his own day</note>. But these learned men themselves protest that they are of a different mind; their own commentaries cry out and the arguments produced above prove it. They want the names of the Churches to be Symbolic and Emblematic. Therefore, they claim those Letters do not so much describe the condition of the Churches of Asia as they were in John's time, but rather the condition of the universal Church in those periods of time which enigmatically correspond to each emblem. Because of this, they say many things are stated here that were never found in those literal Churches of Asia. To this opinion, this fourth argument is directly opposed.

## FIFTH ARGUMENT.

<margin>
LXIX. These Letters contain nothing that was not fulfilled in the Asian Churches.
</margin>
LXIX. FIFTHLY. Nothing is contained in these Letters which was not proven by the facts themselves in those Asian Churches; there is nothing that forces us to look toward another subject in which we might anxiously seek the truth of what is said here. This must now be demonstrated regarding the individual Letters, though briefly. Regarding the exhortations to repentance, constancy, patience, and other duties of that kind, as well as the threats against deserters and the lukewarm, and the promises of grace and glory to be bestowed on those who prove themselves faithful to the Lord until the end, there can be no doubt that they could have been proposed to each Church in that manner. All the difficulty concerns the Historical elements, and any rare Prophetic elements that may intervene. But that there is no difficulty even here, the following observations will make clear.

### ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

"He spent a longer time practicing philosophy around Smyrna and Ephesus" <note>original: Τὸν μὲν πλείω χρόνον ἐφιλοσόφει περὶ τὴν Σμύρναν καὶ τὴν Ἔφεσον</note>; "the Ephesians were astonished, as they were present in great numbers when he spoke" <note>original: ἐκπεπληγμένης τῆς Ἐφέσου, ἥτις διαλεγομένῳ παρῆν πᾶσα</note>. For by his deceptive tricks he <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous pagan philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the first century</note> had attained such a reputation that he was regarded as a god; certainly in no way considered less than Christ. It is added that the Church could not endure evil men, and tested those who called themselves Apostles but were not, and found them to be liars. These were those "ravenous wolves" who did not spare the flock, and men speaking perverse things to lead away disciples after them, as Paul had prophesied in Acts 20:29-30. Ebion, surely, and Cerinthus <note>Early heretical teachers who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, and similar vipers <note>original: *excetræ*, literally water-snakes or hydras, used here to describe the spreading nature of heresy</note>, were then wandering through Asia; who is unaware that John even had conflicts with them? This praise fits perfectly with the words of **Ignatius** <note>Ignatius of Antioch, an early Christian martyr and bishop</note>, who wrote to the Ephesians not long after John: "Onesimus himself highly praises your good order in God, because you all live according to the truth, and because no heresy dwells among you; nor do you listen to anyone more than Jesus Christ speaking in truth" <note>original: Αὐτὸς μὲν οὖν Ὀνήσιμος ὑπερεπαινεῖ ὑμῶν τὴν ἐν Θεῷ εὐταξίαν...</note>. An ancient translator rendered it thus: *Onesimus himself therefore highly praises your Divine arrangement: since you all live according to the truth, and because not one heresy dwells in you; but neither do you hear anyone further than Jesus Christ speaking in truth.* And a little later: "I have known certain people passing through from there, having an evil doctrine, whom you did not allow to sow among you, having blocked your ears, so as not to receive the things sown by them" <note>original: Ἔγνων δὲ καὶ παροδεύσαντάς τινας ἐκεῖθεν...</note>.

Meanwhile, the Church is blamed for its <term>neglect <note>original: ἄφεσιν (*aphesin*), meaning a letting go, abandonment, or cooling of intensity</note></term>, that is, the omission or relaxation of its "first love." There seems to have been more than one cause for this. For it could easily have happened that the former zeal of many cooled down, partly out of faint-heartedness because they saw both Jews and Gentiles stubbornly opposing them; partly because of the tricks of that Apollonius we mentioned, who was believed by many to perform miracles equal to those of the Apostles; partly from human prudence suggesting some kind of moderation, lest the minds of their opponents be further exasperated by a more stubborn zeal; and partly also because of the absence of John, who had been banished to Patmos by the Emperor Domitian. John's sermons, always breathing love, and his example, modeled after the pattern of Christ, had until then powerfully nurtured the glow of sacred love.

<margin>LXXI. The Nicolaitans</margin>
LXXI. Mention is also made of the Nicolaitans nesting in this Church. All the ancient writers consistently report that their sect was most foul; they denied the true Deity of Christ and advocated for promiscuous sexual intercourse, nor did they abstain from things sacrificed to idols...

For Nicholas, the minister of the Apostles <note>referring to Nicholas, one of the seven deacons mentioned in Acts 6:5</note>, was not such a man. See also **Tertullian**, *On Prescription against Heretics*, Chapter 45; **Epiphanius**, *Against Heresies*, 25; **Augustine**, *On Heresies*, Chapter 5; and others after them, as well as **Baronius**, who collected many things from the Ancients for the year 68 AD.

<margin>
Number 9 and following.
</margin>
Nor were these things asserted by the ancients without reason. This is gathered partly from this passage, where "the works" <note>original: τὰ ἔργα</note>—the deeds and actions—of the Nicolaitans are mentioned, a phrase which suggests that their heresy was primarily *practical* <note>meaning focused on behavior and lifestyle rather than just abstract doctrine</note>. It is also gathered from the testimonies of **Peter** and **Jude**. Peter describes certain heretics of his time as those who "walk according to the flesh in the lust of uncleanness," and "count it pleasure to riot in the daytime." They are "spots and blemishes," sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with Christians; "having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin; beguiling unstable souls," having "followed the way of Balaam" <note>quoting 2 Peter 2:13-15</note>. **Oecumenius** and others observe that the Nicolaitans are designated by these words; and the facts themselves speak to this, since Peter joins them to the followers of Balaam, just as the Holy Spirit does in the Epistle to the Pergamenians. **Jude** depicts the same people as those who "turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and deny the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ," and being "dreamers, they defile the flesh," "feeding themselves without fear" <note>quoting Jude 4, 8, 12</note>. Such heretics, therefore, existed under the name of Nicolaitans in the age of the Apostles; and why not in **Ephesus**, the largest and wealthiest city of Asia Minor, where luxury is never usually lacking?

<margin>
LXXII. The origin of the name is uncertain.
</margin>
LXXII. It is not necessary for us to determine now from whence these foul heretics of the Nicolaitans obtained their name: whether from **Nicholas the Deacon**, and whether that was done justly or unjustly; or from some other Nicholas. For this is irrelevant to the present matter, provided it is established that shameful men of this sort—who were called Nicolaitans for whatever reason—were present at that time both elsewhere and in Ephesus. And if no religious tradition of antiquity binds us here, what reason forces us to derive that name from some unknown founder of a sect? Why is it not permitted to believe that those wicked men were named from the reality of the matter, from their opinion, or from their practice? What if we establish, along with the most learned **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot, a 17th-century English churchman and Hebraist known for using rabbinical literature to interpret the New Testament</note>, that the name of the sect was derived from the Chaldean word *Nicola* <note>original Hebrew/Chaldaic: ניכולא</note>, which means "Let us eat"? For since nothing was more important to these most worthless little men than to encourage one another to eat things sacrificed to idols <note>term: idolothyta, food offered to pagan gods</note>, saying to each other and to others, as we may guess: "*Nicola*, let us eat,"

# ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

...we grant, how aptly they could be called *Nicolaitans* by the Orthodox? Compare the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> on Isaiah 22:13: "They say, *NICOL*, let us eat meat." <note>original: אמרין ניכול בשר. This is a scholarly pun: the Aramaic word "Nikhol" (let us eat) sounds like the name "Nicholas." The author suggests the Nicolaitans were named not just after a leader, but after their reputation for gluttony and indulgence.</note> Be that as it may, let it suffice for us now that those who deny that these heretics—foul with debauchery and feasting and known by the name Nicolaitans—existed in the Apostles' age, in the Church (and why not also in Ephesus?), contradict all antiquity and Scripture itself.

<margin>LXXIII. The affliction of the Smyrneans.</margin>
LXXIII. In the *Epistle to the Smyrneans* <note>Referring to the message to the church in Smyrna in Revelation 2:8-11.</note> almost everything is clear. Mentioned are their affliction and poverty due to the confiscation and plundering of their goods (as Christians of those times were frequently stripped of their resources for the sake of religion), and the *blasphemy of those who falsely called themselves Jews*. Foretold also are the imprisonments of certain people and a *ten-day affliction*. What kind of present or past affliction this was, in which the Smyrneans proved their patience by bravely enduring, can be gathered from that which the Spirit prophesies as future, and which is described more at length in historical records.

<margin>LXXIV. In the time of Polycarp.</margin>
<margin>Book IV, Chapter XV. According to the Greek, Chapter XIV in the Latin.</margin>
LXXIV. These records tell how, when almost all of Asia was being disturbed by the greatest storms of persecution, a massive tempest specifically weighed upon the Church at Smyrna. The Blessed **Polycarp**—a student of **John the Apostle** and appointed Bishop of the Smyrneans by him—settled this storm with the blood of his martyrdom. How cruel that affliction was, the Smyrneans themselves described elegantly and pathetically in the letter that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> provides, where they skillfully set forth how lofty and upright a firmness of mind the blessed martyrs showed in enduring the bites of pain.

> For those standing around on every side (I am quoting the words of the letter itself), when they saw before them that some were torn by whips even to the innermost veins and arteries—so that now the entrails and other hidden parts buried in the deep recesses of the body were exposed to the eyes of all—while others were afflicted by being pressed onto sea shells <note>term: sea shells (buccinarum testis). Sharp, broken fragments of shells used as instruments of torture.</note> brought from the ocean and certain very sharp stones, and dragged through every kind of punishment and torment, and finally handed over to savage beasts to be torn apart; when they saw before them, I say, that they sustained all these things with such tolerance, they were struck with almost incredible wonder.

<margin>LXXV. Incensed by the calumnies of the Jews.</margin>
LXXV. For, incited by an insane hatred against the Christian religion, they stirred up everywhere both magistrates and commoners against the faithful...

The people of Smyrna complain in their letter <note>The "Letter of the Smyrneans," which describes the martyrdom of their bishop, Polycarp, in approximately 155 AD.</note> that this same thing happened to them several times. When Polycarp had publicly and steadfastly protested that he was a Christian, *the entire multitude of both Gentiles and Jews living in Smyrna, burning with uncontrollable anger and a loud voice, shouted: "This is the Teacher of Asia! This is the Father of the Christians!"* 

When that same man, while still alive, was condemned to the pyre, a frequent crowd of men immediately began gathering wood and brushwood from the workshops and baths, *and especially the Jews were eagerly assisting in this deed, as is their custom in such matters.* Once the martyr was dead, these same Jews advised the common people and urgently insisted that they plead with the Governor not to give his body to anyone: *“Lest,” they blasphemed, “leaving the Crucified one, they begin to worship this man.”* They also carefully watched the Christians who intended to take him out of the fire. Compare also the history of *Pionius* the Martyr <note>A priest of Smyrna martyred in 250 AD; his account highlights the ongoing tensions between the Jewish and Christian communities there.</note>, likewise of Smyrna, in which the pride and cruelty of the Jews is noted, in the works of *Baronius*, Volume II, for the year 254, Numbers 5 and 13. <note>Cardinal Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) wrote the "Annales Ecclesiastici," a massive history of the Church.</note>

### ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

...is contended by a smaller number. A ten <note>The number "ten" (decas) vs "one" (monas).</note> compared to one is much; compared to a hundred, it is little. Genesis 24:55: *Let the young woman remain with us at least ten days.* That is, for a short time. Compare Amos 5:8 and 6:9, as well as Genesis 18:33 and Numbers 11:19. That this brief time is nevertheless sufficient for a trial is supported by Daniel 1:12. The connection of the words also encourages this interpretation. For they are arranged in such a way as to encourage the faithful toward patience and constancy, using an argument drawn from the brevity of afflictions—a strategy the Holy Spirit uses elsewhere. Isaiah 26:20; 2 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Peter 1:6. Indeed, the historical reality itself almost compels this view. For that storm of persecution spent its rage with the death of Polycarp. <note>original Greek: Ὅστις ὥσπερ ἐπισφραγίσας διὰ τῆς μαρτυρίας αὑτοῦ κατέπαυσε τὸν διωγμόν.</note> *He, as if sealing it through his own martyrdom, brought the persecution to a rest.*

<margin>LXXVII. What historical matters are contained in the Letter to the Pergamenes.</margin>
LXXVII. In the letter to the *Pergamenes*, these historical elements occur: that there was in that city the **Throne of Satan**, and that **Antipas**, the faithful martyr of Christ, was killed in that place; also that there were those who held to the **doctrine of Balaam** and the **doctrine of the Nicolaitans**, against whom the Lord would fight with the sword of his mouth. The explanation of all these things does not seem very difficult.

<margin>LXXVIII. Pergamum is called the Throne of Satan because of the temple of Aesculapius, in which the Devil was worshiped.</margin>
LXXVIII. I will not say, along with *Bullinger* <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a Swiss Reformer.</note>, *Brightman* <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607), an English clergyman and early commentator on Revelation.</note>, and others, that the Proconsul of Asia had the seat of his jurisdiction at Pergamum, and from there raged against the Christians—both there and elsewhere in his province—with cruel edicts suggested and dictated by **Satan**. For not without reason do others believe that the Proconsul of Asia Minor resided at Ephesus. It is more useful to observe that there was in that city a very famous temple and oracle of **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of healing, often symbolized by a snake-entwined staff.</note>, to whom vows were made and gifts were sent even from the most remote places. Thus, by Earinus, a freedman of Domitian, hair was sent to the Pergamene *Aesculapius* along with a jeweled box and a mirror, as *Statius Papinius* indicates. And regarding this same hair of Earinus, *Martial* writes thus:

> — And his sweet locks
> He placed as sacred gifts for the Pergamene God.

BOOK III. CHAPTER III.

...whenever the Gentiles perform sacred rites to their gods, they do so for demons (1 Corinthians 10:20). This applies specifically here because snakes and dragons were sacred to **Aesculapius** <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing, often depicted with a serpent-entwined staff. Pergamum was home to a world-famous sanctuary dedicated to him.</note> and were raised in his temples at public expense; just as he was believed to have come to Rome from Epidaurus in the form of a serpent. But is not Satan the *Dragon* and the *ancient serpent*? (Revelation 12:9). To protect his kingdom, he incited his followers against Christians with as much aggression as possible. For this reason, **Arethas** <note>An early 10th-century commentator on the Apocalypse.</note> rightly says, <note>original Greek: θρόνον δὲ τοῦ σατανᾶ τὴν πέργαμον καλεῖ, ὡς κατείδωλον οὖσαν ὑπὲρ τὴν Ἀσίαν πᾶσαν.</note> "he calls Pergamum the throne of Satan because it was more filled with idols than all the rest of Asia."

<margin>LXXIX. Who was Antipas?</margin>
**LXXIX.** Regarding **ANTIPAS**, these things are handed down by more recent writers: that he was the Bishop of Pergamum who, while preaching Christ publicly and forcing demons to confess they were being put to flight by the name of Christ, was captured by the city prefect. He was dragged to the temple of **Diana** <note>The Roman name for Artemis.</note> and cast into a **bronze bull** <note>A notorious torture device, often called a "Brazen Bull," designed to roast a person alive while their screams sounded like the lowing of a bull.</note> glowing with intense fire. He completed his life in glorious martyrdom around the year 93 AD, in the tenth year of **Domitian**, the same year in which John was relegated to exile. Furthermore, this bronze bull in which Antipas was burned is said to have been moved from Pergamum to Constantinople and placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles. So say *Arethas, Metaphrastes, Cedrenus, Pererius, Baronius, Surius,* and *Cornelius a Lapide*. 

Let each person grant these accounts as much weight as they wish. At the very least, his status as a Bishop is uncertain, and the story of the bronze bull seems entirely legendary. It must be admitted, meanwhile, that no mention of this Antipas is found in ancient history; just as many things from that first century are unknown because there were few or no writers at that time, besides the Divine ones. Yet, to infer from a lack of historical records that no martyr named Antipas existed at Pergamum is completely irrational and goes against the reverence due to Holy Scripture. The Scriptures alone are sufficient for our faith. Who would tolerate a person who thought it permissible to doubt whether those distinguished men greeted by Paul in Romans 16 actually existed in Rome, simply because there is deep silence regarding most of them in ancient monuments? And by what probable reason do we permit ourselves more liberty with these Divine Epistles than with others, or more than a bold breed of critics would think allowed to them in the works of any classic author? <margin>Boethius, On the Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose VII.</margin> *“How many men, most famous in their own times, has a lack of writers destroyed through oblivion!”* exclaims **Boethius**. Let us say, therefore—and let us say it confidently because the Lord Himself says it—that there was a certain pious and zealous man at Pergamum who was cruelly slaughtered for the name of Christ, even if we are ignorant of the man’s social standing, the manner of his death, and similar circumstances.

### ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.

<margin>...either they are the same heretics, or certainly very similar.</margin>
...is clear from those things which we brought forward in section 71. Just as they infested the Church at Smyrna, they were not absent from Pergamum either. And it is quite believable that the followers of this Balaamite doctrine <note>A reference to the biblical figure Balaam, who led the Israelites into sin by encouraging them to participate in pagan festivals; here used to describe Christians who compromised with local pagan customs.</note> were the source of advice to the rest of the faithful, suggesting that they should fearlessly attend the pagan banquets of their fellow citizens where they ate food sacrificed to idols. They did this under the pretext of both liberty and "Christian prudence," so that the flames of persecution would not be ignited more fiercely by excessive scrupulosity and an unnecessary separation from society.

<margin>Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, Book II, near the end.</margin>
And so they strove to transform Christ's sheep into pigs, which—as I remember **Jerome** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his translation of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> elegantly writing to someone—"they might fatten as bacon for Gehenna <note>original Latin: *gehennæ succideam nutrirent*. Jerome uses the image of fattening a pig for slaughter to describe those indulging in worldly pleasures before judgment.</note>." Moreover, those profane banquets were easily accompanied or followed by fornication, both spiritual and physical. For this reason, the eating of things sacrificed to idols and sexual immorality are forbidden to the faithful in the same breath by the decree of the Apostolic Synod, as vices that love to walk with an equal stride. *Acts 15:29.* Furthermore, the Lord threatens that he will *fight with the sword of his mouth* against those Balaamites and Nicolaitans. For since they were swollen with pride and endowed with excessive vanity (*2 Peter 2:18*), they *provoked the Lord to jealousy, as if they were stronger than he. (1 Corinthians 10:22).* Hence there is war against them, in which nothing is easier for the Lord than to finish them off with the sword of his mouth alone, by uncovering, convicting, and confounding their foul impiety with his most holy oracles, and by setting out the punishments he had defined in his word, both in body and soul, both in this life and the future one; according to the Gospel of Peter (*2 Peter 2:11, 13*) and Jude (*verses 11-14*).

<margin>LXXXI. Hidden Manna, and the white stone.</margin>
**LXXXI.** To the one who overcomes, the Lord promises *the eating of the hidden manna and a white stone*: of which things, the latter signifies the sense of free justification <note>The theological concept of being declared righteous by God's grace.</note>, and the former the sweetest taste of Divine sweetness. This is most appropriate. For such was the lot of the faithful in that idolatrous city, that they were held as sacrificial victims of common hatred—especially those who were forbidden by the fear of God and a holy tenderness of conscience from frequenting the wicked feasts of the Gentiles. Against that unjust hatred of the citizens, the Lord opposes the promise of his favor and his friendship: declaring that they would be more acceptable to him the more they were hated by the world. And certainly, nothing more pleasant can happen to a faithful person than to please Christ, and to be defended by him against the crooked judgments of the world. *1 Corinthians 4:3-4.* This is implied by the *white stone* <note>In the ancient world, a white stone was often used in courts to signify acquittal, while a black stone signified conviction.</note>. Unless perhaps—because there is talk of a reward to be given to the victor, and mention was made shortly before of the manna to be given—reference is being made to the sacred contests of the Greeks, in which <term>eiselastika</term> <note>original Greek: εἰσελασικὰ. LXXXIII.
On the very abundant harvest of such pseudo-prophetesses in the ancient Church.
</margin>
LXXXIII. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that so much influence was attributed to those impious women at that time. Because the gift of Prophecy flourished in the Church—with which God had enriched and adorned not only men, but also women, according to the prophecy in Joel 2:28 <note>“I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy...”</note> and the example of the four daughters of Philip the Evangelist in Acts 21:8–9—therefore, certain handmaidens of the Devil, who were impure but clever dogs, did not blush to boast of a Prophetic Spirit. Heretics and false prophets of the earliest times craftily abused the efforts of these women to entice the simpler folk. Who is unaware of *Simon Magus’s* *Selene* (or *Helena*), or *Carpocrates’s* *Marcellina*, or *Apelles’s* *Philomene*, or *Montanus’s* *Priscilla*, *Maximilla*, and *Quintilla*, and the other sorceresses like them? **Jerome** observed that almost all heresies were propagated through women. <margin>To Ctesiphon.</margin> *Simon Magus*, he says, *founded a heresy, assisted by the help of the prostitute Helena.* *Nicholas of Antioch*, the inventor of all uncleanness, led female choirs. *Marcion* sent a woman ahead of him to Rome to prepare people's minds for his deception. *Apelles* had *Philomene* as a companion for his doctrines. *Montanus*, a preacher of an unclean spirit, first corrupted many Churches with gold through *Prisca* and *Maximilla*—noble and wealthy women—and then polluted them with heresy. I will leave behind the ancient examples and move to those closer to us. *Arius*, in order to deceive the world, first deceived the sister of the Prince. *Donatus* was assisted by the wealth of *Lucilla* throughout Africa so that he might pollute all the unfortunate people with his stinking waters. In Spain, *Agape* led *Elpidius*—a woman leading a man, the blind leading the blind—into the pit; and she had as her successor *Priscillian*, a man most devoted to the magic of *Zoroaster* <note>An ancient Persian prophet associated in the Roman mind with magic and occult arts.</note> and a Bishop made from a Magician. Joined to him was *Galla*, who left her sister running here and there as the heir to another neighboring heresy. Who then would wonder that what was so frequent also happened at Thyatira—that a woman became the leader of a wicked deed and led some Christians away from the faith toward impurities by her charms?

The impurities of this Harlot are called "the depths of Satan" because of the secret wisdom she claimed.

LXXXIV. The Lord calls these impurities of Jezebel’s doctrine **the depths of Satan** <note>original Greek: τὰ βάθη τοῦ σατανᾶ</note>. It was the habit of heretics to boast of great mysteries and a hidden, secret doctrine which, they claimed, far exceeded the "boring" simplicity of the Gospel with its more profound wisdom. An example of this is found among the <term>Gnostics</term> <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that claimed salvation came through secret knowledge (gnosis) rather than faith alone.</note>, who were the offspring of the Nicolaitans and had been trained in wickedness in the same school as Jezebel. They called themselves "Gnostics" because of the excellence of their knowledge, claiming to have penetrated deeper into the mysteries of God than all others. **Gregory** wisely says: *Heretics pretend they hear a hidden word, so that they may strike the minds of their listeners with a certain...*

<margin>Book 5 of the *Moralia*, chapter 17.</margin>
...they drape a veil of reverence over their [false] calling. For this reason, they preach in secret, so that their preaching might appear as holy as it is hidden. They shun common knowledge lest they be considered equal to others; they always seek out hidden or new things so that, while others remain ignorant, they themselves may boast in a "uniqueness of knowledge" <note>original: "scientiæ singularitate"</note> before the minds of the unlearned. As we have said, they introduce these things as "hidden" because, in order to display something worthy of admiration, they insist they have received these teachings in private. However, the Lord declares that these "mysteries" belong not to God, but to Satan; He praises those who neither know nor approve of them, but instead shudder at, detest, and curse them.

<margin>LXXXV. The punishment of Jezebel and her children.</margin>
LXXXV. Furthermore, the Lord accuses the woman of obstinacy, because she abused His *patience* <note>Greek: μακροθυμία (makrothymia), meaning long-suffering or divine forbearance</note> and refused to be led to repentance. Therefore, once the time of His long-suffering has passed, He announces that she—who had shamefully abused beds for profane and lustful banquets—shall be cast into a "bed," namely one of pain and death, with every hope of returning to health being cut off. The same fate awaited her "children," whether you understand this as her natural offspring or metaphorically as her closest disciples, through whose efforts she propagated her wicked doctrine. He says He will destroy all of these with "death" <note>often interpreted as pestilence or mortal judgment</note>, in an elegant allusion to the sons of the ancient Jezebel, who were all slain by Jehu (2 Kings 10:6–7). 

Furthermore, a distinction can be made between the children of Jezebel and those *who committed adultery with her*, that is, those who were seduced by others to become followers of her impurities. Upon these the Lord does not yet threaten death, but rather "great affliction," during which they may have time to come to their senses. It is no more necessary to search through history books to find exactly how these things occurred in the Church of Thyatira than it is for what Paul wrote to the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 11:30: *For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep* <note>meaning they have died</note>.

That which the Lord Jesus properly does is attributed to the faithful because they are one with Christ; thus far they do the same things with Christ and in Him, being sharers of His glory, especially since all the fruit of this victory overflows unto them.

Promises made to individuals under conditions are not prophecies about the state of the Church on earth.

LXXXVIII. Instead, these are conditional promises made to individual believers, provided they run the race set before them with eagerness and constancy. The fulfillment of these promises is not to be sought on earth, where only the "firstfruits" <note>the initial taste or down payment of spiritual blessings</note> are given, but rather in heaven.

LXXXIX.
The condition of the Church of Sardis.

LXXXIX. In the letter to the Sardians, there is nothing at all that presents a difficulty. It describes the state of a Church that certainly held pure doctrine, untainted by any heresies; it also possessed a significant knowledge of the truth and openly and freely confessed Christ. For this reason, it had even earned the name of *life* <note>meaning it had a reputation for being spiritually alive</note>. Otherwise, however, their conduct did not match their doctrine, nor did their deeds match their reputation. Their works were not "complete" in the sight of God, nor were they of such a nature that they could be considered fit evidence of spiritual life, or of regeneration <note>spiritual rebirth</note> and sanctification <note>the process of being made holy</note>. If any good still remained, it was quite thin and weak, seemingly struggling against death itself. Yet, amidst such corruption of morals, a few individuals are praised because they "have not defiled their garments." This means they kept themselves chaste and clean from the foul lusts of the Nicolaitans <note>an early sect accused of practicing sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols</note>, hating even the "tunic" that is stained by contact with the flesh (Jude verse 23).
