...who has investigated these things more accurately? Why should we be forced to understand this precisely as the peace given to the Church in this world, to justify a pious cause? Why shouldn't we believe, with Ludovicus de Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642) was a Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist</note>, that it refers to the Priestly custom of the Jews? Whenever there was a question about their lineage, those who were found to be rejected were ordered to leave the court veiled in black clothes, while the genuine ones, dressed in white, remained in the temple to serve with their brothers. This is taught by Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and scholar</note> in *The Entry into the Sanctuary* <note>original: "Biath Hammikdas"</note>, section XI.

<margin>
90. The Key
of David.
</margin>
90. Let us now examine the Letter to the *Philadelphians*. Not without reason does the Lord Jesus claim for Himself the *key of David, with which He opens and no one shuts; He shuts and no one opens*; that is, the supreme power over His Church, so that He may receive into the communion of the saints and the blessed, or exclude them, as He sees fit, and block all access for enemies to harass His citizens. This is an elegant allusion to Isaiah's prophecy about Eliakim, who was the prefect of the Royal court (whom the people of Constantinople used to call the *master of the palace* <note>original Greek: "ϰαραπαλάτην" (karapalaten), referring to the high Byzantine office of Curopalates</note>), the sign of whose dignity was a *key* woven into his shoulder-cloth. Therefore it is said, *the key of the house of David will be placed upon his shoulder.* Isaiah 22:21, 22. The Lord wisely mentions this power here: for since the Philadelphians were of the lowest condition among all the cities of Asia mentioned here—not supported by size, wealth, or any human protection—which is why they are said to have *little strength* <note>original Greek: "μικρὰν δύναμιν" (mikran dynamin)</note>, the most wise and kind Jesus suggests to them that He will be their true Eliakim—the God who raises up and establishes, *upon whose shoulders is the government* (Isaiah 9:5)—clearly provided for their protection. He would be like a *father* to them, just as Eliakim was to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the house of Judah. They indeed lived scattered in the countryside, fearing the frequent tremors of the city <note>Philadelphia was known for frequent earthquakes</note>; but the Lord claims for Himself the keys of those spiritual gates, in the trust of which they may be safe and secure from every hostile invasion, like *a garden enclosed, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.* Song of Solomon 4:12. He also shows to whom it is owed that a flourishing Church was gathered in a town of no great reputation.

91. An o-
pen door,
and the
Jews as sup-
pliants.
</margin>
91. The following words pertain to the same: *Behold, I give you an open door,* etc. That is, an opportunity for success and for spreading the Gospel excellently among both fellow citizens and neighbors. In the same way, Paul testifies that a *great and effective door was opened* to him at both Ephesus and Troas. 1 Corinthians 16:9, 2 Corinthians 2:12. The Lord adds that He will give to them some from the Synagogue of Satan, who, in the same way as those of Smyrna, falsely claimed to be Jews. He was not only going to restrain their impudence but also effectively convert them, so that as suppliants they would seek pardon for their sins and join themselves to the Church...

->### ARGUMENTS FOR THE HISTORICAL SENSE.<-

...they might join themselves. By these words, that universal conversion of the Israelite nation is not designated—of which Paul speaks in Romans 11—but only that of certain Philadelphian Jews who had previously harassed the Church. For the discussion is not about the whole of the people, but about a certain Synagogue; and not even that in its entirety, but certain individuals from the Synagogue.

<margin>XCII. Preservation from the hour of universal trial.</margin>
XCII. Finally, the Lord promises that He will *keep them from the time of trial which was to come upon the whole world.* This is most appropriately referred to the persecution under Trajan <note>Trajan (reigned 98–117 AD) was the Roman Emperor who presided over a significant period of Christian trials, though often local rather than empire-wide</note>, which fell upon the Christian world not long after the Apocalypse was written. This town's Church was perhaps less troubled than many others—which were larger, more prominent, and more subject to envy—because it was poor and therefore held in less reputation and name among the Gentiles.

<margin>XCIII. Some details about the Philadelphians from Ignatius.</margin>
XCIII. History contains nothing specific, as I recall, regarding the Philadelphians of those times. But, as we have already noted several times, the Word of God does not borrow its strength from any human monuments. Nevertheless, something is found in the *Epistles of Ignatius* <note>Ignatius of Antioch was an early Christian bishop and martyr who wrote several letters while being transported to Rome for execution</note> from which some light may shine upon what has been said. When that blessed martyr of Christ, during the reign of Trajan, was being led bound from Antioch (where the Church was harassed by a very heavy persecution) to Rome, he stayed for a short while in Smyrna. When the bonds of this most holy man, famous throughout the entire East, became known to the Churches of Asia, each one immediately sent legates to him to pay their respects, while neighboring Bishops also hurried to him as quickly as possible. After he had been brought to Troas, the Bishop of the Philadelphian Church met him. Acknowledging this duty of Christian courtesy with a grateful heart, Ignatius sent a letter full of kindness and piety to the same Church. From this we gather that those virtues for which the Church is praised here were also flourishing at that time. For just as the constancy of the Bishop is proclaimed here in "keeping the word of patience" and "not denying the name of Christ," so also Ignatius testifies that he knew him—<note>original Greek: "μηδὲ μετὰ κενοδοξίαν, ἀλλ' ἐν ἀγάπη Θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ"</note> "as possessing an administration fitting for the community, not of himself nor through men, nor according to vainglory, but in the love of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Indeed, he says he was struck by the man’s <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἐπιείκειαν, ὃς σιγῶν πλείονα δύναται τῶν μάταια λαλούντων"</note> gentleness, "who, by remaining silent, has more power than those who speak empty things." He further praises <note>original Greek: "τό ἀκίνητον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀόργητον αὐτοῦ ἐν πάση ἐπιεικεία Θεοῦ ζῶντος"</note> "his steadfastness and lack of anger, in all the gentleness of the living God." Moreover, he describes the Church itself as <note>original Greek: "ἐλεημένην"</note> "having received mercy"...

<margin>
94. The Letter to the Laodiceans is clearly adapted to the condition of their city. Book 12.

XCIV. The Letter addressed to the Laodiceans is so adapted to the condition of that city that it seems impossible to twist it toward any other meaning without doing violence to the text. It has long been observed by learned men, drawing from Tacitus, Strabo, and others, that Laodicea was a most wealthy city—so much so that when it was cast down by an earthquake, it was restored by its own resources. <note>Tacitus (a Roman historian) records that Laodicea rebuilt itself after the earthquake of 60 AD without the usual imperial subsidy from Rome, a testament to its immense wealth.</note> Furthermore, that wealth was based both on other merchandise and especially on wool. *The places,* says Strabo <note>Strabo was a Greek geographer and historian of the Augustan era.</note>, *which are around Laodicea raise excellent sheep, surpassing even those of Miletus not only in the softness of their wool, but also in a color that rivals the blackness of crows; from which they derive ample revenues.* This wealth, as often happens, gave birth to luxury, and luxury to security, lukewarmness, and arrogance, even within the Church. Hence, they neglected self-examination and daily admonition. Hence arose a superficial <term>superfunctorium</term> study of spiritual and heavenly matters, as men easily flattered themselves regarding what they thought they had already acquired, boasting that they were no less enriched by the riches of the Spirit than by the riches of the world. 

The Lord sharply rebukes these traits in them, as they deserve. He teaches them that other riches must be sought, far more precious than those they possessed in their beautiful but black fleeces—namely, gold refined by fire, the treasures of faith and charity, and white garments, representing both the righteousness of Christ and purity and holiness. Who does not see the elegance of these metaphors? All their beauty perishes if these things are referred to a "Church of the last times" (which has nothing to do with Laodicea) as if they were spoken of her.

</margin>

There is nothing that either commands or persuades us to look toward another subject in which to anxiously seek the truth of the Lord’s words. And...

-># EXAMINATION OF THE ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE<-

...is beset by disadvantages. The following observations will make this clear.

<margin>
XCVII.
Just because the names of cities are symbolic in some places, it does not mean they are here. Compare section XVII.
</margin>
XCVII. Let us, therefore, call each individual argument to account in the order they were proposed. We certainly do not doubt that the names of ancient regions, cities, and nations in Sacred Scripture are frequently symbolic, enigmatically signifying other groups of people. However, simply because it is thought to happen sometimes, or because it happens elsewhere, it does not necessarily follow that it happens here. Learned men could no more prove by that argument that Ephesus or Smyrna are symbolic names in this context, than they could for Rome, Corinth, Philippi, or Thessalonica in the Epistles of Paul. Nor is there any reason for them to object that the nature of those Epistles—which are undoubtedly dogmatic <note>Instructive or teaching-oriented, rather than visionary.</note>—is one thing, while these—which are inserted into a Prophetic book—are another, and must therefore be explained according to the style of prophecies. For not everything written in a prophetic book is for 그 reason prophetic, nor should it be considered symbolic on that account any more than if it were narrated elsewhere. The history of Hezekiah in the book of the prophet Isaiah must be interpreted no less literally than in the books of Kings or Chronicles.

<margin>
XCVIII.
Indeed, not even the same names that are symbolic in some places are so everywhere. Section LIII and following.
</margin>
XCVIII. Added to this is the fact that nothing should be established as a symbol or an <term>allegory</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλληγορούμενον (allēgoroumenon), meaning something treated as an allegory.</note> of another thing, unless it can be demonstrated to be such according to the rules of sacred <term>types</term> <note>A "type" is a person, place, or event in the Bible meant to foreshadow something in the future.</note> previously confirmed by us. I do not think the learned men will even attempt this in the present matter. Furthermore, even if a certain city or nation serves as a type in one place, it cannot be inferred that the same is also typical elsewhere. It is not permissible to explain everything told about Egypt, Babylon, or Tyre as symbolic, even in prophetic records. Nor, if the learned men want Ephesus to be symbolic in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, will they contend that it is also symbolic in the Acts of the Apostles or in Paul’s Epistle to them. Much less can it be inferred from a collection of similar examples that something is symbolic when that very point is what is being questioned.

<margin>
XCIX.
It cannot be proven by any example that the Churches of the New Testament were established by God as symbols for other Churches.
</margin>
XCIX. Moreover, the examples produced are not truly similar: thus, any appearance of probability that was previously believed to exist in this argument completely vanishes. For nothing is proved by them, except that certain cities or nations flourishing during the Economy <note>The "Economy" refers to God's specific way of managing or relating to humanity during a certain period of history.</note> of the Old Testament were types and emblems of those gatherings that were to come under the New Testament dispensation; or even, that things done on earth are types of heavenly things. But that any Churches of the New Testament, or their names, were given by God as symbols of other subsequent Churches, is proved neither by any authority nor by any suitable example.

### EXAMINATION OF THE ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE

...is beset by inconveniences. This the following observations will make clear.

<margin>
97. Just because the names of cities are sometimes symbolic does not mean they are so here. Compare Section 17.
</margin>
XCVII. Let us therefore bring each argument back to examination in the order in which they were proposed. We do not doubt that the names of ancient regions, cities, and nations are frequently symbolic in Sacred Scripture, and enigmatically signify other gatherings of people. But just because it is thought to happen sometimes, or happens elsewhere, it does not necessarily happen here too. Learned men will no more prove by this argument that Ephesus or Smyrna are symbolic names here, than they would for Rome, Corinth, Philippi, or Thessalonica in the Pauline Epistles. Nor is there reason for them to object that the nature of those Epistles—which are undoubtedly dogmatic <note>Focusing on teaching doctrine</note>—is one thing, while these, being inserted into a Prophetic book, are another and should therefore be explained according to the prophetic style. For not everything written in a prophetic book is therefore "prophetic" in nature, nor should it be considered symbolic any more than if it were narrated elsewhere. The history of Hezekiah <note>referring to Isaiah 36-39</note> in the prophet Isaiah is to be interpreted no less literally than in the books of Kings or Chronicles.

<margin>
98. Indeed, not even the same names that are symbolic in some places are so everywhere. Section 53 and following.
</margin>
XCVIII. It follows that nothing should be established as a symbol or <term>allegory <note>original: *ἀλληγορούμενον* (allegoroumenon) - something treated as an allegory or figure of speech</note></term> of another thing unless it can be demonstrated to be such, according to the rules of sacred <term>types <note>A "type" is a biblical person, place, or event that foreshadows a future reality</note></term> previously confirmed by us. I do not think learned men will even attempt this in the present matter. Furthermore, even if some city or nation acts as a type somewhere, it cannot be inferred that the same is also typical elsewhere. It is not right to interpret everything told about Egypt, Babylon, or Tyre typically, even in prophetic records. Nor, if learned men want Ephesus to be typical in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, will they contend that it is also typical in the Acts of the Apostles or Paul’s letter to them. Much less can it be inferred from a collection of similar examples that something—whose typical status is in question—is indeed typical.

<margin>
99. It can be proven by no example that the Churches of the New Testament were established by God as symbols for other churches.
</margin>
XCIX. But the examples produced are not even similar: thus every appearance of probability that was previously believed to reside in this argument completely vanishes. For nothing is proved by them except that certain cities or nations flourishing during the <term>Economy <note>The "Economy" refers to God's management or arrangement of human history</note></term> of the Old Testament were types and emblems of those gatherings which were to be under the New Testament dispensation, or even that things done on earth are types of heavenly things. But that some churches of the New Testament, or their names, were given by God as symbols of other subsequent churches is proved neither by any authority nor by any suitable example.

### BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>
100. It can be debated whether Isaiah 14:12, etc., should be understood as referring to the Roman Prelate <note>The Pope</note>. See section 18.
</margin>

C. The specimens that have been produced as examples show indeed how much liberty learned men allow themselves in the explanation of Prophecies; however, such interpretations are of a kind that they can hardly find an end for themselves, let alone provide a rule for other similar cases. If they can persuade the Catholics that in *Isaiah 14:12, 13, 14* the Roman Prelate <note>The Pope</note> is being described, I for my part shall certainly allow it; yet, along with the most excellent of our own scholars, I believe these things are to be understood primarily and literally as referring to the Babylonian **Nebuchadnezzar**.

<margin>
101. It is not likely that the Moabites in Isaiah 15 and 16 designate the Jews visited by Christ.
</margin>

CI. Moreover, I can by no means bring myself to believe that in *Isaiah 15 and 16*, the Moabites designate the *Jews visited by Christ*.
**I.** Because the Prophet, after he had set forth the heavy prophecies of the nations neighboring the Israelites in these and the following chapters—namely, the Moabites, Ethiopia, Egypt, Babylon, Edom, and Arabia—only then, in chapter 22, descends to the "valley of vision," and in chapter 28 to Ephraim, and in chapter 29 to Ariel <note>A symbolic name for Jerusalem</note>. He distinguishes the remaining nations clearly enough from the Israelites, unfolding for each their own distinct fates.
**II.** Because in chapter 16:1, the Moabites are expressly distinguished from the Israelites when they are commanded to *send the lamb to the Ruler of the land* (or *the lamb of the Ruler of the land*, which was his by every right) *to the mount of the daughter of Zion*. That is, they were to confess that they were tributaries to the house of David (referencing 2 Samuel 8:2) and to Hezekiah, the legitimate successor of David, now paying those lambs and wool-bearing rams which they had previously paid to the Kings of the ten tribes (2 Kings 3:4). A great part of these could also be used for sacrifices to Jehovah, for the purpose of their own atonement.
**III.** Because Jeremiah, prophesying in the same way about the *Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, Tyrians, and Sidonians*, is commanded to send thongs and bonds to the Kings of those nations through the messengers who were to come to Jerusalem to King Zedekiah (Jeremiah 27:3). This would be utterly contrary to all reason unless the things he predicted were actually going to happen to those very nations. Why send a yoke and a strap to the King of the Moabites if the Jews are designated by the "Moabites"? Does Jeremiah really mean the Moabites literally, while Isaiah means them symbolically? But what is the reason for such a difference, since one egg is not more like another <note>A Latin idiom meaning they are identical</note> than the prophecies of both concerning Moab? One need only compare Jeremiah chapter 48 with *Isaiah 15 and 16*. Will you say that this last Prophecy of Jeremiah is of a different kind than the one set forth in chapter 27? By what judgment do you distinguish it? For Jeremiah himself asserts that *all these prophecies* are **against the nations** <note>original Hebrew: על הגוים (*al ha-goyim*)</note> (Chapter 46:1—for this is the general inscription of all that follows) and he deals with those Moabites who are the people of Chemosh <note>The national god of the Moabites</note> (Chapter 48:13, 46). The Jews in the time of Christ were certainly most far removed from the worship of that Idol.
**IV.** Because the calamities predicted here also notably afflicted the Moabites, partly at the time...

### EXAMINATION OF THE ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE

<margin>
*Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 10, Chapter 11.
</margin>
...in the time of Shalmaneser <note>King of Assyria, 8th century BCE</note>, who, while conquering the Israelites, likewise defeated their neighbors the Moabites; and partly also in the time of Nebuchadnezzar <note>King of Babylon, 6th century BCE</note>, whom Josephus <note>A famous 1st-century Jewish historian</note>—a rich witness—records as having thoroughly subdued the Ammonites and Moabites in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem. However, to demand every single detail in the midst of such silence and lack of historical records would be the mark of a truly troublesome man. 

**V.** If the whole of the Moabites denotes the whole of the carnal Jews <note>A term used by early modern scholars to refer to Jews who followed the law literally but, in their view, lacked spiritual insight</note>, what will the individual cities signify, which both Isaiah and Jeremiah enumerate so at length? Was that lengthiness sought only for the sake of ornament? Or do the individual towns have certain Jewish cities corresponding to them for a specific reason? Learned men still owe us this labor, so that we might also understand which cities of the Israelites correspond to which cities of the Moabites, and in what manner.

<margin>
102. Nor is any reason brought forward that would persuade one of it.
</margin>
CII. It is added that no probable reason is assigned for why the *Jews* should be called *Moabites*. Is it because they overcame some cities of the Moabites in war and settled in them? But by the same logic, you would transform the Babylonians into Israelites, the Persians into Assyrians, the Greeks into Persians, and the Romans into Greeks, and you would call the former by the names of the latter, since they occupied not just a few cities, but entire kingdoms and regions. Is it because they were joined to the Moabites in religion? Certainly not by idolatry: they did not perform sacred rites to Chemosh <note>original: "Camoso"; the national god of the Moabites</note>, as did their ancestors, who nevertheless were never called Moabites for that reason. On the contrary, once the Moabites were subdued, they forced them to take up their own sacred rites: and since from that time the Moabites were counted among the Jews—"becoming Jews" <note>Hebrew: *mityahadim*</note>—it was more appropriate to give them the name of Jews than the reverse. But certainly they were joined in superstition, clinging to external worship without the true love of God. I might believe that. But the Jews did not first learn this from the Moabites. Rather, the Moabites learned from them, emulating their bad examples after they had been forced to "live like Jews" <note>Greek: *ioudaizein*</note>.

<margin>
103. Those things which are built upon such a flimsy foundation collapse by themselves.
</margin>
CIII. Therefore, since it cannot be proven that the Moabites are to be understood as the Jews visited by Christ, whatever is built upon such a ruinous foundation is nothing but difficult speculations <note>Greek: *meteoriai*, meaning lofty or unfounded theories</note>. Why should we transform **Jazer** and the vine of **Sibmah**, **Heshbon**, and **Elealeh** <note>Ancient Moabite cities mentioned in Isaiah 16</note> into Jerusalem, so that from the tears of the sorrowful Prophet we might squeeze out the tears of Christ weeping over Jerusalem? For even if God is introduced as the speaker in the preceding and following parts, nothing prevents the Prophet from sometimes speaking in his own person. Indeed, learned men themselves often warn that in Prophecies and Psalms there is sometimes a silent alternation of persons, and it must be judged based on what is said about the subjects. If you want a few words out of many from a Great Interpreter, here they are.

*And **dialogues** <note>original: διαλογισμοὶ (dialogismoi), referring to the interplay of different voices or thoughts</note> ought to be noticed in some places, since from time to time various characters are introduced as speaking, even when the transition in **personification** <note>original: prosopopæia, the literary device of representing an imaginary or absent person as speaking</note> is not explicitly marked. But is it not also much simpler to explain the "glory of Moab" as the wealth and pride of that people, rather than as the Temple of Jerusalem? Why do we labor in calculating the years of the Jewish war just to find a three-year period within them? For the Prophet is not describing how many years the slaughter would last, but rather designating the time when—counting from this prophetic calculation—that slaughter would happen to the Moabites. For this is how the words sound:* "But now the Lord speaks, saying: Within three years, as the years of a **hired worker** <note>original: mercenarii; an idiom for a strictly measured, exact period of time</note>—who is accustomed to measuring the time of his labor exactly—the glory of Moab shall be brought into contempt." In the fourth year of Hezekiah, Shalmaneser <note>King of Assyria</note> marched against Samaria (2 Kings 18:9), at which time he seems to have occupied the cities of the Moabites, so as not to leave anything behind him that might be harmful to himself or his troops. How much better are these explanations than those modern commentaries?

...is veiled to them. And indeed, nothing stands in the way of this being understood as referring to Tyre properly so-called, according to the literal sense. A most learned man <note>likely referring to a contemporary commentator such as Vitringa or a similar scholar</note> collected a brief history of that city up to our own times in his commentaries on Ezekiel 26. From this, it is clear that it was laid waste several times and rebuilt several times; and as *Curtius* <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian who chronicled the deeds of Alexander the Great</note> says, it has fulfilled many fates and was reborn after its destruction. Today, however, as the *Travelogues* <note>original: Itineraria; referring to the accounts of early modern travelers to the Levant</note> testify by consensus, it is nothing but a heap of ruins with some fishermen's huts; there is no house left that is intact, except for one. The remaining houses are destroyed, and nothing survives except for arches and crypts, in which nearly two hundred people dwell.

CV. Kittim is not Spain, nor was Charles V devastated in Spain.

CV. But let us not add another word about the translation. By what appearance can those things which are either imagined or said be applied to Charles V? <note>Charles V (1500–1558) was the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain during the Reformation.</note> He did not come from the land of *Kittim*: for whether that is *Cilicia*, or *Macedonia*, or *Italy* (on which matter *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant scholar of biblical geography</note> may be consulted), certainly no one, I think, has said until now, and no one believed, that it was *Spain*. Nor was *Charles* devastated in *Spain*; rather, having briefly subdued the rebels, he held the kingdom in a state of peace. And he hardly ever managed his affairs more vigorously or successfully than while he was in *Spain*. At that time—by a rare sign of heavenly favor inclining toward Charles—*Hadrian* his tutor was elected Pope <note>Pope Hadrian VI, the only Dutch pope, who had been Charles's tutor</note>: than which, in the judgment of *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou, a famous French historian and statesman</note>, nothing more fortunate or desirable could have happened to the *Emperor*. Not much later, in the year 1525, on the 10th day before the Kalends of February—which was the *Emperor’s* birthday—he held *Francis I*, the King of France, captive after defeating him at *Pavia* <note>original: Ticinum, the Roman name for Pavia, where a decisive battle occurred in the Italian Wars</note>. Is this what it means to be "devastated in Spain"?

The *Emperor*, though he feigned sorrow, was rejoicing in his heart, and was seriously deliberating about taking the Pope away to *Spain*; he did not release him until six full months had passed, and then only on the condition that he would not oppose the *Emperor* in the affairs of *Milan* or *Naples*, but rather grant him some ecclesiastical revenues. A fine "stronghold of Tyre" indeed! ### BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

Through the expedition of Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566), the Ottoman Sultan whose expansions into Europe posed a constant threat to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, who captured Timișoara, Lipova, Szolnok, and other fortresses, the Emperor was devastated, yet he remained nonetheless the most powerful Prince in Europe. CVII. Furthermore, it is quite strange that the time when Tyre began to be consigned to oblivion is precisely pushed back to the year 1552. This is supposedly because the *Peace of Passau* <note>original: "transactio Passaviensis"; a treaty signed in 1552 that provided a foundation for the legal coexistence of Lutheranism and Catholicism in Germany.</note> took place then, which learned men think they must mention very frequently in their commentaries. Meanwhile, all shall maintain peace, and no one shall be harassed because of religion. Whatever shall be decreed by the common counsel of the estates concerning the method of pacifying religion, with the Emperor’s authority intervening—specifically, that the disagreement be settled by peaceful, pious, and fair means—that shall be firm and ratified.*

Universal History, p. 70.

Is this Peace (praised indeed, as Boxhornius <note>Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a Dutch scholar and historian.</note> says, but not sufficiently observed) of such great importance that you would establish the era of "forgotten Tyre" upon it? I am inclined to add here what the most learned Leipzig scholars <note>The editors of the *Acta Eruditorum*, the first scientific journal of the German lands.</note> noted regarding the historical errors <note>original: "ἀνιστορησίαν" (anhistoresian); a Greek term meaning a lack of historical knowledge.</note> of Varillas <note>Antoine Varillas (1624–1696), a French historian notorious for his inaccuracies.</note>, in the *Acts of the Year 1688*, page 497. They say: "Certainly, something was agreed upon then (at Passau) regarding religious business; but in a very brief style, with the explanation deferred to the calling of a Diet; and the *right of autonomy in sacred matters* <note>original: "jus autonomiæ circa sacra"</note> which the Protestants obtained rests not only on that pacification, but most especially on the decree of the *Diet of Augsburg in the year 1555*." 
> *This is what is also primarily cited by the Protestants whenever it is necessary. Anyone who compares that decree (or what they call the Recess of Augsburg) with the formula of the Passau convention in matters regarding religion, will find it five times longer and more laborious, not only in words but in substance. This is especially because at Passau (as we have said) most things were deferred to Diets, or even to Colloquies and Councils; but at Augsburg everything was handled and defined more broadly and accurately. And while the previous negotiations granted nothing but truces for a time, or until the decisions of a Council, now for the first time it was publicly agreed and guaranteed that, even if harmony in religion could not be reached through colloquies or Councils, eternal liberty and peace of Religion would be preserved in Germany.*

From these things it is clear that the Peace of Passau is not to be made as significant as the Most Learned Interpreter <note>The author is likely refuting a specific commentator who linked the fall of Tyre to the year 1552.</note> usually estimates it—likely because he notices that doing so serves his own arguments. And if any decree whatsoever concerning religious liberty were sufficient to establish this era, it...

<margin>
108. It is asserted awkwardly that the Pope is the roof of the Church, and is called Gog for that reason. See paragraph XVI.

CVIII. The things that follow regarding Gog and Magog <note>Ezekiel 38-39 mentions Gog of the land of Magog; here, the author is debunking a symbolic interpretation of these names.</note> have "neither a roof in heaven," as they say, "nor a foundation on earth" <note>A proverbial expression meaning the argument has no basis in reality.</note>. For besides the fact that "roof" in Hebrew is never called **Gog**, but always *Gag* <note>original: "Gag"; the author is correcting a linguistic error where his opponent confused the name Gog with the Hebrew word for roof.</note>, and likewise **Magog** nowhere denotes "that which is covered," these meanings of the words are invented and proven by no authority. Furthermore, what is more awkward than for the Roman Pope to be called a "roof" because he interposes himself between God and men, blocking the influx of celestial rays and the descent of fertile rain from the earth thus covered—that is, from the assembly of men believing in him? Is this the use of a roof? Did any mortal ever, or anywhere, build a roof for the purpose of precluding a free view of the sky for himself, or to keep rain away from that part of the earth which ought to be fertilized by showers? Is it not rather so that he might have a refuge from rains, shade from heat, a retreat from winds, and a protection against all injuries of the air? By what elegance of emblem shall someone be compared to a roof because of something that happens to it—contrary to the roof's intended use—from that inconvenience which accompanies all human comforts?

<margin>114. Those things which belong to the Universal Church are rightly attributed to particular ones, in their own part. Section 25.</margin>
114. In the *Fourth Argument*, many points are heaped together, though neither individually nor combined do they offer any proof. <margin>115. It is uncertain whether the seven lamps of the Mosaic Lampstand designated seven periods of the New Testament Church.</margin>
115. I would not deny that John’s vision alludes to the golden lampstand of the Mosaic Tabernacle <term>Mosaic Tabernacle: The portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites, described in the Book of Exodus.</term>. However, I do not think it is so certain that its seven lamps designated seven distinct *periods* of the New Testament Church. Why shouldn't the number seven—which in Scripture is a symbol of completion—signify that abundant, perfect, and sufficient light which is granted to the Church through the influence of the Spirit, like a celestial oil, given most bountifully <note>original: "ἀφθόνως" (aphthonos) — plentifully or without envy.</note>? Every particular Church can also be called a lampstand. For it must be carefully noted here that John did not see *one* lampstand equipped with seven lamps; rather, he saw seven *complete* lampstands, each of which likely had more than one lamp.

<margin>116. Nor is it unbecoming for Christ the King, when the matter requires it, to be named after some part of His Kingdom.</margin>
116. The glory of the Lord Jesus is not diminished by the fact that He displays the seven Churches of Asia on His insignia, or that He is said to walk in their midst, since He is the Lord of all. For He who is Lord of all is, by that very fact, Lord of these as well. He demonstrates elsewhere that He is the Lord of all things, bearing this name inscribed on His thigh: *King of Kings, and Lord of Lords.* Because He had now set His mind to specifically remind these particular Churches of their duty, He wished to be identified by them here. This is no less fitting for the Majesty of Christ than the fact that He is elsewhere named after specific individuals.

117. This is because He had so adorned those seven Churches with His gifts, and governed them so solicitously by His providence, as if each individual church had a Spirit peculiar to itself; so much did that one Spirit suffice for all...

If the number seven is frequently Sacred and Symbolic, must it therefore *always* be so, and thus here as well? Was it a mystical thing that Laban pursued Jacob with a *seven-day journey*? (Genesis 31:23). Or that Jethro had *seven daughters*? (Exodus 2:16). Or that the *Israelites served the Midianites for seven years*? (Judges 6:1). Or that *Jephthah led Israel for the same number of years*? (Judges 12:9). Or that *seven days* were given for Samson’s wedding? (Judges 14:12). Or that the men of Jabesh asked for *seven days* for themselves to deliberate? (1 Samuel 11:3). Who does not see that in these and similar cases, the number seven is to be understood simply, without any connotation of symbol or mystery? Why not here too? Where seven local Churches are described, each with its own name, in order, and according to the actual location they occupy.

### EXAMINATION OF ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE

...understand what the most wise of the interpreters have understood concerning God? But let us grant that these are the "eyes" of the Church; and let us not object to the idea that the Church is distinguished by seven periods. But does every period have its own peculiar "eye"? Does not the whole Church look upon Christ with that same single eye of faith—a faith, I say, that does not vary according to the variation of periods? How much better, therefore, would it be to interpret these things as the diligent effort of the whole Church looking toward Christ with all the intensity of its faith? In this view, the number seven serves as a symbol for fullness and perfection. More on this soon.

<margin>
122.
What the seven steps of the temple signified enigmatically, and whether it is more modest to remain ignorant of something than to define it.
</margin>
**122.** Is it really so certain that the *seven steps to the temple gates* signified seven periods of afflictions that must be overcome before the glorious temple of the Lord is seen, that learned men must use this as an argument for their demonstration? What if someone does not feel like believing this based on their mere word? What if they demand proof for this assertion? What proof, I ask, will they give? They ask indeed: what else could they have prefigured? What if I answer that I do not know what that number prefigured; indeed, I do not even know if it prefigured anything at all. Is it necessary for us to establish that whatever was in the temple was *significant* <note>original: "σημαντικὸν" — meaning-bearing or symbolic</note> even down to the smallest details which the *precision* <note>original: "ἀκρίβεια" — technical exactness</note> of the architectural art required, and which were employed for the ornament of the building? Can these most learned men tell us what the five-fold arrangement of curtains in the Mosaic tabernacle meant, or the fifty blue loops and the golden clasps by which those curtains were joined? Or if they do say something, can they prove it? Just as in parables some things are sprinkled in for the beauty of the speech so that the narration of the story may seem more lifelike—in which it would be a task of superfluous and useless diligence to search for individual mysteries—so too it seems we must think about the form of the tabernacle and the temple. Regarding the steps of temples, <margin>On Roman Magistrates, Book II, Ch. V.</margin> *Lipsius* <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a famous Flemish humanist and scholar who wrote extensively on Roman history and antiquities.</note> noted that they pertained to majesty and were therefore commonly used in Roman sacred buildings; in such a way that after every set of SEVEN or nine steps, small platforms were placed where the weary might plant their feet and catch their breath. Is it not enough to say generally that those steps signify that the faithful are lifted on high by various divine gifts to behold God more closely? Then what is the meaning of the number EIGHT for the steps to the inner court? Ezekiel 40:31. It is amazing how much the most learned interpreter sweats over this. First, he advises that each of the faithful has especially *eight* things in which to exercise themselves so they do not appear unfruitful. 2 Peter 1:5, 6, 7. What Peter calls *support* <note>original: "ἐπιχορηγίαν" — the act of providing or supplying; in this context, the "adding" of virtues to one another</note> fits beautifully with the emblem of the steps. For just as the second virtue proceeds from faith, and the third from the second, *so step stands upon and clings to step, and from the first to the second* [ascent...]

Does not the whole Church look upon Christ with the same eye of one faith—a faith, I say, that does not vary according to the variation of the periods? How much better would it be to interpret these things as the intensity of the entire Church’s faith as it busily gazes upon Christ? In this view, the number seven serves as a symbol of fullness and perfection. More on this shortly.

<margin>
122. What the seven steps of the temple signified enigmatically, and whether it is more modest to remain ignorant of something than to define it.
</margin>

**122.** Is it even so certain that the seven steps at the gates of the temple signified seven periods of afflictions which must be overcome before the glorious temple of the Lord is seen, that learned men must use this as a core argument for their demonstration? What if someone does not wish to believe this based on their mere word? What if one demands proof for this assertion? What proof, I ask, will they give? They ask indeed, "what else could it have prefigured?" What if I respond that I do not know what that number prefigured—indeed, I do not even know if it prefigured anything at all. Is it necessary for us to determine that everything in the temple was symbolic <note>original: σημαντικὸν (*sēmantikon*)</note>, even down to the smallest details which the precision <note>original: ἀκρίβεια (*akribeia*)</note> of the architectural art required, and which were employed for the decoration of the building? Could these most learned men tell us what the number five meant for the curtains in the Mosaic tabernacle, or the fifty violet loops and golden clasps by which those curtains were joined? Or if they say something, can they prove it? Just as in parables some details are scattered for the sake of the narrative's beauty, so that the historical account might seem more realistic—details in which hunting for individual mysteries would be a task of superfluous and useless diligence—so too should we think about the form of the tabernacle and the temple.

<margin>
From *Roman Antiquities*, Book II, Chapter V.
</margin>

Concerning the steps of temples, *Lipsius* <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous humanist scholar who wrote extensively on Roman history and architecture.</note> noted that they pertain to "Majesty," and therefore were commonly used in the sacred buildings of the Romans; specifically in such a way that after every sequence of **SEVEN** or nine steps, small level areas were placed where the weary might plant their feet and catch their breath. Is it not enough to say generally that by those steps it is signified that the faithful are raised on high by various divine gifts to see God more closely? Then what does the **EIGHT**-fold number of steps mean for the inner court? (Ezekiel 40:31). It is amazing how much the most learned interpreter sweats over this. First, he advises that "each of the faithful has eight things in particular in which they should exercise themselves, so that they do not appear unfruitful" (2 Peter 1:5, 6, 7). What Peter calls "supplementing" <note>original: ἐπιχορηγίαν (*epichorēgian*); referring to the "adding" of virtues to faith in the biblical text.</note> fits beautifully with the emblem of the steps. For, just as the second follows from faith, and the third from the second, so step stands upon and clings to step, and from the first to the second...

# BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

...the ascent is easy. When he had finished discussing these matters, since it happened conveniently that Peter <note>The author likely refers to a contemporary commentator, possibly Petrus van Mastricht or a similar theologian who attempted to harmonize these symbols.</note> enumerates eight virtues, he soon subjoins—as if not quite satisfied with himself: *I consider it worth investigating in the meantime whether the eight steps might also signify periods of time in relation to the universal Church.* Thus one might wonder whether a single step should be added to the previous seven (which seem to be attained by those entering the outer court), or whether seven new periods of time, distinguished by a variety of notable events, should be understood here. "However," I say, "if the steps mark periods of time, and those periods are only seven in number, whose is this *eighth* step? Whether it is believed to be in its proper place here, or counted among the previous seven, it spoils that sacred and holy number seven either here or there. Furthermore, if those steps signify eight virtues, I truly do not understand how the same steps can signify seven periods of time. If some mystery lies hidden in the number, I prefer to profess ignorance of it, rather than risk my reputation for modesty by boldly prophesying <note>original: *hariolando* — literally 'acting like a soothsayer' or guessing wildly</note> and dictating many things that are inconsistent with one another."

<margin>
Book III. Chapter XXVI.
</margin>
There exists in Maimonides’ *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *Doctor Perplexorum* — the famous 12th-century philosophical work by the Jewish scholar Maimonides.</note> an excellent chapter where he argues that while all Mosaic precepts indeed have a cause and a goal, these cannot always be explained in every specific detail. *So,* he says, *if someone asks why there must be seven lambs in the offering and not eight? The same could be asked if there had been eight, or ten, or twenty. You, therefore, should hold this and impress it upon your mind: that when our sages say everywhere that all precepts have their causes, and that Solomon likewise knew the causes of all the precepts, this must be understood as referring to the use or goal of the precepts* GENERALLY, *but not to* EVERY INDIVIDUAL PART AND CIRCUMSTANCE.

<margin>
123. The number seven is sometimes used for an uncertain, yet large and full [amount].
</margin>
**123.** But why are these most fair-minded men so angry with us because we believe the number seven is sometimes used for an uncertain, yet large and full amount? This is not arrogance, but modesty. Is some specific number designated when *the Lord threatens that He will add sevenfold to their punishment?* Leviticus 26:18. Or when it is said *the righteous man falls seven times?* Proverbs 24:16. Or that *seven abominations are in the heart of the wicked?* Proverbs 26:25. Or that *repayment must be made sevenfold to neighbors?* Psalm 79:12. Or that *the light of the sun will be seven times greater?* Isaiah 30:26. Or that *seven women shall take hold of one man?* Isaiah 4:1. Unwisely, I had added Psalm 12:6 <note>original: Psalm 12:2; numbering differs in the Latin Vulgate</note>, where the word of God is compared to silver melted in an iron furnace, *poured out seven times.* But since I see learned men <note>Referencing the Cocceian school of interpreters who sought seven distinct historical periods in every biblical mention of the number seven.</note> find their seven periods in that place as well, I am deleting and striking it out. There are enough examples in the preceding verses. If anyone desires more, I will give many: for they are like dust <note>original: ὡσεὶ κόνις (*hōsei konis*)</note>.

### EXAMINATION OF ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE

<margin>
124. Finally, the question is not what the number seven signifies elsewhere, but what it signifies here.
</margin>

CXXIV. Furthermore, even if we were to grant our brothers <note>The "Brothers" likely refers to the Cocceian school of theologians who saw the history of the Church reflected in every detail of the Apocalypse.</note> that the seven pillars, the seven eyes, and the seven steps of the temple pre-signified seven periods of time; what gain would they find for the present controversy? Is this consequence correctly deduced from that premise: "Therefore the seven Apostolic Letters are Prophetic, and they set out those seven periods in order"? What is the link between the conclusion and the premise? What logic governs the sequence? Who would not marvel at such great confidence in such a weak <note>original: *elumba* — literally "lame" or "weak-loined," suggesting an argument that lacks structural strength</note> line of reasoning?

<margin>
125. When and in what manner the Holy Spirit teaches through proper names.
</margin>

CXXV. The sixth argument, derived from the names of the cities, reeks of Jewish Cabbala <note>Cabbala refers to a tradition of Jewish mysticism that seeks hidden meanings in the letters and sounds of names. The author uses it here pejoratively to suggest the interpretation is more superstitious than scholarly.</note>, and contains nothing solid. It is not that we deny that the Holy Spirit sometimes teaches through proper names; rather, we believe this occurs only in those names which were first given to things by the command of the Holy Spirit, or were subsequently changed by Him, or at least whose symbolic teaching the Holy Spirit himself has indicated in the Scriptures. For we recognize no other teaching of the Spirit now besides that which has been declared in the sacred monuments of the Scriptures. Indeed, all those examples brought forward by learned men are of this sort. But for us to root around <note>original: *ruspemur* — to search diligently or scratch about</note> by our own wit for the etymologies of Gentile cities, and to refer them to the condition of the Christian Church by a kind of metaphorical leap—without any authority of Divine testimony—and then to hawk the thoughts of our own brains as the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, seems to me a reckless and audacious deed. It is certainly well-established that those who first gave these names to the cities of Asia had nothing less in mind than that the periods of the Christian Church should be symbolically designated by those names. Nor is it established that God, beyond the intention of the original namers, used those words for mystical meanings. But if they assert it is established, let them produce even one testimony from God to which we must yield.

<margin>
126. Concerning what is said about the Etymologies of the Cities of Asia.
</margin>

CXXVI. Many of the things that learned men assume regarding the etymologies <note>The study of the origins and historical development of words.</note> of these names are uncertain or even empty. To say that *Ephesus* is so named as if it were *aphesis* <note>original Greek: *ἄφεσιν* — meaning "letting go," "release," or "remission."</note> because of a "remission" or cooling of love, is a bit more than ridiculous; I could wish that such a thing had not slipped from a theologian who is otherwise quite serious. *Smyrna* was not named after "myrrh," but, as the ancients record, from the *Amazon Smyrna* who occupied Ephesus; or as others prefer, from *Smyrna, the wife of Theseus the Thessalian*, in memory of whom it is said to have been founded by him. More than one origin is handed down for *Pergamum*. Some want it so named because it was situated on a cliff, for higher places are called *Pergama*; others, because honorable marriages were almost entirely abolished there, "from the passing away of marriages" <note>original Greek: *ὑπὸ τὸ περᾶν τὰς γάμους* — a linguistic pun connecting the city name to the Greek words for "beyond" and "marriage."</note>; some because *parchment* <note>original: *Pergamena*</note> first began to be manufactured there. Yet it is more probable that *parchment* is named after *Pergamum*, than the other way around. *Pliny and Strabo* say of *Thyatira*...

### BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

They say that **Thyatira** <note>A city in modern-day Turkey, one of the seven churches of Revelation.</note> was named by Seleucus, the son of Nicanor, because of the news brought to him of the birth of a daughter. Others tell that when the Mysians asked an oracle about founding a city, the response was to build it where a struck and running stag should appear; therefore it was called Thyatira, from the phrase "the sacrificing and the running of the stag." <note>original: διὰ τὸ θύειν καὶ τροχάζειν τὸν ἔλαφον (*dia to thuein kai trochazein ton elaphon*)</note> As for the name of **Sardis**, some refer it to the Hebrew words *Sered* or *Sarid*, which signify a Prince, a Ruler, or a Survivor. If anyone wishes to call this the "elegant play of an ingenious man," they are free to do so by my leave—provided they admit it is indeed a game, and one I find hardly appropriate in Divine matters. **Philadelphia**, the city discussed here, received its name from its founder, King Attalus Philadelphus. **Laodicea**, as we have said, was named after Laodice, the wife of Antiochus. What do these historical origins have in common with the "mysteries" which some people, without any sacred authority, carve out of them?

<margin>127. *Grotius's thoughts on these names.*</margin>
CXXVII. If anyone is not weary of wasting their leisure and talent, they could manufacture other meanings from those names in a cabbalistic fashion <note>The author uses "cabbalistic" to describe the practice of seeking hidden, mystical meanings in the letters or sounds of words, a practice he views with skepticism.</note> that are no less pleasing. Indeed, the thoughts of **Hugo Grotius** <note>A famous Dutch jurist and theologian (1583–1645) known for his rational approach to scripture.</note> seem more ingenious to me; he arranged them in this way: All these names beautifully remind Christians of their duty. **Ephesus** warns that they ought to be kindled with a desire for eternal things, for *ephesis* means "desire." **Smyrna** suggests they should be incorrupt, just as *myrrh* is. **Pergamum** suggests they should think on sublime things; for according to the scholars Hesychius, Suidas, and Servius (in his notes on the *Aeneid*), all high places were called *Pergama* by the people of Asia. **Thyatira** comes from "sacrificing the untamed," <note>original: θύειν ἀτειρέα (*thuein ateirea*)</note> meaning to kill one's untamed passions in honor of God. **Sardis** means to keep the precepts of Christ well-impressed upon the soul, just as the *Sarda* <note>The sardius or carnelian gemstone, which was commonly used for engraving seals.</note> gemstone takes a seal-impression better than all other gems. **Philadelphia** points toward brotherly love, and **Laodicea** toward demonstrating justice to all people. Thus far Grotius. However, these ideas and others of that kind, however much they may delight, prove nothing.

In verses 27 and 33, it says that *Ararat, Menni, and Ashkenaz* <note>Ancient kingdoms mentioned in the Bible; here Gerhard uses creative etymology to link them to Martin Luther's biography.</note> shall crush Babylon. Now, *Menni* and *Ashkenaz* were "metal-workers," as is clear from history and the Hebrew language. Therefore, it denotes **Luther**, the son of a metal-worker <note>Martin Luther’s father, Hans Luder, was a copper miner and smelter.</note> from Eisleben, born in the County of Mansfeld, which is said to derive its name from *Menni*. He, with the hammer of the Word, [breaks] the spiritual Baby-

We shall present only a specimen of the first verse: *To the chief musician* <note>Hebrew: למנצח (*lamnatzeach*)</note>, *For the sons of Korah* <note>Hebrew: לבני קרח (*filiis Core*)</note>, *upon the mysteries: a song* <note>Hebrew: על עלמות (*al alamot*)</note>. The word **KORAH** <note>original: *CORE*</note> is a proper name meaning **BALD**, or **CALVIN** <note>The author is highlighting a linguistic pun: the Hebrew *Korah* means "bald," the Latin for "bald" is *Calvus*, which is the root of the name *Calvin*. And as for what follows—it is wearying to pursue the rest. Who does not exclaim, how great it is to be wise! Bravo! Splendid! *Wisely!* <note>Greek: *Σοφῶς!* (*Sophōs!*)</note> Nothing could be higher!

<margin>129. What other qualities of these cities are observed.</margin>
CXXIX. But indeed, these learned men do not stop at the bare shell of names; they observe other qualities of the cities in which a notable similarity is found with the Church of that specific period, to which the city typically corresponds. Thus, **Ephesus**, once terribly shameful, represents the excellently converted Gentiles. **Pergamum**, located on a high rock, represents the Church in a dominant city, which boasts of its origin from Troy, and thus from Pergamum <note>Pergamum was often associated with Trojan ancestry in classical mythology.</note>. CXXX. However, many things can be opposed to these observations. I. ### BOOK III. CHAPTER IV.

...is not solid. When we have learned a mystery from the words testifying to that mystery, that ought to be enough. Once that has been demonstrated, it is of little help to either faith or understanding to manufacture figures and allegories from historical accounts based on some slight similarity. Those who are devoted to such things make themselves suspect, as if they lacked solid proofs. Truly, this was spoken prudently and piously! If only people had religiously remained within these boundaries!

III. All those similarities are silent as far as the Spirit is concerned in the Scriptures, and they cannot be learned from anywhere except secular histories; consequently, they rely on nothing but human testimony. I do not know how it can be proven that the Spirit of God intended to teach mysteries through things that are not handed down in the Scriptures, or that it is necessary for the faithful to unroll foreign histories—and those sometimes of fleeting reliability—in order to attain knowledge of them.

<margin>On Psalm 42, § 2.</margin>
Let us hear again the warning of Johannes Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who developed "Federal Theology," but here he is cited as a voice of caution against excessive allegory.</note> which he offers on a similar occasion. *I know that for those who delight in allegories, there is material ready for playing here. But, by my advice, anyone will be content with explaining the metaphors and similarities of Scripture, and will abstain from fashioning new ones while he explains the Scriptures.* Add another remark by the same author, especially worthy of note here.

<margin>On Isaiah 6, § 15.</margin>
The most certain <term>hermeneutic</term> <note>original: ἑρμηνευτικὴ (*hermeneutike*); the art or science of interpretation, especially of the Bible.</note> rule for hieroglyphs, emblems, or riddles is this: *the signs and emblems of Scripture signify through the total analogy they have with the sacred things which Scripture and history according to Scripture exhibit.* THEREFORE, IN THE APPLICATION OF THESE EMBLEMS, ONE MUST NOT THINK OF OTHER THINGS THAN THOSE WHICH SCRIPTURE TREATS: and *those things ought to be understood under them which have an analogy in all their parts with all the parts of the emblem; moreover, that analogy is both clear in the things themselves and is also recognized by the metaphors and parables of the Scriptures.*

IV. It is supposed that certain periods of the Church correspond to individual cities, and with that supposed, certain similarities are sought: however, that ought not to have been supposed, since it is the <term>point in dispute</term> <note>original: τὸ ἀμφισβητήμενον (*to amphisbetemenon*); the very thing that remains to be proven.</note>.

<margin>CXXXI. Many parallelisms can be imagined, perhaps no less clever, but lacking solidity.</margin>
CXXXI. If anyone wishes to indulge his own genius, it will be easy for him to devise many similarities of that kind at his pleasure; yet not even the most impudent person would assert that these were given by God as a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament or history believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament or the future.</note>. -># EXAMINATION OF ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE<-

...the blind are an object of contempt, yet they are sweet to God and the Angels in the songs of Israel. Because Pergamum was situated on a rock, and was given to the Romans by the will of King Attalus, and because parchment <note>The word "parchment" (Latin: *membranæ*) is historically derived from the name Pergamum, where it was perfected.</note> was discovered there which they used to use for writing, and finally because Galen—the most celebrated of physicians after the old man of Cos <note>The "old man of Cos" is Hippocrates, the father of medicine.</note>—was born there: it might as well be said that the Church is represented there, which calls itself a city set on a hill, whose Prince is the Roman High Priest <note>A reference to the Pope, often called the *Antistes Romanus* in this period.</note>, who possesses entire provinces by the donation of Emperors; a Church which boasts of the multitude and antiquity of its parchments and published books; and which, finally, though spiritually sick, was not destitute of skilled Physicians, if only she had wished to employ their hands. Because Laodicea, as Strabo testifies, had land that was **abundant in wine** <term>πολύοινον</term> <note>Greek: polyoinon</note>, it might be said that the Church is figured there—first indeed overwhelmed by the drunkenness of a secure lethargy, but then to be abundantly watered by the sweetest liquid of the mystical spirit. And because (as found in *Stephanus of Byzantium*) it was once called *Ramitho*, a word, as it seems, derived from the Syriac <term>רמתה</term> **Ramatha**, which denotes **high** <note>original Syriac: *Ramatha*, meaning "heights" or "exalted"</note>, or because a certain shepherd struck by lightning in those fields supposedly exclaimed **Ramanthas** <term>רם אתה</term>, **You are exalted** <note>original Hebrew: *Ram athas*</note>: we might call this a prelude to the Church being raised to the summit of spiritual happiness on earth, whose shepherds, seized with awe and surrounded by heavenly light, are to cry out to God, *Truly You are the Most High*. Once one has entered upon this path, what end will there be to such clever subtleties? To these things, indeed, I have thus far lent my mind and pen not without a certain shuddering of a trembling heart.

<margin>132. It is in vain to claim an agreement between historical events in the Church and the words of the Epistles.</margin>
CXXXII. In their seventh argument, these most learned men compare the events that have occurred in the Church over the passing centuries with these Epistles, inferring from the agreement of both that the things which happened were already figured before as prophecies in those words. They argue it is entirely impossible for such an exact agreement of facts and words to be found unless it was the intention of the Holy Spirit. But, if I may say so with all due respect to them, nothing is brought forward by them that is exact or consistent with the reckoning of time. They confuse their own periods at will; they transfer what belongs to the first period into the second and vice versa; they twist words into foreign meanings against all ancient usage; they coin new significations for terms; things that are distinguished by an entire decade of centuries they compress not just into one period, but into a single section of a period. The patience of God toward **Jezebel** <note>Jezebel in Revelation 2:20 is often interpreted by these scholars as a symbol of heresy or a specific historical figure.</note>, by which He gave her time for repentance, they place seven or eight years later than the burial of that same Jezebel; and they pile up many more absurdities, which we shall soon demonstrate at greater length. It is far from the case that the things they have scraped together from histories—often with little judgment—match the words of the Epistles with any precision. <margin>133. Not all Prophecies can be demonstrated from Histories. See §. 46. 47.</margin>
CXXXIII. The eighth argument has two parts: first, it contends that these letters contain certain things that cannot be demonstrated from history to have happened in the Churches of Asia; second, it asserts somewhat more boldly that some things are mentioned which can be demonstrated *not* to have happened. I respond to the first part. There are many Prophecies whose fulfillment in the Church can only be shown from the Prophecies themselves, due to the lack of historical records from those times. Out of many, I will bring forward a few examples. Joel, in chapters 1 and 2, describes a massive desolation caused by caterpillars, locusts, beetles, and cockchafers. Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian known for his historical-critical approach to the Bible.</note>, since he could not find a history of such a devastation in the lands of Israel or Judah, explained it enigmatically as referring to *Pul, Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, and Sennacherib* <note>These were all Assyrian kings who invaded Israel.</note>; others, moved by the same reasoning, understand them to be the *Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, and Romans*. This displeases the most celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who emphasized the "covenants" of the Bible and often disagreed with Grotius's more secular historical interpretations.</note>, who thinks the simplicity of the literal letter should be followed; and rightly so. Yet neither he, nor anyone else, can show from history when these things happened in Judah, or even if they happened at all. He does indeed compare them with the drought mentioned in Jeremiah 14:1–6. But besides the fact that he himself admits it is entirely uncertain what time Joel lived, Jeremiah describes a drought, but makes no mention of devastating insects. Add to this that the drought Jeremiah describes was not so great that it matched what is predicted of this plague in Joel 1:2—that nothing like it or nearly like it had ever existed before in the times of their ancestors. For it is not believable that it was as long-lasting or as parched as in the age of Elijah. Finally, the history of this drought, as far as I know, cannot be sought from anywhere other than Jeremiah. Cornelius a Lapide <note>A prominent Jesuit Bible commentator (1567–1637) known for his encyclopedic knowledge of previous commentaries.</note> says it well:

<margin>On Joel 1:4.</margin>
> *The Prophets threaten many things, all of which we believe truly happened, even if they are not narrated elsewhere.*

Similarly, in Amos 4:7, the Lord cries out to the ten tribes: *And I also withheld the rain from you when there were yet three months to the harvest; and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city.* But what history mentions this? For the most celebrated Interpreter <note>Likely referring to Cocceius again.</note> himself warns that this cannot be referred to that great drought <term>ἀομβρίαν</term> <note>Greek: aombrian, meaning "lack of rain."</note> of Elijah. Where also is the history of the *famine* found which Isaiah predicts in Chapter 9:19? Where is the History of the *pestilences* and *earthquakes* in Judea which the Lord prophesied would precede the destruction of Jerusalem in Matthew 24:7? Would it not be bold and rash for someone to demand that all these things be explained symbolically <note>original: "symbolice"</note> because of the silence or ignorance of history? Modestly indeed, the great Interpreter wrote elsewhere:

<margin>In Daniel 5, § 2.</margin>
> *We are forced to be ignorant of many things from a prior age; if we are calmly ignorant of them, and for that reason do not fight with anyone, we shall perhaps be no more foolish; so many good things surpass...*

### EXAMINATION OF ARGUMENTS FOR THE PROPHETIC SENSE.

...learn what we are able to know, etc. Let this be applied to our present purpose: and add that there are very few things of which there is not at least some mention in historical accounts; those things enumerated in this argument can hardly be referred to as <term>hidden things <note>original: "äδηλα" (adēla) — referring to things that are obscure, non-manifest, or not recorded in history</note></term>, as we have shown above. <margin>§. 69. & following.</margin> Regarding the latter point, I say that while it is asserted confidently, we have clearly demonstrated the opposite in the preceding sections, where we resolved all the difficulties that were raised. <margin>134. The opinion of the Ancient Theologians on this matter. See § 49.</margin>
CXXXIV. Those Interpreters who are cited in support of this cause for the *ninth argument* are either Ancients or more Modern. Neither group says what these learned men—with whom we are engaged in this dispute—claim: namely, that by the intention of the Holy Spirit, the words of these letters properly and literally describe not what was happening in the Churches of Asia in John's time, but what was to happen in the universal Church across seven successive periods of time. It is not evident that such an idea even entered the mind of any of the ancients. Rather, *Augustine*, *Bede*, *Aretas* <note>Aretas of Caesarea (c. 860–935) was a bishop and significant commentator on the Apocalypse</note>, and all the others, when they said that by these seven Churches the "entire Church" is written to (because the "totality" is usually designated by the number seven), they meant nothing else than what has been judiciously observed by *Ribera* <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a Jesuit scholar</note> and *Gomarus* <note>Franciscus Gomarus (1563–1641), a famous Dutch Reformed theologian</note>: that those things said to these seven Churches can be adapted to all. Although the Epistles were addressed only to the Asians, they were written to everyone by reason of the communication and the utility to be perceived from their warnings and examples. This is exactly how *Tertullian* responded to *Marcion* <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century heretic who edited the letters of Paul to fit his own theology</note>, who was eager to alter the title of the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians: <margin>Book 5, Chapter 7.</margin>
> *It matters nothing concerning the title, since the Apostle wrote to everyone while writing to some.* <note>original: "Nihil autem de titulo interest, quum ad omnes Apostolus scripserit dum ad quosdam."</note>
To which another of his statements refers: <margin>On the Spectacles, Chapter 3.</margin>
> *For even things pronounced specifically have a general sense. When God warns the Israelites about discipline, or rebukes them, he certainly addresses all. When he threatens destruction to Egypt or Ethiopia, he passes judgment against every sinful nation. Thus, every nation is called Egypt and Ethiopia.* <note>original: "Nam & specialiter quædam pronunciata generaliter sapiunt. Quum Deus Israëlitas admonet disciplinæ... Sic omnis gens vocatur Ægyptus & Æthiopia."</note>

<margin>135. As also Bullinger's opinion, Sermon 3.</margin>
CXXXV. *Bullinger* <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a key figure in the Swiss Reformation</note> is of the same opinion as those Ancients, and is often—and rightly—praised by learned men in the explanation of the Apocalypse. For he says:
> *This greeting, this book, and the entire doctrine of Jesus Christ, recorded by John, belongs to the universal Church of Christ existing in the whole world and throughout all ages. Hence it also belongs to all of us, as many as are in the Church of Christ. For even if the Epistles were addressed to the Romans and Galatians, it does not therefore follow that they are not ours.* <note>original: "Pertinet hæc salutatio, hic liber, & tota doctrina Jesu Christi... ad universalem Christi... Ecclesiam."</note>

CXXXVI. Among the more recent authors, I admit that Brightman <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607) was an influential English clergyman whose work on the Apocalypse was foundational for later Protestant interpretations</note> and Forbes come closest to them—and who would deny that these men are renowned for their praise of erudition and piety? <margin>137. Forbes' views. On Chapter 1, Section III.</margin>
CXXXVII. Forbes <note>Patrick Forbes (1564–1635) was a Scottish bishop and commentator on the Book of Revelation</note> is quite emphatic on this point: *These matters are of two kinds, according to the diversity of times, purposes, and means of revelation; from which two parts of the narrative emerge. The first part concerns those things which are, and those which are to be hereafter—that is, things which existed at that time in the truth of History, truly expressed according to the constitution of those seven Churches and for their instruction. Yet this is done in such a way that future things are also revealed therein for the instruction of all people in all ages. This is because those seven (as it seems) have a <term>typical relation <note>A "typical relation" in theology means that a historical person or event (the type) serves as a prophetic model or foreshadowing of something else (the antitype).</note></term> to the entire <term>Church militant <note>The "Church militant" refers to the Christian Church on earth, which is seen as being in a state of spiritual warfare against sin and evil.</note></term>, according to its various degrees and conditions, as the <term>mystery of iniquity <note>A biblical reference (2 Thessalonians 2:7) to the hidden workings of evil or the Antichrist in the world.</note></term> grows to its peak and the Church itself emerges again from evil. Hence, between the first part of the narrative (comprised in the first three chapters) and the second part, a distinction arises in their purposes and modes of revelation. For although the first part is to some extent about future things—by which the whole Church may be taught—this is only through a typical relation to things existing at that time, and primarily for the use of those particular churches. Whereas the second part, continued through the rest of the book, concerns things that will happen hereafter in such a way that nothing existing on earth at that time is assumed to signify them. Just as its use primarily and properly regards the whole Church militant. Therefore, to perceive it, John had need to ascend into heaven.* Thus far Forbes. Even today's Interpreters will not deny that these views differ greatly from their own thoughts.

First. The edification which the Churches of Asia both could and should have perceived from the Letters addressed to them is, by this new explanation—if not entirely removed—certainly greatly diverted and diminished. For they are commanded to keep in mind the Churches of other places and times, so that they may find in them the truth of those things written to themselves. To the Ephesians the Lord writes, *I know your works and your labor* etc. The Learned Men explain this regarding the tireless diligence in preaching the Gospel of the Apostles who shared the world among themselves. He praises the *turning away from evil*, an example of which they say stands in Peter, who at Jerusalem took vengeance on the wickedness of Ananias and Sapphira, and at Samaria put Simon Magus to shame.
