I do not emphasize now that those who insist upon seven periods agree among themselves in their distribution of time no better than the clocks of a great city; for **Brightman** <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607), an English clergyman whose work *Apocalypsis Apocalypseos* popularized the idea that the Seven Churches represented seven ages of church history.</note> determines them one way, **Forbes** <note>Patrick Forbes (1564–1635), a Scottish bishop who also wrote a commentary on Revelation.</note> another, and the most celebrated **Cocceius** <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian who developed "Covenant Theology" and a highly influential system of interpreting the Book of Revelation as a timeline of church history.</note> in yet another way. My concern now is with those who have chosen this most famous Interpreter <note>Referring to Cocceius.</note> as the leader of their studies. I assert that these men recklessly disturb the very calculations of their own periods. It pleased that Great Man <note>original: "Viro Magno" (referring to Cocceius)</note> to compare these sections—or, if you prefer, these passages—to the curtains and boards of the Tabernacle. <note>In the Book of Exodus, the Tabernacle was constructed with specific boards and curtains that interlocked perfectly. Cocceius used this as a metaphor for how "periods" of history should fit together.</note> However, these curtains and boards were not heaped one upon another in confusion, but had either knots or circles and rings by which they were joined, fastened, and fitted together. Thus, it is only right that those periods should have fixed limits and boundaries by which they begin and end. Yet our Interpreters mix or transpose these whenever it is convenient. The matter will become manifest through examples.

<margin>143. Moreover, this prophetic explanation strangely confuses and disturbs these. See §. XXXIX.</margin>
CXLIII. They say that the **Ephesian** period ends around the close of the first century and corresponds to the **first seal** and the **first trumpet**. <note>In Revelation, the opening of Seven Seals and the sounding of Seven Trumpets are often paired with the Seven Churches in these historical schemes.</note> To the **Smyrnean** Period they assign the second and third centuries, and they wish for the **second seal and trumpet** to correspond to it. Let us see how beautifully these things agree, even if we follow their own hypotheses and commentaries. The most celebrated **Cocceius** observes that the letter to the **Ephesians** was dictated after the destruction of Jerusalem, in the time of Domitian, the brother of Titus and son of Vespasian. <note>The destruction of Jerusalem occurred in 70 AD; Domitian reigned 81–96 AD.</note> Therefore, it would not be without cause if we said that the rebuke concerning "abandoning their first love" (examples of which others find in the Galatians, Corinthians, Hebrews, and in Demas, while Paul was still living) was most applicable to that time. Nevertheless, the destruction of Jerusalem and the events that preceded it are represented—according to the interpretation of the "Great Man" and the whole dutiful crowd of his followers—by the **second seal** and the **second trumpet**. For when the **second seal** was opened, 
<margin>Revelation 6:4.</margin> 
*there went out a red horse, and it was given to its rider to take peace from the earth*—that is, from the Jewish people—*which was done through Gessius Florus, the procurator under Caesar Nero, the first incendiary of the Jewish war.* <note>Gessius Florus was the Roman official whose actions sparked the Great Jewish Revolt in 66 AD.</note> The beginning of this war was in the 12th year of Nero, the year of Christ 64 or 65, according to the calculation of **Louis Cappel**. <note>Ludovicus Cappellus (1585–1658), a French Protestant scholar and pioneer of Hebrew studies.</note> *And when the second Angel sounded his trumpet, something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea,* Revelation 8:8. *That is, a certain distinguished polity in the world, the wrath of God having been kindled against it, and already broken by manifold consumption, was abolished so that it might no longer stand out in the world; and the rest...*

# DISADVANTAGES OF THE PROPHETIC INTERPRETATION

...who, from that State <note>original: *Politiæ*; here referring to the Jewish nation</note>, are dispersed among all nations. This undoubtedly refers to the Jews, along with their temple, city, and region. Regarding this "mountain," Christ also says in *Matthew 17:20* and *Luke 17:6*: *You will say to this mountain: move from here to there.* So the learned men dictate. I do not inquire now how solid that claim is. I only ask this one thing: if the *Letter to Ephesus* is supposed to fit the time period following the destruction of *Jerusalem*, how can that letter exactly correspond to the first seal and the first trumpet? After all, that very destruction, and the years that preceded it, are only narrated when the second seal is opened and the second trumpet sounds. Similarly, when they explain what is said about the poverty of the *Church of Smyrna*, they recall what *Paul* says about the *Hebrews* suffering the plundering of their goods, and what *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> tells of the *poor kinsmen of Christ* mocked by *Domitian*. Yet these events belong to the *first century and the Ephesian* period. By the same logic, someone adds the example of *Sylvester* <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335 AD), who according to legend was raised from a cave to high status by Emperor Constantine.</note>, who was raised by *Constantine* from a cave to great dignities in the Church—just as *Joseph* was raised from prison. But these things happened in the *fourth century* and belong to the *Pergamene* period. So that the "ten-day persecution" predicted for the *Smyrnaeans* can be found, they transcribe the persecutions of *Nero and Domitian* from the *Ephesian* period into this one. And where will it end, if we wished to examine every detail to the quick? <note>original Greek: *exonychizesthai*, an idiom meaning to examine something as minutely as a sculptor checks a statue for flaws with a fingernail.</note>

<margin>144. This is shown specifically regarding the Thyatiran period. See section 41.</margin>

CXLIV. I cannot omit one point: how ignorantly they disturb the chronology of the *Thyatiran period*. The Holy Spirit accurately distinguishes between the time when *Jezebel* <note>In this prophetic system, "Jezebel" was often used by Protestant commentators as a symbol for the Roman Catholic Church.</note> flourished and taught, the time given to her to repent, and the time when she was cast into a *bed of punishment*, sickness, and death. Here, everything is strangely confounded. They begin the "time of patience" granted to *Jezebel* for repentance from the year 366 AD, when the Roman Church was liberated from the persecution of *Julian* <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note>. But at that time, the Roman *Jezebel* had hardly, if at all, begun to "seduce the servants of Christ to commit adultery"—which, according to the explanation of these learned men, means to worship the Saints and the images dedicated to them—and to "eat food sacrificed to idols," meaning to participate in the "idolatrous" Mass. But what is completely ridiculous is that they place the final moment of Divine patience toward *Jezebel* at the victory reported over the Turks under the leadership of *John of Austria* <note>Don John of Austria, who led the Holy League to victory at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571.</note> in the year 1581. Yet by then, *Jezebel* had long since been cast into the bed of sickness and death—indeed, she was already buried—if, as the Great Interpreter <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), whose system of interpretation the author is likely critiquing.</note> teaches, *Gog* with all his forces was buried at the *Council of Trent* (the final session of which was held on December 4, 1563). For in the minds of these scholars, this *Jezebel* and her children certainly belong to those forces. Furthermore, they attribute the calamities with which *Italy* was afflicted by the *Vandals, Goths, Huns, and Saracens* to the "bed of punishment" into which *Jezebel* was cast. I will remain silent for now on the fact that all history...

This is so, unless the learned men would have us remember the straits into which God recently cast the persecutors and the Roman Clergy. But what a monstrous leap it is if those things which pertain to the Thyatiran period—that is, the fourth period <note>The "Thyatiran period" refers to the Middle Ages in the historicist scheme of the Seven Churches of Revelation.</note>—are sought in our own times, that is, at the end of the sixth or the beginning of the seventh period? And this is supposedly the exact chronological reckoning that should give us faith in prophetic explanation!

<margin>
CXLV. The Balaamites and Nicolaitans are not so named because they oppress the people of God by human authority.
</margin>
CXLV. In explaining the mystery of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, learned men take more upon themselves than modesty allows. It is injurious to the ancient Doctors of the Church—who were most God-fearing—to suggest that they merely handed down a "history" of the Nicolaitans based on guesswork prompted by this passage of scripture. For this, if you set aside the sought-after elegance of words <note>original Greek: *λόγων εὐμορφίαν*</note> and, as the rustic Macedonian says, "call a fig a fig and a boat a boat" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to speak plainly or "call a spade a spade."</note>, it is as much as saying that they recklessly and without reason forged a history from their own hearts of things that never happened; and having forged it, they imprudently (if not impudently) smeared it upon the page. Regarding the author and origin of that sect, I find diverse and even uncertain accounts handed down, which, to tell the truth, are somewhat obscure to me. However, to say that they *invented* the history of the sect is entirely foreign to modesty. This is especially true since the doctrines of the sect recorded by the Church Fathers agree so well with the testimonies of Peter and Jude previously cited, and because *Ignatius*, in that passage from his *Epistle to the Trallians* quoted above, speaks of the Nicolaitans as heretics still existing in his own time. But let us see what these learned men bring forward that is supposedly more sound or certain.

<margin>
See sections XXXVIII and XLVII.
</margin>
They say that "to be a Nicolaitan is to start a sect, and to call it by a man's name instead of the name of Christ." By what argument? Because in Greek, *Nicolaus* signifies "he who overcomes the people" <note>original Greek: *ὁ νικῶν τὸν λαὸν*</note>, and *Balaam* in Hebrew signifies "he who is Lord of the people" <note>This refers to the etymological theory that both names symbolize clerical dominance over the laity.</note>. But who made these learned men so wise as to decide the nature of this sect must be learned from the origin of names? Who has proven by certain reasons that the "Nicolaitans" must be derived from the Greek *Nicolaus*, and not from the Chaldean *Nicola*, meaning "let us eat" <note>original Chaldean: *ניכולה*</note>? Furthermore, *Nicolaus* and *Balaam* do not mean exactly the same thing. "To overcome" <note>original Greek: *νικᾶν*</note> is one thing; "Lord" <note>original Hebrew: *בעל* / *Ba'al*</note> is another. But most importantly, Sacred Scripture nowhere testifies that Balaam claimed leadership over the people of God; nor do the writers on ancient heresies say that the Nicolaitans attempted to introduce human authority or worldly dominion into the Church. The Holy Spirit does not mention it by even a single word.

# DISADVANTAGES OF THE PROPHETIC SENSE.
## Eeee 3
<meta>catchword: proclaimer</meta>

But in that, he establishes the heresy of Balaam and the Nicolaitans; because they placed a stumbling block before the children of God, so that they might eat things sacrificed to idols and commit fornication. How weak and fragile it is, then, to describe the sect of the Nicolaitans in the Church by the designation of a human name based solely on the etymology of words—contrary to Scripture and against all of antiquity?

<margin>CXLVI. Antipas cannot denote an advocate.</margin>
**CXLVI. Sixth.** They use the same confidence in their new exposition of the name *Antipas*, which I believe was unheard of before the illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669) was a Dutch theologian who pioneered a "covenant" or "federal" theology, often interpreting biblical names as historical ciphers.</note>. The Oriental versions—the Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic—are ignorant of the name of this Martyr. In its place, the Syriac version of Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist who published a Syriac version of the Epistles and Revelation.</note> has *athleta* <note>original: אנתותא (anthuta), likely a corruption or variant of "athlete" or "witness."</note>, which he translates as *an advocate set forth for a spectacle.* He adds in the notes: *Perhaps in this way he wished to explain the force of the consubstantiality* <note>original: τοῦ ὁμοουσίου (tou homoousiou), the core doctrine of the Council of Nicaea that Christ is of the same substance as the Father.</note>, *a word composed of Antipas, as if he were "one set forth as an example before all."* <note>original: ὁ ἐναντίον πάντων παραδειγματιθείς (ho enantion panton paradeigmatitheis).</note> Furthermore, this is mere guesswork; I do not know how probable it is. Our authors speak more confidently. *Antipas*, they say, *is truncated from Antipater*, and signifies the same thing as that name. I do not deny this. Furthermore: *Antipater denotes one who is equal to the Father.*

<margin>See Section XL.</margin>
I have some doubt about this; I have not yet found it among the Greeks. Nor do the learned men bring forth examples. It could denote this from the use of the particle *anti* <note>The Greek prefix 'anti-' can mean "against," "in place of," or "equal to."</note>: but whether it ever does, I do not know. Let the men most skilled in literature teach this. I find that *Antipater* denotes one who *opposes the Father*. For in Theocritus <note>Theocritus was a 3rd-century BC Greek poet; the reference is to the mythological Titanomachy where Zeus overthrew his father, Cronus.</note>, it is an epithet of Jupiter, because with a hostile mind he stripped his Father of the kingdom and thrust him down to the underworld. Certainly, the parents who gave the name of Antipater to their sons did not foresee hostility: but neither should it be thought that they were so seized by love for themselves that they would so solemnly desire and omen sons to be exactly like themselves. It is more credible that they called them *Antipatros* as if they were *to come into the place of their departing parents*: as in Matthew 2:22, *in the room of Herod his father.* <note>original: ἀντὶ Ἡρῴδου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ (anti Herodou tou patros autou).</note> But I am not being stubborn. I will even consider it demonstrated that *Antipater* signifies one who is equal to the Father. What then? Therefore, *Christ can be called Antipas because of the consubstantiality.* He could be. But where was he ever so called? By whom? When? To whom was he known by this name? The Greek Doctors of the Church were so anxiously concerned about a little word, a syllable, or a letter of the "consubstantiality" <note>Referring to the fierce debates between 'homoousios' (same substance) and 'homoiousios' (similar substance) during the Arian controversy.</note>, yet none of them thought of *Antipas*, a word found in the text, which happily expressed exactly what they wanted. It is a pity that the learned men of our century did not live then, who could have advised those men so indifferent to such a great matter. But let Christ be called *Antipas* because he is *equal to the Father* <note>original: ἰσόπατρος (isopatros).</note>. What finally follows? Therefore, *the name could not have been more fitly made to signify the advocates of the consubstantiality, whose task it is to say the Son is equal to the Father.* <note>original: ἴσον τῷ Πατρί (ison to Patri).</note> Oh, what a failure of logic! <note>original: Φεῦ τῆς ἀσυλλογισίας! (Pheu tes asyllogisias!).</note> Who could bear such—

### BOOK III. CHAPTER V.
<meta>catchword: denouncing</meta>

...[is he] therefore named God, because he was the proclaimer of the Divinity of Christ; [is he called] consubstantial <note>original: *homoousion*. This refers to the Nicene Creed’s definition that Christ is of the same substance as the Father.</note>, as a champion for the "consubstantial" <note>original: *τῷ ὁμοουσίῳ* (tō homoousiō)</note>; [is he called] eternal, as a defender of the eternity of our Lord; and [is he called] "equal with the Father" <note>original: *ἰσόπατρον* (isopatron)</note>, as a teacher of equality with the Father?

<margin>CXLVII. There is no mention in these Epistles of a glorious Kingdom on earth.</margin>
CXLVII. Seventh. It is the constant opinion of very learned men that a glorious Kingdom of Christ on earth is to be expected in the final times, the scene of which is depicted and most beautifully adorned in the last chapters of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. However, these Epistles, which [some] claim summarize the fates of the entire Church until the end, result in nothing less than such glory. For in the last of them <note>The letter to the church at Laodicea.</note>, the state of the Church is described as distressed, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. There is no mention of that blessed condition.

<margin>CXLVIII. For it is in vain to twist here those words of the Lord by which he proclaims that he stands at the door and knocks.</margin>
CXLVIII. For as to what the Lord writes about *standing at the door and knocking*; if we are to retain the explanation of the Brethren <note>Likely referring to the Cocceian school or similar interpreters who viewed "knocking" as a specific historical signal.</note>, this does not mean he is withdrawing himself from the sight of men, but rather that he is exerting force and striving for entry into hearts through the effective and public preaching of the word; this is not a benefit unique to the final period, nor is it a mark of a glorious kingdom. For from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, Christ has traveled throughout the entire world in this way, and according to the manifold <note>original: *πολυποικίλῳ* (polypoikilō)</note> dispensation of his grace, he has come with the ever-greater effectiveness of his word and Spirit now to this province, now to that. Moreover, he was knocking at the hearts of the Laodiceans more vehemently than usual through this Epistle sent to them from heaven.

<margin>CXLIX. Or to each individual who opens, he promises a shared supper:</margin>
CXLIX. Nor does he promise this to the Church restricted to a certain specific period, but to all and every individual opening to him, at whatever time or place, that *he will enter to them with his grace and favor (John 14:23) and dine with them*, in the sharing of spiritual gifts and the exchange of the sweetest love. The faithful experience the truth of this promise in every age: *tasting and seeing how good the Lord is. Psalm 34:8; 1 Peter 2:3.*

<margin>CL. And for each who overcomes, a seat on His Throne.</margin>
CL. Nor is there any reason to drag the promise of the Throne, upon which *he who overcomes* is said to sit, into this [historical interpretation]. For these words do not contain a prophecy by which the condition of the entire Church on earth is figured, but rather a promise of a heavenly reward, which is assigned to individual victors—that is, to sincere and constant Christians. This is just as each of the Epistles concludes with a promise of heavenly glory of that kind, under various different emblems. Christ does not console the pious who were at Laodicea by saying: "Be of good cheer in this hateful lukewarmness and lethargy which has occupied almost everyone's souls; the time is near when I will change the whole face of the Church and send down the New Jerusalem from high heaven. Endure, and save yourselves for favorable things." Instead, [he speaks] his anger to the lukewarm...

<header>DISADVANTAGES OF THE PROPHETIC INTERPRETATION</header>
<meta>catchword: Who</meta>

[the Lord] denounces: he exhorts each individual to their duty; he promises the Throne of glory to all who repent—a glory which they do not actually achieve on this earth just before the end of all things, however many may have repented or do repent at this exhortation of the Lord. But just as he himself possesses his glorious kingdom in the heavens, where he sits at the right hand of God the Father, so he promises a communion in that same glorious Kingdom in heaven to each and every victor. The learned <term>Ludovicus de Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642) was a prominent Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist known for his expertise in Semitic languages.</note></term> observed that the throne of a King among Eastern peoples is ample and wide, like a couch, raised somewhat above the ground on supports and adorned with carpets, so that besides the seat proper to the King, others whom the King wishes to honor may also have a place on the same throne. If the Lord alludes to this—as he certainly seems to—what can be inferred from this in favor of that [supposed] earthly kingdom? We certainly do not begrudge the Church that hope for a holier and more blessed condition on this earth, which we also desire with fervent prayers; but for us to expect it with full assurance of mind, we need firmer supports <note>original: *tibicinibus* (literally "props" or "pillars")</note> for our faith than those provided by this epistle to the Laodiceans. *In the meantime, You, Lord Jesus, the sole leader and Author of our Salvation, hasten the work which You have labored upon from eternity, willing and propitious; and at the appointed time, to the astonishment of your enemies, the joy of the Angels, the wealth of the Nations, and the glory of your people Israel, wisely, strongly, and happily approach, achieve, and perfect it. Amen.*

# BOOK IV. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
I. The Apocalyptic Locusts.
</margin>

Those leaders of the Roman Clergy who plotted the extermination of the Reformed Churches in France <note>original: *in Galliis* (literally "in the Gauls")</note> shrewdly decided that they should use not only force, but also arts and deceptions. Surely some pretext must be sought for their cruelty: so that while they lie in wait for the property, the freedom, and finally the lives of most innocent men, they may seem to thirst for nothing but their salvation. And that this would be so was predicted long ago in the sacred Apocalypse of John. *The locusts coming forth from the pit of the Abyss, and from the smoke of lies reduced into articles of faith* <note>The author interprets the "smoke" from Revelation 9 as the confusing or false dogmas of the Roman Church.</note>, are the false rulers of the Church—given not for building it up, but as a plague. They are indeed partly *like horses prepared for battle*, breathing nothing but contentions and persecutions, *and they have lion's teeth*, preying upon the flock of the Lord with diabolical savagery; *and iron breastplates*, surely not those of justice, with which they might resist the fiery darts of Satan, but other breastplates of wickedness, with which they harden themselves against the force of truth through various reasonings and sophistries. *Finally, they have scorpion tails and stings in their tails*, wounding the souls of the unwary with the poison of depraved doctrine, and defiling the reputation of godly men with their stinging words. Yet these same ones *have crowns on their heads like gold*, while they carry themselves as elders <note>The author uses the term *presbyteris* to contrast the clergy's self-image with their actual behavior.</note> who have been made Priests and Kings by Christ; *and they have faces like those of humans*, putting forward a name, words, and certain deeds in which the image of God shines; and they insinuate themselves into the souls of the improvident with a painted kindness: for *they also have hair like women*, while they adorn and paint themselves with every kind of seductive charm. Revelation 9:1–10.

<margin>
II. They are an Emblem of the Roman Clergy.

Book IV. Chapter I.

...[described] movingly, by those very people who suffered, and narrated by others with a wretched voice and pen. From this, it happened that the famous <term>Conference of Carthage</term> <note>original: "Collatio illa Carthaginiensis"; refers to the 411 AD meeting between Catholic and Donatist bishops</note>, so recently talked about, passed into silence and oblivion, while the entire world stood stunned at the events taking place, and even—as they say—the Roman Pontiff himself detested such great cruelty. And so the value of my labor had perished, for no one was curious anymore about that ancient Conference, which is never to be renewed. 

However, when I recently took those commentaries of mine back into my hands, I seemed to discover that not a few things are contained in them which serve to illustrate ancient history; and they are suitable to provide light, at least for my students, in the study of sacred Antiquity. For my students, I say. For who am I, that I should foolishly and arrogantly hope to teach the learned anything? I have several times declared that I have spent my writing efforts on my listeners and those like them, who are more students than experts in our affairs.

<margin>V. Melchior Leidecker’s *History of the African Church* is praised.</margin>
V. There is one thing, however, which almost deterred me—and perhaps should have deterred me—from publishing this <term>Exercise</term> <note>original: "Exercitatione"; a formal scholarly essay or dissertation</note>. Namely, **Melchior Leidecker**, a most distinguished man and a colleague to be respected by me for many reasons, has adorned and enlarged the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>original: "Rempublicam Literariam"; the international community of scholars and intellectuals</note> with his *History of the African Church*, published after I had already scribbled these papers in my usual manner. It is indeed a massive work, which he collected with incredible labor and indefatigable diligence, and in which the troubles of the Donatist faction make up no small part. Since these things are laid out there in a long narrative, I do not even hide the fact that my own writing might seem less necessary. 

Indeed, if there is any place or value in my recommendation, I urge the reader who desires to bathe himself in a full river to hurry there instead, rather than stopping at my works, where he will find only thin rivulets, or perhaps nothing but small cups to quench a thirst. That most learned man has a way of pouring out his treasures from a vast treasury of extensive reading, which, scattered throughout his vast work, enriches the mind of the greedy reader. My own house is narrower, and my furniture more meager <note>The author uses "curtior suppellex" as a metaphor for his more limited scholarly resources and scope</note>; therefore, it must be arranged in a tighter order, to provide either some concealment or some solace for my poverty. Let him who delights in abundance go to **Leidecker’s** *African History*; he will find something to congratulate himself upon. Let him who is content with a more succinct series of events not be displeased by this little work of mine. To whoever chooses to compare the two, just as he will rightly prefer that abundance with good judgment, so he will perhaps discover that my brevity is not entirely dry or lifeless. 

Let this at least be noted: just as the most distinguished Leidecker, rich in his own resources, had no need of my observations, so his riches have not profited me now; for I had already set my hand...

# On the Schism of the DONATISTS.

...applied himself to the work, I had already finished mine. I do not say this because I wish to owe him nothing—for I owe him much in other matters—but rather so that we do not appear to have acted by collusion in this writing on the same subject, like **merchants in the oil market** <note>original: "velut in velabro olearii"; a Roman idiom referring to the Velabrum district, implying a secret agreement between sellers to fix prices or cooperate</note>.

<margin>VI. The summary and goal of this our Study.</margin>
VI. But enough of prefaces: let us begin the matter itself. I intend to trace the history of the Donatist faction from the very beginning—**from the egg** <note>original: "ab ovo"</note>, as they say—and lead it in a continuous series to the times of that famous **Conference** <note>The Great Conference of Carthage in 411 AD, a turning point in the Donatist controversy</note>. I do this not only because it contains many things worth knowing, and because our Study will be rendered much more robust and substantial for it; but also because I am confident that through a faithful narration of these deeds, I shall achieve two goals which I judge to be of great importance. *First*, that it might be plain to see what an injustice is done to the men of our profession <note>The author's fellow Protestants</note> when they are compared with the Donatists—those factious, stubborn, turbulent, and indeed, I dare say, wicked men—with whose principles and customs our people wish to have nothing in common. *Second*, to show that the modern leaders of the Roman Church have departed far from that path which the ancient Catholics followed. For there appears here <note>in the ancient Catholic Church</note> as much sincerity, charity, and gentleness as there appears there <note>in the modern Roman Church</note> fraud, cunning, and cruelty.

### C H A P T E R  II.

->The Origin of the Donatist Schism, under Majorinus.<-

*I. Caecilianus is ordained Bishop of Carthage by Felix of Aptunga. II. A lawsuit is brought against him because of the gold and silver vessels of the Church which were demanded back by the elders. III. And Felix, his ordainer, is traduced by the name of **traitor** <note>original: "traditoris"; a technical term for those who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman persecutors</note>. IV. Majorinus the Reader is ordained Bishop of Carthage by the faction. V. Two men named Donatus were involved in this party: one from Casae Nigrae, the other the successor of Majorinus. VI. <margin>I. Caecilianus is ordained Bishop of Carthage by Felix of Aptunga.</margin>
The first origin of the Donatist Schism <term>Schism; a formal division or split within a church body</term> took place in this manner. When, after the abdication of Maximian, Constantius Chlorus (the father of Constantine the Great) had succeeded him in the Empire—though not a Christian himself, he was nonetheless a man of mild character and favorable to the affairs of Christians—the Church, both in Africa and elsewhere, was joyfully enjoying the goods of a long-desired peace. It happened at that time, around the year of our Lord 306 according to *Balduinus and Baronius*, or 311 according to *Valesius* (whose calculation seems more certain), that Mensurius, the Bishop of that city [Carthage], passed away. In his place, with the neighboring bishops called together and by the vote of all the people, the Deacon Caecilianus was elected; and he was ordained by the laying on of hands by Felix, the Bishop of Aptunga. Botrus and Calesius took this very poorly; as they had ambitiously considered themselves more worthy of that see <note>original: "sede"; the seat or office of a bishop</note>, they were vehemently indignant at having lost such hope. And so, joining their counsels, they were already planning a schism in their minds, waiting for a convenient opportunity. Which soon presented itself.

<margin>II. A dispute is brought against him by the elders for the return of the Church's gold and silver vessels.</margin>
II. Mensurius, who had sat at Carthage before Caecilianus, had entrusted the sacred vessels of the Church—made of gold and silver—to the elders <term>seniores; lay leaders or respected older members of the congregation who assisted in church administration</term> so that the persecutors would not seize them. For, as I may mention in passing, such was the piety toward God among Christians in those times, even under tyrants, and such was their liberality in his worship, that they contributed very many ornaments of gold and silver to it. Thus *Augustine in Book III against Cresconius, Chapter XXIX* indicates that in the time of Diocletian and the persecution stirred up by him, the Church of Cirta had two gold chalices, six silver ones, and a silver lamp. However, lest anyone think it was a matter of ambitious superstition that such things were in the Church’s treasures, let them know that whenever necessity and the pious cause of feeding the poor demanded it, they were easily sold off <note>original: "distracta fuisse"</note>. See, if you please, *Balduinus’s Annotations on Optatus, pages 87 and 88.* But this is a side note. Caecilianus...

# Concerning the DONATIST SCHISM

Caecilianus, therefore, attending to the duties of his office, rightfully ordered that the church vessels which had been entrusted in good faith to the elders by Mensurius <note>the previous Bishop of Carthage</note> be returned, so that they might be restored to the Church now that its state was more peaceful. This did not please those elders of the worst character, who had "swallowed the prey" committed to the jaws of their greed (to use the words of *Optatus of Milevis* <note>a 4th-century bishop and historian who wrote against the Donatists</note>). When, therefore, they were compelled to return them, they withdrew the common people from communion. They were joined by *Lucilla*, a powerful and factious woman, who had long ago harbored immense anger in her soul after being rebuked by *Caecilianus* (while he was still a Deacon) on account of her superstition <note>Lucilla was known for kissing the bone of a supposed martyr before receiving the Eucharist, a practice Caecilianus condemned as unauthorized</note>. Not only did she herself refuse to join in communion, but she also drew away all those she could by means of arts that were hardly honorable. Thus, with three causes and three types of persons converging, malice achieved its unfortunate effect upon the Church. *Therefore, ambition gave birth to the schism, greed nourished it, and the frantic rage of a woman strengthened it.*

<margin>III. And the administrator Felix is slandered with the name of a "traditor."</margin>
III. However, so that the rift might gape wider, the troublemakers alleged that many things had been done contrary to order in the ordination of *Caecilianus*. They threw about hateful rumors—some against *Felix* (the one who ordained *Caecilianus*), and others against *Caecilianus* himself. They claimed that the former [Felix] had been a <term>traditor; literally "a hand-overer"—someone who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman authorities during the Great Persecution to avoid punishment</term>, and that the latter [Caecilianus] had forbidden provisions from being brought to Christian captives in prison. Furthermore, so that they might find the Primate of *Numidia* <note>a Roman province in modern-day Algeria</note> and his bishops more favorable to them, they denied that the ordination of *Caecilianus* could have been done rightfully and in order without consulting them. These Numidians, therefore, having been summoned to *Carthage*, were received with hospitality by the greedy, the ambitious, and the angry. Seditious gatherings were formed; the case of *Caecilianus* was debated. Meanwhile, not one of them approached the Basilica <note>the main church building</note> where the "flower of the city" <note>the faithful congregation</note> stayed with *Caecilianus*. At that time, a message was sent by *Caecilianus*: *if anything can be proven against me, let the accuser come forward and prove it.* In that moment, among so many enemies, nothing could be fabricated against him personally. Only those stale stories about *Felix* were repeated.

<margin>IV. Majorinus the Reader is ordained as Bishop of Carthage by the factionalists.</margin>
IV. *Caecilianus*, weary of the disputes, sent word to them that if *Felix* had conferred nothing upon him (as they believed), they themselves should ordain *Caecilianus* as if he were still a Deacon. *Purpurius*, one of the factionalists—a man of many crimes and even a manifest murderer (for he had killed his sister's son)—abused this openness, saying: *"Let him come out here as if hands were being laid on him for the Episcopacy, and let his head be broken in penance."* A barbaric voice from a wicked heart! When these things were discovered, the whole Church held *Caecilianus* back, lest he expose himself to bandits. In the meantime, they created *Majorinus* bishop; he had performed the duties of a <term>Lector; a "reader," one of the lower orders of the clergy</term> while *Caecilianus* was a Deacon. He was, moreover, a member of *Lucilla's* household, and it was through her support that he obtained this dignity by most unworthy means.

<margin>V. This party became associated with Donatus.</margin>
V. Yet, what is remarkable is that this sect did not take its name from *Botrus* or *Celesius*, who were the first authors of this schism, nor from *Majorinus*, the first bishop of the schismatics; but from

## BOOK IV. CHAPTER II.

<margin>
Two men were born:
one from the Black Huts,
the other the successor to Majorinus.
</margin>
Whether it was that *Donatus* who was named for his place of origin, the *Black Huts* <note>original: "Casis Nigris"; a small village in the region of Numidia</note>, and who had long ago caused disturbances; or whether it was that *Donatus* who succeeded *Majorinus* <note>the first rival bishop set up by the schismatics</note> in the schismatic seat at Carthage. It was certainly after this latter man that the *Donatians* or *Donatists* preferred to be named, for they did not only value his learning and eloquence most highly, but also esteemed his holiness so much that, according to the testimony of *Augustine*, *they regarded him almost as Christ himself, bearing it more patiently if Christ were disparaged than if Donatus were.*

<margin>
VI. A man endowed with incredible insolence and pride.
</margin>
VI. This is that *Donatus* who reached such a peak of insolence and pride that he considered no man to be his equal; he demanded such subservience from his fellow Bishops that they all venerated him with no less fear than they did God, and they would swear by his name as if by a divine power <note>original: "numen"</note>. Not content with provoking the Prefects with insults, he hurled reproaches and shames upon the Emperors themselves. Indeed, he did not hesitate to write to the Prefect *Gregory*: *Gregory, you stain on the Senate, you disgrace of prefects.* <note>Gregory was the Praetorian Prefect of Italy and Africa around 336 AD</note> Furthermore, when the Emperor's legates came to settle the matters, he was inflamed with his usual fury and burst out into these insane words:

> What has the Emperor to do with the Church?
<note>original: "Quid Imperatori cum Ecclesia?" – a famous phrase in church history regarding the separation of church and state</note>

And from this fountain of fickleness, he poured out many curses. In order to win greater trust among his followers, this most cunning man feigned that God had spoken to him from heaven. Thus, this boast was spread by his attendants:

> Donatus prayed, and God answered him from heaven.

Finally, he was rarely called "Bishop" in the mouth of the people, as if that title were too common, but was simply called *Donatus of Carthage*.

<margin>
VII. The factionalists accuse Caecilianus before Constantine.
</margin>
VII. Let us, however, follow the actions taken by *Caecilianus* and against him. He himself defended the seat entrusted to him by Divine Providence with a brave and unconquered spirit: partly because he was joined in communion with the Bishop of the Roman Church, and partly because he found the Emperor *Constantine* to be benevolent toward him; for Constantine, in most kind letters, promised him his help against those who were attempting to turn the people away from the Most Holy and Catholic Church with evil and ruinous corruption. Yet these things did not deter the schismatics: having labored in vain and being unable to drive *Caecilianus* from his seat through their unofficial councils, they incited *Anulinus*, the Proconsul of Africa, against him and set about provoking *Constantine* himself. This was so close to their hearts that they traveled from Africa into *Gaul* <note>modern-day France, where Constantine was staying at the time</note> to *Constantine* and requested that judges from *Gaul* be granted to them. The Emperor granted this, though not willingly, yielding to their persistent petitions; he added this rebuke:

> You seek a judgment from me in this world, when I myself await the judgment of Christ.
<note>original: "petitis a me in seculo judicium, quum ego ipse Christi judicium exspectem"</note>

<margin>
VIII. But the cause was brought to Melchiades the Pontiff...
</margin>
VIII. ### CONCERNING THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

<margin>
The case was brought to the Roman Pontiff; Caecilian is acquitted.
</margin>
...the bishops, so that he might judge the dispute. Having been warned by *Anulinus* <note>The Proconsul of Africa who handled the initial appeals to Emperor Constantine</note> about the dissensions growing daily, and that it was necessary to observe a legitimate form of judgment to settle them, he ordered *Caecilian* to travel to *Rome* together with ten Bishops of his party, along with ten from the *Donatists*, so that they might argue the case in person before *Melchiades* <note>Also known as Pope Miltiades</note> and the other delegated judges. Therefore, three *Gauls* and fifteen *Italians* came to the city of *Rome*. The case was argued, concerning both *Donatus*—specifically the one named from the *Black Huts* <note>original: "Casis Nigris"</note>—and *Caecilian*. *Donatus* was convicted and confessed that he had rebaptized <note>the practice of performing a second baptism on those who had already been baptized, which the mainstream Church considered a grave error</note> and had laid hands on <term>lapsed bishops</term> <note>bishops who had surrendered sacred books or renounced faith during Roman persecutions</note>, which was deemed contrary to the Church. The witnesses brought forward by *Donatus* confessed that they had nothing to say against *Caecilian*. Thus, by the votes of everyone, *Caecilian* was declared innocent and confirmed in his Bishopric.

<margin>
IX. But the Donatists are not moved from their seats.
</margin>
IX. But the *Donatists* were not moved from their seats. *Melchiades*, having found *Donatus* alone to be the chief author of the entire evil, blamed him most severely, but gave the others a free choice to recover their spiritual health. He declared himself ready to send <term>communicatory letters</term> even to those who were known to have been ordained by *Majorinus*, the rival of *Caecilian*. He also decreed that in whatever places there were two Bishops because of the doubled dissent, the one who had been ordained first should be confirmed, while another people should be provided for the other to rule. When *Augustine* recounted these things, he broke out into affectionate praise for *Melchiades*: *O, what a best of men! O, Son of Christian peace, and Father of the Christian people!*

<margin>
X. Communicatory and Formal letters are granted, and what they are is explained.
</margin>
X. To understand what we have just said regarding *Communicatory letters*, it must be known that it was the custom among the ancients that those traveling among strangers, so that they might be received with hospitality and enjoy the other duties of Christian charity, would request a sign from the Bishop of their own Church for the journey. *Tertullian*, in *On Prescription*, Chapter 20, calls this the *communion of peace and the shared token of hospitality*. For the sake of greater certainty, so that such a sign or token could not be forged, the Bishops added letters which were called *Communicatory*, because by their exchange, the fellowship of the same faith and religion was shown. He who was equipped with these could be admitted to prayers and the <term>synaxis</term> <note>the gathering or assembly for worship and the Eucharist</note> as an Orthodox Christian in other Churches. They were also called *Formatae* <note>Formed or Formal letters</note> because they were written with a specific formula and certain marks. *Optatus of Milevis* says in Book I: *With us, the whole world agrees in one society of communion through the exchange of "Formed" letters.* *Augustine*, in Letter 163, speaking of Eleusius and his companions, says: *I was asking whether they could send the communicatory letters, which we call "formed," wherever they wished.* The Greeks called them *canonical*, *peaceful*, or *commendatory* <note>original Greek: κανονικὰς, εἰρηνικὰς, συστατικάς</note>. Such communicatory letters, for the purpose of testif—

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER II.

<margin>XI. Again they appeal to the Emperor; but to their own great harm.</margin>

XI. But such is the spirit of heretics and schismatics: to hate peace. They insolently despised such timely and much-desired conditions for peace—which would have been accepted had their minds not been so perverse—rendered even harder by the very mercy shown to them by others. *Optatus* <note>Optatus of Milevis, a 4th-century bishop and historian of the schism</note> relates that they appealed from the judgment of the Bishops to the Emperor: but to their own great harm. For when *Donatus* dared to pursue that appeal before *Constantine*, the Emperor responded with indignation: *O rabid audacity of madness! Just as is customary in the cases of the pagans, they have interposed an appeal.* <note>original: "O rabida furoris audacia! Sicut in caussis Gentilium fieri solet, appellationem interposuerunt."</note> And in a letter given to the Bishops assembled at *Rome*, Constantine sharply attacked the *Donatists* as malicious, rabid, and daring men who disparaged the law; he confirmed the sentence passed against them with his own assent, threatening the rebels with every dire consequence. Thus *Balduinus*, *Baronius*, *Petavius*, and others establish the history following *Optatus*. However, *Valesius* <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar</note> charges them with error, fighting with many arguments to show that this appeal was later than the Council of *Arles* (which must be discussed soon), as was that Letter of *Constantine*.

<margin>XII. Their incredible stubbornness.</margin>

XII. Whatever the case may be, since the Emperor greatly desired peace, he did not yet permit the *Donatists*—being so agitated—to return to *Africa*; he reckoned, correctly, that if they were dismissed in such a state, they would be fueled by fury to become the instigators of even greater discords. He therefore summoned *Caecilian* to meet him at *Brixia* <note>Modern-day Brescia, Italy</note>; he likewise ordered his adversaries to be present, promising that if they could prove even a single crime against him in the Emperor's presence, he would treat it as if all the charges they had intended to bring were proven. But when even such a great mediator of mutual reconciliation could achieve nothing due to their refusal, he sent two Bishops to *Carthage* to attempt a path toward peace. But when they too withdrew after forty days of useless litigation without completing the matter, everyone was dismissed and permitted to go to *Africa*, both the *Catholics* and the *Donatists*; the latter, with marvelous speed, arrived before *Caecilian*. There, these most insolent men refused to accept the settlement reached by the Roman Synod, but grew increasingly rabid, resorting to violence, stirring up crowds, and turning the entire state of the African Church upside down. When *Constantine* understood this, in order to strip away every pretext for their stubbornness, he decreed a new judgment—namely, the Council of many Bishops to be lawfully convened at *Arles*, in *Gaul*, where he himself was then staying.

<margin>XIII. Felix of Aptungi [investigated] by Aelianus</margin>

XIII. Furthermore, so that all things might be made more clear, by a prudent counsel he commanded *Aelianus*, the Proconsul of *Africa*, to examine the case of *Felix*, the Bishop of *Aptungi*. It was *Felix* who had been the <term>ordainer</term> <note>The bishop who performed the laying on of hands to consecrate another</note> of *Caecilian*, and he was accused of being a <term>traditor</term> <note>Literally "one who handed over." During Roman persecutions, this was a person who surrendered sacred scriptures to the authorities to be burned to avoid death.</note> of the sacred books...

# CONCERNING THE DONATIST SCHISM.

The Schismatics <note>The Donatist faction, who broke away from the mainstream church</note> were falsely accusing him of being a "hand-overer." <note>original: "traditorem"; a term for those who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman authorities during the persecutions to avoid punishment.</note> However, after he had diligently explored everything as ordered, once all urgent matters were set aside; *Claudius Saturninus*, the Curator of the Republic, was heard, who had been in the city of *Felix* at the time of the persecution and was still Curator when this case was being demanded; others were also heard with him who could not have been ignorant if any such thing had been done by *Felix*, and they were indeed heard even with the application of torture: it was discovered from the responses of all that the life of Bishop *Felix* had been stained by no such blemish. Whereupon this sentence was pronounced by the Proconsul and written back to the Emperor:

-> IT IS MANIFEST THAT FELIX, THE DEVOUT BISHOP, IS FREE FROM THE BURNING OF THE DIVINE INSTRUMENTS: <note>original: "instrumentorum deificorum"; referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> SINCE NO ONE HAS BEEN ABLE TO PROVE ANYTHING AGAINST HIM, THAT HE HANDED OVER OR BURNED THE MOST RELIGIOUS SCRIPTURES. <-

<margin>
XIV. The entire case is committed to the Council of Arles.
</margin>
XIV. And the Schismatics, not even being satisfied by this, returned to the Emperor: complaining that the judgment had not been right, nor had the entire case been heard. Truly, he [Constantine] permitted all things to the judgment of a Council to be summoned by himself. And the city of *Arles* <note>original: "Arelatensis"</note> in *Gaul* seemed a suitable place for such a great business, as he was staying there at the time. Therefore, having sent letters to certain principal Bishops of the Western Church, he invited them to the Council. He also ordered *Caecilian* to be present, together with chosen men from *Byzacena*, *Tripolitania*, the *Numidias* and *Mauretanias*, and from the individual Provinces. But he also called the *Donatists*, providing them with public transport <note>original: "evectione publica"</note> through *Africa* and *Mauretania* and from there to the *Spains*.

<margin>
XV. To which the Donatists themselves are also invited by *Travel Warrants*. What they are.
</margin>
XV. So that everyone might gather more eagerly from all sides, he took care that TRAVEL WARRANTS <term>Tractoriae: official letters or diplomas issued by the Emperor that granted the bearer access to the public postal system, including horses and lodging.</term> should be granted to each. Since we shall have to mention this word in what follows, it is pleasing to explain its use and meaning here for the sake of studious youth: especially since it can provide some light not only to this history, but to all of antiquity. *Travel Warrants* were public <term>Diplomata: official documents or charters issued by high Roman officials.</term> which were given to those sent or summoned by the Prince, who were using the public post, with designated stopping places <note>original: "stativis"</note>—that is, inns and lodgings—where they would be maintained at public expense. Such *Diplomas* were held in such high esteem that they were not even usually given by proconsuls without the Emperor’s consent. That anxious excuse of *Pliny* to *Trajan* gives credit to this observation, because he had granted the use of them to his wife—who wished to rush to her aunt after hearing of her grandfather’s death—without consulting the Emperor.
> *Up to this time, Lord, to no one,* so he writes in *Book 10, Letter 122, have I granted travel warrants, nor have I sent them for any matter except your own; which perpetual observance of mine a certain necessity has broken.* <note>original: "Usque in hoc tempus, Domine, neque cuiquam... Diplomata commodavi, neque in rem ullam nisi tuam misi; quam perpetuam servationem meam quædam necessitas rupit."</note>

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER II.

<margin>
XVI. The template for these warrants.
</margin>

XVI. Furthermore, so that we may rightly judge the generosity and magnificence of the Emperors of that age, it will be by no means useless to display here a certain form of the Diplomas or *Travel Warrants*. <note>original: "Tractoriarum"; these were official permits that allowed travelers to use the state-run postal and transport system.</note> We owe this to Cujacius <note>Jacques Cujas, a renowned 16th-century legal scholar.</note> in his commentary *On the Title of Travel Warrants, Code Book XII*, extracted from the book of *Marculphus the Monk*, which reads as follows:

> That Prince to all officials in that place. We have directed Gaius <note>A placeholder name, like "John Doe."</note> to those parts for the sake of an embassy: therefore we command that at convenient places, both transport and hospitality be provided to the same by us: that is, so many post-horses or extra horses, so many loaves of bread, so many measures of wine, so many measures of beer, so many pounds of bacon, so much meat, so many pigs, so many piglets, so many sheep, so many lambs, so many geese, so many pheasants, so many chickens, so many eggs, so many pounds of oil, so many pounds of fish sauce, <note>original: "gari"; garum was a popular fermented fish condiment in the Roman world.</note> so much honey, so much vinegar, so much cumin, so much pepper, so much costus, <note>An aromatic root used in perfumes and spice.</note> so many cloves, so much spikenard, so much cinnamon, so many grains of mastic, so many dates, so many pistachios, so many almonds, so many pounds of wax, so much salt, so many carts of vegetables and legumes, so many torches, so many carts of fodder for the horses. All these things, both in going and returning, are to be administered to the same in the usual places, and fulfilled without delay by your care.

And this indeed was the form of a *Travel Warrant*. *Schardus, in his Lexicon*, has similar things, with a few changes. It is evident, moreover, that according to the dignity and number of the persons, the number and weight of the items expressed in the diploma were increased or diminished. Constantine certainly gave distinguished evidence of his kindness and generosity when he provided *Travel Warrants* of this kind not only to Catholics, but also to the schismatics summoned to the Council. This was done in the Year 314.

<margin>
XVII. The Council pronounces in favor of Caecilianus.
</margin>

XVII. Allured by such great kindness from the Emperor, about two hundred Fathers assembled, among whom a certain Restitutus, the Bishop of London, <note>original: "Londinensium Præsul"; one of the earliest recorded mentions of a British bishop at a major council.</note> is numbered. Caecilianus was also present with his supporters, nor were the Donatists lacking their own party. Constantine himself also—AS IF APPOINTED BY GOD AS THE COMMON BISHOP OF ALL—did not disdain to be present and sit in the midst of their assembly, taking part in the inquiry. However, although the acts of this Council exist only in many mutilated parts (Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio, a cardinal and church historian.</note> suspects they were corrupted and truncated by the Donatists), it is nevertheless established from the writings of Augustine and Optatus of Milevis that the case of Caecilianus was accurately re-examined; the judgment of the Proconsul Aelianus in the case of Felix, Bishop of Aptungi, was likewise read and held as valid by the Fathers. Thus, with the common vote of all the bishops, the innocence of Caecilianus was approved, and he was confirmed in his see.

<margin>
XVIII. The Donatists, however, do not acquiesce.
</margin>

XVIII. This was not accepted by the adversaries in a single manner. A few, agreeing with the Bishops, followed their opinion; <note>original: "in eorum sententiam pedibus iverunt"; a Roman idiom for voting in favor of a proposal.</note> others resisted with a stubborn spirit and set in motion those things which you would hardly expect except from Donatists—that is, from men driven by an insane sting of an evil mind.

<margin>
XIX. Constantine's leniency toward them.
</margin>

XIV. Notable is the courtesy and leniency of Constantine toward them, which Eusebius praises in *The Life of Constantine, Book I, Chapters 44 and 45*. To him, above all other things, the peace of the Church was a care and close to his heart. Therefore, he moved confidently in their midst like one among many, keeping his protectors and all bodyguards of his person far away, protected instead by the fear of God and walled in by the benevolence of faithful friends. And whomever he noticed were yielding to a sounder opinion and were inclined toward peace and concord, those he praised most highly; however, he turned away from the stubborn and disobedient. Yet he did so in such a way that the Emperor's clemency did not fail even those people. Indeed, he patiently bore some who had attacked him quite harshly, instructing them with a gentle and calm voice that they should act more modestly and not seek to stir up seditions. Of these, some, out of respect for his warnings, abandoned the stubbornness of their minds. Others, who could be recalled to a sound mind by no remedy, he left to the judgment of God, never planning anything harsh against anyone.

<margin>
XX. How the minds of the men were rendered more savage.
</margin>

XX. Certainly, such great leniency from the Emperor ought to have bent the minds of these turbulent men toward obedience; but quite the opposite happened. For they reached such a point of wickedness that they attempted certain reckless crimes; it seems the devil, stung by envy at the current abundance of good things, incited the men to certain grave and atrocious deeds, so that he might ignite the Emperor's mind against them. But envy gained nothing; for the Emperor considered the things being done to be laughable and affirmed that he recognized the impulse of the malignant devil. For he said these were not the deeds of sane men, but of those who were either completely mad <note>original: "amantium," likely a scribal error or variant for "amentium" (senseless/mad), as "amantium" would mean "lovers."</note> or driven by the stings of a most wicked demon: that men of this kind were more worthy of pity than of punishment. *For it is not as much an act of justice to rise up against the madness of men as it is an act of the highest humanity to grieve for their plight.* <note>Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, 1.45.</note> These are almost the exact words of Eusebius.

<margin>
XXI. The Emperor’s generosity toward the ungrateful did not cease, however.
</margin>

XXI. But the Emperor’s generosity did not stop there. For just as he had summoned the Schismatics from Africa to the regions of Gaul <note>Specifically to the Council of Arles in 314 AD.</note> using the public transport system, so too did he support them with the same liberality when they returned, despite the fact that they stubbornly resisted the decrees of the Council and, with incredible audacity, appealed to the Emperor from the Council over which the Emperor himself presided.

XXII. Nay, in a remarkable letter written to all the Bishops and the laity of the Catholic Church throughout Africa, he urged them that whatever their insolence might attempt or do according to their habit of intemperance, they should endure it all by the virtue of tranquility: let no injury be repaid in return; especially since our faith ought to trust that whatever [is done] by such [people...]

Despite their continued civil disobedience and legal appeals, Constantine chose to treat them with pity rather than punishment, urging the Catholic faithful in Africa to practice similar restraint.</summary>

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER II.

<margin>
Let them endure insolence with the virtue of tranquility.
</margin>
...[whatever] we suffer from the madness of men will be of value before God as the grace of <term>martyrdom</term><note>The author frames the endurance of political or religious harassment as a form of "martyrdom," even without physical death.</note>. For what else is it to conquer in the name of God in this age, than to endure with a constant heart the disorderly impulses of men who harass the people of the quiet law? If your sincerity observes this, he says, you will quickly see, through the grace of the highest Divinity, that as the practices or habits of those who offer themselves as the standard-bearers of this most wretched contention wither away, all may know they should not give themselves over to eternal death at the persuasion of a few, when they could be restored to eternal life through the grace of repentance once their errors are corrected.

<margin>
XXIII. Wisely.
</margin>
XXIII. Perhaps such great leniency on the part of *Constantine* might seem excessive; but besides the fact that he wished to give an exceptional example of kindness and clemency in these very beginnings of his Christianity—to make the cruelty of other Tyrants appear more execrable—there were <term>reasons of state</term><note>original: "rationes status"; referring to political necessities and the stability of the government.</note> for which he judged he must act in this way. The *Donatist* faction had entangled the greater part of the Bishops in *Africa* and a huge multitude of the people in their schemes. It did not seem right to the Emperor that, by exacerbating so many thousands of men with untimely severity, that whole Province should be thrown "from the smoke into the flame," as they say, and waver in its obedience. Indeed, the human mind is by nature stubborn, striving toward the contrary and the difficult, especially in matters of religion. Furthermore, sudden coercion often brings more harm to the state, especially when there is a great multitude of offenders who, to be brought to justice, must be defeated in battle. Just as in diseases of the body nothing is more dangerous than immature medicine, so it is in this disease of the soul. Truly, "Time and Rest"<note>original: "Dies & Quies"</note> usually heal those suffering from <term>black bile</term><note>original: "atra bile"; a reference to the four humors of ancient medicine, where black bile was thought to cause melancholy or obsessive anger.</note>.

<margin>
XXIV. Although the outcome did not correspond to the plan.
</margin>
XXIV. These matters were prudently observed by *Constantine*, who certainly earned eternal praise for *Clemency* thereby, even though the outcome did not entirely correspond to his plan. For the *Donatists* abused the Emperor’s leniency and appealed from the <term>Synod</term><note>A formal council of church leaders.</note>, as we have said, to him personally. Although this greatly displeased him, he nevertheless yielded to their importunity and ordered that the parties meet him at *Rome* to argue the case now for a third time. The schismatics were present, but *Caecilian* did not arrive immediately—whether because he thought it unworthy for a Bishop, and the <term>Primate</term><note>The leading bishop of a province.</note> of *Africa* at that, to be subjected for a third time to the judgment of a layman (and one not yet baptized), as *Baronius* was pleased to guess; or whether there was some other cause, which *Augustine* confesses was not clear to him. But he finally arrived at *Milan*<note>original: "Mediolanum"</note>, where the Emperor had also taken the *Donatists*. There, the case having been heard for the third time, the Emperor judged *Caecilian* to be most innocent and the others to be most wicked.

### ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

<margin>XXV. The Donatists cause unrest again, having been condemned for a third time.</margin>
XXV. But what did those men, condemned by a triple sentence, do? Did they acquiesce, lacking any further plan? For who remained to whom they might appeal after the Emperor’s own sentence? Observe the nature of treachery, which can perhaps be refuted by evidence, but cannot be conquered in its will. In the year 316 AD, having returned to Africa, they seized the **Basilica** <note>A large public building used by the Church for worship.</note> which Constantine had seen fit to build in Constantia, a city of Numidia. But see also the character of the Christian faith, which conquers by enduring. Although that Basilica—given to them by Constantine—had been wickedly occupied by the Donatists, the private Catholics endured the loss with Christian patience. Entirely abstaining from stirring up riots, they petitioned the Emperor to grant them a place from public resources where they might build a new sacred house.

<margin>XXVI. The Catholics greatly prove their modesty to the Emperor.</margin>
XXVI. This modesty of the Catholics greatly pleased Constantine, and he praised it immensely in his letters to them. *I have sufficiently congratulated you,* he said, *that you seek no vengeance against the impious and wicked, the sacrilegious and profane, the treacherous and irreligious, those ungrateful to God and enemies of the Church, and that you ask instead that these same people might be shown forgiveness. This is truly to know God from the heart; this is to insist upon His precepts; this is to believe faithfully; this is to feel truly; this is to know that a greater vengeance is provoked against the opponents of the Church when they are spared in this world.* Furthermore, having gladly embraced their petition, he took care that a Basilica be erected at the <term>Fiscal expense</term> <note>original: "sumtu Fiscali"; meaning paid for by the Emperor’s personal treasury or the state's public funds.</note>.

<margin>XXVII. Writing that it is in his mind to arrange a journey to Africa.</margin>
XXVII. In the meantime, he wrote to Celsus the <term>Vicar</term> <note>A high-ranking administrative deputy who governed a "diocese," which was a large grouping of Roman provinces.</note> that it was in his mind to arrange a journey to Africa, hoping that perhaps his presence, like the sun, might be able to scatter those dark clouds of contention. *When,* he says, *by the favor of Divine piety I shall have come to Africa, I am going to demonstrate most fully to everyone—to Caecilian as well as to those who seem to act against him—after a clear judgment has been read, what and what kind of veneration should be offered to the highest Divinity, and by what sort of worship He seems to be delighted. Also, by conducting a diligent examination, those things which some now ignore through the enticements of their minds and think they hide, I am to find out most fully and bring into the light. I shall destroy and scatter those same persons who stir up matters of this kind, and who act so that the most high God is not worshipped with the veneration that is proper. They ought to know and hold as certain, according to the fullest faith (having also invoked health as a witness), that I shall most diligently inquire into the common people as well as those who are leaders among the clergy; and I shall judge that which is manifest to be most true and most religious.* In these words, a purpose of greater severity indeed reveals itself; yet it was not to be exercised until all things had first been explored and attempted.

XXVIII. However, many things intervened so that Constantine was not permitted to set out for Africa. From this, the audacity of those insane men grew,

BOOK IV. CHAPTER II.

<margin>...you, the Emperor himself, those insane men slander.</margin>
The stubbornness of the Donatists grew; and with the same defiance with which they had resisted the judgments of the Bishops, they now slandered the Emperor himself, claiming he had been corrupted by favoritism <note>original: "gratia corruptus"</note> to deliver a most unjust sentence. Greatly moved by this, the Emperor ordered the agitators to be punished and led away. However, soon restraining his indignation—justified though it was—he abstained from bloodshed. He decided that since they were men of the Church, they should be treated with milder punishments, such that they were deprived of their **Basilicas** <term>Large public halls used as churches</term> and sentenced to exile. Yet, after four years had passed, he granted them a pardon even from this exile, leaving those whom neither punishment had corrected nor mercy had softened to be punished by God.

<margin>XXIX. The Donatists send some of their own to Rome.</margin>
XXIX. Around this time, in the year 321 AD, the Donatists became convinced that it would be beneficial to their cause if they appeared to have some form of communion with the Bishop of Rome and his Church. To this end, they dispatched one of their own, whom they had appointed as a Bishop, to Rome so that he might reside there and gather people of their sect. The first of these was **Victor of Garba**, who was followed by five others up until the time when **Optatus** <note>A prominent bishop and author who wrote a history of the schism.</note> wrote against **Parmenian**. They took great care to send those among them who were known to be the most eloquent and famous for a certain reputation of holiness. For they believed that in this way they could best uphold the reputation of their sect in the "Mistress of the World" <note>A common title for the city of Rome.</note>.

<margin>XXX. Those driven from there into the nearby mountains were called Montenses, Campitae, and Rupitani.</margin>
XXX. But the Romans were too sharp-eyed to allow themselves to be deceived by such a trick. Therefore, they expelled the Donatists, forcing them to stay in the nearby mountains and hold their **conventicles** <note>Unauthorized or secret religious meetings.</note> there if they wished. From this, the name **Montenses** <note>Mountain-dwellers.</note> stuck to them; a name which, for a similar reason, had been given to the followers of a certain schismatic named Felicissimus during the time of Cyprian. **Jerome** also called them **Campitae** <note>Field-dwellers.</note> because they gathered in the fields, and **Augustine** called them **Rupitani** <note>Rock-dwellers.</note> from the rocks and crags in which they lived.

### ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

IX. The first Council of Carthage. X. Julian, in order to foster discord among Christians, favors the Donatists. XI. Those who, supported by his protection, rage cruelly against all most sacred things.

<margin>
I. Under Donatus, the Donatists became worse.
</margin>

And these things were indeed carried out by the *Donatists* while they had **MAJORINUS** as the Bishop of their sect at Carthage. Upon his death around the year 331 AD, he was succeeded by that famous **DONATUS**, whose image we provided above. Under his governance, the state of Donatist affairs took on another, and far worse, appearance. At that time, their legal agitators <note>original: "pragmatici"</note> became more and more remarkable, and more "shrewd and crafty slanderers" than any courtroom lawyers ever were in their own forum. They even became more bloodthirsty gladiators than any soldiers raised in military camps—men who "seek to reclaim their property not by joining hands in law, but rather by the sword" <note>This is a reference to the poet Ennius: "non ex jure manu consertum, sed mage ferro," describing the transition from legal process to raw violence.</note>. Since **DONATUS** was endowed with a most proud and fierce nature, he judged nothing to be illicit for himself if it would cause trouble for others and increase the power of his own people.

<margin>
II. Then the Circumcellions arose.
</margin>

II. Therefore, through his teaching and—as is reasonable to believe—his encouragement, the *Circumcellions* <term>A radical, violent faction of Donatists; the name is a corruption of "Circelliones" because they wandered around the "cellas" or country storehouses and shrines</term> arose in Africa. **DONATUS** named them "The Combatants" <note>original: "Agonisticos"</note> and called their leaders the *Captains of the Saints*. They were a rustic and daring class of men who acted as defenders of the sect, fearlessly resisting government officials. Wandering through markets, estates, and villages, they boasted that they were the "vindicators of public justice." Under this plausible pretext, they called slaves to the "cap of liberty" <note>original: "ad pileum," referring to the felt cap given to Roman slaves upon manumission</note> and "freed" those oppressed by debt from their creditors. They would write threatening letters to these creditors, intending death for them unless they canceled the debts and destroyed the legal bonds of agreement.

<margin>
III. A mad race of men.
</margin>

III. Because of this, almost everything was thrown into turmoil. No one was permitted to be secure in their own possessions; the legal bonds of debtors had lost their force, and no creditor had the freedom to demand payment. Everyone was terrified by the letters of these profane men, who impiously boasted that they were the "leaders of the saints." Indeed, they had acquired such authority for themselves that if there was even the slightest delay in carrying out their orders, a mad multitude would soon fly to the spot, compelling the masters of the property—through fear of death—to obedience and to humble, unworthy pleas. Furthermore, the roads were not safe. They forced masters to be thrown out of their own carriages and made them run in front of their own slaves, while the slaves sat confidently in their masters' places. In this way, social conditions were reversed at their whim.

<margin>
IV. First with stakes, then
</margin>

IV. At first, they were armed only with stakes, which they called "The Staves of Israel." With these, whenever they chose to vent their rage, they struck those they encountered so severely that, worn out by the slow...

BOOK IV. CHAPTER III.

<margin>
And armed with weapons.
</margin>
...so they would not feel they were dying by a killing blow; when they preferred to show a kind of mercy, they crushed the brain with a more powerful stroke. But eventually they also used spears and every kind of weapon, raging most severely against Bishops and clerics. During this time, the eyes of some were put out (<note>original: "Augustini haec verbis refero Epist. L." — I report these things in the words of Augustine, Letter 50.</note>); and the hands and tongue of a certain Bishop were cut off: some were even slaughtered. I say nothing of the most cruel murders, and the plundering of houses through night attacks, and the fires set not only to private dwellings, but even to Churches: into which flames there were those who did not hesitate to throw the Divine books <note>The Holy Scriptures.</note>.

<margin>
V. Raging not only against others, but also against themselves.
</margin>
V. Moreover, it almost surpasses belief with what ferocity they raged against themselves, just as they did against others. Some of them were called *Wanderers* <note>original: "Circuitores"</note>: who, as *Philastrius* <note>A 4th-century bishop of Brescia who wrote a catalog of heresies.</note> witnesses, traveling through the lands, forced those they found on the road to kill them, saying they were possessed by a desire for martyrdom. Some of them also, like the *Biothanati* <term>From the Greek for "those who die by violence," often used in the ancient world to refer to those who committed suicide</term>, made great rocks and the horrific precipices of mountains famous by their voluntary deaths. Those who desired the glory of this insane martyrdom were accustomed to signal this long before to those who shared their views. Those followers would then observe them with every kind of duty, serve them, and offer them the most delicious foods, as if they were pre-feeding and fattening certain animals destined for sacrifice. After they had lived for some time quite elegantly and sumptuously in these luxuries, they forced those they encountered to inflict fatal wounds upon them with a sword. And indeed, some achieved their aim, but others failed. For who of sound mind would take upon himself the crime of manifest murder? Therefore, like the *Corybantes* <term>Priests of the goddess Cybele known for their frenzied, wild dancing and behavior</term> raging and raving, they threw themselves headlong from heights: others leaped into fires, others slit their own throats. And they were carried into this insanity with such force that their own Bishops, having employed warnings and Ecclesiastical censures in vain, implored the help of the Magistrates to restrain their fury. For even women, having cast aside all gentleness and the fear of death—which nevertheless seems more innate to them than to men—having professed a religious life and become pregnant from debauchery, threw themselves from heights; and with their wombs burst open, they betrayed their crime, wickedly bound by a double parricide <note>A "double parricide" here refers to the killing of both themselves and their unborn children.</note>. And let these things be said by us once about the *Circumcellions*: not so much in chronological order as by the nature of the events; so that I might give the Reader a view of the fury of these most insane men, as if in a single glance.

</margin>

But just as he provided with laudable concern that under the rule <meta>catchword: rule</meta> of his brother the Emperor...
