# ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS

...condition, the *Eastern* Churches had regained their own Bishops, whom the Arians had driven out through <unclear>wickedness</unclear> and <unclear>violence</unclear> <note>original: "per [im]pidus, Pas- [per] vim"</note>; they were living in peace. Thus, he [the Emperor] judged that he must not neglect the state of the African Church; which, because of its size and nobility, was the glory and ornament of the entire Western Empire subject to him. For this reason, from all those he had found to be faithful and skilled in managing affairs, he appointed *Paul* and *Macarius* as Legates <note>Official representatives or ambassadors.</note> to Africa, men renowned for their piety and prudence. He did this under the pretext that they should relieve the poverty of all the poor through the Emperor’s bounty, but in truth, he hoped that by soothing the people with such great favors from their ingrained ferocity, he might entice them to enter into harmony with their brothers.

<margin>He sends Paul and Macarius to Africa with gifts.</margin>

<margin>VII. Donatus incites his Circumcellions against them.</margin>
VII. *Donatus* easily caught wind of this plan. Hurling cruel insults at the Emperor, he forbade his followers from accepting anything from his generosity. Indeed, sending heralds everywhere, he incited his *Circumcellions* <note>The radical, often violent, militant wing of the Donatist sect.</note> through all the market-fairs to cause troublesome business everywhere for *Paul* and *Macarius* and those souls inclined toward peace. These men, however, rampaged with such force and cruelty that even several Bishops of the Donatist faction, realizing that hatred was being brought upon them by the crimes of these abandoned men, are said to have written to *Count Taurinus* <note>A Roman military commander.</note>. They claimed that men of this sort could not be corrected within the Church and implored his armed discipline. Taurinus did not fail the request: sending soldiers through the markets where the fury of the Circumcellions was accustomed to roam, he sharply suppressed those riots. In the place of *Octava* <note>original: "Octaviensi"</note>, very many were killed and many were mutilated; for a long time afterward, their bodies could be counted by the white-washed altars or tables <note>These were likely shrines the Donatists built to honor their fallen as "martyrs."</note>.

<margin>VIII. Soldiers are opposed to their fury by Count Silvester.</margin>
VIII. *Paul* and *Macarius* themselves were also forced to ask *Count Silvester* for soldiers to ensure the safety of themselves and the treasures they were carrying to be distributed to the poor; not so that they might use force, but so they might prevent the violence organized by *Donatus*. However, when some of the soldiers were received quite insolently by the *Donatists*, they all became moved by anger and made an attack upon them; they were not sufficiently obedient to their officers, who wished in vain to restrain them. From this arose the subsequent complaints of the *Donatists*, who boasted in hateful speeches that they had suffered a dire persecution under the legation of *Paul* and *Macarius*; meanwhile, they inscribed those of their own who had died in this way into the register of blessed martyrs. Yet, in truth, because they resisted the Emperor’s generosity and rioted without any probable cause, they paid the penalties due for their rebellion, as *Optatus* <note>Optatus of Milevis, a 4th-century bishop and historian who wrote against the Donatists.</note> has argued at length. And these are those *Macarian times* <term>original: "Macariana tempora" — a phrase used by Donatists to describe this period as an era of state-sponsored martyrdom, named after the legate Macarius</term>, of which there is frequent mention in the writings of *Augustine*. These times were hated by the *Donatists*, because many from their flock were then restored to the Church while the rest gnashed their teeth in vain; others were forced to flee, and some were even captured and banished far away—especially *Donatus*, [the leader] of the Donatists...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER III.

The Prince <note>Referring here to the Devil.</note>, the source and author of all evils. *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was a prominent Catholic historian whose *Annales Ecclesiastici* is cited here for the date.</note> refers these events to the Year of Christ 348: the 12th year of the reign of *Constans*.

<margin>IX. The first Council of Carthage.</margin>
IX. At that time, through *Gratus*, the Bishop of Carthage of the Orthodox communion, a Council was convened at Carthage so that those things which pertained to the Truth might be confirmed. Truly, we can learn what the state of the African Church was then from no more certain source than from the address of *Gratus* to the Bishops assembled in the Council.

> *“Thanks,” he began in this way, “be to Almighty God and His Christ, who brought an end to the evil schismatics and looked upon His Church, so that He might raise up all the scattered members into her bosom; who commanded the most religious Emperor Constans to cherish the vow of Unity, and to send ministers of the holy work, servants of God, Paul and Macarius; and that today the entire Province of Africa should meet for a council at Carthage by the grace of God.”*

Therefore, gathered for unity by the will of God, let us celebrate Councils throughout the various provinces. In this Council, the matter of <term>Anabaptism: The Donatist practice of re-baptizing those who had already been baptized in the Catholic Church, which the Catholics considered a sacrilege.</term> was addressed, and "false martyrdom" was restrained <note>The Donatists often glorified those who died in violent clashes with imperial authorities or even committed suicide as "martyrs," a claim the Catholic Council sought to invalidate.</note>. It is customary for this to be called the FIRST COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE: not because no council had been celebrated there before it; but because the acts of the others have perished; and of those that survived after Constantine, this very one is proven to be the most ancient.

<margin>X. Julian, in order to foster discord among the Christians, favors the Donatists.</margin>
X. In this way, therefore, some peace was procured for the African Church through *Constans*: but it was not very long-lasting, as it was only preserved until the death of the Emperor *Constans*. When *Julian the Apostate* succeeded him, these same Donatists, with unbridled license, raged more furiously against the Catholics. These ambitious men were not ashamed to decree a legation <note>An official diplomatic mission.</note> to *Julian*, which, by attributing justice to him alone through flattering petitions, sought the restoration of their exiles to their homeland and the return of the basilicas that had been taken from them. This was easily obtained from *Julian*. For it was a pleasure to him both to rescind the decrees and acts of his predecessors, the Christian Princes, and to set Christians against one another. For he hoped, as was wisely observed by *Chrysostom* <note>St. John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, that they would afterwards be defeated with less effort if they had first clashed among themselves. *Optatus* elegantly reproached them for this crime in *Book II*:

> *“Then another [Emperor],” he says, “as is known to all, followed, conceiving sinister vows with you; from a servant of God he became a minister of the enemy: he testified himself an Apostate by his edicts. You petitioned him with prayers so that you might be able to return. If you deny having sent these prayers, we have read them. Nor did he whom you petitioned show any difficulty; he commanded you to go according to his own wish, for he understood that those who would come to disturb the peace with fury were coming. Blush, if there is any shame. By the same voice [edict] liberty was restored to you, by which the temples of idols were ordered to be opened. At almost the same moments your fury returns to Africa, at which the Devil is released from his prisons.”*

# On the SCHISM of the DONATISTS.

...at one time you share common joys with the enemy. <note>original: "uno tempore cum inimico communia gaudia possidetis."</note> Such, however, was that decree of Julian in favor of the Donatists, that many years later the Emperor Honorius ordered it to be posted in the most crowded places as a public notice, along with the legal records in which that petition was inserted, to the disgrace of the Donatists and the mockery of Julian. See Book 38 of the *Theodosian Code* concerning Heretics. <note>The *Codex Theodosianus* was a compilation of Roman laws; Book 16, Title 5, Law 38 specifically deals with the suppression of Donatists.</note>

<margin>XI. Those who, supported by his protection, rage savagely against all most sacred things.</margin>
XI. Nevertheless, both Julian and the Donatists achieved their desire. Indeed, once the pardon for their exile was granted to the Donatists, the most factional leaders of the schism—acting like a band of thugs and robbers—rushed upon the Catholics with the greatest violence. They did this to such an extent that men were torn apart, matrons were dragged away, infants were killed, and pregnancies were violently terminated while the Catholic multitudes were being expelled from their homes. Furthermore, they invaded the basilicas, climbed onto the roofs, and stripped the coverings; they overwhelmed the deacons who were defending the altars by pelted them with roof tiles until they were covered in blood. And, so that you may know the character of these men, they attempted to "purify" the temples with exorcisms and washings, as if they had been polluted by the religious practices of the Catholics. They even ordered the walls to be washed and the enclosed spaces to be sprinkled with "false water." <note>The Donatists believed that only their own baptisms and blessings were valid, viewing Catholic holy water as "false" or "polluted."</note> It is not necessary for me to point out now who their modern-day followers are in such follies. In addition to this, they committed violence against the holy virgins; finally, they even threw the Eucharist itself to the dogs. Yet, if we are to believe Optatus, this did not happen without a sign of Divine judgment: for those same dogs, consumed by rage, tore apart their own masters with avenging teeth as if they were thieves guilty of desecrating the Holy Body, treating them as strangers and enemies. Thus the Donatists, who had seemed almost extinguished under Constantius, became so powerful against the Catholics when supported by the protection of the Emperor Julian, that the Christian Emperors who followed were scarcely able—if at all—to elude their schemes or crush their attempts.

### BOOK IV, CHAPTER VI.

Of the Primianists against the Maximianists. XII. And Salvius the Bishop. XIII. Primianus, however, granted the grace of his communion to the Maximianists.

<margin>
I. Parmenianus, the third Donatist Bishop, defends the cause of his followers through his writings.
</margin>

I. <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial I decorated with floral scrollwork and a small face at the top.</image-desc> After some time had passed, Donatus died. In his place—around the year of Christ 368, during the fifth consulship of Valentinian and Valens—**PARMENIANUS** was substituted. He was a most tenacious defender of the same sect and the third Donatist Bishop at Carthage. As soon as he obtained that seat, he sharpened his pen against the Catholics, publishing writings filled with lies by which, if not others, at least the more simple-minded might have been deceived. But the Catholics did not fail their own side. To refute the man's ravings and to guard against the deceptions arising from his verbal smokescreens, they challenged him to a public assembly of Bishops, where all his writings could be accurately examined. He, however, and those who stood by him, rejected the Catholics as if they were unworthy of their company, because they proclaimed the Catholics to be "unclean" and compromised by communion with the "fallen" <term>lapsi: Christians who had renounced their faith or handed over sacred books during Roman persecutions</term>, while declaring themselves to be holy and pure. Hence, a necessity was imposed upon the godly to defend the public cause and their own innocence, at least through letters.

<margin>
II. Optatus of Milevis responds to him with great gentleness, yet excellently.
</margin>

II. In this matter, Optatus of Milevis, a Bishop in Numidia <note>A Roman province in North Africa, modern-day Algeria</note>, performed outstanding work. He has been mentioned by us often in this writing and will be mentioned often again. He was a man renowned for his learning, as far as that land and those times allowed, and most holy for his proven integrity of character. Parmenianus argued that the Catholic Church existed only within the "faction of Donatus," and that all other churches throughout the whole world were schismatic. With much abusive bitterness, he accused everyone who disagreed with him of being sinners, unclean, wandering outside Christ’s flock, exiles, and finally pagans. Optatus responded to him with an expansive gentleness of spirit and speech, calling him his "Brother" throughout, based on their shared Sacrament—because they had been reborn through one Baptism by one Christian mother religion. "Since," he said, "they prohibit access, block the entrances, avoid sitting together, and deny conversation; let me at least have a discussion with you in this manner, Brother Parmenianus." <note>original: "Quoniam, inquit, & accessum prohibent, & aditus intercludunt, & consessum vitant, & colloquium denegant; vel tecum mihi, Frater Parmeniane, sit isto modo collatio."</note> "And because I have not scorned or despised your treatises, which you wanted to be in the hands and mouths of many, you also should hear the responses of our humility. I wish that modesty—which I judge to be the glory and ornament of learning, and a virtue more worthy than learning itself—would always rule equally, or even more so, in the writings of dissenting Brothers!" As for that point upon which the entire hinge of the question turned—namely, by what distinct signs and specific properties the Catholic Church is defined, so that it might be judged more certainly in whose possession it remains—that, I say, he pursued with those argu-

...is the opinion of **OPTATUS**, which you should neither entirely despise nor approve in every part.

<margin>III. Tyconius’s schism within the Donatist schism.</margin>
III. Certainly, the force of truth compelled **TYCONIUS**, a Bishop of the Donatist sect, to oppose **PARMENIANUS** and defend the Catholic Church of God as being spread throughout the whole world, just as it had been foreseen and predicted through the hearts and mouths of the Saints so long before. By this principle, he undertook to demonstrate against his own people that no man’s sin, however wicked, could invalidate the promises of God; nor could the impiety of anyone established within the Church cause the faith of God—concerning a Church destined to exist and spread to the ends of the earth—to be nullified. However, although Tyconius argued this point vehemently and at great length, stopping the mouths of his detractors with many clear testimonies from the Scriptures, he did not see the logical conclusion: that those Christians in Africa who belonged to the Church spread throughout the whole world were those who were joined to that world through communion, rather than those who were severed from its unity. Yet, in other matters, he held sounder views than many men of his sect. For he wrote—according to the testimony of **AUGUSTINE** in his *48th Letter to Vincentius*—that a Council was held at Carthage by two hundred and seventy Donatist bishops. In that Council, after setting aside all past disputes, they refined their opinion over seventy-five days and decreed that they should commune with the <term>Traditors: "Handers-over"; those who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman authorities to avoid persecution</term>, even those guilty of immense crimes, if they refused to be re-baptized, treating them as if they were uncorrupted. He also says that **DEUTERIUS**, the Bishop of Macrianis of the same communion, merged the gathered congregation of Traditors with the Church and established unity with them according to the statutes of that Council. He notes that **DONATUS** communed continuously with this Deuterius after this act—and not only with Deuterius, but with all the bishops of the Moors for forty years—who, he says, communed with the Traditors without re-baptism until the persecution carried out by Macarius. These things greatly displeased **PARMENIANUS**, a man of obstinate spirit and fiery intellect. When he had tried in vain to restrain Tyconius’s speaking and writing through letters, he struck him with an <term>Anathema: a formal curse or excommunication</term> by the decree of some Council.

<margin>IV. Likewise, another schism by Rogatus.</margin>
IV. Besides this schism of Tyconius within the larger schism, another was attempted by **ROGATUS MAURUS** in <note>original: "Mauritania Cæsareana"</note> Mauretania Caesariensis; those who followed his faction were called "Rogatists" after him. Ancient authors have not recorded the cause of this separation. Nevertheless, the remaining Donatists took this departure, however small, very bitterly. They implored the help of **FIRMUS**, who was exercising a tyranny in Mauretania at that time, to take vengeance for this rash secession. There were also others who formed groups separate from the rest,

# BOOK IV. CHAPTER IV.

614

They were called the Urbanists and the Claudianists: obscure names hardly worth mentioning.

<margin>V. Primianus, the fourth Bishop of the Donatists.</margin>
V. These were indeed the sparks of a growing dissension among the Donatists, but they erupted into an open and widely spreading flame when a fierce dispute arose over the successor of **PARMENIANUS**, who died around the year of Christ 394, in the sixteenth year of the Emperor **THEODOSIUS**. **AUGUSTINE** described this history at great length in his *Commentary on Psalm 36* and in his books *Against Cresconius*. We shall provide a summary here. **PRIMIANUS** was placed in the See of Carthage by the members of his own sect after **PARMENIANUS**, but he soon removed one of his deacons, **MAXIMIANUS**, from communion. **MAXIMIANUS**, unable to endure this censure which he considered unjust, went to other bishops to seek redress, charging **PRIMIANUS** with the most atrocious crimes. A Synod of fifty-three bishops was convened to examine the case at the Caves of Sufes <note>A Roman town in modern-day Tunisia, also known as Sbiba</note>, not far from Carthage. **PRIMIANUS**, though summoned there, refused to appear. The Synodical Fathers, urged by the elders of the Church, traveled to Carthage, where they were received most poorly by him; he not only avoided meeting them but even hired a mob of desperate men and obtained the assistance of <term>Officials: civil officers or local guards</term> to besiege the doors of the Basilicas, denying the Fathers the ability to enter or perform their solemn rites. Because he acted so persistently and insolently, the following sentence is recorded as having been passed against him by them—for it is of interest to know what crimes these men, who in their own opinion were holier than all others, charged against one another.

<margin>VI. Condemned by a notable sentence from the Donatist Synod.</margin>
> VI. *We, all the Priests of God, in the presence of the Holy Spirit, have decreed concerning this same **PRIMIANUS**: first, because he substituted others in place of living bishops; because he mixed unholy people <note>original: "incestos," referring here to those spiritually polluted or ritually unclean</note> with the holy communion; because he attempted to force priests into a conspiracy in that same place; because he caused the priest **FORTUNATUS** to be thrown into a sewer <note>original: "cloacam"</note> after he had assisted the sick with baptism; because he denied communion to Bishop **DEMETRIUS** in order to force him to disinherit his son; because that same priest was rebuked for having welcomed bishops into his home; because the aforementioned **PRIMIANUS** sent a mob to destroy the homes of Christians; because bishops and clergy were besieged together and afterwards stoned by his henchmen; because the elders were beaten in the Basilica because they were indignant that the Claudianists were admitted to communion; because he thought innocent clergy should be condemned; because he refused to present himself to be heard by us, while he blocked the doors of the Basilicas with a mob and officials so that we could not enter; because he insultingly rejected the legates sent by us to him; because he usurped many places first by force and then by judicial authority; besides his other illicit acts, which we have kept silent for the sake of the decency of our writing—*

# CONCERNING THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

619

...we judge: that he be forever condemned by the Sacerdotal choir, lest by being coddled, the Church of God be stained by contagion or any crime. For this reason, all Priests, and all Clerics, and all people who remember they are Christians, are warned by this *Circular Letter* <note>original: *Tractatoria*; an official letter or decree sent to multiple parties to communicate a decision</note> that they should, with diligent care, shrink from his communion as one condemned.

<margin>VII. Maximianus is substituted for him: from which arose the new schisms of the Primianists and Maximianists.</margin>
VII. Shortly after, a second Council was gathered at **CEBARSUSSI** <note>A Roman town in the province of Bizacena, modern-day Tunisia</note> of a hundred or more Bishops; where **PRIMIANUS** was again and more fully condemned, with the Deacon of his own *Church*, **MAXIMIANUS**—whom he himself had previously condemned—substituted in his place. Hands were laid upon him <note>The ritual of ordination or consecration</note> by twelve Bishops at that Council. And so now one See of Schismatics at Carthage had two Bishops at the same time, **PRIMIANUS** and **MAXIMIANUS**: each with his own followers, of whom the former were called *Primianists*, and the latter *Maximianists*.

<margin>VIII. Maximianus is condemned by a harsh sentence from the Numidians and Moors.</margin>
VIII. **PRIMIANUS**, seeing the Bishops of the Proconsular Province, of **BIZACENA**, and of **TRIPOLITANA** favoring **MAXIMIANUS**, implored the help of the **NUMIDIANS** and **MOORS**. Therefore, at his instigation, a Council was gathered again in the city of **BAGAI** in **NUMIDIA**, where three hundred and ten Bishops assembled. Having examined the case of **PRIMIANUS**, who was present, and **MAXIMIANUS**, who was absent and not summoned as was proper, they absolved the former of the crimes charged against him, but they vented their rage most bitterly against the latter. **AUGUSTINE** presents the words of the sentence in *Against Cresconius, Book III, Chapter LIII* and *Book IV, Chapter XXXI*. We shall provide some parts as a sample. They rage against **MAXIMIANUS** himself with this speech: *Let the lightning-bolt of judgment strike Maximianus—the rival of faith, the adulterer of truth, the enemy of Mother Church, the minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram* <note>Biblical figures from Numbers 16 who led a rebellion against Moses and were swallowed by the earth; they were frequently used as archetypes for schismatics</note>—*from the bosom of peace. He is not only condemned by the just death of his own wickedness, but the chain of sacrilege also drags many others into a partnership of crime: the venom of asps is under the lips of those whose mouths are full of cursing and bitterness, etc. The severed limbs lie there, which a pestilential rot has so corrupted that there is more comfort in their amputation than there is medicine in their recovery.*

<margin>IX. And the XII Bishops who had ordained him.</margin>
IX. Then, turning their speech toward those twelve who had ordained Maximianus (whose names it is unnecessary to list here as they were expressed in the original), they said: *Know that those guilty of a notorious crime, who by a deadly work of perdition have glued together a filthy vessel from collected dregs—and also the Clerics of the Church of Carthage who, while participating in the crime, provided the enticement for this unlawful incest* <note>The council uses 'incest' metaphorically to describe the spiritual violation of church unity and the "marriage" between a bishop and his see</note>—*are condemned by the judgment of the presiding God and the truth-speaking mouth of the Universal Council.*

<margin>X. Pardon, but with great [arrogance]</margin>
X. Soon they offered pardon to others who were involved in a slightly lesser crime, but with such an air of arrogance that it is most unworthy of the humble ministers of Christ.

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>An offer made to those who were believed to have sinned less.</margin>
They proceed thus: "We have permitted those whom the shoots of that sacrilegious branch did not pollute—that is, those who, out of a modest reverence for the faith, withdrew their hands from the head of Maximianus—to return to the Mother Church <note>In this context, 'Mother Church' refers to the Donatist sect led by Primianus, which claimed to be the only true church</note>. And lest the short time remaining for those returning should cut off their hope of salvation due to the pressure of a narrow deadline, we open the door of recognition (or, as others read, of forgiveness) to all who acknowledge their error, while all previous decrees remain in force, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January <note>original: *octavum Kalendarum Januariarum*; December 25th</note> next following. This is so that those who return may have the foundations of their honor and faith intact. But if anyone, through sluggish laziness, fails to enter through this door, let him know that the way to all merciful approaches has been closed by his own will. For the sentence pronounced against them shall remain, and a fixed penance shall be set for those returning after the appointed day." Truly, these words reveal a soul that is unmerciful and haughty, far removed from that gentleness which the Lord commended to His followers by both His voice and His example.

<margin>XI. The cruelty of the Primianists toward the Maximianists.</margin>
**XI.** But they did not remain within these boundaries of Ecclesiastical excommunication. While the Primianists boasted that they were the true Catholics and pursued the others as heretics and criminals guilty of monstrous deeds through harsh accusations before the Civil Magistrate, they succeeded—with the Proconsuls either approving or at least looking the other way—in acting against the Maximianists as if by public laws. From this, they dared to send a herald to proclaim at Siniti: **WHOEVER HAS COMMUNICATED WITH MAXIMIANUS, HIS HOUSE SHALL BE BURNED.**

<margin>XII. And toward Bishop Salvius.</margin>
**XII.** But what they perpetrated against Salvius, the Bishop of Membresa, almost surpasses all insolence. He was one of those who had ordained Maximianus and had resisted their violence with a little more confidence than the others. Having captured the old man, they tied dead dogs around his neck and forced him to dance with them for as long as they pleased. Augustine records that this was well-known to him, and he elegantly compares it to the tortures of the Etruscan Kings, who used to bind dead bodies together with the living.

<margin>XIII. Nevertheless, Primianus granted the grace of his communion to the Maximianists.</margin>
**XIII.** By these arts, it came about that Primianus and his followers easily held the upper hand everywhere. He labored to bring the Maximianists back to himself by any means necessary, receiving them into his communion even though they had been condemned for the gravest crimes, and even validating the baptism performed by the Maximianists. In this matter, the Catholics <note>The mainstream Christian Church recognized by the Roman Empire, as opposed to the Donatist sect</note> proclaimed a singular work of Divine Providence. For although all the Donatists charged that the Orthodox in Africa had lost the true face of the Church because they were in communion with Caecilianus <note>The Bishop whose disputed election triggered the Donatist schism</note>, the Donatists themselves were granting the grace of their communion to those whom they had reproached for far greater crimes. Augustine frequently used this argument to fight against them, and he reduced them to silence <note>original: *εχέμυθίαν* (echemythian); a Pythagorean term for a vow of silence or being hused</note>. This matter seemed so significant to the Catholics after those events gathered at Carthage—

# CHAPTER V.

## The efforts of Augustine and other Orthodox believers toward the Donatists.

*I. Augustine offering brotherly conferences to the Donatists. II. He is haughtily rejected by them. III. Not without plots laid against his life. IV. He himself intercedes with the Magistrate on behalf of those guilty of attempted murder <note>original: "parricidis"; though literally 'parricides,' it here refers to those attempting to kill Augustine, their spiritual father</note>. V. The Council of Carthage acts with the same leniency toward them. VI. The notable deed of Maximianus of Vaga, a former Donatist turned Catholic. VII. The prodigious license of the Donatists in recruiting converts. VIII. The courtesy of another Council of Carthage toward the Donatists. IX. The dull-witted pride of Crispinus of Calama, a Donatist Bishop, against Possidius. X. The furious violence of another Crispinus against the same. XI. For whom Possidius nevertheless intercedes before the Proconsul.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a landscape with a tower and buildings.</image-desc>
<margin>I. Augustine offering brotherly conferences to the Donatists.</margin>
At that time, AUGUSTINE flourished most notably, having been appointed as a colleague to Valerius in the Bishopric of Hippo, and soon to be his successor, in the first year of the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of Christ 395. He, because of his sublime learning and extraordinary zeal for the Christian cause, thought he should spare himself no labor to bring the Donatists back into the unity of the Church. Not only in his own city of Hippo or neighboring towns did he eagerly teach the Donatists, inviting them kindly and opposing them firmly; but wherever even the slightest hope of building up the faith shone through, he established—or certainly offered—brotherly conferences with them. Truly, it will perhaps be better to set these things out in the words of Possidius <note>Possidius was a close friend and biographer of Augustine, as well as the Bishop of Calama</note>.

<margin>Life of Augustine, Chapter IX.</margin>
Who, after many other things which would be long to describe, says: *“And these things,”* he says, *“were done continually by Augustine, day and night. For he continually sent private letters to any Bishops of that same error, and also to prominent laymen, giving reasons, warning and exhorting them that they should either correct themselves from that depravity or at least come to discussions. But they, out of distrust of their cause, never even wished to write back, but instead spoke furious words in their anger, and condemned Augustine both privately and publicly as a seducer and deceiver of souls. And they said and argued that he ought to be killed like a wolf in the defense of their flock; and they believed without doubt that all sins could be forgiven by God for those who were able to do and accomplish this: fearing neither God nor feeling shame before men.”*

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>
II. He is haughtily rejected by them.
</margin>

II. Augustine himself frequently complained about this matter. "The charity of Christ," he wrote to the Donatists, "for whose sake we wish to win every person—so far as our own will is concerned—does not permit us to remain silent. If you hate us for this reason, because we preach Catholic peace to you, we are serving the Lord who says, *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God* <note>Matthew 5:9</note>. And it is written in the Psalm: *With those who hated peace, I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they fought against me for no reason* <note>original: "Cum iis qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus; quum loquebar eis debellabant me gratis." Psalm 120:7</note>." Because of this, certain priests of your party sent word to us, saying: DEPART FROM OUR PEOPLE IF YOU DO NOT WANT US TO KILL YOU. Then, <margin>Letter 166 to the Donatists.</margin> he says, "Your Bishops, when approached by us, never wanted to confer with us peacefully, as if fleeing from speaking with sinners." When they used this pretext everywhere to avoid meeting with the Catholics, the Clergy of Hippo <note>The city where Augustine served as Bishop; modern-day Annaba, Algeria</note> humbled themselves so far as to argue that Christ himself had spoken about the law with the Devil, and that Paul had conferred not only with the Jews but also with the Epicureans <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who were often viewed as atheistic or materialistic by early Christians</note>. Yet, no progress was made through all these efforts. The Donatists, with their usual persistence, made the excuse that logical <term>dialectics</term> <note>The art of investigating or discussing the truth of opinions through logical argumentation</note> were not appropriate for the Christian religion; they claimed Augustine was nothing more than a contentious debater who should be avoided and shunned rather than refuted and conquered. On this matter, let him be heard again:

<margin>
Book IV. Against Cresconius.
</margin>

> "Because we have often wished to confer with your people so that, with error removed, brotherly charity might be joined by the bond of peace, you criticize this zeal for fighting for the truth," he says, "calling it by the disgraceful names of 'contention' and 'animosity'."

But he notes that the Donatists offered this excuse because, as he says, they preferred to cover a bad cause with an excuse rather than end it with a discussion. Nor does he hesitate to say this to Cresconius's <note>A Donatist layman and grammarian who wrote against Augustine</note> face, as it were:

> "I think," he says, "that you can very easily understand that it is not for the sake of avoiding contention—which does not exist when the truth is sought and one does not struggle for vain glory—but because of a bad lack of confidence that you do not wish to confer with us."

<margin>
III. Not without plots against his life discovered. Life of Augustine, Chapter XII.
</margin>

III. These furious men were so exasperated by Augustine's zeal that they laid traps for his life on more than one occasion. Let Possidius <note>A close friend of Augustine and his first biographer</note>, a particularly reliable author, tell this again:

> "Several times those same <term>Circumcelliones</term> <note>Radical and often violent groups of Donatist extremists known for their wandering lifestyle and attacks on Catholic clergy</note>, being armed, waylaid the servant of God, Augustine, while he happened to be traveling at someone's request to visit, instruct, and exhort the Church populations, as he very frequently did. And it happened once that those who were lying in wait lost their chance to capture him." The example of this that he adds is quite memorable. For he continues: "It happened by the providence of God that, through the error of the man acting as guide, the priest arrived where he was headed by a different road with his companions; and through this error, which he later discovered, he escaped those impious hands. And while he gave thanks to God his Deliverer in all things, those men, in their usual fashion, spared neither laity nor clergy."

# On the SCHISM of the DONATISTS.

<margin>IV. He intercedes before the Magistrate on behalf of the murderers.</margin>
IV. However, all these things did not prevent **Augustine** from demonstrating his gentleness, his readiness to forgive, and a truly Christian charity—even toward his enemies—in a truly remarkable way. For when they <note>The Donatists or their extremist wing, the Circumcellions.</note> had killed **Restitutus**, a priest of Hippo, after abusing him for twelve days with mockery and lashings; and after they had brought death upon **Innocentius**, also a priest, having first gouged out his eye and cut off his finger; and when the investigation of that case was brought before **Marcellinus**, the Magistrate serving in Africa, Augustine earnestly pleaded with him in a long and careful letter not to demand from them the punishments they deserved according to the severity of the laws.

<margin>Letter 159.</margin>
> "I implore your faith," he says, "which you hold in Christ, through the mercy of the Lord Christ himself, that you neither do this, nor permit it to be done at all. For although we could ignore the death of those who seem to have been brought to trial not because of our accusations, but through the reports of those responsible for guarding the public peace, we nevertheless do not wish the sufferings of the servants of God to be avenged with equal punishments, as if by the law of retaliation <note>original: "vice talionis" — the 'eye for an eye' principle of justice.</note>."

Lest anyone should think this was some trick of **Augustine’s** to seek the praise of popularity while being indifferent to what happened to the Donatists, the powerful reasons with which he argued this case cut off any occasion for such malicious suspicion. And indeed, what could have been said more effectively than the speech with which he urged his request?

> "Since I am speaking to a Christian, especially in such a case, I would not be speaking arrogantly: it is fitting for you to listen to a Bishop giving a command, most distinguished Lord, and deservedly renowned and dearest Son."

<margin>V. The Council of Carthage acts with the same leniency toward them.</margin>
V. The entire African Council held the same spirit; it was celebrated in Carthage in the seventh year of the reigns of Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of Christ 401. For when it was discovered that nothing was being gained through the emperors' edicts—since the stubbornness of the Schismatics seized upon them as material for slanders against the Church, as if they were being dealt with by the authority and force of Magistrates rather than the weight of reason—**Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage**, called a general Synod from all the provinces of the African Church for the month of September, so that by everyone's decision, they might treat with all the Donatists for a universal peace. There, it was decreed by unanimous vote that they should act with leniency rather than severity.

<margin>African [Council], Chapter 36.</margin>
And because it was considered shameful for professors of the Orthodox faith to overcome their adversaries by any means other than reason, they applied the greatest care to this: that from the very records of the **Donatists** with the **Maximianists** <note>The Maximianists were a breakaway group from the Donatists; Augustine used their history to show that the Donatists themselves had split over minor issues, proving their hypocrisy in leaving the main Church.</note>, of whom we have spoken before, they might be convicted of manifest error. But that decree also seemed especially conducive to entering into peace and unity: that from **Anastasius**, the Prelate of the Roman See, and other bishops across the sea, this favor should be sought on behalf of the **Donatists**...

### BOOK IV, CHAPTER IV.

<margin>
II. He is scornfully rejected by them.
</margin>

II. Augustine himself frequently complained about this matter. He wrote to the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian sect in North Africa who claimed that only they were the "pure" church.</note> that the charity of Christ—"to which we wish to win over every man, as far as our will allows—does not permit us to remain silent. If you hate us for this reason, because we preach Catholic peace to you, we serve the Lord who says: *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.* And it is written in the Psalm: *With those who hated peace, I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause.* <note>original: "Cum iis qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus ; quum loquebar eis debellabant me gratis."</note> For this reason, certain priests of your party sent word to us, saying: **STAY AWAY FROM OUR FLOCKS, IF YOU DO NOT WANT US TO KILL YOU.**" Then, <margin>Letter 166 to the Donatists.</margin> he says, "Your Bishops, when approached by us, never wanted to confer with us peacefully, as if they were fleeing from speaking with sinners." When they used this pretext everywhere to excuse themselves from meeting with the Catholics, the clergy of Hippo <note>Augustine was the Bishop of Hippo Regius, in modern-day Algeria.</note> humbled themselves so far as to point out that Christ himself spoke with the Devil about the law, and that Paul conferred not only with the Jews but even with the Epicurean philosophers. However, nothing was gained by all these efforts. The Donatists, with their usual stubbornness, mocked him, claiming that logical debates <note>original: "Dialecticas disputationes"</note> did not suit the Christian religion, and that Augustine was nothing more than a contentious debater who should be avoided and shunned rather than refuted and overcome. Regarding this, <margin>Book IV, Against Cresconius.</margin> let his own words be heard again: "Because we have often wished to confer with your people so that error might be removed and brotherly charity joined by the bond of peace, you criticize our zeal for fighting for the truth by calling it the shameful name of 'contention' and 'animosity.'" But he notes that the Donatists offered this excuse because, as he says, "they would rather cover up a bad cause with an excuse than end it through discussion." Nor does he hesitate to say this right to the face of Cresconius <note>A Donatist layman and grammarian who wrote in defense of his sect.</note>: "I think you can very easily understand that it is not for the sake of avoiding contention—which does not exist when the truth is sought and one does not struggle for empty glory—but because of a lack of confidence in a bad cause that you do not wish to confer with us."

<margin>

*Life of Augustine*, Chapter 12.
</margin>

III. Furthermore, these furious men were so provoked by Augustine’s zeal that they laid traps for his life more than once. Let Possidius <note>Augustine’s friend and first biographer.</note>, a most reliable author, tell it again: "Several times those same armed **Circumcellions** <note>The violent, militant wing of the Donatist movement.</note> blocked the roads against the servant of God, Augustine, while he happened to be going, as requested, to visit, instruct, and encourage the local church congregations—something he did very frequently. And it once happened that those who had hidden in ambush lost their prey." The example he adds is quite memorable. For he continues: "It happened indeed by the providence of God that, due to a mistake by the man guiding him, the priest arrived at his destination by a different road with his companions. Through this error, which he only realized later, he escaped those impious hands. And while he gave thanks to God the Liberator in all things, those men, in their usual fashion, spared neither laypeople nor clergy."

### On the Donatist Schism.

IV. However, none of these atrocities prevented **Augustine** from demonstrating his gentleness, his readiness to forgive, and a truly Christian charity, even toward his enemies, in an altogether marvelous way. For when the Donatists had killed **Restitutus**, a priest of Hippo, after abusing him for twelve days with mockery and lashings; and when they had brought death to **Innocentius**, also a priest, after gouging out his eye and cutting off his finger; and when the judicial inquiry into this matter was brought before **Marcellinus**, the Magistrate acting in Africa, **Augustine** earnestly implored him in a long and meticulous letter not to demand the punishments they deserved according to the severity of the law. 

<margin>
Letter CLIX.
</margin>

"I entreat your faith," he says, "which you have in Christ, by the mercy of the Lord Christ himself, that you neither do this nor permit it to be done at all. For although we could look away from the death of those who seem to have been presented for examination not by our accusation, but by the report of those whose duty it was to maintain public peace; nevertheless, we do not want the sufferings of the servants of God to be avenged by equal punishments, as if by a law of retaliation." <note>original: "quasi vice talionis paribus suppliciis vindicari" — the "lex talionis" refers to the ancient principle of "an eye for an eye."</note> Lest anyone think this was some act of Augustine's to catch the praise of popularity, while being unconcerned about what might happen to the Donatists thereafter, the powerful reasons with which he argued this case cut off any occasion for such a malicious suspicion. And what, indeed, could have been said more effectively than the speech with which he urged his petition? "Since I speak to a Christian, especially in such a cause, I would not be speaking arrogantly: it is fitting for you to hear a Bishop giving a command, most excellent Lord, and deservedly distinguished, and most dear Son."

<margin>

</margin>

V. The entire African Council, which was held at Carthage in the seventh year of Arcadius and Honorius (the year of Christ 401), possessed the same spirit. For when it was discovered that the edicts of the Emperors were achieving nothing—in fact, the stubbornness of the schismatics seized upon them as material for slanders against the Church, as if they were being dealt with by the authority and force of Magistrates rather than the weight of reason—Aurelius, the Bishop of Carthage, called a general Synod from all the provinces of the African Church for the month of September, so that a decision could be made by everyone regarding a universal peace with all the Donatists. There it was decreed by equal vote that they should act with leniency rather than severity. 

<margin>
African Council, Chapter XXXVI.
</margin>

Furthermore, a decree was made which seemed especially conducive to entering into peace and unity: that from the Bishop of the Roman See, **Anastasius**, and other bishops across the sea, a concession <note>original: "indulgentia"</note> should be sought in favor of the Donatists...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER IV.

...indulgence, so that it might be permitted for those wishing to return to the Church to persevere in the orders <note>The "orders" refers to their rank or office as priests or bishops.</note> they had previously received among their own people. We mentioned above that this had also been granted formerly in the time of Pope **Melchiades** <note>Also known as Miltiades, he was Pope from 311 to 314 AD.</note> during the **Roman Council** to the **Donatists**. But since, as minds turned to the contrary, it was later provided in an overseas Synod <note>original: "transmarina Synodo" — likely referring to a council held in Italy or Gaul, across the Mediterranean from Africa.</note> that those returning to the Church should not be received with the honors they previously held; now the African Bishops request once again that this be granted to them. Furthermore, it was decided that legates should be sent from the number of the Synod for the sake of preaching peace and unity, without which salvation cannot be obtained for a Christian (I am relating the very words of the Fathers), to the **Donatists** themselves, whether to those they hold as Bishops or to the common people; through these legates, it might be brought to the knowledge of all how they have nothing just that they can say against the Catholic Church.

<margin>VI. The remarkable deed of Maximianus of Vaga, a Catholic converted from the Donatists. 

Augustine, Letter 238.</margin>
VI. Very few, even when confronted with such great kindness from the Church, deserted the camps of the Donatists. Among these, **Maximianus of Vaga**, a Bishop, earned a great and memorable name. After his conversion to the Church, when he was not received by the people with the affection that was appropriate, he consulted the good of peace and renounced his seat through a voluntary abdication, asking for another to be substituted in his place. He offered a petition on this subject to the **First Council of Milevum**, which was assembled during the fifth consulship of **Arcadius and Honorius**, on the **sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of Christ** 402. **Augustine and Alypius** celebrated this resolution of **Maximianus** with great praise in a letter to **Castorius**, the brother of **Maximianus** and his successor in the Episcopate. They write: "It is far more glorious to have laid down the burden of the episcopate for the sake of the Church to avoid dangers, than to have taken it up for the sake of exercising governance. For he demonstrates that he could have worthily received the honor if the requirement of peace allowed it, who does not unworthily defend what he received. Therefore, God wished to show the enemies of the Church, even through your brother, our son **Maximianus**, that there are those in the bowels of Christ who do not seek their own interests, but those of **Jesus Christ**. For he did not desert that ministry of dispensing the mysteries of God because he was overcome by some secular greed, but he laid it down moved by peaceful piety, lest because of his honor a foul and dangerous, or perhaps even ruinous, dissension should arise among the members of Christ."

<margin>VII. The monstrous license of the Donatists in recruiting converts.</margin>
VII. But just as this laudable example of a Catholic Bishop converted from a **Donatist** earned the praise of **Augustine**, so no words could sufficiently tear into the monstrous conduct of the **Donatists**, from which one may easily judge their character. For while they demand to be held as holier than others, they look down with a high brow upon Christians who are better than themselves but who shrink from schism. To such people they cry out, as it is in the Prophet: "Do not touch me, for I am holier than you" <note>original: "ne tangito me, quia sanctior te sum" — a reference to Isaiah 65:5.</note>. Meanwhile, they admit those who wish to involve themselves in their own minute super-

<page-num>621</page-num>
<header>On the Schism of the Donatists.</header>

<margin>Letter 168.</margin>
...they readily receive those involved in superstitious disputes just to increase their numbers. You may also see how these ill-intentioned deserters often find the cause for their dissent from the Church in their own lifestyle, which is so poorly aligned with the standard of the Gospel <term>standard of the Gospel; original: "Evangelii amussim" — an 'amussis' was a mason's rule or level, used here as a metaphor for moral perfection</term> that they dread the strict discipline of the Church, though she is their mother. I will explain the event in **Augustine’s** words: *A young man is rebuked by his Bishop; he is maddened by frequent beatings of his mother, and does not pull back his impious hands from the very womb that bore him, even on those days when the severity of the law spares even the most wicked criminals <note>original: "legum severitas sceleratissimis parcit" — likely referring to the Lenten season or public festivals when executions and corporal punishments were legally suspended.</note>. He threatens his mother that he will cross over to the party of **Donatus**, and that he will kill her whom he usually beats with unbelievable fury. He threatens her; he crosses to the party of **Donatus**; he is rebaptized in his madness; and while still raging for his mother's blood, he is made white in white garments <note>original: "albis vestibus candidatur" — the traditional white robes worn by those newly baptized to symbolize purity.</note>. He is placed within the chancel rails <note>original: "intra cancellos" — the screened-off area of the church reserved for clergy, indicating he was given a position of honor.</note>, prominent and conspicuous; and he who meditates on matricide is presented to the eyes of all who groan for him as if he were a man renewed. Oh, the monstrous license and madness of hypocrites in winning over proselytes for themselves!*

<margin>VIII. Of another Council of Carthage regarding the Donatists.</margin>
VIII. In the following year, 403 AD, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September <note>August 25th</note>, a general Council was again held in Africa at **Carthage**. There it was decreed that each of the **Orthodox** Bishops, either by himself or joined by a neighboring colleague, should meet the leaders of the **Donatists** in his own city; and in other cities, he should ensure they are met through the local magistrates or elders. A formula for this meeting was also established in the **Synod**, which proceeded in this manner:

<margin>African Council, Chapter 59.</margin>
> We meet with you, sent by the authority of the **Catholic Council**, desiring to rejoice in your correction, and mindful of the charity of the Lord, who said, *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God*, and who also warned through the Prophet to say even to those who say *they are not our brothers: You are our brothers.* Therefore, you ought not to despise this peaceful communion of ours, which comes from charity. If you think you possess any truth, do not hesitate to assert it; that is, once your Council has gathered, choose from among yourselves those to whom you may entrust the defense of your position. We shall do the same, so that from our Council men may also be chosen who, at a set time and place, may peacefully discuss with those you have selected whatever question it is that separates your communion from us. Thus, at long last, with the help of our God, this long-standing error may come to an end, lest because of the stubbornness of men, our weak and ignorant people should perish in sacrilegious dissent. For if you receive this in a brotherly spirit, the truth will easily become known.

And thus far is the formula for the Meeting.

<margin>IX. Of Crispinus, Donatist Bishop of Calama</margin>
IX. However much this contains of the spirit of the Lord and the gentleness of His bride <note>A common theological metaphor for the Church.</note>, the responses given by those hot-headed men when so addressed contained just as much of the pride of the enemy. Let **Crispinus**, the **Donatist** Bishop of **Calama**, serve as an example...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER V.

<margin>Foolish pride against Possidius.</margin> ...the proud stupidity of the Donatist <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who claimed that only they were the "pure" church, refusing to recognize the validity of sacraments administered by those who had wavered during earlier Roman persecutions.</note>; who, when he was fraternally invited to a meeting by *Possidius*, the Orthodox Bishop of the same city—a man of exceptional modesty—first deferred the matter to his own Council, promising that he would deliberate with his followers there on what answer he should give. Thus far, it was not entirely handled poorly; this can certainly be tolerated. But when, after a delay of no small amount of time, he was approached again, he responded with these words: *“Do not fear the words of a sinful man.”* <note>original: "Verba viri peccatoris ne timueris" — a quote from 1 Maccabees 2:62.</note> And again, *“Take care not to say anything in the ears of the unwise, lest when he hears it he mocks your sensible words.”* <note>original: "in aures imprudentis cave ne quicquam dixeris..." — a quote from Proverbs 23:9.</note> Finally, I define this response of mine in Patriarchal language: *“Let the wicked depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways.”* <note>original: "Recedant a me impii, vias eorum nosse nolo" — an echo of Psalm 119:115 and Job 21:14.</note> These things, which were conducted and recorded in the Proconsular Acts <term>Proconsular Acts; original: "Acta Proconsularia" — the official legal records of the Roman provincial government</term> and are recounted from them by **Augustine**, how turgid they are! With what an inflated mind and swelling spirit were they delivered? How unworthy they are of Christian humility and gentleness!
<margin>Against Cresconius, Book III, Chapter XLVI.</margin>

<margin>X. The furious violence of another Crispinus against the same [Possidius].</margin> X. From this humility, the deed of another *Crispinus* departed by no small distance. He was a Priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> of this sect and was said to be a relative of the [Donatist] Bishop. When he saw that his own Bishop was not prevailing in debate—whose long years of learning, as it was regarded among his own people, were so openly yielding to a novice like *Possidius*—he decided he must act with open force. Therefore, when *Possidius* was setting out on a journey to some place, *Crispinus* set an ambush with an armed band of men from his faction. When these men were spotted and reported, *Possidius* fled to a certain estate, where he believed either that the man would dare nothing further, or that he would not prevail; certainly, if he did anything, he would be unable to deny it. But the other, following immediately with a maddened mind, now thought it shameful to hide. Soon he surrounded the house in which *Possidius* had shut himself with his companions with armed men, battered it with stones, encircled it with flames, and forced an entry from every side. The prayers of the inhabitants were in vain, as were the attempts to extinguish the fires. He pressed on with his undertaking no less sluggishly: equally fervent and inexorable. The door gave way to the blows; they entered, and after slaughtering the pack animals they found in the lower part of the house, they dragged the Bishop down from the upper rooms, heavily burdened with blows and insults, nearly casting him down headlong. *Crispinus* himself finally intervened where they might have turned more cruelly violent, seemingly moved by the pleas of others—though he appeared not so much to care for mercy in his anger as to dread the testimony of his crime.

<margin>XI. For whom, nevertheless, Possidius intercedes before the Proconsul.</margin> XI. Laws were not lacking by which such crimes could be punished, but as if they were lacking, they remained quiet in the hands of the Orthodox, who preferred to demonstrate their own gentleness rather than punish the audacity of the others. The Proconsul, having understood all the facts, imposed a fine of only ten pounds of gold upon *Crispinus*; yet, because *Possidius* interceded on his behalf, he was not compelled to pay it. Several times the Catholics displayed a similar equity.

<header>Concerning the DONATIST SCHISM.</header>
<meta>catchword: They are said [to have...]</meta>

# CHAPTER VI.

## Imperial Edicts against the Donatists.

*I. The African Fathers, having applied milder remedies in vain, finally implore the authority of the Emperors against the Donatists. II. III. IV. Three edicts of Honorius against them. V. The Fathers pleaded against the excessive severity of these edicts. VI. The minds of the Emperors were provoked by the crimes of the Donatists. VII. Those who, having evaded the edicts, continued to rage against the Catholics. VIII. Hence a new complaint and stricter Edicts.*

---

<margin>I. The African Fathers, having applied milder remedies in vain, finally implore the authority of the Emperors against the Donatists.</margin>
I. However, so far were the minds of the *Donatists* <note>A breakaway Christian sect in North Africa that claimed only they were the true church.</note> from being softened by these measures, that on the contrary, the efforts of these stubborn men withdrew even further from unity. Therefore, the African Fathers, indignant at such great obstinacy, decreed another embassy to the Emperor Honorius <note>Western Roman Emperor (reigned 395–423 AD).</note> at another Council held in Carthage in the year 404. By this mission, they intended to both commend the pursuit of unity and request punishments against the persistent spirits of the *Donatists* and the fury of the *Circumcellions* <note>A radical, often violent group of wandering Donatist extremists known for attacking Catholic clergy and property.</note>. This is fully evident from Canon 93, where among other things they say:

> *The Donatists, having spurned peaceful conference, have turned to immense violence, so that they have overwhelmed many Bishops and many Clerics (to say nothing of the Laity) with ambushes, and have even invaded some Churches and attempted to invade others.*

And soon after:

> *For the detestable band of the Circumcellions is well known and often denounced in laws; they rage with a madness that has been condemned by frequent sanctions of religious leaders and even of Princes. Against their fury, we ask to obtain protections that are neither unusual nor foreign to the Holy Scriptures.*

Among other things, they also decreed to petition that the Law—which denies Heretics the ability to receive or leave anything through gifts or Wills—should be renewed by the Emperors' piety, so as to take away the right of leaving or receiving from those who, blinded by the fury of stubbornness, choose to persevere in the error of the *Donatists*.

<margin>II. Three edicts of Honorius against them.</margin>
II. By that embassy, the Catholics obtained three edicts from Honorius against the rebaptizing <note>The Donatists insisted that any Catholic joining them had to be "re-baptized," as they considered Catholic sacraments invalid; this was a major point of theological conflict.</note> Donatists, issued on the day before the Ides of February [February 12] at Ravenna, during the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius—that is, in the year 405. In the second of these, which is the most comprehensive of all, after having said:

> *We have seen fit to extirpate the adversaries of the Catholic faith by the authority of this decree: and therefore we have decided that this sect, which preferred the title of "schism" <note>A "schism" was generally seen as a formal split over discipline, whereas "heresy" was a split over core doctrine. The Emperor here refuses to accept their milder self-definition.</note> so as not to be called a "Heresy," must be specifically forbidden by a new constitution.*

For they are said to have progressed so far into crime...

It marks a turning point where the Roman state officially classified the Donatists as heretics, stripping them of legal rights regarding inheritance and property.</summary>

BOOK IV. CHAPTER V.

<margin>The foolish pride shown toward Possidius.</margin>
...the proud foolishness of the Donatist <note>A member of a North African Christian sect that broke away from the Catholic Church over issues of clerical purity; they were known for their uncompromising and often hostile stance toward mainstream Christians.</note>; for when he was brotherly challenged by Possidius, the Orthodox <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the Catholic Church in communion with the bishop of Rome, as opposed to the Donatist schismatics.</note> Bishop of that same city—a man of exceptional modesty—he first deferred to his own Council, promising that he would deliberate there with his followers on what answer he should give. Up to this point, it was not entirely handled badly. This much can certainly be tolerated. But when, after a delay of no small time, he was addressed again, he replied with these words: *“Do not fear the words of a sinful man.”* <note>original: "Verba viri peccatoris ne timueris"</note> And again: *“Take care that you say nothing into the ears of an unwise person, lest when he hears it, he mocks your sensible words.”* <note>original: "in aures imprudentis cave ne quicquam dixeris, ne quum audierit irrideat sensatos sermones tuos" — a paraphrase of Proverbs 23:9.</note> <margin>Against Cresconius, Book III, Chapter 46.</margin> Finally, I define this response of mine with the words of the Psalmist: *“Let the wicked depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways.”* <note>original: "Recedant a me impii, vias eorum nosse nolo" — a variation of Psalm 119:115.</note> These things, which were done and written in the Proconsular Acts <note>Official records of the Roman provincial government.</note> and are recounted from them by Augustine, how turgid they are, and with what an inflated mind and swelling spirit were they uttered? How unworthy they are of Christian humility and gentleness?

<margin>X. The furious violence of the other Crispinus against the same man.</margin>
X. From which humility the deed of the other Crispinus—who was a Presbyter <note>A priest or elder within the church hierarchy.</note> of the former man and said to be a relative—departed by no small distance. He, when he saw that his own Bishop was not prevailing in speech—whose learned old age, as it was regarded among his own people, so openly yielded to a "recruit" of yesterday such as Possidius proved to be—decided he must act with open force. Therefore, when Possidius was setting out on a journey to some place or other, Crispinus set an ambush with an armed band of men from his faction. When these men were spotted and reported, Possidius fled to a certain farm, where he believed either that the man would dare nothing or that he would not prevail; certainly, if he did do something, he could not deny it. But that man, immediately infected with a maddened mind, now thought it shameful to hide. Soon he began to surround the house in which Possidius had shut himself with his companions with armed men, to pelt it with stones, to encircle it with flames, and to force an entrance from every side. The prayers of the inhabitants were in vain; the attempts to extinguish the fires were in vain. He pressed on with his undertakings no less sluggishly, being equally fervent and inexorable. The door gave way to the blows; they entered, and after slaughtering the beasts of burden they found in the lower part of the house, they all but cast down the Bishop from the upper rooms, having heavily burdened him with blows and insults. That they did not rage even more severely was due to the intervention of Crispinus himself, who acted as if moved by the pleas of others; though it seemed he cared not so much for their entreaties in his anger, as he feared the testimony against his crime.

<margin>XI. Nevertheless, Possidius intercedes for him before the Proconsul.</margin>
XI. There was no lack of laws by which such crimes could be punished; but, as if they were lacking, they lay dormant in the hands of the Orthodox, who preferred to demonstrate their own gentleness rather than punish the audacity of the others. The Proconsul, having understood all the facts, imposed a fine of only ten pounds of gold upon Crispinus; however, because Possidius interceded, he was not compelled to pay it. The Catholics demonstrated similar equity <note>Fairness or mercy that goes beyond the strict letter of the law.</note> on several occasions.

# On the Schism of the Donatists.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### Imperial Edicts against the Donatists.

> I. The African Fathers, having used gentler remedies in vain, finally implore the authority of the Emperors against the Donatists. II. III. IV. Three edicts of Honorius against them. V. The Fathers pleaded against the excessive severity of these edicts. VI. The minds of the Emperors were embittered by the crimes of the Donatists. VII. Those who, having eluded the edicts, continued to rage against the Catholics. VIII. Hence new complaints and more severe Edicts.

<margin>I. The African Fathers, having used gentler remedies in vain, finally implore the authority of the Emperors against the Donatists.</margin>
I. However, the minds of the **Donatists** <note>A breakaway Christian sect in North Africa that claimed only they were the "true" pure church, rejecting any clergy who had wavered during earlier Roman persecutions.</note> were so far from being softened by these measures that, on the contrary, the efforts of these stubborn men withdrew even further from unity. Therefore, the African Fathers, indignant at such great obstinacy, decreed a mission to the Emperor Honorius during another Council held at Carthage in the **year 404**. This mission was intended to both commend their own desire for unity and to request punishments against the persistent spirits of the **Donatists** and the fury of the **Circumcellions** <note>Extremist bands associated with the Donatists, often described as violent wandering monks who attacked Catholic clergy and property.</note>. This is fully evident from Canon 93, where among other things they say: *“The Donatists, having despised a peaceful conference, have turned to monstrous violences, such that they have overwhelmed many Bishops and many Clerics (to say nothing of the Laity) with ambushes, and have even invaded some Churches and attempted to invade others.”* And soon after: *“For the detestable band of the Circumcellions who rage is well known and often denounced by laws, which has been condemned by frequent sanctions of the Religious Princes; we ask to obtain protections against their fury that are neither unusual nor foreign to the holy scriptures.”* Among other things, they also decided to petition that the Law—which denies heretics the capacity to receive or leave anything through gifts or wills—be extended by his Piety's authority, so as to take away the right of leaving or receiving property from those who, blinded by the fury of stubbornness, wish to persevere in the error of the Donatists.

<margin>II. Three edicts against them.</margin>
II. Through that mission, the Catholics obtained three edicts from Honorius against the Donatist "rebaptizers" <note>Donatists believed Catholic baptism was invalid and forced converts to be baptized again, a practice the mainstream Church considered a grave sacrilege.</note>, issued on **February 12th at Ravenna, during the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius** <note>original: "Prid. Id. Feb. Rav. Stilicone II, & Honorii Anthemio Coss." — Stilicho was a high-ranking general and regent for the young Emperor Honorius.</note>. This was in the year 405. In the second of these edicts, which is the most comprehensive of all, after having said: *“We have provided by the authority of this decree to uproot the adversaries of the Catholic faith: and therefore we have decided that this sect should be specially forbidden by a new constitution, which, to avoid being called a heresy, preferred the name of a schism.”* For they are said to have progressed into such great crime...

BOOK IV. CHAPTER VI.

...those whom they call **Donatists** <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa that claimed to be the only true, pure church and practiced the rebaptism of those who joined them from the Catholic Church.</note>, so that *they repeat the sacrosanct Baptism after the mysteries have been trampled upon, with harmful boldness, and infect men who were once washed by the gift of Divinity (as has been handed down) with the contagion of a profane repetition.* <note>original Latin: "Baptisma sacrosanctum mysteriis recalcatis, temeritate noxia, iterent, & homines semel, ut traditum est, munere Divinitatis ablutos, contagione profanae repetitionis infecerint."</note> Thus it happened that a heresy was born from a schism. Soon after, he adds a penal sanction: *Wherefore we decree by this law, that whoever hereafter shall be detected to have rebaptized, shall be brought before the Judge who presides over the Province, so that, punished by the confiscation of all his goods, he may suffer the penalty of poverty, by which he shall be perpetually afflicted. Provided that for their children, if they dissent from the wickedness of their father’s society, those things which were their father's shall not be lost.* These are found in *Book 16 of the **Theodosian Code**, Title 6, Law 4.* <note>The Theodosian Code was a compilation of laws of the Roman Empire under the Christian emperors since 312.</note>

III. Another *Edict* was added, given on the same day against the *Donatist Agitators* <note>original: "Turbones Donatisticos." The term suggests "whirlwinds" or "instigators of crowds."</note>, in the same Book, *Title 5, Law 38: Let no one recall the **Manichaean** <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that the Roman state considered particularly dangerous and often grouped with other "heretics."</note>, let no one recall the **Donatist**, who especially (as we have found) do not cease to rage.* This means, as the commentator <note>scholiastes</note> well observes, that they are not permitted to exist at all—indeed, that they should not even be named any longer. And shortly after: *But if anyone should dare to involve himself in interdicted and illicit acts, he shall not escape the snares of both the innumerable past constitutions and the law recently brought forth by our Clemency; and if crowds should assemble, the instigator of the sedition should not doubt that the stings of a sharper punishment must be brought forth. Given at Ravenna on the day before the Ides [February 12], in the second consulship of Stilicho and Anthemius, in the year 405.*

IV. Another law followed in the same year, on the 6th day before the Ides of December [December 8]: *We decree that the heretics of the Donatist superstition, in whatever place, whether confessing or convicted, shall pay the due penalty without delay, the tenor of the law being observed.* Truly, the gold fine <term>multa auraria</term> <note>A specific fine paid in gold coins, usually reserved for serious administrative or religious offenses.</note> of ten pounds of gold imposed by **Theodosius the Great** <note>The Roman Emperor (reigned 379–395) who made Nicene Christianity the state religion.</note> upon the clerical ministers of heretics in the year 392, is extended by this constitution of his son **Honorius** to the **Donatist Heretics**, who nevertheless denied that they were heretics. However, as **Gothofredus** <note>Jacques Gothofredus (1587–1652), a famous jurist and commentator on the Theodosian Code.</note> observes, by this word "Heretics," it seems the Ministers, Clerics, and Bishops of the Donatists are to be understood. For this penalty was not imposed on all Donatists by this law, nor were all Donatists fined; for that was finally done in *Laws 52 and 54*, of which we shall speak in their proper time.

<margin>V. The Fathers pleaded against the excessive severity of these edicts.</margin>
V. I find that the Emperor generally proceeded a little further in his edicts than the prayers of the churchmen requested; for in that same Canon of their council which we praised above, they decreed that it should also be asked that they command the law to be confirmed—the one promulgated by their father **Theodosius** of religious memory regarding the ten pounds of gold against heretical ordainers or those ordained, or even against owners of property where their congregation is discovered—in such a way that it would be effective against those on whose account the Catholics, provoked by their snares, had filed a formal protest <note>contestationem</note>. They hoped that at least by this terror...
