# ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

...retreat from schismatic or heretical depravity, those who ignore being improved and corrected by the consideration of eternal punishment. *Augustine* discusses these matters somewhat more extensively and distinctly in *Letter 50 to Boniface, Count of Military Affairs.* <note>original: "Augustinus Epist. L. ad Bonifacium, Comitem rei militaris." Augustine’s Letter 185 (formerly 50) is a famous defense of using imperial law to correct religious dissent.</note> There he mentions that it seemed to several brothers, among whom he himself was one, that although the madness of the Donatists was raging everywhere, *they should not ask the Emperors to order that the heresy itself should absolutely not exist, by establishing a punishment for those who wished to remain in it; but rather they should decree this: that those who were either preaching the Catholic truth by speaking or reading it by establishing it should not suffer their [the Donatists'] furious violence.* <note>original Latin: "non esse petendum ab Imperatoribus, ut ipsam hæresin juberent omnino non esse... sed hoc potius constituerent, ut eorum furiosas violentias non paterentur."</note> The African Fathers believed this could be done to some extent if the Emperors would confirm the law of Theodosius against Heretics in general—which fined any bishop or cleric ten pounds of gold wherever they were found—specifically against the Donatists in such a way *that not all should be struck by that fine, but only those in whose regions the Catholic Church suffered some violence from the Clerics, the **Circumcellions**, or their people; the Bishops or Ministers of those regions would be held responsible for paying the fine through the care of the local orders.* <note>The Circumcellions were bands of radical Donatist peasants known for violent attacks on Catholic clergy and property.</note> For the Fathers thought that if they were terrified and dared to do no such thing, THE CATHOLIC TRUTH COULD BE FREELY TAUGHT AND HELD, SO THAT NO ONE WOULD BE FORCED INTO IT, BUT WHOEVER WANTED TO COULD FOLLOW IT WITHOUT FEAR, LEST THEY SHOULD HAVE FALSE AND PRETENDED CATHOLICS. This was certainly their opinion in the Council.

<margin>VI. The hearts of the Emperors were embittered by the crimes of the Donatists.</margin>
VI. But very serious complaints from Bishops had reached the legates from other places; these bishops had suffered many evils from them and had been driven out of their seats. Especially the horrific and unbelievable slaughter of **Maximianus**, the Catholic Bishop of the Church of *Vaga*, embittered the hearts of the Emperors. <note>Vaga is modern-day Béja, Tunisia. Maximianus was reportedly brutally beaten and left for dead by Donatist attackers.</note> Thus it happened that before the arrival of the legates, a law was promulgated stating that *a heresy of such monstrosity—to which it seemed more cruel to show mercy than the heresy itself was savage—should not only be prevented from being violent, but should not be allowed to exist with impunity at all.* Not, however, by capital punishment, so that Christian mercy might be preserved even toward the unworthy: but by proposing financial losses and decreeing exile for their Bishops or ministers.

<margin>VII. Those who, having eluded the edicts, continued to rage against Catholics.</margin>
VII. But indeed, the Emperors did not profit from all these edicts to the point that they saw the stubbornness of the Donatists restrained. On the contrary, they found or made a way for themselves to escape. Here was the pretext: after **Stilicho** was killed in the year 408, the Pagans and Heretics immediately began to boast that the laws passed against them were not so much those of Honorius as of Stilicho. <note>Stilicho was a high-ranking general and regent who was executed for treason, after which many of his policies were challenged.</note> For they claimed the Emperor, driven by Stilicho's authority, had only lent his name to them. Hence they intended that the laws were void and should be rescinded along with the other acts of Stilicho. Indeed, on this occasion...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER VI.

The Catholics dared to rise up, and [the Donatists] attempted to use force against them: to such an extent, indeed, that the Donatists killed several of the Catholic Bishops throughout Africa.

<margin>VIII. From this arose new complaints and stricter edicts.</margin>

VIII. From this arose new complaints, both in a letter from *Augustine* to *Olympius*—the Count and Master of Offices—(Letter 129), and to *Donatus*, the Proconsul of Africa, as well as from other Bishops to the Emperor. In these, they requested that the ancient laws be renewed and confirmed. *Augustine*, however, carefully took precautions that they should not be punished with the death penalty.

> *We ask (thus he writes to the Proconsul) that when you hear the cases of the Church, no matter how wicked the injuries you find it has suffered or been targeted by, you forget that you have the power of execution, and do not forget our request.* <note>Augustine was famous for his "plea for leniency" (intercessio), arguing that while the state should restrain heretics, it should not execute them, as the Church sought their conversion, not their death.</note>

Furthermore, when these matters had been reported to the Emperor, it seemed appropriate to look after the Republic and the peace of the Church with three edicts. The first was given on the 15th of November at *Rome, during the consulship of Bassus and Philippus*, in the year 408. <note>original: "xvii. Kal. Dec." By Roman inclusive counting, this is the 15th of November.</note>

> *All things which have been decreed by us by the authority of general laws against the Donatists (who are also called Mountaineers), the Manichaeans, or the Priscillianists, or against the Pagans, we decree not only shall remain in force, but shall be brought to the fullest execution and effect.* <note>The "Mountaineers" (Montenses) was a nickname for the Donatists in Rome because they gathered on a hill outside the city. The Manichaeans and Priscillianists were other groups deemed heretical by the state.</note>

Soon after:

> *Furthermore, the proposed law must hold as convicted those who have confessed themselves to be Donatists, or have refused the communion of the Catholics under the pretext of religion, even though they pretend to be Christians.*

The second [was given] on the 24th of November of the same year.

> *A new audacity of the Donatists, the Heretics, and the Jews has been uncovered (that is, has been revealed): that they wish to disturb the sacraments of the Catholic faith. Your Gravity shall see to it that this pestilence and contagion does not spread further.*

For this is how the most learned Scholiast <note>A "scholiast" is an ancient or medieval commentator on a text; here referring to a legal scholar.</note> corrects the corrupted passage.

> *Therefore, against those who have attempted anything contrary and opposed to the Catholic sect, we command that the punishment of just legal action be brought forth.*

Gothofredus <note>Jacques Godefroy (1587–1652), a famous jurist and editor of the Theodosian Code.</note> warns that the death penalty is indicated by these words. Soon a third edict was added on the 27th of November.

> *The watch of the Defenders, the City Councilors, and all Offices shall guard against anyone within any city, or in any secret part of a territory, who dissents from the priest of the Catholic Church, having the opportunity for unlawful assembly. We also decree that the places themselves be joined to public law [confiscated], with every excuse set aside; and those who dare to dispute and assert things which Divine institution condemns shall be driven into proscription and exile.*

In the following year, the Emperor, lest the Donatists or other heretics should think that the statutes of the laws previously passed against them had grown cold, stated:

> *Let all Judges know,* says the Emperor, *that they must obey these commands with faithful devotion, and they should not doubt that whatever we have decreed against them must be executed among the highest priorities. But if any of the Judges should omit the execution of the present law through a pretense of ignorance, let him know that, having lost his rank, he will undergo a more severe movement of our Clemency.* <note>original: "nostræ Clementiæ." A formal title for the Emperor.</note>

Finally, the extreme point of severity was reached in the year 410, by Law 51: by which it is provided that the Donatists, enemies of the sacred law, are to be punished with the penalty of—

<margin>I. The Conference at Carthage was arranged primarily by Augustine.</margin>
I. These edicts of the Emperors against the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who believed the church must be pure and that sacraments performed by "lapsed" priests were invalid.</note> were indeed severe, and truly too severe. But the Catholics promised themselves more good from a "Friendly Conference." Therefore, the Catholics used imperial edicts to compel the Donatists to attend the very Conference they were trying to avoid. From this was born that famous **CONFERENCE AT CARTHAGE**, about which we must now speak diligently. Possidius <note>Possidius was the Bishop of Calama and a close friend and biographer of Augustine.</note>, who was present, writes that it was arranged chiefly by Augustine to the great benefit of the Church, with the help (as he says) of the most glorious and religious Emperor Honorius. To accomplish this, Honorius even sent the Tribune and Notary Marcellinus from his own side to Africa as a judge. Indeed, on the advice of Augustine, the African Catholics sent legates to Italy to Honorius to request this. For they saw that without the authority and protection of the Prince <note>Referring to the Emperor Honorius.</note>, such a meeting could not be called, nor the adversaries forced to attend, nor could they be kept from evading the discussion.

<margin>II. While the Donatists pretended to seek the same thing.</margin>
II. But Marcellinus also records in his own edict, which he ordered to be read at the Conference, that the Donatists had requested the same. He says, "The harmonious petition of both parties has called forth this imperial decision." For just as the Conference was recently requested by the Catholics, so too there is no doubt that a very short time ago the Donatist Bishops requested a Conference in a trial before illustrious powers. And because the imperial clemency <note>A standard honorific for the Emperor's administrative grace and mercy.</note> freely granted its assent and decreed that a universal council be held within Africa, with both sides equally requesting it, etc. However, there is no doubt that the Donatists did this deceptively and with malicious intent; they made it clear through all their actions how much they abhorred a legitimate Conference. But it must be attributed to the prudence of Marcellinus that, by ignoring the tricks of these shifty men, he craftily ensnared them with their own words, as if those words had come from a sincere heart.

<margin>III. But secretly against the authority of the Emperors.</margin>
III. Otherwise, they did not dare to publicly disapprove of the Conference requested from the Emperor, because they themselves had also requested it at one time, and [they were searching for a] cause... <note>original: "cauſſam"</note>

It notes that while the Donatists pretended to want the conference, they were actually attempting to evade a formal debate.</summary>

<header>Concerning the SCHISM of the DONATISTS.</header>

<margin>
Concerning those murmuring against authority in Ecclesiastical matters.
</margin>
Although they had previously referred the case of Caecilian <note>Caecilian was the Bishop of Carthage whose election in 311 AD sparked the Donatist schism.</note> to Constantine, they nevertheless secretly whispered some complaint. *Augustine says (in his book "After the Conference"): "They stir up hatred against us, because we are conducting the cause of the Church before the Emperor. Hence that saying of the Donatist Primian <note>Primian was the Donatist Bishop of Carthage during the time of Augustine.</note>: 'They carry the sacred decrees of many Emperors; we carry only the Gospels.'"* To the same point belongs another reproach of *Petilian* <note>Petilian of Constantine was a leading Donatist spokesperson and a former lawyer.</note>, mentioned elsewhere by *Augustine*: *"What have we to do with the Kings of this world, whom Christianity has never known except as enemies?"* <note>original: "Quid nobis cum Regibus seculi, quos nunquam Christianitas nisi invidos sensit?"</note> But truly, these claims are mere rust and the ink of the black cuttlefish <note>A Latin idiom meaning "pure malice" or "slander."</note>. For, as Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note> well observed in the Preface to Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*: *From the time they began to be Christians, the affairs of the church depended on them (the Emperors), and the greatest Synods were and are held by their judgment.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀφ' οὗ χρισιανίζειν ἤρξαντο, τὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας πράγματα ἐξ αὐτῶν (Βασιλέων) ἤρτητο, καὶ αἱ μέγιςαι Σύνοδοι τῇ αὐτῶν γνώμῃ γεγονάσί τε καὶ γίνονται."</note> The 103rd Chapter of Macarius of Ancyra <note>A Greek theologian and bishop.</note> is entirely about this: *That no one has the authority to command an Ecumenical or National Synod to be assembled, except the Emperor of the Romans.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι σύνοδον ὀικουμενικὴν ἢ τοπικὴν οὐδεὶς ἐπ' ἀδείας ἔχει προςάξαι συναθροισθῆναι, εἰ μὴ ὁ Βασιλεὺς τῶν Ῥωμαίων."</note> And there is no one even slightly learned who is ignorant of the fact that the first Ecumenical Councils were called in this way. Nor did the Orthodox ever hesitate, when the situation required it, to implore the authority of the Emperors to call Synods. This surely should have been enough for the Donatists, if anything could ever be enough for them.

<margin>
IV. Augustine records that this [authority] was implored by the Orthodox only out of compelling necessity. Book: *Against Julian*.
</margin>
IV. But *Augustine* also defends the Orthodox in another way in this matter—namely, out of necessity, which has no law. The Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who taught that human nature was not corrupted by original sin and that humans could choose good without special divine grace.</note>, after the provincial councils of the Bishops, appealed to some sort of "Ecumenical Synod," as they call it, and had obtained letters from the Emperor for that purpose. The Catholics refused this, understanding that it was sought no less deceitfully than ambitiously. The Pelagians raised the very example we are discussing. Augustine responds to them: *"Do not deceive yourselves or others, as if you have a voice against us such as we had against the Donatists, whom we compelled to come to the Conference by Imperial orders. For their madness had occupied all of Africa, and they would not allow the truth to be preached by Catholics against their error. They were devastating many things and terrifying everyone with violent attacks, robberies, lootings, fires, and murders. We could achieve nothing with them before the Bishops, whom we did not hold in common. What our ancestors had done with them nearly a hundred years before was no longer held in the memory of the people. Therefore, NECESSITY COMPELLED us, so that at last, with the Acts of our Conference completed, we might crush their shamelessness and restrain their boldness."*

<header>BOOK IV. CHAPTER VII.</header>

<margin>
V. Honorius's notable decree concerning the Conference.
</margin>
V. We have seen so far at whose request this conference was arranged. Now let us see by whose authority it was ordered and proclaimed. It was, as has been said several times already, the Emperor Honorius, from whose decree to Marcellinus <note>Marcellinus of Carthage was a high-ranking imperial official and friend of St. Augustine, appointed by Honorius to preside over the conference.</note> on this matter it is useful to excerpt a few things. It begins thus: *Among the greatest cares of our empire, reverence for the Catholic law <note>The "Catholic law" here refers to the official, orthodox Christian faith recognized by the Roman state.</note> is always either first or alone. For we do nothing else either by the labors of war or the counsels of peace, except to ensure that the devoted common people of our world guard the true worship of God.* <note>original: "Inter imperii nostri maximas curas, Catholicæ legis reverentia aut prima semper, aut sola est. Neque enim aliud aut belli laboribus agimus, aut pacis consiliis ordinamus, nisi ut verum Dei cultum orbis nostri plebs devota custodiat."</note> Soon he turns to the *Donatists*, complaining that they have stained Africa—that is, the greatest part of the Kingdom, and one faithfully serving in secular duties—with vain error and superfluous dissension. Then he says he must take care lest, if something were generated against the Catholic law during his time, posterity might impute it to him by a just judgment. Hence, out of a desire for peace and grace, he says he has freely admitted the delegation of the Venerable Bishops, which had desired that the Donatist Bishops be gathered for a meeting in a very famous city <note>Carthage</note>, so that, with priests chosen by each side, the manifest truth might refute superstition through held discussions. He orders this matter to be resolved within four months. But if within the prescribed time the eager Donatist Bishops should decline to meet, he wishes the time for the defiant ones to be concluded by a threefold edict of summons; once these have passed, if those summoned despise being present, he says, "let the people, who will have known their teachers were defeated by silence, yield along with the Churches, and let them eventually be grateful they were conquered, and let them know they must serve, if not our commands, then the true commands of the Catholic law."

<margin>
VI. During a most turbulent and hostile time.
</margin>
VI. But it is also worthwhile to learn at what time this Conference was instituted. From the inscription of the Records, it is clear that it was held "P.C.," that is, after the Consulate of VARANES, to indicate that year which followed his consulate. Furthermore, it is established from the Chronicle of Prosper and Cassiodorus <note>Two important 5th and 6th-century chroniclers who recorded the fall of Rome.</note> that the city of Rome was captured by the Goths during the consulate of Varanes and Tertullus. But because the memory of Tertullus was rarer and more obscure, it is written in Marcellinus’s Chronicle that it was captured during the sole consulate of Varanes. It was captured in the Year of Christ 410. Therefore, this Conference was held in the following year <note>411 AD</note>. Not without reason does Balduinus <note>François Baudouin (1520–1573), a renowned French jurist and historian of church law.</note> proclaim the admirable providence of God in this matter. Honorius was then residing at Ravenna, in the greatest disturbance and even desperation of his affairs, especially since Stilicho <note>The powerful general and regent Stilicho had been executed in 408, leaving the Western Empire vulnerable.</note> was already dead. The Goths had taken Rome and were devastating all of Italy, and they were threatening all the provinces of the Roman Empire. And yet, for all that, the unhappy and stunned Honorius did not fail to hear the prayers of the African Church. And finally, he seems to have taken greater care for that Church than for his own Rome and Italy.

### ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

Should this not rightly seem a marvel to anyone who knows how much this Prince <note>Referring to Emperor Honorius.</note> otherwise suffered from either sluggishness, laziness, or—to use *Cicero’s* word—carelessness, and how great the confusion of those times was?

<margin>VII. Emperors used to send Legates to be moderators of ecclesiastical assemblies.</margin>
**VII.** When *Constantine* had ordered the Synod to meet at *Tyre*, a city of *Syria*, to handle the case of *Athanasius* <note>Saint Athanasius (c. 296–373), the Bishop of Alexandria and a major figure in the defense of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>, he sent *Dionysius, a man of consular rank*, to be an observer of the proceedings, and especially of good order. <note>original Greek: "τῶν πραττομένων, ἐξαιρέτως δὲ τῆς εὐταξίας κατάσκοπον"</note> For thus says *Constantine’s* Letter to the Council, found in *Theodoret’s Ecclesiastical History, Book I, Chapter XXVII*. Therefore, when the Emperor was not free to be present himself, those who were sent in the Emperor's name to moderate those assemblies presided over such Disputations and Conferences concerning Religion.

<margin>VIII. Marcellinus was appointed as Investigator and Judge for this conference by Honorius.</margin>
**VIII.** The same thing was done here. For *Honorius* appointed *Marcellinus, a most distinguished man*, a <term>Tribune and Notary</term> <note>The rank of *Tribunus et Notarius* was a high-level imperial administrative post, often serving as a personal secretary or special envoy to the Emperor.</note>, as the <term>Investigator and Judge</term> <note>original: "Cognitorem & Judicem"</note> in this dispute. Indeed, this *Marcellinus* was conspicuous not only for his illustrious dignity but also for his many virtues and his dexterity in managing affairs. *Augustine* not only sent various letters to him but also inscribed his most select books to him: *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, against the Pelagians*; *On the Spirit and the Letter*; and especially those most learned books *On the City of God*, begun a little after the city <note>Rome, which fell to the Goths in 410 AD.</note> was captured, which was around the time of the *Conference of Carthage*. *Orosius* <note>Paulus Orosius, a historian and student of Augustine.</note> testifies that *he was a man of particular prudence and industry, and most eager for all good studies.* By these virtues, he managed to be promoted to the highest honors in the Republic.

<margin>IX. Adorned with the "Spectabilis" dignity of a Notary.</margin>
**IX.** For the office of the <term>Notaries</term> was of great dignity. They were the Emperor's private secretaries, as *Cassiodorus* teaches in his *Formulary, Book VI, Formula XVI*. That office brought with it Senatorial dignity and the honor of the <term>Spectabilis</term> rank. <note>A title of high nobility in the later Roman Empire, ranking between "Clarissimus" (Illustrious) and "Illustris" (Distinguished).</note> For the Catholic Bishops honored him with such a title in their letters. There exists in *Book XII of the Code, Title VII, Concerning the Primicerius and the Notaries*, where *Tribune-Notaries* are also discussed. *Theodosius* says: *The chief intention of our piety concerns the name of the Notaries.* And *Emperor Zeno* says: *We believe that the excellent and noble service of the Honorable Tribune-Notaries, who bring no small benefit and ornament to the Republic by their glorious obedience, should be fortified and increased by various titles of benefit.*

<margin>X. In what sense he was given as an Investigator.</margin>
**X.** Therefore, *Honorius* gave such a great and significant man as the INVESTIGATOR for this case: for he is called by this name throughout the Conference. *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> defines the function of the Investigator's role in the year 411 thus: *namely, that it is his duty to manage those things which pertain to peace and a quiet assembly, and to ensure...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the role of Marcellinus as the imperial moderator at the Conference of Carthage (411 AD). It explores the specific nature of his judicial authority and his diplomatic efforts to ensure the Donatists' attendance.</meta>

<page-num>632</page-num>
<header>BOOK IV. CHAPTER VII.</header>

...and that nothing should be done in a tumultuous or disorderly manner among the bishops conferring with one another, nor should anything be attempted through force or evil deceit by either party, and that in all things the agreed-upon pacts should be preserved **intact and well-maintained**. <note>original Latin: "sarta tecta," a legal idiom meaning "in good repair" or "fully preserved."</note> In the proper arranging of these matters, he was to have the faculty of interjecting—not indeed according to his own whim, but as justice itself demanded—and finally, he was to pronounce which of the two parties held the stronger legal rights.

<margin>XI. Also a Judge.</margin>
**XI.** Furthermore, in the imperial decree of *Honorius*, *Marcellinus* is called a **JUDGE**: *“In which disputation we wish you to preside as **JUDGE** in the first place.”* *Balduinus* <note>François Baudouin (1520–1573), a famous jurist and historian who wrote extensively on the Donatist schism.</note> explains the meaning of these words by saying that, since the *Donatists* were merely repeating old arguments, *Marcellinus* was an arbiter of law that was by no means new or doubtful. He was an investigator of **fact** rather than of **law**, and was granted an **investigation** <note>original: "cognitionem"</note> rather than full **jurisdiction**. Finally, he was given his role "with a formula," just as in former times private judges of private matters were appointed by a <term>Praetor</term> <note>A Roman magistrate who oversaw the administration of justice.</note>. Yet even here, *Marcellinus* did not wish to sit unless the participants were also seated; whereas in a civil trial, the Judge sits alone while the litigants are ordered to stand. Finally, he conducted himself as *Constantine* did at the *Council of Nicaea*, sitting on the lowest bench. So says *Balduinus*.

<margin>XII. His remarkable courtesy to entice the Donatists to the Conference.</margin>
**XII.** It is truly incredible with what great equity, courtesy, and indulgence *Marcellinus* acted to entice the *Donatists* to the assembly and Conference. First, in the very same edict or imperial order by which he summoned them, he ensured that the **Basilicas** <note>In this context, the church buildings that had been seized or contested.</note> were returned to those who promised they would come. Then, he thought it a necessary concession that they might choose for themselves any Judge they wished to be appointed alongside him for the judgment. Regarding himself, he promised by **oath** that he would judge nothing except what the truth persuaded him. He added many other things suitable for soothing their minds. And as much as can be gathered from *Augustine*, he also performed this duty of kindness for them: he summoned them through <term>Tractoriae</term> letters. <margin>Against the Donatists, After the Conference, Chapter XXIV.</margin> As we recently explained, these letters granted them use of the **public transport system** and supplied them with an abundance of everything necessary for their travel.

<margin>XIII. The differing arrivals of the Donatists and the Catholics into the City.</margin>
**XIII.** Enticed by so many inducements, the *Donatists* finally came to *Carthage*, one hundred and fifty-nine in number, but with such a grand and showy procession that they turned the eyes and minds of that great city toward themselves. They boasted that they had more than four hundred bishops, but claimed many were detained at home by various infirmities or necessities and could not be present. The **Catholics**, though more numerous, entered *Carthage* separately and one by one to avoid any display unworthy of Christian character—unlike the prideful *Donatists*. There were two hundred and eighty-six of them, while nearly a hundred had remained in their own churches, hindered by old age and illness.

<margin>XIV. The meeting place defined at the Baths of Gargilius.</margin>
**XIV.** First, before they formally convened, there was a deliberation about deciding on the meeting place. They reached the opinion that the assembly should be held in the **Baths of Gargilius** <note>The *Thermae Gargilianae* were large public baths in Carthage, often used for major public gatherings due to their size and central location.</note>. This place was in the very heart of the city itself, spacious, well-lit, and providing a safe refuge against the summer heat. The **Donatists** were not pleased with the Basilica of Faustus or of Restitutus, in which many Carthaginian Synods are recorded to have been held. For they shuddered at the churches of the Catholics, which they falsely claimed were "Synagogues of Satan" <note>original Latin: "Satanæ Synagogas." The Donatists viewed the mainstream Catholic Church as corrupted by those who had surrendered sacred books during the Great Persecution.</note>. Hence it happened that as often as they gained possession of them by invasion, they would not claim them for themselves unless they had been washed, purified, and the altars demolished, along with other lustrations <note>Ritual purifications intended to "cleanse" a space of perceived spiritual pollution.</note> applied in their own manner.

<margin>XV. Number of participants on each side restricted to 18.</margin>
**XV.** The next deliberation was concerning the number of those who would have a place in the public meetings. For **Marcellinus** proposed that, to prevent the riot that easily arises from too great a crowd of people flocking together, eighteen chosen from each side—thirty-six in total—should enter the place of the session. The duties were divided such that seven from each side were assigned to the debate; the same number, when needed, to writing; and the remaining four would oversee the transcribing and guarding of the **Acts** <note>The "Acts" (*Acta*) refers to the official legal record of the proceedings.</note>.

<margin>XVI. The remarkable fairness of the Catholics regarding this matter.</margin>
**XVI.** At first, the **Donatists** refused to do this, requesting free and open access to the assembly for all their members. The **Catholics** declared in a letter that they would obey Marcellinus in all things; however, they bound themselves in that same letter to offer every grace to the Donatists. Indeed, they went so far as to say that it would not be their fault if all the Donatists did not enter the place designated for the meeting; but that they themselves were ready to have no more than eighteen come.

<margin>XVII. An even greater and almost incredible [fairness] concerning the principal cause.</margin>
**XVII.** Finally, when Marcellinus had signaled to both parties that each should set forth in writing what they thought would lead to holding the Conference peacefully, the Catholic bishops—nearly three hundred of them—agreed among themselves by common consent to promise the Donatists: if they were overcome by the Donatists' arguments, they would voluntarily resign from the **Episcopacy** <note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note>; but if they won, and the Donatists returned to union, none of them would be deprived of the honor of the Episcopacy. Instead, the Donatist bishop would sit in the same church together with the Catholic bishop as a partner in honor and duty, with each anticipating the other with mutual honor. For, they said, **"where the command of charity has dilated hearts, the possession of peace does not become narrow."** <note>original: "ubi præceptio charitatis dilataverit corda, possessio pacis non fit angusta." This poetic phrase suggests that spiritual love creates enough room for everyone.</note> Furthermore, if it happened that one of the two died, thereafter single bishops would succeed one another in the ancient manner. And if by chance the congregations were satisfied with single bishops and could not tolerate the partnership of two in such an unusual state of affairs...

<margin>XVIII. And this, with finally no one dissenting, was the [will] of all.</margin>
**XVIII.** This was truly a great thing, and it seemed hardly obtainable from such a great multitude of men, among whom it is rare not to find some who are unwilling, for the sake of another’s favor, to deprive themselves of their own comforts. When the matter was first discussed, those who were most ready to sacrifice their own interests for peace, as *Augustine* confesses, were silently marking in their minds some from whom they hardly dared hope to obtain this. However, when it was publicly referred to the universal Council of nearly three hundred Bishops, it so pleased everyone, and they all burned with such passion, that they were ready to lay down their **Episcopacy** <term>The office or rank of a bishop</term> for the sake of Christ’s unity—not to lose it, but to commend it more safely to God. Scarcely two were found there who were displeased: one aged old man, who even dared to speak this more freely; the other signified his will with a silent face. But after the fraternal correction of all overwhelmed that old man speaking so freely, as he changed his opinion, this other one also changed his expression. These things *Augustine* [records] in *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* <note>original: "De Gestis cum Emerito." This is a work by St. Augustine documenting his debate with the Donatist bishop Emeritus.</note>.

<margin>XIX. Their excellent speech to Marcellinus.</margin>
**XIX.** Excellent are the words with which they explained their mind to **Marcellinus** <note>Flavius Marcellinus, the imperial representative sent by Emperor Honorius to preside over the conference.</note>, and worthy to be proposed as an example to all faithful ministers of Christ the Lord.

-> "For why," they speak thus, "should we hesitate to offer the sacrifice of this humility to our Redeemer? Did he truly descend from the heavens into human limbs so that we might be his members, and shall we, lest his very members be torn apart by cruel division, fear to descend from our chairs? <note>original: "de cathedris descendere." The "cathedra" is the bishop's seat of authority.</note> For ourselves, nothing is more sufficient than that we be faithful and obedient Christians. Let us, therefore, always be this. We are ordained as Bishops, however, for the sake of Christian peoples. What, therefore, benefits Christian peoples for Christian peace, let us do this concerning our Episcopacy. If we are useful servants, why do we envy the Lord’s eternal gains for the sake of our temporal heights? The Episcopal dignity will be more fruitful for us if, by being laid aside, it gathers Christ’s flock, rather than dispersing it by being retained. <note>original: "Episcopalis dignitas fructuosior nobis erit, si gregem Christi magis deposita collegerit, quam retenta disperserit."</note> For with what face shall we hope for the honor promised by Christ in the world to come, if our honor hinders Christian unity in this world?" <-

O truly Christian hearts! O noble counsels! Whose praise shall endure in the Church of God, the more glorious as they had once, have even now, and perhaps will have hereafter, few imitators and rivals.

<margin>XX. Of the Nicene Canon concerning one [bishop] at the same time in the Church.</margin>

For it foresaw the inconveniences of such a partnership: but this was set aside for the sake of fostering peace; thus also, where the reasoning for reconciliation...

An explanation according to equity <note>original Greek: κατ' ἐπιείκειαν (*kat' epieikeian*), meaning fairness or the spirit of the law over the letter.</note> regarding the same Bishop in the same Church.

...it seemed to require that two [bishops] be tolerated, since one could hardly be expelled; it was necessary to look at the purpose and intent of the Canon <term>A church rule or law</term> rather than its literal words.

<margin>
XXI. The proud rigor of the Donatists.
</margin>
**XXI.** And so indeed the Catholics, in order to deal more fairly with the *Donatists*, did not refuse to undergo an unfair condition themselves while offering a beneficial one to their adversaries. However, I find nothing offered by the *Donatists’* side that might lead toward restoring union. On the contrary, *Primianus*, the Bishop of Carthage and a leading figure among the *Donatists*, when approached by the Catholics to hold the Conference under the fairest conditions, struck their ears and wounded their spirits with a particularly harsh and proud saying: <note>original: "indignum esse dictans, ut in unum conveniant filii Martyrum, & progenies Traditorum."</note> *asserting it to be unworthy for the sons of Martyrs and the offspring of Traitors to meet in one place.* <note>"Traitors" (Traditores) was a technical term for those who had allegedly handed over sacred scriptures to Roman persecutors.</note>

<margin>
XXII. The order of the Conference most accurately established.
</margin>
**XXII.** Nevertheless, on the day appointed for holding the Conference, everyone gathered at the Baths of Gargilius <note>The *Thermae Gargilianas*, a common meeting place in Carthage.</note>, both Catholics and Donatists. Seven were chosen from each side to speak for the cause of all; likewise, seven others were chosen whom the speakers could call into council if needed; and four others were appointed to oversee the writing and guarding of the records, so there would be no opportunity for or suspicion of falsehood. Four **Notaries** <term>Scribes or court reporters</term> were also provided by each side, so that pairs of them could alternate with the Judge's own recorders, ensuring no one could claim they had said something that was not recorded. To this diligence was added the requirement that each individual, as well as the Judge himself, should subscribe to <note>Sign or certify</note> their own words, lest anyone say that something in those Acts had been corrupted afterward.

<margin>
XXIII. The case to be conducted solely from the Scriptures.
</margin>
**XXIII.** And when the *Donatists* contended that their case should be conducted not according to the prescriptions of civil law, but by Divine Scripture, the Catholics embraced this with "both arms," as the saying goes. Nor did *Augustine* wish to dispute otherwise with *Petilianus*, their advocate, in his book *On the Unity of the Church*. <note>original: "Non audiamus, HÆC DICO, HÆC DICIS, sed audiamus, HÆC DICIT DOMINUS."</note> *“Let us not hear,”* he said, *“‘I SAY THIS’ or ‘YOU SAY THIS,’ but let us hear, ‘THUS SAYS THE LORD.’ There are surely the Lord's books, to whose authority we both submit. There let us seek the Church; there let us discuss our case.”*

<margin>
XXIV. The Donatists, with peevish pride, refuse to sit, and reject the name of "Brothers."
</margin>
**XXIV.** The Catholics, having set aside all hesitation, now desired to come to the matter at hand. But it soon became clear that the Donatists had nothing less in mind; intent only on evasions and quibbling, they would not even sit down when asked by Marcellinus <note>The imperial representative acting as judge.</note>. For they were whispering from their mouths that verse of the Psalmist: <note>original: "Odivi Ecclesiam malignantium, & cum impiis non sedebo."</note> *“I have hated the assembly of the malignant, and with the impious I will not sit.”* To which the Catholics pointedly replied: that they had already done what David says in the same Psalm, <note>original: "& cum iniquis non ingrediar."</note> *“and with the wicked I will not enter.”* And indeed, as wisely observed by Balduinus <note>François Baudouin, a 16th-century jurist and historian.</note>, it is strange that the Donatists, being so foolishly peevish, preferred to stand rather than sit; since...

...since the former <note>standing</note> belongs to the accused, while the latter <note>sitting</note> belongs to the judges. Indeed, when the accused was ordered to sit, he was considered acquitted. Their ancestors had used no other formula of absolution in that first **Council of Cirta**. The pride of these hypocrites was truly incredible. But it happened by the just judgment of God that they refused the honor too generously offered to them, of which they were unworthy. Yet another proof of their pride followed. For when the Catholic Bishops, while debating with them, called them BROTHERS according to the precept of Christian Charity, they indignantly and haughtily rejected this most sweet and honorable name.

<margin>
XXV. The true status of the question.
</margin>
**XXV.** However, *Marcellinus* <note>The imperial representative and judge of the conference.</note> did not think he should allow himself to be moved even the slightest bit from the fairness of a calm and composed mind by all these things. He therefore insisted that they finally treat the matter in which the chief weight of the case resided. But the "shunners of light" <note>original: *lucifugae*, a derogatory term for those who avoid the truth</note>, seeking subterfuges, clamored that the question concerning the persons involved must be held first, and they wanted to know exactly who had requested the Conference <term>original: *Collatio*, the official meeting for comparing views</term> from the Emperor. They argued over this matter with great persistence for a long time. For they were looking for something to gnaw at in that category as well. And when it was said, as the matter itself made plain, that it was the **Catholics** who had requested the Conference be held by offering a petition to the Emperor, they contended that *they* were the **Catholics**. Lest there be a fruitless dispute over a name, *Marcellinus* foresightedly warned that this name should not be pulled into any prejudice of the case, but should be accepted in the received sense, insofar as it designated the adversaries of the **Donatists**. Shut out by this, they turned to another evasion. Namely, that since the question concerned the Catholic Church, it was not only the **Africans** who should be heard—who boasted of the Catholic communion of the whole world—but also the overseas Bishops, lest they should complain of a prejudice done to them and eventually rescind the acts. How futile these things are, everyone sees: since the matter concerned the curing of a disease in the **African** Churches, which, once successfully cured, all the Churches of Christ could not help but congratulate both them and themselves. Thus they dragged delay out of delay, repeatedly groaning the same hateful repetitions. Finally, it came to the point that the Judge ordered the records to be read of what had been done under **Proconsul Anulinus**, at the very beginning of the schism. Then they cried out in pain:

> *We are being led gradually into the case; your Power is gradually leading us into an internal case.* <note>original: "sensim inducimur in caussam: Potestas tua sensim nos in caussa interna deducit."</note>

It would be a long task to relate with what foolish quibbles and foul litigations they wasted time and exhausted the Judge and the Catholics. I confess that I have read **Augustine’s Abridgment** <note>original: *Augustini breviculum*, a summary of the conference written by St. Augustine</note> not without great weariness, but I read the **Acts of the Conference** themselves with much greater effort; these were first brought to light through the labor and study of **Papirius Masson**, and then by **P. Pithou** with manuscripts...

# On the Schism of the Donatists.

...were published, compared and corrected, from the Commelinus Press in the year 96 of the previous century [1596]. This is the copy I used. Taught by my own experience, I did not wish to serve my reader the same boredom and distaste.

<margin>
XXVI. The true status of the question.
</margin>
**XXVI.** The core of the question turned chiefly on this hinge: *Whether those Africans who were in communion with Caecilian—whom the Donatists called a Traitor <term>original: "Traditor," a term for those who surrendered sacred scriptures to Roman authorities during times of persecution to avoid punishment</term>—and other Christians across the sea who maintained communion with those Africans, were so corrupted by that communion that they lost the dignity and privileges of the Church. This was based on the claim that the Catholic Church cannot exist where it is composed of a mixture of wicked men. Because the Donatists had carefully and constantly fled from such a mixture, they contended that the Catholic Church resided solely with them.* Therefore, the controversy was twofold: one of *fact*, whether Caecilian had been a Traitor and was for that reason unworthy of the Bishopric; the other of *law*, which was again twofold. This second part had a *more universal* aspect: whether the Church is so corrupted by the mixing in of certain wicked people that it ceases to be the Church; and a *more specific* aspect: whether the Church in Africa belonged to the Donatists or to those who were called Catholics. These issues should have been dealt with separately, but all more sensible observers easily perceive that this was not done with the proper diligence and accuracy in this *Conference* <note>original: "Collatio," referring to the Conference of Carthage in 411 AD</note>, mostly due to the insolence and stubbornness of the Donatists.

<margin>
XXVII. The Catholics, setting aside personal matters, are eager to approach the heart of the matter.
</margin>
**XXVII.** The Catholics, following a truly laudable plan so that the status of the more serious case could be addressed more quickly, wished to disconnect and separate the case of Caecilian. For that case was both private and personal, having nothing in common with the other general and essential case. Thus, they did not refuse to grant of their own accord what the Donatists falsely alleged—that Caecilian had been a traitor. For they argued that even then, one should not have separated from the Church that had communicated with him. In the *Conference, Chapter 187*, Augustine said: *If, therefore, the question is what the Church is, how great it is, and of what sort it is, Divine testimonies alone will be sufficient to demonstrate it. If they attack men, if they charge men with crimes—even though the cause of the Church must be distinguished from the cause of men, and the hope of the Church must not be placed in men if they are good, nor must the Church be judged to have perished if they are evil—nevertheless, we take up their cause as that of our brothers, and if they can be shown to us to be criminals, we will excommunicate <note>original: "anathematizamus," to formally banish from the church</note> them today. Yet we do not, because of them, desert or abandon the Church promised and shown by God.* Nevertheless, the Donatists persisted in that legal quibbling, rather than allowing themselves to be drawn toward the question of law concerning the Church. And though at other times they were accustomed to have that legal maxim on their lips, *Neither does case prejudice case, nor person prejudice person* <note>original: "Nec caussa caussae, nec persona personae praejudicat," a principle that legal cases and individual guilt should be judged independently</note>, they nonetheless took offense when this exception was raised against them, as they were joining Caecilian's case with the Church's case in such a way that the latter...

# BOOK IV. CHAPTER VII.

...they wished those things to depend. Petilian, the Advocate of the Donatists, cried out: "Every case begins with the persons involved." 
*Conference, Chapter 56.*

<margin>
XXVIII. Proving the perpetuity and universality of the Church in writing.
</margin>
**XXVIII.** After long disputes, they finally reached the heart of the matter. At the very start of the Conference (Chapter 18), the Catholics had submitted a letter in which they briefly proved that the fate of the Church on earth is to have the wicked mixed with the good. They emphasize this point using the parables of the mixed weeds <term>original: "zizania," referring to the Parable of the Tares in Matthew 13</term>, the chaff, and the bad fish, which remain together until the time of the harvest, the winnowing, and the shore. From this they conclude that even if Caecilian and his fellow bishops had a bad case, the wider Christian world could not have been judged or harmed by it. <note>The Catholics argued that the spiritual validity of the global Church does not depend on the personal moral standing of a single bishop like Caecilian.</note> "Unless," they argued, "a sinning man has more power against the Church than a swearing God has for the Church; and what iniquity has lost is greater than what truth has promised." <note>original: "Nisi forte plus contra Ecclesiam valuit homo peccans quam pro Ecclesia Deus jurans; & iniquitas quod amisit, quam veritas quod promisit."</note> They also report that they found countless testimonies where the future Church is promised to be in all nations and the whole world—just as in the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistles, one reads of the very places, cities, and provinces through which it grew, beginning from Jerusalem, so that it might spread from there even into Africa—not by moving away from other places, but by growing into new ones. They deny, however, that they have found any testimony in the Divine words where it is said that the Church would perish from the other parts of the world and remain only in the "party of Donatus" in Africa.

<margin>
XXIX. And refuting the Donatists from their own hypotheses.
</margin>
**XXIX.** Furthermore, they tried to convict the Donatists using their own actions. Specifically, they noted that the Donatists claimed many of their own people had remained unpolluted despite being in communion with the "sacrilegious sprout" of Maximian <note>Maximian was a rival Donatist claimant who started a schism within the Donatist group. The Catholics used this to show the Donatists didn't actually believe their own "purity" rules when it came to their own internal politics.</note>. They had not dared to cancel or repeat the baptism given either by those they had condemned or by their associates, even though it was performed outside their group in a state of schism. "By this action," the Catholics inferred, "they certainly judged enough that the things they were doing against us were condemned by their own example. But it is to be believed that they now understand how unworthy and intolerable it is that, while they sit in Episcopal Chairs with these men and with Primian <note>The Donatist Bishop of Carthage</note> himself—the condemners and the condemned sitting together for his sake—so that there might be peace in the party of Donatus, the whole Christian world is defamed over the case of Caecilian, all to prevent the unity of Christ from living in peace." The Catholics presented these points at the beginning, eager to dive into the case itself.

<margin>
XXX. To which the Donatists respond with a lengthy letter.
</margin>
**XXX.** The Donatists, however, finally respond with a lengthy letter, which is inserted into the *Acts of the Conference, Chapter 258.* In it, they produce many testimonies gathered together from the Prophets, the Song of Songs, and Paul, in which the remarkable purity of the Church—"without spot or wrinkle" <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27</note>—is proclaimed with magnificent words. They also urge those passages where the "polluted" are ordered to be separated from the midst of holy priests, where it is said that chaff has nothing to do with wheat, and where communion of the faithful with the unfaithful, and of light with darkness, is forbidden. Finally, they teach that the wrath of God is provoked against those who...

# On the Schism of the Donatists.

...they do not take care against the contamination of mixing <note>The Donatists believed that associating with "unclean" people spiritually contaminated the whole community.</note>. They also press the examples of Zephaniah, Elijah, Elisha, Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, Haggai, and Malachi, who detested the sacrifices of the impious and wished to have nothing in common with them. They argued that while these prophets lived among the wicked, it was a matter of dwelling near them, not of being in spiritual communion with them. Furthermore, they prove from Moses, Isaiah, and Paul that it is the duty of a Christian to be separated from the wicked not only in character but also in physical presence, as these scriptures command one to depart from the tabernacles of the wicked and from their midst, and to "touch nothing unclean." 

They also respond to the arguments brought forward by the Catholics. First, regarding the field in which the weeds <term>original: "zizania," referring to the weeds in the Parable of the Tares</term> grew alongside the good seed, they argue that—following Christ's own interpretation—one must understand "the field" to be the World, not the Church. As for the Catholic claim that the chaff must remain with the wheat in the Church, they contend this contradicts Jeremiah, who asks: *What has the straw to do with the grain?* <note>Jeremiah 23:28</note>. Regarding the bad fish in the net, they argue these represent hidden criminals; because the net is cast in the sea, the fishermen (that is, the priests) do not know what is inside until it is pulled to the shore, where the good and bad are finally revealed for sorting. Therefore, they argued that the Catholic thesis—that the Church cannot be stained by the crimes of the wicked, even manifest ones—could in no way be proven. 

Furthermore, they reproach the Catholics for inciting the secular Princes to put them to death, and for forcing people into their communion through threats and proscriptions <note>A "proscription" was a legal decree of condemnation or exile</note> against the command of God. With a vehement speech, they complain that through the officials *Leontius*, *Ursacius*, *Macarius*, *Paul*, *Taurinus*, *Romanus*, and other executors, many venerable priests were killed, others driven into exile, Christianity was widely harassed, virginity was violated, the wealthy were outlawed, the poor were plundered, basilicas were seized, and priests were forced into flight. They claimed these things did not even cease in their own time, since in the single town of *Bagai* <note>Referring to a violent clash in 347 AD where Roman troops attacked Donatists</note>, the blood of many Christians was shed for the sake of their adversaries.

<margin>XXXI. Where the dispute arises on both sides.</margin>
**XXXI.** After these things were heard patiently by the Catholics, *Augustine* began his response. He prudently distinguished that two kinds of matters—objections and facts—had been inserted into that letter. One concerned the Divine Scriptures and the words of the holy law; the other concerned human accusations, which he said certain people thought should be brought forward more out of spite than truth. As he attempted to respond to each point in order, the *Donatists* continually interrupted him, so that the entire dispute took on the appearance of a disorderly altercation rather than a legitimate conference. There was much litigation over the word *World* <term>original: "Mundus"</term>: when the Lord says "the field is the *World*," *Augustine* contended that the World should be understood as the Church, as it often is elsewhere; *Petilian*, on the other hand, argued the Church...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER VII.

...the Church is distinguished from the world and opposed to it, as is seen everywhere in the Gospels. Both sides fought with their own testimonies, which would be too long to review here. And with this disagreement, the *Acts of the Conference* <note>original: "Collationis Gesta," the official record of the Council of Carthage</note> that have been published come to an end. The remaining parts, which are missing, must be sought from Augustine’s *Short Summary* <note>original: "Augustini breviculo," a condensed report written by St. Augustine for those who could not read the massive official transcript</note> and his *Book on the things done after the Conference*.

<margin>XXXII. Finally, the Catholics refute the arguments of the Donatists in order.</margin>
XXXII. The Catholics proceeded in such a way that they explained that the testimonies brought forward by the Donatists regarding the Church's exceptional purity referred to that time when she will be eternal in the world to come; whereas the other testimonies they themselves had brought forward, regarding the mixing of the wicked, referred to this present time in this age. They admitted that the good must depart from the wicked, but that this departure happens primarily in the heart and through a difference in conduct. Nevertheless, they maintained that Church discipline should meanwhile remain vigilant to correct such people, not only with words but also through excommunications and removals from rank <term>original: "degradationibus," the process of stripping a cleric of their office and status</term>. Regarding the examples of the Prophets, they said there was only one temple which everyone used, and none of the Prophets who spoke so strongly against the wicked ever established another temple, sacrifices, or priests for themselves. This is how the Catholics responded to the Donatists' reasoning.

<margin>XXXIII. They point out that their own arguments were mostly left untouched by the Donatists.</margin>
XXXIII. They also pointed out that their own arguments were for the most part left untouched by the Donatists. Augustine observes that in that lengthy document, the Donatists offered no response to the parable of the threshing floor, which has the chaff mixed with the wheat until the time of winnowing. He also notes that they wrongly misused the testimony of Jeremiah, who was speaking not about the Church, but about the divine visions of the Prophets and the dreams of men, refusing to allow them to be compared in any way. Furthermore, they said nothing regarding the likeness of the sheep and the goats, who graze together until they are separated at the end of the age. For they could not say in that instance that the goats were unknown to the shepherds in the shared pastures, just as they had previously claimed that the bad fish in the sea were not seen by the fishermen within the nets. Regarding the objections raised about the Maximianists <note>The Maximianists were a breakaway sect of Donatists. The Catholics pointed out that the Donatists were hypocritical because they had welcomed the Maximianists back without re-baptizing them</note>—specifically, that the Donatists had received back those they had previously condemned while letting them keep their full honors, that they had denied that the associates of Maximian were "polluted" by him, and that they preferred to approve rather than cancel and repeat the baptism given by them while in schism—the Donatists did not even offer a slight response; instead, they passed over these points in a strange silence, as if they had never been mentioned.

<margin>XXXIV. The things they call "persecutions" happened to them because of crimes, not because of their religious communion.</margin>
XXXIV. Regarding the complaints they later made about their "persecutions," Augustine records that these things happened to them not because of the communion of Donatus, but because of the crimes through which some of them raged with such violence that they had to be punished by public laws. Moreover, they falsely and unfairly blamed the Catholics for the madness that the Circumcellions <term>original: "Circumcelliones," a radical and often violent militant wing of the Donatists known for attacking Catholics and sometimes committing ritual suicide</term> inflicted upon themselves. He adds that it was surprising they even dared to mention the town of Bagai <note>The Donatists had used state force to suppress the Maximianists at Bagai, which undermined their argument that the "true" church is always the one being persecuted, never the persecutor</note>, since nothing else

# On the Schism of the Donatists.

<margin>...not because of the Donatist name, but because of their own crimes.</margin>
...nothing else was done there except to resist their violence, which they attempted to inflict [in the name of] the Donatist sect. Meanwhile, they committed horrific things in that place, so much so that even a Basilica was burned, and Holy Books <note>original: "Codices Sancti," referring to the scriptures</note> were cast into the fire. This indeed is the summary of those things which the Catholics recorded in writing against the Donatists, in which the mixture of the evil with the good in the Church is debated.

<margin>XXXV. The question of who truly constitutes the Church was not handled properly or in order during the Conference.</margin>
**XXXV.** Regarding the other question—with whom the Church resided, whether with those called *Catholics* or with the *Donatists*—hardly anything seems to have been conducted properly or in order during the Conference. The *Catholics* generally brought forward many testimonies to prove that the Church is spread throughout the entire world, and that many churches founded by the labors of the Apostles belong to this single Church, with which it is clear the *Donatists* do not communicate. But the *Donatists* remained silent on this point, nor did they bring forward any testimony in their very long letter to assert that the Church of the *Donatist* party <note>original: "partis Donati," the specific sect of Donatus</note> had been predicted or foretold. And indeed, if we wish to speak the truth, that question was both very difficult and unnecessary, because on both sides the doctrine sounded almost the same, and the form of the rituals appeared very similar. Thus, to distinguish the Church, other indicators were needed besides Doctrine and Sacraments. Whether there are indeed other solid indicators besides these can be doubted with good reason—or perhaps they cannot even be found. In fact, if the *Donatists*, as *Baudouin* <note>François Baudouin (1520–1573), a noted jurist and historian of church law</note> rightly noted, communicated with the Catholic Church both in the doctrine of faith and in rites and ceremonies, even if they did not communicate with certain persons whom they avoided as if polluted, it seems to have been nothing but a schism of a certain stubbornness <note>original: "morositatis schisma," suggesting the split was based on personality and history rather than fundamental theology</note>.

<margin>XXXVI. The absurd arguments of the Donatists concerning the origin of the Schism.</margin>
**XXXVI.** After long disputes, they began to discuss the Origin of the Schism and the case of *Caecilian* <note>Caecilian was the Bishop of Carthage whose disputed election in 311 AD sparked the Donatist movement</note>. But new disputes arose from the *Donatists'* side. Listen to a ridiculous example of these. When the occasion arose, the *Catholics* accused them of having recently blinded the eyes of the faithful with lime and vinegar; in this, they had even surpassed the Devil himself in cruelty, who, although granted power by God over the body of *Job*, had never attempted anything of the kind. The *Donatists* soon twisted this into a ridiculous legal quibble to stir up hatred against the Catholics, as if the Catholics were acting as patrons for the Devil. But I return to the case of *Caecilian*. When the *Judge* <term>original: "Cognitor," the imperial official presiding over the trial, in this case, Marcellinus</term> ordered that the cause of the first split be investigated, the *Catholics* asked that the documents they were offering be read aloud. When he ordered this to be done, the *Donatists* resisted more stubbornly, saying that *Christ* ought to be the judge of this cause, and accusing the *Catholics* of having made a human man their judge. The *Catholics* replied that they should not stir up hatred against them for requesting a human judge, since they themselves [had done the same] regarding the case of the *Max-*

BOOK IV. CHAPTER VII.

...judged the Maximianists <note>A breakaway group from the main Donatist sect</note>, and brought the case of Caecilianus <note>The Bishop of Carthage whose disputed election sparked the entire schism</note> himself before the Emperor Constantine as accusers. This was certainly not the action of a man who—as was previously claimed—would reserve judgment for Christ alone. Furthermore, from the *Proconsular Acts* (the reading of which the *Donatists* frequently interrupted with calculated objections), it was clearly demonstrated that Caecilianus’s case had been judged properly and lawfully in the Council held at Rome under Melchiades <note>also known as Pope Miltiades, r. 311–314 AD</note>. Caecilianus was acquitted, while Donatus and his followers were convicted of slander. To escape the weight of this, they even accused Melchiades himself of "handing over" the Divine books <note>original: "traditionis," the crime of surrendering scriptures to Roman authorities to avoid persecution; those who did so were called "traditors"</note>, yet they did so without any suitable evidence. The innocence of Caecilianus was also shown through the records of the Council of Arles and the letters of Constantine. The Donatists, on the other hand, sought support for their failing cause from the writings of Optatus of Milevis <note>A Catholic bishop who wrote a famous history of the schism</note>. But once the passage concerning Caecilianus's acquittal—which Optatus mentions in very clear words—was read out, they became a laughingstock to everyone.

<margin>XXXVII. Marcellinus declares that the Donatists have been overcome by the Catholics through the manifestation of all evidence.</margin>

**XXXVII.** Finally, when the legal records produced under Proconsul Aelianus were read in favor of Caecilianus's acquittal, and the adversaries could find no response other than hateful repetitions, the Judge <note>original: "Cognitori," referring to Flavius Marcellinus, the imperial representative presiding over the conference</note> decided to leave the proceedings of that Conference in writing, confirmed by proper testimony. He then pronounced: <term>BY THE MANIFESTATION OF ALL EVIDENCE, THE DONATISTS HAVE BEEN OVERCOME BY THE CATHOLICS</term>. Consequently, they were ordered to hand over the Basilicas (which Marcellinus had allowed them to use until the day of the verdict) to the Catholics without any delay. The madness and insolence of the *Circumcellions* <note>Radical, often violent groups of wandering ascetics who acted as the "shock troops" of the Donatist movement</note> were also ordered to be suppressed. Furthermore, a mandate was issued to the local officials, feudal lords, agents, and managers—not only of private estates but also of the Imperial household <note>original: "domus Divinae"</note>—that they should prohibit the gatherings of the *Donatists* in all cities and places. Indeed, at the end of the sentence or Edict, he ordered that the offerings, contributions, and gifts made to the Donatist churches be handed over to the Catholic bishops.

<margin>XXXVIII. After this sentence, the Donatists made many excuses, but in vain.</margin>

**XXXVIII.** After the pronouncement of this sentence, the Donatists made many excuses. At first, they refused to sign the Acts <note>the official record of the proceedings</note> of that day, so that they might have a basis for building a false accusation, being able to deny they said what they had said, or eventually pretend that the records had been corrupted by the Judge. But finally overcome with shame, because it had been agreed from the start that both parties would sign the records, they allowed themselves to be persuaded to sign. In this way, the Acts of the Conference were finished and perfected, fortified with every mark of authenticity, and ordered to be preserved in the public Archives to provide a record of the event for posterity. Meanwhile, however, there were those who slanderously claimed that *the Donatists had not been permitted to say everything for their side before the Power that heard the case, because the Judge, being of the Catholic communion, favored his own Church.* But the reality of the matter was far otherwise...

The Donatists were ordered to surrender their churches, and their radical wing, the Circumcellions, was suppressed.</summary>

### ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

<meta>catchword: us</meta>

...that was how things stood. For the Judge <note>Marcellinus, the Imperial Tribune and notary who presided over the conference</note>, wishing through his patience to cut off every future opportunity for them to complain, set aside the water-clock <note>original: "clepsydram"; an ancient device used to time legal speeches. By removing it, Marcellinus allowed the Donatists unlimited time to speak</note> and allowed them to say whatever they wished, rather than interrupt the proceedings. Nor did he deliver his verdict until they had finished speaking and had admitted that they themselves had said their piece. Others falsely claimed that Marcellinus had been bribed; but they said this with the same impudence as when they had previously appealed to Constantine. When that Emperor had acquitted Caecilianus and condemned Donatus, they had likewise quibbled that the Emperor had been corrupted.

Furthermore, they complained that force had been used against them, because they were supposedly shut up against their will in a single room as if in a prison. Yet the Catholics were in that same place—a spacious, bright, and cool room. The Judge was also there; and no one felt they were "shut in," except perhaps those who harbored suspicions because they wanted to flee. And so we may understand that they seized upon every possible thing to slander, they even complained that Marcellinus had given judgment at night. In truth, they themselves had wasted the entire day with quibbling so that they might escape under the cover of darkness. The Judge had listened to them with admirable patience. And because it was their own fault, through their empty evasions, that the final part of the case reached into the night, the Judge did not allow his sentence to be evaded simply because he had judged it later than usual. But who does not see how futile these complaints are? They are scarcely worth reporting, let alone refuting.

<margin>
XXXIX.
*The outcome of the Conference.*
</margin>

XXXIX. And this is indeed the history of that most famous *Conference* <note>The "Collatio," a formal legal and theological debate</note> held between the Catholics and the Donatists at Carthage. Its outcome and success must be considered in this final section. Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century historian and student of Augustine</note> describes it in a few words in *Book VII, Chapter XLII*:

> *In these days, by the command of Honorius <note>Western Roman Emperor, r. 395–423 AD</note>, peace and unity were restored to the Catholic Church throughout all Africa. The body of Christ (which we are) was healed by the restoration of the decision. The execution of this holy mandate was entrusted to Marcellinus the Tribune, a man of exceptional prudence and industry, and most eager for all good studies. Count Marinus killed him at Carthage (it is uncertain whether he was spurred by jealousy or corrupted by gold). Marinus was immediately recalled from Africa and stripped of his rank, left to his own conscience for either punishment or repentance, etc.*

But these matters must be clarified further, and we must explain more distinctly what outcome the Conference had regarding the Donatists, Honorius, and Marcellinus.

<margin>
XL. *Many of the Donatists were joined to the Catholic Church.*
</margin>

XL. As far as the Donatists are concerned, their primary leaders were so far from being brought back to "better fruit" <note>meaning repentance or a productive outcome</note> that, on the contrary, they were made even more stubborn. They could be defeated, but they could not be persuaded. However, Augustine testifies that many who were curable did come to their senses. In *On the Acts against Emeritus the Donatist*, he says: "In the name of Christ, we have received the Donatists into the Catholic fold in great part, so that we rejoice that almost all have been joined to the Catholic communion." He says the same in *Letter 50 to Boniface*: "Especially after the Conference which was held between..."

It concludes by citing historical evidence that the conference successfully brought many Donatists back to the Catholic Church, despite the stubbornness of their leaders.</summary>

...us and their Bishops at Carthage were for the most part corrected. This is especially to be understood regarding the common people, not even excluding those who were once seized by the madness of the **Circumcellions** <note>original: "Circumcellionum"; a radical and often violent sect of Donatists, largely composed of the rural peasantry, who sought martyrdom and attacked those they deemed enemies of their faith</note>. For thus says the same Augustine *to Gaudentius, Book 1, Chapter 29:*

> How much consolation do you think we have, seeing that from such a great madness of the Donatist party (where not only was there the error of a wicked division, but even the law of madness was established) many more thousands are being liberated beyond all comparison? For those who perish are not to be counted as equal to the salvation of these others, who are now held in the order of discipline from that very same group; having lost both the work and the name of the **Circumcellions**, they now serve by cultivating the fields, preserve their chastity, and hold to the unity of the Church. How much less are those lost souls—of both sexes, not only boys and girls, young men and maidens, but also married couples and the elderly—equal to the innumerable multitude who, from the wicked dissension of the Donatists, pass into the true and Catholic peace of Christ.

<margin>XLI. Wicked Catholics experienced Divine vengeance.</margin>
XLI. The observation of Balduin <note>François Baudouin (1520–1573), a legal scholar and historian who wrote extensively on church history</note> is worth mentioning here. This Conference, he says, achieved what the greatest and otherwise best Councils could scarcely ever achieve. But I would also wish that it had achieved what *Augustine* hoped for: that the wicked Catholics, whose depravity provoked the Donatists, might have been corrected and amended by these very turmoils. But instead, they became much worse, as is testified by *Salvian of Marseille in his book on Providence and Judgment* <note>Salvian (c. 400–470 AD) was a Christian writer who argued that the barbarian invasions were a divine punishment for the moral corruption of Roman Christians</note>, where he describes the incredible infamy and reckless wickedness of the people of Carthage. Therefore, not long after the Conference, it happened that enemies far more cruel than the Donatists flooded into Africa <note>The Vandals, a Germanic tribe who invaded Roman Africa in 429 AD</note>. They provided a terrible example of Divine vengeance against such desperate wickedness, destroying more than four hundred churches and finally overturning Carthage itself. As *Augustine* was dying, he so lamented such a calamity that, even in his groaning, he recognized it as the just judgment of God, as *Possidius* <note>The friend and biographer of Saint Augustine</note> relates.

<margin>XLII. A decree from Honorius restrained the stubborn Donatists.</margin>
XLII. But I return to the Donatists. There were those who, having become more obstinate and combative, partly proceeded with public violence and partly attempted to render the conference void through scattered slanders and lies, trying to frighten the souls of the simpler folk away from the unity of the Church. To blunt these slanders and elude their schemes, a Council was held in the city of Cirta in Numidia in the year following the Conference, 412 AD. And a very severe <term>rescript</term> <note>original: "rescriptum"; an official imperial response or decree issued by the Roman Emperor</note> exists from the Emperor *Honorius* against them. He, having approved everything that had been done by *Marcellinus* and having revoked the leniency of the previous year, was so indignant at such stubbornness that he ordered the agitators to be strictly punished.
