# On the Schism of the Donatists.

<margin>
XLIII. The Imperial formula.
</margin>

XLIII. Having annulled those maneuvers which **legal experts** <note>original: "Pragmatici"; lawyers or petitioners who sought special imperial favors</note> or notes by our own hand were able to obtain, and while those things which were even recently defined on this matter remain in force, and the decree of the ancient Princes is preserved; unless from the day this law is issued all **Donatists**, both **Priests** and **Clergy** as well as **Laity**, return to the **Catholics** those things which they sacrilegiously abandoned: then the **Illustrious** <note>original: "Illustres"; the highest rank of the Roman aristocracy</note> shall be compelled to pay individually to our **Treasury** <note>original: "Fisco"</note> fifty pounds of gold as a penalty, the **Respectable** <note>original: "Spectabiles"; the middle senatorial rank</note> thirty pounds of gold, the **Most Distinguished** <note>original: "Clarissimi"; the basic senatorial rank</note> twenty pounds, the **Provincial Priests** <note>original: "Sacerdotales"; a high-ranking civic title</note> thirty pounds of gold, the **Leading Citizens** <note>original: "Principales"</note> twenty pounds, the **Town Councilors** <note>original: "Decuriones"</note> five pounds of gold, the **Merchants** <note>original: "Negotiatores"</note> five pounds of gold, and the **Circumcellions** <note>original: "Circumcelliones"; radical, often violent Donatist extremists</note> ten pounds of silver. If these individuals are not presented for the collection of the fine by the **Landlords** <note>original: "Conductoribus"</note> under whom they reside, or by their agents, the landlords themselves shall be held liable for the penalty: so that not even the men of our own household shall be considered immune from this assessment. A separate fine shall also constrain their wives individually from their husbands. For those whom the imposed losses have by no means corrected, the confiscation of all their property will follow. Moreover, the master's warning to **slaves**, or more frequent beatings for **tenant farmers** <note>original: "colonos"</note>, shall call them back from this wicked religion, unless they prefer to be held responsible for the aforementioned expenses themselves (even if they are Catholic). Indeed, the **Clergy** and their ministers, and the most ruinous **Provincial Priests**, having been removed from African soil, which they polluted with their sacrilegious ritual, shall be sent into exile individually to each separate region under suitable guard. Their churches, meeting houses, and estates (if the wicked generosity of heretics has bestowed any upon their churches) are to be claimed for Catholic ownership and authority (as we have long since decreed). Given on the 30th of January at **Ravenna**, during the eighth consulship of **Honorius** and the fifth of **Theodosius**, Augusti. In the year of our Lord 412.

<margin>
XLIV. To which another more severe law was added.
</margin>

XLIV. Furthermore, when the Emperor learned that the insolence of the Donatists could not be restrained even by that edict, in the year 414, on the 22nd of June, during the consulship of **Constantius** and **Constans**, he issued a law against them, than which hardly any was more severe. First, indeed, it declares them **legally incapable** <note>original: "intestabiles"; individuals stripped of the right to make or witness a will, effectively losing their civil standing and ability to inherit</note>, and that they have no power to enter into any contract, but branded with perpetual infamy, they are to be segregated from honorable gatherings and from public assembly. Then, those places in which their dreadful superstition had been observed until now were to be joined to the Venerable Catholic Church. Moreover, their **Bishops**, **Presbyters**, and all their **Prelates** and **Ministers**, stripped of all property, were to be sent into exile to various individual islands and provinces. In addition to this, if anyone should receive these people while they are fleeing the intended vengeance for the purpose of hiding them, his patrimony is to be added to the treasury's gains, such that he undergoes the same penalty proposed for them. It also imposes the loss of inheritance and monetary fines upon men, women, individual persons, and those of high rank according to their status. And this so strictly, that as often as anyone [has] approached such a communion...

<margin>
XLV. The sad death of Marcellinus through the betrayal of the Donatists.
</margin>

XLV. The end of **Marcellinus** <note>Flavius Marcellinus, the imperial representative who presided over the Council of Carthage in 411</note> was a sad one. **Heraclianus** <note>A Roman general and consul who revolted against Emperor Honorius</note> the consul attempted a revolution in Africa, and after withholding the African **grain supply** <note>original: "annona"</note> outside the normal order for some time, he finally hurried toward Rome with an immense fleet of ships. Turning to flight, he seized a ship and returned to Carthage alone, where he was immediately killed by a military hand. Marinus, crossing into Africa to pursue the enemies of the empire, ordered our Marcellinus to be killed. This occurred because Marcellinus suffered under a false accusation, through the betrayal of the Donatists, claiming he favored the faction of Heraclianus. However, he was recorded in the Church registers under the title of **Martyr**.

<margin>
XLVI. Honorius judged it unjust for the Acts of the Conference to be undermined by his death.
</margin>

XLVI. The question was raised whether the **Acts of the Conference** <note>The official records of the Council of Carthage</note> were undermined by his death. The Donatists desired this immensely. But it was beyond all reason, and it appeared otherwise to Honorius. His **Rescript** <note>A formal imperial response to a legal query</note> on this matter to Julian, the Proconsul of Africa, still exists: *“Those things which were carried out against the Donatists through the study and care of Marcellinus of respectable memory, which we wish to have perpetual firmness having been transferred into public monuments. For the public faith ought not to perish by the death of the judge. Given on the 3rd day before the Kalends of September at Rome, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans.”* <note>August 30, 414 AD</note> Furthermore, the Emperor wished for Marcellinus’s Acts regarding the crimes of the Donatists after the Conference of Carthage to be posted in the **Theopropria** <note>A significant public building or imperial audience hall in Carthage</note>; where, it seems, a frequent multitude gathered as if in the most famous place in Carthage, and he desired those same acts to be read throughout the Churches.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->The end of the Donatist faction.<-

# ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS

<margin>1. The corrupt morals of the Africans, and especially the Carthaginians.</margin>
**A**nd such indeed was the outcome of that most famous Conference of Carthage. From that time, the African Church took on a far different appearance. For a few years later, the Vandal storm broke upon them—that terrible and long-lasting invasion. The morals of the Africans had fallen far from the ancient holiness of Christianity, even the morals of those who were called Catholics. Carthage itself—the leader and mother of African cities, that city which was always a rival to the Roman heights, once in arms and bravery, later in splendor and dignity, and recently made noble by such distinguished Bishops, such excellent martyrs, and such remarkable examples of piety and steadfastness—became so contaminated with crimes that Salvian wrote:

<margin>From *On the True Judgment and Providence of God*, Book 7.</margin>
> What part of the city was not full of filth? What street or path within the city was not a brothel? Almost all the crossroads and all the ways were cut off as if by pits of lust, or covered over as if by nets, so that even those who utterly abhorred such things could hardly avoid them.

All the citizens of that city, if I may say so, reeked with the mud of lust, inhaling the foul stench of their mutual indecency. But those horrific things were not horrific to them, because the same horror had infected them all. You would think they shared a single mind of lusts and fornications, like a mire collected from every filth of the streets and sewers. I say nothing of the rest—most offensive to chaste eyes and ears—which that pious man <note>Salvian of Marseille (c. 400–470 CE), a Christian writer who blamed the fall of the Roman Empire on the moral failures of its citizens.</note>, having lived in that city, deplores in his most serious discourse.

<margin>2. Idolatry regarding the "Heavenly Goddess."</margin>
2. This cannot be overlooked: that even the nobles and the powerful, though Christian by profession, harbored an internal crime within their native walls—worshiping some "HEAVENLY ONE" <note>original: "COELESTEM"; referring to Caelestis, the Roman name for the ancient Punic goddess Tanit, who remained popular in Carthage long after the city's Christianization</note>, a demon of the Africans, after Christ, or even alongside him. Their sacrilege and impiety must be considered all the more monstrous because it persisted even after the great efforts of their Bishop, **Aurelius** <note>Aurelius of Carthage (died c. 430 CE), a close friend of Saint Augustine who worked to reform the African church</note>, to demolish the idol and its profane shrine; after so many efforts by Proconsuls and Tribunes toward this very end; after so many imperial laws and decrees given in Africa against idolaters; and finally, after so many Councils celebrated in Carthage by the same Bishop and his colleagues to utterly banish impiety and corrupt morals—alongside public sermons and secret warnings from holy men—yet such a massive crime still flourished with impunity among the powerful.

<margin>3. Hatred toward those who warn.</margin>
3. Finally, there was added to the peak of Carthaginian crimes a hatred toward holy men, through whom they might have been brought back to a better life, whether by word, prayer, or example. For they mocked, hounded, detested, and tore apart such men with insults, daring to do everything against them that the impiety of the Jews did against Christ and the Apostles.

# BOOK IV. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>IV. Why these crimes were not reproached by the Donatists.</margin>
IV. Sometimes it has occurred to me to wonder how it happened that the Donatists—those sharp-eyed and bitter censors of the Catholics—did not heap these crimes upon them with constant insults, while they persisted so stubbornly in their foolishness and fabrications about *Caecilian* <note>Caecilian was the Bishop of Carthage whose election in 311 CE sparked the Donatist schism.</note> and others. Because of this, I believe it is credible that they themselves were stained by the same or similar impurities; thus, they could not object to anything in the Catholics that could not immediately be thrown back at them. Oh, the deplorable state of the Church! Where, while they dispute over trifles, those things are neglected, despised, trampled upon, and profaned in which the very substance of Christianity, so to speak, is placed.

<margin>V. Severely punished by God through the Goths and Vandals.</margin>
V. It could not be otherwise than that God's exhausted patience would finally blaze out against so many crimes of his people. Therefore, he used the Goths and *Vandals*, and crowds of other barbarian nations roused from their ancestral homes, as ministers of his justice. Having made an inroad into *Africa*, they devastated everything with plundering, slaughter, and every kind of cruelty. They raged cruelly not only against property and bodies, but also against the souls and consciences of the Orthodox. For the *Vandals*, infected by the *Arian* heresy <note>Arianism was a theological belief that denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ, teaching that he was a created being rather than co-equal with God the Father.</note>, showed themselves extremely hostile to the Orthodox, not only through edicts but also through punishments. Thus says *Paul the Deacon* in *Book XVI* at the end: *In Africa, Huneric, through Arian treachery, having driven more than 334 Catholic Bishops into exile and flight and seized their churches, afflicted the people with various punishments. Indeed, cutting off the hands of countless people, he cut out their tongues. Yet he could not take away the speech of the Catholic confession.* <note>original: "Nec tamen loquelam Catholicae confessionis eripere potuit." This refers to a famous late-antique account of a miracle where martyrs spoke without tongues.</note> Regarding this miracle, I remember having spoken elsewhere.

<margin>VI. In which calamity the Donatists allied themselves with the Arian Vandals.</margin>
VI. They remembered that their ancestors under the *Emperor Constantius* <note>Constantius II (reigned 337–361), who favored Arianism.</note> had entered into a treaty with the *Arians* against the *Catholics*, and therefore they received them not as enemies, but as allies, since they were joined in the same impiety in the sign of *Anabaptism* <note>Literally "rebaptism." The Donatists and some Arians both insisted on rebaptizing converts, a practice the Catholic Church rejected.</note>, though for different reasons. Why indeed would they hesitate to join the *Vandals*, since we remembered above that they even sent legates to the *Apostate Emperor* <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363), who briefly restored paganism and allowed exiled Donatists to return to Africa to sow discord among Christians.</note> in the *East* against the *Catholics*? *Augustine* records that he heard some of them, wishing to win over the *Goths* when they saw they had some power, said that they believe what the Goths believe. *Epistle 50 to Marcellinus.* Witness is also given by the example of *Nicasius the Donatist*, whose foul death *Victor of Vita* <note>A 5th-century bishop who wrote the 'History of the Vandal Persecution'.</note> compares with the terrible end of *Huneric* in *Book III at the end*. # THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

Huneric <note>The Vandal King who ruled from 477 to 484 CE and was known for persecuting Nicene Christians.</note> completed his reign over the kingdom in seven years and ten months, meeting a death that matched his merits: for his body appeared to be buried while still alive, putrefying and seething with worms—or rather, it seemed to be mere pieces of a body. And that law-giver and transgressor, Nicasius, who had formerly joined them from the heresy of the Donatists, perished shortly thereafter in a similar death.

<margin>
VII. Justinian's decree against them.
</margin>

VII. After Justinian had expelled the Barbarians and subjected a liberated Africa once again to the Roman Empire, he took it upon himself to restrain the license of the Donatists, just as he had done with the Arians. His decree <note>original: *rescriptum* — a formal imperial response to a legal query.</note> to Solomon, the Praetorian Prefect in Africa, still exists, in which the following is found: *“It shall be the concern of Your Excellency <note>original: *Sublimitati tuæ* — an honorific title for high-ranking officials.</note> that no other communion whatsoever be granted to the Arians, nor to the* DONATISTS, *nor to the Jews, nor to others who are known to not practice the Orthodox religion at all, specifically regarding Ecclesiastical rites; rather, they shall be entirely excluded from sacred places and their own wicked temples. No permission shall be granted to them at all to ordain Bishops or Clergy, or to baptize any persons whatsoever and draw them into their own madness: because sects of this kind have been condemned not only by us, but also by previous laws, and they are practiced by most wicked and defiled men. Furthermore, we command that all heretics, according to our laws which we have imposed, be removed from public duties, so that heretics are permitted to perform no public service at all, nor to command the Orthodox: since it is enough for them to live, and not to claim any authority for themselves, and thereby cause some harm to Orthodox men and the most upright worshippers of Almighty God. However, we in no way allow those who have been Rebaptized <note>A reference to the Donatist practice of re-baptizing Catholics who joined them, which was a major point of theological conflict.</note> to serve in the military.”* After a few intervening words: *“But neither do we allow their Synagogues to stand; rather, we wish them to be remodeled into the form of Churches. For we do not permit Jews, nor Pagans, nor* DONATISTS, *nor Arians, nor any other heretics whatsoever, to have dens or to perform anything as if by Ecclesiastical rite: since it is quite absurd to permit impious men to perform sacred rites. See Baronius at the year 535.”* <note>Cesare Baronio was a 16th-century Cardinal and historian who wrote the 'Annales Ecclesiastici'.</note>

<margin>
VIII. Nevertheless, because of the laziness of the Catholics, neither their number nor their authority was diminished. Book 5, Epistle 63.
</margin>

VIII. Nevertheless, the severity of Justinian could not ensure that the Donatists did not retain their Churches and Bishoprics, and eventually they became a heavy burden to the Orthodox—who were certainly far too sluggish—in both number and authority. It reached such a point that when the Catholic Primate of Numidia died, the bishop who was the oldest in terms of his ordination in that province from among the Donatist schismatics openly demanded and claimed that dignity of Primate for himself. From this came the complaints of Gregory of Rome <note>Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote extensively about the revival of Donatism in Africa.</note> to the Emperor Maurice: *“The imperial laws are being set aside with careless indifference, so that neither the judgment of God is held in fear in Africa, nor do the Princely commands take effect: since the Catholic faith is publicly for sale because of the prevailing bribes of the Donatists. Nor were there lacking Bishops, by whom—through bribery—the people under their care...”*

...behaved toward our Fathers, or still behave toward us—those who now arrogantly claim the prestigious name of the *Catholic Church* <note>original: "Ecclesiæ Catholicæ"</note> for themselves, just as the *Catholics* of old behaved toward the *Donatists* <note>A 4th-century North African sect that broke away from the main Christian church, claiming they were the only pure church because they refused to recognize clergy who had surrendered sacred texts during Roman persecutions.</note>; but the paths and reasons of both groups are as far apart from each other as the East is from the West. Indeed, what we are saying is not shrouded in the deep gloom of many disputes; rather, it exists in the clearest light of facts: and it has been so brilliantly explained by the leaders of our profession that it does not require any further commentary from us. However, since we have reached this point, and to ensure our exercise remains complete, it will not be troublesome to summarize what has been extensively treated by great men.

<margin>II. *The Donatists sought the pretext for their Schism solely in the ordination of Caecilian.*</margin>
II. Regarding the *Donatists*, they professed the same faith as the Catholics in Africa, held the same worship of the Divine power, and used the same sacraments and ceremonies; there was no controversy between them on these matters. The only question concerned the Ordination of *Caecilian* <note>Caecilian was the Bishop of Carthage whose 311 CE election was disputed by the Donatists because one of his consecrators was accused of being a "traditor" (one who handed over Bibles to Roman authorities).</note>, which they contended had not been performed according to the proper way and order. They argued that because of this single act, the entire African Church was so polluted by "communion in crime" that it fell away from the title and privileges of the Christian Church; and not only the African Church, but also the other churches across the sea that remained in communion with it. Thus, they claimed the true Christian Church had perished everywhere in the world and remained only in the party of Donatus. This was the sole cause they offered for their separation. Furthermore, the separation itself was so stubborn that, although they were invited to unity with every equity and kindness, they vehemently rejected it. They refused to sit in the same place as Catholics, indignantly rejected the name of "Brothers" given to them by Catholics, and would not admit those coming over from the Catholics to their side unless they underwent a repeated Baptism <note>Re-baptism was a core Donatist practice, as they believed sacraments performed by "corrupt" Catholics were invalid.</note>; as if only then they became Christians from non-Christians. Such was the manner of the *Donatists*.

<margin>III. *Our ancestors noted a universal corruption of morals in the Roman Clergy.*</margin>
III. However, our ancestors in the previous century <note>The 16th-century Protestant Reformers.</note> proceeded in a far different manner. After it pleased the Divine mercy to illuminate the minds of certain godly men with the light of His Spirit and lead them to an understanding of the sacred volumes, they began to discover many things in the *Roman Church* <note>original: "Ecclesia Romana"</note>, in whose communion they were living, which seemed to them to be very far removed from—even directly opposed to—ancient and simple Christianity as it is handed down in the sacred scriptures. They were not quarreling over the crime of some Bishop or Pope, whether it was fabricated or true; but they saw, as the whole world saw with them, that the morals of the *Monks, Priests, Bishops, Cardinals*, and finally the *Popes* themselves, had generally become so corrupt that not even a shadow of civil honesty remained in many of them. Therefore, it seemed difficult for them to believe in...

This was not some untimely stubbornness on the part of our ancestors, but rather the complaint of everyone who still possessed any care for the ancient right. The writings of *Nicholas of Clémanges, Alvaro Pelayo, Dietrich of Niem, Wycliffe, Wessel of Groningen, Cassander, Rainerius*, and countless others cry out this fact. <margin>IV. An incredible ignorance of Divine matters.</margin>
IV. Furthermore, our ancestors perceived an incredible *ignorance of Divine matters* in those to whom the care of teaching the Church had been entrusted. To many of them, the Holy Bible was unknown and had not even been looked upon. Others did not even understand the very words they were muttering to God; those who were considered the most learned of all had spent their lives in the intricacies of Scholastic Philosophy <note>A medieval method of learning that emphasized logic and dialectic, often criticized by Reformers for being overly complex and detached from the Bible</note>, which contributed nothing at all to true wisdom. They fed the souls of their listeners with that chaff, while those listeners gasped in vain for the food of celestial life and the pure Manna. Thus, the study of good literature was stifled, barbarism was introduced, stupor was promoted by every craft, the true light was struck out, and the word of God was suppressed. In its place were substituted the inventions of dull fables: the deeds of *Dominic, Francis, and Veronica* were hammered into people's minds, along with other legends stuffed and sewn together from old wives' delusions. The Gospel history was turned into theatrical works; the most sacred memory of the Lord’s passion was converted into stage acts and concluded with what they called the *Easter Laughter* <note>original: "risu Paschali"; a medieval custom where preachers used jokes, funny stories, or even lewd antics in the pulpit on Easter Sunday to make the congregation laugh, symbolizing the joy of the Resurrection after the somber Lenten season</note>, which was meant to wipe away the grief contracted from the Lenten fast and mortification. If the Holy Bible was ever touched upon, that Divine seed was immediately choked, as if in the blade, by the convoluted and thorny interpretations of the Seraphic Doctors <note>A title given to the most influential medieval Scholastic theologians</note>: *Lombard, Comestor, Thomas, Scotus, Bonaventure, Durand, Ockham*, and others of that sort. What could our ancestors expect from such Doctors that would make them better prepared for the eternal life which they sought above all else?

V. They also perceived that public worship was nearly overwhelmed by infinite *superstitions*, which men had rashly fashioned for themselves beyond and against the word of God. Whatever was flashy in Jewish ceremonies, whatever was florid in Gentile superstition, whatever was glittering in the scraps of ancient heretics—whatever, in short, seemed powerful for soothing and enchanting the eyes, ears, and minds of men—they saw stuffed into Ecclesiastical decrees, publi-

...and so received by custom. In place of that spiritual Christianity—by which God, who is spirit, wishes to be worshipped in spirit and truth—they perceived that almost all religion had been reduced to the joints of the fingers, the murmurs of the lips, the lowing of sacrifices, the tonsures of the cloister, the hair-shirts of hermits, the veneration of rags, combs, and sandals, the marketing of indulgences, the "bugbears" <note>original Greek: μορμολυκεῖα (mormolykeia); frightening masks or hobgoblins used to scare children</note> of ghosts, spirits, and will-o’-the-wisps, and other charms of that kind, suited for distracting and occupying the common folk. <margin>VI. Capital Errors.</margin>
VI. Besides all these things, our ancestors detected **Capital Errors** introduced into religion, by which the chief foundations of the faith were shaken. They heard various blasphemies spewed out against the Divine Scriptures, and those Scriptures accused not only of obscurity and insufficiency, but their authority so depressed beneath the Roman Church that, if her testimony were set aside, they were to be valued no more than the histories of *Livy* or *Polybius* <note>Titus Livius and Polybius were famous secular historians of Rome and Greece; the author is shocked that the Bible would be treated as "merely human" history</note>—nay, lest anything be lacking to their impiety, no more than the fables of *Aesop*. They saw that sacred deposit <note>The Bible</note>, as if it were a most dangerous thing, shaken out of the hands of the Christian people. They saw Bibles in the common tongue—from which, it was claimed, more harm than benefit arises due to the rashness of men—counted among prohibited books, whether printed or handwritten, along with all their parts. They heard other Mediators, of both Intercession and Redemption, commended besides Christ; another Purgatory besides his blood; another Propitiatory Sacrifice besides that which he once offered on the cross; another merit besides his own obedience; another head of the Universal Church besides him. They heard the powers of free will greatly extolled, as well as the validity of one's own merits—both "from fitness" <term>Latin: *ex congruo*; a medieval theological term for merit earned by doing one's best before receiving grace</term> and "from worthiness" <term>Latin: *ex condigno*; merit based on the inherent value of a good work performed under the influence of grace</term>—along with the depression of grace. Thus, they saw the heresy of the Pharisees and False Apostles renewed, who either tried to establish their own righteousness or busied themselves with mixing works and faith in a fatal mixture. Furthermore, they saw the dogmas of the *Pelagians* and *Semi-Pelagians* <note>Groups in the early church who emphasized human effort and denied the total necessity of God’s grace for the beginning of faith</note> dug up again, who, in order to make men free, made them sacrilegious. What shall I say of the most absurd fiction of *Transubstantiation* and the sacrifice of the Mass? Of the sacrilegious removal of the Eucharistic cup from the laity? Of sacred rites performed in a language not understood? Of the proud presumption of perfection and sinlessness? Of the Pope's immense authority over the Church, and many other things of that kind, which our ancestors—informed of the truth by the word of God—could only consider as the gravest errors.

BOOK IV. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>VII. Finally, a horrific idolatry.</margin>
VII. Finally, they discovered a horrific **idolatry** <note>original: "idololatria"</note> spreading through the Roman Church: in the religious worship of the **Blessed Virgin**, concerning whom it is a marvel how foolishly obsessed <note>original: "stolide insanierint"</note> they became—not only the common folk, but also the seducers of the folk, those ill-advised Theologians. This idolatry was seen in the adoration of **Angels**, which was so clearly forbidden by Paul <note>A reference to Colossians 2:18, where the Apostle Paul warns against the "worship of angels."</note>; in the invocation of **Saints**, whom the immense power of the Pope inserted into the "Catalogue of the Divine" at his own whim, much like the **Pagan Apotheosis** <note>original Greek: "Apotheoseos"; the process by which ancient Greeks and Romans deified their heroes or emperors</note>. This included even those saints whom the more prudent knew and admitted were never even men, nor had they ever existed in the natural world. It was seen in the worship of **images**, which goes against the express command of God, and in the veneration of **relics**, whose value was established by nothing other than frauds, impositions, and "sewn-together" deceits—often so evident that they openly contradicted one another. Indeed, our ancestors saw that these very practices were defended by the same arguments used by the ancient Pagans to protect their own religious rites.

<margin>VIII. All these things were a stumbling block to our ancestors.</margin>
VIII. These were the things, along with many others like them, which our ancestors declared to be a **stumbling block** <note>original: "scandalo"; here meaning a cause for spiritual offense or a barrier to faith</note> for them; they argued against them using the Word of God, and they sought a **Reformation** of these things accurately and at great length. I am well aware that the Romanists reply that some things are unfairly blamed on the Roman Church, that many things are exaggerated or amplified to cause ill-will, and that other things held to be "most grave errors" are actually trivial or even contain the sound doctrine of the Christian religion. However, those matters which consist of facts can easily be demonstrated from the primary writers of the Roman Church themselves—and have been demonstrated by our own writers. As for the dispute concerning doctrine, it cannot be settled except by the **Holy Scriptures**, which our ancestors were fully persuaded stood entirely on their side. But that is not the issue at hand now: the only thing that needed to be shown was that in this matter, our ancestors were very different from the **Donatists** <note>A 4th-century North African sect that broke away from the Church; the author argues the Reformers had much better reasons for their separation than the Donatists did</note>, because they alleged far more numerous, entirely different, and more significant reasons for their separation from the Roman Church than the Donatists once offered for their schism.

<margin>IX. Those who sought their reformation.</margin>
IX. Yet, even for these reasons, many and grave as they were, they did not immediately sever themselves from the communion of the Roman Church. Instead, they faithfully communicated the truth, which they believed they had been taught by God, to their fellow citizens through speech and writing. They attempted by every skill to apply a medicine to the corruption creeping everywhere; they carefully refuted common errors using the Word of God once the light of truth was uncovered. They did not cease to demand the **Reformation of the Church**—so necessary and so long sought and desired by the prayers of the godly—with repeated petitions to those who had been entrusted with that care. In the meantime, they were so eager to preserve union that they hardly...

# ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.
<meta>catchword: nibus</meta>

...they refused the conditions of peace, except for those from which the total destruction of religion would have followed.

<margin>X. But in vain: with the leaders of the Roman Church resisting.</margin>

X. Furthermore, they discovered in reality that no hope of true reformation was left to them by the leaders of the Roman Church. Such was the mindset of the Roman Curia <term>Curia Romana</term><note>The administrative apparatus and court of the Pope in Rome.</note>, which **Cardinal Volateranus** <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar and official in the Roman Curia.</note> explained in a careful speech to **Pope Adrian VI**. He argued that it was by no means to be hoped that the **Lutherans** would be wiped out or exterminated through an improvement of the Roman Curia's morals; rather, such an improvement would be the very means of increasing their reputation and their stubbornness. For the uneducated commoners, who usually judge by outcomes, would—once they realized that the Papal government of the Church had been rightly corrected in some part—easily persuade themselves that the reasons for proposing other changes were no less just. They would believe these other matters required similar correction. Furthermore, the authors of the heresies themselves, having achieved victory in one area, would never stop attacking and finding fault. In all human affairs, it is common that once someone has been granted a single demand, they begin to pile demand upon demand, desiring to obtain everything and believing it is their right. Those who study ancient histories will find it clear that from the time heresies first arose plucking at the authority of the Roman Church, all of them have held up the corrupt morals of the Curia as a pretext for their efforts. Moreover, no Pope had ever followed the path of reform as if it were useful to his own affairs; instead, after first issuing warnings and commands, they immediately summoned Princes to protect the Church. What had succeeded happily in the past should be strictly maintained and observed: the Commonwealth is overturned by no means more quickly than by a change in the form of government. To open the door to new and unusual things is the same as exposing oneself to great dangers; it is far safer to walk the path of previous Popes, whose undertakings had a successful end. None of them cut out heresies with reforms, but rather by stirring up what they call **Crusades** <note>original: "Cruciatis"</note>—inciting Princes and peoples, marked with the Symbol of the Cross, against them. He reminded him that Innocent III had crushed the **Albigenses** <note>A dualist sect in Southern France suppressed by a crusade in the 13th century.</note> in **Narbonnese Gaul** by this path; and following the same path, the Popes had extinguished in various places the **Waldensians**, the **Picards**, the **Poor of Lyon**, the **Arnoldists**, the **Speronists**, and the **Patarenes**, of whom nothing remains except their bare names.

<margin>XI. And raging against them in every way.</margin>

XI. Indeed, far from those who desired a Reformation of the Church gaining anything by their protests, they were instead treated with rage in every possible way, as if they were disturbers of the public peace and most pestilential heretics. **Adrian** himself—although, as he used to say, he was by nature, habit, and a certain way of life more inclined toward clemency than any severity—nevertheless warned the princes of **Germany** gathered at **Nuremberg** most severely: that since slow and mild...

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>VII. Finally, a horrible idolatry.</margin>
VII. Finally, they discovered a **horrible idolatry** spreading through the Roman Church: in the religious worship of the Blessed Virgin <note>original: "Beatæ Virginis"</note>, concerning whom it is remarkable how foolishly obsessed not only the common people but even their leaders—ill-advised theologians—became. They saw it also in the adoration of Angels, which was so clearly forbidden by the Apostle Paul; in the invocation of Saints, whom the immense reach of Papal power inserted into the catalogue of the Divine <note>original: "Divorum catalogo," a term echoing pagan Roman religion</note> at its own whim, much like a pagan **Apotheosis** <term>Apotheosis</term><note>The ancient practice of deifying a human being, raising them to the status of a god.</note>. They protested the worship of images, which goes against the most express command of God, and the veneration of relics, whose value was based on nothing other than frauds, impostures, and "sewn-together" deceits—often so obvious that they openly contradicted one another. Our ancestors saw that these very practices were defended with the same arguments that the ancient Gentiles used to protect the purity of their own religions.

<margin>VIII. All these things were a scandal to our ancestors.</margin>
VIII. They argued against these practices using the Word of God and sought a thorough and extensive Reformation of them. I am not unaware that the Romanists respond by saying some of these charges were unfairly attributed to the Roman Church, that many were exaggerated to cause hatred, and that others—though held to be very grave errors—are actually trivial or even contain the sound doctrine of the Christian religion. However, those matters which consist of historical facts can easily be demonstrated from the primary writers of the Roman Church, and have been demonstrated by our own scholars. They attempted by every skill to provide a medicine for the corruption spreading everywhere. They diligently refuted common errors using the Word of God once the light of truth was uncovered. They did not cease to demand the Reformation of the Church—so necessary and so longed for by the prayers of so many godly people—with repeated petitions to those who had been entrusted with that care. # ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS.

...they would refuse the conditions of peace, except for those from which the total destruction of all religion would have followed.

<margin>X. But in vain: with the leaders of the Roman Church resisting.</margin>
X. Furthermore, they discovered in reality that no hope of true reformation remained for them from the leaders of the Roman Church. Such was the mindset of the *Roman Curia* <term>Curia</term><note>The administrative apparatus and court through which the Pope governs the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, which *Cardinal Volateranus* <note>Francesco Soderini (1453–1524), the Cardinal of Volterra, a key diplomat and advisor to the Papacy.</note> explained in a precise speech to *Pope Hadrian VI*. He argued that it was by no means to be hoped that the *Lutherans* would be wiped out or exterminated through an improvement of the *Roman Curia's* morals; on the contrary, such a course would only increase their reputation and their stubbornness. *For the unlearned common people, who usually judge by results, once they discovered from a started reform that the Papal governance of the Church was rightly criticized in some part, would easily persuade themselves that the reasons for proposing other changes—which require similar correction—were no less just; and the authors of the heresies themselves, having won a victory in one matter, would never stop attacking and finding fault.* In all human affairs, it happens that whoever is satisfied in one demand will pile demand upon demand, desiring to obtain everything and believing it is theirs by right. To those who turn the pages of ancient history, it is clear that from the time heresies were born that plucked at the authority of the *Roman Church*, all of them used the corrupt morals of the *Curia* as a pretext for their efforts. Furthermore, no Pope had ever followed the path of reform as if it were useful to his own affairs; instead, after first issuing warnings and instructions, they immediately called upon Princes to protect the Church. What had succeeded happily in former times must be strictly held and observed: for there is no faster way to overturn a Commonwealth than by changing the form of government. To open a door to new and unusual things is the same as exposing oneself to great dangers; it is far safer to walk the path of previous Popes, whose undertakings had happy results. None of them had cut out heresies through reforms, but rather by raising *Crusades* <note>original: "Cruciatis"</note>, as they are called, against them, inciting Princes and peoples marked with the Symbol of the Cross. Let him remember that *Innocent III* crushed the *Albigenses* <note>A dualist medieval sect in Southern France, the target of a brutal crusade in the early 13th century.</note> in *Narbonnese Gaul* by this path; and the Popes who followed him extinguished, in various places, the *Waldensians*, the *Picards*, the *Poor of Lyon*, the *Arnoldists*, the *Speronists*, and the *Patavines*, of whom nothing remains besides their bare names.

<margin>XI. And raging against them in every way.</margin>
XI. Indeed, so far were those who desired a Reformation of the Church from achieving anything by their protests, that on the contrary, they were raged against in every way as disturbers of public peace and most pestilential heretics. *Hadrian* himself, although he claimed to be more inclined by nature, habit, and a certain way of life toward mercy than toward any severity, nevertheless most sternly warned the princes of Germany assembled at *Nuremberg* in his letters: *Since by slow and gen-* <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the next page likely continues with "gentle remedies."</note>

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER IX.

...since nothing is achieved by all these remedies with *Martin* <note>Referring to Martin Luther.</note> and the *sectarians*, they should resort to harsh measures: the sword and the fire. They should cut off the rotten members from the rest of the body, just as was done long ago with *Dathan, Abiram, Ananias, and Sapphira* <note>Biblical figures who were punished by God for rebellion or deception: Dathan and Abiram were swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16), while Ananias and Sapphira fell dead after lying to the Apostles (Acts 5).</note>, and with *Jovinian and Vigilantius* <note>Early Christian writers who questioned asceticism and the veneration of relics, condemned as heretics in the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>, and as was done by their ancestors to *Jan Hus and Jerome of Prague* at the *Council of Constance* <note>A 15th-century council that ended the Great Western Schism but also executed these two Bohemian reformers.</note>: whose examples, the situation now being hopeless, they ought to emulate.

<margin>XII. To the extent that they neither ought to have wished to persevere in the communion of the Roman Church, nor could they have, even if they had wished to.</margin>
XII. In that state of affairs, what were our ancestors to do? They could not remain in the communion of the Roman Church on the condition that they would have to renounce the truths which they firmly believed they had learned from the very word of God. For this would have been to betray their conscience, to put men before God, to sell the treasure of the *Gospel* for the comforts of this world, and finally, to play recklessly with the salvation of their own souls. But the Roman Church did not even permit them to remain in its communion while professing the truth; instead, what they cherished as the truth, the Romans cursed as detestable heresies to be uprooted by fire and sword. Nor was it permitted for them to keep their beliefs silent in their hearts while maintaining an outward communion in public worship; for just as one believes with the heart unto righteousness, so confession must be made with the mouth unto salvation. And by what logic, I ask, or by what conscience could they participate in the sacred rites of the Mass? For they considered it—I do not ask now by what right, but they considered it nonetheless—to be a denial of the unique sacrifice of Christ and a horrific idolatry. And even if they had very much wished to remain silent, they were not allowed to do so in many places because of the *Inquisition* <term>Inquisition</term><note>A powerful judicial body of the Roman Church tasked with finding and punishing heresy, often using secret interrogations.</note>, which searched the secret recesses of the soul with a terrifying examination. Since they were therefore driven out and ejected from the Roman Church itself, and since they were forbidden "water and fire" <note>A classical legal formula for banishment or total social exclusion.</note> unless they submitted to drowning or being burned alive; what remained, but that the Roman Church be told to "keep its things to itself," and that they should profess the *Gospel* truths among those to whom God had given a teachable spirit? These would be people who would worship God according to the rule of His word in the shared witness of prayers and the sacraments; just as the *Orthodox* <note>Referring here to those holding the traditional Nicene faith.</note> once did in the time when the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ; they held significant political power in the 4th century and occupied many churches.</note>, having gained control of affairs, had seized nearly all the temples. Our ancestors were driven to act in this way by an inevitable necessity. They could do no other, unless they had been willing to be openly harmful to Divine truth and the eternal salvation of their souls—a course which is unbecoming of good and wise men.

<margin>XIII. If they had looked at worldly things, there was nothing that would not have discouraged their withdrawal.</margin>
XIII. And indeed, if you except that one voice of conscience, all other things not only failed to persuade them toward that withdrawal, but seemed openly to oppose it. For since our fathers could hope for no profit or advantage from it, if they looked at worldly affairs—but rather could expect nothing but loss and disadvantage—certainly if they had followed "flesh and blood" <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or worldly instincts as opposed to spiritual revelation.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Protestant Reformers did not leave the Roman Church out of a desire for division (schism), but out of a necessity of conscience. # PROTESTANTS ARE WRONGLY COMPARED TO THE DONATISTS.

...if they had consulted <note>original: "consuluissent" — referring back to the previous page's argument about the Reformers weighing their personal safety against their duty to God.</note> their own worldly interests, they never should have seceded. For they foresaw—indeed, they were already experiencing it through their own suffering—that they could not depart from that society without incurring the indignation of Magnates and Princes, the ill-will of the common people and citizens, and the hatred of everyone. They knew they would lose their property, titles, friends, homeland, and all those things that are usually sweetest and dearest to us in this life. Finally, they would expose themselves to poverty, disgrace, exile, persecution, torture, death, and every possible hardship. On the other hand, they were certainly persuaded that if they had chosen to remain in the communion of Rome, they would have suffered no such things; rather, they would have enjoyed all things prosperous and happy. What, then, was the reason why, by seceding, they preferred a life that was outwardly most miserable to one that was most pleasant and flourishing? Unless we conclude they were out of their minds, there must have been some most grave reasons, more powerful than all worldly things, which drove them to despise what nature usually delights in, and to choose voluntarily—and endure most constantly—those things from which we normally shrink. See, if you please, Turretin <note>François Turretin (1623–1687), a high-profile Swiss-Italian Reformed theologian who defended the necessity of the Protestant separation from Rome.</note> in his work *On Our Necessary Separation from the Church of Rome*, where he disputes these and other similar matters elegantly and at length.

<margin>XIV. All hope of restoring union was removed by the anathemas of the Council of Trent.</margin>

XIV. Since then, every hope of reconciliation and of mending the union was cut off by the leaders of the Roman Church. For they decreed that all those errors must be accepted as articles of faith through the decrees of the *Council of Trent* <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Roman Catholic Church's formal response to the Protestant Reformation, where it clarified doctrine and condemned Protestant teachings.</note>, striking with an anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication pronounced by the Church.</note> anyone who testified that their conscience made such acceptance a sin. They cursed our ancestors with every possible malediction as infamous heretics and pests of the human race. They pursued them with the most cruel tortures, stripping them of their fortunes, honors, homeland, and finally life itself, with a savagery and cruelty to which the times of *Nero*, *Diocletian*, or the *Arians* <note>Nero and Diocletian were Roman Emperors famous for persecuting early Christians; the Arians were a group in the 4th century whose theological disputes with the mainstream Church often led to state-sanctioned violence.</note> hardly showed anything similar. To sum it up in a word: just as our ancestors had to leave the Roman Church to fulfill their duty toward God, the Gospel, and the salvation of their own souls—once all hope of *Reformation* <note>The attempt to change the Church's practices from within.</note> had failed—so too were they cruelly cast out from it. And we, following in those same footsteps, are excluded from the communion of that same Roman Church by harsh anathemas. Does this have even the slightest appearance of a resemblance to the *Donatist* <note>The Donatists were a group in North Africa in the 4th century who broke away from the Church, often cited by Catholic writers as the classic example of "schismatics" or people who cause division for the wrong reasons.</note> schism?

## CHAPTER X.

### The Romanists Never Granted a Just Conference to the Protestants.

I. *The Catholics* <note>original: "Catholici" — here referring to the early Christian Church fathers of the 4th and 5th centuries, such as Augustine, who opposed the Donatist schism.</note> *acted with the greatest leniency in examining and repeatedly reviewing the case of the* **Donatists**. <note>The Donatists were a rigorist Christian sect in North Africa who broke away from the main church; the author is comparing their treatment to that of the Protestants.</note>

<margin>I. In other times, the Catholics* <note>original: "Catholicè" — referring to the early Christian Church fathers of the 4th and 5th centuries.</note> *acted with the greatest leniency regarding the investigation and frequent re-examination of the case of the* **Donatists**.</margin>
Thus far we have shown that the **Secession** which our ancestors were forced to make from the communion of the **Roman Church** had entirely different causes and necessities than those the **Donatists** ever claimed for their schism; it was established in such a way that it cannot be compared with the crowds of those factious men without a notable injustice to [our] innocence. It remains for us to show that the leaders of the Roman Church by no means acted with our ancestors as the **Catholics** once did with the **Donatists**. History reveals how much equity and courtesy the latter showed toward the schismatics. As for the injustice, unfairness, and cruelty of the former toward the **Protestants**, both then and now, the matter speaks for itself. The Catholics, of both the ecclesiastical and political orders, heard the complaints of **Donatus** <note>The leader from whom the Donatists took their name.</note> with the greatest patience; they weighed the importance and reasons of the case on both sides; they examined everything brought against **Caecilian** and **Felix** <note>Bishops accused by the Donatists of being "traditors" (those who handed over scriptures during persecution).</note> with all their arguments; and although the innocence of **Caecilian** and **Felix** was proven, they did not refuse to have the same case re-examined a second, third, and even further time by other judges and in other places. They acted meanwhile to soothe the hardened minds of the factious with incredible leniency and prepare them for peace.

<margin>II. The Romanists never granted the Protestants the protection of a just defense.</margin>
II. But those who, in the time of our ancestors, applied their mind and hand to healing the diseases of the **Roman Church**, correcting errors, and uncovering the truth, were heard only with hostile ears by the **Pope**, the **Cardinals**, and the entire **Roman Curia**; they were never granted the protection of a legitimate and just defense.

<margin>III. This is shown by the example of Luther before Cajetan.</margin>
III. This will become manifest even by the single example of **Luther**. When he, in his writings, censured the most base and inexcusable abuses, he was summoned to **Augsburg** to **Cajetan**, the legate of **Leo X**, not so that he might give an account of his doctrine and be heard in those things he had to say for himself, but so that he might be compelled, without any investigation of the case, to revoke what he had written. For this was the mandate of the Pope explained to him at the first meeting—

BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.
660

<margin>Sleidanus</margin>
The Cardinal <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading theologian and cardinal who interviewed Luther at Augsburg in 1518.</note> urged him to return to spiritual health <note>original: "sanitatem" — often used in ecclesiastical Latin to mean "orthodoxy" or "right thinking."</note> and to revoke the errors he had spread. To this, **Luther** replied that he was not conscious of any error, and he asked that any such error be demonstrated to him. He did not deny that he could slip or be deceived—for that is only human—and therefore he submitted himself to the knowledge of the legitimate and holy Church, leaving the whole case to its judgment. Not only that, but he offered to give an account of his doctrine in any place, and did not refuse to have the judgment of the German Universities, or even the University of Paris, placed upon it. He also asked **Cajetan** in writing to deal kindly with him and point out his error; for he believed the power of what he had brought forth from the **Holy Scriptures** was so great that he relied on its truth, which he could not abandon, because "one must obey God rather than men." <note>A reference to Acts 5:29.</note> He therefore requested that the harsh condition of recanting be waived and that he be reconciled with the **Pope**. He claimed he had not entered this arena <note>original: "palæstram" — a Greek-derived term for a wrestling school or place of public contest.</note> out of arrogance or a desire for glory. He added that nothing more desirable could happen to him than for the truth to be made clear, especially if something more learned and pious were brought forward by someone else; he prayed that he might not be forced to wound his own conscience. Truly, nothing could be more fair than these requests. But what happened? Cajetan took the document Luther offered, and having read it, he thought little of it. Although he promised to send it to the Pope, he insisted strongly that Luther recant. Unless he did so, the Cardinal threatened the punishments already decreed by the Pope; at the same time, he ordered Luther to leave and to stay away from his presence in the future unless he changed his mind.

<margin>IV. Charles V.</margin>
IV. Next, **Luther** wrote a letter to the newly elected Emperor **Charles V**, in which he explained his goals. He said that, following the example of **Athanasius**, <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), who frequently appealed to imperial authority during the Arian controversy.</note> he was fleeing to him as if to an altar and a sanctuary of the laws. He prayed that the Emperor would take up the protection of Christian doctrine and defend him against all violence and injustice until the case was settled. He asked for no defense if he were convicted of upholding a bad cause; he asked only for a formal hearing <note>original: "cognitio" — a legal term for a judicial examination or trial.</note> and that no judgment be pronounced beforehand. Certainly, the **Donatists** never asked for anything like this, as they avoided every formal examination of their cause as much as possible. But the very thing the ancient Catholics were so ready to grant, **Luther** could never obtain from the Romanists.

<margin>V. Leo X.</margin>
V. Meanwhile, **Leo X**, with the consent and will of the Cardinals, condemned **Luther’s** doctrine. By the power he claimed to possess, he commanded everyone to shun it, establishing heavy penalties for each person according to their status, rank, and way of life. He also commanded the magistrates, especially the German ones, not to approve or defend any of that doctrine. He ordered Luther’s books, in which these things were contained, to be handed over and burned. He commanded **Luther** to cease from his duty of teaching; then he set a period of sixty days within which Luther was to return to spiritual health, destroy his own books, and publicly detest his own doctrine. <margin>VII. Before the Emperor and Princes at Worms.</margin>
VII. I admit that *Luther* was heard again at *Worms* <note>original: "Wormaciae"</note>: but in what manner? Not so that his cause might be investigated; but only so that it might be understood from him, first, whether he recognized as his own the books published under his name, and then whether he wished to retract anything in them, or rather to defend what had been written. There, when *Luther* had acknowledged his books and requested time for deliberation, he finally responded that he could not retract anything unless an error was first demonstrated to him. Among other things which he discussed excellently, he also used this speech: *However, I would not want these things to be taken as if I assume for myself that I cannot err: but rather, because it is characteristic of man to be deceived and to err, I take for the defense of my cause that saying of our Savior, who spoke of his own teaching, when he was struck by a certain servant: "If I have spoken evilly, bear witness of the evil"* <note>A reference to John 18:23, where Jesus defends himself before the high priest.</note>. *If Christ, in whom all perfection resides, did not refuse to hear testimony against Himself from the lowest servant, how much more should I, who am a sinner by my whole nature, and can err in more than one way, present myself when called, and listen if anyone wishes to testify and bring forward anything against my teaching? Therefore, I vehemently pray by all that is sacred, if there is anyone among all of you who has anything against the doctrine I profess, let him come forward and demonstrate the error by the testimonies of Scripture. If this is done, I will be so far from being stubborn that I will be the first of all to cast my own books into the fire.* Could anything be said more modestly, or more in agreement with reason? Did any of the *Donatists* <note>A 4th-century schismatic group in North Africa; the author suggests Luther is far more reasonable and open to correction than historical heretics.</note> ever seek to have their cause investigated in such a manner? But what did *Luther* obtain? *Eck* <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543), a prominent Catholic theologian and defender of the Papacy who acted as the interrogator at the Diet.</note>, who spoke in the name of the Emperor, with a harsh expression, said: *"You do not respond to the point; nor is it your place to call back into question or doubt those things which were long ago defined by the authority of Councils. A plain and simple answer is sought from you: Whether you wish your writings to be ratified."* Then *Luther* said: *"Since you command, Great Emperor, and most Illustrious Princes, that I respond plainly, I shall obey. This, therefore, is my opinion: that unless I am convicted by the testimonies of Holy Scripture, or by evident reason, I cannot revoke anything of those things which I have written and taught. For I will not commit myself to wounding my own conscience; I do not believe the Roman Pontiff or Councils alone; nor do I accept their authority, for they have erred quite often, and have said things contradictory to themselves."* Who, even if he were more of a *Momus* <note>In Greek mythology, Momus was the personification of satire and mockery; the author means even the most cynical critic could find no fault here.</note> than Momus himself, could find anything in that speech that would seem unworthy of a good and serious man? <margin>VIII. Where he was condemned without a legitimate investigation of the cause.</margin>
VIII. But nothing of the sort was done. Such a fair speech <note>Referring to Luther’s defense at Worms mentioned on the previous page.</note> seemed sufficient cause for the speaker's condemnation. Which followed shortly. For the Emperor <note>Charles V (1500–1558), who was 21 years old at the time of the Diet of Worms in 1521.</note>, who had then passed his twenty-first year, proscribed Luther by a public decree: in which he says the monstrosity of his [Luther's] madness <note>The Latin text here is slightly broken at "ra-" and continues with "condemnabilem," likely intended as "rabiem" (madness/rage).</note> is so damnable that it cannot be sufficiently explained by any speech: *that it is not a man who acts thus, but rather a demon in human form.* Therefore he condemns him as the author of a schism, and as a manifest and persistent heretic: he also commands everyone, under threat of severe punishment, to recognize him as such, and that after twenty-one days (the time granted for his return), everyone should strive to capture him and bring him, once captured, into his own power. By your faith! You Romanists <note>A term for those loyal to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, did *Constantine* <note>Constantine the Great, the first Christian Roman Emperor.</note> act thus with the *Donatists* <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa during the 4th and 5th centuries.</note>?

<margin>IX. Edicts against the Donatists were milder and mostly without effect.</margin>
IX. Furthermore, this must also be accurately observed: the Edicts of the Emperors, at least the earlier ones published against the Donatists, did not establish a punishment so much for their error, or even for their stubbornness, as for the seditions and violence with which they disturbed the public peace; and yet it is known that the Catholic Bishops zealously interceded with the Emperors so that either such edicts would not be published, or, if published, they would not be executed. The rescripts of later Emperors which followed, although more severe, established mostly fines; they hardly ever proceeded to the death penalty.

<margin>X. Against the Protestants [the edicts were] most cruel and effective.</margin>
X. Truly, how far from that mercy of the ancients do the examples of the most monstrous cruelty exercised against our ancestors stand? Which the mind shudders to remember and shrinks from saying. Imperial edicts were written not in ink, but in blood, and on account of the leniency of judges, they were repeated seven times and aimed repeatedly. <margin>Grotius, *Annals*, Book 1.</margin> *Those who had discussed Divine scripture, or been present at private gatherings for the sake of sacred rites—the sword is decreed for men, and burying alive under the ground for women, with their goods confiscated; provided, however, that they first acknowledged their fault: for the stubborn were punished with flames. Even if some, caught in false opinion but otherwise innocent, should repent, they were barred from all dignity. Those who had helped with hospitality, and those who had not informed [on others], were subjected to the punishments of the guilty: on the contrary, for the sake of inciting informants, impunity and rewards were offered. Many harsh things were done against the suspected and fugitives, and even more cruel things against those who relapsed; and the judges were terrified by punishments, lest they bend the laws under the appearance of mercy.* <note>This quote from the Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius describes the "Placards" or bloody edicts issued by Charles V in the Netherlands to suppress the Reformation.</note>

<margin>XI. With the churchmen inciting to cruelty.</margin>

...to avoid persecution? Where did he find laws that shut citizens in their cities and homes, as if in prisons, for immense punishments, unless they turn their sails as the wind of religion blows? Let us hide nothing: in our century, the glory of such inventions has been reserved for the Gallican Church and the Empire of *Louis the Great* <note>original: "Ludovici Magni," referring to King Louis XIV of France and his "Dragonnades" against the Huguenots.</note>.

<margin>The Romanists were always averse to any free Council and Brotherly conference.</margin>
XIII. But it is loathsome to relate these things at greater length. We hasten to other matters. What did the Romanists <note>The supporters of the Pope and the Roman Catholic Church.</note> ever offer or grant to our people that has even a shadow of similarity to the *Conference of Carthage* <note>A 411 AD meeting between Catholic and Donatist bishops intended to resolve their schism.</note>? It was not they, but our ancestors who sought a free council for ending religious controversies, in which everything would be defined according to Holy Scripture; but the Romanists loathed such a Council more than a dog or a snake. *Clement VII* <note>Pope from 1523 to 1534.</note> certainly shuddered at the very name of a Council, not only from fear of moderating the Pontifical authority or cutting off the advantages of his court, but most of all out of consideration for his own affairs. <margin>History of the Council of Trent, book 1, p. 37.</margin> For although *Leo* [X], his relative, when about to enroll him among the Cardinals, had tried to prove that a marriage contract had been made between his mother and his father *Giuliano*; nevertheless, the falsehood of the proof was well-known to everyone <note>Clement VII was the illegitimate son of Giuliano de' Medici; canon law technically barred illegitimate children from high ecclesiastical office.</note>. He also feared lest strength should be added to even this empty pretext by the power of the Emperor [Charles V], who supported the cause of his enemies as much as he could. But this especially kept him most anxious: lest (being well-aware of by what arts he had ascended to the height of the Supreme Pontiff, and how easy it would be for Cardinal Colonna to prove it; finally, by how rigid a decree *Julius II* had declared a simoniacal election <note>An election bought with money or favors.</note> as null and void, and forbade that it could be strengthened by subsequent consent) he should encounter the same danger to his dignity and life as *Balthasar Cossa*, called *John XXIII* <note>An antipope deposed by the Council of Constance in 1415 for various crimes.</note>. Afterwards, however, the same Clement, thinking he must use dissimulation, sent a nuncio to Germany and testified that the petition for a Council by *Emperor Charles* and the other Princes of Germany was very pleasing to him; but those conditions concerning the manner, time, and place of holding the Council...

# BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.
<meta>catchword: ...to be rooted out</meta>

...[conditio]nes <note>The text begins mid-word with the suffix of "conditiones" (conditions).</note> he proposed, which he knew the Protestants would never agree to. For no Council could satisfy the Protestants unless it was one where neither the Pope’s opinion nor anyone's power could prejudice the case, and where judgment was made according to Holy Scripture, rather than Papal laws or the opinions of the Scholastics <note>Medieval theologians whose philosophy-based approach was often rejected by Reformers in favor of "Sola Scriptura" (Scripture alone).</note>. While these things were happening in Germany, the Pope—who had easily foreseen how the Germans would respond to his demands—prevailed upon the King of France <note>Francis I</note> to negotiate with the Protestants. He specifically focused on the Landgrave of Hesse <note>Philip I, a prominent political leader of the Reformation</note>, who was then preparing for a journey to France. The King was to urge them to stop asking for a Council and to promise them, in his own name, that if they found any other way to resolve the disputes, he would sincerely and effectively apply all his effort to promote that way when the time was right. How much sincerity and openness there once was among Catholics is matched here by fraud and deception.

<margin>XIV. Paul III calls the Council of Mantua, but it was equally displeasing to both the Protestants and the Papal supporters.</margin>

XIV. Paul III, the successor of Clement, by that "fullness of power" <note>original: *potestatis plenitudine*; a technical term for the Pope's claimed supreme authority</note> which he claimed to possess and with the consent of his fellow Cardinals, announced a public Council for the entire Christian world. It was to be held at Mantua on May 27, 1537, to decree those things by which the Church might be reformed, heresies utterly removed, and war waged against the enemies of religion. Furthermore, in two decrees—one by which he announced the Council, and another in which he feigned a reform of the Roman Court—he openly declared that ***the Council was being summoned by him to root out the Lutheran heresy***. Because of this, the Protestants were forced to reject such a Council and to publish their reasons for this refusal in writing, so as to wash away the slanders of their adversaries. Finally, they implored the help of Kings and Princes to protect them, as innocent men, from injury, promising that if a legitimate Council were called at any later time, they would defend their cause and prove their actions before impartial judges. Specifically, they sent letters to the ***King of France***, to which he replied that ***he felt the same as they did about the Council, and would never approve of any except a legitimate one gathered in a safe place;*** he added that the King of Scotland <note>James V</note>, his son-in-law, would undoubtedly agree with his opinion. The King of ***England*** <note>Henry VIII</note> also, in his own name and that of the nobles of his kingdom, published a writing against the Council called by the Pope: ***that he indeed heartily desired a Christian Council, but would neither come to a Papal one nor send ambassadors.*** Thus, such a Papal Council seemed unjust not only to the Protestants but even to those Princes devoted to the Roman Church.

<margin>XV. And finally, to the Pope himself.</margin>

XV. Yet the Pope himself was not particularly pleased with the calling of the Council, condemning his own lack of judgment for having proceeded so far in this matter. Certainly, he clearly saw that for rooting out heresies... <note>original catchword: *pandis*, likely the end of *exstirpandis* (to be rooted out).</note>

# LUTHER WAS NEVER GRANTED A JUST DEFENSE.

...revealing that a Council was not, as he once thought, a useful remedy; but rather, that for the good of Italy, the goal was better achieved by arms, or by the inquisition of heretical depravity <note>A technical term for the legal office of the Inquisition, tasked with rooting out "heresy" or "depravity" (deviance from Church doctrine).</note>. Meanwhile, however, he reflected that he could not—without the gravest offense and danger—betray the true intention of his mind and dissolve that small gathering which had already assembled, not at Mantua, but (by a change of the Pope's plan) at Trent. Therefore, the Council of Trent was begun, and it was decided that its first session should be held on the 7th day of January in the year 1543 <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the definitive Catholic response to the Reformation. Though the text notes 1543, the formal opening is historically dated to December 1545.</note>.

<margin>XVI. The Council of Trent was anything but free.</margin>

XVI. But what kind of Council was it? Was it similar to the Conference of Carthage <note>A famous 411 AD meeting between Catholics and Donatists to resolve a schism, often cited as a model of debate.</note>? Let *Andreas Dudith* <note>A Hungarian nobleman and bishop who later became a Protestant; he was a representative at the Council of Trent.</note>, *Bishop of the Five Churches* <note>original: Quinqueecclesiensis; the Latin name for Pécs in Hungary.</note>, speak on my behalf. He was present at the Council himself, and in a letter written to the Emperor Maximilian II, he speaks thus: *“What could be achieved in that Council, where votes were merely counted, not weighed by their own importance? If the cause had been fought with reason, if even a few allies had been there with us, we would have defeated the vast forces of our adversaries, few as we were. But since the battle was decided by numbers alone—in which we were far inferior—we could not depart as victors in the best of causes. The Pope could oppose each one of us with a hundred of his own followers; and if a hundred seemed too few, he could suddenly create a thousand more to send as reinforcements for his struggling party. Thus, one could see every day hungry and needy Bishops—for the most part little bearded youths <note>original: "barbatulos adolescentes"; a mocking reference to their lack of maturity and experience.</note> lost in luxury—flying toward Trent, hired to give their votes according to the Pope's will. They were indeed unlearned and foolish, yet useful in their impudence and audacity. When these joined the Pope's old flatterers, then indeed did iniquity triumph and exult. No decision could be made except in favor of those who considered it the highest religion to defend the Pope’s power and luxury. If there was any grave and learned man who could not bear such an indignity, he was led away—as if he were not a good Catholic—by terror, threats, and persecution, until he approved what he did not wish to. In short, matters were brought to such a state by the wickedness of those who had come there pre-trained and instructed, that the Council seemed to consist not of Bishops, but of ghosts; not of men, but of puppets moved by the strings of others, just as the statues of Daedalus <note>A mythological inventor said to have created statues so lifelike they moved on their own.</note> are said to have been. Most of those hired Bishops were like bagpipes <note>original: "utres, rusticorum musicum instrumentum"; literally "skins, a peasant's musical instrument."</note> which must be inflated to produce a sound. The Holy Spirit had no dealings with that assembly. Everything was the result of human schemes, which were exhausted in defending the excessive and truly shameful domination of the Popes. From there, answers were expected as if from Delphi or Dodona <note>Ancient Greek oracles.</note>. From there, clearly, that Holy Spirit—whom they boast presides over their Councils—was sent enclosed in a courier’s saddlebags <note>A famous and scathing contemporary joke: that the "Holy Spirit" guiding the Council actually arrived in the mail from Rome in the form of the Pope's instructions.</note>. And what is truly ridiculous: when the rivers happened to swell with rain, the Spirit could not fly there before...*
