### BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

...could, as soon as the floods had subsided. Thus it happened that the Spirit was carried not *over* the waters, as it says in Genesis, but *beside* the waters <note>This is a famous contemporary sarcasm directed at the Council of Trent. Critics joked that the "Holy Spirit" arrived at the Council in the courier's mailbags sent from Rome, rather than descending from heaven upon the gathered bishops.</note>. Oh, monstrous and singular madness! Nothing that the Bishops decreed—treating them like the common people—could be considered ratified unless the Pope himself became its author.

<margin>XVII. The protests of Emperor Ferdinand and the King of France against the Council.</margin>

XVII. If these reasons are not enough to excuse the Protestants for thinking it unjust to submit their cause to such a Council, then let Emperor Ferdinand <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564), Holy Roman Emperor, who sought to reconcile the religious factions in his empire.</note> be heard. While the Council was still in progress, he wrote a letter to Pope Pius <note>Pope Pius IV (reigned 1559–1565), who oversaw the final sessions of the Council of Trent.</note> complaining heavily that *the Council was not proceeding in the manner and order that godly men wished, or that the afflicted state of the Christian world required; that business was being handled sluggishly; that the Fathers were distracted by contentions and disagreements; and that the Council did not possess its full and intact liberty, among other such complaints.* He even sent a volume of demands to the Council, such as: *that the Pope graciously allow himself and the Roman Curia to be reformed; that the number of Cardinals be reduced; that provision be made so that scandalous dispensations <note>Special permissions to bypass Church law, often sold or given as favors.</note> are no longer granted; that exemptions granted everywhere against common law be revoked; that the holding of multiple benefices <note>A "benefice" was a church office that provided an income; "plurality" meant one person collecting income from many offices without actually serving them.</note> be completely abolished; that Bishops be strictly compelled to live in their dioceses; that communion under both kinds <note>original: "communio sub utraque specie"—the practice of giving the laity both the bread and the wine during the Eucharist, a major demand of the reformers.</note> be decreed; that something of the ancient rigor regarding the eating of meat and fasting be relaxed; and that the marriage of Priests be granted to certain nations.*

Both the letters and these Articles can be found in the works of Goldast <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss jurist and historian who compiled imperial documents.</note>, in the second part of his *Imperial Constitutions*. However, the Legates at Trent were violently moved by this writing of Ferdinand's, judging it to be the work of those *who were exerting all their effort to diminish the dignity of the Synod and its leaders, and to lessen the splendor of the Papacy; they therefore decided not to even hand it over to the Assembly, but to suspend it for as long as it took for their Nuncios to talk Ferdinand out of that duty,* as Pallavicino <note>Sforza Pallavicino (1607–1667), a Jesuit cardinal who wrote a history of the Council of Trent from the Catholic perspective.</note> records in his *History of the Council of Trent*, Book XVII, Chapter 1, Section 6.

Similar articles were sent to the Council by the King of France, as the same Goldast relates in his third part, adding a solemn protest by the King against the Council, in which the French spoke as follows: *We French were hungry and starving, seeking bread from the Most Blessed Pope as from a common Father—not indeed natural bread, of which France (a most fertile region) has no need, but that Divine Supersubstantial bread of the Angels <note>original: "supersubstantialem"—a term for the Eucharist or spiritual food, derived from the Latin Vulgate's version of the Lord's Prayer.</note>, for which there was first such high cost, and now such a shortage in almost the entire Christian world, that it has scarcely ever been greater since the birth of Christ. But he did not give the bread we asked for, but a scorpion, whose tail with a single sting might strike at once two most powerful Kings, the Gallican Church <note>The Catholic Church in France, which traditionally maintained a degree of independence from the Pope.</note>, and the doctrine of the Parisian theologians.*

After other things said in a denunciatory manner <note>original: "στηλιτευτικῶς" (stēliteutikōs)—a Greek term for a public, written shaming or pillorying.</note> against Pope Pius, these same Fathers also addressed the Council: *What is proposed to you for judgment, or what judgment of yours is published, that was not first sent from Rome, and by Pius...*

# HISTORY OF THE COLLOQUY OF POISSY.

...if it should please them? They conclude: *We refuse the command of Pius IV; whatever his judgments and opinions may be, we reject, spurn, and despise them.* And again, they address the Fathers of the Council in this way: *Since nothing is done by you, but everything instead is done at Rome rather than at Trent, and since what is published here is rightly considered the whims of Pius IV rather than the decrees of the Council of Trent; we declare and protest that whatever is decreed and published in this gathering—that is, by the whim and will of Pius IV alone—the Most Christian King <note>A traditional title for the King of France.</note> will not approve, nor will the Gallican Church <term>Gallican Church</term><note>The Roman Catholic Church in France, which historically maintained a degree of independence from the Pope's administrative control.</note> regard as a decree of an Ecumenical Council.* From all of this, it is clear that the Papal Council of Trent has nothing in common or similar to the Conference of Carthage <note>The author frequently references the 411 AD Conference of Carthage as a model of fair debate between Catholics and Donatists, contrasting it with the perceived unfairness of Trent.</note>, nor could our ancestors have recognized its authority unless, with a madness utterly without precedent, they had willfully intended to hand themselves over to their enemies to be slaughtered.

<margin>XVIII. History of the Colloquy of Poissy.</margin>
XVIII. The beginnings of the Colloquy of Poissy <term>Colloquy of Poissy</term><note>A religious conference held in 1561 in Poissy, France, intended to reconcile French Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots).</note> were somewhat more favorable. The history of this Colloquy is certainly no less remarkable than whatever we have mentioned so far regarding the Conference of Carthage. It is also highly relevant to our cause, as it will make clear that the professors of our Religion <note>The author identifies with the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note> displayed the brilliance and sincerity of true Catholics <note>The author uses "Catholic" here in its original sense of "universal" or "orthodox," claiming the title for the Protestants against the Roman Church.</note> in a new and striking example; while, by contrast, the prelates of the Roman Church sought all their defense in the haughty evasions and deceptive arts of the *Donatists* <note>The author compares the Roman Catholic clergy to the Donatists, an early Christian sect known for being difficult and schismatic.</note>. Therefore, I believe I will be doing something worthwhile if I briefly collect here what has been recorded about the *Colloquy of Poissy* by the most trustworthy authors. The matter stands thus: while *Charles IX* <note>King of France (reigned 1560–1574) who was a minor at the time of the Colloquy.</note> held the scepter in France, various plans regarding religion were debated on both sides. Lest excessive partisan zeal should cause public disturbances, a time and place were appointed by a solemn royal decree, where several chosen men from both dissenting parties would meet to find a way, if possible, toward moderation, peace, and the avoidance of riots. The King of Navarre <note>Antoine de Bourbon, a key political leader who fluctuated between the Catholic and Protestant parties.</note> sent legates and letters to the Senate of Geneva, asking that *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), the primary successor to John Calvin and the lead representative for the Protestants at Poissy.</note> be allowed to attend the assembly, as it was being held for such a great and serious cause. The Queen Mother <note>Catherine de' Medici, who was acting as regent for her son Charles IX and sought to prevent civil war.</note> requested *Peter Martyr Vermigli* <note>A prominent Italian Reformed theologian then living in Zurich.</note> from the people of Zurich for the same purpose. The Papal prelates had gathered from all the provinces of France, even though they insisted that those who had long ago been condemned for heresy should not be heard, and they refused to confer with them. There also came ministers of the churches from various parts of France, famous among their own people for their learning and piety; the King's edict had provided for their safety by public guarantee, so that it was free for all and each of them to come, stay, and depart whenever they saw fit.

<margin>XIX. Beza, to whom the task of speaking...</margin>
XIX. They arrived at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on August 23rd, *in the year* 1561.

BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

<margin>A preparatory meeting with Cardinal Lorraine requested by the Protestants of the provinces.</margin>
They elected Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a French Protestant reformer and the successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note> by common vote to speak on a matter of such great importance in so august an assembly. Towards nightfall, he was led into the chamber of the *King of Navarre*: where the *Queen* <note>Catherine de' Medici, who was serving as regent for her young son, Charles IX.</note>, the *King of Navarre* himself, the *Prince of Condé*, the *Cardinals Bourbon* and *Lorraine*, along with many other nobles, were present. *Beza* briefly recounted the reasons for his arrival, though they were not unknown to them. The *Queen* replied with congratulations, saying she hoped that public peace would be primarily considered. However, the *Cardinal of Lorraine*—for it is difficult for churchmen not to reveal their true nature—received *Beza* with harsher words: *Just as you gave occasion for serious disturbances while absent,* he said, *so it is to be hoped by all of us that you will now apply all your counsel to quiet them in person.* To which *Beza* replied: *that he was of too humble a condition to be capable of stirring up such a great and powerful kingdom. By nature and will, he had always been most averse to disturbances; moreover, his zeal and duties, or rather his devotion toward God, King, and Country, would never be lacking.* After some mutual conversation, *Cardinal Lorraine* testified to the *Queen* that he was greatly satisfied by *Beza*. He said he hoped for the desired outcome of the Colloquy if matters were handled calmly and with right reason. After the assembly was dismissed, he addressed *Beza* very affectionately, saying: *I am glad that I have heard you speak, and I invite you, by the immortal God, to mutual conference. For I hope that, with the arguments on both sides well-weighed and balanced, a way to concord will certainly be found in a short time.* *Beza* thanked him profusely, pleading that the Cardinal himself would also persevere in the holy work and zeal of securing public concord; for his part, he would wholeheartedly contribute whatever gifts he had received from God to that end, and would not allow anything to be found wanting in himself. I have recorded these things in such detail so that it might be clear how far the theologians of our party were from the proud and utterly inhumane rigidity of the Donatists <term>Donatists</term><note>A 4th-century Christian sect in North Africa known for their uncompromising and rigid stance against those they considered "fallen" or impure. <margin>XX. Conditions under which the public Colloquy is to be held.</margin>
XX. All controversies should be settled by the Word of God alone <note>original: "ex uno Dei verbo" — a reference to the Protestant principle of Sola Scriptura.</note>. Whatever is determined in that Colloquy should be recorded in public commentaries and acts by the Royal Notaries. The King's response to this was that he would discuss the matter with the men of his Council, so that, if possible, the whole matter might be brought to a peaceful conclusion with the consent of the Bishops. The Bishops protested that this freedom of debating had already long ago been condemned...

# HISTORY OF THE COLLOQUY OF POISSY

...should by no means be granted to those born <note>The text likely refers here to the rights or legal standing of those born into the Reformed faith.</note> into it, they deferred the matter for several days. Finally, the Queen <note>Catherine de' Medici, acting as Regent for her young son.</note> replied to them that the bishops themselves would by no means be the judges: instead, some of the King's secretaries would be assigned to them, unless they preferred to record the proceedings themselves. They were to testify publicly that the matter was to be settled based on the Word of God alone, and that the King and the Princes of the blood would be present at this Colloquy. She advised them to conduct themselves with modesty and to seek the glory of God alone, as she believed them to be devoted to Him. She added that it was not expedient to grant them anything in writing, since her own words ought to be more than enough.

Once the deputies of the Reformed Churches had received this response and departed, some of the Sorbonne doctors <note>Theologians from the University of Paris, known for their staunch defense of Catholic orthodoxy.</note> immediately approached the Queen. They begged her not to listen to these men of a "new religion." They argued that if she was determined to hear them, she should at least ensure the young King was not present during their speeches; there was a very great danger, they claimed, that he might be deceived at his tender age. Those who had long ago been convicted as heretics, they insisted, should not be heard at all. The Queen replied only that she would do nothing without mature counsel, and that the reality would make it clear that the matter was not being conducted according to the whims of those men whom they claimed followed a "new doctrine." Here again, I offer it to fair-minded readers to consider whose demands more closely resemble those of the Catholics, and whose those of the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a 4th-century Christian sect; the author is making a polemical comparison between ancient schismatics and the religious factions of the 16th century.</note>.

<margin>XXI. Its beginning.</margin>
XXI. On the 4th of September, they gathered in the great hall of the Monastery of Poissy. Present were the King <note>Charles IX, who was only 11 years old at the time.</note>, the Queen Mother, the Duke of Orléans (the King’s brother), Marguerite (the King’s sister), the King and Queen of Navarre, the Prince of Condé, and a great number of other nobles. Among the Catholic prelates were Cardinals, Archbishops, and Bishops—about fifty in total—surrounded by a large circle of Sorbonne doctors and Canon lawyers. Standing nearby were the pastors of the Reformed Churches, numbering about thirty.

<margin>XXII. The King's speech. From de Thou, Book XXVIII.</margin>
XXII. The King, about to open the proceedings, said that they knew for what reason they had been summoned here: namely, that a healthy remedy might be sought, according to their judgment, for the disturbances arising everywhere in his kingdom. Therefore, they should see to it that, with every cause of offense cut away, those things needing correction be amended, and that public peace be provided for in a lawful manner, as best as could be done. He desired that they not depart until they had applied every effort so that, once the disagreements were finally settled, mutual harmony and sincere friendship might be restored among the peoples subject to his majesty. If they did this, as he trusted they would, he would not allow them to ever again need to seek from him or his magistrates the patronage under which they were once protected by his ancestors.

<margin>XXIII. The speech of de l'Hôpital, the King's Chancellor.</margin>
XXIII. ### Book IV. Chapter X.

<margin>Setting forth his mind at greater length.</margin>
...it was maturely deliberated in the most noble assembly of princes and the council, that indeed through this specific and particular <term>colloquy|A formal academic discussion or conference, used here for the religious summit at Poissy</term> the matters of religious controversy might be peacefully compared between the two dissenting parties. He argued that the remedy of a General <term>Council|A universal gathering of church leaders from the entire Christian world</term> was certainly expected in vain, and thus sought in vain—much as if someone, despising domestic remedies that are easiest to prepare, were to fly off to explore the Indies to find a cure. He said that remedies for our diseases will be more easily prepared by us than by foreign and external men who are completely ignorant of the state of our affairs and our people; yet it is from this very class of foreign men that a general council would have to be composed. He noted that more abundant fruits have often come from national councils than from general ones, seeing that the general Council of Ariminum <note>original: "Ariminense Concilium." Held in 359 AD, this council was initially seen as a victory for Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, which clearly favored the Arians, was corrected by particular synods. This was also true in our own Gaul through the industry and faith of Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers <note>A 4th-century champion of orthodoxy against Arianism in France.</note>, who by these methods once prevented the Arian heresy from spreading in these regions. Therefore, there was no doubt that the greatest benefits would come from this assembly, especially since the King is so zealously devoted to it and will undoubtedly contribute all his strength and authority. He urged the legates of both sides to ensure they did their duty: to aspire toward concord with mutual spirits, that the majority should not despise the minority, and that the matter should not be conducted through curious disputations. Let every matter be judged by the word of God alone, for once this is properly understood, there is no need for many books. He cautioned the bishops not to treat those whom they say follow "new doctrine" as enemies, as they still retain the name of Christian through Baptism. He stated the King had given them the power to meet so that the reasons they held might be made manifest to all; let the bishops strive to refute them with firm arguments. Then, once the disputation was made public, it would be clear to everyone that those men were condemned for the best of reasons, and not by the vain authority of men. He exhorted them again and again to ensure nothing was done out of ambition; let them know they do not sit as judges, but should instead be devoted to the truth. God would thus bless these methods and the King’s most constant will in this matter.

<margin>XXIV. Not greatly approved by the Bishops.</margin>
XXIV. Indeed, it cannot be denied that a speech of this kind comes very close to the fairness of the ancient Catholics; nor do I refuse to compare it to the proceedings conducted by Marcellinus at Carthage <note>A reference to the Conference of Carthage in 411 AD, where St. Augustine debated the Donatists under the mediation of the imperial official Marcellinus.</note>. But it happened somewhat unexpectedly for the bishops. The Cardinals of Tournon and Lorraine demanded that L'Hôpital <note>original: "Hospitalius." Michel de L'Hôpital (1507–1573), the Chancellor of France, who sought religious toleration.</note> deliver what he had said in writing. L'Hôpital, however, refused, because the matter had been fully understood by everyone. Indeed, Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous historian of the period.</note> says he had "caught the scent" and knew this was being done so they could create trouble for him and, in the meantime, throw a delay in the way of the business.

<margin>XXV. Beza’s speech from the Divine Spirit.</margin>
XXV. Finally, once the ministers of the Reformed Church were given the power to speak, Theodore Beza spoke to this effect: "Since all things, both greatest and smallest, and especially those which pertain to the worship of God—which is our..."

> "Since, O Lord," he said, "today you so favor your useless servants that they may, before their King and this most illustrious assembly, profess the knowledge of your truth: may you be willing, according to your accustomed goodness, O Father of Lights <note>A biblical title for God from the Epistle of James, referring to God as the source of all wisdom.</note>, to so illuminate our minds, govern all our affections, and form them to teachability: so direct our speeches, that those things which you have imparted to us according to our small measure concerning the knowledge of your truth, we may bring forth in public with both heart and mouth, for the glory of your name, the prosperity of our King and all his people, and the peace and tranquility of the Christian Republic <note>original: "Christianæque Reipublicæ." In the 16th century, this term referred to the collective body of Christian nations, or Christendom.</note> and especially this Kingdom."

<margin>XXVI. Soon he turns to the King.</margin>

Because this speech is less well known and remarkably demonstrates the spirit with which men of our profession <note>Meaning those of the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note>, according to the nature of their religion, are disposed toward Kings and Princes, it will not be troublesome to present at least some part of it here.

> "That is indeed accounted as the greatest happiness," he said, "by those who faithfully honor and respect their Princes, O most illustrious King, if they can gaze upon the face of those Princes of theirs: which, representing as it were a certain visible majesty of God, cannot fail to deeply move the souls of loyal subjects. For we are so naturally constituted that those things we have seen with our own eyes touch our senses more effectively than those things we have perceived by a bare and simple mental concept. But if it should happen that subjects are not only able to see their Prince, but are also seen by the Prince, and what is more, are heard, and finally approved by him: then indeed they seem to have achieved the very sum of all their prayers. Of these four things, O King, it pleased God that some of your faithful subjects should be deprived for a time, indeed with great grief and inconvenience: until that same God, in his infinite mercy, granting something to our continuous tears and groans, so favored us that on this day he has given us a good more desired than hoped for—namely, the opportunity to behold your Majesty—so that we might be both seen and heard by you in this most illustrious theater of nearly the whole world. If we had never received any other benefit, nor were to have any hereafter, the remaining course of our life would certainly not be sufficient to celebrate and proclaim so great a blessing from God, and to give immortal thanks, as is fitting, to your Majesty. But, since to those previous benefits this also [is joined...]"

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

...we add that this day not only provides us access but even invites us—indeed, in a certain sweet and kind manner suited to your Majesty, it almost compels us—to testify with one heart concerning the name of our God and the obedience we owe you. We must undoubtedly admit that our minds are hardly capable of receiving such great benefits, and our tongues are even less sufficient to express the feelings and wills of our hearts. Therefore, since this favor surpasses all human eloquence, we prefer to confess our weakness with modest silence rather than diminish its greatness with a poverty of words. Only one thing remains for us to hope: that our service today may be pleasing to your Majesty. This we hope will be the case, provided (God willing) our arrival brings an end not so much to the miseries of our past afflictions (the memory of which is wiped out on this happy day) as to that matter which has always seemed to us even heavier than death: namely, the disturbances in this kingdom stirred up long ago because of Religion <note>original: "Religionem." Beza is referring to the French Wars of Religion and the tensions between Catholics and the Reformed Protestants.</note> to the great ruin of many. 

Now indeed, there are many circumstances which until this day prevented us from enjoying such a great benefit, and would even now take away all hope of achieving it, unless we leaned on and were supported by other things. First, there is an opinion fixed and deeply rooted in the minds of many—by some evil or the unfairness of the times—that we are turbulent, ambitious men, entirely devoted to our own opinions, and enemies of peace and tranquility. 

There are also those who, though they do not think we entirely shrink from peace and harmony, believe nevertheless that we seek it under such unfair and heavy conditions that we should in no way be received—as if we wanted to turn the whole world upside down <note>A common accusation against the Reformers, echoing the biblical charge against the Apostles in Acts 17:6.</note> to build a new one according to our own judgment, and even want to drive some from their property to occupy it ourselves. There are other great obstacles of this kind: but we prefer their memory be buried rather than rub and renew old wounds by mentioning them, especially now, when not complaints should be brought forward, but remedies for complaints should be provided and dispatched. 

Who, indeed, among so many obstacles gives us courage? Certainly not any protection of ours, O King, since we are the humblest of all men; nor is it arrogance or some vain persuasion. Our lowly and obscure condition does not allow this. But this confirms us: our good conscience <note>original: "Bona nostra conscientia."</note>: which rests on the goodness of our cause—our cause, I say—for which we hope God, through the mediation of your Majesty, will be the defender and avenger. Likewise your kindness, O King, which is wonderfully visible in your expression, face, and speech; the fairness inherent in your mind, most illustrious Queen <note>A reference to Catherine de' Medici, the Queen Mother and Regent of France.</note>; the goodness of your heart, O King, and of the most illustrious Princes, kinsmen of our King; the op-

<margin>XXVII.

XXVII. Having spoken these grave words to the King, he turned his speech toward the Catholic Prelates <note>original: "Pontificios Antistites." Such is our persuasion regarding you. Indeed, by the name of that great God who has gathered us here, who will be the witness and judge of our thoughts and words, we pray and entreat you that, whatever has been said, written, or done over these last forty years, you would lay aside with us all prejudices and passions which could hinder the fruit of this most laudable plan. And concerning us, if you please, hope for that which, by God’s blessing, you shall find: namely, a teachable mind, ready to receive whatever shall be demonstrated from the pure Word of God. Do not think that we come here to uphold any error, but rather so that whatever has been sinned by us or by you may be corrected. Do not think us so arrogant that we wish to abolish that which is eternal, namely the Church of our God. Do not think we seek ways to make you equal to this wretched and lowly condition of ours—in which, however, by the greatest grace of God, we are most content. This is our will: that the ruins of Jerusalem <note>A biblical metaphor for the Church in need of reform.</note> be restored; that the spiritual temple be built up; that the house of God, constructed of living stones, might recover its former luster; and that the scattered and dissipated flocks may be gathered and brought back into the fold of that one and highest Shepherd. This is our counsel, this our will, this our prayer; and if until this day you have not believed it, we hope you will believe it then, when we have conferred with you in all patience and gentleness. Would that, in place of disputations and arguments, we might with one voice sing a song to God, joining hands with one another—as once happened, it is said, between two battle lines, even among the unfaithful. Truly, it would be a shame for us if, while both preaching the doctrine of concord and peace, we are easily divided and only with difficulty reconciled. But what of it? These things can and ought to be desired by men, but it belongs to God alone to bring them to pass; which He will surely do when, in His goodness, He covers our sins and scatters our darkness with His light.*

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

<margin>The doctrine of the Reformed Churches is beautifully summarized.</margin>
...those matters regarding the obedience owed to Kings, Princes, and Magistrates, which are consistently taught among us. And at last, he concludes his speech in this manner:

> If it has happened, or should happen in the future, that some people, falsely using the name of our doctrine <note>original: "doctrinæ nostræ nomen ementientes"</note>, are found to be rebellious even in the slightest against your ministers: we testify before God and your Majesty, O King, that such men are by no means of our number, and will have no sharper adversaries than us (so far as our humble condition allows). Therefore, O King, our zeal for promoting the glory of God, the obedience and service owed to your Majesty, our love for our country, and especially for the Church of God, have brought us to this place: hoping that God the Best and Greatest, according to His accustomed mercy, will grant the same benefit to you as He did to the young Josiah <note>Josiah was a biblical king of Judah who began his reign as a boy and was famous for his religious reforms and returning the people to the law of God.</note>, and that through your happy governance, O Queen; and through your counsel, O King, and yours, most illustrious Princes and Councilors, the ancient memory of the famous Queen Clotilda <note>Clotilda was the wife of Clovis I, the first King of the Franks; she is credited with converting her husband to Christianity, thus "disseminating the knowledge of God" throughout France.</note> shall be renewed: by whose efforts God saw fit to spread the knowledge of Himself through this Kingdom. This is our hope, most powerful King, for which we are prepared to spend our very lives: so that by obeying you in this most pious and laudable matter, we may see that truly golden age, in which our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ is acknowledged and worshipped, so that all honor and glory may always be given to Him.

<margin>XXIX. The Confession of Faith of those same Churches is presented to the King.</margin>
XXIX. Then, having offered the Confession of the French Churches to the King, he said:

> We pray your Majesty not to look at our unrefined and unpolished speech, but at a spirit entirely dedicated to your service. Since the main points of our doctrine are contained more clearly and fully in this Confession of Faith, we pray your Majesty to receive it: we hope, by the favor of our God, that after we have conferred with all sobriety and reverence, we may come to some agreement. But if our iniquities should snatch this blessing from us, we do not doubt that your Majesty will provide for all things fairly and well, according to equity and goodness, without prejudice to either side.

Who would not admire and proclaim in all these things the piety, sincerity, candor, modesty, and prudence, joined with equal skill in Divine matters and eloquence? # HISTORY OF THE COLLOQUY OF POISSY.

...uttered such shameful things <note>original: "vitiosa effutirent"</note> that would offend the ears of the King himself and of all godly people; for this reason, he had intervened from the beginning to prevent the King from attending this assembly. Therefore, he now entreated his Royal Majesty to place no trust in what had just been said, but to suspend his judgment for a time and not allow his mind *to be preoccupied by their false opinions until the bishops had demonstrated otherwise:* for then the King and the entire assembly would understand the difference between truth and falsehood. He therefore requested a day to respond. Meanwhile, he prayed that the King would follow in the footsteps of his ancestors regarding religion. Finally, he added: had they not shown regard for the King and his commands, the bishops would have risen up against those horrendous and abominable words just pronounced, and would not have allowed the speech to proceed any further.

<margin>XXXI. The cause of the anger was certain words of Beza regarding the Supper.</margin>
XXXI. Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a contemporary historian and statesman whose works provide a primary account of the French Wars of Religion.</note> further records the cause of such great an outcry in these words. When Beza, in his dissertation on the mystery of the Supper <term>The Supper: Referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</term>, was carried away by the heat of the debate, he proceeded to the point that—although he admitted that all the faithful partake in the body and blood of Christ in an ineffable <note>Too great or sacred to be expressed in words.</note> way, just as they see the sacraments with their eyes, touch them with their hands, and bring them to their mouths—he nevertheless affirmed that if one considers the distance of locations (as he said was necessary when discussing the presence of the body and its humanity distinctly considered), *the body of Christ is as far from the bread and wine as the highest heaven is from the earth.* This was not heard without an outcry from those present, and at those words Tournon <note>Cardinal François de Tournon, the presiding official of the assembly and a staunch opponent of the Reformation.</note> became so incensed. Thus far Thuanus. However, it was easy for Beza to prove that what he said was correct and entirely consistent with the Holy Scriptures and the doctors of the early Church, as he abundantly demonstrated in letters written to the Queen.

<margin>XXXII. The bishops deliberate whether and how to respond to Beza.</margin>
XXXII. But a pretext was sought to break off the colloquy. The bishops therefore met, and after communicating the matter with several doctors of the Sorbonne <note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris, known for its rigorous defense of Catholic orthodoxy.</note> and doctors of Canon Law, they deliberated on what response should be set against the speech of the Reformed Church. Here the Cardinal of Lorraine <note>Charles of Lorraine, a powerful member of the House of Guise and a chief negotiator for the Catholic side.</note> is reported to have said, *“I wish either he had been mute, or we had been deaf.”* After the matter was debated in various ways by both sides, it was finally decided that only two chapters of that speech should be answered: namely, concerning the Church and the Supper. It was also deliberated whether it would be advantageous for a Confession of Faith to be written out and offered first to the Ministers; if they refused to embrace it, then a sentence of condemnation would immediately be brought against them as heretics, and thus an end would be put to the Colloquy. However, this deliberation did not fully prevail among them, as some of the bishops opposed it. When this matter reached the Ministers of the Reformed Church, they complained to the King and Queen, praying that the fruit of the Colloquy not be hindered by such schemes.

...spewed forth shameful things, which would offend the ears of the King himself and of all pious people; for this reason, they had initially interceded to prevent the King from attending this assembly. Therefore, they now pleaded with the *Royal Majesty* not to place the slightest faith in what had just been said, but to suspend his judgment for a time and not allow his mind to be preoccupied by their false opinions, until the *Prelates* <note>The high-ranking Catholic bishops and cardinals present at the colloquy.</note> had demonstrated otherwise. For then the *King* and the entire *Assembly* would understand the distinction between truth and falsehood. They therefore requested a day to respond. In the meantime, they urged the *King* to follow in the footsteps of his ancestors in *Religion*. Finally, he <note>The Cardinal of Tournon, who was acting as the spokesperson for the Catholic party.</note> added: that if they had not taken the *King* and his commands into account, the *Prelates* would have risen up at those horrendous and abominable words which had just been uttered, and would not have allowed the speech to proceed any further.

<margin>XXXI. The cause of the anger was certain words of *Beza* concerning the *Supper*.</margin>
XXXI. *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman whose works are a primary source for this period.</note> further records the cause of such great outcry in these words. When *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), the primary representative of the Reformed party and successor to John Calvin.</note> was proceeding in his Dissertation on the mystery of the *Supper* <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, he had been carried away by the heat of the debate to such an extent that, although he admitted all the faithful participate in the body and blood of Christ in an inexpressible way—just as they see the sacraments themselves with their eyes, touch them with their hands, and bring them to their mouths—he nevertheless affirmed that, if one considers the distance of locations (as he said was necessary when discussing the presence of the body and His humanity considered distinctly), *the body of Christ is as far distant from the bread and wine as the highest heaven is from the earth.* <note>original Latin: "corpus Christi tantum a pane & vino abesse, quantum altissimum cælum a terra distat"</note> This was not heard without an outcry from those present, and at those words *Tournon* <note>Cardinal François de Tournon, a staunch defender of Catholic orthodoxy.</note> became so incensed. Thus far *Thuanus*. However, it was easy for *Beza* to prove that these things were rightly spoken by him and were entirely consistent with the Sacred Scriptures and the Doctors of the early Church, as was abundantly demonstrated by him in letters written to the Queen.

<margin>XXXII. The *Prelates* deliberate whether, and in what way, *Beza* should be answered.</margin>
XXXII. But a pretext had to be found for breaking off the colloquy. Therefore, the *Prelates* met, and having communicated the matter with several doctors of the *Sorbonne* <note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note> and of *Canon Law*, they deliberated on what response should be opposed to the speech of the *Reformed Church*. Here the Cardinal of *Lorraine* <note>Charles de Guise, Cardinal of Lorraine, a powerful leader of the Catholic faction and a skilled orator.</note> is reported to have said: *“Would that either he had been mute, or we had been deaf.”* <note>original Latin: "Utinam aut ille mutus, aut nos surdi fuissemus"</note> After the matter was debated back and forth in various ways, it was finally decided that only two chapters of that speech should be answered: namely, concerning the Church and the *Supper*. They also deliberated whether it would be beneficial for a *Confession* of faith to be drafted, which would first be offered to the *Ministers* <note>The Protestant pastors.</note>; if they refused to embrace it, then a sentence of condemnation would immediately be passed against them as heretics, and thus an end would be put to the Colloquy. This deliberation, however, did not entirely prevail among them, as some of the *Prelates* opposed it. When this matter reached the *Ministers of the Reformed Church*, they complained to the *King and Queen*, praying that the fruit of the Colloquy not be hindered by such schemes.

### BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

<margin>XXXIII. The Oration of Lorraine.</margin>
XXXIII. Therefore, the **Colloquy** <note>A formal theological conference between parties intended to settle religious differences.</note> was restored on September 16th. Once again, the King <note>Charles IX, who was only eleven years old at the time.</note>, the Queen <note>Catherine de' Medici, the Queen Mother and Regent.</note>, the King of Navarre, and others were present at the same location, though with a smaller crowd. There, the **Cardinal of Lorraine** <note>Charles of Lorraine (1524–1574), a powerful prelate and member of the House of Guise.</note> delivered a long and long-meditated oration. He had greatly desired this meeting—to use the words of **Thuanus** <note>original: "Thuani verbis loquor." Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a famous historian whose accounts are a primary source for this text.</note>—lest his own reputation perish, despite the contrary opinion of the **Cardinal of Tournon** and many other theologians. He disputed with no little skill regarding the **Church** and the **Supper** <note>The Lord's Supper or Eucharist.</note> according to the mind of his own party. Speaking in the name of the **Prelates**, he testified that he wished to live and die in this doctrine which he had explained.

<margin>XXXIV. The others agree with him.</margin>
XXXIV. After him, all the **Prelates** who were present stood up and approached closer to the King. On their behalf, **Cardinal Tournon** testified that this was the confession of their faith, which they were willing to seal with their own blood; he declared it to be the indubitable truth of **Holy Mother Church**, and that the King, according to the custom and institution of his ancestors, ought to hold firmly to it. If, however, those who had separated themselves from the **Roman Church** were willing to subscribe to that confession, then they might certainly be received and heard more fully on other heads of doctrine in which they said they wished to be instructed. Otherwise, he argued that all hearing ought to be denied to them, and that it was the King’s duty to expel them from his jurisdiction. He stated that he vehemently prayed for this on behalf of all his colleagues.

<margin>XXXV. Beza denied the opportunity to respond on that day.</margin>
XXXV. Then **Beza** immediately asked the King for the opportunity to respond to Lorraine's oration on the spot. For the **Ministers** <note>The Protestant Reformed clergy.</note> feared that the power of meeting together would no longer be granted to them. A rumor was spreading everywhere that the **Prelates** had decided, once that day had passed, to deal with them no further except through the lightning bolts of **excommunication**. Indeed, it was suspected by some that a discussion concerning the opinion of the **Germans** <note>Referring to the Lutherans, whose views on the Eucharist differed from the Reformed/Calvinist views represented by Beza.</note>—which had been somewhat inopportunely introduced by **Beza** and ingeniously seized upon by **Lorraine**—would become an opportunity to both elude the **Conference** <note>original: "Collationis."</note> and to set the German and Reformed churches against one another with a ridiculous outcome. Nevertheless, the opportunity for the **Ministers** to respond was denied on that day, and the matter was delayed until another day. This, too, was procrastinated by various obstacles thrown in the way.

<margin>XXXVI. The Ministers seek the continuation of the Colloquy.</margin>
XXXVI. Therefore, the **Ministers**, fearing these delays would cause the entire matter to be interrupted, finally decided to offer a petition to the King. They argued that since they had come there from such distant regions by his command, so that matters might be peacefully communicated and compared with the **Prelates** to reach an agreement on uprooting the errors that had oppressed the **Church** for so many years, they asked that the power to conduct the **Colloquy** and to state and explain their cause be granted. They asserted it was entirely the duty of the King—adorned with that August title of **"Most Christian"** <note>The traditional title held by the Kings of France.</note>—to undertake the patronage of **Religion**. They argued that this was the way to secure both the Kingdom for himself and peace and tranquility for his Kingdom...

XXXVII. Thus, the assembly, which had been interrupted for several days, was finally restored with a small number of people: the Queen <note>Catherine de' Medici.</note>, the King <note>Charles IX.</note>, the Queen of Navarre, the **Prelates**, twelve chosen **Ministers**, and very few others being present. The **Cardinal of Lorraine** opened by saying that this assembly had met so that they might hear those things which the **Ministers** wished to answer in response to the speech he had recently delivered. Then **Beza** spoke: *“Having first called upon the name of God,”* he said, *“that He might wish to be present with us in a matter of such great importance, and to bring it about that this assembly should meet for the glory of His name, for your dignity, O Queen, and for the peace and tranquility of the entire Christian Commonwealth and especially of this Kingdom: we shall respond briefly to those things which were recently proposed to us in the name of the **Prelates** against two chapters of our **Confession**—namely, concerning the **Church** and concerning the **Lord's Supper**. If the opportunity to respond immediately had been granted to us while the memory of the things proposed was still fresh, or if a transcript of the delivered oration had been provided, we could have responded more distinctly and perhaps more appropriately; nevertheless, we shall say those things which God grants us: so that it may be understood in what matters we agree, and in which matters we likewise disagree with them. May a firm concord regarding these things be entered into.”*

<margin>
XXXVIII.
The speech of d'Espence.
</margin>

XXXVIII. After **Beza** had spoken at length regarding the **Church**, **Claude d'Espence** <note>A moderate Catholic theologian and doctor of the Sorbonne known for his learning and desire for reform within the church.</note>, a learned man and one eager for the peace of the **Church**, was ordered by the **Cardinal of Lorraine** to speak. He began by saying that he had long desired this opportunity for mutual conference, and stated that he had always completely shrunk from those cruel punishments hitherto used against those who embraced that religion. He also acknowledged that the things just said by **Beza** regarding the **Church**—namely, its marks and its succession—were true; but he began a dispute regarding the authority of the "calling" <note>term: Vocation (The legitimate authorization or 'calling' by which a person is appointed to the ministry of the Church).</note> by which the **Reformers** relied upon to enter the **Church** and receive the office of teaching. Then he also insisted upon something regarding the physical presence of Christ in the **Supper**. He even read several passages from the books of **Calvin**, and it was said that he had introduced this speech by the command of the **Cardinal of Lorraine**, in an arranged manner, so that a convenient opportunity for breaking off the **Colloquy** might be found.

The disordered shouting of the monk Sainctes.

This refers to the Premonstratensians or Norbertines, an order of canons regular who wear white habits.</note> from the **Sorbonne School**, named **Sainctes** <note>Claude de Sainctes (1525–1591), a scholar of the Sorbonne and a fierce opponent of the Reformation.</note>, rose up in a confrontational manner, repeating at length and unpleasantly what had been said by **d'Espence**: *“Traditions rest upon a firmer foundation than the Scripture itself: because the Scripture can certainly be turned and translated this way and that by a variety of interpretations.”* He added many more things of this kind. He himself, however, responded accurately to the speech of *Espencæus* <note>Claude d'Espence, a moderate Catholic theologian who sought reconciliation.</note>. XL. Lorraine strives to pit the French theologians against the Germans.

XL. Afterward, the Cardinal recalled the Ministers <note>The Protestant pastors.</note> to the controversy regarding the **Supper** <note>The Eucharist or Lord's Supper, the central point of theological division.</note>: craftily acting so as to collide them with the German theologians who were devoted to the *Augsburg* Confession <note>The primary statement of faith for Lutherans; Lorraine hoped to exploit differences between the Lutheran and Calvinist views of the Eucharist.</note>. These Germans had been summoned to France at the instigation of *Francis Balduinus*, but since they arrived too late, they had stopped at *Paris*. After many things were discussed on both sides, *Beza* persisted with his companions in this: that he had come there to defend the confession of his own churches, and that he held this single mandate from his churches. While he responded to *Espencæus* concerning the speech on "calling" <note>The "vocation" or right of Protestant ministers to preach.</note>, he said many things which served more to irritate the minds of the prelates than to win their favor.

<margin>
XLI. The insolent speech of Laynez the Jesuit and another Sorbonnist.
</margin>

XLI. Then a certain Spaniard from the Jesuit society rose up, who had been sent by *Ippolito d'Este*, the Cardinal of Ferrara, who had recently been sent as a legate to the King by *Pius IV*. This was *James Laynez* <note>Diego Laynez (1512–1565), the second Superior General of the Society of Jesus.</note>, who had been appointed by *Ignatius* as the first Provost General of his society. Having interrupted, and after he had poured out many insults against the Protestants—calling them "monkeys," "foxes," and "monsters"—and saying they should be sent away to the Council <note>The Council of Trent.</note> summoned by the Pope, he finally rebuked the Queen because she was undertaking the knowledge of these matters which did not belong to her at all, but rather to the Pope, the Cardinals, and the Bishops. He said it was not lawful, while a General Council was being celebrated, for a private Colloquy to be established here by the Queen's authority. The Queen bore the man's arrogance with impatience, but out of respect for the Legate, she concealed her offense. Thus, filling the air with a chaos of shouting, they dragged out the day in various ways. And a certain Sorbonnist, threatening *Beza* with his finger, said, *"O, if only we held you once within the walls of our Sorbonne!"* They would have done to him, I believe, the same thing that the Donatists <note>A schismatic group in the early Church known for their rigorism and occasional violence.</note> once did to *Restitutus*, a priest of Hippo, or to *Maximianus* of Vaga.

</margin>

XLII. At last the assembly was dismissed, and hereafter it was not held in the same form: because *Lorraine*, as was publicly reported, feared that if the speech were made common and known to the Princes and Nobles who were present, the matter would become clearer...

Therefore, from that day the form of the Colloquy was changed: and then from the number of both the Prelates <note>original: "Antistitum", referring here to the high-ranking Catholic clergy</note> and the Ministers, five were chosen from each side for this Colloquy, so that they might confer together peacefully. From the Papists: Jean de Monluc, Bishop of Valence; Pierre de Val, Bishop of Séez <note>original: "Vallius, Episcopus Senensis"</note>; Boutillier, the Abbot of Bourgueil; and Claude d'Espence, a doctor of the **Sorbonne** <note>The prestigious theology faculty in Paris</note>. From the Reformed Churches: Peter Martyr Vermigli, Theodore Beza, Nicolas des Gallars, Augustin Marlorat, and Jean de l'Espine. Then the order of business, the place, the time, and the notaries who would record the dispute were agreed upon.

<margin>XLIII. These men draft a formula of consensus regarding the article on the Supper.</margin>
XLIII. And although it seemed fair to everyone that the Confession of the Churches <note>The Reformed confession of faith</note> should be discussed in order, they nevertheless pursued the dispute concerning the **Supper** <note>The Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note>, since that had already been brought into the open: specifically that chapter regarding the presence of the Lord in the Supper. After the matter was variously debated among them, at last the delegates of both parties agreed upon this sentiment: *Insofar as faith makes the things promised present, and truly receives the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ by the power of the Holy Spirit: by this reasoning we confess the presence of his body and blood in the holy Supper: in which he offers, grants, and truly exhibits to us the substance of his body and blood by the operation of the Holy Spirit: in which we receive and eat spiritually and through faith that body which died for us, so that we may be bones of his bones, flesh of his flesh, and be quickened by it and perceive whatever serves our salvation.*

<margin>XLIV. In which they satisfy the parties very little.</margin>
XLIV. Yet this formula of sentiment was by no means fully accepted by the college of Prelates. Therefore, the next day another was presented to the Ministers in their name, in which something had been changed: for it attributed to the Word what that former formula attributed to the fruitfulness of faith. The Ministers did not wish to accept that formula on account of its ambiguity, lest it give birth to more serious errors. But lest there seem to be a struggle over words, by the consensus of all the delegates they drafted it in these words: *we confess that Jesus Christ in the Supper offers, gives, and truly exhibits to us the substance of his body and blood by the operation of the Holy Spirit: and that we receive and eat spiritually and through faith that true body which died for us: so that we may be bones of his bones, flesh of his flesh: to this end, that we may be quickened by it, and perceive whatever serves our salvation: And since faith, relying on the word of God, makes the things perceived present; and through this faith we truly and effectively receive the true and natural body and blood of Jesus Christ by the power of the Holy Spirit: in this respect we confess the presence of his body and blood in the Supper.* With these things thus established, the delegates of both sides brought the matter back to their own people, so that both might freely decide what they thought. At first glance, therefore, many of the Prelates accepted the formula as drafted: but once the matter was communicated to the **Sorbonnists**, they later rejected it by common sentiment. Nevertheless, their delegates, as had been established with the Ministers, persisted in their opinion—

## BOOK IV. CHAPTER X.

Those who persisted <note>The moderate Catholic delegates who had agreed to the compromise formula</note> were accused of forming a secret union with the Ministers, and they were no longer granted the opportunity to speak or confer with them. Therefore, since the means of communication had been cut off, the Ministers sent this explanation of their formula to the delegates of the Prelates: *We affirm that no distance of space can hinder the communion we have with Christ’s body and blood: for the Lord’s Supper is a heavenly thing; and although on earth we receive with the mouth bread and wine, which are the true signs of his body and blood: nevertheless, by faith and the operation of the Holy Spirit, our minds (for which this is the primary food) are lifted up into heaven and enjoy the present body and blood. And in this respect, we say that the body truly joins itself to the bread, and the blood to the wine: yet in no other way than by a Sacramental reckoning—that is, neither in a local nor a natural manner—but because those signs effectively signify that God gives those things to the faithful communicants, and that the faithful perceive them truly and certainly by faith.* This is the clear opinion of the Reformed Churches concerning the presence of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Sacrament of the Supper.

<margin>XLV. The outcome of the Colloquy.</margin>
XLV. And this was indeed the outcome of the Colloquy of Poissy, for which many had gathered for three months for the sake of that disputation: it bore no fruit at that time, and afterward, the greatest disturbances of uprisings and wars followed <note>Referring to the outbreak of the French Wars of Religion shortly after the talks failed</note>.

<margin>XLVI. The fickleness of Lorraine in religion.</margin>
XLVI. Meanwhile, it is most worthy of note what Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman</note> says regarding the Cardinal of Lorraine: that at the time this Colloquy was held, he undoubtedly agreed with the German Protestants on most points; *but being an ambitious man,* he says, *and otherwise fickle, lest he lose the favor of the popular breeze which he uniquely pursued, he later changed his mind.* He was accustomed to defend himself with this excuse: saying that he had indeed previously felt the same as the Protestants of Germany, but after the questions under dispute had been decided by the Council of Trent <note>The major Roman Catholic reform council (1545–1563) that defined many dogmas against Protestantism</note>, he had acquiesced to its decrees. Is it believable that any religion is held by a man who is so changeable, and for whom the decisions of a Council—such as that of Trent was—are the sole foundation for his change? I now call upon readers of every kind to compare the history of the Conference of Carthage <note>A 411 AD conference between Catholics led by St. Augustine and the Donatist schismatics</note> with that of the Colloquy of Poissy, and to decide in their own minds without prejudice which party’s theologians are further removed from the spirit and actions of the Donatists.

<margin>XLVII. The recent Prelates intended a Conference like Carthage with bad intent toward the Reformed.</margin>
XLVII. Indeed, it never happened that the Romanists offered our ancestors any Conference similar to that of Carthage. Nor did the recent prelates of the Gallican Church have that in mind, although they claimed it with smooth words. In this matter, their cunning and—if I may say so—the "depths of Satan" <note>A biblical reference to Revelation 2:24</note> shine forth alongside the most holy providence of God. The Prelates had nothing else in mind but the <term>πανολεθρίαν</term> <note>original: "panolethrian," meaning total destruction or utter ruin</note> of the Reformed Religion in France, to be procured by any means; and they had now brought the matter to the point where, contrary to the edicts...

<meta>This page continues the account of the aftermath of the Colloquy of Poissy. The previous page detailed the failure of the theological compromise regarding the Eucharist and the subsequent breakdown of communication between the Reformed ministers and the Catholic prelates.</meta>

# HISTORY OF THE COLLOQUY OF POISSY

...breaking every promise and contrary to public safety, the Reformed <margin>the [Catholic party] showed these things.</margin> were stripped of most of their churches, with only a few survivors remaining at that time. Whole provinces, having been fruitlessly pressured into apostasy <note>abandoning one’s faith</note>, were exposed to the fury of soldiers. These soldiers served as "Apostles" for the Roman Church; their horrible curses, which they used to drive miserable, reluctant people to join the Communion of the Mass, served as their version of "preaching the Gospel." Elsewhere, slaughter and the latest forms of execution were raged against those who held a good conscience and the salvation of their souls dearer than life itself. While these things were being carried out at the instigation of the Prelates—and in some places even under their leadership and guidance—they acted as if the matter were still undecided. They put on a show of complete friendliness, mentioned the Colloquy and "fraternal conference," and protested that they disliked the use of force and arms in matters of religion. With deceptive speeches, they congratulated the King on the return of so many thousands of his subjects to the bosom of the Church, claiming it was achieved solely by the lure of goodness, clemency, and generosity, and by a path that was—as one of them put it—*strewn with nothing but lilies* <note>original: "non nisi liliis sparsa." This refers to the Bourbon lily, the symbol of the French monarchy, suggesting the conversion was a peaceful royal triumph.</note>.

<margin>XLVIII. So that their most heavy persecution might have the appearance of fairness.</margin>
XLVIII. Why was there such a great discrepancy and contradiction between their actions and their words? Clearly, the few survivors remaining in France had to be persuaded that they were far from their own destruction, and a lethargy of unhealthy security had to be induced in them. The Prelates had to put on a certain appearance of Christian zeal for the conversion of souls; and, if nothing else, they certainly had to speak of those means by which nature itself teaches all mortals that truth can be persuaded and the mind convinced. Meanwhile, they knew with absolute certainty that before those hopes they were dangling from a distance could be realized, the power of Royal authority alone would ensure no Reformed Church remained in the kingdom of France.

<margin>XLIX. By which thing they admit, even unwillingly, that conversion by force is not true conversion.</margin>
XLIX. These were the schemes of cunning men; meanwhile, we must look up to Divine Providence, which makes holy use of their trickery. For one may learn from the very mouths and pens of our adversaries that a true conversion—and the enrichment of the holy Catholic Church by the addition of new members—is that which is accomplished by instruction, persuasion, the evidence of arguments, and the conviction of the mind through these things, with the grace of the Holy Spirit added. It is not that which seizes bodies and hardens minds through the authority of any man, the cruelty of Royal edicts, force, arms, or punishments. Since it is manifest to all of Europe from the light of these deeds that the destroyers of the Reformed Religion in France did not follow the former path but the latter, we conclude that the "conversion" they labored for is a mere perversion.

> Arise, Lord Jesus, and by Your protection, show the cause of the Gospel truth—which is also Your cause—to be safe and invincible.

**XXXIX.** The unruly shouts of the monk **de Sainctes**. <note>Claude de Sainctes, a militant Catholic polemicist.</note> *In the same place.*
**XL.** **Lorraine** *strives to pit the French theologians against the* **Germans**. <note>A tactical move to exploit the doctrinal differences between French Calvinists and German Lutherans.</note> 680
**XLI.** *The petulant speech of the Jesuit* **Lainez** <note>Diego Lainez, the second Superior General of the Jesuits.</note> *and another from the* **Sorbonne**. *In the same place.*
**XLII.** *The format of the Conference was changed again: five chosen from each side who might confer peacefully.* *In the same place.*
**XLIII.** *These men draft a formula of consensus regarding the article on the* **Lord's Supper**. 681
**XLIV.** *In which they satisfy the parties very little.* *In the same place.*
**XLV.** *The end of the Conference.* 882
**XLVI.** The fickleness of **Lorraine** *in* Religion. *In the same place.*
**XLVII.** *The* Prelates *recently showed a conference similar to the* **Conference of Carthage** <note>The 411 AD conference where the Roman authorities forced a resolution against the Donatists; the author suggests the Poissy conference was a similar "setup" against the Protestants.</note> *to the* Reformed *with ill intent.* 883
**XLVIII.** *So that their very severe persecution of them might have the appearance of fairness.* 884
**XLIX.** *Wherefore, even if unwillingly, they admit that it is not a true conversion which is made by force.* *In the same place.*

The author frames the conference as a manipulative attempt by the Catholic hierarchy to justify subsequent persecution of the Reformed movement.</summary>
